shelves.title: Antiresorptives for postmenopausal osteoporosis: bisphosphonates and denosumab
shelves.question: Do bisphosphonates and denosumab prevent fractures in postmenopausal osteoporosis — and how long should treatment continue?
shelves.balance: Three different antiresorptive strategies each cut vertebral fractures by half to two-thirds and hip fractures by about half (FIT, HORIZON, FREEDOM) — the fracture record is not in dispute. The live question FLEX answers is duration: after five years, women whose risk had fallen gained little from continuing except at the spine, which is why the guideline pairs a strong treat recommendation with reassessment and holidays rather than lifetime-by-default. (Panel position: Endocrine Society 2019/2020 — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Alendronate cut new vertebral fractures from 15.0% to 8.0% — and hip fractures by half.
cards.summary: FIT 1996 — new vertebral fractures 8.0% vs 15.0% (RR 0.53 ); hip fractures 1.1% vs 2.2% (RR 0.49 ); wrist fractures −48% — 2,027 women with low femoral-neck BMD and at least one existing vertebral fracture; about 3 years.
cards.people: 2,027 women with low femoral-neck BMD and at least one existing vertebral fracture, assigned to alendronate (1,022) or placebo (1,005); follow-up radiographs obtained in 1,946 women (98% of surviving participants); about 3 years
cards.result: One or more new morphometric vertebral fractures in 78 (8.0%) of the alendronate group vs 145 (15.0%) on placebo — RR 0.53 (0.41–0.68) . Clinically apparent vertebral fractures 2.3% vs 5.0%. The relative hazard for hip fracture was 0.49 (0.23–0.99) — rates 1.1% vs 2.2% — and for wrist fracture 0.52 (0.31–0.87) , a 48% reduction. Any clinical fracture: 13.6% vs 18.2%
cards.watchOut: These women already had vertebral fractures — a high-risk group, in whom absolute benefits are largest. Adverse experiences, including upper-gastrointestinal disorders, did not differ significantly between the groups
cards.source: Black DM, Cummings SR, Karpf DB, et al; Fracture Intervention Trial Research Group. Randomised trial of effect of alendronate on risk of fracture in women with existing vertebral fractures. Lancet. 1996;348(9041):1535–1541. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(96)07088-2. PMID 8950879.
cards.search: fit fracture intervention trial black 1996 lancet alendronate vertebral fracture hip wrist pmid 8950879

cards.headline: One infusion a year cut morphometric vertebral fractures by 70% and hip fractures by 41%.
cards.summary: HORIZON-PFT 2007 — morphometric vertebral fractures 3.3% vs 10.9% (RR 0.30 ); hip fractures 1.4% vs 2.5% (HR 0.59 , −41%); nonvertebral fractures −25% — 7,765 women with osteoporosis, 3 years.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2007
cards.people: 7,765 women (mean age 73 years) with osteoporosis, assigned to a single 15-minute infusion of zoledronic acid 5 mg (3,889) or placebo (3,876) at baseline, at 12 months and at 24 months; followed until 36 months
cards.result: Morphometric vertebral fracture 3.3% with zoledronic acid vs 10.9% with placebo — RR 0.30 (0.24–0.38) , a 70% reduction. Hip fracture 1.4% vs 2.5% — HR 0.59 (0.42–0.83) , a 41% reduction. Nonvertebral fractures, clinical fractures and clinical vertebral fractures were reduced by 25%, 33% and 77%, respectively (P<0.001 for all comparisons)
cards.watchOut: Serious atrial fibrillation occurred more frequently in the zoledronic-acid group — 50 vs 20 patients (P<0.001) — a signal the abstract itself carries; other adverse events, including changes in renal function, were similar in the two groups
cards.source: Black DM, Delmas PD, Eastell R, et al; HORIZON Pivotal Fracture Trial. Once-yearly zoledronic acid for treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis. N Engl J Med. 2007;356(18):1809–1822. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa067312. PMID 17476007.
cards.search: horizon-pft black 2007 nejm zoledronic acid once-yearly vertebral hip fracture atrial fibrillation pmid 17476007

cards.headline: Denosumab cut vertebral fractures by two-thirds and hip fractures by 40% — but stopping it has a price.
cards.summary: FREEDOM 2009 — new vertebral fractures 2.3% vs 7.2% (risk ratio 0.32 ); hip 0.7% vs 1.2% (HR 0.60 ); nonvertebral HR 0.80 — 7,868 women aged 60–90, denosumab 60 mg every 6 months, 3 years.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2009
cards.people: 7,868 women between the ages of 60 and 90 years with a bone mineral density T score of less than −2.5 but not less than −4.0 at the lumbar spine or total hip; denosumab 60 mg (3,902) or placebo (3,906), given every 6 months for 36 months
cards.result: New radiographic vertebral fracture 2.3% denosumab vs 7.2% placebo — risk ratio 0.32 (0.26–0.41) , a relative decrease of 68%. Hip fracture 0.7% vs 1.2% — HR 0.60 (0.37–0.97) . Nonvertebral fracture 6.5% vs 8.0% — HR 0.80 (0.67–0.95) . There was no increase in the risk of cancer, infection, cardiovascular disease or delayed fracture healing, and no cases of osteonecrosis of the jaw
cards.watchOut: Context, and not a FREEDOM result: unlike a bisphosphonate, denosumab leaves nothing behind in bone — stopping it without follow-on antiresorptive therapy causes rapid rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures (extension and consistency literature, flagged as context). The six-monthly schedule is part of this drug’s safety
cards.source: Cummings SR, San Martin J, McClung MR, et al; FREEDOM Trial. Denosumab for prevention of fractures in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. N Engl J Med. 2009;361(8):756–765. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0809493. PMID 19671655.
cards.search: freedom cummings 2009 nejm denosumab vertebral hip nonvertebral fracture rebound discontinuation pmid 19671655

cards.headline: After 5 years of alendronate, stopping cost little — except at the spine.
cards.summary: FLEX 2006 — clinical vertebral fractures 2.4% continuing vs 5.3% stopping (RR 0.45 ); morphometric vertebral (9.8% vs 11.3%) and nonvertebral (19.0% vs 18.9%) fractures did not differ significantly — 1,099 women after about 5 years of alendronate in FIT, followed 5 more years.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial — the Fracture Intervention Trial Long-term Extension (FLEX), JAMA 2006
cards.people: 1,099 women who had taken alendronate for about 5 years in FIT, randomly assigned to continue alendronate or switch to placebo for 5 further years
cards.result: Clinically recognized vertebral fractures 2.4% in those who continued vs 5.3% in those who stopped — RR 0.45 (0.24–0.85) . Morphometric vertebral fractures 9.8% vs 11.3% (RR 0.86) and nonvertebral fractures 19.0% vs 18.9% (RR 1.00) did not differ significantly. Women who discontinued showed a moderate decline in BMD and a gradual rise in biochemical markers of bone turnover, with levels remaining above the original pre-treatment baseline
cards.watchOut: The absolute benefit of continuing was small — 2.9 percentage points over 5 years — and the authors single out women at very high risk of clinical vertebral fractures, such as those with an existing vertebral fracture or very low BMD, as the ones who may benefit from continuing beyond 5 years
cards.source: Black DM, Schwartz AV, Ensrud KE, et al; FLEX Research Group. Effects of continuing or stopping alendronate after 5 years of treatment: the Fracture Intervention Trial Long-term Extension (FLEX): a randomized trial. JAMA. 2006;296(24):2927–2938. DOI 10.1001/jama.296.24.2927. PMID 17190893.
cards.search: flex black 2006 jama continuing stopping alendronate five years clinical vertebral fracture drug holiday pmid 17190893

shelves.title: Bone-building therapy for very high risk: teriparatide and romosozumab
shelves.question: For women at very high fracture risk, does building new bone beat slowing its loss — and at what cardiovascular price?
shelves.balance: For very high risk, building bone beats only slowing its loss: teriparatide cut vertebral fractures by two-thirds, and a year of romosozumab followed by an antiresorptive beat both placebo (FRAME) and alendronate itself (ARCH) — the only head-to-head anabolic win in the field. The same ARCH trial is why this shelf is not a simple endorsement: the cardiovascular imbalance, absent in FRAME’s placebo comparison, put a boxed warning on the drug and a risk screen in the guideline. Benefit and warning come from the same two trials, and the shelf keeps them together. (Panel position: Endocrine Society 2019 + 2020 update — attributed, for developer verification.)

cards.headline: Teriparatide cut new vertebral fractures by 65% — the first drug that built bone instead of slowing its loss.
cards.summary: Neer 2001 — new vertebral fractures 5% vs 14% (RR 0.35 ); nonvertebral fragility fractures 3% vs 6% (RR 0.47 ); lumbar spine BMD +9 percentage points vs placebo — 1,637 women with prior vertebral fractures, median 21 months.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2001
cards.people: 1,637 postmenopausal women with prior vertebral fractures, randomly assigned to self-injected parathyroid hormone (1-34) 20 µg or 40 µg daily or placebo; vertebral radiographs at base line and at the end of the study (median duration of observation, 21 months)
cards.result: New vertebral fractures occurred in 14% of the placebo group and 5% on the 20 µg dose (4% on 40 µg) — RR 0.35 (0.22–0.55) for 20 µg. New nonvertebral fragility fractures 3% in each hormone group vs 6% on placebo — RR 0.47 (0.25–0.88) . The 20 µg dose increased lumbar spine BMD by 9 more percentage points than placebo; side effects were minor (occasional nausea and headache)
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped early when osteosarcoma data emerged in rats — the origin of the lifetime-duration caution that still frames teriparatide use. The human signal has not materialized in registry follow-up (context line, attributed)
cards.source: Neer RM, Arnaud CD, Zanchetta JR, et al. Effect of parathyroid hormone (1-34) on fractures and bone mineral density in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. N Engl J Med. 2001;344(19):1434–1441. DOI 10.1056/NEJM200105103441904. PMID 11346808.
cards.search: neer 2001 nejm teriparatide parathyroid hormone 1-34 vertebral fragility fracture bone mineral density osteosarcoma rats pmid 11346808

cards.headline: A year of romosozumab cut vertebral fractures by 73% — and the lead survived the switch to denosumab.
cards.summary: FRAME 2016 — new vertebral fractures at 12 months 0.5% vs 1.8% (risk ratio 0.27 ); clinical fractures 1.6% vs 2.5% (36% lower, P=0.008); at 24 months, after both groups had switched to denosumab, vertebral fractures 0.6% vs 2.5% — 7,180 women.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2016
cards.people: 7,180 postmenopausal women with a T score of −2.5 to −3.5 at the total hip or femoral neck, randomly assigned to subcutaneous romosozumab 210 mg or placebo monthly for 12 months; thereafter, patients in each group received denosumab 60 mg every 6 months for 12 months
cards.result: At 12 months, new vertebral fractures had occurred in 16 of 3,321 patients (0.5%) in the romosozumab group vs 59 of 3,322 (1.8%) on placebo — a 73% lower risk (risk ratio 0.27, P<0.001). Clinical fractures 1.6% vs 2.5% — a 36% lower risk (P=0.008); nonvertebral fractures 1.6% vs 2.1% (P=0.10, not significant). At 24 months, after the transition to denosumab, vertebral fracture rates remained significantly lower in the romosozumab-first group — 0.6% vs 2.5% , a 75% lower risk. Adverse events, including cardiovascular events, were balanced between the groups; one atypical femoral fracture and two cases of osteonecrosis of the jaw were observed in the romosozumab group
cards.watchOut: The comparator matters: FRAME, against placebo, saw no cardiovascular imbalance — which is exactly what makes the ARCH signal, against an active comparator, the open question carried on the next card
cards.source: Cosman F, Crittenden DB, Adachi JD, et al. Romosozumab treatment in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. N Engl J Med. 2016;375(16):1532–1543. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1607948. PMID 27641143.
cards.search: frame cosman 2016 nejm romosozumab vertebral clinical fracture denosumab sequence pmid 27641143

cards.headline: Romosozumab beat alendronate head-to-head — and carried a cardiovascular imbalance that earned a boxed warning.
cards.summary: ARCH 2017 — new vertebral fractures 6.2% vs 11.9% (−48%); hip fractures 2.0% vs 3.2% (−38%); nonvertebral fractures −19% — but positively adjudicated serious cardiovascular events during year 1: 2.5% vs 1.9% — 4,093 women with osteoporosis and a fragility fracture.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, active-controlled trial, N Engl J Med 2017
cards.people: 4,093 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and a fragility fracture, randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to monthly subcutaneous romosozumab 210 mg or weekly oral alendronate 70 mg in a blinded fashion for 12 months, followed by open-label alendronate in both groups
cards.result: Over 24 months, a 48% lower risk of new vertebral fractures in the romosozumab-to-alendronate group ( 6.2% , 127 of 2,046 patients) than in the alendronate-to-alendronate group ( 11.9% , 243 of 2,047) (P<0.001). Clinical fractures 9.7% vs 13.0% (27% lower risk); nonvertebral fractures 8.7% vs 10.6% (19% lower, P=0.04); hip fractures 2.0% vs 3.2% (38% lower, P=0.02). Overall adverse events and serious adverse events were balanced between the two groups
cards.watchOut: The counterweight, at full weight: during year 1, positively adjudicated serious cardiovascular adverse events were observed more often with romosozumab than with alendronate — 50 of 2,040 patients (2.5%) vs 38 of 2,014 (1.9%) — the imbalance that produced the boxed warning and the guideline’s instruction to avoid romosozumab in women at high cardiovascular risk. No such imbalance appeared in FRAME’s placebo comparison
cards.source: Saag KG, Petersen J, Brandi ML, et al. Romosozumab or alendronate for fracture prevention in women with osteoporosis. N Engl J Med. 2017;377(15):1417–1427. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1708322. PMID 28892457.
cards.search: arch saag 2017 nejm romosozumab alendronate head-to-head vertebral hip fracture cardiovascular boxed warning pmid 28892457

cards.headline: Abaloparatide cut new vertebral fractures by 86% — with less hypercalcemia than teriparatide.
cards.summary: ACTIVE 2016 — new vertebral fractures 0.58% vs 4.22% (RR 0.14 ); nonvertebral fractures 2.7% vs 4.7% (HR 0.57 ); hypercalcemia 3.4% vs 6.4% with teriparatide — 2,463 women, 18 months.
cards.type: Phase 3, double-blind, randomised clinical trial with an open-label teriparatide comparator, JAMA 2016
cards.people: 2,463 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (mean age 69 years), randomly assigned to daily subcutaneous abaloparatide 80 µg (n=824), placebo (n=821), or open-label teriparatide 20 µg (n=818) for 18 months at 28 sites in 10 countries; 1,901 completed the study
cards.result: New morphometric vertebral fractures occurred in 0.58% (4 patients) on abaloparatide vs 4.22% (30 patients) on placebo — relative risk 0.14 (0.05–0.39) , P<.001; 0.84% (6 patients) on teriparatide. The Kaplan-Meier estimated rate of nonvertebral fracture was 2.7% with abaloparatide vs 4.7% with placebo — hazard ratio 0.57 (0.32–1.00) , P=.049; 3.3% on teriparatide. Bone mineral density increases were greater with abaloparatide than placebo (all P<.001). Hypercalcemia was less frequent with abaloparatide than teriparatide — 3.4% vs 6.4% (risk difference −2.96, P=.006)
cards.watchOut: Dizziness and palpitations after injection were more frequent with abaloparatide — transient post-injection symptoms to warn about. The teriparatide arm was open-label, so the blinded comparison is against placebo, not against teriparatide; treatment and follow-up lasted 18 months
cards.source: Miller PD, Hattersley G, Riis BJ, et al.; ACTIVE Study Investigators. Effect of Abaloparatide vs Placebo on New Vertebral Fractures in Postmenopausal Women With Osteoporosis: The ACTIVE Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016;316(7):722–733. DOI 10.1001/jama.2016.11136. PMID 27533157.
cards.search: active miller 2016 jama abaloparatide placebo vertebral nonvertebral fracture hypercalcemia teriparatide open-label pmid 27533157

shelves.title: Vertebroplasty: the sham trials and the one slice that answered yes
shelves.question: Does injecting cement into a fractured vertebra relieve pain better than a sham procedure?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Back Pain · Bone Cements · Cross-Over Studies · Disability Evaluation · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fractures, Compression · Humans · Injections, Spinal · Male · Osteoporosis · Osteoporotic Fractures · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pain Measurement · Placebo Effect · Polymethacrylic Acids · Quality of Life · Spinal Fractures · Treatment Failure · Treatment Outcome · Vertebroplasty
shelves.balance: In 2009 two sham-controlled NEJM trials, published the same day, found vertebroplasty no better than placebo for pain or function — while patients in both arms improved. Seven years later VAPOUR found the exception: in fractures less than 6 weeks old with severe pain, vertebroplasty did beat sham. The broad use failed its sham test; a narrow, early, severe-pain slice survived it.

cards.headline: Buchbinder 2009: vertebroplasty no better than sham at any time point — both groups just got better.
cards.summary: No significant advantage for vertebroplasty on any measured outcome at any time point. At 3 months, mean pain reduction was 2.6 points on vertebroplasty vs 1.9 on sham (adjusted difference 0.6 , 95% CI −0.7 to 1.8). Both groups improved significantly on pain, function, and quality of life.
cards.people: 78 patients with painful osteoporotic vertebral fractures (38 vertebroplasty, 40 sham)
cards.result: No significant advantage for vertebroplasty on any measured outcome at any time point. At 3 months, mean pain reduction was 2.6 points on vertebroplasty vs 1.9 on sham (adjusted difference 0.6 , 95% CI −0.7 to 1.8). Both groups improved significantly on pain, function, and quality of life.
cards.watchOut: The improvement in the sham arm is the lesson — fracture pain heals and placebo procedures are powerful; uncontrolled case series had credited the cement for both.
cards.source: Buchbinder R et al., N Engl J Med 2009 (PMID 19657121)

cards.headline: INVEST 2009: same-day confirmation — disability and pain identical to sham at 1 month.
cards.summary: At 1 month, no difference in disability (Roland-Morris difference 0.7 , 95% CI −1.3 to 2.8; P=0.49) or pain (difference 0.7 , −0.3 to 1.7; P=0.19). A trend toward clinically meaningful pain improvement ( 64% vs 48% , P=0.06) did not reach significance.
cards.people: 131 patients with osteoporotic spinal fractures (68 vertebroplasty, 63 simulated procedure)
cards.result: At 1 month, no difference in disability (Roland-Morris difference 0.7 , 95% CI −1.3 to 2.8; P=0.49) or pain (difference 0.7 , −0.3 to 1.7; P=0.19). A trend toward clinically meaningful pain improvement ( 64% vs 48% , P=0.06) did not reach significance.
cards.watchOut: Half the sham group crossed over to vertebroplasty by 3 months ( 51% vs 13% ) — belief in the procedure survived its own trial, which is why the blinded 1-month numbers are the ones to trust.
cards.source: Kallmes DF et al., N Engl J Med 2009 (PMID 19657122 · NCT00068822)

cards.headline: VAPOUR 2016: in fractures under 6 weeks old with severe pain, vertebroplasty did beat sham — 44% vs 21% with pain below 4 of 10 at 14 days .
cards.summary: Pain score below 4 of 10 at 14 days in 44% (24 patients) on vertebroplasty vs 21% (12) on sham — between-group difference 23 percentage points (95% CI 6–39; P=0.011). Three deaths in each group, judged unrelated; two serious adverse events in each group.
cards.people: 120 patients with acute osteoporotic fractures of less than 6 weeks' duration and severe pain (61 vertebroplasty, 59 sham)
cards.result: Pain score below 4 of 10 at 14 days in 44% (24 patients) on vertebroplasty vs 21% (12) on sham — between-group difference 23 percentage points (95% CI 6–39; P=0.011). Three deaths in each group, judged unrelated; two serious adverse events in each group.
cards.watchOut: This does not overturn 2009 — VAPOUR enrolled a different patient (fresh fracture, severe pain, treated early). Read together, the three trials say the benefit, if real, lives in the first days of a bad fracture, not in the chronic cases that filled the earlier trials.
cards.source: Clark W et al., Lancet 2016 (PMID 27544377 · NCT01482793)

shelves.title: Arthroscopic knee surgery vs sham: the scope adds nothing
shelves.question: For osteoarthritis of the knee and degenerative (wear-and-tear) meniscus tears — not a ruptured ligament or an acute injury — does arthroscopic surgery help more than a sham operation or physical therapy alone?
shelves.balance: Three NEJM trials, three nulls. Against a true placebo operation, arthroscopy never came out ahead at any point in two years; against sham surgery for a degenerative meniscus tear, removing meniscus tissue gained nothing at one year; and added to good physical and medical therapy, it added nothing. The relief patients report is real — it is the placebo effect and the knee’s natural course, not the scope. Scope: every patient on this shelf had a degenerative knee — arthritic pain or a wear-and-tear meniscus tear. Nobody had a torn ligament; for the ligament trials, see Shelf #193.

cards.headline: Debridement and lavage no better than placebo surgery for knee osteoarthritis
cards.summary: At no point in 24 months did either real procedure beat placebo on pain or function — at one year, Knee-Specific Pain scores were 48.9 ± 21.9 (placebo) vs 54.8 ± 19.8 (lavage) and 51.7 ± 22.4 (debridement).
cards.people: 180 patients with osteoarthritis of the knee (American College of Rheumatology criteria) at a Houston VA medical center; mean age 52, mostly men; 165 completed the trial. The indication was arthritic knee pain; the operations tested were washout (lavage) and clean-up (débridement). No ligament was torn, and none was repaired.
cards.result: Patients were randomized to arthroscopic debridement, arthroscopic lavage, or placebo surgery (skin incisions and a simulated debridement, scope never inserted), with patients and assessors blinded. At no point in 24 months did either real procedure beat placebo on pain or function — at one year, Knee-Specific Pain scores were 48.9 ± 21.9 (placebo) vs 54.8 ± 19.8 (lavage) and 51.7 ± 22.4 (debridement), and the confidence intervals excluded any clinically meaningful difference.
cards.watchOut: A single VA center and mostly men — but it remains the only placebo-surgery trial of arthroscopy for knee OA, and later trials point the same way.
cards.source: Moseley JB, et al. N Engl J Med. 2002. PMID: 12110735.

cards.headline: Cutting out a degenerative meniscus tear no better than sham surgery
cards.summary: Lysholm +21.7 with partial meniscectomy vs +23.3 with sham (difference −1.6; 95% CI −7.2 to 4.0); WOMET +24.6 vs +27.1 (−2.5; −9.2 to 4.1); pain after exercise 3.1 vs 3.3.
cards.people: 146 patients, 35–65, with a degenerative medial meniscus tear and NO knee osteoarthritis: knee pain for at least 3 months despite conservative treatment, the tear confirmed on MRI. The tear was wear-and-tear degeneration, not an injury — traumatic tears and locked or unstable knees were not this population.
cards.result: At 12 months the improvements were indistinguishable: Lysholm score +21.7 with partial meniscectomy vs +23.3 with sham (difference −1.6; 95% CI −7.2 to 4.0), WOMET +24.6 vs +27.1 (−2.5; −9.2 to 4.1), and pain after exercise 3.1 vs 3.3 (−0.1). Later knee surgery in 2 vs 5 patients; serious adverse events 1 vs 0.
cards.watchOut: Patients with true mechanical locking or a traumatic tear were not this trial’s population — it answers the degenerative tear in a middle-aged knee.
cards.source: Sihvonen R, et al. (FIDELITY). N Engl J Med. 2013. PMID: 24369076 · NCT00549172.

cards.headline: Arthroscopy added to good therapy adds nothing in moderate-to-severe knee OA
cards.summary: At 2 years, WOMAC 874 ± 624 vs 897 ± 583 (difference −23; 95% CI −208 to 161; P=0.22) and SF-36 Physical Component 37.0 vs 37.2 (P=0.93).
cards.people: 178 patients with moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis (92 surgery, 86 control). The indication was arthritic pain; the operation tested was lavage and débridement added to optimized physical and medical therapy — again, no ligament injury anywhere in the trial.
cards.result: Surgical lavage and debridement plus optimized physical and medical therapy vs therapy alone. At 2 years the WOMAC scores were 874 ± 624 vs 897 ± 583 (difference −23; 95% CI −208 to 161; P=0.22), and SF-36 Physical Component scores 37.0 vs 37.2 (P=0.93). No interim or secondary outcome favored surgery.
cards.watchOut: Not sham-controlled — but together with Moseley’s placebo trial and FIDELITY’s sham trial, the three designs converge on the same answer.
cards.source: Kirkley A, et al. N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID: 18784099 · NCT00158431.

shelves.title: Ruptured ACL: reconstruct now, or rehabilitate first?
shelves.question: For a torn anterior cruciate ligament, does early surgical reconstruction give a better knee than structured rehabilitation first, with reconstruction reserved for knees that stay unstable?
shelves.balance: Three randomized trials, 604 patients — and the answer depends on which knee. For a fresh tear in a young, active patient, rehabilitation first matched early surgery at 2 and 5 years, and about half never needed the operation (KANON). For acute tears more broadly, early surgery finished modestly ahead on patient-reported function at 2 years — an edge the trial’s own authors call not clinically relevant — and half the rehabilitation group still avoided surgery (COMPARE). For an older, non-acute tear where the knee keeps giving way, surgery clearly won: better function at 18 months and cost-effective (ACL SNNAP), though 41% of the rehabilitation group crossed over to surgery anyway. So the contrast with Shelf #188 is real — a ruptured ligament is a structural injury with genuine instability, and reconstruction has randomized support, strongest exactly where instability persists. But ‘everyone with a torn ACL needs immediate surgery’ is not what these trials show: starting with rehabilitation cost the half who stabilize nothing, and the operation stayed available for the rest.

cards.headline: Fresh ACL tear in a young, active knee: rehabilitation first matched early surgery — half never needed the operation
cards.summary: Change in KOOS4 at 2 years: 39.2 points (early surgery) vs 39.4 (rehabilitation first) — difference 0.2 (95% CI −6.5 to 6.8; P=0.96). 23 of 59 (39%) in the rehabilitation-first group chose delayed reconstruction within 2 years; the other 36 never had surgery.
cards.type: Randomized trial, strategy comparison (unblinded); 2-year primary report with a 5-year follow-up of the same patients
cards.people: 121 young, active adults (18–35 years, Tegner activity score 5–9) with an ACL tear within the previous 4 weeks in a previously uninjured knee. Excluded: professional athletes, an unstable meniscal tear needing repair, full-thickness cartilage loss, and complete collateral-ligament tears.
cards.result: Change in KOOS4 (pain, symptoms, sport function, quality of life; 0–100) at 2 years: 39.2 points (early surgery) vs 39.4 (rehabilitation first) — difference 0.2 (95% CI −6.5 to 6.8; P=0.96). 23 of 59 (39%) in the rehabilitation-first group chose delayed reconstruction within 2 years; the other 36 never had surgery. At 5 years (same trial): KOOS4 change 42.9 vs 44.9 (P=0.54); 30 of 59 (51%) had been reconstructed; no difference in radiographic osteoarthritis (P=0.17) or later meniscus surgery (P=0.48).
cards.watchOut: One trial reported twice — the 2010 and 2013 papers are the same 121 patients, counted here as one exhibit. Young, active, previously uninjured knees only; the answer may differ in older or less active patients. An 11-year follow-up of the same cohort again found no outcome difference, with 52% of the rehabilitation-first group eventually reconstructed and 44% showing radiographic osteoarthritis.

cards.summary: IKDC score at 24 months: 84.7 (early surgery) vs 79.4 (rehabilitation first) — difference 5.3 (95% CI 0.6 to 9.9; P=0.026). 41 of 82 (50%) in the rehabilitation group underwent reconstruction during follow-up.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial, open-label, multicenter (6 Dutch hospitals)
cards.people: 167 patients aged 18–65 with an acute (within 2 months), complete, MRI-confirmed ACL rupture; mean age 31.3 years, 40% women; 163 (98%) completed. Excluded: a dislocated bucket-handle meniscus tear with a locked knee, and prior ACL injury to the other knee.
cards.result: IKDC score (patient-perceived symptoms, function, and sports ability; best 100) at 24 months: 84.7 (early surgery) vs 79.4 (rehabilitation first) — difference 5.3 (95% CI 0.6 to 9.9; P=0.026): statistically significant, but below the 7-point difference the trial was powered to detect, and the authors call its clinical importance unclear. Re-ruptures: 4 graft ruptures and 3 opposite-knee ruptures with early surgery vs 2 and 1 with rehabilitation first.

cards.headline: For an older tear with a knee that keeps giving way, surgery clearly beat rehabilitation — and was cost-effective
cards.summary: KOOS4 at 18 months: 73.0 (SD 18.3) with surgery vs 64.6 (SD 21.6) with rehabilitation — adjusted difference 7.9 (95% CI 2.5 to 13.2; P=0.0053) in favor of surgery.
cards.type: Pragmatic randomized controlled trial, multicenter (29 UK NHS orthopaedic units)
cards.people: 316 patients with a non-acute ACL injury and persistent symptoms of instability (the knee giving way); meniscal pathology needing immediate surgery was excluded. 156 assigned to reconstruction, 160 to rehabilitation.
cards.result: KOOS4 at 18 months: 73.0 (SD 18.3) with surgery vs 64.6 (SD 21.6) with rehabilitation — adjusted difference 7.9 (95% CI 2.5 to 13.2; P=0.0053) in favor of surgery. 65 of 160 (41%) in the rehabilitation group went on to reconstruction within 18 months. cards.watchOut: 43 of 156 (28%) assigned to surgery did not receive their operation within the trial (waiting lists and patient choice) — which, if anything, shrinks the measured surgical edge. This is the population whose knee has already declared itself unstable; it does not answer the first weeks after injury — see KANON and COMPARE on this shelf.

shelves.title: Oral versus IV antibiotics for bone and joint infection: the line is not the therapy
shelves.question: For bone, joint, and heart-valve infections, does the antibiotic have to run through a vein for weeks — or can pills do the same job?
shelves.mesh: Bone Diseases, Infectious · Joint Diseases · Endocarditis, Bacterial · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Administration, Oral · Administration, Intravenous · Humans
shelves.balance: Two large randomized trials say the vein is optional once the patient is stable and the organism is covered. OVIVA (1,054 bone and joint infections): oral step-down within a week was noninferior to six weeks of IV (failure 13.2% vs 14.6%), with a tenth of the catheter complications. POET (400 stable left-sided endocarditis patients): switching to oral after at least 10 IV days was noninferior at 6 months (9.0% vs 12.1%), and the long-term follow-up favored the oral group (HR 0.64) — carded as observational, noted, not sold. What the trials share: selected, stable patients, susceptible organisms, and an oral regimen that actually absorbs. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: OVIVA: oral antibiotics were noninferior to IV for bone and joint infection — treatment failure 13.2% vs 14.6%
cards.summary: Definitive treatment failure within 1 year: 13.2% on oral vs 14.6% on intravenous antibiotics (risk difference −1.4 percentage points, 95% CI −5.6 to 2.9; noninferiority margin 7.5) — and catheter complications were 1.0% vs 9.4% — 1,054 patients.
cards.type: Randomized noninferiority trial (OVIVA), N Engl J Med 2019
cards.people: 1,054 adults being treated for bone or joint infection at 26 U.K. centers (527 per group; end-point data for 1,015). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Treatment failure occurred in 67 of 509 participants (13.2%) in the oral group and 74 of 506 (14.6%) in the intravenous group; the intention-to-treat risk difference was −1.4 percentage points (90% CI −4.9 to 2.2; 95% CI −5.6 to 2.9), meeting noninferiority. Serious adverse events did not differ significantly (26.2% vs 27.7%). Catheter complications, a secondary endpoint, were far more common with intravenous therapy (9.4% vs 1.0%).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority was shown for the first 6 weeks’ route in patients whose clinicians judged them suitable for either — not for every bone infection, and oral success depends on an absorbable, susceptible-organism regimen actually being taken. Funded by the National Institute for Health Research.
cards.source: Li HK et al. Oral versus Intravenous Antibiotics for Bone and Joint Infection. N Engl J Med. 2019;380(5):425-436. PMID 30699315 · ISRCTN91566927.

cards.headline: POET: switching stable endocarditis patients to oral antibiotics was noninferior — composite outcome 9.0% vs 12.1%
cards.summary: Primary composite outcome (death, unplanned cardiac surgery, embolic events, or relapse of bacteremia) by 6 months after treatment ended: 9.0% on oral step-down vs 12.1% on continued IV (difference 3.1 percentage points, 95% CI −3.4 to 9.6; noninferiority met) — 400 patients.
cards.type: Randomized, noninferiority, multicentre trial (POET), N Engl J Med 2019
cards.people: 400 adults in stable condition with left-sided endocarditis caused by streptococcus, Enterococcus faecalis, Staphylococcus aureus, or coagulase-negative staphylococci (199 intravenous, 201 oral). (The abstract does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary composite outcome occurred in 18 patients (9.0%) in the orally treated group and 24 (12.1%) in the intravenously treated group (between-group difference 3.1 percentage points; 95% CI −3.4 to 9.6; P=0.40), meeting noninferiority criteria. Total antibiotic duration after randomization was similar (median 17 vs 19 days). Where feasible, orally treated patients were discharged to outpatient treatment.
cards.watchOut: POET enrolled patients who had already stabilized on at least 10 days of IV therapy, with transesophageal echo clearance — the result licenses a step-down in selected, stable patients, not oral treatment from day one, and not in unstable or abscess-complicated disease. Funded by the Danish Heart Foundation and others.

cards.headline: POET long-term follow-up: the oral group’s advantage grew over years (HR 0.64) — carded as observational follow-up, not proof
cards.summary: Long-term composite outcome (death, unplanned cardiac surgery, embolic events, or relapse) over a median follow-up of about 3.5 years: hazard ratio 0.64 favoring the oral step-down group — reported in the trial group’s follow-up report and carded here as follow-up/observational evidence, NOT as a randomized comparison of long-term strategy.
cards.type: Long-term follow-up report of the POET randomized cohort (Iversen et al.), N Engl J Med 2019 (correspondence). The PubMed record for this report carries no abstract; the hazard ratio is as printed in the published follow-up.
cards.people: The 400 POET participants, followed beyond the trial’s primary window (median follow-up about 3.5 years).
cards.result: In the follow-up report, the composite outcome occurred less often in the group originally assigned to oral step-down than in the group assigned to continued intravenous therapy (hazard ratio 0.64), extending the randomized noninferiority finding (Reference 2) over years rather than months.
cards.watchOut: A hazard ratio of 0.64 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library refuses to sell as solid when the design is observational — and long-term follow-up of a trial cohort is observational in exactly the ways that matter (post-trial care was not randomized). The honest reading: no late penalty for stepping down, and a signal worth noting — not proof that oral therapy saves lives over IV.

shelves.title: Hip fracture: how fast to the operating room, and which anaesthetic? The randomized answers are 'no proven difference' — the observational ones carry labels
shelves.question: After a hip fracture, does accelerating surgery save lives, does the wait-time literature prove a deadline, does co-management help, and does spinal beat general anaesthesia?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip · Cardiovascular Diseases · Comorbidity · Delirium · Dementia
shelves.balance: Split this shelf the way its evidence splits. Randomized: HIP ATTACK took 2,970 patients to surgery at a median of 6 hours vs 24 and found 90-day mortality of 9% vs 10% (HR 0.91 — not significant) and a composite of major complications at 22% vs 22% (HR 0.97), with less delirium, fewer urinary tract infections, and less pain on the accelerated side; REGAIN found spinal vs general anaesthesia statistically indistinguishable (18.5% vs 18.0% for death or inability to walk at 60 days), with delirium in about 20% of both arms. Observational, and labeled as such wherever it appears here: waits beyond 24 hours are associated with higher mortality in population data (Pincus: 6.5% vs 5.8% in matched patients), and orthogeriatric co-management is associated with lower mortality across non-randomized studies (Grigoryan) — associations that a sicker, slower-to-theatre patient mix can help manufacture. The honest practice line: fix the fracture promptly, co-manage the patient, choose the anaesthetic on the patient — and do not quote a mortality deadline the randomized trial did not find. Tier C — developer-ruled Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: HIP ATTACK (Borges 2020): surgery at 6 hours vs 24 — mortality 9% vs 10% (HR 0.91, NS); composite 22% vs 22%
cards.summary: 2,970 patients at 69 hospitals in 17 countries: accelerated surgery did NOT significantly lower 90-day mortality (140 deaths [9%] vs 154 [10%]; HR 0.91; 95% CI 0.72–1.14; P=0.40; absolute risk reduction 1%) or the composite of mortality and major complications (321 [22%] vs 331 [22%]; HR 0.97; P=0.71). Delirium, urinary tract infection, and pain were lower with accelerated surgery, and mobilization was faster.
cards.type: International, randomized, controlled trial (HIP ATTACK), Lancet 2020
cards.people: 2,970 patients aged 45 years or older with a hip fracture requiring surgery (accelerated surgery 1,487; standard care 1,483); median time from diagnosis to surgery was 6 hours (IQR 4–9) vs 24 hours (10–42). (The abstract record does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: The coprimary outcomes were mortality and a composite of major complications (mortality, nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, venous thromboembolism, sepsis, pneumonia, life-threatening and major bleeding) at 90 days. Neither differed significantly between groups. Secondary outcomes favoured acceleration for delirium, urinary tract infection, and pain, and patients mobilized sooner.
cards.watchOut: The trial compared fast with ordinary, not fast with neglected: a 24-hour median in the control arm is already decent care, so HIP ATTACK does not acquit multi-day delays — that territory belongs to the observational card, with its confounding label attached. What acceleration demonstrably bought was comfort and fewer minor complications, not survival.
cards.source: Borges FK et al. (HIP ATTACK Investigators). Accelerated surgery versus standard care in hip fracture (HIP ATTACK): an international, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet. 2020. PMID 32050090 · NCT02027896. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(20)30058-1

cards.headline: Pincus 2017: the timing signal — waits beyond 24 hours associated with higher mortality (observational; labeled)
cards.summary: 42,230 Ontario patients: in propensity-matched comparisons, surgery after 24 hours carried 30-day mortality of 6.5% vs 5.8% with earlier surgery (absolute risk difference 0.79 points; 95% CI 0.23–1.35) and a higher composite of death or medical complications (12.2% vs 10.1%; difference 2.16 points). Association, not randomization.
cards.type: Population-based retrospective cohort study with propensity-score matching, JAMA 2017 — OBSERVATIONAL
cards.people: 42,230 adults undergoing hip-fracture surgery at 72 hospitals in Ontario, Canada, 2009–2014 (mean age 80.1 years; 70.5% women); overall 30-day mortality 7.0%. The matched analysis compared 13,731 patients operated after 24 hours with 13,731 matched patients operated earlier.
cards.result: Risk-adjusted spline models showed the probability of each complication beginning to increase when wait times exceeded 24 hours, irrespective of the complication considered. In matched patients, delayed surgery was associated with higher 30-day mortality (898 [6.5%] vs 790 [5.8%]) and a higher composite of mortality, myocardial infarction, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, and pneumonia (1,680 [12.2%] vs 1,383 [10.1%]).
cards.watchOut: Why this card cannot set a deadline by itself: patients wait longer because they are sicker, anticoagulated, or awaiting workup — the delay is partly a marker of the risk it is blamed for. Propensity matching narrows but cannot close that gap. Read together with HIP ATTACK: the randomized trial found no mortality gain from 6 vs 24 hours, and this cohort cannot prove one beyond 24. Together they support 'prompt, and don't dawdle' rather than a proven hour-by-hour cliff. The beyond-48-hour harm signal in the wider literature is likewise observational and is labeled so wherever this shelf cites it.
cards.source: Pincus D et al. Association between wait time and 30-day mortality in adults undergoing hip fracture surgery. JAMA. 2017. PMID 29183076. DOI 10.1001/jama.2017.17606 (Observational study — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: Grigoryan 2014: orthogeriatric co-management associated with lower mortality — a non-randomized literature, graded POSSIBLE
cards.summary: 18 studies, 9,094 patients: orthogeriatric collaboration was associated with lower in-hospital mortality (RR 0.60, relative) and lower long-term mortality (RR 0.83, relative), and with shorter length of stay — across studies that were not randomized comparisons of the models.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of predominantly non-randomized studies, Journal of Orthopaedic Trauma 2014
cards.people: 9,094 hip-fracture patients in 18 studies (1992–2012) of inpatient models pairing an orthopaedic surgeon with a geriatrician, grouped as routine geriatric consultation, geriatric ward with orthopaedic consultation, or shared care.
cards.result: Orthogeriatric collaboration was associated with significantly lower in-hospital mortality (relative risk 0.60; 95% CI 0.43–0.84) and long-term mortality (RR 0.83; 0.74–0.94), and a modestly shorter length of stay (standardized mean difference −0.25), strongest in the shared-care model — though heterogeneity limited that interpretation.
cards.watchOut: Hospitals that build co-management services differ from hospitals that don't — in staffing, volume, and much else — and pooling does not adjust that away. An RR of 0.60 for a service model is also large enough to invite suspicion. The shelf grades this strand POSSIBLE: plausible, consistent, unproven by randomization. It is the strand most aligned with Shelf #340's randomized Marcantonio card — a geriatrician at the bedside is delirium prevention wearing a service-delivery coat.
cards.source: Grigoryan KV et al. Orthogeriatric care models and outcomes in hip fracture patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. J Orthop Trauma. 2014. PMID 23912859. DOI 10.1097/BOT.0b013e3182a5a045 (Systematic review — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: REGAIN (Neuman 2021): spinal vs general anaesthesia — no significant difference; delirium about 20% in both arms
cards.summary: 1,600 patients: death or inability to walk at 60 days occurred in 18.5% on spinal anaesthesia vs 18.0% on general anaesthesia (relative risk 1.03; 95% CI 0.84–1.27; P=0.83); death within 60 days 3.9% vs 4.1%; delirium in about one patient in five in BOTH groups.
cards.type: Pragmatic, randomized, superiority trial (REGAIN), New England Journal of Medicine 2021
cards.people: 1,600 previously ambulatory patients aged 50 years or older undergoing surgery for hip fracture at 46 US and Canadian hospitals (mean age 78 years; 67.0% women): spinal anaesthesia 795, general anaesthesia 805.
cards.result: The primary composite — death or inability to walk about 10 feet independently or with a walker or cane at 60 days — occurred in 132 of 712 patients (18.5%) assigned to spinal and 132 of 733 (18.0%) assigned to general anaesthesia. Inability to walk independently (15.2% vs 14.4%), death within 60 days (3.9% vs 4.1%), time to discharge, and delirium (about 20% in each arm) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: A superiority trial that found no superiority — spinal anaesthesia remains a reasonable choice for other reasons (patient preference, pulmonary considerations), but 'spinal prevents delirium' is not among its proven benefits: delirium struck about a fifth of both arms, which is itself an argument for the prevention bundles of Shelf #340. Note that 83.8% of the spinal group actually received spinal anaesthesia; crossovers were analysed as randomized.

shelves.title: Opioids versus non-opioids in chronic pain: no advantage on function — and worse symptoms on opioids
shelves.question: In chronic back and joint pain, does an opioid strategy beat a non-opioid strategy over a year — and what does the wider trial literature say?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic · Analgesics, Opioid · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Back Pain · Chronic Pain
shelves.balance: SPACE is the trial this question always needed: 240 VA patients with chronic back pain or hip/knee osteoarthritis pain, randomized to an opioid or a non-opioid medication strategy for 12 months. Pain-related function: 3.4 vs 3.3 (P=0.58) — no advantage. Pain intensity actually favoured the non-opioid arm (4.0 vs 3.5), and medication-related symptoms were twice as burdensome on opioids (1.8 vs 0.9). The standard critique is printed fairly on SPACE's own card: the opioid arm's mean dose was modest, about 21 morphine milligram equivalents a day, so the trial convicts a cautious opioid strategy rather than maximal dosing. Busse's 96-trial meta-analysis converges: opioids beat placebo by 0.69 cm on a 10-cm pain scale — under the 1-cm threshold for clinical importance — and showed no edge over non-opioid alternatives. OPAL extends the null to acute back and neck pain, the gateway prescription. The harm card is explicitly observational, and is labeled as such. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: SPACE (Krebs 2018): pain-related function 3.4 vs 3.3 over 12 months (P=0.58) — no advantage; symptoms worse on opioids (1.8 vs 0.9)
cards.summary: 240 patients with chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis pain: pain-related function (Brief Pain Inventory interference, 0–10) averaged 3.4 in the opioid group vs 3.3 in the nonopioid group over 12 months (difference 0.1; 95% CI −0.5 to 0.7; overall P=0.58). Pain intensity favoured the non-opioid strategy (4.0 vs 3.5). Medication-related symptoms were worse on opioids (1.8 vs 0.9).
cards.type: Pragmatic, 12-month, randomized trial with masked outcome assessment (SPACE), JAMA 2018
cards.people: 240 patients (mean age 58.3 years; 13.0% women) with moderate-to-severe chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis pain despite analgesic use, recruited from Veterans Affairs primary care clinics; 234 (97.5%) completed the trial. Both interventions followed a treat-to-target strategy with stepped medication options within the assigned class (opioid arm beginning with immediate-release morphine, oxycodone, or hydrocodone/acetaminophen; non-opioid arm beginning with acetaminophen or an NSAID).
cards.result: Groups did not differ significantly on pain-related function over 12 months. Pain intensity over 12 months was lower (better) in the nonopioid group. The main adverse outcome — patient-reported medication-related symptoms on a 0–19 checklist — was higher in the opioid group (1.8 vs 0.9). No opioid use disorder or overdose occurred during the trial's monitored year.
cards.watchOut: The critique, printed fairly: the opioid group's mean dose was modest — about 21 morphine milligram equivalents per day — because the strategy titrated cautiously and many patients settled at low doses or stopped. SPACE therefore tests the opioid strategy as actually practiced more than it tests high-dose therapy, which remains untested at one year in a trial like this and carries Card 4's harms at higher rates. A 1-point change on the BPI scales was prespecified as clinically important; the function difference was 0.1.
cards.source: Krebs EE et al. Effect of opioid vs nonopioid medications on pain-related function in patients with chronic back pain or hip or knee osteoarthritis pain: the SPACE randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID 29509867 · NCT01583985. DOI 10.1001/jama.2018.0899

cards.headline: Busse 2018: 96 trials — opioids beat placebo by 0.69 cm on a 10-cm scale, below the 1-cm line that matters; no edge over alternatives
cards.summary: 96 randomized trials, 26,169 participants with chronic noncancer pain: vs placebo, opioids reduced pain by a weighted mean difference of −0.69 cm (95% CI −0.82 to −0.56) on a 10-cm visual-analogue scale whose minimally important difference is 1 cm, improved physical functioning only modestly (below its 5-point importance threshold), and increased vomiting. In comparisons with non-opioid alternatives, pain relief was similar.
cards.people: 26,169 participants (61% women; median age 58 years) in 96 randomized trials of opioids for chronic noncancer pain: neuropathic pain (25 trials), nociceptive pain (32), central-sensitization pain (33), and mixed pain (6).
cards.result: Compared with placebo, opioid use was associated with reduced pain (−0.69 cm on a 10-cm scale), a small improvement in physical functioning, and increased vomiting; the modeled proportion achieving the minimally important pain difference was 11.9%. Against non-opioid alternatives — NSAIDs, tricyclic antidepressants, and anticonvulsants among them — opioids were not superior for pain.
cards.watchOut: Most included trials ran for weeks, not the years over which opioids are actually taken, and many used enriched designs that select responders before randomization — so the pooled 0.69 cm is, if anything, a generous estimate of the average effect. The functioning result tells the same story as SPACE in a different dialect: statistically detectable, clinically small.
cards.source: Busse JW et al. Opioids for chronic noncancer pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. JAMA. 2018. PMID 30561481. DOI 10.1001/jama.2018.18472 (Systematic review — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: OPAL (Jones 2023): acute back and neck pain — opioid no better than placebo (2.78 vs 2.25 at 6 weeks; P=0.051)
cards.summary: 347 adults with acute low back or neck pain: mean pain severity at 6 weeks was 2.78 on opioid (oxycodone-naloxone) vs 2.25 on placebo (adjusted mean difference 0.53; 95% CI −0.00 to 1.07; P=0.051) — no significant benefit, with the point estimate favouring placebo. At least one adverse event: 35% vs 30%.
cards.people: 347 adults (49% women) presenting to 157 primary-care or emergency department sites in Sydney, Australia, with 12 weeks or less of at least moderately severe low back and/or neck pain: guideline-recommended care plus opioid (174) or guideline care plus identical placebo (173), for up to 6 weeks; the opioid was oxycodone-naloxone up to 20 mg of oxycodone per day.
cards.result: The primary outcome — pain severity at 6 weeks on the 10-point Brief Pain Inventory severity subscale — did not differ significantly between groups (adjusted mean difference 0.53; P=0.051), analysed in 151 opioid and 159 placebo participants with post-randomization scores. Opioid-related adverse events (such as constipation, 7.5% vs 3.5%) were more frequent on the opioid. The authors' conclusion: opioids should not be recommended for acute non-specific low back pain or neck pain.
cards.watchOut: Acute pain is the gateway prescription — the first opioid most patients ever receive — and in its commonest presentation it beat placebo not at all. A different question from SPACE's chronic-pain null, with the same answer. The trial used a judicious short course by design; that is precisely the regimen guidelines used to endorse.
cards.source: Jones CMP et al. Opioid analgesia for acute low back pain and neck pain (the OPAL trial): a randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2023. PMID 37392748 · ACTRN12615000775516. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(23)00404-X

cards.headline: Vowles 2015: the harm denominator — misuse in 21–29% and addiction in 8–12% of chronic-pain patients prescribed opioids (observational literature)
cards.summary: Systematic review of the rates literature: among patients with chronic pain prescribed opioids, rates of misuse averaged between 21% and 29% and rates of addiction between 8% and 12%, across studies with widely varying definitions, settings, and screening methods.
cards.type: Systematic review and data synthesis, Pain 2015 — OBSERVATIONAL rates literature, labeled as such
cards.people: Patients with chronic pain receiving opioid therapy, across the studies captured by the review (literature to 2014), spanning primary care through specialty pain clinics; the ranges are averages over heterogeneous populations and definitions.
cards.result: Averaging across studies, misuse behaviors occurred in roughly one in four patients on chronic opioid therapy (21–29%) and addiction in roughly one in ten (8–12%). Estimates varied widely with the population studied and the instrument used.
cards.watchOut: This card carries no randomized evidence and claims none: misuse and addiction rates cannot be randomized into existence, and the underlying studies define their terms inconsistently — hence the wide ranges, printed as ranges. It is on the shelf because a fair opioid ledger needs a harm denominator beside SPACE's benefit numerator of zero — and because the developer's 0.5–2.0 caution applies to inflated harm claims too: these are descriptive rates, not relative effects.
cards.source: Vowles KE et al. Rates of opioid misuse, abuse, and addiction in chronic pain: a systematic review and data synthesis. Pain. 2015. PMID 25785523. DOI 10.1097/01.j.pain.0000460357.01998.f1 (Systematic review — no registry number applies.)

shelves.title: Arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease: no benefit over sham — and at ten years, more arthritis progression in the operated knee
shelves.question: In a degenerative knee — osteoarthritis or a degenerative meniscus tear — does arthroscopic surgery beat sham surgery, therapy, or time?
shelves.mesh: Arthroscopy · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Therapy · Intention to Treat Analysis · Knee Injuries · Menisci, Tibial
shelves.balance: The sham trials anchor this shelf, and two of them are re-cards from Shelf #188, where they are counted. FIDELITY randomized 146 patients with a degenerative meniscus tear to partial meniscectomy or sham surgery: at 12 months the groups were indistinguishable. Its ten-year follow-up (Kalske, NEJM 2026 — dated 2026, as published) is the uncomfortable coda: radiographic osteoarthritis progression in 81% of the operated knees vs 70% of the sham knees, and knee replacement or osteotomy in 12% vs 4%. METEOR found surgery plus therapy no better than therapy alone — with 30% of the therapy group crossing over to surgery, printed on its card, where it cuts both ways. Moseley's 2002 placebo-surgery trial said it first. Cochrane's 2022 synthesis puts the average pain benefit at 2.4 mm on a 100-mm scale — printed with its scale, because 2.4 mm is what 'trivial' looks like numerically. The carve-outs are printed, not implied: a truly locked knee, traumatic tears in young patients, and meniscal root tears are different questions these trials did not ask. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: FIDELITY (Sihvonen 2013): meniscectomy no better than SHAM surgery at 12 months (re-card; home: Shelf #188)
cards.summary: 146 patients with a degenerative medial meniscus tear and no knee osteoarthritis: Lysholm score improved +21.7 with arthroscopic partial meniscectomy vs +23.3 with sham surgery (difference −1.6; 95% CI −7.2 to 4.0); WOMET +24.6 vs +27.1 (−2.5); pain after exercise 3.1 vs 3.3 — all non-significant. Later knee surgery: 2 vs 5 patients. (Re-card; home: Shelf #188.)
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (FIDELITY), New England Journal of Medicine 2013. Re-card — home: Shelf #188
cards.people: 146 patients aged 35–65 with knee pain for at least 3 months despite conservative treatment and an MRI-confirmed degenerative medial meniscus tear, without knee osteoarthritis; traumatic tears and knees with true mechanical locking were not this population. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #188; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.result: At 12 months the improvements were indistinguishable between real and sham surgery on the Lysholm score, the WOMET score, and pain after exercise; confidence intervals excluded a clinically meaningful advantage for meniscectomy. Serious adverse events were rare in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The sham operation was a real anaesthetic, real incisions, and a simulated procedure — the strongest control surgery can offer, and the real operation could not beat it. Ten-year outcomes are the next card. Note the population fence, which is also the shelf's carve-out: degenerative tears in middle-aged knees — not a young athlete's traumatic tear, and not a locked knee.
cards.source: Sihvonen R et al. Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy versus sham surgery for a degenerative meniscal tear. N Engl J Med. 2013. PMID 24369076 · NCT00549172. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1305189

cards.headline: Kalske 2026: FIDELITY at TEN years — osteoarthritis progression 81% vs 70%; knee replacement or osteotomy 12% vs 4% (dated 2026)
cards.summary: Ten-year follow-up of the FIDELITY cohort, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2026: radiographic osteoarthritis progression in 81% of the meniscectomy group vs 70% of the sham group; total knee replacement or osteotomy in 12% vs 4%; WOMET scores favoured the sham group by 9.4 points. The symptom equivalence of year 1 had become a structural deficit by year 10.
cards.type: Ten-year follow-up of a randomized sham-controlled trial (FIDELITY), New England Journal of Medicine 2026
cards.people: The FIDELITY trial cohort — 146 patients randomized in Finland with degenerative medial meniscus tears (Reference 1) — reassessed at ten years. (The PubMed record for this report carries no abstract; the figures on this card are as published in the journal report, and the population is the parent trial's.)
cards.result: At ten years, radiographic osteoarthritis had progressed in 81% of knees assigned to arthroscopic partial meniscectomy vs 70% assigned to sham surgery; 12% vs 4% had undergone total knee replacement or osteotomy; and knee-specific quality-of-life/function scores (WOMET) favoured the sham group by 9.4 points.
cards.watchOut: Long-term follow-up of a 146-patient trial is a small denominator for percentages — read 81 vs 70 and 12 vs 4 as a direction with wide uncertainty, not as precise personal risks. The direction is mechanistically coherent: removing meniscal tissue removes load-sharing tissue. The card is dated 2026 because the report is 2026 — this shelf distinguishes the follow-up from its 2013 parent trial explicitly.
cards.source: Kalske R et al. Arthroscopic partial meniscectomy for a degenerative tear — 10-year outcomes. N Engl J Med. 2026. PMID 42054686. DOI 10.1056/NEJMc2516079 (Ten-year follow-up of FIDELITY, NCT00549172; the PubMed record prints no abstract and carries no MeSH headings.)

cards.headline: METEOR (Katz 2013): surgery plus therapy vs therapy alone — no significant difference; 30% crossed over to surgery
cards.summary: 351 patients with a meniscal tear and mild-to-moderate osteoarthritis: WOMAC physical-function improvement at 6 months was 20.9 points with surgery plus physical therapy vs 18.5 with physical therapy alone (mean difference 2.4; 95% CI −1.8 to 6.5) — not significant; results at 12 months were similar. Thirty percent of patients assigned to therapy alone had undergone surgery by 6 months.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, controlled trial (METEOR), New England Journal of Medicine 2013
cards.people: 351 symptomatic patients aged 45 years or older with a meniscal tear and evidence of mild-to-moderate osteoarthritis on imaging, at seven US centres, randomized to surgery with postoperative physical therapy or to a standardized physical-therapy regimen with the option to cross over. (The abstract record does not print the sex mix.)
cards.result: The primary outcome — change in WOMAC physical-function score (0–100) at 6 months — did not differ significantly between groups (difference 2.4 points; 95% CI −1.8 to 6.5), nor at 12 months. The frequency of adverse events did not differ significantly between groups. Nine patients assigned to surgery (6%) had not undergone it.
cards.watchOut: The crossover, printed both ways: 30% of the therapy-first group chose surgery within 6 months, which dilutes the intention-to-treat contrast toward the null — AND demonstrates that a therapy-first strategy still left 70% of patients un-operated at a year with the same average outcome. METEOR's population (tear WITH osteoarthritis) complements FIDELITY's (tear WITHOUT osteoarthritis); both answers are no.
cards.source: Katz JN et al. Surgery versus physical therapy for a meniscal tear and osteoarthritis. N Engl J Med. 2013. PMID 23506518 · NCT00597012. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1301408

cards.headline: Moseley 2002: the original placebo-surgery trial — debridement and lavage no better than placebo at any point in 24 months (re-card; home: Shelf #188)
cards.summary: 180 patients with knee osteoarthritis: at one year, Knee-Specific Pain scores were 48.9 ± 21.9 after placebo surgery vs 54.8 ± 19.8 after lavage and 51.7 ± 22.4 after debridement — and at NO point in 24 months did either real procedure beat placebo on pain or function; confidence intervals excluded any clinically meaningful difference. (Re-card; home: Shelf #188.)
cards.type: Randomized, placebo-controlled (sham surgery), double-blind trial, New England Journal of Medicine 2002. Re-card — home: Shelf #188
cards.people: 180 patients with osteoarthritis of the knee at a Houston VA medical centre (mean age 52; mostly men); 165 completed the trial. The operations tested were arthroscopic lavage and arthroscopic debridement for arthritic knee pain — no torn ligament was involved. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #188; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.result: Patients were randomized to arthroscopic debridement, arthroscopic lavage, or placebo surgery (skin incisions and a simulated debridement, with the scope never inserted), with patients and outcome assessors blinded. At no point during 24 months did either real procedure outperform placebo on pain or function scores.
cards.watchOut: A single VA centre and a mostly male population — and still, two decades on, the reference placebo-surgery trial of arthroscopy for knee osteoarthritis itself, with every later trial pointing its way. The placebo operation also improved patients' scores: the size of surgery's ritual effect is part of what this card measures.
cards.source: Moseley JB et al. A controlled trial of arthroscopic surgery for osteoarthritis of the knee. N Engl J Med. 2002. PMID 12110735. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa013259 (Pre-registration era — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: Cochrane 2022: across 16 trials, arthroscopy's average pain benefit is 2.4 mm on a 100-mm scale — trivial, printed with its scale
cards.summary: 16 randomized trials, 2,105 participants with degenerative knee disease: arthroscopic surgery (debridement, partial meniscectomy, or both) vs placebo surgery or non-surgical treatment gave a mean pain benefit of about 2.4 mm on a 100-mm scale — below any plausible threshold of clinical importance — with no important functional advantage. Four trials (380 participants) used placebo-surgery controls.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2022
cards.people: 2,105 participants in 16 randomized trials of symptomatic degenerative knee disease (osteoarthritis, degenerative meniscal tears, or both); average ages ranged from 46 to 65 years and 56% of participants were women. Comparators were placebo surgery (4 trials, 380 participants), exercise (8 trials, 1,371 participants), and other non-surgical treatments.
cards.result: Arthroscopic surgery produced little or no clinically important benefit in pain or function compared with placebo surgery or non-surgical care — the headline pain difference being about 2.4 mm on a 100-mm visual-analogue scale — while exposing patients to surgical risks and to subsequent knee surgery (replacement or osteotomy), which the review tracked as a harm outcome and which Reference 2 of this shelf follows to ten years.
cards.watchOut: The synthesis agrees with every anchor card on this shelf, which is why it closes it. Guidelines — including the BMJ Rapid Recommendations — now advise strongly against arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease. The carve-outs in this shelf's balance stand apart from that advice: a truly locked knee, traumatic tears in young patients, and meniscal root tears are different questions, untested by these trials.
cards.source: O'Connor D et al. Arthroscopic surgery for degenerative knee disease (osteoarthritis including degenerative meniscal tears). Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2022. PMID 35238404. DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD014328 (Systematic review — no registry number applies.)

shelves.title: Imaging and injections for low back pain: routine imaging does not help, most scans of pain-free backs look 'abnormal', and epidural steroid added nothing to lidocaine
shelves.question: For low back pain and spinal stenosis, do routine imaging and epidural steroid injections improve outcomes — or mostly label normal aging as disease?
shelves.mesh: Low Back Pain · Spinal Stenosis · Injections, Epidural · Glucocorticoids · Intervertebral Disc Degeneration · Magnetic Resonance Imaging
shelves.balance: Three different designs converge on restraint. Randomized trials pooled: imaging people sooner does not make them better (6 trials, 1,804 patients, no significant difference in pain or function at any horizon). Anatomy explains why: in people with NO pain at all, disc degeneration is present in 37% at age 20 and 96% at age 80 — a scan finding is usually a birthday, not a diagnosis. And the injection most often offered for spinal stenosis failed its best test: in the 400-patient LESS trial, adding glucocorticoid to epidural lidocaine improved 6-week disability by −1.0 points on a 24-point scale (P=0.07 — not significant, and below any plausible importance threshold), with adverse events numerically higher on the steroid arm (21.5% vs 15.5% in the trial report). What this shelf does not say: imaging for red flags — cancer, infection, cauda equina, fracture, progressive deficit — remains essential; these trials excluded suspected serious disease. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Chou 2009: routine immediate imaging vs usual care — no benefit in 6 randomized trials (n=1,804)
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Lancet : 6 randomized trials, 1,804 patients with low back pain and no sign of serious disease — immediate lumbar imaging (X-ray, MRI, or CT) vs usual care without it: no significant differences in pain or function at short-term (up to 3 months) or long-term (6–12 months) follow-up, and no differences in quality of life, mental health, or satisfaction.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Lancet 2009
cards.people: 6 trials, 1,804 patients, mostly acute or subacute low back pain assessed in primary-care settings; patients with features suggesting serious underlying conditions were not the population studied.
cards.result: Meta-analyses found no significant differences between immediate imaging and usual care for the primary outcomes at either short-term follow-up (standardised mean difference 0.19 [−0.01 to 0.39] for pain; 0.11 [−0.29 to 0.50] for function) or long-term follow-up (−0.04 [−0.15 to 0.07] for pain; 0.01 [−0.17 to 0.19] for function). Other outcomes — quality of life, mental health, overall patient-reported improvement, satisfaction — did not differ significantly. Trial quality, imaging method, and pain duration did not change the results.
cards.watchOut: The desk brief for this shelf carried this paper as 'Chou 2011'; the record itself is Lancet 2009 (the 6-trial, n=1,804 numbers match this paper exactly), and the card cites the record. The null applies to routine imaging without red flags — it is not an argument against imaging suspected cancer, infection, fracture, or cauda equina, populations these trials did not enrol.
cards.source: Chou R, Fu R, Carrino JA, Deyo RA. Imaging strategies for low-back pain: systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet. 2009;373:463–472. PMID 19200918. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(09)60172-0

cards.headline: Brinjikji 2015: in pain-free people, disc degeneration runs from 37% at age 20 to 96% at age 80 — your scan is not your pain
cards.summary: Systematic review of imaging in 3,110 asymptomatic individuals (33 studies, CT or MRI): prevalence of disc degeneration 37% at age 20 → 96% at age 80 ; disc bulge 30% → 84%; disc protrusion 29% → 43%; annular fissure 19% → 29%. Degeneration on a scan is the normal appearance of an aging spine — in people with no pain at all.
cards.type: Systematic literature review of imaging prevalence in asymptomatic populations, AJNR 2015
cards.people: 33 articles reporting imaging findings in 3,110 asymptomatic individuals; age-specific prevalence estimated by decade from age 20 to 80.
cards.result: The prevalence of disc degeneration in asymptomatic individuals increased from 37% of 20-year-old individuals to 96% of 80-year-old individuals. Disc bulge prevalence rose from 30% at age 20 to 84% at age 80; disc protrusion from 29% to 43%; annular fissure from 19% to 29%. The authors' conclusion, printed as the card's point: imaging findings of spinal degeneration are present in high proportions of asymptomatic individuals, increase with age, and are likely part of normal aging, unassociated with pain in many cases.
cards.watchOut: This card is the interpretive key for Card 1: if nearly every 80-year-old's scan is 'degenerate', a degenerative scan cannot by itself explain an 80-year-old's pain — and labeling it as the cause invites the cascade of injections and surgery tested on Card 3. The review pools cross-sectional prevalence; it does not follow individuals, and some findings (e.g., Modic changes, severe stenosis with concordant signs) carry more clinical weight than disc degeneration alone.
cards.source: Brinjikji W et al. Systematic literature review of imaging features of spinal degeneration in asymptomatic populations. AJNR Am J Neuroradiol. 2015;36:811–816. PMID 25430861. DOI 10.3174/ajnr.A4173

cards.headline: LESS (Friedly 2014): epidural steroid plus lidocaine vs lidocaine alone — disability difference −1.0 points, P=0.07, at 6 weeks
cards.summary: 400 patients with lumbar spinal stenosis and moderate-to-severe leg pain and disability, double-blind: epidural glucocorticoid plus lidocaine vs lidocaine alone — Roland-Morris disability difference −1.0 points on a 0–24 scale (95% CI −2.1 to 0.1; P=0.07 ) and leg-pain difference −0.2 (P=0.48) at 6 weeks. The trial report records adverse events in 21.5% vs 15.5% — the steroid arm paying more for no proven gain.
cards.type: Double-blind, multisite, randomized trial (LESS), New England Journal of Medicine 2014
cards.people: 400 patients with lumbar central spinal stenosis and moderate-to-severe leg pain and disability, randomly assigned to epidural glucocorticoids plus lidocaine or lidocaine alone; one or two injections before the 6-week primary evaluation. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix; the registry ID below was verified against the record's own ClinicalTrials.gov databank entry.)
cards.result: At 6 weeks there were no significant between-group differences in the Roland-Morris Disability Questionnaire score (adjusted difference −1.0 points [−2.1 to 0.1]; P=0.07) or in leg-pain intensity (−0.2 points [−0.8 to 0.4]; P=0.48). The prespecified subgroup analysis by injection route (interlaminar vs transforaminal) likewise showed no significant differences. The authors' conclusion: epidural glucocorticoid plus lidocaine offered minimal or no short-term benefit compared with lidocaine alone. The full trial report's adverse-event counts — 21.5% of the glucocorticoid-lidocaine group vs 15.5% of the lidocaine-alone group reported at least one adverse event — are carried on this card so the null does not travel without its cost column.
cards.watchOut: Two fences. First, the comparator was an active injection (lidocaine), not a sham — the trial shows the steroid adds nothing to the injection ritual, not that the ritual itself is inert; both groups improved from baseline. Second, this is stenosis with leg pain, at 6 weeks: it does not test steroid injections for acute radicular pain from disc herniation, a different question where any benefit is brief at most. A −1.0-point average on a 24-point scale would be trivial even if it had reached significance.

shelves.title: Bisphosphonate drug holidays: after 3–5 years, lower-risk patients lose little by stopping — vertebral fractures are the exception that stratifies the decision
shelves.question: After several years on a bisphosphonate, who can safely take a drug holiday — and who should keep taking it?
shelves.mesh: Diphosphonates · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal · Bone Density · Spinal Fractures · Osteoporotic Fractures · Zoledronic Acid · Alendronate
shelves.balance: One-home note: FLEX already lives on Shelf #91, where it is counted; its card here is a labeled re-card, and nothing on this shelf changes #91. The holiday evidence is two extension trials, and both tell the same two-part story. Stopping costs almost nothing on the outcomes patients fear most — in FLEX, nonvertebral fractures were identical after stopping alendronate (RR 1.00) — except at the spine, where continuing protected: clinical vertebral fractures 2.4% continuing vs 5.3% stopped in FLEX, and morphometric vertebral fractures roughly halved by continuing zoledronic acid in the HORIZON extension (14 vs 30 patients, OR ≈0.51, relative). Bone density drifts down off drug (hip −2.4% in FLEX) but stays above pretreatment levels for years — the drug lingers in bone, which is the whole pharmacologic basis of a holiday. The ASBMR rule that closes the shelf is therefore stratified, not universal: reassess after 5 years oral or 3 years IV; holiday for 2–3 years if risk is not high; continue up to 10/6 years if it is. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: FLEX (Black 2006): stopping alendronate after 5 years — nonvertebral fractures identical (RR 1.00); clinical vertebral fractures 5.3% stopped vs 2.4% continued (re-card; home: Shelf #91)
cards.summary: 1,099 postmenopausal women who had taken alendronate for ~5 years in FIT, re-randomized to 5 more years of alendronate or placebo: nonvertebral fracture risk 19.0% vs 18.9% (RR 1.00 [0.76–1.32]) — no cost to stopping. Clinical vertebral fractures: 2.4% continuing vs 5.3% stopped (RR 0.45, labeled relative). Total hip BMD fell −2.4% off drug but stayed above levels from 10 years earlier. (Re-card; home: Shelf #91.)
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind extension trial (FLEX — Fracture Intervention Trial Long-term Extension), JAMA 2006. Re-card — home: Shelf #91
cards.people: 1,099 postmenopausal women at 10 US centers who had been randomized to alendronate in FIT (mean 5 years of prior treatment), assigned to alendronate 5 mg/d (n=329), 10 mg/d (n=333), or placebo (n=437) for 5 years. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #91; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.result: Compared with continuing alendronate, switching to placebo for 5 years resulted in declines in BMD at the total hip (−2.4% [−2.9 to −1.8]; P<0.001) and spine (−3.7%), but mean levels remained at or above pretreatment levels from 10 years earlier, and bone-turnover markers rose yet stayed below pretreatment levels. The cumulative risk of nonvertebral fractures did not differ (RR 1.00 [0.76–1.32]; 19.0% continuing vs 18.9% discontinuing). Continuing significantly lowered clinically recognized vertebral fractures (2.4% vs 5.3%; RR 0.45 [0.24–0.85], a relative effect) but not morphometric vertebral fractures (9.8% vs 11.3%; RR 0.86 [0.60–1.22]). An 18-patient biopsy substudy showed no qualitative bone abnormalities.
cards.watchOut: Read the two fracture results as a pair, because guidelines do: the holiday is free for hip and nonvertebral fractures — the fractures that disable — and costs something only at the spine, in the subset whose vertebral risk remains high. A low hip T-score predicted who benefited from continuing, which is the empirical seed of the risk-stratified rule on Card 3. Registry ID verified against the record's own databank entry.
cards.source: Black DM et al.; FLEX Research Group. Effects of continuing or stopping alendronate after 5 years of treatment: the Fracture Intervention Trial Long-term Extension (FLEX): a randomized trial. JAMA. 2006;296:2927–2938. PMID 17190893 · NCT00398931 (verified against the record). DOI 10.1001/jama.296.24.2927
