cards.headline: HORIZON extension (Black 2012): 3 more years of zoledronic acid halved morphometric vertebral fractures (14 vs 30 patients; OR 0.51, relative)
cards.summary: 1,233 postmenopausal women who had received 3 annual zoledronic acid infusions in HORIZON-PFT, re-randomized to 3 more years or placebo: new morphometric vertebral fractures 14 vs 30 patients (odds ratio 0.51 , labeled relative; P=0.035); other fracture types did not differ. Femoral-neck BMD held on drug and dipped slightly off it (between-group difference 1.04%), remaining above pretreatment levels in both groups.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled extension trial (HORIZON-PFT extension), Journal of Bone and Mineral Research 2012
cards.people: 1,233 postmenopausal women who had received zoledronic acid for 3 years in the core HORIZON-PFT trial, randomized to 3 additional years of zoledronic acid (n=616) or placebo (n=617).
cards.result: In years 3–6, femoral-neck BMD remained constant in the continue group and dropped slightly in the stop group (between-treatment difference 1.04% [0.4 to 1.7]; P=0.0009) but remained above pretreatment levels in both. Biochemical markers stayed constant on drug and rose slightly off it, remaining well below pretreatment in both. New morphometric vertebral fractures were fewer with continued treatment (14 vs 30 patients; OR 0.51; P=0.035), whereas other fractures were not different. The desk brief for this shelf carried vertebral rates of 3.0% vs 6.2%; the record's abstract prints patient counts and the odds ratio, so the card prints counts and the odds ratio.
cards.watchOut: Harms of continuing, printed from the same abstract: nonsignificant increases in atrial fibrillation serious adverse events (2.0% vs 1.1%; P=0.26) and stroke (3.1% vs 1.5%; P=0.06) in the continue group — small numbers, not significant, and part of why indefinite continuation is not the default. The vertebral benefit concentrated in women with low hip T-scores or prior fractures — again, stratification, not universality.
cards.source: Black DM et al. The effect of 3 versus 6 years of zoledronic acid treatment of osteoporosis: a randomized extension to the HORIZON-Pivotal Fracture Trial (PFT). J Bone Miner Res. 2012;27:243–254. PMID 22161728 · NCT00145327. DOI 10.1002/jbmr.1494

cards.headline: ASBMR 2016: the risk-stratified holiday rule — reassess at 5 years oral / 3 years IV; holiday 2–3 years if risk is not high
cards.summary: American Society for Bone and Mineral Research task force, built on FLEX and the HORIZON extension (the only two long-term trials): after 5 years of oral or 3 years of IV bisphosphonate, reassess risk. High risk (older age, low hip T-score, prior major fracture, fracture on therapy) — consider continuing up to 10 years oral / 6 years IV . Not high risk — a drug holiday of 2–3 years can be considered. The report's own fence: the approach rests on limited evidence, for vertebral fracture reduction, in mostly white postmenopausal women.
cards.type: Task force report / guidance synthesis (American Society for Bone and Mineral Research), Journal of Bone and Mineral Research 2016
cards.people: Guidance addressed to patients on long-term bisphosphonate therapy for osteoporosis, principally postmenopausal women; the task force notes it may apply to men and glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis with adaptations.
cards.result: The task force suggests that after 5 years of oral bisphosphonate or 3 years of intravenous bisphosphonate, reassessment of risk should be considered. In women at high risk — older women, those with a low hip T-score or high fracture risk score, those with a previous major osteoporotic fracture, or who fracture on therapy — continuation of treatment for up to 10 years (oral) or 6 years (intravenous), with periodic evaluation, should be considered. For women not at high fracture risk after 3–5 years of treatment, a drug holiday of 2–3 years can be considered. On harms: the risk of atypical femoral fracture, but not osteonecrosis of the jaw, clearly increases with treatment duration — but such rare events are outweighed by vertebral fracture risk reduction in high-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: This is a guidance card, not a trial card, and it is labeled as such: the task force itself states the approach is based on limited evidence and 'does not replace the need for clinical judgment', and that future trials are unlikely to settle it. The shelf's POSSIBLE stamp covers exactly this structure — two consistent extension trials, one vertebral exception, and a consensus rule interpolating between risk strata.
cards.source: Adler RA et al. Managing Osteoporosis in Patients on Long-term Bisphosphonate Treatment: Report of a Task Force of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. J Bone Miner Res. 2016;31:16–35. PMID 26350171. DOI 10.1002/jbmr.2708

shelves.title: Treat-to-target in rheumatoid arthritis: the strategy is the treatment — measure on schedule, escalate to a target, and the drugs you already have work better
shelves.question: In rheumatoid arthritis, does managing to a measured disease-activity target — rather than treating by impression — improve outcomes, whichever drugs are used?
shelves.mesh: Arthritis, Rheumatoid · Antirheumatic Agents · Methotrexate · Remission Induction · Disease Progression · Humans
shelves.balance: Four strategy trials, one shared ingredient — a number, a schedule, and a rule that the number triggers action. TICORA (Reference 1) tripled-to-quadrupled remission over routine care (65% vs 16%); CAMERA (Reference 2) won with the same single drug in both arms, differing only in visit cadence and a computer enforcing the target; CAMERA-II (Reference 3) showed a defined steroid dose inside the strategy adds structural protection; BeSt (Reference 4) showed four different strategies converging clinically once all were aimed at the same target. The claim stamped LIKELY is the strategy itself — measured, protocolized escalation to a disease-activity target — and this shelf deliberately credits no molecule: the drug shelves are graded elsewhere, on their own trials. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: TICORA (Grigor 2004, Lancet): tight control put 65% in remission vs 16% on routine care — remission defined by the target, reached by escalation
cards.summary: 111 patients with rheumatoid arthritis, randomized to intensive outpatient management — monthly review, disease-activity scoring, protocolized escalation including intra-articular and intramuscular steroid — vs routine care. Mean fall in disease activity score: −3.5 vs −1.9 (difference 1.6 [1.1–2.1], P<0.0001). A good response came in 82% vs 44% (OR 5.8 [2.4–13.9], a relative measure) and remission (DAS <1.6) in 65% vs 16% (OR 9.7 [3.9–23.9], relative) — absolute rates printed beside the odds ratios, as this shelf's rule requires. Radiographic progression, physical function, and quality of life all favored intensive management at no additional cost. Deaths were 1 (intensive) vs 3 (routine), none judged attributable to treatment — printed because this library prints mortality beside its claims.
cards.type: Single-blind randomized controlled trial (TICORA), Lancet 2004 — two teaching hospitals. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 183 patients screened; 111 randomized (55 intensive, 55 routine analyzed) with rheumatoid arthritis. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Mean fall in disease activity score was greater with intensive management (−3.5 vs −1.9; difference 1.6 [95% CI 1.1–2.1]; P<0.0001). Good response (DAS <2.4 with a fall >1.2): 45/55 (82%) vs 24/55 (44%), OR 5.8 [2.4–13.9], P<0.0001. Remission (DAS <1.6): 36/55 (65%) vs 9/55 (16%), OR 9.7 [3.9–23.9], P<0.0001. Radiographic progression, physical function, and quality of life also favored intensive management at no additional cost. Three patients on routine care and one on intensive management died; none was judged attributable to treatment.
cards.watchOut: TICORA is small and single-blind, and its intensive arm bundled several things at once — visit frequency, scoring, steroid injections, escalation rules — so the trial credits the strategy , not any ingredient. That limitation is also the shelf's thesis: what won here was measuring against a target and acting on the measurement, which is why the supporting cards (CAMERA, BeSt) test the same idea with different drugs and machinery.
cards.source: Grigor C et al. Effect of a treatment strategy of tight control for rheumatoid arthritis (the TICORA study): a single-blind randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2004;364(9430):263–269. PMID 15262104

cards.headline: CAMERA (Verstappen 2007): monthly, computer-guided methotrexate escalation produced remission in 50% vs 37% on conventional care
cards.summary: 299 patients with early rheumatoid arthritis, both arms on methotrexate aimed at remission: the intensive arm was seen monthly , with dose adjustments dictated by predefined response criteria through a computerized decision program; the conventional arm was seen every 3 months and treated by common practice, with cyclosporine added for inadequate response in either arm. Over 2 years, 50% of the intensive group achieved at least one period of remission vs 37% of the conventional group (P=0.03) , and areas under the curve for nearly all clinical variables favored intensive management. Same drug, same target — the difference was the cadence and the protocol. That is the treat-to-target claim in its purest form.
cards.type: Two-year multicentre open-label strategy trial (CAMERA), Ann Rheum Dis 2007. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 299 patients with early rheumatoid arthritis randomized to intensive strategy or conventional strategy, both receiving methotrexate. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Seventy-six (50%) patients in the intensive strategy group achieved at least one period of remission during the 2-year trial, vs 55 (37%) in the conventional strategy group (P=0.03). Areas under the curve for nearly all clinical variables were significantly lower — a better clinical effect — in the intensive group. Rheumatologists reported the computerized decision program was a helpful tool in daily practice.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and strategy-level, like TICORA: CAMERA cannot separate the computer program from the monthly visits or the escalation rules, and it was never meant to. Read with TICORA it answers the obvious objection — that TICORA's win was a steroid-injection artifact — by winning with methotrexate titration alone. What neither trial can do is credit a molecule; the molecule shelves live elsewhere in this library.
cards.source: Verstappen SM et al. Intensive treatment with methotrexate in early rheumatoid arthritis: aiming for remission. Computer Assisted Management in Early Rheumatoid Arthritis (CAMERA, an open-label strategy trial). Ann Rheum Dis. 2007;66(11):1443–1449. PMID 17519278

cards.headline: CAMERA-II (Bakker 2012): adding prednisone 10 mg to the tight-control strategy reduced erosive damage and raised sustained remission
cards.summary: 236 patients with early RA (duration <1 year) on a methotrexate-based, monthly, tight-control strategy, randomized to start with prednisone 10 mg/day or placebo alongside. After 2 years, erosive joint damage was limited in both groups and less with prednisone (the record reports the direction, not a pooled figure, and this card prints none); the prednisone strategy also reduced disease activity and disability faster, achieved sustained remission more often, and more often avoided escalation to cyclosporine or a biologic. Adverse events were similar overall — some occurred less often in the prednisone group. A strategy refinement, carded as one: inside an already-tight protocol, a small daily steroid dose bought structural protection.
cards.type: 2-year, prospective, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind, multicenter trial (CAMERA-II), Ann Intern Med 2012 — 7 hospitals in the Netherlands. Registry verified against the record's own databank: ISRCTN70365169.
cards.people: 236 patients with early rheumatoid arthritis (duration <1 year): 117 assigned to methotrexate plus prednisone, 119 to methotrexate plus placebo, all managed to a remission target at monthly visits. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Erosive joint damage after 2 years was limited and less in the group receiving methotrexate and prednisone than in the group receiving methotrexate and placebo. The prednisone strategy was also more effective in reducing disease activity and physical disability, achieving sustained remission, and avoiding the addition of cyclosporine or a biologic agent. Adverse events were similar in both groups, though some occurred less in the prednisone group. The authors note monthly tight-control visits are not always feasible.
cards.watchOut: This card refines, and slightly complicates, the shelf: part of tight control's power can be pharmacologic after all, when the drug is started early inside the strategy. It does not license casual long-term prednisone outside a protocol — the trial's steroid was a defined 10 mg inside monthly monitoring with a remission target and escalation rules, which is a different exposure from open-ended prescribing.

cards.headline: BeSt (Goekoop-Ruiterman 2007): four strategies, one target — initial combinations acted faster and spared joints, and by year 2 all arms converged at 42% remission
cards.summary: 508 patients with early active RA, all adjusted every 3 months toward low disease activity, randomized to sequential monotherapy, step-up combination, initial combination with tapered high-dose prednisone, or initial combination with infliximab. The initial-combination arms improved faster in year 1; by year 2 all groups reached a mean functional ability score of 0.6 and 42% were in remission, with no significant between-strategy differences in clinical outcomes (P=0.690 for remission) , while radiographic damage stayed better suppressed in the initial-combination arms (median Sharp–van der Heijde progression 2.0, 2.0, 1.0, 1.0; P=0.004). Toxicity did not differ significantly, and combination therapy could be withdrawn successfully — by year 2 over half the infliximab arm was on single-drug therapy. BeSt's lesson completes the shelf: the target discipline equalized the strategies clinically; the head start bought joint structure .
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial with blinded assessors (the BeSt study, 2-year report), Ann Intern Med 2007 — 20 Dutch centers. The record carries no registry databank entry; no registry ID is stated because none appears on the record.
cards.people: 508 patients with early active rheumatoid arthritis randomized to four treatment strategies, with trimonthly adjustments to achieve low disease activity. Patients and physicians were aware of the allocated group; assessors were blinded. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Groups 3 and 4 (initial combinations) had more rapid clinical improvement during the first year; all groups improved further to a mean Health Assessment Questionnaire score of 0.6 (overall P=0.257) and 42% were in remission (overall P=0.690) during the second year. Progression of joint damage remained better suppressed in groups 3 and 4 (median scores 2.0, 2.0, 1.0, and 1.0 in groups 1–4; P=0.004). After 2 years, 33%, 31%, 36%, and 53% of patients in groups 1–4 respectively were receiving single-drug therapy. There were no significant differences in toxicity.
cards.watchOut: BeSt is the shelf's discipline against overselling intensity: given the same measured target and the same permission to escalate, starting simple caught up clinically within two years — what the aggressive starts bought was speed and structure, not a different destination. It also means the strategy claim cannot be reduced to 'more drugs sooner': the common ingredient across all four arms, and across TICORA and CAMERA, is scheduled measurement against a target with mandated action.
cards.source: Goekoop-Ruiterman YP et al. Comparison of treatment strategies in early rheumatoid arthritis: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2007;146(6):406–415. PMID 17371885

shelves.title: Tofacitinib safety after ORAL Surveillance: cancers LIKELY increased in older, cardiovascular-risk patients — MACE POSSIBLE, noninferiority missed for both
shelves.question: In older patients with rheumatoid arthritis and cardiovascular risk, is tofacitinib as safe as a TNF inhibitor for heart events and cancer?
shelves.mesh: Arthritis, Rheumatoid · Cardiovascular Diseases · Neoplasms · Janus Kinase Inhibitors · Treatment Outcome · Humans
shelves.balance: One large, purpose-built safety trial drives this shelf, and its two endpoints earn different grades. Malignancies excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer: HR 1.48 with an interval [1.04–2.09] that excludes no-effect, on absolute rates of 4.2% vs 2.9% over a median 4 years — LIKELY, in patients who look like ORAL's: 50 or older, cardiovascular-risk-bearing, methotrexate-experienced RA. MACE: HR 1.33 [0.91–1.94] — the point estimate leans against tofacitinib and noninferiority was missed, but the interval includes benefit, so increased cardiovascular events are POSSIBLE, not established. Both stamps are fenced to the studied population; the trial says nothing direct about younger, low-risk patients, and neither does this shelf. The class-wide boxed warnings that followed are regulatory prudence built on this single trial's shape — the shelf reports the trial, and grades only what the trial showed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: ORAL Surveillance (Ytterberg 2022, NEJM): tofacitinib missed noninferiority for both coprimary endpoints — MACE HR 1.33 [0.91–1.94], malignancies HR 1.48 [1.04–2.09]
cards.summary: 4,362 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate, aged 50 or older with at least one additional cardiovascular risk factor , randomized to tofacitinib 5 mg or 10 mg twice daily or a TNF inhibitor, median follow-up 4.0 years. MACE occurred in 3.4% on combined tofacitinib vs 2.5% on TNF inhibitor (HR 1.33 [0.91–1.94]); cancers excluding nonmelanoma skin cancer in 4.2% vs 2.9% (HR 1.48 [1.04–2.09]) — hazard ratios (relative) printed beside their absolute rates. The prespecified noninferiority margin of 1.8 was missed for both : the intervals could not exclude an 80% relative excess. The cancer interval excludes 1.0; the MACE interval does not — which is why this shelf splits its stamp. Opportunistic infections, all herpes zoster, and nonmelanoma skin cancer were also more frequent on tofacitinib; efficacy was similar across arms. The FDA extended boxed warnings across the JAK-inhibitor class on this trial.
cards.type: Randomized, open-label, noninferiority, postauthorization safety-endpoint trial (ORAL Surveillance), N Engl J Med 2022. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02092467.
cards.people: 4,362 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate, aged ≥50 years with ≥1 additional cardiovascular risk factor: 1,455 received tofacitinib 5 mg twice daily, 1,456 tofacitinib 10 mg twice daily, 1,451 a TNF inhibitor. Median follow-up 4.0 years. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: During follow-up, incidences of MACE and cancer were higher with the combined tofacitinib doses (3.4% [98 patients] and 4.2% [122 patients]) than with a TNF inhibitor (2.5% [37 patients] and 2.9% [42 patients]). Hazard ratios were 1.33 [95% CI 0.91–1.94] for MACE and 1.48 [95% CI 1.04–2.09] for cancers; the noninferiority of tofacitinib was not shown for either coprimary endpoint against the 1.8 margin. Incidences of adjudicated opportunistic infections (including herpes zoster and tuberculosis), all herpes zoster, and adjudicated nonmelanoma skin cancer were higher with tofacitinib. Efficacy was similar in all three groups.
cards.watchOut: The fence is the population: ORAL Surveillance deliberately enriched for risk — older patients, cardiovascular risk factors required, a smoking-enriched cohort — and its verdicts travel only as far as that population. Nothing here measures risk in a 35-year-old without cardiovascular risk, and this shelf does not generalize the signal to them; equally, 'noninferiority missed' is not 'harm proven' for MACE, whose interval spans 0.91 to 1.94. The malignancy claim is the one whose interval excludes no-effect, and it is stamped accordingly.
cards.source: Ytterberg SR et al. Cardiovascular and cancer risk with tofacitinib in rheumatoid arthritis. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(4):316–326. PMID 35081280 · NCT02092467 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2109927

shelves.title: Tocilizumab for giant cell arteritis: sustained remission quadrupled while the prednisone burden halved
shelves.question: Giant cell arteritis relapses as prednisone tapers, and prednisone itself maims. Does IL-6 blockade hold remission while the steroid falls away?
shelves.mesh: Giant Cell Arteritis · Tocilizumab · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Prednisone · Remission Induction · Humans
shelves.balance: GiACTA is the rare trial that wins on both axes of its disease: sustained glucocorticoid-free remission at one year in 56% vs 14% against the like-for-like taper, and a cumulative prednisone exposure cut from ~3,300 mg to ~1,860 mg — efficacy and steroid-sparing in the same result, with serious adverse events running lower on the drug than on placebo-plus-steroid. The fences are printed on the card: a one-year horizon, remission judged while IL-6 blockade suppresses the CRP clinicians usually watch, and no mortality claim of any kind. Within them, this is among the cleanest biologic verdicts in rheumatology. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: GiACTA (Stone 2017, NEJM): sustained remission at week 52 in 56% on weekly tocilizumab vs 14% on placebo — with the prednisone dose roughly halved
cards.summary: 251 patients with giant cell arteritis: subcutaneous tocilizumab 162 mg weekly or every other week, each with a 26-week prednisone taper, vs placebo with a 26-week or 52-week taper. Sustained glucocorticoid-free remission at week 52: 56% (weekly tocilizumab) and 53% (every-other-week) vs 14% (placebo + 26-week taper) and 18% (placebo + 52-week taper) , P<0.001 for both tocilizumab comparisons. Cumulative median prednisone over 52 weeks: 1,862 mg in each tocilizumab group vs 3,296 mg (26-week taper) and 3,818 mg (52-week taper) on placebo — the steroid-sparing is the clinical point, since glucocorticoid toxicity is giant cell arteritis's second disease. Serious adverse events were less frequent on tocilizumab (15% and 14%) than on placebo (22% and 25%). One case of anterior ischemic optic neuropathy occurred in the every-other-week tocilizumab group. No mortality claim is made on this card or anywhere on this shelf.
cards.type: 1-year randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (GiACTA), N Engl J Med 2017. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01791153.
cards.people: 251 patients with giant cell arteritis, randomized 2:1:1:1 to tocilizumab weekly, tocilizumab every other week (each with a 26-week prednisone taper), placebo with a 26-week taper, or placebo with a 52-week taper. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Sustained remission at week 52 occurred in 56% on weekly tocilizumab and 53% on every-other-week tocilizumab, vs 14% on placebo with a 26-week taper and 18% on placebo with a 52-week taper (P<0.001 for the comparisons of either tocilizumab regimen with placebo). Cumulative median prednisone dose over 52 weeks was 1,862 mg in each tocilizumab group vs 3,296 mg (placebo, 26-week taper) and 3,818 mg (placebo, 52-week taper), P<0.001. Serious adverse events occurred in 15% (weekly), 14% (every-other-week), 22% (placebo/26-week) and 25% (placebo/52-week). Anterior ischemic optic neuropathy developed in one patient on every-other-week tocilizumab.
cards.watchOut: One year is the whole horizon: whether remission survives tocilizumab withdrawal, and the drug's long-run infection and laboratory profile in an elderly population, sit beyond this trial — as its authors state. IL-6 blockade also silences CRP, giant cell arteritis's usual activity gauge, so 'remission' on tocilizumab is partly a clinical judgment made without its customary laboratory witness. Neither caveat dents the randomized comparison itself: quadruple the sustained-remission rate at half the steroid, in the disease's defining trial. LIKELY.

shelves.title: Rituximab for ANCA-associated vasculitis: cyclophosphamide's equal for induction, clearly better than azathioprine for maintenance
shelves.question: Can rituximab replace cyclophosphamide to induce remission in ANCA-associated vasculitis — and what holds the remission afterward?
shelves.mesh: Antineutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibodies · Vasculitis · Rituximab · Cyclophosphamide · Azathioprine · Remission Induction · Humans
shelves.balance: The induction claim rests on RAVE (Reference 1): noninferior remission at 6 months (64% vs 53%), superior in relapsing disease, with no early adverse-event separation — equal efficacy, with cyclophosphamide's cumulative toxicities avoided by substitution rather than measured head-to-head. RITUXVAS (Reference 2) sets the boundary in severe renal disease: a rituximab-based combination matched intravenous cyclophosphamide (76% vs 82% sustained remission; 18% mortality in both arms in a very sick cohort) without proving superiority. Maintenance is the decisive card: MAINRITSAN (Card 3, labeled annex) cut major relapse to 5% vs 29% against azathioprine at matched severe-event rates. Serious infection ran similar across arms wherever the records report it — the expectation that rituximab would prove dramatically gentler in the short run is not what these trials show, and this shelf does not claim it. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: RAVE (Stone 2010, NEJM): rituximab noninferior to cyclophosphamide for remission at 6 months — 64% vs 53% — and superior in relapsing disease, 67% vs 42%
cards.summary: 197 patients with severe ANCA-associated vasculitis (Wegener's granulomatosis or microscopic polyangiitis): rituximab 375 mg/m² weekly × 4 vs daily oral cyclophosphamide, both with glucocorticoids tapered off. The primary endpoint — remission without prednisone at 6 months — was reached by 64% on rituximab vs 53% on cyclophosphamide , meeting noninferiority (P<0.001 for noninferiority). In patients entering with relapsing disease, rituximab was outright superior: 67% vs 42% (P=0.01). Efficacy held in major renal disease and alveolar hemorrhage. Adverse-event rates did not differ significantly between the groups — rituximab matched cyclophosphamide's effect without yet proving itself gentler in this window, and this card claims no more than that.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, double-dummy, noninferiority trial (RAVE), N Engl J Med 2010 — 9 centers. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00104299.
cards.people: 197 ANCA-positive patients with Wegener's granulomatosis or microscopic polyangiitis; baseline disease activity, organ involvement, and the proportion with relapsing disease were similar between groups. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Sixty-three patients in the rituximab group (64%) reached the primary endpoint vs 52 (53%) in the control group, meeting the criterion for noninferiority (P<0.001). The rituximab-based regimen was more efficacious for relapsing disease: 34 of 51 (67%) vs 21 of 50 (42%) reached the endpoint (P=0.01). Rituximab was as effective as cyclophosphamide in major renal disease and alveolar hemorrhage. There were no significant differences between the groups in rates of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Six months and a remission endpoint: RAVE does not answer relapse after induction (that is MAINRITSAN's question, Card 3) or cumulative cyclophosphamide harms — infertility, bladder cancer — that accrue over years and motivated the comparison in the first place. The trial's honest shape: equal induction, better re-induction of relapsers, no early safety separation. Later maintenance data, not this card, carry the argument further.
cards.source: Stone JH et al. Rituximab versus cyclophosphamide for ANCA-associated vasculitis. N Engl J Med. 2010;363(3):221–232. PMID 20647199 · NCT00104299 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0909905

cards.headline: RITUXVAS (Jones 2010, NEJM): in severe renal vasculitis, a rituximab-based regimen matched intravenous cyclophosphamide — remission 76% vs 82%, deaths 18% in both arms
cards.summary: 44 patients with newly diagnosed ANCA-associated vasculitis and renal involvement (median GFR 18 ml/min), randomized 3:1 to rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly × 4) plus two intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses with glucocorticoids, vs intravenous cyclophosphamide for 3–6 months followed by azathioprine. Sustained remission at 12 months: 76% vs 82% (P=0.68) — rituximab was not superior , and this card prints that plainly. Severe adverse events: 42% vs 36% (P=0.77). Deaths: 6 of 33 (18%) vs 2 of 11 (18%) — identical proportions in a population whose severity shows in that number; mortality is printed here because this library prints it beside every claim. GFR recovery was similar (median increase 19 vs 15 ml/min). A combination regimen, graded as one: it shows a rituximab-based path works in the sickest renal patients, not that rituximab alone replaces cyclophosphamide there.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (RITUXVAS), N Engl J Med 2010. Registry verified against the record's own databank: ISRCTN28528813.
cards.people: 44 patients with newly diagnosed ANCA-associated vasculitis and renal involvement (median age 68 years; median GFR 18 ml/min/1.73 m²): 33 assigned to the rituximab-based regimen, 11 to intravenous cyclophosphamide. The record does not state a sex split.
cards.result: Sustained remission at 12 months occurred in 25 of 33 (76%) on the rituximab-based regimen and 9 of 11 (82%) on intravenous cyclophosphamide (P=0.68). Severe adverse events occurred in 42% vs 36% (P=0.77). Six of 33 (18%) and 2 of 11 (18%) patients died (P=1.00). Median GFR increase from 0 to 12 months was 19 vs 15 ml/min (P=0.14). The authors conclude the rituximab-based regimen was not superior and was not associated with reductions in early severe adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Eleven control patients is a small denominator — every control death moves that arm by 9 points — and the rituximab arm still received two cyclophosphamide pulses, so the trial cannot isolate rituximab's solo contribution in renal disease. Its role on this shelf is boundary-setting: in the severest renal presentations, the rituximab path produced no early safety dividend and no efficacy loss, which is what 'an acceptable alternative' means in numbers.
cards.source: Jones RB et al. Rituximab versus cyclophosphamide in ANCA-associated renal vasculitis. N Engl J Med. 2010;363(3):211–220. PMID 20647198 · ISRCTN28528813 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa0909169

cards.headline: MAINRITSAN (Guillevin 2014, NEJM) — annex, maintenance: rituximab held remission far better than azathioprine — major relapse 5% vs 29% at month 28
cards.summary: Labeled an annex card: this is maintenance, not induction. 115 patients with ANCA-associated vasculitis in complete remission after cyclophosphamide-glucocorticoid induction, randomized to rituximab 500 mg on days 0 and 14 and at months 6, 12, and 18, vs daily azathioprine to month 22. At month 28, major relapse had occurred in 3 patients (5%) on rituximab vs 17 (29%) on azathioprine (HR for relapse 6.61 [1.56–27.96] against azathioprine; P=0.002) — the azathioprine-to-rituximab hazard printed as the record states it, with absolute rates beside it. Severe adverse events were similar (25 patients in each group); severe infections numbered 8 (azathioprine) vs 11 (rituximab); cancer developed in 2 vs 1 patients; two azathioprine patients died (sepsis, pancreatic cancer) and no rituximab patient did — small numbers, printed because this library prints deaths.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (MAINRITSAN), N Engl J Med 2014. Registries verified against the record's own databank: NCT00748644 · EudraCT 2008-002846-51.
cards.people: 115 patients (87 granulomatosis with polyangiitis, 23 microscopic polyangiitis, 5 renal-limited vasculitis) in complete remission after a cyclophosphamide-glucocorticoid regimen: 57 assigned to rituximab, 58 to azathioprine. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At month 28, major relapse had occurred in 17 azathioprine patients (29%) and 3 rituximab patients (5%) (hazard ratio for relapse, 6.61; 95% CI 1.56–27.96; P=0.002). Severe adverse events were similar: 25 patients in each group had severe adverse events (44 events on azathioprine, 45 on rituximab); severe infections occurred in 8 vs 11 patients; cancer in 2 vs 1; two patients in the azathioprine group died (1 sepsis, 1 pancreatic cancer).
cards.watchOut: Maintenance after cyclophosphamide induction is a selected population — everyone here had already survived and responded to induction — so the 5% vs 29% applies to that doorway, not to diagnosis day. The trial was open-label, and relapse ascertainment leaned on activity scores plus organ involvement. Even fenced, a six-fold relative separation on major relapse, with matched severe-event counts, is why rituximab became the maintenance standard; the card is labeled annex so no reader mistakes it for induction evidence.
cards.source: Guillevin L et al. Rituximab versus azathioprine for maintenance in ANCA-associated vasculitis. N Engl J Med. 2014;371(19):1771–1780. PMID 25372085 · NCT00748644 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1404231

shelves.title: Belimumab for lupus: a modest, twice-replicated responder gain in SLE — and a real renal gain in lupus nephritis
shelves.question: Does blocking B-lymphocyte stimulator with belimumab help systemic lupus — in the joints-and-rash disease, and in the kidney disease that decides its prognosis?
shelves.mesh: Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic · Lupus Nephritis · Belimumab · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · B-Cell Activating Factor · Humans
shelves.balance: Belimumab's case is accumulation, not drama: BLISS-52 (Reference 1) gained 14 SRI points over placebo, BLISS-76 (Reference 2) gained 10 and attenuated by week 76 — both printed at full size — and BLISS-LN (Reference 3) moved the outcome that matters most in lupus, renal response (43% vs 32%) with renal events or death at HR 0.51 relative. Safety across the program ran close to placebo for serious infection, with no malignancy signal in the trials; the monitored neuropsychiatric caution from labeling is stated on Card 1 and belongs in prescribing, not hidden from it. Modest absolute gains, consistently in one direction, across two organ systems: LIKELY. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: BLISS-52 (Navarra 2011, Lancet): belimumab 10 mg/kg raised the SRI response to 58% vs 44% on placebo at week 52
cards.summary: 867 seropositive patients with active SLE (SELENA-SLEDAI ≥6) in Latin America, Asia-Pacific, and eastern Europe, on standard care, randomized to belimumab 1 or 10 mg/kg or placebo. The SLE Responder Index at week 52 — a ≥4-point SLEDAI fall with no new major organ flare and no overall worsening — was reached by 58% on belimumab 10 mg/kg (OR 1.83 [1.30–2.59], P=0.0006) and 51% on 1 mg/kg (OR 1.55 [1.10–2.19]) vs 44% on placebo : relative odds printed beside the absolute rates; the drug's gain is the 14-point gap at the approved dose. Serious infection ran 4% (10 mg/kg), 8% (1 mg/kg), and 6% (placebo) — no dose-ordered infection penalty. No malignancies were reported. The neuropsychiatric signal that later labeling watches — depression and suicidality in a disease that itself causes both — is carded in the shelf balance, with the trial's own AE rates similar across arms.
cards.type: Multicentre randomized, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (BLISS-52), Lancet 2011. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00424476.
cards.people: 867 patients aged ≥18 years, seropositive with SELENA-SLEDAI ≥6, randomized to belimumab 1 mg/kg (n=289), 10 mg/kg (n=290), or placebo (n=288), plus standard of care, for 48 weeks. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: SRI rates at week 52 were significantly higher with belimumab 1 mg/kg (148 [51%]; OR 1.55 [95% CI 1.10–2.19]; P=0.0129) and 10 mg/kg (167 [58%]; OR 1.83 [1.30–2.59]; P=0.0006) than placebo (125 [44%]). SELENA-SLEDAI falls of ≥4 points, BILAG flare criteria, and Physician's Global Assessment non-worsening each favored belimumab. Adverse-event rates were similar across groups; serious infection was reported in 8% (1 mg/kg), 4% (10 mg/kg), and 6% (placebo); severe or serious hypersensitivity reactions on an infusion day in two patients (<1%) in each belimumab group and none on placebo. No malignant diseases were reported.
cards.watchOut: BLISS-52's population is the first fence: enrolled outside North America and western Europe, seropositive and moderately-to-severely active — the twin trial in a different population (Reference 2) produced a smaller effect, so the 58% is not a universal constant. The SRI itself is a composite built for these trials; a 14-point absolute responder gain is real but modest, and this shelf's LIKELY rests on two concordant trials plus a renal win (Reference 3), not on BLISS-52 alone.
cards.source: Navarra SV et al. Efficacy and safety of belimumab in patients with active systemic lupus erythematosus: a randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet. 2011;377(9767):721–731. PMID 21296403 · NCT00424476 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(10)61354-2

cards.headline: BLISS-76 (Furie 2011): the same drug, a smaller effect — SRI 43.2% vs 33.5% at week 52, attenuated to 38.5% vs 32.4% by week 76
cards.summary: 819 ANA- or anti-dsDNA-positive patients with SELENA-SLEDAI ≥6, same design, longer follow-up. At week 52, SRI response on belimumab 10 mg/kg was 43.2% vs 33.5% on placebo (P=0.017) — a 10-point absolute gain, smaller than BLISS-52's 14 — with 1 mg/kg at 40.6% (P=0.089, not significant). By week 76 the effect had attenuated: 38.5% (10 mg/kg) vs 32.4% (placebo) , printed here because durability is part of the claim. Severe-flare risk over 76 weeks fell relatively by 34% at 1 mg/kg (P=0.023) and 23% at 10 mg/kg (P=0.13). Serious and severe adverse events — including infections, malignancies, and deaths — were comparable across groups , as the record states. Two trials, same drug, same endpoint, effects of 14 and 10 points: that consistency-with-variation is the honest summary of belimumab in non-renal SLE.
cards.type: Phase III, multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled trial (BLISS-76), Arthritis Rheum 2011. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00410384.
cards.people: 819 antinuclear antibody-positive or anti-double-stranded DNA-positive SLE patients with SELENA-SLEDAI scores ≥6, randomized 1:1:1 to belimumab 1 mg/kg, 10 mg/kg, or placebo plus standard therapy for 72 weeks. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Belimumab 10 mg/kg met the primary endpoint: SRI response at week 52 was 43.2% vs 33.5% on placebo (P=0.017); 1 mg/kg gave 40.6% (P=0.089). At week 76, response rates were 32.4% (placebo), 39.1% (1 mg/kg), and 38.5% (10 mg/kg). In post hoc analyses at higher SELENA-SLEDAI thresholds, 10 mg/kg discriminated better at weeks 52 and 76. Severe-flare risk over 76 weeks was reduced relatively by 34% (1 mg/kg; P=0.023) and 23% (10 mg/kg; P=0.13). Serious and severe adverse events, including infections, laboratory abnormalities, malignancies, and deaths, were comparable across groups.
cards.watchOut: The week-76 attenuation deserves its line: whether it reflects waning drug effect, placebo-group catch-up as nonresponders exit, or the composite endpoint's behavior over time cannot be separated in this record. BLISS-76 is also why this shelf does not stamp belimumab's SLE effect higher than LIKELY: a real, twice-replicated, single-digit-to-low-teens absolute responder gain is useful medicine for a disease with few options — and it is not a transformation.
cards.source: Furie R et al. A phase III, randomized, placebo-controlled study of belimumab, a monoclonal antibody that inhibits B lymphocyte stimulator, in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus. Arthritis Rheum. 2011;63(12):3918–3930. PMID 22127708 · NCT00410384 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1002/art.30613

cards.headline: BLISS-LN (Furie 2020, NEJM): in lupus nephritis, renal response 43% vs 32% — and renal events or death HR 0.51 (relative)
cards.summary: 448 adults with biopsy-proven active lupus nephritis, belimumab 10 mg/kg or placebo added to standard therapy (mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide-azathioprine), 104 weeks. The primary efficacy renal response — urine protein-to-creatinine ≤0.7 with eGFR preserved and no rescue therapy — came in 43% vs 32% (OR 1.6 [1.0–2.3], P=0.03) ; complete renal response 30% vs 20% (OR 1.7 [1.1–2.7]). The endpoint patients feel: time to a renal-related event or death favored belimumab, HR 0.51 [0.34–0.77] — a relative effect, printed with its label; the record does not separate the death component, and this card does not invent one. Safety was consistent with the earlier trials. Nephritis is where lupus kills kidneys, and this is the shelf's strongest card: a renal endpoint, two years, a halved relative event hazard.
cards.type: Phase 3, multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (BLISS-LN), N Engl J Med 2020 — 107 sites in 21 countries. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT01639339.
cards.people: 448 adults with biopsy-proven, active lupus nephritis, randomized 1:1 to intravenous belimumab 10 mg/kg (n=224) or placebo (n=224), in addition to standard therapy, for 104 weeks. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: At week 104, significantly more patients on belimumab had a primary efficacy renal response (43% vs 32%; OR 1.6 [95% CI 1.0–2.3]; P=0.03) and a complete renal response (30% vs 20%; OR 1.7 [95% CI 1.1–2.7]; P=0.02). The risk of a renal-related event or death was lower with belimumab (HR 0.51 [95% CI 0.34–0.77]; P=0.001). The safety profile was consistent with previous belimumab trials.
cards.watchOut: Eleven points of absolute renal response is the claim — meaningful in a disease where the alternative trajectory is dialysis, short of dramatic. The composite event endpoint mixes renal events with death, and its HR 0.51 flatters if read as a mortality effect, which this card explicitly refuses to do. Belimumab also carries a monitored neuropsychiatric caution (depression, suicidality) from its labeling; the BLISS trials' own adverse-event rates, including infections, ran similar to placebo, and both facts belong in the same conversation with the patient.

shelves.title: Anifrolumab for lupus: one phase 3 trial missed its primary, the other hit a different one — POSSIBLE
shelves.question: Does blocking the type I interferon receptor with anifrolumab reduce lupus activity — and why do its two phase 3 trials disagree?
shelves.mesh: Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic · Anifrolumab · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Receptor, Interferon alpha-beta · Humans
shelves.balance: This shelf exists to teach discordance. TULIP-1 (Reference 1) prespecified SRI-4 and missed it outright — 36% vs 40% on placebo. TULIP-2 (Reference 2) prespecified BICLA instead, the endpoint that had leaned positive inside TULIP-1, and hit it cleanly: 47.8% vs 31.5%. Both facts are on the shelf at full size, in that order. The drug plausibly works — interferon biology, a consistent BICLA direction across both trials, steroid-sparing secondaries — but a library that demands two concordant trials cannot stamp LIKELY on a split pair, and the zoster cost (7.2%) plus a pneumonia death on the winning card argue against generosity. POSSIBLE: a real option for active SLE despite standard care, prescribed with the disagreement disclosed. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: TULIP-1 (Furie 2019): the primary endpoint was MISSED — SRI-4 response 36% on anifrolumab 300 mg vs 40% on placebo (P=0.41)
cards.summary: Printed first, because on this shelf the null leads. 457 patients with moderate-to-severe SLE on standard care, randomized to anifrolumab 300 mg, anifrolumab 150 mg, or placebo every 4 weeks for 48 weeks. The primary outcome — SRI-4 response at week 52 — occurred in 36% on anifrolumab 300 mg vs 40% on placebo (difference −4.2 points [−14.2 to 5.8]; P=0.41) : numerically worse than placebo, nowhere near significance. SRI-4 at week 24 and in the interferon-signature-high subgroup also did not differ. What leaned the other way was secondary: BICLA response 37% vs 27% (difference 10.1 [0.6–19.7]), steroid reduction and skin responses in the same direction, flare rate ratio 0.83 [0.60–1.14]. Serious adverse events were similar (14% vs 16%). A failed primary with interesting secondaries is a hypothesis, not a result — remember that shape when Card 2 changes the endpoint.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomized, controlled, phase 3 trial (TULIP-1), Lancet Rheumatol 2019 — 123 sites in 18 countries. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02446912.
cards.people: 457 patients aged 18–70 years with moderate-to-severe SLE on stable standard care: 180 assigned to anifrolumab 300 mg, 93 to anifrolumab 150 mg, 184 to placebo, every 4 weeks for 48 weeks. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: The proportion with an SRI-4 response at week 52 was similar between anifrolumab 300 mg (65 [36%] of 180) and placebo (74 [40%] of 184; difference −4.2 [95% CI −14.2 to 5.8]; P=0.41). SRI-4 at week 24 and at week 52 in the interferon gene signature test-high subgroup also did not differ. Sustained corticosteroid reduction was achieved by 41% vs 32% (difference 8.9 [−4.1 to 21.9]); CLASI ≥50% reduction by week 12 by 42% vs 25% (difference 17.0 [−0.3 to 34.3]); annualized flare rates were 0.60 vs 0.72 (rate ratio 0.83 [0.60–1.14]). BICLA response was 37% vs 27% (difference 10.1 [0.6 to 19.7]). Serious adverse events occurred in 14% (anifrolumab 300 mg) vs 16% (placebo). The primary endpoint was not reached.
cards.watchOut: TULIP-1's lesson is about endpoint choice in a composite-score disease: SRI-4 and BICLA weigh the same clinical events differently, and the trial that 'failed' and the trial that 'succeeded' (Reference 2) differ first in which composite they crowned. That does not make TULIP-2's result illegitimate — BICLA was prespecified there — but it does mean the drug's evidence is one positive trial on a swapped primary against one negative trial on the original. That is exactly the shape this library stamps POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Furie RA et al. Type I interferon inhibitor anifrolumab in active systemic lupus erythematosus (TULIP-1): a randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial. Lancet Rheumatol. 2019;1(4):e208–e219. PMID 38229377 · NCT02446912 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S2665-9913(19)30076-1

cards.headline: TULIP-2 (Morand 2020, NEJM): with BICLA as the primary endpoint, anifrolumab won — 47.8% vs 31.5% — and herpes zoster ran 7.2%
cards.summary: 362 patients with active SLE, anifrolumab 300 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 48 weeks, with the primary endpoint taken from TULIP-1's secondary shelf: BICLA response at week 52 — improvement in all moderately-to-severely active organ systems with no worsening anywhere. BICLA response: 47.8% vs 31.5% (difference 16.3 points [6.3–26.3]; P=0.001) , consistent in the interferon-signature-high subgroup (48.0% vs 30.7%). Glucocorticoid reduction and skin severity also favored anifrolumab; joint counts and flare rate did not reach significance. The harm line: herpes zoster in 7.2% of anifrolumab patients (the record's abstract does not state the placebo zoster rate, and this card prints none) and bronchitis in 12.2%. One patient in the anifrolumab group died of pneumonia — printed beside the benefit, as this library requires.
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (TULIP-2), N Engl J Med 2020. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT02446899.
cards.people: 362 patients with active SLE received the randomized intervention: 180 anifrolumab 300 mg, 182 placebo, intravenously every 4 weeks for 48 weeks. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: BICLA response at week 52 occurred in 47.8% on anifrolumab vs 31.5% on placebo (difference 16.3 percentage points [95% CI 6.3–26.3]; P=0.001). In the high interferon gene signature subgroup, responses were 48.0% vs 30.7%; in the low subgroup, 46.7% vs 35.5%. Glucocorticoid-dose and skin-severity endpoints significantly favored anifrolumab; swollen/tender joint counts and annualized flare rate did not. Herpes zoster occurred in 7.2% and bronchitis in 12.2% of anifrolumab patients. There was one death from pneumonia in the anifrolumab group.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen points of BICLA response is a respectable lupus effect — and it was obtained by promoting a secondary endpoint after the prespecified primary failed in the sister trial (Reference 1). Prespecification within TULIP-2 keeps the result honest as a trial; the two-trial pattern keeps the shelf at POSSIBLE as a claim. Interferon blockade's zoster risk is the practical tax: vaccination status belongs in the prescribing conversation.
cards.source: Morand EF et al. Trial of anifrolumab in active systemic lupus erythematosus. N Engl J Med. 2020;382(3):211–221. PMID 31851795 · NCT02446899 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1912196

shelves.title: Treating the acute gout flare: low-dose colchicine is the dose, steroids equal NSAIDs — and the practice points matter as much as the drugs
shelves.question: A joint is hot, red, and exquisitely painful at 2 a.m. Which treatment relieves an acute gout flare, at what dose, and what should not be done?
shelves.mesh: Gout · Colchicine · Prednisolone · Naproxen · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Canakinumab · Humans
shelves.balance: Three interchangeable first moves, each with its trial: low-dose colchicine 1.8 mg early in the flare (Card 1 — equal to high-dose, placebo-like harms; the high-dose ritual survives only as this shelf's cautionary tale); an NSAID or a 5-day oral prednisolone course, proven equivalent head-to-head (Reference 2), chosen by the patient's kidneys, stomach, and anticoagulation rather than by efficacy. Canakinumab (Reference 3) wins on pain in patients who have failed or cannot take those — and stays fenced there by its phase II evidence, its immunosuppression, and its cost. Printed practice points: treat as early in the flare as possible — AGREE's window was the first 36 hours — and do not stop allopurinol during a flare : a flare is treated on top of urate lowering, never by interrupting it. Long-term flare prevention is a urate question, graded on Shelf #168 and Shelf #382 . Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: AGREE (Terkeltaub 2010): low-dose colchicine worked as well as high-dose — ≥50% pain relief in 37.8% vs 15.5% on placebo — with a placebo-like harm profile
cards.summary: 184 patients with an early acute gout flare, self-administering colchicine within 36 hours: low dose (1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg an hour later — 1.8 mg total), high dose (4.8 mg over 6 hours), or placebo. The primary endpoint, ≥50% pain reduction at 24 hours without rescue medication: 37.8% low-dose, 32.7% high-dose, 15.5% placebo (P=0.005 and P=0.034 vs placebo) — low dose matched high dose on effect. On harm they diverged completely: diarrhea in 76.9% on high dose (19.2% severe; 17.3% vomiting) vs 23.0% on low dose (none severe, no vomiting), an adverse-event profile the authors call indistinguishable from placebo. Rescue medication within 24 hours: 31.1% (low), 34.6% (high), 50.0% (placebo). The old hourly-until-diarrhea ritual is what this trial retired: the dose is 1.8 mg, started early.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group dose-comparison trial (the AGREE trial), Arthritis Rheum 2010. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00506883.
cards.people: 184 patients in the intention-to-treat analysis with acute gout flare, self-administering treatment early in the flare: 74 low-dose colchicine, 52 high-dose, 58 placebo. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: Responders (≥50% pain reduction at 24 hours without rescue medication) were 28 of 74 (37.8%) on low-dose colchicine, 17 of 52 (32.7%) on high-dose, and 9 of 58 (15.5%) on placebo (P=0.005 and P=0.034 vs placebo). Rescue medication within 24 hours was taken by 31.1% (low-dose; P=0.027 vs placebo), 34.6% (high-dose), and 50.0% (placebo). The low-dose group's adverse-event profile was similar to placebo (OR 1.5 [95% CI 0.7–3.2]). High-dose colchicine caused diarrhea in 76.9% (OR 21.3 [7.9–56.9]), severe diarrhea in 19.2%, and vomiting in 17.3%; low-dose caused diarrhea in 23.0% (OR 1.9 [0.8–4.8]), with no severe diarrhea and no vomiting.
cards.watchOut: The trial treated flares early — colchicine's window is the first day or so, and the AGREE numbers should not be quoted for a flare already three days old. Colchicine also carries real drug-interaction and organ-impairment fences (strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors, advanced kidney or liver disease) that sit outside this efficacy record and inside its labeling. Within the early-flare window: low dose is the dose, and 'low-dose equals high-dose with placebo-like harms' is one of the cleanest dose lessons in this library.
cards.source: Terkeltaub RA et al. High versus low dosing of oral colchicine for early acute gout flare: twenty-four-hour outcome of the first multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group, dose-comparison colchicine study. Arthritis Rheum. 2010;62(4):1060–1068. PMID 20131255 · NCT00506883 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1002/art.27327

cards.headline: Prednisolone vs naproxen (Janssens 2008, Lancet): a 5-day oral steroid course was equivalent to an NSAID for gout pain — the alternatives are genuinely interchangeable
cards.summary: 120 primary-care patients with crystal-proven monoarticular gout: prednisolone 35 mg once daily or naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 5 days, double-blind. Pain fell by 44.7 mm (prednisolone) vs 46.0 mm (naproxen) on a 100 mm scale at 90 hours — a difference of 1.3 mm [−9.8 to 7.1], inside the prespecified 10% equivalence margin by both per-protocol and intention-to-treat analyses. Adverse effects were similar, minor, and resolved by 3 weeks. Carded as the shelf's equivalence evidence: for the patient whose kidneys, stomach, or anticoagulant rules out an NSAID — a large share of the gout population — a short oral steroid course is not a compromise but an equal. Glucocorticoids and NSAIDs together form the interchangeable first line with colchicine (Reference 1); the choice among them is made on the patient's other organs, not on efficacy.
cards.type: Double-blind, randomized equivalence trial, Lancet 2008 — primary care. Registry verified against the record's own databank: ISRCTN14648181.
cards.people: 120 patients with gout confirmed by monosodium urate crystals in primary care: 60 assigned to prednisolone 35 mg daily, 60 to naproxen 500 mg twice daily, for 5 days (59 per group in per-protocol analysis). The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: After 90 hours, the reduction in pain score was 44.7 mm with prednisolone and 46.0 mm with naproxen (difference 1.3 mm; 95% CI −9.8 to 7.1), suggesting equivalence within the a priori 10% margin; the intention-to-treat difference in change was 1.57 mm [−8.65 to 11.78]. Adverse effects were similar between groups, minor, and resolved by the 3-week follow-up. The authors conclude oral prednisolone and naproxen are equally effective in the initial treatment of gout arthritis over 4 days.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence in crystal-proven monoarticular gout in primary care — polyarticular flares and hospital patients are extrapolations, reasonable ones. Five days of prednisolone 35 mg is a defined, short exposure; the card does not endorse open-ended steroid use for recurrent flares, where the correct move is urate lowering (whose cardiovascular safety is graded on Shelf #382), not a standing prescription for flare suppression.
cards.source: Janssens HJ et al. Use of oral prednisolone or naproxen for the treatment of gout arthritis: a double-blind, randomised equivalence trial. Lancet. 2008;371(9627):1854–1860. PMID 18514729 · ISRCTN14648181 (verified against the record's own databank). DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(08)60799-0

cards.headline: Canakinumab for difficult gout flares (So 2010): pain relief beat an injected steroid — in patients who had already failed or could not take the standard drugs
cards.summary: 200 patients with acute gouty arthritis refractory to, or with contraindications to, NSAIDs and/or colchicine — the fence is the population — randomized to a single subcutaneous dose of canakinumab (10–150 mg) or intramuscular triamcinolone 40 mg. At 72 hours a dose response was significant; canakinumab 150 mg reduced pain more than triamcinolone at every time point from 24 hours to 7 days (differences of −11.5 to −19.2 mm on a 100 mm scale; P<0.05 throughout), and the risk of a recurrent flare fell significantly at all doses (relative risk reduction 94% at 150 mg — a relative figure, printed as such). Overall adverse events were similar (41% vs 42%), mostly mild or moderate. Why it is fenced despite winning: this is a phase II dose-ranging trial in a selected difficult population, and IL-1 blockade is systemic immunosuppression bought at biologic prices for a self-limited flare — its place is the patient who has exhausted Cards 1 and 2, not the first flare in the clinic.
cards.type: 8-week, single-blind, double-dummy, phase II dose-ranging randomized study, Arthritis Rheum 2010. Registry verified against the record's own databank: NCT00798369.
cards.people: 200 patients with acute gouty arthritis refractory to or with contraindications to NSAIDs and/or colchicine: 143 received a single subcutaneous canakinumab dose (10, 25, 50, 90, or 150 mg), 57 intramuscular triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg. The record does not state a mean age or sex split.
cards.result: A statistically significant dose response for pain was observed at 72 hours; all canakinumab doses gave numerically less pain than triamcinolone. Canakinumab 150 mg reduced pain intensity more than triamcinolone at 24, 48, and 72 hours (differences −11.5 mm [P=0.04], −18.2 mm [P=0.002], −19.2 mm [P<0.001]) and at 4, 5, and 7 days (all P<0.05). Canakinumab significantly reduced recurrent-flare risk vs triamcinolone (P≤0.01 for all doses; relative risk reduction 94% at 150 mg). Overall adverse-event incidence was similar (41% vs 42%), mostly mild or moderate.
cards.watchOut: Superior pain scores in a phase II trial do not make a first-line drug: the comparator here was a single steroid injection in patients chosen because standard therapy had failed or was barred, and neither infection outcomes over years nor cost-effectiveness are answered by 8 weeks of data. The card's job on this shelf is to mark the end of the escalation path — colchicine or NSAID or steroid for nearly everyone; IL-1 blockade reserved for the difficult few — and to keep 'superior on pain' from drifting into general practice.
cards.source: So A et al. Canakinumab for the treatment of acute flares in difficult-to-treat gouty arthritis: results of a multicenter, phase II, dose-ranging study. shelves.title: Fibromyalgia treatment: the drugs help about one patient in ten — exercise is the better bet, and neither is strong
shelves.question: Pain everywhere, exhaustion, no lesion to fix. What actually helps fibromyalgia — the licensed drugs, the old tricyclic, or exercise?
shelves.mesh: Fibromyalgia · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Milnacipran · Pregabalin · Amitriptyline · Exercise Therapy · Resistance Training · Humans
shelves.balance: Three Cochrane drug reviews agree on the shape: duloxetine, milnacipran, and pregabalin each give substantial pain relief to roughly one patient in ten beyond placebo (References 1–2) — a real effect, honestly small, with most patients getting nothing but the side effects. Amitriptyline, the oldest prescription in this clinic, has no first- or second-tier evidence at all; its reputation rests on small old trials (Reference 2). Exercise (Reference 3) buys a similar-sized benefit with low-certainty evidence and almost no harm, which is why it grades a step higher here. Nothing on this shelf modifies the disease, and nothing claims a mortality effect — fibromyalgia does not kill; it grinds. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Duloxetine and milnacipran (Cochrane reviews): substantial relief for about 1 in 10 beyond placebo
cards.summary: Two Cochrane reviews of the licensed SNRIs. Duloxetine (Lunn 2014; six fibromyalgia studies, 2,249 participants): at 60 mg daily, ≥50% pain reduction at 12 weeks had a risk ratio of 1.57 [1.20–2.06] vs placebo (a relative effect), NNTB 8 [4–21]; 16% of participants stopped the drug because of adverse effects. Milnacipran (Cording 2015; six studies, 4,238 participants): at least 30% pain relief in about 40% on drug vs 30% on placebo — NNT 6 to 10, rising to 11 under a stricter responder definition; adverse events in 86% vs 78%, nausea the standout (NNH 5.7), serious adverse events under 2% and no different from placebo. Read plainly: treat ten people, roughly one is substantially better because of the drug.
cards.type: Two Cochrane systematic reviews of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (Lunn 2014, CD007115; Cording 2015, CD008244). Systematic reviews — no registry number applies.
cards.people: Adults with fibromyalgia in the pooled trials: 2,249 participants in the duloxetine fibromyalgia studies and 4,238 in the milnacipran studies, treated 8–28 weeks. The reviews pool many trials; no single mean age or sex mix applies.
cards.result: Duloxetine 60 mg daily was effective for fibromyalgia over 12 weeks (RR for ≥50% pain reduction 1.57 [95% CI 1.20 to 2.06]; NNTB 8 [4 to 21]), with a similar magnitude over 28 weeks (RR 1.58 [1.10 to 2.27]). Milnacipran 100–200 mg gave at least 30% pain relief to about 40% of participants vs 30% on placebo (NNT 6 to 10; NNT 11 under a stricter, more conservative analysis). Adverse events were common on milnacipran (86% vs 78% on placebo); nausea (NNH 5.7), constipation (NNH 13), and headache (NNH 29) showed the greatest differences; serious adverse events did not differ (under 2%).
cards.watchOut: The benefit is real and concentrated: most patients treated get no meaningful relief, and the reviews cannot say in advance who the one in ten will be. Lunn notes almost every duloxetine study was performed or sponsored by the manufacturer, and Cording flags that the imputation method used in the milnacipran trials could overestimate the effect. Trial durations were weeks, not years — neither review shows benefit persisting beyond about six months.

cards.headline: Pregabalin: the same one-in-ten shape. Amitriptyline: no unbiased evidence at all (Cochrane)
cards.summary: Pregabalin (Derry 2016; five classic-design trials, 3,283 participants): substantial benefit (≥50% pain relief) in 22–24% on 300–600 mg vs 14% on placebo — about 9 percentage points attributable to the drug; moderate benefit (≥30%) in 39–43% vs 28%. Amitriptyline (Moore, CD011824; nine studies, only 649 participants, none with 50 or more per arm): there was no first-tier or second-tier evidence for benefit at all. The third-tier pool gives RR 3.0 [1.7–4.9] (relative) and NNT 4.1 for ≥50% relief — numbers the reviewers themselves grade very low quality — against adverse events in 78% vs 47% (NNH 3.3). The most traditional prescription on this shelf has the weakest file in it.
cards.type: Two Cochrane systematic reviews (Derry 2016, CD011790; Moore, CD011824 — record updated 2019). Systematic reviews — no registry number applies. Neither PubMed record carries a MeSH heading list, so no MeSH is printed for these two reviews: this library copies MeSH from the record itself and invents none.
cards.people: Adults with fibromyalgia: 3,283 participants in pregabalin's classic-design trials (8–13 weeks of stable treatment, doses 150–600 mg) and 649 across amitriptyline's nine small trials (6–24 weeks, doses 25–50 mg).
cards.result: Pregabalin 300–600 mg increased substantial benefit (RR 1.8 [1.4 to 2.1] at 450 mg; high-quality evidence): about 9% more participants than placebo achieved ≥50% relief, and about 11% more achieved ≥30% relief. For amitriptyline there was no first- or second-tier evidence; third-tier analysis gave RR 3.0 [95% CI 1.7 to 4.9] for ≥50% relief (NNT 4.1 [2.9 to 6.7], very low quality evidence). More participants had at least one adverse event on amitriptyline than placebo (78% vs 47%; RR 1.5 [1.3 to 1.8]; NNH 3.3). Lack-of-efficacy withdrawals were more common on placebo (12% vs 5%).
cards.watchOut: Do not quote amitriptyline's NNT of 4.1 beside pregabalin's percentages: the NNT comes from tiny, old, bias-prone trials — the reviewers' own verdict is that there is no supportive unbiased evidence for a beneficial effect, which is disappointing for a first-line drug but is the finding. Pregabalin's cleaner trials used last-observation-carried-forward imputation, which can overestimate effect. Both drugs' benefits, where real, are symptomatic only. Pregabalin's fibromyalgia data also appear, from a different review, on Shelf #345; this card's home for the fibromyalgia-specific reviews is here.

cards.headline: Exercise — aerobic and resistance (Cochrane): modest gains in pain and function, almost no harm — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Aerobic exercise (Bidonde 2017; 13 RCTs, 839 people): versus no-exercise control, pain intensity improved by a mean difference of −11.06 points [−18.34 to −3.77] on a 0–100 scale — an absolute improvement of about 11% — and health-related quality of life by −7.89 points [−13.23 to −2.55]; the evidence for pain was low quality. Resistance training (Busch 2013; five studies, 219 women): pain improved by −3.3 cm on a 10-cm scale [−6.35 to −0.26] and multidimensional function by −16.75 points on the 100-point Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire [−23.31 to −10.19] versus control. Harms across the exercise reviews were few and minor — the price is effort and attrition, not adverse events.
cards.type: Two Cochrane systematic reviews of randomized trials (Bidonde 2017, CD012700; Busch 2013, CD010884). Systematic reviews — no registry number applies.
cards.people: Adults with fibromyalgia: 839 participants across 13 aerobic-exercise RCTs (interventions 6–24 weeks) and 219 women across five resistance-training studies (8–21 weeks).
cards.result: Aerobic exercise vs control — pain intensity MD −11.06 (95% CI −18.34 to −3.77; six studies, 351 participants; low-quality evidence); HRQL MD −7.89 (−13.23 to −2.55); stiffness MD −7.96 (−14.95 to −0.97). Resistance training vs control — pain MD −3.3 cm on a 10-cm scale (−6.35 to −0.26); FIQ total MD −16.75 units (−23.31 to −10.19); self-reported physical function MD −6.29 units (−10.45 to −2.13); muscle strength improved (leg extension +27.32 kg force [18.28 to 36.36]).
cards.watchOut: The trials are small, short, and unblindable — participants know they are exercising, and every major outcome is self-reported, so expectation is baked into these effect sizes; that is why exercise grades POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. Effects are averages across programs of very different intensity, and what happens after the supervised program ends is largely unmeasured. Even discounted, an ~11-point pain improvement with no drug toxicity is the best risk-adjusted offer on this shelf.

shelves.title: ACL tears: early surgery vs rehab first — KANON trial
shelves.question: In acute anterior cruciate ligament tears, is early reconstruction better than structured rehabilitation first, with reconstruction only if needed?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries · Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Joint Instability · Knee Injuries · Male · Menisci, Tibial · Osteoarthritis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: For young, active adults with an acute ACL tear, the KANON strategy trial found rehabilitation plus early reconstruction was not superior to rehabilitation with optional delayed reconstruction at 5 years (mean KOOS4 change 42.9 versus 44.9 points; between-group difference 2.0 points, 95% CI -8.5 to 4.5; P=0.54), and about half of the rehab-first group never needed surgery by 5 years (30 of 59, 51%, had delayed reconstruction). But the primary 2-year KANON report, the COMPARE trial and ACL SNNAP are already carded elsewhere in the library and are not re-carded here, the remaining syntheses rate the evidence low quality, and younger, more active patients disproportionately fail rehab first — so the shelf is POSSIBLE, and it does not cover non-acute tears with persistent instability, where the balance differs. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: KANON at 5 years: early reconstruction was not better than rehab first with optional delayed surgery
cards.summary: KANON at 5 years (young active adults): KOOS4 improved 42.9 points with early reconstruction and 44.9 with rehab plus optional delayed surgery — difference 2.0 points, not significant; 30 of 59 (51%) of the rehab-first group had crossed over to reconstruction by 5 years.
cards.people: 121 young, active adults (mean age 26 years) with acute ACL injury to a previously uninjured knee at two hospitals in Sweden; one patient was lost to 5-year follow-up. The abstract does not state sex mix. Groups: 62 assigned to early ACL reconstruction, 59 to optional delayed reconstruction.
cards.result: Thirty (51%) patients assigned to optional delayed ACL reconstruction had delayed reconstruction (seven between two and five years). The mean change in KOOS(4) score from baseline to five years was 42.9 points for rehabilitation plus early ACL reconstruction and 44.9 for rehabilitation plus optional delayed reconstruction (between-group difference 2.0 points, 95% confidence interval -8.5 to 4.5; P=0.54 after adjustment for baseline score). At five years there were no significant between-group differences in KOOS(4) (P=0.45), any KOOS subscale (P>=0.12), SF-36 (P>=0.34), Tegner activity scale (P=0.74), incident radiographic osteoarthritis of the index knee (P=0.17), or knees having meniscus surgery (P=0.48).
cards.watchOut: Single trial in young, active adults with acute tears; results do not automatically extend to older patients, chronic tears or knees with persistent instability, and adverse events were common in both strategies in the primary report.
cards.source: Frobell RB et al. Treatment for acute anterior cruciate ligament tear: five year outcome of randomised trial. BMJ. 2013 Jan 24;346:f232. PMID: 23349407. Registry ID: ISRCTN84752559 (Current Controlled Trials), as stated in the record's databank.

cards.headline: KANON at 11 years: ACL continuity on 5-year MRI was associated with worse, not better, reported outcomes
cards.summary: KANON at 11 years, the counter-intuitive card: among nonsurgically managed patients, an ACL that looked continuous on 5-year MRI was associated with worse 11-year KOOS4 than delayed reconstruction (adjusted difference −20.2 [−31.9 to −8.6]) — a subgroup analysis, hypothesis-generating, and a warning against reading structure as outcome.
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised controlled trial (KANON)
cards.people: 105 of 121 (87%) active adults with acute ACL ruptures randomised in KANON completed 11-year follow-up; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix in this analysis.
cards.result: Of patients managed nonsurgically, 58% (n=14) had ACL continuity and 42% (n=10) had ACL discontinuity on 5-year MRI. ACL continuity was associated with worse 11-year KOOS(4) scores compared with delayed ACL reconstruction (adjusted mean difference -20.2, 95% CI -31.9 to -8.6) and early ACL reconstruction (adjusted mean difference -15.5, 95% CI -26.4 to -4.7), and similar or worse scores compared with ACL discontinuity (adjusted mean difference -11.4, 95% CI -26.5 to 3.6). The proportion with tibiofemoral radiographic osteoarthritis ranged from 14% (ACL continuity) to 23% (delayed reconstruction), and patellofemoral osteoarthritis from 11% (ACL discontinuity) to 41% (early reconstruction).
cards.watchOut: Small, exploratory secondary analysis (only 24 nonsurgically managed patients in the continuity comparison); association, not a randomised comparison, and the groups were not randomised by healing status.
cards.source: Filbay SR et al. Association Between ACL Continuity on Magnetic Resonance Imaging at 5 Years After an Acute ACL Rupture and 11-Year Outcomes: A Secondary Analysis From the KANON Trial. Am J Sports Med. 2025 Jul;53(8):1893-1900. PMID: 40387842. Registration: ISRCTN 84752559, as stated in the record.

cards.headline: Who fails rehab first in COMPARE: younger, more active patients with instability and pain
cards.summary: COMPARE’s failure analysis: 41 of 82 rehab-first patients had delayed reconstruction (median 6.4 months), 90% of them for instability — younger, more active patients with instability and pain are who fails rehab first.
cards.type: Exploratory subgroup analysis of a randomised controlled trial (COMPARE)
cards.people: Subgroup of 82 patients randomised to rehabilitation plus optional delayed reconstruction within the COMPARE trial, in which 167 patients with an ACL rupture were randomised overall; the abstract does not state sex mix.
cards.result: During 2-year follow-up, 41 of the 82 patients received a delayed ACL reconstruction after a median of 6.4 months (interquartile range, 3.9-10.3 months); most reconstructions occurred between 3 and 6 months (n=17; 41.5%). Ninety percent (n=37) reported knee instability concerns as a reason for surgery. Patients who required reconstruction were significantly younger (27.4 versus 35.3 years; P=.001) and had a higher preinjury activity level than those who did not, and during follow-up their International Knee Documentation Committee scores were lower and pain scores higher.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory, non-randomised comparison within one trial arm — it identifies who crosses over, it does not prove those patients would have done better with early surgery.
cards.source: van der Graaff SJA et al. Why, When, and in Which Patients Nonoperative Treatment of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury Fails: An Exploratory Analysis of the COMPARE Trial. Am J Sports Med. 2022 Mar;50(3):645-651. PMID: 35048733. Registry ID: no registry ID appears in this record's own databank.

cards.headline: 2024 meta-analysis: no certain evidence reconstruction beats nonoperative care for isolated ACL tears — low-quality evidence
cards.summary: The 2024 meta-analysis rated the evidence low quality : no certain advantage for reconstruction over nonoperative care in isolated ACL tears, with a trend toward less radiographic osteoarthritis without surgery (OR 1.84 [0.90–3.75] as printed for the comparison).
cards.people: 5 studies (2 randomised controlled trials and 3 retrospective non-randomised studies) comparing reconstruction with nonoperative treatment in isolated ACL tears, searched to 25 October 2021; the abstract does not state total participant number, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Nonoperatively treated knees showed a trend toward lower odds of developing radiological signs of osteoarthritis (odds ratio 1.84, 95% CI 0.90 to 3.75 — a relative measure, reported as printed for the comparison in the abstract, with no absolute rates given beside it), while surgically reconstructed knees had significantly better stability (mean difference -2.44, 95% CI -3.21 to -1.66) and a trend toward better but clinically not meaningful Lysholm scores (mean difference 2.88, 95% CI -1.09 to 6.85). The authors conclude there is no certain evidence reconstruction is superior to nonoperative treatment, and rate the quality of evidence low because of higher risk of bias and inconsistency; a moderate risk of bias was found in 2 studies and serious risk in 1 study.
cards.watchOut: Only 5 studies, mixing randomised and retrospective designs, with low-quality evidence — this synthesis cannot settle the question and its osteoarthritis odds ratio is not statistically significant.
cards.source: de Jonge R et al. Nonoperative Treatment as an Option for Isolated Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Orthop J Sports Med. 2024 Apr 8;12(4):23259671241239665. PMID: 38601190. Registration: PROSPERO CRD42021285901, as stated in the record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: rehab first is a defensible primary strategy for acute tears — with a large crossover and thin evidence beyond KANON
cards.summary: Rehab first is a defensible primary strategy — it avoided surgery in about half of KANON — with a large crossover and thin evidence beyond one trial family: POSSIBLE, and the gap is stated on the card.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the KANON trial cohort (121 young, active adults, mean age 26 years, followed to 5 and 11 years), an 82-patient COMPARE rehab-first subgroup, and a 5-study meta-analysis.
cards.result: At 5 years KANON found no significant difference between strategies (KOOS(4) change 42.9 versus 44.9 points; difference 2.0 points, 95% CI -8.5 to 4.5; P=0.54), with 30 of 59 (51%) of the rehab-first group having had delayed reconstruction — so rehab first avoided surgery in about half, while the COMPARE analysis shows the other half who cross over are younger (27.4 versus 35.3 years) and more active, usually between 3 and 6 months. The 2024 meta-analysis rates the overall evidence low quality. This shelf is stamped POSSIBLE. Note on in-flight and already-carded evidence: the primary KANON 2-year report (PMID 20660401), ACL SNNAP (PMID 35988569) and the COMPARE primary report (PMID 33687926) are already carded elsewhere in the library and are deliberately not re-carded here under the one-home rule; the 2026-11-08 sweep found no new primary early-surgery-versus-rehab-first randomised trial and no in-flight head-to-head trial could be verified from the fetched records, so none is named.
cards.watchOut: This shelf covers acute tears in young, active adults. It must not be read as covering non-acute tears with persistent instability — ACL SNNAP, already carded elsewhere, addressed that different population — nor paediatric tears.
