shelves.title: PRP injections for tendons and knees: the null shelf
shelves.question: Does platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection beat placebo/saline injection for knee osteoarthritis or tendinopathy?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cartilage, Articular · Female · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Knee Joint · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Pain · Pain Management · Pain Measurement · Platelet-Rich Plasma
shelves.balance: LIKELY — the treatment made no difference is the finding: in blinded, placebo-controlled trials PRP did not beat saline for knee osteoarthritis pain or cartilage volume (RESTORE), for Achilles tendinopathy on top of eccentric exercise (de Vos), or for lateral epicondylitis pain at 3 months (Krogh). Both arms typically improve, which is why uncontrolled series look positive. This shelf does not support paying for PRP for these indications; other PRP preparations and joints were not tested in these trials. Proposed stamp LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: RESTORE: PRP no better than saline for knee OA pain or cartilage at 12 months
cards.summary: RESTORE (288 participants, placebo-controlled): PRP changed knee pain by −2.1 points versus −1.8 with saline at 12 months — difference −0.4 [−0.9 to 0.2], far short of the 1.8-point clinically important difference; cartilage volume loss was identical (−1.4% vs −1.2%).
cards.people: 288 community participants aged 50 years or older with symptomatic mild-to-moderate medial knee OA; mean age 61.9 (SD 6.5) years, 59% women (169/288)
cards.result: Pain change at 12 months -2.1 points with PRP vs -1.8 with saline (difference -0.4, 95% CI -0.9 to 0.2; P=.17) on a 0-10 scale, well short of the 1.8-point minimum clinically important difference. Medial tibial cartilage volume change -1.4% vs -1.2% (difference -0.2%, 95% CI -1.9% to 1.5%; P=.81). Of 31 prespecified secondary outcomes, 29 showed no significant between-group difference.
cards.watchOut: One leukocyte-poor commercial PRP product, 3 weekly injections, Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2-3 medial OA only; other preparations/grades are extrapolation, not evidence of benefit.
cards.source: Bennell KL et al. JAMA. 2021;326(20):2021-2030. PMID: 34812863. Registry: ACTRN12617000853347 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, from the record's abstract).

cards.headline: de Vos: PRP adds nothing to eccentric exercise in chronic Achilles tendinopathy
cards.summary: De Vos (Achilles tendinopathy): PRP plus eccentric exercise improved VISA-A by 21.7 points versus 20.5 with saline plus exercise — adjusted difference −0.9 [−12.4 to 10.6]; the interval excludes the predefined 12-point relevant difference in PRP’s favour.
cards.people: 54 patients aged 18-70 years with chronic midportion Achilles tendinopathy (27 PRP, 27 saline), single centre in the Netherlands; sex distribution not stated in the abstract
cards.result: VISA-A score improved by 21.7 points (95% CI 13.0-30.5) with PRP plus eccentric exercises vs 20.5 points (95% CI 11.6-29.4) with saline plus eccentric exercises at 24 weeks; adjusted between-group difference -0.9 (95% CI -12.4 to 10.6), a confidence interval that did not include the predefined 12-point relevant difference in favour of PRP.
cards.watchOut: Small trial (n=54); both groups received eccentric exercise, so the trial tests PRP as an add-on, not PRP alone. Improvement in both arms is the natural history/exercise effect PRP is often credited with.
cards.source: de Vos RJ et al. JAMA. 2010;303(2):144-149. PMID: 20068208. Registry: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00761423.

cards.headline: Krogh: neither PRP nor glucocorticoid beat saline for tennis elbow pain at 3 months
cards.summary: Krogh (tennis elbow): at 3 months neither PRP (−2.7 vs saline) nor glucocorticoid (−3.8) beat saline significantly; glucocorticoid’s 1-month advantage (−8.1) had already vanished — the steroid pattern in miniature.
cards.people: 60 patients with chronic lateral epicondylitis randomised 1:1:1 to PRP, glucocorticoid or saline; mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract
cards.result: At the 3-month primary end point, pain reduction did not differ significantly between groups: PRP vs saline mean difference -2.7 (95% CI -8.8 to 3.5) and glucocorticoid vs saline -3.8 (95% CI -9.9 to 2.4) on the Patient-Rated Tennis Elbow Evaluation. Glucocorticoid did reduce pain more at 1 month (vs saline -8.1, 95% CI -14.3 to -1.9), a short-term effect only.
cards.watchOut: Small (about 20 per arm) and a single injection; the 1-month steroid advantage should not be read as a durable benefit, and tendon thickness/Doppler changes with steroid did not translate into 3-month pain benefit.
cards.source: Krogh TP et al. Am J Sports Med. 2013;41(3):625-635. PMID: 23328738. Registry: none in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: for knee OA and these tendons, PRP is a null — do not pay for the placebo effect
cards.summary: Three double-blind saline-controlled trials, three nulls on their primary outcomes — knee, Achilles, elbow. LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): for these indications PRP offers the placebo effect at a price.
cards.people: Across the three placebo-controlled trials above: 288 older adults with knee OA, 54 adults with Achilles tendinopathy, and 60 adults with lateral epicondylitis
cards.result: No trial found a significant benefit of PRP over saline on its primary outcome: knee pain difference -0.4 points (95% CI -0.9 to 0.2), Achilles VISA-A adjusted difference -0.9 points (95% CI -12.4 to 10.6), and tennis-elbow pain difference -2.7 points (95% CI -8.8 to 3.5) for PRP vs saline. Stamp proposed: LIKELY (that PRP offers no meaningful benefit for these indications).
cards.watchOut: A null shelf is indication- and preparation-specific: it does not settle PRP for other joints, other preparations, or post-surgical use, and no in-flight trial is named here because none in the 2024-2026 sweep was a large placebo-controlled trial positioned to overturn these three.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bennell 2021 (PMID: 34812863), de Vos 2010 (PMID: 20068208) and Krogh 2013 (PMID: 23328738); no additional source.

shelves.title: Tendinopathy: loading programmes vs injections
shelves.question: For tendinopathy, do loading (exercise) programmes beat, match or lose to injections — and which loading programme?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Adult · Aged · Bursitis · Exercise Therapy · Female · Hip Joint · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Education as Topic · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the one direct head-to-head (LEAP, gluteal tendinopathy) found education plus exercise beat a corticosteroid injection on global improvement at both 8 weeks (absolute risk difference 19.9%) and 52 weeks (20.4%), while pain at 52 weeks no longer differed; the steroid's advantage is early and short-lived. Among loading programmes themselves, heavy slow resistance matched eccentric training for Achilles tendinopathy and progressive tendon-loading beat eccentric exercise for patellar tendinopathy — so loading works, the exact recipe matters less, and no loading-vs-injection trial exists for Achilles or patellar tendons in this pack. That single direct injection comparison is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not higher. Proposed stamp POSSIBLE — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: LEAP: education plus exercise beat corticosteroid injection for gluteal tendinopathy
cards.summary: LEAP (gluteal tendinopathy, 204 patients): education-plus-exercise beat corticosteroid injection on global improvement at 8 weeks — 51/66 vs 38/65 , absolute difference 19.9% , NNT 5 — and still led at 52 weeks (absolute difference 20.4%), though pain scores no longer differed at a year.
cards.people: 204 people aged 35-70 years with gluteal tendinopathy over 3 months; 167 women, mean age 54.8 (SD 8.8) years; education+exercise (EDX) n=69, corticosteroid injection (CSI) n=66, wait-and-see n=69
cards.result: Global improvement success at 8 weeks: EDX 51/66, CSI 38/65, wait-and-see 20/68 — EDX vs CSI absolute risk difference 19.9% (95% CI 4.7% to 35.0%), NNT 5.0. Pain at 8 weeks: EDX 1.5 vs CSI 2.7 vs wait-and-see 3.8 (EDX vs CSI mean difference -1.04, 95% CI -1.72 to -0.37). At 52 weeks global success remained higher with EDX than CSI (51/65 vs 36/63; absolute risk difference 20.4%, 95% CI 4.9% to 35.9%), but pain no longer differed (EDX vs CSI -0.26, 95% CI -1.06 to 0.55).
cards.watchOut: One injection vs a 14-session, 8-week physiotherapy programme — effort and contact time differ greatly; single-blinded, patient-reported primary outcome, greater trochanteric/gluteal tendon only.
cards.source: Mellor R et al (LEAP). BMJ. 2018;361:k1662. PMID: 29720374. Registry: ACTRN12612001126808 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry, from the record's abstract).

cards.headline: Beyer: heavy slow resistance matched eccentric training for Achilles tendinopathy
cards.summary: Beyer (Achilles): heavy slow resistance and eccentric training improved VISA-A, pain, tendon thickness and neovascularisation to the same degree, maintained at 52 weeks — the loading method matters less than loading.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (loading vs loading — no injection arm)
cards.people: 58 patients with chronic (>3 months) midportion Achilles tendinopathy randomised to eccentric training or heavy slow resistance (HSR) for 12 weeks; mean age and sex distribution not stated in the abstract
cards.result: Both groups improved significantly on VISA-A and pain (visual analog scale) from 0 to 12 weeks (P<.0001), maintained at 52 weeks, with significant reductions in tendon thickness and neovascularisation — and none of these clinical or structural improvements differed between groups (no between-group figures given in the abstract). Patient satisfaction at 12 weeks tended higher with HSR (100% vs 80%; P=.052) but not at 52 weeks (96% vs 76%; P=.10); compliance was 92% with HSR vs 78% with eccentric training (P<.005).
cards.watchOut: This card compares two loading recipes, not loading vs injection — it supports 'loading works, recipe is flexible', not any claim about injections. Small trial (n=58) with no untreated or injection control.
cards.source: Beyer R et al. Am J Sports Med. 2015;43(7):1704-1711. PMID: 26018970. Registry: none in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: Breda: progressive tendon-loading beat eccentric exercise for patellar tendinopathy
cards.summary: Breda (patellar tendinopathy): progressive tendon loading beat eccentric exercise on VISA-P at 24 weeks ( 28 vs 18 points ; adjusted difference 9 [1–16]); return to sport (43% vs 27%) was a trend only, and satisfaction identical.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (loading vs loading — no injection arm)
cards.people: 76 patients with clinically diagnosed, ultrasound-confirmed patellar tendinopathy; mean age 24 (SD 4) years, 58 (76%) male, median symptom duration 2 years; 38 per arm
cards.result: VISA-P improvement at 24 weeks was 28 points with progressive tendon-loading exercise vs 18 points with eccentric exercise (adjusted mean between-group difference 9, 95% CI 1 to 16; P=.023). Return to sport was 43% vs 27% (P=.13, a trend only); patient satisfaction (81% vs 83%; P=.54) and adherence (40% vs 49%; P=.33) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Young athletic population (mean age 24) — not generalisable to older or non-sporting patellar tendinopathy; again no injection arm, so it refines the loading prescription rather than settling loading vs injection.
cards.source: Breda SJ et al. Br J Sports Med. 2021;55(9):501-509. PMID: 33219115. Registry: none in the PubMed record.

cards.headline: Synthesis: loading first, injection for short-term relief only — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Loading first: the one head-to-head trial beats injection early and late on global improvement, and the loading-vs-loading trials show durable gains either way. Injection’s role is short-term relief — POSSIBLE, on small unblinded trials.
cards.people: Direct injection comparison: 204 adults with gluteal tendinopathy (LEAP); loading-recipe comparisons: 58 adults with Achilles and 76 young athletes with patellar tendinopathy
cards.result: LEAP is the pack's only loading-vs-injection trial: education+exercise beat corticosteroid injection on global improvement by an absolute 19.9% at 8 weeks and 20.4% at 52 weeks, with no pain difference at 52 weeks (-0.26, 95% CI -1.06 to 0.55). Beyer and Breda show loading programmes produce lasting improvement and that progressive/heavy loading is at least as good as classic eccentric work. Stamp proposed: POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Thin where it matters most: no loading-vs-injection RCT for Achilles or patellar tendinopathy is carded here, and the shelf should be revisited if such a head-to-head (or a large LEAP replication in another tendon) is published — none was identified in the 2024-2026 sweep. Extrapolating LEAP's gluteal result to every tendon is the main misuse to guard against.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mellor 2018 (PMID: 29720374), Beyer 2015 (PMID: 26018970) and Breda 2021 (PMID: 33219115); no additional source.

shelves.title: Treating glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis
shelves.question: Which bone therapy best prevents fractures and bone loss in patients on long-term glucocorticoids?
shelves.mesh: Alendronate/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Bone Density/drug effects · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects · Osteoporosis/chemically induced/drug therapy/prevention & control · Prednisone · Spinal Fractures/epidemiology/prevention & control · Alendronate/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — LIKELY for bone-density benefit; POSSIBLE for fracture prevention: Alendronate raised lumbar-spine bone density by 2.1% (5 mg) and 2.9% (10 mg) over 48 weeks while placebo lost 0.4% in Saag 1998, and in the head-to-head trial teriparatide raised spine density more than alendronate at 36 months (11.0% vs 5.3%) with fewer new vertebral fractures (1.7% vs 7.7%). The fracture evidence is thinner than the density evidence: Saag 1998's vertebral-fracture difference was not significant (2.3% vs 3.7%; relative risk 0.6, 95% CI 0.1 to 4.4) and the teriparatide fracture result comes from one active-comparison trial, so fracture prevention is stamped POSSIBLE while the density benefit is LIKELY.

cards.headline: Saag 1998: alendronate increased bone density in patients on glucocorticoids — spine +2.9% on 10 mg vs −0.4% on placebo
cards.summary: Saag 1998: spine density +2.9% on alendronate 10 mg vs −0.4% on placebo; the fracture difference was not significant (relative risk 0.6 — inside the 0.5–2.0 band, printed as such).
cards.people: 477 men and women, 17 to 83 years of age, receiving glucocorticoid therapy, in two 48-week studies of alendronate 5 mg or 10 mg daily versus placebo; the abstract does not state the sex mix or mean age.
cards.result: Lumbar-spine bone density increased by 2.1% (±0.3) on 5 mg and 2.9% (±0.3) on 10 mg of alendronate (P<0.001) and decreased by 0.4% (±0.3) on placebo. Femoral-neck density increased by 1.2% and 1.0% in the alendronate groups and decreased by 1.2% on placebo. New vertebral fractures were proportionally fewer on alendronate (overall incidence 2.3%) than on placebo (3.7%), but the difference was not significant (relative risk 0.6, 95% CI 0.1 to 4.4 — a ratio inside the 0.5–2.0 band, not solid evidence of fracture prevention). Markers of bone turnover decreased significantly on alendronate. There were no differences in serious adverse effects, with a small increase in nonserious upper gastrointestinal effects on 10 mg.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint was bone density, a surrogate; the fracture result is a non-significant secondary finding and must not be quoted as fracture protection.
cards.source: Saag KG et al. Alendronate for the prevention and treatment of glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis. N Engl J Med. 1998 Jul 30;339(5):292-299. PMID: 9682041. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: Teriparatide vs alendronate at 36 months: bigger density gains and fewer vertebral fractures on teriparatide — 1.7% vs 7.7%
cards.summary: Teriparatide vs alendronate at 36 months: spine density +11.0% vs +5.3% ; new vertebral fractures 1.7% vs 7.7% .
cards.people: 428 subjects with glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, ages 22–89 years, who had received at least 5 mg/day of prednisone equivalent for at least 3 months, randomised to teriparatide 20 micrograms/day or alendronate 10 mg/day; fracture data were available for 173 teriparatide and 169 alendronate subjects; the abstract does not state the sex mix or mean age.
cards.result: At 36 months, bone-density increases from baseline were significantly greater on teriparatide than alendronate: lumbar spine 11.0% vs 5.3%, total hip 5.2% vs 2.7%, femoral neck 6.3% vs 3.4% (P<0.001 for all). Fewer subjects had new vertebral fractures on teriparatide (3 [1.7%] of 173) than on alendronate (13 [7.7%] of 169) (P=0.007), most occurring in the first 18 months. Nonvertebral fractures did not differ (7.5% vs 7.0%; P=0.843). Elevated predose serum calcium was commoner on teriparatide (21% vs 7%; P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: There is no placebo arm — this ranks two active drugs, it does not measure either against no treatment; the vertebral-fracture analysis covers the subset with follow-up radiographs, not all 428 randomised subjects.
cards.source: Saag KG et al. Effects of teriparatide versus alendronate for treating glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis: thirty-six-month results of a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial. Arthritis Rheum. 2009 Nov;60(11):3346-3355. PMID: 19877063. Registry ID: no registry ID appears in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: treat the bone, expect density gains — LIKELY; expect fracture protection — POSSIBLE, on one head-to-head trial
cards.summary: Density benefit LIKELY; fracture protection POSSIBLE, resting on one head-to-head trial — split as proposed.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Saag 1998 (477 patients on glucocorticoids, alendronate vs placebo) and Saag 2009 (428 patients, teriparatide vs alendronate for 36 months).
cards.result: Alendronate prevents the bone-density loss of glucocorticoid therapy (spine +2.9% on 10 mg vs −0.4% on placebo at 48 weeks), and teriparatide builds more density than alendronate over 36 months (spine 11.0% vs 5.3%) with fewer vertebral fractures in the radiographed subset (1.7% vs 7.7%). shelves.title: Hip protectors for fracture prevention
shelves.question: Do external hip protectors prevent hip fractures in older people at high risk?
shelves.mesh: Fractures, Bone/epidemiology/prevention & control · Frail Elderly · Hip Fractures/epidemiology/prevention & control · Orthopedic Equipment/adverse effects · Patient Compliance · Poisson Distribution · Risk
shelves.balance: SPLIT — POSSIBLE in nursing or residential care; MAYBE (weak evidence) in the community: The arc of this literature runs from an early strikingly positive trial to later, larger nulls. Kannus 2000 found hip fractures at 21.3 vs 46.0 per 1000 person-years (relative hazard 0.4). The later individually randomised van Schoor trial found no difference (18 vs 20 fractures; hazard ratio 1.05). The Cochrane synthesis in its Parker 2005 form pooled a marginally significant reduction in nursing/residential care (relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.97, with significant heterogeneity) and no reduction in the community (1.16, 0.85 to 1.59); its 2014 update softened the care-setting estimate further (0.82, 0.67 to 1.00; absolute effect 11 fewer per 1000, CI from 20 fewer to 0) and confirmed little or no community effect (1.15, 0.84 to 1.58). Acceptance and long-term adherence were poor throughout. Both halves of the arc stay printed: the early positive result is not deleted, and it does not outrank the later nulls.

cards.headline: Kannus 2000: the early positive trial — hip fracture rates 21.3 vs 46.0 per 1000 person-years with a hip protector
cards.summary: Kannus 2000: hip fracture rates 21.3 vs 46.0 per 1,000 person-years (relative hazard 0.4) — the early positive trial.
cards.people: 1,801 ambulatory but frail elderly adults (1,409 women and 392 men; mean age 82 years), randomised in a 1:2 ratio to a group wearing an anatomically designed external hip protector or to a control group; follow-up continued until the end of the first full month after 62 hip fractures had occurred in the control group.
cards.result: During follow-up, 13 subjects in the hip-protector group had a hip fracture versus 67 in the control group — rates of 21.3 and 46.0 per 1000 person-years (relative hazard 0.4, 95% CI 0.2 to 0.8; P=0.008 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it). Pelvic fractures were slightly but not significantly fewer on protectors (2 vs 12 subjects; relative hazard 0.4, 0.1 to 1.8), and other fractures were similar. Within the protector group, 4 subjects fractured while wearing the protector (among 1,034 falls) and 9 while not wearing it (among 370 falls) (relative hazard 0.2, 0.05 to 0.5).
cards.watchOut: This is the first and most positive trial in the field, with a 1:2 allocation and an event-driven stopping rule; later larger trials (next card) did not reproduce it, and the within-group wearing comparison is not randomised.
cards.source: Kannus P et al. Prevention of hip fracture in elderly people with use of a hip protector. N Engl J Med. 2000 Nov 23;343(21):1506-1513. PMID: 11087879. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial).

cards.headline: van Schoor 2003: the later, individually randomised trial found no effect — 18 vs 20 hip fractures, hazard ratio 1.05
cards.summary: van Schoor 2003: 18 vs 20 hip fractures (hazard ratio 1.05) — no effect in the later, individually randomised trial.
cards.people: 561 elderly persons aged 70 years or older with low bone density and high fall risk, living in apartment houses for the elderly, homes for the elderly and nursing homes in Amsterdam and surroundings, enrolled March 1999 to March 2001; mean follow-up 69.6 weeks; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Eighteen hip fractures occurred in the intervention group versus 20 in the control group; four intervention-group fractures occurred while a protector was being worn and at least four late at night or early in the morning. There was no significant difference in time to first hip fracture in univariate analysis (log-rank P=0.86) or multivariate analysis (hazard ratio 1.05, 95% CI 0.55 to 2.03). The per-protocol analysis in compliant participants was also non-significant (hazard ratio 0.77, 0.25 to 2.38). The authors conclude the hip protector studied was not effective in preventing hip fractures.
cards.watchOut: Compliance was the field's recurring problem and this trial is no exception — but its intention-to-treat null in an individually randomised design is exactly the evidence that tempers Kannus, and this shelf prints both.
cards.source: van Schoor NM et al. Prevention of hip fractures by external hip protectors: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2003 Apr 16;289(15):1957-1962. PMID: 12697798. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Parker Cochrane 2005: pooling gave a marginal reduction in care settings (relative risk 0.77) and none in the community (1.16)
cards.summary: Parker Cochrane 2005: care settings pooled to a marginal relative risk 0.77 ; the community pooled to 1.16 — nothing.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: 15 included trials; pooling covered 11 trials in nursing or residential care settings (including 6 cluster-randomised studies) and 3 individually randomised trials with 5,135 community-dwelling participants; one further trial contributed compliance data only; the abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Pooling the care-setting trials showed a marginally statistically significant reduction in hip fracture incidence (relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.97), with significant statistical heterogeneity. Pooling the three individually randomised community trials showed no reduction (relative risk 1.16, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.59). There was no significant effect on pelvic or other fractures. No important adverse effects were reported, but compliance, particularly long term, was poor. The authors' conclusion: accumulating evidence casts some doubt on the effectiveness of providing hip protectors.
cards.watchOut: The care-setting pooled estimate rests partly on cluster-randomised trials pooled on an exploratory basis, and heterogeneity was significant — it is a marginal pooled signal, not a settled effect.

shelves.title: Displaced femoral neck fracture: total hip arthroplasty vs hemiarthroplasty
shelves.question: In ambulatory older adults with a displaced femoral neck fracture, does total hip arthroplasty reduce secondary procedures or improve function versus hemiarthroplasty?
shelves.mesh: Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip/adverse effects · Femoral Neck Fractures/physiopathology,surgery · Hemiarthroplasty/adverse effects · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Postoperative Complications · Proportional Hazards Models · Recovery of Function
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the large HEALTH trial (1495 independently ambulating patients), total hip arthroplasty did not significantly reduce secondary hip procedures within 24 months versus hemiarthroplasty (7.9% vs 8.3%), produced only a clinically unimportant improvement in function and quality of life, caused more hip instability/dislocation (4.7% vs 2.4%), and had similar mortality (14.3% vs 13.1% — reported alongside, with no mortality claim made). A smaller earlier trial in fitter elderly patients was concordant on similar final pain and function. A single pivotal trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Mortality was a secondary outcome with no between-group difference; because this shelf makes no mortality or cardiovascular benefit claim, it is not flagged Tier C under the build rule (see summary.md).

cards.headline: HEALTH (Bhandari) 2019: total hip arthroplasty did not reduce secondary procedures vs hemiarthroplasty (7.9% vs 8.3% at 24 months)
cards.summary: HEALTH (Bhandari) 2019: total hip arthroplasty did not reduce secondary procedures vs hemiarthroplasty ( 7.9% vs 8.3% at 24 months); mortality was similar (14.3% vs 13.1%), printed on the card.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (80 centres in 10 countries)
cards.people: 1495 patients aged 50 years or older with a displaced femoral neck fracture, all able to ambulate without another person's assistance before the fracture, randomly assigned to total hip arthroplasty or hemiarthroplasty. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, a secondary hip procedure within 24 months, occurred in 57 of 718 (7.9%) with total hip arthroplasty vs 60 of 723 (8.3%) with hemiarthroplasty (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.40; P=0.79). Hip instability or dislocation occurred in 34 (4.7%) vs 17 (2.4%) patients (hazard ratio 2.00, 99% CI 0.97 to 4.09 — a relative figure whose interval includes no effect). WOMAC total, pain, stiffness and function scores modestly favoured total hip arthroplasty, an improvement the investigators describe as clinically unimportant. Mortality was similar (14.3% vs 13.1%, P=0.48), and serious adverse events occurred in 300 (41.8%) vs 265 (36.7%) patients.
cards.watchOut: Enrolled only patients who walked independently before fracture — the subgroup most expected to benefit from a total hip; results do not cover frailer, non-ambulatory patients. Function differences, though statistically detectable, were below clinical importance by the authors' own reading.
cards.source: Bhandari M et al. (HEALTH Investigators). Total Hip Arthroplasty or Hemiarthroplasty for Hip Fracture. N Engl J Med. 2019;381(23):2199-2208. PMID: 31557429. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00556842, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Parker 2019: in 105 fitter elderly patients, total hip replacement gave similar final pain and function with more complications than hemiarthroplasty
cards.summary: Parker 2019: in 105 fitter elderly patients, total hip replacement gave similar final pain and function with more complications.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with blinded functional assessment, minimum one-year follow-up
cards.people: 105 patients described as the 'fitter' elderly with a displaced intracapsular fracture, randomised to a cemented polished tapered stem hemiarthroplasty or a cemented total hip arthroplasty with a cemented acetabular cup. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Final outcome measures of residual pain and regain of function were similar for both methods. The total hip group tended to a longer hospital stay and had more medical complications and more surgical complications than the hemiarthroplasty group, with longer operative times and greater operative blood loss. The authors recommended caution regarding increased promotion of total hip replacement for intracapsular fractures until further studies are completed. (The record's abstract prints internally inconsistent numerals for the complication counts and operative times, so this card reports the trial's direction and conclusions only, not those figures.)
cards.watchOut: Only 105 patients from a single programme, and its abstract's numeric details are unreliable as printed (see the provenance note in the result); it is carded as qualitative corroboration of HEALTH, not as an independent quantitative estimate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no reoperation advantage, a whisper of function, more dislocations — implant choice is a judgement call, not a mandate
cards.summary: No reoperation advantage, more dislocations — implant choice is a judgement call: POSSIBLE. (Mortality reported in HEALTH; no mortality claim is made.)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: HEALTH (1495 patients, 10 countries) and Parker 2019 (105 fitter elderly patients).
cards.result: HEALTH's primary endpoint was null (7.9% vs 8.3% secondary procedures), mortality was similar (14.3% vs 13.1%), and the price of total hip arthroplasty was roughly double the dislocation count (4.7% vs 2.4%) against a function gain the trialists themselves call clinically unimportant. Parker points the same way. This shelf does not cover hip-fracture timing or anaesthesia, which live on Shelf #342, and makes no mortality claim: the death rates are printed because the topic file flagged the shelf for a Tier C check, and the check's outcome (no claim, no flag) is recorded in summary.md.
cards.watchOut: HEALTH's population — previously independent walkers — is exactly where guidelines most often favour total hip replacement; the trial narrows, but does not erase, the case for selecting it in the most active patients.

shelves.title: Carpal tunnel syndrome: surgery vs splinting, and steroid injection
shelves.question: Does surgical release beat night splinting for carpal tunnel syndrome — and how durable is a corticosteroid injection?
shelves.mesh: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome/physiopathology,surgery,therapy · Decompression, Surgical · Severity of Illness Index · Splints · Carpal Tunnel Syndrome/drug therapy,physiopathology,surgery · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Injections
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Surgery beat night splinting on every outcome in the one randomised head-to-head trial (success 80% vs 54% at 3 months; 90% vs 75% at 18 months, by which time 41% of the splint group had crossed to surgery). A methylprednisolone injection beat placebo on symptom severity at 10 weeks and delayed or reduced surgery at one year in the one placebo-controlled trial — yet about three of four injected patients still had surgery within a year. Each comparison rests on a single trial, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE for both halves of the question.

cards.headline: Gerritsen 2002: surgery beat night splinting — success 80% vs 54% at 3 months, 90% vs 75% at 18 months
cards.summary: Gerritsen 2002: surgery beat night splinting — success 80% vs 54% at 3 months, 90% vs 75% at 18 months.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (13 neurological outpatient clinics, Netherlands)
cards.people: 176 patients with clinically and electrophysiologically confirmed idiopathic carpal tunnel syndrome assigned to night wrist splinting for at least 6 weeks (89) or open carpal tunnel release (87); 147 (84%) completed the 18-month follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In intention-to-treat analyses, surgery was more effective than splinting on all outcome measures (general improvement, nights woken by symptoms, symptom severity). Success rates at 3 months were 80% for surgery (62 of 78) vs 54% for splinting (46 of 86), a difference of 26% (95% CI 12% to 40%; P<0.001). At 18 months success was 90% (61 of 68) vs 75% (59 of 79), a difference of 15% (3% to 27%; P=0.02) — but by then 41% of splint-group patients (32 of 79) had also undergone surgery, so the long-term comparison is partly surgery-now versus surgery-later.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded (unavoidable), with heavy crossover by 18 months: the clean contrast is the 3-month result. Patients were referred, electrophysiologically confirmed cases, not undifferentiated wrist symptoms in primary care.
cards.source: Gerritsen AAM et al. Splinting vs surgery in the treatment of carpal tunnel syndrome: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2002;288(10):1245-1251. PMID: 12215131. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the trial predates routine registration reporting in MEDLINE records.

cards.headline: Atroshi 2013: methylprednisolone injection improved symptoms at 10 weeks but not 1 year; 73–81% still had surgery within a year
cards.summary: Atroshi 2013: methylprednisolone injection improved symptoms at 10 weeks but not 1 year; 73–81% still had surgery within a year.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial (single regional referral orthopaedic department, Sweden)
cards.people: 111 patients aged 18 to 70 years with carpal tunnel syndrome and no previous steroid injections, in three groups of 37 receiving 80 mg methylprednisolone, 40 mg methylprednisolone, or placebo; all had previously failed wrist splinting. All patients had 1-year data.
cards.result: Improvement in symptom severity score at 10 weeks was greater with 80 mg (difference in change from baseline −0.64, 95% CI −1.06 to −0.21; P=0.003) and 40 mg (−0.88, −1.30 to −0.46; P<0.001) than placebo on the 1-to-5 scale, but there were no significant differences at 1 year. One-year surgery rates were 73% (80 mg), 81% (40 mg) and 92% (placebo); versus placebo, the 80-mg group was less likely to have surgery (odds ratio 0.24, 0.06 to 0.95 — a relative figure), and time-to-surgery analyses favoured both steroid doses (hazard ratios 0.46 and 0.57 — relative figures). The authors note 3 of 4 injected patients had surgery within 1 year.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, 111 patients, all splinting failures — a more severe spectrum than newly diagnosed carpal tunnel syndrome; the 1-year symptom null is as much a part of the answer as the 10-week benefit.
cards.source: Atroshi I et al. Methylprednisolone injections for the carpal tunnel syndrome: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Ann Intern Med. 2013;159(5):309-317. PMID: 24026316. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00806871, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: splinting is the weaker first step, injection buys months not a cure, surgery is the durable option in this trial base
cards.summary: Splinting is the weaker first step, injection buys months, surgery is durable — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Gerritsen 2002 (176 patients, surgery vs splinting) and Atroshi 2013 (111 patients, injection vs placebo).
cards.result: Read together: splinting loses to surgery early (26-point success gap at 3 months) and 41% of splinted patients end up operated anyway; an injection in splint-failures wins about 10 weeks of symptom relief and shifts the surgery curve (hazard ratios 0.46–0.57, relative) without changing 1-year symptoms, and three quarters still proceed to release. The two trials study different rungs of the ladder (treatment-naive versus splint-failures), so they corroborate a sequence rather than compete.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial compares injection directly with surgery, and endoscopic versus open release is not tested anywhere on this shelf.

shelves.title: Subacromial shoulder pain: decompression surgery vs sham and exercise
shelves.question: Does arthroscopic subacromial decompression improve pain and function more than sham (diagnostic arthroscopy) or exercise therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acromion/injuries · Arthroscopy/methods · Decompression, Surgical/methods · England · Exercise Therapy/methods · Osteophyte/complications · Shoulder Pain/physiopathology,surgery
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two independent sham-controlled randomised trials — CSAW (313 patients, UK) and FIMPACT (210 patients, Finland) — found arthroscopic subacromial decompression no better than diagnostic arthroscopy alone on pain and function: CSAW's Oxford Shoulder Score difference was −1.3 points (95% CI −3.9 to 1.3) at 6 months, and FIMPACT's 24-month pain differences (−4.6 at rest, −9.0 on activity, on 0–100 scales) did not reach its 15-point minimal clinically important difference. Two concordant placebo-surgery trials justify LIKELY for the null; knee arthroscopy shelves (#188, #347) are different joints and operations and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: CSAW (Beard) 2018: decompression was no better than arthroscopy alone (−1.3 Oxford Shoulder Score points, CI −3.9 to 1.3)
cards.summary: CSAW (Beard) 2018: decompression was no better than arthroscopy alone ( −1.3 Oxford Shoulder Score points, CI −3.9 to 1.3).
cards.type: Multicentre, pragmatic, placebo-controlled, three-group randomised surgical trial (32 UK hospitals)
cards.people: 313 patients with subacromial pain for at least 3 months, intact rotator cuff tendons, eligible for arthroscopic surgery, who had completed non-operative management including exercise therapy and at least one steroid injection; assigned to decompression (106), arthroscopy only (103) or no treatment (104). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months, mean Oxford Shoulder Score (0 worst to 48 best) did not differ between decompression (32.7, SD 11.6) and arthroscopy only (34.2, SD 9.2): mean difference −1.3 points (95% CI −3.9 to 1.3; p=0.3141). Both surgical groups scored slightly better than no treatment (29.4; differences 2.8 and 4.2 points), differences the authors state were not clinically important and may reflect placebo effect or postoperative physiotherapy. Six study-related complications occurred, all frozen shoulders (two per group). Substantial minorities did not receive their assigned treatment by 6 months (23% decompression, 42% arthroscopy only, 12% no treatment).
cards.watchOut: High non-receipt of allocated treatment (especially the arthroscopy-only arm) dilutes the contrast, though intention-to-treat analysis preserves randomisation; patients had already failed exercise and injection, so this is a refractory-pain population.
cards.source: Beard DJ et al. Arthroscopic subacromial decompression for subacromial shoulder pain (CSAW): a multicentre, pragmatic, parallel group, placebo-controlled, three-group, randomised surgical trial. Lancet. 2018;391(10118):329-338. PMID: 29169668. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01623011, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: FIMPACT (Paavola) 2018: decompression gave no clinically relevant benefit over diagnostic arthroscopy at 24 months
cards.summary: FIMPACT (Paavola) 2018: decompression gave no clinically relevant benefit over diagnostic arthroscopy at 24 months; its 10-year follow-up is fenced in the currency sweep.
cards.type: Multicentre, three-group, randomised, double-blind, sham-controlled trial (three Finnish public hospitals)
cards.people: 210 patients with symptoms consistent with shoulder impingement syndrome, assigned to arthroscopic subacromial decompression, diagnostic arthroscopy (placebo), or exercise therapy, with two-year follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the primary intention-to-treat comparison at 24 months, mean pain change (visual analogue scale 0–100) for decompression vs diagnostic arthroscopy differed by −4.6 points at rest (95% CI −11.3 to 2.1; P=0.18) and −9.0 points on arm activity (−18.1 to 0.2; P=0.054) — neither clinically relevant against the prespecified 15-point minimal important difference, and no secondary outcomes or adverse events differed between the surgical groups. Against exercise therapy, decompression differed by −7.5 points at rest and −12.0 on activity (statistically significant but below the 15-point threshold); the authors flag that comparison as unblinded and likely biased in decompression's favour by selective exclusions.
cards.watchOut: The exercise comparison is explicitly confounded per the authors; the trial's decisive comparison is the sham one. Two-year horizon — very late divergence is not addressed.

cards.headline: Synthesis: when the bone removal is the only thing removed, nothing changes — the operation's specific effect is nil in two sham trials
cards.summary: The operation's specific effect is nil in two sham trials — LIKELY the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CSAW (313 patients) and FIMPACT (210 patients), both sham-controlled.
cards.result: CSAW and FIMPACT independently isolate the same contrast — everything about the operation except the decompression itself — and both land on no clinically important difference (−1.3 shoulder-score points; −4.6 and −9.0 pain points against a 15-point importance threshold). Small advantages of 'surgery' over no treatment in CSAW are attributable to context effects, as its authors state. This is the shoulder counterpart of the knee arthroscopy story on Shelves #188 and #347, which stay home there and are not re-carded.

shelves.title: Lumbar disc herniation with sciatica: early surgery vs prolonged conservative care
shelves.question: Does early discectomy relieve sciatica faster than conservative care with surgery if needed — and do outcomes converge by one year?
shelves.mesh: Area Under Curve · Disability Evaluation · Diskectomy · Intervertebral Disc Displacement/complications,surgery,therapy · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lumbar Vertebrae/surgery · Physical Therapy Modalities
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Early surgery relieves sciatica faster, but outcomes converge. In the Peul trial (283 patients), early microdiscectomy and conservative care with surgery if needed produced no significant difference in disability over the first year, leg-pain relief and perceived recovery were faster with early surgery (recovery hazard ratio 1.97, a relative figure), and perceived recovery at one year was 95% in both groups — with 39% of the conservative group crossing to surgery. SPORT's randomised trial likewise found substantial improvement in both groups with small, non-significant intention-to-treat differences (its observational cohort, carded separately, favoured surgery but is confounded by self-selection). Gabapentinoid drugs for sciatica live on Shelf #345 and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Peul 2007: early surgery sped relief (recovery hazard ratio 1.97) but 1-year recovery was 95% in both groups
cards.summary: Peul 2007: early surgery sped relief (recovery hazard ratio 1.97, relative) but 1-year recovery was 95% in both groups .
cards.people: 283 patients with severe sciatica for 6 to 12 weeks, assigned to early surgery (141) or prolonged conservative treatment with surgery if needed (142). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Of the early-surgery group, 125 (89%) underwent microdiscectomy after a mean of 2.2 weeks; of the conservative group, 55 (39%) had surgery after a mean of 18.7 weeks. There was no significant overall difference in Roland Disability Questionnaire scores during the first year (P=0.13). Relief of leg pain was faster with early surgery (P<0.001), as was perceived recovery (hazard ratio 1.97, 95% CI 1.72 to 2.22 — a relative figure; P<0.001). The probability of perceived recovery at 1 year was 95% in both groups.
cards.watchOut: Nearly four in ten conservative patients crossed to surgery, so the trial tests a strategy of early versus delayed-if-needed surgery, not surgery versus never; unblinded patient-reported outcomes favour the group that got the intervention it may have preferred.

cards.headline: SPORT randomised trial (Weinstein) 2006: both groups improved substantially; intention-to-treat differences were small and not significant
cards.summary: SPORT randomised trial (Weinstein) 2006: both groups improved substantially; intention-to-treat differences were small and not significant.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (13 multidisciplinary spine clinics in 11 US states)
cards.people: 501 surgical candidates (mean age 42 years; 42% women) with imaging-confirmed lumbar intervertebral disc herniation and persistent radiculopathy signs and symptoms for at least 6 weeks, assigned to standard open discectomy or individualised nonoperative treatment.
cards.result: Adherence was limited: 50% of patients assigned to surgery received it within 3 months, while 30% of those assigned to nonoperative treatment crossed to surgery in the same period. Intention-to-treat analyses showed substantial improvements for all primary (SF-36 bodily pain and physical function, modified Oswestry Disability Index) and secondary outcomes in both groups over 2 years; between-group differences consistently favoured surgery but were small and not statistically significant for the primary outcomes. The authors state that the large two-way crossover means conclusions about superiority or equivalence are not warranted from the intention-to-treat analysis.

cards.summary: Surgery buys speed, not a different destination — LIKELY, on the randomised record.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Peul 2007 (283 randomised), SPORT randomised trial (501 randomised) and SPORT observational cohort (743, non-randomised).
cards.result: The two randomised trials agree: faster pain relief and perceived recovery with early surgery (Peul hazard ratio 1.97, relative) and convergence by one year (95% perceived recovery in both Peul groups; SPORT's primary-outcome differences small and non-significant). The observational cohort's larger pro-surgery differences are exactly what self-selection predicts and are labelled accordingly on their own card. For a patient whose priority is speed of relief and who accepts operative risk, early discectomy is supported; for a patient content to wait, conservative care forfeits little by one year, at a ~39% chance of later surgery (Peul).
cards.watchOut: Do not cite the cohort's effect sizes as trial evidence; and neither randomised trial addresses cauda equina, progressive deficit, or other absolute surgical indications.

shelves.title: Psoriatic arthritis: IL-17 inhibition (secukinumab, ixekizumab)
shelves.question: Do IL-17A inhibitors improve joint responses (ACR20) and skin disease in active psoriatic arthritis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Arthritis, Psoriatic/complications,drug therapy · Drug Administration Schedule · Injections, Subcutaneous · Interleukin-17/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two double-blind phase 3 trials of two IL-17A inhibitors agree on joint responses at 24 weeks. Secukinumab (FUTURE 1, 606 patients): ACR20 responses of 50.0% (150 mg) and 50.5% (75 mg) versus 17.3% on placebo. Ixekizumab in biologic-naive patients (SPIRIT-P1, 417 patients): ACR20 of 62.1% (every 2 weeks) and 57.9% (every 4 weeks) versus 30.2% on placebo, with less structural-damage progression and greater skin clearance. Both trials also showed more infections on active treatment; FUTURE 1 recorded small numbers of strokes (4) and myocardial infarctions (2) in secukinumab groups across the whole study period versus none on placebo — reported on its card as a safety observation, not a benefit or harm claim. Skin biologics for psoriasis itself are Shelf #377 and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: FUTURE 1 2015: secukinumab doubled-to-tripled ACR20 responses at week 24 (50.0% and 50.5% vs 17.3% on placebo)
cards.summary: FUTURE 1 2015: secukinumab doubled-to-tripled ACR20 responses at week 24 ( 50.0% and 50.5% vs 17.3% on placebo).
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (intravenous loading, then subcutaneous dosing; placebo switched to secukinumab at week 16 or 24)
cards.people: 606 patients with psoriatic arthritis, randomised 1:1:1 to intravenous secukinumab 10 mg/kg at weeks 0, 2 and 4 followed by subcutaneous secukinumab 150 mg or 75 mg every 4 weeks, or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: ACR20 response at week 24 was 50.0% on secukinumab 150 mg and 50.5% on 75 mg versus 17.3% on placebo (P<0.001 for both); ACR50 responses and joint structural damage were also significantly better than placebo, and improvements were sustained through 52 weeks. Infections, including candida, were more common on secukinumab. Across the whole study (mean secukinumab exposure 438.5 days; mean placebo exposure 128.5 days), four secukinumab patients had a stroke (0.6 per 100 patient-years, 95% CI 0.2–1.5) and two a myocardial infarction (0.3 per 100 patient-years, 0.0–1.0), versus none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The stroke and infarction counts are small, unadjudicated as a trial endpoint, and accrued over much longer secukinumab than placebo exposure — they are a watch item, not evidence of cardiovascular harm or benefit, and no cardiovascular claim is carded on this shelf.
cards.source: Mease PJ et al. Secukinumab Inhibition of Interleukin-17A in Patients with Psoriatic Arthritis. N Engl J Med. 2015;373(14):1329-1339. PMID: 26422723. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01392326, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SPIRIT-P1 2017: ixekizumab achieved ACR20 in 62.1% (2-weekly) and 57.9% (4-weekly) versus 30.2% on placebo in biologic-naive psoriatic arthritis
cards.summary: SPIRIT-P1 2017: ixekizumab achieved ACR20 in 62.1% (2-weekly) and 57.9% (4-weekly) vs 30.2% on placebo in biologic-naive psoriatic arthritis.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with an adalimumab active-reference arm (24-week controlled period)
cards.people: 417 biologic-naive patients with active psoriatic arthritis: placebo 106, adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks 101 (active reference), ixekizumab 80 mg every 2 weeks 103, ixekizumab 80 mg every 4 weeks 107 (both ixekizumab regimens after a 160 mg starting dose). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24 was achieved by 62.1% on 2-weekly and 57.9% on 4-weekly ixekizumab versus 30.2% on placebo (p≤0.001, non-responder imputation). Disease activity and functional disability improved significantly at weeks 12 and 24, structural-damage progression at week 24 was significantly less (p≤0.01), and plaque-psoriasis clearance was greater than placebo (p≤0.001); the adalimumab reference arm also improved significantly versus placebo. Treatment-emergent adverse events were more frequent on ixekizumab (65.7–66.4%) and adalimumab (64.4%) than placebo (47.2%).
cards.watchOut: The adalimumab arm is a reference for assay sensitivity, not a powered head-to-head comparison — SPIRIT-P1 cannot rank ixekizumab against adalimumab, and its population is biologic-naive only.

shelves.question: Do secukinumab (MEASURE) and upadacitinib (SELECT-AXIS) improve disease activity in active ankylosing spondylitis versus placebo?

shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two drug classes, three placebo-controlled trials on this shelf. Secukinumab's MEASURE programme (two trials, 590 patients): ASAS20 responses at week 16 of 61% and 60% (150 mg and 75 mg after intravenous loading) versus 29% on placebo in MEASURE 1, and 61% (150 mg) versus 28% in MEASURE 2. Upadacitinib (SELECT-AXIS 1, 187 biologic-naive patients): ASAS40 at week 14 in 52% versus 26% on placebo (treatment difference 26%, 95% CI 13–40). Each class clears its placebo bar comfortably on symptom-response composites; the trials are short (14–16 week controlled periods) and do not test structural progression.

cards.headline: MEASURE 1 & 2 2015: secukinumab 150 mg achieved ASAS20 in 61% versus 29% and 28% on placebo at week 16
cards.summary: MEASURE 1 & 2 2015: secukinumab 150 mg achieved ASAS20 in 61% vs 29% and 28% on placebo at week 16.
cards.type: Two double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (reported in one paper)
cards.people: 590 patients with active ankylosing spondylitis across the two trials: MEASURE 1 randomised 371 patients (intravenous secukinumab 10 mg/kg or placebo at weeks 0, 2 and 4, then subcutaneous 150 mg or 75 mg every 4 weeks from week 8) and MEASURE 2 randomised 219 patients (subcutaneous secukinumab 150 mg or 75 mg, or placebo, at baseline, weeks 1–3, then every 4 weeks); placebo patients were reassigned to secukinumab at week 16. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: In MEASURE 1, ASAS20 response at week 16 was 61% on subcutaneous secukinumab 150 mg, 60% on 75 mg, and 29% on placebo (P<0.001 for both doses). In MEASURE 2, rates were 61% (150 mg), 41% (75 mg) and 28% (placebo) (P<0.001 for 150 mg; P=0.10 for 75 mg). Improvements were sustained through 52 weeks. Infections, including candidiasis, were more common with secukinumab in MEASURE 1's controlled period; pooled exposure-adjusted rates of grade 3–4 neutropenia, candida infection and Crohn's disease were 0.7, 0.9 and 0.7 per 100 patient-years.
cards.watchOut: Two trials reported as one record, with placebo arms ending at week 16; the 75 mg dose missed significance in MEASURE 2, so the carded claim belongs to the 150 mg regimen.

shelves.title: Gout: nurse-led treat-to-target urate lowering
shelves.question: Does a nurse-led, treat-to-target allopurinol strategy achieve target urate and fewer flares more often than GP usual care?
shelves.mesh: Allopurinol/administration & dosage · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Disease Management · England · General Practice/methods · Gout/drug therapy,economics,nursing · Gout Suppressants/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large randomised trial answers the question directly, and a single trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Doherty 2018 (517 community patients with a gout flare in the previous 12 months) found nurse-led care — individualised education, shared decision-making and treat-to-target urate lowering — put 95% of patients below the 360 μmol/L (6 mg/dL) urate target at 2 years versus 30% on GP usual care (risk ratio 3.18, 95% CI 2.42–4.18), with all secondary outcomes, including flare frequency in year 2, favouring nurse-led care, at £5,066 per QALY gained. No second treat-to-target RCT was pinned at build, so the shelf is labelled single-trial throughout. Febuxostat cardiovascular safety is Shelf #382 and acute-flare treatment is Shelf #390; neither is re-carded here.

cards.headline: Doherty 2018: nurse-led treat-to-target care put 95% of gout patients at target urate at 2 years, versus 30% with GP usual care
cards.summary: Doherty 2018: nurse-led treat-to-target care put 95% of gout patients at target urate at 2 years, vs 30% with GP usual care (risk ratio 3.18, relative).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (community, 2 years; intention-to-treat with multiple imputation)
cards.people: 517 adults who had had a gout flare in the previous 12 months, randomised 1:1 to nurse-led care (255) — research nurses trained in best-practice gout management, individualised information and shared decision-making, with treat-to-target urate-lowering therapy — or GP-led usual care (262). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome, serum urate below 360 μmol/L (6 mg/dL) at 2 years, was achieved by 95% on nurse-led care versus 30% on usual care (risk ratio 3.18, 95% CI 2.42–4.18; p<0.0001) — a relative measure beyond the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with the absolute rates as stated. Nurse-led care was associated with high uptake of and adherence to urate-lowering therapy; at 2 years all secondary outcomes (including flare frequency in year 2, tophi and quality of life) favoured the nurse-led group. The cost per QALY gained was £5,066 at 2 years.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of a care-delivery package — education, engagement and titration together — in UK primary care; it cannot separate the nurse effect from the treat-to-target effect, and usual-care performance (30% at target) is part of the contrast.

shelves.title: Knee osteoarthritis: physical therapy vs glucocorticoid injection, and the cartilage question
shelves.question: Does physical therapy beat an intra-articular glucocorticoid injection for knee OA symptoms at one year — and do repeated steroid injections cost cartilage?
shelves.mesh: Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Hospitals, Military · Injections, Intra-Articular · Military Personnel · Osteoarthritis, Knee/drug therapy,physiopathology,rehabilitation · Pain Management/methods · Pain Measurement
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — physical therapy beats injection at 1 year · POSSIBLE — repeated triamcinolone loses cartilage without pain benefit. Each half rests on a single trial, so each is capped at POSSIBLE. Deyle 2020 (156 patients, US Military Health System primary care) found 1-year WOMAC totals of 37.0 with physical therapy versus 55.8 after glucocorticoid injection (between-group difference 18.8 points, 95% CI 5.0–32.6, favouring therapy). McAlindon 2017 (140 patients, triamcinolone 40 mg vs saline every 3 months for 2 years) found significantly greater cartilage volume loss with steroid (−0.21 mm vs −0.10 mm change in index-compartment thickness; difference −0.11 mm, −0.20 to −0.03) and no significant pain difference (−1.2 vs −1.9; difference −0.6, −1.6 to 0.3).

cards.headline: Deyle 2020: physical therapy beat glucocorticoid injection at 1 year — WOMAC 37.0 versus 55.8
cards.summary: Deyle 2020: physical therapy beat glucocorticoid injection at 1 year — WOMAC 37.0 vs 55.8 .
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (primary care, 1 year; unblinded by nature of the interventions)
cards.people: 156 patients with osteoarthritis in one or both knees in the US Military Health System, mean age 56 years, randomised 1:1 to physical therapy (78) or intra-articular glucocorticoid injection (78); baseline WOMAC scores were 107.1 (SD 42.4) and 108.8 (SD 47.1) respectively. cards.result: At 1 year the mean total WOMAC score (0–240, higher is worse) was 37.0 (SD 30.7) with physical therapy versus 55.8 (SD 53.8) with injection — a mean between-group difference of 18.8 points (95% CI 5.0–32.6) favouring physical therapy. Secondary outcomes (Alternate Step Test time, Timed Up and Go time, Global Rating of Change) changed in the same direction. One patient fainted while receiving an injection.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, unblindable interventions and a self-reported primary outcome in a military health-system population; the injection arm received injections per usual practice rather than a fixed repeated schedule, so this is a strategy comparison, not a drug-efficacy test.

cards.headline: McAlindon 2017: triamcinolone every 3 months for 2 years lost more cartilage than saline (−0.21 vs −0.10 mm) with no pain advantage
cards.summary: McAlindon 2017: triamcinolone every 3 months for 2 years lost more cartilage than saline (−0.21 vs −0.10 mm) with no pain advantage.
cards.people: 140 patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (ACR criteria, Kellgren-Lawrence grades 2–3) with ultrasound features of synovitis, at a single US centre; mean age 58 (SD 8) years, 75 women (54%); 70 received intra-articular triamcinolone 40 mg and 70 saline every 12 weeks for 2 years; 119 (85%) completed the study. cards.result: Triamcinolone produced significantly greater cartilage volume loss than saline: mean change in index-compartment cartilage thickness −0.21 mm versus −0.10 mm (between-group difference −0.11 mm, 95% CI −0.20 to −0.03). cards.watchOut: The minimal clinically important difference for cartilage volume loss is not yet defined, so the clinical weight of an extra 0.11 mm over 2 years is uncertain; the regimen tested is fixed quarterly injection, not occasional injection for flares.

cards.headline: Synthesis: therapy first for symptoms; repeated scheduled steroid costs cartilage without buying pain relief — split POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Therapy first for symptoms; repeated scheduled steroid costs cartilage without buying pain relief — split POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Deyle 2020 (156 patients, strategy trial) and McAlindon 2017 (140 patients, injection vs saline).
cards.result: The two trials interlock: the strategy trial says a course of physical therapy leaves patients better at 1 year than an injection strategy (WOMAC difference 18.8 points), and the mechanistic trial says the injection strategy's repeated form — quarterly triamcinolone for 2 years — loses cartilage (−0.11 mm difference) while buying no significant pain relief. shelves.title: Exercise therapy for knee and hip osteoarthritis
shelves.question: Does land-based exercise therapy reduce pain and improve function in knee and hip osteoarthritis versus no exercise?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Arthralgia/physiopathology,prevention & control · Exercise Therapy/methods · Osteoarthritis, Knee/physiopathology,therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Arthralgia/therapy · Exercise Therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two Cochrane syntheses of randomised trials point the same way for both joints. For knee OA (Fransen 2015; 54 studies identified, 44 trials pooled), land-based exercise reduced pain by 12 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI 10–15) and improved physical function by 10 points (8–13) immediately after treatment, with smaller benefits sustained 2–6 months after formal treatment ended (pain 6 points, 3–9). For hip OA (Fransen 2014; 10 RCTs, with high-quality evidence from 9 trials and 549 participants), exercise reduced pain (standardised mean difference −0.38, −0.55 to −0.20) and improved function (SMD −0.38) immediately after treatment. The reviewers themselves flag vulnerability to selection, attrition and detection bias — exercise trials cannot blind participants — which is why the effect sizes, not just their significance, are printed on the cards. Exercise for other indications is carded across Shelves #452–#461 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Fransen 2015 (Cochrane): land-based exercise reduced knee OA pain by 12 points/100 and improved function by 10 points/100 across 44 pooled trials
cards.summary: Fransen 2015 (Cochrane): land-based exercise reduced knee OA pain by 12 points/100 and improved function by 10 points/100 across 44 pooled trials.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised clinical trials (searches to May 2013)
cards.people: 54 studies of land-based therapeutic exercise versus non-exercise control in knee osteoarthritis; pooled results from 44 trials for pain and function. Only 19 of 54 studies (35%) reported adequate random sequence generation, allocation concealment and accounting for incomplete outcome data. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Immediately after treatment, exercise significantly reduced pain (12 points on a 100-point scale, 95% CI 10–15) and improved physical function (10 points, 8–13) to a moderate degree, and improved quality of life by a small amount (4 points, 2–5; 13 studies). Sustainability data from 12 studies showed pain still significantly reduced 2–6 months after formal treatment ended (6 points, 3–9), and function improved in 10 studies (3 points, 1–5). The reviewers state the results may be vulnerable to selection, attrition and detection bias.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis, not a single trial: heterogeneous exercise programmes pooled together, searches ending in 2013, and unblindable interventions with self-reported outcomes — the 12-point average conceals wide variation between programmes.

shelves.title: Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow): corticosteroid injection — short-term win, long-term loss
shelves.question: Does a corticosteroid injection for tennis elbow beat physiotherapy or wait-and-see at one year, despite winning at six weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Chronic Disease · Combined Modality Therapy · Physical Therapy Modalities · Recovery of Function · Tennis Elbow/drug therapy,physiopathology · Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials, in the same Brisbane research programme, show the same reversal. Coombes 2013 (165 patients, 2×2 factorial): corticosteroid injection produced lower complete recovery or much improvement at 1 year than placebo injection (83% vs 96%; relative risk 0.86, 99% CI 0.75–0.99) and far greater 1-year recurrence (54% vs 12%; recurrence relative risk for placebo vs steroid 0.23) — while physiotherapy made no significant 1-year difference (91% vs 88%). Bisset 2006 (198 patients): injections were significantly better at 6 weeks, but 47 of 65 early successes subsequently regressed, and injection outcomes were significantly poorer than physiotherapy in the long term; physiotherapy beat wait-and-see early, with no difference by 52 weeks. The relative risks sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band individually; the LIKELY rests on two concordant trials plus the large absolute recurrence split (54% vs 12%).

cards.headline: Coombes 2013: corticosteroid injection lowered 1-year recovery (83% vs 96% on placebo injection) and multiplied recurrence (54% vs 12%)
cards.summary: Coombes 2013: corticosteroid injection lowered 1-year recovery ( 83% vs 96% on placebo injection) and multiplied recurrence (54% vs 12%).
cards.type: 2×2 factorial, randomised, injection-blinded, placebo-controlled trial (1-year follow-up)
cards.people: 165 patients aged 18 years or older with unilateral lateral epicondylalgia of more than 6 weeks' duration, at a university centre and 16 primary-care settings in Brisbane, Australia: corticosteroid injection 43, placebo injection 41, corticosteroid plus physiotherapy 40, placebo plus physiotherapy 41. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Corticosteroid injection resulted in lower complete recovery or much improvement at 1 year than placebo injection (83% vs 96%; relative risk 0.86, 99% CI 0.75–0.99; P=0.01) — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with the absolute rates as stated — and greater 1-year recurrence (54% vs 12%; relative risk 0.23, 99% CI 0.10–0.51 for the placebo comparison; P<0.001). Physiotherapy versus no physiotherapy did not differ at 1 year on recovery (91% vs 88%; RR 1.04, 0.90–1.19) or recurrence (29% vs 38%). Similar patterns held at 26 weeks, with the steroid's early advantage reversed.
cards.watchOut: One research programme's population (Brisbane primary care) and a global-rating outcome; the factorial design pools physiotherapy arms for the injection contrast, which the analysis prespecified.

cards.headline: Bisset 2006: injections won at 6 weeks, then 47 of 65 successes regressed and long-term outcomes were poorer than physiotherapy
cards.summary: Bisset 2006: injections won at 6 weeks, then 47 of 65 successes regressed and long-term outcomes were poorer than physiotherapy.

Physiotherapy was superior to wait and see in the short term, with no difference at 52 weeks, when most participants in both groups reported a successful outcome. shelves.title: Dupuytren's contracture: collagenase injection vs surgery
shelves.question: Does collagenase clostridium histolyticum correct Dupuytren's contracture versus placebo — and how does it compare with limited fasciectomy on recurrence and recovery?
shelves.mesh: Hathewaya histolytica/enzymology · Dupuytren Contracture/drug therapy,physiopathology · Injections, Intralesional · Microbial Collagenase/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Range of Motion, Articular · Tendon Injuries/etiology · Collagenases/administration & dosage,adverse effects,economics
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — collagenase corrects contracture versus placebo · POSSIBLE — fasciectomy gives better 1-year hand-health scores. Against placebo (CORD, 308 patients), collagenase took 64.0% of treated cords to within 5 degrees of full extension versus 6.8% on placebo, and improved total range of motion from 43.9 to 80.7 degrees versus 45.3 to 49.5 — a large, blinded win. Head-to-head (DISC, 672 patients, pragmatic unblinded), collagenase was NOT non-inferior to limited fasciectomy on the 1-year Patient Evaluation Measure (17.8 vs 11.9 points, higher is worse; difference 5.9, 95% CI 3.1–8.8, against a 6-point margin; one-sided P=0.49 for non-inferiority), with fewer moderate/severe complications on collagenase (1.8% vs 5.1%) but far more reintervention for recurrence (14.6% vs 3.4%). The head-to-head half is a single trial, hence POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: CORD 2009: collagenase corrected 64.0% of contracted cords to near-full extension versus 6.8% on placebo
cards.summary: CORD 2009: collagenase corrected 64.0% of contracted cords to near-full extension vs 6.8% on placebo.
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multicentre trial
cards.people: 308 patients with joint contractures of 20 degrees or more from Dupuytren's disease; the primary metacarpophalangeal or proximal interphalangeal joint was assigned to up to three injections of collagenase clostridium histolyticum 0.58 mg or placebo into the contracted cord at 30-day intervals, with manipulation the day after injection. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — reduction of contracture to 0–5 degrees of full extension 30 days after the last injection — was met by 64.0% of collagenase-injected cords versus 6.8% on placebo (P<0.001), and all 26 secondary endpoints favoured collagenase (P≤0.002). Overall range of motion improved from 43.9 to 80.7 degrees with collagenase versus 45.3 to 49.5 degrees with placebo (P<0.001). Common adverse events were localised swelling, pain, bruising, pruritus and transient regional lymph-node enlargement; three treatment-related serious events were reported — two tendon ruptures and one complex regional pain syndrome. No significant changes in flexion or grip strength and no systemic allergic reactions occurred.
cards.watchOut: A 30-day post-injection endpoint in trial-selected cords: it proves correction, not durability — recurrence over years is the DISC trial's territory, and tendon rupture, though rare, is the signature serious harm.

cards.headline: Synthesis: collagenase works versus placebo but does not match fasciectomy's 1-year hand health — split verdict
cards.summary: Collagenase works vs placebo (LIKELY) but does not match fasciectomy's 1-year hand health (POSSIBLE).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: CORD (308 patients, collagenase vs placebo) and DISC (672 patients, collagenase vs fasciectomy).

shelves.title: Frozen shoulder: capsular release, manipulation, or structured physiotherapy (UK FROST)
shelves.question: In primary frozen shoulder, do arthroscopic capsular release or manipulation under anaesthesia beat early structured physiotherapy on shoulder function?
shelves.mesh: Bursitis/therapy · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Injections, Intra-Articular · Joint Capsule Release · Manipulation, Orthopedic · Physical Therapy Modalities · Range of Motion, Articular
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large three-arm trial programme, reported at two horizons on this shelf, found no clinically superior option. UK FROST (503 patients) reported 12-month Oxford Shoulder Scores of 40.3 for arthroscopic capsular release, 38.3 for manipulation under anaesthesia and 37.2 for early structured physiotherapy — mean differences of 3.06 points (release vs physiotherapy), 1.05 (manipulation vs physiotherapy) and 2.01 (release vs manipulation), all below the trial's target differences (5 and 4 points), so none of the three was clinically superior. Capsular release carried more serious adverse events (8 vs 2 with manipulation), and the linked economic evaluation found manipulation the most cost-effective option at £20,000 per QALY (probability 0.8632), with capsular release costing £1,734 more than physiotherapy and essentially no chance (0.0002) of being cost-effective. A single trial programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and both cards are the SAME trial (ISRCTN48804508) at two reports — labelled as such, never as two trials.

cards.headline: UK FROST 2020: no intervention was clinically superior at 12 months — Oxford Shoulder Scores 40.3 (release), 38.3 (manipulation), 37.2 (physiotherapy)
cards.summary: UK FROST 2020: no intervention was clinically superior at 12 months — Oxford Shoulder Scores 40.3 (release), 38.3 (manipulation), 37.2 (physiotherapy).
cards.type: Multicentre, pragmatic, three-arm, superiority randomised trial (35 UK hospital sites)
cards.people: 503 adults (≥18 years) with unilateral primary frozen shoulder (passive external rotation restricted by ≥50%) referred to secondary care, randomised 2:2:1 to manipulation under anaesthesia (201 analysed), arthroscopic capsular release (203), or early structured physiotherapy with steroid injection (99); 12-month Oxford Shoulder Score data were available for about 94% in each arm. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 months the mean Oxford Shoulder Score (0–48, higher is better) was 40.3 (95% CI 38.9–41.7) for capsular release, 38.3 (36.9–39.7) for manipulation and 37.2 (35.3–39.2) for physiotherapy. Mean differences were 2.01 points (0.10–3.91) for release versus manipulation, 3.06 (0.71–5.41) for release versus physiotherapy and 1.05 (−1.28 to 3.39) for manipulation versus physiotherapy — all below the prespecified target differences (5 points against physiotherapy; 4 between the surgical options), so none of the three interventions was clinically superior. Eight serious adverse events were reported with capsular release and two with manipulation. Manipulation had the highest probability of cost-effectiveness at £20,000 per QALY (0.8632, vs 0.1366 physiotherapy and 0.0002 release).
cards.watchOut: One trial, in secondary-care referrals with severe restriction; all arms included steroid injection and physiotherapy elements, so the comparison is between strategies built on shared components, not surgery versus nothing.
cards.source: Rangan A et al. Management of adults with primary frozen shoulder in secondary care (UK FROST): a multicentre, pragmatic, three-arm, superiority randomised clinical trial. Lancet. 2020;396(10256):977-989. PMID: 33010843. Registry ID: ISRCTN48804508, stated in the record's abstract; the MEDLINE record carries no databank SI field.

cards.headline: UK FROST economic evaluation 2021: capsular release cost £1,734 more than physiotherapy with worse QALYs; manipulation was the cost-effective option
cards.summary: UK FROST economic evaluation 2021: capsular release cost £1,734 more than physiotherapy with worse QALYs; manipulation was the cost-effective option.
cards.type: Within-trial cost-utility analysis of the UK FROST randomised trial (NHS perspective, 1 year)
cards.people: The same UK FROST trial population as the card above (503 adults with primary frozen shoulder in UK secondary care); costs in 2018 GBP and QALYs over 1 year, analysed by regression methods. This is a second report of the same trial, not a second trial.
cards.result: Arthroscopic capsular release was £1,734 more costly than early structured physiotherapy (95% CI £1,529–£1,938) and £1,457 more costly than manipulation (£1,283–£1,632); manipulation was £276 (£66–£487) more expensive than physiotherapy. Capsular release had worse QALYs than manipulation (−0.0293; −0.0616 to 0.0030), while manipulation had better QALYs than physiotherapy (0.0396; −0.0008 to 0.0800). At £20,000 per QALY, the probability of being cost-effective was 0.8632 for manipulation, 0.1366 for physiotherapy and 0.0002 for capsular release; results were robust to sensitivity analyses.
cards.watchOut: A 1-year NHS cost perspective: it prices the strategies as delivered in UK secondary care and does not capture longer-horizon recurrence or patient preference for avoiding anaesthesia.
