shelves.title: Polymyalgia rheumatica: IL-6 blockade to spare steroids
shelves.question: Does sarilumab (SAPHYR) or tocilizumab (SEMAPHORE) sustain remission of polymyalgia rheumatica during glucocorticoid taper versus taper alone?
shelves.mesh: Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Polymyalgia Rheumatica/drug therapy · Prednisone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Recurrence · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Drug Tapering/methods · C-Reactive Protein/analysis
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — sarilumab sustains remission in relapsing disease · POSSIBLE — tocilizumab spares steroids in new-onset disease. SAPHYR (118 patients relapsing during taper) found sustained remission at 52 weeks in 28% on sarilumab plus a 14-week prednisone taper versus 10% on placebo plus a 52-week taper (difference 18 percentage points, 95% CI 4–32; P=0.02), with median cumulative glucocorticoid doses of 777 mg versus 2,044 mg. For tocilizumab, the SEMAPHORE primary report could not be pinned at build (see summary.md); the carded tocilizumab trial is PMR-SPARE (36 patients with new-onset disease), which found glucocorticoid-free remission at week 16 in 63.2% versus 11.8% (odds ratio 12.9, 2.2–73.6) under a rapid 11-week taper. Both halves are single trials — one small — so both are capped at POSSIBLE. Tocilizumab for giant cell arteritis is Shelf #385 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: SAPHYR 2023: sarilumab tripled sustained remission at 52 weeks (28% vs 10%) and cut cumulative prednisone from 2,044 mg to 777 mg
cards.summary: SAPHYR 2023: sarilumab tripled sustained remission at 52 weeks ( 28% vs 10% ) and cut cumulative prednisone from 2,044 mg to 777 mg.
cards.people: 118 patients with polymyalgia rheumatica who had relapsed during glucocorticoid tapering; 60 received sarilumab 200 mg subcutaneously twice monthly plus a 14-week prednisone taper and 58 received placebo plus a 52-week prednisone taper. Sustained remission required resolution of signs and symptoms by week 12, sustained CRP normalisation, no flare, and adherence to the taper from weeks 12–52. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Sustained remission at week 52 occurred in 17 of 60 patients (28%) on sarilumab versus 6 of 58 (10%) on placebo (difference 18 percentage points, 95% CI 4–32; P=0.02). The median cumulative glucocorticoid dose was 777 mg with sarilumab versus 2,044 mg with placebo (P<0.001). The most common adverse events on sarilumab versus placebo were neutropenia (15% vs 0%), arthralgia (15% vs 5%) and diarrhoea (12% vs 2%); treatment-related discontinuations were 12% versus 7%.
cards.watchOut: The comparison bundles two differences at once — sarilumab versus placebo AND a 14-week versus 52-week taper — so the trial tests a sarilumab-enabled fast taper strategy, not the drug against an identical taper; absolute remission rates remain modest in both arms.

cards.headline: PMR-SPARE 2022: tocilizumab achieved glucocorticoid-free remission at week 16 in 63.2% versus 11.8% on placebo under a rapid taper
cards.summary: PMR-SPARE 2022: tocilizumab achieved glucocorticoid-free remission at week 16 in 63.2% vs 11.8% on placebo under a rapid taper — a very small trial.
cards.type: Double-blind, multicentre phase 2/3 randomised controlled trial (16 weeks' treatment; outcomes to week 24)
cards.people: 36 patients with new-onset polymyalgia rheumatica at three centres, randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous tocilizumab 162 mg weekly (19) or placebo (17), all receiving oral prednisone tapered from 20 mg to zero over 11 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Glucocorticoid-free remission at week 16 was achieved by 12 of 19 patients on tocilizumab (63.2%) versus 2 of 17 on placebo (11.8%; p=0.002), corresponding to an odds ratio of 12.9 (95% CI 2.2–73.6) — a relative measure with a very wide interval from a very small trial, carded with its absolute rates. Mean time to first relapse was 130 (SD 13) versus 82 (SD 11) days (p=0.007), and median cumulative glucocorticoid dose was 727 mg (IQR 721–842) versus 935 mg (861–1,244) (p=0.003). Serious adverse events occurred in five placebo patients and one tocilizumab patient.
cards.watchOut: Only 36 patients and a deliberately rapid taper that most placebo patients were destined to fail; the topic file named the SEMAPHORE trial for this half — its primary report could not be pinned at build, so PMR-SPARE is carded as the verified tocilizumab RCT and the substitution is disclosed here and in summary.md.

shelves.title: Systemic sclerosis-associated interstitial lung disease: nintedanib
shelves.question: Does nintedanib slow the decline in lung function in systemic sclerosis-associated ILD (SENSCIS) — and does tocilizumab preserve lung function in early diffuse disease?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Disease Progression · Enzyme Inhibitors/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Indoles/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Lung Diseases, Interstitial/drug therapy,etiology,physiopathology · Protein-Tyrosine Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — nintedanib slows FVC decline · MAYBE (weak evidence) — tocilizumab preserves lung function. SENSCIS (576 patients) found an adjusted annual FVC decline of −52.4 mL on nintedanib versus −93.3 mL on placebo over 52 weeks (difference 41.0 mL per year, 95% CI 2.9–79.0; P=0.04) — a single trial on a physiological endpoint, with no significant difference in skin score or respiratory quality of life, and diarrhoea in 75.7% versus 31.6%; sensitivity analyses gave P values of 0.06–0.10, so the half is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. For tocilizumab (focuSSced, 210 patients with early diffuse cutaneous disease), the primary skin endpoint was NOT met (modified Rodnan change difference −1.73, 95% CI −3.78 to 0.32; p=0.10); the lung signal — a 4.2-percentage-point difference in FVC% predicted — comes from a secondary endpoint at nominal significance, which is exactly weak evidence: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: SENSCIS 2019: nintedanib slowed annual FVC decline from −93.3 mL to −52.4 mL over 52 weeks, with no skin or quality-of-life benefit

cards.people: 576 patients with systemic sclerosis (first non-Raynaud symptom within 7 years) and CT fibrosis affecting at least 10% of the lungs, who received at least one dose of nintedanib 150 mg twice daily or placebo; 51.9% had diffuse cutaneous disease and 48.4% were receiving mycophenolate at baseline. cards.result: The adjusted annual rate of FVC change was −52.4 mL per year on nintedanib versus −93.3 mL per year on placebo (difference 41.0 mL per year, 95% CI 2.9–79.0; P=0.04); sensitivity analyses using multiple imputation gave P values from 0.06 to 0.10. Key secondary endpoints did not differ: modified Rodnan skin score difference −0.21 (95% CI −0.94 to 0.53; P=0.58) and St George's Respiratory Questionnaire difference 1.69 (−0.73 to 4.12). Diarrhoea, the most common adverse event, was reported in 75.7% on nintedanib versus 31.6% on placebo.

cards.people: 210 adults with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis of 60 months or less and modified Rodnan skin scores of 10–35, at 75 sites in 20 countries; 104 received subcutaneous tocilizumab 162 mg weekly and 106 placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was not met: least-squares mean change in modified Rodnan skin score at week 48 was −6.14 on tocilizumab versus −4.41 on placebo (adjusted difference −1.73, 95% CI −3.78 to 0.32; p=0.10). Health Assessment Questionnaire disability and patient/physician global scores did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: The lung result is a secondary endpoint in a trial that missed its primary endpoint, reported at nominal (multiplicity-unadjusted) significance, in early diffuse disease selected for skin severity — not in a population recruited for ILD. That is why this half is stamped MAYBE (weak evidence).

shelves.title: Rotator cuff tears: tendon repair versus physiotherapy (Moosmayer; Kukkonen)
shelves.question: For small-to-medium rotator cuff tears, does surgical repair beat physiotherapy — in traumatic tears, and in non-traumatic tears in older patients?
shelves.mesh: Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Muscle Strength/physiology · Musculoskeletal Pain/etiology,physiopathology · Patient Satisfaction · Physical Therapy Modalities · Range of Motion, Articular/physiology · Recovery of Function
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE both ways, because the two trials ask different questions. In Moosmayer's trial of tears up to 3 cm (many traumatic; repair vs physiotherapy with optional secondary repair), primary repair was statistically better at 5 years — Constant score by 5.3 points (P=0.05), ASES by 9.0 points, pain by 1.1 cm — but the authors themselves state the differences were small and may be below clinical importance, and 12 of 51 physiotherapy patients crossed to repair. In Kukkonen's trial of non-traumatic supraspinatus tears in older patients, repair, acromioplasty and physiotherapy alone did not differ on the Constant score at 2 years (changes 22.6 vs 20.5 vs 18.4 points; P=0.38), while repair cost significantly more. One trial per sub-question caps both halves at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Moosmayer 2014: primary tendon repair beat physiotherapy at 5 years by small margins (Constant +5.3 points) that the authors say may be below clinical importance
cards.summary: Moosmayer 2014: tendon repair beat physiotherapy at 5 years by small margins (Constant +5.3 points ) that may be below clinical importance.
cards.type: Single-centre, pragmatic randomised controlled trial with 5-year follow-up (repair vs physiotherapy with optional secondary repair)
cards.people: 103 patients with a rotator cuff tear not exceeding 3 cm (52 primary tendon repair, 51 physiotherapy); 5-year follow-up rate 98%; 12 of the 51 physiotherapy patients underwent secondary tendon repair. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Primary repair was superior on the Constant score (between-group mean difference 5.3 points; P=0.05), the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons score (9.0 points; P<0.001), pain on a 10-cm visual analogue scale (1.1 cm; P<0.001) and patient satisfaction (1.0 cm; P=0.03). In 37% of tears treated with physiotherapy only, tear size increased by more than 5 mm on ultrasound over 5 years, and this was associated with an inferior outcome. The authors conclude the differences favouring repair were small and may be below clinical importance.
cards.watchOut: The physiotherapy arm is a strategy (physiotherapy first, repair if needed — used by 12 of 51), so the trial compares 'repair now' with 'repair only if physiotherapy fails', not repair with no repair ever. The headline Constant difference sits exactly at P=0.05.

cards.headline: Kukkonen 2015: for non-traumatic supraspinatus tears, repair and acromioplasty did not beat physiotherapy alone on the Constant score at 2 years
cards.summary: Kukkonen 2015: for non-traumatic supraspinatus tears, repair did not beat physiotherapy alone on the Constant score at 2 years.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, three cumulatively designed arms (physiotherapy alone vs acromioplasty + physiotherapy vs repair + acromioplasty + physiotherapy)
cards.people: 180 shoulders with symptomatic, non-traumatic supraspinatus tears randomised; 167 shoulders (160 patients) were analysed at 2 years. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix; the trial's population is described by its authors as older patients.
cards.result: There were no significant differences (P=0.38) in mean change in Constant score: 18.4 points (95% CI 14.2 to 22.6) with physiotherapy alone, 20.5 (16.4 to 24.6) with acromioplasty and physiotherapy, and 22.6 (18.4 to 26.8) with repair, acromioplasty and physiotherapy. Visual analogue pain scores (P=0.45) and patient satisfaction (P=0.28) also did not differ. At 2 years the mean sagittal tear size was smaller in the repair group (4.2 mm vs 11.0 mm), and repair and acromioplasty were significantly more expensive than physiotherapy alone (P<0.01). The authors conclude conservative treatment is a reasonable first option for isolated, symptomatic, non-traumatic supraspinatus tears in older patients.
cards.watchOut: Two years may be too short to price tear progression — the authors flag that non-repaired tears may progress and warrant further follow-up, which is exactly what Moosmayer's 5-year imaging showed in a third of physiotherapy-only tears.
cards.source: Kukkonen J et al. Treatment of Nontraumatic Rotator Cuff Tears: A Randomized Controlled Trial with Two Years of Clinical and Imaging Follow-up. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2015;97(21):1729-1737. PMID: 26537160. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: tear type decides — a small, late repair advantage in Moosmayer's tears; no advantage at all in older patients' non-traumatic tears
cards.summary: Tear type decides — a small, late repair advantage in traumatic tears; none in older patients' non-traumatic tears — Split: POSSIBLE · POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Moosmayer 2014 (103 patients, tears ≤3 cm, 5 years) and Kukkonen 2015 (180 shoulders, non-traumatic tears, 2 years).
cards.result: Read together: physiotherapy-first is a defensible default in both populations — in Kukkonen it matched surgery outright at 2 years at lower cost; in Moosmayer the repair-now strategy ended 5.3 Constant points ahead at 5 years, a margin its authors question clinically, while a third of unrepaired tears enlarged. Neither trial supports urgent repair for every tear, and neither supports 'never repair'. Subacromial decompression for pain without a full tear lives on Shelf #654 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not average the two trials into one verdict: traumatic versus non-traumatic tears in different age groups are different decisions, which is why the stamp splits.

shelves.title: Acute Achilles tendon rupture: surgery versus non-operative treatment (Myhrvold; Willits; CARTA)
shelves.question: Does operative repair of an acute Achilles rupture improve function or reduce re-rupture versus non-operative treatment with functional rehabilitation?
shelves.mesh: Achilles Tendon/injuries,surgery · Acute Disease · Ankle Injuries/surgery,therapy · Conservative Treatment · Minimally Invasive Surgical Procedures · Rupture/surgery,therapy · Tendon Injuries/surgery,therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Surgery does not improve function, and it trades one complication profile for another. Myhrvold (554 randomised) found no difference in Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score change at 12 months between non-operative treatment, open repair and minimally invasive surgery (−17.0 vs −16.0 vs −14.7 points; P=0.57), but re-rupture was higher without surgery (6.2% vs 0.6% in each surgical group) while nerve injuries clustered in the surgical groups (5.2% minimally invasive, 2.8% open, 0.6% non-operative). Willits (144 patients, both arms on accelerated functional rehabilitation) likewise found no clinically important difference in strength, motion or scores, with re-rupture in 2 operative vs 3 non-operative patients and more soft-tissue complications with surgery. The newer CARTA trial (300 patients) found an ultrasound-guided individualised algorithm did not improve heel-rise work at 12 months, but cut re-rupture versus default non-operative care (3% vs 11%) while operating on 36% fewer patients than routine surgery. Function: no surgical advantage, across three concordant trials. Re-rupture: surgery (or selecting for it) prevents most re-ruptures, at the price of surgical complications.

cards.headline: Myhrvold 2022: surgery did not improve rupture scores at 12 months (−17.0 non-operative vs −16.0 open vs −14.7 minimally invasive) but cut re-rupture (6.2% vs 0.6%)
cards.summary: Myhrvold 2022: surgery did not improve rupture scores at 12 months (−17.0 non-operative vs −16.0 open vs −14.7 minimally invasive) but cut re-rupture.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial, three arms (non-operative vs open repair vs minimally invasive surgery)
cards.people: 554 adults with acute Achilles tendon rupture presenting to four Norwegian centres were randomised; 526 were included in the final analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean changes in the Achilles' tendon Total Rupture Score at 12 months were −17.0 points in the non-operative group, −16.0 in the open-repair group and −14.7 in the minimally invasive group (P=0.57), with no evidence of pairwise differences; physical performance and patient-reported physical function were also similar. Re-ruptures were more frequent in the non-operative group (6.2%) than in the open-repair or minimally invasive groups (0.6% in each). Nerve injuries occurred in 9 patients in the minimally invasive group (5.2%), 5 in the open-repair group (2.8%) and 1 in the non-operative group (0.6%).
cards.watchOut: Function scores are reported as change-from-baseline on a scale where the groups converge; the trial's decisive separation is in complications, which pull in opposite directions — re-rupture without surgery, nerve injury with it. Both surgical techniques behaved alike.
cards.source: Myhrvold SB et al. Nonoperative or Surgical Treatment of Acute Achilles' Tendon Rupture. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(15):1409-1420. PMID: 35417636. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01785264, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Willits 2010: with accelerated functional rehabilitation in both arms, operative and non-operative treatment were clinically similar on every measured outcome
cards.summary: Willits 2010: with accelerated functional rehabilitation in both arms, operative and non-operative treatment were clinically similar on every measured outcome.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (operative repair vs non-operative treatment, both with early weight-bearing and early range of motion)
cards.people: 144 patients with acute Achilles tendon rupture (72 operative, 72 non-operative); 118 were men and 26 women; mean age 40.4 years (SD 8.8).
cards.result: Re-rupture occurred in 2 patients in the operative group and 3 in the non-operative group. There was no clinically important difference between groups in isokinetic strength, the Leppilahti score, range of motion or calf circumference at 3, 6, 12 or 24 months. Complications numbered 13 in the operative group and 6 in the non-operative group, the main difference being more soft-tissue-related complications with surgery. The authors conclude the accelerated-rehabilitation non-operative protocol avoids serious complications related to surgical management while giving clinically similar outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Small by modern standards (144 patients): its re-rupture counts (2 vs 3) cannot measure the re-rupture difference Myhrvold later quantified (6.2% vs 0.6%). Its contribution is the rehabilitation insight — outcomes converge when BOTH arms mobilise early — from an era when non-operative care usually meant prolonged casting.
cards.source: Willits K et al. Operative versus nonoperative treatment of acute Achilles tendon ruptures: a multicenter randomized trial using accelerated functional rehabilitation. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2010;92(17):2767-2775. PMID: 21037028. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: CARTA (Toft 2026): an ultrasound-guided individualised algorithm did not improve heel-rise work, but cut re-rupture vs default non-operative care (3% vs 11%, a relative reduction of 73%) with fewer operations than routine surgery
cards.summary: CARTA 2026 (carded from the sweep): an ultrasound-guided individualised algorithm did not improve heel-rise work, but cut re-rupture vs default non-operative care ( 3% vs 11% ).
cards.type: Multicentre, three-arm randomised controlled trial (individualised CARTA algorithm vs non-operative vs operative treatment), carded from the 2024–2026 currency sweep
cards.people: 300 adults with acute Achilles tendon rupture randomised (of 970 screened); 76% men and 24% women; mean age 41 years (SD 1, as printed in the abstract). In the CARTA arm, surgery was indicated if ultrasound showed less than 25% tendon overlap or at least 7% elongation; 64% of CARTA patients were operated on. Twelve-month data were available for 98 CARTA, 100 non-operative and 97 operative patients.
cards.result: There were no significant between-group differences in the primary outcome, heel-rise work at 12 months. CARTA reduced re-rupture compared with non-operative treatment (3%, 95% CI 1 to 8, vs 11%, 6 to 19; P=0.03) — described by the authors as a 73% relative reduction, with the absolute rates (3% vs 11%) printed beside it — improved the Achilles tendon Total Rupture Score by 8 points (1 to 15; P=0.02) and the resting angle by −2° (−4 to −1; P=0.01). No difference was found between CARTA and operative treatment except that 36% fewer patients underwent surgery under CARTA.
cards.watchOut: The functional primary outcome was null; the re-rupture and score gains are secondary outcomes in a 300-patient trial, and the algorithm's thresholds (25% overlap, 7% elongation) come from the same group's programme. It refines patient selection; it does not resurrect routine surgery, which it matched while operating on a third fewer patients.
cards.source: Toft M et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: function is equivalent whichever route is chosen; the real choice is re-rupture risk without surgery versus surgical complications with it — LIKELY
cards.summary: Function is equivalent whichever route is chosen; the real choice is re-rupture risk versus surgical complications — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Myhrvold 2022 (526 analysed), Willits 2010 (144) and CARTA 2026 (300) — three randomised trials spanning cast-era, accelerated-rehabilitation and ultrasound-selected care.
cards.result: All three agree on the headline: no functional advantage to routine surgery (rupture-score and heel-rise outcomes statistically indistinguishable in each trial). They also agree on the trade: non-operative care carries a re-rupture rate around 6–11% that surgery or ultrasound-selected surgery brings down to around 1–3%, while surgery brings nerve injury (up to 5.2%) and soft-tissue complications that non-operative care largely avoids. Tendinopathy loading programmes for intact tendons live on Shelf #460 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Quote re-rupture and nerve-injury rates together or not at all: quoting either side alone turns a trade-off into a sales pitch.

shelves.title: Femoroacetabular impingement: hip arthroscopy versus conservative care (FASHIoN, FAIT)
shelves.question: In symptomatic femoroacetabular impingement, does hip arthroscopy improve hip-related quality of life more than personalised hip therapy / physiotherapy with activity modification?
shelves.mesh: Arthroscopy · Conservative Treatment · Femoracetabular Impingement/diagnosis,rehabilitation,surgery · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Physical Therapy Modalities · Range of Motion, Articular · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two multicentre randomised trials — unblindable by nature, assessor-blinded — agree that arthroscopy beats good conservative care by a modest, clinically relevant margin. UK FASHIoN (348 participants): iHOT-33 improved to 58.8 with arthroscopy vs 49.7 with personalised hip therapy at 12 months (adjusted mean difference 6.8 points, 95% CI 1.7–12.0), just exceeding the 6.1-point minimum clinically important difference. FAIT (222 participants): Hip Outcome Score ADL at 8 months was 10.0 points higher with arthroscopy (95% CI 6.4–13.6), above its 9-point clinically important difference. The price in FASHIoN was more patient-reported adverse events (147 vs 102 events) including one post-operative hip joint infection; FAIT reported no serious adverse events. Benefit is real but single-digit-to-10 points on 100-point scales — an average gain, not a transformation.

cards.headline: UK FASHIoN (Griffin 2018): hip arthroscopy beat personalised hip therapy on iHOT-33 at 12 months by 6.8 points, just above the clinically important difference
cards.summary: UK FASHIoN 2018: hip arthroscopy beat personalised hip therapy on iHOT-33 at 12 months by 6.8 points , just above the clinically important difference.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, assessor-blinded randomised controlled trial (23 UK NHS hospitals; patients and clinicians unmasked)
cards.people: 348 participants with femoroacetabular impingement syndrome, at least 16 years old, with cam or pincer morphology and no osteoarthritis (171 arthroscopy, 177 personalised hip therapy); follow-up at the primary outcome was 92% (319 of 348). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 months, mean iHOT-33 scores had improved from 39.2 (SD 20.9) to 58.8 (27.2) with arthroscopy and from 35.6 (18.2) to 49.7 (25.5) with personalised hip therapy; the adjusted mean difference was 6.8 points (95% CI 1.7–12.0) in favour of arthroscopy (P=0.0093), exceeding the minimum clinically important difference of 6.1 points. Patient-reported adverse events numbered 147 (in 100 of 138 patients) in the arthroscopy group vs 102 (in 88 of 146) in the therapy group, muscle soreness being most common; of six serious adverse events in the arthroscopy group, five were treatment-related, and one patient developed a hip joint infection after surgery. There were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded patients reporting their own outcomes is the standing weakness of surgery-versus-therapy trials: some of the 6.8-point gap may be expectation. The margin above the clinically important threshold is thin (6.8 vs 6.1), and cost-effectiveness was left to further follow-up.
cards.source: Griffin DR et al. Hip arthroscopy versus best conservative care for the treatment of femoroacetabular impingement syndrome (UK FASHIoN): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2018;391(10136):2225-2235. PMID: 29893223. Registry ID: ISRCTN64081839, as stated in the record's abstract.

cards.headline: FAIT (Palmer 2019): arthroscopic hip surgery gave a 10.0-point higher Hip Outcome Score ADL than physiotherapy and activity modification at 8 months
cards.summary: FAIT 2019: arthroscopic hip surgery gave a 10.0-point higher Hip Outcome Score ADL than physiotherapy at 8 months.
cards.type: Two-group parallel, assessor-blinded, pragmatic randomised controlled trial (seven NHS England sites)
cards.people: 222 participants aged 18–60 years with symptomatic FAI confirmed clinically and on imaging (112 arthroscopic surgery, 110 physiotherapy and activity modification); patients with previous surgery, recent targeted physiotherapy, established osteoarthritis or hip dysplasia were excluded. At 8 months, data were available for 100 surgery patients (89%) and 88 physiotherapy patients (80%). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean Hip Outcome Score ADL was 78.4 (95% CI 74.4 to 82.3) after arthroscopic surgery vs 69.2 (65.2 to 73.3) after physiotherapy; after adjustment for baseline score, age, sex and site, the mean score was 10.0 points higher (6.4 to 13.6; P<0.001) with surgery — above the prespecified minimum clinically important difference of 9 points. The physiotherapy programme was a goal-based programme of up to eight sessions over five months. No serious adverse events were reported in either group.
cards.watchOut: Shorter horizon than FASHIoN (8 months) and differential follow-up completeness (89% vs 80%); FASHIoN's adverse-event count is the more honest picture of surgery's price. Both trials recruited patients already referred to secondary/tertiary care — not everyone with hip pain and cam morphology.

cards.summary: Two concordant trials put arthroscopy ahead by roughly one clinically important difference — LIKELY, with modest expectations.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: UK FASHIoN (348 participants, 12 months) and FAIT (222 participants, 8 months); the currency sweep also surfaced FAIT's medium-term follow-up report (PMID 39592214), which is a follow-up of the carded FAIT trial and is fenced here, not re-carded.

shelves.title: Unstable ankle fracture in older adults: close contact casting versus surgery (Willett; CROSSBAT)
shelves.question: In adults over 60 with an unstable ankle fracture, does close contact casting give equivalent ankle function to surgery, with fewer complications — and what does the younger-adult CROSSBAT trial add?
shelves.mesh: Ankle Fractures/diagnostic imaging,surgery,therapy · Casts, Surgical · Fracture Fixation/adverse effects,instrumentation,methods · Surgical Wound Dehiscence/epidemiology,etiology · Surgical Wound Infection/epidemiology,etiology · Ankle Fractures/physiopathology,therapy · Australia/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The older-adult question rests on one large equivalence trial. Willett (620 adults over 60) found close contact casting equivalent to surgery on the Olerud-Molander Ankle Score at 6 months (64.5 vs 66.0; mean difference −0.6, 95% CI −3.9 to 2.6, inside the ±6-point equivalence margin; P for equivalence=.001), with far fewer infections and wound breakdowns (1% vs 10%; odds ratio 7.3) and fewer additional operations (1% vs 6%), but more radiological malunion (15% vs 3%; odds ratio 6.0) and a 19% conversion rate from casting to surgery. CROSSBAT, in younger adults (18–65) with a less severe fracture pattern, independently found surgery not superior to non-surgical care (function scores 49.8 vs 53.0) with more adverse events after surgery (32% vs 14%) — supportive, but a different population and fracture, so the older-adult equivalence claim stays at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Willett 2016: close contact casting was equivalent to surgery for ankle function at 6 months in over-60s (OMAS 64.5 vs 66.0), with fewer infections (1% vs 10%) but more malunion (15% vs 3%)
cards.summary: Willett 2016: close contact casting was equivalent to surgery for ankle function at 6 months in over-60s (OMAS 64.5 vs 66.0), with fewer infections (1% vs 10%).
cards.type: Pragmatic, equivalence, randomised clinical trial with blinded outcome assessors (24 UK centres)
cards.people: 620 adults older than 60 years with an acute, overtly unstable ankle fracture (309 surgery, 311 casting); mean age 71 years; 460 (74%) were women; 593 (96%) completed the study and 93% received their allocated treatment; 52 of 275 (19%) who initially received casting later converted to surgery.
cards.result: At 6 months, ankle function was equivalent: Olerud-Molander Ankle Score 66.0 (95% CI 63.6–68.5) for surgery vs 64.5 (61.8–67.2) for casting (mean difference −0.6, −3.9 to 2.6; P for equivalence=.001, margin ±6 points). Infection and wound breakdown were more common with surgery (29 of 298 [10%] vs 4 of 275 [1%]; odds ratio 7.3, 95% CI 2.6–20.2), as were additional operating-room procedures (6% vs 1%; odds ratio 5.8, 1.8–18.7); radiological malunion was more common with casting (38 of 249 [15%] vs 8 of 274 [3%]; odds ratio 6.0, 2.8–12.9) — relative figures with absolute rates beside them. Casting used 54 fewer operating-room minutes per participant. Quality of life, pain, ankle motion, mobility and satisfaction did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence at 6 months in function, not identity of outcomes: casting trades surgical complications for malunion and a one-in-five chance of ending up in theatre anyway. The trial's three-year follow-up report (PMID 29584832) exists but its PubMed abstract carries no extractable outcome figures, so it is disclosed here rather than carded.

cards.headline: CROSSBAT (Mittal 2017): in adults 18–65 with type B ankle fractures, surgery was not superior to non-surgical management and caused more adverse events (32% vs 14%)
cards.summary: CROSSBAT 2017: in adults 18–65 with type B ankle fractures, surgery was not superior to non-surgical management and caused more adverse events.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, single-blinded combined randomised and observational study (22 hospitals, Australia and New Zealand)
cards.people: 160 people aged 18–65 years with an isolated type B ankle fracture and minimal talar shift were randomised (80 surgical fixation, 80 non-surgical, both followed by 6 weeks in a walking boot); 139 were analysed by intention to treat. A parallel observational cohort of 276 patients was also followed. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the randomised cohort, surgery was not superior to non-surgery on the Foot and Ankle Outcomes Questionnaire (49.8 vs 53.0; mean difference 3.2, 95% CI 0.4 to 5.9; P=0.028, favouring non-surgery) or on the SF-12 physical component score (53.7 vs 53.2; mean difference 0.6, −2.9 to 1.8; P=0.63). Adverse events occurred in 23 participants (32%) in the surgical group and 10 (14%) in the non-surgical group. Similar results were found in the observational cohort.
cards.watchOut: A different decision from Willett's: younger patients, a stable-enough fracture pattern with minimal talar shift, and boot immobilisation rather than close contact casting. It corroborates 'surgery is not automatically better' without answering the older, unstable-fracture question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: for unstable ankle fracture in older adults, casting-first is equivalent at 6 months and safer — POSSIBLE on one pivotal trial
cards.summary: For unstable ankle fracture in older adults, casting-first is equivalent at 6 months and safer — POSSIBLE on one pivotal trial.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Willett 2016 (620 adults over 60, unstable fractures) and CROSSBAT 2017 (160 randomised adults 18–65, type B fractures). The currency sweep's SUPER-FIN trial (cast vs surgery for unstable lateral malleolus fractures, PMID 41534905) addresses a neighbouring fracture population and is fenced here, not carded.
cards.result: The older-adult claim rests on Willett alone: function equivalent at 6 months (difference −0.6 points against a ±6 margin), surgical-site harm clearly lower with casting (infection/wound breakdown 1% vs 10%), anatomical harm higher (malunion 15% vs 3%), and 19% of casted patients converting to surgery. CROSSBAT's null in younger adults is consistent background, not a second older-adult trial — hence POSSIBLE. Hip fracture timing and implant choices live on Shelves #342 and #652 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence of a 6-month function score is not equivalence of every outcome that matters at 3 years; malunion's long-term cost is the open question on this shelf.

shelves.title: Chronic plantar heel pain: plantar fascia–specific stretching (DiGiovanni)
shelves.question: Does a programme of plantar fascia–specific stretching relieve chronic plantar heel pain and keep patients off surgery versus standard Achilles stretching — and what does the shock-wave trial add?
shelves.mesh: Achilles Tendon/physiopathology · Activities of Daily Living · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Celecoxib · Chronic Disease · Combined Modality Therapy · Exercise Therapy/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One pivotal randomised trial and its own two-year follow-up support plantar fascia–specific stretching: DiGiovanni randomised 101 patients with plantar fasciitis of at least 10 months' duration and found the fascia-specific programme superior to standard Achilles stretching at 8 weeks on worst pain (P=0.02) and first-step morning pain (P=0.006), with better satisfaction; at two years, after all patients had been taught the fascia programme, 92% of respondents reported total satisfaction or satisfaction with minor reservations and 94% reported decreased pain. The confirmatory trial carded here tests a different intervention — Gerdesmeyer's radial shock-wave therapy beat placebo at 12 weeks (VAS composite reduction 72.1% vs 44.7%; overall success 61.0% vs 42.2%) — which supports 'mechanical loading/stimulation treatments can beat controls in recalcitrant heel pain' without confirming stretching itself. One trial for the shelf's own question caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: DiGiovanni 2003: plantar fascia–specific stretching beat Achilles stretching at 8 weeks on worst pain (P=0.02) and first-step pain (P=0.006) in chronic plantar fasciitis
cards.summary: DiGiovanni 2003: plantar fascia–specific stretching beat Achilles stretching at 8 weeks on worst pain and first-step pain in chronic plantar heel pain.
cards.type: Prospective randomised study (both groups also received prefabricated soft insoles, a 3-week course of celecoxib and an educational video)
cards.people: 101 patients with chronic proximal plantar fasciitis for at least 10 months (mean age 46 years); 82 returned for the 8-week follow-up evaluation. The abstract does not state the sex mix or the per-group numbers randomised.
cards.result: The pain subscale of the Foot Function Index showed significantly better results for the plantar fascia–stretching programme on item 1 (worst pain; P=0.02) and item 2 (pain with first steps in the morning; P=0.006), and response-rate analyses showed significant differences in pain, activity limitations and patient satisfaction, all favouring the fascia-specific programme. Baseline covariates did not differ between groups except duration of symptoms (P<0.01). The authors present the programme as an effective alternative in the non-operative treatment of chronic, disabling plantar heel pain.
cards.watchOut: A small, short, unblindable trial reported largely through P-values rather than effect sizes, with 19 of 101 patients missing at 8 weeks; the comparator (Achilles stretching) was the era's standard, not an inert control, which strengthens the comparison but limits how large the true advantage can be estimated.
cards.source: DiGiovanni BF et al. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain. A prospective, randomized study. J Bone Joint Surg Am. 2003;85(7):1270-1277. PMID: 12851352. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (2003).

cards.summary: DiGiovanni 2006 two-year follow-up: after all patients were taught the fascia programme, 92% reported satisfaction (uncontrolled follow-up of the same trial).
cards.type: Two-year follow-up of the randomised trial carded above — the same cohort, not a second trial
cards.people: The 82 patients who completed the initial 8-week trial; complete two-year data sets were obtained from 66 patients, by mailed questionnaire.
cards.result: At the 8-week point, all patients were instructed in the plantar fascia–stretching protocol. At two years there were no significant differences between the original groups in worst pain or first-step morning pain. cards.headline: Gerdesmeyer 2008: radial shock-wave therapy beat placebo at 12 weeks in recalcitrant plantar fasciitis (success 61.0% vs 42.2%) — a different intervention, carded as the shelf's confirmatory mechanical-treatment trial
cards.summary: Gerdesmeyer 2008: radial shock-wave therapy beat placebo at 12 weeks (success 61.0% vs 42.2% ) — a different intervention than stretching, carded as what it is.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial (three treatments of radial extracorporeal shock-wave therapy vs placebo, no anaesthesia)
cards.people: 245 patients with chronic, recalcitrant plantar fasciitis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 12 weeks, shock-wave therapy was superior to placebo on the visual analogue scale composite score (reduction 72.1% vs 44.7%; P=0.0220) and on overall success rate (61.0% vs 42.2%; P=0.0020); superiority was more pronounced at 12 months, and all secondary measures (single VAS scores, Roles and Maudsley score, SF-36, patient and investigator global judgment) favoured shock-wave therapy (P<0.025, one-sided). No relevant side effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: This trial confirms that a mechanical intervention can beat placebo in this condition — it does not confirm stretching, and the topic file's 'shockwave-versus-stretching' framing could not be honoured because the verified Gerdesmeyer trial is shock-wave versus placebo. One-sided P-values and a composite percentage-reduction outcome also deserve a cooler read than the headline.

shelves.title: Total knee replacement versus non-surgical treatment for knee osteoarthritis (Skou / MEDIC)
shelves.question: In moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis eligible for replacement, does total knee replacement beat a supervised non-surgical programme on pain and function at one year — and at what serious-adverse-event price?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/rehabilitation · Combined Modality Therapy · Exercise Therapy · Foot Orthoses · Intention to Treat Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: A single randomised trial (Skou / MEDIC, 100 patients) found total knee replacement followed by 12 weeks of non-surgical care improved the KOOS4 score more than the same non-surgical programme alone at 12 months (improvement 32.5 vs 16.0 points; adjusted mean difference 15.8, 95% CI 10.0–21.5), but the replacement group had more serious adverse events (24 vs 6; P=0.005). Notably, 26% of the non-surgical group crossed over to replacement within the year while most did not — the authors' own framing is that replacement works better on average and that most patients assigned to non-surgical care still avoided it at one year. No second randomised trial of replacement versus conservative care was found (the currency sweep confirms the gap), so a single 100-patient unblindable trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Skou 2015 (MEDIC): total knee replacement improved KOOS4 by 15.8 points more than non-surgical care alone at 12 months, with more serious adverse events (24 vs 6)
cards.summary: Skou 2015 (MEDIC): total knee replacement improved KOOS4 by 15.8 points more than non-surgical care alone at 12 months, with more serious adverse events.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (replacement + 12 weeks of non-surgical treatment vs 12 weeks of non-surgical treatment alone; unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 100 patients with moderate-to-severe knee osteoarthritis eligible for unilateral total knee replacement; 95 completed the 12-month follow-up. The non-surgical programme (exercise, education, dietary advice, insoles, pain medication) was delivered by physiotherapists and dietitians in both arms. In the non-surgical group, 13 patients (26%) underwent replacement before 12 months; in the replacement group, 1 patient (2%) received only non-surgical treatment. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the total-knee-replacement group had greater improvement in the KOOS4 score (pain, symptoms, activities of daily living and quality of life; 0–100) than the non-surgical group (32.5 vs 16.0; adjusted mean difference 15.8, 95% CI 10.0 to 21.5). The total-knee-replacement group had a higher number of serious adverse events than the non-surgical group (24 vs 6; P=0.005).
cards.watchOut: One hundred patients, one country, unblinded patient-reported outcomes, and a quarter of the control arm crossing to surgery (which biases the intention-to-treat contrast toward the null, yet the difference survived). Serious adverse events are counted as events (24 vs 6), not patients, and the abstract does not itemise them.
cards.source: Skou ST et al. A Randomized, Controlled Trial of Total Knee Replacement. N Engl J Med. 2015;373(17):1597-1606. PMID: 26488691. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01410409, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.question: Does a progressive Nordic hamstring eccentric programme reduce overall, new and recurrent hamstring injuries in male footballers?

shelves.balance: LIKELY: Petersen's cluster-randomised trial (54 teams, 942 players) found overall hamstring injury rates of 3.8 vs 13.1 per 100 player seasons with the Nordic programme (adjusted rate ratio 0.293, 95% CI 0.150–0.572), with new injuries at 3.1 vs 8.1 (rate ratio 0.410) and recurrent injuries at 7.1 vs 45.8 per 100 player seasons (rate ratio 0.137); the number needed to treat was 13 players to prevent one injury. The Al Attar meta-analysis of programmes including the Nordic exercise (5 studies) independently pooled an injury risk ratio of 0.490 (0.291–0.827), described as up to a 51% relative reduction. Two concordant sources with large relative effects and absolute rates printed beside them earn LIKELY. ('Preventing' here is ordinary sports-injury language for a training programme, not a diabetes-onset claim.)

cards.headline: Petersen 2011: Nordic hamstring training cut overall injuries to 3.8 vs 13.1 per 100 player seasons (adjusted rate ratio 0.293); NNT 13
cards.summary: Petersen 2011: Nordic hamstring training cut injuries to 3.8 vs 13.1 per 100 player seasons (adjusted rate ratio 0.293); NNT 13.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised controlled trial (54 Danish professional and amateur teams; 10-week progressive programme then weekly in-season maintenance)
cards.people: 942 male soccer players (461 intervention, 481 control) followed for one full season; the control group followed its usual training programme. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Fifty-two acute hamstring injuries were registered in the control group compared with 15 in the intervention group. Overall injury rates were 3.8 vs 13.1 per 100 player seasons (adjusted rate ratio 0.293, 95% CI 0.150–0.572; P<0.001); new injury rates were 3.1 vs 8.1 (rate ratio 0.410, 0.180–0.933; P=0.034); recurrent injury rates were 7.1 vs 45.8 per 100 player seasons among previously injured players (rate ratio 0.137, 0.037–0.509; P=0.003) — relative figures with the absolute rates beside them. The number needed to treat to prevent one acute hamstring injury (new or recurrent) was 13 players (95% CI 9–23); for a new injury, 25; for a recurrent injury, 3.
cards.watchOut: Cluster design by team with injury registration by team staff who knew the allocation; amateur and professional Danish men's football is the tested setting, and adherence outside a trial is the usual reason real-world effects shrink. The recurrent-injury rate ratio rests on few events in previously injured players.
cards.source: Petersen J et al. Preventive effect of eccentric training on acute hamstring injuries in men's soccer: a cluster-randomized controlled trial. Am J Sports Med. 2011;39(11):2296-2303. PMID: 21825112. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Al Attar 2017: programmes including the Nordic hamstring exercise pooled an injury risk ratio of 0.490 across five studies
cards.summary: Al Attar 2017: programmes including the Nordic hamstring exercise pooled an injury risk ratio of 0.490 (a relative figure) across five studies.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled and interventional studies (searches to December 2015)
cards.people: Five studies meeting inclusion criteria, of programmes including the Nordic hamstring exercise in soccer players; the pooled outcome was total injuries per 1,000 hours of exposure. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age or total participant count.
cards.result: Programmes that included the Nordic hamstring exercise were associated with a hamstring injury risk ratio of 0.490 (95% CI 0.291–0.827; P=0.008) — a relative figure; the authors summarise this as reducing hamstring injury rates by up to 51% in the long term compared with teams using no injury-prevention measures. (The Petersen trial carded above is the largest study of this kind and is within this pooling's era; the meta-analysis is corroboration of the class, not an independent second trial of the same size.)
cards.watchOut: Five studies of varying designs (not all randomised) with a wide interval; a pooled relative risk of 0.490 sits just inside the developer's 0.5 solid-evidence line and should be quoted with its interval and with Petersen's absolute rates, not as false precision.
cards.source: Al Attar WSA et al. Effect of Injury Prevention Programs that Include the Nordic Hamstring Exercise on Hamstring Injury Rates in Soccer Players: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Sports Med. 2017;47(5):907-916. PMID: 27752982. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review; its PROSPERO registration (CRD42015019912) is stated in its abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: Nordic eccentric training roughly halves-to-thirds hamstring injury rates in male footballers — LIKELY
cards.summary: Nordic eccentric training roughly halves-to-thirds hamstring injury rates in male footballers — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Petersen 2011 (942 players, cluster-randomised) and Al Attar 2017 (5-study pooling).
cards.result: The trial gives absolute rates (3.8 vs 13.1 injuries per 100 player seasons; NNT 13 players for one season) and the pooling gives the same direction at class level (risk ratio 0.490). Few injury-prevention interventions have a randomised base this consistent. The claim is bounded to male football (soccer) players and to programmes actually performed progressively; concussion management is a different injury and lives on Shelf #461.
cards.watchOut: Compliance is the effect modifier nobody randomised: Petersen's programme was supervised within a trial structure, and later currency-sweep trials measure strength gains, not injuries — strength is a surrogate here.

shelves.title: Trigger finger: ultrasound-guided versus blind corticosteroid injection
shelves.question: Does ultrasound guidance improve the success of a first corticosteroid injection for trigger finger versus landmark-guided ('blind') injection, measured by symptom resolution and need for surgery?
shelves.mesh: Trigger Finger Disorder/diagnostic imaging,drug therapy · Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Ultrasonography, Interventional · Case-Control Studies · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Injections/methods · Methylprednisolone/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The two randomised comparisons of ultrasound-guided versus blind injection disagree, and both are small. Tunçez 2023 (66 patients) found faster triggering resolution, earlier return to work and better QDASH/VAS scores at weeks 1 and 4 with ultrasound guidance, but no significant difference at 12 or 24 weeks. Cecen 2015 (74 patients) found both groups improved significantly with no significant difference between them at 6 weeks or 6 months, and second injections were needed by 6 blind-group vs 3 ultrasound-group patients (all of those needing a second injection had diabetes). Durability data come from a different comparison: Hansen's trial of open surgery versus ultrasound-guided injection found success falling from 86% at 3 months to 49% at 12 months after injection, versus 99% and 99% after surgery. Whether guidance improves injection success at all is genuinely unsettled — MAYBE (weak evidence). A related ultrasound-versus-landmark randomised paper in this field was retracted (PMID 30947606); it is not carded and its existence is disclosed in the summary.

cards.headline: Tunçez 2023: ultrasound-guided injection resolved triggering faster and scored better at weeks 1–4, but QDASH and VAS did not differ at 12 or 24 weeks
cards.summary: Tunçez 2023: ultrasound-guided injection resolved triggering faster and scored better at weeks 1–4, but QDASH and VAS did not differ at 12 or 24 weeks.
cards.type: Prospective controlled study with randomised allocation (ultrasound-guided vs blinded corticosteroid injection around the A1 pulley)
cards.people: 66 patients with persistent symptoms of a single trigger finger (34 ultrasound-guided, 32 blinded); mean age 52.66 years (range 29–73); 18 were men and 48 women. Seventeen patients with diabetes mellitus received re-injections (11 blinded group, 6 ultrasound group; P<0.05).
cards.result: In the ultrasound-guided group, triggering resolved faster, return to work was earlier and the medication period was shorter (P<0.05), and QDASH and VAS scores were significantly lower at the 1st and 4th weeks (P<0.05); at the 12th and 24th weeks there was no significant difference between the groups (P>0.05). The authors conclude ultrasound guidance is more effective, with better early results and faster return to work.
cards.watchOut: Sixty-six patients, single centre, and the durable endpoints are null: the benefit shown is speed in the first month, not success. The abstract gives P-values without the score values, so the size of the early advantage cannot be verified from the record — one reason the shelf stamp is low.
cards.source: Tunçez M et al. Ultrasound guided versus blinded injection in trigger finger treatment: a prospective controlled study. J Orthop Surg Res. 2023;18(1):459. PMID: 37365603. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Cecen 2015: ultrasound-guided and blind injection improved equally — no significant difference at 6 weeks or 6 months
cards.summary: Cecen 2015: ultrasound-guided and blind injection improved equally — no significant difference at 6 weeks or 6 months.
cards.type: Prospective randomised case-control study (40 mg methylprednisolone acetate into the flexor tendon sheath; half ultrasound-guided, half blinded)
cards.people: 74 patients with persistent or increasing symptoms of a single trigger digit were enrolled; 4 were excluded for lack of follow-up, leaving 70 analysed. The abstract does not state mean age; there were significantly more female patients in the ultrasound group (32 versus 23%).
cards.result: After injection, all patients improved significantly in pain level and Quinnell grading at 6 weeks and 6 months compared with before injection. There were no significant differences between the ultrasound-guided and blinded groups on these outcomes. Nine patients (13%) needed a second injection (6 blinded, 3 ultrasound-guided); all nine had diabetes mellitus. No local complications were seen. The authors conclude ultrasound-guided injection may cost extra time and effort with no superior clinical benefit over the blinded technique.
cards.watchOut: Small and single-centre like its counterpart, with a sex imbalance between groups; 'no significant difference' in 70 patients cannot exclude a modest benefit — which is precisely why two small discordant trials land on MAYBE (weak evidence) rather than a null stamp.
cards.source: Cecen GS et al. Corticosteroid injection for trigger finger: blinded or ultrasound-guided injection? Arch Orthop Trauma Surg. 2015;135(1):125-131. PMID: 25381472. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Hansen 2017: open surgery beat ultrasound-guided injection by 12 months (success 99% vs 49%) — the durability context for any injection-technique claim
cards.summary: Hansen 2017: open surgery beat ultrasound-guided injection by 12 months (success 99% vs 49% ) — the durability context for any injection claim.
cards.type: Single-centre randomised controlled trial with 1-year follow-up (open A1 pulley release vs ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection)
cards.people: 165 patients with trigger finger (81 open surgery, 84 ultrasound-guided injection); groups were similar at baseline except lower alcohol consumption in the surgery group. Success meant normal finger movement, or normal movement with discomfort, at latest follow-up.
cards.result: At 3 months, 86% of the injection group and 99% of the surgery group were successfully treated; at 12 months, success was 49% after corticosteroid injection vs 99% after open surgery. Pain score at latest follow-up was significantly higher in the injection group. Complications after open surgery were more severe, including 3 superficial infections and 1 iatrogenic nerve lesion; after injection, 11 patients had a steroid flare and 2 had fat necrosis at the injection site.
cards.watchOut: This trial does not compare guidance techniques — it uses the ultrasound-guided injection as the injection arm. Its role on this shelf is to show that even the best-delivered injection loses half its successes by one year, which bounds what any guidance improvement could be worth.
cards.source: Hansen RL et al. Open Surgery Versus Ultrasound-Guided Corticosteroid Injection for Trigger Finger: A Randomized Controlled Trial With 1-Year Follow-up. J Hand Surg Am. 2017;42(5):359-366. PMID: 28341069. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: guidance may speed early relief; whether it improves success is unproven — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Guidance may speed early relief; whether it improves success is unproven — MAYBE (weak evidence). A neighbouring guided-vs-blind RCT is retracted and was NOT carded.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Tunçez 2023 (66 patients) and Cecen 2015 (70 analysed) on guidance; Hansen 2017 (165 patients) on injection durability versus surgery. The currency sweep's percutaneous-release versus steroid-injection trial (PMID 41029287) compares treatments, not guidance, and is fenced here.
cards.result: The guidance question has exactly two small randomised answers and they conflict: early-only benefit (Tunçez) versus no difference at any point (Cecen). The fair summary for practice is that blind injection by an experienced hand is not shown to be inferior, ultrasound guidance is not shown to be superior beyond the first month, and injection of any technique is a time-limited treatment — 49% success at 12 months against surgery's 99% in Hansen. Carpal tunnel injection and surgery live on Shelf #653, a different entrapment.
cards.watchOut: Every alias and label on this shelf is interrogative or MAYBE (weak evidence) by design: the evidence does not support a declarative claim in either direction.

shelves.title: Patellar tendinopathy: heavy slow resistance versus corticosteroid injection versus eccentric training (Kongsgaard)
shelves.question: In patellar tendinopathy, how do heavy slow resistance training, eccentric decline-squat training and corticosteroid injection compare at 12 weeks and beyond?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage · Patellar Ligament/diagnostic imaging,injuries,physiopathology · Resistance Training/methods · Tendinopathy/drug therapy,etiology,physiopathology · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised trial (Kongsgaard, 39 men) carries the whole three-way comparison. All three treatments improved VISA-p function scores and activity pain (VAS) at 12 weeks; by the half-year follow-up, the corticosteroid group's gains had deteriorated while the eccentric and heavy-slow-resistance groups maintained theirs, and treatment satisfaction was highest with heavy slow resistance. Tendon swelling fell in the corticosteroid (−13%) and heavy-slow-resistance (−12%) groups at 12 weeks, and vascularisation fell in both (−52% and −45%), while tendon mechanical properties were unchanged by any treatment. The pattern — injection wins early, training wins late — is clinically coherent and matches wider tendinopathy experience, but 39 patients in one trial is POSSIBLE, never LIKELY. The heavy-slow-resistance trial in Achilles tendinopathy (Beyer) is already carded on Shelf #460 and is fenced here, not re-carded.

cards.headline: Kongsgaard 2009: corticosteroid injection's gains deteriorated by 6 months while eccentric and heavy-slow-resistance gains held; satisfaction highest with heavy slow resistance
cards.summary: Kongsgaard 2009: corticosteroid injection's gains deteriorated by 6 months while eccentric and heavy-slow-resistance gains held; satisfaction was highest with heavy slow resistance.
cards.type: Randomised-controlled, single-blind trial, three arms (peritendinous corticosteroid injection vs eccentric decline-squat training vs heavy slow resistance training, 12 weeks, with half-year follow-up)
cards.people: 39 male patients with patellar tendinopathy, randomised across the three arms. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: All groups improved in VISA-p function and activity pain (VAS) from 0 to 12 weeks (P<0.05). Improvements were maintained at follow-up in the eccentric and heavy-slow-resistance groups but deteriorated in the corticosteroid group (P<0.05). Tendon swelling decreased in the corticosteroid (−13±9%) and heavy-slow-resistance (−12±13%) groups (P<0.05) and vascularisation decreased in both (−52±49% and −45±23%; P<0.01) at 12 weeks. Tendon mechanical properties were similar in healthy and injured tendons and unaffected by treatment; heavy slow resistance yielded elevated collagen network turnover. At half-year follow-up, treatment satisfaction differed between groups, with the heavy-slow-resistance group most satisfied. The abstract reports the clinical outcomes as within-group changes with P-values rather than between-group effect sizes.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-nine men, one centre, and headline clinical results reported as significance tests rather than magnitudes — the direction (injection fades, training persists) is clear, its size is not. No women were studied, and athletes in-season may not tolerate heavy loading the way this cohort did.
cards.source: Kongsgaard M et al. Corticosteroid injections, eccentric decline squat training and heavy slow resistance training in patellar tendinopathy. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2009;19(6):790-802. PMID: 19793213. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: for patellar tendinopathy, train for the long term; expect injection relief to fade — POSSIBLE on one small trial
cards.summary: For patellar tendinopathy, train for the long term; expect injection relief to fade — POSSIBLE on one small trial.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Kongsgaard 2009 (39 men, three arms). The currency sweep's blood-flow-restriction versus heavy-slow-resistance trial (PMID 41452311) is a two-arm loading comparison in the same condition and is fenced here, not carded.
cards.result: Within its limits, the trial supports the sequence clinicians already suspect: corticosteroid injection gives good short-term relief that deteriorates by six months, while both loading programmes (eccentric decline squats and heavy slow resistance) hold their gains, with heavy slow resistance most satisfying to patients and accompanied by structural improvement (less swelling and vascularisation). Tendinopathy loading programmes in general — including the Achilles heavy-slow-resistance trial — live on Shelf #460, whose trials are fenced to their home and not re-carded here; this shelf owns only the patellar three-way comparison.
cards.watchOut: Do not extend the injection warning beyond the peritendinous patellar context of this trial, and do not quote satisfaction rankings from 39 patients as if they were population estimates.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kongsgaard M et al. Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2009;19(6):790-802. PMID: 19793213. Registry ID as on the card above.

shelves.title: Lumbar spinal stenosis: surgery versus non-surgical treatment (Delitto; SPORT)
shelves.question: In symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis, does surgical decompression improve physical function more than a structured physical-therapy programme at two years — against the SPORT programme's as-treated signal?
shelves.mesh: Decompression, Surgical/adverse effects · Intention to Treat Analysis · Lumbar Vertebrae/surgery · Physical Therapy Modalities · Reoperation · Sex Factors · Spinal Stenosis/surgery,therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The randomised (intention-to-treat) evidence is close to null, and the pro-surgery signal lives in analyses that crossover contaminates. Delitto (169 surgical candidates) found mean physical-function improvement at 2 years of 22.4 points with surgery vs 19.2 with physical therapy (intention-to-treat difference 0.9 points, 95% CI −7.9 to 9.6), with 57% of the therapy group crossing to surgery — and causal-effects sensitivity analyses accounting for crossover still showed no significant difference. SPORT's randomised cohort (289 patients) found a significant intention-to-treat advantage for surgery only on bodily pain (mean difference 7.8, 1.5–14.1), not on physical function or the Oswestry Disability Index; its combined as-treated analysis (randomised plus observational cohorts, 654 patients) favoured surgery on all primary outcomes by 3 months, sustained at 2 years — but as-treated comparisons after 43–67% treatment switching are observational in effect. Honest stamp: POSSIBLE that surgery helps some patients more than therapy; the randomised comparisons do not prove a functional advantage.

cards.headline: Delitto 2015: surgery and physical therapy improved physical function equally at 2 years (22.4 vs 19.2 points; difference 0.9), despite 57% of the therapy group crossing to surgery
cards.summary: Delitto 2015: surgery and physical therapy improved physical function equally at 2 years (difference 0.9 points), despite 57% crossover to surgery.
cards.type: Multisite randomised controlled trial (surgical decompression vs a structured physical-therapy programme; masked outcome testers)
cards.people: 169 surgical candidates aged 50 years or older with symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis (87 surgery, 82 physical therapy), randomised between November 2000 and September 2007; 24-month follow-up was completed by 74 surgery and 73 therapy participants. The abstract does not state the sex mix numerically beyond stratification by sex.
cards.result: Mean improvement in the SF-36 physical function score at 2 years was 22.4 (95% CI 16.9 to 27.9) in the surgery group and 19.2 (13.6 to 24.8) in the physical-therapy group; intention-to-treat analysis showed no difference between groups (24-month difference 0.9, −7.9 to 9.6). Sensitivity analyses using causal-effects methods to account for the high crossover from therapy to surgery (57%) showed no significant differences in physical function. The authors note that without a control group, success cannot be attributed to either intervention, and call for shared decision-making with full disclosure of the surgical and non-surgical evidence.
cards.watchOut: Both groups improved by about 20 points — with no untreated control, regression to the mean and natural history are unmeasured contributors in both arms. The trial enrolled people who had already consented to be surgical candidates, the population most likely to cross over.
cards.source: Delitto A et al. Surgery versus nonsurgical treatment of lumbar spinal stenosis: a randomized trial. Ann Intern Med. 2015;162(7):465-473. PMID: 25844995. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00022776, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SPORT stenosis (Weinstein 2008): intention-to-treat favoured surgery only for bodily pain (difference 7.8), not function; the as-treated analysis favoured surgery on all outcomes
cards.summary: SPORT 2008: intention-to-treat favoured surgery only for bodily pain (difference 7.8), not function; as-treated analyses favoured surgery more.
cards.type: Randomised cohort within the Spine Patient Outcomes Research Trial, analysed alongside a parallel observational cohort (13 US spine clinics)
cards.people: 289 patients in the randomised cohort and 365 in the observational cohort — surgical candidates with at least 12 weeks of symptoms and imaging-confirmed spinal stenosis without spondylolisthesis. At 2 years, 67% of patients randomised to surgery had undergone it, while 43% of those randomised to non-surgical care had also undergone surgery. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis of the randomised cohort, surgery showed a significant treatment effect on the SF-36 bodily pain scale (mean difference in change from baseline 7.8, 95% CI 1.5 to 14.1) but no significant difference on physical function or the modified Oswestry Disability Index. In the combined as-treated analysis of both cohorts, adjusted for potential confounders, surgery showed significantly more improvement in all primary outcomes by 3 months, sustained at 2 years.
cards.watchOut: With 43–67% of participants not receiving their assigned treatment, the randomised contrast is heavily diluted and the as-treated contrast is confounded by whoever chose to switch — SPORT is best read as 'surgery as actually taken looks better; surgery as assigned barely separates from usual care'. Its non-surgical arm was usual care, not Delitto's structured programme.
cards.source: Weinstein JN et al. Surgical versus nonsurgical therapy for lumbar spinal stenosis. N Engl J Med. 2008;358(8):794-810. PMID: 18287602. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00000411, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Aspirin versus anticoagulants after hip or knee arthroplasty: CRISTAL and EPCAT II
shelves.question: After hip or knee arthroplasty, is aspirin enough? Does aspirin beat enoxaparin on symptomatic venous thromboembolism (CRISTAL), and is aspirin non-inferior to rivaroxaban for extended prophylaxis after an initial rivaroxaban run-in (EPCAT II)?
shelves.mesh: Anticoagulants/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip/adverse effects · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/adverse effects · Aspirin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Australia · Chemoprevention · Enoxaparin/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY on both halves, because the two large trials answer two different questions and both answers are firm. Used from the start as monotherapy, aspirin was worse: CRISTAL (9,711 patients, cluster-randomised across 31 Australian hospitals, stopped early) found symptomatic VTE within 90 days in 3.45% on aspirin versus 1.82% on enoxaparin — non-inferiority failed and enoxaparin was significantly superior (p=0.007). Used as the extended phase after 5 days of rivaroxaban for everyone, aspirin was non-inferior: EPCAT II (3,424 patients) found VTE in 0.64% on aspirin versus 0.70% on continued rivaroxaban (difference 0.06 percentage points; p<0.001 for non-inferiority), with major bleeding in 0.47% versus 0.29%. The discordance is the shelf: timing and run-in, not the molecule, explain it. Mortality was a secondary outcome in CRISTAL, reported among six secondary outcomes with none significantly better in the enoxaparin group; no mortality claim is made on this shelf.

cards.headline: CRISTAL (2022): symptomatic VTE within 90 days occurred in 3.45% on aspirin versus 1.82% on enoxaparin — non-inferiority failed, enoxaparin superior (p=0.007)
cards.summary: CRISTAL (2022): symptomatic VTE within 90 days in 3.45% on aspirin vs 1.82% on enoxaparin — non-inferiority failed, enoxaparin superior.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised, crossover, registry-nested trial (31 Australian hospitals; enrolment stopped early at an interim analysis)
cards.people: 9,711 patients aged 18 or older undergoing hip or knee arthroplasty (5,675 in the aspirin group, 4,036 in the enoxaparin group; median age 68 years; 56.8% female), treated with aspirin 100 mg/day or enoxaparin 40 mg/day for 35 days after hip arthroplasty and 14 days after knee arthroplasty; 95% completed the trial; enrolment stopped at 62% of the prespecified 15,562 after an interim analysis met the stopping rule.
cards.result: Symptomatic VTE within 90 days occurred in 256 patients overall (pulmonary embolism 79, above-knee deep-vein thrombosis 18, below-knee 174): 3.45% in the aspirin group versus 1.82% in the enoxaparin group (estimated difference 1.97%, 95% CI 0.54 to 3.41). This failed the 1% non-inferiority criterion and was significantly superior for enoxaparin (p=0.007). Of six secondary outcomes (including death and major bleeding), none was significantly better in the enoxaparin group.
cards.watchOut: Cluster randomisation by hospital with early stopping can exaggerate the difference, and most of the excess events were below-knee thromboses (174 of 256) — the outcome mix matters when weighing a 1.6-percentage-point absolute difference against injection burden and cost.

cards.headline: EPCAT II (Anderson 2018): after 5 days of rivaroxaban for all, extended aspirin was non-inferior to continued rivaroxaban (VTE 0.64% vs 0.70%); major bleeding 0.47% vs 0.29%
cards.summary: EPCAT II (2018): after 5 days of rivaroxaban for all, extended aspirin was non-inferior to continued rivaroxaban (VTE 0.64% vs 0.70% ).
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised, controlled non-inferiority trial (switch design after a universal run-in)
cards.people: 3,424 patients undergoing total hip (1,804) or total knee (1,620) arthroplasty, all given rivaroxaban 10 mg once daily until postoperative day 5, then randomly assigned to continue rivaroxaban (1,717) or switch to aspirin 81 mg daily (1,707) for a further 9 days after knee arthroplasty or 30 days after hip arthroplasty, with 90 days of follow-up. cards.result: Symptomatic venous thromboembolism occurred in 11 of 1,707 (0.64%) in the aspirin group and 12 of 1,717 (0.70%) in the rivaroxaban group (difference 0.06 percentage points, 95% CI −0.55 to 0.66; p<0.001 for non-inferiority, p=0.84 for superiority). cards.result: The two trials look contradictory only if the run-in is ignored. shelves.title: Burosumab, an anti-FGF23 antibody, in X-linked hypophosphataemia: adults and children
shelves.question: Does burosumab heal the skeleton in X-linked hypophosphataemia — against placebo on phosphate and fracture healing in adults, and against conventional phosphate-and-vitamin-D therapy on rickets severity in children?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Biomarkers/metabolism · Bone Remodeling/drug effects · Calcium/metabolism · Familial Hypophosphatemic Rickets/drug therapy,physiopathology · Fibroblast Growth Factor-23
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two phase 3 trials in the two age populations agree: in adults, burosumab normalised mean serum phosphate in 94.1% vs 7.6% on placebo and healed active fractures far more often (43.1% vs 7.7% fully healed at week 24) with improved stiffness; in children, it beat conventional therapy on rickets severity at week 40 (Radiographic Global Impression of Change +1.9 vs +0.8). Phosphate, rickets and fracture-healing outcomes; no mortality claim is made. (The paediatric record carries a published erratum, PMID 31305251; not a retraction.)

cards.headline: Insogna 2018 (adults): burosumab normalised phosphate in 94.1% vs 7.6% and healed fractures — 43.1% vs 7.7% fully healed at week 24
cards.summary: Insogna (2018, adults): burosumab normalised phosphate in 94.1% vs 7.6% and healed fractures — 43.1% vs 7.7% fully healed at week 24.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (24-week primary analysis)
cards.people: 134 symptomatic adults with X-linked hypophosphataemia and hypophosphataemia and pain, assigned 1:1 to burosumab 1 mg/kg (68) or placebo (66) subcutaneously every 4 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Across midpoints of dosing intervals, 94.1% of burosumab-treated participants attained mean serum phosphate above the lower limit of normal vs 7.6% on placebo (p<0.001). WOMAC stiffness improved significantly more with burosumab (least-squares mean difference -8.1±3.24; p=0.012); physical function (-4.9±2.48; p=0.048) and worst pain (-0.5±0.28; p=0.092) did not reach significance after Hochberg adjustment. At week 24, 43.1% (burosumab) vs 7.7% (placebo) of baseline active fractures were fully healed — the odds of healing were 16.8-fold greater with burosumab (p<0.001), a relative measure with the absolute rates beside it. Bone-turnover markers rose significantly; the safety profile was similar to placebo, with no treatment-related serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Week-24 analysis of a lifelong disease, in adults selected for pain and hypophosphataemia: enthesopathy, osteoarthritis and dental disease — much of the adult XLH burden — were not endpoints, and the registry ID is absent from this record (see source line).
cards.source: Insogna KL et al. A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Phase 3 Trial Evaluating the Efficacy of Burosumab, an Anti-FGF23 Antibody, in Adults With X-Linked Hypophosphatemia: Week 24 Primary Analysis. cards.headline: Imel 2019 (children): burosumab beat conventional therapy on rickets severity at week 40 (global impression +1.9 vs +0.8)
cards.summary: Imel (2019, children): burosumab beat conventional therapy on rickets severity at week 40 (global impression +1.9 vs +0.8 ).
cards.type: Randomised, active-controlled, open-label phase 3 trial (64 weeks; primary endpoint at week 40)
cards.people: 61 children aged 1-12 years with X-linked hypophosphataemia (Thacher rickets severity score at least 2.0, fasting phosphorus below 0.97 mmol/L, confirmed PHEX mutation or family pattern) who had received conventional therapy for at least 6-12 months; 29 assigned to burosumab 0.8 mg/kg every 2 weeks (16 girls, 13 boys) and 32 to continue conventional therapy (18 girls, 14 boys).
cards.result: At week 40, the Radiographic Global Impression of Change global score improved by a least-squares mean of +1.9 (SE 0.1) with burosumab vs +0.8 (0.1) with conventional therapy (difference 1.1; 95% CI 0.8 to 1.5; p<0.0001). Rickets severity, growth and biochemistries all improved significantly more with burosumab. Treatment-related adverse events were more frequent with burosumab (17 of 29 patients [59%] vs 7 of 32 [22%]); three serious adverse events occurred in each group, all judged unrelated and resolved.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a radiographic primary endpoint assessed as global impression: large and consistent effects, but families and investigators knew the treatment, and conventional therapy dosing was investigator-prescribed rather than protocol-fixed.
