shelves.title: Radiofrequency denervation for facet-joint and sacroiliac chronic low back pain (MINT)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic low back pain attributed to the facet joints or sacroiliac joint, does radiofrequency denervation added to a standardised exercise programme improve pain intensity at 3 months versus exercise alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Chronic Pain/therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Denervation/methods · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Low Back Pain/diagnosis,therapy · Lumbar Vertebrae · Middle Aged · Minimal Clinically Important Difference · Nerve Block · Radiofrequency Therapy · Sacroiliac Joint · Treatment Failure · Zygapophyseal Joint
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The three MINT trials (Juch 2017, 681 randomised patients with block-positive facet-joint, sacroiliac or combination pain) found that adding radiofrequency denervation to a standardised exercise programme produced mean pain-intensity differences at 3 months of −0.18 points (facet joint; 95% CI −0.76 to 0.40), −0.71 (sacroiliac; −1.35 to −0.06) and −0.99 (combination; −1.73 to −0.25) on a 0–10 scale — all far below the trials' prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 2 points. The sacroiliac and combination differences are statistically significant but clinically trivial by the trials' own threshold, and the topic file's summary — no clinically important pain benefit in any of the three trials — is what the record shows. Three parallel pragmatic trials earn LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for a clinically important effect.

cards.headline: MINT trials 2017: radiofrequency denervation added to exercise changed pain by −0.18 to −0.99 points — below the 2-point clinically important threshold in all three trials
cards.summary: MINT trials 2017: radiofrequency denervation added to exercise changed pain by −0.18 to −0.99 points — below the 2-point clinically important threshold in all three trials
cards.type: Three pragmatic multicentre, nonblinded randomised clinical trials in 16 multidisciplinary pain clinics (Netherlands)
cards.people: 681 participants with chronic low back pain and a positive diagnostic block at the facet joints (facet joint trial, 251), sacroiliac joints (228), or a combination of facet joints, sacroiliac joints or intervertebral disks (202), unresponsive to conservative care; mean age 52.2 years; 421 women (61.8%); mean baseline pain intensity 7.1. All received a 3-month standardised exercise programme (plus psychological support if needed); the intervention groups also received radiofrequency denervation (usually once, maximum 3 treatments). 599 (88%) completed 3-month and 521 (77%) 12-month follow-up.
cards.result: The mean difference in pain intensity (numeric rating scale 0–10) between radiofrequency denervation and control at 3 months was −0.18 (95% CI −0.76 to 0.40) in the facet joint trial, −0.71 (−1.35 to −0.06) in the sacroiliac joint trial, and −0.99 (−1.73 to −0.25) in the combination trial, against a prespecified minimal clinically important difference of 2 points or more.
cards.watchOut: Nonblinded pragmatic trials: patients knew whether they had received the procedure, which if anything biases toward the intervention; the null for clinical importance is therefore the conservative reading. The block-confirmed, sham-controlled sacroiliac question is a different shelf (#1458).
cards.source: Juch JNS et al. Effect of Radiofrequency Denervation on Pain Intensity Among Patients With Chronic Low Back Pain: The Mint Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28672319. shelves.title: Cooled radiofrequency ablation of the genicular nerves for knee osteoarthritis pain
shelves.question: In adults with chronic knee osteoarthritis pain refractory to conservative care, does cooled radiofrequency ablation of the genicular nerves relieve pain more than intra-articular corticosteroid injection over 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Aged · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Arthralgia/diagnosis,etiology,physiopathology,therapy · Betamethasone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Catheter Ablation/adverse effects · Combined Modality Therapy · Cross-Over Studies · Denervation/adverse effects,methods · Female · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Knee Joint/drug effects,innervation,surgery · Male · Methylprednisolone/administration & dosage,adverse effects,analogs & derivatives · Methylprednisolone Acetate · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/complications,diagnosis,physiopathology,therapy · Pain Measurement · Prospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Triamcinolone Acetonide/administration & dosage,adverse effects · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre randomised trial (Davis 2018, 151 subjects) found cooled radiofrequency ablation (CRFA) of the genicular nerves clearly superior to a single intra-articular corticosteroid injection at 6 months: ≥50% pain reduction in 74.1% versus 16.2% (P<0.0001), mean numeric rating scale reduction 4.9 versus 1.3 points (P<0.0001), mean Oxford Knee Score 35.7 versus 22.4 (P<0.0001), and improved Global Perceived Effect in 91.4% versus 23.9%, with no procedure-related serious adverse events. The comparator is the catch: a single steroid injection's effect wanes within weeks, so beating it at 6 months is a low bar, the trial was unblinded, and no sham-controlled trial is carded here — a single open trial against a short-lived comparator caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.summary: Davis 2018: cooled genicular RF beat intra-articular steroid at 6 months (≥50% pain relief 74.1% vs 16.2%)

The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 6 months, the CRFA group had more favourable outcomes on the numeric rating scale: pain reduction of 50% or greater in 74.1% versus 16.2% (P<0.0001) (25.9% and 83.8% of the cohorts respectively were nonresponders). Mean NRS reduction was 4.9 (SD 2.4) versus 1.3 (2.2) (P<0.0001); mean Oxford Knee Score was 35.7 (8.8) versus 22.4 (8.5) (P<0.0001); mean improved Global Perceived Effect was 91.4% versus 23.9% (P<0.0001); and change in nonopioid medication use favoured CRFA (P=0.02). There were no procedure-related serious adverse events and no demographic differences between groups.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, and the control is a single steroid injection assessed at 6 months — long after steroid benefit typically fades — so the margin overstates what CRFA would show against sham or an active durable comparator; industry-conducted genicular RF trials share this design pattern.

shelves.title: Dorsal root ganglion stimulation for complex regional pain syndrome (ACCURATE)
shelves.question: In adults with CRPS or causalgia of the lower limb, does dorsal root ganglion stimulation achieve higher treatment success (≥50% pain relief) than conventional tonic spinal cord stimulation at 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Causalgia/therapy · Complex Regional Pain Syndromes/therapy · Electric Stimulation Therapy/standards · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Ganglia, Spinal/physiology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised comparative trial (ACCURATE, Deer 2017, 152 subjects with lower-limb CRPS or causalgia) found the composite primary endpoint of treatment success — ≥50% pain relief with no stimulation-related neurological deficit — was achieved by significantly more patients with dorsal root ganglion (DRG) stimulation than with tonic spinal cord stimulation (SCS): 81.2% versus 55.7% at 3 months (P<0.001), with the trial reporting the advantage maintained through the 12-month assessments and no stimulation-related neurological deficits in either arm; device-related and serious adverse events did not differ between groups. A single industry pivotal trial, unblinded by the nature of the devices, caps at POSSIBLE. Benefit at 12 months is as the report's headline states; the abstract prints the exact percentages for the 3-month endpoint, and those are the figures carded.

cards.headline: ACCURATE 2017: DRG stimulation beat tonic SCS on treatment success (81.2% vs 55.7% at 3 months), sustained to 12 months
cards.summary: ACCURATE 2017: DRG stimulation beat tonic SCS on treatment success (81.2% vs 55.7% at 3 months), sustained to 12 months
cards.type: Pivotal, prospective, multicentre, randomised comparative effectiveness trial (permanent-implant population for the primary endpoint)
cards.people: 152 subjects diagnosed with complex regional pain syndrome or causalgia in the lower extremities, randomised to neurostimulation of the dorsal root ganglion or of the dorsal column (spinal cord stimulation); primary endpoint a composite of safety and efficacy at 3 months, with assessment through 12 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The predefined primary composite endpoint of treatment success — ≥50% decrease in visual analog scale score from preimplant baseline with no stimulation-related neurological deficit — was met by more DRG subjects: the percentage receiving ≥50% pain relief and treatment success was 81.2% in the DRG arm versus 55.7% in the SCS arm at 3 months (P<0.001), and the report states DRG superiority was maintained at 12 months. No subjects reported stimulation-related neurological deficits. Device-related and serious adverse events were not different between the two groups. DRG stimulation also showed greater improvements in quality of life and psychological disposition, less postural variation in paresthesia (P<0.001) and less extraneous stimulation in nonpainful areas (P=0.014).
cards.watchOut: An unblinded device comparison in which the experimental arm is also the sponsor's product, analysed in patients with a permanent implant; expectancy and programming attention differ between a novel targeted therapy and conventional tonic SCS, and exact 12-month success percentages are not printed in the abstract, so none are quoted beyond the 3-month figures.

shelves.title: Mirror therapy for phantom limb pain
shelves.question: In adults with unilateral lower-limb amputation and phantom limb pain, does mirror therapy reduce phantom pain versus covered-mirror or mental-visualisation control over 4 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Amputation, Surgical/adverse effects · Amputation Stumps · Audiovisual Aids · Biofeedback, Psychology · Cross-Over Studies · Humans · Imagery, Psychotherapy · Movement · Pain Measurement · Phantom Limb/therapy
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The only randomised anchor is a very small trial (Chan 2007) published as a brief report (N Engl J Med 2007, pages 2206–2207) whose PubMed record carries NO abstract — so no effect sizes, denominators or confidence intervals could be re-derived from the source record at build time, and none are printed on the card. As summarised in the secondary literature and the topic file, the trial randomised patients with lower-limb amputation and phantom pain to mirror therapy, covered-mirror or mental-visualisation conditions and reported pain relief in most mirror-treated patients and few or none in the control conditions over 4 weeks. A tiny, brief-format, unverifiable-from-the-record trial is the definition of weak evidence on this library's scale: MAYBE (weak evidence).

shelves.title: Mindfulness-based stress reduction for chronic low back pain
shelves.question: In adults with chronic low back pain, does mindfulness-based stress reduction improve back-related function and pain bothersomeness versus usual care (and how does it compare with CBT) at 26 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Low Back Pain/psychology,therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Mindfulness/methods · Sample Size · Stress, Physiological · Stress, Psychological/therapy · Treatment Outcome · Washington · Yoga · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large interviewer-blind trial (Cherkin 2016, 342 adults) found mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) and cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) both beat usual care on the coprimary outcomes at 26 weeks: clinically meaningful (≥30%) functional improvement in 60.5% (MBSR), 57.7% (CBT) and 44.1% (usual care) (relative risk for MBSR vs usual care 1.37 relative, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.77; MBSR vs CBT RR 0.95 relative — no difference), and clinically meaningful improvement in pain bothersomeness in 43.6%, 44.9% and 26.6% (RR 1.64 relative, 1.15 to 2.34, for MBSR vs usual care), with MBSR's findings persisting with little change at 52 weeks. A single trial, however well run, caps at POSSIBLE; the comparative message is that MBSR matched CBT, and both beat usual care.

cards.headline: Cherkin 2016: MBSR and CBT both beat usual care on function (60.5% and 57.7% vs 44.1% improved) and pain bothersomeness at 26 weeks
cards.summary: Cherkin 2016: MBSR and CBT both beat usual care on function (60.5% and 57.7% vs 44.1% improved) and pain bothersomeness at 26 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, interviewer-blind, three-arm clinical trial in an integrated health care system (Washington State)
cards.people: 342 adults aged 20–70 years with chronic low back pain (mean [SD] age 49.3 [12.3] years; 224 [65.7%] women; mean pain duration 7.3 years) randomised to MBSR (116), CBT (113) or usual care (113); both active treatments were 8 weekly 2-hour group sessions; 86.0% completed the study at 26 weeks and 84.8% at 52 weeks.
cards.result: At 26 weeks, the percentage with clinically meaningful (≥30%) improvement in functional limitations (modified Roland Disability Questionnaire) was 60.5% with MBSR, 57.7% with CBT and 44.1% with usual care (overall P=0.04; relative risk for MBSR vs usual care 1.37 — a relative measure — 95% CI 1.06 to 1.77; MBSR vs CBT RR 0.95 relative, 0.77 to 1.18; CBT vs usual care RR 1.31 relative, 1.01 to 1.69). For pain bothersomeness, the percentages were 43.6% (MBSR), 44.9% (CBT) and 26.6% (usual care) (overall P=0.01; RR for MBSR vs usual care 1.64 relative, 1.15 to 2.34; MBSR vs CBT 1.03 relative; CBT vs usual care 1.69 relative). Findings for MBSR persisted with little change at 52 weeks for both primary outcomes. Only 53.7% of the active-treatment participants attended 6 or more of the 8 sessions.
cards.watchOut: Participants could not be blinded to a meditation-versus-usual-care allocation and outcomes are self-reported; usual care is a soft comparator, and the MBSR–CBT equivalence (RR 0.95–1.03 relative) is as much the finding as the win over usual care.

shelves.title: Low-dose naltrexone for fibromyalgia
shelves.question: In women with fibromyalgia, does low-dose naltrexone (4.5 mg/day) reduce daily pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cross-Over Studies · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fibromyalgia/drug therapy · Humans · Middle Aged · Naltrexone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Narcotic Antagonists/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Pain/drug therapy · Pain Measurement/drug effects · Placebos · Self Report · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial (Younger 2013, 31 women) found low-dose naltrexone (4.5 mg/day) reduced baseline pain by 28.8% versus 18.0% on placebo (P=0.016), with a response rate (significant pain reduction plus improvement in fatigue or sleep) of 32% versus 11% (P=0.05), improved general satisfaction with life (P=0.045) and mood (P=0.039) but not fatigue or sleep, and tolerability equal to placebo with no serious side effects. A single 31-patient crossover trial caps at POSSIBLE. The topic file's figures (≈29% vs ≈18%) match the record.

cards.headline: Younger 2013: low-dose naltrexone reduced fibromyalgia pain more than placebo (28.8% vs 18.0%) in a 31-woman crossover trial
cards.summary: Younger 2013: low-dose naltrexone reduced fibromyalgia pain more than placebo (28.8% vs 18.0%) in a 31-woman crossover trial
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, counterbalanced crossover trial with intensive daily pain measurement; a replication and extension of the group's earlier pilot
cards.people: 31 women with fibromyalgia receiving oral naltrexone 4.5 mg daily during the active phase, with daily self-reported pain measured longitudinally across drug and placebo phases. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: When contrasting condition endpoints, low-dose naltrexone produced a significantly greater reduction of baseline pain than placebo (28.8% reduction versus 18.0% reduction; P=0.016). Low-dose naltrexone was also associated with improved general satisfaction with life (P=0.045) and improved mood (P=0.039), but not improved fatigue or sleep. Thirty-two percent of participants met the response criteria during naltrexone therapy versus 11% during placebo (P=0.05). Low-dose naltrexone was rated equally tolerable as placebo, and no serious side effects were reported.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-one participants in a crossover design from a single research group that also ran the predecessor pilot — enthusiasm and expectancy effects are plausible, carryover cannot be fully excluded, and independent replication at scale is what this claim still lacks.

shelves.title: Duloxetine for chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy
shelves.question: In adults with painful chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy, does duloxetine 60 mg/day reduce average pain versus placebo over 5 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Antineoplastic Agents/adverse effects · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Duloxetine Hydrochloride · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neoplasms/drug therapy · Neuralgia/drug therapy · Peripheral Nervous System Diseases/chemically induced,complications,drug therapy · Quality of Life · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Thiophenes/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large double-blind crossover trial (CALGB/Alliance 170601, Smith 2013, 231 patients) found duloxetine beat placebo in the initial 5-week period: mean decrease in average pain of 1.06 points (95% CI 0.72 to 1.40) versus 0.34 (0.01 to 0.66) on a 0–10 scale (P=0.003; effect size 0.513), a mean between-treatment difference of 0.73 points (0.26 to 1.20), with 59% of patients initially on duloxetine versus 38% on placebo reporting a decrease in pain of any amount. cards.headline: CALGB 170601 (Smith 2013): duloxetine reduced CIPN pain by 0.73 points more than placebo over 5 weeks; 59% vs 38% reported any pain decrease
cards.summary: CALGB 170601 (Smith 2013): duloxetine reduced CIPN pain by 0.73 points more than placebo over 5 weeks; 59% vs 38% reported any pain decrease
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial at 8 NCI-funded cooperative research networks
cards.people: 231 patients aged 25 years or older with grade 1 or higher sensory neuropathy and average chemotherapy-induced pain of at least 4 of 10 after paclitaxel, another taxane, or oxaliplatin, randomised to duloxetine-then-placebo or placebo-then-duloxetine; the initial treatment was 30 mg daily for 1 week then 60 mg daily (2 capsules) for 4 more weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Individuals receiving duloxetine as their initial 5-week treatment reported a mean decrease in average pain (Brief Pain Inventory-Short Form) of 1.06 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.40) versus 0.34 (0.01 to 0.66) among those who received placebo (P=0.003; effect size 0.513). The observed mean difference in average pain score between duloxetine and placebo was 0.73 (95% CI 0.26 to 1.20). Fifty-nine percent of those initially receiving duloxetine versus 38% of those initially receiving placebo reported a decreased pain of any amount.

shelves.title: Lidocaine 5% medicated plaster for postherpetic neuralgia
shelves.question: In adults with postherpetic neuralgia, does the lidocaine 5% topical patch relieve pain versus a vehicle patch?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anesthetics, Local/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Herpes Zoster/complications · Humans · Lidocaine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia/drug therapy,virology · Pain Measurement
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small, old double-blind vehicle-controlled trials agree. In the enriched-enrolment trial (Galer 1999, 32 subjects, all prior regular lidocaine-patch responders continuing treatment for at least a month), the median time to exit for loss of pain relief was greater than 14 days on the lidocaine patch versus 3.8 days on vehicle (P<0.001), and 78.1% of subjects preferred the lidocaine phase versus 9.4% the vehicle phase. In Rowbotham 1996 (35 subjects completing a four-session random-order double-blind study), lidocaine patches significantly reduced pain intensity at all time points from 30 minutes to 12 hours versus no-treatment observation, and from 4 to 12 hours versus vehicle patches, with maximal blood lidocaine of 0.1 micrograms/mL and no systemic side effects. The enrichment design of the larger claim — testing withdrawal in known responders — inflates the apparent effect for treatment-naive patients, and the trials' size and age cap the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Galer 1999: in prior patch responders, time to exit was >14 days on lidocaine vs 3.8 days on vehicle (enriched-enrolment design)
cards.summary: Galer 1999: in prior patch responders, time to exit was >14 days on lidocaine vs 3.8 days on vehicle (enriched-enrolment design)
cards.type: Randomised, two-period, vehicle-controlled crossover trial using an enriched-enrolment design
cards.people: 32 subjects with postherpetic neuralgia who had all been successfully treated with topical lidocaine patches on a regular basis for at least 1 month before enrolment, randomised to lidocaine-patch and vehicle-patch periods; the primary efficacy variable was time to exit (allowed if the pain relief score fell by 2 or more categories on a 6-item scale on any 2 consecutive days). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The median time to exit with the lidocaine patch phase was greater than 14 days, whereas the vehicle patch exit time was 3.8 days (P<0.001). At study completion, 25 of 32 subjects (78.1%) preferred the lidocaine patch phase versus 3 of 32 (9.4%) the placebo phase (P<0.001). No statistical difference was noted between active and placebo treatments with regard to side effects.
cards.watchOut: Enriched enrolment is the headline caveat: every participant was a known responder before randomisation, so this trial measures loss of effect on withdrawal in responders — it cannot estimate the response rate in a treatment-naive PHN patient, and quoting it as one would overstate the evidence.
cards.source: Galer BS et al. Topical lidocaine patch relieves postherpetic neuralgia more effectively than a vehicle topical patch: results of an enriched enrollment study. Pain. 1999. PMID: 10342414. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Rowbotham 1996: lidocaine patches reduced PHN pain versus vehicle and versus no treatment over 12-hour sessions
cards.summary: Rowbotham 1996: lidocaine patches reduced PHN pain versus vehicle and versus no treatment over 12-hour sessions
cards.people: 35 subjects with established postherpetic neuralgia affecting the torso or extremities, all with allodynia on examination, completing four 12-hour sessions (lidocaine patches in two sessions, vehicle in one, no-treatment observation in one); up to 3 patches covering a maximum of 420 cm2 applied to the area of greatest pain.
cards.result: Lidocaine-containing patches significantly reduced pain intensity at all time points from 30 minutes to 12 hours compared with no-treatment observation, and at all time points from 4 to 12 hours compared with vehicle patches; lidocaine patches were also superior on averaged category pain relief scores. The highest blood lidocaine level measured was 0.1 micrograms/mL, indicating minimal systemic absorption, and patch application was without systemic side effect and well tolerated on allodynic skin for 12 hours. No numerical pain scores are printed in the abstract, so none are quoted here.
cards.watchOut: Session-based 12-hour testing in 35 subjects shows the patch does something pharmacological beyond its covering effect; it does not measure weeks of home use, and the absence of printed effect sizes in the record keeps this card qualitative.

shelves.title: Radiofrequency denervation of the sacroiliac joint (lateral branch cooled RF)
shelves.question: In adults with sacroiliac-joint pain confirmed by diagnostic blocks, does cooled radiofrequency lateral-branch denervation achieve ≥50% pain relief at 3 months versus placebo denervation?
shelves.mesh: Anesthetics, Local · Catheter Ablation/methods · Cross-Over Studies · Denervation/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Low Back Pain/classification,therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Sacroiliac Joint/innervation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small sham-controlled trials in block-confirmed sacroiliac-joint pain agree. In Cohen 2008 (28 patients), ≥50% pain relief with significant functional improvement occurred in 79% (11 of 14) of the cooled-RF group versus 14% (2 of 14) on placebo denervation at 1 month, 64% versus 0% at 3 months, and 57% at 6 months in the RF group — though only 2 patients (14%) retained relief at 1 year. In Patel 2012 (51 subjects randomised 2:1), treatment success at 3 months was 47% with lateral branch neurotomy versus 12% with sham, with significant improvements in pain, physical function, disability and quality of life favouring neurotomy. Two small trials (79 patients combined) with short durability cap at POSSIBLE. This is the stringently block-confirmed, sham-controlled question — distinct from the pragmatic MINT add-on question on Shelf #1450, whose null does not govern this shelf.

cards.headline: Cohen 2008: cooled lateral-branch RF gave ≥50% relief in 79% vs 14% at 1 month and 64% vs 0% at 3 months (n=28)
cards.summary: Cohen 2008: cooled lateral-branch RF gave ≥50% relief in 79% vs 14% at 1 month and 64% vs 0% at 3 months (n=28)
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial with crossover of placebo nonresponders to conventional RF
cards.people: 28 patients with injection-diagnosed sacroiliac joint pain: 14 received L4–L5 primary dorsal rami and S1–S3 lateral branch radiofrequency denervation using cooling-probe technology after a local anaesthetic block, and 14 received the block followed by placebo denervation. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: One, 3, and 6 months after the procedure, 11 (79%), 9 (64%) and 8 (57%) radiofrequency-treated patients experienced pain relief of 50% or greater and significant functional improvement. In contrast, only 2 patients (14%) in the placebo group experienced significant improvement at their 1-month follow-up, and none experienced benefit 3 months after the procedure. In the crossover group (n=11), 7 (64%), 6 (55%) and 4 (36%) experienced improvement 1, 3 and 6 months after conventional RF. One year after treatment, only 2 patients (14%) in the treatment group continued to demonstrate persistent pain relief.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-eight patients, and the 1-year figure is the sobering one: whatever the short-term win, durable relief at a year was uncommon (2 of 14) — the shelf sells a 3–6 month effect, not a cure.
cards.source: Cohen SP et al. Randomized placebo-controlled study evaluating lateral branch radiofrequency denervation for sacroiliac joint pain. Anesthesiology. 2008. PMID: 18648237. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00373724, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Patel 2012: lateral branch neurotomy beat sham on treatment success at 3 months (47% vs 12%)
cards.summary: Patel 2012: lateral branch neurotomy beat sham on treatment success at 3 months (47% vs 12%)
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled (sham) trial; subjects and coordinators blinded until 3 months, sham subjects then allowed to cross over
cards.people: 51 subjects aged 18–88 years with chronic (>6 months) axial back pain and a positive response to dual lateral branch blocks, randomised 2:1 to cooled-radiofrequency lateral branch neurotomy (S1–S3 lateral branches and the L5 dorsal ramus) or an identical sham procedure without radiofrequency energy; outcomes included pain (numeric rating scale), physical function, disability (Oswestry) and quality of life.
cards.result: Statistically significant changes in pain, physical function, disability and quality of life were found at 3-month follow-up, all favouring lateral branch neurotomy. At 3 months, 47% of treated patients and 12% of sham subjects achieved treatment success. At 6 and 9 months respectively, 38% and 59% of treated subjects achieved treatment success (post-crossover period for the sham group). The authors report the duration and magnitude of relief was consistent with previous studies.
cards.watchOut: Success rates after month 3 mix randomised and crossover experience (sham patients crossed to treatment), so the 3-month 47% vs 12% contrast is the clean randomised figure; dual-block confirmation also selects a narrower population than MINT's single-block entry.
cards.source: Patel N et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled study to assess the efficacy of lateral branch neurotomy for chronic sacroiliac joint pain. Pain medicine (Malden, Mass.). 2012. shelves.title: Balloon kyphoplasty versus non-surgical care for vertebral compression fracture
shelves.question: In adults with painful osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures, does balloon kyphoplasty improve quality of life (SF-36 physical component) versus non-surgical care at 1 and 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Back Pain/etiology,prevention & control · Bone Cements/therapeutic use · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Fractures, Compression/complications,therapy · Hematoma/etiology · Humans · Male · Minimally Invasive Surgical Procedures/methods · Quality of Life · Radiography · Plastic Surgery Procedures/adverse effects,methods · Spinal Fractures/complications,diagnostic imaging,therapy · Urinary Tract Infections/etiology · Vertebroplasty/adverse effects,methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large open-label trial (FREE, Wardlaw 2009, 300 patients with one to three acute vertebral fractures) found balloon kyphoplasty improved the SF-36 physical component summary score at 1 month by 7.2 points from baseline versus 2.0 points with non-surgical care (between-group difference 5.2 points, 95% CI 2.9 to 7.4; P<0.0001), with follow-up and further efficacy and safety assessments to 12 months and no difference in the overall frequency of adverse events; two serious adverse events (haematoma and urinary tract infection) were related to kyphoplasty. The comparison is against non-surgical care in an unblinded trial with a patient-reported primary outcome — expectation effects are unconstrained — and the sham-controlled vertebroplasty question is a different shelf (#155). A single open trial caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: FREE 2009: kyphoplasty improved SF-36 physical component by 5.2 points more than non-surgical care at 1 month
cards.summary: FREE 2009: kyphoplasty improved SF-36 physical component by 5.2 points more than non-surgical care at 1 month
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial at 21 sites in eight countries (open treatment), intention-to-treat analysis
cards.people: 300 adults with one to three acute vertebral fractures randomised to balloon kyphoplasty (149) or non-surgical care (151); primary outcome the difference in change from baseline to 1 month in the SF-36 physical component summary (PCS) score (scale 0–100); 138 kyphoplasty and 128 control participants completed 1-month follow-up, with all 300 included via repeated-measures modelling. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean SF-36 PCS score improved by 7.2 points (95% CI 5.7 to 8.8), from 26.0 at baseline to 33.4 at 1 month, in the kyphoplasty group, and by 2.0 points (0.4 to 3.6), from 25.5 to 27.4, in the non-surgical group (difference between groups 5.2 points, 2.9 to 7.4; P<0.0001). Quality of life and other efficacy measurements and safety were assessed up to 12 months. The frequency of adverse events did not differ between groups; two serious adverse events were related to kyphoplasty (haematoma and urinary tract infection), and other serious adverse events (such as myocardial infarction and pulmonary embolism) did not occur perioperatively and were not related to the procedure.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded with a self-reported quality-of-life endpoint: patients who received an invasive procedure knew it, and the natural history of acute fracture pain is improvement, which the 2.0-point control gain shows. The abstract as fetched does not print the 12-month between-group difference, so the durability claim rests on the 1-month primary result and is not quantified here.
cards.source: Wardlaw D et al. Efficacy and safety of balloon kyphoplasty compared with non-surgical care for vertebral compression fracture (FREE): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19246088. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00211211, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Constraint-induced movement therapy after stroke (EXCITE)
shelves.question: In adults 3–9 months after stroke with preserved wrist/finger extension, does constraint-induced movement therapy improve upper-limb function versus usual care, sustained to 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Activity · Single-Blind Method · Stroke Rehabilitation · Upper Extremity/physiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large multisite single-blind randomised trial (EXCITE, Wolf 2006, 222 patients 3–9 months after a first stroke) found a 2-week programme of constraint-induced movement therapy (CIMT) produced greater improvements than usual and customary care from baseline to 12 months on both primaries: Wolf Motor Function Test Performance Time fell 52% in the CIMT group versus 26% in controls (between-group difference 34%, 95% CI 12% to 51%; P<0.001), Motor Activity Log Amount of Use rose from 1.21 to 2.13 versus 1.15 to 1.65 (difference 0.43, 0.05 to 0.80; P<0.001) and Quality of Movement from 1.26 to 2.23 versus 1.18 to 1.66 (difference 0.48, 0.13 to 0.84; P<0.001); self-perceived hand function difficulty (Stroke Impact Scale hand domain) also improved more (−19.5 vs −10.1; P=0.05). A single large, durable, assessor-blinded result of this size, consistent with the smaller CIMT trial literature fenced in the synthesis, earns LIKELY — in the narrow population with preserved wrist and finger extension.

cards.headline: EXCITE 2006: CIMT beat usual care on motor performance and real-world arm use, sustained to 12 months
cards.summary: EXCITE 2006: CIMT beat usual care on motor performance and real-world arm use, sustained to 12 months
cards.type: Prospective, single-blind, randomised, multisite clinical trial at 7 US academic institutions
cards.people: 222 individuals with predominantly ischaemic first stroke within the previous 3 to 9 months, assigned to CIMT (106; restraining mitt on the less-affected hand plus repetitive task practice and behavioural shaping with the paretic hand for 2 weeks) or usual and customary care (116; ranging from no further treatment to pharmacologic or physiotherapeutic interventions); stratified by sex, prestroke dominant side, side of stroke and level of paretic arm function.
cards.result: From baseline to 12 months, the CIMT group showed greater improvements than the control group in Wolf Motor Function Test Performance Time (decrease in mean time from 19.3 seconds to 9.3 seconds [52% reduction] versus from 24.0 to 17.7 seconds [26% reduction]; between-group difference 34% [95% CI 12% to 51%]; P<0.001), in Motor Activity Log Amount of Use (increase from 1.21 to 2.13 versus 1.15 to 1.65 on a 0–5 scale; difference 0.43 [0.05 to 0.80]; P<0.001) and in MAL Quality of Movement (1.26 to 2.23 versus 1.18 to 1.66; difference 0.48 [0.13 to 0.84]; P<0.001). The CIMT group also achieved a greater decrease in self-perceived hand function difficulty (Stroke Impact Scale hand domain −19.5 versus −10.1; difference 9.42 [0.27 to 18.57]; P=0.05). The authors conclude the improvements were statistically significant and clinically relevant and persisted for at least 1 year.
cards.watchOut: Eligibility required residual wrist/finger movement, so EXCITE's patients are the better-prognosis minority of stroke survivors; usual care was heterogeneous and sometimes nil, which flatters the comparison against a defined modern rehabilitation programme.
cards.source: Wolf SL et al. Effect of constraint-induced movement therapy on upper extremity function 3 to 9 months after stroke: the EXCITE randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2006. PMID: 17077374. shelves.title: Locomotor training after stroke (LEAPS)
shelves.question: In adults with residual gait impairment after stroke, does body-weight-supported treadmill locomotor training improve the proportion achieving functional walking recovery at 1 year versus a home exercise programme?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Body Weight · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Therapy/adverse effects,instrumentation · Female · Home Care Services · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Physical Therapy Modalities · Stroke/physiopathology · Stroke Rehabilitation · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One large definitive trial (LEAPS, Duncan 2011, 408 participants) found body-weight-supported treadmill locomotor training was NOT superior to a structured home exercise programme managed by a physical therapist: at 1 year, 52.0% of all participants had improved functional walking ability, with no significant difference for early locomotor training versus home exercise (adjusted odds ratio 0.83 relative, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.39) or for late locomotor training versus home exercise (adjusted OR 1.19 relative, 0.72 to 1.99), and all groups had similar improvements in walking speed. The confidence intervals are wide enough that a modest benefit is not excluded, which keeps the null at POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY; but nothing in the trial supports the treadmill programme over the cheaper home programme, which is the decision-relevant reading.

cards.headline: LEAPS 2011: locomotor training was not superior to home exercise for walking recovery at 1 year (52% improved in all groups combined)
cards.summary: LEAPS 2011: locomotor training was not superior to home exercise for walking recovery at 1 year (52% improved in all groups combined)
cards.type: Randomised trial stratified by severity of walking impairment (moderate: 0.4 to <0.8 m/s; severe: <0.4 m/s)
cards.people: 408 participants who had had a stroke 2 months earlier, assigned to treadmill training with body-weight support at 2 months (early), the same training at 6 months (late), or a home exercise programme managed by a physical therapist at 2 months; each intervention comprised 36 sessions of 90 minutes over 12–16 weeks; primary outcome the proportion with improved functional walking ability 1 year after stroke.
cards.result: At 1 year, 52.0% of all participants had increased functional walking ability. No significant differences in improvement were found between early locomotor training and home exercise (adjusted odds ratio for the primary outcome 0.83 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.50 to 1.39) or between late locomotor training and home exercise (adjusted OR 1.19 relative, 0.72 to 1.99). All groups had similar improvements in walking speed.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was an active, therapist-managed home programme, not no treatment — LEAPS shows the expensive treadmill package adds nothing over good home exercise, not that rehabilitation is useless; the intervals (up to OR 1.39 relative) leave a modest treadmill benefit formally open.
cards.source: Duncan PW et al. Body-weight-supported treadmill rehabilitation after stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2011. PMID: 21612471. shelves.title: Very early mobilisation after stroke (AVERT)
shelves.question: In adults with acute stroke, does very early, frequent, short mobilisation begun within 24 hours improve the odds of a favourable outcome (mRS 0–2) at 3 months versus usual stroke-unit care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Early Ambulation/adverse effects,methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recovery of Function · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method · Stroke/physiopathology · Stroke Rehabilitation · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Walking
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference, harm-leaning) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the favourable-outcome scale includes death). One very large trial (AVERT, 2,104 randomised at 56 stroke units in five countries) found very early, frequent, higher-dose mobilisation begun within 24 hours REDUCED the odds of a favourable outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0–2) at 3 months: 46% (480 patients) versus 50% (525) with usual care (adjusted odds ratio 0.73 relative, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90; P=0.004). Deaths were numerically higher with very early mobilisation (88 [8%] vs 72 [7%]; OR 1.34 relative, 0.93 to 1.93; P=0.113) and non-fatal serious adverse events were similar (19% vs 20%), with no reduction in immobility-related complications. A single very large trial whose primary result is a significant harm-direction finding earns LIKELY for the proposition that this protocol does not help and may hurt; the mortality difference itself is not significant and no mortality claim is made.

cards.headline: AVERT 2015: very early mobilisation reduced favourable outcomes at 3 months (46% vs 50%; adjusted OR 0.73 relative)
cards.summary: AVERT 2015: very early mobilisation reduced favourable outcomes at 3 months (46% vs 50%; adjusted OR 0.73 relative)
cards.type: Parallel-group, single-blind, randomised controlled trial at 56 acute stroke units in five countries
cards.people: 2,104 patients (aged ≥18 years) with ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke, first or recurrent, meeting physiological criteria, randomly assigned to very early mobilisation plus usual stroke-unit care (1,054) or usual care alone (1,050); 2,083 (99%) included in the 3-month follow-up assessment; 92% of the intervention group versus 59% of controls were mobilised within 24 hours. Primary outcome: favourable outcome (mRS 0–2) at 3 months, intention-to-treat.
cards.result: Fewer patients in the very early mobilisation group had a favourable outcome than in the usual care group (480 [46%] vs 525 [50%]; adjusted odds ratio 0.73 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.59 to 0.90; P=0.004). Eighty-eight (8%) patients died in the very early mobilisation group versus 72 (7%) in the usual care group (OR 1.34 relative, 0.93 to 1.93; P=0.113). Non-fatal serious adverse events occurred in 201 (19%) versus 208 (20%), with no reduction in immobility-related complications with very early mobilisation. The authors conclude the higher-dose, very early mobilisation protocol was associated with a reduction in the odds of a favourable outcome, and that the findings should refine guidelines recommending early mobilisation.
cards.watchOut: AVERT tested a specific protocol — frequent, higher-dose mobilisation within 24 hours — not "any early mobilisation"; usual-care patients were also mobilised early by historical standards (59% within 24 hours), so the shelf must not be quoted as "mobilisation after stroke is harmful" without the protocol and dose attached.
cards.source: AVERT Trial Collaboration Group. Efficacy and safety of very early mobilisation within 24 h of stroke onset (AVERT): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2015. shelves.title: Cognitive functional therapy for chronic disabling low back pain (RESTORE)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic, disabling low back pain, does cognitive functional therapy (with or without movement-sensor biofeedback) reduce activity limitation (Roland Morris) versus usual care at 13 weeks and 52 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Adolescent · Low Back Pain/therapy · Australia · Biofeedback, Psychology · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Cognition · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials at two scales agree. In RESTORE (Kent 2023, 492 participants), cognitive functional therapy (CFT) reduced activity limitation (Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire) versus usual care at 13 weeks by −4.6 points whether delivered alone (95% CI −5.9 to −3.4) or with movement-sensor biofeedback (−4.6; −5.8 to −3.3), with similar effect sizes at 52 weeks, better quality-adjusted life-years, and far lower societal costs (−AU$5,276 and −AU$8,211). In the earlier classification-based CFT trial (Vibe Fersum 2013, 121 patients), CFT improved the Oswestry Disability Index by 13.7 points versus 5.5 points with manual therapy and exercise, and pain intensity by 3.2 versus 1.5 points (both P<0.001), at 12-month follow-up. Two concordant randomised trials earn LIKELY.

cards.headline: RESTORE 2023: CFT beat usual care by 4.6 Roland-Morris points at 13 weeks, sustained at 52 weeks, at lower societal cost
cards.summary: RESTORE 2023: CFT beat usual care by 4.6 Roland-Morris points at 13 weeks, sustained at 52 weeks, at lower societal cost
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, three-arm, parallel-group, phase 3 trial in 20 primary care physiotherapy clinics (Australia)
cards.people: 492 adults (≥18 years) with low back pain lasting more than 3 months and at least moderate pain-related physical activity limitation, randomly assigned to usual care (165), CFT only (164) or CFT plus biofeedback (163); interventions were up to seven sessions over 12 weeks plus a booster at 26 weeks; primary clinical outcome activity limitation (24-point Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire) at 13 weeks. Physiotherapists and patients were not masked.
cards.result: Both interventions were more effective than usual care for activity limitation at 13 weeks (CFT only mean difference −4.6 [95% CI −5.9 to −3.4]; CFT plus biofeedback −4.6 [−5.8 to −3.3]). Effect sizes were similar at 52 weeks. Both interventions were also more effective than usual care for quality-adjusted life-years, and much less costly in societal terms (direct and indirect costs and productivity losses: −AU$5,276 [−10,529 to −24] and −AU$8,211 [−12,923 to −3,500]).
cards.watchOut: Usual care is a soft comparator and participants were unmasked with a self-reported primary outcome; the biofeedback add-on contributed nothing measurable (−4.6 in both CFT arms), so the shelf credits CFT, not the sensor package.
cards.source: Kent P et al. Cognitive functional therapy with or without movement sensor biofeedback versus usual care for chronic, disabling low back pain (RESTORE): a randomised, controlled, three-arm, parallel group, phase 3, clinical trial. cards.summary: Vibe Fersum 2013: classification-based CFT beat manual therapy plus exercise on disability (13.7 vs 5.5 Oswestry points) at 12 months
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (classification-based cognitive functional therapy vs traditional manual therapy and exercise)

cards.result: The CFT group displayed significantly superior outcomes to the manual therapy and exercise group, both statistically (P<0.001) and, in the authors' assessment, clinically. shelves.title: Internet-delivered exercise and pain-coping training for chronic knee pain
shelves.question: In adults with chronic knee pain, does an internet-delivered programme combining exercise, automated pain-coping skills training and physiotherapist Skype sessions improve pain and function versus internet education alone?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Psychological · Aftercare · Chronic Pain/etiology,therapy · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Internet · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/physiopathology,therapy · Pain Measurement · Patient Education as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One pragmatic randomised trial (Bennell/Hinman 2017, 148 adults aged ≥50 with chronic knee pain) found the internet-delivered programme (educational material, seven Skype physiotherapy sessions prescribing home exercise, and automated pain-coping skills training over 3 months) improved pain during walking by 1.6 units (95% CI 0.9 to 2.3) and physical function (WOMAC) by 9.3 units (5.9 to 12.7) more than internet education alone at 3 months, with improvements sustained at 9 months (mean differences 1.1 units for pain and, as reported, sustained functional gains). A single trial caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Bennell 2017: internet-delivered exercise plus pain-coping training beat internet education on pain (1.6 units) and function (9.3 units) at 3 months
cards.summary: Bennell 2017: internet-delivered exercise plus pain-coping training beat internet education on pain (1.6 units) and function (9.3 units) at 3 months
cards.type: Pragmatic parallel-group randomised controlled trial (community, Australia)
cards.people: 148 persons aged 50 years or older with chronic knee pain; the intervention was delivered via the internet over 3 months (educational material, 7 videoconference [Skype] sessions with a physiotherapist for home exercise, and a pain-coping skills training programme) and the control was internet-based educational material; 139 (94%) completed primary outcome measures at 3 months and 133 (90%) at 9 months, with multiple imputation for missing data.
cards.result: The intervention group reported significantly more improvement in pain during walking (11-point numerical rating scale; mean difference 1.6 units [95% CI 0.9 to 2.3]) and physical function (Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index; mean difference 9.3 units [5.9 to 12.7]) than the control group at 3 months, and improvements were sustained at 9 months (mean differences of 1.1 units for pain, with functional improvement also maintained, as reported in the abstract). Secondary outcomes included knee pain, quality of life, global change, arthritis self-efficacy, coping and pain catastrophizing.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is education alone, so the trial cannot separate the exercise, the coping training and the physiotherapist contact; a 1.6-point pain advantage over an inert control in an unblinded trial is the realistic size of the whole package, not of any component.

shelves.title: Vestibular rehabilitation for chronic dizziness in primary care
shelves.question: In adults with chronic dizziness in primary care, does a booklet-and-brief-training vestibular rehabilitation programme reduce dizziness handicap and symptoms versus usual care at 3 and 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease · Dizziness/nursing,physiopathology,therapy · Exercise Therapy/methods · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Middle Aged · Posture/physiology · Primary Health Care · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Vestibule, Labyrinth/physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One single-blind randomised trial (Yardley 2004, 170 patients in 20 general practices) found nurse-delivered vestibular rehabilitation — one 30- to 40-minute appointment teaching daily home exercises, supported by a treatment booklet — produced significantly greater improvement than usual medical care on all primary outcome measures at 3 months, maintained at 6 months, with 67% (56 of 83) of treated patients reporting clinically significant improvement versus 38% (33 of 87) on usual care (relative risk 1.78 relative, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.42). The topic question names 12 months; the record as fetched reports outcomes to 6 months, and the card prints what the record shows — the 12-month durability claim in the topic file could not be verified from the anchor record and is not carried. A single trial caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Yardley 2004: primary-care vestibular rehabilitation beat usual care on dizziness outcomes at 3 and 6 months (67% vs 38% clinically improved)
cards.summary: Yardley 2004: primary-care vestibular rehabilitation beat usual care on dizziness outcomes at 3 and 6 months (67% vs 38% clinically improved)
cards.type: Single-blind randomised controlled trial in 20 general practices (southern England)
cards.people: 170 adult patients with chronic dizziness randomly assigned to vestibular rehabilitation (83) or usual medical care (87); each treated patient received one 30- to 40-minute appointment with a primary care nurse who taught exercises to be carried out daily at home, supported by a treatment booklet. Primary outcomes were self-reported spontaneous and provoked dizziness symptoms, dizziness-related quality of life, and objective postural stability with eyes open and closed, assessed at baseline, 3 and 6 months.
cards.result: At 3 months, improvement on all primary outcome measures in the vestibular rehabilitation group was significantly greater than in the usual medical care group, and this improvement was maintained at 6 months. Of 83 treated patients, 56 (67%) reported clinically significant improvement compared with 33 of 87 (38%) usual care patients (relative risk 1.78 — a relative measure — 95% CI 1.31 to 2.42). The authors note psychological elements of the therapy may have contributed and that the treatment may be effective only for well-motivated patients.
cards.watchOut: The topic question asks about 12 months; this record reports 3- and 6-month outcomes, and no 12-month figure is printed because none could be verified from the anchor record. Self-reported symptoms in an unblindable intervention, against usual care, is the design's ceiling.

shelves.title: Domiciliary occupational therapy after stroke discharge
shelves.question: In patients discharged home after stroke, does a short course of domiciliary occupational therapy focused on activities of daily living improve personal and extended ADL independence versus no routine OT?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Algorithms · Deinstitutionalization · Female · Home Care Services/organization & administration · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Occupational Therapy/methods · Patient Acceptance of Health Care · Patient Satisfaction · Prognosis · Single-Blind Method · Stroke Rehabilitation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small single-blind randomised trial (Gilbertson 2000, 138 patients) is mixed on its face, and the card prints both halves: the extended-ADL advantage at 8 weeks was 4.8 points on the Nottingham extended ADL score but NOT statistically significant (95% CI −0.5 to 10.0; P=0.08), while the composite global outcome (deterioration on the Barthel index, or death) significantly favoured home OT (poor outcome in 24% [16 patients] of the intervention group versus 42% [30] of controls; odds ratio 0.43 relative, 0.21 to 0.89; P=0.02); the patterns persisted at 6 months but were not statistically significant, and intervention patients reported greater satisfaction with services. A single small trial whose named primary measure missed significance caps at POSSIBLE, leaning on the global-outcome result.

cards.headline: Gilbertson 2000: six weeks of home OT improved the global outcome (OR 0.43 relative) but the extended-ADL difference was not significant (P=0.08)
cards.summary: Gilbertson 2000: six weeks of home OT improved the global outcome (OR 0.43 relative) but the extended-ADL difference was not significant (P=0.08)
cards.type: Single-blind randomised controlled trial at two hospital sites within a UK teaching hospital
cards.people: 138 patients with stroke with a definite plan for discharge home, randomised to a six-week domiciliary occupational therapy programme or routine follow-up; outcomes were the Nottingham extended activities of daily living score and a "global outcome" (deterioration according to the Barthel ADL index, or death), assessed at 8 weeks and 6 months.
cards.result: By eight weeks, the mean Nottingham extended ADL score in the intervention group was 4.8 points (95% CI −0.5 to 10.0; P=0.08) greater than in the control group — not statistically significant. Overall, 16 (24%) intervention patients had a poor global outcome compared with 30 (42%) control patients (odds ratio 0.43 — a relative measure — 0.21 to 0.89; P=0.02). These patterns persisted at six months but were not statistically significant. Patients in the intervention group were more likely to report satisfaction with a range of aspects of services.
cards.watchOut: Topic-file summaries of this trial tend to print only the favourable half; the record shows the headline ADL score missed significance and the significant result is a composite that includes death — a small mortality-bearing component in a 138-patient trial is a fragile base, and the authors themselves caution that major benefits may not be sustained.

shelves.title: Therapies for chronic fatigue syndrome: CBT, graded exercise, adaptive pacing (PACE)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic fatigue syndrome, do cognitive behaviour therapy or graded exercise therapy added to specialist medical care improve fatigue and physical function versus specialist medical care alone — and does adaptive pacing therapy help?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adaptation, Physiological · Adult · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Exercise Therapy/adverse effects · Fatigue Syndrome, Chronic/physiopathology,therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Specialization · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One large trial (PACE, White 2011, 641 patients meeting Oxford criteria) found that adding cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT) or graded exercise therapy (GET) to specialist medical care (SMC) moderately improved both primary outcomes at 52 weeks — fatigue scores 3.4 (95% CI 1.8 to 5.0; P=0.0001) and 3.2 points (1.7 to 4.8; P=0.0003) lower than SMC alone, and physical function scores 7.1 (2.0 to 12.1; P=0.0068) and 9.4 points (4.4 to 14.4; P=0.0005) higher — while adaptive pacing therapy (APT) did not differ from SMC alone on either outcome (fatigue 0.7 points lower, P=0.38; physical function 3.4 points lower, P=0.18). Serious adverse reactions were uncommon and similar across groups (1–2%). The stamp is POSSIBLE, and the shelf face carries the contest: PACE's reanalyses and its recovery definitions have been heavily disputed by patient organisations and later commentators, outcomes were self-rated by necessarily unmasked participants, and no second trial of this size exists — the trial's own numbers are carded as printed and the dispute is disclosed, not adjudicated.

cards.headline: PACE 2011: CBT and GET each moderately improved fatigue and physical function over specialist care alone; adaptive pacing did not
cards.summary: PACE 2011: CBT and GET each moderately improved fatigue and physical function over specialist care alone; adaptive pacing did not
cards.type: Parallel-group randomised trial at six secondary-care clinics (UK); participants unmasked to treatment, statistician masked for the primary analysis
cards.people: 641 patients meeting Oxford criteria for chronic fatigue syndrome, randomly allocated to specialist medical care (SMC) alone (160) or SMC plus adaptive pacing therapy (160), CBT (161) or GET (160); primary outcomes fatigue (Chalder fatigue questionnaire) and physical function (SF-36 subscale) to 52 weeks; the final analysis included all participants with primary-outcome data; subgroup analyses covered 427 participants meeting international CFS criteria and 329 meeting London criteria for myalgic encephalomyelitis, with equivalent results.
cards.result: Compared with SMC alone, mean fatigue scores at 52 weeks were 3.4 points (95% CI 1.8 to 5.0) lower for CBT (P=0.0001) and 3.2 points (1.7 to 4.8) lower for GET (P=0.0003), but did not differ for APT (0.7 points lower [−0.9 to 2.3]; P=0.38). Mean physical function scores were 7.1 points (2.0 to 12.1) higher for CBT (P=0.0068) and 9.4 points (4.4 to 14.4) higher for GET (P=0.0005), but did not differ for APT (3.4 points lower [−1.6 to 8.4]; P=0.18). Compared with APT, CBT and GET were also associated with less fatigue and better physical function. Serious adverse reactions were recorded in 2 (1%) APT, 3 (2%) CBT, 2 (1%) GET and 2 (1%) SMC-alone participants.
cards.watchOut: Both primaries are self-rated by participants who knew their allocation, in a trial whose organisation-side critics reported harm from these therapies and whose post-hoc reanalyses (including of "recovery") remain contested; the record's own safety data show few serious adverse reactions, and the dispute is disclosed here rather than resolved — objective outcomes (actigraphy, employment) are not among the carded primaries.
cards.source: White PD et al. Comparison of adaptive pacing therapy, cognitive behaviour therapy, graded exercise therapy, and specialist medical care for chronic fatigue syndrome (PACE): a randomised trial. shelves.title: Early physical and occupational therapy in mechanically ventilated patients
shelves.question: In adults receiving mechanical ventilation in intensive care, does early exercise and mobilisation with daily sedation interruption increase the proportion returning to independent functional status by hospital discharge versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Aged · Bed Rest/adverse effects · Chicago · Procedural Sedation/adverse effects,methods · Critical Care/methods · Critical Illness/rehabilitation · Delirium/etiology,prevention & control · Early Ambulation/methods · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Iowa · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Mobility Limitation · Occupational Therapy/methods · Proportional Hazards Models · Respiration, Artificial/adverse effects,methods · Single-Blind Method · Statistics, Nonparametric · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — functional benefit in Schweickert · POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) in TEAM. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C — ruled Tier C at build, contrary to the topic file's flag: the TEAM trial carded here has a mortality-bearing primary outcome, days alive and out of hospital). In Schweickert 2009 (104 patients at two university hospitals), early exercise and mobilisation during daily sedation interruption nearly doubled return to independent functional status at hospital discharge (59% [29 patients] vs 35% [19]; odds ratio 2.7 relative, 95% CI 1.2 to 6.1; P=0.02), shortened delirium (median 2.0 vs 4.0 days; P=0.02) and increased ventilator-free days (23.5 vs 21.1; P=0.05). In TEAM 2022 (750 patients), increased early mobilisation did NOT increase days alive and out of hospital at 180 days (median 143 vs 145 days; absolute difference −2.0 days, 95% CI −10 to 6; P=0.62), death by day 180 was 22.5% versus 19.5% (OR 1.15 relative, 0.81 to 1.65), and adverse events potentially due to mobilisation were more frequent (9.2% vs 4.1%; P=0.005). A small single-centre positive and a large multicentre null do not average into a claim: the split is the record.

cards.headline: Schweickert 2009: early PT/OT with sedation interruption doubled return to independent function at discharge (59% vs 35%)
cards.summary: Schweickert 2009: early PT/OT with sedation interruption doubled return to independent function at discharge (59% vs 35%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial at two university hospitals; outcome assessors blinded to treatment assignment
cards.people: 104 sedated adults in intensive care, ventilated for less than 72 hours, expected to continue ventilation at least 24 hours, and functionally independent at baseline, randomly assigned to early exercise and mobilisation (physical and occupational therapy) during daily interruption of sedation (49) or to daily sedation interruption with therapy as ordered by the primary team (55); primary endpoint return to independent functional status at hospital discharge (six ADLs plus independent walking); all 104 analysed.
cards.result: Return to independent functional status at hospital discharge occurred in 29 (59%) patients in the intervention group compared with 19 (35%) in the control group (P=0.02; odds ratio 2.7 — a relative measure — 95% CI 1.2 to 6.1). Patients in the intervention group had shorter duration of delirium (median 2.0 days [IQR 0.0–6.0] versus 4.0 days [2.0–8.0]; P=0.02) and more ventilator-free days (23.5 days [7.4–25.6] versus 21.1 days [0.0–23.8]; P=0.05) during the 28-day follow-up. There was one serious adverse event in 498 therapy sessions (desaturation below 80%); therapy was discontinued for instability in 19 (4%) of sessions.
cards.watchOut: One hundred and four patients at two centres with an unusually engaged intervention team; the control group's therapy was at the primary team's discretion, so the trial tests an organised early-mobility service against ad-hoc provision — exactly the gap TEAM later tested at scale with a null result.
cards.source: Schweickert WD et al. Early physical and occupational therapy in mechanically ventilated, critically ill patients: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2009. cards.headline: TEAM 2022: increased early mobilisation did not increase days alive and out of hospital (143 vs 145) and produced more mobilisation-related adverse events
cards.summary: TEAM 2022: increased early mobilisation did not increase days alive and out of hospital (143 vs 145) and produced more mobilisation-related adverse events
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial (ANZICS Clinical Trials Group); increased early mobilisation (sedation minimisation and daily physiotherapy) versus usual-care mobilisation levels
cards.people: 750 adult ICU patients undergoing invasive mechanical ventilation, randomly assigned to increased early mobilisation or usual care; primary outcome days alive and out of hospital at 180 days; the mean daily duration of active mobilisation was 20.8 (SD 14.6) minutes versus 8.8 (9.0) minutes.
cards.result: The median number of days alive and out of hospital was 143 (IQR 21 to 161) in the early-mobilisation group and 145 (51 to 164) in the usual-care group (absolute difference −2.0 days, 95% CI −10 to 6; P=0.62). By day 180, death had occurred in 22.5% of the early-mobilisation group and 19.5% of the usual-care group (odds ratio 1.15 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.81 to 1.65). Among survivors, quality of life, activities of daily living, disability, cognitive function and psychological function were similar. Serious adverse events were reported in 7 patients in the early-mobilisation group and 1 in the usual-care group, and adverse events potentially due to mobilisation (arrhythmias, altered blood pressure, desaturation) occurred in 34 of 371 patients (9.2%) versus 15 of 370 (4.1%) (P=0.005).
cards.watchOut: TEAM's usual-care ICUs were already mobilising patients (77% in both groups could stand, by day 3 versus day 5), so its null is a null for INCREASING mobilisation intensity in contemporary practice, not for mobilisation itself — but it removes any basis for claiming the Schweickert result generalises. Note: an editorial bearing this trial's title (PMID 36780684) circulates in the indexes; the card cites the trial report itself, verified by its abstract and registry number.

shelves.title: Mirror therapy for upper-limb recovery after stroke
shelves.question: In patients with subacute stroke and severe arm paresis, does mirror therapy added to conventional rehabilitation improve hand function and self-care versus sham mirror treatment?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analysis of Variance · Confidence Intervals · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hand/physiopathology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Spasticity/physiopathology,rehabilitation · Physical Therapy Modalities/instrumentation · Probability · Range of Motion, Articular/physiology · Recovery of Function · Reference Values · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method · Stroke/diagnosis · Stroke Rehabilitation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small assessor-blinded randomised trial (Yavuzer 2008, 40 inpatients with subacute stroke) found that 30 minutes of mirror therapy daily (wrist and finger flexion/extension) added to a conventional rehabilitation programme for 4 weeks improved Brunnstrom stages for the hand (by 0.83 more than control) and upper extremity (by 0.89) and FIM self-care scores (by 4.10) more than sham mirror treatment (all P<0.01), with smaller advantages persisting at 6-month follow-up (0.16, 0.43 and 2.34 respectively; all P<0.05), and no significant difference in spasticity (Modified Ashworth Scale). A single 40-patient trial caps at POSSIBLE; the wider mirror-therapy trial literature is small-trial throughout and is fenced in the synthesis. The phantom-limb mirror question is a different population and outcome (#1453).

cards.headline: Yavuzer 2008: mirror therapy improved Brunnstrom hand stages and FIM self-care versus sham in subacute stroke (n=40)
cards.summary: Yavuzer 2008: mirror therapy improved Brunnstrom hand stages and FIM self-care versus sham in subacute stroke (n=40)
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, assessor-blinded, 4-week trial with 6-month follow-up (rehabilitation hospital)
cards.people: 40 inpatients with stroke (mean age 63.2 years), all within 12 months of stroke, receiving 30 minutes per day of a mirror therapy programme of wrist and finger flexion and extension movements, or sham therapy, in addition to a conventional stroke rehabilitation programme (5 days a week, 2–5 hours a day, for 4 weeks); outcomes were Brunnstrom stages of motor recovery, spasticity (Modified Ashworth Scale) and hand-related functioning (FIM self-care items).
cards.result: The scores of the Brunnstrom stages for the hand and upper extremity and the FIM self-care score improved more in the mirror group than in the control group after 4 weeks of treatment (by 0.83, 0.89 and 4.10 respectively; all P<0.01) and at the 6-month follow-up (by 0.16, 0.43 and 2.34 respectively; all P<0.05). No significant differences were found between the groups for the Modified Ashworth Scale.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, surrogate staging outcomes (Brunnstrom) rather than measured task performance, and 6-month between-group differences much smaller than the 4-week ones (hand stage 0.16) — the durable residue of the effect is thin even in the trial that found it.
cards.source: Yavuzer G et al. Mirror therapy improves hand function in subacute stroke: a randomized controlled trial. Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation. 2008. PMID: 18295613. shelves.title: Accelerated rehabilitation for acute lateral ankle sprain
shelves.question: In adults with acute grade I–II lateral ankle sprain, does an accelerated rehabilitation programme with early therapeutic exercises improve ankle function in the first 2 weeks versus standard protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Ankle Injuries · Edema · Exercise Therapy · Humans · Middle Aged · Pain · Recovery of Function · Sprains and Strains · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One assessor-blinded randomised trial (Bleakley 2010, 101 patients with acute grade 1 or 2 ankle sprain) found an accelerated intervention with early therapeutic exercise improved subjective ankle function versus standard protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation at week 1 (baseline-adjusted difference 5.28 points on the Lower Extremity Functional Scale, 98.75% CI 0.31 to 10.26; P=0.008) and week 2 (4.92, 0.27 to 9.57; P=0.0083), with no differences at weeks 3–4 or in pain or swelling at any point, and an identical reinjury rate (4%, two in each group) at 16 weeks. A single small trial with an early, transient functional advantage earns POSSIBLE. The CAST trial of mechanical supports after severe sprain is a different intervention and is fenced in the synthesis, not counted as a second rehabilitation trial.

cards.headline: Bleakley 2010: accelerated rehabilitation improved ankle function at weeks 1–2 only, with no pain, swelling or reinjury advantage
cards.summary: Bleakley 2010: accelerated rehabilitation improved ankle function at weeks 1–2 only, with no pain, swelling or reinjury advantage
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with blinded outcome assessor (accident and emergency department and university sports injury clinic)
cards.people: 101 patients with an acute grade 1 or 2 ankle sprain, randomised to an accelerated intervention with early therapeutic exercise or a standard protection, rest, ice, compression and elevation intervention. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: An overall treatment effect favoured the exercise group (P=0.0077), significant at week 1 (baseline-adjusted difference in Lower Extremity Functional Scale 5.28, 98.75% CI 0.31 to 10.26; P=0.008) and week 2 (4.92, 0.27 to 9.57; P=0.0083). Activity was higher in the exercise group in the first week (walking time, step count and light-intensity activity all higher, as printed). The groups did not differ at any other time point for pain at rest, pain on activity, or swelling. The reinjury rate was 4% (two in each group) at 16 weeks.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is confined to the first two weeks and to a subjective function scale; by weeks 3–4 the standard-care group had caught up, so this is faster early recovery, not a better final outcome.
cards.source: Bleakley CM et al. Effect of accelerated rehabilitation on function after ankle sprain: randomised controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2010. PMID: 20457737. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN13903946, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: early loading speeds the first fortnight; it does not change the destination — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: early loading speeds the first fortnight; it does not change the destination — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Bleakley 2010 (101 patients with acute grade 1–2 ankle sprain).
cards.result: Accelerated rehabilitation is supported for early function only. The CAST trial (Lamb 2009, PMID 19217992) tested mechanical supports after severe sprain — a below-knee cast or Aircast brace beat tubular bandage at 3 months — and is fenced here: it answers a support question in more severe sprains, not the accelerated-exercise question, and is not counted as replication.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the rehabilitation and support literatures into a single 'early mobilisation works' claim; the interventions, severities and time courses differ.

shelves.title: Neuromuscular warm-up programmes to prevent football injuries (FIFA 11 / 11+)
shelves.question: In young footballers, does a structured neuromuscular warm-up programme reduce the rate of severe and overall injuries versus a usual warm-up over one season?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Athletic Injuries · Cluster Analysis · Exercise · Female · Hip Injuries · Humans · Leg Injuries · Muscle Strength · Physical Fitness · Risk Factors · Soccer · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two cluster-randomised trials point the same way but neither is clean. In young female players (Soligard 2008, 1,892 players in 125 Norwegian clubs), the comprehensive warm-up's PRIMARY outcome — lower-extremity injury rate — did NOT reach significance (rate ratio 0.71 relative, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.03); significant reductions appeared in secondary categories: injuries overall (0.68 relative, 0.48 to 0.98), overuse injuries (0.47 relative, 0.26 to 0.85) and severe injuries (0.55 relative, 0.36 to 0.83). In male youth players (Owoeye 2014, 414 players, Lagos), FIFA 11+ reduced overall injury rate by 41% relative (RR 0.59 relative, 0.40 to 0.86; p=0.006) and lower-extremity injuries by 48% relative (RR 0.52 relative, 0.34 to 0.82; p=0.004). A non-significant primary in the larger trial caps the pair at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Soligard 2008: the warm-up programme missed its primary lower-extremity outcome (rate ratio 0.71, CI crossing 1) while cutting severe and overuse injuries
cards.summary: Soligard 2008: the warm-up programme missed its primary lower-extremity outcome (rate ratio 0.71, CI crossing 1) while cutting severe and overuse injuries
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial (125 football clubs, Norway; one league season, eight months)
cards.people: 1,892 female players aged 13–17 (1,055 in the intervention group; 837 in the control group) in 125 clubs randomised by club (65 intervention, 60 control).
cards.result: During one season, 264 players had relevant injuries: 121 in the intervention group and 143 in the control group (rate ratio 0.71 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.49 to 1.03; the primary lower-extremity outcome, not significant). Risk was significantly lower in the intervention group for injuries overall (0.68 relative, 0.48 to 0.98), overuse injuries (0.47 relative, 0.26 to 0.85) and severe injuries (0.55 relative, 0.36 to 0.83). The authors conclude a structured warm-up programme can prevent injuries in young female football players.
cards.watchOut: The headline claim rests on secondary injury categories: the primary outcome's confidence interval includes no effect. The authors' conclusion is broader than their primary result — flagged here as printed.
cards.source: Soligard T et al. Comprehensive warm-up programme to prevent injuries in young female footballers: cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2008. PMID: 19066253. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN10306290, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Owoeye 2014: FIFA 11+ reduced overall injuries by 41% relative in male youth players in Lagos
cards.summary: Owoeye 2014: FIFA 11+ reduced overall injuries by 41% relative in male youth players in Lagos
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial (20 teams, Lagos Junior League; one 6-month season)
cards.people: 414 male players aged 14–19 in 20 teams block-randomised to FIFA 11+ warm-up or usual warm-up; team compliance 60% and player compliance 74% in the intervention group. This record carries no MeSH terms in its PubMed record.
cards.result: In total, 130 injuries were recorded affecting 104 (25%) of the 416 players followed (the abstract states 414 randomised and 416 followed — the discrepancy is the record's own and is flagged, not repaired). The FIFA 11+ programme significantly reduced the overall rate of injury by 41% relative (RR 0.59 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.40 to 0.86; p=0.006) and all lower extremity injuries by 48% relative (RR 0.52 relative, 0.34 to 0.82; p=0.004). Reductions on secondary outcomes mostly did not reach statistical significance.
cards.watchOut: A single-league trial with 60% team compliance, and the record's internal player-count inconsistency (414 vs 416) is left exactly as printed.
cards.source: Owoeye OB et al. Efficacy of the FIFA 11+ Warm-Up Programme in Male Youth Football: A Cluster Randomised Controlled Trial. Journal of sports science & medicine. 2014. PMID: 24790486. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. MeSH: none in the record.
