cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent direction, one missed primary — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Soligard 2008 (1,892 female players) and Owoeye 2014 (414 male players).
cards.result: Across sexes and continents, structured neuromuscular warm-ups reduced severe, overuse and overall injuries; the largest trial's primary endpoint, however, was not significant, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.

shelves.title: Early targeted aerobic exercise after sport-related concussion
shelves.question: In adolescents with sport-related concussion, does early prescribed aerobic exercise at a sub-symptom heart-rate threshold shorten time to recovery versus a placebo stretching programme?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Athletic Injuries · Brain Concussion · Exercise · Exercise Therapy · Female · Heart Rate · Humans · Male · Muscle Stretching Exercises · Patient Compliance · Post-Concussion Syndrome
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials from the same programme, in the same population, agree. The pilot (Leddy 2019, 103 adolescents) found recovery in a median of 13 days (IQR 10–18.5) on subsymptom-threshold aerobic exercise versus 17 days (IQR 13–23) on placebo-like stretching (P=.009). The multicentre replication (Leddy 2021, 118 adolescents) found aerobic-exercise patients more likely to recover within 4 weeks, with a 48% relative reduction in the risk of persistent post-concussive symptoms (hazard ratio for stretching vs aerobic exercise 0.52 relative, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.97; p=0.039), and no adverse events in either trial. Two concordant randomised trials with a placebo-like control earn LIKELY — for adolescents seen within 10 days of injury. Note: the topic draft's '≈14 vs ≈19 days' median figures appear in NEITHER abstract; the carded figures are the records' own (13 vs 17 days in the pilot; the replication reports the hazard ratio, not medians).

cards.headline: Leddy 2019 (pilot): aerobic exercise recovered adolescents in a median 13 days versus 17 days on stretching
cards.summary: Leddy 2019 (pilot): aerobic exercise recovered adolescents in a median 13 days versus 17 days on stretching
cards.type: Multicenter prospective randomised clinical trial at university concussion centers
cards.people: 103 adolescent athletes aged 13–18 presenting within 10 days of sport-related concussion (aerobic exercise n=52, 24 female [46%]; stretching n=51, 24 female [47%]); mean time from injury to first visit 4.9 (SD 2.2) days (aerobic) and 4.8 (SD 2.4) days (stretching).
cards.result: Aerobic exercise participants recovered in a median of 13 (IQR 10–18.5) days, whereas stretching participants recovered in 17 (IQR 13–23) days (P=.009). Delayed recovery (≥30 days) occurred in 2 participants (4%) in the aerobic group versus 7 (14%) in the placebo group — a non-significant difference (P=.08). Recovery required being asymptomatic, physician confirmation blinded to treatment group, and normal exercise tolerance on treadmill testing.
cards.watchOut: The delayed-recovery difference — the outcome with the longest shadow — was not significant in this pilot; the significant result is time to recovery.
cards.source: Leddy JJ et al. Early Subthreshold Aerobic Exercise for Sport-Related Concussion: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA pediatrics. 2019. PMID: 30715132. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02710123, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Leddy 2021 (replication): aerobic exercise raised 4-week recovery and halved the relative risk of persistent symptoms
cards.summary: Leddy 2021 (replication): aerobic exercise raised 4-week recovery and halved the relative risk of persistent symptoms
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial at three community and hospital-affiliated sports medicine concussion centres, USA
cards.people: 118 adolescents aged 13–18 presenting within 10 days of sport-related concussion, randomly assigned to individualised subsymptom threshold aerobic exercise (61) or stretching exercise (57), at least 20 minutes daily for up to 4 weeks, with heart-rate-monitor adherence measurement; all 118 in the intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: On survival analysis, controlling for sex, site, and mean daily exercise time, patients assigned to aerobic exercise were more likely to recover within 4 weeks after injury compared with stretching, with a 48% relative reduction in the risk of persistent post-concussive symptoms (hazard ratio for stretching vs aerobic exercise 0.52 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.28 to 0.97; p=0.039). No adverse events were reported. The abstract reports no median recovery times for this trial.
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from one research programme in one country's sports-medicine centres; independent replication outside that programme does not yet exist in the carded record.
cards.source: Leddy JJ et al. Early targeted heart rate aerobic exercise versus placebo stretching for sport-related concussion in adolescents: a randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. shelves.title: Radial extracorporeal shock-wave therapy for chronic plantar fasciitis
shelves.question: In adults with chronic recalcitrant plantar fasciitis, does radial extracorporeal shock-wave therapy improve heel-pain treatment success at 12 weeks versus placebo shock-wave?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Fasciitis, Plantar · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonic Therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial (Gerdesmeyer 2008, 245 patients with chronic plantar fasciitis) found three sessions of radial shock-wave therapy beat placebo at 12 weeks on the visual analogue scale composite score (reduction 72.1% vs 44.7%; P=.0220) and on overall treatment success (61.0% vs 42.2%; P=.0020), with superiority more pronounced at 12 months and no relevant side effects. A single positive trial — with percentage reductions printed without the underlying absolute scores — earns POSSIBLE. Plantar fascia–specific stretching is a different intervention, homed elsewhere.

cards.headline: Gerdesmeyer 2008: radial shock-wave therapy beat placebo on pain composite and treatment success at 12 weeks
cards.summary: Gerdesmeyer 2008: radial shock-wave therapy beat placebo on pain composite and treatment success at 12 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial (Level of evidence, 1, as printed in the record)
cards.people: 245 patients with chronic plantar fasciitis receiving three interventions of radial extracorporeal shock wave therapy (0.16 mJ/mm2; 2000 impulses) or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Radial shock-wave therapy was significantly superior to placebo at 12 weeks: reduction of the visual analog scale composite score 72.1% compared with 44.7% (P=.0220), and overall success rate 61.0% compared with 42.2% in the placebo group (P=.0020). Superiority was even more pronounced at 12 months, and all secondary outcome measures (single VAS scores, Roles and Maudsley score, SF-36, global judgments) supported shock-wave therapy (P<.025, 1-sided, as printed). No relevant side effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: The abstract prints percentage reductions and success rates without absolute VAS scores, and several secondary P values are 1-sided as printed; the placebo success rate of 42.2% also shows how much of the outcome is natural history and expectation.
cards.source: Gerdesmeyer L et al. Radial extracorporeal shock wave therapy is safe and effective in the treatment of chronic recalcitrant plantar fasciitis: results of a confirmatory randomized placebo-controlled multicenter study. The American journal of sports medicine. 2008. PMID: 18832341. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-run placebo-controlled trial, a real but modest margin — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-run placebo-controlled trial, a real but modest margin — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Gerdesmeyer 2008 (245 patients with chronic recalcitrant plantar fasciitis).

shelves.title: External ankle bracing to prevent recurrent ankle sprain
shelves.question: In athletes recovering from a lateral ankle sprain, does wearing an ankle brace during sport reduce recurrent sprains over 12 months versus neuromuscular training or their combination?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Ankle Injuries · Athletic Injuries · Braces · Exercise Therapy · Female · Home Care Services · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Secondary Prevention · Self Report · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One three-arm randomised trial (Janssen 2014, 384 athletes aged 18–70 after a lateral ankle sprain) found self-reported recurrence over 1 year in 27% with neuromuscular training, 15% with bracing, and 19% with the combination; bracing beat training (relative risk 0.53 relative, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.97), while the combination was not significantly better than either and no group differed on time loss or costs. A single trial with a self-reported primary outcome earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Janssen 2014: bracing halved self-reported recurrences versus neuromuscular training (15% vs 27%)
cards.summary: Janssen 2014: bracing halved self-reported recurrences versus neuromuscular training (15% vs 27%)
cards.type: Three-arm randomised controlled trial with 1-year follow-up
cards.people: 384 athletes, aged 18–70, who had sustained a lateral ankle sprain (training group n=120; brace group n=126; combination group n=138), receiving an 8-week home-based neuromuscular training programme, a semirigid ankle brace worn during all sports activities for 12 months, or both (brace for 8 weeks). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: During the 1-year follow-up, 69 participants (20%) reported a recurrent ankle sprain: 29 (27%) in the training group, 17 (15%) in the brace group and 23 (19%) in the combi group. The relative risk for a recurrent ankle sprain in the brace group versus the training group was 0.53 (a relative measure; absolute rates 15% vs 27%, as above) (95% CI 0.29 to 0.97). No significant differences were found for time losses or costs due to ankle sprains between the intervention groups.
cards.watchOut: Recurrence was self-reported and participants could not be blinded to wearing a brace; the combination arm — the intuitively strongest option — did not win, which argues some of the brace effect may be adherence- or reporting-related.
cards.source: Janssen KW et al. Bracing superior to neuromuscular training for the prevention of self-reported recurrent ankle sprains: a three-arm randomised controlled trial. British journal of sports medicine. 2014. PMID: 24398222. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.question: In military recruits, does a pre-exercise static stretching programme reduce the risk of lower-limb injury over a 12-week training period versus no stretching?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Ankle Injuries · Athletic Injuries · Exercise Therapy · Humans · Leg Injuries · Male · Physical Fitness · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large randomised trial (Pope 2000, 1,538 male army recruits) found pre-exercise static stretching did not reduce injury risk over 12 weeks of training: all-injuries hazard ratio 0.95 relative (95% CI 0.77 to 1.18), soft-tissue injury 0.83 relative (0.63 to 1.09), bone injury 1.22 relative (0.86 to 1.76) — 158 injuries in the stretch group and 175 in controls. A second recruit trial (Herbert & Gabriel) is reported in the topic literature as agreeing with the null and is fenced in the synthesis without carded figures. A large, precise null earns LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Pope 2000: pre-exercise stretching did not reduce lower-limb injury in 1,538 army recruits
cards.summary: Pope 2000: pre-exercise stretching did not reduce lower-limb injury in 1,538 army recruits
cards.type: Randomized trial over a 12-week training period
cards.people: 1,538 male army recruits randomly allocated to stretch or control groups; both groups performed active warm-up exercises, and the stretch group additionally performed one supervised 20-second static stretch for each of six major leg muscle groups during every warm-up. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: 333 lower-limb injuries were recorded, including 214 soft-tissue injuries: 158 in the stretch group and 175 in the control group. There was no significant effect of preexercise stretching on all-injuries risk (hazard ratio 0.95 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.77 to 1.18), soft-tissue injury risk (HR 0.83 relative, 0.63 to 1.09), or bone injury risk (HR 1.22 relative, 0.86 to 1.76). Fitness (20-m shuttle run score), age, and enlistment date predicted injury risk (P<0.01 each); height, weight and BMI did not.
cards.watchOut: Young male military recruits in high-volume training: the null is solid for this population and protocol, and fitness — not stretching — was the modifiable predictor the trial actually found.
cards.source: Pope RP et al. A randomized trial of preexercise stretching for prevention of lower-limb injury. Medicine and science in sports and exercise. 2000. PMID: 10694106. shelves.title: Cold-water immersion for post-exercise recovery
shelves.question: In athletes, does post-exercise cold-water immersion improve recovery of sprint performance and reduce muscle soreness versus passive recovery?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Athletes · Biomarkers · C-Reactive Protein · Cold Temperature · Creatine Kinase · Humans · Immersion · Interleukin-6 · Male · Muscle, Skeletal · Myalgia · Oxidative Stress · Recovery of Function · Running · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The carded recovery trial is very small (Leeder 2019, 21 trained male games players in a simulated tournament): cold-water immersion was associated with improved recovery of sprint speed 24 hours after the final match simulation (effect size 0.83 ± 0.59; p=.034) and attenuated creatine kinase efflux, while the authors themselves conclude immersion was 'in the main ineffective' at managing the tournament's physiological stress and provides only limited benefits. Set against it, a randomised strength-training study (Roberts 2015) found regular post-exercise cold-water immersion blunted anabolic signalling, satellite-cell responses and long-term strength and hypertrophy gains. One tiny, mixed recovery trial plus a real adaptation cost is MAYBE (weak evidence) for any net benefit.

cards.headline: Leeder 2019: in 21 players, cold-water immersion improved one sprint-recovery marker and a damage marker, and little else
cards.summary: Leeder 2019: in 21 players, cold-water immersion improved one sprint-recovery marker and a damage marker, and little else
cards.type: Randomised trial (simulated tournament: Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test three times in five days)
cards.people: 21 trained male games players (age 19 ± 2 years; body mass 78.0 ± 8.8 kg) randomised to cold-water immersion (n=11) or control (n=10).
cards.result: Cold water immersion was associated with improved recovery of sprint speed 24 h after the final shuttle test (effect size 0.83 ± 0.59; p=.034) and attenuated the efflux of creatine kinase pre- and post the third test (p<.01). The simulated tournament perturbed some but not all stress markers, and the authors conclude that, in the main, cold water immersion was ineffective at managing it, is not harmful in this setting, and provides limited benefits. The abstract reports no muscle-soreness effect size.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-one participants and many markers: one significant sprint result among a panel of mostly null outcomes is exactly the pattern that earns MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.source: Leeder JDC et al. Cold water immersion improves recovery of sprint speed following a simulated tournament. European journal of sport science. 2019. PMID: 30957673. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Roberts 2015: regular cold-water immersion after strength training blunted muscle adaptation
cards.summary: Roberts 2015: regular cold-water immersion after strength training blunted muscle adaptation
cards.type: Two randomised studies (12-week strength-training study and an acute single-leg exercise study)
cards.people: 21 physically active men strength trained for 12 weeks (2 days per week) with either 10 minutes of cold-water immersion or active recovery after each session; a second study involved nine active men performing single-leg strength exercise. All participants were male; mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Strength and muscle mass increased more in the active-recovery group than in the cold-water-immersion group (P<0.05). Isokinetic work (19%), type II muscle fibre cross-sectional area (17%) and myonuclei per fibre (26%) increased in the active-recovery group (all P<0.05) but not in the immersion group, and satellite-cell and p70S6 kinase responses were greater after active recovery. The authors conclude the use of cold-water immersion as a regular post-exercise recovery strategy should be reconsidered.
cards.watchOut: This card answers the adaptation question, not acute tournament recovery — but any athlete using immersion daily is in this card's population, not only the tournament card's.
cards.source: Roberts LA et al. Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training. The Journal of physiology. 2015. PMID: 26174323. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: a narrow, weak acute benefit bought with an adaptation penalty — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a narrow, weak acute benefit bought with an adaptation penalty — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Leeder 2019 (21 male games players) and Roberts 2015 (21 men in the training study; 9 in the acute study).
cards.result: For a congested tournament, immersion may help next-day sprint speed slightly; as a daily habit during strength training, the randomised evidence says it costs muscle adaptation. Neither trial is large enough to grade either claim higher.
cards.watchOut: Soreness — the outcome athletes most often cite — has no carded effect size in either record; do not quote one.

shelves.title: Arthroscopic stabilisation versus non-operative care for first-time traumatic shoulder dislocation in young active patients
shelves.question: In young active patients with a first-time traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation, does early arthroscopic stabilisation reduce recurrence versus non-operative treatment over 2–3 years?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Acute Disease · Adult · Arthroscopy · Athletic Injuries · Biocompatible Materials · Humans · Immobilization · Male · Military Personnel · Orthopedic Fixation Devices · Prospective Studies · Shoulder Dislocation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small prospective randomised trial (Bottoni 2002, military patients with acute traumatic first-time dislocation) found recurrent instability in 1 of 9 followed patients (11.1%) after arthroscopic Bankart repair versus 9 of 12 (75%) after immobilisation and rehabilitation over an average 36 months; six of the nine non-operative recurrences went on to open Bankart repair. The effect is very large, but the trial randomised only 24 patients and lost 3 to follow-up — POSSIBLE, not more. A second randomised trial reported in the topic literature (Jakobsen) could not be pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced in the synthesis.

cards.headline: Bottoni 2002: recurrence 11% after arthroscopic stabilisation versus 75% with non-operative care — in 21 followed patients
cards.summary: Bottoni 2002: recurrence 11% after arthroscopic stabilisation versus 75% with non-operative care — in 21 followed patients
cards.type: Prospective, randomized clinical trial (military treatment facility)
cards.people: Young athletes with acute, traumatic, first-time anterior shoulder dislocation: 14 assigned to non-operative treatment (4 weeks of immobilisation then supervised rehabilitation) and 10 to arthroscopic Bankart repair with a bioabsorbable tack followed by the same rehabilitation; three patients were lost to follow-up, leaving 12 non-operative and 9 operative patients, followed an average of 36 months. All participants were male military personnel per the record's MeSH.
cards.result: Nine of 12 non-operatively treated patients (75%) developed recurrent instability, and six of the nine required subsequent open Bankart repair. Of the nine operatively treated patients available for follow-up, one (11.1%) developed recurrent instability.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four randomised, 21 followed: percentages this dramatic rest on single-digit numerators, and a bioabsorbable-tack Bankart repair from 2002 is not today's anchor-based technique — direction is informative, the exact rates are era-bound.
cards.source: Bottoni CR et al. A prospective, randomized evaluation of arthroscopic stabilization versus nonoperative treatment in patients with acute, traumatic, first-time shoulder dislocations. The American journal of sports medicine. 2002. PMID: 12130413. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: a huge relative effect in a tiny, dated trial — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a huge relative effect in a tiny, dated trial — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Bottoni 2002 (24 randomised; 21 followed to ~36 months).
cards.result: Early arthroscopic stabilisation very probably reduces recurrence in young, high-demand patients after a first traumatic dislocation — 75% versus 11% is hard to explain away — but the evidence base carded here is one small trial in male soldiers. cards.watchOut: Do not transport the 75% non-operative recurrence rate to older or lower-demand patients, whose recurrence risk is far lower.

shelves.title: Blood-flow-restriction training in post-surgical musculoskeletal rehabilitation
shelves.question: In patients rehabilitating after ACL reconstruction, does low-load blood-flow-restriction resistance training produce strength and hypertrophy gains comparable with conventional heavy-load training, with less joint pain?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injuries · Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction · Constriction · Female · Hamstring Muscles · Humans · Male · Muscle Strength · Pain · Pain Management · Quadriceps Muscle · Range of Motion, Articular · Regional Blood Flow · Resistance Training · Single-Blind Method · State Medicine · Torque · United Kingdom · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small single-assessor-blinded randomised trial (Hughes 2019, 28 ACL-reconstruction patients; 24 completed) found 8 weeks of low-load blood-flow-restriction training (30% of 1-repetition maximum) produced strength and muscle-thickness gains statistically indistinguishable from heavy-load training (70% 1RM) — scaled 10RM strength rose 104 ± 30% versus 106 ± 43% in the injured limb, muscle thickness 5.8 ± 0.2% versus 6.7 ± 0.3% — with greater reductions in knee joint pain (67 ± 15% vs 39 ± 12%) and effusion and larger self-reported function gains. A single 28-patient trial earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Hughes 2019: BFR training matched heavy-load training on strength and hypertrophy, with less knee pain and effusion
cards.summary: Hughes 2019: BFR training matched heavy-load training on strength and hypertrophy, with less knee pain and effusion
cards.type: Parallel-group, two-arm, single-assessor blinded, randomised clinical trial (UK NHS setting)
cards.people: 28 patients scheduled for unilateral ACL reconstruction with hamstring autograft, block randomised after surgery to heavy-load resistance training at 70% repetition maximum (n=14) or blood-flow-restriction training at 30% 1RM (n=14), completing 8 weeks of biweekly unilateral leg-press training (16 sessions) alongside standard hospital rehabilitation; 24 participants completed the study (12 per group), with no adverse events. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Scaled 10RM strength increased in the injured limb by 104 ± 30% (BFR) and 106 ± 43% (heavy load) and in the non-injured limb by 33 ± 13% and 39 ± 17%, with no group differences. Muscle thickness increased comparably (5.8 ± 0.2% and 6.7 ± 0.3%) and pennation angle similarly, with no group differences; greater attenuation of some peak-torque losses was seen with BFR at higher speeds. Significantly greater increases in several self-reported function measures (50–218 ± 48% vs 35–152 ± 56%), Y-balance performance and range of motion, and reductions in knee joint pain (67 ± 15% vs 39 ± 12%) and effusion (6 ± 2% vs 2 ± 2%), were observed with BFR compared with heavy-load training, as printed.
cards.watchOut: Twelve completers per arm and a very wide spray of percentage changes: the equivalence claim is 'no difference detected' in a trial powered for neither equivalence nor harm, and the function percentages as printed are unusually large and imprecise.
cards.source: Hughes L et al. Comparing the Effectiveness of Blood Flow Restriction and Traditional Heavy Load Resistance Training in the Post-Surgery Rehabilitation of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Patients: A UK National Health Service Randomised Controlled Trial. Sports medicine (Auckland, N.Z.). 2019. PMID: 31301034. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Active training for long-standing adductor-related groin pain in athletes
shelves.question: In athletes with long-standing adductor-related groin pain, does an active physical training programme (strengthening, coordination, core) increase the proportion returning to sport without pain versus conventional physiotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Athletic Injuries · Cumulative Trauma Disorders · Exercise Therapy · Groin · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Management · Physical Therapy Modalities · Single-Blind Method · Soccer
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Hölmich 1999, 68 athletes with median 40 weeks of adductor-related groin pain) found 23 of the active-training group versus 4 of the conventional-physiotherapy group returned to sport at the same level without groin pain (odds ratio 12.7 relative, 95% CI 3.4 to 47.2, multiple-logistic-regression). The second carded trial (Weir 2011) complicates the exercise story: a multimodal manual-therapy programme returned athletes to sport faster than exercise therapy (12.8 vs 17.3 weeks; p=0.043), with only 50–55% in either group fully returned — exercise helps, but slowly and incompletely, and manual multimodal care beat exercise alone on speed. Two small trials, one dramatic and one sobering, earn POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Hölmich 1999: active training returned 23 athletes to pain-free sport versus 4 with conventional physiotherapy
cards.summary: Hölmich 1999: active training returned 23 athletes to pain-free sport versus 4 with conventional physiotherapy
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial with blinded outcome examination (intention-to-treat analysis)
cards.people: 68 athletes with long-standing (median 40 weeks) adductor-related groin pain, randomly assigned to an active training programme aimed at strength and coordination of the pelvic and adductor muscles or to physiotherapy without active training, over 8–12 weeks, with standardised examination 4 months after treatment ended. All participants were male per the record's MeSH; mean age is not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: 23 patients in the active-training group and four in the physiotherapy group returned to sports at the same level without groin pain (odds ratio 12.7 — a relative measure — 95% CI 3.4 to 47.2, by multiple-logistic-regression analysis; the abstract does not print the per-group denominators alongside the counts). Subjective global assessments showed a significant (p=0.006) linear trend towards a better effect in the active-training group, and a per-protocol analysis did not differ appreciably.
cards.watchOut: A striking odds ratio on small counts (23 vs 4 successes), with the comparator being passive physiotherapy rather than a modern exercise programme — the margin over today's exercise care would likely be smaller.
cards.source: Hölmich P et al. Effectiveness of active physical training as treatment for long-standing adductor-related groin pain in athletes: randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 1999. PMID: 9989713. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Weir 2011: multimodal manual therapy beat exercise therapy on time to return (12.8 vs 17.3 weeks); only half fully returned either way
cards.summary: Weir 2011: multimodal manual therapy beat exercise therapy on time to return (12.8 vs 17.3 weeks); only half fully returned either way
cards.type: Single blinded, prospective, randomised controlled trial
cards.people: Athletes with pain at the proximal adductor insertion on palpation and resisted adduction for at least two months, randomised to exercise therapy (home-based exercise plus a structured return-to-running programme, instructed on three occasions) or a multi-modal treatment programme (heat, manual therapy, stretching and return to running). The abstract does not state the total sample size, mean age or sex mix in the portion reporting the primary results.
cards.result: Athletes who received multi-modal treatment returned to sports quicker (12.8 weeks, SD 6.0) than athletes in the exercise therapy group (17.3 weeks, SD 4.4; p=0.043). Only 50–55% of athletes in both groups made a full return to sport (as printed).
cards.watchOut: Carded exactly as its record prints: the trial says exercise therapy is not the fastest route back and that even the winning programme left roughly half of athletes short of full return by the assessment window.
cards.source: Weir A et al. Manual or exercise therapy for long-standing adductor-related groin pain: a randomised controlled clinical trial. Manual therapy. 2011. PMID: 20952244. cards.summary: Synthesis: active training works for adductor groin pain, over months, incompletely — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Hölmich 1999 (68 athletes) and Weir 2011 (athletes with ≥2 months of adductor-related groin pain).
cards.result: Read together, the trials support progressive strengthening-based training as the core treatment — and warn that return to full sport takes three to four-plus months and fails for a substantial minority whichever programme is used.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate current groin-pain classification (Doha agreement); 'adductor-related' here is the trials' own clinical definition.

shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The carded primary trial (Chevalier 2010, 253 patients) found a single 6 ml hylan G-F 20 injection beat placebo on WOMAC pain over 26 weeks by −0.15 points (SE 0.076; p=0.047) — statistically significant and described by the authors as 'clinically relevant', a characterisation the margin does not obviously support. The explicitly labelled review card beside it (Rutjes 2012, systematic review and meta-analysis of 89 trials, 12,667 adults) found that in the 18 large trials with blinded outcome assessment (5,094 patients) the effect size was −0.11 (95% CI −0.18 to −0.04) — clinically irrelevant — with an increased risk of serious adverse events (relative risk 1.41 relative, 1.02 to 1.97). A borderline small positive trial plus a large-trial literature at clinically irrelevant size is MAYBE (weak evidence) for any meaningful benefit.

cards.headline: Chevalier 2010: single hylan injection beat placebo on WOMAC pain by −0.15 points at p=0.047
cards.summary: Chevalier 2010: single hylan injection beat placebo on WOMAC pain by −0.15 points at p=0.047
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, double-blind (one injector/one blinded observer), placebo controlled, multicentre trial
cards.people: 253 patients with primary symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (Kellgren-Lawrence grade II or III) randomly assigned to arthrocentesis plus a single 6 ml intra-articular injection of hylan G-F 20 or placebo, evaluated at 4, 8, 12, 18 and 26 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Patients receiving hylan G-F 20 experienced statistically significantly greater improvements in WOMAC A pain scores than placebo (−0.15, SE 0.076, p=0.047), and in several secondary measures (WOMAC A1, patient and observer global assessments). There was no difference in safety results between groups, and no increased risk of local adverse events in the open repeat-treatment phase. The authors describe the pain relief as clinically relevant; the printed between-group difference is −0.15 points.
cards.watchOut: The authors' 'clinically relevant' conclusion overclaims a −0.15-point difference that reached significance at p=0.047 — flagged on the card face. Single-injection hylan results do not automatically extend to multi-injection or other hyaluronan products.

cards.headline: Rutjes 2012 (REVIEW card): in large blinded trials the pain effect was clinically irrelevant, with more serious adverse events
cards.summary: Rutjes 2012 (REVIEW card): in large blinded trials the pain effect was clinically irrelevant, with more serious adverse events
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis — explicitly a review card, carded beside the primary trial, not as a trial
cards.people: 89 randomised trials involving 12,667 adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis comparing viscosupplementation with sham or nonintervention control; 68 trials had a sham control, 40 had follow-up beyond 3 months, and 22 used cross-linked hyaluronic acid forms.
cards.result: Overall, 71 trials (9,617 patients) showed viscosupplementation moderately reduced pain (effect size −0.37, 95% CI −0.46 to −0.28), but with important heterogeneity and an asymmetrical funnel plot: five unpublished trials (1,149 patients) showed an effect size of −0.03 (−0.14 to 0.09), and 18 large trials with blinded outcome assessment (5,094 patients) showed a clinically irrelevant effect size of −0.11 (−0.18 to −0.04). Six trials (811 patients) showed a non-significant increase in flare-ups (relative risk 1.51 relative, 0.84 to 2.72), and 14 trials (3,667 patients) showed an increased risk of serious adverse events (relative risk 1.41 relative, 1.02 to 1.97). Trial quality was generally low and safety data often unreported.
cards.watchOut: This is a review, carded as a review: its large-trial subgroup is the most trustworthy stratum of this literature and it is the reason the shelf does not grade the Chevalier result higher.
cards.source: Rutjes AW et al. Viscosupplementation for osteoarthritis of the knee: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Annals of internal medicine. 2012. PMID: 22868835. shelves.title: Repeated intra-articular triamcinolone for knee osteoarthritis: cartilage and pain
shelves.question: In adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, does intra-articular triamcinolone 40 mg every 3 months for 2 years reduce knee pain versus saline — and what does it do to cartilage volume?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Arthralgia · Cartilage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Glucocorticoids · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Linear Models · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Sample Size · Sodium Chloride · Synovitis · Triamcinolone Acetonide
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One definitive 2-year double-blind randomised trial (McAlindon 2017, 140 patients with symptomatic knee OA and ultrasound synovitis) found intra-articular triamcinolone 40 mg every 3 months caused significantly GREATER cartilage volume loss than saline (index-compartment cartilage thickness change −0.21 mm vs −0.10 mm; between-group difference −0.11 mm, 95% CI −0.20 to −0.03) and NO significant pain difference (−1.2 vs −1.9 on the WOMAC Likert pain subscale; between-group difference −0.6, −1.6 to 0.3), against a minimal clinically important pain improvement of 3.94 points that neither group approached. Repeated scheduled steroid injection, as tested, loses cartilage and does not relieve pain: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on benefit, with structural harm. Single as-needed injections are a different question, homed elsewhere.

cards.headline: McAlindon 2017: two years of quarterly triamcinolone lost more cartilage than saline and did not reduce pain
cards.summary: McAlindon 2017: two years of quarterly triamcinolone lost more cartilage than saline and did not reduce pain
cards.type: Two-year, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial (Tufts Medical Center)
cards.people: 140 patients fulfilling American College of Rheumatology criteria for symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, Kellgren-Lawrence grades 2 or 3, with ultrasonic features of synovitis (mean age 58 [SD 8] years; 75 women [54%]), receiving intra-articular triamcinolone 40 mg (n=70) or saline (n=70) every 12 weeks for 2 years; 119 (85%) completed the study.
cards.result: Intra-articular triamcinolone resulted in significantly greater cartilage volume loss than saline (mean change in index compartment cartilage thickness −0.21 mm vs −0.10 mm; between-group difference −0.11 mm, 95% CI −0.20 to −0.03 mm) and no significant difference in pain (−1.2 vs −1.9; between-group difference −0.6, 95% CI −1.6 to 0.3) on the WOMAC Likert pain subscale (range 0–20; minimal clinically important improvement 3.94). The saline group had 3 treatment-related adverse events versus 5 in the triamcinolone group, and a small between-group difference in hemoglobin A1c change (−0.2%; −0.5% to −0.007%) favoured saline. The authors conclude the findings do not support this treatment.
cards.watchOut: The minimal clinically important difference for the cartilage outcome is not yet defined, as the record itself states — but the direction (more loss on the drug) plus a flat pain result leaves no benefit story to protect.
cards.source: McAlindon TE et al. Effect of Intra-articular Triamcinolone vs Saline on Knee Cartilage Volume and Pain in Patients With Knee Osteoarthritis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28510679. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01230424, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Sprifermin for knee osteoarthritis (structure modification)
shelves.question: In adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, does intra-articular sprifermin (recombinant FGF-18) increase femorotibial cartilage thickness on MRI versus placebo at 2 years?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cartilage, Articular · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factors · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Knee Joint · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (cartilage thickness) · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (symptoms) — PROPOSED: The FORWARD trial (Hochberg 2019, 549 participants with symptomatic radiographic knee OA) found intra-articular sprifermin 100 µg increased total femorotibial cartilage thickness versus placebo at 2 years (+0.05 mm, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.07, every 6 months; +0.04 mm, 0.02 to 0.06, every 12 months), with the 30 µg doses non-significant — a statistically real MRI effect whose clinical importance the authors themselves call uncertain, with the minimal clinically important difference for the primary outcome unknown. On symptoms there was NO significant difference in total WOMAC score change for any dose — a clean null. One trial, a surrogate structural endpoint, and a symptom null: the split is the honest stamp. Neither half is Tier C (no mortality or event claim).

cards.headline: FORWARD 2019: sprifermin 100 µg thickened cartilage by 0.04–0.05 mm on MRI at 2 years; WOMAC symptoms did not differ
cards.summary: FORWARD 2019: sprifermin 100 µg thickened cartilage by 0.04–0.05 mm on MRI at 2 years; WOMAC symptoms did not differ
cards.type: 5-year, dose-finding, multicenter randomized clinical trial (10 sites); primary outcome at 2 years, follow-up analysis at 3 years
cards.people: 549 participants aged 40 to 85 years with symptomatic, radiographic knee osteoarthritis and Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2 or 3 (median age 65.0 years; 379 female [69.0%]), randomised to sprifermin 100 µg every 6 months (n=110) or every 12 months (n=110), 30 µg every 6 months (n=111) or every 12 months (n=110), or placebo every 6 months (n=108), each treatment being weekly injections over 3 weeks; 474 (86.3%) completed 2-year follow-up.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, changes from baseline to 2 years in total femorotibial joint cartilage thickness were 0.05 mm (95% CI 0.03 to 0.07 mm) for 100 µg sprifermin every 6 months; 0.04 mm (0.02 to 0.06) for 100 µg every 12 months; 0.02 mm (−0.01 to 0.04) for 30 µg every 6 months; and 0.01 mm (−0.01 to 0.03) for 30 µg every 12 months. There were no statistically significant differences in mean absolute change in total WOMAC scores for any sprifermin group versus placebo. The most frequently reported treatment-emergent adverse event was arthralgia (placebo 43.0%; sprifermin groups 36.0–45.0%). The authors state the improvement was statistically significant but of uncertain clinical importance, and durability of response was also uncertain; the minimal clinically important difference for the primary outcome is unknown.
cards.watchOut: Five hundredths of a millimetre of MRI cartilage, with no symptom separation at any dose: structure and symptoms dissociate here, and any 'disease-modifying' claim beyond the MRI number outruns this record.
cards.source: Hochberg MC et al. Effect of Intra-Articular Sprifermin vs Placebo on Femorotibial Joint Cartilage Thickness in Patients With Osteoarthritis: The FORWARD Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 31593273. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01919164, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Tanezumab (anti-nerve growth factor) for osteoarthritis pain
shelves.question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis pain inadequately controlled by standard analgesics, does tanezumab reduce pain and improve function versus placebo — and what joint and sensory harms accompany it?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Female · Headache · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Pain · Pain Measurement · Paresthesia · Receptor, Nerve Growth Factor · Respiratory Tract Infections · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised double-blind trials agree the anti-NGF antibody reduces OA pain: the proof-of-concept trial (Lane 2010, 450 patients with knee OA) found mean reductions in knee pain while walking of 45–62% across tanezumab doses versus 22% on placebo (P<0.001), with OMERACT-OARSI response rates of 74–93% versus 44% and paresthesia in 7%; and the phase 3 trial (Schnitzer 2019, 698 patients with hip or knee OA) found statistically significant but MODEST advantages on all three co-primaries at 16 weeks (WOMAC Pain least-squares mean differences −0.60 and −0.73 on a 0–10 scale), alongside rapidly progressive osteoarthritis only in tanezumab patients (2.2% and 0.4%) and more total joint replacements (3.5% and 6.9% vs 1.7%). Real analgesia, small phase-3 margins, and a joint-safety problem that shadows the class: POSSIBLE. Joint and sensory harms are not cardiovascular events, so the shelf is not Tier C.

cards.headline: Lane 2010: tanezumab cut walking knee pain by 45–62% versus 22% on placebo, with paresthesia in 7%
cards.summary: Lane 2010: tanezumab cut walking knee pain by 45–62% versus 22% on placebo, with paresthesia in 7%
cards.type: Proof-of-concept randomised trial (tanezumab intravenous on days 1 and 56)
cards.people: 450 patients with osteoarthritis of the knee randomly assigned to tanezumab (10, 25, 50, 100, or 200 µg per kilogram of body weight) or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: When averaged over weeks 1 through 16, mean reductions from baseline in knee pain while walking ranged from 45 to 62% with various doses of tanezumab, compared with 22% with placebo (P<0.001). Patient global assessment improvements were 29–47% versus 19% (P≤0.001), and OMERACT-OARSI response rates ranged from 74 to 93% with tanezumab versus 44% with placebo (P<0.001). Adverse event rates were 68% (tanezumab) and 55% (placebo); the most common in tanezumab patients were headache (9%), upper respiratory tract infection (7%), and paresthesia (7%).
cards.watchOut: Percentage reductions from a proof-of-concept dose-ranging trial flatter the drug: the later phase 3 margins on the same constructs were fractions of a point, and this early record predates the class's joint-safety reckoning.
cards.source: Lane NE et al. Tanezumab for the treatment of pain from osteoarthritis of the knee. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20942668. cards.headline: Schnitzer 2019: phase 3 gains were fractions of a point — and rapidly progressive OA appeared only on tanezumab
cards.summary: Schnitzer 2019: phase 3 gains were fractions of a point — and rapidly progressive OA appeared only on tanezumab
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, multicenter trial (subcutaneous tanezumab at day 1 and week 8; outcomes at week 16)
cards.people: 698 patients aged 18 years or older with hip or knee osteoarthritis, inadequate response to OA analgesics, and no radiographic evidence of prespecified joint safety conditions, randomised to tanezumab 2.5 mg (n=231), tanezumab 2.5 mg then 5 mg (n=233), or placebo (n=232); 696 received at least one dose (mean [SD] age 60.8 [9.6] years; 65.1% women) and 582 (83.6%) completed the trial.
cards.result: From baseline to 16 weeks, WOMAC Pain (0–10) fell from 7.1 to 3.6 (tanezumab 2.5 mg) and 7.3 to 3.6 (2.5/5 mg) versus 7.3 to 4.4 (placebo): least-squares mean differences versus placebo −0.60 (95% CI −1.07 to −0.13; P=.01) and −0.73 (−1.20 to −0.26; P=.002). WOMAC Physical Function differences were −0.66 (P=.007) and −0.89 (P<.001), and patient global assessment differences −0.22 (P=.01) and −0.25 (P=.004). Rapidly progressive OA occurred only in tanezumab-treated patients (2.5 mg: n=5, 2.2%; 2.5/5 mg: n=1, 0.4%). Total joint replacements occurred in 8 (3.5%), 16 (6.9%), and 4 (1.7%) patients in the 2.5 mg, 2.5/5 mg, and placebo groups. The authors call the improvements modest and note tanezumab patients had more joint safety events and replacements.
cards.watchOut: Patients with radiographic joint-safety risk features were excluded before randomisation, yet rapidly progressive OA still appeared only on drug — the screened population is the best case for this class's joint safety.
cards.source: Schnitzer TJ et al. Effect of Tanezumab on Joint Pain, Physical Function, and Patient Global Assessment of Osteoarthritis Among Patients With Osteoarthritis of the Hip or Knee: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2019. cards.headline: Synthesis: genuine analgesia, modest phase-3 size, a class-defining joint harm — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: genuine analgesia, modest phase-3 size, a class-defining joint harm — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Lane 2010 (450 patients) and Schnitzer 2019 (698 patients).
cards.result: The arc from 2010 to 2019 is the shelf's lesson: dramatic early percentage effects settled into sub-point phase-3 differences, while the harm signal (rapidly progressive OA, more joint replacements) grew clearer. Efficacy and harm are both real; POSSIBLE prices both.
cards.watchOut: Neither carded trial used tanezumab alongside chronic NSAIDs — the combination in which the joint-safety signal was historically worst — so even these harm rates may understate unscreened real-world use.

shelves.title: Gluteal tendinopathy: education plus exercise versus corticosteroid injection versus wait-and-see (LEAP)
shelves.question: In adults with gluteal tendinopathy (greater trochanteric pain syndrome), does education plus exercise improve global outcome and pain versus corticosteroid injection or a wait-and-see approach at 8 weeks and 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Adult · Aged · Bursitis · Exercise Therapy · Female · Hip Joint · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Education as Topic · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Tendinopathy · Watchful Waiting · Weight-Bearing
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large, well-run three-arm single-blinded randomised trial (LEAP, Mellor 2018, 204 participants with MRI-confirmed gluteal tendinopathy) found education plus exercise (EDX) beat both alternatives on global improvement at 8 weeks (success 51/66 EDX vs 38/65 corticosteroid injection vs 20/68 wait-and-see; EDX vs wait-and-see risk difference 49.1%, 95% CI 34.6% to 63.5%; EDX vs injection 19.9%, 4.7% to 35.0%) and remained better than injection at 52 weeks (success 51/65 vs 36/63; difference 20.4%, 4.9% to 35.9%), while pain at 52 weeks no longer differed between EDX and injection (mean difference −0.26, −1.06 to 0.55). A single trial, but large, pragmatic and decisive on its primary outcome: LIKELY.

cards.headline: LEAP 2018: education plus exercise beat injection and wait-and-see on global improvement at 8 weeks and 12 months
cards.summary: LEAP 2018: education plus exercise beat injection and wait-and-see on global improvement at 8 weeks and 12 months
cards.type: Prospective, three arm, single blinded, randomised clinical trial (Brisbane and Melbourne, Australia)
cards.people: 204 individuals aged 35–70 years with lateral hip pain for more than three months, pain at least 4/10, and gluteal tendinopathy confirmed clinically and by MRI, with no corticosteroid injection in the previous 12 months (167 women; mean age 54.8 years [SD 8.8]), randomised to a physiotherapy-led education and exercise programme of 14 sessions over eight weeks (n=69), one corticosteroid injection (n=66), or wait and see (n=69); 189 (92.6%) completed 52-week follow-up.
cards.result: Success on the global rating of change at eight weeks was reported by 51/66 EDX, 38/65 CSI, and 20/68 WS participants. EDX and CSI had better global improvement than WS (risk difference 49.1% [95% CI 34.6% to 63.5%], number needed to treat 2.0 [1.6 to 2.9]; and 29.2% [13.2% to 45.2%], 3.4 [2.2 to 7.6]; respectively). EDX beat CSI (19.9% [4.7% to 35.0%]; NNT 5.0 [2.9 to 21.1]). Pain (0–10) at eight weeks was 1.5 (SD 1.5) EDX, 2.7 (2.4) CSI, 3.8 (2.0) WS. At 52 weeks, success was 51/65 EDX, 36/63 CSI, 31/60 WS — EDX better than CSI (20.4% [4.9% to 35.9%]; NNT 4.9) and WS (26.8% [11.3% to 42.3%]). Pain at 52 weeks was 2.1 (2.2), 2.3 (1.9) and 3.2 (2.6); EDX did not differ from CSI (−0.26 [−1.06 to 0.55]) but both beat WS.
cards.watchOut: The topic draft's phrasing — that the injection's 'early edge did not persist as an advantage over exercise' — understates the record: the injection never led exercise at any timepoint in this trial; exercise led from week 8 onward on global outcome.
cards.source: Mellor R et al. Education plus exercise versus corticosteroid injection use versus a wait and see approach on global outcome and pain from gluteal tendinopathy: prospective, single blinded, randomised clinical trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2018. PMID: 29720374. Registry ID: ACTRN12612001126808 (Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry), as stated in the record's abstract — no ClinicalTrials.gov databank entry appears in the record. cards.result: The clinically useful ordering is EDX > injection > wait-and-see for global improvement, sustained to a year; injection still beats doing nothing, which matters for patients who cannot engage with a 14-session programme.

shelves.title: Partial versus total knee replacement for medial compartment osteoarthritis (TOPKAT)
shelves.question: In adults with isolated medial compartment knee osteoarthritis suitable for either procedure, does partial (unicompartmental) knee replacement match total knee replacement on patient-reported outcome (Oxford Knee Score) at 5 years, and how do costs and reoperations compare?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Health Care Costs · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Operative Time · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Postoperative Pain · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · Reoperation · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large multicentre pragmatic randomised trial (TOPKAT, Beard 2019, 528 patients with isolated medial compartment knee OA suitable for either operation) found no difference in Oxford Knee Score at 5 years between partial and total knee replacement (mean difference 1.04, 95% CI −0.42 to 2.50; p=0.159), a similar incidence of reoperations and complications, and better cost-effectiveness for partial replacement (0.240 additional quality-adjusted life-years, 0.046 to 0.434; £910 less expensive, −1503 to −317, in UK 2017 prices). A single large trial with 94% five-year follow-up earns LIKELY for equivalence of patient-reported outcome in the eligible population.

cards.headline: TOPKAT 2019: partial and total knee replacement tied on Oxford Knee Score at 5 years; partial cost less and gained more QALYs
cards.summary: TOPKAT 2019: partial and total knee replacement tied on Oxford Knee Score at 5 years; partial cost less and gained more QALYs
cards.type: Multicentre, pragmatic randomised controlled trial at 27 UK sites (combined expertise-based and equipoise-based surgeon allocation)
cards.people: 528 patients with isolated osteoarthritis of the medial compartment of the knee who satisfied general requirements for a medial partial knee replacement, randomly assigned (1:1) to partial or total knee replacement between January 2010 and September 2013; 94% responded to the 5-year follow-up survey. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At the 5-year follow-up there was no difference in Oxford Knee Score between groups (mean difference 1.04, 95% CI −0.42 to 2.50; p=0.159). Partial knee replacement was more effective (0.240 additional quality-adjusted life-years, 95% CI 0.046 to 0.434) and less expensive (−£910, −1503 to −317) than total replacement over 5 years, from slightly better outcomes, lower surgery costs, and lower follow-up health-care costs. Both procedures were effective, with a similar incidence of re-operations and complications, as reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Eligibility required suitability for a partial replacement — most knee OA patients are not in this trial's population — and registry data outside trials have historically shown higher revision rates for partial replacements, a tension this 5-year trial does not fully resolve.
cards.source: Beard DJ et al. The clinical and cost-effectiveness of total versus partial knee replacement in patients with medial compartment osteoarthritis (TOPKAT): 5-year outcomes of a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2019. PMID: 31326135. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01352247, from the record's databank fields (the abstract also states ISRCTN03013488). shelves.title: Spinal manipulation, medication, or home exercise for neck pain
shelves.question: In adults with acute or subacute mechanical neck pain, does spinal manipulation or home exercise with advice relieve pain more than medication over 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen · Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Manipulation, Spinal · Middle Aged · Neck Pain · Pain Measurement · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Bronfort 2012, 272 adults with nonspecific neck pain of 2–12 weeks) found spinal manipulation had a statistically significant pain advantage over medication after 8, 12, 26 and 52 weeks (P≤0.010 at each), home exercise with advice was superior to medication at 26 weeks (P=0.02), and manipulation and home exercise did not differ importantly at any time point. The abstract prints P values without pain-score effect sizes, participants and providers could not be blinded, and no clinically-important-difference criteria were prespecified — a single unblindable trial with incompletely printed figures earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Bronfort 2012: manipulation and home exercise both beat medication on neck pain; they tied each other
cards.summary: Bronfort 2012: manipulation and home exercise both beat medication on neck pain; they tied each other
cards.type: Randomized, controlled trial (1 university research center and 1 pain management clinic, Minnesota)
cards.people: 272 persons aged 18 to 65 years with nonspecific neck pain for 2 to 12 weeks, receiving 12 weeks of spinal manipulation therapy, medication, or home exercise with advice. The abstract does not state the per-group numbers, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: For participant-rated pain, spinal manipulation had a statistically significant advantage over medication after 8, 12, 26, and 52 weeks (P≤0.010), and home exercise with advice was superior to medication at 26 weeks (P=0.02). No important differences in pain were found between manipulation and home exercise at any time point. Results for most secondary outcomes (disability, global improvement, medication use, satisfaction, SF-36) were similar to the primary outcome. The abstract prints no pain-score effect sizes, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: Participants and providers could not be blinded, and the record itself notes no criteria for clinically important group differences were prespecified — statistical separation from medication is shown, its clinical size is not printed.
cards.source: Bronfort G et al. Spinal manipulation, medication, or home exercise with advice for acute and subacute neck pain: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2012. PMID: 22213489. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00029770, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Ultrasound-guided needling and lavage (barbotage) for rotator-cuff calcific tendinitis
shelves.question: In adults with rotator-cuff calcific tendinitis, does ultrasound-guided percutaneous needling and lavage improve shoulder function versus subacromial corticosteroid injection at 1 year?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Calcinosis · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Male · Methylprednisolone · Methylprednisolone Acetate · Middle Aged · Radiography · Regression Analysis · Shoulder Pain · Tendinopathy · Therapeutic Irrigation · Ultrasonography, Interventional
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised trial (de Witte 2013, 48 patients) found ultrasound-guided needling and lavage combined with subacromial corticosteroid injection produced significantly better shoulder function at 1 year than subacromial corticosteroid injection alone — mean Constant score 86.0 (95% CI 80.3 to 91.6) versus 73.9 (67.7 to 80.1); P=.005 — with greater calcification shrinkage (−11.6 ± 6.4 mm vs −5.1 ± 5.7 mm; P=.001) and a baseline-adjusted treatment effect of 20.5 points in favour of barbotage (P=.05). NOTE — topic-file correction: the draft described this trial as 'not superior'; the record shows it WAS superior on its primary outcome at 1 year, and the card follows the record. One small trial earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: de Witte 2013: barbotage plus injection beat injection alone on Constant score at 1 year (86.0 vs 73.9; P=.005)
cards.summary: de Witte 2013: barbotage plus injection beat injection alone on Constant score at 1 year (86.0 vs 73.9; P=.005)
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial; Level of evidence, 1 (as printed in the record)
cards.people: 48 patients with rotator-cuff calcific tendinitis (25 female, 52.1%; mean age 52.0 ± 7.3 years; mean baseline Constant score 68.7 ± 11.9), randomised to ultrasound-guided needling and lavage combined with subacromial corticosteroid injection (group 1, 23 patients) or isolated subacromial corticosteroid injection (group 2); no patients were lost to follow-up.
cards.result: At 1-year follow-up, the mean Constant score in group 1 was 86.0 (95% CI 80.3 to 91.6) versus 73.9 (67.7 to 80.1) in group 2 (P=.005). Mean calcification size decreased by 11.6 ± 6.4 mm in group 1 and 5.1 ± 5.7 mm in group 2 (P=.001); total resorption occurred in 13 patients in group 1 and 6 in group 2 (P=.07). With regression correcting for baseline Constant score and Gärtner type, the mean treatment effect was 20.5 points (P=.05) in favour of barbotage. Four patients in group 1 and 11 in group 2 (P=.06) had an additional barbotage procedure or surgery during follow-up for persisting symptoms. DASH and WORC results were similar in direction.
cards.watchOut: Both groups received the subacromial corticosteroid injection — the trial tests barbotage as an add-on, not barbotage instead of injection — and 48 patients is a small base for a 12-point score difference.
cards.source: de Witte PB et al. Calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff: a randomized controlled trial of ultrasound-guided needling and lavage versus subacromial corticosteroids. The American journal of sports medicine. 2013. PMID: 23696211. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Mesenchymal stem-cell injections for knee osteoarthritis
shelves.question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, does an intra-articular injection of adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells improve pain and function versus conservative care at 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Adipose Tissue · Female · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Male · Mesenchymal Stem Cell Transplantation · Mesenchymal Stem Cells · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Transplantation, Autologous · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The carded randomised trial (Freitag 2019) randomised only 30 participants into three groups (single injection, two injections, or conservative-care control) and its abstract prints NO numerical results at all — it states that both treatment groups showed 'clinically significant pain and functional improvement' at 12 months and that MRI scoring 'indicated modification of disease progression', without effect sizes, confidence intervals or P values. A conclusion of 'safe and effective… may prevent disease progression' drawn on unprinted numbers in 30 patients is the definition of MAYBE (weak evidence) on this library's scale, and the gap between the abstract's claims and its printed data is flagged on the card face. No serious adverse events were observed.

cards.headline: Freitag 2019: a 30-patient stem-cell trial whose abstract claims benefit but prints no numbers
cards.summary: Freitag 2019: a 30-patient stem-cell trial whose abstract claims benefit but prints no numbers
cards.people: 30 participants with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis randomized into three groups: a single intra-articular injection of autologous adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cells (100 × 10^6 cells), two injections (baseline and 6 months), or a control group continuing conservative management. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: As printed in the record's abstract: no serious adverse events were observed; both treatment groups receiving stem cells showed clinically significant pain and functional improvement at completion of follow-up at 12 months; and radiological analysis using the Magnetic Resonance Imaging Osteoarthritis Knee Score indicated modification of disease progression. The abstract reports no effect sizes, score changes, confidence intervals or P values for any of these statements, so none are carded. The authors conclude the therapy 'appears to be a safe and effective therapy for knee osteoarthritis and may have the potential to prevent disease progression'.
cards.watchOut: The authors' conclusion overclaims its own printed record: with ~10 patients per group and no numbers in the abstract, neither efficacy nor disease modification can be weighed. Anyone quoting score improvements for this trial is quoting beyond the verified record.
cards.source: Freitag J et al. Adipose-derived mesenchymal stem cell therapy in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial. Regenerative medicine. 2019. PMID: 30762487. Registry ID: ACTRN12614000814673, as stated in the record's abstract (trial registration number) — no databank registry field appears in the record. shelves.title: Intensive diet and exercise for knee osteoarthritis in overweight older adults (IDEA)
shelves.question: In overweight or obese older adults with knee osteoarthritis, does intensive dietary weight loss combined with exercise reduce knee joint loads, inflammation (IL-6) and pain versus exercise alone over 18 months?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Biomarkers · Biomechanical Phenomena · Body Mass Index · Diet, Reducing · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Inflammation · Interleukin-6 · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Overweight · Pain Measurement · Quality of Life · Self Report · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Weight Loss · Weight-Bearing
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The IDEA trial (Messier 2013, 454 overweight and obese older adults with knee OA) found diet plus exercise produced 11.4% weight loss versus 2.0% with exercise alone over 18 months, with less pain (3.6 vs 4.7 on a 0–20 scale; P=.004 for the exercise comparison), better function (14.1 vs 18.4; P<.001), lower IL-6 (2.7 vs 3.1 pg/mL) and lower knee compressive force in the diet groups (2487 N diet vs 2687 N exercise; pairwise difference 200 N, 95% CI 55 to 345; P=.007). The programme's earlier ADAPT trial (316 participants) agrees: diet plus exercise beat the healthy-lifestyle control on function, pain and mobility. Two concordant randomised trials from one programme earn LIKELY.

cards.headline: IDEA 2013: diet plus exercise lost 11.4% of body weight and beat exercise alone on pain, function, IL-6 and joint load
cards.summary: IDEA 2013: diet plus exercise lost 11.4% of body weight and beat exercise alone on pain, function, IL-6 and joint load
cards.type: Single-blind, 18-month, randomized clinical trial (Wake Forest University)
cards.people: 454 overweight and obese older community-dwelling adults (age ≥55 years, body mass index 27–41) with pain and radiographic knee OA, assigned to intensive diet-induced weight loss plus exercise, intensive diet-induced weight loss alone, or exercise alone; 399 participants (88%) completed the study. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Mean weight loss was 10.6 kg (11.4%) for diet + exercise, 8.9 kg (9.5%) for diet, and 1.8 kg (2.0%) for exercise. After 18 months, knee compressive forces were lower in diet participants (mean 2487 N; 95% CI 2393 to 2581) than exercise participants (2687 N; 2590 to 2784; pairwise difference 200 N, 55 to 345; P=.007). IL-6 was lower in diet + exercise (2.7 pg/mL) and diet (2.7) than exercise (3.1). The diet + exercise group had less pain (3.6; 3.2 to 4.1) and better function (14.1; 12.6 to 15.6) than both the diet group (4.8; 4.3 to 5.2) and the exercise group (4.7; 4.2 to 5.1; difference for pain 1.02, 0.33 to 1.71; P=.004; for function 4.29, 2.07 to 6.50; P<.001), and better physical health-related quality of life than exercise (44.7 vs 41.9; P=.005).

shelves.title: Botulinum toxin A for post-stroke upper-limb spasticity
shelves.question: In adults with wrist and finger spasticity after stroke, does intramuscular botulinum toxin A improve muscle tone (Modified Ashworth) and global function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies · Botulinum Toxins, Type A · Persons with Disabilities · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fingers · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Spasticity · Neuromuscular Agents · Recovery of Function · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation · Wrist
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (Brashear 2002, 126 subjects with wrist and finger flexor spasticity after stroke) met its primary outcome: at week 6, 62% of botulinum toxin A subjects versus 27% on placebo reported improvement of at least one point on the Disability Assessment Scale in their self-chosen principal target of treatment (P<0.001), with greater improvement in the principal target at weeks 4, 6, 8 and 12 and greater improvement in flexor tone at all follow-up visits through 12 weeks (P<0.001 for all tone comparisons; the abstract prints no tone scores, so none are carded — and the trial's primary outcome was disability, not the Modified Ashworth framing in the shelf question, which is disclosed on the card). No major adverse events were associated with injection. The wider botulinum-toxin programme named in the topic draft was not pinned at build; on the pinned record, one trial: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Brashear 2002: botulinum toxin A doubled the rate of disability improvement in the patient's chosen target (62% vs 27% at week 6) and improved flexor tone through 12 weeks
cards.summary: Brashear 2002: botulinum toxin A doubled the rate of disability improvement in the patient's chosen target (62% vs 27% at week 6) and improved flexor tone through 12 weeks
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicenter trial (one-time injections; 12 weeks of follow-up)
cards.people: 126 subjects with increased flexor tone in the wrist and fingers after a stroke, receiving one-time intramuscular injections of botulinum toxin type A (200 to 240 units; 64 subjects) or placebo (62); at baseline each subject selected one of four disability areas (personal hygiene, dressing, pain, limb position) with moderate-to-severe disability as the principal target of treatment. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome was self-reported disability on the Disability Assessment Scale in the principal target of treatment at 6 weeks. Subjects treated with botulinum toxin A had greater improvement in the principal target at weeks 4, 6, 8 and 12 (P<0.001, P<0.001, P=0.03 and P=0.02 respectively); at week 6, 40 of 64 (62%) in the botulinum toxin group versus 17 of 62 (27%) on placebo reported improvement of at least one point in the principal target (P<0.001) — an absolute difference of about 35 percentage points. Subjects receiving botulinum toxin A also had greater improvement in flexor tone in the wrist and fingers at all follow-up visits through 12 weeks (P<0.001 for all comparisons; no tone scores are printed in the abstract). There were no major adverse events associated with the injection.
cards.watchOut: The question foregrounds Modified Ashworth tone; the trial's primary outcome was patient-chosen disability, and tone is reported only as significance. A self-reported disability primary outcome in a trial where injection effects can be felt is vulnerable to partial unblinding — the size of the gap (62% vs 27%) is nonetheless large.
cards.source: Brashear A et al. Intramuscular injection of botulinum toxin for the treatment of wrist and finger spasticity after a stroke. The New England journal of medicine. 2002. PMID: 12167681. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Functional electrical stimulation versus ankle–foot orthosis for foot drop after stroke
shelves.question: In adults with foot drop from chronic stroke, does peroneal-nerve functional electrical stimulation improve gait speed and walking outcomes comparably with a standard ankle–foot orthosis over 30 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Ankle · Chronic Disease · Electric Stimulation Therapy · Female · Foot · Foot Orthoses · Gait Disorders, Neurologic · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Peroneal Nerve · Quality of Life · Recovery of Function · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre randomised trial (Bethoux 2014, 495 Medicare-eligible individuals at least 6 months post-stroke, wearing FES or an AFO for 6 months; 399 completed) found peroneal-nerve functional electrical stimulation NONINFERIOR to an ankle-foot orthosis on all primary endpoints (10-Meter Walk Test, a Stroke Impact Scale composite, and device-related serious adverse event rate), with both groups improving significantly on the walk test and NO between-group differences on secondary endpoints — the authors' conclusion is equivalence, not superiority, and outcome assessments were unblinded. The abstract prints no walk-speed figures, so none are carded. One large trial answering a comparability question: POSSIBLE. The Kottink trial series named in the topic draft was not pinned at build and is fenced.

cards.headline: Bethoux 2014: FES was noninferior to AFO on all primary endpoints over 6 months, with no between-group differences — equivalence, not superiority (495 randomised)
cards.summary: Bethoux 2014: FES was noninferior to AFO on all primary endpoints over 6 months, with no between-group differences — equivalence, not superiority (495 randomised)
cards.type: Multicenter randomized controlled trial (6 months of device use; unblinded outcome assessments; multiply imputed intention-to-treat analyses)
cards.people: 495 Medicare-eligible individuals at least 6 months post-stroke with foot drop, randomised to wear peroneal-nerve functional electrical stimulation or an ankle-foot orthosis for 6 months; 399 subjects completed the study. Primary endpoints were the 10-Meter Walk Test, a composite of the Mobility, Activities of Daily Living/Instrumental ADL and Social Participation subscores of the Stroke Impact Scale, and device-related serious adverse event rate. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: FES proved noninferior to the AFO for all primary endpoints. Both the FES and AFO groups improved significantly on the 10-Meter Walk Test. Within the FES group, significant improvements were found for the SIS composite score, total modified Emory Functional Ambulation Profile score, individual floor and obstacle course times, Functional Ambulation Profile and Berg Balance Scale — but no between-group differences were found on secondary endpoints. The authors conclude use of FES is equivalent to the AFO. No numerical gait-speed or scale values are printed in the abstract, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority with unblinded outcome assessment, in a trial losing 96 of 495 participants before completion: equivalence is the claim, and it is also the ceiling. Preference advantages sometimes quoted for FES are not between-group results in this record.
cards.source: Bethoux F et al. The effects of peroneal nerve functional electrical stimulation versus ankle-foot orthosis in patients with chronic stroke: a randomized controlled trial. Neurorehabilitation and neural repair. 2014. PMID: 24526708. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01087957, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Aerobic (treadmill) exercise training after stroke
shelves.question: In adults with chronic stroke and residual gait deficits, does a 6-month progressive treadmill aerobic exercise programme improve peak fitness (VO2) and ambulatory function versus a stretching control?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Analysis of Variance · Brain Ischemia · Cardiovascular System · Double-Blind Method · Exercise · Exercise Test · Exercise Therapy · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Gait · Gait Disorders, Neurologic · Hemiplegia · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Physical Endurance · Physical Fitness · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation · Surveys and Questionnaires · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised controlled trial (Macko 2005, 61 adults with chronic hemiparetic gait after ischemic stroke; 45 completed — 25 treadmill, 20 control) found 6 months of progressive treadmill aerobic exercise (3 times weekly) beat a reference programme of stretching plus low-intensity walking on cardiovascular fitness (VO2 peak +17% vs +3%; P<0.005 — only the treadmill group improved fitness), 6-minute walk performance (+30% vs +11%; P<0.02) and Walking Impairment Questionnaire distance scores (+56% vs +12%; P<0.05), with all figures printed as percentage changes rather than absolute values. A single small trial with 26% attrition earns POSSIBLE. The Cochrane fitness-after-stroke summary named in the topic draft is a review, not pinned or carded as evidence beside the primary trial.

cards.headline: Macko 2005: treadmill training improved VO2 peak (+17% vs +3%), 6-minute walk (+30% vs +11%) and mobility scores versus stretching control in chronic stroke
cards.summary: Macko 2005: treadmill training improved VO2 peak (+17% vs +3%), 6-minute walk (+30% vs +11%) and mobility scores versus stretching control in chronic stroke
cards.type: Randomized, controlled trial (6 months, 3 sessions per week)
cards.people: 61 adults with chronic hemiparetic gait after ischemic stroke (more than 6 months), randomized to 6 months of progressive treadmill aerobic exercise (T-AEX) or a reference rehabilitation program of stretching plus low-intensity walking (R-CONTROL); 25 patients completed T-AEX and 20 completed R-CONTROL. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Only treadmill training increased cardiovascular fitness (VO2 peak +17% versus +3% change, T-AEX versus R-CONTROL; P<0.005). Group-by-time analyses showed treadmill training improved ambulatory performance on 6-minute walks (+30% versus +11%; P<0.02) and mobility function on Walking Impairment Questionnaire distance scores (+56% versus +12%; P<0.05). Within the treadmill group, increasing training velocity predicted improved VO2 peak (r=0.43; P<0.05) but not walking function, while increasing session duration predicted improved 6-minute walk (r=0.41; P<0.05) but not fitness gains. All outcome figures in the abstract are percentage changes from baseline; absolute VO2 and walk-distance values are not printed and none are carded.
cards.watchOut: Sixteen of 61 randomised patients did not complete — a completers-heavy reading of a demanding 6-month intervention — and percentage gains on small baselines can look larger than the absolute functional change. The control was an active stretching/low-intensity programme, so the contrast is intensity and mode, not exercise versus nothing.
cards.source: Macko RF et al. Treadmill exercise rehabilitation improves ambulatory function and cardiovascular fitness in patients with chronic stroke: a randomized, controlled trial. Stroke. 2005. PMID: 16151035. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.
