shelves.title: Self-managed computerised speech and language therapy for chronic aphasia after stroke (Big CACTUS)
shelves.question: In adults with chronic post-stroke aphasia, does self-managed computerised word-finding therapy improve word retrieval versus usual care or attention control at 6 months — and does it improve functional conversation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aphasia · Attention · Female · Humans · Language Therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Single-Blind Method · Speech Therapy · Stroke · Stroke Rehabilitation · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — split by outcome, and the split is the finding: One large pragmatic multicentre single-blinded randomised trial (Big CACTUS, Palmer 2019, 278 participants with aphasia at least 4 months post-stroke) found 6 months of self-managed computerised speech and language therapy plus usual care improved personally relevant word finding by 16.2 percentage points versus usual care (95% CI 12.7 to 19.6; P<0.0001) and by 14.4 points versus attention control (10.8 to 18.1), comfortably beyond the 10% difference prespecified as clinically meaningful — but produced NO improvement in functional communication on masked ratings of video-recorded conversation (mean difference in change versus usual care −0.03, −0.21 to 0.14; P=0.709). POSSIBLE for word retrieval; the record shows no benefit for functional conversation, and the shelf says both.

cards.headline: Big CACTUS 2019: computer therapy improved word finding by 16.2 points versus usual care but did not improve functional conversation (P=0.709)
cards.summary: Big CACTUS 2019: computer therapy improved word finding by 16.2 points versus usual care but did not improve functional conversation (P=0.709)
cards.type: Pragmatic, superiority, three-arm, individually randomised, single-blind, parallel group trial (21 UK speech and language therapy departments)
cards.people: 278 participants aged 18 years or older with aphasia post-stroke at least 4 months before randomisation (101 usual care; 97 computerised speech and language therapy [CSLT] plus usual care; 80 attention control plus usual care); the modified intention-to-treat population comprised 86 (usual care), 83 (CSLT) and 71 (attention control) participants with 6-month outcomes. Outcome assessors and the trial statistician were masked.
cards.result: Mean word finding improvements were 1.1% (SD 11.2) with usual care, 16.4% (15.3) with CSLT and 2.4% (8.8) with attention control. Word finding improvement was 16.2% (95% CI 12.7 to 19.6; P<0.0001) higher with CSLT than usual care and 14.4% (10.8 to 18.1) higher than attention control. Mean changes in functional communication (Therapy Outcome Measures, masked ratings of video-recorded conversations) were 0.05 (SD 0.59) for usual care, 0.04 (0.58) for CSLT and 0.10 (0.61) for attention control; the mean difference in change between CSLT and usual care was −0.03 (−0.21 to 0.14; P=0.709) — no benefit on the co-primary functional outcome, against a standardised mean difference of 0.45 prespecified as clinically meaningful.
cards.watchOut: Two co-primary outcomes pointing opposite ways: naming the trained words improved substantially while conversation — the outcome patients ultimately care about — did not measurably change. Quoting only the word-finding result misrepresents this trial.
cards.source: Palmer R et al. Self-managed, computerised speech and language therapy for patients with chronic aphasia post-stroke compared with usual care or attention control (Big CACTUS): a multicentre, single-blinded, randomised controlled trial. shelves.question: In patients with dementia or Parkinson's disease who aspirate thin liquids on videofluoroscopy, does a chin-down posture or nectar/honey-thickened liquids reduce the 3-month incidence of pneumonia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Deglutition Disorders · Dementia · Drinking · Female · Frail Elderly · Honey · Humans · Incidence · Male · Middle Aged · Parkinson Disease · Patient Compliance · Pneumonia, Aspiration · Posture · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): One large randomised trial (Robbins 2008, 515 patients aged 50 or older with dementia or Parkinson disease who aspirated thin liquids on videofluoroscopy; 504 followed) found NO significant difference in 3-month pneumonia incidence between chin-down posture (9.8%) and thickened liquids (11.6%; hazard ratio 0.84 relative, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.45; P=0.53), and no significant difference between nectar-thick (8.4%) and honey-thick (15.0%; HR 0.50 relative, 0.23 to 1.09; P=0.083) — with more dehydration (6% vs 2%), urinary tract infection (6% vs 3%) and fever (4% vs 2%) on thickened liquids. The authors state no definitive conclusions about superiority can be made, and there was no untreated control group, so the null is a null between strategies, not proof that all strategies are useless. The companion videofluoroscopy study (Logemann 2008, 711 patients) found honey-thick liquids most often eliminated aspiration immediately, then nectar-thick, then chin-down. The topic draft attributed the pneumonia trial to Logemann; its first author is Robbins J — corrected on the card. One trial programme: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Pneumonia incidence is the primary outcome; it is not a mortality/CV claim, so this shelf is not Tier C.

cards.headline: Robbins 2008: pneumonia incidence did not differ between chin-down posture (9.8%) and thickened liquids (11.6%) at 3 months (HR 0.84; P=0.53)
cards.summary: Robbins 2008: pneumonia incidence did not differ between chin-down posture (9.8%) and thickened liquids (11.6%) at 3 months (HR 0.84; P=0.53)
cards.type: Randomized, controlled, parallel-design trial (47 hospitals and 79 subacute care facilities; 3-month follow-up)
cards.people: 515 patients age 50 years or older with dementia or Parkinson disease who aspirated thin liquids on videofluoroscopy, randomly assigned to drink all liquids in a chin-down posture (n=259) or to drink nectar-thick (n=133) or honey-thick (n=123) liquids in a head-neutral position; 504 were followed until death or for 3 months. Care providers were not blinded. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Fifty-two participants developed pneumonia, an overall estimated 3-month cumulative incidence of 11%. The 3-month cumulative incidence was 0.098 with chin-down posture versus 0.116 with thickened liquids (hazard ratio 0.84 — a relative measure — [95% CI 0.49 to 1.45]; P=0.53), and 0.084 with nectar-thick versus 0.150 with honey-thick liquids (HR 0.50 relative [0.23 to 1.09]; P=0.083). More patients assigned to thickened liquids than to chin-down posture had dehydration (6% vs 2%), urinary tract infection (6% vs 3%) and fever (4% vs 2%). The authors conclude that no definitive conclusions about the superiority of any tested intervention can be made, note the absence of a no-treatment control group, and observe that the observed pneumonia incidence was much lower than expected.
cards.watchOut: A null between active strategies with wide confidence intervals (the chin-down interval 0.49 to 1.45 relative admits meaningful benefit or harm) and no untreated arm: the trial says the strategies did not separate, not that aspiration management does not matter. The nectar-versus-honey contrast trends AGAINST the thicker liquid — the opposite of the immediate-aspiration result in the companion study below.
cards.source: Robbins J et al. Comparison of 2 interventions for liquid aspiration on pneumonia incidence: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2008. PMID: 18378947. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00000362, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Logemann 2008 (companion study): honey-thick liquids most often eliminated aspiration immediately on videofluoroscopy — an immediate-effect study, not a pneumonia trial
cards.summary: Logemann 2008 (companion study): honey-thick liquids most often eliminated aspiration immediately on videofluoroscopy — an immediate-effect study, not a pneumonia trial
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (all 3 interventions applied in randomly assigned order during the videofluorographic swallow study)
cards.people: 711 patients ages 50 to 95 years with dementia and/or Parkinson's disease who aspirated on thin liquids as assessed videofluorographically; every patient received chin-down posture, nectar-thickened liquids and honey-thickened liquids in a randomly assigned order during the study. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Immediate elimination of aspiration on thin liquids occurred most often with honey-thickened liquids for patients in each diagnostic category, followed by nectar-thickened liquids and chin-down posture. Patients with the most severe dementia exhibited the least effectiveness on all interventions. Patient preference was best for chin-down posture, followed closely by nectar-thickened liquids. The abstract prints no percentages for elimination rates, so none are carded. The authors conclude a videofluorographic assessment is needed to identify the best short-term intervention for an individual patient, and that the longer-term impact of short-term prevention requires further study.
cards.watchOut: Immediate elimination of aspiration on a swallow study is a surrogate for the pneumonia outcome in the Robbins trial above — and the two point in different directions for honey-thick liquids (best immediately, worst pneumonia trend). Carding this study as pneumonia evidence would be an error; it is carded as the immediate-effect companion it is.
cards.source: Logemann JA et al. A randomized study of three interventions for aspiration of thin liquids in patients with dementia or Parkinson's disease. Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR. 2008. PMID: 18230864. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: strategies did not separate on pneumonia; immediate aspiration control and 3-month outcomes disagree — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: strategies did not separate on pneumonia; immediate aspiration control and 3-month outcomes disagree — POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Robbins 2008 (515 patients, 3-month pneumonia) and Logemann 2008 (711 patients, immediate videofluoroscopic elimination) — one trial programme, two linked studies.
cards.result: The programme's combined message is uncomfortable and important: the strategy that best stops aspiration on the day (honey-thick) carried the highest pneumonia point estimate at 3 months and the most dehydration, while no strategy beat another significantly on pneumonia (overall incidence 11%). Individual videofluoroscopic tailoring, per the companion study, remains the programme's practical residue.
cards.watchOut: There is no no-treatment arm anywhere in this programme, so 'do nothing' is not an evidence-based reading of the null.
cards.source: Synthesis of Robbins J et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2008. PMID: 18378947; Logemann JA et al. Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR. 2008. PMID: 18230864. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Whole-body vibration for bone density and postural control in postmenopausal women
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women, does 6 months of whole-body vibration training improve hip bone mineral density, muscle strength and postural control versus resistance training or no exercise?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Bone Density · Exercise · Female · Hip · Humans · Middle Aged · Muscle, Skeletal · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal · Pilot Projects · Postmenopause · Postural Balance · Posture · Radiography · Time Factors · Vibration
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised controlled PILOT trial (Verschueren 2004, 70 postmenopausal women aged 58–74) found 24 weeks of whole-body vibration training (3 times weekly) increased hip bone mineral density by +0.93% (P<0.05) while resistance training (−0.60%) and no-exercise control (−0.62%) showed no significant change, and improved isometric (+15%) and dynamic (+16%) muscle strength (both P<0.01), with no vibration-related side effects and no change in serum bone-turnover markers in any group. The stamp is POSSIBLE and no higher: 70 women, a surrogate endpoint (DXA hip BMD), and a pilot design. The record's rationale cites ANIMAL models of vibration loading; no animal data are carded — the human trial is the only evidence on this shelf. Postural-control results are not reported with figures in the abstract, so none are carded.

cards.headline: Verschueren 2004: whole-body vibration raised hip BMD by +0.93% and strength by 15–16% over 24 weeks in a 70-woman pilot trial
cards.summary: Verschueren 2004: whole-body vibration raised hip BMD by +0.93% and strength by 15–16% over 24 weeks in a 70-woman pilot trial
cards.type: Randomized controlled pilot study (24 weeks; three parallel groups)
cards.people: 70 postmenopausal women volunteers aged 58–74 years, randomly assigned to whole body vibration training (WBV, n=25; static and dynamic knee-extensor exercises on a vibration platform at 35–40 Hz, 2.28–5.09 g, three times weekly), resistance training (RES, n=22; dynamic leg press and leg extension progressing from 20 RM to 8 RM) or a no-training control group (CON, n=23), for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Vibration training significantly increased hip bone mineral density by +0.93% (P<0.05); no changes in hip BMD were observed in the resistance training (−0.60%) or control (−0.62%) groups (not significant). Vibration training also improved isometric and dynamic muscle strength (+15% and +16% respectively; P<0.01). Serum markers of bone turnover did not change in any group, and no vibration-related side effects were observed. The authors conclude WBV may be a feasible way to modify risk factors for falls and fractures and call for further human studies.
cards.watchOut: A +0.93% BMD difference is a surrogate movement, not a fracture outcome, in a pilot of 25 treated women; the record's opening rationale rests on animal models (fenced — none carded), and the abstract reports no fracture, fall or postural-control figures despite the trial's title naming postural control.
cards.source: Verschueren SM et al. Effect of 6-month whole body vibration training on hip density, muscle strength, and postural control in postmenopausal women: a randomized controlled pilot study. Journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. 2004. PMID: 15040822. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small positive pilot on a bone-density surrogate — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small positive pilot on a bone-density surrogate — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Verschueren 2004 (70 postmenopausal women).
cards.result: Whole-body vibration was the only arm to gain hip BMD and it gained strength as well, against two comparators that did neither. Pilot scale and a surrogate endpoint hold the stamp at POSSIBLE; the fracture question is unaddressed by this record.

shelves.title: Prefabricated foot orthoses for patellofemoral pain
shelves.question: In adults with patellofemoral pain, do prefabricated foot orthoses improve global outcome versus flat inserts, physiotherapy, or their combination over 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Orthotic Devices · Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome · Physical Therapy Modalities · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One prospective single-blind factorial randomised trial (Collins 2008, 179 participants aged 18–40 with patellofemoral pain in Brisbane, Australia) found prefabricated foot orthoses beat flat inserts on global improvement at 6 weeks (relative risk reduction 0.66 as printed, 99% CI 0.05 to 1.17; NNT 4, 99% CI 2 to 51), but found NO significant differences between foot orthoses and physiotherapy, or between physiotherapy and physiotherapy plus orthoses, and all groups showed clinically meaningful improvements over 52 weeks with no between-group separation at 12 months. The honest summary is a short-term edge over a flat insert only: POSSIBLE. The 'relative risk reduction' line as printed carries a confidence interval extending above 1.0 — an internal awkwardness in the record, flagged on the card and carded as printed.

cards.headline: Collins 2008: orthoses beat flat inserts at 6 weeks (NNT 4) but matched physiotherapy, added nothing to it, and did not separate at 12 months
cards.summary: Collins 2008: orthoses beat flat inserts at 6 weeks (NNT 4) but matched physiotherapy, added nothing to it, and did not separate at 12 months
cards.type: Prospective, single blind, randomised clinical trial (2×2 factorial elements; single centre, community setting, Brisbane, Australia)
cards.people: 179 participants (100 women) aged 18 to 40 years with a clinical diagnosis of patellofemoral pain syndrome of more than six weeks' duration and no foot orthoses or physiotherapy in the preceding 12 months, receiving 6 weeks of off-the-shelf foot orthoses, flat inserts, multimodal physiotherapy (patellofemoral joint mobilisation, patellar taping, quadriceps retraining, education), or foot orthoses plus physiotherapy; outcomes at 6, 12 and 52 weeks.
cards.result: Foot orthoses produced improvement beyond flat inserts in the short term, notably at six weeks (relative risk reduction 0.66, 99% confidence interval 0.05 to 1.17; NNT 4 (99% CI 2 to 51)) — the printed interval for a 'risk reduction' extending above 1.0 is internally awkward and is carded exactly as printed. No significant differences were found between foot orthoses and physiotherapy, or between physiotherapy and physiotherapy plus orthoses. All groups showed clinically meaningful improvements in primary outcomes over 52 weeks. The authors conclude orthoses are superior to flat inserts by participants' overall perception, similar to physiotherapy, and do not improve outcomes when added to physiotherapy, while possibly hastening recovery.
cards.watchOut: The only beaten comparator is a flat insert at 6 weeks; against active physiotherapy the orthosis is a match, not an addition. Global improvement is a participant-perception outcome in a single-blind trial — the perception is the outcome by design, and also its weakness.
cards.source: Collins N et al. Foot orthoses and physiotherapy in the treatment of patellofemoral pain syndrome: randomised clinical trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2008. PMID: 18952682. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00118521, from the record's databank fields (the abstract text also names Australian Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN012605000463673). shelves.title: Hip abductor and external rotator strengthening for patellofemoral pain
shelves.question: In women with patellofemoral pain, does an 8-week programme of isolated hip abductor and external rotator strengthening reduce pain and improve function versus no intervention?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Analysis of Variance · Biomechanical Phenomena · Confidence Intervals · Exercise Therapy · Female · Health Status · Hip Joint · Humans · Isometric Contraction · Muscle Strength · Muscle Strength Dynamometer · Muscle Weakness · Pain Measurement · Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome · Physical Therapy Modalities · Radiography · Self Report · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised controlled trial (Khayambashi 2012, 28 women with patellofemoral pain; 14 exercise, 14 no-exercise control) found significant group-by-time interactions for every outcome: an 8-week programme of isolated hip abductor and external rotator strengthening (3 times weekly) improved pain (visual analog scale), health status (WOMAC) and bilateral hip strength versus control, with pain and health-status gains sustained at 6 months in the exercise group. The stamp is POSSIBLE and no higher: 28 participants, and the abstract prints NO numerical pain or function values — significance and direction only — so no effect sizes are carded. The Dolak et al. trial named in the topic draft was not pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced without figures.

cards.headline: Khayambashi 2012: isolated hip strengthening improved pain, health status and hip strength versus no exercise in 28 women — no effect sizes printed
cards.summary: Khayambashi 2012: isolated hip strengthening improved pain, health status and hip strength versus no exercise in 28 women — no effect sizes printed
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (8-week intervention; 6-month follow-up of the exercise group)
cards.people: 28 females with patellofemoral pain, sequentially assigned to an exercise group (n=14) completing bilateral hip abductor and external rotator strengthening 3 times per week for 8 weeks, or a no-exercise control group (n=14); pain (visual analog scale), health status (WOMAC) and hip strength (handheld dynamometer) were assessed at baseline and postintervention, with pain and health status also evaluated at 6 months in the exercise group. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Significant group-by-time interactions were observed for each variable of interest. Post hoc testing showed pain, health status and bilateral hip strength improved in the exercise group following the 8-week intervention and did not change in the control group; improvements in pain and health status were sustained at 6-month follow-up in the exercise group. The abstract reports no numerical values for pain, WOMAC or strength outcomes, so none are carded. The authors conclude isolated hip strengthening was effective and should be considered in rehabilitation programmes for females with patellofemoral pain (therapy, level 2b, as the record states).
cards.watchOut: 'Sequentially assigned' in a 28-person trial, no printed magnitudes, and a 6-month follow-up measured only in the exercise group (no controlled durability claim is possible): this is a promising small trial, and the card must not be inflated beyond it.
cards.source: Khayambashi K et al. The effects of isolated hip abductor and external rotator muscle strengthening on pain, health status, and hip strength in females with patellofemoral pain: a randomized controlled trial. The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy. 2012. PMID: 22027216. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Lateral wedge insoles for medial knee osteoarthritis
shelves.question: In adults with medial knee osteoarthritis, do lateral wedge insoles reduce knee pain and slow cartilage loss versus flat control insoles over 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Arthralgia · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Orthotic Devices · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Patient Compliance · Patient Satisfaction · Shoes · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One well-conducted randomised controlled trial (Bennell 2011, 200 people aged 50 or more with mild to moderately severe medial knee osteoarthritis in Melbourne, Australia) found 12 months of full-length 5-degree lateral wedge insoles provided NO symptomatic or structural benefit versus flat control insoles: the between-group difference in change in overall knee pain was −0.3 points (95% CI −1.0 to 0.3) and in medial tibial cartilage volume −0.4 mm3 (−15.4 to 14.6), with confidence intervals that did not include minimal clinically important differences, and no differences in any secondary outcome. A large, precise null on both co-primary questions carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The earlier wedge trials named in the topic draft were not pinned at build and are not needed for the stamp.

cards.headline: Bennell 2011: lateral wedge insoles gave no pain or cartilage benefit over flat insoles at 12 months (pain difference −0.3 points; cartilage −0.4 mm3)
cards.summary: Bennell 2011: lateral wedge insoles gave no pain or cartilage benefit over flat insoles at 12 months (pain difference −0.3 points; cartilage −0.4 mm3)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (community setting, Melbourne, Australia; 12 months)
cards.people: 200 people aged 50 or more with a clinical and radiographic diagnosis of mild to moderately severe medial knee osteoarthritis, wearing full-length 5-degree lateral wedged insoles or flat control insoles inside their shoes daily for 12 months. Primary outcomes were change in overall knee pain (past week, 11-point numerical rating scale) and change in medial tibial cartilage volume on MRI. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Between-group differences did not differ significantly for either primary outcome: change in overall pain −0.3 points (95% confidence interval −1.0 to 0.3) and change in medial tibial cartilage volume −0.4 mm3 (−15.4 to 14.6), and the confidence intervals did not include minimal clinically important differences. None of the changes in secondary outcomes (pain, function, stiffness, health-related quality of life, progression of medial cartilage defects and bone marrow lesions) showed differences between groups. The authors conclude lateral wedge insoles worn for 12 months provided no symptomatic or structural benefits compared with flat control insoles.
cards.watchOut: The null is strong for THIS prescription (full-length 5-degree wedges, all-day wear, mild-to-moderate disease): it does not test other wedge angles, heel-only wedges, or bracing — knee bracing is a separate question on Shelf #1529.
cards.source: Bennell KL et al. Lateral wedge insoles for medial knee osteoarthritis: 12 month randomised controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2011. PMID: 21593096. shelves.title: Knee bracing (neoprene sleeve and valgus unloader brace) for knee osteoarthritis
shelves.question: In adults with varus gonarthrosis, does a valgus unloader brace or a neoprene sleeve improve pain and function versus no brace over 6 months?
shelves.mesh: Bone Diseases, Developmental · Braces · Female · Humans · Knee · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One prospective parallel-group randomised clinical trial (Kirkley 1999, 119 patients with osteoarthritis with varus deformity of the knee) found both a neoprene sleeve and a custom-made valgus-producing unloader brace, each added to medical treatment, significantly improved disease-specific quality of life (P=0.001) and function (P≤0.001) at 6 months versus medical treatment only, with the unloader brace significantly better than the sleeve on pain after the six-minute walking test (P=0.021) and the thirty-second stair-climbing test (P=0.016), and only a trend on the WOMAC aggregate (P=0.062). The abstract prints significance levels without effect sizes, so no magnitudes are carded. A single older, unblinded-by-nature device trial earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Kirkley 1999: both a neoprene sleeve and an unloader brace improved quality of life and function versus medical treatment alone at 6 months; the unloader won on pain after walking and stair tests
cards.summary: Kirkley 1999: both a neoprene sleeve and an unloader brace improved quality of life and function versus medical treatment alone at 6 months; the unloader won on pain after walking and stair tests
cards.type: Prospective, parallel-group, randomized clinical trial (computer-generated block randomization, sealed envelopes; stratified by age, deformity and ACL status)
cards.people: 119 patients with varus gonarthrosis randomised to medical treatment only (control; 40 patients, 31 men and 9 women, mean age 60.9 years), medical treatment plus a neoprene sleeve (38 patients, 27 men and 11 women, mean age 58.2 years), or medical treatment plus a custom-made valgus-producing functional unloader brace (41 patients, 28 men and 13 women, mean age 59.5 years); 9 patients withdrew. Disease-specific quality of life was measured with the WOMAC and MACTAR questionnaires and function with the six-minute walking and thirty-second stair-climbing tests; the primary outcome was the analysis of covariance of change between baseline and six months.
cards.result: At the six-month follow-up, there was a significant improvement in disease-specific quality of life (P=0.001) and in function (P≤0.001) in both the neoprene-sleeve group and the unloader-brace group compared with the control group. The unloader brace differed significantly from the neoprene sleeve on pain after the six-minute walking test (P=0.021) and after the thirty-second stair-climbing test (P=0.016); the difference between unloader brace and sleeve on change in WOMAC aggregate (P=0.062) and WOMAC physical function (P=0.081) was a strong trend, not significance. The abstract prints no score changes, so no effect sizes are carded. The authors conclude patients with varus gonarthrosis may benefit significantly from a knee brace in addition to standard medical treatment, with the unloader brace on average more effective than the sleeve.
cards.watchOut: A brace cannot be blinded against no brace, the outcomes are patient-reported or effort-dependent, and the record is from 1999 — background medical treatment has changed since. The WOMAC trend (P=0.062) must not be upgraded to a brace-versus-sleeve quality-of-life advantage; the significant brace-versus-sleeve differences are confined to post-test pain.
cards.source: Kirkley A et al. The effect of bracing on varus gonarthrosis. The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume. 1999. PMID: 10225800. shelves.title: Six versus twelve weeks of antibiotics for pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis
shelves.question: In adults with pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, is 6 weeks of antibiotic therapy non-inferior to 12 weeks for cure at one year?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteomyelitis · Single-Blind Method · Spinal Diseases · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — one pivotal trial. In the Bernard trial (359 randomised patients with microbiologically confirmed pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis, 71 French centres), cure at one year was identical: 160 of 176 (90.9%) on 6 weeks versus 159 of 175 (90.9%) on 12 weeks (difference 0.05%; 95% CI −6.2 to 6.3), inside the prespecified 10% noninferiority margin. Adverse events were similar (50 vs 51 patients), including deaths (14 [8%] in the 6-week group vs 12 [7%] in the 12-week group — printed here beside the cure result, as the record gives them). The trial was open-label with a masked validation committee. Note for the developer: the drafting note cites the journal as Lancet Infectious Diseases; the record's journal is The Lancet. One trial, one country, an open-label design: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Bernard 2015: 6 weeks cured as many vertebral osteomyelitis patients as 12 weeks (90.9% in both arms; difference 0.05%)
cards.summary: Bernard 2015: 6 weeks cured as many vertebral osteomyelitis patients as 12 weeks (90.9% in both arms; difference 0.05%)
cards.type: Open-label, non-inferiority randomised controlled trial with masked endpoint validation
cards.people: 359 adults with microbiologically confirmed pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis and typical radiological features, at 71 centres in France; after 8 post-randomisation exclusions, 176 patients were analysed in the 6-week group and 175 in the 12-week group, with antibiotic choice by the treating physician under French guidelines. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The proportion classified as cured at 1 year by a masked independent validation committee was 160 of 176 (90.9%) with 6 weeks of treatment and 159 of 175 (90.9%) with 12 weeks (difference 0.05%; 95% CI −6.2 to 6.3), demonstrating noninferiority within the prespecified absolute margin of 10%. Adverse events occurred in 50 patients (6-week) and 51 (12-week); the most common was death (14 [8%] vs 12 [7%]), followed by antibiotic intolerance.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority was shown against a 10% margin — the interval excludes a penalty larger than about 6 points, which most clinicians would accept for halving treatment duration, but the margin itself is a judgement the reader should see. Open-label treatment assignment with masked adjudication is the standard compromise for duration trials. Microbiologically confirmed cases only: culture-negative vertebral osteomyelitis is outside the record.
cards.source: Bernard L et al. Antibiotic treatment for 6 weeks versus 12 weeks in patients with pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis: an open-label, non-inferiority, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2015. PMID: 25468170. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00764114; EudraCT 2006-000951-18, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Rifampin combination therapy for staphylococcal prosthetic-device infection (Zimmerli)
shelves.question: In staphylococcal infections of stable orthopaedic implants managed with debridement and implant retention, does ciprofloxacin plus rifampin cure more infections than ciprofloxacin alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Anti-Infective Agents · Antibiotics, Antitubercular · Ciprofloxacin · Disease-Free Survival · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Floxacillin · Hip Prosthesis · Humans · Knee Prosthesis · Male · Middle Aged · Orthopedic Fixation Devices · Penicillins · Prosthesis-Related Infections · Rifampin · Staphylococcal Infections · Treatment Outcome · Vancomycin
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single small pre-registration-era trial, flagged for the developer as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: it remains, decades later, the only randomised trial of rifampin combination therapy for staphylococcal implant infection, and no second trial exists to satisfy the gate. In the Zimmerli trial (33 randomised patients with culture-proven staphylococcal infection of stable orthopaedic implants and short symptom duration), among the 24 patients who completed the trial, cure at a median of roughly 3 years was 12 of 12 (100%) with ciprofloxacin–rifampin versus 7 of 12 (58%) with ciprofloxacin–placebo (P=0.02). Nine of 33 patients dropped out (adverse events, noncompliance, protocol violations); 7 of the dropouts were later treated with rifampin combinations and 5 were cured without device removal. The effect is large and mechanistically grounded in rifampin's biofilm activity, but it rests on 24 completers from 1990s Switzerland, with fluoroquinolone-susceptible staphylococci: POSSIBLE, and fragile.

cards.headline: Zimmerli 1998: ciprofloxacin–rifampin cured 12 of 12 completers versus 7 of 12 on ciprofloxacin alone (P=0.02) — in a 33-patient trial
cards.summary: Zimmerli 1998: ciprofloxacin–rifampin cured 12 of 12 completers versus 7 of 12 on ciprofloxacin alone (P=0.02) — in a 33-patient trial
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial (conducted 1992–1997; pre-registration era)
cards.people: 33 patients with culture-proven staphylococcal infection associated with stable orthopaedic implants and a short duration of symptoms (exclusion limit under 1 year; actual experience 0–21 days), at two Swiss infectious-disease services; 18 were allocated to ciprofloxacin–rifampin and 15 to ciprofloxacin–placebo, after initial debridement and a 2-week intravenous course of flucloxacillin or vancomycin with rifampin or placebo. Twenty-four patients completed the trial, with follow-up of 35 and 33 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix. No registry ID appears in the record's databank fields — a 1990s trial, predating registration; none is invented.
cards.result: Cure (absence of clinical and laboratory signs of infection, C-reactive protein under 5 mg/L, and no radiological loosening or infection at final follow-up) was achieved in 12 of 12 patients (100%) in the ciprofloxacin–rifampin group versus 7 of 12 (58%) in the ciprofloxacin–placebo group (P=0.02), among patients who fully completed the trial. Nine of 33 randomised patients dropped out (adverse events 6, noncompliance 1, protocol violations 2); 7 of these were subsequently treated with rifampin combinations, of whom 5 were cured without removal of the device.
cards.watchOut: The headline is a completers analysis: the intention-to-treat cure rates are diluted by the 27% dropout, and the rifampin rescue of dropouts, while supportive, is uncontrolled. Entry required stable implants and symptoms of days, not weeks — chronic, loose, or sinus-forming infections are outside the record, as are rifampin- or fluoroquinolone-resistant organisms. The trial's influence on guidelines vastly exceeds its size, which is exactly why the shelf flags itself as a two-trial-gate exception candidate.
cards.source: Zimmerli W et al. Role of rifampin for treatment of orthopedic implant-related staphylococcal infections: a randomized controlled trial. Foreign-Body Infection (FBI) Study Group. JAMA. 1998. PMID: 9605897. No registry ID in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial); none is invented. shelves.title: Pilocarpine for Sjögren's-related dry mouth
shelves.question: In patients with Sjögren's syndrome, does oral pilocarpine improve salivary flow and dry-mouth symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Lacrimal Apparatus/drug effects · Male · Middle Aged · Parasympathomimetics/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pilocarpine/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Salivation/drug effects · Sjogren's Syndrome/complications/physiopathology · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two placebo-controlled randomised trials agree, with an anchor correction disclosed here: the topic file pinned Johnson 1993 (PMID 8326972) as the Sjögren's trial, but that record is post-IRRADIATION xerostomia in head-and-neck cancer patients — a different population answering a different question — so it is not carded on this shelf. The actual Sjögren's pivotal trial is Vivino 1999 (n=373): pilocarpine 5 mg four times daily significantly improved global dry-mouth and dry-eye assessments versus placebo (P≤.01) and raised salivary flow two- to three-fold (P<.001); the abstract does not print the responder percentages, and none are supplied. A small Taiwanese trial (Wu 2006, n=44) found the same pattern of significant symptomatic and salivary improvement, likewise without printed effect sizes. Sweating is the characteristic cost in both. LIKELY on direction and consistency; the absence of printed responder rates in both abstracts is stated plainly.

cards.headline: Vivino 1999 (P92-01): pilocarpine 5 mg four times daily significantly improved dry mouth and dry eyes in Sjögren's syndrome; salivary flow rose 2- to 3-fold
cards.summary: Vivino 1999 (P92-01): pilocarpine 5 mg four times daily significantly improved dry mouth and dry eyes in Sjögren's syndrome; salivary flow rose 2- to 3-fold
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, fixed-dose randomised trial (12 weeks)
cards.people: 373 patients with primary or secondary Sjögren's syndrome and clinically significant dry mouth and dry eyes, randomised to pilocarpine 2.5 mg, pilocarpine 5 mg, or placebo tablets four times daily for 12 weeks. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: A significantly greater proportion of patients on 5 mg pilocarpine showed improvement versus placebo (P≤.01) in global assessments of dry mouth, dry eyes and other dryness symptoms (P≤.05) — the abstract does not print the responder percentages, and none are supplied here. Salivary flow increased significantly, two- to three-fold (P<.001), after the first dose and was maintained across the 12 weeks. The most common adverse effect was sweating; no serious drug-related adverse experiences were reported.
cards.watchOut: The headline outcomes are global subjective assessments; the objective anchor is salivary flow. The 2.5 mg dose did not carry the headline result — the benefit belongs to 5 mg four times daily (20 mg/day), a demanding regimen whose adherence these records do not report.

shelves.title: Upadacitinib in giant cell arteritis (SELECT-GCA)
shelves.question: In patients with giant cell arteritis, does upadacitinib with a glucocorticoid taper achieve sustained remission more often than placebo with a taper?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Drug Tapering/methods · Drug Therapy, Combination/adverse effects/methods · Giant Cell Arteritis/drug therapy · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Janus Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects/administration & dosage · Remission Induction/methods · Cardiovascular Diseases/chemically induced/epidemiology · Treatment Outcome · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — in the single phase 3 trial, upadacitinib 15 mg daily with a 26-week glucocorticoid taper produced sustained remission at week 52 in 46.4% versus 29.0% on placebo with a slower 52-week taper; the 7.5 mg dose did not beat placebo. The comparison builds the faster steroid taper into the upadacitinib strategy, so the shelf's claim is about the combined strategy, not the drug at equal steroid exposure. No major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in the upadacitinib groups during 52 weeks. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. Scope boundary: IL-6 blockade with tocilizumab in giant cell arteritis is a different question, homed on Shelf #385.

cards.headline: SELECT-GCA: sustained remission at week 52 in 46.4% on upadacitinib 15 mg versus 29.0% on placebo; the 7.5 mg dose was not superior
cards.summary: SELECT-GCA: sustained remission at week 52 in 46.4% on upadacitinib 15 mg versus 29.0% on placebo; the 7.5 mg dose was not superior
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (52 weeks; 2:1:1 randomisation; upadacitinib arms used a 26-week glucocorticoid taper, the placebo arm a 52-week taper)
cards.people: 428 patients with new-onset (70%) or relapsing giant cell arteritis: 209 received upadacitinib 15 mg daily, 107 received 7.5 mg daily and 112 received placebo. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — sustained remission at week 52 (no signs or symptoms of giant cell arteritis from week 12 through week 52, with adherence to the assigned glucocorticoid taper) — was met by 46.4% (95% CI 39.6 to 53.2) on upadacitinib 15 mg versus 29.0% (95% CI 20.6 to 37.5) on placebo (P=0.002). Upadacitinib 15 mg was also superior on the prespecified key secondary endpoints (sustained complete remission, time to flare, cumulative glucocorticoid exposure, patient-reported outcomes). Upadacitinib 7.5 mg was not superior to placebo on the primary endpoint (41.1%, 95% CI 31.8 to 50.4). Safety outcomes over 52 weeks were similar across groups, and no major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in the upadacitinib groups.
cards.watchOut: The design confounds drug with taper speed: the upadacitinib groups tapered steroids twice as fast, and remission required adherence to the assigned taper — a strategy trial, not a pure drug-versus-placebo test at matched steroid exposure. JAK-inhibitor class concerns (cardiovascular events, malignancy, serious infection) cannot be settled by 428 patients over 52 weeks, even with no MACE observed.
cards.source: Blockmans D et al. A Phase 3 Trial of Upadacitinib for Giant-Cell Arteritis. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 40174237. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03725202, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: upadacitinib 15 mg with a fast taper holds remission in giant cell arteritis — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: upadacitinib 15 mg with a fast taper holds remission in giant cell arteritis — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: SELECT-GCA (Blockmans 2025), 428 patients with giant cell arteritis.
cards.result: A selective JAK inhibitor at 15 mg daily, paired with a 26-week steroid taper, kept about 46% of patients in sustained remission at one year versus 29% on placebo with a 52-week taper, and won on flare timing and cumulative steroid exposure. The lower dose did not separate from placebo. It is the first oral targeted therapy to show this in giant cell arteritis — on one trial, with the taper difference built into the comparison.

shelves.title: Tapering low-dose glucocorticoids in senior rheumatoid arthritis (the GLORIA programme)
shelves.question: In patients aged 65 and over with rheumatoid arthritis who have taken low-dose prednisolone for two years in the GLORIA trial, can the glucocorticoid be tapered and stopped over three months without loss of disease control — and what did the two years of treatment itself achieve?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Methotrexate/therapeutic use · Prednisolone/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the GLORIA trial showed two years of add-on prednisolone 5 mg/day modestly improved disease activity and joint damage in patients aged 65+, at the cost of more (mostly non-severe) adverse events; its blinded tapering study then showed that stopping over three months returned disease activity to placebo-group levels, with a numerical (not significant) excess of flares and no evidence of adrenal insufficiency. Both analyses used one-sided testing for their primary comparisons, which is flagged on the cards. The tapering study is a post-trial withdrawal phase in trial completers, not a fresh randomisation, and is carded as such. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: GLORIA: two years of prednisolone 5 mg/day lowered disease activity by 0.37 DAS28 points, with 24% more patients harmed (mostly non-severe infections)
cards.summary: GLORIA: two years of prednisolone 5 mg/day lowered disease activity by 0.37 DAS28 points, with 24% more patients harmed (mostly non-severe infections)
cards.type: Pragmatic, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (2 years; minimal exclusion criteria, all cotreatments allowed except long-term open-label glucocorticoids)
cards.people: 451 patients aged 65+ with established, active rheumatoid arthritis (mean age 72, mean disease duration 11 years, mean DAS28 4.5, mean 2.1 comorbidities); 79% were on disease-modifying drugs including 14% on biologics. The abstract does not print the sex split.
cards.result: Disease activity (DAS28, a co-primary endpoint) was 0.37 points lower on prednisolone (95% confidence limit 0.23; p<0.0001, one-sided testing) and joint-damage progression was 1.7 points lower (95% confidence limit 0.7; p=0.003). The harm co-primary endpoint — at least one adverse event of special interest — occurred in 60% on prednisolone versus 49% on placebo (adjusted relative risk 1.24, 95% confidence limit 1.04; p=0.02), with the largest contrast in mostly non-severe infections; other glucocorticoid-specific events were rare. Trial completion was 63% versus 61%.
cards.watchOut: The trial's primary analyses used one-sided testing, which makes the printed p-values and confidence limits more favourable than the two-sided convention; read them accordingly. The benefit (0.37 DAS28 points) is modest at group level, and the trial's pragmatic senior population — multimorbid, long disease duration — is exactly the group in whom steroid harms accumulate.
cards.source: Boers M et al. Low dose, add-on prednisolone in patients with rheumatoid arthritis aged 65+: the pragmatic randomised, double-blind placebo-controlled GLORIA trial. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2022. PMID: 35641125. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02585258, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: After GLORIA: blinded 3-month tapering and discontinuation was feasible — DAS28 rose 0.2 points, flares 45% versus 33% (not significant), no adrenal insufficiency
cards.summary: After GLORIA: blinded 3-month tapering and discontinuation was feasible — DAS28 rose 0.2 points, flares 45% versus 33% (not significant), no adrenal insufficiency
cards.type: Placebo-controlled, double-blind tapering phase after the GLORIA trial (protocol-specified 3-month linear taper of blinded study medication in patients completing the 2-year trial)
cards.people: 191 GLORIA completers were eligible for the tapering analysis; 36 met treatment-related flare criteria and contributed to the flare analysis only. Disease-activity change was assessed in 76 patients from the prednisolone group and 79 from the placebo group. Age and sex are as in the GLORIA population (card above); this record does not print them separately.
cards.result: Mean DAS28 change after tapering was +0.2 (SD 1.0) in the prednisolone group versus 0.0 (SD 1.2) in the placebo group; the baseline-adjusted between-group difference in DAS28 increase was 0.16 (95% confidence limit -0.06; p=0.12, one-sided test) — that is, disease activity rose to the level of the group that had never taken prednisolone, remaining on average in the low-activity range. Flares occurred in 45% of prednisolone patients versus 33% of placebo patients (relative risk 1.37, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.98; p=0.12, two-sided). There was no evidence of adrenal insufficiency, including in the subset with cortisol and ACTH measured after tapering.
cards.watchOut: This was not a new randomisation: it compares the original trial arms among completers, a selected group who had tolerated and stayed on therapy for two years. The flare difference is compatible with anything from a small protective effect of stopping to a near-doubling of risk; 'feasible and safe' is the authors' framing of a non-significant result. This record carries no registry ID in its databank fields; the parent trial's registration is on the GLORIA card.

cards.headline: Synthesis: low-dose prednisolone works modestly in senior RA, and can usually be stopped — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: low-dose prednisolone works modestly in senior RA, and can usually be stopped — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: GLORIA (Boers 2022), 451 patients aged 65+, and its blinded tapering phase (Almayali 2023), 191 completers.
cards.result: Two years of prednisolone 5 mg/day bought a modest, real improvement in disease activity and less joint damage, paid for with about a quarter more patients experiencing mostly non-severe adverse events, chiefly infections. When the drug was then tapered and stopped blindly over three months, disease activity drifted back to untreated levels, roughly four in ten patients flared in both groups, and no adrenal insufficiency appeared — stopping is feasible, but the benefit stops with the drug.
cards.watchOut: One-sided primary testing in both reports flatters the precision; and the tapering evidence comes from completers of a trial, not from unselected long-term steroid users in clinic, in whom tapering is often harder.

shelves.title: Methotrexate for painful knee osteoarthritis (PROMOTE)
shelves.question: In adults with painful knee osteoarthritis, does weekly oral methotrexate added to usual analgesia reduce knee pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Methotrexate/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Osteoarthritis, Knee/drug therapy/complications · Double-Blind Method · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Administration, Oral · Antirheumatic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aged · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome · Arthralgia/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single multicentre double-blind trial found a statistically significant but small average pain benefit at 6 months: 0.79 points on a 0-to-10 scale, with a confidence interval (0.08 to 1.51) that reaches from negligible to worthwhile. Stiffness and function also favoured methotrexate, and an adherence analysis suggested a dose-response. The card prints the effect's size plainly; whether an average gain under one point justifies weekly methotrexate's monitoring burden is a clinical judgement this record informs but does not settle. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. A later biomarker substudy of PROMOTE (PMID 42413648) reports the pain response concentrated in participants with elevated baseline hs-CRP — a subgroup finding, fenced in the synthesis card, not carded as evidence.

cards.headline: PROMOTE: knee pain at 6 months fell 0.79 points more on methotrexate than on placebo (95% CI 0.08 to 1.51; P=0.030)
cards.summary: PROMOTE: knee pain at 6 months fell 0.79 points more on methotrexate than on placebo (95% CI 0.08 to 1.51; P=0.030)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (15 UK secondary-care clinics; methotrexate escalated 10 to 25 mg once weekly over 6 weeks, continued to 12 months, on top of usual analgesia)
cards.people: 155 adults with symptomatic radiographic knee osteoarthritis and knee pain of at least 4 out of 10 on most days despite current medication were randomised (77 methotrexate, 78 placebo); 64% were women and the mean age was 60.9 years; half had Kellgren-Lawrence grade 3 to 4 disease. Follow-up at 6 months was 86%.
cards.result: Mean knee pain (0-to-10 numerical rating scale) fell from 6.4 at baseline to 5.1 at 6 months on methotrexate and from 6.8 to 6.2 on placebo; the intention-to-treat treatment difference was 0.79 points in favour of methotrexate (95% CI 0.08 to 1.51; P=0.030). WOMAC stiffness (0.60 points, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.18; P=0.045) and function (5.01 points, 95% CI 1.29 to 8.74; P=0.008) also favoured methotrexate, and a treatment-adherence analysis supported a dose-response effect. Four serious adverse events were reported, all judged unrelated (2 in each group).
cards.watchOut: The average effect is small and its confidence interval nearly touches zero; a group average of 0.79 points can hide a mixture of responders and non-responders, and this record does not report a responder analysis. Registry IDs are stated in the record's design section rather than its databank fields.
cards.source: Kingsbury SR et al. Pain Reduction With Oral Methotrexate in Knee Osteoarthritis : A Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Clinical Trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2024. PMID: 39074374. Registry IDs: ISRCTN77854383 and EudraCT 2013-001689-41, as stated in the record (design section). cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but small average pain benefit from weekly methotrexate — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but small average pain benefit from weekly methotrexate — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: PROMOTE (Kingsbury 2024), 155 adults with painful knee osteoarthritis.
cards.result: Once-weekly oral methotrexate, added to usual analgesia, beat placebo on pain, stiffness and function at 6 months in a properly blinded trial — the first solid randomised signal for a cheap, familiar drug in knee osteoarthritis. But the average pain gain was under one point on a ten-point scale, and the trial does not identify in advance who the responders are.
cards.watchOut: Two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial. shelves.title: Hydroxychloroquine withdrawal in stable systemic lupus erythematosus
shelves.question: In patients with clinically stable systemic lupus erythematosus, does withdrawing hydroxychloroquine increase the risk of disease flare versus continuing it?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hydroxychloroquine/therapeutic use · Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic/drug therapy/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisone/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome/physiopathology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the only randomised withdrawal trial (47 patients, 1991) found that switching stable patients to placebo roughly doubled-to-tripled flare risk over 24 weeks (relative risk 2.5, 95% CI 1.08 to 5.58; flares in 16 of 22 versus 9 of 25). The direction has never been contradicted and underlies the modern practice of continuing hydroxychloroquine indefinitely, but the evidence is one small trial from before modern background therapy. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: Canadian Hydroxychloroquine Study Group: withdrawing hydroxychloroquine raised flare risk 2.5-fold over 24 weeks
cards.summary: Canadian Hydroxychloroquine Study Group: withdrawing hydroxychloroquine raised flare risk 2.5-fold over 24 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled withdrawal trial (6 months; patients stable on hydroxychloroquine were randomised to continue it or switch to placebo)
cards.people: 47 patients with clinically stable systemic lupus erythematosus (25 continued hydroxychloroquine at their existing dose, 22 received placebo); 10 patients in each group were also taking prednisone. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: Clinical flare-ups occurred in 16 of 22 patients (73%) switched to placebo versus 9 of 25 (36%) who continued hydroxychloroquine — a relative risk of 2.5 (95% confidence interval 1.08 to 5.58), and time to flare was shorter on placebo (P=0.02). Severe exacerbations requiring withdrawal from the study occurred in 5 of 22 versus 1 of 25 (relative risk 6.1, 95% CI 0.72 to 52.44 — a relative measure with a very wide interval, printed beside the absolute counts). Prednisone dose changes did not differ between the groups.
cards.watchOut: A very small, single-centre-era trial from 1991: the severe-exacerbation estimate rests on six events, and background lupus therapy has changed substantially since. The trial predates trial registration; the record carries no registry ID.
cards.source: Canadian Hydroxychloroquine Study Group A randomized study of the effect of withdrawing hydroxychloroquine sulfate in systemic lupus erythematosus. cards.headline: Synthesis: stopping hydroxychloroquine in stable lupus invites flares — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: stopping hydroxychloroquine in stable lupus invites flares — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Canadian Hydroxychloroquine Study Group (1991), 47 patients with stable lupus.
cards.result: In the only randomised test, taking stable patients off hydroxychloroquine caused about three quarters of them to flare within six months, versus about a third of those who stayed on it. Small and old as it is, this trial is the randomised root of the rule that hydroxychloroquine, once started in lupus, is continued.
cards.watchOut: Two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single small trial. Its age cuts both ways — modern cohorts are observational only, so this remains the best randomised evidence; a modern withdrawal trial would supersede it and should trigger a re-sweep.

shelves.title: Mycophenolate versus cyclophosphamide in scleroderma lung disease (SLS I and SLS II)
shelves.question: In patients with systemic-sclerosis interstitial lung disease, does immunosuppression improve forced vital capacity — cyclophosphamide versus placebo, and two years of mycophenolate mofetil versus one year of oral cyclophosphamide?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Autoimmune Diseases/drug therapy · Bronchoalveolar Lavage Fluid/immunology · Cyclophosphamide/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Leukopenia/chemically induced · Lung Diseases, Interstitial/drug therapy/immunology/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Regression Analysis · Respiratory Function Tests · Scleroderma, Systemic/drug therapy/immunology · Treatment Outcome · Vital Capacity/drug effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY — the programme's two randomised trials together support both drugs. SLS I showed one year of oral cyclophosphamide beat placebo on forced vital capacity by 2.53 percentage points of predicted value. SLS II then compared the two active strategies head-to-head: its prespecified primary analysis was negative for the hypothesis that mycophenolate would prove superior at 24 months (p=0.24), with FVC improving within both groups (2.19 and 2.88 points) and mycophenolate clearly better tolerated (leucopenia in 4 versus 30 patients; premature withdrawal 20 versus 32). Deaths over 24 months in SLS II were 5 (7%) on mycophenolate versus 11 (15%) on cyclophosphamide, mostly from progressive lung disease — printed beside the primary results as the record reports them; SLS II was not powered for mortality. Scope boundary: nintedanib and tocilizumab in systemic-sclerosis ILD are a different question, homed on Shelf #688. PROPOSED: LIKELY.

cards.headline: SLS I: one year of oral cyclophosphamide improved FVC by 2.53 percentage points versus placebo (P<0.03)

cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (13 US centres; cyclophosphamide up to 2 mg/kg/day for 1 year, then a further year of follow-up)
cards.people: 158 patients with systemic sclerosis, restrictive lung physiology, dyspnoea and evidence of active alveolitis or interstitial lung disease on lavage or high-resolution CT; 145 completed at least 6 months of treatment and were analysed. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — forced vital capacity as a percentage of predicted at 12 months, adjusted for baseline — favoured cyclophosphamide by an absolute 2.53 percentage points (95% confidence interval 0.28 to 4.79; P<0.03). Differences in dyspnoea, skin thickening and quality of life also favoured cyclophosphamide, and the FVC difference was maintained at 24 months, a year after treatment stopped. Adverse events were more frequent on cyclophosphamide, without a significant difference in serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The benefit is modest (about 2.5 points of FVC percent predicted) and bought with a cytotoxic drug; the analysis excluded 13 randomised patients who did not complete 6 months. The record carries no registry ID in its databank fields (a 2006 report).
cards.source: Tashkin DP et al. Cyclophosphamide versus placebo in scleroderma lung disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2006. PMID: 16790698. cards.headline: SLS II: mycophenolate was not superior to cyclophosphamide on the primary analysis (p=0.24) — but FVC improved in both groups and toxicity was lower
cards.summary: SLS II: mycophenolate was not superior to cyclophosphamide on the primary analysis (p=0.24) — but FVC improved in both groups and toxicity was lower
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, double-dummy, parallel-group trial (14 US centres; mycophenolate target 1500 mg twice daily for 24 months versus oral cyclophosphamide target 2.0 mg/kg/day for 12 months then placebo)
cards.people: 142 patients with scleroderma-related interstitial lung disease meeting dyspnoea, pulmonary-function and CT criteria were randomised (69 mycophenolate, 73 cyclophosphamide); 126 (63 per group) were included in the primary analysis. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The course of percent-predicted FVC over 24 months did not differ significantly between groups in the prespecified joint-model primary analysis (p=0.24) — the trial was negative for its hypothesis that mycophenolate would be more effective. Within-group, FVC improved by 2.19 points (95% CI 0.53 to 3.84) on mycophenolate and 2.88 points (1.19 to 4.58) on cyclophosphamide in a post-hoc analysis. Sixteen patients (11%) died: 5 (7%) on mycophenolate and 11 (15%) on cyclophosphamide, most from progressive interstitial lung disease. Leucopenia (30 versus 4 patients) and thrombocytopenia (4 versus 0) were much commoner on cyclophosphamide; fewer mycophenolate patients withdrew prematurely (20 versus 32) or met treatment-failure criteria (0 versus 2).
cards.watchOut: Read the stamp carefully: SLS II did not prove mycophenolate superior, and because it had no placebo arm, the within-group FVC gains lean on SLS I's placebo-controlled benchmark from a different era and population. The mortality difference is a secondary count in a trial powered for lung function. The preference for mycophenolate rests on tolerability, which this trial measured directly and decisively.
cards.source: Tashkin DP et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: both drugs hold lung function in scleroderma ILD; mycophenolate wins on tolerability — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: both drugs hold lung function in scleroderma ILD; mycophenolate wins on tolerability — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: SLS I (Tashkin 2006), 158 patients, and SLS II (Tashkin 2016), 142 patients.
cards.result: Cyclophosphamide is genuinely better than placebo for scleroderma lung disease (SLS I). Mycophenolate, given for two years, produced the same trajectory of lung-function improvement as one year of cyclophosphamide (SLS II), with a fraction of the marrow toxicity and fewer dropouts — which is why mycophenolate became the default despite SLS II's formally negative primary comparison.
cards.watchOut: The chain of inference has one soft link: SLS II's lack of a placebo arm means its within-group gains are interpreted against SLS I's older benchmark. Absolute benefits are small in FVC terms, and neither trial shows a mortality effect.

shelves.title: Autologous stem-cell transplantation in severe systemic sclerosis (ASTIS and SCOT)
shelves.question: In patients with severe early diffuse systemic sclerosis, does autologous haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation improve event-free and overall survival versus monthly cyclophosphamide — and at what early cost?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Autografts · Cyclophosphamide/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Female · Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplantation/adverse effects · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Male · Middle Aged · Scleroderma, Diffuse/drug therapy · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two randomised trials in different health systems point the same way: an early hazard from transplant-related deaths, then a widening long-term survival advantage over cyclophosphamide. In ASTIS, 8 treatment-related deaths occurred in the first year in the transplant arm versus none on cyclophosphamide, yet by 2 to 4 years the hazard of death or major organ failure was about a third (time-varying HR 0.35 and 0.34). In SCOT, overall survival at 72 months was 86% versus 51% in the per-protocol population, with treatment-related mortality of 6% by 72 months versus 0%. PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C): overall survival is a headline outcome. Both trials are small (156 and 75 patients) and enrolled a selected, severely affected population treated at expert centres.

cards.headline: ASTIS: transplantation caused 8 treatment-related deaths in year one, then cut the event hazard to about a third by years 2-4
cards.summary: ASTIS: transplantation caused 8 treatment-related deaths in year one, then cut the event hazard to about a third by years 2-4
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, open-label trial (29 centres in 10 countries; HSCT versus 12 monthly intravenous cyclophosphamide pulses; median follow-up 5.8 years)
cards.people: 156 patients with early diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis, randomised to HSCT (79) or cyclophosphamide (77) and followed to 2013. The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was event-free survival (time to death or persistent major organ failure). Fifty-three events occurred: 22 in the HSCT group (19 deaths and 3 irreversible organ failures) and 31 in the control group (23 deaths and 8 irreversible organ failures). The first year reversed the final verdict: 13 events (16.5%), including 8 treatment-related deaths, occurred in the HSCT group versus 8 events (10.4%) with no treatment-related deaths in the control group. Cumulative events equalised by 2 years (14 versus 14) and separated by 4 years (15 [19%] versus 20 [26%]); time-varying hazard ratios for event-free survival were 0.35 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.74) at 2 years and 0.34 (0.16 to 0.74) at 4 years.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the survival curves cross — any single hazard ratio misdescribes this trial; the record's time-varying analysis is the honest summary. Eight of 79 transplanted patients died of the treatment in year one: the long-term benefit is real only for patients who survive the procedure, in centres that do it often.
cards.source: van Laar JM et al. Autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation vs intravenous pulse cyclophosphamide in diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 25058083. Registry ID: ISRCTN54371254, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: SCOT: overall survival at 72 months was 86% with myeloablative transplantation versus 51% with cyclophosphamide (per-protocol)
cards.summary: SCOT: overall survival at 72 months was 86% with myeloablative transplantation versus 51% with cyclophosphamide (per-protocol)
cards.type: Randomised trial (myeloablative CD34-selected autologous HSCT versus 12 monthly cyclophosphamide infusions; primary endpoint a global rank composite score at 54 months)
cards.people: 75 adults aged 18 to 69 with severe scleroderma were randomised (36 transplantation, 39 cyclophosphamide). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary global rank composite score at 54 months favoured transplantation: 67% of 1404 pairwise comparisons favoured transplantation and 33% cyclophosphamide (P=0.01). In the per-protocol population, event-free survival at 54 months was 79% versus 50% (P=0.02); at 72 months, Kaplan-Meier event-free survival was 74% versus 47% (P=0.03) and overall survival 86% versus 51% (P=0.02). Only 9% of the transplantation group had started disease-modifying drugs by 54 months versus 44% of the cyclophosphamide group (P=0.001). Treatment-related mortality with transplantation was 3% at 54 months and 6% at 72 months, versus 0% with cyclophosphamide.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-five patients: the survival percentages come from small denominators and a per-protocol analysis for the 54-month figure. SCOT used a myeloablative regimen, ASTIS a non-myeloablative one — the trials agree in direction, not in protocol, and neither was blinded (transplantation cannot be).
cards.source: Sullivan KM et al. Myeloablative Autologous Stem-Cell Transplantation for Severe Scleroderma. The New England journal of medicine. 2018. PMID: 29298160. cards.headline: Synthesis: pay early mortality, gain long-term survival — the transplant bargain in severe scleroderma, LIKELY (Tier C)
cards.summary: Synthesis: pay early mortality, gain long-term survival — the transplant bargain in severe scleroderma, LIKELY (Tier C)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ASTIS (van Laar 2014), 156 patients, and SCOT (Sullivan 2018), 75 patients.
cards.result: For carefully selected patients with severe early diffuse systemic sclerosis, autologous stem-cell transplantation trades a real risk of dying from the treatment in the first year (8 of 79 in ASTIS; 6% treatment-related mortality by 6 years in SCOT) for substantially better long-term event-free and overall survival than monthly cyclophosphamide. Two independent randomised trials, two regimens, one shape of result.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are small and were run in expert networks on patients sick enough to justify the risk yet fit enough to survive it. The estimates should not be generalised to milder disease, older patients, or low-volume centres.

shelves.title: Inebilizumab in IgG4-related disease (MITIGATE)
shelves.question: In patients with active IgG4-related disease, does the CD19 B-cell-depleting antibody inebilizumab reduce the risk of disease flare versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Antigens, CD19/immunology/metabolism · B-Lymphocytes/drug effects/immunology/metabolism · Double-Blind Method · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Immunoglobulin G/blood · Immunoglobulin G4-Related Disease/diagnosis/drug therapy/immunology · Infusions, Intravenous · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Lymphocyte Depletion/methods · Remission Induction/methods · Symptom Flare Up · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — in the first randomised trial in this disease, inebilizumab cut one-year flare risk from 60% to 10% (hazard ratio 0.13), with higher rates of flare-free, glucocorticoid-free complete remission. Serious adverse events were numerically more frequent on inebilizumab (18% versus 9%). The effect size is very large, but it rests on a single 135-patient trial in a rare disease with no approved-therapy comparator landscape. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. Scope boundary: inebilizumab in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is a different question, homed on Shelf #1118.

cards.headline: MITIGATE: flares in 10% on inebilizumab versus 60% on placebo over 52 weeks (HR 0.13)
cards.summary: MITIGATE: flares in 10% on inebilizumab versus 60% on placebo over 52 weeks (HR 0.13)
cards.type: Phase 3, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (52 weeks; both groups received identical glucocorticoid tapers; inebilizumab 300 mg on days 1 and 15 and at week 26)
cards.people: 135 adults with active IgG4-related disease were randomised (68 inebilizumab, 67 placebo). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — first treated, adjudicated disease flare during the 52-week treatment period — occurred in 7 participants (10%) on inebilizumab versus 40 (60%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.13, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.28; P<0.001 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates). The annualised flare rate was also lower (rate ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.31; P<0.001). Flare-free, treatment-free complete remission (odds ratio 4.68, 95% CI 2.21 to 9.91) and flare-free, glucocorticoid-free complete remission (odds ratio 4.96, 95% CI 2.34 to 10.52) were both more frequent on inebilizumab. Serious adverse events occurred in 12 participants (18%) on inebilizumab versus 6 (9%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A hazard ratio of 0.13 in a 135-patient trial is an unusually large effect; single-trial estimates of this size usually shrink on replication. Background immunosuppressants were prohibited, so the comparison is against steroid taper alone. Longer-term B-cell-depletion risks (infection, hypogammaglobulinaemia) are not mapped by 52 weeks.
cards.source: Stone JH et al. Inebilizumab for Treatment of IgG4-Related Disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2025. PMID: 39541094. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04540497, from the record's databank fields.
