shelves.title: Abaloparatide in postmenopausal osteoporosis (ACTIVE)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does abaloparatide reduce new vertebral fractures versus placebo — and how does it compare with teriparatide on fractures and hypercalcaemia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Density Conservation Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Femur Neck/diagnostic imaging/physiology · Humans · Hypercalcemia/chemically induced · Injections, Subcutaneous · Lumbar Vertebrae/injuries/physiopathology · Middle Aged · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal · Osteoporotic Fractures/prevention & control · Parathyroid Hormone-Related Protein/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pelvic Bones/drug effects/physiology · Placebos/therapeutic use · Postmenopause · Radiography · Spinal Fractures/prevention & control · Teriparatide/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Thoracic Vertebrae/injuries
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — ACTIVE is a large (2463 women), double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in which abaloparatide reduced new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures over 18 months and raised BMD more than placebo, with less hypercalcaemia than the open-label teriparatide arm (3.4% versus 6.4%). One verification limit must be stated plainly: the record's abstract reports the fracture results qualitatively ('occurred less frequently'; a lower Kaplan-Meier nonvertebral event rate) and does NOT print the arm-level fracture rates, which appear only in the paper's tables — so no fracture percentages are carded on this shelf, and the exact size of the fracture benefit cannot be quoted from the verified record. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. Distinct angle versus Shelf #92: that shelf asks the class question (bone-building versus antiresorptive therapy at very high risk, with ACTIVE as one of several carded trials); this shelf is the dedicated ACTIVE record — the placebo-controlled fracture outcomes and the prespecified hypercalcaemia comparison with teriparatide. Flagged for the developer's one-home ruling at insert.

cards.headline: ACTIVE: abaloparatide reduced vertebral and nonvertebral fractures versus placebo over 18 months; hypercalcaemia 3.4% versus 6.4% on teriparatide
cards.summary: ACTIVE: abaloparatide reduced vertebral and nonvertebral fractures versus placebo over 18 months; hypercalcaemia 3.4% versus 6.4% on teriparatide
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with an additional open-label teriparatide arm (28 sites in 10 countries; daily subcutaneous injections for 18 months)
cards.people: 2463 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (mean age 69 years, range 49 to 86; BMD T-score -2.5 to -5.0 with prior vertebral or nonvertebral fracture, or higher-risk criteria for women over 65) were randomised to placebo (821), abaloparatide 80 micrograms (824) or open-label teriparatide 20 micrograms (818); 1901 completed the study.
cards.result: New morphometric vertebral fractures — the primary endpoint — occurred less frequently in both active groups than on placebo, and the Kaplan-Meier estimated rate of nonvertebral fracture was lower with abaloparatide than placebo; BMD increases at total hip, femoral neck and lumbar spine were greater with abaloparatide than placebo (all P<.001). The prespecified safety comparison found less hypercalcaemia with abaloparatide than with teriparatide: 3.4% versus 6.4% (risk difference -2.96 percentage points, 95% CI -5.12 to -0.87; P=.006). The record's abstract does not print the numerical fracture rates for any arm (they are in the paper's tables), so they are not carded here.
cards.watchOut: The trial was powered and positive, but the verified abstract supports direction, not magnitude, for the fracture endpoints — any source quoting exact fracture percentages for ACTIVE is drawing on the full text, not this record. The teriparatide arm was open-label, so the hypercalcaemia and BMD contrasts with teriparatide are less protected than the placebo comparison; the trial was not powered for an abaloparatide-versus-teriparatide fracture comparison.
cards.source: Miller PD et al. Effect of Abaloparatide vs Placebo on New Vertebral Fractures in Postmenopausal Women With Osteoporosis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. PMID: 27533157. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01343004, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Zoledronic acid after denosumab-teriparatide combination therapy (DATA-HD extension)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women who have completed combined high-dose denosumab and teriparatide (DATA-HD), does a single zoledronic acid infusion preserve the bone microarchitecture and strength gains after the combination stops?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Teriparatide/therapeutic use · Denosumab/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Zoledronic Acid/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Bone Density Conservation Agents/therapeutic use · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/drug therapy · Bone Density
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — this is a single-arm extension, not a randomised comparison: all 53 participants received zoledronic acid, so nothing here estimates zoledronic acid's effect against not giving it. The answer the record gives is largely negative for peripheral bone: despite zoledronic acid, volumetric BMD at the radius drifted back to baseline values over 27 months and estimated stiffness and failure load fell progressively (remaining above baseline only at the tibia). A correction to the topic file, which described zoledronic acid as having 'largely maintained the microarchitecture and strength gains': that maintenance claim belongs to DXA-measured spine and hip BMD in the parent DATA-HD report (as summarised in this record's introduction); for the HR-pQCT microarchitecture and strength outcomes this extension actually measured, the authors conclude a single dose was NOT as effective at maintaining the gains. The question has been kept as filed because the record answers it — mostly in the negative. PROPOSED: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: DATA-HD extension: after one zoledronic acid dose, peripheral volumetric BMD fell back towards baseline and estimated strength declined over 27 months
cards.summary: DATA-HD extension: after one zoledronic acid dose, peripheral volumetric BMD fell back towards baseline and estimated strength declined over 27 months
cards.type: Single-arm extension study (no comparator group; all participants received one 5 mg intravenous zoledronic acid dose 24-35 weeks after the last denosumab dose; HR-pQCT at the distal radius and tibia at months 27 and 42)
cards.people: 53 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis who had completed the 15-month DATA-HD trial (of 76 originally randomised to teriparatide 20 or 40 micrograms overlapped with denosumab) entered the extension. The abstract does not print mean age.
cards.result: Despite zoledronic acid, total and cortical volumetric BMD gradually decreased over the 27 months after the infusion, reaching values similar to pretreatment baseline at the radius while remaining significantly above baseline at the tibia. Cortical porosity fell below baseline at month 27 but rose again from month 27 to 42; trabecular parameters did not change significantly. Estimated stiffness and failure load at both sites decreased progressively from month 15 to 42, remaining above baseline only at the tibia. The authors conclude that, in contrast to the largely maintained DXA spine and hip BMD reported for the parent study, a single zoledronic acid dose was not as effective at maintaining the peripheral volumetric-density and microarchitecture gains.
cards.watchOut: No control group: the observed declines are what happened after zoledronic acid, not a comparison with withholding it, so zoledronic acid may still have slowed losses this design cannot see. Only 53 of the 76 DATA-HD participants entered the extension (a completer population), and all outcomes are imaging surrogates — no fractures were assessed. The record carries no registry ID in its databank fields; the parent trial's registration is on the DATA-HD shelf (#1827).

cards.result: Whatever zoledronic acid does for DXA-measured spine and hip density after combination therapy, the finer peripheral measurements tell a weaker story: radius density returned to baseline and estimated bone strength declined at both measured sites. shelves.title: Zoledronic acid versus risedronate in Paget's disease of bone
shelves.question: In patients with Paget's disease of bone, is a single zoledronic acid infusion superior to a course of oral risedronate for biochemical response, and is the response more durable?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Alkaline Phosphatase/blood · Biomarkers/blood · Bone Remodeling/drug effects · Bone and Bones/drug effects/pathology · Diphosphonates/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Etidronic Acid/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Imidazoles/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Osteitis Deformans/blood/drug therapy · Quality of Life · Risedronic Acid · Zoledronic Acid
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two identical randomised double-blind trials, pooled in a single report (as with FIT-1 and FIT-2 on Shelf #1800, they are carded as what they are: two trials in one publication), found a single zoledronic acid infusion clearly superior to 60 days of risedronate: therapeutic response 96.0% versus 74.3% at six months, faster normalisation of alkaline phosphatase, and far more durable responses in post-trial follow-up (loss of response 1 of 113 versus 21 of 82). The endpoints are biochemical (alkaline phosphatase), which is the accepted activity measure in Paget's disease, not a fracture or pain outcome — pain scores improved in both groups without a reported between-group difference. The record carries no registry ID (a 2005 report). PROPOSED: LIKELY.

cards.headline: Reid 2005 (two pooled trials): response 96.0% with one zoledronic acid infusion versus 74.3% with risedronate; loss of response 1 versus 21 in follow-up
cards.summary: Reid 2005 (two pooled trials): response 96.0% with one zoledronic acid infusion versus 74.3% with risedronate; loss of response 1 versus 21 in follow-up
cards.type: Two identical randomised, double-blind, active-controlled trials of 6 months, pooled in one report (single 15-minute infusion of zoledronic acid 5 mg versus risedronate 30 mg daily for 60 days)
cards.people: 347 patients with Paget's disease of bone (176 zoledronic acid, 171 risedronate). The abstract does not print mean age or the sex split.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — therapeutic response at 6 months (normalisation of alkaline phosphatase, or a reduction of at least 75% in total alkaline phosphatase excess) — was achieved by 169 of 176 patients (96.0%) on zoledronic acid versus 127 of 171 (74.3%) on risedronate (P<0.001). Alkaline phosphatase normalised in 88.6% versus 57.9% (P<0.001), and the median time to first response was 64 versus 89 days (P<0.001). Quality-of-life physical-component scores improved more with zoledronic acid at 3 months; pain scores improved in both groups. In post-trial follow-up (median 190 days), loss of therapeutic response occurred in 1 of 113 zoledronic-acid patients versus 21 of 82 risedronate patients (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: Alkaline phosphatase response is a biochemical surrogate; the report does not show differences in fractures, deformity or hearing outcomes. The durability comparison comes from a post-trial follow-up subset (113 and 82 patients), not the full randomised cohort. The record carries no registry ID — the trials predate routine registration reporting.
cards.source: Reid IR et al. Comparison of a single infusion of zoledronic acid with risedronate for Paget's disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 16135834. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: one infusion beats two months of tablets for Paget's biochemical control — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: one infusion beats two months of tablets for Paget's biochemical control — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Reid 2005, two pooled randomised trials, 347 patients with Paget's disease.
cards.result: A single 15-minute zoledronic acid infusion produced quicker, deeper and much longer-lasting suppression of Paget's disease activity than a 60-day risedronate course — near-universal response (96%) versus three quarters, with relapse in follow-up almost confined to the risedronate group. This is the trial pair that made single-infusion zoledronic acid the standard first-line treatment for active Paget's disease.
cards.watchOut: The evidence is biochemical-response evidence; symptom and structural outcomes were secondary and largely similar. Two trials reported as one pooled analysis — counted as two, quoted as pooled, as the report presents them.

shelves.title: Strontium ranelate in postmenopausal osteoporosis (SOTI and TROPOS)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does strontium ranelate reduce vertebral fractures (SOTI) and nonvertebral fractures (TROPOS) versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Biomarkers/blood · Biopsy · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone and Bones/metabolism/pathology · Calcium/therapeutic use · Clinical Trials, Phase III as Topic · Double-Blind Method · Female · Femur Neck · Fractures, Spontaneous/prevention & control · Humans · Lumbar Vertebrae/diagnostic imaging/injuries · Middle Aged · Organometallic Compounds/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/complications/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Radiography · Risk · Secondary Prevention · Spinal Fractures/etiology/prevention & control · Strontium/blood · Thiophenes/adverse effects/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Thoracic Vertebrae/diagnostic imaging/injuries · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — two large double-blind placebo-controlled trials, each powered for its own fracture family: SOTI (1649 women with prevalent vertebral fracture) reduced new vertebral fractures (relative risk 0.59 over three years), and TROPOS (5091 women) reduced nonvertebral fractures by a relative 16%, with a relative 36% hip-fracture reduction confined to a prespecified-age-and-BMD high-risk subgroup (flagged as a subgroup on the card). Both abstracts report relative measures without arm-level absolute fracture rates, so the cards print relative effects only and flag the missing absolutes — the absolute gains are smaller than the relative ones suggest. Adverse-event incidence was similar to placebo in both trials. Neither record carries a registry ID (2004-2005 reports). PROPOSED: LIKELY.

cards.headline: SOTI: vertebral fracture relative risk 0.59 over three years on strontium ranelate (49% relative reduction in year one)
cards.summary: SOTI: vertebral fracture relative risk 0.59 over three years on strontium ranelate (49% relative reduction in year one)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (strontium ranelate 2 g daily for 3 years; calcium and vitamin D in both groups)
cards.people: 1649 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and at least one vertebral fracture. The abstract does not print mean age.
cards.result: New vertebral fractures were fewer on strontium ranelate than placebo: a relative risk reduction of 49% in the first year and 41% over the three-year study period (relative risk 0.59, 95% confidence interval 0.48 to 0.73 — a relative measure; the abstract does not print the absolute fracture rates for either arm, so none are carded). Bone mineral density at month 36 was higher with strontium ranelate by 14.4% at the lumbar spine and 8.3% at the femoral neck relative to placebo (P<0.001 for both). There were no significant differences in serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The absence of absolute fracture rates in the record matters: a 41% relative reduction applied to an unstated baseline risk cannot be turned into a number-needed-to-treat from this record. The record carries no registry ID (a 2004 report, pre-registration era).
cards.source: Meunier PJ et al. The effects of strontium ranelate on the risk of vertebral fracture in women with postmenopausal osteoporosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2004. PMID: 14749454. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: TROPOS: nonvertebral fractures reduced by a relative 16%; hip fractures by a relative 36% in the high-risk subgroup only
cards.summary: TROPOS: nonvertebral fractures reduced by a relative 16%; hip fractures by a relative 36% in the high-risk subgroup only
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (strontium ranelate 2 g daily; 5-year study with the main analysis at 3 years)
cards.people: 5091 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. The abstract does not print mean age.
cards.result: Over three years, strontium ranelate reduced all nonvertebral fractures by a relative 16% (P=0.04) and major fragility fractures (hip, wrist, pelvis and sacrum, ribs and sternum, clavicle, humerus) by a relative 19% (P=0.031), versus placebo; vertebral fractures were reduced by a relative 39% (P<0.001) in the 3640 patients with spinal radiographs. In the subgroup at high hip-fracture risk (age 74 or over and femoral-neck T-score -3 or lower; 1977 women), hip fractures were reduced by a relative 36% (P=0.046). Adverse-event incidence was similar in both groups. As in SOTI, the abstract prints relative reductions without absolute arm-level fracture rates, so none are carded.
cards.watchOut: The headline nonvertebral effect is a modest relative 16% with P=0.04 — statistically fragile — and the hip-fracture result comes from a subgroup comprising about two fifths of the trial, not the whole randomised population; it should never be quoted as the trial's overall hip result. The record carries no registry ID (a 2005 report).

cards.summary: Synthesis: strontium ranelate prevents vertebral and, modestly, nonvertebral fractures — LIKELY, on relative measures

shelves.question: In men with osteoporosis, does annual zoledronic acid reduce vertebral fractures versus placebo?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single large double-blind trial (1199 men) found two annual zoledronic acid infusions cut new morphometric vertebral fractures over 24 months from 4.9% to 1.6% (relative risk 0.33). Clinical vertebral and nonvertebral fractures were also fewer but not significantly so (few events). Deaths (2.6% versus 2.9%) and serious adverse events (25.3% versus 25.2%) did not differ — printed beside the fracture results, as safety counts in a trial not powered for mortality. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: Boonen 2012: morphometric vertebral fractures in 1.6% on zoledronic acid versus 4.9% on placebo over 24 months (RR 0.33)
cards.summary: Boonen 2012: morphometric vertebral fractures in 1.6% on zoledronic acid versus 4.9% on placebo over 24 months (RR 0.33)
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (zoledronic acid 5 mg or placebo at baseline and 12 months; calcium and vitamin D in both groups; 24 months)
cards.people: 1199 men aged 50 to 85 with primary osteoporosis or osteoporosis associated with low testosterone. The abstract does not print the mean age.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — one or more new morphometric vertebral fractures over 24 months — occurred in 1.6% of the zoledronic acid group versus 4.9% of the placebo group (relative risk 0.33, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.70; P=0.002 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates). Moderate-to-severe vertebral fractures were fewer (P=0.03) and height loss less (P=0.002) with zoledronic acid; clinical vertebral and nonvertebral fractures were numerically fewer but not statistically significant, with few events. BMD was higher and bone-turnover markers lower on zoledronic acid (P<0.05). Deaths (2.6% versus 2.9%) and serious adverse events (25.3% versus 25.2%) were similar.
cards.watchOut: One trial in men, with a morphometric (radiographic) primary endpoint: most of the fractures counted were not clinical events. Results were similar in men with low testosterone, as reported. The trial predates no safety signal but cannot exclude rare harms such as osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical femoral fracture.
cards.source: Boonen S et al. Fracture risk and zoledronic acid therapy in men with osteoporosis. The New England journal of medicine. 2012. PMID: 23113482. shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit, with harm) — the Riggs randomised trial (202 women, 4 years) is the definitive test of high-dose fluoride: lumbar spine BMD rose by a median 35%, yet new vertebral fractures were not reduced (163 versus 136 fractures) and nonvertebral fractures were significantly MORE frequent on fluoride (72 versus 24; P<0.01), with dose reductions for side effects in 54 versus 24 women. The 1994 extended observations (a single-arm follow-up of 50 treated women) found spine BMD kept rising for 6 years and speculated that lower doses might thread the needle — an authors' hypothesis from uncontrolled data, flagged as such on its card, not a finding. One trial programme: the shelf stands as a two-trial-gate exception candidate, kept because the harm answer is clinically important and unlikely ever to be re-tested at this dose. PROPOSED: POSSIBLE (no benefit, with harm), as a two-trial-gate exception candidate.

cards.headline: Riggs 1990: fluoride raised spine BMD by 35% but did not reduce vertebral fractures — and nonvertebral fractures rose (72 versus 24)
cards.summary: Riggs 1990: fluoride raised spine BMD by 35% but did not reduce vertebral fractures — and nonvertebral fractures rose (72 versus 24)
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (4 years; sodium fluoride 75 mg/day versus placebo, both groups with calcium 1500 mg/day)
cards.people: 202 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis and vertebral fractures were randomised; 66 women in the fluoride group and 69 in the placebo group completed the trial. The abstract does not print mean age.
cards.result: Median bone mineral density rose 35% in the lumbar spine (P<0.0001), 12% in the femoral neck and 10% in the trochanter on fluoride, but fell 4% in the radial shaft (predominantly cortical bone; P<0.02) — all versus placebo. The number of new vertebral fractures was similar (163 on fluoride versus 136 on placebo; not significant — counts of fractures, not of women). Nonvertebral fractures were more frequent on fluoride (72 versus 24; P<0.01). Side effects severe enough to require dose reduction occurred in 54 women on fluoride versus 24 on placebo, chiefly gastrointestinal symptoms and lower-extremity pain. The authors concluded that fluoride increases cancellous but decreases cortical BMD and increases skeletal fragility.
cards.watchOut: Only 135 of 202 randomised women completed the trial, and fracture counts (not patient-level proportions) are what the record prints — do not convert them into percentages of women. The trial predates registration; the record carries no registry ID.
cards.source: Riggs BL et al. Effect of fluoride treatment on the fracture rate in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. The New England journal of medicine. 1990. PMID: 2407957. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Riggs 1994 extended observations: in 50 treated women followed to 6 years, spine BMD kept rising; the vertebral-fracture rate traced a U-shape against achieved BMD
cards.summary: Riggs 1994 extended observations: in 50 treated women followed to 6 years, spine BMD kept rising; the vertebral-fracture rate traced a U-shape against achieved BMD
cards.type: Extended observations and additional analysis of the Riggs trial (single-arm: 50 women from the fluoride group followed for up to 6 years of treatment; no concurrent control)
cards.people: 50 women from the fluoride arm of the 1990 trial, followed during continued treatment. Doses had been reduced for side effects in 54 of the 101 women randomised to fluoride during the trial, permitting dose-response analyses.
cards.result: Lumbar spine BMD increased linearly over 6 years (median rate 8.7% per year). Serum fluoride correlated with spine BMD gain (r=0.61, P<0.001). Grouped by achieved spine BMD, the vertebral fracture rate per 100 person-years fell to a nadir of 24 as mean BMD rose from 0.6 to 1.2 g/cm2, then doubled to 52 in the group at 1.6 g/cm2; multivariate analysis suggested fracture rate falls with rising BMD except when the rise is rapid or serum fluoride climbs steeply. The authors raised the possibility that lower fluoride doses might moderately reduce vertebral fractures.
cards.watchOut: This is an uncontrolled extension: there is no placebo group at 6 years, the women analysed are trial survivors and compliers, and the 'lower doses might work' suggestion is a hypothesis fitted to observational patterns within one arm — it has never been confirmed in a randomised comparison and is flagged here as speculation, not evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: fluoride builds bone density but not bone strength at this dose — POSSIBLE (no benefit, with harm)
cards.summary: Synthesis: fluoride builds bone density but not bone strength at this dose — POSSIBLE (no benefit, with harm)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Riggs 1990 (202 women, randomised) and its 1994 extended observations (50 women, single-arm).
cards.result: Fluoride is the classic cautionary tale of osteoporosis therapeutics: a drug can raise measured bone density by a third and still leave vertebral fractures unchanged while increasing fractures elsewhere — the new bone is not normal bone. The extended follow-up's suggestion that gentler dosing might succeed remains untested speculation three decades on.
cards.watchOut: One randomised trial carries the verdict; it is large and clear enough on harm that the question will not be re-randomised at 75 mg/day. The shelf should be read as dose-specific: it condemns high-dose fluoride, not every fluoride exposure (dental fluoride is a different question, Shelves #464 and #471).
cards.source: Synthesis of Riggs BL et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1990 (PMID: 2407957) and Riggs BL et al. Journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. 1994 (PMID: 8140940). Registry IDs as on the trial cards.

shelves.title: High-dose versus standard-dose teriparatide, each combined with denosumab (DATA-HD)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does doubling the teriparatide dose within denosumab combination therapy (40 versus 20 micrograms daily) increase spine and hip BMD more over 15 months?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Bone Density/drug effects/physiology · Bone Density Conservation Agents/therapeutic use · Bone Resorption · Denosumab/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/drug therapy/physiopathology · Teriparatide/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — with a correction to the topic file, disclosed here: the filed question asked whether the combination beats 'either agent alone'. That is the parent DATA study's question, not DATA-HD's. The verified DATA-HD record randomised women between two doses of teriparatide (40 versus 20 micrograms), with denosumab added in BOTH arms — there is no monotherapy arm — and the shelf's question has been re-scoped to the comparison the trial actually made. On that question, the high-dose combination produced substantially larger BMD gains (spine +17.5% versus +9.5% at 15 months). PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single, small (76 women), open-label trial with a surrogate BMD endpoint; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. How the gains are (or are not) held after the combination stops is the DATA-HD extension's question, Shelf #1821.

cards.headline: DATA-HD: spine BMD rose 17.5% on teriparatide 40 micrograms plus denosumab versus 9.5% on the 20-microgram combination (difference 8.1 points; p<0.0001)
cards.summary: DATA-HD: spine BMD rose 17.5% on teriparatide 40 micrograms plus denosumab versus 9.5% on the 20-microgram combination (difference 8.1 points; p<0.0001)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, controlled phase 4 trial with masked outcome assessors (single centre; teriparatide for 9 months with denosumab 60 mg added at months 3 and 9, for 12 months; endpoints at 15 months)
cards.people: 76 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis were randomised to teriparatide 20 micrograms daily (39) or 40 micrograms daily (37), all receiving denosumab from month 3; 69 completed at least one post-baseline visit and entered the modified intention-to-treat analysis. The abstract does not print mean age.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — percentage change in spine areal BMD at 15 months — was +17.5% (SD 6.0) in the 40-microgram group versus +9.5% (SD 3.2) in the 20-microgram group (difference 8.1 percentage points, 95% CI 5.5 to 10.6; p<0.0001). Femoral neck BMD rose 6.8% versus 4.3% (difference 2.5 points, 95% CI 0.5 to 4.5; p=0.04) and total hip BMD 6.1% versus 3.9% (difference 2.2 points, 95% CI 0.6 to 3.8; p<0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 77-78% of both groups; serious adverse events were reported in 7 (18%) of the standard-dose group and 2 (5%) of the high-dose group. No deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received the combination — this trial says nothing about combination versus single-agent therapy (that was the parent DATA study, a different record, not carded here). Open-label treatment (assessors masked), one centre, 76 women, and a density surrogate: no fracture outcomes. The higher-dose arm's numerically fewer serious adverse events is a small-numbers pattern, not a safety finding.
cards.source: Tsai JN et al. Combination denosumab and high dose teriparatide for postmenopausal osteoporosis (DATA-HD): a randomised, controlled phase 4 trial. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2019. PMID: 31447409. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02176382, from the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: within the combination, the higher teriparatide dose builds markedly more bone — POSSIBLE

shelves.title: Romosozumab versus teriparatide after oral bisphosphonates (STRUCTURE)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis transitioning from oral bisphosphonate therapy, does romosozumab increase total-hip BMD more than teriparatide over 12 months?
shelves.mesh: No MeSH terms in the record
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a single open-label phase 3 trial (436 women, all previously on oral bisphosphonates) found total-hip BMD rose 2.6% over 12 months on romosozumab while falling 0.6% on teriparatide (difference 3.2 percentage points). Hypercalcaemia was much less frequent on romosozumab (under 1% versus 10%). The endpoint is a density surrogate — no fracture outcomes — and prior bisphosphonate exposure is precisely the setting where teriparatide's effect is blunted, which the authors state as the trial's premise. PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception. Scope boundary: romosozumab's fracture efficacy (FRAME, ARCH) is carded on Shelf #92.

cards.headline: STRUCTURE: total-hip BMD +2.6% on romosozumab versus -0.6% on teriparatide through 12 months (difference 3.2 points; p<0.0001)
cards.summary: STRUCTURE: total-hip BMD +2.6% on romosozumab versus -0.6% on teriparatide through 12 months (difference 3.2 points; p<0.0001)
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, active-controlled phase 3 trial (46 sites; romosozumab 210 mg monthly versus teriparatide 20 micrograms daily, for 12 months; primary endpoint the mean of months 6 and 12)
cards.people: 436 postmenopausal women (aged 55 to 90) with osteoporosis who had taken an oral bisphosphonate for at least 3 years and alendronate in the preceding year, with a BMD T-score of -2.5 or lower and a history of fracture; 218 were assigned to each treatment, with 206 and 209 in the primary efficacy analysis. The abstract does not print mean age.
cards.result: Through 12 months, mean total-hip areal BMD changed by +2.6% (95% CI 2.2 to 3.0) on romosozumab versus -0.6% (95% CI -1.0 to -0.2) on teriparatide — a difference of 3.2 percentage points (95% CI 2.7 to 3.8; p<0.0001). Adverse events were generally balanced; the most frequent were nasopharyngitis (13% versus 10%), hypercalcaemia (under 1% versus 10%) and arthralgia (10% versus 6%). Serious adverse events occurred in 17 (8%) on romosozumab and 23 (11%) on teriparatide, none judged treatment-related; withdrawals for adverse events were 3% versus 6%.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with a surrogate primary endpoint and no fracture outcomes; and the deck is stacked by design — participants were selected for prior bisphosphonate exposure, which is known to blunt teriparatide's bone-forming effect (the record states this premise). The result supports romosozumab as the better transition agent after bisphosphonates; it does not compare the two drugs in treatment-naive patients. The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Langdahl BL et al. Romosozumab (sclerostin monoclonal antibody) versus teriparatide in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis transitioning from oral bisphosphonate therapy: a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial. Lancet (London, England). 2017. PMID: 28755782. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01796301, from the record's databank fields. MeSH: the record carries no MeSH terms.

shelves.title: Nasal salmon calcitonin in established osteoporosis (PROOF)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with established osteoporosis, does nasal salmon calcitonin reduce new vertebral fractures versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Analysis of Variance · Bone Density/drug effects · Calcitonin/administration & dosage · Chi-Square Distribution · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fractures, Spontaneous/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Humans · Middle Aged · Nasal Cavity · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy · Reference Values · Secondary Prevention · Spinal Fractures/epidemiology/etiology/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the single large trial (PROOF, 1255 women, 5 years) found a significant vertebral-fracture reduction at exactly one of its three doses: 200 IU daily (relative risk 0.67; 51 of 287 versus 70 of 270), while 100 IU (RR 0.85) and 400 IU (RR 0.84) were not significant. A benefit confined to the middle dose, with no dose-response, is a fragile pattern that multiplicity can manufacture, and the cards flag it as such; the 200 IU result is nonetheless the trial's prespecified primary comparison. Attrition was heavy (only 511 of 1255 women completed 5 years). PROPOSED as a two-trial-gate exception candidate: a single trial; the shelf should be withdrawn or re-scoped if the developer rejects the exception.

cards.headline: PROOF: vertebral fractures reduced at the 200 IU dose only (RR 0.67); 100 IU and 400 IU not significant
cards.summary: PROOF: vertebral fractures reduced at the 200 IU dose only (RR 0.67); 100 IU and 400 IU not significant
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (5 years; nasal salmon calcitonin 100, 200 or 400 IU daily versus placebo; all participants received calcium 1000 mg and vitamin D 400 IU daily)
cards.people: 1255 postmenopausal women with established osteoporosis were randomised; 1108 had at least one follow-up spinal radiograph, 783 completed 3 years and 511 completed 5 years. The abstract does not print mean age.
cards.result: The primary comparison — new vertebral fractures on 200 IU versus placebo — was positive: 51 of 287 versus 70 of 270 women, relative risk 0.67 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.97; P=0.03). In the 817 women with one to five prevalent vertebral fractures at enrolment, the 200 IU risk reduction was similar (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.96; P=0.03 — a subgroup of the trial population, as the record presents it). The 100 IU (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.21) and 400 IU (relative risk 0.84, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.18) groups did not differ significantly from placebo. Lumbar spine BMD rose 1 to 1.5% in all active groups (P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: The missing dose-response is the story: if 200 IU works and double the dose does not, chance and multiplicity are live explanations, even though 200 IU was the prespecified primary dose. Nearly 60% of randomised women did not complete 5 years, so the fracture analysis rests on a completer-heavy subset. The trial predates registration reporting; the record carries no registry ID.
cards.source: Chesnut CH et al. A randomized trial of nasal spray salmon calcitonin in postmenopausal women with established osteoporosis: the prevent recurrence of osteoporotic fractures study. PROOF Study Group. The American journal of medicine. 2000. PMID: 10996576. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Tai chi for fibromyalgia (Wang)
shelves.question: In adults with fibromyalgia, does tai chi improve symptoms and function versus aerobic exercise (and versus wellness education with stretching)?
shelves.mesh: Comparative Effectiveness Research · Exercise · Female · Fibromyalgia · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Tai Ji · Treatment Outcome · United States
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials, both from one research group, both single-blind, both positive on symptom scores. The larger comparative-effectiveness trial (226 patients, BMJ 2018) found tai chi improved the revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire 5.5 points more than aerobic exercise at 24 weeks (95% CI 0.6 to 10.4, P=0.03) — a modest edge, and larger (16.2 points) when the dose and duration were matched. The earlier trial (66 patients, NEJM 2010) found a much larger difference against wellness education and stretching (FIQ change −18.4 points, P<0.001). Participants cannot be blinded to exercise, the outcomes are symptom scores, and no independent group has replicated the comparison — so the evidence is moderate, not strong. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Wang 2018: tai chi beat aerobic exercise on FIQR by 5.5 points at 24 weeks — 16.2 points when dose and duration were matched
cards.summary: Wang 2018: tai chi beat aerobic exercise on FIQR by 5.5 points at 24 weeks — 16.2 points when dose and duration were matched
cards.people: 226 adults with fibromyalgia (ACR 1990 and 2010 criteria) at an urban tertiary academic hospital in the United States, randomised to supervised aerobic exercise (24 weeks, twice weekly) or one of four classic Yang-style tai chi interventions (12 or 24 weeks, once or twice weekly); 151 tai chi, 75 aerobic exercise; followed for 52 weeks. Primary outcome was change in the revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (FIQR) at 24 weeks.
cards.result: FIQR scores improved in all five groups. The combined tai chi groups improved 5.5 points more than aerobic exercise at 24 weeks (95% confidence interval 0.6 to 10.4, P=0.03), with larger gains on patient global assessment (0.9 points, P=0.005), anxiety (1.2 points, P=0.006), self-efficacy (1.0 points, P=0.0004) and coping strategies (2.6 points, P=0.005). Tai chi at the same intensity and duration as aerobic exercise (24 weeks, twice weekly) beat it by 16.2 FIQR points (8.7 to 23.6, P<0.001); 24 weeks of tai chi beat 12 weeks by 9.6 points (2.6 to 16.6, P=0.007); once weekly was no worse than twice weekly. Attendance was better for tai chi than for aerobic exercise. No serious adverse events related to the interventions were reported.
cards.watchOut: The between-group edge over aerobic exercise (5.5 points) is modest and its confidence interval nearly reaches zero — the headline comparison is the matched-dose 16.2-point figure, which is a subgroup contrast, not the primary analysis. Participants could not be blinded to the exercise they received.
cards.source: Wang C et al. Effect of tai chi versus aerobic exercise for fibromyalgia: comparative effectiveness randomized controlled trial. BMJ. 2018. PMID: 29563100. cards.headline: Wang 2010: tai chi beat wellness education and stretching by 18.4 FIQ points at 12 weeks in a small trial
cards.summary: Wang 2010: tai chi beat wellness education and stretching by 18.4 FIQ points at 12 weeks in a small trial

shelves.title: Bed rest for acute sciatica and low back pain (Vroomen; Malmivaara)
shelves.question: In patients with acute sciatica (or acute low back pain), does prescribed bed rest speed recovery versus watchful waiting and staying active?
shelves.mesh: Absenteeism · Adult · Analgesics · Bed Rest · Diskectomy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pain Measurement · Patient Satisfaction · Sciatica · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials in the New England Journal of Medicine, consistent. In sciatica (183 patients), bed rest for two weeks produced improvement in 70% versus 65% with watchful waiting (adjusted odds ratio 1.2, 95% CI 0.6 to 2.3), and by 12 weeks 87% of both groups had improved, with no differences in pain, function, absenteeism or surgery. In acute low back pain (186 patients), bed rest was the slowest of three strategies — continuing ordinary activities as tolerated recovered significantly faster than either bed rest or exercises on pain duration and intensity, disability and days absent from work. Bed rest does not speed recovery, and in back pain it delayed it. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Vroomen 1999: bed rest for sciatica — 70% improved vs 65% with watchful waiting at two weeks; 87% in both groups by 12 weeks
cards.summary: Vroomen 1999: bed rest for sciatica — 70% improved vs 65% with watchful waiting at two weeks; 87% in both groups by 12 weeks
cards.people: 183 patients with a lumbosacral radicular syndrome (sciatica) severe enough that bed rest was usually justified, randomly assigned to bed rest for two weeks or watchful waiting over the same period. Outcome assessors and analysts were blinded to allocation. Primary outcomes were the investigator's and patient's global assessments of improvement at 2 and 12 weeks; secondary outcomes included pain and functional scores, absenteeism and surgical intervention.
cards.result: After two weeks, 64 of 92 patients in the bed-rest group (70%) reported improvement versus 59 of 91 (65%) in the watchful-waiting group (adjusted odds ratio 1.2, 95% confidence interval 0.6 to 2.3). After 12 weeks, 87% of patients in both groups reported improvement. Pain intensity, bothersomeness of symptoms and functional status did not differ significantly between groups at any point, and absenteeism from work and rates of surgical intervention were similar. The authors concluded that bed rest is not a more effective therapy than watchful waiting for sciatica.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (0.6 to 2.3) cannot exclude a modest benefit or harm from bed rest at two weeks — but with 87% of both groups improved by 12 weeks and no advantage on any secondary measure, the room for a clinically important benefit is small.
cards.source: Vroomen PC et al. Lack of effectiveness of bed rest for sciatica. N Engl J Med. 1999. PMID: 9971865. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era (no registry ID in the record). cards.headline: Malmivaara 1995: for acute low back pain, ordinary activity recovered fastest and bed rest was the slowest strategy
cards.summary: Malmivaara 1995: for acute low back pain, ordinary activity recovered fastest and bed rest was the slowest strategy
cards.people: 186 employees of the city of Helsinki presenting to occupational health care with acute, nonspecific low back pain, randomly assigned to bed rest for two days (67 patients), back-mobilising exercises (52) or continuation of ordinary activities as tolerated (67). cards.result: At both 3 and 12 weeks, the ordinary-activity group recovered better than either the bed-rest or exercise groups, with statistically significant differences favouring ordinary activity in duration of pain, pain intensity, lumbar flexion, subjective ability to work, the Oswestry back-disability index and number of days absent from work. shelves.title: Antibiotics for chronic low back pain with Modic changes (Albert; AIM)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic low back pain and Modic type 1 changes after a disc herniation, does a 100-day course of amoxicillin (± clavulanate) reduce pain and disability versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amoxicillin-Potassium Clavulanate Combination · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Bone Diseases · Disability Evaluation · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Edema · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intervertebral Disc Displacement · Low Back Pain · Lumbar Vertebrae · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pain Measurement · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The classic shrinkage, carded in full. Albert 2013 (162 patients, single centre) reported dramatic gains from 100 days of amoxicillin–clavulanate in Modic type 1 disease — disability (RMDQ) fell from 15 to 5.7 at one year against 15 to 14 on placebo. The larger AIM trial (180 patients, six Norwegian centres, BMJ 2019) found a between-group RMDQ difference of −1.6 points (−3.1 to 0.0, P=0.04) — statistically significant but well below its own predefined clinically important difference of 4 points; in type 1 changes the difference was −2.3, in type 2 it was −0.1. Drug-related adverse events: 56% on amoxicillin versus 34% on placebo. The stamp follows the mature multicentre data: at most a small benefit of doubtful clinical importance, bought with three months of antibiotics. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Albert 2013: antibiotics cut RMDQ disability from 15 to 5.7 at one year versus 15 to 14 on placebo — a very large effect in a small single-centre trial
cards.summary: Albert 2013: antibiotics cut RMDQ disability from 15 to 5.7 at one year versus 15 to 14 on placebo — a very large effect in a small single-centre trial
cards.people: 162 patients with chronic low back pain of more than six months after a previous disc herniation, with vertebral bone oedema (Modic type 1 changes) adjacent to the herniation, randomised double-blind to 100 days of amoxicillin–clavulanate (Bioclavid) or placebo; 144 were evaluated at one-year follow-up. Primary outcomes were disease-specific disability (RMDQ) and lumbar pain.
cards.result: At baseline, end of treatment and one year, RMDQ changed: antibiotic group 15, 11, 5.7; placebo group 15, 14, 14. Leg pain fell from 5.3 to 1.4 with antibiotics versus 4.0 to 4.3 with placebo; lumbar pain from 6.7 to 3.7 versus 6.3 to 6.3. Improvements were statistically significant on all primary and secondary outcomes, exceeded predefined clinically important thresholds, and continued between the end of treatment and one year, with a trend to a dose–response relationship.
cards.watchOut: An effect this large (a disability gap of more than eight RMDQ points) from a single-centre trial of 162 patients is exactly the pattern that shrinks on replication — and it did, in AIM. The trial tested amoxicillin–clavulanate, while AIM tested amoxicillin alone; the drug regimens are not identical.
cards.source: Albert HB et al. cards.headline: AIM 2019: in 180 patients the RMDQ difference was −1.6 points — significant, but below the predefined clinically important difference of 4
cards.summary: AIM 2019: in 180 patients the RMDQ difference was −1.6 points — significant, but below the predefined clinically important difference of 4
cards.people: 180 patients with chronic low back pain, previous disc herniation and Modic changes (type 1 in 118, type 2 in 62) at six Norwegian hospitals, randomised double-blind to three months of oral amoxicillin 750 mg three times daily or placebo. The primary outcome was RMDQ score (0–24) at one year, with a minimal clinically important between-group difference predefined as 4 points.
cards.result: In the total cohort at one year, the between-group difference in mean RMDQ score was −1.6 (95% confidence interval −3.1 to 0.0, P=0.04). In type 1 Modic changes the difference was −2.3 (−4.2 to −0.4, P=0.02); in type 2 changes it was −0.1 (−2.7 to 2.6, P=0.95). Fifty patients (56%) in the amoxicillin group had at least one drug-related adverse event versus 31 (34%) on placebo. The authors concluded that three months of amoxicillin did not provide a clinically important benefit and does not support antibiotic treatment for chronic low back pain with Modic changes.
cards.watchOut: The overall P value is 0.04 with a confidence interval ending at 0.0 — a fragile significance. AIM used amoxicillin alone rather than the amoxicillin–clavulanate of Albert, so it is a near-replication, not an exact one; the type 1 subgroup result keeps a small benefit genuinely possible.

shelves.title: Colchicine for knee osteoarthritis (COLKOA)
shelves.question: In patients with knee osteoarthritis, does low-dose colchicine reduce pain and inflammation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Biomarkers · Colchicine · Cytokines · Disease Progression · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Inflammation · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Synovial Fluid · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: One double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (COLKOA, 109 patients, 16 weeks of colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily). The primary endpoint — at least 30% improvement in total WOMAC score at week 16 — was met by 39% of the colchicine group and 49% of the placebo group (P=0.284; odds ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.41), and no clinical secondary endpoint differed. Colchicine did reduce inflammatory and bone-turnover biomarkers (serum hs-CRP and synovial-fluid CTX I fell significantly), so the drug engaged its targets without relieving symptoms. A single small trial cannot make this LIKELY, but a blinded trial with no symptom signal in any endpoint justifies the no-difference lean. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: COLKOA: 39% responded on colchicine vs 49% on placebo — no symptom benefit, despite biomarker movement
cards.summary: COLKOA: 39% responded on colchicine vs 49% on placebo — no symptom benefit, despite biomarker movement
cards.people: 109 patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis randomised double-blind to colchicine 0.5 mg orally twice daily or placebo for 16 weeks. The primary endpoint was at least 30% improvement in total WOMAC score at week 16; secondary endpoints included pain, WOMAC pain, patient global assessment, function, quality of life and serum, urine and synovial-fluid biomarkers of cartilage metabolism and inflammation.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met by 39% (95% confidence interval 27–52%) of the colchicine group and 49% (36–62%) of the placebo group (P=0.284; odds ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.41). No strong evidence of treatment difference was identified on any clinical secondary endpoint. Treatment significantly reduced mean serum hs-CRP (P=0.008) and synovial-fluid CTX I (P=0.002) and tended to reduce other inflammatory markers without reaching significance. The authors concluded colchicine reduced inflammation and high bone-turnover biomarkers but did not reduce knee osteoarthritis symptoms over 16 weeks, and called for a longer study of possible slow-acting disease-modifying effects.
cards.watchOut: Only 109 patients and 16 weeks: the confidence interval around the response odds ratio (0.31 to 1.41) leaves room for a modest benefit, and a slow disease-modifying effect over years was not tested. The null is for symptoms at four months.
cards.source: Leung YY et al. Colchicine lack of effectiveness in symptom and inflammation modification in knee osteoarthritis (COLKOA): a randomized controlled trial. Osteoarthritis Cartilage. 2018. PMID: 29426008. Registry ID: NCT02176460, from the record. shelves.title: Methotrexate for hand osteoarthritis (Ferrero; HERO as companion)
shelves.question: In patients with hand osteoarthritis refractory to usual treatment, does weekly methotrexate reduce pain versus placebo — and what did hydroxychloroquine do in the parallel question?
shelves.mesh: Antirheumatic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Methotrexate · Osteoarthritis · Prospective Studies · Synovitis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: CORRECTION to the topic draft: the draft's claim that methotrexate reduced pain is not what the trial found. In Ferrero 2021 (64 patients with erosive hand osteoarthritis), the decrease in pain VAS at three months was 21.1 mm on methotrexate versus 11.7 mm on placebo (p=0.2), and the authors' own conclusion is that weekly 10 mg methotrexate showed no superiority over placebo for pain relief at 3 or 12 months; the only significant signal was structural (more eroded joints progressing to a remodelling phase, 27% vs 15%, p=0.03). The companion hydroxychloroquine trial, HERO (248 patients), was a firm null: hand pain at six months 5.66 on hydroxychloroquine versus 5.49 on placebo, difference −0.16 (−0.73 to 0.40, P=0.57). Two anti-rheumatic drugs, no analgesic benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Ferrero 2021: methotrexate did NOT significantly reduce hand OA pain — the topic draft's claim is contradicted by the trial's own conclusion
cards.summary: Ferrero 2021: methotrexate did NOT significantly reduce hand OA pain — the topic draft's claim is contradicted by the trial's own conclusion
cards.people: 64 patients with symptomatic erosive hand osteoarthritis refractory to usual treatment, randomised double-blind at a single centre to methotrexate 10 mg weekly or placebo for one year. The primary endpoint was change in pain on a visual analogue scale from baseline to 3 months; secondary endpoints included pain at 12 months, function, radiographic scores and MRI features.
cards.result: At 3 months there was no significant difference in the mean decrease in pain VAS (methotrexate 21.1 mm [SD 27.4], placebo 11.7 mm [24.3]; p=0.2). At 12 months, by the Verbruggen–Veys radiographic score, erosive joints progressed significantly more to a remodelling phase in the methotrexate group than the placebo group (27% vs 15%; p=0.03), and joints with space loss appeared to erode less on methotrexate (8% vs 29%; p=0.2). Baseline MRI synovitis was associated with erosive progression of non-erosive joints (p=0.02). The authors concluded: weekly doses of 10 mg methotrexate showed no superiority over placebo in terms of pain relief at 3 or 12 months.
cards.watchOut: The trial was small and the pain outcome imprecise (standard deviations around 25 mm), so a modest analgesic benefit is not excluded — but the primary endpoint missed and the trial's conclusion is null. The remodelling signal is structural, from a secondary analysis, and does not answer the pain question this shelf asks.

cards.headline: HERO: hydroxychloroquine for hand osteoarthritis — hand pain 5.66 vs 5.49 on placebo at six months (P=0.57)
cards.summary: HERO: hydroxychloroquine for hand osteoarthritis — hand pain 5.66 vs 5.49 on placebo at six months (P=0.57)
cards.people: 248 participants (82% women, mean age 62.7 years) with symptomatic (pain at least 4 of 10) and radiographic hand osteoarthritis at 13 primary and secondary care centres in England, randomised double-blind to hydroxychloroquine 200–400 mg daily or placebo for 12 months with ongoing usual care; 210 (84.7%) completed the 6-month primary endpoint of average hand pain over the previous two weeks (0–10 scale).
cards.result: At 6 months, mean hand pain was 5.49 points in the placebo group and 5.66 in the hydroxychloroquine group — a treatment difference of −0.16 point (95% confidence interval −0.73 to 0.40) (P=0.57). Results were robust to adjustment for adherence, missing data and rescue medication, and no significant treatment differences existed at 3, 6 or 12 months for any secondary outcome, including function, grip strength and quality of life. Baseline synovitis on ultrasound (94% of scanned participants) did not affect treatment response. Fifteen serious adverse events were reported (7 hydroxychloroquine, 8 placebo). The authors concluded hydroxychloroquine was no more effective than placebo for pain relief in moderate-to-severe hand osteoarthritis.
cards.watchOut: The trialists note hydroxychloroquine dosage restrictions may have reduced efficacy. Otherwise this is a large, well-conducted null — the strongest card on the shelf, and it is for hydroxychloroquine, not methotrexate.

shelves.title: Emergency-department care and physiotherapy for acute whiplash (MINT)
shelves.question: In patients presenting to emergency departments with acute whiplash, does a physiotherapy package (or active management advice) improve recovery versus usual-care advice alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Health Care Costs · Humans · Male · Physical Therapy Modalities · Treatment Outcome · Whiplash Injuries
shelves.balance: One large two-step pragmatic trial (MINT, ISRCTN33302125). Step 1 (cluster-randomised, 3,851 patients in 15 emergency departments): training staff to give active-management consultations made no difference to the Neck Disability Index at 12 months versus usual consultations (difference 0.5, 95% CI −1.5 to 2.5). Step 2 (599 patients with persisting symptoms): a package of up to six physiotherapy sessions gave a modest benefit at 4 months versus a single advice session (NDI difference −3.7, −6.1 to −1.3) that was gone by 8 and 12 months, and the package was not cost-effective. The trial's own recommendation — usual consultations plus a single advice session — is what the evidence supports. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: MINT Step 1: active-management consultations in the ED made no difference — NDI difference 0.5 (−1.5 to 2.5) at 12 months in 3,851 patients
cards.summary: MINT Step 1: active-management consultations in the ED made no difference — NDI difference 0.5 (−1.5 to 2.5) at 12 months in 3,851 patients
cards.people: 3,851 patients with acute whiplash-associated disorder grades I–III attending 15 emergency departments in 12 NHS Trusts, in a pragmatic cluster-randomised trial: hospitals were randomised to consultations by staff trained in active management, or usual consultations. 1,598 patients were assigned to usual care and 2,253 to active management; 2,704 (70%) provided data at 12 months. The primary outcome was the Neck Disability Index (NDI); outcome investigators were masked, though patients and clinicians could not be.
cards.result: The NDI score did not differ between active-management and usual-care consultations (difference at 12 months 0.5, 95% confidence interval −1.5 to 2.5). No treatment-related serious adverse events or deaths were noted. Active-management consultations were more expensive than usual care.
cards.watchOut: A cluster design with 30% loss to follow-up — but the confidence interval excludes any worthwhile benefit from the consultation package, so the null for Step 1 is firm. 'Active management' here is a specific staff-training intervention, not simply good advice-giving.

shelves.title: Paracetamol for acute low back pain (PACE)
shelves.question: In patients with acute low back pain, does regular or as-needed paracetamol speed recovery versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen · Acute Pain · Adult · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Low Back Pain · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Socioeconomic Factors · Treatment Outcome · Drug Monitoring
shelves.balance: One large, rigorous double-blind trial (PACE, 1,652 patients) with a precise result. Median time to recovery was 17 days with regular paracetamol, 17 days with as-needed paracetamol and 16 days with placebo (regular vs placebo hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.14; as-needed vs placebo 1.05, 0.92 to 1.19), with no differences on secondary outcomes and identical adverse-event rates (about 18.5% in every group). Paracetamol was the recommended first-line analgesic for acute low back pain when the trial ran; this is the trial that removed its evidence base. Correction to the topic draft: the placebo group's median recovery was 16 days, not 17. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: PACE: median recovery 17 days (regular), 17 days (as-needed), 16 days (placebo) in 1,652 patients — paracetamol changed nothing
cards.summary: PACE: median recovery 17 days (regular), 17 days (as-needed), 16 days (placebo) in 1,652 patients — paracetamol changed nothing
cards.people: 1,652 patients with acute low back pain recruited at 235 primary care centres in Sydney, Australia, randomised double-dummy and double-blind to up to 4 weeks of regular paracetamol (three times daily, 3,990 mg/day), as-needed paracetamol (maximum 4,000 mg/day) or placebo. All participants received best-evidence advice and were followed for 3 months. The primary outcome was time to recovery — a pain score of 0 or 1 on a 0–10 scale sustained for 7 consecutive days.
cards.result: 550 participants were assigned to regular paracetamol, 549 to as-needed and 553 to placebo. Median time to recovery was 17 days (95% confidence interval 14–19) in the regular group, 17 days (15–20) in the as-needed group and 16 days (14–20) in the placebo group (regular vs placebo hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.14; as-needed vs placebo 1.05, 0.92 to 1.19; regular vs as-needed 1.05, 0.92 to 1.20). There was no difference between groups for time to recovery (adjusted p=0.79), and the number reporting adverse events was the same in all groups (99 [18.5%], 99 [18.7%] and 98 [18.5%]). The authors concluded the findings question the universal endorsement of paracetamol for acute low back pain.
cards.watchOut: The confidence intervals exclude a worthwhile speeding of recovery, so the null is solid for the question asked — but the trial measured time to recovery, not the immediate hour-by-hour analgesia patients take paracetamol for; it does not prove paracetamol can never take the edge off a painful evening.
cards.source: Williams CM et al. Efficacy of paracetamol for acute low-back pain: a double-blind, randomised controlled trial (PACE). Lancet. 2014. PMID: 25064594. Registry ID as printed in the record: ANZCTR ACTN12609000966291. shelves.title: Motor control exercise for chronic low back pain (Costa)
shelves.question: In patients with chronic non-specific low back pain, does motor control (specific stabilisation) exercise improve activity limitation and pain versus placebo (detuned ultrasound and diathermy)?
shelves.mesh: Chronic Disease · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Low Back Pain · Male · Middle Aged · Movement · Pain Measurement · Posture · Recovery of Function
shelves.balance: Two Australian randomised trials that answer two halves of the question. Against placebo (detuned ultrasound and diathermy), Costa 2009 (154 patients) found motor control exercise improved activity by 1.1 points (95% CI 0.3 to 1.8) and global impression of recovery by 1.5 points (0.4 to 2.5) at two months — but the effect on pain itself was 0.9 points (−0.01 to 1.8), not significant. Against another active exercise, Macedo 2012 (172 patients) found no significant difference between motor control exercise and graded activity at any time point for any outcome (pain effect at 2 months 0.0, −0.7 to 0.8). So: exercise of this kind gives small short-term functional gains over doing nothing real, but there is nothing specifically superior about the motor control approach. PROPOSED POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Costa 2009: motor control exercise beat placebo on activity (+1.1) and global recovery (+1.5) at 2 months — but not on pain (+0.9, CI crossing zero)
cards.summary: Costa 2009: motor control exercise beat placebo on activity (+1.1) and global recovery (+1.5) at 2 months — but not on pain (+0.9, CI crossing zero)
cards.people: 154 patients with chronic low back pain of more than 12 weeks' duration at an outpatient physical therapy department in Australia, randomised to 12 sessions over 8 weeks of motor control exercise (training specific trunk muscles and control of posture and movement) or placebo (detuned ultrasound and detuned short-wave diathermy). Primary outcomes at 2 months were pain intensity, activity (Patient-Specific Functional Scale) and global impression of recovery.
cards.result: At 2 months, the mean effect of exercise on activity was 1.1 points (95% confidence interval 0.3 to 1.8), on global impression of recovery 1.5 points (0.4 to 2.5), and on pain 0.9 points (−0.01 to 1.8), all on 11-point scales — so the exercise improved activity and perceived recovery but did not clearly reduce pain. Secondary outcomes also favoured motor control exercise, and most short-term effects were maintained at the 6- and 12-month follow-ups. Clinicians could not be blinded to the intervention they delivered.
cards.watchOut: Effects of about one point on 11-point scales are small, the treating clinicians were unblinded, and the placebo (detuned machines) controls attention and touch only partly. The pain outcome — the symptom patients care most about — did not reach significance.

shelves.title: Teriparatide versus risedronate in severe osteoporosis (VERO): fewer vertebral and clinical fractures on the anabolic
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with severe osteoporosis and prevalent vertebral fractures, does daily teriparatide prevent new fractures better than weekly risedronate — the rare head-to-head fracture trial between an anabolic and an antiresorptive?
shelves.mesh: Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/drug therapy · Osteoporotic Fractures/prevention & control · Risedronic Acid/therapeutic use · Teriparatide/therapeutic use · Humans · Female · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: In the only large head-to-head fracture trial between an anabolic and an antiresorptive, teriparatide beat risedronate. In 1,360 postmenopausal women with severe osteoporosis and prevalent vertebral fractures (VERO, 24 months), new radiographic vertebral fractures occurred in 5.4% on teriparatide versus 12.0% on risedronate (risk ratio 0.44 — a 56% relative reduction, 6.6 percentage points absolute), and clinical fractures in 4.8% versus 9.8% (hazard ratio 0.48). Non-vertebral fragility fractures did not differ significantly (4.0% versus 6.1%; HR 0.66, p=0.10). The benefit was consistent across subgroups in the prespecified subgroup report. This is a single trial, industry-funded, in a high-risk population — the comparison is against an active drug, not placebo, so both drugs work; teriparatide worked better on vertebral and clinical fractures. PROPOSED LIKELY — one large, double-blind, fracture-endpoint head-to-head trial with a clear result on its primary outcome.

cards.headline: VERO (Kendler 2018): new vertebral fractures 5.4% on teriparatide vs 12.0% on risedronate over 24 months (RR 0.44)
cards.summary: VERO (Kendler 2018): new vertebral fractures 5.4% on teriparatide vs 12.0% on risedronate over 24 months (RR 0.44)
cards.people: 1,360 postmenopausal women with severe osteoporosis — at least two moderate or one severe vertebral fracture and BMD T-score ≤−1.50 — randomised to teriparatide 20 μg daily plus weekly oral placebo, or risedronate 35 mg weekly plus daily placebo injections, for 24 months (680 per group). Primary outcome: new radiographic vertebral fractures.
cards.result: New vertebral fractures: 28 (5.4%) on teriparatide versus 64 (12.0%) on risedronate (risk ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.29–0.68; p<0.0001 — a relative measure, printed beside the absolute rates). Clinical fractures: 30 (4.8%) versus 61 (9.8%) (hazard ratio 0.48, 95% CI 0.32–0.74; p=0.0009). Non-vertebral fragility fractures: 25 (4.0%) versus 38 (6.1%) (HR 0.66; 95% CI 0.39–1.10; p=0.10, not significant).
cards.watchOut: Single head-to-head trial, funded by Lilly (teriparatide's maker). The population was already severely affected (prevalent vertebral fractures), so absolute benefits are larger than they would be in lower-risk osteoporosis. Teriparatide is a daily injection, usually time-limited; risedronate is a weekly pill — the trial answers efficacy, not convenience or cost.
cards.source: Kendler DL et al. Effects of teriparatide and risedronate on new fractures in post-menopausal women with severe osteoporosis (VERO): a multicentre, double-blind, double-dummy, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2018. PMID: 29129436. Registry ID: NCT01709110, from the record (also EudraCT 2012-000123-41). cards.headline: VERO subgroups (Geusens 2018): the teriparatide advantage did not differ across age, prior fractures, prior drugs, or BMD subgroups
cards.summary: VERO subgroups (Geusens 2018): the teriparatide advantage did not differ across age, prior fractures, prior drugs, or BMD subgroups
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (VERO)
cards.people: The same 1,360 VERO women (680 per group; mean age 72.1 years; mean 2.7 prevalent vertebral fractures; 55.4% with BMD T-score <−2.5; 43.2% osteoporosis drug-naïve; 39.3% recent bisphosphonate users), in prospectively planned subgroup analyses predefined by age, prevalent fracture number/severity, glucocorticoid use, prior osteoporosis drugs, and baseline BMD.
cards.result: As previously reported in the primary paper, new vertebral fractures and clinical fractures were significantly reduced on teriparatide versus risedronate. For most fracture endpoints, the risk reduction did not significantly differ in any subgroup (treatment-by-subgroup interaction p>0.1), with most subgroups mirroring the total study population.
cards.watchOut: Subgroup analyses of a single trial — consistency is reassuring but cannot substitute for a second trial. The draft for this shelf pinned this subgroup paper (PMID 29329484) as the anchor; the primary VERO report (PMID 29129436) is carded first above because it carries the fracture rates.

shelves.title: Zoledronate after stopping denosumab: partial protection against rebound bone loss, no winning timing
shelves.question: In patients discontinuing denosumab, does a zoledronate infusion (and at what timing) prevent the rapid rebound bone loss and vertebral fracture risk that follow denosumab cessation?
shelves.mesh: Bone Density · Bone Density Conservation Agents/therapeutic use · Denosumab/therapeutic use · Humans · Osteoporosis/drug therapy · Zoledronic Acid/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Stopping denosumab without follow-on treatment causes rapid rebound bone loss; zoledronate softens that loss but does not prevent it. In a Taiwanese randomised trial of 101 patients who had taken denosumab for at least 2 years, one zoledronate infusion lost lumbar spine BMD in year 1 (median −0.68%) while continued denosumab gained (+1.30%; p=.03), though hip BMD was preserved in both groups; loss was worse after 3 or more years of denosumab (−3.20%). In a Danish randomised timing study of 61 patients stopping after a mean 4.6 years, spine BMD fell about 4% by 24 months whichever timing was used (6 months, 9 months, or turnover-guided), with BMD then maintained during year 2. Neither trial tested fractures. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — two small randomised trials agree zoledronate only partially protects, BMD endpoints only, and no timing strategy has been shown superior.

cards.headline: Lee 2024: spine BMD fell on zoledronate (−0.68%) while continuing denosumab gained (+1.30%) in year 1; hip BMD preserved in both
cards.summary: Lee 2024: spine BMD fell on zoledronate (−0.68%) while continuing denosumab gained (+1.30%) in year 1; hip BMD preserved in both
cards.type: Randomised, open-label, parallel-group trial (Denosumab Sequential Therapy)
cards.people: 101 patients (95 women; median age 72) in Taiwan who had received denosumab for at least 2 years, randomised (stratified, open-label) to continued denosumab 60 mg twice yearly (group A, n=25) or a single zoledronate 5 mg dose in year 1 (group ZOL, n=76). Coprimary outcomes: percentage change in lumbar spine, total hip, and femoral neck BMD at 1 year.
cards.result: Median lumbar spine BMD change in year 1 was −0.68% (IQR −3.22% to 2.75%) on zoledronate versus +1.30% (−0.68% to 5.24%) on continued denosumab (P=.03). Total hip (median +1.12% vs 0%; P=.24) and femoral neck (+0.17% vs +0.18%; P=.71) did not differ significantly. In the zoledronate subgroup with 3 or more years of prior denosumab, spine BMD fell −3.20% (IQR −7.89% to 0.68%) versus +1.30% on continued denosumab (P=.003). The authors conclude zoledronate does not fully prevent spine bone loss after denosumab discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is continued denosumab, not no treatment — so this trial shows zoledronate is worse than staying on denosumab for spine BMD, not how much better it is than stopping outright. Unequal group sizes (25 vs 76), open-label, BMD endpoint only; the planned 2-year follow-up is not in this report.
cards.source: Lee CC et al. Zoledronate Sequential Therapy After Denosumab Discontinuation to Prevent Bone Mineral Density Reduction: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2024. PMID: 39527056. Registry ID: NCT03868033, from the record. cards.headline: Sølling 2021: spine BMD fell ~4% by 24 months after zoledronate whatever the timing (6 months, 9 months, or turnover-guided), then held in year 2
cards.summary: Sølling 2021: spine BMD fell ~4% by 24 months after zoledronate whatever the timing (6 months, 9 months, or turnover-guided), then held in year 2
cards.people: 61 postmenopausal women and men over 50 discontinuing denosumab after 4.6 ± 1.6 years, randomised open-label to zoledronate at 6 months (6M), at 9 months (9M), or when bone turnover increased (observation, OBS), with retreatment if p-CTX rose ≥1.26 μg/L or BMD fell ≥5%; 58 completed 24 months.
cards.result: From baseline to 24 months, lumbar spine BMD decreased 4.0 ± 0.8% (6M), 4.1 ± 0.8% (9M), and 4.3 ± 1.5% (OBS) (p<.001 within groups; no between-group differences). From 12 to 24 months spine BMD was maintained (+0.9 ± 0.9%, +0.4 ± 0.8%, +0.3 ± 0.7%; no between-group differences), and hip BMD did not change in year 2. Significant bone loss at some site by 24 months occurred in 60% (6M), 37% (9M), and 53% (OBS); 9 patients were retreated at month 24 for BMD loss ≥5%, and 2 patients sustained a non-vertebral fracture in year 2.
cards.watchOut: No untreated control group, small groups (~20 each), and most loss happened in year 1 (reported in the earlier 12-month paper, not this record). Timing made no detectable difference, but the trial was not powered to find a modest one. Fracture protection after switching remains untested in both carded trials.
cards.source: Sølling AS et al. Treatment With Zoledronate Subsequent to Denosumab in Osteoporosis: A 2-Year Randomized Study. J Bone Miner Res. 2021. PMID: 33813753. Registry ID: NCT03087851, from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: zoledronate after denosumab blunts but does not prevent rebound loss; no timing wins — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: zoledronate after denosumab blunts but does not prevent rebound loss; no timing wins — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: 101 patients in Lee 2024 (zoledronate vs continued denosumab) and 61 in Sølling 2021 (zoledronate timing strategies).
cards.result: Spine BMD fell after switching to zoledronate in both trials (median −0.68% at 1 year vs +1.30% if denosumab continued; ~−4% by 24 months across timings), hip BMD was largely preserved, and loss was greater after longer denosumab exposure. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Both trials measure BMD, not the rebound vertebral fractures that make denosumab cessation dangerous. Nothing here supports stopping denosumab without a follow-on plan; it shows the standard follow-on plan is incomplete protection, especially after long denosumab courses.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lee CC et al. JAMA Netw Open. 2024 (PMID: 39527056) and Sølling AS et al. J Bone Miner Res. 2021 (PMID: 33813753). Registry IDs as on the trial cards.

shelves.title: Semaglutide for knee osteoarthritis (STEP 9): weight −13.7% vs −3.2% and WOMAC pain −41.7 vs −27.5 points at 68 weeks
shelves.question: In people with obesity and moderate knee osteoarthritis with at least moderate pain, does once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg reduce knee pain and body weight compared with placebo, on top of lifestyle counselling?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Body Mass Index · Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Injections, Subcutaneous · Obesity/complications, therapy · Osteoarthritis, Knee/complications, therapy · Weight Loss/drug effects · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage, adverse effects · Counseling · Caloric Restriction · Arthralgia/diagnosis, etiology, therapy · Pain Measurement · Semaglutide
shelves.balance: Weight loss relieves knee osteoarthritis pain, and STEP 9 is the first large trial of a GLP-1 drug aimed at the knee itself. In 407 people with obesity (mean BMI 40.3) and moderate knee osteoarthritis with at least moderate pain, once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg for 68 weeks — with physical-activity and reduced-calorie counselling in both arms — produced weight loss of −13.7% versus −3.2% on placebo, and a WOMAC pain improvement of −41.7 versus −27.5 points (both p<0.001), with physical function also better (+12.0 vs +6.5 SF-36 points). Serious adverse events were similar; discontinuations for adverse events were 6.7% vs 3.0%, mostly gastrointestinal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). Tier C: a single trial carries the claim, and how much of the pain effect is weight loss itself — versus any joint-specific action — the trial cannot separate.

cards.headline: STEP 9: semaglutide −13.7% body weight vs −3.2%; WOMAC pain −41.7 vs −27.5 points at 68 weeks (both p<0.001)
cards.summary: STEP 9: semaglutide −13.7% body weight vs −3.2%; WOMAC pain −41.7 vs −27.5 points at 68 weeks (both p<0.001)
cards.people: 407 participants (mean age 56; 81.6% women; mean BMI 40.3; mean WOMAC pain 70.9/100) with obesity and clinical plus radiological moderate knee osteoarthritis, at 61 sites in 11 countries, randomised 2:1 to semaglutide 2.4 mg once weekly or placebo for 68 weeks, both with activity and diet counselling.
cards.result: Weight change: −13.7% vs −3.2% (p<0.001). WOMAC pain change: −41.7 vs −27.5 points (p<0.001). SF-36 physical function: +12.0 vs +6.5 points (p<0.001). Serious adverse events were similar between groups; permanent discontinuation for adverse events 6.7% vs 3.0%, gastrointestinal disorders the commonest reason.
cards.watchOut: One trial, in people with obesity — it does not answer for knee OA without obesity, for other GLP-1 agents, or for structural progression (no cartilage outcome), and pain relief tracks the weight difference closely.
cards.source: Bliddal H et al.. Once-Weekly Semaglutide in Persons with Obesity and Knee Osteoarthritis. The New England journal of medicine. 2024. PMID: 39476339. Registry ID: NCT05064735.
