shelves.title: Vitamin C after a wrist fracture: two positive trials, one null replication
shelves.question: In adults with a wrist (distal radius) fracture, does vitamin C 500 mg daily for about 50 days prevent complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antioxidants · Ascorbic Acid · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Fractures, Bone · Humans · Radius Fractures · Reflex Sympathetic Dystrophy · Wrist Injuries
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials from one Dutch group found vitamin C after a wrist fracture cut complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS, formerly reflex sympathetic dystrophy): 7% versus 22% in Zollinger 1999 — an absolute difference of 15 percentage points (95% CI 2–26) — and, in the 2007 dose-response trial, 2.4% on pooled vitamin C versus 10.1% on placebo, with the 500 mg dose at a relative risk of 0.17 relative to placebo and no extra gain at 1,500 mg. The independent replication went the other way: Ekrol 2014 (Edinburgh, n = 336) made function its primary outcome and found no benefit on the DASH score at any point, no overall difference in CRPS, and a few early secondary outcomes favouring placebo. Both positive trials come from a single research group and the one independent test was null on function and on CRPS overall; the pill is cheap and, at 500 mg daily for about 50 days, low-risk, but the evidence is split. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a plausible, inexpensive prophylactic backed by two positive trials from one group and contradicted by one independent null replication.

cards.headline: Zollinger 1999: reflex sympathetic dystrophy in 7% on vitamin C versus 22% on placebo — absolute difference 15 percentage points
cards.summary: Zollinger 1999: reflex sympathetic dystrophy in 7% on vitamin C versus 22% on placebo — absolute difference 15 percentage points
cards.people: 123 adults with 127 conservatively treated wrist fractures, randomly allocated in a double-blind trial to 500 mg vitamin C or placebo daily for 50 days, with follow-up lasting 1 year; eight patients were withdrawn after randomisation, leaving 119 fractures analysed (54 on vitamin C, 65 on placebo).
cards.result: Reflex sympathetic dystrophy occurred in four wrists (7%) in the vitamin C group and 14 (22%) in the placebo group — an absolute difference of 15 percentage points (95% CI for the difference 2–26). Complaints while wearing the cast and fracture type were also significant prognostic variables for its occurrence.
cards.watchOut: The 1999 terminology is reflex sympathetic dystrophy, the predecessor label for complex regional pain syndrome type I. Only 18 events in total, and the confidence interval runs from 2 to 26 percentage points, so the true effect could be much smaller than the point estimate.
cards.source: Zollinger PE et al.. Effect of vitamin C on frequency of reflex sympathetic dystrophy in wrist fractures: a randomised trial. Lancet. 1999. PMID: 10636366. cards.headline: Zollinger 2007: CRPS 2.4% on pooled vitamin C versus 10.1% on placebo (p = 0.002); 500 mg relative risk 0.17, with a dose plateau
cards.summary: Zollinger 2007: CRPS 2.4% on pooled vitamin C versus 10.1% on placebo (p = 0.002); 500 mg relative risk 0.17, with a dose plateau
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre dose-response trial
cards.people: 416 patients with 427 wrist fractures in a double-blind, prospective, multicentre trial, randomly allocated to placebo (99 patients with 99 fractures) or vitamin C 200, 500 or 1,500 mg daily for fifty days (317 patients with 328 fractures).
cards.result: The prevalence of complex regional pain syndrome was 2.4% (8 of 328) in the vitamin C group and 10.1% (10 of 99) in the placebo group (p = 0.002); all of the affected patients were elderly women. By dose, prevalence was 4.2% (4 of 96) at 200 mg (relative risk 0.41, 95% CI 0.13 to 1.27), 1.8% (2 of 114) at 500 mg (relative risk 0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.77) and 1.7% (2 of 118) at 1,500 mg (relative risk 0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.75) — relative risks, with the absolute rates beside them. Early cast-related complaints predicted CRPS (relative risk 5.35, 95% CI 2.13 to 13.42). The authors recommend a daily dose of 500 mg for fifty days.
cards.watchOut: The same Dutch group as the 1999 trial, so this is confirmation by the originators, not independent replication. Only 18 CRPS events in total, and every case occurred in elderly women — how far the result generalises to men and younger patients is untested.
cards.source: Zollinger PE et al.. Can vitamin C prevent complex regional pain syndrome in patients with wrist fractures? A randomized, controlled, multicenter dose-response study. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. American Volume. 2007. PMID: 17606778. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ekrol 2014: no benefit on function — its primary outcome — and no overall CRPS difference; a few early outcomes favoured placebo
cards.summary: Ekrol 2014: no benefit on function — its primary outcome — and no overall CRPS difference; a few early outcomes favoured placebo
cards.people: 336 adult patients with an acute fracture of the distal aspect of the radius, recruited over one year in Edinburgh and randomised to 500 mg of vitamin C or placebo daily for fifty days after the fracture; the primary outcomes were the DASH (Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand) score at six weeks and at one year, with complications, motion, grip and pinch strength, pain and a CRPS score as secondary variables.
cards.result: There was no significant effect of vitamin C on the DASH score throughout the study period, and no significant difference in the rate of CRPS overall or in time to fracture healing. At six weeks, patients in the vitamin C group with a nondisplaced fracture had a significantly greater wrist flexion deficit (p = 0.008) and pinch strength deficit (p = 0.020) and a greater rate of CRPS (p = 0.022), but there was no difference in the CRPS rate at any other time point. At twenty-six weeks, there was a higher rate of complications (p = 0.043) and greater pain with use (p = 0.045) in patients with a displaced fracture treated with vitamin C.
cards.watchOut: An independent group asking a broader question — function first, CRPS among the secondary outcomes — and its null on both is the strongest counterweight to the Dutch trials. The early signals favouring placebo come from subgroup and secondary comparisons among many, so read them as 'no benefit shown', not as proof of harm.
cards.source: Ekrol I et al.. The influence of vitamin C on the outcome of distal radial fractures: a double-blind, randomized controlled trial. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. cards.headline: Synthesis: two positive trials from one Dutch group, one independent null replication — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two positive trials from one Dutch group, one independent null replication — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: Adults with wrist (distal radius) fractures across the three randomised trials above: Zollinger 1999 (119 fractures analysed), Zollinger 2007 (427 fractures) and Ekrol 2014 (336 patients).
cards.result: Vitamin C cut reflex sympathetic dystrophy from 22% to 7% in the first Dutch trial and CRPS from 10.1% to 2.4% (pooled doses) in the Dutch dose-response trial, with a plateau at 500 mg; the independent Edinburgh trial found no functional benefit and no overall CRPS difference. That is a split record — real promise, one research group, no independent confirmation — for a cheap and low-risk pill. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: CRPS definitions and ascertainment differed between the Dutch trials and Ekrol 2014, and event counts are small in every trial, so all the percentage differences rest on few cases. The evidence split — not the pill's price or safety — is what holds the stamp at POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Heat wraps for acute back pain: beat placebo, ibuprofen and acetaminophen over the first days — small effects, short trials
shelves.question: Does a wearable heat wrap relieve acute low back pain better than painkillers or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen · Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hot Temperature · Humans · Ibuprofen · Low Back Pain · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Cramp · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — continuous low-level heat wrap therapy (40 °C, worn 8 hours a day) beat oral placebo (day-1 pain relief 1.76 vs 1.05 on a 0–5 scale) and beat both ibuprofen and acetaminophen in head-to-head trials, and the Cochrane review calls the evidence moderate for a small short-term reduction in pain and disability. The catch: the wrap trials are short (2–3 days), come from one research group, and measure days, not recovery.

cards.headline: Heat wrap beat ibuprofen and acetaminophen on day-1 pain relief (2.0 vs 1.51 and 1.32 on a 0–5 scale) in 371 patients
cards.summary: Heat wrap beat ibuprofen and acetaminophen on day-1 pain relief (2.0 vs 1.51 and 1.32 on a 0–5 scale) in 371 patients
cards.people: 371 subjects with acute nonspecific low back pain randomised to heat wrap (40 °C, 8 hours/day; n = 113), acetaminophen 4,000 mg/day (n = 113), ibuprofen 1,200 mg/day (n = 106), oral placebo (n = 20) or unheated wrap (n = 19); outcomes over 2 treatment days and 2 follow-up days, investigator-blinded
cards.result: Day-1 pain relief: heat wrap 2.0 vs ibuprofen 1.51 (P = 0.0007) and acetaminophen 1.32 (P = 0.0001). Extended relief on days 3–4: 2.61 vs 1.68 and 1.95. The wrap also improved lateral trunk flexibility (mean change 4.28 cm vs 2.51 cm ibuprofen) and reduced muscle stiffness and day-4 disability more than either drug. No adverse events were serious; the highest rate (10.4%) was with ibuprofen.
cards.watchOut: Patients cannot be blinded to a heated wrap, and the placebo/unheated arms were small blinding checks — expectation is part of any heat effect. The abstract does not name the wrap's brand.
cards.source: Nadler SF et al.. Continuous low-level heat wrap therapy provides more efficacy than Ibuprofen and acetaminophen for acute low back pain. Spine. 2002. PMID: 12004166. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: Nine trials, 1,117 participants, of superficial heat or cold for low back pain, pooled in the Cochrane review
cards.result: In two trials of 258 participants with acute/sub-acute pain, heat wrap reduced pain after five days versus oral placebo (weighted mean difference 1.06, 95% CI 0.68–1.45, on a 0–5 scale). cards.headline: Synthesis: a reasonable first move for acute back pain — expect modest relief for a few days
cards.summary: Synthesis: a reasonable first move for acute back pain — expect modest relief for a few days
cards.people: 1,117 participants across the Cochrane pooling; 590 in the two head-to-head wrap trials carded
cards.result: Continuous low-level heat wraps relieve acute low back pain slightly more than placebo and at least as much as standard doses of ibuprofen or acetaminophen over the first days, with fewer drug side effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Nothing here covers chronic back pain, sciatica, or pain with red flags (trauma, fever, bladder or bowel change, progressive weakness) — those need assessment, not heat. Most acute back pain improves on its own within weeks, which is the backdrop every short trial exploits.

shelves.title: Kinesio tape for shoulder pain: no added benefit over sham tape or over rehabilitation alone
shelves.question: Does kinesio taping relieve shoulder pain or improve recovery from rotator cuff problems?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Bandages · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Orthopedic Procedures · Pain Measurement · Prospective Studies · Range of Motion, Articular · Shoulder Pain · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the double-blind sham-controlled trial, kinesio tape changed nothing except immediate pain-free abduction range; added to a proper rehabilitation programme in a 52-patient trial it produced no extra benefit on any outcome at any time point; and the meta-analysis finds a small pain advantage only against minimal intervention, none against real treatment. The tape's benefits, where they appear, track the comparison's weakness, not the shoulder's recovery.

cards.headline: Double-blind sham-controlled trial: only immediate pain-free abduction improved (+16.9°); pain and disability did not
cards.summary: Double-blind sham-controlled trial: only immediate pain-free abduction improved (+16.9°); pain and disability did not
cards.people: 42 college students with rotator cuff tendonitis/impingement randomised to therapeutic kinesio tape or sham tape, each worn for two consecutive 3-day intervals
cards.result: The therapeutic tape group showed an immediate improvement in pain-free shoulder abduction after application (mean increase 16.9° ± 23.2°, P = 0.005). No other differences between groups in range of motion, pain or disability scores were found at any time interval. The authors conclude use of kinesio tape for decreasing pain intensity or disability is not supported.
cards.watchOut: Young college students over six days — the kindest possible test conditions, and still pain and disability did not move.

cards.result: Versus minimal intervention, taping gave superior pain relief (pooled standardised mean difference −0.36, 95% CI −0.64 to −0.09; P = 0.009) but disability was not significantly different (−0.41, −0.83 to 0.01). cards.watchOut: 'Minimal intervention' comparators (a leaflet, waiting) cannot blind anyone — the one positive pooled result comes from exactly the comparisons where expectation effects live.

cards.headline: Synthesis: harmless, colourful, and not a treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: harmless, colourful, and not a treatment
cards.people: 42 students in the sham-controlled trial, 52 patients in the rehabilitation trial, 17 trials in the meta-analysis
cards.result: Kinesio tape does not reduce shoulder pain or disability beyond sham taping, does not augment rehabilitation, and beats only minimal intervention in pooled chronic-pain data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Skin irritation is the main harm. The risk is opportunity cost: taping instead of the exercise rehabilitation that the trials show actually improves shoulders.

shelves.title: Foam rolling for sore muscles: soreness feels less and performance dips less — effects are small and trials are tiny
shelves.question: Does foam rolling reduce post-exercise muscle soreness and speed recovery?
shelves.mesh: Exercise · Humans · Male · Muscle Fatigue · Muscle, Skeletal · Myalgia · Pain Measurement · Pain Threshold · Physical Therapy Modalities · Quadriceps Muscle · Sports · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — foam rolling after hard exercise reduces the perception of muscle soreness (meta-analytic effect g = 0.47) and slightly blunts the temporary loss of sprint and strength performance, and before exercise it gives a small short-term flexibility gain. The direct trials are tiny (the anchor trial has 8 participants), effects are small, and nothing here shows faster true recovery of the muscle — only that it feels better.

cards.headline: The anchor trial has 8 men: foam rolling cut quadriceps tenderness (effect sizes 0.59–0.84) after 100 heavy squats
cards.summary: The anchor trial has 8 men: foam rolling cut quadriceps tenderness (effect sizes 0.59–0.84) after 100 heavy squats
cards.people: 8 healthy, physically active men in a controlled laboratory crossover-style study; 10 sets of 10 back squats at 60% of one-repetition maximum, followed by 20 minutes of foam rolling immediately, 24 and 48 hours after exercise, or no foam rolling
cards.result: Foam rolling substantially improved quadriceps muscle tenderness (pressure-pain threshold) in the days after exercise (Cohen d 0.59–0.84), with substantial effects on sprint time (d 0.68–0.77), power (d 0.48–0.87) and dynamic strength-endurance (d = 0.54).
cards.watchOut: Eight participants — the effect sizes are real arithmetic on a sample too small to trust; this card is why the stamp cannot rise above POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Pearcey GE et al.. Foam rolling for delayed-onset muscle soreness and recovery of dynamic performance measures. J Athl Train. 2015. PMID: 25415413. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 21 studies: rolling after exercise reduced muscle pain perception (g = 0.47) and blunted performance dips
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 21 studies: rolling after exercise reduced muscle pain perception (g = 0.47) and blunted performance dips
cards.people: 21 studies of foam rolling or roller massage before or after exercise, pooled by Wiewelhove and colleagues; 14 used foam rollers, 7 roller massager bars
cards.result: Post-exercise rolling reduced muscle pain perception (+6.0%, g = 0.47) and attenuated decreases in sprint performance (+3.1%, g = 0.34) and strength (+3.9%, g = 0.21), with a trivial effect on jump performance. Pre-exercise rolling slightly improved sprint (+0.7%, g = 0.28) and flexibility (+4.0%, g = 0.34). The authors judge the effects 'rather minor and partly negligible' but potentially relevant. The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies are small and heterogeneous, and soreness is self-reported by people who know they rolled — expectation is built into the outcome.

cards.headline: Systematic review of 14 studies: short-term range-of-motion gains without a performance penalty
cards.summary: Systematic review of 14 studies: short-term range-of-motion gains without a performance penalty
cards.people: 14 studies of self-myofascial release with a foam roll or roller massager, appraised with the PEDro scale (Cheatham 2015)
cards.result: Foam rolling or roller massage appears to increase joint range of motion short-term without negatively affecting muscle performance, and may attenuate performance decrements and delayed-onset muscle soreness after intense exercise; short bouts before exercise did not appear to affect performance. cards.watchOut: A qualitative review of small studies; it supports plausibility, not magnitude.

cards.headline: Synthesis: worth doing for soreness — a comfort tool, not a recovery drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: worth doing for soreness — a comfort tool, not a recovery drug
cards.people: 21 studies in the meta-analysis; 8 participants in the largest single direct trial carded
cards.result: Foam rolling modestly reduces how sore muscles feel after hard exercise and slightly preserves sprint and strength performance; pre-exercise it adds a little short-term flexibility. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Cold-water immersion for post-exercise recovery is a separate question with its own shelf (#1476). Rolling does not treat injury; pain that is focal, sharp or persistent needs assessment.

shelves.title: Cupping for chronic neck pain: three small trials beat waiting lists — none could blind, none used a sham
shelves.question: Does cupping therapy relieve chronic neck pain?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Complementary Therapies · Female · Health Status · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neck · Neck Pain · Pain Measurement · Pain Threshold · Pilot Projects · Quality of Life · Self Report · Sensation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — three small German trials (50 patients each) of cupping for chronic neck pain all beat waiting-list or usual care on pain scores (by about 11–23 mm on a 100 mm scale), but none could blind patients, none used a sham-cupping control, and all come from one research environment. The effect may be cupping, attention, or expectation — the trials cannot separate them, which is exactly why the stamp is POSSIBLE and not higher.

cards.headline: Five dry-cupping sessions: pain at rest 22.5 mm lower than waiting-list control (P = 0.00002) in 50 patients
cards.summary: Five dry-cupping sessions: pain at rest 22.5 mm lower than waiting-list control (P = 0.00002) in 50 patients
cards.people: 50 patients with chronic nonspecific neck pain randomised to five dry cupping treatments over two weeks or a waiting-list control group; pain on 100 mm visual analogue scales, neck disability and quality of life measured before and after
cards.result: Pain at rest was 22.5 mm lower in the cupping group than control (Δ−22.5 mm, P = 0.00002) and movement-related pain 17.8 mm lower (P = 0.01); pain-diary scores diverged after the fifth session (Δ−1.1 on a 0–10 scale, P = 0.001). Pressure-pain thresholds also differed between groups. Registry ID: NCT01289964 (stated in the record).
cards.watchOut: A pilot against a waiting list — the control group received nothing and knew it; effects of this size against no treatment routinely shrink against a credible sham.
cards.source: Lauche R et al.. The influence of a series of five dry cupping treatments on pain and mechanical thresholds in patients with chronic non-specific neck pain--a randomised controlled pilot study. BMC Complement Altern Med. 2011. PMID: 21843336. Registry ID: NCT01289964. cards.summary: Pulsating cupping device vs standard care: pain diary 2.72 vs 4.44 after treatment (P = 0.001) in 50 patients
cards.people: 50 patients with chronic nonspecific neck pain randomised to five pneumatic pulsation (moving and stationary pulsating cupping) treatments over two weeks (n = 25) or standard medical care (n = 25)

cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent small-trial wins against no treatment — sham-controlled proof does not exist
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent small-trial wins against no treatment — sham-controlled proof does not exist
cards.people: 150 patients across the three randomised trials carded, all from German research groups
cards.result: Cupping in its dry, pulsating and massage forms reduced chronic neck pain by roughly 11–23 mm on a 100 mm scale versus waiting-list or usual care over 2–3 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Bruising and skin marks are intrinsic to cupping; burns and infection are reported with aggressive techniques outside trials. Persistent neck pain with arm weakness, numbness or trauma needs medical assessment first.

shelves.title: Night guards for jaw pain: better than a sham appliance and than nothing — no better than other conservative care
shelves.question: Does wearing an occlusal splint (night guard) relieve temporomandibular (jaw) pain?
shelves.mesh: Acupuncture Therapy · Humans · Occlusal Splints · Pain Measurement · Physical Therapy Modalities · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Relaxation Therapy · Temporomandibular Joint Dysfunction Syndrome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — a stabilisation splint (the acrylic night guard a dentist makes) beat a non-occlusal sham appliance in a 60-patient trial and shows weak evidence of benefit over no treatment in the Cochrane review, but the same review found no advantage over any other active treatment, and a prefabricated guard matched the custom splint in a 48-patient trial. Reasonable to try; not proven superior to simpler care.

cards.headline: Cochrane: weak evidence of benefit vs no treatment; no difference vs any other active treatment (12 trials)
cards.summary: Cochrane: weak evidence of benefit vs no treatment; no difference vs any other active treatment (12 trials)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials of stabilisation splint therapy for temporomandibular pain dysfunction syndrome, compared against acupuncture, bite plates, biofeedback, relaxation, jaw exercises, non-occluding appliances and minimal or no treatment
cards.result: There was no evidence of a statistically significant difference between stabilisation splint therapy and other active treatments. There was weak evidence that splints reduce pain severity, at rest and on palpation, compared with no treatment. The reviewers conclude there is insufficient evidence either for or against splint therapy and call for better trials.
cards.watchOut: The trials pooled are old and small; note the later (2016) update of this review was withdrawn, so the 2004 review remains the carded synthesis — its 'insufficient evidence' verdict stands unreplaced.
cards.source: Al-Ani MZ et al.. Stabilisation splint therapy for temporomandibular pain dysfunction syndrome. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2004. PMID: 14973990. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stabilisation appliance beat a non-occlusal control appliance in 60 patients with muscle-origin jaw pain
cards.summary: Stabilisation appliance beat a non-occlusal control appliance in 60 patients with muscle-origin jaw pain
cards.people: 60 patients with temporomandibular disorders of mainly myogenous (muscle) origin randomised to a stabilisation appliance or a non-occlusal control appliance for 10 weeks
cards.result: Improvement in overall subjective symptoms was reported significantly more often in the stabilisation group than in controls (P < 0.001 as reported). Daily or constant pain fell significantly more in the treatment group (P = 0.028), as did the number of tender masticatory muscles (P = 0.018).
cards.watchOut: Ten weeks, muscle-origin pain only — joint-origin (arthralgia/disc) pain may behave differently, and the control appliance still covers the teeth, which may itself change habits.
cards.source: Ekberg E et al.. The efficacy of appliance therapy in patients with temporomandibular disorders of mainly myogenous origin. A randomized, controlled, short-term trial. cards.headline: A prefabricated guard (Relax) matched the custom stabilisation splint: ~60% achieved 30% pain reduction in both arms
cards.summary: A prefabricated guard (Relax) matched the custom stabilisation splint: ~60% achieved 30% pain reduction in both arms
cards.people: 48 patients with temporomandibular joint arthralgia in a multicentre randomised trial of a prefabricated appliance (Relax, named in the record) vs a custom stabilisation appliance, followed to 12 months
cards.result: A 30% reduction in pain intensity was reported by 62.5% (prefabricated) vs 58.3% (stabilisation) at 10 weeks, and 41.7% in both groups at 12 months; pain and physical function improved in both groups with no significant group differences, and no side effects occurred.
cards.watchOut: No untreated arm — both groups improving equally is consistent with both working, or with time and attention; it does tell patients the cheaper one-visit option performed as well.
cards.source: Christidis N et al.. Effectiveness of a prefabricated occlusal appliance in patients with temporomandibular joint pain: a randomized controlled multicenter study. J Oral Facial Pain Headache. 2014. PMID: 24822236. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a reasonable, reversible first step for jaw pain — with honest limits
cards.summary: Synthesis: a reasonable, reversible first step for jaw pain — with honest limits
cards.people: 12 trials in the Cochrane review; 108 patients in the two direct trials carded
cards.result: Splints probably help jaw pain somewhat versus doing nothing and beat a sham appliance in muscle-origin pain, but have never beaten other active conservative treatments, and prefabricated guards performed as well as custom splints. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Splints treat symptoms, not causes; irreversible dental work (grinding teeth, rebuilding the bite) for jaw pain is not supported by this evidence and should be viewed with suspicion. Jaw pain with locking, trauma or swelling needs prompt dental assessment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Al-Ani MZ et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2004 (PMID: 14973990); Ekberg E et al. J Orofac Pain. 2003 (PMID: 12836501); Christidis N et al. J Oral Facial Pain Headache. 2014 (PMID: 24822236).

shelves.title: Vitamin K2 (MK-7) for bones: one 3-year trial says slower loss, one 1-year trial says nothing — fractures never measured
shelves.question: Does vitamin K2 (menaquinone-7, MK-7) protect bone density or arterial health after menopause?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aging · Bone Density · Bone Density Conservation Agents · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Femur Neck · Hip Joint · Humans · Lumbar Vertebrae · Middle Aged · Osteocalcin · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal · Osteoporotic Fractures · Spinal Fractures · Vitamin K 2
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the two bone trials disagree: three years of MK-7 180 µg/day slowed bone-density decline at the spine and femoral neck in 244 Dutch women, while one year of MK-7 360 µg/day changed nothing in 334 Norwegian women. The Dutch trial's vascular arm found improved arterial stiffness, mainly in women who started stiffest. No trial anywhere measured fractures — the outcome that matters — so the shelf holds at POSSIBLE on a split record.

cards.headline: Three years of MK-7 180 µg/day significantly slowed bone loss at spine and femoral neck (n = 244)
cards.summary: Three years of MK-7 180 µg/day significantly slowed bone loss at spine and femoral neck (n = 244)
cards.people: 244 healthy postmenopausal women randomised to MK-7 180 µg/day or placebo for 3 years; bone density by DXA at lumbar spine, total hip and femoral neck, with bone-strength indices and vertebral fracture assessment
cards.result: MK-7 significantly decreased the age-related decline in bone mineral content and density at the lumbar spine and femoral neck (but not total hip), favourably affected femoral-neck bone strength, and significantly decreased loss of vertebral height in the lower thoracic region. Vitamin K status (uncarboxylated osteocalcin ratio) improved as expected.
cards.watchOut: Density and strength surrogates only — vertebral 'fracture assessment' here measured height loss, not clinical fractures; and the abstract gives no absolute BMD numbers, so the size of the slowing cannot be stated from the record. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Knapen MH et al.. Three-year low-dose menaquinone-7 supplementation helps decrease bone loss in healthy postmenopausal women. Osteoporos Int. 2013. PMID: 23525894. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: The contrary trial: MK-7 360 µg/day for one year did not influence bone loss at any site (n = 334)
cards.summary: The contrary trial: MK-7 360 µg/day for one year did not influence bone loss at any site (n = 334)
cards.people: 334 healthy Norwegian women aged 50–60, one to five years after menopause; MK-7 360 µg/day as Natto capsules vs identical olive-oil placebo capsules for 12 months, double-blind; bone density at hip, femoral neck, spine and whole body
cards.result: After 12 months there were no statistical differences in bone-loss rates between groups at the total hip or any other site, even though vitamin K status markers moved as expected (carboxylated osteocalcin up, undercarboxylated down; P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Double the dose of the positive trial and still null — duration (1 vs 3 years) and how soon after menopause treatment began are the candidate explanations, and neither is proven. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Emaus N et al.. Vitamin K2 supplementation does not influence bone loss in early menopausal women: a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Osteoporos Int. 2010. PMID: 19937427. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Same Dutch cohort, arteries: MK-7 improved arterial stiffness, chiefly in women who started stiffest
cards.summary: Same Dutch cohort, arteries: MK-7 improved arterial stiffness, chiefly in women who started stiffest
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (Knapen 2015, vascular outcomes of the 2013 cohort)
cards.people: The same 244 postmenopausal women (124 placebo, 120 MK-7 180 µg/day as MenaQ7, named in the record) followed for 3 years with carotid echotracking and pulse-wave velocity
cards.result: Carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity and the stiffness index β decreased significantly in the MK-7 group overall; local carotid measures (distension, compliance, distensibility, Young's modulus, local pulse wave velocity) improved significantly in women whose baseline stiffness index was above the median (10.8). The calcification marker dp-ucMGP fell 50% versus placebo; inflammatory and endothelial markers did not change.
cards.watchOut: A secondary-outcome paper from the same single trial — it does not add an independent population, and arterial stiffness is a surrogate for events, not an event.
cards.source: Knapen MH et al.. Menaquinone-7 supplementation improves arterial stiffness in healthy postmenopausal women. A double-blind randomised clinical trial. Thromb Haemost. 2015. PMID: 25694037. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a split bone record and a surrogate vascular signal — fractures unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: a split bone record and a surrogate vascular signal — fractures unknown
cards.people: 578 postmenopausal women across the two independent bone trials; one cohort of 244 behind both positive papers
cards.result: MK-7 slowed measured bone loss over three years in one trial and did nothing over one year in a larger one; arterial stiffness improved on a surrogate measure in the positive trial's cohort. No fracture data exist. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Vitamin K antagonises warfarin — anyone anticoagulated with warfarin must not start K2 supplements without their clinician. Proven osteoporosis treatments (on their own shelves) are judged on fracture reduction, a bar MK-7 has never been tested against.
cards.source: Synthesis of Knapen MH et al. Osteoporos Int. 2013 (PMID: 23525894); Emaus N et al. Osteoporos Int. 2010 (PMID: 19937427); Knapen MH et al. Thromb Haemost. 2015 (PMID: 25694037).

shelves.title: Tart cherry juice for muscle soreness: strength loss 4% vs 22% in the first trial — three small trials, one direction
shelves.question: Does tart cherry juice reduce exercise-induced muscle soreness and speed recovery?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Biomechanical Phenomena · Cross-Over Studies · Elbow · Exercise · Fruit · Humans · Male · Muscle Contraction · Muscle, Skeletal · Phytotherapy · Plant Preparations · Prunus · Elbow Injuries
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — three small randomised trials of tart cherry juice around strenuous exercise (14, 54 and 20 participants) all favour it: strength loss after eccentric exercise was 4% vs 22% in the crossover trial, post-race pain rose 12 mm vs 37 mm in runners, and marathon runners recovered strength faster with lower inflammatory markers. Samples are tiny, outcomes are short-term surrogates, and the juices differ between trials — a consistent signal, not a proven one.

cards.headline: Crossover trial in 14 students: strength loss after eccentric exercise was 4% on cherry juice vs 22% on placebo
cards.summary: Crossover trial in 14 students: strength loss after eccentric exercise was 4% on cherry juice vs 22% on placebo
cards.people: 14 male college students in a randomised placebo-controlled crossover; 12 fl oz of a tart cherry juice blend or placebo twice daily for 8 days, with a bout of maximal eccentric elbow-flexion contractions on day 4, then crossover after two weeks using the opposite arm
cards.result: Strength loss averaged over the four days after exercise was 4% with cherry juice vs 22% with placebo (time-by-treatment P < 0.0001), and pain was significantly less (P = 0.017). Muscle tenderness (P = 0.81) and relaxed elbow angle (P = 0.85) did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen young men and one elbow-flexor exercise model — a proof of concept, with a strikingly large effect that larger trials rarely preserve. The record names the product only as a tart cherry juice blend; no brand is stated. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Connolly DA et al.. Efficacy of a tart cherry juice blend in preventing the symptoms of muscle damage. Br J Sports Med. 2006. PMID: 16790484. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: 54 relay runners: post-race pain rose 12 mm on cherry juice vs 37 mm on placebo (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: 54 relay runners: post-race pain rose 12 mm on cherry juice vs 37 mm on placebo (P < 0.001)
cards.people: 54 healthy runners (mean age 35.8) in a long-distance relay (average 26.3 km per runner over 24 hours); 355 mL bottles of tart cherry juice or a placebo cherry drink twice daily for 7 days before and on race day, double-blind
cards.result: Pain on a 100 mm visual analogue scale rose by 12 ± 18 mm in the cherry juice group vs 37 ± 20 mm on placebo (P < 0.001). Cherry-juice runners were also more willing to use the drink again and more satisfied with the pain reduction they attributed to it. The record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.summary: 20 marathon runners: strength recovered faster (P = 0.024) and inflammatory markers were lower on cherry juice
cards.people: 20 recreational marathon runners randomised to tart cherry juice or placebo for 5 days before, the day of, and 48 hours after a marathon; muscle damage, inflammation and oxidative-stress markers measured before and after the race
cards.result: Isometric strength recovered significantly faster in the cherry juice group (P = 0.024). shelves.title: Avacopan in ANCA-associated vasculitis: remission matched high-dose prednisone at 26 weeks and beat it on sustained remission at 52 (65.7% vs 54.9%)
shelves.question: In ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis or microscopic polyangiitis), can avacopan replace most of the glucocorticoid taper without losing remission?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aniline Compounds/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Anti-Neutrophil Cytoplasmic Antibody-Associated Vasculitis/*drug therapy · Azathioprine/administration & dosage · Cyclophosphamide/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucocorticoids/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Nipecotic Acids/adverse effects/*therapeutic use · Prednisone/*administration & dosage/adverse effects · Receptor, Anaphylatoxin C5a/*antagonists & inhibitors · Recurrence · Remission Induction · Rituximab/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: In the phase 3 ADVOCATE trial (Jayne 2021), yes on both counts that matter. Avacopan — an oral complement C5a-receptor blocker, added to cyclophosphamide or rituximab induction with only a short low-dose steroid lead-in — matched a standard 20-week prednisone taper for remission at week 26 (72.3% versus 70.1%; noninferior, not superior) and beat it for sustained remission at week 52 (65.7% versus 54.9%; difference 12.5 percentage points, 95% CI 2.6 to 22.3; P = 0.007 for superiority). Serious adverse events were slightly less frequent on avacopan (37.3% versus 39.0%), and glucocorticoid-related toxicity — the harm the drug exists to avoid — accumulates on the steroid side of the ledger. The phase 2 trial (Jayne 2017) had shown the same shape: faster, at-least-as-good early response (86.4% and 81.0% versus 70.0% at week 12) with reduced-dose or no prednisone. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one phase 3 trial with a superiority win on the endpoint that counts, supported by its phase 2 — short of LIKELY because the phase 3 evidence base is a single trial and remission was not superior at the primary timepoint. The vasculitis shelf's other disease-modifying questions (rituximab, plasma exchange, reduced-dose glucocorticoids) are on shelf #386.

cards.headline: Jayne 2021 (ADVOCATE): avacopan noninferior to prednisone for remission at 26 weeks (72.3% vs 70.1%) and superior for sustained remission at 52 weeks (65.7% vs 54.9%)
cards.summary: Jayne 2021 (ADVOCATE): avacopan noninferior to prednisone for remission at 26 weeks (72.3% vs 70.1%) and superior for sustained remission at 52 weeks (65.7% vs 54.9%)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind active-controlled trial, 52 weeks (ADVOCATE) (Jayne 2021)
cards.people: 331 patients with newly diagnosed or relapsing antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis received cyclophosphamide (followed by azathioprine) or rituximab as background induction, and were randomised double-dummy to avacopan 30 mg twice daily or oral prednisone on a 20-week tapering schedule. The first endpoint was remission (Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score 0, no glucocorticoids in the previous 4 weeks) at week 26; the second was sustained remission from weeks 26 through 52.
cards.result: Remission at week 26 occurred in 72.3% on avacopan versus 70.1% on prednisone (estimated common difference 3.4 percentage points; 95% CI −6.0 to 12.8) — noninferiority met (P < 0.001) but superiority not shown (P = 0.24). Sustained remission at week 52 occurred in 65.7% versus 54.9% (difference 12.5 percentage points; 95% CI 2.6 to 22.3; P = 0.007 for superiority). Serious adverse events occurred in 37.3% of the avacopan group and 39.0% of the prednisone group.
cards.watchOut: Avacopan did not replace glucocorticoids from day one: both groups could receive intravenous and oral steroids before and around randomisation as part of induction, so the trial tests avacopan plus a short steroid lead-in against a full taper — a steroid-minimising strategy, not a steroid-free one. Every patient also received rituximab or cyclophosphamide, so nothing here isolates avacopan as induction therapy by itself.
cards.source: Jayne DRW et al. Avacopan for the Treatment of ANCA-Associated Vasculitis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021. PMID: 33596356. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02994927, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Jayne 2017 (phase 2): avacopan with reduced-dose or no prednisone reached the week-12 response endpoint in 86.4% and 81.0% versus 70.0% on standard-dose prednisone
cards.summary: Jayne 2017 (phase 2): avacopan with reduced-dose or no prednisone reached the week-12 response endpoint in 86.4% and 81.0% versus 70.0% on standard-dose prednisone
cards.people: 67 patients with newly diagnosed or relapsing ANCA-associated vasculitis needing cyclophosphamide or rituximab were randomised to standard-dose prednisone (60 mg daily, tapered) plus placebo, avacopan 30 mg twice daily with reduced-dose prednisone (20 mg daily, tapered), or avacopan 30 mg twice daily with no prednisone. The primary endpoint was a reduction of at least 50% in the Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score by week 12 with no worsening in any system.
cards.result: The endpoint was reached by 14 of 20 patients (70.0%) on control, 19 of 22 (86.4%) on avacopan plus reduced-dose prednisone, and 17 of 21 (81.0%) on avacopan without prednisone; noninferiority of the avacopan regimens was declared (P = 0.002 for the reduced-dose group, P = 0.01 for the no-prednisone group). Renal response, urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio and urinary MCP-1 fell faster on avacopan. Adverse events matched the control group overall. Serious adverse events were numerically more frequent on avacopan — 11 of 44 patients (25%) versus 4 of 23 (17%) on control — concentrated in the no-prednisone arm (8 of 22, 36%; versus 3 of 22, 14%, with reduced-dose prednisone) (full-text Table 3).
cards.watchOut: Sixty-seven patients and a 12-week activity-score endpoint: a feasibility signal, not proof — and the trial's own percentages ride on denominators of 20–22 patients, so each percentage point is a fraction of a person. Its value on this shelf is directional support for the phase 3 result, and it carries no registry ID in its PubMed record.
cards.source: Jayne DRW et al. Randomized Trial of C5a Receptor Inhibitor Avacopan in ANCA-Associated Vasculitis. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2017. PMID: 28400446. cards.headline: Synthesis: avacopan lets most of the steroid taper go, and the remission it buys lasts longer — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.summary: Synthesis: avacopan lets most of the steroid taper go, and the remission it buys lasts longer — POSSIBLE (benefit)
cards.people: One phase 3 trial (ADVOCATE, 331 patients) and its phase 2 predecessor (67 patients), both adding avacopan to rituximab- or cyclophosphamide-based induction in ANCA-associated vasculitis.
cards.result: Remission at 26 weeks was statistically indistinguishable from a standard prednisone taper (72.3% vs 70.1%, noninferiority met, superiority not shown); sustained remission at 52 weeks favoured avacopan by 12.5 percentage points (65.7% vs 54.9%), the only superiority result in the programme and the clinically decisive one, since relapse and cumulative steroid damage are the disease's twin burdens. Phase 2 response rates (81–86% vs 70%) point the same way. Serious adverse events were no worse than on prednisone.
cards.watchOut: One phase 3 trial is one phase 3 trial: no independent replication exists, follow-up stops at a year, and the trial cannot answer whether avacopan helps in the most severe presentations (its population was newly diagnosed or relapsing disease fit for the protocol) or what happens when it is combined with the reduced-dose steroid regimens that have themselves become standard since (shelf #386).
cards.source: Synthesis of Jayne DRW et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33596356); Jayne DRW et al. Journal of the American Society of Nephrology. 2017 (PMID: 28400446).

shelves.title: CAR T cells for severe autoimmune disease: all 15 patients in the founding series improved and stopped immunosuppression — uncontrolled evidence only, now with a 24-patient basket trial behind it
shelves.question: In severe refractory autoimmune disease (lupus, inflammatory myositis, systemic sclerosis), can CD19 CAR T-cell therapy induce drug-free remission?
shelves.mesh: Humans · *Antigens, CD19/administration & dosage · Cytokine Release Syndrome/etiology · Follow-Up Studies · *Immunotherapy, Adoptive · *Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic/therapy · *Myositis/therapy · *Scleroderma, Systemic/therapy · *Myeloablative Agonists/administration & dosage · Cyclophosphamide/administration & dosage · Infections/etiology · Treatment Outcome · Vidarabine/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: The results are dramatic and the evidence is weak — both halves of that sentence matter. In the founding Erlangen series (Müller 2024), 15 patients with severe, treatment-refractory disease — 8 with lupus, 3 with inflammatory myositis, 4 with systemic sclerosis — received CD19 CAR T cells after fludarabine–cyclophosphamide lymphodepletion: every lupus patient reached DORIS remission, every myositis patient had a major clinical response, every sclerosis patient improved on the EUSTAR activity index, and all 15 stopped immunosuppression entirely, over a median follow-up of 15 months. The CASTLE basket trial (Müller 2026) extends this to 24 patients with the engineered product zorpocabtagene autoleucel: 22 of 24 met their disease-specific efficacy endpoints at 24 weeks, including DORIS remission in 9 of 10 lupus patients, again with everyone off glucocorticoids and immunosuppression. Toxicity so far is milder than in oncology use — cytokine-release syndrome grade 1 in most, no ICANS in CASTLE, one pneumonia hospitalisation in the first series. What is missing is everything that makes evidence strong: no control group, no randomisation, no blinding, 39 patients in total worldwide in these reports, follow-up measured in months for diseases that relapse over years, and the near-certainty that the most spectacular responders are the ones written up. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — the display label for exactly this situation: a possibly transformative therapy whose evidence is two uncontrolled series from one research network. Tier C: taken to the developer personally. Rituximab and conventional immunosuppression shelves (for example lupus nephritis #1413) carry the controlled evidence for these diseases.

cards.headline: Müller 2024: CD19 CAR T cells in 15 patients with severe lupus, myositis or systemic sclerosis — remissions or major responses in all, immunosuppression stopped in all
cards.summary: Müller 2024: CD19 CAR T cells in 15 patients with severe lupus, myositis or systemic sclerosis — remissions or major responses in all, immunosuppression stopped in all
cards.type: Case series, 15 patients, single research programme (Müller 2024)
cards.people: 15 patients with severe, refractory autoimmune disease — 8 with systemic lupus erythematosus, 3 with idiopathic inflammatory myositis and 4 with systemic sclerosis — received a single infusion of CD19 CAR T cells after lymphodepletion with fludarabine and cyclophosphamide. Median follow-up was 15 months (range 4 to 29).
cards.result: All patients with lupus achieved remission according to the DORIS criteria, all patients with myositis achieved a major clinical response (ACR–EULAR), and all patients with systemic sclerosis had decreased scores on the EUSTAR activity index. Immunosuppressive therapy was completely stopped in all patients. B-cell aplasia lasted a mean of 112±47 days before B cells reconstituted. Ten patients had grade 1 cytokine-release syndrome and one grade 2; one patient had grade 1 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome, and one was hospitalised with pneumonia.
cards.watchOut: A case series with no comparator, assembled by the programme that pioneered the treatment: regression to the mean, the lymphodepletion chemotherapy itself (cyclophosphamide is an active lupus and sclerosis drug), and publication selection are all live alternative explanations for part of the effect. The record carries no registry ID. Fifteen patients across three different diseases is five patients per disease of evidence, however striking each story is.
cards.source: Müller F et al. CD19 CAR T-Cell Therapy in Autoimmune Disease - A Case Series with Follow-up. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024. PMID: 38381673. cards.headline: Müller 2026 (CASTLE): zorpocabtagene autoleucel in 24 patients — 22 of 24 met disease-specific efficacy endpoints at 24 weeks; no cytokine-release syndrome above grade 2, no ICANS
cards.summary: Müller 2026 (CASTLE): zorpocabtagene autoleucel in 24 patients — 22 of 24 met disease-specific efficacy endpoints at 24 weeks; no cytokine-release syndrome above grade 2, no ICANS
cards.people: 24 patients with severe, refractory, progressive autoimmune disease — 10 with systemic lupus erythematosus, 9 with systemic sclerosis and 5 with idiopathic inflammatory myopathy — received zorpocabtagene autoleucel, a fully human CD19 CAR T-cell product, after standard lymphodepletion. Efficacy endpoints were disease-specific (DORIS remission for lupus, ACR–EULAR major improvement for myositis, no progression of interstitial lung disease for systemic sclerosis) at week 24.
cards.result: Twenty-two of 24 patients met the efficacy endpoints at 24 weeks, including DORIS remission in 9 of 10 patients with lupus, and all patients remained free of glucocorticoids and other immunosuppression. By disease, the endpoints were met by 9 of 10 patients with lupus (DORIS remission), 9 of 9 with systemic sclerosis (no progression of interstitial lung disease) and 4 of 5 with inflammatory myopathy (ACR major/moderate response) (full text). Cytokine-release syndrome occurred in 18 of 24 patients (75%) — grade 1 in 17 and grade 2 in 1, never above grade 2; no immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome occurred; the abstract reports no deaths or treatment-related discontinuations. Endpoints were assessed at 24 weeks; median follow-up was 13 months (range 8–19), with no relapses in any patient (full text).
cards.watchOut: Still single-arm, still the same research network as the founding series, and 24 weeks is a very short leash for diseases measured in decades — B cells return within months, and whether remission survives their return is the whole question. A basket design pools three diseases into one headline number (22 of 24), which reads stronger than any single disease's evidence is.
cards.source: Müller F et al. CD19 CAR-T cells for treatment-refractory autoimmune diseases: the phase 1/2 CASTLE basket trial. Nature Medicine. 2026. PMID: 41501497. cards.headline: Synthesis: unanimous responses in 39 uncontrolled patients — a signal too strong to ignore and too weak to stamp higher — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: unanimous responses in 39 uncontrolled patients — a signal too strong to ignore and too weak to stamp higher — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Two uncontrolled reports from one research network: a 15-patient case series across lupus, myositis and systemic sclerosis (median follow-up 15 months) and the 24-patient CASTLE phase 1/2 basket trial of zorpocabtagene autoleucel (endpoints at 24 weeks; median follow-up 13 months, no relapses).
cards.result: Every lupus patient in the series reached DORIS remission; 22 of 24 CASTLE patients met their disease-specific endpoints; immunosuppression was stopped in all 39 patients; and toxicity was far milder than CAR T therapy in cancer (no cytokine-release syndrome above grade 2 in CASTLE, no ICANS, one pneumonia hospitalisation in the series). If even half of this effect is real and durable, it rewrites the treatment of refractory autoimmune disease — which is precisely why the stamp must stay at MAYBE until a controlled trial exists: the history of medicine is unkind to uncontrolled unanimity.
cards.watchOut: Selection is the confounder that cannot be adjusted away: these are patients chosen for a pioneering programme, treated at expert centres, and reported by their inventors. Lymphodepletion chemotherapy is itself immunosuppressive treatment. The randomised trials now being designed will decide whether this shelf becomes the most important one in its area or a cautionary tale; until then the card texts, not the stamp, carry the excitement.
cards.source: Synthesis of Müller F et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 38381673); Müller F et al. Nature Medicine. 2026 (PMID: 41501497).

shelves.title: Pegloticase for refractory gout: urate normalised in 42% on the drug alone and 60% with methotrexate cover, tophi completely resolved in about half — in the minority who keep responding
shelves.question: In adults with refractory chronic gout, does pegloticase lower serum urate and resolve tophi versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Allopurinol/therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Resistance · Enzymes, Immobilized/*administration & dosage · Female · Gout/*drug therapy · Gout Suppressants/therapeutic use · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Polyethylene Glycols/*administration & dosage · Treatment Outcome · Urate Oxidase/*administration & dosage · Uric Acid/*blood
shelves.balance: In gout that has failed or cannot tolerate conventional urate lowering, pegloticase does what no oral drug in these patients could: in the twin placebo-controlled trials (Sundy 2011, PMID: 21846852), sustained urate below 6.0 mg/dL was achieved by 42% of patients on biweekly pegloticase and 35% on monthly dosing, against 0 of 43 on placebo. Tophi — the visible burden of the disease — completely resolved in at least one tophus in 45% of biweekly patients versus 8% on placebo at six months (Baraf 2013, PMID: 24286509). The catch is immunogenicity: most patients eventually make anti-drug antibodies, lose the urate response and face infusion reactions, which is why covering pegloticase with methotrexate raised the 12-month responder rate to 60.0% versus 30.8% with placebo cover in the MIRROR randomised trial (Botson 2023, PMID: 37385296), with complete resolution of at least one tophus in 53.8% versus 31.0%. Deaths in the phase 3 trials were 4 on pegloticase and 3 on placebo among 225 patients. PROPOSED LIKELY — strong, replicated randomised evidence for urate lowering and tophus resolution in a population with no working alternative, with the responder minority and the infusion-reaction risk stated on the face of the shelf. Tier C: taken to the developer personally (harm profile and a surrogate primary endpoint).

cards.headline: Sundy 2011 (twin phase 3 trials): sustained urate below 6.0 mg/dL in 42% on biweekly pegloticase, 35% on monthly — and 0% on placebo
cards.summary: Sundy 2011 (twin phase 3 trials): sustained urate below 6.0 mg/dL in 42% on biweekly pegloticase, 35% on monthly — and 0% on placebo
cards.type: Two replicate randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials, 225 patients (Sundy 2011)
cards.people: 225 adults with severe chronic gout, serum urate at least 8.0 mg/dL and allopurinol intolerance or refractoriness, at 56 rheumatology practices in the US, Canada and Mexico, given 12 biweekly intravenous infusions of pegloticase 8 mg every infusion, pegloticase alternating with placebo (monthly), or placebo alone. The primary endpoint was plasma urate below 6.0 mg/dL in both months 3 and 6.
cards.result: Pooled across the two trials, the primary endpoint was reached by 36 of 85 patients on biweekly pegloticase (42%; 95% CI 32% to 54%), 29 of 84 on monthly dosing (35%; 24% to 46%) and 0 of 43 on placebo (0%; 0% to 8%) (p < 0.001 for each comparison). Seven deaths occurred between randomisation and database closure — four in patients receiving pegloticase and three on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a blood level, not a patient outcome, and the response pattern is close to all-or-nothing: patients who develop anti-pegloticase antibodies typically lose urate lowering entirely, so the 42% figure is a responder minority, not an average effect. The abstract does not quantify infusion reactions or flare rates; the drug carries an anaphylaxis warning in practice, and urate is checked before each infusion because loss of urate lowering signals antibody formation and rising reaction risk.
cards.source: Sundy JS et al. Efficacy and tolerability of pegloticase for the treatment of chronic gout in patients refractory to conventional treatment: two randomized controlled trials. JAMA. 2011. PMID: 21846852. Registry ID: NCT00325195, from the record. cards.headline: Baraf 2013: complete resolution of at least one tophus in 45% on biweekly pegloticase versus 8% on placebo at six months
cards.summary: Baraf 2013: complete resolution of at least one tophus in 45% on biweekly pegloticase versus 8% on placebo at six months
cards.type: Tophus-burden analysis of the phase 3 randomised trials and their open-label extension (Baraf 2013)
cards.people: The 212 patients randomised in the two phase 3 pegloticase trials, of whom 155 (73%) had at least one measurable subcutaneous tophus at baseline (547 tophi photographed and measured), treated with biweekly or monthly pegloticase or placebo for six months, with responders continuing into an open-label extension.
cards.result: Complete resolution of at least one tophus, without new or enlarging tophi, occurred in 45% of the biweekly group (p = 0.002 versus placebo), 26% of the monthly group and 8% on placebo at six months. Counting individual tophi, complete response rates were 28%, 19% and 2% respectively. Patients who met the sustained urate-lowering endpoint were far more likely to clear a tophus (54%) than non-responders (20%) or placebo patients (8%).
cards.watchOut: Tophus response tracks urate response, so this is largely the same responder minority seen through a clinical lens — it confirms the drug melts urate deposits when it works, but adds no evidence for the roughly 58% who never sustain urate lowering. Photographic tophus measurement captures visible subcutaneous deposits only.
cards.source: Baraf HS et al. Tophus burden reduction with pegloticase: results from phase 3 randomized trials and open-label extension in patients with chronic gout refractory to conventional therapy. Arthritis Research & Therapy. 2013. PMID: 24286509. Registry ID: NCT00325195 and NCT01356498, from the record. cards.headline: Botson 2023 (MIRROR randomised trial): methotrexate cover doubled the 12-month responder rate — 60.0% versus 30.8% — and raised complete tophus resolution to 53.8% versus 31.0%
cards.summary: Botson 2023 (MIRROR randomised trial): methotrexate cover doubled the 12-month responder rate — 60.0% versus 30.8% — and raised complete tophus resolution to 53.8% versus 31.0%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial of methotrexate co-therapy, 152 patients (MIRROR RCT, Botson 2023)
cards.people: 152 adults with uncontrolled gout (urate at least 7 mg/dL despite oral therapy, or intolerance, plus tophi, frequent flares or gouty arthropathy) randomised 2:1 to pegloticase 8 mg every two weeks with blinded oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly or with placebo, for 52 weeks. A responder kept urate below 6 mg/dL for at least 80% of the assessment month.
cards.result: At month 12 the responder rate was 60.0% (60 of 100) with methotrexate versus 30.8% (16 of 52) with placebo cover (difference 29.1 percentage points, 95% CI 13.2 to 44.9; p = 0.0003). Complete resolution of at least one tophus by week 52 occurred in 53.8% (28 of 52 assessed) versus 31.0% (9 of 29). Fewer methotrexate patients stopped pegloticase for loss of urate lowering (22.9% versus 63.3%), pharmacokinetics showed higher pegloticase exposure and lower immunogenicity with methotrexate, and no infusion reactions occurred after week 24.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is pegloticase-plus-methotrexate against pegloticase-plus-placebo, so this trial shows how to make pegloticase work better, not whether pegloticase beats nothing — that was the Sundy trials' job. Methotrexate brings its own toxicity and exclusions (kidney disease, cytopenias, alcohol), and the tophus denominators (52 and 29) are the subsets with measurable tophi, not all randomised patients.
cards.source: Botson JK et al. A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Multicenter Efficacy and Safety Study of Methotrexate to Increase Response Rates in Patients With Uncontrolled Gout Receiving Pegloticase: 12-Month Findings. ACR Open Rheumatology. 2023. PMID: 37385296. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: the record carries no MeSH terms

cards.headline: Botson 2022 (MIRROR open-label pilot): 79% responded at six months with methotrexate cover — in 14 patients, with flares in 13 of 14 during the first 12 weeks
cards.summary: Botson 2022 (MIRROR open-label pilot): 79% responded at six months with methotrexate cover — in 14 patients, with flares in 13 of 14 during the first 12 weeks
cards.type: Single-arm open-label pilot study, 14 patients (MIRROR open-label, Botson 2022)
cards.people: 14 men with uncontrolled gout (mean age 49 years, mean gout history 13.8 years, baseline urate 9.2 mg/dL) given oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly starting four weeks before pegloticase and continued through 52 weeks of infusions; patients with immunocompromise, G6PD deficiency, severe kidney disease or methotrexate contraindications were excluded.
cards.result: The six-month responder rate was 79%, against the 42% historical rate for pegloticase alone. Ten patients remained in the study to week 52, of whom eight completed treatment as 12-month responders; mean urate fell by 8.2 mg/dL to 1.1 mg/dL among those remaining. Flares were near-universal early (13 of 14 patients in weeks 1–12) and became less frequent over time (2 of 8 in weeks 36–52). One patient recovered from sepsis (a serious adverse event); the non-responders developed high anti-drug antibody titres.
cards.watchOut: Fourteen patients, no control group and a historical comparator: this pilot generated the hypothesis that the randomised MIRROR trial then confirmed, and it is carded as that — a feasibility signal, not evidence in its own right. Its flare figures are the shelf's clearest picture of how rough the first three months of pegloticase treatment feel.
cards.source: Botson JK et al. A multicentre, efficacy and safety study of methotrexate to increase response rates in patients with uncontrolled gout receiving pegloticase (MIRROR): 12-month efficacy, safety, immunogenicity, and pharmacokinetic findings during long-term extension of an open-label study. cards.headline: Synthesis: pegloticase normalises urate and dissolves tophi in the patients it works for — the whole game is keeping antibodies from switching it off — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: pegloticase normalises urate and dissolves tophi in the patients it works for — the whole game is keeping antibodies from switching it off — LIKELY
cards.people: Four records in refractory or uncontrolled gout: the twin placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (225 patients), their tophus analysis (155 patients with tophi), a 14-patient open-label methotrexate pilot, and the 152-patient randomised trial of methotrexate versus placebo as pegloticase cover.
cards.result: Against placebo, pegloticase produced sustained urate below 6.0 mg/dL in 42% (biweekly) versus 0%, and complete resolution of at least one tophus in 45% versus 8% at six months. Adding methotrexate cover raised the 12-month responder rate from 30.8% to 60.0% and complete tophus resolution from 31.0% to 53.8%. Nothing here shows benefit for the majority who lose response to anti-drug antibodies, and no trial was powered for mortality or joint-destruction endpoints.
cards.watchOut: Every efficacy number on this shelf is conditional on response: the honest summary for a patient starting pegloticase is roughly a coin-flip of transformative urate control, improved to about 60:40 with methotrexate cover, against early flares in nearly everyone and infusion reactions concentrated in those losing response. Flares, pain scores and function — the outcomes patients feel — are reported far less completely than urate.

shelves.title: Topical diclofenac for knee and hand osteoarthritis: beats its vehicle in six double-blind trials and matches oral diclofenac for pain — the trade is skin irritation instead of stomach and blood-test harms
shelves.question: In adults with knee or hand osteoarthritis, does topical diclofenac reduce pain versus placebo or oral NSAIDs?

shelves.balance: LIKELY: Topical diclofenac is one of the better-tested rub-on treatments in the library. Against vehicle or placebo it won in every large double-blind trial carded here: the 1.5% solution in knee osteoarthritis (Roth 2004, PMID: 15477437, n = 326; Bookman 2004, PMID: 15313991, n = 248 — WOMAC pain change −3.9 versus −2.5 on both control solutions), the same solution in a 775-patient five-arm trial (Simon 2009, PMID: 19380203), the 1% gel in knee osteoarthritis (Barthel 2009, PMID: 19932833, n = 492) and in hand osteoarthritis (Altman 2009, PMID: 19648310, n = 385, NCT00171665). Against oral diclofenac it was not beaten: a 622-patient double-dummy equivalence trial (Tugwell 2004, PMID: 15468367) and Simon 2009 both found no significant efficacy difference, while gastrointestinal adverse events and abnormal liver-function, haemoglobin and creatinine-clearance results were significantly fewer with the topical route. The price is local: application-site dryness, rash or irritation in roughly a fifth to two-fifths of users depending on formulation, leading few to stop. The effect sizes are modest — these are symptom scores moving a few points further than vehicle, not joints restored — and almost all trials were industry-run and short (4–12 weeks). The class-level Cochrane synthesis, covering ketoprofen as well, is homed at shelf #577; shelf #330 covers diclofenac only as the oral comparator in gastroprotection strategies. PROPOSED LIKELY (not Tier C: a symptom claim with no mortality or cardiovascular benefit asserted).

cards.headline: Roth 2004: topical diclofenac solution beat vehicle on every outcome in 326 patients with knee osteoarthritis over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Roth 2004: topical diclofenac solution beat vehicle on every outcome in 326 patients with knee osteoarthritis over 12 weeks
cards.people: 326 patients with primary osteoarthritis of the knee (radiographic changes and a pain flare on entry), randomised double-blind to 1.5% diclofenac sodium solution in a dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) carrier, 40 drops four times daily, or the vehicle-control solution without diclofenac, for 12 weeks. Primary outcomes: WOMAC pain and physical function subscales and patient global assessment.
cards.result: Topical diclofenac was significantly more effective than vehicle on all measures: pain P = .001, physical function P = .002, patient global assessment P = .003, stiffness P = .005, pain on walking P = .004. Minor skin irritation occurred in 68 of 164 diclofenac patients (41.5%) — dryness 36.6%, rash 11.0% — with no significant difference between groups in gastrointestinal complaints or dropouts for adverse effects. The abstract reports p-values rather than the absolute score changes.
cards.watchOut: The vehicle contains DMSO, an active-feeling carrier that itself produces skin sensations — blinding against it is imperfect, and symptom scores are exactly the outcomes imperfect blinding inflates. The abstract gives significance levels without the size of the score differences, so the size of the benefit must be read from Bookman and Simon, which print changes.
cards.source: Roth SH et al. Efficacy and safety of a topical diclofenac solution (pennsaid) in the treatment of primary osteoarthritis of the knee: a randomized, double-blind, vehicle-controlled clinical trial. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15477437. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Bookman 2004: diclofenac solution improved WOMAC pain by −3.9 points versus −2.5 on vehicle-control and −2.5 on placebo over 4 weeks
cards.summary: Bookman 2004: diclofenac solution improved WOMAC pain by −3.9 points versus −2.5 on vehicle-control and −2.5 on placebo over 4 weeks
cards.people: 248 men and women in southern Ontario with primary knee osteoarthritis and at least moderate pain, randomised to 1.5% diclofenac solution in a DMSO carrier, the DMSO vehicle-control solution, or a placebo solution with a token amount of DMSO for blinding, applied for 4 weeks. Primary endpoint: WOMAC LK3.0 pain subscale change.
cards.result: Mean pain change was −3.9 (95% CI −4.8 to −2.9) on diclofenac versus −2.5 (−3.3 to −1.7) on vehicle-control (p = 0.023) and −2.5 on placebo (p = 0.016). Physical function (−11.6), stiffness (−1.5), pain on walking (−0.8) and patient global assessment all significantly favoured diclofenac. Skin irritation, mostly minor dryness, occurred in 30 of 84 diclofenac patients (36%) and caused 5 (6%) to stop. Gastrointestinal event rates did not differ; no serious gastrointestinal or renal events were detected.
cards.watchOut: Four weeks is short for a lifelong condition, and the absolute advantage over an active-feeling vehicle is about 1.4 WOMAC pain points — real, and the same order as the class effect at #577, but a patient expecting transformation will be disappointed. Two control solutions were needed because the DMSO carrier cannot be perfectly mimicked, which tells its own story about blinding.
cards.source: Bookman AA et al. Effect of a topical diclofenac solution for relieving symptoms of primary osteoarthritis of the knee: a randomized controlled trial. CMAJ. 2004. PMID: 15313991. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Tugwell 2004: topical diclofenac matched oral diclofenac for knee osteoarthritis symptoms in 622 patients — with significantly fewer gastrointestinal events and laboratory abnormalities
cards.summary: Tugwell 2004: topical diclofenac matched oral diclofenac for knee osteoarthritis symptoms in 622 patients — with significantly fewer gastrointestinal events and laboratory abnormalities
cards.people: 622 men and women with radiological primary knee osteoarthritis and mild-to-severe symptoms, randomised double-blind, double-dummy for 12 weeks to topical 1.5% diclofenac solution (50 drops three times daily) plus placebo capsules, or placebo solution plus oral diclofenac 50 mg capsules three times daily. Equivalence was judged in the per-protocol group against predefined clinically-significant-difference ranges for WOMAC pain, physical function and patient global assessment.
cards.result: Between-treatment differences in change scores (topical minus oral) were 13.3 mm for pain (95% CI −8.6 to 35.2; total scale 500 mm), 71.0 mm for physical function (−2.4 to 144.5; scale 1700 mm) and 4.3 mm for global assessment (−1.2 to 9.8; scale 100 mm) — every confidence interval inside its predefined equivalence range (±75, ±255 and ±20 mm respectively). Minor skin irritation occurred in 83 of 311 topical patients (27%), mostly dryness; total and severe gastrointestinal adverse events (dyspepsia, abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea) were significantly less frequent on topical treatment, and significantly fewer topical patients developed abnormal liver-function tests, haemoglobin or creatinine clearance.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence here means 'within a generous predefined margin' — the pain margin (±75 mm on a 500-mm scale) would swallow effects patients can feel, and per-protocol analysis flatters equivalence. Oral diclofenac 50 mg three times daily is also a full-dose comparator with a known harm profile, so 'as good as oral' is a claim about this dose, not about NSAIDs in general.
cards.source: Tugwell PS et al. Equivalence study of a topical diclofenac solution (pennsaid) compared with oral diclofenac in symptomatic treatment of osteoarthritis of the knee: a randomized controlled trial. The Journal of Rheumatology. 2004. PMID: 15468367. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Simon 2009: in 775 patients, topical diclofenac beat placebo and its DMSO vehicle, did not differ from oral diclofenac, and adding it to oral diclofenac added nothing
cards.summary: Simon 2009: in 775 patients, topical diclofenac beat placebo and its DMSO vehicle, did not differ from oral diclofenac, and adding it to oral diclofenac added nothing
cards.people: 775 subjects with radiologically confirmed symptomatic primary knee osteoarthritis in a 12-week double-blind, double-dummy, five-arm trial: topical diclofenac in DMSO vehicle (40 drops four times daily), placebo solution, DMSO vehicle alone, oral diclofenac, or topical plus oral diclofenac. Co-primary outcomes: WOMAC pain and physical function and patient overall health assessment.
cards.result: Topical diclofenac was superior to placebo for pain (−6.0 vs −4.7, P = 0.015), physical function (−15.8 vs −12.3, P = 0.034), overall health (−0.95 vs −0.37, P < 0.0001) and patient global assessment (−1.36 vs −1.01, P = 0.016), and superior to the DMSO vehicle on all efficacy variables. The DMSO vehicle was no better than placebo. No significant difference was observed between topical and oral diclofenac. The commonest adverse event on topical diclofenac was dry skin (18.2%); digestive-system and laboratory abnormalities were fewer than with oral diclofenac.
cards.watchOut: The placebo group's pain also fell by 4.7 points — most of what a patient experiences on the gel is the ritual, the rubbing and the disease's own fluctuation; the drug adds about 1.3 WOMAC pain points on top. 'No significant difference' from oral diclofenac in a trial not designed as an equivalence study is weaker than Tugwell's formal equivalence result.
cards.source: Simon LS et al. Efficacy and safety of topical diclofenac containing dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) compared with those of topical placebo, DMSO vehicle and oral diclofenac for knee osteoarthritis. Pain. 2009. PMID: 19380203. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Barthel 2009: diclofenac 1% gel beat vehicle in 492 patients with knee osteoarthritis over 12 weeks, with gastrointestinal rates no higher than vehicle
cards.summary: Barthel 2009: diclofenac 1% gel beat vehicle in 492 patients with knee osteoarthritis over 12 weeks, with gastrointestinal rates no higher than vehicle
cards.people: 492 adults aged 35 or over with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis of at least 6 months, randomised double-blind to diclofenac sodium 1% gel (n = 254) or vehicle gel (n = 238), 4 g applied four times daily for 12 weeks. Primary outcomes at week 12: WOMAC pain and physical function subscales and global rating of disease.
cards.result: At week 12 the gel group had significantly greater improvement than vehicle in WOMAC pain (P = 0.01), WOMAC physical function (P = 0.001) and global rating of disease (P < 0.001), with significant differences from week 1. Application-site reactions occurred in 5.1% on gel versus 2.5% on vehicle; gastrointestinal disorders were reported by 5.9% on gel and 5.0% on vehicle. The abstract reports p-values rather than absolute score changes.
cards.watchOut: A different formulation from the DMSO solution trials — the gel's skin-reaction rate (5.1%) is far lower than the solution's, so harms cannot be pooled across formulations carelessly. As with Roth, significance is reported without the absolute score changes in the abstract, limiting bedside translation.
cards.source: Barthel HR et al. Randomized controlled trial of diclofenac sodium gel in knee osteoarthritis. Seminars in Arthritis and Rheumatism. 2009. PMID: 19932833. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Altman 2009: diclofenac 1% gel beat vehicle in hand osteoarthritis — pain intensity down 42–45% on gel, significantly better than vehicle at weeks 4 and 6
cards.summary: Altman 2009: diclofenac 1% gel beat vehicle in hand osteoarthritis — pain intensity down 42–45% on gel, significantly better than vehicle at weeks 4 and 6
cards.people: 385 men and women aged 40 or over with primary osteoarthritis of the dominant hand, randomised double-blind to diclofenac sodium 1% gel (n = 198) or vehicle (n = 187), self-applied to both hands four times daily for 8 weeks. Primary outcomes: pain intensity (100-mm visual analogue scale), total AUSCAN score and global rating of disease activity at weeks 4 and 6. Registered as NCT00171665.
cards.result: On diclofenac gel, pain intensity scores fell by 42–45%, total AUSCAN scores by 35–40% and global disease rating by 36–40% (within-group relative changes). Differences favouring gel over vehicle were significant at week 4 for pain intensity and AUSCAN, with a trend for global rating, and at week 6 gel was significantly better on every primary outcome. The commonest treatment-related adverse event was application-site paraesthesia; most events were mild, and no cardiac events, gastrointestinal bleeding or ulcers were reported.
cards.watchOut: The 42–45% pain fall is the within-group change on gel, not the advantage over vehicle — vehicle-treated hands also improved, and the abstract does not print the vehicle's percentage fall, so the drug-attributable share cannot be computed from this record. Hand osteoarthritis has far fewer treatment trials than knee, so this single gel trial carries the hand half of the shelf's question.
cards.source: Altman RD et al. Diclofenac sodium gel in patients with primary hand osteoarthritis: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Journal of Rheumatology. 2009. PMID: 19648310. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00171665, from the record's databank fields.
