cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent vehicle-controlled wins in knee and hand, parity with oral diclofenac, skin irritation as the trade — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent vehicle-controlled wins in knee and hand, parity with oral diclofenac, skin irritation as the trade — LIKELY
cards.people: Six double-blind randomised trials, 2004–2009, totalling about 2,700 patients: three of the 1.5% DMSO solution in knee osteoarthritis (Roth, Bookman, Simon), one topical-versus-oral equivalence trial (Tugwell), and two of the 1% gel (Barthel, knee; Altman, hand).
cards.result: Every trial found topical diclofenac superior to its vehicle or placebo on pain and function; the two head-to-head trials found no efficacy difference from oral diclofenac, with significantly fewer gastrointestinal events and laboratory abnormalities on the topical route. Harms were dominated by application-site reactions — dryness or irritation in 18–42% with the solution, about 5% with the gel. Absolute benefits over vehicle are modest (about 1.3–1.4 WOMAC pain points where changes are printed).
cards.watchOut: Nearly all of this evidence is manufacturer-sponsored, short (4–12 weeks), and built on symptom scores against vehicles designed to feel active; there is no trial of years-long use, no structural outcome, and no direct trial against topical ketoprofen or other rub-on NSAIDs — the cross-drug comparison lives in the Cochrane synthesis at shelf #577. 'Matches oral diclofenac' should not be read as 'matches all oral NSAIDs at all doses'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Roth SH et al. Archives of Internal Medicine. 2004 (PMID: 15477437); Bookman AA et al. CMAJ. 2004 (PMID: 15313991); Tugwell PS et al. shelves.title: Milnacipran for fibromyalgia: three positive phase 3 trials, but a small benefit — and one in five patients stopped the drug for side effects in the largest trial
shelves.question: In adults with fibromyalgia, does milnacipran improve pain and global status versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Capsules · Constipation/chemically induced · Cyclopropanes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Dizziness/chemically induced · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Fatigue/drug therapy · Female · Fibromyalgia/diagnosis/drug therapy/physiopathology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Milnacipran · Pain/drug therapy/physiopathology · Pain Measurement/methods · Patient Satisfaction/statistics & numerical data · Placebos · Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome · Vomiting/chemically induced
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Milnacipran passed its pivotal trials — three large double-blind phase 3 studies (Clauw 2008, PMID: 19108787, n = 1,196, NCT00098124; Mease 2009, PMID: 19132781, n = 888; Branco 2010, PMID: 20156949, n = 884, NCT00436033) each found significantly more composite responders — patients simultaneously achieving at least 30% pain improvement, a global rating of much or very much improved, and in two trials a physical-function gain — on milnacipran 100 or 200 mg/day than on placebo, with a smaller phase 2 trial (Vitton 2004, PMID: 15378666) showing at least 50% pain reduction in 37% on twice-daily milnacipran versus 14% on placebo. The catch is size and price: the phase 3 abstracts report significance without printing the responder percentages, the Cochrane synthesis homed at shelf #391 puts substantial pain relief at roughly one patient in ten beyond placebo for this drug class, and adverse events drove 19.5–23.7% of milnacipran patients out of Clauw 2008 versus 9.5% on placebo, with nausea in about a third. Benefit persisted to a year in extension studies (Goldenberg 2010, PMID: 20002596), but extensions keep the patients who already tolerated and responded to the drug. Three positive industry-run pivotal trials clear the two-trial gate; the small absolute benefit and the dropout burden keep the stamp at moderate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (not Tier C: no mortality or cardiovascular claim; benefit rests on multiple randomised trials, not a single trial or observational data).

cards.headline: Vitton 2004: in the 125-patient phase 2 trial, at least 50% pain reduction in 37% on twice-daily milnacipran versus 14% on placebo; overall improvement 75% versus 38%
cards.summary: Vitton 2004: in the 125-patient phase 2 trial, at least 50% pain reduction in 37% on twice-daily milnacipran versus 14% on placebo; overall improvement 75% versus 38%
cards.people: 125 patients with fibromyalgia in a double-blind, placebo-controlled, flexible-dose-escalation trial: 4 weeks of escalation to up to 200 mg/day, then 8 weeks at constant dose. Outcomes included pain intensity, fatigue, depressed mood and sleep.
cards.result: 75% of milnacipran-treated patients reported overall improvement versus 38% on placebo (p < 0.01). Among twice-daily patients, 37% achieved at least 50% reduction in pain intensity versus 14% on placebo (p < 0.05) — absolute rates as reported. 84% of milnacipran patients escalated to the full 200 mg/day; most adverse events were mild to moderate and transient.
cards.watchOut: Small, short and flexible-dose — a dose-finding study, not a confirmatory one. The same 125-patient trial was reported again by Gendreau 2005 (PMID: 16206355); it is one trial, not two, and is carded once here. A 23-percentage-point absolute advantage on the strictest pain outcome is the most favourable number anywhere in this shelf's record, from its smallest trial — the usual direction of shrinkage followed in the phase 3 programme.
cards.source: Vitton O et al. A double-blind placebo-controlled trial of milnacipran in the treatment of fibromyalgia. Human Psychopharmacology. 2004. PMID: 15378666. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Clauw 2008: 1,196 patients — both milnacipran doses significantly beat placebo on composite responder endpoints; nausea in about a third, and 1 in 5 stopped for adverse events
cards.summary: Clauw 2008: 1,196 patients — both milnacipran doses significantly beat placebo on composite responder endpoints; nausea in about a third, and 1 in 5 stopped for adverse events
cards.people: 1,196 adults meeting 1990 ACR criteria for fibromyalgia (96.2% female), randomised to milnacipran 100 mg/day (n = 399), 200 mg/day (n = 396) or placebo (n = 401) for 15 weeks. Primary endpoints: FM composite responders (at least 30% pain improvement plus much/very much improved global status plus at least 6-point SF-36 physical-component gain) and FM pain composite responders (pain plus global criteria). Registered as NCT00098124.
cards.result: Significantly more milnacipran patients were FM composite responders (100 mg/day P = 0.01; 200 mg/day P = 0.02) and FM pain composite responders (P = 0.03 and P = 0.004) than placebo patients; pain improved significantly from week 1, and global status, physical function and fatigue also improved. The abstract reports p-values without printing the responder percentages, so the absolute size of the advantage cannot be read from this record. Commonest adverse events: nausea (34.3% and 37.6%), headache (18.0% and 17.7%) and constipation (14.3% and 17.9%); adverse events caused discontinuation in 19.5% (100 mg) and 23.7% (200 mg) versus 9.5% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A registration trial designed and run by the sponsor, with a composite endpoint whose components can be met by small simultaneous nudges; the missing responder percentages in the abstract are the single most important number in the study, and a reader of this record cannot compute an NNT from it. The discontinuation gap (about 10–14 percentage points over placebo) is the honest counterweight to every efficacy figure on this shelf.
cards.source: Clauw DJ et al. Milnacipran for the treatment of fibromyalgia in adults: a 15-week, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multiple-dose clinical trial. Clinical Therapeutics. 2008. PMID: 19108787. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00098124, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Mease 2009: 888 patients over 27 weeks — FM responders significantly more frequent on both doses (p = 0.028 and p = 0.017); pain responders at 200 mg/day p = 0.032
cards.summary: Mease 2009: 888 patients over 27 weeks — FM responders significantly more frequent on both doses (p = 0.028 and p = 0.017); pain responders at 200 mg/day p = 0.032
cards.people: 888 patients with fibromyalgia in a 27-week randomised, double-blind, multicentre trial of milnacipran 100 mg/day, 200 mg/day or placebo, with the primary endpoint assessed after 3 months of stable-dose treatment. Responder definitions matched the sister trial: pain (24-hour morning-recall visual analogue scale), patient global impression of change, and SF-36 physical component for the full FM composite.
cards.result: At the primary endpoint, significantly more milnacipran patients met FM responder criteria versus placebo (200 mg/day p = 0.017; 100 mg/day p = 0.028), and more 200 mg/day patients met FM pain responder criteria (p = 0.032). Significant pain reductions appeared after week 1 at both doses; at 15 weeks the 200 mg/day dose also significantly improved global status (p < 0.001), fatigue (p = 0.016), cognition (p = 0.025) and multiple SF-36 domains. As in the sister trial, the abstract gives p-values rather than responder percentages. Nausea and headache were the commonest adverse events.
cards.watchOut: A second sponsor-run pivotal trial replicating the first's design and its reporting habit — significance without absolute responder rates. Two trials with the same sponsor, same endpoints and same analysis population are replication of a sort, but not independent replication; no academic or independently funded trial of milnacipran in fibromyalgia exists in this record.
cards.source: Mease PJ et al. The efficacy and safety of milnacipran for treatment of fibromyalgia. a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Journal of Rheumatology. 2009. PMID: 19132781. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Branco 2010: the European phase 3 trial (884 patients) — composite responders significantly favoured milnacipran 200 mg/day (p = 0.0003), FIQ also improved (p = 0.015)
cards.summary: Branco 2010: the European phase 3 trial (884 patients) — composite responders significantly favoured milnacipran 200 mg/day (p = 0.0003), FIQ also improved (p = 0.015)
cards.people: 884 outpatients meeting 1990 ACR criteria for fibromyalgia at European centres, randomised to milnacipran 200 mg/day (n = 435) or placebo (n = 449) for 17 weeks (4-week escalation, 12-week stable dose, 9-day down-titration). Primary criterion: a 2-measure composite of at least 30% pain improvement plus much/very much improved global status; the Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire was the additional key measure. Registered as NCT00436033.
cards.result: At week 16, milnacipran 200 mg/day significantly beat placebo on the 2-measure composite responder criterion (p = 0.0003) and on FIQ total score (p = 0.015), with significant gains also in SF-36 physical (p = 0.025) and mental (p = 0.007) components, fatigue (p = 0.006) and self-reported cognition (p = 0.041). The abstract again reports no absolute responder percentages. Nausea, hyperhidrosis (sweating) and headache were the commonest adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Only the 200 mg/day dose was tested, so this trial cannot speak to the marketed 100 mg/day regimen's European performance; and a p-value of 0.0003 on a composite endpoint can coexist with a small absolute responder gap — which, once more, the abstract does not print. Hyperhidrosis joins nausea as a signature burden of the drug at this dose.
cards.source: Branco JC et al. A European multicenter randomized double-blind placebo-controlled monotherapy clinical trial of milnacipran in treatment of fibromyalgia. The Journal of Rheumatology. 2010. PMID: 20156949. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00436033, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Goldenberg 2010: benefit persisted through a 6-month extension, and patients switched from placebo improved after re-randomisation to milnacipran — in a population pre-selected for tolerating the drug
cards.summary: Goldenberg 2010: benefit persisted through a 6-month extension, and patients switched from placebo improved after re-randomisation to milnacipran — in a population pre-selected for tolerating the drug
cards.people: 449 patients who had completed a 6-month lead-in trial (87.7% of those eligible) entered a 6-month double-blind extension: those already on milnacipran 200 mg/day continued it (n = 209); those previously on placebo or milnacipran 100 mg/day were re-randomised to 100 mg/day (n = 48) or 200 mg/day (n = 192). Outcomes: visual analogue pain, FIQ total score and patient global impression of change.
cards.result: Patients continuing milnacipran maintained their pain reduction over the full 12 months, with global and FIQ benefits also maintained. Patients re-randomised from placebo or 100 mg/day to 200 mg/day improved further in pain, FIQ and global ratings at 1 year. The most common newly emergent adverse event was nausea. The abstract reports trajectories without absolute responder rates.
cards.watchOut: Extension populations are survivors: everyone who could not tolerate milnacipran, or got nothing from it, has already left, so durability here means 'durability in the minority who stayed'. There is no placebo arm continuing through the extension, so the maintained improvement cannot be separated from natural history and expectation in this record.
cards.source: Goldenberg DL et al. Durability of therapeutic response to milnacipran treatment for fibromyalgia. Results of a randomized, double-blind, monotherapy 6-month extension study. Pain Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20002596. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised double-blind extension study (goldenberg 2010) 449 patients who had completed a 6-month lead-in trial (87.7% of those eligible) entered a 6-month double-blind extension: those already on milnacipran 200 mg/day continued it (n = 209); those previously on placebo or milnacipran 100 mg/day were re-randomised to 100 mg/day (n = 48) or 200 mg/day (n = 192). outcomes: visual analogue pain, fiq total score and patient global impression of change. patients continuing milnacipran maintained their pain reduction over the full 12 months, with global and fiq benefits also maintained. patients re-randomised from placebo or 100 mg/day to 200 mg/day improved further in pain, fiq and global ratings at 1 year. the most common newly emergent adverse event was nausea. the abstract reports trajectories without absolute responder rates. extension populations are survivors: everyone who could not tolerate milnacipran, or got nothing from it, has already left, so durability here means 'durability in the minority who stayed'. there is no placebo arm continuing through the extension, so the maintained improvement cannot be separated from natural history and expectation in this record. goldenberg dl et al. durability of therapeutic response to milnacipran treatment for fibromyalgia. results of a randomized, double-blind, monotherapy 6-month extension study. pain medicine. 2010. pmid: 20002596. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adrenergic uptake inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · adult · aged · cyclopropanes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · dose-response relationship, drug · double-blind method · female · fibromyalgia/drug therapy · follow-up studies · humans · male · middle aged · milnacipran · pain measurement · treatment outcome · young adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: three positive pivotal trials and a small, real, expensively tolerated benefit — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: three positive pivotal trials and a small, real, expensively tolerated benefit — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Four randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling about 3,100 patients (phase 2 n = 125; phase 3 n = 1,196, 888 and 884) plus a 449-patient double-blind extension, all sponsor-run, in adults meeting 1990 ACR fibromyalgia criteria, overwhelmingly women.
cards.result: Every trial met its composite responder endpoint significantly. The only absolute responder figures in the abstracts come from the smallest trial (at least 50% pain reduction: 37% versus 14%). The class-level Cochrane synthesis at shelf #391 estimates substantial pain relief for roughly one patient in ten beyond placebo across the licensed fibromyalgia drugs including milnacipran. Against the benefit: nausea in about a third of patients, and adverse-event discontinuation of 19.5–23.7% versus 9.5% on placebo in the largest trial.
cards.watchOut: The evidence answers 'does milnacipran beat placebo on composite responder endpoints over 3–6 months' — yes, consistently. It does not answer how it compares with duloxetine, pregabalin, amitriptyline or exercise (no head-to-head trials carded here; the comparative picture is at #391), what happens after a year in unselected patients, or whether the benefit survives stopping. Milnacipran also raises blood pressure and pulse as a noradrenergic drug — a monitoring point the trial abstracts underplay.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vitton O et al. Human Psychopharmacology. 2004 (PMID: 15378666); Clauw DJ et al. Clinical Therapeutics. 2008 (PMID: 19108787); Mease PJ et al. shelves.title: Allopurinol versus febuxostat, both titrated to target: the older, cheaper drug was noninferior for flares in STOP Gout — and numerically ahead
shelves.question: In adults with gout, when allopurinol and febuxostat are each titrated to a serum urate target, how do they compare on gout flares and safety?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · *Allopurinol/therapeutic use/adverse effects · *Febuxostat/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Glomerular Filtration Rate · *Gout/drug therapy/complications/blood · *Gout Suppressants/therapeutic use/adverse effects · *Renal Insufficiency, Chronic/drug therapy/complications · Treatment Outcome · Uric Acid/blood
shelves.balance: One large double-blind trial answers this directly, and its answer is unfashionable: titrated to the same urate target, allopurinol was noninferior to febuxostat for the outcome patients feel — flares. In STOP Gout (O'Dell 2022, PMID: 35434725; 940 participants, at least a third with stage 3 chronic kidney disease), 36.5% of allopurinol patients had one or more flares in the observation phase versus 43.5% on febuxostat (P<0.001 for noninferiority against an 8-percentage-point margin); 80% of both groups reached target urate, and serious adverse events, including cardiovascular events, did not differ. The trial's prespecified kidney subgroup (Helget 2024, PMID: 38906504) found the same shape in stage 3 CKD — flares 32% versus 45% (P=0.02) at equal urate control — with one caution: acute kidney injury was more common on allopurinol in that subgroup. A post-hoc look at the initiation phase (Barry 2024, PMID: 38925627) found starting and escalating either drug carried similar flare risk when prophylaxis (90% colchicine) was given. This shelf is about flare control under treat-to-target dosing; it is distinct from shelf #382, which asks the separate cardiovascular-safety question (CARES and FAST), and from shelf #681 (nurse-led treat-to-target care versus usual GP care). PROPOSED LIKELY (no meaningful difference — allopurinol noninferior) (Tier C: the comparison rests on a single trial and its own sub-analyses).

cards.headline: O'Dell 2022 (STOP Gout): in 940 patients, flares in 36.5% on allopurinol versus 43.5% on febuxostat — allopurinol noninferior, with equal urate control and no difference in serious adverse events
cards.summary: O'Dell 2022 (STOP Gout): in 940 patients, flares in 36.5% on allopurinol versus 43.5% on febuxostat — allopurinol noninferior, with equal urate control and no difference in serious adverse events
cards.type: Randomised double-blind noninferiority trial (O'Dell 2022, STOP Gout)
cards.people: 940 participants with gout and hyperuricaemia (serum urate ≥6.8 mg/dL), at least 33% with stage 3 chronic kidney disease, in a US Veterans Affairs double-blind noninferiority trial. Allopurinol started at 100 mg daily (maximum 800 mg) and febuxostat at 40 mg daily (maximum 120 mg), each titrated to a serum urate target over 24 weeks, maintained to week 48, then observed to week 72, with anti-inflammatory prophylaxis during titration and maintenance. 20.1% withdrew, similarly in both arms.
cards.result: During the observation phase (weeks 49–72), 36.5% of allopurinol-treated participants had one or more flares compared with 43.5% on febuxostat (P<0.001 for noninferiority; prespecified margin 8 percentage points). Overall, 80% of participants achieved mean target urate levels during maintenance, with no difference by treatment. There were no treatment differences in serious adverse events, including cardiovascular events.
cards.watchOut: A VA population — overwhelmingly older men (the companion initiation analysis reports 98.4% male, mean age 62.1 years) — so the result transfers to women and younger patients by extrapolation, not by data. Noninferiority was the design; the 7-point absolute gap favouring allopurinol is a secondary reading of a trial powered on its margin, and one in five participants withdrew.
cards.source: O'Dell JR et al. Comparative Effectiveness of Allopurinol and Febuxostat in Gout Management. NEJM Evidence. 2022. PMID: 35434725. Registry ID: NCT02579096. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Helget 2024: in the trial's stage 3 CKD subgroup, flares were 32% on allopurinol versus 45% on febuxostat (P=0.02) at equal urate control — but acute kidney injury was more common on allopurinol
cards.summary: Helget 2024: in the trial's stage 3 CKD subgroup, flares were 32% on allopurinol versus 45% on febuxostat (P=0.02) at equal urate control — but acute kidney injury was more common on allopurinol
cards.type: Prespecified subgroup analysis of a randomised trial (Helget 2024)
cards.people: Prespecified subcohort of the STOP Gout trial: 351 of 940 participants with chronic kidney disease (eGFR 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m²), of whom 277 were assessed for the primary outcome of a gout flare during weeks 49–72. Both drugs were titrated to serum urate <6.0 mg/dL (<5.0 with tophi).
cards.result: Fewer patients randomised to allopurinol had a flare during phase 3 (32% vs 45%; P=0.02) despite similar attainment of the urate goal by the end of phase 2 (79% vs 81%; P=0.6). Acute kidney injury was more common in participants with stage 3 CKD randomised to allopurinol compared with febuxostat. The authors conclude the two drugs are similarly efficacious and well tolerated in CKD under a treat-to-target regimen, with fewer flares on allopurinol.
cards.watchOut: A subgroup of a trial whose overall result was noninferiority: the flare difference here (P=0.02) is hypothesis-strengthening, not a second trial, and the analysis had limited power for infrequent safety events. The acute kidney injury signal runs the other way and is the card's real clinical payload — in stage 3 CKD, allopurinol's flare advantage came with more AKI in this dataset.
cards.source: Helget LN et al. Efficacy and Safety of Allopurinol and Febuxostat in Patients With Gout and CKD: Subgroup Analysis of the STOP Gout Trial. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2024. PMID: 38906504. Registry ID: none in the record (subgroup report of NCT02579096). cards.headline: Barry 2024: during initiation and dose escalation, flare risk was similar for the two drugs (hazard ratio 1.17, febuxostat vs allopurinol, not significant) when 90% received colchicine prophylaxis
cards.summary: Barry 2024: during initiation and dose escalation, flare risk was similar for the two drugs (hazard ratio 1.17, febuxostat vs allopurinol, not significant) when 90% received colchicine prophylaxis
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of a randomised trial (Barry 2024)
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of all 940 STOP Gout participants during weeks 0–24, when urate-lowering therapy was initiated and titrated to a serum urate goal of <6 mg/dL (<5 mg/dL with tophi). Participants were 98.4% male, mean age 62.1 years, mean baseline serum urate 8.5 mg/dL; all received anti-inflammatory prophylaxis (90% colchicine). Flares were assessed by structured participant interviews.
cards.result: In a multivariable Cox model there were no significant associations of treatment assignment (hazard ratio 1.17 for febuxostat vs allopurinol), dose escalation (HR 1.18 vs no escalation), prophylaxis type, or individual comorbidity with flare, and no interaction with dose escalation. Factors independently associated with flare risk during initiation were younger age, higher baseline serum urate, and absence of tophi.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and observational within the trial: 'no significant association' for a hazard ratio of 1.17 is not proof of equivalence, and the reassuring initiation picture depends on near-universal colchicine prophylaxis and gradual titration — it does not describe starting either drug at full dose without cover.
cards.source: Barry A et al. Comparison of Gout Flares With the Initiation of Treat-to-Target Allopurinol and Febuxostat: A Post-Hoc Analysis of a Randomized Multicenter Trial. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2024. PMID: 38925627. Registry ID: none in the record (post-hoc analysis of NCT02579096). cards.headline: Synthesis: under treat-to-target dosing the drugs are interchangeable for flare control, with allopurinol numerically ahead — LIKELY (no meaningful difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: under treat-to-target dosing the drugs are interchangeable for flare control, with allopurinol numerically ahead — LIKELY (no meaningful difference)
cards.people: One double-blind noninferiority trial of 940 patients with gout (a third with stage 3 CKD), its prespecified CKD subgroup (n=351), and its post-hoc initiation-phase analysis.
cards.result: Flares after titration: 36.5% (allopurinol) versus 43.5% (febuxostat), noninferiority P<0.001; in stage 3 CKD 32% versus 45% (P=0.02); target urate reached by 80% on both; serious adverse events, including cardiovascular events, not different; initiation-phase flare risk similar under colchicine prophylaxis. The one counter-signal is more acute kidney injury on allopurinol in the CKD subgroup. Nothing here supports paying febuxostat's price for better flare control; the cardiovascular-safety comparison lives on shelf #382.
cards.watchOut: A single trial family carries this shelf: the subgroup and post-hoc cards are the same 940 patients re-read, not independent confirmation, and the population is almost entirely older male veterans. Febuxostat keeps legitimate niches this trial does not address — true allopurinol intolerance or hypersensitivity risk, and dosing convenience in advanced kidney disease beyond stage 3.
cards.source: Synthesis of O'Dell JR et al. NEJM Evidence. 2022 (PMID: 35434725); Helget LN et al. American Journal of Kidney Diseases. 2024 (PMID: 38906504); Barry A et al. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2024 (PMID: 38925627).

shelves.title: Aspirin after hip fracture (PEP): pulmonary embolism cut 43% relative and fatal PE 58% relative versus placebo — but the aspirin-versus-heparin trial has never been done
shelves.question: After hip fracture, is aspirin as effective as heparin for preventing venous thromboembolism?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip · Aspirin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Cause of Death · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Femoral Neck Fractures/surgery · Hip Fractures/surgery · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Male · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Postoperative Complications/mortality/prevention & control · Pulmonary Embolism/mortality/prevention & control · Survival Rate · Thrombophlebitis/mortality/prevention & control
shelves.balance: The question as posed has never been tested — and the shelf says so on its face, because the nearest evidence is routinely misquoted as if it had been. The PEP trial (PMID: 10776741; 13,356 hip-fracture patients) randomised aspirin 160 mg daily against placebo, layered on whatever other prophylaxis clinicians chose. Aspirin reduced pulmonary embolism by 43% relative (95% CI 18 to 60) and symptomatic DVT by 29% relative; confirmed PE or DVT occurred in 1.6% versus 2.5% (9 fewer events per 1,000 treated), and fatal PE fell by 58% relative (18 vs 43 deaths). There was no effect on other causes of death, and the price was bleeding: 6 extra transfused postoperative bleeds per 1,000, though bleeding deaths were equal (13 vs 15). Because some PEP patients also received heparin and aspirin's effect looked similar in that subgroup, PEP is consistent with aspirin adding benefit alongside heparin — it cannot rank aspirin against heparin. So: aspirin after hip fracture is better than no aspirin (POSSIBLE, one trial, Tier C); whether it is as effective as heparin is unknown. Prophylaxis after elective arthroplasty — where head-to-head evidence does exist — is shelf #1127, and the wider hip-fracture care bundle is shelf #342.

cards.headline: PEP Trial 2000: in 13,356 hip-fracture patients, aspirin cut pulmonary embolism by 43% relative and fatal PE by 58% relative versus placebo — confirmed PE or DVT 1.6% versus 2.5% — at a cost of 6 extra transfused bleeds per 1,000
cards.summary: PEP Trial 2000: in 13,356 hip-fracture patients, aspirin cut pulmonary embolism by 43% relative and fatal PE by 58% relative versus placebo — confirmed PE or DVT 1.6% versus 2.5% — at a cost of 6 extra transfused bleeds per 1,000
cards.type: Randomised placebo-controlled trial (PEP Trial Collaborative Group 2000)
cards.people: 13,356 patients undergoing surgery for hip fracture in 148 hospitals (Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Sweden, UK), randomised to aspirin 160 mg daily or placebo, started preoperatively and continued for 35 days, on top of any other thromboprophylaxis their clinicians chose (some also received heparin). A further 4,088 elective arthroplasty patients were randomised in the same trial and are reported separately in the paper. Follow-up covered mortality and in-hospital morbidity to day 35.
cards.result: Among hip-fracture patients, aspirin produced a 43% relative reduction in pulmonary embolism (95% CI 18 to 60; P = 0.002) and a 29% relative reduction in symptomatic deep-vein thrombosis (95% CI 3 to 48; P = 0.03). Confirmed PE or DVT occurred in 105/6,679 (1.6%) on aspirin versus 165/6,677 (2.5%) on placebo — an absolute reduction of 9 per 1,000 and a 36% relative reduction (95% CI 19 to 50; P = 0.0003). Fatal PE was prevented in 4 per 1,000 patients (18 vs 43 deaths; 58% relative reduction, 95% CI 27 to 76; P = 0.002), with no effect on deaths from other vascular (hazard ratio 1.04, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.26) or non-vascular causes (1.01, 0.84 to 1.23). Deaths from bleeding were 13 versus 15, but aspirin caused an excess of 6 postoperative transfused bleeding episodes per 1,000 (P = 0.04). Effects were similar in subgroups, including patients also receiving subcutaneous heparin; proportional effects in the arthroplasty cohort were compatible.
cards.watchOut: PEP randomised aspirin against placebo, not against heparin: patients received whatever other prophylaxis their clinicians chose, so the trial proves aspirin adds protection over no aspirin — it does not prove aspirin equals heparin, and no large trial has randomised the two head-to-head after hip fracture. It is also 1992–98 practice: thromboprophylaxis, anaesthesia and mobilisation norms have all changed, which likely lowers the absolute event rates a modern patient faces, in both arms.
cards.source: PEP Trial Collaborative Group. Prevention of pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis with low dose aspirin: Pulmonary Embolism Prevention (PEP) trial. Lancet. 2000. PMID: 10776741. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Synthesis: aspirin beats placebo after hip fracture by a clinically important margin; the heparin comparison is an evidence gap, not a result — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: aspirin beats placebo after hip fracture by a clinically important margin; the heparin comparison is an evidence gap, not a result — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.people: One large randomised placebo-controlled trial (PEP; 13,356 hip-fracture patients, plus a separately reported arthroplasty cohort). No randomised aspirin-versus-heparin trial after hip fracture was found in screening.
cards.result: Pulmonary embolism: 43% relative reduction (95% CI 18 to 60). Symptomatic DVT: 29% relative reduction (3 to 48). Confirmed PE/DVT: 1.6% vs 2.5% (absolute reduction 0.9 percentage points). Fatal PE: 58% relative reduction (27 to 76); 4 fewer deaths per 1,000. Other-cause mortality: no effect. Harm: 6 extra transfused bleeds per 1,000; bleeding deaths 13 vs 15.
cards.watchOut: Tier C: a single trial, now a quarter-century old, answering a neighbouring question (aspirin versus placebo) rather than the one posed (aspirin versus heparin). The stamp grades the placebo comparison; the equivalence question should be presented to patients and guideline committees as unanswered, not as settled by PEP.
cards.source: Synthesis of PEP Trial Collaborative Group. Lancet. 2000 (PMID: 10776741).

shelves.title: Tramadol for osteoarthritis and chronic musculoskeletal pain: a pain benefit too small to feel, bought with more adverse events, more dropouts and a mortality signal
shelves.question: In chronic musculoskeletal and osteoarthritic pain, does tramadol help enough to justify its dependence and harm risks?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/*therapeutic use · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/drug therapy · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis/*complications, drug therapy · Osteoarthritis, Knee/drug therapy · Pain/*drug therapy, etiology, prevention & control · Pain Management · Pain Measurement · Tramadol/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: The benefit is real but smaller than the threshold patients can feel. The Cochrane synthesis (Toupin April 2019, PMID: 31132298) pooled 22 randomised trials in osteoarthritis: tramadol, alone or with acetaminophen, improved pain by 4% absolute over placebo — judged no important benefit — although slightly more people achieved a 20% improvement (15 of 100 versus 10 of 100). Function showed the same 4% pattern. The harms are not symmetrical with that small gain: adverse events were a third more common (risk ratio 1.34; a 17% absolute increase), nausea, dizziness and tiredness leading; withdrawal because of adverse events was 2.6 times as common (a 12% absolute increase); and serious adverse events were more frequent (110/2459 versus 22/1153; risk ratio 1.78). The trials averaged about two months, so they cannot measure dependence, falls in older users, or long-term outcomes at all. The one large long-horizon dataset is observational and points the wrong way: in 88,902 propensity-matched UK patients aged 50 and over with osteoarthritis (Zeng 2019, PMID: 30860559), starting tramadol was followed by higher one-year mortality than starting naproxen (23.5 versus 13.8 deaths per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 1.71), diclofenac, celecoxib or etoricoxib — though not codeine — and the authors themselves warn that confounding by indication (tramadol is prescribed to frailer patients) may explain it. The class-level opioid synthesis (Busse 2018, PMID: 30561481) is homed at shelf #346 and is not re-carded here; its pooled opioid effect was likewise below the minimally important difference. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit) / POSSIBLE (harm): a drug whose average benefit sits below what patients can feel, whose trial harms are certain, and whose dependence and mortality questions the trials never ran long enough to answer (Tier C: the mortality claim rests on observational data).

cards.headline: Toupin April 2019 (Cochrane): tramadol improved osteoarthritis pain by 4% absolute over placebo — no important benefit — while adverse-event withdrawals rose 12% absolute
cards.summary: Toupin April 2019 (Cochrane): tramadol improved osteoarthritis pain by 4% absolute over placebo — no important benefit — while adverse-event withdrawals rose 12% absolute
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, 22 RCTs (Toupin April 2019, Cochrane)
cards.people: 22 randomised trials (21 in the meta-analyses) of oral tramadol alone (17 trials) or tramadol plus acetaminophen (5 trials) versus placebo or active control in osteoarthritis, mostly hip or knee, in predominantly female participants with a mean age of 63 and moderate-to-severe pain; 3,871 participants were randomised to tramadol or the combination and 2,625 to placebo or active control. Doses ranged from 37.5 mg to 400 mg daily; mean trial duration was about two months.
cards.result: Pain: tramadol alone improved pain by 4% absolute versus placebo (95% CI 3% to 5%; 8 studies, 3,972 participants) and the combination by 4% (2% to 6%) — rated no important benefit; 15 of 100 on tramadol versus 10 of 100 on placebo achieved a clinically important (≥20%) pain improvement. Function improved by the same 4% absolute. Harms: any adverse event, risk ratio 1.34 (1.24 to 1.46) for tramadol alone — a 17% absolute increase — with nausea, dizziness and tiredness most frequent; withdrawal because of adverse events, risk ratio 2.64 (2.17 to 3.20), a 12% absolute increase; serious adverse events, risk ratio 1.78 (1.11 to 2.84; 110/2459 versus 22/1153). Evidence was moderate quality, downgraded for risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: Short trials in a chronic disease: a mean of two months of treatment cannot capture dependence, tolerance, falls or fractures — the harms that dominate tramadol's real-world risk profile accrue over the years-long exposures these trials never studied. Most trials were industry-funded, only four reported adequate sequence generation and allocation concealment, and 10 of 22 had incomplete outcome data.
cards.source: Toupin April K et al.. Tramadol for osteoarthritis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019. PMID: 31132298. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Zeng 2019: starting tramadol for osteoarthritis was followed by higher one-year mortality than starting an NSAID (hazard ratios 1.70–2.04) — but not than starting codeine
cards.summary: Zeng 2019: starting tramadol for osteoarthritis was followed by higher one-year mortality than starting an NSAID (hazard ratios 1.70–2.04) — but not than starting codeine
cards.people: Sequential propensity-score-matched cohorts from a UK general-practice database (The Health Improvement Network, 2000–2015): 88,902 patients aged 50 or over with osteoarthritis newly prescribed tramadol (n = 44,451 before matching) or one of five comparators — naproxen, diclofenac, celecoxib, etoricoxib or codeine. Outcome: all-cause mortality within one year of the first prescription.
cards.result: Deaths in the tramadol cohort ran at 23.5 per 1,000 person-years versus 13.8 for naproxen (rate difference 9.7 per 1,000 person-years, 95% CI 6.3 to 13.2; hazard ratio 1.71, 1.41 to 2.07). Mortality was likewise higher against diclofenac (36.2 versus 19.2 per 1,000 person-years; HR 1.88, 1.51 to 2.35), celecoxib (31.2 versus 18.4; HR 1.70, 1.33 to 2.17) and etoricoxib (25.7 versus 12.8; HR 2.04, 1.37 to 3.03), but not against codeine (32.2 versus 34.6; HR 0.94, 0.83 to 1.05).
cards.watchOut: Observational, and the authors say so plainly: propensity matching cannot remove confounding by indication — tramadol is channelled to older, frailer patients and to those in whom NSAIDs are judged unsafe, which is itself a mortality risk. The comparison with codeine (a drug with a similar channelling pattern) showing no difference is the internal hint that channelling, not tramadol pharmacology, may drive the signal. It is a reason for caution and for randomised evidence, not proof that tramadol kills.
cards.source: Zeng C et al.. Association of Tramadol With All-Cause Mortality Among Patients With Osteoarthritis. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 30860559. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a sub-perceptible average benefit, certain short-term harms, and long-term questions the trials never asked
cards.summary: Synthesis: a sub-perceptible average benefit, certain short-term harms, and long-term questions the trials never asked
cards.people: One Cochrane synthesis of 22 osteoarthritis trials (about 6,500 participants) and one propensity-matched UK cohort of 88,902 patients followed for one year after a first prescription.
cards.result: Pain and function improve by about 4% absolute over placebo — below clinical importance — with 5 extra people in 100 achieving a 20% pain improvement. Against that: 17 extra people in 100 with an adverse event, 12 extra in 100 stopping treatment because of one, and a near-doubling of serious adverse events in trials; observational data associate starting tramadol with higher one-year mortality than starting an NSAID. Dependence is unmeasured in the trial base because the trials lasted weeks.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the mortality hazard ratios as tramadol's proven effect — they are associations in channelled prescribing data. Equally, do not quote 'no important benefit' as 'no one benefits': one in twenty extra patients gets a worthwhile pain improvement, which is why the honest stamp is a split, not a dismissal.
cards.source: Synthesis of Toupin April K et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2019 (PMID: 31132298); Zeng C et al. JAMA. 2019 (PMID: 30860559).

shelves.title: Cyclobenzaprine in fibromyalgia: patients feel better overall and sleep better, pain improves early — fatigue and tender points do not move
shelves.question: In fibromyalgia and chronic back spasm, does cyclobenzaprine improve sleep and pain?
shelves.mesh: Amitriptyline/*analogs & derivatives, *therapeutic use · Databases, Factual · Fatigue/drug therapy, etiology, physiopathology · Female · Fibromyalgia/complications, *drug therapy, physiopathology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Relaxants, Central/*therapeutic use · Pain/drug therapy, etiology, physiopathology · Placebos · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The fibromyalgia evidence is old, small and consistent in shape. Pooling five randomised placebo-controlled trials, Tofferi 2004 (PMID: 14872449) found patients on cyclobenzaprine three times as likely to report global improvement (odds ratio 3.0, 95% CI 1.6 to 5.6; risk difference 0.21, so about five patients treated for one to improve), with pain better early and sleep the symptom that improved most — but no improvement in fatigue or tender points at any time point. A later mechanistic trial using very low bedtime doses (1–4 mg) in 36 patients (Moldofsky 2011, PMID: 21885490) found the same pattern over eight weeks — pain, tenderness, fatigue and depression scores improved versus placebo — and tied it to sleep physiology: nights of restorative, normalised cyclic-alternating-pattern sleep increased on the drug and correlated with the symptom gains. For the back-spasm half of the question, the muscle-relaxant class synthesis (Cashin 2021, PMID: 34233900) is homed at shelf #786 and is not re-carded here: it found small, not clinically important pain reductions in acute low back pain on very-low-to-low certainty evidence, and considerable uncertainty for chronic use. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but symptomatic effect, strongest on sleep and global impression, in trials too small and short to define its place against modern fibromyalgia therapy.

cards.headline: Tofferi 2004: cyclobenzaprine tripled the odds of global improvement in fibromyalgia (OR 3.0; NNT about 5) — sleep and early pain improved, fatigue and tender points never did
cards.summary: Tofferi 2004: cyclobenzaprine tripled the odds of global improvement in fibromyalgia (OR 3.0; NNT about 5) — sleep and early pain improved, fatigue and tender points never did
cards.people: Five randomised, placebo-controlled trials of cyclobenzaprine in people with fibromyalgia, identified from Medline, Embase, PsycLIT, the Cochrane Library and unpublished sources. Outcomes abstracted: global improvement, pain, fatigue, sleep and tender points over time.
cards.result: The odds ratio for global improvement on cyclobenzaprine was 3.0 (95% CI 1.6 to 5.6), with a pooled risk difference of 0.21 (0.09 to 0.34) — a number needed to treat of 4.8 (3.0 to 11) for one patient to experience symptom improvement. Pain improved early in treatment; sleep improved; there was no improvement in fatigue or tender points at any time point.
cards.watchOut: Five small trials from an earlier fibromyalgia era, with diagnostic criteria and background care that predate modern practice; the pooled estimate rests on few patients and on global-impression outcomes, the measures most sensitive to unblinding by a sedating, dry-mouth-causing drug. No registry identifier exists for this review — it predates review registration.
cards.source: Tofferi JK et al.. Treatment of fibromyalgia with cyclobenzaprine: A meta-analysis. Arthritis and Rheumatism. 2004. PMID: 14872449. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Moldofsky 2011: bedtime very-low-dose cyclobenzaprine (1–4 mg) improved pain, tenderness, fatigue and mood over 8 weeks — alongside measurably more restorative sleep
cards.summary: Moldofsky 2011: bedtime very-low-dose cyclobenzaprine (1–4 mg) improved pain, tenderness, fatigue and mood over 8 weeks — alongside measurably more restorative sleep
cards.people: 36 patients with fibromyalgia, unrefreshing sleep and the alpha-nonREM EEG anomaly at screening, randomised to bedtime very-low-dose cyclobenzaprine 1–4 mg (dose-escalating, n = 18) or placebo (n = 18) for 8 weeks. Outcomes: pain, tenderness, fatigue, Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale scores, and cyclic alternating pattern (CAP) sleep EEG at weeks 2, 4 and 8.
cards.result: On cyclobenzaprine, musculoskeletal pain and fatigue decreased and tenderness improved; total HAD and HAD-depression scores fell; patient- and clinician-rated fatigue improved. None of these measures changed significantly on placebo, and at 8 weeks cyclobenzaprine was significantly better than placebo for pain, tenderness and the depression subscore. Significantly more cyclobenzaprine patients gained nights of restorative sleep (normalised CAP ratio ≤33%), and those gains correlated with improvements in fatigue and mood.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six patients, one sleep laboratory, and a surrogate EEG biomarker: this is a mechanism-confirming pilot, not a basis for effect sizes. The doses (1–4 mg at bedtime) are far below the 10 mg three-times-daily dosing of the older trials and of routine prescribing — the two carded studies are not testing the same exposure.
cards.source: Moldofsky H et al.. Effects of bedtime very low dose cyclobenzaprine on symptoms and sleep physiology in patients with fibromyalgia syndrome: a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled study. cards.headline: Synthesis: a sleep-first drug in fibromyalgia — global improvement for about one patient in five treated, with fatigue and tenderness unmoved in the pooled trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: a sleep-first drug in fibromyalgia — global improvement for about one patient in five treated, with fatigue and tenderness unmoved in the pooled trials
cards.people: Five pooled placebo-controlled trials (Tofferi 2004) and one 36-patient bedtime-dosing trial with EEG endpoints (Moldofsky 2011), all in fibromyalgia.
cards.result: Global improvement: odds ratio 3.0 (1.6–5.6), NNT ≈ 5. Sleep: the most consistent beneficiary. Pain: improved early in the older trials and, at very low bedtime doses, sustained over 8 weeks. Fatigue and tender points: no improvement in the pooled trials. Nothing in this evidence base addresses chronic back spasm directly — the class evidence for back pain lives at shelf #786.
cards.watchOut: Every trial predates or ignores the current fibromyalgia standards (duloxetine, milnacipran, pregabalin, exercise), and none compares against them. Sedation and dry mouth — cyclobenzaprine is structurally a tricyclic — both unblind and limit daytime dosing; the bedtime low-dose strategy exists precisely to work around that.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tofferi JK et al. Arthritis and Rheumatism. 2004 (PMID: 14872449); Moldofsky H et al. The Journal of Rheumatology. 2011 (PMID: 21885490).

shelves.title: Spa therapy and hydrotherapy: a three-week spa course left half of knee osteoarthritis patients improved at six months, and warm-water therapy eases fibromyalgia pain a little
shelves.question: In knee osteoarthritis and fibromyalgia, does balneotherapy or hydrotherapy improve pain and function?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Balneology/*methods · Combined Modality Therapy · Epidemiologic Methods · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/*therapy · Pain Measurement · Patient Satisfaction · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two different water-based interventions share this shelf, and the evidence differs by disease. For knee osteoarthritis, the load-bearing trial is large: 382 patients randomised (by a Zelen design, so patients did not know an alternative existed) to 18 days of spa therapy — massage, showers, mud and pool sessions — plus home exercise and usual care, or to exercise and usual care alone; at six months, 50.8% of the spa group versus 36.4% of controls had achieved a minimal clinically important improvement in pain or function (P = 0.005), though quality of life and patient-acceptable symptom state did not differ (Forestier 2010, PMID: 19734131). For fibromyalgia, the pooled hydrotherapy trials show a small pain reduction (standardised mean difference −0.42, 95% CI −0.61 to −0.24; eight studies, 462 participants) and a small quality-of-life gain, with no effect on depressive symptoms or tender point count; the reviewers graded the evidence moderate-to-strong but called for larger trials with long-term follow-up (Naumann 2014, PMID: 25000940). Neither literature can blind its participants — you know whether you have been sent to a spa — so expectation and the holiday itself are unmeasured co-interventions in every estimate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine but modest symptomatic gain, inseparable from context, with durability shown to six months only in the knee trial.

cards.headline: Forestier 2010: after a 3-week spa course, 50.8% of knee osteoarthritis patients reached a clinically important improvement at 6 months versus 36.4% with exercise and usual care alone
cards.summary: Forestier 2010: after a 3-week spa course, 50.8% of knee osteoarthritis patients reached a clinically important improvement at 6 months versus 36.4% with exercise and usual care alone
cards.people: 382 patients with American College of Rheumatology knee osteoarthritis attending French spa resorts as outpatients (195 spa therapy, 187 control), randomised by the Zelen method. Both groups continued usual treatment and daily standardised home exercises; the spa group also received 18 days of spa therapy (massages, showers, mud and pool sessions). Primary endpoint: minimal clinically important improvement (MCII) at 6 months — ≥19.9 mm on a visual analogue pain scale and/or ≥9.1 points on normalised WOMAC function, without knee surgery.
cards.result: At 6 months, 99/195 (50.8%) of the spa group and 68/187 (36.4%) of controls achieved MCII (χ² = 8.05; P = 0.005) — about one extra responder for every seven treated. There was no improvement in Short Form 36 quality of life or in patient acceptable symptom state at 6 months. Treatment was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Unblindable, and the control group got no equivalent attention, travel or rest: the 14-point responder gap prices in the whole spa experience, not a specific property of mineral water. Zelen randomisation (consent after allocation) protects against resentment effects, but the self-assessed endpoints remain expectation-sensitive.
cards.source: Forestier R et al.. Spa therapy in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: a large randomised multicentre trial. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2010. PMID: 19734131. cards.headline: Naumann 2014: hydrotherapy reduced fibromyalgia pain by a small standardised effect (−0.42) across 8 trials — no effect on depression or tender points
cards.summary: Naumann 2014: hydrotherapy reduced fibromyalgia pain by a small standardised effect (−0.42) across 8 trials — no effect on depression or tender points
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Naumann 2014)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trials of balneotherapy (mineral/thermal water) and hydrotherapy (water-based treatment) in fibromyalgia syndrome, searched to April 2013 across Medline, CENTRAL, Embase and CAMBASE. The hydrotherapy pain meta-analysis pooled 8 studies with 462 participants (3 low-risk-of-bias studies, 223 participants); quality of life pooled 7 studies with 398 participants.
cards.result: At end of treatment, hydrotherapy reduced pain with a standardised mean difference of −0.42 (95% CI −0.61 to −0.24; P < 0.00001; I² = 0%) and improved health-related quality of life (SMD −0.40, −0.62 to −0.18). No effect was seen on depressive symptoms or tender point count. The reviewers rated the evidence moderate-to-strong for the pain and quality-of-life outcomes and called for larger, high-quality trials focused on long-term results.
cards.watchOut: Small, short trials of heterogeneous water treatments (temperature, minerals, exercise content all vary), pooled at end of treatment — the moment expectation effects peak. Whether any benefit survives months after the last bath is exactly what this literature does not show; the knee-osteoarthritis trial on this shelf is the only carded evidence with a six-month horizon.
cards.source: Naumann J et al.. Therapeutic benefit of balneotherapy and hydrotherapy in the management of fibromyalgia syndrome: a qualitative systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Arthritis Research & Therapy. 2014. PMID: 25000940. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: modest symptomatic benefit in both diseases — a 14-point responder advantage at 6 months in knee osteoarthritis, a small pooled pain effect in fibromyalgia
cards.summary: Synthesis: modest symptomatic benefit in both diseases — a 14-point responder advantage at 6 months in knee osteoarthritis, a small pooled pain effect in fibromyalgia
cards.people: One 382-patient randomised spa trial in knee osteoarthritis with 6-month follow-up, and a meta-analysis of randomised hydrotherapy/balneotherapy trials in fibromyalgia (pain: 8 studies, 462 participants).
cards.result: Knee osteoarthritis: MCII 50.8% versus 36.4% at 6 months (NNT ≈ 7), no quality-of-life difference. Fibromyalgia: pain SMD −0.42 and quality-of-life SMD −0.40 at end of treatment; depression and tender points unchanged. Harms in the carded evidence are negligible; the intervention's real costs are time, travel and money.
cards.watchOut: No carded study isolates the water itself: heat, buoyancy, massage, exercise, rest and being on holiday travel together in every trial. Claims for specific mineral compositions or named spas go beyond anything randomised — and no specific product or resort is named in the carded records.

shelves.title: Abatacept in early rheumatoid arthritis: adding it to methotrexate roughly doubles early remission and slows damage — and a small group stay in remission after everything is stopped
shelves.question: In early rheumatoid arthritis, does abatacept with methotrexate induce remission and halt joint damage versus methotrexate alone?
shelves.mesh: Abatacept · Adult · Antirheumatic Agents/adverse effects, *therapeutic use · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/diagnostic imaging, *drug therapy · Disease Progression · Drug Therapy, Combination · Epidemiologic Methods · Female · Humans · Immunoconjugates/adverse effects, *therapeutic use · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use · Male · Methotrexate/adverse effects, *therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Prognosis · Quality of Life · Radiography · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two phase 3 trials in early, seropositive disease point the same way. In methotrexate-naive patients with poor prognostic factors (AGREE; Westhovens 2009, PMID: 19124524), abatacept plus methotrexate put 41.4% into DAS28 remission at one year versus 23.3% on methotrexate alone (P < 0.001) and slowed radiographic progression (mean Genant–Sharp change 0.63 versus 1.06; P = 0.040), with adverse events, serious infections and malignancies no more frequent than on methotrexate alone. In AVERT (Emery 2015, PMID: 25367713), subcutaneous abatacept plus methotrexate achieved DAS28 remission at 12 months in 60.9% versus 45.2% (P = 0.010); after all treatment was then withdrawn in patients with low disease activity, 14.8% versus 7.8% remained in remission at both 12 and 18 months (P = 0.045) — the drug-free-remission signal that makes this shelf more than a 'stronger suppression' story, though it applies to a small minority. Abatacept monotherapy (42.5% remission at 12 months) sat between the combination and methotrexate alone. The head-to-head AMPLE trial against adalimumab was in established, methotrexate-inadequate disease — a different question — and is not carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): consistent randomised evidence in early disease for more remission and less damage, with a safety profile in these trials indistinguishable from methotrexate alone.

cards.headline: AGREE 2009: in methotrexate-naive early RA with poor prognostic factors, abatacept + methotrexate doubled remission (41.4% vs 23.3%) and slowed joint damage at one year
cards.summary: AGREE 2009: in methotrexate-naive early RA with poor prognostic factors, abatacept + methotrexate doubled remission (41.4% vs 23.3%) and slowed joint damage at one year
cards.type: Randomised double-blind phase IIIb trial (Westhovens 2009; AGREE)
cards.people: Patients with rheumatoid arthritis of two years or less, methotrexate-naive, seropositive for rheumatoid factor and/or anti-CCP2 (96.5% and 89.0% respectively) with radiographic erosions, randomised 1:1 to intravenous abatacept (approximately 10 mg/kg) plus methotrexate or placebo plus methotrexate. Mean DAS28 at baseline was 6.3, mean Genant-modified Sharp score 7.1, mean disease duration 6.5 months. Co-primary endpoints: DAS28 (CRP) remission and joint-damage progression at year 1.
cards.result: Remission at year 1: 41.4% on abatacept plus methotrexate versus 23.3% on methotrexate alone (P < 0.001). Radiographic progression was significantly less (mean change in total Sharp score 0.63 versus 1.06; P = 0.040). Over one year, adverse events (84.8% versus 83.4%), serious adverse events (7.8% versus 7.9%), serious infections (2.0% versus 2.0%), autoimmune disorders (2.3% versus 2.0%) and malignancies (0.4% versus 0%) were comparable between groups.
cards.watchOut: A selected, worst-prognosis slice of early RA (seropositive with erosions already present) — the absolute remission advantage may not transfer to seronegative or non-erosive early disease. The record carries no registry identifier. One year is also short for a drug intended to be taken for decades.
cards.source: Westhovens R et al.. Clinical efficacy and safety of abatacept in methotrexate-naive patients with early rheumatoid arthritis and poor prognostic factors. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2009. PMID: 19124524. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: AVERT 2015: abatacept + methotrexate reached remission in 60.9% versus 45.2% at 12 months — and after all drugs were stopped, 14.8% versus 7.8% were still in remission at 18 months
cards.summary: AVERT 2015: abatacept + methotrexate reached remission in 60.9% versus 45.2% at 12 months — and after all drugs were stopped, 14.8% versus 7.8% were still in remission at 18 months
cards.people: Patients with early active rheumatoid arthritis (symptoms under two years, DAS28 (CRP) ≥3.2, anti-CCP2 positive, 95.2% rheumatoid-factor positive) randomised double-blind to weekly subcutaneous abatacept 125 mg plus methotrexate, abatacept 125 mg monotherapy, or methotrexate alone for 12 months. Patients with low disease activity at month 12 entered a further 12 months with all RA treatment withdrawn. Co-primary endpoints: DAS28 (CRP) <2.6 at month 12, and at both months 12 and 18, for the combination versus methotrexate.
cards.result: Remission at 12 months: 60.9% for abatacept plus methotrexate versus 45.2% for methotrexate (P = 0.010); abatacept monotherapy achieved 42.5%. After withdrawal of all therapy, remission at both 12 and 18 months held in 14.8% versus 7.8% (P = 0.045), and in 12.4% of the monotherapy group. Both abatacept arms had a safety profile comparable with methotrexate alone over the treatment period.
cards.watchOut: The drug-free remission figure — the result most often quoted from AVERT — is 14.8%: striking as proof of mechanism, but it means most combination patients who reached the withdrawal phase still needed treatment again. Withdrawal was offered only to patients already in low disease activity, a selected subgroup, and 12 months off treatment is not a cure horizon.
cards.source: Emery P et al.. cards.headline: Synthesis: in early seropositive RA, adding abatacept to methotrexate adds roughly 16–18 points of remission and measurably slows damage, at no measured safety cost over 1–2 years
cards.summary: Synthesis: in early seropositive RA, adding abatacept to methotrexate adds roughly 16–18 points of remission and measurably slows damage, at no measured safety cost over 1–2 years
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials in early (≤2 years), seropositive rheumatoid arthritis: AGREE (intravenous abatacept + methotrexate versus methotrexate, one year) and AVERT (subcutaneous abatacept ± methotrexate versus methotrexate, 12 months' treatment plus 12 months' withdrawal).
cards.result: Remission: 41.4% versus 23.3% (AGREE, year 1) and 60.9% versus 45.2% (AVERT, month 12). Damage: Genant–Sharp progression 0.63 versus 1.06 in AGREE. Drug-free remission after withdrawal: 14.8% versus 7.8%. Safety: adverse events, serious infections and malignancies comparable with methotrexate alone in both trials.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled the seropositive, erosive, poor-prognosis end of early RA, where the case for early biologic therapy is strongest; neither answers whether abatacept beats a treat-to-target methotrexate strategy with glucocorticoid bridging, the comparison modern early-RA practice actually poses.
cards.source: Synthesis of Westhovens R et al. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2009 (PMID: 19124524); Emery P et al. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2015 (PMID: 25367713).

shelves.title: Zoledronic acid for knee osteoarthritis with bone-marrow lesions: a promising six-month signal in 59 patients, extinguished by a 223-patient two-year trial
shelves.question: In knee osteoarthritis with bone-marrow lesions, does zoledronic acid reduce pain or lesion size?
shelves.mesh: Acute-Phase Reaction/drug therapy, etiology, pathology · Aged · Arthralgia/*drug therapy, pathology, physiopathology · Bone Density Conservation Agents/administration & dosage, *therapeutic use · Bone Marrow Diseases/complications, *drug therapy, pathology · Diphosphonates/administration & dosage, *therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Imidazoles/administration & dosage, *therapeutic use · Infusions, Intravenous · Knee Joint/drug effects, pathology, physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/complications, *drug therapy, pathology · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome · Zoledronic Acid
shelves.balance: The two trials disagree in proportion to their size. The small one came first: in 59 patients with knee osteoarthritis and MRI bone-marrow lesions, a single zoledronic acid infusion reduced pain at six months (−14.5 mm on a visual analogue scale, 95% CI −28.1 to −0.9) and shrank total lesion area more than placebo (−175.7 mm², −327.2 to −24.3), with 39% versus 18% achieving a clinically significant lesion reduction — but the pain effect was absent at 3 and 12 months and function scores never separated (Laslett 2012, PMID: 22355040). The definitive test, ZAP, randomised 223 similar patients to yearly infusions for two years and found nothing: cartilage volume loss was identical (−878 versus −919 mm³; difference 41, −79 to 161; P = .50), pain scores numerically favoured placebo, lesion size did not differ, and adverse events were more common on zoledronic acid (96% versus 83%), driven by acute post-infusion reactions (87% versus 56%) (Cai 2020, PMID: 32315057). The authors' conclusion — these findings do not support the use of zoledronic acid in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis — is the one the larger trial earns. PROPOSED SPLIT: the small-trial six-month signal is on the record and was honestly generated, but a treatment decision today rests on ZAP.

cards.headline: Laslett 2012: one zoledronic acid infusion cut knee pain and lesion size at 6 months in 59 patients — the effect was gone by 12 months
cards.summary: Laslett 2012: one zoledronic acid infusion cut knee pain and lesion size at 6 months in 59 patients — the effect was gone by 12 months
cards.people: 59 adults aged 50–80 with clinical knee osteoarthritis and MRI bone-marrow lesions (mean baseline pain 54 mm on a visual analogue scale; mean total lesion area 468 mm²), randomised to a single intravenous infusion of zoledronic acid 5 mg or placebo, with MRI at baseline, 6 and 12 months and pain/function measured by VAS and KOOS.
cards.result: At 6 months, pain was lower on zoledronic acid (−14.5 mm versus placebo, 95% CI −28.1 to −0.9) and total bone-marrow lesion area fell further (−175.7 mm², −327.2 to −24.3); 39% versus 18% achieved a clinically significant lesion reduction (P = 0.044). At 3 and 12 months the pain difference was not significant, the 12-month lesion difference was a trend only (−146.5 mm², −307.5 to +14.5), and KOOS function scales never differed. Acute-phase reactions were frequent in both arms.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-nine patients and a thicket of time points and outcomes: the significant results sit at exactly one time point (6 months) of several tested, the classic geometry of a small-trial false positive. This trial is best read as the hypothesis ZAP was built to test — and ZAP tested it at four times the size and twice the duration.

cards.headline: ZAP 2020: two yearly zoledronic acid infusions changed nothing in knee osteoarthritis with bone-marrow lesions — cartilage, pain and lesions all null at 24 months
cards.summary: ZAP 2020: two yearly zoledronic acid infusions changed nothing in knee osteoarthritis with bone-marrow lesions — cartilage, pain and lesions all null at 24 months
cards.people: 223 adults aged 50 or over with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis and MRI subchondral bone-marrow lesions, enrolled at four Australian sites, randomised to intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg (n = 113) or saline placebo (n = 110) at baseline and 12 months; 190 (85%) completed. Primary outcome: change in tibiofemoral cartilage volume over 24 months; prespecified secondaries included VAS and WOMAC pain and lesion-size change.
cards.result: Cartilage volume change did not differ (−878 versus −919 mm³; between-group difference 41 mm³, 95% CI −79 to 161; P = .50). No prespecified secondary outcome differed: VAS pain change −11.5 versus −16.8 (difference 5.2, −2.3 to 12.8; P = .17), WOMAC pain difference 20.5 (−11.2 to 52.2; P = .21), lesion-size difference −27 mm² (−127 to 73; P = .60). Adverse events were more frequent on zoledronic acid (96% versus 83%), mainly acute reactions within three days of infusion (87% versus 56%). The authors conclude the findings do not support zoledronic acid in knee osteoarthritis.
cards.watchOut: A null on the lesion hypothesis, not on bisphosphonates generally: this trial says nothing about zoledronic acid for osteoporosis or post-fracture care, where its evidence lives on other shelves. Cartilage volume's minimal clinically important difference is unestablished, but the pain and lesion outcomes — the ones patients and the hypothesis cared about — were null with confidence intervals excluding the Laslett effect.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the small trial's six-month signal did not survive a proper test — zoledronic acid does not treat knee osteoarthritis, with or without bone-marrow lesions
cards.summary: Synthesis: the small trial's six-month signal did not survive a proper test — zoledronic acid does not treat knee osteoarthritis, with or without bone-marrow lesions
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials of intravenous zoledronic acid in knee osteoarthritis with MRI bone-marrow lesions: n = 59 with a single infusion and 12-month follow-up (Laslett 2012), and n = 223 with yearly infusions and 24-month follow-up (Cai 2020).
cards.result: Small trial: pain −14.5 mm and lesion −175.7 mm² at 6 months only. Large trial: cartilage difference 41 mm³ (P = .50), pain difference +5.2 mm favouring placebo numerically, lesion difference −27 mm² (P = .60), adverse events 96% versus 83%. Where they overlap in time (6–12 months), the large trial's null is the estimate to use.
cards.watchOut: Bone-marrow lesions remain a marker of painful, progressing osteoarthritis — what failed is this treatment for them, not their prognostic meaning. A single negative drug result also does not close the lesion-targeted idea for other agents; it closes it for zoledronic acid at this dose and schedule.
cards.source: Synthesis of Laslett LL et al. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2012 (PMID: 22355040); Cai G et al. JAMA. 2020 (PMID: 32315057).

shelves.title: Calcium and vitamin D in female Navy recruits: 2,000 mg calcium with 800 IU vitamin D cut stress fractures from 6.6% to 5.3% over eight weeks of basic training
shelves.question: In military recruits, do calcium and vitamin D supplementation prevent stress fractures?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Calcium/*administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fractures, Stress/*prevention & control · Humans · *Military Personnel · Placebos · United States · Vitamin D/*administration & dosage
shelves.balance: A single large trial answers this question, and it has never been repeated at scale. Lappe 2008 (PMID: 18433305) randomised 5,201 female US Navy recruits, double-blind, to 2,000 mg calcium plus 800 IU vitamin D daily or placebo through eight weeks of basic training — a population with a high, uniform mechanical load and a baseline stress-fracture incidence of about 6–7%. Supplementation reduced stress fractures by a fifth relative: 5.3% versus 6.6% on intention-to-treat (P = 0.0026), an absolute reduction of 1.3 percentage points — roughly one fracture prevented for every 77 recruits supplemented — and 6.8% versus 8.6% in the per-protocol analysis of the 3,700 who completed. The authors estimate that supplementing an entire intake cohort of 14,416 women would have prevented about 187 fractures. What the trial cannot say: whether the effect holds in men (none enrolled), in less extreme training loads, at lower doses, or whether calcium, vitamin D, or only the combination does the work. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) (Tier C: one trial, one sex, one training system).

cards.headline: Lappe 2008: calcium 2,000 mg + vitamin D 800 IU daily cut stress fractures in 5,201 female Navy recruits from 6.6% to 5.3% over 8 weeks (P = 0.0026)
cards.summary: Lappe 2008: calcium 2,000 mg + vitamin D 800 IU daily cut stress fractures in 5,201 female Navy recruits from 6.6% to 5.3% over 8 weeks (P = 0.0026)
cards.people: 5,201 female US Navy recruit volunteers at Great Lakes, randomised double-blind to calcium 2,000 mg plus vitamin D3 800 IU daily or placebo for the eight weeks of basic training. Stress fractures were ascertained when recruits presented to clinic with symptoms and were confirmed by radiography or technetium scan; 309 recruits in total were diagnosed (overall incidence 5.9% per eight weeks).
cards.result: Intention-to-treat: stress-fracture incidence 5.3% on supplementation versus 6.6% on placebo (P = 0.0026) — a 20% relative reduction (labelled relative) and 1.3 percentage points absolute. Per-protocol (3,700 completers): 6.8% versus 8.6% (P = 0.02), a 21% relative reduction. Generalised to the 14,416 women who entered training at the base over the recruitment period, the authors estimate about 187 fractures would have been prevented.
cards.watchOut: One trial, in young women only, during eight weeks of exceptionally uniform, high-volume training, with a calcium dose (2,000 mg/day) at the tolerable upper intake level. The record carries no registry identifier. It does not establish benefit for male recruits, athletes in ordinary training, or lower doses — and it cannot separate calcium's contribution from vitamin D's.
cards.source: Lappe J et al.. Calcium and vitamin d supplementation decreases incidence of stress fractures in female navy recruits. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2008. PMID: 18433305. shelves.title: Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound for fresh fractures: the large sham-controlled TRUST trial and the low-bias trial set both say no
shelves.question: In fresh fractures, does low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) speed healing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Fracture Fixation, Intramedullary/methods · Humans · Male · Single-Blind Method · Tibial Fractures/surgery, *therapy · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonic Therapy/*methods · Ultrasonic Waves
shelves.balance: This is a literature whose answer flips with trial quality, and the high-quality end is unambiguous. TRUST randomised 501 patients with operatively fixed tibial fractures to daily self-administered LIPUS or an identical sham device for a year: functional recovery (SF-36 physical component) differed by 0.55 points (95% CI −0.75 to 1.84) against a minimally important difference of 3–5, and time to radiographic healing did not differ (hazard ratio 1.07, 0.86 to 1.34) (Busse 2016, PMID: 27797787). The accompanying systematic review of 26 randomised trials found the same split personality — trials at high risk of bias suggested benefit, trials at low risk of bias showed none, for return to work, reoperation, weight bearing, pain and radiographic healing alike (interaction P < 0.001) (Schandelmaier 2017, PMID: 28348110). Earlier positive small trials are the high-bias tail of that distribution. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): for fresh fractures, the trustworthy trials show LIPUS neither heals bone faster nor returns function sooner. Established nonunion, a different question, is not what these trials studied.

cards.headline: TRUST 2016: in 501 tibial fractures, daily LIPUS did not improve function (difference 0.55 points, MID 3–5) or radiographic healing (HR 1.07) versus a sham device
cards.summary: TRUST 2016: in 501 tibial fractures, daily LIPUS did not improve function (difference 0.55 points, MID 3–5) or radiographic healing (HR 1.07) versus a sham device
cards.people: 501 skeletally mature patients with open or closed tibial fractures treated with intramedullary nailing at 43 North American academic trauma centres, randomised centrally to self-administered daily LIPUS (n = 250) or sham device (n = 251) until radiographic healing or one year. Primary registry outcome: time to radiographic healing; functional outcome: SF-36 physical component summary (PCS) scores.
cards.result: No difference in SF-36 PCS between groups (mean difference 0.55, 95% CI −0.75 to 1.84; P = 0.41) — the confidence interval excludes the 3–5-point minimally important difference — and no difference in time to radiographic healing (hazard ratio 1.07, 0.86 to 1.34; P = 0.55), return to work, weight bearing or other functional measures. Safety outcomes did not differ. Compliance was moderate: 73% of patients delivered at least half of the recommended treatments.
cards.watchOut: Operatively fixed tibial fractures only, and compliance was imperfect — a defender can argue the device was under-used. But the sham-controlled design is exactly the test the earlier uncontrolled literature never faced, and no effect appeared in any functional or radiographic measure.

cards.headline: Schandelmaier 2017: across 26 trials, LIPUS benefited patients only in the trials at high risk of bias — the trustworthy trials showed no effect on any patient-important outcome
cards.summary: Schandelmaier 2017: across 26 trials, LIPUS benefited patients only in the trials at high risk of bias — the trustworthy trials showed no effect on any patient-important outcome
cards.people: 26 randomised controlled trials of LIPUS versus sham or no device in patients with any fracture or osteotomy (median sample size 30; range 8–501), from Medline, Embase, CINAHL, CENTRAL and trial registries to November 2016, with GRADE certainty ratings and a parallel BMJ Rapid Recommendation panel.
cards.result: In the low-risk-of-bias trials (tibia and clavicle fractures), LIPUS did not reduce time to return to work (2.7% later, 95% CI 7.7% earlier to 14.3% later; moderate certainty) or subsequent operations (risk ratio 0.80, 0.55 to 1.16), and did not reduce days to weight bearing (4.8% later; high certainty), pain at 4–6 weeks (mean difference 0.93 points lower on a 0–100 scale; high certainty) or days to radiographic healing (1.7% earlier; moderate certainty). For pain, weight bearing and healing, high-bias trials suggested benefit while low-bias trials showed none (interaction P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Most included trials are tiny (median 30 patients), which is how a literature can look positive for decades: small studies of a device with a radiographic endpoint. The review's conclusion is about fresh fracture and osteotomy healing — it does not test LIPUS as salvage therapy for established nonunion.
