cards.search: schandelmaier 2017: across 26 trials, lipus benefited patients only in the trials at high risk of bias — the trustworthy trials showed no effect on any patient-important outcome schandelmaier 2017: across 26 trials, lipus benefited patients only in the trials at high risk of bias — the trustworthy trials showed no effect on any patient-important outcome in fresh fractures, does low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (lipus) speed healing? systematic review and meta-analysis, 26 rcts (schandelmaier 2017) 26 randomised controlled trials of lipus versus sham or no device in patients with any fracture or osteotomy (median sample size 30; range 8–501), from medline, embase, cinahl, central and trial registries to november 2016, with grade certainty ratings and a parallel bmj rapid recommendation panel. in the low-risk-of-bias trials (tibia and clavicle fractures), lipus did not reduce time to return to work (2.7% later, 95% ci 7.7% earlier to 14.3% later; moderate certainty) or subsequent operations (risk ratio 0.80, 0.55 to 1.16), and did not reduce days to weight bearing (4.8% later; high certainty), pain at 4–6 weeks (mean difference 0.93 points lower on a 0–100 scale; high certainty) or days to radiographic healing (1.7% earlier; moderate certainty). for pain, weight bearing and healing, high-bias trials suggested benefit while low-bias trials showed none (interaction p < 0.001). most included trials are tiny (median 30 patients), which is how a literature can look positive for decades: small studies of a device with a radiographic endpoint. the review's conclusion is about fresh fracture and osteotomy healing — it does not test lipus as salvage therapy for established nonunion. schandelmaier s et al.. low intensity pulsed ultrasound for bone healing: systematic review of randomized controlled trials. bmj. 2017. pmid: 28348110. registry id: none in the record. mesh: *fracture healing · fractures, bone/*therapy · humans · randomized controlled trials as topic · *ultrasonic therapy

cards.headline: Synthesis: when the trials are blinded and adequately sized, LIPUS does nothing measurable for fresh fracture healing
cards.summary: Synthesis: when the trials are blinded and adequately sized, LIPUS does nothing measurable for fresh fracture healing
cards.people: One 501-patient sham-controlled trial in nailed tibial fractures and a 26-trial systematic review spanning all fracture types and osteotomy.
cards.result: Function: +0.55 SF-36 points (−0.75 to 1.84) — null against a 3–5-point MID. Radiographic healing: HR 1.07 (0.86–1.34). Reoperation: RR 0.80 (0.55–1.16). Every patient-important outcome in low-bias trials is compatible with no effect, and the apparent benefits in the older literature track bias, not dose or fracture type.
cards.watchOut: Do not extend this verdict to established nonunion or to patients who cannot have surgery — those uses were not randomised in the carded evidence and remain genuinely untested rather than disproven. The claim closed here is narrower: routine LIPUS to speed fresh-fracture healing.
cards.source: Synthesis of Busse JW et al. BMJ. 2016 (PMID: 27797787); Schandelmaier S et al. BMJ. 2017 (PMID: 28348110).

shelves.title: Triple therapy in rheumatoid arthritis: three cheap oral drugs matched etanercept plus methotrexate on disease activity — in early disease and after methotrexate failure alike
shelves.question: In adults with rheumatoid arthritis responding inadequately to methotrexate, does triple therapy (methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine) match a tumour-necrosis-factor inhibitor plus methotrexate?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antirheumatic Agents/adverse effects, *therapeutic use · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/*drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Etanercept · Female · Humans · Hydroxychloroquine/adverse effects, *therapeutic use · Immunoglobulin G/adverse effects, *therapeutic use · Male · Methotrexate/adverse effects, *therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Receptors, Tumor Necrosis Factor/*therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Sulfasalazine/adverse effects, *therapeutic use · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: Two blinded randomised trials, in the two populations where the question arises, give the same answer on disease activity. After methotrexate failure, RACAT randomised 353 patients to triple therapy (methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine) or etanercept + methotrexate, with a blinded switch to the other strategy at 24 weeks for non-responders: DAS28 improvement at 48 weeks was −2.1 versus −2.3 (P = 0.26), formally noninferior (upper confidence limit 0.41 against a 0.6 margin; P = 0.002), with no differences in radiographic progression, pain, quality of life or major adverse events, and 27% of each group needing the switch (O'Dell 2013, PMID: 23755969). In early aggressive disease, TEAR's factorial design compared immediate triple therapy, immediate etanercept + methotrexate, and step-up from methotrexate to either: over weeks 48–102 there was no DAS28 difference between the oral triple and the biologic combination, whichever way patients reached them — though etanercept + methotrexate did win the secondary radiographic comparison at 102 weeks (Moreland 2012, PMID: 22508468). PROPOSED LIKELY (no difference in disease activity): an oral regimen costing a small fraction of a biologic performs equivalently on the outcome patients feel, with radiographic protection the one place the biologic kept an edge in early disease.

cards.headline: RACAT 2013: after methotrexate failure, triple therapy was noninferior to etanercept + methotrexate at 48 weeks (DAS28 −2.1 vs −2.3), with identical switch rates
cards.summary: RACAT 2013: after methotrexate failure, triple therapy was noninferior to etanercept + methotrexate at 48 weeks (DAS28 −2.1 vs −2.3), with identical switch rates
cards.people: 353 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate, randomised double-blind (VA Cooperative Studies Program) to triple therapy — methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine — or etanercept plus methotrexate for 48 weeks. Patients not improving by a prespecified threshold at 24 weeks were switched, still blinded, to the other therapy. Primary outcome: change in DAS28 at week 48.
cards.result: Both groups improved significantly in the first 24 weeks; 27% of each group required the blinded switch, and switchers improved on the second therapy without a between-group difference (P = 0.08). DAS28 change at 48 weeks: −2.1 with triple therapy versus −2.3 with etanercept + methotrexate (P = 0.26); the 95% upper confidence limit for the difference (0.41) sat below the 0.6 noninferiority margin (P = 0.002 for noninferiority). No significant differences in radiographic progression, pain, health-related quality of life, or major adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority on a 0.6 DAS28 margin is a chosen tolerance, not identity — the trial licenses 'not unacceptably worse', and its population (largely male US veterans) is narrower than the clinic population. A quarter of each arm failed its assigned strategy within six months; the trial compares strategies with a rescue switch, not two regimens taken in isolation.
cards.source: O'Dell JR et al.. Therapies for active rheumatoid arthritis after methotrexate failure. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23755969. cards.headline: TEAR 2012: in early aggressive RA, oral triple therapy and etanercept + methotrexate produced indistinguishable disease activity over two years — immediate combination beat step-up early, whichever combination was used
cards.summary: TEAR 2012: in early aggressive RA, oral triple therapy and etanercept + methotrexate produced indistinguishable disease activity over two years — immediate combination beat step-up early, whichever combination was used
cards.people: Patients with early aggressive rheumatoid arthritis randomised in a 2×2 factorial, double-blind design to immediate methotrexate + etanercept, immediate oral triple therapy (methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine), or step-up from methotrexate monotherapy to one of the two combinations at week 24 if DAS28-ESR remained ≥3.2, with matching placebos throughout. Primary outcome: DAS28-ESR over weeks 48–102. The record's abstract does not state the total enrolment.
cards.result: At week 24, immediate-combination groups had lower DAS28-ESR than step-up groups (3.6 versus 4.2; P < 0.0001), with no difference between the two combinations. Over weeks 48–102, step-up patients caught up completely, and there was no significant DAS28-ESR difference between oral triple therapy and methotrexate + etanercept in any comparison. One secondary outcome did separate: radiographic change at week 102 favoured methotrexate + etanercept over triple therapy (statistically significant).
cards.watchOut: The radiographic edge for the biologic is real and should not be averaged away: TEAR says the two strategies control symptoms and activity equally, not that they protect joints identically over two years. Early aggressive disease is also not the RACAT population — the two trials agree on activity, in different patients.

cards.headline: Synthesis: on disease activity, three generic oral drugs equal a TNF inhibitor plus methotrexate — tested after methotrexate failure and in early aggressive disease
cards.summary: Synthesis: on disease activity, three generic oral drugs equal a TNF inhibitor plus methotrexate — tested after methotrexate failure and in early aggressive disease
cards.people: Two double-blind randomised strategy trials: RACAT (n = 353, active RA despite methotrexate, 48 weeks, blinded switch design) and TEAR (early aggressive RA, 2×2 factorial, 102 weeks).
cards.result: DAS28 change: −2.1 (triple) versus −2.3 (etanercept + MTX) in RACAT, noninferiority formally met; no DAS28 difference over weeks 48–102 in TEAR. Switch/rescue rates identical (27% each arm, RACAT). Radiographic progression: no difference in RACAT; a statistically significant advantage to etanercept + MTX at 102 weeks in TEAR. Major adverse events: no significant differences in either trial.
cards.watchOut: Both trials used etanercept as the biologic comparator; equivalence to other TNF inhibitors or other biologic classes is an extrapolation. Cost and access arguments built on this shelf are legitimate — but they depend on the radiographic caveat staying attached.
cards.source: Synthesis of O'Dell JR et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2013 (PMID: 23755969); Moreland LW et al. Arthritis and Rheumatism. 2012 (PMID: 22508468).

shelves.title: Lumbar fusion versus cognitive intervention and exercise for chronic low back pain: three randomised trials and their pooled 11-year follow-up show no advantage for surgery
shelves.question: In chronic degenerative low back pain, does lumbar fusion beat structured exercise and cognitive rehabilitation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Chronic Disease · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods* · Exercise Therapy/methods* · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Intervertebral Disc Displacement/complications/surgery/therapy* · Low Back Pain/etiology/surgery/therapy* · Lumbar Vertebrae/surgery* · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Single-Blind Method · Spinal Fusion/methods* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference): Every randomised comparison of lumbar fusion with a structured cognitive-and-exercise programme for chronic degenerative low back pain has found the same thing — both groups improve, and surgery does not beat rehabilitation. In the Norwegian trial, Oswestry disability fell from 41 to 26 after fusion and from 42 to 30 after cognitive intervention and exercises at one year (between-group difference 2.3 points, 95% CI −6.7 to 11.4; P = 0.33), with an 18% early complication rate in the surgical group (Brox JI et al., PMID: 12973134). The UK MRC trial (349 patients) found a marginal 2-year Oswestry difference of −4.1 points (95% CI −8.1 to −0.1; P = 0.045) favouring surgery — a difference its own authors called marginal, just reaching the predefined minimal clinical difference, with no difference in walking capacity or any other outcome (Fairbank J et al., PMID: 15911537). At four years in the merged Norwegian trials, 24% of the rehabilitation group had crossed over to surgery and 23% of the fusion group had undergone re-operation, with no difference in disability or return to work (Brox JI et al., PMID: 19635718). The pooled long-term follow-up of all three trials (473 patients; mean 11.4 years) found an adjusted Oswestry difference of −0.7 points (95% CI −5.5 to 4.2) (Mannion AF et al., PMID: 24200413). Two boundaries: the Swedish Lumbar Spine Study (Fritzell P et al., PMID: 11725230) compared fusion with unstructured usual care rather than a structured programme and is cross-referenced here, not carded; and fusion added to decompression for spinal stenosis is a different question, not answered by this shelf.

cards.headline: Brox 2003: fusion and cognitive intervention with exercises improved disability equally at 1 year (Oswestry 41→26 vs 42→30; difference 2.3, P = 0.33) — with an 18% early complication rate after surgery
cards.summary: Brox 2003: fusion and cognitive intervention with exercises improved disability equally at 1 year (Oswestry 41→26 vs 42→30; difference 2.3, P = 0.33) — with an 18% early complication rate after surgery
cards.people: 64 patients aged 25–60 with low back pain lasting more than a year and radiographic disc degeneration at L4–L5 and/or L5–S1, randomised to instrumented lumbar fusion with posterior transpedicular screws plus postoperative physiotherapy, or to cognitive intervention (a lecture establishing that ordinary physical activity would not harm the disc, with advice to use and bend the back) reinforced by three daily exercise sessions for 3 weeks. The main outcome was the Oswestry Disability Index; 97% were examined at 1 year.
cards.result: The Oswestry index fell from 41 to 26 after surgery and from 42 to 30 after cognitive intervention and exercises (mean difference 2.3 points, 95% CI −6.7 to 11.4; P = 0.33). Improvements in back pain, analgesic use, emotional distress, life satisfaction and return to work did not differ; an independent observer rated treatment success in 70% after surgery and 76% after non-operative care. Fear-avoidance beliefs and fingertip-to-floor distance improved more without surgery; lower-limb pain improved more with surgery. The early complication rate in the surgical group was 18%.
cards.watchOut: A single-blind trial of 64 patients: the confidence interval (−6.7 to 11.4) cannot exclude a modest benefit for either approach, and the comparator was a specific intensive 3-week programme — not physiotherapy as usually delivered.

cards.headline: Fairbank 2005 (MRC spine stabilisation trial): a marginal Oswestry difference favouring surgery (−4.1 points, P = 0.045) that its authors judged no clear evidence of benefit — and no difference in walking
cards.summary: Fairbank 2005 (MRC spine stabilisation trial): a marginal Oswestry difference favouring surgery (−4.1 points, P = 0.045) that its authors judged no clear evidence of benefit — and no difference in walking
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial (MRC spine stabilisation trial, Fairbank 2005)
cards.people: 349 patients aged 18–55 with chronic low back pain of at least one year who were considered candidates for spinal fusion, at 15 UK centres; 176 were assigned to lumbar fusion surgery and 173 to an intensive rehabilitation programme based on cognitive behavioural principles. The primary outcomes were the Oswestry disability index and the shuttle walking test at two years; 284 patients (81%) provided follow-up data.
cards.result: Oswestry scores improved in both groups (surgery 46.5 → 34.0; rehabilitation 44.8 → 36.1). The estimated between-group difference was −4.1 points (95% CI −8.1 to −0.1; P = 0.045) in favour of surgery, just reaching the predefined minimal clinical difference; there were no significant differences in the shuttle walking test or any other outcome measure. The authors conclude that no clear evidence emerged that primary fusion is more beneficial than intensive rehabilitation, and that the risk and additional cost of surgery count against it.
cards.watchOut: This is the one nominally positive result in the shelf, and it is fragile: one of two primary outcomes, a confidence interval ending at −0.1, and 19% loss to follow-up. It should not be quoted as 'fusion works' without its authors' own conclusion attached.

cards.headline: Brox 2010 (4-year follow-up of the Norwegian trials): no long-term difference — and by 4 years 24% of the rehabilitation group had undergone surgery while 23% of the fusion group had been re-operated
cards.summary: Brox 2010 (4-year follow-up of the Norwegian trials): no long-term difference — and by 4 years 24% of the rehabilitation group had undergone surgery while 23% of the fusion group had been re-operated
cards.type: Four-year follow-up report of two merged randomised trials (Brox 2010) — same trial programme as card 1, flagged
cards.people: 124 patients from two merged Norwegian randomised trials comparing instrumented transpedicular fusion with cognitive intervention and exercises in chronic low back pain with disc degeneration, with or without previous surgery for disc herniation, followed for four years. This report is the long-term follow-up of the trial programme that includes Brox 2003 (card 1), not an independent trial.
cards.result: The intention-to-treat treatment effect on the Oswestry index was 1.1 points (95% CI −5.9 to 8.2), and −1.6 (−8.9 to 5.6) in the as-treated analysis; there was no difference in return to work. Crossover ran in both directions: 14 patients (24%) assigned to cognitive intervention and exercises had also undergone surgery by four years, and 15 (23%) assigned to fusion had undergone re-operation.
cards.watchOut: With a quarter of each group receiving the other treatment (or further surgery), the intention-to-treat comparison increasingly tests 'which strategy first' rather than the procedures themselves — but that is precisely the decision patients face, and on that question the two strategies remained equal.

cards.headline: Mannion 2013 (pooled follow-up of all three trials, mean 11.4 years): adjusted Oswestry difference −0.7 points (95% CI −5.5 to 4.2) — no difference a decade out
cards.summary: Mannion 2013 (pooled follow-up of all three trials, mean 11.4 years): adjusted Oswestry difference −0.7 points (95% CI −5.5 to 4.2) — no difference a decade out
cards.type: Pooled long-term follow-up of three randomised trials (Mannion 2013) — same trial populations as cards 1–3, flagged
cards.people: 473 patients with at least a year of chronic low back pain, all considered candidates for spinal fusion, enrolled in the three Norwegian and UK randomised trials of fusion versus multidisciplinary cognitive-behavioural and exercise rehabilitation; 261 (55%) completed long-term follow-up at a mean of 11.4 years (range 8–15). This is a pooled re-follow-up of the same trial populations as cards 1–3, not a new randomisation.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis, adjusted for baseline Oswestry score, previous surgery, duration of pain, sex, age and smoking, the mean treatment effect of fusion was −0.7 points on the 0–100 Oswestry scale (95% CI −5.5 to 4.2); the as-treated effect was −0.8 (−5.9 to 4.3). Secondary outcomes — pain intensity and frequency, medication use, work status, quality of life, satisfaction with care and global outcome — showed no relevant group differences.
cards.watchOut: Only 55% of the original patients completed follow-up, so a late divergence in either direction could hide in the missing data; and because it re-reports the same three trials, this card adds duration of observation, not independent confirmation.

cards.headline: Synthesis: across three trials and a decade of follow-up, fusion for degenerative low back pain never beat a structured cognitive-and-exercise programme
cards.summary: Synthesis: across three trials and a decade of follow-up, fusion for degenerative low back pain never beat a structured cognitive-and-exercise programme
cards.people: Three randomised trials (64 and 349 patients, plus the second Norwegian trial within the merged 124) with follow-up reports at 4 years and a pooled mean of 11.4 years.
cards.result: Oswestry between-group differences: 2.3 points (P = 0.33) at 1 year; −4.1 (P = 0.045, judged marginal by its own authors) at 2 years; 1.1 at 4 years; −0.7 at about 11 years — every interval includes or grazes no effect, and no secondary outcome (pain, work, quality of life) ever separated the groups. Surgery carried an 18% early complication rate in the Norwegian trial and a 23% re-operation rate by 4 years.
cards.watchOut: All comparators were intensive, well-delivered rehabilitation programmes; the trials do not show that fusion equals doing nothing, and they do not cover fusion for instability, deformity, fracture or spinal stenosis — different questions with different evidence. Patients whose problem is a clear surgical lesion were not the population studied.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brox JI et al. Spine. 2003 (PMID: 12973134); Fairbank J et al. BMJ. 2005 (PMID: 15911537); Brox JI et al. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2010 (PMID: 19635718); Mannion AF et al. The Spine Journal. 2013 (PMID: 24200413).

shelves.title: IL-1 blockade for difficult gout flares: canakinumab beat an injected steroid on pain and cut new-flare risk by more than half; anakinra matched usual care and triamcinolone in two trials — at the price of more infections
shelves.question: In gout flares in patients who cannot take NSAIDs or colchicine, do IL-1 blockers (anakinra, canakinumab) relieve the flare?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use* · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use* · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Arthritis, Gouty/drug therapy* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gout Suppressants/therapeutic use* · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In patients whose flares cannot be treated with NSAIDs or colchicine, IL-1 blockade works about as well as — and for canakinumab somewhat better than — the steroid injection it replaces. In the two β-RELIEVED trials (456 patients with frequent flares in whom NSAIDs and/or colchicine were contraindicated, not tolerated or unresponsive), a single 150 mg dose of canakinumab gave lower pain at 72 hours than 40 mg intramuscular triamcinolone (25.0 vs 35.7 mm on a 100-mm scale; difference −10.7 mm, 95% CI −15.4 to −6.0) and reduced the risk of a new flare by 62% relative over the core studies (hazard ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.57) and by 56% relative over the full 24 weeks (HR 0.44, 0.32 to 0.60) — but with more adverse events (66.2% vs 52.8%), more serious adverse events (8.0% vs 3.5%), and more infections, neutropenia and thrombocytopenia (Schlesinger N et al., PMID: 22586173). Anakinra was non-inferior to a clinician's choice of colchicine, naproxen or prednisone in a small double-blind trial of 88 patients with crystal-proven flares (Janssen CA et al., PMID: 30602035), and matched triamcinolone for pain relief in a 165-patient phase II trial restricted to patients for whom NSAIDs and colchicine were unsuitable (pain reduction −41.2 vs −39.4 points; P = 0.688) (Saag KG et al., PMID: 33605029). The earlier phase II canakinumab dose-ranging study (So A et al., PMID: 20533546) is carded at shelf #390 and is cross-referenced here, not re-carded. No placebo-controlled trial exists in this population — every comparison is against an active steroid — and canakinumab's infection signal is a large part of why these drugs sit behind steroids in practice despite the trial results.

cards.headline: β-RELIEVED 2012: canakinumab beat triamcinolone on 72-hour pain (25.0 vs 35.7 mm) and cut new-flare risk by 62% relative — with serious adverse events in 8.0% vs 3.5%
cards.summary: β-RELIEVED 2012: canakinumab beat triamcinolone on 72-hour pain (25.0 vs 35.7 mm) and cut new-flare risk by 62% relative — with serious adverse events in 8.0% vs 3.5%
cards.type: Two randomised double-blind active-controlled trials with extensions (β-RELIEVED and β-RELIEVED-II, Schlesinger 2012)
cards.people: 456 patients with frequently flaring gouty arthritis for whom NSAIDs and/or colchicine were contraindicated, not tolerated or unresponsive (82.6% had comorbidities), in two 12-week randomised, multicentre, double-blind, active-controlled core trials with double-blind 12-week extensions. A single dose of canakinumab 150 mg subcutaneously (n = 230) or triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg intramuscularly (n = 226) was given at baseline and again upon a new flare; co-primary endpoints were pain intensity at 72 hours and time to first new flare.
cards.result: Mean 72-hour pain was 25.0 mm on canakinumab versus 35.7 mm on triamcinolone (difference −10.7 mm, 95% CI −15.4 to −6.0; P < 0.0001), with significantly less physician-assessed tenderness and swelling. Canakinumab delayed the first new flare and reduced flare risk by 62% relative in the core studies (HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.57) and by 56% relative over the entire 24-week period (HR 0.44, 0.32 to 0.60). Over 24 weeks, adverse events were reported in 66.2% (canakinumab) vs 52.8% (triamcinolone) and serious adverse events in 8.0% vs 3.5%; infections, low neutrophil count and low platelet count were more frequent with canakinumab.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a single moderate steroid injection, not placebo and not an oral steroid course; part of the flare-prevention advantage reflects canakinumab's long action against a one-off injection. The safety gradient — roughly double the serious adverse events — is the clinically decisive number for most patients.
cards.source: Schlesinger N et al. Canakinumab for acute gouty arthritis in patients with limited treatment options: results from two randomised, multicentre, active-controlled, double-blind trials and their initial extensions. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2012. PMID: 22586173. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Janssen 2019: anakinra non-inferior to treatment as usual (colchicine, naproxen or prednisone) for gout-flare pain in a small double-blind trial
cards.summary: Janssen 2019: anakinra non-inferior to treatment as usual (colchicine, naproxen or prednisone) for gout-flare pain in a small double-blind trial
cards.people: 88 patients with a crystal-proven acute gout flare, randomised (1:1) to anakinra or to treatment as usual (free choice of colchicine, naproxen or prednisone); 43 received anakinra and 45 usual care. The primary endpoint was the change in pain between baseline and the averaged pain score on days 2–4 on a five-point scale, with a non-inferiority limit of 0.4 points in favour of usual care.
cards.result: Anakinra was non-inferior to treatment as usual in both the per-protocol (mean difference −0.13, 95% CI −0.44 to 0.18) and intention-to-treat (−0.18, −0.44 to 0.08) populations. Secondary outcomes — pain, swelling, tenderness and treatment response after 5 days — improved similarly and significantly in both groups, and no unexpected or uncommon serious adverse events were observed in either arm.
cards.watchOut: Eighty-eight patients cannot exclude meaningful differences, and the comparator was a clinician-chosen menu of three standard drugs: the trial shows anakinra is a credible substitute when those drugs cannot be used, not that it beats any one of them. The record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Janssen CA et al. Anakinra for the treatment of acute gout flares: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, active-comparator, non-inferiority trial. Rheumatology. 2019. cards.headline: Saag 2021: in patients for whom NSAIDs and colchicine were unsuitable, anakinra relieved flare pain as much as triamcinolone (−41.2 vs −39.4 points; P = 0.688) — not superior, but comparable
cards.summary: Saag 2021: in patients for whom NSAIDs and colchicine were unsuitable, anakinra relieved flare pain as much as triamcinolone (−41.2 vs −39.4 points; P = 0.688) — not superior, but comparable
cards.people: 165 patients for whom NSAIDs and colchicine were not suitable treatments, randomised in a multicentre double-blind study to anakinra 100 or 200 mg/day for 5 days (n = 110) or a single triamcinolone 40 mg injection (n = 55), with follow-up for up to 2 years; 301 flares were treated in total (214 with anakinra, 87 with triamcinolone). Median age was 55 years, 87% were men, mean disease duration 8.7 years, and patients reported a mean of 4.5 flares in the prior year. The primary endpoint was change in patient-assessed pain in the most affected joint from baseline to 24–72 hours.
cards.result: For the first flare, mean pain decline was −41.2 points (0–100 scale) on anakinra (both doses combined) and −39.4 on triamcinolone (P = 0.688): the designed superiority comparison was not met, but both treatments gave clinically meaningful relief, and anakinra performed better on most secondary endpoints. There were no unexpected safety findings, and antidrug antibodies were not associated with adverse events or altered pain reduction.
cards.watchOut: A phase II trial that missed its superiority endpoint: 'comparable to a steroid injection' is the supported claim, in a population with no NSAID or colchicine option. The two anakinra doses were combined for the headline comparison.
cards.source: Saag KG et al. A Randomized, Phase II Study Evaluating the Efficacy and Safety of Anakinra in the Treatment of Gout Flares. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2021. PMID: 33605029. Registry ID: NCT03002974 (verified against the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: IL-1 blockers relieve flares in patients with no NSAID/colchicine option — canakinumab somewhat better than a steroid injection, anakinra about equal — with a real infection cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: IL-1 blockers relieve flares in patients with no NSAID/colchicine option — canakinumab somewhat better than a steroid injection, anakinra about equal — with a real infection cost
cards.people: Three randomised programmes in NSAID/colchicine-limited populations: canakinumab vs triamcinolone (456 patients), anakinra vs treatment as usual (88), and anakinra vs triamcinolone (165).
cards.result: Pain: canakinumab was 10.7 mm better than triamcinolone at 72 hours; anakinra was non-inferior to usual care and statistically indistinguishable from triamcinolone (−41.2 vs −39.4 points). Flares: canakinumab reduced new-flare risk by 56–62% relative versus a single steroid injection. Harms: serious adverse events 8.0% vs 3.5% and more infections with canakinumab; no unexpected safety signals for anakinra in two small trials.
cards.watchOut: No trial in this population used placebo or an oral steroid comparator, none was powered for rare harms, and the patients studied — frequent flares, heavy comorbidity, standard drugs exhausted — are not ordinary gout patients. Cost and infection risk, not efficacy, are what keep these agents in reserve.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schlesinger N et al. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2012 (PMID: 22586173); Janssen CA et al. Rheumatology. 2019 (PMID: 30602035); Saag KG et al. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2021 (PMID: 33605029).

shelves.title: Cherries and gout: eating cherries was associated with 35% fewer attacks in a case-crossover study — but the only randomised trial found cherry concentrate did not lower urate at all
shelves.question: In gout, do cherries or cherry concentrate prevent flares?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alcohol Drinking/epidemiology · Comorbidity · Cross-Over Studies · Eating* · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gout/drug therapy/epidemiology*/prevention & control* · Gout Suppressants/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Obesity/epidemiology · Prospective Studies · Prunus* · Recurrence · Risk Factors · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The flare claim rests on a single observational study — a well-designed one, but one. In a case-crossover study of 633 gout patients followed online for a year, with each patient serving as their own control, cherry intake in the 2 days before a hazard period was associated with a 35% lower risk of a gout attack than no intake (odds ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.85 — a relative figure); cherry extract showed a similar association (OR 0.55, 0.30 to 0.98), and cherry intake combined with allopurinol use was associated with an attack risk 75% lower than periods with neither exposure (OR 0.25, 0.15 to 0.42) (Zhang Y et al., PMID: 23023818). The proposed mechanism — urate lowering — failed its randomised test: in 50 gout patients given placebo or one of four doses of tart cherry concentrate for 28 days, the concentrate had no effect on serum urate, urinary urate excretion or flare frequency (P = 0.76) (Stamp LK et al., PMID: 31891407). A systematic review found six small studies pointing in the same direction as Zhang but too heterogeneous to pool (Chen PE et al., PMID: 31885677). So: a consistent association with fewer attacks, no demonstrated urate mechanism, and no randomised flare trial — a large tart-cherry flare trial exists only as a registered protocol. Tier C: observational-dependent.

cards.headline: Zhang 2012: cherry intake in the previous 2 days was associated with a 35% lower risk of a gout attack (OR 0.65) in a 633-patient case-crossover study
cards.summary: Zhang 2012: cherry intake in the previous 2 days was associated with a 35% lower risk of a gout attack (OR 0.65) in a 633-patient case-crossover study
cards.people: 633 individuals with gout, recruited and followed online for one year. For each gout attack, participants reported exposures — including daily cherry and cherry-extract intake — during the 2-day period before the attack, and the same information was collected for 2-day control periods; associations were estimated with conditional logistic regression, so each patient serves as their own control.
cards.result: Cherry intake over a 2-day period was associated with a 35% lower risk of gout attacks compared with no intake (multivariate OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.85 — a relative measure). Cherry extract intake showed a similar inverse association (OR 0.55, 0.30 to 0.98). The association persisted across subgroups stratified by sex, obesity status, purine intake, alcohol use, diuretic use and antigout medication use. Cherry intake combined with allopurinol use was associated with a 75% lower attack risk than periods with neither exposure (OR 0.25, 0.15 to 0.42).
cards.watchOut: The case-crossover design removes fixed between-person confounding, but not recall bias — patients reported intake around attacks they knew had occurred — or time-varying confounders. An odds ratio from self-reported diet is hypothesis-raising, not proof, and no standardised cherry dose was tested.
cards.source: Zhang Y et al. Cherry consumption and decreased risk of recurrent gout attacks. Arthritis & Rheumatism. 2012. PMID: 23023818. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stamp 2020: randomised dose trial — tart cherry concentrate did not lower serum urate, increase urate excretion, or reduce flares over 28 days (P = 0.76)
cards.summary: Stamp 2020: randomised dose trial — tart cherry concentrate did not lower serum urate, increase urate excretion, or reduce flares over 28 days (P = 0.76)
cards.people: 50 people with gout and serum urate above 0.36 mmol/L (≈6.0 mg/dL) — half taking allopurinol, half on no urate-lowering therapy — randomised to tart cherry juice concentrate (placebo, 7.5, 15, 22.5 or 30 mL twice daily) for 28 days, with blood sampling at baseline, at 1, 3 and 5 hours after dosing, and on days 1, 3, 7, 14, 21 and 28.
cards.result: Cherry concentrate dose had no significant effect on the reduction in serum urate area under the curve, on urine urate excretion, on the change in urinary anthocyanin between day 0 and day 28, or on the frequency of gout flares over the 28-day study period (P = 0.76). There were 24 reported adverse events, of which one (hyperglycaemia) was considered possibly related to the concentrate. Allopurinol use did not modify the effect. The authors conclude that if cherry concentrate affects flares over a longer period, it is not likely to be mediated by a reduction in serum urate.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-eight days and 50 patients cannot test flare prevention — flares were a secondary count in a urate-mechanism trial. The record describes the treatment as tart cherry juice concentrate by dose only, naming no brand or manufacturer: the record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Stamp LK et al. Lack of effect of tart cherry concentrate dose on serum urate in people with gout. Rheumatology. 2020. PMID: 31891407. cards.headline: Chen 2019: systematic review of six studies — cherry intake associated with fewer flares and lower urate, but too heterogeneous to meta-analyse
cards.summary: Chen 2019: systematic review of six studies — cherry intake associated with fewer flares and lower urate, but too heterogeneous to meta-analyse
cards.people: Six studies of cherries in reducing uric acid and gout, identified from PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Library to August 2019 and assessed with the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool; the set overlaps the case-crossover and small trials discussed on this shelf.
cards.result: The included studies reported decreases in the incidence and severity of gout after cherry ingestion, and gout patients regularly ingesting cherry extract or juice reported fewer flare-ups than those who did not supplement; the reviewers observed a positive correlation between tart cherry juice consumption and decreased serum uric acid. They were unable to conduct a meta-analysis because of the lack of relevant studies and the high variation in methodologies and metrics, and conclude that comprehensive trials or long-term follow-up studies are required.
cards.watchOut: A narrative synthesis in a complementary-medicine journal, resting substantially on the same Zhang study carded above — it adds breadth, not independent weight. The record carries no MeSH terms.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one well-designed observational study says fewer attacks after cherries; the only randomised test says the obvious mechanism (urate lowering) does not happen
cards.summary: Synthesis: one well-designed observational study says fewer attacks after cherries; the only randomised test says the obvious mechanism (urate lowering) does not happen
cards.people: One case-crossover study (633 patients), one 28-day randomised dose-ranging trial (50 patients), and one six-study systematic review.
cards.result: Attacks: OR 0.65 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.85) for cherry intake in the prior 2 days, and OR 0.25 (0.15 to 0.42) for cherry intake plus allopurinol versus neither (both relative measures). Urate: no effect of concentrate at any dose over 28 days (P = 0.76). Harms: minimal — one possibly related hyperglycaemia report in the trial.
cards.watchOut: Until a randomised trial with flares as the endpoint reports, 'cherries prevent gout attacks' remains an association looking for a mechanism. Nothing here supports substituting cherries for urate-lowering therapy; the Zhang association was strongest alongside allopurinol, not instead of it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zhang Y et al. Arthritis & Rheumatism. 2012 (PMID: 23023818); Stamp LK et al. Rheumatology. 2020 (PMID: 31891407); Chen PE et al. Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine. 2019 (PMID: 31885677).

shelves.title: Vitamin C for gout: the only trial in gout patients found a trivial 0.23 mg/dL urate fall against allopurinol's 1.9 mg/dL — and flares have never been tested
shelves.question: In gout, does vitamin C lower serum urate or prevent flares?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Allopurinol/administration & dosage · Ascorbic Acid/administration & dosage*/blood · Creatinine/blood · Dietary Supplements* · Female · Gout/drug therapy* · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · New Zealand · Pilot Projects · Treatment Outcome · Uric Acid/blood*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no difference that matters): Vitamin C does lower urate slightly in the general population — a meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials (556 participants, mostly people without gout) found a mean reduction of −0.35 mg/dL (95% CI −0.66 to −0.03) at a median dose of 500 mg/day (Juraschek SP et al., PMID: 21671418). But in the only randomised trial in patients with gout, vitamin C 500 mg/day for 8 weeks lowered serum urate by just 0.014 mmol/L (0.23 mg/dL), against 0.118 mmol/L (1.9 mg/dL) in patients starting or increasing allopurinol (P < 0.001) (Stamp LK et al., PMID: 23681955). No trial in any population has measured gout flares as an outcome of vitamin C. An effect roughly an eighth the size of a low allopurinol dose, from a pilot of 40 patients, is the whole gout-specific evidence base: enough to say vitamin C is not a urate-lowering treatment for gout, not enough to exclude a trivial physiological effect. Tier C: the gout claim rests on a single small pilot trial.

cards.headline: Stamp 2013: in gout patients, vitamin C 500 mg/day lowered urate by 0.23 mg/dL over 8 weeks versus 1.9 mg/dL with allopurinol (P < 0.001) — 'clinically insignificant'
cards.summary: Stamp 2013: in gout patients, vitamin C 500 mg/day lowered urate by 0.23 mg/dL over 8 weeks versus 1.9 mg/dL with allopurinol (P < 0.001) — 'clinically insignificant'
cards.people: 40 patients with gout and serum urate above 0.36 mmol/L (6 mg/dL). Twenty patients already taking allopurinol were randomised to an increase in allopurinol dose or to commence vitamin C 500 mg/day; twenty not taking allopurinol were randomised to start allopurinol (up to 100 mg/day) or vitamin C 500 mg/day. Plasma ascorbate, creatinine and serum urate were measured on day 0 and at week 8.
cards.result: Plasma ascorbate increased significantly in the vitamin C patients, confirming exposure. The reduction in serum urate over 8 weeks was significantly smaller with vitamin C than with starting or increasing allopurinol: a mean reduction of 0.014 mmol/L (0.23 mg/dL) versus 0.118 mmol/L (1.9 mg/dL) (P < 0.001). The authors conclude that a modest dose of vitamin C (500 mg/day) for 8 weeks had no clinically significant urate-lowering effect in patients with gout, whether given alone or combined with allopurinol — results that differ from earlier findings in healthy hyperuricaemic volunteers.
cards.watchOut: A pilot: 40 patients, 8 weeks, a urate endpoint only — no flare outcomes, and a single modest dose. It excludes a clinically useful effect at 500 mg/day; it does not test gram doses or longer treatment, though the burden of proof now sits with anyone proposing them.
cards.source: Stamp LK et al. Clinically insignificant effect of supplemental vitamin C on serum urate in patients with gout: a pilot randomized controlled trial. Arthritis & Rheumatism. 2013. PMID: 23681955. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Juraschek 2011: across 13 trials in mostly non-gout volunteers, vitamin C lowered urate by −0.35 mg/dL — statistically real, clinically small, and not in gout
cards.summary: Juraschek 2011: across 13 trials in mostly non-gout volunteers, vitamin C lowered urate by −0.35 mg/dL — statistically real, clinically small, and not in gout
cards.people: 13 randomised controlled trials of oral vitamin C supplementation with concurrent control groups (556 participants in total; trial sizes 8–184; median vitamin C dose 500 mg/day; median duration 30 days; pretreatment serum urate 2.9–7.0 mg/dL). Trials enrolling children or dialysis patients were excluded; the populations were largely healthy or hyperuricaemic volunteers rather than gout patients.
cards.result: The combined effect of vitamin C supplementation was a significant reduction in serum uric acid of −0.35 mg/dL (95% CI −0.66 to −0.03; P = 0.032), with significant heterogeneity (I² = 77%); subgroup analyses indicated larger reductions in placebo-controlled trials. The authors conclude that vitamin C lowers urate in aggregate and that future trials are needed to determine whether it can reduce hyperuricaemia or prevent incident and recurrent gout.
cards.watchOut: Pooling small, short trials in people without gout answers a physiology question, not the clinical one — and the one trial in gout patients (card 1) found an even smaller effect in the target population. Heterogeneity of 77% means the pooled figure describes no single real regimen well.
cards.source: Juraschek SP et al. Effect of oral vitamin C supplementation on serum uric acid: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Arthritis Care & Research. 2011. PMID: 21671418. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: vitamin C moves urate by a fraction of a milligram in volunteers and by almost nothing in gout — it is not a gout treatment, and flare prevention is untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: vitamin C moves urate by a fraction of a milligram in volunteers and by almost nothing in gout — it is not a gout treatment, and flare prevention is untested
cards.people: One pilot randomised trial in gout (40 patients, 8 weeks) and one meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials in mostly non-gout populations (556 participants).
cards.result: Urate change: −0.23 mg/dL on vitamin C versus −1.9 mg/dL on allopurinol in gout patients (P < 0.001); −0.35 mg/dL pooled across volunteer trials. Flares: no data in any trial. Harms at 500 mg/day: none highlighted in either record.
cards.watchOut: The honest negative is narrow: modest-dose vitamin C does not lower urate enough to matter in established gout. This shelf cannot speak to high-dose regimens, to people with hyperuricaemia but no gout, or to any effect on flares — none has been tested.

shelves.title: Colchicine prophylaxis in pseudogout: a 10-patient before-and-after series from 1986 is nearly the whole evidence base — attacks fell from 3.2 to 1 per patient-year, and no randomised trial has ever tested it
shelves.question: In calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, does colchicine prevent recurrent pseudogout flares?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Arthritis/drug therapy/etiology/prevention & control · Chondrocalcinosis/complications/drug therapy/prevention & control* · Colchicine/administration & dosage/therapeutic use* · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recurrence
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): Prophylactic colchicine for recurrent pseudogout is widespread practice built on almost no evidence. The only primary study with numbers is a 1986 before-and-after series: 10 patients with recurrent attacks recorded 32 attacks in the year before starting colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily (3.2 per patient-year) and 10 attacks in the year taking it (1 per patient-year; P < 0.001), with 90% of patients judged to benefit (Alvarellos A et al., PMID: 3772928). A second 1987 report (González T et al., PMID: 3625651) reaches the same conclusion in its title, but its PubMed record carries no abstract, so no figures from it are printed on this shelf. The systematic review of all CPPD management (Parperis K et al., PMID: 33360232) found 22 studies and 403 patients across every treatment for the disease, only three randomised trials in total (of methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and magnesium carbonate — not colchicine), and states plainly that colchicine, NSAIDs and corticosteroids have not been evaluated by randomised trials in CPPD. Regression to the mean — patients start prophylaxis after a bad year — can manufacture exactly the pattern the 1986 series reports. Tier C: a single tiny uncontrolled series.

cards.headline: Alvarellos 1986: 10 patients — attacks fell from 32 in the year before colchicine to 10 in the year on it (3.2 → 1 per patient-year; P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Alvarellos 1986: 10 patients — attacks fell from 32 in the year before colchicine to 10 in the year on it (3.2 → 1 per patient-year; P < 0.001)
cards.people: 10 patients with recurrent attacks of pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis), each followed for one year before and one year after starting oral colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily. There was no control group: each patient's own pre-treatment year is the comparator.
cards.result: Thirty-two episodes of acute arthritis were recorded in the year before the drug was started (3.2 per patient per year) and only 10 while taking it (1 per patient per year; P < 0.001). Ninety percent of the patients were judged to benefit from the drug. The authors conclude that oral colchicine is an effective prophylactic agent in recurring pseudogout.
cards.watchOut: Ten patients, no blinding, no parallel control, and a design guaranteed to flatter the drug: patients start prophylaxis after an unusually bad year, so attacks would be expected to fall with no treatment at all (regression to the mean). The P value cannot repair a design problem.

cards.headline: Parperis 2021: systematic review of all CPPD treatment — 22 studies, 403 patients, three randomised trials in the whole disease, and colchicine never among them
cards.summary: Parperis 2021: systematic review of all CPPD treatment — 22 studies, 403 patients, three randomised trials in the whole disease, and colchicine never among them
cards.people: All studies evaluating specific treatment agents for calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition disease from database inception to May 2020: 22 eligible studies with 403 unique patients (3 randomised double-blind controlled trials, 10 case series and 9 cohort studies); case reports were excluded.
cards.result: The only three randomised trials in CPPD evaluated methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and magnesium carbonate. Commonly administered agents such as NSAIDs, colchicine and corticosteroids have not been evaluated by randomised trials; the rest of the evidence consists of case series and cohorts, in which intramuscular and intra-articular glucocorticoids, ACTH, and the biologics anakinra and tocilizumab appeared efficacious for acute attacks. The reviewers conclude that high-quality evidence in CPPD is limited and urgently needed.
cards.watchOut: A review of absence: it certifies how thin the record is rather than estimating any colchicine effect size, and its search ended in May 2020. The situation it documents — no colchicine trial in this disease — is the reason this shelf cannot carry a stronger stamp.

cards.headline: Synthesis: prophylactic colchicine in pseudogout rests on one 10-patient uncontrolled series from 1986 — plausible, widely used, and untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: prophylactic colchicine in pseudogout rests on one 10-patient uncontrolled series from 1986 — plausible, widely used, and untested
cards.people: One before-and-after series (10 patients) and one systematic review of the entire CPPD treatment literature (22 studies, 403 patients).
cards.result: Attacks per patient-year: 3.2 in the year before colchicine and 1.0 in the year on colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily (P < 0.001, uncontrolled). Randomised trials of colchicine in CPPD: none, per the 2021 systematic review.
cards.watchOut: Colchicine's gout record (shelf #390) cannot be imported into CPPD — a different crystal and a different disease — and this shelf's question is prophylaxis, not treatment of the acute attack. In the elderly patients who dominate CPPD, colchicine's renal and drug-interaction cautions apply with full force, against a benefit this uncertain.

shelves.title: Methotrexate in polymyalgia rheumatica: the 10 mg weekly trial got patients off prednisone sooner with fewer flares; the 7.5 mg trial found nothing — dose may be the difference
shelves.question: In polymyalgia rheumatica, does adding methotrexate allow faster steroid tapering without more relapses?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Antirheumatic Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Leucovorin/therapeutic use · Male · Methotrexate/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Placebos · Polymyalgia Rheumatica/drug therapy* · Prednisone/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two small double-blind trials disagree, and the clearest difference between them is the dose. Caporali's multicentre trial (72 patients with newly diagnosed polymyalgia rheumatica) added methotrexate 10 mg weekly to a 24-week prednisone taper: by 76 weeks, 28 of 32 methotrexate patients versus 16 of 30 placebo patients were no longer taking prednisone (risk difference 34 percentage points, 95% CI 11 to 53; P = 0.003), fewer methotrexate patients had flared (15 of 32 vs 22 of 30; P = 0.04), and the median cumulative prednisone dose was 2.1 g versus 2.97 g (P = 0.03), with similar adverse events (Caporali R et al., PMID: 15466766). The earlier Dutch trial used methotrexate 7.5 mg weekly in 40 patients (six of whom also had giant cell arteritis) and found no difference in time to remission, relapses or cumulative prednisone dose (van der Veen MJ et al., PMID: 8733437). The Caporali cohort's follow-up at about six years found the steroid-sparing advantage had narrowed to non-significance (cumulative prednisone 2.6 g vs 3.2 g, P = 0.6; still taking steroids 31% vs 39.3%), while a third of all patients still needed steroids beyond six years (Cimmino MA et al., PMID: 18578959). IL-6 blockade for polymyalgia rheumatica is a separate question, at shelf #687.

cards.headline: Caporali 2004: methotrexate 10 mg weekly got 28 of 32 patients off prednisone by 76 weeks versus 16 of 30 on placebo (risk difference 34 points; P = 0.003), with fewer flares
cards.summary: Caporali 2004: methotrexate 10 mg weekly got 28 of 32 patients off prednisone by 76 weeks versus 16 of 30 on placebo (risk difference 34 points; P = 0.003), with fewer flares
cards.people: 72 patients with newly diagnosed polymyalgia rheumatica at five Italian rheumatology clinics, in a multicentre randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Prednisone started at 25 mg/day, was tapered to zero within 24 weeks and adjusted if flare-ups occurred; oral methotrexate 10 mg or placebo was given weekly for 48 weeks, with folinic acid supplementation (7.5 mg). Outcomes at 76 weeks were the proportion no longer taking prednisone, the number of flare-ups and the cumulative prednisone dose; 62 patients (32 methotrexate, 30 placebo) contributed to the analysis.
cards.result: Twenty-eight of 32 patients in the methotrexate group and 16 of 30 in the placebo group were no longer taking prednisone at 76 weeks (P = 0.003; risk difference 34 percentage points, 95% CI 11 to 53). Fifteen of 32 methotrexate patients and 22 of 30 placebo patients had at least one flare-up (P = 0.04). The median cumulative prednisone dose was 2.1 g in the methotrexate group and 2.97 g in the placebo group (P = 0.03). The rate and severity of adverse events were similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Ten of 72 patients (14%) discontinued treatment or were lost to follow-up, the starting prednisone dose was relatively high, a high dose of folinic acid was used, and 76 weeks is short in a disease that often runs for years — the six-year follow-up of this same cohort (card 3) shows the advantage fading.
cards.source: Caporali R et al. Prednisone plus methotrexate for polymyalgia rheumatica: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15466766. cards.headline: van der Veen 1996: methotrexate 7.5 mg weekly showed no steroid-sparing effect at all — no difference in remission, relapses or cumulative prednisone dose
cards.summary: van der Veen 1996: methotrexate 7.5 mg weekly showed no steroid-sparing effect at all — no difference in remission, relapses or cumulative prednisone dose
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (van der Veen 1996)
cards.people: 40 patients with polymyalgia rheumatica, six of whom also had clinical symptoms of giant cell arteritis (a temporal artery biopsy was available from 37 patients and showed GCA in six). All patients started prednisone 20 mg/day, tapered as soon as symptoms disappeared and ESR/CRP normalised, and were randomised double-blind to a weekly capsule of methotrexate 7.5 mg or placebo; 21 patients were followed for two years, or at least one year after discontinuing medication.
cards.result: No differences were found between the methotrexate and placebo groups in time to achieve remission, duration of remission, number of relapses, or cumulative prednisone doses. On the rapid tapering regimen, the mean daily prednisone dose was reduced by 50% after 21 weeks, 40% of all patients were able to discontinue prednisone within two years, and the median duration of steroid treatment was 47.5 weeks. No serious complications from GCA were encountered.
cards.watchOut: A lower methotrexate dose than Caporali (7.5 vs 10 mg weekly), a mixed PMR/GCA population, and only 21 patients with long follow-up: this trial can rule out a large effect of low-dose methotrexate, not the regimen the later trial tested.
cards.source: van der Veen MJ et al. Can methotrexate be used as a steroid sparing agent in the treatment of polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis? Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 1996. cards.headline: Cimmino 2008 (six-year follow-up of the Caporali cohort): the steroid-sparing gap had closed to non-significance — and a third of patients still needed steroids after six years
cards.summary: Cimmino 2008 (six-year follow-up of the Caporali cohort): the steroid-sparing gap had closed to non-significance — and a third of patients still needed steroids after six years
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of a randomised trial cohort (Cimmino 2008) — same cohort as card 1, flagged
cards.people: 57 of the 72 patients enrolled in the Caporali randomised trial (card 1), reviewed about five to six years after starting therapy, with information collected by direct visit, chart review or interviews with relatives. This is the long-term follow-up of that trial's cohort, not an independent study.
cards.result: At about six years, 31% of methotrexate-treated patients were still taking steroids, versus 39.3% of controls. Mean cumulative prednisone dose was 2.6 g with methotrexate versus 3.2 g in controls (P = 0.6). PMR flare-ups occurred in 30.8% of methotrexate patients and 44.4% of controls (P = 0.39). Inflammatory markers remained slightly lower with methotrexate (CRP 2.7 vs 10.2 mg/L; P = 0.04), while steroid-related side effects were similarly frequent (58 vs 55 events). The authors note that PMR is not a benign condition: a third of patients need steroid treatment for more than six years.
cards.watchOut: Attrition (57 of 72 patients) and non-significance cut both ways: the early Caporali advantage may genuinely have faded, or the smaller remainder may conceal it. Either way, methotrexate did not deliver a demonstrable reduction in steroid side effects — the outcome patients care about most.
cards.source: Cimmino MA et al. Long-term follow-up of polymyalgia rheumatica patients treated with methotrexate and steroids. Clinical and Experimental Rheumatology. 2008. PMID: 18578959. cards.headline: Synthesis: methotrexate 10 mg weekly probably shortens prednisone treatment in PMR's first two years; 7.5 mg does nothing measurable, and long-term sparing is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: methotrexate 10 mg weekly probably shortens prednisone treatment in PMR's first two years; 7.5 mg does nothing measurable, and long-term sparing is unproven
cards.people: Two double-blind randomised trials (72 and 40 patients) at different methotrexate doses, plus the positive trial's cohort follow-up at about six years (57 patients).
cards.result: Off prednisone at 76 weeks: 28 of 32 (88%) vs 16 of 30 (53%) in the 10 mg trial. At least one flare: 15 of 32 (47%) vs 22 of 30 (73%) at 10 mg; no difference at 7.5 mg. Cumulative prednisone: median 2.1 vs 2.97 g at 76 weeks (P = 0.03), converging to a non-significant 2.6 vs 3.2 g by about six years. Adverse events were similar between groups in both trials.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are small, the positive one used a relatively high starting prednisone dose and generous folinic acid cover, and no study shows fewer steroid complications. On this evidence methotrexate is an option for PMR patients at high risk of steroid toxicity — not a default addition for everyone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Caporali R et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2004 (PMID: 15466766); van der Veen MJ et al. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 1996 (PMID: 8733437); Cimmino MA et al. Clinical and Experimental Rheumatology. 2008 (PMID: 18578959).

shelves.title: Abatacept in giant cell arteritis: in the single randomised trial, continuing abatacept after a shared 12-week induction kept 48% of patients relapse-free at 12 months versus 31% on placebo, with remission lasting 9.9 versus 3.9 months
shelves.question: In adults with giant cell arteritis, does abatacept increase relapse-free remission?
shelves.mesh: Abatacept/therapeutic use* · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Female · Giant Cell Arteritis/drug therapy* · Humans · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small randomised-withdrawal trial supports abatacept in giant cell arteritis. All 49 enrolled patients (newly diagnosed or relapsing GCA) received abatacept 10 mg/kg intravenously plus prednisone for 12 weeks; the 41 who were in remission at week 12 were then randomised double-blind to continue monthly abatacept or switch to placebo, with prednisone tapered on a standardised schedule and discontinued in all patients at week 28. Relapse-free survival at 12 months was 48% for those continuing abatacept and 31% for those switched to placebo (P = 0.049), and median duration of remission was 9.9 versus 3.9 months (P = 0.023), with no difference in the frequency or severity of adverse events, including infection (Langford CA et al., PMID: 28133925). The design flatters the drug in one specific way: only patients who had already responded to 12 weeks of abatacept were randomised, so the trial estimates the value of continuing it, not of starting it — and with 41 randomised patients, the headline P value of 0.049 rests on a handful of events. IL-6 blockade with tocilizumab in GCA is shelf #385 and upadacitinib is shelf #1812; no head-to-head comparison among these agents exists. Tier C: single small trial.

cards.headline: Langford 2017: relapse-free survival at 12 months was 48% on continued abatacept vs 31% after switching to placebo (P = 0.049); median remission 9.9 vs 3.9 months
cards.summary: Langford 2017: relapse-free survival at 12 months was 48% on continued abatacept vs 31% after switching to placebo (P = 0.049); median remission 9.9 vs 3.9 months
cards.people: 49 eligible patients with newly diagnosed or relapsing giant cell arteritis, all treated with abatacept 10 mg/kg intravenously on days 1, 15 and 29 and at week 8, together with daily prednisone. At week 12, the 41 patients in remission underwent double-blind randomisation to continue monthly abatacept or switch to placebo; both arms followed a standardised prednisone taper, reaching 20 mg daily at week 12 with discontinuation in all patients at week 28. The primary endpoint was duration of remission (relapse-free survival).
cards.result: The relapse-free survival rate at 12 months was 48% for patients receiving abatacept and 31% for those receiving placebo (P = 0.049). Median duration of remission was longer with abatacept (9.9 months) than with placebo (3.9 months; P = 0.023). There was no difference in the frequency or severity of adverse events, including infection, between the treatment arms.
cards.watchOut: A randomised-withdrawal design in 41 patients: everyone randomised had already tolerated and responded to 12 weeks of abatacept, so the trial cannot say what abatacept adds when started at diagnosis, and a few relapses falling the other way would erase the statistical significance. The 17-percentage-point difference rests on small absolute numbers.
cards.source: Langford CA et al. A Randomized, Double-Blind Trial of Abatacept (CTLA-4Ig) for the Treatment of Giant Cell Arteritis. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2017. PMID: 28133925. randomised double-blind withdrawal trial (langford 2017) 49 eligible patients with newly diagnosed or relapsing giant cell arteritis, all treated with abatacept 10 mg/kg intravenously on days 1, 15 and 29 and at week 8, together with daily prednisone. at week 12, the 41 patients in remission underwent double-blind randomisation to continue monthly abatacept or switch to placebo; both arms followed a standardised prednisone taper, reaching 20 mg daily at week 12 with discontinuation in all patients at week 28. the primary endpoint was duration of remission (relapse-free survival). the relapse-free survival rate at 12 months was 48% for patients receiving abatacept and 31% for those receiving placebo (p = 0.049). median duration of remission was longer with abatacept (9.9 months) than with placebo (3.9 months; p = 0.023). there was no difference in the frequency or severity of adverse events, including infection, between the treatment arms. a randomised-withdrawal design in 41 patients: everyone randomised had already tolerated and responded to 12 weeks of abatacept, so the trial cannot say what abatacept adds when started at diagnosis, and a few relapses falling the other way would erase the statistical significance. the 17-percentage-point difference rests on small absolute numbers. langford ca et al. a randomized, double-blind trial of abatacept (ctla-4ig) for the treatment of giant cell arteritis. arthritis & rheumatology. 2017. pmid: 28133925. registry id: nct00556439 (verified against the record). mesh: abatacept/therapeutic use* · aged · aged, 80 and over · double-blind method · female · giant cell arteritis/drug therapy* · humans · male · middle aged

cards.headline: Synthesis: continuing abatacept after induction kept more patients relapse-free over the first year in the only trial — a real but fragile, single-study signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: continuing abatacept after induction kept more patients relapse-free over the first year in the only trial — a real but fragile, single-study signal
cards.people: One multicentre randomised-withdrawal trial: 49 patients induced with abatacept plus prednisone, 41 randomised at week 12.
cards.result: Relapse-free at 12 months: 48% vs 31% (a 17-percentage-point difference; P = 0.049). Median remission duration: 9.9 vs 3.9 months (P = 0.023). Adverse events, including infections: no difference detected.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, withdrawal design, 41 randomised patients — the weakest architecture that can still be called randomised evidence. It supports abatacept as one steroid-sparing option among several for GCA (tocilizumab at shelf #385, upadacitinib at shelf #1812), with no comparative data between them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Langford CA et al. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2017 (PMID: 28133925).

shelves.title: Hydroxychloroquine and rituximab in primary Sjögren syndrome: three placebo-controlled trials, three negative primary endpoints — the two most-used systemic treatments do not improve dryness, pain or fatigue
shelves.question: In primary Sjögren syndrome, do hydroxychloroquine or rituximab improve systemic disease and dryness?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use* · Fatigue/drug therapy/etiology · Female · Humans · Hydroxychloroquine/therapeutic use* · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Sjogren's Syndrome/complications/drug therapy* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The two systemic treatments most used in primary Sjögren syndrome have each failed their primary endpoint in placebo-controlled trials. Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day in JOQUER (120 patients): 17.9% versus 17.2% met the responder endpoint at 24 weeks (odds ratio 1.01) (Gottenberg JE et al., PMID: 25027140). Rituximab in TEARS (120 patients): no difference at week 24 (difference 1.0 percentage point), with transient early gains in fatigue that did not persist (Devauchelle-Pensec V et al., PMID: 24727841). Rituximab again in TRACTISS (133 patients, two courses): response 39.8% versus 36.8% after imputation (adjusted odds ratio 1.13), no improvement in any outcome except unstimulated salivary flow, and not cost-effective at £10,752 versus £2,672 per patient (Bowman SJ et al., PMID: 28296257). What does help dry mouth symptomatically — pilocarpine — is shelf #1796.

cards.headline: Gottenberg 2014 (JOQUER): hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day did no better than placebo — 17.9% vs 17.2% met the responder endpoint at 24 weeks (OR 1.01; P = .98)
cards.summary: Gottenberg 2014 (JOQUER): hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day did no better than placebo — 17.9% vs 17.2% met the responder endpoint at 24 weeks (OR 1.01; P = .98)
cards.people: 120 patients with primary Sjögren syndrome (American-European Consensus Group criteria) at 15 French university hospitals, randomised double-blind to hydroxychloroquine 400 mg/day or placebo for 24 weeks; all patients then received hydroxychloroquine to week 48. The primary endpoint was a 30% or greater reduction in 2 of 3 numeric analog scales (dryness, pain, fatigue) at week 24.
cards.result: At 24 weeks, 17.9% (10/56) on hydroxychloroquine and 17.2% (11/64) on placebo met the primary endpoint (odds ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.78; P = .98). Mean dryness, pain and fatigue scores moved little in either group between weeks 0 and 24. Hydroxychloroquine showed no efficacy in patients with anti-SSA autoantibodies, high IgG levels, or systemic involvement. Serious adverse events were similar (2 versus 3 in the first 24 weeks). All but one patient in the hydroxychloroquine group had detectable blood levels of the drug — non-adherence does not explain the result.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of 120 patients whose confidence interval (0.37 to 2.78) is too wide to exclude a modest benefit — but the point estimate is exactly null and no symptom scale or subgroup moved. Twenty-four weeks may be short for a slow-acting drug, and the trial cannot speak to very long-term outcomes.
cards.source: Gottenberg JE et al. Effects of hydroxychloroquine on symptomatic improvement in primary Sjögren syndrome: the JOQUER randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014. PMID: 25027140. Registry ID: NCT00632866 (verified against the record). cards.headline: Devauchelle-Pensec 2014 (TEARS): rituximab missed its week-24 primary endpoint (difference 1.0 percentage point; 95% CI −16.7 to 18.7) — early fatigue gains faded
cards.summary: Devauchelle-Pensec 2014 (TEARS): rituximab missed its week-24 primary endpoint (difference 1.0 percentage point; 95% CI −16.7 to 18.7) — early fatigue gains faded
cards.people: 120 patients with recent-onset (less than 10 years) biologically active or systemic primary Sjögren syndrome, with scores of 50 mm or more on at least 2 of 4 visual analogue scales (global disease, pain, fatigue, dryness), at 14 French university hospitals; rituximab 1 g at weeks 0 and 2 versus placebo, double-blind. Primary endpoint: improvement of at least 30 mm in 2 of 4 VAS by week 24.
cards.result: No significant difference between groups in the primary endpoint (difference 1.0%, 95% CI −16.7% to 18.7%). More rituximab patients met the responder definition at week 6 (22.4% vs 9.1%; P = 0.036), and improvement of at least 30 mm in the fatigue VAS was more common with rituximab at weeks 6 (P < 0.001) and 16 (P = 0.012), with greater fatigue improvement from baseline to week 24 — but the composite primary endpoint at week 24 was not met. Adverse events were similar between groups except for a higher rate of infusion reactions with rituximab.
cards.watchOut: The early time-point wins are secondary looks at a negative trial — benefit at week 6 that is gone by week 24 is the signature of placebo response and regression to the mean. The authors concede low baseline disease activity and a possibly insensitive primary outcome; the trial does not test rituximab for severe systemic manifestations such as vasculitis or lung disease, where use rests on case series.
cards.source: Devauchelle-Pensec V et al. Treatment of primary Sjögren syndrome with rituximab: a randomized trial. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2014. PMID: 24727841. Registry ID: NCT00740948 (verified against the record). cards.headline: Bowman 2017 (TRACTISS): two courses of rituximab — response 39.8% vs 36.8% (adjusted OR 1.13; 95% CI 0.50 to 2.55), and not cost-effective
cards.summary: Bowman 2017 (TRACTISS): two courses of rituximab — response 39.8% vs 36.8% (adjusted OR 1.13; 95% CI 0.50 to 2.55), and not cost-effective
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial with cost-effectiveness analysis (Bowman 2017, TRACTISS)
cards.people: 133 anti-Ro-positive patients with primary Sjögren syndrome, symptomatic fatigue and oral dryness, recruited from 25 UK rheumatology clinics; intravenous rituximab 1,000 mg or saline placebo in 2 courses at weeks 0, 2, 24 and 26, with corticosteroid pre- and post-infusion medication. Primary endpoint: the proportion achieving a 30% reduction in either fatigue or oral dryness VAS at 48 weeks.
cards.result: Among patients with complete data, 21 of 56 on placebo and 24 of 61 on rituximab achieved the primary endpoint; after multiple imputation of missing outcomes, response rates were 36.8% (placebo) and 39.8% (rituximab) (adjusted odds ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.50 to 2.55). There were no significant improvements in any outcome measure except unstimulated salivary flow. Mean cost per patient was £10,752 ± 264.75 for rituximab versus £2,672 ± 241.71 for placebo. Serious adverse events numbered 10 in each group. The authors conclude rituximab is neither clinically effective nor cost-effective in this patient population.
cards.watchOut: A symptom trial in anti-Ro-positive patients with fatigue and dryness — it does not address rituximab for organ-threatening systemic disease. The one positive signal, unstimulated salivary flow, is a surrogate among many outcomes tested.
cards.source: Bowman SJ et al. Randomized Controlled Trial of Rituximab and Cost-Effectiveness Analysis in Treating Fatigue and Oral Dryness in Primary Sjögren's Syndrome. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2017. PMID: 28296257. Registry ID: ISRCTN65360827 and EudraCT 2010-021430-64 (as listed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised trials, no durable benefit — hydroxychloroquine and rituximab do not improve the symptoms of primary Sjögren syndrome
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials, no durable benefit — hydroxychloroquine and rituximab do not improve the symptoms of primary Sjögren syndrome
cards.people: Three double-blind placebo-controlled trials: JOQUER (hydroxychloroquine, n = 120), TEARS (rituximab, n = 120) and TRACTISS (rituximab, n = 133).
cards.result: Primary endpoints: 17.9% vs 17.2% responders (JOQUER, OR 1.01); difference 1.0 percentage point (TEARS); 39.8% vs 36.8% (TRACTISS, adjusted OR 1.13). Early fatigue signals in TEARS did not survive to week 24. Harms were modest (infusion reactions with rituximab); the clearest cost is money — rituximab cost roughly four times more per patient than placebo care in TRACTISS, with nothing to show for it.
cards.watchOut: All three trials tested symptoms and patient-reported disease activity, not prevention of glandular damage or lymphoma, and none enrolled the severe systemic phenotypes for which rituximab is still used on observational grounds. Within the questions they asked, though, the answer is consistent: no benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gottenberg JE et al. JAMA. 2014 (PMID: 25027140); Devauchelle-Pensec V et al. Annals of Internal Medicine. 2014 (PMID: 24727841); Bowman SJ et al. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2017 (PMID: 28296257).
