shelves.title: Rituximab in refractory myositis: in the RIM trial 83% of patients improved — but with no placebo-only arm, the trial cannot show the drug caused it
shelves.question: In adults with inflammatory myopathies, does rituximab improve strength and disease activity?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Murine-Derived/therapeutic use* · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use* · Child · Dermatomyositis/drug therapy* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Weakness/drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Placebos · Polymyositis/drug therapy* · Rituximab · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The RIM trial randomised 200 adults and children with refractory polymyositis, dermatomyositis or juvenile dermatomyositis to rituximab early or about 8 weeks late — everyone received the drug, so there was no placebo-only comparison. The early and late groups reached the definition of improvement at the same speed (median 20.0 vs 20.2 weeks; P = 0.74), yet 83% of all patients met the improvement definition over 44 weeks on background glucocorticoids and immunosuppressants (Oddis CV et al., PMID: 23124935). A post-hoc biomarker analysis of the same trial found improvement concentrated in patients with anti-synthetase, Mi-2 or non-myositis-associated antibodies and high interferon-regulated chemokine scores (Reed AM et al., PMID: 26382217) — hypothesis-generating only. For dermatomyositis specifically, intravenous immunoglobulin has the cleaner placebo-controlled evidence (shelf #2718). Tier C: a single trial whose placebo-phase design cannot isolate the drug's effect.

cards.headline: Oddis 2013 (RIM): early vs late rituximab — no difference in time to improvement (median 20.0 vs 20.2 weeks; P = 0.74); 83% of patients met the definition of improvement by week 44
cards.summary: Oddis 2013 (RIM): early vs late rituximab — no difference in time to improvement (median 20.0 vs 20.2 weeks; P = 0.74); 83% of patients met the definition of improvement by week 44
cards.people: 200 randomised patients with refractory disease — 76 with adult polymyositis, 76 with adult dermatomyositis and 48 with juvenile dermatomyositis — all receiving rituximab either early or late in a double-blind, placebo-phase design, with glucocorticoid or immunosuppressive therapy allowed at entry. The primary endpoint compared time to achieve the International Myositis Assessment and Clinical Studies Group preliminary definition of improvement (DOI) between the early and late groups.
cards.result: Among 195 patients analysed, there was no difference in time to achieving the DOI between the rituximab late (n = 102) and rituximab early (n = 93) groups (median 20.2 and 20.0 weeks respectively; P = 0.74 by log rank test). The secondary endpoints — time to at least 20% improvement in muscle strength, and the proportions achieving the DOI at week 8 — also did not differ significantly. However, 161 patients (83%) met the DOI during the trial, and individual core set measures improved in both groups throughout the 44 weeks.
cards.watchOut: The design is the story: with rituximab given to everyone within the first weeks, the trial compares timing, not drug versus no drug. The 83% improvement rate could reflect rituximab, the background steroids and immunosuppressants, the natural fluctuation of refractory disease, or regression to the mean — RIM cannot separate them. It is randomised evidence about when, not whether.
cards.source: Oddis CV et al. Rituximab in the treatment of refractory adult and juvenile dermatomyositis and adult polymyositis: a randomized, placebo-phase trial. Arthritis and Rheumatism. 2013. PMID: 23124935. Registry ID: NCT00106184 (verified against the record). cards.headline: Reed 2015 (RIM biomarker substudy): improvement after rituximab clustered in anti-synthetase, Mi-2 and non-MAA antibody groups with high interferon chemokine scores
cards.summary: Reed 2015 (RIM biomarker substudy): improvement after rituximab clustered in anti-synthetase, Mi-2 and non-MAA antibody groups with high interferon chemokine scores
cards.type: Post-hoc biomarker analysis of a randomised trial (Reed 2015, RIM substudy)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of the RIM trial — a further report of the same trial as the Oddis 2013 card above, not an independent study. Serum samples from 177 rituximab-treated patients were analysed at baseline and after treatment for type-1 interferon-regulated and other chemokine and cytokine scores, and correlated with myositis autoantibodies (anti-synthetase n = 28, TIF1-γ n = 19, Mi-2 n = 25, SRP n = 21, MJ n = 18, non-MAA n = 24, unidentified autoantibody n = 9, no autoantibodies n = 33).
cards.result: Interferon chemokine scores at baseline were higher in subjects with anti-synthetase (median 43), TIF1-γ (31) and Mi-2 (30) antibodies than in other groups (P < 0.001). At 16 weeks after rituximab, anti-synthetase and Mi-2 positive subjects and the non-MAA group showed the greatest improvement in chemokine scores (−6.7, −6.1 and −7.2; P < .001). High chemokine scores and Mi-2, non-MAA or undefined autoantibody status tracked with the greatest clinical improvement on the muscle VAS (muscle-interaction P = 0.075).
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc, within-trial and uncontrolled: with no untreated comparator, 'predictors of improvement' may predict improvement on anything — or spontaneous improvement. The key clinical interaction was not conventionally significant (P = 0.075). Useful for designing the next trial; not a basis for selecting patients today.

cards.headline: Synthesis: rituximab may help refractory myositis — RIM's 83% improvement rate is encouraging and unproven in equal measure
cards.summary: Synthesis: rituximab may help refractory myositis — RIM's 83% improvement rate is encouraging and unproven in equal measure
cards.people: One randomised placebo-phase trial (n = 200) and its biomarker substudy (serum from 177 patients).
cards.result: No early-versus-late difference (median time to improvement 20.0 vs 20.2 weeks; P = 0.74); 83% met the definition of improvement by week 44 on background therapy. Biomarker-defined subgroups (anti-synthetase, Mi-2, high interferon chemokine score) improved most, in a post-hoc analysis of the same trial.
cards.watchOut: There is still no placebo-controlled trial of rituximab in myositis with a no-treatment arm. The honest statement is 'widely used, biologically plausible, and compatible with a real effect of unknown size' — which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.
cards.source: Synthesis of Oddis CV et al. Arthritis and Rheumatism. 2013 (PMID: 23124935); Reed AM et al. BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders. 2015 (PMID: 26382217).

shelves.title: Intravenous immunoglobulin in dermatomyositis: 79% versus 44% responded at 16 weeks in ProDERM — with thromboembolism among the harms
shelves.question: In dermatomyositis, does intravenous immunoglobulin improve strength and function?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Creatine Kinase/analysis · Dermatomyositis/drug therapy/therapy* · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Immunoglobulins, Intravenous/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two placebo-controlled trials, 29 years apart, point the same way. ProDERM randomised 95 adults with active dermatomyositis to IVIG 2.0 g/kg every 4 weeks or placebo: at 16 weeks, 79% versus 44% achieved at least minimal improvement on the Total Improvement Score (difference 35 percentage points, 95% CI 17 to 53; P < 0.001), with at least moderate and major improvement also favouring IVIG (Aggarwal R et al., PMID: 36198179). The small 1993 crossover trial (15 patients with treatment-resistant disease) found significant gains in muscle strength scores on IVIG, and major improvement in 9 of the 12 patients who received it, versus none of 11 on placebo (Dalakas MC et al., PMID: 8247075). The price is real: in ProDERM, 9 serious adverse events were considered related to IVIG, including 6 thromboembolic events, and headache affected 42% of patients.

cards.headline: Aggarwal 2022 (ProDERM): IVIG 2.0 g/kg every 4 weeks — 79% (37/47) vs 44% (21/48) achieved at least minimal improvement at 16 weeks (difference 35 points; 95% CI 17 to 53; P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Aggarwal 2022 (ProDERM): IVIG 2.0 g/kg every 4 weeks — 79% (37/47) vs 44% (21/48) achieved at least minimal improvement at 16 weeks (difference 35 points; 95% CI 17 to 53; P < 0.001)
cards.people: 95 adults with active dermatomyositis randomised 1:1 to IVIG at 2.0 g per kilogram or placebo every 4 weeks for 16 weeks; patients on placebo, and those without confirmed deterioration on IVIG, could enter a 24-week open-label extension. The primary endpoint was a response — a Total Improvement Score (TIS, a weighted composite of six core measures of myositis activity, range 0 to 100) of at least 20, indicating at least minimal improvement, with no confirmed deterioration up to week 16.
cards.result: At 16 weeks, 79% of the IVIG group (37 of 47) and 44% of the placebo group (21 of 48) had a TIS of at least 20 (difference 35 percentage points, 95% CI 17 to 53; P < 0.001). Secondary endpoints — at least moderate improvement (TIS ≥40), major improvement (TIS ≥60) and change in the cutaneous disease score — were generally in the same direction; the exception was creatine kinase level, which did not differ meaningfully. Over 40 weeks, 282 treatment-related adverse events occurred in the IVIG group, including headache (in 42% of patients), pyrexia (19%) and nausea (16%); 9 serious adverse events were considered related to IVIG, including 6 thromboembolic events.
cards.watchOut: Funded by Octapharma, an IVIG manufacturer; the record names the funder but no brand name for the immune globulin product. Sixteen weeks is short for a chronic disease, the placebo response (44%) was high, and the thromboembolic events — in a disease that itself raises clotting risk — need weighing in older patients and those with vascular risk factors.
cards.source: Aggarwal R et al. Trial of Intravenous Immune Globulin in Dermatomyositis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36198179. Registry ID: NCT02728752 (verified against the record). cards.headline: Dalakas 1993: in 15 patients with treatment-resistant dermatomyositis, IVIG significantly improved muscle strength (P < 0.018) — 9 of 12 who received it improved majorly, versus 0 of 11 on placebo
cards.summary: Dalakas 1993: in 15 patients with treatment-resistant dermatomyositis, IVIG significantly improved muscle strength (P < 0.018) — 9 of 12 who received it improved majorly, versus 0 of 11 on placebo
cards.people: 15 patients (age 18 to 55 years) with biopsy-proved, treatment-resistant dermatomyositis, all continuing prednisone (mean daily dose 25 mg), randomly assigned double-blind to one infusion of immune globulin (2 g per kilogram) or placebo per month for 3 months, with the option of crossing over to the alternative therapy for 3 more months. Response was gauged by muscle strength, neuromuscular symptoms and changes in the rash, with repeated muscle biopsies in some patients.
cards.result: The 8 patients assigned to immune globulin had a significant improvement in muscle strength scores (P < 0.018) and neuromuscular symptoms (P < 0.035); the 7 assigned to placebo did not. With crossovers, 12 patients in total received immune globulin: 9 with severe disabilities had a major improvement to nearly normal function (mean muscle strength scores rose from 74.5 to 84.7), 2 had mild improvement and 1 had no change. Of 11 placebo-treated patients, none had a major improvement, 3 had mild improvement, 3 had no change and 5 worsened. Repeat biopsies in 5 patients whose strength improved showed increased muscle-fibre diameter and resolution of complement deposits on capillaries.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen patients, 1993, no trial registration, and crossover counting mixes randomised and open experience — the '9 of 12' figure is not itself a randomised comparison. Its value is that a small, rigorous-for-its-time trial pointed the same way as the large modern one.
cards.source: Dalakas MC et al. A controlled trial of high-dose intravenous immune globulin infusions as treatment for dermatomyositis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1993. PMID: 8247075. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Synthesis: IVIG works in active dermatomyositis — the best-supported systemic treatment in this disease, with a clotting caution
cards.summary: Synthesis: IVIG works in active dermatomyositis — the best-supported systemic treatment in this disease, with a clotting caution
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials: ProDERM (n = 95, 2022) and Dalakas 1993 (n = 15, crossover).
cards.result: Response at 16 weeks in ProDERM: 79% vs 44% (difference 35 percentage points, 95% CI 17 to 53). Dalakas: significant strength gains on IVIG and none on placebo, with major improvement in 9 of 12 patients exposed to IVIG. Harms in ProDERM: headache in 42% of patients, and 9 related serious adverse events including 6 thromboembolic events.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled active, largely refractory disease and ran 16 weeks or less; neither answers duration of therapy, maintenance strategy, or use in juvenile or clinically amyopathic disease. Cost and supply of IVIG are substantial practical constraints the trials do not address.

shelves.title: Apremilast for Behçet oral ulcers: fewer ulcers and less pain in two placebo-controlled trials — the phase 3 ulcer-burden AUC was 129.5 versus 222.1
shelves.question: In Behçet disease with recurrent oral ulcers, does apremilast reduce ulcer number and pain?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Area Under Curve · Behcet Syndrome/complications/drug therapy* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Oral Ulcer/drug therapy/etiology* · Phosphodiesterase 4 Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Quality of Life · Thalidomide/adverse effects/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Apremilast 30 mg twice daily beat placebo for the cardinal manifestation of Behçet syndrome in two randomised trials. In the phase 3 RELIEF trial (207 patients with active oral ulcers and no major organ involvement), the area under the curve for the total number of oral ulcers over the 12-week placebo-controlled period was 129.5 on apremilast versus 222.1 on placebo (least-squares mean difference −92.6, 95% CI −130.6 to −54.6; P < 0.001), and the Behçet's Disease Quality of Life score improved more (−4.3 vs −1.2 points) (Hatemi G et al., PMID: 31722152). The earlier phase 2 trial (111 patients) found 0.5 versus 2.1 oral ulcers per patient at week 12 and a greater fall in ulcer pain (−44.7 vs −16.0 mm on a 100-mm scale) (Hatemi G et al., PMID: 25875256). The adverse-event pattern is gastrointestinal — diarrhoea, nausea and headache — and neither trial speaks to eye, vascular or neurological Behçet, whose patients were excluded or absent.

cards.headline: Hatemi 2019 (RELIEF): apremilast cut the oral-ulcer burden over 12 weeks — AUC 129.5 vs 222.1 (least-squares mean difference −92.6; 95% CI −130.6 to −54.6; P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Hatemi 2019 (RELIEF): apremilast cut the oral-ulcer burden over 12 weeks — AUC 129.5 vs 222.1 (least-squares mean difference −92.6; 95% CI −130.6 to −54.6; P < 0.001)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Hatemi 2019, RELIEF)
cards.people: 207 patients with Behçet syndrome with active oral ulcers but no major organ involvement, who had not previously received biologic agents, randomised 1:1 to apremilast 30 mg or placebo orally twice daily for 12 weeks, followed by a 52-week extension phase. The primary endpoint was the area under the curve (AUC) for the total number of oral ulcers during the 12-week placebo-controlled period, with lower values indicating fewer ulcers; there were 13 secondary endpoints, including complete response of oral ulcers and change in ulcer pain.
cards.result: The AUC for the number of oral ulcers was 129.5 for apremilast compared with 222.1 for placebo (least-squares mean difference −92.6, 95% CI −130.6 to −54.6; P < 0.001). The change from baseline in the Behçet's Disease Quality of Life score was −4.3 points in the apremilast group versus −1.2 points in the placebo group (least-squares mean difference −3.1 points, 95% CI −4.9 to −1.3). Adverse events with apremilast included diarrhoea, nausea and headache.
cards.watchOut: An ulcer-count AUC is a burden measure, not a responder count — the abstract does not report the complete-response rates among its secondary endpoints. Patients with major organ disease were excluded, so this licenses no inference about ocular, vascular or CNS Behçet. Funded by Celgene, the manufacturer.
cards.source: Hatemi G et al. Trial of Apremilast for Oral Ulcers in Behçet's Syndrome. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31722152. cards.headline: Hatemi 2015 (phase 2): apremilast left patients with 0.5 oral ulcers at week 12 versus 2.1 on placebo (P < 0.001), and ulcer pain fell further (−44.7 vs −16.0 mm)
cards.summary: Hatemi 2015 (phase 2): apremilast left patients with 0.5 oral ulcers at week 12 versus 2.1 on placebo (P < 0.001), and ulcer pain fell further (−44.7 vs −16.0 mm)
cards.people: 111 patients with Behçet syndrome who had two or more oral ulcers, randomised to apremilast 30 mg twice daily or placebo for 12 weeks, followed by a 12-week extension in which the placebo group was switched to apremilast and a 28-day post-treatment observational phase. The primary endpoint was the number of oral ulcers at week 12; secondary outcomes included ulcer pain on a 100-mm visual analogue scale, genital ulcers, disease activity and quality of life.
cards.result: The mean number of oral ulcers per patient at week 12 was 0.5 ± 1.0 in the apremilast group versus 2.1 ± 2.6 in the placebo group (P < 0.001). The mean decline in pain from oral ulcers was −44.7 ± 24.3 mm with apremilast versus −16.0 ± 32.5 mm with placebo (P < 0.001). Nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea were more common in the apremilast group (22, 9 and 12 incidents respectively among 55 patients) than in the placebo group (10, 1 and 2 among 56 patients). There were two serious adverse events in patients receiving apremilast.
cards.watchOut: Small and short, as the authors state: neither large enough nor long enough to assess long-term efficacy, effects on other manifestations of Behçet syndrome, or uncommon serious adverse events. Its role is corroboration — the phase 3 trial is the load-bearing evidence.
cards.source: Hatemi G et al. Apremilast for Behçet's syndrome--a phase 2, placebo-controlled study. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2015. PMID: 25875256. cards.headline: Synthesis: apremilast reduces oral ulcer number and pain in Behçet syndrome — a mucocutaneous answer only
cards.summary: Synthesis: apremilast reduces oral ulcer number and pain in Behçet syndrome — a mucocutaneous answer only
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials: RELIEF phase 3 (n = 207) and the phase 2 trial (n = 111), each with 12 weeks of placebo-controlled treatment.
cards.result: Ulcer burden AUC 129.5 vs 222.1 (RELIEF); oral ulcers per patient 0.5 vs 2.1 and pain change −44.7 vs −16.0 mm (phase 2). Quality of life improved modestly more with apremilast (−4.3 vs −1.2 points). Harms: diarrhoea, nausea, headache — gastrointestinal intolerance is the limiting factor.
cards.watchOut: No trial evidence here for genital ulcers as a primary target, for arthritis, or for any major-organ manifestation; patients with major organ involvement were excluded from RELIEF. Comparative safety beyond the extension phases is observational.

shelves.title: IL-1 blockade in colchicine-resistant familial Mediterranean fever: canakinumab produced complete responses in 61% versus 6% — and anakinra halved attack rates in its small trial
shelves.question: In colchicine-resistant familial Mediterranean fever, do interleukin-1 inhibitors control attacks?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Child · Child, Preschool · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Familial Mediterranean Fever/drug therapy* · Female · Fever/drug therapy* · Hereditary Autoinflammatory Diseases/drug therapy* · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Interleukin-1beta/antagonists & inhibitors* · Male · Mevalonate Kinase Deficiency/drug therapy* · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised placebo-controlled trials support interleukin-1 blockade when colchicine fails. In CLUSTER, patients with genetically confirmed colchicine-resistant familial Mediterranean fever randomised at the time of a flare to canakinumab 150 mg subcutaneously every 4 weeks or placebo achieved a complete response — resolution of the flare and no new flare until week 16 — in 61% versus 6% (P < 0.001), rising to 71% when patients whose dose was increased to 300 mg are included (De Benedetti F et al., PMID: 29768139). In the smaller anakinra trial (25 patients), attacks per month were 1.7 ± 1.7 on anakinra versus 3.5 ± 1.9 on placebo (P = 0.037), and 6 of 12 anakinra patients versus 0 of 13 on placebo averaged less than one attack per month (Ben-Zvi I et al., PMID: 27860460). Infections are the main harm signal with canakinumab (173.3 events per 100 patient-years in the FMF cohort; serious infections 6.6 per 100 patient-years).

cards.headline: De Benedetti 2018 (CLUSTER): canakinumab in colchicine-resistant FMF — complete response at week 16 in 61% vs 6% (P < 0.001); 71% including dose escalation to 300 mg
cards.summary: De Benedetti 2018 (CLUSTER): canakinumab in colchicine-resistant FMF — complete response at week 16 in 61% vs 6% (P < 0.001); 71% including dose escalation to 300 mg
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (De Benedetti 2018, CLUSTER)
cards.people: Patients with genetically confirmed colchicine-resistant familial Mediterranean fever — one of three autoinflammatory cohorts in CLUSTER, alongside mevalonate kinase deficiency and TRAPS — randomised at the time of a flare to 150 mg of canakinumab subcutaneously or placebo every 4 weeks; patients whose flare did not resolve received an add-on injection of 150 mg. The primary outcome was complete response: resolution of the flare and no flare until week 16. Complete responders then underwent a second randomisation to canakinumab or placebo every 8 weeks up to week 40.
cards.result: At week 16, complete response in the FMF cohort was 61% with canakinumab versus 6% with placebo (P < 0.001); including patients whose dose was increased to 300 mg every 4 weeks, 71% achieved a complete response. After week 16, the extended every-8-weeks regimen maintained disease control in 46% of FMF patients. The most frequently reported adverse events among canakinumab patients were infections — 173.3 per 100 patient-years in the FMF cohort — with serious infections at 6.6 per 100 patient-years. (The parallel cohorts responded less completely at the starting dose: mevalonate kinase deficiency 35% versus 6%, TRAPS 45% versus 8%.)
cards.watchOut: The FMF cohort is one limb of a three-disease trial, so its patient count is a fraction of the whole; enrolment at the time of a flare enriches for active disease. Funded by Novartis. Long-term prevention of amyloidosis — the outcome that ultimately matters in FMF — is inferred from attack control, not measured here.
cards.source: De Benedetti F et al. Canakinumab for the Treatment of Autoinflammatory Recurrent Fever Syndromes. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29768139. cards.headline: Ben-Zvi 2017: anakinra in colchicine-resistant FMF — 1.7 vs 3.5 attacks per month (P = 0.037); 6 of 12 vs 0 of 13 patients averaged under one attack per month
cards.summary: Ben-Zvi 2017: anakinra in colchicine-resistant FMF — 1.7 vs 3.5 attacks per month (P = 0.037); 6 of 12 vs 0 of 13 patients averaged under one attack per month
cards.people: 25 patients with colchicine-resistant FMF still receiving colchicine (dosage 1.5 to 3 mg/day), randomly assigned double-blind to receive anakinra or placebo (vehicle) for 4 months. Primary efficacy outcomes were the number of attacks per month and the number of patients with a mean of less than 1 attack per month; quality of life was assessed on a 0–10 visual analog scale.
cards.result: The mean number of attacks per patient per month was 1.7 ± 1.7 in those receiving anakinra and 3.5 ± 1.9 in those receiving placebo (P = 0.037). Six patients in the anakinra group, compared to none in the placebo group, had less than 1 attack per month (P = 0.005). Joint attacks per month were fewer with anakinra (0.8 ± 1.6 versus 2.1 ± 1.1; P = 0.019), and quality of life was better (VAS 7.7 ± 2.3 versus 4.2 ± 2.9; P = 0.045). The number of adverse events per patient per month was comparable between groups (2.03 ± 1.75 versus 3.34 ± 2.5; P = 0.22), and there were no severe adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-five patients and 4 months — the smallest trial in this batch, and daily injections are a real burden. It corroborates the class effect shown at scale in CLUSTER rather than standing alone.
cards.source: Ben-Zvi I et al. Anakinra for Colchicine-Resistant Familial Mediterranean Fever: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2017. PMID: 27860460. cards.headline: Synthesis: IL-1 blockade controls attacks in colchicine-resistant FMF — large effects in both trials
cards.summary: Synthesis: IL-1 blockade controls attacks in colchicine-resistant FMF — large effects in both trials
cards.people: Two double-blind placebo-controlled trials: CLUSTER (canakinumab; FMF cohort of a three-disease trial) and Ben-Zvi 2017 (anakinra, n = 25).
cards.result: Complete response 61% vs 6% with canakinumab at 16 weeks (71% including dose escalation); attacks per month 1.7 vs 3.5 with anakinra. Harms: infections predominate with canakinumab (serious infections 6.6 per 100 patient-years in the FMF cohort); no severe adverse events in the small anakinra trial.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are short relative to a lifelong disease, and neither measured amyloidosis or renal outcomes. Colchicine remains the foundation — these drugs are for the minority in whom it fails (the record puts colchicine resistance at 10–20% of patients), which is the population both trials enrolled.
cards.source: Synthesis of De Benedetti F et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29768139); Ben-Zvi I et al. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2017 (PMID: 27860460).

shelves.title: Methotrexate alone is not enough in psoriatic arthritis: etanercept beat it on ACR20 (60.9% vs 50.7%) and minimal disease activity — and adding methotrexate to etanercept added nothing
shelves.question: In psoriatic arthritis, is methotrexate alone enough, or does early TNF inhibition beat it?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use* · Arthritis, Psoriatic/drug therapy* · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Etanercept/therapeutic use* · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate/therapeutic use* · Middle Aged · Tumor Necrosis Factor Inhibitors/therapeutic use*
shelves.balance: LIKELY: SEAM-PsA randomised 851 patients with psoriatic arthritis, double-blind, to methotrexate monotherapy, etanercept monotherapy, or the combination. At week 24, ACR20 response rates were significantly greater with etanercept monotherapy than with methotrexate monotherapy (60.9% versus 50.7%; P = 0.029), and with combination therapy than with methotrexate (65.0% versus 50.7%; P = 0.005); minimal disease activity was achieved by 35.9% and 35.7% versus 22.9% respectively (both P = 0.005). Outcomes were similar in the combination and etanercept monotherapy groups, except for some skin endpoints — combining methotrexate and etanercept did not improve the efficacy of etanercept — and both etanercept arms showed less radiographic progression at week 48 than methotrexate alone (Mease PJ et al., PMID: 30747501). Methotrexate still worked for half the patients: the trial demotes it from default monotherapy, it does not make it useless.

cards.headline: Mease 2019 (SEAM-PsA): ACR20 at week 24 — etanercept 60.9% and combination 65.0% versus methotrexate 50.7%; minimal disease activity 35.9% / 35.7% versus 22.9%
cards.summary: Mease 2019 (SEAM-PsA): ACR20 at week 24 — etanercept 60.9% and combination 65.0% versus methotrexate 50.7%; minimal disease activity 35.9% / 35.7% versus 22.9%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind three-arm phase III trial (Mease 2019, SEAM-PsA)
cards.people: 851 patients with psoriatic arthritis (mean age 48.4 ± 13.1 years; mean duration of PsA 3.2 ± 6.3 years, median 0.6) randomised double-blind to one of three weekly regimens: oral methotrexate 20 mg plus subcutaneous placebo (n = 284), subcutaneous etanercept 50 mg plus oral placebo (n = 284), or etanercept 50 mg plus methotrexate 20 mg (n = 283). The primary endpoint was ACR20 response at week 24 and the key secondary endpoint was Minimal Disease Activity (MDA) response at week 24; radiographic progression was assessed at week 48.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 60.9% on etanercept monotherapy versus 50.7% on methotrexate monotherapy (P = 0.029), and 65.0% on combination therapy versus 50.7% on methotrexate (P = 0.005). MDA: 35.9% (etanercept) and 35.7% (combination) versus 22.9% (methotrexate) (both P = 0.005). ACR50 and ACR70 response rates, Very Low Disease Activity and PsA disease activity scores were consistent with the primary results. Patients in both etanercept arms showed less radiographic progression at week 48 than patients on methotrexate monotherapy. Outcomes were similar in the combination and etanercept monotherapy groups except for some skin endpoints. No new safety signals were seen.
cards.watchOut: An industry-run head-to-head with a fixed oral methotrexate dose of 20 mg and no treat-to-target escalation — methotrexate was not optimised the way a determined clinician might (parenteral switch, dose titration), so the trial answers the starting-strategy question better than 'methotrexate pushed to its limit'. The population was early (median disease duration 0.6 years), matching the question's early-treatment framing.
cards.source: Mease PJ et al. Etanercept and Methotrexate as Monotherapy or in Combination for Psoriatic Arthritis: Primary Results From a Randomized, Controlled Phase III Trial. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2019. PMID: 30747501. Registry ID: NCT02376790 (verified against the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: start with the TNF inhibitor, not methotrexate alone — and the combination adds nothing for joints
cards.summary: Synthesis: start with the TNF inhibitor, not methotrexate alone — and the combination adds nothing for joints
cards.people: One double-blind phase III trial, 851 patients, three arms.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 60.9% (etanercept), 65.0% (combination), 50.7% (methotrexate). MDA: 35.9% / 35.7% / 22.9%. Less radiographic progression at week 48 in both etanercept arms. Combination therapy was essentially etanercept monotherapy on joint outcomes, differing only on some skin endpoints.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, albeit a large and definitive one, and etanercept is the only TNF inhibitor tested this way; whether the result generalises to other biologics, or to optimised methotrexate, is inference. Methotrexate's 50.7% ACR20 means half of patients do respond to the cheap oral drug — the trial informs sequencing, not abandonment.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mease PJ et al. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2019 (PMID: 30747501).

shelves.title: Methotrexate for pseudogout: the only randomised trial (26 patients, crossover) found nothing — a 10-patient refractory series is the entire case for it
shelves.question: In adults with calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout), does methotrexate reduce flare frequency or joint damage?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use · Chondrocalcinosis/drug therapy/pathology* · Chronic Disease · Cross-Over Studies · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate/therapeutic use* · Middle Aged · Recurrence · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The randomised evidence is a single small crossover trial: 26 patients with chronic or recurrent calcium pyrophosphate deposition arthropathy received weekly subcutaneous methotrexate 15 mg or placebo for 3 months per period; the disease activity score (DAS44) changed by −0.08 on methotrexate versus −0.13 on placebo (P = 0.44), pain levels remained stable, and the trial's only serious adverse event (bicytopenia) occurred on methotrexate (Finckh A et al., PMID: 25315665). Against that, a retrospective series of 10 patients with refractory disease — persistent polyarthritis, persistent oligoarthritis or very frequently recurring monoarthritis — rated methotrexate a median 7.4 of 10, with physicians judging the response excellent in 2, good in 5 and medium in 3; 2 patients stopped for toxicity, including transient bone marrow aplasia (Andres M et al., PMID: 22832286). Neither study measured flare frequency as its primary outcome, and neither measured joint damage at all — those outcomes in the question are, strictly, untested. Colchicine prophylaxis for the same disease is shelf #2713. Tier C: one tiny trial plus a case series.

cards.headline: Finckh 2014: methotrexate 15 mg/week for 3 months did not beat placebo in chronic-recurrent CPPD — DAS44 change −0.08 vs −0.13 (P = 0.44)
cards.summary: Finckh 2014: methotrexate 15 mg/week for 3 months did not beat placebo in chronic-recurrent CPPD — DAS44 change −0.08 vs −0.13 (P = 0.44)
cards.people: 26 patients with definite CPPD arthropathy — recurrent arthritis or persistent polyarthritis, with an insufficient response to NSAIDs, glucocorticoids or colchicine — randomised double-blind in a crossover trial to weekly subcutaneous injections of methotrexate 15 mg/week or placebo for 3 months per period; 25 treatment periods on methotrexate and 21 on placebo were compared on an intention-to-treat basis. The primary outcome was improvement in the disease activity score based on 44 joints (DAS44).
cards.result: The evolution of the DAS44 was not significantly different between groups (median DAS44 decreased by −0.08 on methotrexate versus −0.13 on placebo after 3 months; P = 0.44). Pain levels remained stable in both groups (median change in VAS pain −1 unit on methotrexate and 0 on placebo; P = 0.43), and none of the secondary outcomes was significantly different. Minor adverse events did not differ in frequency, but the only serious adverse event occurred on methotrexate (bicytopenia). The authors conclude the results suggest no strong effect of methotrexate on disease activity in this older population with chronic or recurrent CPPD arthropathy.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-six patients in a crossover cannot exclude a modest effect, and 3 months of 15 mg/week may under-run a slow-acting DMARD. But it is the only randomised test methotrexate has ever had in this disease, and its point estimates favour placebo.
cards.source: Finckh A et al. Methotrexate in chronic-recurrent calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease: no significant effect in a randomized crossover trial. Arthritis Research & Therapy. 2014. PMID: 25315665. Registry ID: EudraCT 2007-003479-37 (as stated in the record). cards.headline: Andres 2012: in 10 patients with refractory CPP crystal arthritis, methotrexate was rated a median 7.4 of 10 by patients — and stopped for toxicity in 2
cards.summary: Andres 2012: in 10 patients with refractory CPP crystal arthritis, methotrexate was rated a median 7.4 of 10 by patients — and stopped for toxicity in 2
cards.people: Retrospective observational series of 10 patients with refractory calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease — 5 with persistent polyarthritis, 3 with persistent oligoarthritis and 2 with very frequently recurring monoarthritis — treated with methotrexate when NSAIDs, colchicine and glucocorticoids were ineffective, contraindicated or not tolerated. Treatment response was evaluated by the physician (excellent, good, medium, poor or absent) and by the patient on a 10-cm visual analog scale (0 = no effect; 10 = complete resolution of symptoms).
cards.result: The median methotrexate evaluation by patients was 7.4 of 10, and physicians considered the response excellent in 2 patients, good in 5 and medium in 3 — none poor or absent. The safety profile was generally good, but methotrexate was discontinued in 2 patients because of adverse effects: transient bone marrow aplasia and elevation of liver enzymes. The authors conclude methotrexate could be an effective and safe option for refractory CPP arthritis, while noting that additional studies are necessary.
cards.watchOut: Ten selected, refractory patients, no comparator, retrospective — this design cannot distinguish drug effect from natural history, concurrent treatment changes, or the optimism of clinicians who chose the drug. Read alongside Finckh, it says 'worth studying in refractory disease', not 'works'.
cards.source: Andres M et al. Methotrexate is an option for patients with refractory calcium pyrophosphate crystal arthritis. Journal of Clinical Rheumatology. 2012. PMID: 22832286. Registry ID: none in the record (retrospective observational study). cards.headline: Synthesis: unproven — a negative micro-trial and an encouraging anecdote series leave methotrexate in CPPD a MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: unproven — a negative micro-trial and an encouraging anecdote series leave methotrexate in CPPD a MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: One randomised crossover trial (n = 26) and one retrospective series (n = 10): the entire comparative evidence base for methotrexate in CPPD.
cards.result: Randomised: DAS44 change −0.08 vs −0.13 (P = 0.44), pain unchanged, one serious adverse event (bicytopenia) on methotrexate. Observational: median patient rating 7.4 of 10 in refractory disease, with 2 of 10 patients stopping for bone-marrow or liver toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Flare frequency and joint damage — the outcomes in the question — were not the primary outcomes of either study. Any use today is extrapolation, and the marrow toxicity seen in both reports is the predictable price of methotrexate in an elderly population.
cards.source: Synthesis of Finckh A et al. Arthritis Research & Therapy. 2014 (PMID: 25315665); Andres M et al. Journal of Clinical Rheumatology. 2012 (PMID: 22832286).

shelves.title: Plantar fasciitis: a corticosteroid injection buys about a month of modest pain relief and nothing beyond it — fascia rupture and infection are rare but real
shelves.question: In adults with plantar fasciitis, does a corticosteroid injection give more than short-term relief, and what harms follow?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cohort Studies · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage/analogs & derivatives · Double-Blind Method · Fasciitis, Plantar/complications/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · Female · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Injections · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/diagnostic imaging/etiology/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome · *Ultrasonography, Interventional
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by time. The one well-blinded placebo-controlled trial found a real but brief effect: in 82 patients, a single ultrasound-guided dexamethasone injection beat saline by 10.9 points on a 0–100 pain scale at 4 weeks (95% CI 1.4 to 20.4; P = .03), with no significant pain difference at 8 or 12 weeks, though fascia thickness stayed lower for three months (McMillan AM et al., PMID: 22619193). The Cochrane synthesis of 39 trials (2,492 adults) agrees and adds the scale of the benefit: versus placebo or no treatment, heel pain was lower by a mean of 6.38 points on a 0–100 scale in the first month (low-quality evidence; the confidence interval includes only a marginal clinical benefit against a minimal important difference of 8), and there was no difference at 1–6 months (mean difference −3.47; 95% CI −8.43 to 1.48) (David JA et al., PMID: 28602048). Harms are uncommon but not zero: pooling 21 trials that reported adverse events, there were two plantar fascia ruptures and three injection-site infections among 699 participants in steroid arms, plus 27 less serious short-term events — and the reviewers warn that harms were under-reported, so a higher risk cannot be ruled out; the case-report harms patients ask about (fat-pad atrophy) were not quantified in any trial. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (small benefit in the first month) / LIKELY (no difference beyond the short term). Tier C: the pooled evidence is rated low to very low quality and the harm estimates rest on incomplete reporting.

cards.headline: McMillan 2012: one ultrasound-guided dexamethasone injection beat placebo by 10.9 pain points at 4 weeks — and by nothing significant at 8 or 12 weeks
cards.summary: McMillan 2012: one ultrasound-guided dexamethasone injection beat placebo by 10.9 pain points at 4 weeks — and by nothing significant at 8 or 12 weeks
cards.people: 82 people with a clinical and ultrasound diagnosis of plantar fasciitis unrelated to systemic inflammatory disease, in a randomised, investigator- and participant-blinded, placebo-controlled trial at a university clinic in Melbourne. Intervention: ultrasound-guided injection of 1 mL of 4 mg/mL dexamethasone sodium phosphate versus 1 mL normal saline, both after an ultrasound-guided posterior tibial nerve block. Outcomes: foot-health pain score (0–100) and ultrasound fascia thickness at 4, 8 and 12 weeks.
cards.result: Pain reduction at 4 weeks favoured dexamethasone by 10.9 points (95% CI 1.4 to 20.4; P = .03); the number needed to treat for one successful pain outcome at 4 weeks was 2.93. Between-group pain differences at 8 and 12 weeks were not statistically significant. Fascia thickness favoured dexamethasone at 4 weeks (−0.35 mm), 8 weeks (−0.39 mm) and 12 weeks (−0.43 mm). No adverse events associated with the intervention were reported.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own conclusion is the shelf's message: significant pain relief did not continue beyond four weeks. The persistent thinning of the fascia on ultrasound is an imaging finding, not a patient benefit — pain, the outcome patients feel, had converged by 8 weeks. A single trial of 82 patients also cannot measure rare harms such as fascia rupture.
cards.source: McMillan AM et al. Ultrasound guided corticosteroid injection for plantar fasciitis: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2012. PMID: 22619193. Registry ID: ACTRN12610000239066. cards.headline: David 2017 (Cochrane): 39 trials, 2,492 adults — steroid injection may slightly reduce heel pain for up to one month (mean 6.4 points on a 100-point scale) and not after; two fascia ruptures and three infections were reported among 699 steroid-arm participants
cards.summary: David 2017 (Cochrane): 39 trials, 2,492 adults — steroid injection may slightly reduce heel pain for up to one month (mean 6.4 points on a 100-point scale) and not after; two fascia ruptures and three infections were reported among 699 steroid-arm participants
cards.people: Cochrane review of 39 studies (36 randomised and 3 quasi-randomised trials) of corticosteroid injection for plantar heel pain in 2,492 adults, mostly small trials (median 59 participants) in outpatient specialty clinics in 17 countries, with follow-up from one month to over two years. Eight trials (724 participants) compared steroid injection with placebo or no treatment.
cards.result: Versus placebo or no treatment, steroid injection may lower heel pain in the short term (< 1 month): mean difference −6.38 points on a 0–100 visual analogue scale (95% CI −11.13 to −1.64; 350 participants, 5 studies; low-quality evidence) — against a minimal clinically important difference of 8, the interval includes only a marginal benefit, and the benefit shrank further when restricted to the three placebo-controlled trials. In the medium term (1–6 months) there was no difference (mean difference −3.47; 95% CI −8.43 to 1.48; low-quality evidence), and very low-quality evidence for no effect on function and fewer treatment failures. In an exploratory pooling of 21 trials reporting adverse events (699 participants in steroid arms): two ruptures of the plantar fascia, three injection-site infections, and 27 less serious short-term adverse events. The reviewers rated almost all evidence very low quality and warned harms were under-reported.
cards.watchOut: Nearly every trial was at high risk of bias in at least one domain, chiefly blinding — so even the modest one-month benefit may be overstated. The review could not quantify the harms patients most fear with repeated injections (fat-pad atrophy, rupture with multiple doses): absence of quantification is not absence of risk. Comparisons with shock-wave therapy, platelet-rich plasma and other injectables were all rated very low quality; shock-wave therapy for chronic recalcitrant plantar fasciitis is homed at shelf #1473 and stretching at #1024.
cards.source: David JA et al. Injected corticosteroids for treating plantar heel pain in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28602048. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: an injection is a one-month analgesic, not a treatment for the condition — SPLIT (POSSIBLE short-term / no difference beyond)
cards.summary: Synthesis: an injection is a one-month analgesic, not a treatment for the condition — SPLIT (POSSIBLE short-term / no difference beyond)
cards.people: One blinded placebo-controlled trial (n = 82) and a Cochrane synthesis of 39 trials (2,492 adults) of corticosteroid injection for plantar heel pain/fasciitis.
cards.result: Short term (< 1 month): pain lower by ~6–11 points on 0–100 scales versus placebo — at or below the threshold patients can reliably feel. Medium term (1–6 months): no difference (pooled mean difference −3.47, CI crossing zero). Harms in trial reporting: 2 fascia ruptures and 3 injection-site infections per 699 injected participants, with under-reporting acknowledged. A patient choosing an injection is choosing a few weeks of somewhat less pain while the condition runs its course — a legitimate choice when made with that expectation, and a misleading one when sold as a cure.
cards.watchOut: Both sources concern a single injection in trial settings; neither licenses a programme of repeated injections, whose cumulative harm (rupture, fat-pad atrophy) has never been trialled. Plantar fasciitis usually resolves over months with load management — the natural history is the invisible third arm of every trial here.
cards.source: Synthesis of McMillan AM et al. BMJ. 2012 (PMID: 22619193); David JA et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28602048).

shelves.title: Lesinurad added to allopurinol: urate target reached by 54–66% versus 23–28% in two large trials — flares and tophi unmoved, kidneys paying at the higher dose, and the drug later discontinued
shelves.question: In adults with gout whose serum urate remains above target on allopurinol, does adding lesinurad increase the proportion reaching target urate — and does it reduce flares or tophi?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Allopurinol/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Female · Gout/drug therapy · Gout Suppressants/administration & dosage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Thioglycolates/administration & dosage · Triazoles/administration & dosage · United States · Uricosuric Agents/administration & dosage · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the blood test, not yet for the disease. Two large phase 3 trials agree closely: adding lesinurad 200 mg to allopurinol put 54.2% (CLEAR 1, Saag KG et al., PMID: 27564409) and 55.4% (CLEAR 2, Bardin T et al., PMID: 27821644) of patients at the <6.0 mg/dL urate target at month 6, versus 27.9% and 23.3% on allopurinol alone (p<0.0001 in both). But in neither trial did the outcomes patients feel — gout flare rates in months 7–12, or complete resolution of tophi — differ significantly, so the proven benefit is a surrogate. The harm is renal and dose-related: creatinine elevations of at least 1.5× baseline occurred in 5.9% on 200 mg and 15.0% on the unmarketed 400 mg dose versus 3.4% on allopurinol alone in CLEAR 2, with serious treatment-emergent events at 9.5% on 400 mg versus 3.9% on allopurinol alone. Lesinurad was discontinued in the United States in February 2019 for business reasons, not for safety or efficacy findings — so this shelf now reads as the evidence record for a drug patients can no longer be started on there. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): lesinurad reliably delivers urate target on top of allopurinol at the 200 mg dose with a modest renal price; a flare or tophus benefit was never shown.

cards.headline: Saag 2017 (CLEAR 1): urate target at month 6 in 54.2% on lesinurad 200 mg and 59.2% on 400 mg versus 27.9% on allopurinol alone (p<0.0001) — flares and tophi not significantly different
cards.summary: Saag 2017 (CLEAR 1): urate target at month 6 in 54.2% on lesinurad 200 mg and 59.2% on 400 mg versus 27.9% on allopurinol alone (p<0.0001) — flares and tophi not significantly different
cards.people: 603 predominantly male US patients (mean age 51.9 years, mean gout duration 11.8 years, baseline serum urate 6.94 mg/dL) taking at least 300 mg allopurinol (200 mg in moderate renal impairment) with screening urate ≥6.5 mg/dL and at least two gout flares in the previous year, randomised to lesinurad 200 mg or 400 mg daily added to allopurinol, or placebo added to allopurinol, for 12 months.
cards.result: The proportion reaching serum urate <6.0 mg/dL at month 6 was 54.2% on lesinurad 200 mg and 59.2% on 400 mg versus 27.9% on allopurinol alone (p<0.0001 for both comparisons), with the absolute rates printed alongside. Lesinurad was not significantly superior on the key secondary endpoints: mean gout flare rate requiring treatment in months 7–12, and complete resolution of at least one target tophus by month 12. The 200 mg dose's safety profile was comparable to allopurinol alone except for higher incidences of predominantly reversible serum creatinine elevations.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a laboratory target at month 6 in patients pre-selected for flares — yet flares themselves did not fall over the following six months, the interval the trial allowed. A urate surrogate that does not convert into fewer flares within a year may still convert later (urate lowering is slow to dissolve crystal load), but that conversion is asserted, not shown, in this record.
cards.source: Saag KG et al. Lesinurad Combined With Allopurinol: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study in Gout Patients With an Inadequate Response to Standard-of-Care Allopurinol (a US-Based Study). Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2017. PMID: 27564409. Registry ID: NCT01510158. cards.headline: Bardin 2017 (CLEAR 2): target reached by 55.4% (200 mg) and 66.5% (400 mg) versus 23.3% — renal adverse events 5.9% and 15.0% versus 4.9%, creatinine ≥1.5× baseline in up to 15.0%
cards.summary: Bardin 2017 (CLEAR 2): target reached by 55.4% (200 mg) and 66.5% (400 mg) versus 23.3% — renal adverse events 5.9% and 15.0% versus 4.9%, creatinine ≥1.5× baseline in up to 15.0%
cards.people: 610 predominantly male patients in a multinational trial (mean age 51.2 years, mean gout duration 11.5 years, baseline serum urate 6.9 mg/dL) on allopurinol at least 300 mg (200 mg in moderate renal impairment) with screening urate ≥6.5 mg/dL and at least two flares in the prior year, randomised to lesinurad 200 mg or 400 mg added to allopurinol or allopurinol alone for 12 months.
cards.result: Serum urate <6.0 mg/dL at month 6 was achieved by 55.4% on lesinurad 200 mg and 66.5% on 400 mg versus 23.3% on allopurinol alone (p<0.0001 for both). No key secondary endpoint (flare rate in months 7–12; complete resolution of one or more target tophi) differed significantly in lesinurad's favour. Renal-related adverse events occurred in 5.9% (200 mg), 15.0% (400 mg) and 4.9% (allopurinol alone); serum creatinine elevation of at least 1.5× baseline in 5.9%, 15.0% and 3.4% respectively; serious treatment-emergent adverse events in 4.4%, 9.5% and 3.9%.
cards.watchOut: The 400 mg dose — the one with the best urate numbers — carried a threefold renal-event rate and was not the marketed dose; quoting CLEAR results without the dose split overstates the usable benefit. Both CLEAR trials enrolled patients with preserved-enough renal function to receive the drug, so the renal signal in real-world kidney disease would plausibly be worse.
cards.source: Bardin T et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant trials, one surrogate won, every clinical endpoint drawn — and a renal cost that rises steeply with dose
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant trials, one surrogate won, every clinical endpoint drawn — and a renal cost that rises steeply with dose
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind phase 3 trials totalling 1,213 patients with gout inadequately controlled on allopurinol (CLEAR 1, US; CLEAR 2, multinational), each testing lesinurad 200 mg and 400 mg added to allopurinol over 12 months.
cards.result: Urate target <6.0 mg/dL at month 6: 54.2% and 55.4% on 200 mg, 59.2% and 66.5% on 400 mg, versus 27.9% and 23.3% on allopurinol alone. Flares (months 7–12) and tophus resolution: no significant benefit in either trial. Renal harm: creatinine ≥1.5× baseline in 5.9% (200 mg) and 15.0% (400 mg) versus 3.4% (CLEAR 2). Availability: lesinurad was discontinued in the US in February 2019 for business reasons, not safety or efficacy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with the harm on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Urate is a surrogate with an unusually strong causal claim in gout, which is why this is POSSIBLE (benefit) rather than MAYBE — but the trials' own flare and tophus endpoints are the honest counterweight, and any future uricosuric should be held to the same split presentation. Tier C is not set: the base is two large concordant phase 3 trials.
cards.source: Synthesis of Saag KG et al. Arthritis & Rheumatology. 2017 (PMID: 27564409); Bardin T et al. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2017 (PMID: 27821644).

shelves.title: Noisy knees do predict arthritis symptoms: crepitus 'always' carried 3.0-fold odds of incident symptomatic knee osteoarthritis in 3,495 people — but most cases arose in knees already abnormal on X-ray
shelves.question: Do noisy, clicking knees (crepitus) mean arthritis is coming — and does anything prevent it or help?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Biomechanical Phenomena · Female · Humans · Incidence · Knee Joint/diagnostic imaging/physiopathology · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/diagnostic imaging/epidemiology/physiopathology · Prognosis · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Sound · Time Factors · United States/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — as a prognostic signal, not a treatment effect. In the Osteoarthritis Initiative cohort (3,495 people without symptomatic knee osteoarthritis at baseline, followed to 48 months), the odds of developing symptomatic knee osteoarthritis rose stepwise with crepitus frequency: adjusted odds ratios 1.5 (rarely), 1.8 (sometimes), 2.2 (often) and 3.0 (always) versus never (p<0.0001 for trend). The catch matters for the visitor's question: knees that already had radiographic osteoarthritis without symptoms were 26% of observations but contributed over 75% of the incident cases — crepitus mostly flags knees whose joint is already changed, and this record tests no treatment or prevention. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): frequent knee crepitus is a genuine risk marker for symptomatic osteoarthritis within four years, strongest where X-ray change already exists; nothing in this evidence says the noise itself damages the joint or that any intervention prevents the outcome.

cards.headline: Lo 2018: adjusted odds of incident symptomatic knee OA rose 1.5 → 1.8 → 2.2 → 3.0 across crepitus frequency (never to always), p<0.0001 for trend, in 3,495 people
cards.summary: Lo 2018: adjusted odds of incident symptomatic knee OA rose 1.5 → 1.8 → 2.2 → 3.0 across crepitus frequency (never to always), p<0.0001 for trend, in 3,495 people
cards.people: 3,495 participants (42.2% male; mean age 61.1 ± 9.2 years; mean BMI 28.2 ± 4.7 kg/m²) without symptomatic knee osteoarthritis at baseline in the multicentre US Osteoarthritis Initiative cohort; crepitus assessed by questionnaire at baseline and 12, 24 and 36 months; frequent pain and radiographs annually to 48 months; symptomatic OA defined as frequent symptoms plus Kellgren/Lawrence grade ≥2.
cards.result: The odds of incident symptomatic osteoarthritis were higher with greater crepitus frequency (adjusted for age, sex and BMI): rarely 1.5, sometimes 1.8, often 2.2, always 3.0, versus never as referent (p<0.0001 for trend). The group with radiographic OA at baseline but no symptoms contributed 26% of observations but more than 75% of incident symptomatic cases.
cards.watchOut: Observational and prognostic: crepitus may simply be the audible sign of cartilage change already present (most cases came from radiographically abnormal knees), patellofemoral OA was not systematically evaluated, and adjustment covered only age, sex and BMI. No intervention was tested — the record cannot say whether anything prevents or helps.
cards.source: Lo GH et al. Subjective Crepitus as a Risk Factor for Incident Symptomatic Knee Osteoarthritis: Data From the Osteoarthritis Initiative. Arthritis Care & Research. 2018. PMID: 28470832. shelves.title: Baricitinib beats adalimumab head-to-head in RA-BEAM: ACR20 at week 12 in 70% versus 61% (and 40% on placebo), with less radiographic progression than placebo
shelves.question: In rheumatoid arthritis with inadequate response to conventional DMARDs, does baricitinib beat adalimumab on disease activity when both are combined with methotrexate?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Administration, Oral · Adult · Antirheumatic Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · Azetidines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Janus Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · Joints/diagnostic imaging/pathology · Male · Methotrexate/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Purines · Pyrazoles · Radiography · Sulfonamides/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in RA-BEAM, 1,307 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis and inadequate response to methotrexate (all continuing methotrexate) were randomised to baricitinib 4 mg daily, adalimumab 40 mg every other week, or placebo. ACR20 at week 12: 70% on baricitinib versus 61% on adalimumab (p=0.014) and 40% on placebo (p<0.001). Radiographic progression at week 24 was lower on baricitinib than placebo (mean mTSS change 0.41 versus 0.90; p<0.001). The trial's patient-reported-outcome analysis found baricitinib also beat adalimumab on function, pain, fatigue and quality of life at week 12, maintained to week 52. Adverse events including infections were more frequent on baricitinib and adalimumab than placebo through week 24; cancers were reported in five patients (two on baricitinib, three on placebo); baricitinib lowered neutrophil counts and raised creatinine and LDL cholesterol. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): one large phase 3 trial puts the oral JAK inhibitor ahead of adalimumab on response, structure and symptoms — a single-trial superiority claim, so Tier C.

cards.headline: Taylor 2017 (RA-BEAM): ACR20 at week 12 in 70% on baricitinib versus 61% on adalimumab (p=0.014) and 40% on placebo; mTSS progression 0.41 versus 0.90 at week 24
cards.summary: Taylor 2017 (RA-BEAM): ACR20 at week 12 in 70% on baricitinib versus 61% on adalimumab (p=0.014) and 40% on placebo; mTSS progression 0.41 versus 0.90 at week 24
cards.people: 1,307 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis receiving background methotrexate, randomised 3:3:2 to placebo (switched to baricitinib after 24 weeks), baricitinib 4 mg once daily, or adalimumab 40 mg every other week, over 52 weeks.
cards.result: ACR20 response at week 12 (primary endpoint): 70% with baricitinib versus 40% with placebo (p<0.001) and 61% with adalimumab (p=0.014 for baricitinib versus adalimumab). Radiographic progression (mTSS) at week 24: mean change 0.41 on baricitinib versus 0.90 on placebo (p<0.001). Adverse events, including infections, were more frequent through week 24 with baricitinib and adalimumab than placebo; cancers in five patients (two baricitinib, three placebo); baricitinib was associated with reduced neutrophil counts and increased creatinine and LDL cholesterol.
cards.watchOut: One trial, sponsored by the manufacturer, with the placebo arm switched to baricitinib at week 24 — so long-term structure and safety comparisons rest on the active-comparator period; superiority over adalimumab is a 9-percentage-point ACR20 difference, real but not large.
cards.source: Taylor PC et al. Baricitinib versus Placebo or Adalimumab in Rheumatoid Arthritis. New England Journal of Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28199814. Registry ID: NCT01710358. cards.headline: Keystone 2017 (RA-BEAM outcomes analysis): baricitinib beat both placebo and adalimumab on function, pain, fatigue, morning stiffness and quality of life at week 12, maintained to week 52
cards.summary: Keystone 2017 (RA-BEAM outcomes analysis): baricitinib beat both placebo and adalimumab on function, pain, fatigue, morning stiffness and quality of life at week 12, maintained to week 52
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised phase 3 trial (Keystone 2017, RA-BEAM)
cards.people: The RA-BEAM population: placebo n=488, baricitinib 4 mg daily n=487, adalimumab 40 mg biweekly n=330, all with background methotrexate; patient-reported outcomes included HAQ-DI, pain, FACIT-F fatigue, SF-36, EQ-5D, work productivity and daily-diary morning joint stiffness, worst tiredness and worst joint pain.
cards.result: Compared with placebo and adalimumab, baricitinib showed statistically significant improvements (p≤0.05) in HAQ-DI, patient's global assessment, pain, FACIT-F, SF-36 physical component score, EQ-5D index scores and WPAI-RA daily activity at week 12, maintained for measures assessed to week 52; diary measures (morning stiffness duration and severity, worst tiredness, worst joint pain) also significantly favoured baricitinib over placebo and adalimumab at week 12.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the same single trial, reporting significance across many correlated patient-reported outcomes without absolute effect sizes in the abstract — supportive texture for RA-BEAM, not independent confirmation.

shelves.title: ADACTA: tocilizumab alone beats adalimumab alone when methotrexate cannot be used — DAS28 fell 3.3 versus 1.8 points at 24 weeks
shelves.question: In rheumatoid arthritis when methotrexate cannot be used, is tocilizumab monotherapy superior to adalimumab monotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/therapy · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — ADACTA randomised 325 patients with severe rheumatoid arthritis who were intolerant to methotrexate or inappropriate for it to tocilizumab 8 mg/kg intravenously every 4 weeks or adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks (each with the other's placebo) for 24 weeks. Mean DAS28 change was −3.3 on tocilizumab versus −1.8 on adalimumab (difference −1.5, 95% CI −1.8 to −1.1; p<0.0001). Serious adverse events were similar (12% tocilizumab versus 10% adalimumab); tocilizumab produced more raised LDL cholesterol, raised alanine aminotransferase, and reduced platelet and neutrophil counts. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the one head-to-head monotherapy trial favours tocilizumab clearly on disease activity — a single-trial claim, so Tier C.

cards.headline: Gabay 2013 (ADACTA): DAS28 change −3.3 on tocilizumab versus −1.8 on adalimumab at week 24 (difference −1.5, p<0.0001); serious adverse events 12% versus 10%
cards.summary: Gabay 2013 (ADACTA): DAS28 change −3.3 on tocilizumab versus −1.8 on adalimumab at week 24 (difference −1.5, p<0.0001); serious adverse events 12% versus 10%
cards.people: 326 enrolled patients (intention-to-treat 325: tocilizumab n=163, adalimumab n=162) aged at least 18 years with severe rheumatoid arthritis for at least 6 months who were intolerant to methotrexate or inappropriate for continued methotrexate, at 76 centres in 15 countries; double-dummy design (tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks plus placebo SC every 2 weeks, or adalimumab 40 mg SC every 2 weeks plus placebo IV every 4 weeks) for 24 weeks.
cards.result: Week-24 mean change in DAS28 was −3.3 in the tocilizumab group versus −1.8 in the adalimumab group (difference −1.5, 95% CI −1.8 to −1.1; p<0.0001). Serious adverse events: 19 of 162 (12%) on tocilizumab versus 16 of 162 (10%) on adalimumab. More patients on tocilizumab had increased LDL cholesterol, increased alanine aminotransferase, and reduced platelet and neutrophil counts.
cards.watchOut: A single 24-week, sponsor-run superiority trial in a selected methotrexate-inappropriate population; DAS28 contains an acute-phase component that IL-6 blockade suppresses directly, which flatters tocilizumab on this particular score — a known interpretive caveat for the −1.5 difference.
cards.source: Gabay C et al. Tocilizumab monotherapy versus adalimumab monotherapy for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (ADACTA): a randomised, double-blind, controlled phase 4 trial. randomised phase 4 trial (gabay 2013, adacta) 326 enrolled patients (intention-to-treat 325: tocilizumab n=163, adalimumab n=162) aged at least 18 years with severe rheumatoid arthritis for at least 6 months who were intolerant to methotrexate or inappropriate for continued methotrexate, at 76 centres in 15 countries; double-dummy design (tocilizumab 8 mg/kg iv every 4 weeks plus placebo sc every 2 weeks, or adalimumab 40 mg sc every 2 weeks plus placebo iv every 4 weeks) for 24 weeks. week-24 mean change in das28 was −3.3 in the tocilizumab group versus −1.8 in the adalimumab group (difference −1.5, 95% ci −1.8 to −1.1; p<0.0001). serious adverse events: 19 of 162 (12%) on tocilizumab versus 16 of 162 (10%) on adalimumab. more patients on tocilizumab had increased ldl cholesterol, increased alanine aminotransferase, and reduced platelet and neutrophil counts. a single 24-week, sponsor-run superiority trial in a selected methotrexate-inappropriate population; das28 contains an acute-phase component that il-6 blockade suppresses directly, which flatters tocilizumab on this particular score — a known interpretive caveat for the −1.5 difference. gabay c et al. tocilizumab monotherapy versus adalimumab monotherapy for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis (adacta): a randomised, double-blind, controlled phase 4 trial. the lancet. 2013. pmid: 23515142. registry id: nct01119859. mesh: adalimumab · adult · aged · antibodies, monoclonal, humanized/therapeutic use · antirheumatic agents/therapeutic use · arthritis, rheumatoid/therapy · double-blind method · female · humans · male · middle aged

shelves.title: Guselkumab works in psoriatic arthritis in both DISCOVER trials: ACR20 at week 24 in 52–64% versus 22–33% on placebo, in biologic-naive and TNF-experienced patients alike
shelves.question: In active psoriatic arthritis, does guselkumab improve joint and skin responses versus placebo — in biologic-naive patients and after TNF inhibitors?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Psoriatic/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two phase 3 trials agree. DISCOVER-1 (381 patients, about 30% previously treated with TNF inhibitors): ACR20 at week 24 in 59% on guselkumab every 4 weeks and 52% every 8 weeks versus 22% on placebo (differences 37 and 30 percentage points; both p<0.0001). DISCOVER-2 (741 biologic-naive patients): 64% and 64% versus 33% (differences 31 points each; both p<0.0001). Serious adverse events to week 24 were no more frequent on guselkumab than placebo in either trial (DISCOVER-1: 0% and 3% versus 4%; DISCOVER-2: 3% and 1% versus 3%), and no guselkumab-treated patient died in DISCOVER-1 or had more serious infections than placebo overall. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two large concordant trials, both dosing schedules, across biologic-naive and TNF-experienced disease.

cards.headline: Deodhar 2020 (DISCOVER-1): ACR20 at week 24 in 59% (every 4 weeks) and 52% (every 8 weeks) versus 22% on placebo — differences 37 and 30 points, both p<0.0001

cards.people: 381 adults with active psoriatic arthritis (at least three swollen and three tender joints, CRP ≥0.3 mg/dL) despite standard therapies at 86 sites in 13 countries, about 30% previously treated with one or two TNF inhibitors, randomised to guselkumab 100 mg every 4 weeks (n=128), guselkumab 100 mg at weeks 0 and 4 then every 8 weeks (n=127), or placebo (n=126); 362 continued to week 24.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 59% (76/128) on guselkumab every 4 weeks and 52% (66/127) every 8 weeks versus 22% (28/126) on placebo — percentage differences 37% (95% CI 26–48) and 30% (19–41), both p<0.0001. Serious adverse events to week 24: none on every-4-weeks guselkumab, four (3%) on every-8-weeks, five (4%) on placebo; one placebo patient died of cardiac failure and two had serious infections; no guselkumab-treated patient died or had a serious infection.
cards.watchOut: Placebo comparison ends at week 24 by design, and skin outcomes — half the candidate question — are reported in the full text rather than the abstract record carded here; the joint result is the verified core of this shelf.

cards.people: 741 biologic-naive patients with active psoriatic arthritis (at least five swollen and five tender joints, CRP ≥0.6 mg/dL) despite standard therapies at 118 sites in 13 countries, randomised to guselkumab 100 mg every 4 weeks (n=246), guselkumab at weeks 0 and 4 then every 8 weeks (n=248), or placebo (n=247); 739 started treatment and 716 continued to week 24.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24: 64% (156/245) on guselkumab every 4 weeks and 64% (159/248) every 8 weeks versus 33% (81/246) on placebo — percentage differences 31% (95% CI 22–39) and 31% (23–40), both p<0.0001. No deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: Biologic-naive patients with high baseline activity (≥5 swollen and tender joints) — response rates will be lower in milder or heavily pre-treated real-world disease; 24 weeks says nothing about long-term joint damage or drug survival.

shelves.title: HOPE: six weeks of prednisolone 10 mg relieves inflammatory hand osteoarthritis pain — finger pain fell 21.5 points versus 5.2 on placebo
shelves.question: In inflammatory hand osteoarthritis, does a short course of prednisolone 10 mg reduce finger pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Hand · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis/drug therapy · Prednisolone/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the HOPE trial randomised 92 patients with painful hand osteoarthritis and ultrasound/clinical signs of synovial inflammation to prednisolone 10 mg daily or placebo for 6 weeks (then a 2-week taper and 6 weeks off treatment). Finger pain (100-mm VAS) fell by 21.5 points on prednisolone versus 5.2 on placebo — a between-group difference of −16.5 (95% CI −26.1 to −6.9; p=0.0007). Non-serious adverse events were similar; five serious adverse events occurred (one myocardial infarction on prednisolone; four events on placebo). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a short prednisolone course works for an inflammatory hand-OA flare — in one small, carefully phenotyped trial of patients selected for synovitis and an NSAID-washout flare, so Tier C.

cards.headline: Kroon 2019 (HOPE): finger pain change −21.5 on prednisolone versus −5.2 on placebo at week 6 (difference −16.5, p=0.0007); 91% completed in both arms
cards.summary: Kroon 2019 (HOPE): finger pain change −21.5 on prednisolone versus −5.2 on placebo at week 6 (difference −16.5, p=0.0007); 91% completed in both arms
cards.people: 92 adults with symptomatic hand osteoarthritis and signs of inflammation in DIP/PIP joints (≥4 joints with nodes, ≥1 with soft swelling or erythema, ≥1 with power Doppler signal or grade ≥2 synovial thickening, and finger pain ≥30 mm on a 100-mm VAS that flared ≥20 mm during a 48-hour NSAID washout) at two Dutch rheumatology sites, randomised to prednisolone 10 mg daily (n=46) or placebo (n=46) for 6 weeks, followed by a 2-week taper and 6-week follow-up; 42 per group completed the 14-week study.
cards.result: Mean change in VAS finger pain at week 6: −21.5 (SD 21.7) on prednisolone versus −5.2 (24.3) on placebo — between-group difference −16.5 (95% CI −26.1 to −6.9; p=0.0007). Non-serious adverse events were similar between groups. Five serious adverse events: one in the prednisolone group (myocardial infarction) and four in the placebo group. Discontinuation for adverse events: one (2%) on prednisolone, three (7%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-two highly selected patients — most screened patients were excluded, usually for absent synovial inflammation or no washout flare — so the result applies to inflammatory flares of hand OA, not everyday hand OA pain; durability beyond the taper is limited in this record.
cards.source: Kroon FPB et al. Results of a 6-week treatment with 10 mg prednisolone in patients with hand osteoarthritis (HOPE): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. 2019. PMID: 31727410. Registry ID: NTR5263. shelves.title: Metformin for knee osteoarthritis pain: 11.4 mm better than placebo on a 100-mm scale at 6 months — statistically real, below the 15-mm difference patients were said to need
shelves.question: In overweight or obese adults with knee osteoarthritis, does metformin reduce knee pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Metformin/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Obesity/complications/drug therapy · Osteoarthritis, Knee/drug therapy/complications · Overweight/complications/drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Diarrhea/chemically induced/epidemiology · Arthralgia/diagnosis/drug therapy/etiology · Treatment Outcome · Visual Analog Scale · Follow-Up Studies · Delayed-Action Preparations/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a community-based telemedicine trial randomised 107 people with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis and BMI ≥25 to metformin 2,000 mg/day or placebo for 6 months. Knee pain (100-mm VAS) fell 31.3 mm on metformin and 18.9 mm on placebo — a between-group difference of −11.4 mm (95% CI −20.1 to −2.6; p=0.01; standardised effect 0.43). That is smaller than the trial's own stated minimum clinically important difference of 15 mm. Diarrhoea occurred in 15% on metformin versus 8% on placebo, and abdominal discomfort in 13% versus 9%. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real but modest average pain effect in one small trial, awaiting the larger confirmatory trial the authors call for — Tier C.

cards.headline: Pan 2025: pain change −31.3 mm on metformin versus −18.9 mm on placebo (difference −11.4 mm, p=0.01); diarrhoea 15% versus 8%
cards.summary: Pan 2025: pain change −31.3 mm on metformin versus −18.9 mm on placebo (difference −11.4 mm, p=0.01); diarrhoea 15% versus 8%
cards.people: 107 community-recruited participants in Victoria, Australia, with knee pain for at least 6 months, pain score >40 mm on a 100-mm VAS, and BMI ≥25 (mean age 58.8 years, 68% female), randomised to oral metformin 2,000 mg/day (n=54) or identical placebo (n=53) for 6 months in a double-blind telemedicine trial; 88 (82%) completed.
cards.result: Mean change in VAS knee pain at 6 months: −31.3 mm on metformin versus −18.9 mm on placebo (between-group difference −11.4 mm, 95% CI −20.1 to −2.6; p=0.01), a standardised effect size of 0.43 (0.02–0.83). The trial's stated minimum clinically important difference was 15 mm. Most common adverse events: diarrhoea in 8 (15%) on metformin versus 4 (8%) on placebo; abdominal discomfort in 7 (13%) versus 5 (9%).
cards.watchOut: A single modest-sized trial whose average effect sits below its own clinical-importance threshold — some patients may gain meaningfully while the average does not reach 15 mm; remote recruitment and follow-up, and 18% non-completion, add uncertainty. The authors state confirmation in a larger trial is warranted.
