shelves.title: Genicular artery embolisation no better than a sham procedure for knee osteoarthritis pain: 21.4 versus 18.4 points of pain reduction at 4 months
shelves.question: For symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, does genicular artery embolisation reduce pain versus sham embolisation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Osteoarthritis, Knee/therapy · Female · Male · Embolization, Therapeutic/methods · Middle Aged · Double-Blind Method · Aged · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome · Netherlands
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in a double-blind sham-controlled trial, 58 adults with symptomatic mild-to-moderate knee osteoarthritis not improving with conservative treatment were randomised to real or sham genicular artery embolisation. At 4 months, KOOS pain improved 21.4 points (95% CI 13.9–28.8) with embolisation and 18.4 points (11.6–25.1) with sham — a between-group difference of 3.0 points (−7.1 to 13.0), effect size d=0.15, with group allocation not a significant contributor (p=0.31). No serious adverse events occurred; 23 mild adverse events occurred in the embolisation group and 5 in the sham group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the large improvements after an invasive knee procedure were produced equally by its sham — the honest headline for embolisation in mild-to-moderate disease.

cards.headline: van Zadelhoff 2024: KOOS pain reduction 21.4 (GAE) versus 18.4 (sham) at 4 months — difference 3.0 points (CI −7.1 to 13.0), p=0.31; mild adverse events 23 versus 5
cards.summary: van Zadelhoff 2024: KOOS pain reduction 21.4 (GAE) versus 18.4 (sham) at 4 months — difference 3.0 points (CI −7.1 to 13.0), p=0.31; mild adverse events 23 versus 5
cards.people: 58 adults with symptomatic mild-to-moderate knee osteoarthritis not improving with conservative treatment at a single university centre in Rotterdam, Netherlands, randomised to genicular artery embolisation (n=29) or sham embolisation (n=29), double-blind, with 4-month follow-up; all participants completed the study.
cards.result: Mean pain reduction (KOOS pain subscale, 0–100) after 4 months: 21.4 points (95% CI 13.9–28.8) in the embolisation group and 18.4 points (11.6–25.1) in the sham group; between-group difference 3.0 (95% CI −7.1 to 13.0), Cohen's d=0.15 (−0.37 to 0.66); group allocation was not a significant contributor to pain reduction (p=0.31). No serious adverse events occurred; 23 mild adverse events in the embolisation group and 5 in the sham group.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 58 patients with mild-to-moderate disease and only 4 months of follow-up — it cannot exclude a small effect (the CI spans −7.1 to 13.0) or speak to severe OA; but it is exactly the sham-controlled design this procedure needed, and it found the procedure's ritual, not its embolisation, doing the work.

shelves.title: Topical capsaicin eases osteoarthritis pain for up to 3 months (SMD −0.84) — and burns: application-site burning RR 5.56, number-needed-to-harm 3
shelves.question: Does topical capsaicin cream relieve osteoarthritis pain versus placebo cream?
shelves.mesh: Capsaicin/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Humans · Osteoarthritis/drug therapy · Administration, Topical · Pain/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a 2024 systematic review pooled eight double-blind RCTs (498 patients) of topical capsaicin (0.0125%–5%) versus placebo in osteoarthritis: pain severity on visual analogue scale was lower with capsaicin (standardised mean difference −0.84, 95% CI −1.48 to −0.19; p=0.01). The trade-off is on the face of the result: burning sensation at the application site was far more common (risk ratio 5.56, 1.75–17.69; p=0.004; number-needed-to-harm 3). The reviewers rate the certainty low to very low, with short study durations, small samples and high heterogeneity; follow-up extended only to 3 months. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a genuine short-term pain effect for patients who cannot take NSAIDs, bought with predictable local burning — the publication names no branded product or company, and preparations vary widely in strength.

cards.headline: Tshering 2024: pain SMD −0.84 versus placebo across 8 RCTs (498 patients); burning RR 5.56 with number-needed-to-harm 3; certainty low to very low
cards.summary: Tshering 2024: pain SMD −0.84 versus placebo across 8 RCTs (498 patients); burning RR 5.56 with number-needed-to-harm 3; certainty low to very low
cards.people: Eight double-blind randomised trials involving 498 patients with osteoarthritis, topical capsaicin 0.0125%–5% versus placebo, searched to February 2023; five trials (62.5%) at overall low risk of bias and three (37.5%) at high risk of bias.
cards.result: Topical capsaicin reduced pain severity on visual analogue scale versus placebo (standardised mean difference −0.84, 95% CI −1.48 to −0.19; p=0.01; eight studies). It increased burning sensation at the application site (risk ratio 5.56, 1.75–17.69; p=0.004; number-needed-to-harm 3; five studies). Benefits were shown at follow-ups of up to 3 months.
cards.watchOut: Concentrations spanning 0.0125% to 5% are pooled as one treatment, heterogeneity is high, trials are small and short, and burning itself unblinds patients — which inflates subjective pain contrasts in exactly the direction observed. The reviewers suggest capsaicin for short-term management in patients intolerant to NSAIDs.
cards.source: Tshering G et al. Efficacy and safety of topical capsaicin in the treatment of osteoarthritis pain: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Phytotherapy Research. 2024. PMID: 38761115. shelves.title: Glyceryl trinitrate patches split by tendon: Achilles tendinopathy improved (78% versus 49% asymptomatic at 6 months), patellar tendinopathy did not (no treatment effect, p=0.80)
shelves.question: In chronic Achilles and patellar tendinopathy, do topical glyceryl trinitrate patches improve pain and function versus placebo patches?
shelves.mesh: Achilles Tendon/drug effects · Administration, Topical · Adult · Aged · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitroglycerin/administration & dosage · Physical Therapy Modalities · Prospective Studies · Tendinopathy/drug therapy/therapy · Vasodilator Agents/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by tendon. For chronic noninsertional Achilles tendinopathy, Paoloni 2004 randomised 65 patients (84 tendons) to glyceryl trinitrate patches (1.25 mg/24 h) plus rehabilitation or rehabilitation alone: the GTN group had less pain with activity at 12 and 24 weeks, less night pain and tenderness at 12 weeks, and 78% of tendons (28/36) were asymptomatic in daily activities at 6 months versus 49% (20/41) on placebo (p=0.001) — though the mean effect size across all outcome measures was only 0.14. For chronic patellar tendinopathy, Steunebrink 2013 randomised patients to GTN or placebo patches, both with eccentric training: VISA-P scores improved over time in both groups (to 75.0 and 80.7 at 24 weeks) with no treatment-by-time effect (p=0.80), no difference in pain during sports (p=0.38) or satisfaction (p=0.25); three GTN patients reported rash. PROPOSED SPLIT: a positive Achilles result driven by one small trial with p-value-led reporting, and a clean patellar null — tendon by tendon, not a class effect.

cards.headline: Paoloni 2004 (Achilles): 78% of GTN tendons asymptomatic at 6 months versus 49% on placebo (p=0.001); pain with activity lower at 12 and 24 weeks — mean effect size only 0.14
cards.summary: Paoloni 2004 (Achilles): 78% of GTN tendons asymptomatic at 6 months versus 49% on placebo (p=0.001); pain with activity lower at 12 and 24 weeks — mean effect size only 0.14
cards.people: 65 patients (84 Achilles tendons) with chronic noninsertional Achilles tendinopathy, randomised to continuous topical glyceryl trinitrate 1.25 mg/24 hours plus rehabilitation or placebo patches plus rehabilitation.
cards.result: Compared with controls, the GTN group showed reduced pain with activity at 12 weeks (p=0.02) and 24 weeks (p=0.03), reduced night pain at 12 weeks (p=0.04), reduced tenderness at 12 weeks (p=0.02), lower hop-test pain at 24 weeks (p=0.005), and increased ankle plantar-flexor total work at 24 weeks (p=0.04). At 6 months, 28 of 36 tendons (78%) in the GTN group were asymptomatic with activities of daily living versus 20 of 41 (49%) in the placebo group (p=0.001). The mean effect size for all outcome measures was 0.14.
cards.watchOut: Most endpoints are reported as p-values without absolute differences in the record, and a mean effect size of 0.14 is small despite the significant asymptomatic-proportion contrast; tendons, not patients, are the unit in the headline proportion, and some patients contributed two tendons.
cards.source: Paoloni JA et al. Topical glyceryl trinitrate treatment of chronic noninsertional achilles tendinopathy. A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery. American Volume. 2004. PMID: 15118032. cards.headline: Steunebrink 2013 (patellar): VISA-P improved in both groups to 75.0 (GTN) and 80.7 (placebo) at 24 weeks — no treatment effect (p=0.80), no pain or satisfaction difference
cards.summary: Steunebrink 2013 (patellar): VISA-P improved in both groups to 75.0 (GTN) and 80.7 (placebo) at 24 weeks — no treatment effect (p=0.80), no pain or satisfaction difference
cards.people: Patients with chronic patellar tendinopathy randomised to a 12-week programme of glyceryl trinitrate or placebo patches, both combined with eccentric squats on a decline board, with measurements at baseline, 6, 12 and 24 weeks; primary outcome the VISA-P questionnaire.
cards.result: VISA-P scores improved over the study period in both groups, reaching 75.0 ± 16.2 (GTN) and 80.7 ± 22.1 (placebo) at 24 weeks, with a significant effect for time (p<0.01) but no treatment-by-time effect (p=0.80). Pain scores during sports likewise showed time effects only (treatment-by-time p=0.38), and patient satisfaction did not differ between groups after 24 weeks (p=0.25). Three patients in the GTN group reported some rash.
cards.watchOut: Both groups received an effective co-intervention (eccentric training), so this trial tests GTN as an add-on — a null add-on result does not directly contradict the Achilles trial's design, but it removes any presumption of a class-wide tendon effect.
cards.source: Steunebrink M et al. Topical glyceryl trinitrate treatment of chronic patellar tendinopathy: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2013. PMID: 22930695. shelves.title: Glyceryl trinitrate for rotator cuff tendinopathy: one small trial positive at 6 months (46% versus 24% asymptomatic), a Cochrane review calling the whole field too weak to be sure
shelves.question: In rotator cuff tendinopathy, does topical glyceryl trinitrate improve pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Topical · Adult · Aged · Chronic Disease · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitroglycerin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pain/drug therapy · Placebos · Shoulder · Tendinopathy/physiopathology/rehabilitation · Vasodilator Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — Paoloni 2005 randomised 53 patients (57 shoulders) with chronic supraspinatus tendinopathy to glyceryl trinitrate patches (1.25 mg/24 h) plus rehabilitation or placebo plus rehabilitation: at 24 weeks the GTN group had significantly less pain with activity, at night and at rest, less impingement, better range of motion and greater muscle force, and 46% of GTN patients were asymptomatic in daily activities at 6 months versus 24% on rehabilitation alone (p=0.007) — with a mean effect size across outcomes of 0.26. The Cochrane review of topical GTN for rotator cuff disease (three small studies, one at moderate and two at high risk of bias) could not meta-analyse them, found extractable pain data in only one study, and concluded longer-term benefit is uncertain, with headache a common side effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single small positive trial, honestly framed by a sceptical Cochrane review — Tier C.

cards.headline: Paoloni 2005: 46% on GTN asymptomatic at 6 months versus 24% on rehabilitation alone (p=0.007); pain, motion and force all significantly better at week 24 — mean effect size 0.26
cards.summary: Paoloni 2005: 46% on GTN asymptomatic at 6 months versus 24% on rehabilitation alone (p=0.007); pain, motion and force all significantly better at week 24 — mean effect size 0.26
cards.people: 53 patients (57 shoulders) with chronic supraspinatus tendinopathy randomised to continuous topical glyceryl trinitrate 1.25 mg/24 hours plus rehabilitation or placebo patches plus rehabilitation, followed to 24 weeks.
cards.result: The GTN group had significantly reduced shoulder pain with activity, at night and at rest at week 24 (p=0.03), reduced internal-rotation impingement (p=0.02), increased range of motion in abduction and internal rotation (p=0.04), and increased force at weeks 12 and 24 in supraspinatus testing (p=0.001), external rotation (p=0.04), internal rotation (p=0.01), adduction (p=0.04) and subscapularis pushoff (p=0.01). At 6 months, 46% of GTN patients were asymptomatic with activities of daily living versus 24% with rehabilitation alone (p=0.007). Mean effect size for all outcome measures was 0.26.
cards.watchOut: The record reports p-values rather than absolute score differences for nearly every endpoint, in 53 patients from the same research group as the Achilles trial — a declared p-value-only gap; the one patient-centred absolute (46% vs 24% asymptomatic) is the load-bearing number.
cards.source: Paoloni JA et al. Topical glyceryl trinitrate application in the treatment of chronic supraspinatus tendinopathy: a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled clinical trial. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2005. PMID: 15827365. randomised double-blind trial (paoloni 2005) 53 patients (57 shoulders) with chronic supraspinatus tendinopathy randomised to continuous topical glyceryl trinitrate 1.25 mg/24 hours plus rehabilitation or placebo patches plus rehabilitation, followed to 24 weeks. the gtn group had significantly reduced shoulder pain with activity, at night and at rest at week 24 (p=0.03), reduced internal-rotation impingement (p=0.02), increased range of motion in abduction and internal rotation (p=0.04), and increased force at weeks 12 and 24 in supraspinatus testing (p=0.001), external rotation (p=0.04), internal rotation (p=0.01), adduction (p=0.04) and subscapularis pushoff (p=0.01). at 6 months, 46% of gtn patients were asymptomatic with activities of daily living versus 24% with rehabilitation alone (p=0.007). mean effect size for all outcome measures was 0.26. the record reports p-values rather than absolute score differences for nearly every endpoint, in 53 patients from the same research group as the achilles trial — a declared p-value-only gap; the one patient-centred absolute (46% vs 24% asymptomatic) is the load-bearing number. paoloni ja et al. topical glyceryl trinitrate application in the treatment of chronic supraspinatus tendinopathy: a randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled clinical trial. the american journal of sports medicine. 2005. pmid: 15827365. mesh: administration, topical · adult · aged · chronic disease · double-blind method · female · humans · male · middle aged · nitroglycerin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · pain/drug therapy · placebos · shoulder · tendinopathy/physiopathology/rehabilitation · vasodilator agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use

cards.headline: Cumpston 2009 (Cochrane): three small studies, two at high risk of bias, no meta-analysis possible — 'insufficient evidence to be certain' about longer-term GTN effects in rotator cuff disease
cards.summary: Cumpston 2009 (Cochrane): three small studies, two at high risk of bias, no meta-analysis possible — 'insufficient evidence to be certain' about longer-term GTN effects in rotator cuff disease
cards.people: Three small randomised or controlled trials of topical glyceryl trinitrate for rotator cuff disease (20, 53 and 48 participants): acute supraspinatus tendinitis treated 3 days, chronic supraspinatus tendinopathy treated up to 24 weeks with rehabilitation, and rotator cuff tendinitis versus corticosteroid injection.
cards.result: Meta-analysis was precluded by differing interventions and outcomes, and pain and function data could be extracted from only one study. The one placebo-controlled acute trial (20 participants, 5 mg patches for 3 days) found reduced pain intensity (adjusted mean difference −3.50, 95% CI −3.96 to −3.04). In the injection-comparison trial, 15 of 24 GTN participants reported headache. The authors concluded there is some evidence from one high-risk-of-bias study for acute symptoms, but insufficient evidence to be certain about longer-term effects.
cards.watchOut: The review's chronic-tendinopathy trial is the same Paoloni study carded above — the review adds the field-wide verdict (small, biased, unpoolable), not independent patients. Its search closed in October 2007.
cards.source: Cumpston M et al. Topical glyceryl trinitrate for rotator cuff disease. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2009. PMID: 19588386. shelves.title: Shock wave therapy for midportion Achilles tendinopathy: no better than placebo shock waves in the sham-controlled trial — everyone improved with physiotherapy
shelves.question: In midportion Achilles tendinopathy, does extracorporeal shock wave therapy improve pain and function versus sham or placebo treatment?
shelves.mesh: Achilles Tendon/diagnostic imaging/physiopathology · Adult · Aged · Elasticity Imaging Techniques · Extracorporeal Shockwave Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Physical Therapy Modalities · Single-Blind Method · Tendinopathy/therapy · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — against a true placebo, shock wave therapy has not separated. In the single-blinded placebo-controlled trial (Gatz 2021, PMID: 33586526), VISA-A scores improved in all three arms over 24 weeks (+23 points with point-focused ESWT, +18 with line-focused ESWT, +15 with placebo ESWT), with no significant time-by-group interaction (P = 0.24) — every group also did daily physiotherapy. Against no treatment the picture differs: in Rompe 2007 (PMID: 17244902), 52% on repetitive low-energy shock-wave therapy reported complete recovery or much improvement at 4 months versus 24% on a wait-and-see policy, a result statistically indistinguishable from eccentric loading (60%). So shock waves beat doing nothing, but not their own placebo — the honest reading is a large contextual/physiotherapy effect and no proven specific effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): versus sham treatment, ESWT has not been shown to improve Achilles pain or function beyond placebo plus physiotherapy.

cards.headline: Gatz 2021: VISA-A improved +23 (point ESWT), +18 (line ESWT) and +15 (placebo ESWT) — no significant difference between real and placebo shock waves (P = 0.24)
cards.summary: Gatz 2021: VISA-A improved +23 (point ESWT), +18 (line ESWT) and +15 (placebo ESWT) — no significant difference between real and placebo shock waves (P = 0.24)
cards.people: 66 patients with Achilles tendinopathy in a single-blinded placebo-controlled trial: point-focused ESWT (n = 21), line-focused ESWT (n = 24), or placebo ESWT (n = 21); all groups performed daily physiotherapy for 24 weeks and received 4 treatment sessions in the first 6 weeks; VISA-A measured at baseline, 6 and 24 weeks.
cards.result: VISA-A improved significantly over time in all groups (P < 0.001), most in the point-focused group (+23 points), then line-focused (+18) and placebo (+15), but there was no significant interaction between time and group (F(4, 116) = 1.393; P = 0.24). Ultrasound tissue characterisation, power Doppler and B-mode showed no significant change; only shear-wave elastography showed increased tendon elastic properties with point-focused ESWT. The authors concluded no statistically relevant effect of ESWT over placebo could be detected.
cards.watchOut: Small (66 patients), single-blind, and every arm received daily physiotherapy, so the trial tests ESWT as an add-on, not alone; the cohort mixed presentations and the point estimates favour ESWT numerically — the trial can exclude a large specific effect, not a modest one.
cards.source: Gatz M et al. Line- and Point-Focused Extracorporeal Shock Wave Therapy for Achilles Tendinopathy: A Placebo-Controlled RCT Study. Sports health. 2021. PMID: 33586526. cards.headline: Rompe 2007: shock-wave therapy matched eccentric loading (52% vs 60% recovered/much improved) and beat wait-and-see (24%) at 4 months
cards.summary: Rompe 2007: shock-wave therapy matched eccentric loading (52% vs 60% recovered/much improved) and beat wait-and-see (24%) at 4 months
cards.people: 75 patients with chronic recalcitrant (>6 months) noninsertional (main-body/midportion) Achilles tendinopathy, all previously unsuccessfully treated for over 3 months, randomised to eccentric loading, repetitive low-energy shock-wave therapy, or a wait-and-see policy (25 per group), analysed by intention to treat at 4 months.
cards.result: VISA-A rose from 51 to 76 points with eccentric loading, 50 to 70 with shock-wave therapy, and 48 to 55 with wait-and-see. Pain fell from 7 to 4, 7 to 4, and 8 to 6 points respectively. Complete recovery or much improvement was reported by 15 of 25 (60%) on eccentric loading, 13 of 25 (52%) on shock-wave therapy, and 6 of 25 (24%) on wait-and-see; the two active treatments did not differ significantly from each other and both were significantly better than wait-and-see on all outcome measures.
cards.watchOut: No sham arm and no blinding — patients knew whether they received a machine treatment or nothing, so this trial cannot separate a specific shock-wave effect from expectation and attention effects, which is exactly what the later placebo-controlled trial was designed to test.
cards.source: Rompe JD et al. Eccentric loading, shock-wave treatment, or a wait-and-see policy for tendinopathy of the main body of tendo Achillis: a randomized controlled trial. The American journal of sports medicine. 2007. PMID: 17244902. cards.headline: Synthesis: beats nothing, ties placebo — the specific effect of shock waves on the Achilles is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: beats nothing, ties placebo — the specific effect of shock waves on the Achilles is unproven
cards.people: Two randomised trials in chronic Achilles tendinopathy: one placebo-controlled (n = 66, with universal background physiotherapy) and one three-arm trial against eccentric loading and wait-and-see (n = 75).
cards.result: Versus placebo ESWT: VISA-A gains of +23/+18 versus +15 points, interaction P = 0.24 (no significant specific benefit). Versus wait-and-see: 52% versus 24% recovered or much improved. The pattern — clearly better than no treatment, not better than sham treatment — is the classic signature of a strong non-specific effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) versus sham, Tier C because the sham evidence is a single small trial.
cards.watchOut: Shock-wave protocols, energy levels and tendon sub-types (insertional versus midportion) vary across the wider literature; this shelf answers the sham/placebo question for midportion disease and does not rule out benefit in every protocol or subgroup.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gatz M et al. Sports health. 2021 (PMID: 33586526); Rompe JD et al. The American journal of sports medicine. 2007 (PMID: 17244902).

shelves.title: Cemented hemiarthroplasty for intracapsular hip fracture: modestly better quality of life and far fewer periprosthetic fractures (0.5% vs 2.1%) — no proven survival gain
shelves.question: For an intracapsular hip fracture, does cemented hemiarthroplasty improve quality of life and reduce reoperation versus uncemented hemiarthroplasty?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip/methods · Bone Cements/adverse effects · Female · Femoral Neck Fractures/surgery · Hemiarthroplasty/adverse effects/methods · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Periprosthetic Fractures/epidemiology · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Quality of Life · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — cement wins on the outcomes that separate the two operations, modestly. In WHiTE 5 (Fernandez 2022, PMID: 35139272; 1,225 patients), health-related quality of life at 4 months was better with cement (EQ-5D utility 0.371 vs 0.315; adjusted difference 0.055, 95% CI 0.009 to 0.101; P = 0.02 — at the bottom of the 0.050–0.075 range considered clinically important), and periprosthetic fractures were much less frequent (0.5% vs 2.1%; odds ratio for uncemented vs cemented 4.37). Mortality at 12 months was 23.9% versus 27.8% (odds ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.05) — a difference that was not significant. The earlier meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (Li 2020, PMID: 32080078; 1,577 hips) agrees on the fracture harm of uncemented stems (periprosthetic fracture odds ratio 8.32; loosening/subsidence odds ratio 5.33) and on no significant 12-month mortality difference (odds ratio 1.22, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.59), while noting uncemented surgery is quicker and had fewer pulmonary emboli. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cemented hemiarthroplasty gives a small quality-of-life edge and a clear reduction in periprosthetic fracture, at the price of a longer operation; a survival benefit is unproven.

cards.headline: WHiTE 5 (Fernandez 2022): EQ-5D at 4 months 0.371 cemented vs 0.315 uncemented (difference 0.055, P = 0.02); periprosthetic fracture 0.5% vs 2.1%; 12-month mortality 23.9% vs 27.8% (not significant)
cards.summary: WHiTE 5 (Fernandez 2022): EQ-5D at 4 months 0.371 cemented vs 0.315 uncemented (difference 0.055, P = 0.02); periprosthetic fracture 0.5% vs 2.1%; 12-month mortality 23.9% vs 27.8% (not significant)
cards.people: 1,225 patients aged 60 years or older with an intracapsular hip fracture in a multicentre UK trial, randomised to cemented hemiarthroplasty (n = 610) or modern uncemented hemiarthroplasty (n = 615); primary outcome EQ-5D utility at 4 months (follow-up data available for 71.6% at 4 months).
cards.result: Mean EQ-5D utility at 4 months was 0.371 (cemented) versus 0.315 (uncemented): adjusted difference 0.055 (95% CI 0.009 to 0.101; P = 0.02), against a minimal clinically important difference range of 0.050 to 0.075. The difference was similar at 1 month and smaller at 12 months. Mortality at 12 months was 23.9% versus 27.8% (odds ratio for death 0.80, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.05). Periprosthetic fractures occurred in 0.5% versus 2.1% (odds ratio, uncemented vs cemented, 4.37; 95% CI 1.19 to 24.00); other complication rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: Nearly 30% of patients lacked 4-month quality-of-life data (frail, elderly population with high mortality), and the quality-of-life edge sits at the very bottom of the clinically important range; the trial used modern uncemented designs, so its results do not rehabilitate older uncemented stems.
cards.source: Fernandez MA et al. Cemented or Uncemented Hemiarthroplasty for Intracapsular Hip Fracture. The New England journal of medicine. 2022. PMID: 35139272. Registry ID: ISRCTN18393176. cards.headline: Li 2020 meta-analysis (8 RCTs, 1,577 hips): no mortality difference at 12 months, but periprosthetic fracture odds 8.32× and loosening/subsidence 5.33× higher with uncemented stems
cards.summary: Li 2020 meta-analysis (8 RCTs, 1,577 hips): no mortality difference at 12 months, but periprosthetic fracture odds 8.32× and loosening/subsidence 5.33× higher with uncemented stems
cards.people: 8 randomised trials totalling 1,577 hips (795 cemented, 782 uncemented) in elderly patients with femoral neck fracture, comparing cemented with uncemented hemiarthroplasty.
cards.result: No significant difference in mortality at 12 months (odds ratio 1.22, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.59; P = 0.14), hospital stay, blood loss, or Harris Hip Score. Cemented operations took longer (mean difference about 7.3 minutes). Periprosthetic fracture (odds ratio 8.32, 95% CI 3.85 to 17.98; P < 0.00001) and prosthetic subsidence/loosening (odds ratio 5.33, 95% CI 2.18 to 13.00; P = 0.0002) were significantly more frequent with uncemented stems, while pulmonary embolism was less frequent after uncemented surgery.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials predate WHiTE 5 and include older uncemented designs, so the size of the fracture penalty may overstate the risk with current implants; the pulmonary-embolism signal rests on few events and points the other way from the fracture signal.
cards.source: Li N et al. Cemented versus uncemented hemi-arthroplasty for femoral neck fractures in elderly patients: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32080078. cards.headline: Synthesis: cement for quality of life and stem security; the survival question stays open
cards.summary: Synthesis: cement for quality of life and stem security; the survival question stays open
cards.people: One large multicentre randomised trial (n = 1,225) plus a meta-analysis of 8 earlier randomised trials (1,577 hips), all in older patients with intracapsular/femoral-neck fracture treated by hemiarthroplasty.
cards.result: Quality of life at 4 months: adjusted EQ-5D difference 0.055 in favour of cement (P = 0.02). Periprosthetic fracture: 0.5% versus 2.1% in WHiTE 5; pooled odds ratio 8.32 against uncemented stems in the meta-analysis. shelves.title: Trochanteric hip fracture: intramedullary nail and sliding hip screw tie at one year in the 850-patient INSITE trial — the cheaper screw is an acceptable alternative
shelves.question: For trochanteric (intertrochanteric) hip fractures, does an intramedullary nail give better outcomes than a sliding hip screw?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Aged · Male · Fracture Fixation, Intramedullary/adverse effects/methods · Bone Nails/adverse effects · Quality of Life · Bone Screws/adverse effects · Hip Fractures/surgery/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — with modern implants, the nail's dominance is not matched by better outcomes. In INSITE (Schemitsch 2023, PMID: 37278998; 850 patients), 1-year quality of life was identical in practical terms (EQ-5D mean difference 0.02 points, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.07; P = 0.42), with no between-group differences in revision surgery, fracture healing, adverse events, mobility or hip function, and no interaction with fracture stability. The older Cochrane comparison (Parker & Handoll 2010, PMID: 20824825; 22 trials, 3,749 participants for Gamma nail vs sliding hip screw) if anything leaned against the early nails: the Gamma nail was associated with more operative and later femoral fractures and a higher reoperation rate, with no differences in wound infection, mortality or medical complications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for AO/OTA 31-A1/A2 trochanteric fractures, nail and screw deliver the same 1-year outcomes, so cost and surgeon familiarity can decide.

cards.headline: INSITE (Schemitsch 2023): EQ-5D at 1 year differed by 0.02 points (P = 0.42) — no difference in revisions, healing, mobility or hip function either
cards.summary: INSITE (Schemitsch 2023): EQ-5D at 1 year differed by 0.02 points (P = 0.42) — no difference in revisions, healing, mobility or hip function either
cards.people: 850 ambulatory patients aged 18 years or older (mean age 78.5 years; 64.6% women) with low-energy trochanteric fractures (AO/OTA 31-A1 or 31-A2) at 25 sites in 12 countries, randomised to Gamma3 intramedullary nail (n = 423) or sliding hip screw (n = 427) and followed for 52 weeks; 621 completed 1-year follow-up.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in the primary outcome, EQ-5D health-related quality of life at 1 year (mean difference 0.02 points, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.07; P = 0.42; adjusted regression coefficient 0.00, P = 0.81). No secondary outcome — revision surgery, fracture healing, adverse events, Parker mobility score, Harris hip score — differed between groups, and neither fracture stability nor previous fracture modified the result. The authors conclude the sliding hip screw is an acceptable lower-cost alternative.
cards.watchOut: About 27% of randomised patients did not complete 1-year follow-up, and the trial covers A1/A2 fracture patterns only — it does not answer the separate question of reverse-obliquity or subtrochanteric patterns, where nails are usually preferred on mechanical grounds.

cards.headline: Cochrane 2010 (Parker & Handoll): Gamma nail vs sliding hip screw in 22 trials (3,749 patients) — more femoral fractures and reoperations with the early nails, no mortality difference
cards.summary: Cochrane 2010 (Parker & Handoll): Gamma nail vs sliding hip screw in 22 trials (3,749 patients) — more femoral fractures and reoperations with the early nails, no mortality difference
cards.people: 43 randomised or quasi-randomised trials of cephalocondylic intramedullary nails versus extramedullary implants for extracapsular hip fractures in predominantly older adults; the core comparison, Gamma nail versus sliding hip screw, comprised 22 trials with 3,749 participants with mainly trochanteric fractures.
cards.result: The Gamma nail was associated with an increased risk of operative and later fracture of the femur and an increased reoperation rate compared with the sliding hip screw. There were no major differences between implants in wound infection, mortality, or medical complications. Comparisons of other nails (intramedullary hip screw, proximal femoral nail) against the sliding hip screw likewise showed similar functional outcomes, mortality and postoperative complications, with more fracture-fixation complications for the intramedullary hip screw.
cards.watchOut: These trials tested first-generation nail designs from the 1990s–2000s; their excess femoral-fracture signal may not apply to the modern Gamma3 tested in INSITE — but they remove any presumption that nails were ever the better-evidenced default.
cards.source: Parker MJ et al. Gamma and other cephalocondylic intramedullary nails versus extramedullary implants for extracapsular hip fractures in adults. cards.headline: Synthesis: two decades apart, the same answer — implant choice does not move 1-year outcomes in A1/A2 trochanteric fractures
cards.summary: Synthesis: two decades apart, the same answer — implant choice does not move 1-year outcomes in A1/A2 trochanteric fractures
cards.people: One modern international randomised trial (n = 850, Gamma3 nail vs sliding hip screw) and the Cochrane review of 43 earlier trials (22 trials, 3,749 participants in the Gamma nail comparison).
cards.result: Modern trial: EQ-5D difference 0.02 points (P = 0.42), all secondary outcomes null. Older pooled evidence: no mortality, infection or functional advantage for nails, with more femoral fractures and reoperations for early nail designs. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the nail-versus-screw question in trochanteric fractures.
cards.watchOut: Neither record carded here addresses the most unstable fracture geometries, and implant costs differ substantially between health systems — the equivalence finding is what licenses a cost-based choice, not a mandate for either device.

shelves.title: Romosozumab in men with osteoporosis: spine density up 12.1% vs 1.2% on placebo in a year — a density trial, with a numerical cardiovascular imbalance and no fracture endpoint
shelves.question: In men with osteoporosis, does romosozumab increase bone mineral density versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Absorptiometry, Photon/methods · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Density Conservation Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Cardiovascular Diseases/chemically induced · Double-Blind Method · Femur Neck/physiopathology · Hip Joint/physiopathology · Humans · Lumbar Vertebrae/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoporosis/drug therapy/physiopathology · Osteoporotic Fractures/physiopathology/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for bone density, in the only placebo-controlled trial in men. In BRIDGE (Lewiecki 2018, PMID: 29931216; 245 men), 12 months of monthly romosozumab 210 mg raised lumbar spine BMD by 12.1% versus 1.2% on placebo and total hip BMD by 2.5% versus −0.5% (P < 0.001 for both). That is a large, unambiguous effect on the surrogate the trial was powered for — but the trial reports no fracture outcomes, and its safety table carries the signal that has followed this drug: positively adjudicated cardiovascular serious adverse events in 8 men (4.9%) on romosozumab versus 2 (2.5%) on placebo, a numerical imbalance in a trial far too small to judge it, with overall adverse and serious adverse events otherwise balanced. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): romosozumab clearly increases spine and hip density in men over 12 months; whether that converts into fewer fractures in men, and at what cardiovascular price, this record does not say.

cards.headline: BRIDGE (Lewiecki 2018): lumbar spine BMD +12.1% vs +1.2%, total hip +2.5% vs −0.5% at 12 months (P < 0.001) — cardiovascular serious events 4.9% vs 2.5%
cards.summary: BRIDGE (Lewiecki 2018): lumbar spine BMD +12.1% vs +1.2%, total hip +2.5% vs −0.5% at 12 months (P < 0.001) — cardiovascular serious events 4.9% vs 2.5%
cards.people: 245 men aged 55 to 90 years with osteoporosis (BMD T-score ≤−2.5 at spine, total hip or femoral neck, or ≤−1.5 with a fragility fracture) at 31 centres in Europe, Latin America, Japan and North America, randomised 2:1 to romosozumab 210 mg subcutaneously monthly (n = 163) or placebo (n = 82) for 12 months.
cards.result: The mean percentage change in lumbar spine BMD at month 12 was 12.1% on romosozumab versus 1.2% on placebo, and at the total hip 2.5% versus −0.5% (P < 0.001 for both). Adverse events and serious adverse events were balanced overall, but positively adjudicated cardiovascular serious adverse events occurred in 8 patients (4.9%) on romosozumab versus 2 (2.5%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Bone density is a surrogate: the trial was neither designed nor powered for fractures, and 245 men cannot characterise a cardiovascular harm that matters at the individual level — the 4.9% versus 2.5% split is a flag to weigh, not a measured risk. Tier C: a single trial carrying a benefit claim.
cards.source: Lewiecki EM et al. A Phase III Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trial to Evaluate Efficacy and Safety of Romosozumab in Men With Osteoporosis. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2018. PMID: 29931216. Registry ID: NCT02186171. shelves.title: Teriparatide after osteoporotic fracture: treatment failure 11.0% vs 17.6% — not significant; one meta-analysis finds better function, neither finds faster healing
shelves.question: Does teriparatide speed healing and improve outcomes in osteoporotic fractures versus control treatment?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the healing claim fails, a functional claim survives weakly. Pooling the 5 randomised trials in osteoporotic hip and pelvic fractures (Moon 2020, PMID: 33335866), treatment failure — non-union, varus collapse, screw perforation or revision for mechanical failure — occurred in 11.0% on teriparatide versus 17.6% on control, an odds ratio of 0.81 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.53; P = 0.16) that is not significant. The broader meta-analysis of PTH analogues across fracture types (Eastman 2021, PMID: 33559713) reaches the matching verdict in words: PTH treatment improved functional outcomes but did not affect the fracture healing rate or reduce pain, across trials that were mostly in elderly patients with osteoporosis and of heterogeneous, limited quality. PROPOSED SPLIT: no demonstrated acceleration of healing or reduction in mechanical failure; a possible functional benefit that the underlying trials are too weak to quantify.

cards.headline: Moon 2020 meta-analysis (5 RCTs): treatment failure 11.0% on teriparatide vs 17.6% on control — odds ratio 0.81 (0.42–1.53), P = 0.16, not significant
cards.summary: Moon 2020 meta-analysis (5 RCTs): treatment failure 11.0% on teriparatide vs 17.6% on control — odds ratio 0.81 (0.42–1.53), P = 0.16, not significant
cards.people: 5 randomised controlled trials of teriparatide versus control in osteoporotic hip and pelvic bone fractures (181 teriparatide and 205 control patients in the failure analysis); treatment failure defined as non-union, varus collapse of the proximal fragment, lag-screw perforation, or revision for mechanical failure at final follow-up.
cards.result: Treatment failures numbered 20 of 181 (11.0%) on teriparatide versus 36 of 205 (17.6%) on control: odds ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.42 to 1.53; P = 0.16; I² = 42%) — not statistically significant. The authors conclude there is a lack of evidence to confirm that teriparatide reduces treatment failures in osteoporotic hip and pelvic fractures.
cards.watchOut: Only 386 patients inform the primary analysis, so the confidence interval spans meaningful benefit and meaningful harm; this record carries no MeSH in PubMed. The point estimate favours teriparatide — the honest statement is 'unproven', not 'disproven'.
cards.source: Moon NH et al. Effects of Teriparatide on Treatment Outcomes in Osteoporotic Hip and Pelvic Bone Fractures: Meta-analysis and Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials. Hip & pelvis. 2020. PMID: 33335866. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Eastman 2021 meta-analysis: PTH analogues improved functional outcomes but did not affect fracture healing rate or reduce pain
cards.summary: Eastman 2021 meta-analysis: PTH analogues improved functional outcomes but did not affect fracture healing rate or reduce pain
cards.people: Prospective randomised controlled trials of PTH analogues (teriparatide class) versus placebo, comparator or no treatment in adults with acute fractures of various types; most trials enrolled elderly patients with osteoporosis (search to August 2019).
cards.result: The review's pooled conclusion, as reported in the record, is qualitative: PTH analogue treatment improved functional outcomes across a range of fracture types but did not affect the fracture healing rate or reduce pain, and there was no evidence that PTH treatment caused harm or impeded healing. The record reports no single pooled effect size for the functional benefit.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative 'improved function' conclusion without a pooled number in the record cannot be weighed precisely, and the authors themselves describe the trial base as heterogeneous and of limited quality — this is the weak half of the split, and it is why the shelf is Tier C.
cards.source: Eastman K et al. Effectiveness of parathyroid hormone (PTH) analogues on fracture healing: a meta-analysis. shelves.title: rhBMP-2 for open tibial fractures: 44% relative reduction in reintervention with unreamed nails (Govender) — no healing advantage at all with reamed nails (Aro)
shelves.question: In open tibial fractures, does recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 reduce reintervention for delayed union versus standard care alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Morphogenetic Protein 2 · Bone Morphogenetic Proteins/therapeutic use · Female · Fractures, Open/drug therapy · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Recombinant Proteins · Single-Blind Method · Tibial Fractures/drug therapy · Transforming Growth Factor beta/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer turns on the nail. In the 450-patient BESTT trial (Govender 2002, PMID: 12473698), where fractures were fixed predominantly with unreamed nails, the 1.50 mg/mL rhBMP-2 implant produced a 44% relative reduction in the risk of secondary intervention for delayed union (relative risk 0.56, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.78; p = 0.0005), with faster fracture and wound healing (wound healing at 6 weeks 83% vs 65%) and fewer hardware failures and infections in severe injuries. In the later trial restricted to reamed nail fixation (Aro 2011, PMID: 21454742; 277 patients), the same 1.5 mg/mL dose did nothing measurable: fracture healing at week 20 was 68% with rhBMP-2 versus 67% with standard care, secondary procedures were 12% in each group, and infections were numerically more frequent with rhBMP-2 (19% vs 11%; p = 0.0645). PROPOSED SPLIT: a real reintervention benefit in the unreamed-nail setting of the original trial; no demonstrated benefit when the fracture is fixed with a reamed nail.

cards.headline: Govender 2002 (BESTT): 1.50 mg/mL rhBMP-2 cut the risk of secondary intervention for delayed union by a relative 44% (RR 0.56, 0.40–0.78; p = 0.0005)
cards.summary: Govender 2002 (BESTT): 1.50 mg/mL rhBMP-2 cut the risk of secondary intervention for delayed union by a relative 44% (RR 0.56, 0.40–0.78; p = 0.0005)
cards.people: 450 patients with an open tibial shaft fracture randomised to standard care (intramedullary nail fixation and routine soft-tissue management), standard care plus rhBMP-2 0.75 mg/mL (total 6 mg), or standard care plus rhBMP-2 1.50 mg/mL (total 12 mg) on an absorbable collagen sponge placed at definitive wound closure; 421 patients (94%) completed 12-month follow-up; single-blind, stratified by wound severity.
cards.result: The 1.50 mg/mL group had a 44% relative reduction in the risk of failure — secondary intervention because of delayed union (relative risk 0.56, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.78; pairwise p = 0.0005) — significantly fewer invasive interventions (p = 0.0264), faster fracture healing (p = 0.0022), fewer hardware failures (p = 0.0174), fewer infections in Gustilo-Anderson type III injuries (p = 0.0219), and faster wound healing (83% vs 65% healed at 6 weeks; p = 0.0010). The record reports the effect as a relative risk; arm-level absolute reintervention rates are not given in the record.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind, industry-era trial in which the benefit concentrated in the higher dose and in more severe injuries; the comparator era's nailing was largely unreamed, which the later reamed-nail trial suggests may be the setting where the implant adds something.
cards.source: Govender S et al. Recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2 for treatment of open tibial fractures: a prospective, controlled, randomized study of four hundred and fifty patients. The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume. 2002. PMID: 12473698. cards.headline: Aro 2011: with reamed nails, healing at week 20 was 68% (rhBMP-2) vs 67% (standard care); secondary procedures 12% in both groups; infections 19% vs 11%
cards.summary: Aro 2011: with reamed nails, healing at week 20 was 68% (rhBMP-2) vs 67% (standard care); secondary procedures 12% in both groups; infections 19% vs 11%
cards.people: 277 patients with acute open tibial fractures treated with reamed intramedullary nail fixation, randomised to standard care alone or standard care plus an absorbable collagen sponge with rhBMP-2 1.5 mg/mL (total 12.0 mg) placed at wound closure; 13% of fractures were Gustilo-Anderson type IIIB; intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: Fracture healing was 60% versus 48% at week 13 (p = 0.0541) and 68% versus 67% at week 20 in the rhBMP-2 and standard-care groups — not significantly accelerated. Twelve percent of patients in each group underwent secondary procedures; more invasive procedures accounted for 30% of those in the rhBMP-2 group versus 57% in the standard-care group (p = 0.1271). Infection occurred in 27 patients (19%) on rhBMP-2 versus 15 (11%) on standard care (p = 0.0645).
cards.watchOut: The week-13 healing split (60% vs 48%) nearly reached significance before vanishing by week 20 — at most a small timing effect in this setting; the infection difference is a non-significant numerical excess that nonetheless removes any presumption of harmlessness.
cards.source: Aro HT et al. Recombinant human bone morphogenetic protein-2: a randomized trial in open tibial fractures treated with reamed nail fixation. The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume. 2011. PMID: 21454742. cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive trial, one null trial — separated by how the bone was nailed
cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive trial, one null trial — separated by how the bone was nailed
cards.people: Two randomised trials of the same 12 mg rhBMP-2 implant in open tibial fractures: BESTT (n = 450, predominantly unreamed fixation) and Aro 2011 (n = 277, all reamed fixation).
cards.result: Reintervention/healing: relative risk of secondary intervention 0.56 (0.40–0.78) in BESTT; healing 68% versus 67% and secondary procedures 12% versus 12% in the reamed-nail trial. PROPOSED SPLIT by fixation method — benefit shown only alongside unreamed nailing.
cards.watchOut: Dose, wound severity mix and era differ alongside the nailing difference, so 'reamed versus unreamed' is the most visible explanation for the split, not a proven mechanism; neither record reports long-term safety outcomes such as ectopic bone or malignancy surveillance.

shelves.title: Scaphoid waist fracture: surgery did not beat a cast at one year in SWIFFT (439 patients) — and carried a 14% serious-complication rate against 1%
shelves.question: In adults with a bicortical scaphoid waist fracture, does surgical fixation improve function versus cast immobilisation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Screws · Casts, Surgical · Female · Fracture Fixation · Fracture Fixation, Internal/methods · Fractures, Bone/surgery/therapy · Fractures, Ununited/surgery · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Outcome Assessment · Scaphoid Bone/injuries/surgery · Time-to-Treatment · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on function, with the harms pointing against routine early surgery. In SWIFFT (Dias 2020, PMID: 32771106; 439 adults with bicortical scaphoid waist fractures displaced by 2 mm or less), patient-rated wrist evaluation at 52 weeks was 11.9 after early surgical fixation versus 14.0 with cast immobilisation (adjusted mean difference −2.1, 95% CI −5.8 to 1.6; p = 0.27) — no significant difference. The complication trade was lopsided: potentially serious surgical complications in 31 of 219 patients (14%) in the surgery group versus 3 of 220 (1%) in the cast group, while cast-related complications ran the other way (5 patients [2%] after surgery vs 40 [18%] in the cast group), and medical complications were similar (2% in both groups). The cast strategy in SWIFFT was not 'cast and hope': fractures that failed to unite were fixed promptly. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): initial cast immobilisation with surgery reserved for confirmed non-union gives the same one-year function without exposing everyone to surgical risk.

cards.headline: SWIFFT (Dias 2020): PRWE at 52 weeks 11.9 (surgery) vs 14.0 (cast), difference −2.1 (p = 0.27); serious complications 14% vs 1%
cards.summary: SWIFFT (Dias 2020): PRWE at 52 weeks 11.9 (surgery) vs 14.0 (cast), difference −2.1 (p = 0.27); serious complications 14% vs 1%
cards.people: 439 adults (mean age 33 years; 83% men) with a clear bicortical scaphoid waist fracture displaced by 2 mm or less, presenting to 31 hospitals in England and Wales, randomised to early surgical fixation (n = 219) or below-elbow cast immobilisation with immediate fixation if non-union was confirmed (n = 220); 408 patients contributed to the primary analysis of patient-rated wrist evaluation (PRWE) at 52 weeks.
cards.result: Mean PRWE at 52 weeks was 11.9 in the surgery group and 14.0 in the cast group (adjusted mean difference −2.1, 95% CI −5.8 to 1.6; p = 0.27) — no significant difference. Potentially serious complications from surgery occurred in 31 of 219 patients (14%) versus 3 of 220 (1%) with cast treatment; cast-related complications occurred in 5 (2%) versus 40 (18%); medical complications were similar (4 [2%] vs 5 [2%]). The authors recommend initial cast immobilisation, with confirmed non-unions fixed immediately.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and pragmatic, in fractures displaced by at most 2 mm — the result does not cover clearly displaced or proximal-pole fractures, where surgery has a different rationale. Tier C: a single (albeit large and well-run) trial carries this shelf.
cards.source: Dias JJ et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: same wrist at one year, fewer serious harms — cast first, fix the failures
cards.summary: Synthesis: same wrist at one year, fewer serious harms — cast first, fix the failures
cards.people: One pragmatic multicentre randomised trial of 439 adults with minimally displaced bicortical scaphoid waist fractures (SWIFFT), comparing early fixation with cast-plus-selective-fixation.
cards.result: Function (PRWE at 52 weeks): 11.9 versus 14.0, difference −2.1 (95% CI −5.8 to 1.6), not significant. Serious complications: 14% with early surgery versus 1% with the cast strategy. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) on function, with the harm balance favouring cast-first; Tier C for a single-trial shelf.
cards.watchOut: Long-term arthritis and non-union sequelae beyond one year are not settled by this record; patients whose work or sport makes cast time costly may still reasonably choose surgery knowing function at a year is, on average, the same.

shelves.title: End-stage ankle arthritis: replacement and fusion improved walking/standing scores by statistically indistinguishable amounts at one year in TARVA — different complications, same totals
shelves.question: In end-stage ankle osteoarthritis, does total ankle replacement give better pain and function than ankle arthrodesis (fusion)?
shelves.mesh: Male · Humans · Aged · Female · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Ankle/adverse effects/methods · Ankle Joint/surgery · Ankle/surgery · State Medicine · Treatment Outcome · Osteoarthritis · Arthrodesis/adverse effects/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — at one year, in the only randomised trial. In TARVA (Goldberg 2022, PMID: 36375147; 303 patients aged 50–85), both operations improved Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire walking/standing scores substantially; the adjusted difference in change at 52 weeks was −5.6 points in favour of replacement (95% CI −12.5 to 1.4), which the authors judged neither clinically nor statistically significant. Adverse events were similar in total (109 vs 104) but different in kind: more wound-healing problems and nerve injuries with replacement; more thromboembolic events and nonunion with fusion, whose symptomatic nonunion rate was 7%. A post hoc analysis suggested fixed-bearing replacement implants did beat fusion (−11.1, 95% CI −19.3 to −2.9) — a hypothesis, not the trial's verdict. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on one-year scores the two operations tie; the choice turns on complication profiles, implant longevity questions this trial cannot answer, and patient preference.

cards.headline: TARVA (Goldberg 2022): adjusted difference in MOXFQ walking/standing change −5.6 (95% CI −12.5 to 1.4) — not significant; adverse events 109 vs 104; symptomatic fusion nonunion 7%
cards.summary: TARVA (Goldberg 2022): adjusted difference in MOXFQ walking/standing change −5.6 (95% CI −12.5 to 1.4) — not significant; adverse events 109 vs 104; symptomatic fusion nonunion 7%
cards.people: 303 patients aged 50 to 85 years with end-stage ankle osteoarthritis suitable for either operation, randomised across 17 UK NHS trusts to total ankle replacement or ankle arthrodesis (fusion); mean age 68 years, 71% men; 21 withdrew before surgery and 281 contributed clinical scores; primary outcome change in Manchester-Oxford Foot Questionnaire walking/standing domain at 52 weeks; open-label (no blinding possible).
cards.result: Both groups improved. The adjusted difference in change in walking/standing scores was −5.6 (95% CI −12.5 to 1.4) favouring replacement — not considered clinically or statistically significant. Adverse events numbered 109 (replacement) versus 104 (fusion), with more wound-healing issues and nerve injuries after replacement and more thromboembolic events and nonunion after fusion; the symptomatic nonunion rate for fusion was 7%. A post hoc analysis suggested superiority of fixed-bearing replacement over fusion (−11.1, 95% CI −19.3 to −2.9).
cards.watchOut: Only 52-week data in this record: the questions that most divide the two operations — implant survival and revision burden over 10+ years versus adjacent-joint arthritis after fusion — are exactly the ones a one-year trial cannot answer. The fixed-bearing signal is post hoc. Tier C: single trial.
cards.source: Goldberg AJ et al. Total Ankle Replacement Versus Arthrodesis for End-Stage Ankle Osteoarthritis: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2022. PMID: 36375147. shelves.title: Humeral shaft fracture: surgery did not significantly improve 12-month function in FISH — but one in four braced fractures never united, and pooled data trade nonunion against infection and nerve injury
shelves.question: In fractures of the humeral shaft (diaphysis), does operative plate fixation improve function versus non-operative functional bracing?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Plates · Braces · Closed Fracture Reduction/adverse effects/methods · Disability Evaluation · Female · Fracture Fixation, Internal/adverse effects/methods · Fractures, Ununited/etiology · Humans · Humeral Fractures/surgery/therapy · Male · Middle Aged · Open Fracture Reduction/methods · Recovery of Function
shelves.balance: SPLIT — function ties in the trial; the failure modes do not. In the FISH trial (Rämö 2020, PMID: 32396179; 82 patients), DASH scores at 12 months were 8.9 after plate fixation versus 12.0 with functional bracing (difference −3.1 points, 95% CI −9.6 to 3.3; P = 0.34) — no significant difference, against a 10-point minimal clinically important difference. But 13 of 44 braced patients (30%) crossed over to surgery to promote healing, 11 (25%) developed nonunion, and 3 surgical patients (8%) had a temporary radial nerve palsy. The wider meta-analysis of comparison studies (Beyer 2023, PMID: 37459427; 18 studies, 706 patients) shows the same trade at scale: revision, nonunion and malunion risks were significantly higher with bracing (p < 0.0001, p < 0.0001, p = 0.004), infection and radial nerve injury higher with surgery (p = 0.04 and p = 0.01), and Constant shoulder scores higher after surgery (p = 0.004). PROPOSED SPLIT: average function at a year is similar either way; bracing buys avoidance of surgical complications at the price of roughly a one-in-four nonunion risk and frequent late surgery, while plating buys union at the price of infection and nerve risk.

cards.headline: FISH (Rämö 2020): DASH at 12 months 8.9 (surgery) vs 12.0 (bracing), difference −3.1 (P = 0.34); 30% of braced patients crossed over to surgery; nonunion 25% vs radial nerve palsy 8%
cards.summary: FISH (Rämö 2020): DASH at 12 months 8.9 (surgery) vs 12.0 (bracing), difference −3.1 (P = 0.34); 30% of braced patients crossed over to surgery; nonunion 25% vs radial nerve palsy 8%
cards.people: 82 adults with closed, unilateral, displaced humeral shaft fractures at two Finnish university trauma centres, randomised to open reduction and internal plate fixation (n = 38) or functional bracing (n = 44); mean age 48.9 years; 78 patients (95%) completed the trial; primary outcome Disabilities of Arm, Shoulder and Hand (DASH) score at 12 months (minimal clinically important difference 10 points).
cards.result: Mean DASH at 12 months was 8.9 (95% CI 4.2 to 13.6) after surgery versus 12.0 (95% CI 7.7 to 16.4) with bracing: between-group difference −3.1 points (95% CI −9.6 to 3.3; P = 0.34). Thirteen patients (30%) assigned to bracing underwent surgery during follow-up to promote healing; 11 braced patients (25%) developed fracture nonunion; 3 surgical patients (8%) developed a temporary radial nerve palsy.
cards.watchOut: A small trial (82 patients) with 30% crossover: the intention-to-treat function comparison is diluted precisely because bracing failures were rescued by surgery — so 'no difference in function' and 'one in four braced fractures did not unite' are both true, and both matter. Tier C on that basis.

cards.headline: Beyer 2023 meta-analysis (18 studies, 706 patients): nonunion, malunion and revision significantly higher with bracing; infection and radial nerve injury higher with surgery
cards.summary: Beyer 2023 meta-analysis (18 studies, 706 patients): nonunion, malunion and revision significantly higher with bracing; infection and radial nerve injury higher with surgery
cards.people: 18 comparison studies totalling 706 patients with humeral shaft fractures treated by functional bracing or surgery (open reduction and internal fixation, intramedullary nailing, or locked compression plate), pooled for nonunion, malunion, function scores and complications.
cards.result: Risks of revision, nonunion and malunion were significantly higher in the brace group than the surgical group (p < 0.0001, p < 0.0001 and p = 0.004 respectively). Infection risk was higher with surgery (p = 0.04), as were radial nerve injury rates in the unspecified-surgery group (p = 0.01). Mean Constant shoulder score was significantly higher after surgery (p = 0.004). Within surgery, nailing carried more delayed unions and other complications, plating more infections. The record reports significance levels rather than pooled absolute rates for these comparisons.
cards.watchOut: Most included studies are not randomised trials, so the pooled contrasts inherit selection bias — surgeons choose which fractures to brace; and with p-values but no pooled effect sizes in the record, the size of each trade-off cannot be stated from this card.
cards.source: Beyer J et al. Evaluation of Humeral Shaft Fracture Outcomes by Treatment Method: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis Based on Comparison Studies. JBJS reviews. 2023. PMID: 37459427. cards.headline: Synthesis: pick your failure mode — nonunion and late surgery with a brace, or infection and nerve risk with a plate
cards.summary: Synthesis: pick your failure mode — nonunion and late surgery with a brace, or infection and nerve risk with a plate
cards.people: One randomised trial (n = 82, FISH) and one meta-analysis of 18 comparison studies (706 patients) for humeral shaft fractures.
cards.result: Function at 12 months: DASH difference −3.1 points (P = 0.34), not significant and below the 10-point clinically important threshold. Union: 25% nonunion and 30% crossover in the braced arm of FISH; pooled nonunion/malunion/revision all significantly higher with bracing. Surgical harms: infection and radial nerve injury significantly higher with surgery in pooled data; temporary radial nerve palsy 8% in FISH's surgical arm. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C.

shelves.title: Non-displaced Lisfranc injury: surgery and non-operative care scored 91.8 vs 96.1 at two years — in a trial that recruited 27 of its planned 60 patients and says so itself
shelves.question: In Lisfranc injuries, does operative treatment improve outcomes versus non-operative treatment in non-displaced injuries?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Adult · Middle Aged · Fracture Fixation, Internal/methods · Foot Injuries/therapy/diagnostic imaging · Treatment Outcome · Finland · Open Fracture Reduction/methods · Fractures, Bone/therapy · Young Adult · Pain Measurement
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — the only randomised trial is frankly underpowered. Ponkilainen 2025 (PMID: 39584430) randomised 27 patients with CT-confirmed non-displaced Lisfranc injuries against a target sample of 60: at 2 years the mean VAS Foot and Ankle overall score was 96.1 with non-operative care and 91.8 with open reduction and internal fixation (mean difference 4.3, 95% CI −2.4 to 11) — no statistically significant difference, in the authors' own words an underpowered trial from which robust conclusions cannot be drawn. Both groups ended near the top of the scale, which is itself informative: non-displaced injuries do well. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): no demonstrated advantage for operating on non-displaced Lisfranc injuries, on evidence too thin to close the question.

cards.headline: Ponkilainen 2025: VAS-FA at 2 years 96.1 (non-operative) vs 91.8 (ORIF), difference 4.3 (−2.4 to 11) — no significant difference; trial stopped at 27 of 60 planned patients
cards.summary: Ponkilainen 2025: VAS-FA at 2 years 96.1 (non-operative) vs 91.8 (ORIF), difference 4.3 (−2.4 to 11) — no significant difference; trial stopped at 27 of 60 planned patients
cards.people: 27 patients with computed-tomography-confirmed non-displaced Lisfranc injuries at two hospitals in Finland (2012–2022), randomised to non-operative treatment or open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF); target sample size was 60; primary outcome Visual Analogue Scale Foot and Ankle (VAS-FA) at 2 years, with secondary outcomes at 6 months, 1 and 2 years.
cards.result: Mean VAS-FA overall score at 2 years was 96.1 (95% CI 91.5 to 100) in the non-operative group and 91.8 (95% CI 86.9 to 96.7) in the ORIF group — mean between-group difference 4.3 (95% CI −2.4 to 11), not statistically significant. The authors state plainly that the trial is underpowered to draw robust conclusions.
cards.watchOut: With 27 patients the confidence interval still includes an 11-point advantage for non-operative care and a small advantage for surgery; a decade-long recruitment window (2012–2022) for 27 patients also signals how selected this population is. This is the weakest-evidence shelf in the wave — hence MAYBE (weak evidence) and Tier C.
cards.source: Ponkilainen V et al. Operative versus non-operative treatment for non-displaced Lisfranc injuries: A two-center randomized clinical trial. Scandinavian journal of surgery : SJS : official organ for the Finnish Surgical Society and the Scandinavian Surgical Society. 2025. PMID: 39584430. cards.summary: Synthesis: both roads ended near the top of the scale — but the trial is too small to prove they are equal

shelves.title: Lisfranc surgery: primary fusion beat fixation on function scores in the small 2006 ligamentous-injury trial (88 vs 68.6) — the larger 2024 displaced-injury trial found no difference
shelves.question: In Lisfranc injuries requiring surgery, does primary arthrodesis give better outcomes than open reduction and internal fixation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Arthrodesis · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Fracture Fixation, Internal · Humans · Ligaments, Articular/injuries/physiopathology/surgery · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Satisfaction · Prospective Studies · Recovery of Function/physiology · Tarsal Joints/injuries/physiopathology/surgery · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by injury type and by era. In the prospective randomised trial of primarily ligamentous Lisfranc injuries (Ly & Coetzee 2006, PMID: 16510816; 41 patients), primary arthrodesis of the medial rays produced a mean AOFAS Midfoot score of 88 at two years versus 68.6 after open reduction and screw fixation (p < 0.005); 5 fixation patients developed persistent pain with deformity or osteoarthrosis and went on to arthrodesis, and arthrodesis patients rated their activity at 92% of preinjury level versus 65% (p < 0.005). In the multicentre randomised trial of displaced Lisfranc injuries (Ponkilainen 2024, PMID: 38482816; 43 patients), the primary outcome told the opposite story: VAS-FA overall at 24 months was 86.5 with fixation versus 80.1 with arthrodesis (difference 6.5, 95% CI −5.3 to 18.2) — no evidence of a difference, in a trial that also fell short of its planned 60 patients. PROPOSED SPLIT: fusion ahead for purely ligamentous injuries in one small older trial; no demonstrated difference for displaced injuries in the newer trial — both underpowered, so neither verdict is secure.

cards.headline: Ly & Coetzee 2006: AOFAS Midfoot 88 (arthrodesis) vs 68.6 (ORIF) at 2 years, p < 0.005; 5 of 20 fixation patients later needed arthrodesis for pain, deformity or arthritis
cards.summary: Ly & Coetzee 2006: AOFAS Midfoot 88 (arthrodesis) vs 68.6 (ORIF) at 2 years, p < 0.005; 5 of 20 fixation patients later needed arthrodesis for pain, deformity or arthritis
cards.people: 41 patients with an isolated acute or subacute primarily ligamentous Lisfranc joint injury, randomised prospectively to open reduction and screw fixation (n = 20) or primary arthrodesis of the medial two or three rays (n = 21), followed for a mean of 42.5 months with AOFAS Midfoot Scale, visual analogue pain scale, radiography and questionnaire.
cards.result: Anatomic reduction was achieved in 18 of 20 fixation and 20 of 21 arthrodesis patients. At two years the mean AOFAS Midfoot score was 68.6 after fixation versus 88 after arthrodesis (p < 0.005). Five fixation patients had persistent pain with deformity or osteoarthrosis and were eventually treated with arthrodesis. Patients estimated their postoperative activity at 65% of preinjury level after fixation versus 92% after primary arthrodesis (p < 0.005).
cards.watchOut: A single-surgeon-era trial of 41 patients in a specific injury pattern (primarily ligamentous, not fracture-dislocations); unblinded patient-reported components and a 19-point score gap this large in a sample this small should be read as a strong signal, not a settled effect size.
cards.source: Ly TV et al. Treatment of primarily ligamentous Lisfranc joint injuries: primary arthrodesis compared with open reduction and internal fixation. A prospective, randomized study. The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume. 2006. PMID: 16510816. cards.headline: Ponkilainen 2024: VAS-FA at 24 months 86.5 (ORIF) vs 80.1 (arthrodesis), difference 6.5 (−5.3 to 18.2) — no evidence of a difference in displaced injuries
cards.summary: Ponkilainen 2024: VAS-FA at 24 months 86.5 (ORIF) vs 80.1 (arthrodesis), difference 6.5 (−5.3 to 18.2) — no evidence of a difference in displaced injuries
cards.people: 43 patients with displaced Lisfranc injuries in a national multicentre Finnish randomised trial of open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) versus primary arthrodesis; primary outcome VAS Foot and Ankle (VAS-FA) overall score at 24 months, with subscales and AOFAS Midfoot Scale at 6, 12 and 24 months; planned sample size was 60 and was not reached.
cards.result: Mean VAS-FA overall at 24 months was 86.5 (95% CI 77.9 to 95.1) in the ORIF group and 80.1 (95% CI 72.0 to 88.1) in the arthrodesis group: mean between-group difference 6.5 (95% CI −5.3 to 18.2), Cohen's d = 0.100. The authors found no eligible evidence of a difference and conclude both are viable initial surgical options, noting the trial is underpowered.
cards.watchOut: Underpowered (43 of 60 planned), and its population — displaced injuries, including fracture patterns — is not the purely ligamentous population of the 2006 trial; the two trials may both be right for their own injury types, which is exactly the split this shelf records.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ligamentous injuries leaned fusion in 2006; displaced injuries tied in 2024 — the honest answer is injury-dependent and insecure
cards.summary: Synthesis: ligamentous injuries leaned fusion in 2006; displaced injuries tied in 2024 — the honest answer is injury-dependent and insecure
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 84 surgical Lisfranc patients: primarily ligamentous injuries (n = 41, 2006) and displaced injuries (n = 43, 2024), both below their intended precision.
cards.result: Ligamentous: AOFAS 88 versus 68.6 favouring arthrodesis (p < 0.005), with 5 of 20 fixation patients later fused. Displaced: VAS-FA 86.5 versus 80.1, difference 6.5 (95% CI −5.3 to 18.2), not significant. PROPOSED SPLIT by injury type, Tier C because both trials are small and the split rests on comparing across them.
cards.watchOut: Hardware removal, midfoot arthritis progression and return-to-sport beyond two years are not resolved by either record; a pooled meta-analysis of these and future trials may yet move one side of the split.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ly TV et al. The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume. 2006 (PMID: 16510816); Ponkilainen V et al. Foot & ankle international. 2024 (PMID: 38482816).

shelves.title: Tranexamic acid in hip and knee replacement: intravenous and topical routes tie — combining both cuts blood loss further and more than halves transfusion versus a single route
shelves.question: In primary total knee and hip arthroplasty, how do intravenous, topical and combined tranexamic acid routes compare for blood loss and transfusion?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Administration, Topical · Anemia/epidemiology/metabolism/prevention & control/therapy · Antifibrinolytic Agents/administration & dosage · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip/methods · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/methods · Blood Loss, Surgical/prevention & control · Blood Transfusion/statistics & numerical data · Hemoglobins/metabolism · Humans · Length of Stay · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tranexamic Acid/administration & dosage · Venous Thromboembolism/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the combined route; the two single routes are interchangeable. Pooling 26 randomised trials (Sun 2019, PMID: 30696680), intravenous versus topical tranexamic acid did not differ substantially on total blood loss (weighted mean difference 30.92 mL, p = 0.31), haemoglobin decline, hospital stay, transfusion rate (relative risk 1.08, p = 0.75) or venous thromboembolism (relative risk 1.89, p = 0.15). But single-route patients fared worse than combined-route patients on every bleeding measure: total blood loss was 198.07 mL greater, haemoglobin decline 0.56 g/dL greater, and transfusion rate higher (relative risk 2.51, p < 0.05) — i.e., the combined route roughly halved transfusion relative to a single route. The earlier meta-analysis (Zhang 2017, PMID: 28602763; 6 trials, 704 patients) concurs: combined administration reduced total blood loss by a mean 134.65 mL and the transfusion rate by a risk difference of −0.07 (7 fewer transfusions per 100 patients, 95% CI −0.11 to −0.03). Neither analysis found a venous-thromboembolism penalty for combining routes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): if tranexamic acid is given, give it both ways; if only one way, route does not matter.

cards.people: 26 randomised controlled trials in patients undergoing total knee or total hip arthroplasty comparing intravenous, topical, or combined intravenous-plus-topical tranexamic acid; outcomes included intraoperative and total blood loss, transfusion rate, haemoglobin levels and decline, length of stay and venous thromboembolism (random-effects models).
cards.result: Intravenous versus topical routes did not differ substantially: total blood loss weighted mean difference 30.92 mL (p = 0.31), transfusion rate relative risk 1.08 (p = 0.75), venous thromboembolism relative risk 1.89 (p = 0.15), and no significant differences in drain loss, haemoglobin level or decline, or length of stay. Compared with combined delivery, single-route delivery had significantly greater total blood loss (weighted mean difference 198.07 mL, p < 0.05), greater haemoglobin decline (0.56, p < 0.05) and higher transfusion rates (relative risk 2.51, p < 0.05), with no significant difference in venous thromboembolism.
cards.watchOut: Route-comparison trials are typically small and dose regimens vary (the analysis stratifies by dose and surgery type); the venous-thromboembolism comparisons rest on few events, so 'no detected increase' is weaker than 'proven safe' — and this shelf compares routes among patients already receiving tranexamic acid, not drug versus no drug.

cards.summary: Zhang 2017 meta-analysis (6 RCTs, 704 patients): combined vs single route — total blood loss −134.65 mL, transfusion risk difference −0.07
cards.people: 6 randomised controlled trials totalling 704 patients undergoing primary total knee or hip arthroplasty, comparing combined intravenous-plus-topical tranexamic acid with a single application (intravenous or topical) or saline; primary outcomes total blood loss, haemoglobin decline and transfusion requirements.
cards.result: Combined administration significantly reduced total blood loss (mean difference −134.65 mL, 95% CI −191.66 to −77.64; P < 0.0001), drainage volume (mean difference −40.19 mL; P < 0.00001) and transfusion rate (risk difference −0.07, 95% CI −0.11 to −0.03; P = 0.0004 — 7 fewer transfusions per 100 patients in absolute terms), and preserved postoperative haemoglobin (mean difference 0.74 g/dL; P < 0.0001), without a signal on the recorded tranexamic-acid adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: Only 6 trials and 704 patients, with the authors themselves calling for larger high-quality trials; the absolute transfusion gain (7 per 100) is more modest than the relative figures in the larger 2019 analysis suggest, because baseline transfusion rates differ across eras and protocols.
