shelves.title: Tourniquet in knee replacement: it buys a drier field and a shorter operation — and costs more pain, less early motion, and the highest thrombosis rate in the network analyses
shelves.question: In total knee arthroplasty, does using a tourniquet improve the surgical field without worsening pain, function or thromboembolism?
shelves.mesh: Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/adverse effects/methods · Bayes Theorem · Blood Loss, Surgical · Humans · Pain · Thromboembolism · Tourniquets/adverse effects
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the tourniquet wins the operation and loses the recovery. In the 2022 Bayesian network meta-analysis of pain, function and thromboembolism (Migliorini 2022, PMID: 33967006; 54 articles, 5,497 procedures), the no-tourniquet group had the lowest rate of deep vein thrombosis, the lowest pain scores at 24–48 hours and at 1, 3 and 12 months, the greatest gain of motion at every time point from 3 days to 12 months, and the highest Knee Society scores at 1, 3 and 12 months. In the companion peri-operative network analysis (Migliorini 2021, PMID: 33417033; 68 studies, 7,413 procedures), full-time tourniquet use gave the shortest surgical duration and the lowest intra-operative blood loss, while hospitalisation was shortest with no tourniquet — and the total-blood-loss data were so inconsistent that no conclusion could be drawn on them. PROPOSED SPLIT: the field/duration benefit the question asks about is real but intra-operative only; on every patient-facing outcome the network evidence favours operating without a tourniquet, or limiting its inflation time.

cards.headline: Migliorini 2022 network meta-analysis (54 articles, 5,497 procedures): no tourniquet ranked lowest for DVT and pain, best for motion gain and Knee Society scores
cards.summary: Migliorini 2022 network meta-analysis (54 articles, 5,497 procedures): no tourniquet ranked lowest for DVT and pain, best for motion gain and Knee Society scores
cards.people: 54 clinical trials/articles covering 5,497 knee arthroplasty procedures, comparing tourniquet protocols (full use, partial use, no tourniquet) for pain (visual analogue scale), clinical and functional outcomes (range of motion, Knee Society Rating System) and deep vein thrombosis rate.
cards.result: The no-tourniquet group evidenced the lowest rate of deep vein thrombosis and the lowest visual analogue pain scores at 24–48 hours and at 1, 3 and 12 months. The same group showed the greatest gain of motion at 3 days, 1 week, 1, 3, 6 and 12 months, and the highest Knee Society scores at 1, 3 and 12 months. The authors conclude that, for the endpoints considered, knee arthroplasties performed without a tourniquet perform better overall. The record reports rankings rather than pooled effect sizes for these outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Network rankings across many small trials with varying inflation protocols are less secure than a single large head-to-head trial, and the straight-leg-raise outcome was too inconsistent to use; surgeons' field-quality judgements — the tourniquet's original purpose — are not among the pooled endpoints.

cards.headline: Migliorini 2021 network meta-analysis (68 studies, 7,413 procedures): full-time tourniquet — shortest surgery, least intra-operative blood loss; no tourniquet — shortest hospitalisation; total blood loss data inconsistent
cards.summary: Migliorini 2021 network meta-analysis (68 studies, 7,413 procedures): full-time tourniquet — shortest surgery, least intra-operative blood loss; no tourniquet — shortest hospitalisation; total blood loss data inconsistent
cards.people: 68 studies covering 7,413 knee arthroplasty procedures, comparing tourniquet protocols (no tourniquet, full-time, incision-to-suture, cementation-to-end and other partial protocols) on peri-operative outcomes: surgical duration, blood loss, haemoglobin drop, transfusion and hospitalisation.
cards.result: Full-time tourniquet use resulted in the shortest surgical duration and the lowest intra-operative blood loss, followed in both cases by the incision-to-suture protocol. The incision-to-suture protocol achieved the smallest haemoglobin drop in the first 72 hours and the lowest transfusion rate, followed by full-time tourniquet. Hospitalisation was shortest in the no-tourniquet group. Significant inconsistency was found in the total estimated blood loss data, so no assumption could be made on that outcome.
cards.watchOut: The peri-operative wins are process measures (minutes, intra-operative millilitres) rather than patient outcomes, and the transfusion ranking actually favours a limited-inflation protocol over both extremes — the network supports 'less tourniquet' more cleanly than it supports any single protocol.
cards.source: Migliorini F et al. Impact of tourniquet during knee arthroplasty: a bayesian network meta-analysis of peri-operative outcomes. Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery. 2021. cards.headline: Synthesis: a clearer view for the surgeon, a sorer and stiffer knee for the patient — and no proven total-blood-loss advantage
cards.summary: Synthesis: a clearer view for the surgeon, a sorer and stiffer knee for the patient — and no proven total-blood-loss advantage
cards.people: Two Bayesian network meta-analyses from the same group covering 54 articles (5,497 procedures) for patient outcomes and 68 studies (7,413 procedures) for peri-operative outcomes in knee arthroplasty.
cards.result: Operative outcomes: full-time tourniquet ranked first for surgical duration and intra-operative blood loss. Patient outcomes: no tourniquet ranked first for pain at all time points, motion gain, Knee Society scores, hospital stay and lowest deep vein thrombosis rate. Total blood loss: inconsistent data, no conclusion. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit confined to the operation itself, harm or disadvantage on recovery outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Both networks are by one author group and lean on many small trials; a large pragmatic randomised trial of tourniquet versus none with patient-reported outcomes would outrank this entire structure and could move the stamp.

shelves.title: Cervical disc replacement vs fusion: higher overall success (odds ratio 2.10), half the secondary surgery (0.50) and less adjacent-segment disease (0.46) in pooled long-term trial data
shelves.question: In cervical radiculopathy or myelopathy from disc disease, does cervical disc arthroplasty preserve motion and match fusion on long-term outcomes and reoperation?
shelves.mesh: Arthroplasty · Cervical Vertebrae/surgery · Disability Evaluation · Diskectomy · Humans · Intervertebral Disc Degeneration/surgery · Intervertebral Disc Displacement/surgery · Pain Measurement · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Spinal Fusion · Total Disc Replacement
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — pooled randomised evidence favours the artificial disc on success, satisfaction and reoperation, which is why this shelf sits above POSSIBLE. In the long-term meta-analysis of 11 randomised trials (Wang 2020, PMID: 31863642; 3,505 patients), arthroplasty beat fusion on overall success (odds ratio 2.10, 95% CI 1.70 to 2.59), neurological success (1.65) and patient satisfaction (2.14), with less neck and arm pain, and significantly less symptomatic adjacent-segment disease (odds ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.63), less total secondary surgery (0.50, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.87) and less surgery at both the index level (0.46) and the adjacent level (0.37) — with no significant difference in total adverse events (1.14, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.42). The earlier synthesis of 14 trials (Findlay 2018, PMID: 30062947; 3,160 patients, follow-up to 10 years) concurs: disc replacement was superior on patient-reported outcomes between 4 and 7 years and produced significantly less adjacent-segment disease at both 2 years and 4–7 years. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): arthroplasty matches or beats fusion on function and halves reoperation and adjacent-segment disease in the pooled trial record; the residual uncertainty is prosthesis durability beyond the trial horizon, not the direction of the evidence.

cards.headline: Wang 2020 meta-analysis (11 RCTs, 3,505 patients): overall success OR 2.10, symptomatic adjacent-segment disease OR 0.46, total secondary surgery OR 0.50 — all favouring arthroplasty
cards.summary: Wang 2020 meta-analysis (11 RCTs, 3,505 patients): overall success OR 2.10, symptomatic adjacent-segment disease OR 0.46, total secondary surgery OR 0.50 — all favouring arthroplasty
cards.people: 11 randomised controlled trials totalling 3,505 patients with cervical disc disease (1,913 arthroplasty, 1,592 fusion), comparing cervical disc arthroplasty with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion on long-term success, function, adverse events, adjacent-segment degeneration, secondary surgery and satisfaction.
cards.result: Arthroplasty achieved significantly higher overall success (odds ratio 2.10, 95% CI 1.70 to 2.59), neck disability index success (1.73, 95% CI 1.37 to 2.18), neurological success (1.65, 95% CI 1.24 to 2.20), patient satisfaction (2.14, 95% CI 1.50 to 3.05) and recommendation rates (3.23, 95% CI 1.79 to 5.80), with better neck pain (−5.50), arm pain (−3.78) and SF-36 physical and mental component scores. Symptomatic adjacent-segment disease was lower (odds ratio 0.46, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.63), as were total secondary surgery (0.50, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.87), index-level surgery (0.46) and adjacent-level surgery (0.37). Total adverse events did not differ significantly (1.14, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.42), nor did the neck disability index score itself (−2.88, 95% CI −5.93 to 0.17).
cards.watchOut: Most underlying trials were industry-sponsored device trials in selected patients (typically single-level disease, no major instability or severe facet arthrosis), and 'overall success' is a composite defined by the device-trial programmes; the pooled population is younger and cleaner than everyday cervical practice.
cards.source: Wang QL et al. Long-term Results Comparing Cervical Disc Arthroplasty to Anterior Cervical Discectomy and Fusion: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Orthopaedic surgery. 2020. PMID: 31863642. cards.headline: Findlay 2018 meta-analysis (14 RCTs, 3,160 patients, follow-up to 10 years): disc replacement superior at 2 years and at 4–7 years, with less adjacent-segment disease at both horizons
cards.summary: Findlay 2018 meta-analysis (14 RCTs, 3,160 patients, follow-up to 10 years): disc replacement superior at 2 years and at 4–7 years, with less adjacent-segment disease at both horizons
cards.people: 22 papers from 14 prospective randomised trials totalling 3,160 patients with symptomatic degenerative cervical disc disease, comparing total disc replacement with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion, with follow-up of up to ten years; evidence graded with GRADE.
cards.result: Meta-analysis indicated disc replacement is superior to fusion at two years and between four and seven years. Short-term patient-reported outcome advantages were typically not significant at two years, but between four and seven years significant differences in neck disability index, SF-36 physical component scores, dysphagia and satisfaction all favoured disc replacement. Most trials found significantly less adjacent-segment disease after disc replacement at both two years and between four and seven years. The authors conclude disc replacement is as effective as fusion and superior for some outcomes, with continued uncertainty about degeneration of the prosthesis.
cards.watchOut: Heterotopic ossification can quietly convert a 'motion-preserving' disc into a fused segment over time, and neither synthesis can speak to 20-year prosthesis survival; patients with myelopathy from multilevel disease or instability were largely outside these trials.
cards.source: Findlay C et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: the disc wins the pooled trial record on success, reoperation and the neighbouring segment — durability is the open file
cards.summary: Synthesis: the disc wins the pooled trial record on success, reoperation and the neighbouring segment — durability is the open file
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised trials (11 trials, 3,505 patients; 14 trials, 3,160 patients, overlapping trial sets) comparing cervical disc arthroplasty with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion.
cards.result: Overall success odds ratio 2.10 (1.70–2.59); symptomatic adjacent-segment disease odds ratio 0.46 (0.34–0.63); total secondary surgery odds ratio 0.50 (0.29–0.87); adverse events not significantly different (1.14, 0.92–1.42). Both syntheses find less adjacent-segment disease and better medium-term patient-reported outcomes with arthroplasty. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — strong, concordant randomised evidence, short of Level A certainty because of sponsorship and selection in the underlying trials.
cards.watchOut: The two meta-analyses share most of their trials, so they are corroboration of method rather than independent replication; motion preservation itself is reported as a design feature and range-of-motion outcome in the trial programmes rather than as a pooled number in these records.

shelves.title: Degenerative spondylolisthesis: SLIP's small trial favoured adding fusion (reoperation 14% vs 34%) — the four-times-larger NORDSTEN-DS trial found decompression alone non-inferior at five years (responders 63% vs 63%)
shelves.question: In degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis with stenosis, does laminectomy plus fusion improve outcomes versus laminectomy alone?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Decompression, Surgical · Disability Evaluation · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Laminectomy · Lumbar Vertebrae/surgery · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Reoperation/statistics & numerical data · Spinal Fusion · Spinal Stenosis/complications/surgery · Spondylolisthesis/complications/surgery · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials point in opposite directions, and the larger one is the null. In SLIP (Ghogawala 2016, PMID: 27074067; only 66 patients), adding instrumented fusion produced a greater improvement in SF-36 physical-component scores at 2 years (15.2 vs 9.5; difference 5.7, 95% CI 0.1 to 11.3; P = 0.046) sustained at 3 and 4 years, and a lower cumulative reoperation rate (14% vs 34%; P = 0.05) — but the Oswestry disability change did not differ significantly (−26.3 vs −17.9; P = 0.06), and fusion cost more blood loss and longer hospital stays (P < 0.001 for both). In NORDSTEN-DS (Kgomotso 2024, PMID: 39111800; 267 patients, 5-year follow-up), decompression alone was non-inferior: 63% of each group achieved at least a 30% Oswestry improvement (difference 0.4 percentage points, 95% CI −11.2 to 11.9, against a −15-point non-inferiority margin), with identical mean Oswestry changes (−17.8 in both groups). PROPOSED SPLIT: fusion may protect against reoperation in selected stable grade-I slips (SLIP), but for the average patient the bigger, longer trial says decompression alone does just as well at five years while avoiding the bigger operation.

cards.headline: SLIP (Ghogawala 2016): SF-36 physical +15.2 (fusion) vs +9.5 (laminectomy alone) at 2 years, P = 0.046; reoperation 14% vs 34%, P = 0.05; Oswestry change not significant
cards.summary: SLIP (Ghogawala 2016): SF-36 physical +15.2 (fusion) vs +9.5 (laminectomy alone) at 2 years, P = 0.046; reoperation 14% vs 34%, P = 0.05; Oswestry change not significant
cards.people: 66 patients aged 50 to 80 years with stable grade I degenerative spondylolisthesis (3–14 mm slip) and symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis, randomised to decompressive laminectomy alone or laminectomy with posterolateral instrumented fusion; primary outcome change in SF-36 physical-component summary at 2 years; follow-up 89% at 1 year, 86% at 2 years, 68% at 4 years.
cards.result: The fusion group had a greater increase in SF-36 physical-component scores at 2 years (15.2 vs 9.5; difference 5.7, 95% CI 0.1 to 11.3; P = 0.046), maintained at 3 and 4 years (P = 0.02 for both). Oswestry Disability Index changes at 2 years did not differ significantly (−26.3 fusion vs −17.9 decompression alone; P = 0.06). Cumulative reoperation was 14% in the fusion group versus 34% with decompression alone (P = 0.05). Fusion involved more blood loss and longer hospital stays (P < 0.001 for both).
cards.watchOut: Only 66 patients and a primary-outcome P value of 0.046 with a confidence interval whose lower bound is 0.1 — a fragile result; a third of patients were lost by year 4, and the reoperation contrast (the most decision-relevant number) sits exactly at P = 0.05.
cards.source: Ghogawala Z et al. Laminectomy plus Fusion versus Laminectomy Alone for Lumbar Spondylolisthesis. The New England journal of medicine. 2016. PMID: 27074067. Registry ID: NCT00109213. cards.headline: NORDSTEN-DS 5-year (Kgomotso 2024): Oswestry responders 63% vs 63% (difference 0.4 points, −11.2 to 11.9) — decompression alone non-inferior to decompression plus fusion
cards.summary: NORDSTEN-DS 5-year (Kgomotso 2024): Oswestry responders 63% vs 63% (difference 0.4 points, −11.2 to 11.9) — decompression alone non-inferior to decompression plus fusion
cards.people: 267 patients aged 18 to 80 years with symptomatic lumbar spinal stenosis and degenerative spondylolisthesis of 3 mm or more at the stenotic level, randomised at 16 Norwegian clinics to decompression alone (n = 134) or decompression with instrumented fusion (n = 133); 230 patients (88%) responded at 5 years; primary outcome a ≥30% reduction in Oswestry Disability Index, with a predefined −15-percentage-point non-inferiority margin.
cards.result: In the modified intention-to-treat analysis, 84 of 133 patients (63%) in the decompression-alone group and 81 of 129 (63%) in the fusion group met the primary outcome: difference 0.4 percentage points (95% CI −11.2 to 11.9), above the −15-point non-inferiority margin; per-protocol results were similar (65% vs 66%). Mean Oswestry change was −17.8 in both groups (mean difference 0.02, 95% CI −3.8 to 3.9), and secondary outcomes (claudication questionnaire, leg and back pain scales, EQ-5D) pointed the same way.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority within a generous −15-point margin is not proof of exact equivalence, and this record is the 5-year follow-up report; reoperation counts beyond the 2-to-5-year window mentioned are not fully detailed in the record carded here.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, two answers — weight the larger, longer one, and keep fusion for the unstable exceptions
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, two answers — weight the larger, longer one, and keep fusion for the unstable exceptions
cards.people: Two randomised trials in degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis: SLIP (n = 66, grade I stable slips, US) and NORDSTEN-DS (n = 267, Norway, 5-year follow-up).
cards.result: Function: SF-36 physical difference +5.7 favouring fusion in SLIP (P = 0.046); Oswestry responders identical (63% vs 63%) and non-inferiority met in NORDSTEN-DS. Reoperation: 14% versus 34% favouring fusion in SLIP (P = 0.05). Burden: more blood loss and longer stays with fusion in SLIP. PROPOSED SPLIT — the trials genuinely disagree, plausibly over patient selection (stable grade-I slips with particular features) as much as over the operation.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial enrolled frankly unstable or high-grade slips, where fusion is not controversial; applying NORDSTEN-DS's non-inferiority to those patients would be an extrapolation beyond both records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ghogawala Z et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2016 (PMID: 27074067); Kgomotso EL et al. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2024 (PMID: 39111800).

shelves.title: Starting allopurinol during a gout flare: pain, resolution time and repeat flares all unchanged in two randomised trials — the old 'wait until it settles' rule has no trial support
shelves.question: In acute gout, does starting allopurinol during the flare prolong or worsen the attack versus starting after it settles?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Allopurinol/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Colchicine/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gout/complications/drug therapy · Gout Suppressants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Indomethacin/therapeutic use · Male · Pain Management/methods · Pain Measurement · Recurrence · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — starting during the flare neither prolongs nor worsens it, in two concordant randomised trials. In Taylor 2012 (PMID: 23098865; 57 men with crystal-proven gout), allopurinol 300 mg started at first medical contact versus placebo for 10 days (both groups on indomethacin and colchicine prophylaxis, all on open allopurinol from day 11) produced identical pain trajectories — visual analogue scores fell from 6.72 versus 6.28 at baseline to 0.18 versus 0.27 at day 10, with no significant difference on any day — and similar subsequent flares (2 vs 3 patients; P = 0.60), while urate fell rapidly on allopurinol (7.8 to 5.9 mg/dL by day 3). ELAG (Satpanich 2022, PMID: 34406530; 117 patients) found the same for timing: median time to complete resolution was 6 days in both the day-1 and day-14 start groups (p = 0.14), and median time to clinical resolution was 4 days in both (p = 0.12), with no serious adverse events in either group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the flare runs its course regardless — starting urate lowering during the attack is safe and saves a second visit's worth of delay.

cards.headline: Taylor 2012: day-10 pain 0.18 (immediate allopurinol) vs 0.27 (placebo-first) — no significant difference on any of days 1–10; flares 2 vs 3 patients
cards.summary: Taylor 2012: day-10 pain 0.18 (immediate allopurinol) vs 0.27 (placebo-first) — no significant difference on any of days 1–10; flares 2 vs 3 patients
cards.people: 57 men with crystal-proven gout randomised to allopurinol 300 mg daily or matching placebo for 10 days, all receiving indomethacin 50 mg three times daily for 10 days and colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily for 90 days, with open-label allopurinol from day 11; 51 patients evaluable (26 allopurinol, 25 placebo); outcomes daily visual analogue pain for 10 days and self-reported flares to day 30.
cards.result: Mean daily pain scores did not differ significantly between groups at any point from days 1 to 10 (baseline 6.72 vs 6.28, P = 0.37; day 10, 0.18 vs 0.27, P = 0.54). Subsequent flares occurred in 2 patients on allopurinol versus 3 on placebo (P = 0.60). Urate fell rapidly on allopurinol (7.8 mg/dL at baseline to 5.9 mg/dL at day 3), while sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein did not differ between groups at any point.
cards.watchOut: Small (51 evaluable), all-male, and both arms received full anti-inflammatory cover (indomethacin plus colchicine) — the trial answers 'starting allopurinol under anti-inflammatory cover', which is how it should be done, not starting it bare. The delayed arm waited only 10 days.
cards.source: Taylor TH et al. Initiation of allopurinol at first medical contact for acute attacks of gout: a randomized clinical trial. The American journal of medicine. 2012. PMID: 23098865. cards.summary: ELAG (Satpanich 2022): median time to complete resolution 6 days with both day-1 and day-14 allopurinol starts (p = 0.14); no serious adverse events
cards.people: 117 patients with crystal-proven gout presenting within 72 hours of flare onset, randomised open-label to allopurinol started on day 1 (n = 59, early) or day 14 (n = 58, late); 115 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis; 28-day trial excluding advanced renal failure, patients already on urate-lowering therapy, and HLA-B*5801 carriers.
cards.result: Median time to complete resolution was 6 days (interquartile range 5–14) in the early group and 6 days (5–7) in the late group (p = 0.14); median time to clinical resolution was 4 days (3–6) in both groups (p = 0.12). Arthritis relapse, laboratory parameters and adverse events did not differ significantly, and no serious adverse events occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the early group's wider resolution range (5–14 days) hints at a few slow resolvers the median hides; HLA-B*5801 screening in this Thai population limits direct transfer to settings that do not screen.

cards.result: Pain at day 10: 0.18 versus 0.27 (not significant). Time to complete resolution: median 6 days in both timing groups. shelves.title: Erosive gout: pushing urate below 0.20 mmol/L (≈3.4 mg/dL) instead of 0.30 did not improve CT bone erosion scores over two years — and the intensive target was harder to hit (62% vs 83%) despite much higher drug doses
shelves.question: In erosive gout, does intensive serum urate lowering to a very low target improve outcomes versus standard target treatment?
shelves.mesh: Allopurinol/therapeutic use · Febuxostat/therapeutic use · Gout/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · Gout Suppressants · Humans · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome · Uric Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — more drug, lower urate, same bones. In the 2-year double-blind randomised trial (Dalbeth 2022, PMID: 34927391; 104 patients with erosive gout), an intensive serum urate target of <0.20 mmol/L (≈3.4 mg/dL) versus the standard <0.30 mmol/L (≈5.0 mg/dL) produced significantly lower urate levels over the study (P = 0.002), yet CT bone erosion scores rose slightly in both groups with no between-group difference (P = 0.20), and every OMERACT core outcome — flares, tophi, pain, patient global assessment, quality of life, activity limitation — improved in both groups without between-group differences. The intensive strategy was also harder to execute: only 62% of the intensive group reached their target by year 2 versus 83% of the standard group (P < 0.05), despite a mean allopurinol dose of 746 mg/day versus 497 mg/day (P < 0.001) and significantly more combination therapy (P = 0.0004), with similar adverse-event rates. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): below the standard <0.30 mmol/L (≈5.0 mg/dL) target, further urate lowering bought no measurable structural or clinical gain over two years in erosive gout — at a substantially higher medication burden.

cards.headline: Dalbeth 2022: erosion scores rose slightly in both groups (between-group P = 0.20); intensive target achieved by 62% vs 83%; mean allopurinol dose 746 vs 497 mg/day
cards.summary: Dalbeth 2022: erosion scores rose slightly in both groups (between-group P = 0.20); intensive target achieved by 62% vs 83%; mean allopurinol dose 746 vs 497 mg/day
cards.people: 104 participants with erosive gout already on oral urate-lowering therapy with baseline serum urate ≥0.30 mmol/L (≈5.0 mg/dL), randomised for 2 years to an intensive serum urate target of <0.20 mmol/L (≈3.4 mg/dL) or a standard target of <0.30 mmol/L (≈5.0 mg/dL), with therapy titrated by protocol up to maximum approved doses of allopurinol, probenecid, febuxostat and benzbromarone; primary endpoint total CT bone erosion score.
cards.result: Serum urate was significantly lower in the intensive group over the study (P = 0.002), but fewer intensive-group participants achieved their randomised target by year 2 (62% vs 83%; P < 0.05). CT bone erosion scores increased slightly in both groups with no between-group difference (P = 0.20). All OMERACT core outcome domains improved in both groups with no between-group differences. The intensive group required higher mean allopurinol doses (746 ± 210 vs 497 ± 186 mg/day; P < 0.001) and more combination therapy (P = 0.0004). Adverse and serious adverse event rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: Two years may be short for erosion remodelling, and the intensive arm's failure to actually reach its target in 38% of patients dilutes the contrast — the trial tests the strategy of aiming lower as much as the state of being lower. Tier C: single trial, and the developer reviews erosive-gout target claims personally.

shelves.title: Tranexamic acid in hip fracture surgery: transfusion relative risk 0.72 in the pooled trials — a real reduction, with thromboembolic safety still under-powered rather than proven
shelves.question: In hip fracture surgery, does tranexamic acid reduce blood transfusion versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee · Blood Loss, Surgical/prevention & control · Combined Modality Therapy · Double-Blind Method · Erythrocyte Transfusion · Female · Hemoglobins/analysis · Hemostasis, Surgical/methods · Hip Fractures/surgery · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Perioperative Care/methods · Risk Factors · Tranexamic Acid/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — transfusion falls; the safety file stays open. The pooled randomised evidence (Haj-Younes 2020, PMID: 31835969; 10 trials, 842 patients) shows tranexamic acid reduced the proportion of patients transfused with a relative risk of 0.72 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.88) — a 28% relative reduction — with no significant differences in mortality (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.10), deep vein thrombosis (1.14), pulmonary embolism (0.53), acute coronary syndrome (1.52) or cerebrovascular events (0.78), all on low event counts. The best-known single trial (Zufferey 2010, PMID: 19926634; 110 patients) points the same way on efficacy — transfusion 42% on tranexamic acid versus 60% on placebo (P = 0.06) — while carrying the caution in its own data: vascular events at 6 weeks occurred in 16% versus 6% (P = 0.10), prompting the authors to warn of a possible hypercoagulable state and to call for further safety evaluation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): expect roughly a quarter to a third fewer patients transfused, relatively speaking; do not read the pooled safety rows as proof of thromboembolic innocence.

cards.headline: Zufferey 2010: transfusion 42% (tranexamic acid) vs 60% (placebo), P = 0.06; vascular events 16% vs 6% at 6 weeks, P = 0.10
cards.summary: Zufferey 2010: transfusion 42% (tranexamic acid) vs 60% (placebo), P = 0.06; vascular events 16% vs 6% at 6 weeks, P = 0.10
cards.people: 110 patients requiring surgery for an isolated hip fracture of less than 48 hours, randomised double-blind to tranexamic acid 15 mg/kg at skin incision and 3 hours later (n = 57) or saline placebo (n = 53); transfusion given by protocol at haemoglobin <9 g/dL; primary outcome erythrocyte transfusion to day 8; safety outcome a composite of symptomatic and asymptomatic vascular events to 6 weeks, with blinded adjudication.
cards.result: Erythrocyte transfusion occurred in 42% of the tranexamic acid group versus 60% of the placebo group (P = 0.06) — an absolute difference of 18 percentage points that just missed conventional significance in this small trial. The probability of vascular events at 6 weeks was 16% with tranexamic acid versus 6% with placebo (P = 0.10). The authors' own meta-analysis combining this trial with previous trials found tranexamic acid significantly reduced transfusion in hip fracture surgery, while cautioning that it may promote a hypercoagulable state and requires further safety evaluation.
cards.watchOut: A 110-patient trial cannot settle either its own efficacy (P = 0.06) or its safety signal (P = 0.10); both numbers are hypothesis-grade alone and earn their keep as the cautionary half of this shelf — the efficacy verdict rests on the pooled analysis.
cards.source: Zufferey PJ et al. Tranexamic acid in hip fracture surgery: a randomized controlled trial. British journal of anaesthesia. 2010. PMID: 19926634. cards.headline: Haj-Younes 2020 meta-analysis (10 RCTs, 842 patients): transfusion RR 0.72 (0.59–0.88); mortality RR 1.17 (0.65–2.10); DVT RR 1.14; PE RR 0.53 — all safety intervals wide
cards.summary: Haj-Younes 2020 meta-analysis (10 RCTs, 842 patients): transfusion RR 0.72 (0.59–0.88); mortality RR 1.17 (0.65–2.10); DVT RR 1.14; PE RR 0.53 — all safety intervals wide
cards.people: 10 randomised controlled trials totalling 842 patients undergoing surgery for hip or proximal femoral fractures, comparing perioperative tranexamic acid with placebo; primary outcome proportion of patients requiring blood transfusion; secondary outcomes blood loss, mortality and complications (random-effects meta-analysis).
cards.result: The proportion of patients requiring transfusion was significantly lower with tranexamic acid: relative risk 0.72 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.88) — a 28% relative reduction. There was no significant difference in mortality (relative risk 1.17, 95% CI 0.65 to 2.10), deep venous thrombosis (1.14, 95% CI 0.43 to 3.06), pulmonary embolism (0.53, 95% CI 0.09 to 3.02), acute coronary syndrome (1.52, 95% CI 0.18 to 12.98), cerebrovascular events (0.78, 95% CI 0.16 to 3.68) or wound complications (1.61, 95% CI 0.51 to 5.13). The authors note the small sample size and low adverse-event rates preclude definitive safety conclusions.
cards.watchOut: 842 patients across 10 small trials is a thin base for harm outcomes in a population whose baseline thromboembolic risk is high; several safety intervals include doubling or worse. Dose and timing regimens varied across the pooled trials.
cards.source: Haj-Younes B et al. Tranexamic acid in hip fracture surgery: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of orthopaedic surgery (Hong Kong). 2020. PMID: 31835969. cards.result: Transfusion: pooled relative risk 0.72 (0.59–0.88); in the largest single trial, 42% versus 60% absolute. Mortality and thromboembolic outcomes: no significant differences, with confidence intervals too wide to exclude harm (mortality up to 2.10; acute coronary syndrome up to 12.98). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for transfusion reduction, harm explicitly unresolved on the face of the shelf.

shelves.title: Hip fracture anaemia: iron plus tranexamic acid halved transfusion (15% vs 30%, RR 0.51) in HiFIT — but neither drug alone beat placebo (26% and 27% vs 30%)
shelves.question: In hip fracture patients with anaemia, does intravenous iron — alone or with tranexamic acid — reduce transfusion versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Male · Adult · Humans · Female · Middle Aged · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Tranexamic Acid/therapeutic use/adverse effects · Hip Fractures/surgery/chemically induced/drug therapy · Blood Transfusion · Iron/therapeutic use · Anemia/drug therapy/etiology · Hemoglobins · Double-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Disaccharides · Ferric Compounds
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the combination works; the components, alone, were not shown to. In the HiFIT factorial trial (Lasocki 2023, PMID: 37524101; 413 hip-fracture patients with preoperative haemoglobin 9.5–13.0 g/dL), transfusion during hospitalisation occurred in 31 of 103 patients (30%) on double placebo, versus 16 of 104 (15%) on ferric derisomaltose plus tranexamic acid (relative risk 0.51, 98.3% CI 0.27 to 0.97; p = 0.012) — but in 27 patients (26%) on iron alone (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.29; p = 0.28) and 28 (27%) on tranexamic acid alone (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.33; p = 0.39), neither significantly different from placebo. Adverse events were similar across groups (487 events in total); severe postoperative anaemia (haemoglobin <8 g/dL) was more frequent on double placebo. The trial was stopped early for efficacy at its planned interim analysis. PROPOSED SPLIT: give both or expect little — in this trial the transfusion benefit belonged to the combination, and a single preoperative iron infusion by itself did not significantly reduce transfusion.

cards.headline: HiFIT (Lasocki 2023): transfusion 15% (iron + TXA) vs 30% (double placebo), RR 0.51, p = 0.012 — iron alone 26% (p = 0.28), TXA alone 27% (p = 0.39)
cards.summary: HiFIT (Lasocki 2023): transfusion 15% (iron + TXA) vs 30% (double placebo), RR 0.51, p = 0.012 — iron alone 26% (p = 0.28), TXA alone 27% (p = 0.39)
cards.people: 413 adults hospitalised with hip fracture at 12 French centres with preoperative haemoglobin between 9.5 and 13.0 g/dL (median age 86 years; 76% women), randomised 1:1:1:1 in a 2×2 factorial double-blind design to ferric derisomaltose 20 mg/kg intravenously plus tranexamic acid (1 g bolus, 1 g over 8 hours, plus 3 g topically during surgery), iron plus placebo, tranexamic acid plus placebo, or double placebo (about 103–104 per group); primary outcome transfusion during hospitalisation or by day 30; trial stopped early for efficacy after the planned interim analysis of the first 390 patients.
cards.result: Transfusion occurred in 31 of 103 patients (30%) on double placebo versus 16 of 104 (15%) on both drugs (relative risk 0.51, 98.3% CI 0.27 to 0.97; p = 0.012), 27 (26%) on iron alone (relative risk 0.81, 95% CI 0.50 to 1.29; p = 0.28) and 28 (27%) on tranexamic acid alone (relative risk 0.85, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.33; p = 0.39). A total of 487 adverse events were reported with similar rates among groups; severe postoperative anaemia (haemoglobin <8 g/dL) was more frequent in the double placebo group; common events were sepsis, pneumonia and urinary infection at similar rates in all groups.
cards.watchOut: Early stopping for efficacy tends to inflate effect sizes, and the factorial's single-agent arms were not powered to exclude modest benefits — 'not significant' for iron alone is not proof of no effect. The tranexamic acid regimen here (intravenous plus 3 g topical) is more intensive than in most hip-fracture trials, which may explain why its single-agent arm still missed significance while the combination succeeded. Tier C: single trial.
cards.source: Lasocki S et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: a combination result, not an iron result — HiFIT supports pairing the drugs and warns against crediting either one alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: a combination result, not an iron result — HiFIT supports pairing the drugs and warns against crediting either one alone
cards.people: One multicentre 2×2 factorial double-blind randomised trial of 413 hip-fracture patients with haemoglobin 9.5–13.0 g/dL (HiFIT).
cards.result: Transfusion: 30% double placebo; 15% iron plus tranexamic acid (relative risk 0.51, p = 0.012); 26% iron alone (p = 0.28); 27% tranexamic acid alone (p = 0.39). PROPOSED SPLIT by treatment combination, Tier C as a single early-stopped trial.
cards.watchOut: Patients with haemoglobin below 9.5 g/dL — those at highest transfusion risk — were outside this trial, and the result should not be extrapolated to them; nor does the trial address oral iron, repeated dosing, or transfusion thresholds different from local practice.

shelves.title: Prehabilitation before hip or knee replacement: better early function and pain after knee replacement in pooled trials — but 24 of 28 trials at high risk of bias, and the hip evidence is two contradictory trials
shelves.question: Before total hip or knee arthroplasty, does prehabilitation improve postoperative pain, function and length of stay versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip/rehabilitation · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/rehabilitation · Osteoarthritis, Hip/surgery/rehabilitation · Osteoarthritis, Knee/surgery/rehabilitation · Preoperative Exercise · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Range of Motion, Articular · Recovery of Function · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real-looking early advantage after knee replacement, resting on a weak trial base. Pooling the randomised trials in osteoarthritis arthroplasty (Adebero 2024, PMID: 38349251; 28 trials), prehabilitation improved post-knee-replacement function (standardised mean difference 0.50, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.77), pain (0.44, 0.17 to 0.71), quality of life (0.28), strength (0.72) and functional mobility (0.39) — but 24 of the 28 trials were at high risk of bias, heterogeneity was significant for every outcome, hip-replacement evidence rested on 2 limited and contradictory trials, and the authors state these problems prevent conclusions about effectiveness up to one year. The wider orthopaedic synthesis (Punnoose 2023, PMID: 37052919; 48 trials, 3,570 participants) graded the postoperative evidence for knee replacement function at 6 weeks as moderate certainty (standardised mean difference −0.51, 95% CI −0.85 to −0.17, on scales where lower is better), with most other postoperative differences low to very low certainty. Neither record reports a pooled length-of-stay benefit, so that part of the question is unanswered here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prehabilitation probably improves early recovery after knee replacement; for hip replacement, and for hospital stay, the evidence is not there yet.

cards.headline: Adebero 2024 meta-analysis (28 RCTs): post-TKA function SMD 0.50, pain 0.44, strength 0.72 — with 24 of 28 trials at high risk of bias and only 2 contradictory THA trials
cards.summary: Adebero 2024 meta-analysis (28 RCTs): post-TKA function SMD 0.50, pain 0.44, strength 0.72 — with 24 of 28 trials at high risk of bias and only 2 contradictory THA trials
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Adebero 2024)
cards.people: 28 randomised controlled trials of prehabilitation (preoperative exercise-based programmes) before total knee or total hip arthroplasty for osteoarthritis, with self-reported function, health-related quality of life and pain, and performance-based strength, range of motion, balance and functional mobility, followed to 52 weeks after surgery (searches to August 2022; risk of bias by RoB 2.0).
cards.result: After total knee arthroplasty, prehabilitation improved function (standardised mean difference 0.50, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.77), pain (0.44, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.71), health-related quality of life (0.28, 95% CI 0.12 to 0.43), strength (0.72, 95% CI 0.47 to 0.98), range of motion (0.31, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.59) and functional mobility (0.39, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.73), but not balance (0.28, 95% CI −0.11 to 0.66). High risk of bias was found in 24 of 28 trials, all outcomes showed significant heterogeneity (p < 0.01), and the total hip arthroplasty evidence comprised 2 limited and contradictory trials; the authors conclude these problems prevent conclusions regarding effectiveness up to one year.
cards.watchOut: Standardised mean differences of 0.4–0.5 from mostly unblinded exercise trials with subjective outcomes are exactly the effect sizes bias produces; treat the direction as probably right and the size as probably inflated. Length of stay is not among the pooled outcomes in this record.

cards.headline: Punnoose 2023 meta-analysis (48 trials, 3,570 patients): moderate-certainty postoperative function benefit at 6 weeks after knee replacement (SMD −0.51); most other postoperative evidence low to very low certainty
cards.summary: Punnoose 2023 meta-analysis (48 trials, 3,570 patients): moderate-certainty postoperative function benefit at 6 weeks after knee replacement (SMD −0.51); most other postoperative evidence low to very low certainty
cards.people: 48 randomised trials involving 3,570 participants (61.5% women; mean age 64.1 years) comparing prehabilitation with standard care across orthopaedic surgery, including total knee and total hip replacement and lumbar surgery; outcomes pain, function, muscle strength and health-related quality of life, graded with GRADE (searches 2000 to June 2022).
cards.result: Preoperatively, moderate-certainty evidence favoured prehabilitation for knee replacement function (standardised mean difference −0.70, 95% CI −1.08 to −0.32) and strength/flexion, and for hip replacement quality of life and strength/abduction. Postoperatively, moderate-certainty evidence supported prehabilitation for function at 6 weeks after knee replacement (standardised mean difference −0.51, 95% CI −0.85 to −0.17); other postoperative differences favouring prehabilitation were of low to very low certainty. The authors conclude prehabilitation showed promising results, with high risk of bias and heterogeneity affecting overall quality.
cards.watchOut: The negative standardised differences here reflect scales where lower scores are better — the direction favours prehabilitation, but readers must not mix this sign convention with the positive differences in the Adebero analysis. Durability beyond the early postoperative window is the weak point in both syntheses.
cards.source: Punnoose A et al. Prehabilitation for Patients Undergoing Orthopedic Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA network open. 2023. PMID: 37052919. MeSH: Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Preoperative Exercise · Orthopedic Procedures · Quality of Life · Europe

cards.headline: Synthesis: worth doing before a knee replacement, unproven before a hip replacement — and nobody has shown it shortens the stay
cards.summary: Synthesis: worth doing before a knee replacement, unproven before a hip replacement — and nobody has shown it shortens the stay
cards.people: Two systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised prehabilitation trials: 28 trials in hip/knee osteoarthritis arthroplasty (Adebero 2024) and 48 trials across orthopaedic surgery (Punnoose 2023).
cards.result: Knee replacement: function standardised mean difference 0.50 (0.23–0.77) and 6-week function −0.51 (−0.85 to −0.17, moderate certainty) in the two analyses; pain 0.44 (0.17–0.71); strength 0.72 (0.47–0.98). Hip replacement: 2 limited, contradictory trials. Length of stay: no pooled benefit reported in either record. Trial quality: 24 of 28 trials at high risk of bias in the arthroplasty-specific review. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C for the bias-laden base.
cards.watchOut: Programmes labelled 'prehabilitation' range from a leaflet plus two sessions to supervised multi-week training; the pooled averages cannot tell a patient which dose, if any, drives the benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Adebero T et al. Disability and rehabilitation. 2024 (PMID: 38349251); Punnoose A et al. JAMA network open. 2023 (PMID: 37052919).

shelves.title: NSAIDs and fracture healing: the large adjusted synthesis finds no significant nonunion increase (OR 1.11, 0.99–1.23) — the small randomised-trial pool finds harm (OR 3.47), concentrated in use beyond 4 weeks and in indomethacin
shelves.question: Do NSAIDs delay fracture healing or increase non-union?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use/pharmacology · Fracture Healing/drug effects · Fractures, Ununited · Fractures, Bone
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two evidence layers disagree, and the disagreement is informative. The updated systematic review (Chuang 2024, PMID: 39319252; 20 studies, 523,240 patients, mostly observational) found no significant difference in non-union or delayed union between NSAID users and non-users (pooled adjusted odds ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.23); an initial reoperation association (crude odds ratio 1.42, 95% CI 0.88 to 2.28) also became insignificant on sensitivity analysis. The meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials (Al Farii 2021, PMID: 34746650; 6 trials, 609 patients) found the opposite: nonunion odds ratio 3.47 with NSAIDs — but when trials were split by treatment duration, courses under 2 weeks showed no significant nonunion risk while courses over 4 weeks did, and indomethacin specifically carried odds ratios from 1.66 to 9.03 while other NSAIDs showed no significant risk. PROPOSED SPLIT: short courses look safe in both layers; prolonged use — and indomethacin in particular — carries a randomised-trial harm signal that the big observational pool, with its cruder exposure data, may simply miss. Because this is a harm claim, the shelf is Tier C.

cards.headline: Chuang 2024 updated review (20 studies, 523,240 patients): adjusted OR for non-union/delayed union 1.11 (0.99–1.23) — not significant
cards.summary: Chuang 2024 updated review (20 studies, 523,240 patients): adjusted OR for non-union/delayed union 1.11 (0.99–1.23) — not significant
cards.people: 20 prospective, retrospective and case-control studies totalling 523,240 patients (mean ages 6.7 to 77.0 years; follow-up 3 to 67 months) assessing NSAID use and bone-healing outcomes (non-union, delayed union, reoperation), with a leave-one-out sensitivity approach (searches to July 2023).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in non-union or delayed union between NSAID users and non-users: pooled adjusted odds ratio 1.11 (95% CI 0.99 to 1.23). An initial significant association with reoperation became insignificant on sensitivity analysis (crude odds ratio 1.42, 95% CI 0.88 to 2.28). The authors conclude NSAIDs may have a minimal impact on non-union or delayed-union risk, while cautioning that few studies focus on NSAID type and dosage.
cards.watchOut: The bulk of the weight is observational: people prescribed NSAIDs after fracture differ from those who are not (pain severity, fracture type, comorbidity), and 'NSAID use' in records rarely captures duration — the very variable the randomised analysis suggests matters. An odds ratio of 1.11 with an upper bound of 1.23 also cannot exclude a small real increase.
cards.source: Chuang PY et al. Do NSAIDs affect bone healing rate, delay union, or cause non-union: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis. Frontiers in endocrinology. 2024. PMID: 39319252. cards.headline: Al Farii 2021 RCT meta-analysis (6 trials, 609 patients): nonunion OR 3.47 overall — but no significant risk under 2 weeks of use; indomethacin ORs 1.66–9.03
cards.summary: Al Farii 2021 RCT meta-analysis (6 trials, 609 patients): nonunion OR 3.47 overall — but no significant risk under 2 weeks of use; indomethacin ORs 1.66–9.03
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Al Farii 2021)
cards.people: 6 randomised controlled trials totalling 609 patients comparing nonunion occurrence in patients who received NSAIDs after fracture versus control, with subgroup analyses by duration of NSAID treatment and by drug (searches to October 2018; fixed-effects model). This record carries no MeSH in PubMed.
cards.result: The risk of nonunion was higher in patients given NSAIDs after fracture, with an odds ratio of 3.47. Categorised by duration, patients who received NSAIDs for a short period (<2 weeks) showed no significant risk of nonunion, whereas those treated for a long period (>4 weeks) did. Indomethacin was associated with a significantly higher nonunion rate, with odds ratios ranging from 1.66 to 9.03, compared with other NSAIDs, which did not show a significant nonunion risk.
cards.watchOut: Six small trials and 609 patients — the 3.47 estimate is fragile, the trials are largely older indomethacin-era studies (including heterotopic-ossification prophylaxis contexts), and the record reports no confidence interval for the headline odds ratio; read the duration and drug pattern as the finding, not the point estimate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: duration and drug, not the class label, carry the risk — brief analgesic courses are exonerated by both layers
cards.summary: Synthesis: duration and drug, not the class label, carry the risk — brief analgesic courses are exonerated by both layers
cards.people: Two meta-analyses: a 20-study, 523,240-patient mostly-observational synthesis (Chuang 2024) and a 6-trial, 609-patient randomised-trial synthesis (Al Farii 2021).
cards.result: Overall association: adjusted odds ratio 1.11 (0.99–1.23), not significant, in the large pool; odds ratio 3.47 in the small randomised pool. By duration: no significant risk under 2 weeks; risk present over 4 weeks. By drug: indomethacin odds ratios 1.66–9.03; other NSAIDs not significant. PROPOSED SPLIT by exposure pattern, Tier C as a harm claim resting partly on small old trials.
cards.watchOut: Neither record isolates modern selective COX-2 inhibitors at analgesic doses in typical fracture patients, and spinal-fusion healing (where the concern is greatest) is a distinct literature not covered by these two records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chuang PY et al. Frontiers in endocrinology. 2024 (PMID: 39319252); Al Farii H et al. OTA international : the open access journal of orthopaedic trauma. 2021 (PMID: 34746650).

shelves.title: Knee cartilage defects ≥3 cm²: the MACI implant's pain-and-function advantage over microfracture was maintained at five years in SUMMIT (P = 0.022) — with no difference in MRI defect filling
shelves.question: In knee cartilage defects, does matrix-applied autologous chondrocyte implantation give better outcomes than microfracture?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adolescent · Adult · Animals · Arthroplasty, Subchondral/adverse effects/methods · Cartilage, Articular/diagnostic imaging/injuries/surgery · Chondrocytes/pathology/transplantation · Collagen/therapeutic use · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Knee Injuries/diagnostic imaging/surgery/therapy · Knee Joint/diagnostic imaging/surgery · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/diagnosis · Postoperative Complications/diagnosis · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Reproducibility of Results · Swine · Transplantation, Autologous/adverse effects/methods · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one well-conducted randomised trial, followed to five years. In SUMMIT (Brittberg 2018, PMID: 29565642; 144 patients randomised, 128 in the 5-year extension), symptomatic knee cartilage defects of 3 cm² or larger treated with the MACI implant — autologous cultured chondrocytes on a porcine collagen membrane, as named in the record, which does not name a manufacturer — maintained a clinically and statistically significant advantage over microfracture on the co-primary endpoint of KOOS pain and function at 5 years (P = 0.022), with activities-of-daily-living improvements also significantly better (P = 0.007); quality-of-life and other-symptom scores remained numerically higher but lost statistical significance versus the 2-year analysis. MRI at year 5 (120 patients) showed improved defect filling in both groups with no statistically significant difference between treatments — the structural pictures tie while the patients' scores do not. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): for larger cartilage defects, MACI gives durably better pain and function than microfracture at five years, on the strength of a single trial programme.

cards.headline: SUMMIT 5-year (Brittberg 2018): KOOS pain/function advantage of MACI over microfracture maintained and significant at 5 years (P = 0.022); ADL P = 0.007; MRI filling not significantly different
cards.summary: SUMMIT 5-year (Brittberg 2018): KOOS pain/function advantage of MACI over microfracture maintained and significant at 5 years (P = 0.022); ADL P = 0.007; MRI filling not significantly different
cards.people: 144 patients with symptomatic cartilage defects of the knee (3 cm² or larger) randomised at 14 European sites in the SUMMIT trial to matrix-applied characterised autologous cultured chondrocytes on a porcine collagen membrane (MACI — the product as named in the record; the record does not name a manufacturer) versus microfracture; 128 patients (65 MACI, 63 microfracture) continued into the 5-year extension study; MRI structural evaluation in 120 patients at year 5.
cards.result: The improvements in KOOS Pain and Function domains were maintained over 5 years, and the improvement of MACI over microfracture on the co-primary endpoint remained clinically and statistically significant at 5 years (P = 0.022). Activities of daily living remained significantly better with MACI (P = 0.007); quality of life and other symptoms remained numerically higher but lost statistical significance relative to the 2-year analysis. MRI showed improved defect filling with both treatments and no statistically significant between-group difference.
cards.watchOut: A single trial programme (this is the 5-year extension of the same SUMMIT cohort, not an independent replication), with 16 of 144 patients not continuing into the extension; the record reports significance levels rather than the 5-year point differences for the co-primary endpoint, and MACI is a two-stage, high-cost procedure whose comparator (microfracture) is known to fade — beating a fading comparator at year 5 is a lower bar than beating it at year 2. Tier C: single trial carrying a benefit claim for a named product.
cards.source: Brittberg M et al. Matrix-Applied Characterized Autologous Cultured Chondrocytes Versus Microfracture: Five-Year Follow-up of a Prospective Randomized Trial. The American journal of sports medicine. 2018. PMID: 29565642. shelves.title: First-time kneecap dislocation: operating on the MPFL roughly halves redislocation (22% vs 43% in children; pooled OR 0.17) — but the operated children scored their knees slightly worse
shelves.question: After a first-time traumatic patellar dislocation, does medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction prevent re-dislocation better than rehabilitation or bracing?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Arthroscopy/adverse effects · Braces/statistics & numerical data · Child · Female · Humans · Knee · Knee Injuries/surgery · Knee Joint/surgery · Ligaments, Articular/surgery · Male · Patellar Dislocation/surgery/therapy · Recurrence · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for preventing the next dislocation, with a function caveat and a population flag. In the randomised trial in skeletally immature patients aged 9–14 (Askenberger 2018, PMID: 29847145; 74 patients), arthroscopic-assisted MPFL repair cut 2-year redislocation to 8 of about 37 patients (22%) versus 16 (43%) with a knee brace (P = 0.047) — yet the repair group's mean Kujala score was lower (90.9, 'good') than the brace group's (95.9, 'excellent'), and the KOOS-child sport/play and quality-of-life subscales favoured the brace group among those with redislocations. The 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis (Elnewishy 2024, PMID: 39703292; 6 studies, 325 patients) pools a larger surgical advantage: redislocation odds ratio 0.17 (95% CI 0.09 to 0.32; P < 0.00001) and Kujala scores higher with surgery (mean difference 8.10) — but with severe heterogeneity (I² = 95%) and mostly non-randomised studies. A second randomised trial (Straume-Næsheim 2022, PMID: 35347375) is in recurrent — not first-time — dislocation: persistent instability at 12 months in 2 of 30 (6.7%) after MPFL reconstruction versus 13 of 31 (41.9%) with active rehabilitation (relative risk 6.3 for rehabilitation). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): MPFL surgery prevents redislocation better than bracing or rehabilitation; whether the average first-time dislocator's knee feels better for it is much less clear, and the randomised base is paediatric repair plus a recurrent-dislocation trial, not adult first-time reconstruction — hence Tier C.

cards.headline: Askenberger 2018 RCT (children 9–14): redislocation 22% after MPFL repair vs 43% with knee brace (P = 0.047) — but Kujala 90.9 vs 95.9 favoured the brace
cards.summary: Askenberger 2018 RCT (children 9–14): redislocation 22% after MPFL repair vs 43% with knee brace (P = 0.047) — but Kujala 90.9 vs 95.9 favoured the brace
cards.people: 74 skeletally immature patients aged 9 to 14 years (mean 13.1) with an acute first-time traumatic lateral patellar dislocation, all assessed with examination, radiographs, MRI and diagnostic arthroscopy within 2 weeks, randomised to a knee brace for 4 weeks plus physiotherapy or arthroscopic-assisted MPFL repair with anchors plus 4 weeks in a soft cast splint and physiotherapy; follow-up 2 years.
cards.result: Redislocation at final follow-up occurred in 8 patients (22%) in the repair group versus 16 patients (43%) in the brace group (P = 0.047). However, the mean Kujala score was 90.9 ('good') after repair versus 95.9 ('excellent') with bracing, KOOS-child sport/play and quality-of-life subscales were lower in the repair group (significantly so among patients with redislocations), and an impaired quadriceps Limb Symmetry Index (median 83%) was found only in the repair group. Eighty-one percent of patients had at least 2 anatomic patellar instability risk factors; none was significantly associated with redislocation.
cards.watchOut: Children only, repair (reattachment) rather than the reconstruction the question names, and a P value of 0.047 on the primary outcome — the stability benefit is real but fragile, and it came with measurably worse early knee function and quadriceps symmetry.
cards.source: Askenberger M et al. Operative Repair of Medial Patellofemoral Ligament Injury Versus Knee Brace in Children With an Acute First-Time Traumatic Patellar Dislocation: A Randomized Controlled Trial. cards.headline: Straume-Næsheim 2022 RCT (recurrent dislocation): persistent instability 6.7% after MPFL reconstruction vs 41.9% with active rehabilitation (RR 6.3)
cards.summary: Straume-Næsheim 2022 RCT (recurrent dislocation): persistent instability 6.7% after MPFL reconstruction vs 41.9% with active rehabilitation (RR 6.3)
cards.people: 61 patients aged 12 to 30 years with recurrent lateral patellar dislocation and no significant trochlear dysplasia or tibial-tuberosity–trochlear-groove distance ≥20 mm, randomised to isolated MPFL reconstruction (n = 30) or active physiotherapist-led rehabilitation (n = 31); all underwent diagnostic arthroscopy; primary outcome persistent patellar instability at 12 months. NOTE: this trial enrolled recurrent, not first-time, dislocators.
cards.result: Persistent patellar instability at 12 months was reported by 2 patients (6.7%) in the reconstruction group versus 13 (41.9%) in the rehabilitation group (relative risk 6.3, 95% CI 1.5 to 25.5, for rehabilitation versus reconstruction). Activity levels and patient-reported outcome measures (KOOS, Kujala, Cincinnati, Lysholm, Noyes) did not differ significantly between groups at baseline or follow-up, and patients with persistent instability did not score significantly lower than stable patients.
cards.watchOut: Population mismatch with this shelf's question — recurrent dislocators have already declared themselves high-risk, so the absolute benefit of surgery here overstates what a first-time dislocator should expect; it is carded as directional support for the stabilising effect, and the mismatch is flagged for the coordinator.
cards.source: Straume-Næsheim TM et al. Medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction is superior to active rehabilitation in protecting against further patella dislocations. cards.headline: Elnewishy 2024 meta-analysis (6 studies, 325 patients): redislocation OR 0.17 (0.09–0.32) and Kujala +8.10 with MPFL surgery vs bracing — at I² = 95% heterogeneity
cards.summary: Elnewishy 2024 meta-analysis (6 studies, 325 patients): redislocation OR 0.17 (0.09–0.32) and Kujala +8.10 with MPFL surgery vs bracing — at I² = 95% heterogeneity
cards.people: 6 studies totalling 325 patients directly comparing medial patellofemoral ligament surgery (described as reconstruction) with knee bracing for acute first-time traumatic patellar dislocation, published within the last 10 years; primary outcomes redislocation rate and Kujala functional score. This record carries no MeSH in PubMed.
cards.result: MPFL surgery significantly reduced redislocation rates versus bracing (odds ratio 0.17, 95% CI 0.09 to 0.32; P < 0.00001) and improved functional outcomes (Kujala mean difference 8.10, 95% CI 6.46 to 9.75), with fewer reoperations reported — despite notable heterogeneity across studies (I² = 95%). The authors recommend further high-quality randomised trials to confirm the findings.
cards.watchOut: A pooled odds ratio of 0.17 with I² of 95% means the studies barely agree with each other; the pooled Kujala advantage also contradicts the one paediatric randomised trial carded above, where bracing scored better — the review's functional claim should be weighted below its redislocation claim.
cards.source: Elnewishy A et al. Operative Repair of Medial Patellofemoral Ligament Injury Versus Knee Bracing in Acute First-Time Traumatic Patellar Dislocation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Cureus. 2024. PMID: 39703292. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: surgery stabilises — that much is consistent; whether it leaves a better-feeling knee after a first dislocation is unresolved
cards.summary: Synthesis: surgery stabilises — that much is consistent; whether it leaves a better-feeling knee after a first dislocation is unresolved
cards.people: Two randomised trials (74 children with first-time dislocation, repair vs brace; 61 patients with recurrent dislocation, reconstruction vs rehabilitation) and one meta-analysis of 6 studies (325 patients) in first-time dislocation.
cards.result: Redislocation: 22% versus 43% (first-time, children, P = 0.047); pooled odds ratio 0.17 (0.09–0.32) in first-time dislocation; persistent instability 6.7% versus 41.9% in recurrent dislocation. Function: Kujala favoured bracing in the randomised trial (95.9 vs 90.9) but favoured surgery in the heterogeneous pooled analysis (+8.10). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for redislocation prevention, Tier C.
cards.watchOut: No randomised trial of reconstruction (as opposed to repair) in adults after a first-time dislocation is carded here — that trial is what would settle the question as asked; anatomic risk factors (present in 81% of the paediatric trial's patients) likely identify who gains most, but neither randomised record proves a subgroup rule.

shelves.title: Ankle syndesmosis injury: suture-button fixation beats screws on function scores (AOFAS ~95 vs ~87) and implant problems (breakage 0% vs 25.4%, removal 6.0% vs 22.4%) in pooled randomised trials
shelves.question: For acute ankle syndesmosis (diastasis) injuries, does suture-button fixation give better outcomes than syndesmotic screws?
shelves.mesh: Ankle Fractures/surgery · Ankle Injuries/surgery · Bone Screws · Device Removal · Female · Fracture Fixation, Internal/adverse effects/instrumentation/methods · Humans · Male · Postoperative Complications · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Return to Sport · Suture Techniques/adverse effects · Sutures
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — consistent across two independent meta-analyses of the same small randomised literature. Shimozono 2019 (PMID: 30475639; 5 trials, 285 patients) found suture-button patients scored higher on the American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society scale at a mean of 20.8 months (95.3 vs 86.7; P < 0.001), with no broken implants (0.0% vs 25.4%; P < 0.001), fewer implant removals (6.0% vs 22.4%; P = 0.01) and less joint malreduction (0.8% vs 11.5%; P = 0.05). Onggo 2020 (PMID: 30503612; 5 trials, 280 patients) confirms the pattern with a cooler head: the 1-year AOFAS advantage was a mean difference of 5.46 points (95% CI 0.40 to 10.51; p = 0.03) — statistically significant but, the authors note, of unlikely clinical significance — while implant failure was dramatically lower with the button (odds ratio 0.03, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.15; p < 0.001) and infection/wound problems were marginally, non-significantly higher (odds ratio 1.4, 95% CI 0.4 to 4.85; p = 0.60). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the button's clearest wins are mechanical — nothing to break, rarely anything to remove, better reduction — with a small functional edge on top.

cards.headline: Shimozono 2019 meta-analysis (5 RCTs, 285 patients): AOFAS 95.3 vs 86.7 (P < 0.001); broken implants 0.0% vs 25.4%; removal 6.0% vs 22.4%; malreduction 0.8% vs 11.5%
cards.summary: Shimozono 2019 meta-analysis (5 RCTs, 285 patients): AOFAS 95.3 vs 86.7 (P < 0.001); broken implants 0.0% vs 25.4%; removal 6.0% vs 22.4%; malreduction 0.8% vs 11.5%
cards.people: 5 randomised controlled trials comparing suture-button (n = 143) with syndesmotic screw fixation (n = 142) for ankle syndesmosis injuries; outcomes included American Orthopaedic Foot & Ankle Society (AOFAS) score at a mean follow-up of 20.8 months, implant breakage, implant removal and joint malreduction.
cards.result: The suture-button group had a higher postoperative AOFAS score (95.3 vs 86.7; P < 0.001) and lower rates of broken implants (0.0% vs 25.4%; P < 0.001), implant removal (6.0% vs 22.4%; P = 0.01) and joint malreduction (0.8% vs 11.5%; P = 0.05) than the screw group. The authors conclude the suture-button technique results in improved functional outcomes and lower rates of broken implant and malreduction, warranting a grade A recommendation in their assessment.
cards.watchOut: Five small trials; an 8.6-point AOFAS gap is larger than the second meta-analysis found at a fixed 1-year time point, and AOFAS is a clinician-completed score vulnerable to unblinded assessment — weight the hard mechanical outcomes (breakage, removal, malreduction) more than the score gap.
cards.source: Shimozono Y et al. Suture Button Versus Syndesmotic Screw for Syndesmosis Injuries: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. The American journal of sports medicine. 2019. PMID: 30475639. cards.headline: Onggo 2020 meta-analysis (5 RCTs, 280 patients): AOFAS mean difference +5.46 at 1 year (p = 0.03); implant failure OR 0.03 (p < 0.001); infection OR 1.4, not significant
cards.summary: Onggo 2020 meta-analysis (5 RCTs, 280 patients): AOFAS mean difference +5.46 at 1 year (p = 0.03); implant failure OR 0.03 (p < 0.001); infection OR 1.4, not significant
cards.people: 5 randomised controlled trials totalling 280 patients (140 suture button, 140 syndesmotic screw) with acute ankle diastasis/syndesmotic injuries, comparing clinical outcomes and complication profiles of the two constructs (searches to March 2018).
cards.result: Suture-button fixation gave a significantly higher AOFAS score at 1 year (mean difference 5.46, 95% CI 0.40 to 10.51; p = 0.03) — which the authors judge unlikely to be clinically significant — and a significantly lower implant failure rate (odds ratio 0.03, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.15; p < 0.001). Infection and wound issues were marginally higher with the suture button (odds ratio 1.4, 95% CI 0.4 to 4.85; p = 0.60). No other parameter differed significantly; the authors conclude both constructs yield similar clinical outcomes, with fewer implant failures for the button.
cards.watchOut: The two meta-analyses draw on substantially the same five trials, so this is corroboration, not independent replication; neither record addresses cost (buttons cost more per implant, screws cost more in removals) or outcomes beyond about two years.

cards.summary: Synthesis: pick the button for the hardware outcomes; expect similar knees — ankles — either way on symptoms
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of the same small randomised literature (5 trials each; 285 and 280 patients) comparing suture-button with syndesmotic screw fixation for acute ankle syndesmosis injuries.
cards.result: Function: AOFAS higher with the button by 5.46 points at 1 year (0.40–10.51) in one analysis and 95.3 versus 86.7 at ~21 months in the other. Hardware: broken implants 0.0% versus 25.4%; implant failure odds ratio 0.03; removal 6.0% versus 22.4%; malreduction 0.8% versus 11.5%. Infection: no significant difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), driven by implant-related outcomes with a small functional advantage.
cards.watchOut: Syndesmosis injuries accompanying fractures versus isolated ligamentous diastasis may behave differently, and the pooled trials mix them; long-term arthritis outcomes by reduction quality are beyond both records.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shimozono Y et al. The American journal of sports medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30475639); Onggo JR et al. Foot and ankle surgery : official journal of the European Society of Foot and Ankle Surgeons. 2020 (PMID: 30503612).

shelves.title: One botulinum toxin A injection into the thumb base cut pain more than saline at 3 months in a 60-patient phase 3 trial — with transient thenar weakness in nearly half
shelves.question: In painful base-of-thumb osteoarthritis, does intra-articular botulinum toxin A reduce pain versus placebo injection?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one small, well-blinded trial, a real pain difference, and a conspicuous side effect. In RHIBOT (Nguyen C et al., PMID: 38294016), 60 adults with painful trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis received an ultrasound-guided injection of botulinum toxin A 50 units or saline, both with rigid splinting: at 3 months thumb pain had fallen by -25.7 points (0-100 scale) on botulinum toxin versus -9.7 on saline, an absolute difference of -16.0 points (95% CI -28.1 to -3.9; p=0.043). But 14 of 30 (47%) botulinum patients reported a mild transient motor deficit of the thenar muscle, versus 2 of 30 (7%) on saline, and no serious adverse events occurred in either group. A 2023 narrative review of intra-articular therapies for hand osteoarthritis (Oo WM et al., PMID: 36633823) places this among investigational injectates whose supporting studies are mostly small and short. There is no second randomised trial of botulinum toxin for this joint, no data on repeat injections, and no structural outcome. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a single injection probably eases thumb-base pain for at least 3 months, at the price of temporary thumb weakness in many — one small trial is all there is.

cards.headline: RHIBOT (Nguyen 2022): pain fell -25.7 points on botulinum toxin A versus -9.7 on saline at 3 months (difference -16.0; p=0.043) — thenar weakness in 47% versus 7%
cards.summary: RHIBOT (Nguyen 2022): pain fell -25.7 points on botulinum toxin A versus -9.7 on saline at 3 months (difference -16.0; p=0.043) — thenar weakness in 47% versus 7%
cards.people: 60 adults (mean age 64.9 years, 78% women) with x-ray trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis and baseline thumb pain 60.0/100, at Cochin Hospital, Paris, randomised to ultrasound-guided intra-articular botulinum toxin A 50 Allergan units in 1 mL saline (n=30) or 1 mL saline alone (n=30), both with custom rigid splinting; primary outcome at 3 months.
cards.result: Mean reduction in base-of-thumb pain at 3 months was -25.7 (95% CI -35.5 to -15.8) on botulinum toxin versus -9.7 (-17.1 to -2.2) on saline: absolute difference -16.0 points (-28.1 to -3.9; p=0.043). Adverse events numbered 27 in the botulinum group and 24 in the saline group; mild transient thenar motor deficit occurred in 14/30 (47%) versus 2/30 (7%); no serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients, one centre, 3 months, and a p-value of 0.043 — the confidence interval for the pain difference runs from -28 to -4 points, so the true effect could be modest. The thenar weakness, though transient, is intrinsic to injecting a paralytic next to thumb muscles, and unblinding by weakness is possible.
cards.source: Nguyen C et al. Intra-articular botulinum toxin A injection for painful base-of-thumb osteoarthritis: a double-blind, randomised, controlled, phase 3 trial (RHIBOT). The Lancet. Rheumatology. 2022. PMID: 38294016. Registry ID: NCT03187626. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Oo & Hunter 2023: intra-articular options for hand osteoarthritis are mostly small, short studies — corticosteroids help briefly in finger joints; investigational injectates, botulinum toxin included, rest on thin evidence
cards.summary: Oo & Hunter 2023: intra-articular options for hand osteoarthritis are mostly small, short studies — corticosteroids help briefly in finger joints; investigational injectates, botulinum toxin included, rest on thin evidence
cards.people: Published randomised trials of intra-articular therapies (corticosteroids, hyaluronic acid, and investigational agents including botulinum toxin, platelet-rich plasma and stem cells) for thumb-base and interphalangeal hand osteoarthritis.
cards.result: The review found short-term symptomatic benefit from corticosteroids in interphalangeal osteoarthritis, no significant difference between corticosteroids and hyaluronic acid in thumb-base osteoarthritis in most short-term studies, and investigational agents limited by small sample size, short follow-up and, for some, serious side effects. Imaging guidance gave higher administration accuracy than landmark guidance.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review, not a meta-analysis — it frames how thin the whole injection literature for hand osteoarthritis is rather than adding an independent estimate for botulinum toxin, for which RHIBOT remains the only randomised trial at this joint.
cards.source: Oo WM et al. Efficacy, Safety, and Accuracy of Intra-articular Therapies for Hand Osteoarthritis: Current Evidence. Drugs & aging. 2023. PMID: 36633823. cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive small trial against a field of thin injection evidence — pain relief plausible at 3 months, durability and repeat dosing unknown
cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive small trial against a field of thin injection evidence — pain relief plausible at 3 months, durability and repeat dosing unknown
cards.people: One double-blind phase 3 trial (RHIBOT, n=60) of a single botulinum toxin A injection for trapeziometacarpal osteoarthritis, read against a 2023 narrative review of all intra-articular therapies for hand osteoarthritis.
cards.result: Pain at 3 months: -25.7 points on botulinum toxin versus -9.7 on saline (difference -16.0; p=0.043). Harm on the face: transient thenar motor deficit 47% versus 7%; no serious adverse events. No trial data beyond 3 months, on repeat injections, or on joint structure. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: a single small trial carries this shelf.
cards.watchOut: A single-trial benefit shelf is exactly what Tier C review exists for: the effect size is clinically meaningful if real, but one 60-patient trial with a borderline p-value can mislead, and the weakness side effect will matter to patients who work with their hands.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nguyen C et al. The Lancet. Rheumatology. 2022 (PMID: 38294016); Oo WM et al. Drugs & aging. 2023 (PMID: 36633823).
