shelves.title: Tai chi matched physical therapy for knee osteoarthritis over a full year — WOMAC improvement 167 versus 143 points, a non-significant 24-point gap, with better depression scores on tai chi
shelves.question: For knee osteoarthritis, is tai chi as effective as physical therapy for pain and function?
shelves.mesh: Comparative Effectiveness Research · Depression/therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/psychology/therapy · Physical Therapy Modalities · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Tai Ji · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — between the two active treatments, in the only head-to-head trial. Wang C et al. (PMID: 27183035) randomised 204 adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis to tai chi twice weekly for 12 weeks or standard physical therapy (twice weekly for 6 weeks, then 6 weeks of monitored home exercise). At 12 weeks the WOMAC score had fallen by 167 points on tai chi and 143 points on physical therapy — a between-group difference of 24 points (95% CI -10 to 58) that was not significant — and most secondary outcomes improved similarly in both groups, with benefits maintained to 52 weeks. Tai chi did significantly better on depression and on the physical component of quality of life, and no serious adverse events occurred. This is a comparison of two active therapies, not of tai chi against nothing: the trial cannot say how much of either group's improvement was the treatment itself. One trial, unblindable, at one centre. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): tai chi performed comparably to a standard physical-therapy course over 12 months, with a mood advantage — equivalence shown once, not replicated head-to-head.

cards.headline: Wang 2016: WOMAC fell 167 points on tai chi versus 143 on physical therapy at 12 weeks (difference 24, 95% CI -10 to 58, not significant) — gains maintained to 52 weeks
cards.summary: Wang 2016: WOMAC fell 167 points on tai chi versus 143 on physical therapy at 12 weeks (difference 24, 95% CI -10 to 58, not significant) — gains maintained to 52 weeks
cards.people: 204 adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (mean age 60 years, 70% women) at a US academic hospital, randomised to tai chi twice weekly for 12 weeks or standard physical therapy twice weekly for 6 weeks followed by 6 weeks of monitored home exercise; followed for 52 weeks.
cards.result: WOMAC score reduction at 12 weeks: 167 points (95% CI 145 to 190) on tai chi versus 143 points (119 to 167) on physical therapy; between-group difference 24 points (-10 to 58), not significant. Most secondary outcomes (physical function, medication use, quality of life) improved similarly and were maintained to 52 weeks; depression and the physical component of quality of life improved significantly more on tai chi. No serious adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Participants knew their treatment — expectation effects cannot be excluded, and there was no untreated control, so the trial shows comparability, not that either treatment beats natural history or placebo. One centre, one tai chi protocol, one physical-therapy protocol.
cards.source: Wang C et al. Comparative Effectiveness of Tai Chi Versus Physical Therapy for Knee Osteoarthritis: A Randomized Trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2016. PMID: 27183035. Registry ID: NCT01258985. cards.headline: Synthesis: two active treatments, one trial, no separation on pain or function — tai chi is a reasonable substitute for a physical-therapy course, not a proven superior one
cards.summary: Synthesis: two active treatments, one trial, no separation on pain or function — tai chi is a reasonable substitute for a physical-therapy course, not a proven superior one
cards.people: One randomised comparative-effectiveness trial, 204 patients with knee osteoarthritis, tai chi versus standard physical therapy, 52 weeks of follow-up (Wang 2016).
cards.result: Primary outcome (WOMAC at 12 weeks): 167- versus 143-point improvement, difference 24 points (95% CI -10 to 58), not significant; benefits maintained to 52 weeks in both groups; depression and physical quality-of-life component favoured tai chi significantly; no serious adverse events in either group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) between the two programmes, Tier C: a single-trial equivalence claim.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (-10 to 58) cannot exclude a modest real advantage to either side, and 'as effective as physical therapy' inherits every uncertainty about how effective that physical-therapy course itself was. A second head-to-head trial would change this stamp.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang C et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2016 (PMID: 27183035).

shelves.title: Opioids for acute low back and neck pain (OPAL): pain at 6 weeks no better than placebo — 2.78 versus 2.25 on a 10-point scale, the point estimate favouring placebo — with more opioid-related adverse events
shelves.question: In acute low back pain and neck pain, do opioids relieve pain better than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Male · Female · Adolescent · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects · Oxycodone/adverse effects · Low Back Pain/drug therapy* · Neck Pain/drug therapy · Australia · Acute Pain/drug therapy* · Analgesia*
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a judicious short opioid course did not beat placebo for the commonest acute spinal pain. In OPAL (Jones CMP et al., PMID: 37392748), 347 adults presenting to 157 primary care or emergency department sites in Sydney, Australia, with 12 weeks or less of low back or neck pain (or both) of at least moderate severity were randomly assigned to guideline-recommended care plus an opioid (oxycodone-naloxone, up to 20 mg of oxycodone per day orally; n=174) or guideline-recommended care plus an identical placebo (n=173), for up to 6 weeks, in a triple-blinded design. The primary outcome — pain severity at 6 weeks on the 10-point pain severity subscale of the Brief Pain Inventory, analysed in 151 opioid and 159 placebo participants who provided at least one post-randomisation pain score — was a mean of 2.78 (SE 0.20) in the opioid group versus 2.25 (0.19) in the placebo group (adjusted mean difference 0.53, 95% CI -0.00 to 1.07, p=0.051): no significant difference, and the point estimate favoured placebo. More participants in the opioid group had discontinued by week 6 (33 of 174, 19%, versus 25 of 172, 15%). At least one adverse event was reported by 61 participants (35%) on the opioid versus 51 (30%) on placebo (p=0.30), and opioid-related adverse events were more frequent on the opioid — constipation, for example, in 13 participants (7.5%) versus 6 (3.5%). The authors concluded that opioids should not be recommended for acute non-specific low back pain or neck pain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in one triple-blinded placebo-controlled trial of 347 patients, a short course of oxycodone-naloxone added to guideline care gave no pain advantage over placebo at 6 weeks for acute low back or neck pain, with more opioid-related adverse events.

cards.headline: Jones 2023 (OPAL): pain at 6 weeks 2.78 on opioid versus 2.25 on placebo (adjusted mean difference 0.53, p=0.051) — no significant benefit, and constipation 7.5% versus 3.5%
cards.summary: Jones 2023 (OPAL): pain at 6 weeks 2.78 on opioid versus 2.25 on placebo (adjusted mean difference 0.53, p=0.051) — no significant benefit, and constipation 7.5% versus 3.5%
cards.people: 347 adults (aged 18 years or over) presenting to one of 157 primary care or emergency department sites in Sydney, NSW, Australia, with 12 weeks or less of low back or neck pain (or both) of at least moderate pain severity, randomly assigned (1:1) to guideline-recommended care plus an opioid (oxycodone-naloxone, up to 20 mg of oxycodone per day orally; n=174) or guideline-recommended care plus an identical placebo (n=173), for up to 6 weeks. Of 346 participants with sex recorded, 170 (49%) were female and 176 (51%) male. By week 6, 33 (19%) of 174 participants in the opioid group and 25 (15%) of 172 in the placebo group had discontinued, due to loss to follow-up and participant withdrawals.
cards.result: The primary outcome — pain severity at 6 weeks on the pain severity subscale of the Brief Pain Inventory (10-point scale), analysed in the 151 opioid and 159 placebo participants who provided at least one post-randomisation pain score using a repeated measures linear mixed model — was a mean pain score of 2.78 (SE 0.20) in the opioid group versus 2.25 (0.19) in the placebo group (adjusted mean difference 0.53, 95% CI -0.00 to 1.07, p=0.051): not significantly different, with the point estimate in placebo's favour. Safety, analysed in all randomly assigned eligible participants: 61 (35%) of 174 participants in the opioid group reported at least one adverse event versus 51 (30%) of 172 in the placebo group (p=0.30), but more people in the opioid group reported opioid-related adverse events — for example, constipation in 13 (7.5%) of 174 participants versus six (3.5%) of 173 in the placebo group. The authors concluded that opioids should not be recommended for acute non-specific low back pain or neck pain, given no significant difference in pain severity compared with placebo.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one regimen: a deliberately judicious short course (oxycodone-naloxone capped at 20 mg of oxycodone per day for up to 6 weeks) in acute non-specific spinal pain — the result does not test higher doses, longer courses, or opioids for radicular or specific-cause pain. Attrition was material (19% versus 15% discontinued by week 6) and the primary analysis rested on the 310 participants with post-randomisation scores; the near-miss p-value (0.051) cuts against the opioid, not for it, since the point estimate favoured placebo. Pain had also largely settled in both groups by 6 weeks (means under 3 of 10), which is the natural history of acute spinal pain and leaves little room for any analgesic to show separation.
cards.source: Jones CMP et al. Opioid analgesia for acute low back pain and neck pain (the OPAL trial): a randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2023. PMID: 37392748. Registry ID: ACTRN12615000775516. cards.summary: Synthesis: one triple-blinded trial — no pain advantage over placebo at 6 weeks, more opioid-related adverse events — with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.people: One randomised, triple-blinded, placebo-controlled trial of 347 adults with acute (12 weeks or less) low back or neck pain (OPAL), testing oxycodone-naloxone up to 20 mg of oxycodone per day added to guideline-recommended care against identical placebo plus guideline care, for up to 6 weeks, with 151 and 159 participants in the primary analysis.
cards.result: Pain severity at 6 weeks (10-point Brief Pain Inventory severity subscale): mean 2.78 (SE 0.20) on opioid versus 2.25 (0.19) on placebo (adjusted mean difference 0.53, 95% CI -0.00 to 1.07, p=0.051) — no significant difference. Any adverse event: 61 (35%) versus 51 (30%) (p=0.30); constipation 13 (7.5%) versus 6 (3.5%). Discontinuation by week 6: 33 (19%) versus 25 (15%). shelves.title: Calcitonin eases acute vertebral fracture pain within a week — pooled effect large at week 1 (SMD -1.54, NNT about 2) in two systematic reviews, fading into uncertainty by week 4
shelves.question: In acute painful osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures, does calcitonin relieve pain versus placebo or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain · Aged · Calcitonin · Fractures, Compression · Humans · Middle Aged · Osteoporotic Fractures · Spinal Fractures
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the first days of pain, on pooled small trials. The updated systematic review (Boucher E et al., PMID: 32188529) included 11 studies in adults 60 and over with recent atraumatic compression fractures and found pain lower on salmon calcitonin (100-200 IU daily, injected or nasal) than control at week 1 with high certainty: standardised mean difference -1.54 (95% CI -2.02 to -1.06), a number needed to treat of about 2; by week 4 heterogeneity made the effect unclear, and adverse events overall were not significantly increased (nausea/vomiting risk ratio 2.10, 95% CI 0.87 to 5.08). The earlier review of five double-blind placebo-controlled trials, 246 patients (Knopp JA et al., PMID: 15614441), found the same pattern: pain at rest already lower at week 1 (weighted mean difference 3.08 on a 10-point scale, 95% CI 2.64 to 3.52) and still lower at week 4 (4.03, 3.70 to 4.35), with minor gastrointestinal side effects. Neither review shows any effect on fracture healing, function beyond mobilisation, or later outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): calcitonin is a reasonable short-term analgesic adjunct for the acute fracture week, not a treatment for the osteoporosis itself.

cards.headline: Boucher 2020 (updated review): week-1 pain SMD -1.54 (95% CI -2.02 to -1.06), NNT 2, high certainty — week-4 effect unclear; nausea/vomiting RR 2.10, not significant
cards.summary: Boucher 2020 (updated review): week-1 pain SMD -1.54 (95% CI -2.02 to -1.06), NNT 2, high certainty — week-4 effect unclear; nausea/vomiting RR 2.10, not significant
cards.people: 11 studies (9 in the meta-analysis) of synthetic calcitonins (salmon, eel, human) in adults aged 60+ with a recent atraumatic osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture; treatment from 14 days to 6 months, salmon calcitonin typically 100-200 IU daily intramuscular or nasal.
cards.result: Pain at week 1 was lower on salmon calcitonin than control: standardised mean difference -1.54 (95% CI -2.02 to -1.06; I2=52%), graded high certainty, corresponding to a number needed to treat of 2. At 4 weeks substantial heterogeneity made the analgesic effect unclear. Overall adverse events were not significantly increased (low certainty); nausea and vomiting risk ratio 2.10 (95% CI 0.87 to 5.08).
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are small and old, pain scales and calcitonin preparations vary, and the headline week-1 effect is surprisingly large for an analgesic — exactly the pattern small-trial meta-analyses can exaggerate. Nothing here addresses healing, chronic pain, or fractures.
cards.source: Boucher E et al. Efficacy of calcitonin for treating acute pain associated with osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture: an updated systematic review. CJEM. 2020. PMID: 32188529. cards.headline: Knopp 2005: five double-blind trials, 246 patients — pain at rest lower by 3.08 points at week 1 and 4.03 at week 4 on calcitonin versus placebo
cards.summary: Knopp 2005: five double-blind trials, 246 patients — pain at rest lower by 3.08 points at week 1 and 4.03 at week 4 on calcitonin versus placebo
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (Knopp 2005)
cards.people: Five randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 246 patients with stable, recent osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures, treated with calcitonin or placebo for acute pain.
cards.result: Calcitonin significantly reduced pain severity on a visual analogue scale: pain at rest was lower at week 1 (weighted mean difference 3.08; 95% CI 2.64 to 3.52) and the effect continued weekly to week 4 (weighted mean difference 4.03; 95% CI 3.70 to 4.35), with a similar pattern for pain on sitting, standing and walking. Side effects were gastrointestinal, minor and often self-limited, and time to mobilisation was shortened.
cards.watchOut: Five small trials from an earlier era, with data partly extrapolated from graphs; a 3-4 point weighted difference on the scale used is very large and should be read as 'direction consistent, size uncertain'. These trials predate modern vertebral-fracture care pathways.
cards.source: Knopp JA et al. Calcitonin for treating acute pain of osteoporotic vertebral compression fractures: a systematic review of randomized, controlled trials. Osteoporosis international. 2005. PMID: 15614441. cards.headline: Synthesis: two reviews, fifteen years apart, same answer — early pain relief is real enough to use, the size and duration are not pinned down
cards.summary: Synthesis: two reviews, fifteen years apart, same answer — early pain relief is real enough to use, the size and duration are not pinned down
cards.people: Two systematic reviews (2005: 5 double-blind trials, 246 patients; 2020 update: 11 studies) of calcitonin versus placebo/control for acute osteoporotic vertebral compression fracture pain in older adults.
cards.result: Week 1: SMD -1.54 (95% CI -2.02 to -1.06), NNT about 2 (2020 review); rest-pain weighted mean difference 3.08 points at week 1 (2005 review). Week 4: still positive in the 2005 pooling (4.03 points), unclear amid heterogeneity in the 2020 update. Harms: minor gastrointestinal effects; nausea/vomiting RR 2.10 (0.87 to 5.08), not significant. No data on healing or long-term outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for acute pain only.
cards.watchOut: Both reviews rest on the same small, old trial base — concordance between reviews is not the same as two independent trial programmes. Calcitonin's separate role in osteoporosis treatment is a different shelf's question; this shelf is only about the acute pain week.
cards.source: Synthesis of Boucher E et al. CJEM. 2020 (PMID: 32188529); Knopp JA et al. Osteoporosis international. 2005 (PMID: 15614441).

shelves.title: Denosumab raised spine density 5.7% in a year in men with low bone density (ADAMO) — and 8.0% by two years — but the trial measured density, not fractures
shelves.question: In men with low bone mineral density, does denosumab increase bone density and is it safe over two years?
shelves.mesh: Absorptiometry, Photon · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Biomarkers · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Remodeling/drug effects · Bone and Bones/metabolism · Denosumab · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Testosterone/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for bone density, from a single trial programme. ADAMO randomised 242 men with low bone mineral density to denosumab 60 mg every 6 months or placebo: at 12 months (Orwoll E et al., PMID: 22723310) lumbar spine density had risen 5.7% on denosumab, with gains of 2.4% at total hip, 2.1% at femoral neck, 3.1% at trochanter and 0.6% at the one-third radius, all significant versus placebo, and adverse-event incidence similar between groups. In the 12-month open-label extension (Langdahl BL et al., PMID: 25607608), continued treatment brought cumulative 24-month gains to 8.0% at the spine, 3.4% at total hip and 3.4% at femoral neck, men crossing over from placebo gained similarly in their first denosumab year, and no new safety signals appeared. What ADAMO never measured is the outcome that matters: it was not powered for fractures, so fracture protection in men is extrapolated from the women's trials, not shown here. One trial, one surrogate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab reliably increases bone density in men over two years with a clean short-term safety record in this population; fracture benefit in men is inferred, not demonstrated.

cards.headline: ADAMO year 1 (Orwoll 2012): lumbar spine BMD +5.7% on denosumab versus placebo, with gains at every site measured and similar adverse-event rates
cards.summary: ADAMO year 1 (Orwoll 2012): lumbar spine BMD +5.7% on denosumab versus placebo, with gains at every site measured and similar adverse-event rates
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Orwoll 2012, ADAMO)
cards.people: 242 men with low bone mineral density (mean age 65 years) randomised to denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months or placebo for 12 months; 228 (94.2%) completed the year.
cards.result: At 12 months denosumab increased BMD by 5.7% at the lumbar spine, 2.4% at total hip, 2.1% at femoral neck, 3.1% at trochanter and 0.6% at the one-third radius (adjusted p ≤ 0.0144 for the difference versus placebo at all sites). Serum CTX fell significantly by day 15. The incidence of adverse events was similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Bone density is a surrogate: 242 men followed for one year cannot show whether fractures fall. Men with prostate cancer on androgen deprivation and men with frank osteoporosis were not this trial's population — it enrolled low BMD broadly.
cards.source: Orwoll E et al. A randomized, placebo-controlled study of the effects of denosumab for the treatment of men with low bone mineral density. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2012. PMID: 22723310. Registry ID: NCT00980174. cards.headline: ADAMO year 2 (Langdahl 2015): cumulative spine gain 8.0% at 24 months on continued denosumab; crossover men gained like first-year patients; no new safety signals
cards.summary: ADAMO year 2 (Langdahl 2015): cumulative spine gain 8.0% at 24 months on continued denosumab; crossover men gained like first-year patients; no new safety signals
cards.type: Open-label extension of a randomised trial (Langdahl 2015, ADAMO)
cards.people: 228 men from ADAMO entered a 12-month open-label phase (219 completed): the original denosumab group continued 60 mg every 6 months and the original placebo group crossed over to denosumab.
cards.result: During year 2, continued denosumab added 2.2% at the lumbar spine, 0.9% total hip, 1.3% femoral neck, 1.3% trochanter and 0.2% one-third radius, for cumulative 24-month gains of 8.0%, 3.4%, 3.4%, 4.6% and 0.7% respectively (all p<0.01). Crossover men gained in their first denosumab year much as the original group had. Adverse-event rates were similar between groups and no new safety signals were identified.
cards.watchOut: The second year was open-label with no placebo group — it shows density keeps rising and nothing alarming emerged in 228 men, but rare harms of denosumab (such as osteonecrosis of the jaw or atypical fractures) are far too infrequent for a study this size to see.
cards.source: Langdahl BL et al. A 24-month study evaluating the efficacy and safety of denosumab for the treatment of men with low bone mineral density: results from the ADAMO trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, two years, a consistent density gain at every site — and a fracture question this shelf cannot answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, two years, a consistent density gain at every site — and a fracture question this shelf cannot answer
cards.people: The ADAMO programme: a 242-man double-blind placebo-controlled year (Orwoll 2012) plus a 228-man open-label second year (Langdahl 2015), denosumab 60 mg every 6 months in men with low bone mineral density.
cards.result: Lumbar spine BMD: +5.7% versus placebo at 12 months; +8.0% cumulative at 24 months. Total hip +3.4% and femoral neck +3.4% at 24 months. Safety over 2 years: adverse events similar to placebo in year 1, no new signals in year 2. Fractures: not an endpoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) on the density surrogate, Tier C: a single trial carries the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Prescribers reasonably extrapolate fracture protection from the large women's denosumab trial, but this shelf's own record is density-only — the stamp grades what ADAMO showed, and the well-known rebound in bone turnover after missed denosumab doses is outside this record entirely.

shelves.title: Robotic knee replacement lines the implant up better — alignment outliers roughly halved — but patients feel no difference: WOMAC difference -0.35 points in pooled randomised trials
shelves.question: Does robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty improve alignment, pain or function versus conventional surgery?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/adverse effects · Robotic Surgical Procedures/adverse effects · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Radiography · Knee Joint/diagnostic imaging/surgery
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the x-ray improves, the patient does not (yet). A systematic review of 12 randomised trials, 2,200 patients (Ruangsomboon P et al., PMID: 36805771) found robotic-assisted total knee arthroplasty probably makes little to no difference to patient-reported outcomes (WOMAC mean difference -0.35, 95% CI -0.78 to 0.07) or range of motion (mean difference -0.73 degrees, CI -7.5 to 6.0), while likely reducing mechanical-alignment outliers (risk ratio 0.43, CI 0.27 to 0.67 — a 57% relative reduction) and deviation from neutral alignment (mean difference -0.94 degrees, CI -1.1 to -0.73). A second meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials, 1,942 knees (Alrajeb R et al., PMID: 38133653), found the same split: significantly better anatomical and mechanical restoration on imaging, with clinical and functional scores and complication rates statistically similar. Neither review could settle revision rates — the outcome better alignment is supposed to improve — because follow-up is too short. PROPOSED SPLIT: robotic assistance is a radiological improvement in search of a clinical one; on current randomised evidence patients should not expect to feel better, move better, or have fewer complications.

cards.headline: Ruangsomboon 2023 (12 RCTs, 2,200 patients): WOMAC difference -0.35 (95% CI -0.78 to 0.07) — but alignment outliers RR 0.43 (0.27 to 0.67) favour the robot
cards.summary: Ruangsomboon 2023 (12 RCTs, 2,200 patients): WOMAC difference -0.35 (95% CI -0.78 to 0.07) — but alignment outliers RR 0.43 (0.27 to 0.67) favour the robot
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Ruangsomboon 2023)
cards.people: 12 randomised controlled trials involving 2,200 adults undergoing primary total knee arthroplasty for osteoarthritis, robotic-assisted versus conventional jig-based technique.
cards.result: Patient-reported outcomes: WOMAC mean difference -0.35 (95% CI -0.78 to 0.07), interpreted as probably little to no effect. Range of motion: mean difference -0.73 degrees (CI -7.5 to 6.0). Mechanical alignment: outliers risk ratio 0.43 (CI 0.27 to 0.67) and deviation from neutral mean difference -0.94 degrees (CI -1.1 to -0.73), both favouring robotic surgery. No differences in revision rate or major adverse effects, with evidence on those outcomes rated insufficient.
cards.watchOut: The trials span several robot generations and platforms, mostly with short follow-up; the revision question — the entire clinical rationale for better alignment — needs a decade, and these data do not have it. Industry involvement in the underlying trials is common in this literature.
cards.source: Ruangsomboon P et al. Clinical and radiological outcomes of robotic-assisted versus conventional total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Acta orthopaedica. 2023. cards.headline: Alrajeb 2024 (7 RCTs, 1,942 knees): anatomical and mechanical restoration significantly better with robotics; clinical scores, function and complications statistically similar
cards.summary: Alrajeb 2024 (7 RCTs, 1,942 knees): anatomical and mechanical restoration significantly better with robotics; clinical scores, function and complications statistically similar
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Alrajeb 2024)
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials, 1,942 knees (974 robotic, 968 conventional jig-based), comparing robotic versus conventional total knee replacement on radiological alignment, knee scores, WOMAC, range of motion and complications.
cards.result: Robotic knees had significantly better post-operative anatomical restoration (odds ratio -0.82; 95% CI -1.027 to -0.58; p<0.00001) and mechanical restoration (odds ratio -0.95; 95% CI -1.49 to -0.41; p<0.0006). Range of motion and femoral prosthesis position favoured robotics without reaching significance (p=0.1 and p=0.07). Clinical and functional outcomes and complication rates were statistically similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Effect measures are reported as odds ratios for continuous alignment outcomes, which is hard to translate into millimetres a patient could care about; and this pool (search to June 2022) overlaps the other review's trials — two meta-analyses of largely the same RCTs are one evidence base, not two.
cards.source: Alrajeb R et al. Robotic-assisted versus conventional total knee arthroplasty: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.people: Two meta-analyses (2023: 12 RCTs, 2,200 patients; 2024: 7 RCTs, 1,942 knees, substantially overlapping trial sets) of robotic-assisted versus conventional total knee arthroplasty.
cards.result: Alignment: outliers RR 0.43 (0.27 to 0.67), deviation from neutral -0.94 degrees — consistently better with robotics. Patient outcomes: WOMAC mean difference -0.35 (-0.78 to 0.07); range of motion, clinical scores, complications all statistically similar. Revisions: no difference shown, evidence insufficient. cards.watchOut: Costs, operative time and the learning curve sit outside these records, as does every outcome beyond short-term follow-up. shelves.title: Filgotinib beat placebo in all three FINCH trials — ACR20 up to 77% versus 50% on methotrexate background — and the 200 mg dose matched adalimumab on low disease activity
shelves.question: In rheumatoid arthritis, does filgotinib induce remission versus placebo — and how does it compare with adalimumab?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab/therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate · Middle Aged · Pyridines/therapeutic use · Triazoles/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — three large double-blind phase 3 trials, one direction. In FINCH 1 (Combe B et al., PMID: 33504485; 1,755 patients with inadequate response to methotrexate), ACR20 at week 12 was 76.6% on filgotinib 200 mg and 69.8% on 100 mg versus 49.9% on placebo (both p<0.001), and filgotinib 200 mg was non-inferior to adalimumab for low disease activity (DAS28-CRP ≤3.2) at week 12, while the 100 mg dose was not. In FINCH 2 (Genovese MC et al., PMID: 31334793; 448 patients refractory to biologics), ACR20 was 66.0% (200 mg) and 57.5% (100 mg) versus 31.1% on placebo (both p<0.001). In FINCH 3 (Westhovens R et al., PMID: 33452004; 1,252 methotrexate-naive or limited-exposure patients), ACR20 at week 24 was 81% on filgotinib 200 mg plus methotrexate and 80% on 100 mg plus methotrexate versus 71% on methotrexate alone (p<0.001 and p=0.017), with remission (DAS28-CRP <2.6) in 54% and 43% versus 29%; filgotinib monotherapy (78%) did not significantly beat methotrexate (p=0.058). Adverse events were comparable across arms in each trial; herpes zoster cases appeared on filgotinib in FINCH 2, and none of the trials ran long enough to settle the JAK-class cardiovascular and malignancy questions. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): filgotinib induces response and remission well beyond placebo in every population tested, and at 200 mg stands comparison with adalimumab — with long-term class safety still the open file.

cards.headline: FINCH 1 (Combe 2021): ACR20 76.6% (200 mg) and 69.8% (100 mg) versus 49.9% placebo at week 12 — 200 mg non-inferior to adalimumab, 100 mg not
cards.summary: FINCH 1 (Combe 2021): ACR20 76.6% (200 mg) and 69.8% (100 mg) versus 49.9% placebo at week 12 — 200 mg non-inferior to adalimumab, 100 mg not
cards.people: 1,755 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate, randomised 3:3:2:3 to filgotinib 200 mg, filgotinib 100 mg, adalimumab 40 mg every other week, or placebo (to week 24), all on background methotrexate, for 52 weeks.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 12: 76.6% on filgotinib 200 mg and 69.8% on 100 mg versus 49.9% on placebo (treatment differences 26.7%, 95% CI 20.6 to 32.8, and 19.9%, 13.6 to 26.2; both p<0.001). Filgotinib beat placebo on signs and symptoms, physical function and structural damage. Filgotinib 200 mg was non-inferior to adalimumab on DAS28-CRP ≤3.2 at week 12 (p<0.001 for non-inferiority); 100 mg did not achieve non-inferiority. Adverse events and laboratory abnormalities were comparable among active arms.
cards.watchOut: The adalimumab comparison is non-inferiority on a disease-activity threshold at 12 weeks, not superiority and not a remission endpoint; the placebo group was switched at week 24, so long-term placebo-controlled safety does not exist. Trial populations exclude many real-world comorbid patients.
cards.source: Combe B et al. Filgotinib versus placebo or adalimumab in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and inadequate response to methotrexate: a phase III randomised clinical trial. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2021. PMID: 33504485. Registry ID: NCT02889796. cards.headline: FINCH 2 (Genovese 2019): in biologic-refractory disease, ACR20 66.0% and 57.5% versus 31.1% on placebo — including 70.3% versus 17.6% after three or more prior biologics
cards.summary: FINCH 2 (Genovese 2019): in biologic-refractory disease, ACR20 66.0% and 57.5% versus 31.1% on placebo — including 70.3% versus 17.6% after three or more prior biologics
cards.people: 448 treated adults with moderately to severely active rheumatoid arthritis and inadequate response or intolerance to at least one biologic DMARD (23.4% had used three or more), randomised to filgotinib 200 mg (n=148), 100 mg (n=153) or placebo (n=148) daily on background conventional DMARDs, for 24 weeks.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 12: 66.0% on filgotinib 200 mg and 57.5% on 100 mg versus 31.1% on placebo (differences 34.9%, 95% CI 23.5 to 46.3, and 26.4%, 15.0 to 37.9; both p<0.001). In patients with three or more prior biologics: 70.3%, 58.8% and 17.6% respectively. Commonest adverse events were nasopharyngitis and headache; four uncomplicated herpes zoster cases and one retinal vein occlusion occurred on filgotinib; no opportunistic infections, tuberculosis, malignancies, perforations or deaths.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-four weeks in the hardest-to-treat population shows response, not durability or rare-harm rates; the retinal vein occlusion and zoster cases are the kind of signal only much larger exposure can size. Patients stayed on background conventional DMARDs, so this is add-on efficacy.

shelves.title: Tapering works for many, stopping fails for most: remission held in 81% continuing, 59% tapering and 43% stopping DMARDs (RETRO) — while guided TNF dose reduction matched usual care on major flares (DRESS)
shelves.question: In rheumatoid arthritis in sustained remission on a biologic, can the biologic be tapered or stopped without flare?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage · Antirheumatic Agents/administration & dosage · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy/physiopathology · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Disease Progression · Drug Administration Schedule · Etanercept · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Foot/diagnostic imaging · Hand/diagnostic imaging · Humans · Immunoglobulin G/administration & dosage · Male · Netherlands/epidemiology · Quality of Life · Receptors, Tumor Necrosis Factor/administration & dosage · Recurrence · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: SPLIT — tapering is a reasonable, monitored gamble; stopping is a losing bet for most. In RETRO (Tascilar K et al., PMID: 38297524), 282 patients in sustained remission were randomised to continue full-dose DMARDs, taper to 50%, or taper then stop: remission at 12 months was maintained by 81.2% continuing, 58.6% tapering and 43.3% stopping (p=0.0005 for trend), with relapse hazard ratios of 3.02 for tapering and 4.34 for stopping versus continuing — though most who relapsed regained remission when full dose was reintroduced. The DRESS study (van Herwaarden N et al., PMID: 25858265) asked the narrower biologic question: in 180 patients with low disease activity on adalimumab or etanercept, a disease-activity-guided dose-reduction strategy was non-inferior to usual care for major flare at 18 months (12% versus 10%; difference 2%, 95% CI -12 to 12), with the drug stopped successfully in 20% and the interval extended in 43% — but short-lived flares were far commoner (73% versus 27%). So: about two in three patients can reduce a TNF inhibitor under close monitoring without a major flare; complete withdrawal, in RETRO, kept barely two in five in remission. PROPOSED SPLIT: taper — yes, with monitoring and a restart plan; stop outright — expect relapse in the majority.

cards.headline: RETRO (Tascilar 2021): remission at 12 months 81.2% continuing versus 58.6% tapering versus 43.3% stopping — relapse hazard 3.02 and 4.34 against continuing
cards.summary: RETRO (Tascilar 2021): remission at 12 months 81.2% continuing versus 58.6% tapering versus 43.3% stopping — relapse hazard 3.02 and 4.34 against continuing
cards.people: 303 patients with rheumatoid arthritis for at least 12 months in sustained DAS28-ESR remission (<2.6) at 14 German centres, randomised to continue 100% DMARD dose (n=100), taper to 50% (n=102), or taper to 50% for 6 months then stop (n=101); 282 analysed, assessed every 3 months for 12 months. Treatments included biologics and conventional DMARDs.
cards.result: Sustained remission without relapse at 12 months: 81.2% (95% CI 73.3 to 90.0) continuing, 58.6% (49.2 to 70.0) tapering, 43.3% (34.6 to 55.5) stopping (log-rank trend p=0.0005). Relapse hazard ratios versus continuing: 3.02 (1.69 to 5.40) for tapering and 4.34 (2.48 to 7.60) for stopping. Most patients who relapsed regained remission after reintroduction of the 100% dose. Serious adverse events: 11% continuing, 8% tapering, 14% stopping; none judged intervention-related.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and 'DMARDs' here mixes biologics with conventional drugs, so the stopping number is not a pure biologic-withdrawal estimate. Relapse was usually recaptured by restarting — the real cost of a failed taper in this trial was months of active disease, not permanent loss of control, but structural damage during relapse was not the endpoint.

cards.headline: DRESS (van Herwaarden 2015): guided TNF-inhibitor dose reduction non-inferior for major flare (12% versus 10% at 18 months) — 20% stopped outright, 43% spaced doses, 37% could not reduce
cards.summary: DRESS (van Herwaarden 2015): guided TNF-inhibitor dose reduction non-inferior for major flare (12% versus 10% at 18 months) — 20% stopped outright, 43% spaced doses, 37% could not reduce
cards.type: Randomised open-label non-inferiority strategy trial (van Herwaarden 2015, DRESS)
cards.people: 180 patients with rheumatoid arthritis and low disease activity on adalimumab or etanercept at two Dutch clinics, randomised to a disease-activity-guided dose-reduction strategy (stepwise interval extension every 3 months until flare or discontinuation; n=121) or usual care (n=59), followed 18 months.
cards.result: Major flare (DAS28-CRP flare lasting over 3 months): 12% on the reduction strategy versus 10% on usual care — difference 2% (95% CI -12 to 12), inside the 20% non-inferiority margin. In the reduction group, TNF inhibitor use was stopped successfully in 20% (95% CI 13 to 28) and the interval increased in 43% (34 to 53); no reduction was possible in 37%. Function, quality of life, relevant radiographic progression and adverse events did not differ, but short-lived flares (73% versus 27%) and minimal radiographic progression (32% versus 15%) were more frequent with reduction.
cards.watchOut: The non-inferiority margin was a generous 20 percentage points, the trial was open-label, and 'non-inferior for major flare' coexists with nearly three times as many short flares and twice the minimal radiographic progression — the strategy trades small, recoverable setbacks for less drug, which patients should choose knowingly.
cards.source: van Herwaarden N et al. Disease activity guided dose reduction and withdrawal of adalimumab or etanercept compared with usual care in rheumatoid arthritis: open label, randomised controlled, non-inferiority trial. BMJ. 2015. PMID: 25858265. Registry ID: NTR3216. cards.headline: Synthesis: dose reduction under monitoring is the supported move; outright stopping keeps remission in a minority — and relapse is usually, not always, recaptured
cards.summary: Synthesis: dose reduction under monitoring is the supported move; outright stopping keeps remission in a minority — and relapse is usually, not always, recaptured
cards.people: Two randomised strategy trials: RETRO (282 analysed, sustained remission, continue versus taper versus stop all DMARDs) and DRESS (180 patients, low disease activity on adalimumab/etanercept, guided reduction versus usual care).
cards.result: Continuing keeps remission best (81.2% at 12 months, RETRO). Tapering: 58.6% stay in remission (RETRO); guided TNF reduction non-inferior on major flare, 12% versus 10% (DRESS), with successful stop in 20% and spacing in 43%. Stopping after taper: 43.3% remain in remission (RETRO). Costs of trying: short flares 73% versus 27% (DRESS); most relapses regained remission on restarting (RETRO). PROPOSED SPLIT by strategy, as the balance states.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are open-label and European, with tight 3-monthly monitoring that routine practice may not match; neither answers tapering for non-TNF biologics or JAK inhibitors specifically, and neither was powered for joint damage over years.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tascilar K et al. The Lancet. Rheumatology. 2021 (PMID: 38297524); van Herwaarden N et al. BMJ. 2015 (PMID: 25858265).

shelves.title: Glucocorticoid bridging gets early rheumatoid arthritis down faster, but methotrexate alone catches up on remission by two years — 72% versus 67% in CareRA's low-risk group
shelves.question: In early rheumatoid arthritis, does initial combination therapy with a glucocorticoid bridging scheme beat methotrexate alone for remission and damage?
shelves.mesh: Antirheumatic Agents/administration & dosage · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/diagnosis/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage · Joints/diagnostic imaging · Leflunomide/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Prednisone/administration & dosage · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Radiography · Severity of Illness Index · Sulfasalazine/administration & dosage · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — bridging wins the early months, not the two-year remission count. CareRA (Stouten V et al., PMID: 31236568) randomised 379 DMARD-naive early rheumatoid arthritis patients by prognostic risk. In high-risk patients, methotrexate plus a prednisone step-down bridge (COBRA-Slim, starting 30 mg) put 72% into remission (DAS28-CRP <2.6) at two years — statistically indistinguishable from the heavier COBRA-Classic (65%, prednisone from 60 mg plus sulfasalazine) and COBRA-Avant-Garde (74%, plus leflunomide) regimens, with fewer therapy-related adverse events. In low-risk patients, COBRA-Slim reached 67% remission versus 72% on methotrexate alone without prednisone (Tight Step Up) — no significant difference — although the bridged group ran lower longitudinal disease-activity scores over the two years and needed fewer glucocorticoid injections. The COBRA-light trial (den Uyl D et al., PMID: 23606682) confirms the early pharmacology: prednisolone-based combination therapy drove DAS44 down by about -2.2 to -2.5 points within 6 months, with minimal disease activity in 41-49%. So the honest answer to 'does bridging beat methotrexate alone' is: faster and smoother control early, yes; more remission or less damage at two years, not shown. PROPOSED SPLIT: early benefit, long-term equivalence — and the lightest bridge (methotrexate plus prednisone step-down) did everything the heavier combinations did.

cards.headline: CareRA (Stouten 2019): two-year remission 72% on methotrexate + prednisone bridge versus 65-74% on heavier combinations in high-risk patients — and 67% versus 72% against methotrexate alone in low-risk patients
cards.summary: CareRA (Stouten 2019): two-year remission 72% on methotrexate + prednisone bridge versus 65-74% on heavier combinations in high-risk patients — and 67% versus 72% against methotrexate alone in low-risk patients
cards.people: 379 DMARD- and glucocorticoid-naive early rheumatoid arthritis patients, stratified by prognosis. High-risk (n=289): COBRA-Classic (methotrexate + sulfasalazine + prednisone from 60 mg, n=98), COBRA-Slim (methotrexate + prednisone from 30 mg, n=98), COBRA-Avant-Garde (methotrexate + leflunomide + prednisone from 30 mg, n=93). Low-risk (n=90): COBRA-Slim (n=43) versus Tight Step Up — methotrexate without prednisone (n=47). Followed 2 years.
cards.result: Remission (DAS28-CRP <2.6) at year 2, high-risk: 72% COBRA-Slim, 65% COBRA-Classic, 74% COBRA-Avant-Garde (p=1.00), with other clinical and radiological outcomes and sustainability similar; COBRA-Slim had significantly fewer therapy-related adverse events than Classic (p=0.02) or Avant-Garde (p=0.005). Low-risk: 67% on COBRA-Slim versus 72% on methotrexate alone (p=1.00), but the bridged group had lower longitudinal DAS28-CRP over 2 years and needed fewer glucocorticoid injections, with comparable safety.
cards.watchOut: The only true bridging-versus-no-bridging contrast is the 90-patient low-risk stratum — underpowered for the remission endpoint, and its point estimate actually favours methotrexate alone. CareRA was open-label and treat-to-target adaptations blur the randomised contrast over two years.
cards.source: Stouten V et al. Effectiveness of different combinations of DMARDs and glucocorticoid bridging in early rheumatoid arthritis: two-year results of CareRA. Rheumatology (Oxford, England). 2019. PMID: 31236568. Registry ID: NCT01172639. cards.headline: COBRA-light (den Uyl 2014): prednisolone combination therapy cut DAS44 by -2.50 (full COBRA) and -2.18 (light) at 6 months — minimal disease activity in 49% and 41%
cards.summary: COBRA-light (den Uyl 2014): prednisolone combination therapy cut DAS44 by -2.50 (full COBRA) and -2.18 (light) at 6 months — minimal disease activity in 49% and 41%
cards.type: Randomised open non-inferiority trial (den Uyl 2014, COBRA-light)
cards.people: 164 patients with early active rheumatoid arthritis (mean DAS44 about 4.0-4.1), randomised to original COBRA (prednisolone 60 mg tapering to 7.5 mg, methotrexate 7.5 mg/week, sulfasalazine 2 g/day) or COBRA-light (prednisolone 30 mg tapering to 7.5 mg in 9 weeks, methotrexate escalated to 25 mg/week), both treat-to-target, assessed at 26 weeks.
cards.result: DAS44 fell by -2.50 (SD 1.21) on COBRA and -2.18 (1.10) on COBRA-light at 6 months; the adjusted difference of 0.21 (95% CI -0.11 to 0.53) sat within the predefined 0.5-point non-inferiority margin. Minimal disease activity (DAS44 <1.6) was reached by 49% on COBRA and 41% on COBRA-light.
cards.watchOut: This trial compares two bridging regimens with each other, not bridging with none — it shows how fast and deep early control goes on prednisolone combinations, and that the lighter version suffices, but it cannot by itself prove bridging beats methotrexate alone. Open-label, 26 weeks.
cards.source: den Uyl D et al. A non-inferiority trial of an attenuated combination strategy ('COBRA-light') compared to the original COBRA strategy: clinical results after 26 weeks. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2014. PMID: 23606682. cards.headline: Synthesis: bridging is an accelerator, not a destination-changer — and the lightest effective recipe is methotrexate plus a prednisone step-down
cards.summary: Synthesis: bridging is an accelerator, not a destination-changer — and the lightest effective recipe is methotrexate plus a prednisone step-down
cards.people: CareRA (379 early rheumatoid arthritis patients, 2 years, the only randomised bridging-versus-methotrexate-alone contrast in its low-risk stratum) and COBRA-light (164 patients, 26 weeks, two prednisolone combination regimens).
cards.result: Two-year remission: 67% bridged versus 72% methotrexate alone (low-risk CareRA, not significant); high-risk combinations all 65-74% with no winner and more adverse events on the heavier regimens. Early control: DAS44 down -2.18 to -2.50 by 6 months on prednisolone combinations (COBRA-light); bridged low-risk patients ran lower disease activity longitudinally and needed fewer steroid injections (CareRA). PROPOSED SPLIT: early benefit, two-year remission equivalence.
cards.watchOut: Glucocorticoid harms accumulate with dose and duration and sit largely outside these two records' reporting; the case for bridging rests on speed and symptom control in the first months, weighed by the clinician against steroid exposure in the individual patient.
cards.source: Synthesis of Stouten V et al. Rheumatology (Oxford, England). 2019 (PMID: 31236568); den Uyl D et al. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2014 (PMID: 23606682).

shelves.title: Denosumab slowed structural damage in erosive hand osteoarthritis in one 100-patient trial — joint scores diverged by 14.3 points at 48 weeks and new erosive joints were fewer (OR 0.24)
shelves.question: In erosive hand osteoarthritis, does denosumab slow structural damage versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Denosumab/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Osteoarthritis/diagnostic imaging/drug therapy · RANK Ligand · Treatment Outcome · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for joint structure, from a single small phase 2a trial, with symptoms not the story. Wittoek R et al. (PMID: 38361122) randomised 100 patients with erosive hand osteoarthritis to denosumab 60 mg every 3 months or placebo for 48 weeks. The primary radiographic endpoint — change in the Ghent University Scoring System (GUSS), where positive change means remodelling and negative change erosive progression — favoured denosumab by an estimated 8.9 points at week 24 (95% CI 1.0 to 16.9; p=0.024) and by 14.3 points at week 48 (95% CI 4.6 to 24.0; p=0.003). Fewer new erosive joints developed on denosumab (odds ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72; p=0.009). Adverse events were actually more frequent on placebo (125 events in 90% of patients) than on denosumab (97 events in 80%). What the record does not show is that patients felt better: the demonstrated effect is radiographic, in one centre, in 100 patients, over 48 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): denosumab has genuine structure-modifying signal in erosive hand osteoarthritis — the first for any drug in this disease — but one phase 2a trial is a beginning, not a basis for routine use, and pain benefit is unproven here.

cards.headline: Wittoek 2024: GUSS difference +8.9 points at week 24 (p=0.024) and +14.3 at week 48 (p=0.003) on denosumab versus placebo; new erosive joints OR 0.24 (p=0.009)
cards.summary: Wittoek 2024: GUSS difference +8.9 points at week 24 (p=0.024) and +14.3 at week 48 (p=0.003) on denosumab versus placebo; new erosive joints OR 0.24 (p=0.009)
cards.people: 100 patients with erosive hand osteoarthritis at a single centre (51 denosumab, 41 women; 49 placebo, 37 women), randomised to denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 3 months or placebo for 48 weeks; baseline mean GUSS of target joints 155.9 (SD 69.3) on denosumab and 158.7 (46.8) on placebo.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (change in total GUSS at week 24): estimated between-group difference 8.9 points (95% CI 1.0 to 16.9; p=0.024) favouring denosumab. At week 48 the adjusted GUSS was 163.5 on denosumab versus 149.2 on placebo, difference 14.3 (95% CI 4.6 to 24.0; p=0.003). New erosive joints at week 48 were fewer on denosumab (odds ratio 0.24, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.72; p=0.009). Adverse events: 97 events in 41/51 patients (80%) on denosumab versus 125 events in 44/49 (90%) on placebo.
cards.watchOut: A radiographic score is a surrogate — GUSS improvement means remodelling on x-ray, and this record does not demonstrate less pain or better hand function. One centre, 100 patients, an every-3-months dose borrowed from osteoporosis practice, and no replication yet: phase 2a results in osteoarthritis have a long history of not surviving phase 3.

shelves.title: Hydrodilatation helped frozen shoulder more than placebo in the one low-bias trial in the Cochrane review — but adding it to a steroid injection changed nothing at 8 weeks in a 2025 double-blind trial
shelves.question: In frozen shoulder, does hydrodilatation (arthrographic distension) improve pain and movement versus corticosteroid injection or physiotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Air · Bursitis/therapy · Dilatation/methods · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Range of Motion, Articular · Shoulder Joint · Shoulder Pain/therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — better than placebo or physiotherapy alone in the older small trials; no better than a plain steroid injection in the newest blinded test. The Cochrane review (Buchbinder R et al., PMID: 18254123) found five trials, 196 people: the single low-risk-of-bias trial showed distension with saline and steroid beat placebo for pain (number needed to treat to benefit 2), function (NNTB 3) and range of movement at 3 weeks, with function benefit partly maintained to 12 weeks; a second trial found distension plus physiotherapy beat physiotherapy alone on movement and percentage pain improvement at 8 weeks; three further trials comparing distension against steroid injection alone gave conflicting results, all at high risk of bias. The 2025 double-blind trial (Konarski A et al., PMID: 40495621; 79 patients) directly tested the add-on: steroid injection with hydrodilatation versus steroid injection alone improved similarly (SPADI 57.7 to 32.7 versus 57.4 to 35.8), with no significant difference in any outcome at 8 weeks — and hydrodilatation was the more painful procedure. PROPOSED SPLIT: distension is an active treatment against inert comparators in the short term, but the fluid-stretch itself has not been shown to add anything to the steroid it is usually delivered with.

cards.headline: Buchbinder 2008 (Cochrane, 5 trials, 196 people): distension with saline + steroid beat placebo at 3 weeks (NNTB 2 for pain, 3 for function) — comparisons against steroid injection alone conflicted
cards.summary: Buchbinder 2008 (Cochrane, 5 trials, 196 people): distension with saline + steroid beat placebo at 3 weeks (NNTB 2 for pain, 3 for function) — comparisons against steroid injection alone conflicted
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Buchbinder 2008)
cards.people: Five randomised/controlled trials, 196 adults with adhesive capsulitis: distension with steroid and air versus air alone and versus steroid injection (47 participants); distension with steroid and saline versus placebo (46); distension with steroid versus steroid injection (45 and 22); distension plus physical therapy versus physical therapy alone (36).
cards.result: Only one trial was at low risk of bias; it found arthrographic distension with saline and steroid better than placebo for pain (number needed to treat to benefit 2), function (NNTB 3) and range of movement at 3 weeks, with one of two function scores still better at 6 and 12 weeks (NNT 3). Distension plus physical therapy improved range of movement and median percentage pain improvement (not pain score) versus physical therapy alone at 8 weeks in a high-bias-risk trial. Three high-bias-risk trials comparing distension with steroid against steroid injection alone, or against distension alone, reported conflicting, variable effects. Adverse effects were few and minor, mainly pain during and after the procedure. The review graded the placebo comparison 'silver' level evidence of short-term benefit.
cards.watchOut: Four of five trials were at high risk of bias, no meta-analysis was possible, and the total evidence base is 196 patients — the NNTB of 2 comes from a single 46-patient trial. Frozen shoulder also improves on its own over time, which inflates every uncontrolled impression of benefit.
cards.source: Buchbinder R et al. Arthrographic distension for adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder). The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2008. PMID: 18254123. cards.headline: Konarski 2025: steroid injection with versus without hydrodilatation — SPADI improved 57.7 to 32.7 versus 57.4 to 35.8, no significant difference in any outcome at 8 weeks; hydrodilatation hurt more
cards.summary: Konarski 2025: steroid injection with versus without hydrodilatation — SPADI improved 57.7 to 32.7 versus 57.4 to 35.8, no significant difference in any outcome at 8 weeks; hydrodilatation hurt more
cards.people: 79 patients aged 18-90 with frozen shoulder (mean age 54, 53% women), randomised to glenohumeral cortisone injection alone (contrast, local anaesthetic, steroid) or the same injection followed by saline hydrodilatation until capsular rupture or severe resistance; outcomes at 8 weeks.
cards.result: Range of motion and SPADI improved in both groups (SPADI: injection alone 57.4 to 35.8; hydrodilatation 57.7 to 32.7), as did ASES, Simple Shoulder Test and Constant scores, with no significant between-group differences at 8 weeks. Hydrodilatation was more painful than injection alone. Subgroup patterns differed (men improved external rotation more with hydrodilatation; women, severe-pain presenters and those with symptoms under 120 days favoured injection alone).
cards.watchOut: Eight weeks is early in a condition that evolves over many months, and 79 patients cannot exclude a modest later difference; subgroup findings in a null trial are hypothesis-generating at best. But as the only double-blind head-to-head test, its null carries more weight than the older open comparisons.
cards.source: Konarski A et al. A Double Blind Randomised Controlled Trial Comparing Glenohumeral Cortisone With and Without Hydrodilatation in Patients With Frozen Shoulder. cards.headline: Synthesis: an active procedure whose active ingredient may be the steroid — benefit over doing nothing is supported, benefit over a steroid injection is not
cards.summary: Synthesis: an active procedure whose active ingredient may be the steroid — benefit over doing nothing is supported, benefit over a steroid injection is not
cards.people: Cochrane review of 5 small trials (196 patients, searches to 2006) plus one 2025 double-blind randomised trial (79 patients) of hydrodilatation added to corticosteroid injection.
cards.result: Versus placebo: short-term pain/function benefit, NNTB 2-3, from one low-bias trial. Versus physiotherapy alone: better movement at 8 weeks in one high-bias trial. Versus steroid injection alone: conflicting older results, and no significant difference on any outcome at 8 weeks in the 2025 double-blind trial (SPADI gains 25.0 versus 21.6 points), with more procedural pain on hydrodilatation. PROPOSED SPLIT by comparator, as the balance states.
cards.watchOut: The evidence base is small, old and mostly unblinded; a large modern trial of hydrodilatation versus steroid injection with 6-12 month follow-up could still move this either way. Natural history — frozen shoulder thaws by itself — is the silent third arm in every one of these studies.
cards.source: Synthesis of Buchbinder R et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2008 (PMID: 18254123); Konarski A et al. ANZ journal of surgery. 2025 (PMID: 40495621).

shelves.title: Surgery did not beat a cast for displaced distal radius fractures — wrist scores identical at 12 months in DRAFFT2 and at 24 months in older patients in CROSSFIRE, though 13% of casts later needed fixation
shelves.question: In adults with a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture, does surgical fixation improve function versus cast treatment?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Bone Wires · Casts, Surgical/statistics & numerical data · Female · Fracture Fixation/methods/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Radius Fractures/physiopathology/therapy · Treatment Outcome · United Kingdom · Wrist Joint/physiopathology/surgery · Young Adult
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — to wrist function, in two multicentre randomised trials, with one honest catch. DRAFFT2 (Costa ML et al., PMID: 35045969) randomised 500 adults with dorsally displaced distal radius fractures to moulded cast or K-wire fixation after manipulation: the Patient Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE) score at 12 months was 21.2 on cast versus 20.7 on K-wires (adjusted difference -0.34, 95% CI -4.33 to 3.66; p=0.87), with no difference at 3 or 6 months either. The catch: 33 cast patients (13%) needed surgical fixation for loss of fracture position in the first six weeks, versus one revision in the K-wire group. CROSSFIRE's 24-month analysis (Lawson A et al., PMID: 35476128), in patients 60 and over randomised to volar locking plate or closed reduction and cast, found the same functional equivalence (PRWE 13.6 versus 15.8; difference 2.1, 95% CI -4.2 to 8.5; p=0.50) and similar complications — though more plate patients called their treatment 'very successful' (75.0% versus 44.6%; p=0.002). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): routine fixation does not buy better wrist function than a cast at 1-2 years; what it buys is insurance against the roughly one-in-eight chance the casted fracture slips and needs the operation anyway.

cards.headline: DRAFFT2 (Costa 2022): PRWE at 12 months 21.2 cast versus 20.7 K-wire (difference -0.34, 95% CI -4.33 to 3.66; p=0.87) — but 13% of the cast group needed fixation within 6 weeks
cards.summary: DRAFFT2 (Costa 2022): PRWE at 12 months 21.2 cast versus 20.7 K-wire (difference -0.34, 95% CI -4.33 to 3.66; p=0.87) — but 13% of the cast group needed fixation within 6 weeks
cards.people: 500 adults (mean age 60, 83% women) with a dorsally displaced distal radius fracture needing manipulation, at 36 UK hospitals, randomised to moulded cast (n=255) or surgical fixation with K-wires plus cast (n=245); 395 (79%) completed follow-up.
cards.result: Primary outcome, PRWE score at 12 months (0 best, 100 worst): mean 21.2 (SD 23.1) on cast versus 20.7 (22.3) on K-wires; adjusted mean difference -0.34 (95% CI -4.33 to 3.66; p=0.87). No differences at 3 or 6 months, and quality of life did not differ. In the cast group 33 participants (13%) required surgical fixation for loss of fracture position within six weeks, versus one revision surgery in the K-wire group (odds ratio 0.02, 95% CI 0.001 to 0.10).
cards.watchOut: DRAFFT2 tested K-wires, not modern volar plates, and enrolled fractures the treating team judged suitable for either treatment after manipulation — fractures needing surgery on sight were never in the trial. The 13% crossover is part of the cast strategy's real cost, even though final function equalised.

cards.headline: CROSSFIRE 24-month analysis (Lawson 2022): volar plate versus closed reduction in over-60s — PRWE 13.6 versus 15.8 (difference 2.1; p=0.50), complications similar, 'very successful' ratings 75.0% versus 44.6%
cards.summary: CROSSFIRE 24-month analysis (Lawson 2022): volar plate versus closed reduction in over-60s — PRWE 13.6 versus 15.8 (difference 2.1; p=0.50), complications similar, 'very successful' ratings 75.0% versus 44.6%
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial with parallel observational cohort (Lawson 2022, CROSSFIRE)
cards.people: 300 patients aged 60+ with displaced distal radius fractures at 19 Australian and New Zealand centres: 166 randomised to volar locking plate fixation or closed reduction with cast, plus 134 who declined randomisation and chose treatment in a parallel observational group; 91% of randomised patients followed to 24 months.
cards.result: At 24 months in the randomised cohort, mean PRWE was 13.6 (95% CI 9.1 to 18.1) on plate fixation versus 15.8 (11.3 to 20.2) on closed reduction — mean difference 2.1 (95% CI -4.2 to 8.5; p=0.50), not clinically important. All other outcomes were similar except patient-reported treatment success, favouring the plate (54/72, 75.0%, 'very successful' versus 33/74, 44.6%; p=0.002). Complications were low and similar (deep infection 1/76 on closed reduction versus 0/75 on plate; complex regional pain syndrome 2.6% versus 1.3%). Observational-group outcomes were consistent.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of 24-month data, in older patients only, testing volar plates — the satisfaction gap without a function gap may reflect expectations and the experience of treatment as much as the wrist itself. Patients who chose their treatment in the observational arm are not randomised evidence.
cards.source: Lawson A et al. Plating vs Closed Reduction for Fractures in the Distal Radius in Older Patients: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA surgery. 2022. cards.summary: Synthesis: two fixation technologies, two age spans, one result — function equalises by a year; the decision is about the 13% slip risk and patient preference, not expected function
cards.people: DRAFFT2 (500 adults, K-wires versus cast, 12 months) and CROSSFIRE (166 randomised patients aged 60+, volar plate versus closed reduction, 24 months), both multicentre randomised trials in dorsally displaced/displaced distal radius fractures.
cards.result: PRWE differences: -0.34 points (95% CI -4.33 to 3.66) at 12 months and 2.1 points (-4.2 to 8.5) at 24 months — neither significant nor clinically important. Complications low and similar in CROSSFIRE. Cast-strategy cost: 13% needed fixation for loss of position within 6 weeks (DRAFFT2). Patient-rated 'very successful': 75.0% plate versus 44.6% cast (CROSSFIRE). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) to function.
cards.watchOut: Fractures judged to need surgery at presentation, intra-articular complexity beyond these trials' entry criteria, and younger high-demand patients are under-represented; the null applies to fractures a surgeon could honestly offer either way, which is exactly the population randomised.
cards.source: Synthesis of Costa ML et al. BMJ. 2022 (PMID: 35045969); Lawson A et al. JAMA surgery. 2022 (PMID: 35476128).

shelves.title: Bisphosphonates take about a year to pay off: 12.4 months of treatment to prevent one nonvertebral fracture per 100 women — 20.3 months for one hip fracture per 200
shelves.question: After starting a bisphosphonate, how long until fracture risk actually falls — what is the time to benefit?
shelves.mesh: Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Density Conservation Agents/therapeutic use · Female · Hip Fractures/prevention & control · Humans · Middle Aged · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/prevention & control · Osteoporotic Fractures/prevention & control · Postmenopause · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Spinal Fractures/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — arriving on a measurable schedule, pooled from ten randomised trials. Deardorff WJ et al. (PMID: 34807231) fitted survival curves to 10 randomised trials of alendronate, risedronate and zoledronic acid in 23,384 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (mean ages 63-74, follow-up 12-48 months). The pooled time to benefit was 12.4 months (95% CI 6.3 to 18.4) to prevent one nonvertebral fracture per 100 women treated (absolute risk reduction 0.010); 12.1 months (95% CI 6.4 to 17.8) to prevent one clinical vertebral fracture per 200 women (absolute risk reduction 0.005); and 20.3 months (95% CI 11.0 to 29.7) to prevent one hip fracture per 200 women (absolute risk reduction 0.005). In other words, the drugs work — but a woman whose life expectancy is under about a year is unlikely to live long enough to collect the nonvertebral benefit, and hip protection takes the longest to arrive. These are population averages from trial populations with established osteoporosis, not a promise for any individual. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): bisphosphonate fracture prevention is real but deferred — roughly a year for nonvertebral and vertebral fractures, nearer two years for hip — which is precisely the number deprescribing and goals-of-care conversations need.

cards.headline: Deardorff 2022: time to benefit 12.4 months (nonvertebral, ARR 0.010), 12.1 months (clinical vertebral, ARR 0.005), 20.3 months (hip, ARR 0.005) — pooled from 10 RCTs, 23,384 women
cards.summary: Deardorff 2022: time to benefit 12.4 months (nonvertebral, ARR 0.010), 12.1 months (clinical vertebral, ARR 0.005), 20.3 months (hip, ARR 0.005) — pooled from 10 RCTs, 23,384 women
cards.people: 10 randomised placebo-controlled trials (identified via USPSTF, AHRQ, Cochrane and Endocrine Society reviews) of alendronate, risedronate and zoledronic acid in 23,384 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (existing vertebral fracture or T-score ≤ -2.5); trial sizes 994 to 7,765, mean ages 63 (SD 7) to 74 (3) years, follow-up 12 to 48 months. Random-effects Weibull survival curves estimated absolute risk reduction and time to benefit, pooled by random-effects meta-analysis.
cards.result: Time to benefit for the first nonvertebral fracture at an absolute risk reduction of 0.010 (one fracture prevented per 100 treated): 12.4 months (95% CI 6.3 to 18.4). For hip fracture at ARR 0.005 (one per 200 treated): 20.3 months (95% CI 11.0 to 29.7). For clinical vertebral fracture at ARR 0.005: 12.1 months (95% CI 6.4 to 17.8). The authors conclude bisphosphonate therapy is most likely to benefit women whose life expectancy exceeds about 12.4 months.
cards.watchOut: Time to benefit is a modelled population statistic: it depends on the chosen absolute-risk-reduction threshold and on trial populations at high baseline fracture risk — lower-risk women wait longer for the same absolute benefit. It says nothing about when an individual's bone density or turnover markers change, which is much earlier.
cards.source: Deardorff WJ et al. Time to Benefit of Bisphosphonate Therapy for the Prevention of Fractures Among Postmenopausal Women With Osteoporosis: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials. JAMA internal medicine. 2022. PMID: 34807231. cards.headline: Synthesis: one meta-analysis answers the timing question directly — benefit is back-loaded, so the decision to start (or continue) should be made against life expectancy
cards.summary: Synthesis: one meta-analysis answers the timing question directly — benefit is back-loaded, so the decision to start (or continue) should be made against life expectancy
cards.people: A single meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials, 23,384 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, covering the three first-line bisphosphonates (Deardorff 2022).
cards.result: Nonvertebral fracture: one prevented per 100 women after 12.4 months (95% CI 6.3 to 18.4). Clinical vertebral fracture: one per 200 after 12.1 months (6.4 to 17.8). Hip fracture: one per 200 after 20.3 months (11.0 to 29.7). No competing time-to-benefit estimate exists in this record to contradict it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) with the timing on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: The shelf inherits the parent trials' population — postmenopausal women with osteoporosis by fracture or T-score. Extrapolating the 12.4-month figure to men, to glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis, or to osteopenia without fracture is beyond this record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Deardorff WJ et al. JAMA internal medicine. 2022 (PMID: 34807231).

shelves.title: Low-dose colchicine while allopurinol starts cut gout flares from 2.91 to 0.52 per patient in the one double-blind trial — 43 patients, flares also milder and shorter on colchicine
shelves.question: In gout, does low-dose colchicine prophylaxis during initiation of urate-lowering therapy prevent acute flares versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Arthritis, Gouty/diagnosis/drug therapy · Chronic Disease · Colchicine/administration & dosage · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Probability · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Secondary Prevention · Severity of Illness Index · Statistics, Nonparametric · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large effect in a very small trial, never replicated under blind. Borstad GC et al. (PMID: 15570646) randomised 43 patients with crystal-proven chronic gouty arthritis starting allopurinol to colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily or placebo, continuing study drug until 3 months after serum urate fell below 6.5 mg/dL. Patients on colchicine had fewer total flares (0.52 versus 2.91 per patient; p=0.008), fewer flares in months 0-3 (0.57 versus 1.91; p=0.022) and months 3-6 (0 versus 1.05; p=0.033), less severe flares (visual analogue scale 3.64 versus 5.08; p=0.018) and fewer recurrent flares (p=0.001). Colchicine was well tolerated in this small sample. The relative reduction in flare count is about 82% relative — but it rests on 43 patients studied two decades ago, with no second placebo-controlled trial of prophylaxis at allopurinol initiation in this record, and modern practice (lower starting doses, treat-to-target titration) may flare less at baseline than this trial's placebo arm did. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prophylactic colchicine during allopurinol initiation prevents and softens flares on the best available evidence — which is one small trial, so the shelf is Tier C.

cards.headline: Borstad 2004: total flares 0.52 on colchicine versus 2.91 on placebo (p=0.008); flare severity 3.64 versus 5.08 on VAS (p=0.018); recurrent flares fewer (p=0.001)
cards.summary: Borstad 2004: total flares 0.52 on colchicine versus 2.91 on placebo (p=0.008); flare severity 3.64 versus 5.08 on VAS (p=0.018); recurrent flares fewer (p=0.001)
cards.people: 43 patients with crystal-proven chronic gouty arthritis starting allopurinol, randomised to colchicine 0.6 mg orally twice daily or placebo, continued until 3 months after serum urate reached <6.5 mg/dL; outcomes were flare frequency, severity (visual analogue scale) and duration over the initiation period.
cards.result: Total flares per patient: 0.52 on colchicine versus 2.91 on placebo (p=0.008) — an approximately 82% relative reduction in flare count, with the absolute counts printed alongside. Flares in months 0-3: 0.57 versus 1.91 (p=0.022); months 3-6: 0 versus 1.05 (p=0.033). Flare severity on VAS: 3.64 versus 5.08 (p=0.018). Recurrent flares were less likely on colchicine (p=0.001). Colchicine was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Forty-three patients, one centre, 2004: with numbers this small, a handful of flares moving between arms would change the result, and the trial predates modern low-dose allopurinol initiation and treat-to-target titration, which lower the background flare rate the prophylaxis has to beat. No replication exists.
cards.source: Borstad GC et al. Colchicine for prophylaxis of acute flares when initiating allopurinol for chronic gouty arthritis. The Journal of rheumatology. 2004. PMID: 15570646. cards.headline: Synthesis: a fivefold difference in flare counts from the only blinded trial — direction trusted by guidelines, precision not available anywhere
cards.summary: Synthesis: a fivefold difference in flare counts from the only blinded trial — direction trusted by guidelines, precision not available anywhere
cards.people: One randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, 43 patients with chronic gouty arthritis starting allopurinol, colchicine 0.6 mg twice daily versus placebo (Borstad 2004). No second placebo-controlled prophylaxis trial was found for this shelf.
cards.result: Flares per patient 0.52 versus 2.91 (p=0.008); severity and recurrence also favoured colchicine; tolerability good in-trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the shelf rests on a single small trial for a benefit claim, exactly the pattern Tier C review exists for.
cards.watchOut: The stamp grades prophylaxis during allopurinol initiation only. It does not cover colchicine for treating an established flare, prophylaxis with other urate-lowering drugs, or doses other than 0.6 mg twice daily — each is a different question with its own record.
cards.source: Synthesis of Borstad GC et al. The Journal of rheumatology. 2004 (PMID: 15570646).
