shelves.title: Rilonacept cut gout flares during allopurinol initiation in two blinded trials — 0.21-0.29 flares per patient versus 1.06 on placebo in phase 3, with injection-site reactions the price
shelves.question: In patients starting urate-lowering therapy, does rilonacept (interleukin-1 blockade) prevent gout flares versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Allopurinol/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gout/drug therapy/pathology · Gout Suppressants/therapeutic use · Humans · Hyperuricemia/drug therapy/pathology · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Middle Aged · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two double-blind placebo-controlled trials, same direction, dose response in the larger one. In the phase II trial (Schumacher HR et al., PMID: 22223180), 83 patients starting allopurinol received weekly rilonacept 160 mg (after a 320 mg loading dose) or placebo: mean flares per patient over 12 weeks were 0.15 (6 flares) versus 0.79 (33 flares) (p=0.0011), and the proportion experiencing any flare was 14.6% versus 45.2% (p=0.0037). In the phase III confirmatory trial (Schumacher HR et al., PMID: 22549879), 241 patients starting allopurinol received 16 weekly injections of placebo, rilonacept 80 mg or rilonacept 160 mg: flares per patient over 16 weeks were 1.06 on placebo versus 0.29 on 80 mg and 0.21 on 160 mg (both p<0.001) — about a 73-80% relative reduction, with the absolute counts alongside — and patients with at least one flare numbered 46.8% on placebo versus 18.8% and 16.3%. The cost was injection-site reactions (19.8% on 160 mg versus 1.3% on placebo in phase III); other adverse events were broadly balanced. Rilonacept is a weekly injection for a problem oral colchicine also addresses, and it is not marketed for this indication — the shelf records efficacy, not a recommendation to seek it. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): IL-1 blockade with rilonacept prevents initiation flares as reliably as anything tested, at injection burden and cost the trials do not weigh.

cards.headline: Phase II (Schumacher 2012): flares per patient 0.15 on rilonacept versus 0.79 on placebo over 12 weeks (p=0.0011); any flare 14.6% versus 45.2% (p=0.0037)
cards.summary: Phase II (Schumacher 2012): flares per patient 0.15 on rilonacept versus 0.79 on placebo over 12 weeks (p=0.0011); any flare 14.6% versus 45.2% (p=0.0037)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase II trial (Schumacher 2012)
cards.people: 83 adults with hyperuricaemia and gout (41 rilonacept, 42 placebo) starting allopurinol 300 mg daily titrated to urate <6 mg/dL, receiving weekly subcutaneous rilonacept (320 mg loading, then 160 mg) or placebo; primary endpoint flares per patient through week 12, with 6 further weeks observed after study drug stopped at week 16.
cards.result: Mean gout flares per patient through week 12: 0.15 (6 flares total) on rilonacept versus 0.79 (33 flares) on placebo (p=0.0011), with separation as early as week 4 (p=0.007). Proportion with at least one flare: 14.6% versus 45.2% (p=0.0037). No rebound in flare rate in the 6 weeks after discontinuation. Adverse events were similar between groups, with no deaths or serious infectious events; infections occurred in 14.6% on rilonacept versus 26.2% on placebo, musculoskeletal disorders 14.6% versus 21.4%. Completion of the 12-week evaluation: 98% versus 79% (p=0.015).
cards.watchOut: A small phase II trial (83 patients) sponsored as a proof of concept; the flare-count effect is large but the sample cannot size uncommon harms of IL-1 blockade, and all patients also received titrated allopurinol, so this is add-on prophylaxis, not flare treatment.
cards.source: Schumacher HR et al. Rilonacept (interleukin-1 trap) in the prevention of acute gout flares during initiation of urate-lowering therapy: results of a phase II randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2012. PMID: 22223180. Registry ID: NCT00610363. cards.headline: Phase III (Schumacher 2012): flares per patient 1.06 placebo versus 0.29 (80 mg) and 0.21 (160 mg) over 16 weeks (both p<0.001); injection-site reactions 19.8% versus 1.3% at the higher dose
cards.summary: Phase III (Schumacher 2012): flares per patient 1.06 placebo versus 0.29 (80 mg) and 0.21 (160 mg) over 16 weeks (both p<0.001); injection-site reactions 19.8% versus 1.3% at the higher dose
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase III trial (Schumacher 2012)
cards.people: 241 adults with gout, at least two flares in the past year and serum urate ≥7.5 mg/dL, all starting allopurinol 300 mg daily titrated to <6.0 mg/dL, randomised 1:1:1 to 16 weekly subcutaneous injections of placebo, rilonacept 80 mg or rilonacept 160 mg (double loading dose on day 1).
cards.result: Mean flares per patient through week 16: 1.06 on placebo versus 0.29 on rilonacept 80 mg and 0.21 on 160 mg (both p<0.001) — relative reductions of about 73% and 80%, with the absolute counts alongside. Patients with at least one flare: 46.8% on placebo versus 18.8% (80 mg) and 16.3% (160 mg) (both p<0.001). Completion was higher on rilonacept (80.0% and 86.4%) than placebo (72.5%). Adverse events were generally balanced except injection-site reactions: 1.3% placebo, 8.8% on 80 mg, 19.8% on 160 mg (p=0.0001 for 160 mg versus placebo, post hoc).
cards.watchOut: Sixteen weeks of prophylaxis in trial volunteers with frequent flares; the trial does not compare rilonacept with oral colchicine prophylaxis, does not address cost or the burden of 16 weekly injections, and rilonacept's gout programme did not lead to a marketed gout indication — availability, not efficacy, is the practical barrier.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two concordant blinded trials with a dose gradient — flare prevention is as well shown for rilonacept as for any initiation prophylaxis, practicality aside
cards.summary: Synthesis: two concordant blinded trials with a dose gradient — flare prevention is as well shown for rilonacept as for any initiation prophylaxis, practicality aside
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials (phase II n=83; phase III n=241) of weekly subcutaneous rilonacept versus placebo in patients starting allopurinol, 12-16 weeks.
cards.result: Flares per patient: 0.15 versus 0.79 (phase II, 12 weeks); 0.21-0.29 versus 1.06 (phase III, 16 weeks). Any flare: 14.6% versus 45.2%; 16.3-18.8% versus 46.8%. Harm on the face: injection-site reactions up to 19.8% versus 1.3%; other adverse events balanced; no rebound after stopping. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for flare prevention during urate-lowering initiation.
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from the same development programme with the same sponsor and design — concordant, but not independent in the way two unrelated trial groups would be. The comparator that matters in practice, low-dose colchicine, was never in the ring.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schumacher HR et al. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2012 (PMID: 22223180); Schumacher HR et al. Arthritis care & research. 2012 (PMID: 22549879).

shelves.title: Hip bone structure after menopause: resistance-and-impact exercise and risedronate each nudged some strength estimates versus control — neither beat the other, and density itself did not move
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women, does a programme of resistance and impact exercise — or risedronate — better preserve hip bone structure?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Middle Aged · Risedronic Acid/therapeutic use · Postmenopause · Bone Density · Absorptiometry, Photon · Pelvic Bones · Exercise Therapy · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/drug therapy/prevention & control
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — one 12-month randomised trial in 276 women within 6 years of menopause (mean age 54.5) compared weighted jogging plus progressive resistance exercise, monthly risedronate 150 mg, and control, all with calcium and vitamin D. Volumetric bone density and other pQCT outcomes did not differ between groups. On hip structural analysis, exercise beat control on intertrochanteric cross-sectional area (+2.25%, 95% CI 0.28 to 4.12), moment of inertia (+5.67%, 95% CI 1.47 to 9.87) and section modulus (+4.38%, 95% CI 1.02 to 7.74); risedronate beat control on intertrochanteric moment of inertia (+4.28%) and section modulus (+3.35%) and on several shaft measures. Exercise and risedronate did not differ significantly from each other on the remaining measures, and no fractures were assessed. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): both strategies produced small favourable shifts in estimated hip strength versus control in a single trial, with no winner between them and no fracture evidence.

cards.headline: Blay 2024: exercise and risedronate each improved some hip structural estimates versus control (up to +5.67%); pQCT density outcomes null; exercise versus risedronate not significantly different
cards.summary: Blay 2024: exercise and risedronate each improved some hip structural estimates versus control (up to +5.67%); pQCT density outcomes null; exercise versus risedronate not significantly different
cards.people: 276 postmenopausal women within 6 years of menopause (mean age 54.5 ± 3.2 years, mean 36.7 months postmenopause) randomised to exercise (n=92; weighted jogging and progressive resistance exercise), risedronate 150 mg monthly (n=91), or control (n=93) for 12 months; all groups received calcium and vitamin D. Imaging (pQCT and DXA with hip structural analysis) at baseline, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: No significant between-group differences in pQCT outcomes (volumetric bone mineral density, area, strength estimates). At 12 months, exercise versus control: intertrochanteric cross-sectional area +2.25% (95% CI 0.28 to 4.12; p=0.03), cross-sectional moment of inertia +5.67% (95% CI 1.47 to 9.87; p<0.01), section modulus +4.38% (95% CI 1.02 to 7.74; p=0.01); narrow-neck average cortical thickness +2.37% (95% CI −0.08 to 4.83). Risedronate versus control: intertrochanteric moment of inertia +4.28% (95% CI −0.24 to 8.81), section modulus +3.35% (95% CI −0.21 to 6.91); shaft subperiosteal width +0.82%, moment of inertia +2.53%, section modulus +1.57%. Exercise maintained neck-shaft angle versus both control (+1.27%) and risedronate (+1.31%). All other exercise-versus-risedronate differences were not significant.
cards.watchOut: Surrogate structural estimates over 12 months in recently postmenopausal women — no fracture outcomes, several confidence intervals crossing zero despite significant p-values on the paper's modelling, and multiple correlated HSA endpoints invite selective emphasis. A single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two routes to slightly stronger-looking hips, no density change, no fractures counted
cards.summary: Synthesis: two routes to slightly stronger-looking hips, no density change, no fractures counted
cards.people: One three-arm RCT (276 recently postmenopausal women, 12 months) comparing resistance-and-impact exercise, monthly risedronate, and control.
cards.result: Hip structural analysis favoured both active arms over control on selected measures (exercise: moment of inertia +5.67%; risedronate: +4.28% at the intertrochanteric site); pQCT density and area outcomes were null; exercise versus risedronate was not significantly different. shelves.title: Zoledronate every 18 months in women with osteopenia: fragility fractures in 122 vs 190 women over 6 years (HR 0.63, NNT 15) — one large trial, in women not yet osteoporotic
shelves.question: In older women with osteopenia (bone density below normal but above the osteoporosis threshold), does zoledronate prevent fragility fractures compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute-Phase Reaction/chemically induced · Aged · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Density Conservation Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Bone Diseases, Metabolic/drug therapy · Bone Remodeling/drug effects · Calcium/therapeutic use · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fractures, Bone/prevention & control · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Intention to Treat Analysis · Iritis/chemically induced · Proportional Hazards Models · Zoledronic Acid/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a single, large, well-run trial in exactly the population where most fractures occur. Reid IR et al. (PMID: 30575489) randomised 2,000 women aged 65 or older with osteopenia (T score -1.0 to -2.5) to four infusions of zoledronate 5 mg or saline at 18-month intervals over 6 years. A nonvertebral or vertebral fragility fracture occurred in 122 women on zoledronate versus 190 on placebo (hazard ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.79; number needed to treat 15), with concordant reductions in nonvertebral (HR 0.66), symptomatic (HR 0.73) and vertebral (odds ratio 0.45) fractures. Most fractures in postmenopausal women occur in women with osteopenia, so the population is the right one; but this is one trial, from one country, in women selected for a median 10-year hip fracture risk of only 2.3%, and bisphosphonate treatment of osteopenia commits many women who would never fracture to a drug with rare but serious harms not quantifiable at this sample size. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single-trial benefit claim on a fracture endpoint, for the developer's personal review.

cards.headline: Reid 2018: fragility fracture in 122/1,000 women on zoledronate vs 190/1,000 on placebo over 6 years (HR 0.63) — vertebral fractures OR 0.45
cards.summary: Reid 2018: fragility fracture in 122/1,000 women on zoledronate vs 190/1,000 on placebo over 6 years (HR 0.63) — vertebral fractures OR 0.45
cards.people: 2,000 women aged 65 or older (mean age 71) with osteopenia — T score -1.0 to -2.5 at total hip or femoral neck (mean femoral neck T score -1.6; median 10-year hip fracture risk 2.3%) — randomised to zoledronate 5 mg or normal saline infusions at 18-month intervals (four infusions) for 6 years, in New Zealand. All were advised 1 g/day dietary calcium; those not already taking vitamin D received cholecalciferol.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (first nonvertebral or vertebral fragility fracture) occurred in 122 women in the zoledronate group and 190 in the placebo group (HR 0.63, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.79; p<0.001); the number needed to treat to prevent one woman fracturing was 15. Nonvertebral fractures HR 0.66 (p=0.001), symptomatic fractures HR 0.73 (p=0.003), vertebral fractures OR 0.45 (p=0.002), and height loss was less with zoledronate (p<0.001).
cards.watchOut: One trial, unreplicated, in a single country's population with low baseline hip-fracture risk — the absolute yield (68 fewer women fracturing per 1,000 over 6 years) depends on that baseline. Rare bisphosphonate harms (atypical femoral fracture, osteonecrosis of the jaw) occur below this trial's detection threshold, and the record's registry identifier is the ANZCTR number ACTRN12609000593235.
cards.source: Reid IR et al. Fracture Prevention with Zoledronate in Older Women with Osteopenia. The New England journal of medicine. 2018. PMID: 30575489. Registry ID: ACTRN12609000593235. shelves.title: Alexander technique lessons: 24 lessons cut disability by 3.4 points and pain days from 21 to 3 a month in back pain — and lessons matched acupuncture for chronic neck pain a year on
shelves.question: In adults with chronic or recurrent back pain, or chronic neck pain, do one-to-one Alexander technique lessons reduce pain and disability compared with usual care, massage or exercise advice?
shelves.mesh: Behavior Therapy/methods · Chronic Disease · Counseling · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Low Back Pain/nursing/therapy · Male · Massage/methods · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Patient Satisfaction · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two large UK primary-care trials, one for back pain and one for neck pain, both show durable benefit a year after lessons end. In ATEAM (Little P et al., PMID: 18713809), 579 patients with chronic or recurrent back pain randomised to 24 Alexander lessons had a Roland Morris disability score 3.4 points better than normal care at one year (95% CI -4.76 to -2.03), six lessons gave -1.40 points, and six lessons plus exercise prescription achieved 72% of the effect of 24 lessons alone; median days in pain in the previous four weeks fell from 21 on control to 3 after 24 lessons (reported as -18 days). Massage, by contrast, was not significantly better than control at one year (-0.58, 95% CI -1.94 to 0.77). In ATLAS (MacPherson H et al., PMID: 26524571), 517 people with chronic neck pain had Northwick Park Questionnaire scores 3.79 percentage points lower with Alexander lessons than usual care at 12 months (95% CI 0.91 to 6.66; p=0.010), a 31% relative reduction from baseline, essentially matching acupuncture (3.92 points). No significant harms were reported in ATEAM, and no serious adverse events were judged related in ATLAS. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Alexander lessons from registered teachers produce modest, durable improvements in chronic back and neck pain — the catch is access, cost and the number of lessons needed.

cards.headline: Little 2008 (ATEAM): 24 Alexander lessons beat normal care by 3.4 disability points at 1 year; six lessons plus exercise kept 72% of that effect — massage did not last
cards.summary: Little 2008 (ATEAM): 24 Alexander lessons beat normal care by 3.4 disability points at 1 year; six lessons plus exercise kept 72% of that effect — massage did not last
cards.people: 579 patients with chronic or recurrent low back pain in 64 English general practices, randomised to normal care (144), six massage sessions (147), six Alexander technique lessons (144) or 24 lessons (144); half of each group also received an exercise prescription with nurse behavioural counselling. Follow-up to 1 year.
cards.result: Roland Morris disability versus control (score 8.1): massage -0.58 (95% CI -1.94 to 0.77, not significant), six lessons -1.40 (95% CI -2.77 to -0.03), 24 lessons -3.4 (95% CI -4.76 to -2.03), exercise prescription -1.29 (95% CI -2.25 to -0.34). Exercise after six lessons achieved 72% of the effect of 24 lessons alone (-2.98 versus -4.14). Median days with back pain in the past four weeks: control 21 days; 24 lessons -18 days, six lessons -10 days, massage -7 days. Quality of life improved significantly and no significant harms were reported. Trial registration as reported in the record: National Research Register N0028108728.
cards.watchOut: Participants and teachers cannot be blinded to lessons, so expectation effects are possible; the comparison that matters most (24 lessons) is also the most expensive, and the trial predates modern back-pain pathways. Massage's early benefit fading to null at one year is reported inside this same record.
cards.source: Little P et al. Randomised controlled trial of Alexander technique lessons, exercise, and massage (ATEAM) for chronic and recurrent back pain. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2008. cards.headline: MacPherson 2015 (ATLAS): neck-pain disability 3.79 percentage points lower with Alexander lessons than usual care at 12 months — statistically indistinguishable from acupuncture's 3.92
cards.summary: MacPherson 2015 (ATLAS): neck-pain disability 3.79 percentage points lower with Alexander lessons than usual care at 12 months — statistically indistinguishable from acupuncture's 3.92
cards.people: 517 people in UK primary care with nonspecific neck pain lasting at least 3 months (median duration 6 years) and a Northwick Park Questionnaire (NPQ) score of at least 28%, randomised to 20 one-to-one Alexander lessons (600 minutes total) plus usual care, 12 acupuncture sessions plus usual care, or usual care alone; mean attendance was 14 lessons.
cards.result: Between-group reductions in NPQ score at 12 months versus usual care: Alexander lessons 3.79 percentage points (95% CI 0.91 to 6.66; p=0.010) and acupuncture 3.92 percentage points (95% CI 0.97 to 6.87; p=0.009). Reductions from baseline were 31% relative for lessons and 32% relative for acupuncture. Self-efficacy improved with both interventions versus usual care at 6 months (p<0.001). No reported serious adverse events were considered probably or definitely related to either intervention.
cards.watchOut: The absolute gain is modest — under 4 points on a percentage disability scale — and practitioners came from the two main UK professional associations, which the authors note may limit generalisability. Usual-care controls knew they were not receiving lessons, so some of the effect may be attention and self-efficacy rather than the technique itself.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large pragmatic trials, two spinal regions, one consistent story — real but modest gains that persist to a year
cards.summary: Synthesis: two large pragmatic trials, two spinal regions, one consistent story — real but modest gains that persist to a year
cards.people: Two UK primary-care randomised trials totalling 1,096 patients: ATEAM (579, chronic/recurrent back pain, lessons versus normal care, massage and exercise prescription) and ATLAS (517, chronic neck pain, lessons versus acupuncture and usual care).
cards.result: Back pain: 24 lessons -3.4 Roland Morris points (95% CI -4.76 to -2.03) and pain days down from a median 21 to about 3 in four weeks at 1 year; six lessons plus exercise retained 72% of the 24-lesson effect. Neck pain: lessons -3.79 NPQ percentage points versus usual care at 12 months (p=0.010), matching acupuncture. Harms: none significant in either trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial could blind participants, both are UK primary-care populations taught by registered teachers, and neither shows that a handful of lessons suffices — the dose that worked was 20-24 lessons, or six lessons deliberately paired with exercise. Tier C is not set: two large concordant randomised trials carry the shelf.

shelves.title: Pilates for low back pain: about 14 points better than doing almost nothing on a 100-point pain scale — but no better than other exercise
shelves.question: In adults with non-specific low back pain, does Pilates reduce pain and disability compared with minimal intervention — and is it better than other forms of exercise?
shelves.mesh: Exercise Movement Techniques/adverse effects/methods · Humans · Low Back Pain/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Time Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — against minimal intervention only. The Cochrane review (Yamato TP et al., PMID: 26133923) pooled 10 trials with 510 participants: Pilates reduced pain versus minimal intervention by a mean 14.05 points on a 0-100 scale at short-term follow-up (95% CI -18.91 to -9.19; low-quality evidence) and by 10.54 points at intermediate term (moderate-quality evidence), with disability improved by 7.95 points short term and 11.17 points at intermediate term. Against other exercise, however, there was no significant difference in disability either short term (mean difference -3.29, 95% CI -6.82 to 0.24) or intermediate term (-0.91, 95% CI -5.02 to 3.20). A single-assessor-blinded trial of 60 patients (Natour J et al., PMID: 24965957) found Pilates plus NSAIDs beat NSAIDs alone on pain, function and quality of life (all p<0.001 for pain and function) with fewer NSAIDs taken at 45, 90 and 180 days (p<0.010). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): Pilates is a reasonable exercise choice for back pain — the evidence supports exercise, not Pilates specifically.

cards.headline: Yamato 2015 (Cochrane): pain down 14.05 points versus minimal intervention — and no significant disability difference versus other exercise (-3.29; CI crosses zero)
cards.summary: Yamato 2015 (Cochrane): pain down 14.05 points versus minimal intervention — and no significant disability difference versus other exercise (-3.29; CI crosses zero)
cards.people: 10 randomised trials, 510 participants with acute, subacute or chronic non-specific low back pain; six trials compared Pilates with minimal intervention and four with other exercises. Seven trials were at low risk of bias and three at high risk; outcomes converted to a 0-100 scale.
cards.result: Versus minimal intervention: pain mean difference -14.05 (95% CI -18.91 to -9.19) short term (low-quality evidence) and -10.54 (95% CI -18.46 to -2.62) at intermediate term (moderate-quality evidence); disability -7.95 (95% CI -13.23 to -2.67) short term and -11.17 (95% CI -18.41 to -3.92) intermediate term. Versus other exercise: disability did not differ significantly short term (-3.29, 95% CI -6.82 to 0.24) or intermediate term (-0.91, 95% CI -5.02 to 3.20); pain results were heterogeneous and mixed. Two trials assessed adverse events: one found none, the other only minor events.
cards.watchOut: No comparison in the review rests on high-quality evidence, total numbers are small (510 across 10 trials), and 'minimal intervention' is a soft comparator — beating it shows Pilates works as exercise, not that its specific method adds anything.

cards.headline: Natour 2015: Pilates plus NSAIDs beat NSAIDs alone on pain and function (p<0.001) — and the Pilates group took fewer painkillers at every follow-up
cards.summary: Natour 2015: Pilates plus NSAIDs beat NSAIDs alone on pain and function (p<0.001) — and the Pilates group took fewer painkillers at every follow-up
cards.people: 60 patients with chronic non-specific low back pain randomised to Pilates plus NSAID medication or NSAID medication alone, assessed by a blinded assessor at baseline and at 45, 90 and 180 days for pain (VAS), function (Roland Morris), quality of life (SF-36), flexibility and NSAID intake.
cards.result: Differences favouring the Pilates group were reported for pain (p<0.001), function (p<0.001) and the SF-36 domains of functional capacity (p<0.046), pain (p<0.010) and vitality (p<0.029). NSAID use was lower in the Pilates group at 45, 90 and 180 days (p<0.010). The authors reported no harmful effects. The record reports p-values and directions rather than absolute score changes.
cards.watchOut: A 60-patient single-centre trial whose abstract gives significance levels without the size of the score changes, so the clinical size of its effect cannot be checked from the record; participants could not be blinded to doing Pilates.

cards.summary: Synthesis: Pilates works about as well as exercise works — the honest claim is 'a good way to exercise a bad back', not a superior therapy
cards.people: Cochrane review of 10 trials (510 participants) plus a 60-patient assessor-blinded trial of Pilates added to NSAIDs, in acute-to-chronic non-specific low back pain.
cards.result: Versus minimal intervention, pain fell by 14.05 points (0-100) short term and 10.54 points at intermediate term, and disability by 7.95 and 11.17 points. shelves.title: The McKenzie method for recent back pain: a slight short-term pain dip the Cochrane reviewers judged not clinically important — and no better than motor-control exercise in chronic pain
shelves.question: In adults with non-specific low back pain, does the McKenzie method (directional-preference exercises) reduce pain and disability compared with minimal intervention, manual therapy or other exercise?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Low Back Pain/therapy · Acute Pain/therapy · Exercise Therapy · Treatment Outcome · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the best synthesis is unusually blunt. The 2023 Cochrane review of the McKenzie method for (sub)acute non-specific low back pain (Almeida MO et al., PMID: 37017272; 5 trials, 563 participants) found a slight short-term pain reduction versus minimal intervention (mean difference -7.3 on a 0-100 scale, 95% CI -12.0 to -2.56) that was gone by intermediate term (-5.0, 95% CI -14.3 to 4.3), no disability reduction at either point, and no advantage over manual therapy — with a slight pain increase versus manual therapy at intermediate term (+7.0, 95% CI 0.7 to 13.3). The reviewers concluded the effects were not clinically important and that the method is not an effective treatment for (sub)acute back pain. In chronic back pain with a directional preference, a 70-patient trial (Halliday MH et al., PMID: 27170524) found no significant between-group differences in pain (p=.99) or function (p=.26) between McKenzie and motor-control exercise over 8 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): McKenzie assessment may help clinicians sort patients, but as a treatment it has not beaten booklets, manual therapy or rival exercise by any margin that matters.

cards.headline: Almeida 2023 (Cochrane): pain -7.3 points short term, nothing on disability, nothing lasting — 'not an effective treatment' for (sub)acute back pain
cards.summary: Almeida 2023 (Cochrane): pain -7.3 points short term, nothing on disability, nothing lasting — 'not an effective treatment' for (sub)acute back pain
cards.people: 5 randomised trials, 563 participants with (sub)acute (under 12 weeks) non-specific low back pain from primary or tertiary care; comparisons against minimal intervention (educational booklet or McKenzie added to other care), manual therapy, and massage plus advice. All trials were at high risk of performance and detection bias; none measured adverse events.
cards.result: Versus minimal intervention: pain mean difference -7.3 (95% CI -12.0 to -2.56) short term but -5.0 (95% CI -14.3 to 4.3) at intermediate term; disability -2.5 (95% CI -7.5 to 2.0) short term and -0.9 (95% CI -7.3 to 5.6) intermediate — neither significant. Versus manual therapy: pain -8.7 (95% CI -27.4 to 10.0) short term, and +7.0 (95% CI 0.7 to 13.3) — slightly worse — at intermediate term; disability not significantly different. All evidence low to very low certainty; the authors concluded the effects were not clinically important.
cards.watchOut: The review covers (sub)acute pain only, and every trial was unblinded by design; a small short-term pain dip on a 100-point scale is exactly the pattern expectation effects produce. The verdict is about the method as delivered in trials, not about the wider McKenzie assessment system.

cards.headline: Halliday 2016: in chronic back pain with a directional preference, McKenzie and motor-control exercise tie on pain (p=.99) and function (p=.26)
cards.summary: Halliday 2016: in chronic back pain with a directional preference, McKenzie and motor-control exercise tie on pain (p=.99) and function (p=.26)
cards.people: 70 people with chronic low back pain who demonstrated a directional preference on McKenzie assessment — the subgroup the method is designed for — randomised to 12 treatments over 8 weeks of the McKenzie method or motor-control exercise, with blinded outcome assessment. Registry ID: ACTRN12611000971932 (as reported in the record).
cards.result: No significant between-group difference in trunk muscle thickness (transversus abdominis -5.8%, 95% CI -15.2% to 3.7%). Perceived recovery was slightly superior in the McKenzie group (-0.8 on a -5 to +5 scale, 95% CI -1.5 to -0.1). No significant between-group differences were found for pain (p=.99) or function (p=.26).
cards.watchOut: This is the method's home turf — patients pre-selected for directional preference — and it still did not beat a rival exercise approach on pain or function; the one positive signal is a 0.8-point edge in perceived recovery on an 11-point scale. Seventy patients over 8 weeks cannot exclude small effects.

shelves.title: Massage for low back pain: better than doing nothing for a few weeks (pooled pain SMD -0.75) — the Cochrane reviewers still say they have 'very little confidence' it works
shelves.question: In adults with non-specific low back pain, does massage therapy reduce pain and improve function compared with inactive or active controls, and for how long?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain/therapy · Adult · Bias · Chronic Pain/therapy · Humans · Low Back Pain/therapy · Manipulation, Spinal · Massage/adverse effects/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — short-term only, on low-confidence evidence. The Cochrane review (Furlan AD et al., PMID: 26329399) pooled 25 trials with 3,096 participants: for sub-acute and chronic back pain, massage beat inactive controls for pain in the short term (SMD -0.75, 95% CI -0.90 to -0.60; 761 participants) and function (SMD -0.72, 95% CI -1.05 to -0.39), but not in the long term; against active controls the pain advantage was smaller (SMD -0.37 short term; -0.40 long term) with no functional difference. The reviewers rated the evidence low to very low quality and concluded they have very little confidence massage is effective. The best-known single trial (Cherkin DC et al., PMID: 11322842; 262 patients) found massage superior to self-care education at 10 weeks on symptoms (3.41 versus 4.71 on a 0-10 scale; p=.01) and disability (5.88 versus 8.92; p<.001), but by 1 year massage was no longer better than self-care. Increased pain was the commonest adverse event, reported in 1.5% to 25% of participants across trials; no serious adverse events were reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): expect weeks of relief, not a cure — and the ATEAM trial on shelf #4201 likewise found massage's back-pain benefit gone by one year.

cards.headline: Furlan 2015 (Cochrane): massage beats inactive controls short term (pain SMD -0.75, function SMD -0.72) — long term, the advantage disappears
cards.summary: Furlan 2015 (Cochrane): massage beats inactive controls short term (pain SMD -0.75, function SMD -0.72) — long term, the advantage disappears
cards.people: 25 randomised trials, 3,096 participants with acute (1 trial), sub-acute or chronic non-specific low back pain; massage by hands in most trials, mechanical device in three; comparators grouped as inactive (sham, waiting list, no treatment) or active (manipulation, TENS, acupuncture, exercise, self-care education and others).
cards.result: For sub-acute/chronic pain versus inactive controls: pain SMD -0.75 (95% CI -0.90 to -0.60; 761 participants, 7 studies) and function SMD -0.72 (95% CI -1.05 to -0.39; 725 participants) in the short term, but not the long term. Versus active controls: pain SMD -0.37 (95% CI -0.62 to -0.13) short term and -0.40 (95% CI -0.80 to -0.01) long term, with no differences for function at either point. For acute pain, one 51-patient trial found massage better for pain (SMD -1.24) but not function. No serious adverse events were reported; increased pain intensity was the most common adverse event (1.5% to 25% of participants). Evidence quality: low to very low.
cards.watchOut: Performance and measurement bias dominate — nobody can be blinded to receiving massage — and the reviewers' own conclusion ('very little confidence that massage is an effective treatment') is more cautious than their pooled numbers look. Short-term relief after a pleasant treatment is the easiest effect in medicine to manufacture.

cards.headline: Cherkin 2001: massage beat self-care at 10 weeks (symptoms 3.41 vs 4.71; disability 5.88 vs 8.92) — by 1 year it no longer beat self-care, though it still beat acupuncture
cards.summary: Cherkin 2001: massage beat self-care at 10 weeks (symptoms 3.41 vs 4.71; disability 5.88 vs 8.92) — by 1 year it no longer beat self-care, though it still beat acupuncture
cards.people: 262 patients aged 20-70 with persistent back pain randomised to traditional Chinese medical acupuncture (94), therapeutic massage (78) or self-care educational materials (90), with up to 10 massage or acupuncture visits over 10 weeks; outcomes assessed by telephone interviewers masked to treatment at 4, 10 and 52 weeks; 95% follow-up.
cards.result: At 10 weeks massage was superior to self-care on symptoms (3.41 versus 4.71 on a 0-10 scale; p=.01) and disability (5.88 versus 8.92 on a 0-23 scale; p<.001), and superior to acupuncture on disability (5.89 versus 8.25; p=.01). After 1 year massage was not better than self-care but remained better than acupuncture (symptoms 3.08 versus 4.74; p=.002; dysfunction 6.29 versus 8.21; p=.05). The massage group used the least medication (p<.05) and had the lowest subsequent care costs. No patient withdrew for adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: A single trial from 2001 with an education-booklet comparator — beating a booklet at 10 weeks is a low bar, and the 1-year convergence with self-care is the more durable lesson. Acupuncture's poor showing here is this trial's result, not a general verdict on acupuncture.
cards.source: Cherkin DC et al. Randomized trial comparing traditional Chinese medical acupuncture, therapeutic massage, and self-care education for chronic low back pain. cards.headline: Synthesis: massage is a short-term comfort measure with a consistent expiry date — pooled and single-trial evidence agree
cards.summary: Synthesis: massage is a short-term comfort measure with a consistent expiry date — pooled and single-trial evidence agree
cards.people: Cochrane review of 25 trials (3,096 participants) and the 262-patient Cherkin trial, in acute to chronic non-specific low back pain.
cards.result: Short term versus inactive controls: pain SMD -0.75 and function SMD -0.72; versus active controls, pain SMD -0.37 and no functional gain. Cherkin: clear wins at 10 weeks (symptoms 3.41 versus 4.71; disability 5.88 versus 8.92), no advantage over self-care at 1 year. Harms minor: transiently increased pain in 1.5-25%; no serious events reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), explicitly short-term.
cards.watchOut: The whole field is unblindable and the evidence is graded low to very low, which caps this at POSSIBLE; the claim that survives is 'massage helps for some weeks', and any claim of lasting structural benefit is unsupported. Tier C is not set: the shelf rests on a Cochrane meta-analysis plus a concordant large trial.

shelves.title: Dry needling for trigger-point pain: neck pain down 2.31 points more than sham in the short term — and no measurable effect left by mid-term in either review
shelves.question: In adults with musculoskeletal pain from myofascial trigger points, does dry needling reduce pain and disability compared with sham needling, no treatment or other physical therapy?
shelves.mesh: Acupuncture Therapy/methods · Humans · Musculoskeletal Pain/therapy · Needles · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Pain Management/methods · Pain Measurement · Physical Therapy Modalities · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Trigger Points
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a short-term effect that fades. The broad review (Gattie E et al., PMID: 28158962; 13 randomised trials) found very low- to moderate-quality evidence that dry needling by physical therapists reduced pain more than control, sham or other treatments in the immediate-to-12-week window and raised pressure pain threshold, but at 6-12 months the pain advantage was no longer statistically significant, and functional outcomes beat only no-treatment/sham, not other therapies. The neck-specific update (Navarro-Santana MJ et al., PMID: 33066556; 28 trials) found pain lower than sham/placebo/waiting-list by 1.53 points immediately (95% CI -2.29 to -0.76) and 2.31 points at short term (95% CI -3.64 to -0.99), disability better (SMD -0.87, 95% CI -1.60 to -0.14), but no difference versus other physical therapy interventions and no between-treatment effect on any outcome at mid-term; cervical range of motion did not improve. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): dry needling buys short-term trigger-point pain relief comparable to other hands-on therapy — it has not shown a durable or unique effect.

cards.headline: Gattie 2017: dry needling beats control/sham for pain up to 12 weeks — at 6-12 months the effect is no longer significant
cards.summary: Gattie 2017: dry needling beats control/sham for pain up to 12 weeks — at 6-12 months the effect is no longer significant
cards.people: 13 randomised trials of dry needling performed by physical therapists for any musculoskeletal pain condition, compared with control, sham or other interventions; trial quality scores (PEDro) ranged 4-9 of 10, median 7; eight meta-analyses were performed across outcomes and timepoints.
cards.result: In the immediate-to-12-week period, dry needling decreased pain and increased pressure pain threshold versus control/sham or other treatment. At 6-12 months dry needling was favoured for decreasing pain but the effect was not statistically significant. Functional outcomes were significantly better than control/sham but not better than other treatments. Evidence quality ranged from very low to moderate; the authors state evidence of long-term benefit is currently lacking. The record reports directions and significance rather than pooled point estimates.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen small trials across many different pain conditions is a thin base for a technique now sold for all of them; sham needling is itself an active-feeling intervention, and even so the advantage evaporates by 6-12 months.
cards.source: Gattie E et al. The Effectiveness of Trigger Point Dry Needling for Musculoskeletal Conditions by Physical Therapists: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy. 2017. PMID: 28158962. cards.headline: Navarro-Santana 2020: neck trigger-point pain -1.53 points immediately and -2.31 at short term versus sham — but no effect at mid-term and none on range of motion
cards.summary: Navarro-Santana 2020: neck trigger-point pain -1.53 points immediately and -2.31 at short term versus sham — but no effect at mid-term and none on range of motion
cards.people: 28 randomised trials of dry needling for myofascial trigger points associated with neck pain, compared with sham/placebo/waiting list, manual therapy or other physical interventions; outcomes were pain intensity, pain-related disability, pressure pain thresholds and cervical range of motion. Evidence graded low to moderate.
cards.result: Pain versus sham/placebo/waiting list/other dry needling: mean difference -1.53 (95% CI -2.29 to -0.76) immediately and -2.31 (95% CI -3.64 to -0.99) at short term; versus manual therapy at short term -0.51 (95% CI -0.95 to -0.06); no differences versus other physical therapy interventions. Disability at short term: SMD -0.87 (95% CI -1.60 to -0.14) versus sham-type controls only. Pressure pain threshold improved immediately (MD 55.48 kPa, 95% CI 27.03 to 83.93). No effect on cervical range of motion, and no between-treatment effect on any outcome at mid-term.
cards.watchOut: The record for this review carries no MeSH terms. The largest effects are against sham/waiting-list comparators in the shortest windows — the exact pattern seen with many hands-on therapies — and the mid-term nulls are part of the same dataset, not a separate sceptical study.
cards.source: Navarro-Santana MJ et al. Effectiveness of Dry Needling for Myofascial Trigger Points Associated with Neck Pain Symptoms: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of clinical medicine. 2020. PMID: 33066556. MeSH: none in the record

cards.summary: Synthesis: a real short-term signal against sham, an equally consistent fade — dry needling is an option among hands-on therapies, not a breakthrough
cards.people: Two meta-analyses covering 13 trials (all musculoskeletal conditions) and 28 trials (neck trigger points), with follow-up from immediately post-treatment to 12 months.
cards.result: Pain: better than sham/control up to 12 weeks (neck MD -2.31 at short term, 95% CI -3.64 to -0.99); not significant at 6-12 months in the broad review and null at mid-term in the neck review. Function: better than sham (SMD -0.87) but not better than manual or other physical therapy. Range of motion: no effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), short-term framing on the face of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Evidence is very low to moderate quality, trials are small, and publication bias toward positive needling trials is plausible; the stamp reflects pooled randomised evidence, which is why Tier C is not set, but no one should promise patients lasting relief from this record.

shelves.title: TENS machines: pain is lower while the current is on (SMD -0.96 versus placebo across 91 trials) — the older back-pain-only review found just two trials and they disagreed
shelves.question: In adults with acute or chronic pain, does transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) reduce pain compared with placebo or standard care — and does the effect persist after the device is switched off?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Chronic Pain/therapy · Graft vs Host Disease · Humans · Pain Measurement · Transcutaneous Electric Nerve Stimulation/adverse effects/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — strictly during or immediately after use. The meta-TENS collaboration (Johnson MI et al., PMID: 35144946) pooled 381 randomised trials with 24,532 participants: pain intensity was lower during or immediately after TENS than placebo (91 trials, 4,841 participants; SMD -0.96, 95% CI -1.14 to -0.78; moderate-certainty evidence) and lower than standard-care pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatments (61 trials, 3,155 participants; SMD -0.72, 95% CI -0.95 to -0.50; low-certainty evidence), with adverse events generally mild and no different from comparators. The narrower older Cochrane review for chronic low back pain (Khadilkar A et al., PMID: 16034883) found only two eligible trials (175 patients) which disagreed — one positive, one null across multiple outcomes — and judged the evidence inconsistent for TENS as a single treatment for back pain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a TENS unit is a reasonable, low-harm way to take the edge off pain while it runs; neither review establishes relief that outlasts the session, and back-pain-specific evidence is the weakest part of the record.

cards.headline: Johnson 2022 (meta-TENS): across 91 placebo-controlled trials, pain during/immediately after TENS is lower by SMD -0.96 — moderate-certainty, measured while the device is on
cards.summary: Johnson 2022 (meta-TENS): across 91 placebo-controlled trials, pain during/immediately after TENS is lower by SMD -0.96 — moderate-certainty, measured while the device is on
cards.people: 381 randomised trials, 24,532 adults with acute or chronic pain of any diagnosis, comparing strong non-painful TENS at or near the pain site with placebo or other treatments; primary outcome was pain intensity during or immediately after TENS, plus proportions achieving at least 30% or over 50% pain reductions.
cards.result: Versus placebo: SMD -0.96 (95% CI -1.14 to -0.78) across 91 trials / 92 samples, 4,841 participants — moderate-certainty evidence. Versus standard-care treatments: SMD -0.72 (95% CI -0.95 to -0.50) across 61 trials, 3,155 participants — low-certainty evidence. Trial methodology and pain characteristics did not modify the effect in subgroup analyses. Adverse events were poorly reported, generally mild and not different from comparators; no serious adverse events were attributed.
cards.watchOut: The outcome window is the giveaway: pain was measured during or immediately after stimulation, so this review cannot speak to hours-later or long-term relief. Estimates were downgraded for the many small trials contributing imprecision, and the record's MeSH even carries an unrelated 'Graft vs Host Disease' term, reproduced verbatim as the record gives it.
cards.source: Johnson MI et al. cards.headline: Khadilkar 2005 (Cochrane): for chronic low back pain specifically, only two trials (175 patients) qualified — one positive, one null — 'inconsistent evidence'
cards.summary: Khadilkar 2005 (Cochrane): for chronic low back pain specifically, only two trials (175 patients) qualified — one positive, one null — 'inconsistent evidence'
cards.people: Randomised trials of TENS for chronic low back pain searched to April 2005; only two trials with 175 patients met eligibility, differing in design, quality, inclusion criteria, TENS parameters, treatment schedules, co-interventions and outcomes.
cards.result: In one trial TENS produced significantly greater pain relief than the placebo control; in the other, no statistically significant differences between treatment and control groups were shown for multiple outcome measures. Pre-planned subgroup analyses by stimulation parameters, site, duration and patient characteristics were impossible with two trials. The authors concluded there is inconsistent evidence to support TENS as a single treatment for chronic low back pain and called for larger multicentre trials.
cards.watchOut: This review is two decades old and tiny — it does not refute the later 381-trial pool, but it does show that the condition TENS is most often bought for, chronic back pain, has the thinnest direct evidence. Anyone citing meta-TENS for back pain is extrapolating from mixed pain conditions.
cards.source: Khadilkar A et al. Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) for chronic low-back pain. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2005. PMID: 16034883. shelves.title: Back belts and lumbar supports: moderate evidence they do not prevent back pain — yet one trial in workers with previous pain found 52.7 fewer pain days a year, with no fewer sick days
shelves.question: Do lumbar supports (back belts/braces) prevent low back pain, prevent its recurrence, or treat existing non-specific low back pain?
shelves.mesh: Braces · Evaluation Studies as Topic · Humans · Low Back Pain/prevention & control/therapy · Lumbosacral Region · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — prevention in general: no; recurrence in workers who already have back pain: maybe; treatment: unknown. The Cochrane review (van Duijvenbode IC et al., PMID: 18425875) included seven prevention studies (14,437 people) and eight treatment studies (1,361 people): there was moderate evidence that lumbar supports are not more effective than no intervention or training in preventing low back pain, conflicting evidence on supports as supplements to other prevention, and it remained unclear whether supports beat no treatment or other interventions for treating back pain; only five of fifteen studies met half or more of the internal validity items. Against that background, one well-sized trial (Roelofs PD et al., PMID: 18025444) randomised 360 home care workers with a history of back pain: those given patient-directed lumbar supports reported on average 52.7 fewer days with low back pain over 12 months (95% CI -59.6 to -45.1) than a healthy-working-methods course alone, with small significant advantages in pain intensity and function — but total sick days did not fall (-5 days, 95% CI -21.1 to 6.8). PROPOSED SPLIT: do not buy a belt to prevent a first back problem or to treat one; a support may reduce the number of painful days for people whose work provokes recurrences, without reducing time off work.

cards.headline: van Duijvenbode 2008 (Cochrane): moderate evidence supports do NOT prevent back pain; for treatment, 8 trials still leave it 'unclear'
cards.summary: van Duijvenbode 2008 (Cochrane): moderate evidence supports do NOT prevent back pain; for treatment, 8 trials still leave it 'unclear'
cards.people: Seven randomised prevention studies (14,437 people) and eight randomised treatment studies (1,361 people) of any type of lumbar support for non-specific low back pain, searched to December 2006; evidence graded qualitatively (strong/moderate/limited/conflicting/none) because pooling was not possible.
cards.result: Prevention: moderate evidence that lumbar supports are not more effective than no intervention or training; conflicting evidence on whether supports add anything to other preventive interventions. Treatment: it remained unclear whether lumbar supports are more effective than no intervention or other interventions. Overall methodological quality was rather low — only five of the fifteen studies met 50% or more of the internal validity items — and the authors flagged adequate compliance as the key unsolved trial issue.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative, 2008-vintage synthesis of mostly low-quality trials: 'moderate evidence of no effect' for prevention is the firmest statement the field has produced, and it has not been overturned by a large modern trial. Absence of good trials for treatment is not evidence supports treat pain — it is an open question wearing a product label.
cards.source: van Duijvenbode IC et al. Lumbar supports for prevention and treatment of low back pain. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2008. PMID: 18425875. cards.headline: Roelofs 2007: home care workers with previous back pain had 52.7 fewer pain days in a year with a support — and exactly no reduction in sick days
cards.summary: Roelofs 2007: home care workers with previous back pain had 52.7 fewer pain days in a year with a support — and exactly no reduction in sick days
cards.people: 360 Dutch home care workers with a self-reported history of low back pain, randomised to a short course on healthy working methods with or without patient-directed use of one of four types of lumbar support; primary outcomes were days of low back pain and sick leave over 12 months. Registry ID: ISRCTN73707379.
cards.result: The lumbar support group reported an average of 52.7 fewer days with low back pain over 12 months (95% CI -59.6 to -45.1 days). Total sick days did not decrease (-5 days, 95% CI -21.1 to 6.8). Small but statistically significant differences in pain intensity and function (Quebec Back Pain Disability scale) favoured lumbar support.
cards.watchOut: Participants were unblinded and a substantial amount of missing outcome data required imputation; the headline outcome (days with pain) is self-reported by people who knew they had the belt, while the objective-adjacent outcome (sick leave) did not move. This is secondary prevention in one occupation, not a licence to generalise to first prevention or treatment.
cards.source: Roelofs PD et al. Lumbar supports to prevent recurrent low back pain among home care workers: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2007. PMID: 18025444. Registry ID: ISRCTN73707379. cards.headline: Synthesis: the belt fails as a shield, is unproven as a treatment, and has one credible niche — cutting painful days in people whose backs already play up at work
cards.summary: Synthesis: the belt fails as a shield, is unproven as a treatment, and has one credible niche — cutting painful days in people whose backs already play up at work
cards.people: Cochrane qualitative review of 15 randomised studies (14,437 prevention participants; 1,361 treatment participants) plus one 360-worker secondary-prevention trial with 12-month follow-up.
cards.result: Primary prevention: moderate evidence of no benefit. Treatment: unclear after eight trials. Secondary prevention in home care workers: 52.7 fewer pain days per year (95% CI -59.6 to -45.1) but sick days unchanged (-5, 95% CI -21.1 to 6.8). PROPOSED SPLIT, as the three questions genuinely have three different answers.
cards.watchOut: Compliance — whether people actually wear the support — is the confounder the Cochrane authors singled out, and neither card resolves it. Tier C is not set: the split rests on a Cochrane review plus a large randomised trial, not on a single small study.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Duijvenbode IC et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2008 (PMID: 18425875); Roelofs PD et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2007 (PMID: 18025444).

shelves.title: Low-level laser therapy for neck pain: pain down about 20 mm on a 100 mm scale in the pooled trials, with relief persisting up to 22 weeks in chronic pain
shelves.question: In adults with acute or chronic neck pain, does low-level laser therapy (photobiomodulation) reduce pain compared with placebo or active treatment?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Low-Level Light Therapy · Neck Pain/etiology/radiotherapy · Pain Measurement · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an older but large pooled signal, with mild side effects. The Lancet systematic review (Chow RT et al., PMID: 19913903) pooled 16 randomised trials with 820 patients: in acute neck pain, two trials gave a relative risk of 1.69 for pain improvement with laser versus placebo (95% CI 1.22 to 2.33); in chronic neck pain, five trials reporting categorical data gave a relative risk of 4.05 (95% CI 2.74 to 5.98), and 11 trials reporting visual analogue scores showed pain intensity reduced by 19.86 mm on a 100 mm scale (95% CI 10.04 to 29.68), with relief persisting 1-22 weeks after treatment ended (reduction 22.07 mm, 95% CI 17.42 to 26.72). Side effects were mild and not different from placebo. A double-blind placebo-controlled trial in a narrower group — 60 patients with acute neck pain with radiculopathy (Konstantinovic LM et al., PMID: 20704667) — found significantly better arm pain (p=0.003, effect size d=0.92) and neck extension (p=0.003, d=0.94) after 15 treatments over 3 weeks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): laser therapy probably eases neck pain by a clinically noticeable margin — but the trials span many wavelengths and doses, and the evidence base is from 2009 and earlier.

cards.headline: Chow 2009 (Lancet): chronic neck pain improvement RR 4.05 versus control; VAS pain down 19.86 mm — and still down 22.07 mm up to 22 weeks after treatment
cards.summary: Chow 2009 (Lancet): chronic neck pain improvement RR 4.05 versus control; VAS pain down 19.86 mm — and still down 22.07 mm up to 22 weeks after treatment
cards.people: 16 randomised controlled trials, 820 patients with acute or chronic neck pain, comparing low-level laser therapy at any wavelength with placebo or active control; primary outcome was pain intensity as mean difference in change in mm on a 100 mm visual analogue scale.
cards.result: Acute neck pain (2 trials): relative risk of pain improvement 1.69 (95% CI 1.22 to 2.33) for laser versus placebo. Chronic neck pain: five trials with categorical data gave RR 4.05 (95% CI 2.74 to 5.98) for pain improvement; 11 trials with VAS data showed pain reduced by 19.86 mm (95% CI 10.04 to 29.68). Seven trials with follow-up 1-22 weeks after treatment ended showed persisting relief of 22.07 mm (95% CI 17.42 to 26.72). Side effects were mild and not different from placebo.
cards.watchOut: The trials used different wavelengths, doses and treatment schedules, and most predate modern trial-reporting standards; a relative risk of 4.05 from small categorical trials is exactly the kind of estimate that shrinks when a large rigorous trial is done — none has been. The review's search is from 2009.

cards.headline: Konstantinovic 2010: in acute neck pain with radiculopathy, laser beat sham on arm pain (p=0.003, d=0.92) and neck extension (p=0.003, d=0.94) after 15 sessions
cards.summary: Konstantinovic 2010: in acute neck pain with radiculopathy, laser beat sham on arm pain (p=0.003, d=0.92) and neck extension (p=0.003, d=0.94) after 15 sessions
cards.people: 60 patients with acute neck pain with radiculopathy at a Belgrade rehabilitation clinic, receiving 15 treatments over 3 weeks of active laser (905 nm, 5,000 Hz, 12 mW/cm2, 2 J/cm2 per point) or an inactivated-laser placebo procedure; outcomes were pain (VAS), neck movement, neck disability index and quality of life at the end of treatment.
cards.result: Statistically significant differences favoured laser for intensity of arm pain (p=0.003, with high effect size d=0.92) and for neck extension (p=0.003, d=0.94). The record reports these two significant outcomes with effect sizes; it does not report significant differences for the remaining secondary outcomes in its abstract.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients, one centre, three weeks, and a radiculopathy population — narrower and more acute than the chronic neck pain most laser clinics treat. Large effect sizes (d≈0.9) in small trials usually regress; treat this as confirmation of direction, not of magnitude.
cards.source: Konstantinovic LM et al. Low-level laser therapy for acute neck pain with radiculopathy: a double-blind placebo-controlled randomized study. Pain medicine (Malden, Mass.). 2010. PMID: 20704667. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent direction across a 16-trial pool and a sham-controlled trial — real pain relief, uncertain dose, dated evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent direction across a 16-trial pool and a sham-controlled trial — real pain relief, uncertain dose, dated evidence
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 16 randomised trials (820 patients, acute and chronic neck pain) plus a 60-patient double-blind sham-controlled trial in acute radicular neck pain.
cards.result: Chronic neck pain: VAS down 19.86 mm/100 (95% CI 10.04 to 29.68) and categorical improvement RR 4.05 (95% CI 2.74 to 5.98); acute pain improvement RR 1.69 (95% CI 1.22 to 2.33); follow-up relief 22.07 mm up to 22 weeks. Radiculopathy trial: arm pain and extension significantly better (both p=0.003). Side effects mild, placebo-like. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No large modern confirmatory trial exists and protocols vary so much that 'laser therapy' here is a family of doses, not one treatment; clinics charging per session indefinitely are beyond this evidence, which covers defined short courses. Tier C is not set: a 16-trial meta-analysis carries the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chow RT et al. Lancet (London, England). 2009 (PMID: 19913903); Konstantinovic LM et al. Pain medicine (Malden, Mass.). 2010 (PMID: 20704667).

shelves.title: Shock wave therapy for tennis elbow: 'Platinum' level evidence of little or no benefit across nine placebo trials — one positive trial in tennis players is the exception, and steroid injection beat it head-to-head
shelves.question: In adults with lateral elbow pain (tennis elbow), does extracorporeal shock wave therapy reduce pain and improve function compared with placebo or steroid injection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tennis Elbow/therapy · Ultrasonic Therapy/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the pooled verdict is one of the firmest nulls in this territory. The Cochrane review (Buchbinder R et al., PMID: 16235324) included nine placebo-controlled trials with 1,006 participants: 11 of 13 pooled analyses found no significant benefit of shock wave therapy over placebo — for example, improvement in pain at 4-6 weeks differed by -9.42 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI -20.70 to 1.86) and pain on resisted wrist extension at 12 weeks by -9.04 (95% CI -19.37 to 1.28). The reviewers graded this 'Platinum' level evidence of little or no benefit. Two pooled results favoured treatment (success relative risk 2.2, 95% CI 1.55 to 3.12), but four other trials that could not be pooled did not support them. The best-known positive trial (Rompe JD et al., PMID: 15090392) enrolled only tennis players with MRI-confirmed elbow pain of at least 12 months: 65% achieved at least 50% pain reduction versus 28% on sham (p=.001). In the one head-to-head trial, steroid injection beat shock wave therapy at 3 months (84% versus 60% achieving 50% pain reduction; p<0.05) — though shelf #684 records that steroid's own advantage reverses by one year. Adverse effects were minimal: transient pain, skin reddening and nausea. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): outside a narrow recalcitrant tennis-player subgroup, shock wave therapy for tennis elbow is an expensive placebo-grade intervention on current evidence.

cards.headline: Buchbinder 2005 (Cochrane): nine placebo trials, 1,006 participants — pain improvement -9.42 points (CI -20.70 to 1.86) at 4-6 weeks; 'little or no benefit'
cards.summary: Buchbinder 2005 (Cochrane): nine placebo trials, 1,006 participants — pain improvement -9.42 points (CI -20.70 to 1.86) at 4-6 weeks; 'little or no benefit'
cards.people: Nine randomised trials (1,006 participants) of extracorporeal shock wave therapy versus placebo for lateral elbow pain, plus one trial (93 participants) versus steroid injection; searches to February 2005; each trial independently quality-assessed by two reviewers.
cards.result: Eleven of 13 pooled analyses found no significant benefit over placebo: weighted mean difference for pain improvement at 4-6 weeks -9.42 on a 100-point scale (95% CI -20.70 to 1.86; 3 trials, 446 participants) and for pain on resisted wrist extension at 12 weeks -9.04 (95% CI -19.37 to 1.28; 3 trials, 455 participants). Two pooled analyses favoured treatment, including treatment success RR 2.2 (95% CI 1.55 to 3.12; 2 trials, 192 participants), but four unpooled trials did not support that finding. Steroid injection was more effective at 3 months (21/25, 84%, versus 29/48, 60%, achieving 50% pain reduction; p<0.05). Adverse effects were minimal — transient pain, reddening and nausea, rarely requiring discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: The review is from 2005 and device protocols have changed since; but no later large trial has overturned it, and the burden of proof sits with the newer protocols. The two positive pooled analyses rest on 192 participants against 1,006 in the full set.

cards.headline: Rompe 2004: in tennis players with at least a year of MRI-confirmed elbow pain, 65% versus 28% achieved at least 50% pain reduction (p=.001)
cards.summary: Rompe 2004: in tennis players with at least a year of MRI-confirmed elbow pain, 65% versus 28% achieved at least 50% pain reduction (p=.001)
cards.people: 78 tennis players with recalcitrant, MRI-confirmed lateral epicondylitis of at least 12 months' duration, randomised to three weekly sessions of active low-energy shock wave treatment or identical placebo (sham) treatment; main outcome was pain during resisted wrist extension at 3 months.
cards.result: Improvement in pain during resisted wrist extension at 3 months: mean 3.5 (SD 2.0) in the treatment group versus 2.0 (SD 1.9) on sham (p=.001). Upper Extremity Function Scale improvement: 23.4 (SD 14.8) versus 10.9 (SD 14.9) (p<.001). At least 50% pain reduction was achieved by 65% of treated patients versus 28% on sham (p=.001).
cards.watchOut: A highly selected subgroup — actual tennis players, symptoms over a year, MRI confirmation — treated by the technique's leading research group; the Cochrane reviewers could not pool this trial with the others, and its result has not been reproduced in general elbow-pain populations. It defines a possible niche, not a general indication.

cards.summary: Synthesis: the average patient gets nothing measurable; a narrow, long-duration athletic subgroup might — and even there, one trial is all there is
cards.people: Cochrane review of nine placebo-controlled trials (1,006 participants) and one steroid-comparison trial (93), plus a 78-patient sham-controlled trial in tennis players with at least 12 months of symptoms.
cards.result: Pooled pain differences versus placebo: -9.42 points at 4-6 weeks and -9.04 at 12 weeks, both with confidence intervals crossing zero; 11 of 13 analyses null. Rompe subgroup: 65% versus 28% achieving at least 50% pain reduction. Steroid beat shock wave head-to-head at 3 months (84% versus 60%). Harms minimal. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for lateral elbow pain in general.
cards.watchOut: Shock wave therapy does have positive sham-controlled evidence at other sites (plantar heel pain, shelf #1473) — this null is specific to the elbow and must not be generalised across tendons. Tier C is not set: the null rests on a 1,006-participant Cochrane pool.
cards.source: Synthesis of Buchbinder R et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2005 (PMID: 16235324); Rompe JD et al. The American journal of sports medicine. 2004 (PMID: 15090392).

shelves.title: Morton's neuroma injections: adding steroid to the anaesthetic made no difference in the placebo-controlled trial — ultrasound guidance is where the Cochrane pool finds a gain (pain -15.01 mm at 6 months)
shelves.question: In adults with Morton's neuroma, does a corticosteroid-plus-anaesthetic injection relieve pain better than anaesthetic alone — and does ultrasound guidance improve the result?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Morton Neuroma/therapy · Anesthetics, Local · Quality of Life · Pain · Atrophy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the steroid itself: no proven gain; the guidance: probably a gain. The 2024 Cochrane review (Matthews BG et al., PMID: 38334217; six trials, 373 participants) found low-certainty evidence that corticosteroid plus local anaesthetic results in little to no difference in pain at 3-6 months versus anaesthetic alone (mean difference -6.31 mm on a 100 mm scale, 95% CI -14.23 to 1.61; two trials, 157 participants) and little to no difference in function (SMD -0.30, 95% CI -0.61 to 0.02), while ultrasound-guided injection probably reduces pain versus unguided injection at 6 months (mean difference -15.01 mm, 95% CI -27.88 to -2.14; moderate-certainty) and probably increases function (SMD -0.47, 95% CI -0.84 to -0.10). The double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Lizano-Díez X et al., PMID: 28617064; 41 patients, three injections) found no significant between-group differences in pain or function at 3 and 6 months, and 48.5% of all patients went on to request surgical excision — 44% of the steroid group and 53% of controls (p=1.0). The guidance trial (Mahadevan D et al., PMID: 27037432; 45 feet) itself found pain improved in both groups (from 64 to 29 mm guided; 69 to 37 mm unguided) with no statistical difference between them, and 12-month failure rates of 48% and 55% (p=0.458). Steroid adverse events in the review included skin atrophy (3.9%), hypopigmentation (3.9%) and plantar fat pad atrophy (2.6%). PROPOSED SPLIT: inject if you like — the anaesthetic may be doing the work; if you inject, guidance probably helps; about half of patients still end up wanting surgery within a year.

cards.headline: Matthews 2024 (Cochrane): steroid+anaesthetic versus anaesthetic alone — pain MD -6.31 mm (low certainty); guided versus unguided — pain MD -15.01 mm (moderate certainty)
cards.summary: Matthews 2024 (Cochrane): steroid+anaesthetic versus anaesthetic alone — pain MD -6.31 mm (low certainty); guided versus unguided — pain MD -15.01 mm (moderate certainty)
cards.people: Six randomised trials, 373 participants with Morton's neuroma confirmed by symptoms, a clinical test and ultrasound or MRI; comparisons covered steroid plus local anaesthetic versus anaesthetic alone (2 trials, 157 participants), ultrasound-guided versus unguided steroid injection (2 trials, 116 feet), and plantar versus dorsal neurectomy (1 trial). Risk of bias had 'some concerns' across most outcomes; no study was low risk across all domains.
cards.result: Steroid+anaesthetic versus anaesthetic alone at 3-6 months: pain mean difference -6.31 mm on a 0-100 VAS (95% CI -14.23 to 1.61; p=0.12; low-certainty), function SMD -0.30 (95% CI -0.61 to 0.02; low-certainty), quality of life MD 0.07 (95% CI -0.03 to 0.17; moderate-certainty, little to no difference). Guided versus unguided at 6 months: pain MD -15.01 mm (95% CI -27.88 to -2.14; p=0.02; moderate-certainty), function SMD -0.47 (95% CI -0.84 to -0.10), satisfaction RR 1.71 (95% CI 1.19 to 2.44; low-certainty). Steroid adverse events: mild skin atrophy 3.9%, hypopigmentation 3.9%, plantar fat pad atrophy 2.6%; the adverse-event relative risk versus anaesthetic alone was 9.84 (95% CI 1.28 to 75.56) on very low-certainty evidence.
cards.watchOut: Only six trials exist for every intervention for this common condition combined, and the guidance advantage comes from pooling two small trials — one of which (Mahadevan, carded below) found no significant between-group difference itself. No established minimal clinically important difference exists for the function scales used.
cards.source: Matthews BG et al. Treatments for Morton's neuroma. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2024. PMID: 38334217. MeSH: Humans · Morton Neuroma/therapy · Anesthetics, Local · Quality of Life · Pain · Atrophy

cards.headline: Lizano-Díez 2017: three steroid injections no better than anaesthetic alone at 3 and 6 months — and 48.5% of everyone asked for surgery by the end
cards.summary: Lizano-Díez 2017: three steroid injections no better than anaesthetic alone at 3 and 6 months — and 48.5% of everyone asked for surgery by the end
cards.people: 41 patients with Morton's neuroma randomised to three injections of corticosteroid plus local anaesthetic or local anaesthetic alone (placebo control); patients and the data-collecting researcher were blinded; pain (VAS) and AOFAS score measured at baseline, after each injection, and at 3 and 6 months after the last injection.
cards.result: No significant between-group differences in pain or function improvement at 3 and 6 months versus baseline. By the end of the study 17 patients (48.5%) requested surgical excision of the neuroma: 7 (44%) in the steroid group and 10 (53%) in the control group (p=1.0). The record reports the null result and surgery counts rather than group mean scores in its abstract.
cards.watchOut: Forty-one patients cannot exclude a modest steroid effect, and three injections is a more intensive course than the single injection most clinics give — if anything that biases toward finding a benefit that still did not appear. Surgery request is a patient-driven endpoint, but it is the outcome patients care about.
cards.source: Lizano-Díez X et al. Corticosteroid Injection for the Treatment of Morton's Neuroma: A Prospective, Double-Blinded, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Trial. Foot & ankle international. 2017. PMID: 28617064. cards.headline: Mahadevan 2016: pain fell in both arms (64→29 mm guided; 69→37 mm unguided) with no difference between them — failure 48% versus 55% at 12 months
cards.summary: Mahadevan 2016: pain fell in both arms (64→29 mm guided; 69→37 mm unguided) with no difference between them — failure 48% versus 55% at 12 months
cards.people: 45 feet in 36 patients (mean age 57.8 years) with ultrasound-confirmed Morton's neuroma, randomised to a single injection of 40 mg triamcinolone acetonide plus 2 ml 1% lignocaine given with ultrasound guidance (23 feet) or without it (22 feet), followed for 12 months.
cards.result: Mean pain VAS improved significantly in both groups: guided from 64 mm (SD 25) to 29 mm (SD 27); unguided from 69 mm (SD 23) to 37 mm (SD 25) — with no statistical difference between groups at any time point. Failure within 12 months: 11/23 (48%) guided versus 12/22 (55%) unguided (p=0.458). Short-term (3-month) differences in questionnaire index and satisfaction favoured guidance but did not reach significance (p=0.059 and p=0.066) and were not observed beyond three months.
cards.watchOut: This trial is half of the Cochrane guidance pool yet is itself null between groups — the pooled -15.01 mm depends heavily on the second, smaller trial. Both arms improving by ~30 mm also shows how much of an injection's effect is the procedure, the anaesthetic and time, not the steroid or the scanner.
cards.source: Mahadevan D et al. Corticosteroid injection for Morton's neuroma with or without ultrasound guidance: a randomised controlled trial. The bone & joint journal. 2016. PMID: 27037432. cards.headline: Synthesis: an injection ritual whose active ingredient is unproven, delivered better with a scanner, in a condition where half the patients still choose surgery
cards.summary: Synthesis: an injection ritual whose active ingredient is unproven, delivered better with a scanner, in a condition where half the patients still choose surgery
cards.people: Cochrane review of six trials (373 participants), the 41-patient placebo-controlled steroid trial, and the 45-foot guidance trial, all in imaging- or clinically-confirmed Morton's neuroma.
cards.result: Steroid versus anaesthetic alone: pain MD -6.31 mm (95% CI -14.23 to 1.61), function SMD -0.30 (CI crosses zero); surgery requested by 44% versus 53% in the blinded trial. Guidance versus no guidance: pooled pain MD -15.01 mm at 6 months (moderate certainty) against a null result in the larger of the two pooled trials; 12-month failure ~48-55% either way. Steroid harms: skin/fat-pad atrophy and hypopigmentation in roughly 3-4% each. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: The tension between the Cochrane guidance pool and the Mahadevan trial is declared on the face of this shelf rather than resolved — the coordinator may prefer the guidance claim downgraded. Tier C is not set: the shelf's claims rest on a Cochrane review plus two randomised trials, and its main claim about the steroid is a null.
cards.source: Synthesis of Matthews BG et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2024 (PMID: 38334217); Lizano-Díez X et al. Foot & ankle international. 2017 (PMID: 28617064); Mahadevan D et al. The bone & joint journal. 2016 (PMID: 27037432).
