shelves.title: Foot orthoses for plantar heel pain: a small medium-term edge over sham insoles (SMD -0.27) — custom-made no better than prefabricated, and the head-to-head with steroid injection never reached a difference patients would notice
shelves.question: In adults with plantar heel pain (plantar fasciitis), do foot orthoses reduce pain and improve function compared with sham orthoses, and how do they compare with corticosteroid injection?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Fasciitis, Plantar/therapy · Female · Foot Orthoses · Heel/physiopathology · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/prevention & control · Pain Management · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, delayed and possibly below what patients can feel. The systematic review (Whittaker GA et al., PMID: 28935689) pooled 19 trials with 1,660 participants: in the medium term (7-12 weeks) there was moderate-quality evidence that foot orthoses reduced pain more than sham orthoses (standardised mean difference -0.27, 95% CI -0.48 to -0.06), but no improvement in function; in the short term (0-6 weeks) and longer term (13-52 weeks) the evidence was very low quality and showed no pain or function benefit; customised and prefabricated orthoses did not differ at any time point. The head-to-head SOOTHE trial (Whittaker GA et al., PMID: 31130060; 103 participants) found corticosteroid injection ahead on foot pain at week 4 (adjusted mean difference 8.2 points, 95% CI 0.6 to 15.8) and orthoses ahead at week 12 (8.5 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 16.8) — but neither difference met the pre-calculated minimal important difference of 12.5 points. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a prefabricated arch-supporting insole is a reasonable, low-harm buy for heel pain at around two to three months — paying for custom moulding buys nothing the trials can detect.

cards.headline: Whittaker 2018: 19 trials — orthoses beat sham only in the 7-12 week window (SMD -0.27), function unmoved, custom equals prefabricated
cards.summary: Whittaker 2018: 19 trials — orthoses beat sham only in the 7-12 week window (SMD -0.27), function unmoved, custom equals prefabricated
cards.people: 19 randomised parallel-group trials, 1,660 adults with plantar heel pain, evaluating foot orthoses (customised or prefabricated) against sham orthoses or other comparators; pain and function categorised as short term (0-6 weeks), medium term (7-12 weeks) or longer term (13-52 weeks); literature searched to June 2017.
cards.result: Medium term: moderate-quality evidence that orthoses reduced pain more than sham orthoses (SMD -0.27, 95% CI -0.48 to -0.06), with no improvement in function. Short term and longer term: very low-quality evidence of no pain or function benefit. Customised versus prefabricated orthoses: no difference at any time point. The authors note it is uncertain whether the medium-term pain effect is a clinically important change.
cards.watchOut: An SMD of -0.27 is a small effect — roughly a quarter of a standard deviation — found in exactly one follow-up window, with null results on either side of it and null function throughout. That pattern is as consistent with a transient contextual effect as with a mechanical one.
cards.source: Whittaker GA et al. Foot orthoses for plantar heel pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British journal of sports medicine. 2018. PMID: 28935689. cards.headline: Whittaker 2019 (SOOTHE): injection wins at week 4 (+8.2 points), orthoses win at week 12 (+8.5) — neither reaches the 12.5-point difference patients were calculated to notice
cards.summary: Whittaker 2019 (SOOTHE): injection wins at week 4 (+8.2 points), orthoses win at week 12 (+8.5) — neither reaches the 12.5-point difference patients were calculated to notice
cards.people: 103 community-recruited participants aged 21-72 (63 women) with plantar heel pain, randomised in an assessor-blinded parallel trial to prefabricated arch-contouring foot orthoses or a single ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection; primary outcome was the foot pain subscale of the Foot Health Status Questionnaire at 4 and 12 weeks.
cards.result: Foot pain: corticosteroid injection was more effective at week 4 (adjusted mean difference 8.2 points, 95% CI 0.6 to 15.8) and foot orthoses were more effective at week 12 (adjusted mean difference 8.5 points, 95% CI 0.2 to 16.8). Both differences were statistically significant, but neither met the previously calculated minimal important difference of 12.5 points, so patients may not notice a clinically worthwhile difference between the interventions.
cards.watchOut: A single trial comparing two active treatments with no sham arm — it cannot say whether either beats doing nothing at 12 weeks, and its own authors undercut the headline by reporting the minimal-important-difference failure. It complements shelf #2728 (steroid injection versus placebo) rather than replacing it.
cards.source: Whittaker GA et al. Effectiveness of Foot Orthoses Versus Corticosteroid Injection for Plantar Heel Pain: The SOOTHE Randomized Clinical Trial. The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy. 2019. PMID: 31130060. cards.headline: Synthesis: cheap prefabricated insoles earn a cautious yes at 2-3 months; expensive custom orthotics and superiority claims do not
cards.summary: Synthesis: cheap prefabricated insoles earn a cautious yes at 2-3 months; expensive custom orthotics and superiority claims do not
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 19 trials (1,660 participants) and one 103-patient head-to-head trial against corticosteroid injection, in adults with plantar heel pain.
cards.result: Versus sham: pain SMD -0.27 (95% CI -0.48 to -0.06) at 7-12 weeks only; function unchanged; customised no better than prefabricated at any point. Versus injection: +8.2 points to injection at week 4, +8.5 points to orthoses at week 12, both below the 12.5-point minimal important difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), sized honestly as small.
cards.watchOut: Plantar heel pain usually improves with time, which inflates every uncontrolled impression of insoles; the sham-controlled medium-term signal is the only part of this record that survives that critique, and it is modest. Tier C is not set: a 19-trial meta-analysis carries the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Whittaker GA et al. British journal of sports medicine. 2018 (PMID: 28935689); Whittaker GA et al. The Journal of orthopaedic and sports physical therapy. 2019 (PMID: 31130060).

shelves.title: A night splint for thumb-base arthritis: nothing at 1 month — then pain 14.3 mm better and disability improved at 12 months, in the one randomised trial
shelves.question: In adults with osteoarthritis at the base of the thumb, does wearing a custom-made splint reduce pain and disability compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Disability Evaluation · Equipment Design · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Movement · Osteoarthritis/complications/physiopathology/therapy · Pain/etiology · Pain Management · Patient Compliance · Splints/adverse effects · Thumb/physiopathology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a slow-burn result from a single trial, so this shelf is Tier C. Rannou F et al. (PMID: 19451573) randomised 112 patients (101 women) with base-of-thumb osteoarthritis in two French tertiary hospitals to a custom-made neoprene splint worn at night or usual care. At 1 month there was no difference in pain change (adjusted mean change -10.1 versus -10.7; between-group difference 0.6, 95% CI -7.9 to 9.1; p=0.89). At 12 months the splint group had improved more on pain (adjusted mean change -22.2 versus -7.9; between-group difference -14.3, 95% CI -23.4 to -5.2; p=0.002), on the Cochin Hand Function Scale (between-group difference -6.3, 95% CI -10.9 to -1.7; p=0.008) and on patient-perceived disability (-13.1, 95% CI -21.8 to -4.4; p=0.003). Adherence was high — 86% of the splint group wore it more than five nights a week at 12 months — and no adverse effects were observed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a night splint is cheap and harmless, but patients should be told the trial found nothing at one month — the benefit, if real, took a year of nightly wear.

cards.headline: Rannou 2009: pain difference 0.6 mm at 1 month (p=0.89) becomes -14.3 mm at 12 months (p=0.002) — disability also better on both measures
cards.summary: Rannou 2009: pain difference 0.6 mm at 1 month (p=0.89) becomes -14.3 mm at 12 months (p=0.002) — disability also better on both measures
cards.people: 112 patients (101 women) with base-of-thumb osteoarthritis at two French tertiary care hospitals, randomised to a custom-made neoprene splint (57) or usual care (55), worn at night; primary outcome was change in pain (VAS 0-100 mm) at 1 month, with pain and disability (Cochin Hand Function Scale, 0-90; patient-perceived disability VAS) also assessed at 12 months. Registry ID: NCT00350896. Patients, providers and assessors were not blinded, and outcomes were self-reported.
cards.result: At 1 month: adjusted mean pain change -10.1 (splint) versus -10.7 (control); between-group difference 0.6 (95% CI -7.9 to 9.1; p=0.89). At 12 months: pain change -22.2 versus -7.9 (difference -14.3, 95% CI -23.4 to -5.2; p=0.002); Cochin score change -1.9 versus +4.3 (difference -6.3, 95% CI -10.9 to -1.7; p=0.008); patient-perceived disability -11.6 versus +1.5 (difference -13.1, 95% CI -21.8 to -4.4; p=0.003). At 12 months 86% of the splint group had worn it more than five nights a week; no adverse effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: The trial's own primary endpoint (pain at 1 month) was null — the positive results are 12-month secondary outcomes in an unblinded trial with self-reported measures, the classic setup for expectation drift. One trial, 112 patients, never independently replicated: hence Tier C and no higher stamp.
cards.source: Rannou F et al. Splint for base-of-thumb osteoarthritis: a randomized trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2009. PMID: 19451573. Registry ID: NCT00350896. cards.headline: Synthesis: one unblinded trial, a failed primary endpoint, and a coherent late benefit — enough for a cautious yes to a harmless device, not for a promise
cards.summary: Synthesis: one unblinded trial, a failed primary endpoint, and a coherent late benefit — enough for a cautious yes to a harmless device, not for a promise
cards.people: One multicentre randomised trial, 112 patients with base-of-thumb osteoarthritis, custom neoprene night splint versus usual care, followed 12 months.
cards.result: Pain: difference 0.6 mm at 1 month (p=0.89); -14.3 mm at 12 months (95% CI -23.4 to -5.2; p=0.002). Disability at 12 months: Cochin difference -6.3 points (p=0.008), perceived disability -13.1 mm (p=0.003). Adherence 86% at five-plus nights a week; adverse effects none. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C because a single trial carries it.
cards.watchOut: Guidelines recommended this splint before any trial existed; the trial now supporting it is unblinded with a null primary endpoint, so the honest counselling is 'worth trying, give it months, it costs little and harms nothing in the record'. A sham-splint trial would settle it and has never been done.

shelves.title: Muscle rubs (salicylate rubefacients): the older small trials said they work (acute NNT 3.2) — the larger, more recent trials showed no effect, and Cochrane will not support their use
shelves.question: In adults with acute or chronic musculoskeletal pain, do salicylate-containing rubefacient creams and gels (muscle rubs) relieve pain compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Topical · Adult · Chronic Disease · Humans · Irritants/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Musculoskeletal Pain/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Salicylates/administration & dosage/adverse effects
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a fading signal that lives in the oldest trials. The Cochrane review (Derry S et al., PMID: 25425092) found, for clinical success at seven days in acute conditions (mostly sprains, strains and acute low back pain), a relative risk of 1.9 (95% CI 1.5 to 2.5) and a number needed to treat of 3.2 (95% CI 2.4 to 4.9) for salicylate rubefacients versus placebo — but rated this very low quality evidence and not robust; in chronic conditions (mostly osteoarthritis, bursitis and chronic back pain) the relative risk was 1.6 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.0) with an NNT of 6.2 (95% CI 4.0 to 13), also very low quality. The reviewers state plainly that in both categories any evidence of efficacy came from the older, smaller studies, while the larger, more recent studies showed no effect, and conclude the evidence does not support the use of topical salicylate rubefacients for acute injuries or chronic conditions. The overview of all topical analgesics (Derry S et al., PMID: 28497473; 13 Cochrane reviews, 206 studies, around 30,700 participants) likewise graded salicylate rubefacient evidence low or very low quality — in sharp contrast to topical diclofenac gel in acute pain (78% achieving at least 50% relief versus 20% on placebo; NNT 1.8, 95% CI 1.5 to 2.1), which sits on shelf #577's territory. Adverse events were more common with salicylate than placebo but concentrated in a few studies, and local events were nearly all in one study combining salicylate with another irritant. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): the rub probably does something for a few days in acute aches — the warmth and the rubbing are unmeasured co-treatments — but anyone choosing a rub over a proven topical NSAID gel is choosing the weaker record.

cards.headline: Derry 2014 (Cochrane): acute RR 1.9 (NNT 3.2), chronic RR 1.6 (NNT 6.2) — 'evidence does not support the use', because the big recent trials are null
cards.summary: Derry 2014 (Cochrane): acute RR 1.9 (NNT 3.2), chronic RR 1.6 (NNT 6.2) — 'evidence does not support the use', because the big recent trials are null
cards.people: Randomised double-blind placebo- or active-controlled trials of topical salicylate rubefacients in adults with musculoskeletal pain: six placebo-controlled (560 participants) and one active-controlled (137) in acute pain; seven placebo-controlled (489) and three active-controlled (182) in chronic pain. All studies were potentially at risk of bias, and formulations mixed salicylates with various other potentially active ingredients.
cards.result: Primary outcome, clinical success at seven days in acute conditions: RR 1.9 (95% CI 1.5 to 2.5), NNT 3.2 (95% CI 2.4 to 4.9) versus placebo (fixed-effect; random-effects RR 2.7, 95% CI 1.05 to 7.0) — judged not robust, very low quality evidence. In chronic conditions: RR 1.6 (95% CI 1.2 to 2.0), NNT 6.2 (95% CI 4.0 to 13), very low quality. In both categories, efficacy signals came from older, smaller studies while larger, more recent studies showed no effect. Adverse events were more common than placebo overall but driven by one or two studies; removing them abolished the difference. Data against active controls were insufficient for conclusions.
cards.watchOut: Rubefacients cannot be properly blinded — the treated skin burns and smells — so expectation effects are built into every trial, and even with that advantage the modern trials are null. Products also differ (salicylate plus menthol, camphor or other irritants in varying mixes), so 'muscle rub' is a shelf category, not one drug.
cards.source: Derry S et al. Salicylate-containing rubefacients for acute and chronic musculoskeletal pain in adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 25425092. cards.headline: Derry 2017 (overview): across 206 topical-analgesic studies, rubefacients sit in the low/very-low tier — while diclofenac gel's acute-pain NNT is 1.8 on moderate-to-high quality evidence
cards.summary: Derry 2017 (overview): across 206 topical-analgesic studies, rubefacients sit in the low/very-low tier — while diclofenac gel's acute-pain NNT is 1.8 on moderate-to-high quality evidence
cards.people: 13 Cochrane reviews covering 206 studies and around 30,700 participants, assessing topical analgesics (NSAID gels, salicylate rubefacients, capsaicin, lidocaine) for acute and chronic pain in adults; primary outcome was at least 50% participant-reported pain relief, with efficacy required from at least 200 participants in at least two studies.
cards.result: For salicylate rubefacients the overview judged evidence of efficacy low or very low quality — limited evidence, potentially subject to publication bias, existed for chronic pain, and evidence in acute pain was very low quality with sparse data. By contrast, in acute musculoskeletal pain diclofenac Emulgel achieved at least 50% relief in 78% versus 20% on placebo (2 studies, 314 participants; NNT 1.8, 95% CI 1.5 to 2.1) on moderate- or high-quality evidence, and ketoprofen gel in 72% versus 33% (NNT 2.5). In chronic pain, lack-of-efficacy withdrawals were lower with topical salicylate than placebo (2% versus 7%; NNTp 21, very low-quality evidence), and adverse-event withdrawals were higher (5% versus 1%; NNH 26, very low-quality evidence).
cards.watchOut: An overview inherits every weakness of the reviews beneath it; its value here is comparative — it places rubs in context against the topical NSAID gels a shopper sees on the same shelf, using the same yardstick (at least 50% relief) for both.
cards.source: Derry S et al. Topical analgesics for acute and chronic pain in adults - an overview of Cochrane Reviews. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 28497473. cards.headline: Synthesis: a warm rub feels like treatment and may add a little for acute aches — but the rigorous end of its own literature says no
cards.summary: Synthesis: a warm rub feels like treatment and may add a little for acute aches — but the rigorous end of its own literature says no
cards.people: Cochrane review of salicylate rubefacient trials (about 1,300 participants across acute and chronic comparisons) and a 13-review overview of all topical analgesics (206 studies, around 30,700 participants).
cards.result: Acute: RR 1.9, NNT 3.2 — very low quality, not robust, older small trials only. Chronic: RR 1.6, NNT 6.2 — very low quality. Larger recent trials: no effect in either category. Harms: mostly local, concentrated in few studies. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), the weakest stamp on this wave, reflecting a benefit claim the reviewers themselves decline to support.
cards.watchOut: The stamp is MAYBE rather than a null because the pooled acute estimate is statistically positive and the null modern trials are few; the coordinator may prefer POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference). Either way, the practical advice is identical: if a topical is wanted, the NSAID gels have the stronger record (shelf #577). Tier C is not set: the shelf rests on Cochrane syntheses, not a single trial.

shelves.title: Dextrose prolotherapy for knee osteoarthritis: WOMAC improvement beat blinded saline in both randomised trials (change 15.3 vs 7.6 points at a year; pain difference −10.34 points)
shelves.question: In adults with painful knee osteoarthritis, do dextrose prolotherapy injections improve pain, function and stiffness compared with blinded saline injections?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Adult · Arthralgia/drug therapy · Female · Glucose/administration & dosage · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Knee Joint/drug effects · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Range of Motion, Articular/drug effects · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small blinded trials from different continents point the same way. In the US three-arm trial (Rabago D et al., PMID: 23690322), composite WOMAC scores at 52 weeks improved by 15.3 ± 3.5 points on dextrose prolotherapy versus 7.6 ± 3.4 on blinded saline and 8.2 ± 3.3 on at-home exercise (P<.05), exceeding the WOMAC minimal clinically important difference, with high satisfaction and no adverse events. In the Hong Kong trial (Sit RWS et al., PMID: 32393559), the WOMAC pain difference-in-difference at 52 weeks favoured intra-articular hypertonic dextrose by −10.34 points (95% CI −19.20 to −1.49; P=0.022), with parallel gains in function (−9.55), composite score (−9.65) and visual-analogue pain (−10.98), and no adverse events reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prolotherapy probably improves knee osteoarthritis symptoms beyond a saline injection ritual — by amounts patients can feel — but the trials are small, single-centre and unblinded at the level of the treating clinician in one case, so the stamp stays at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Rabago 2013: WOMAC change at 52 weeks 15.3 (prolotherapy) vs 7.6 (saline) vs 8.2 (exercise) points, P<.05 — beyond the minimal clinically important difference
cards.summary: Rabago 2013: WOMAC change at 52 weeks 15.3 (prolotherapy) vs 7.6 (saline) vs 8.2 (exercise) points, P<.05 — beyond the minimal clinically important difference
cards.people: 90 adults with at least 3 months of painful knee osteoarthritis, randomised to dextrose prolotherapy, blinded saline injections, or at-home exercise; injections (extra- and intra-articular) at weeks 1, 5 and 9 with optional sessions at weeks 13 and 17; injector, assessor and injection-group participants were blinded; primary outcome was the composite WOMAC score (100 points) at 52 weeks.
cards.result: All groups improved from baseline (P<.01). Adjusted for sex, age and body mass index, WOMAC scores improved more with prolotherapy than with saline or exercise at 52 weeks (score change 15.3 ± 3.5 vs 7.6 ± 3.4 and 8.2 ± 3.3 points; P<.05), exceeding the WOMAC-based minimal clinically important difference; individual knee pain scores also improved more (P=.05). Satisfaction with prolotherapy was high and there were no adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Ninety patients, one US centre, and a composite of extra- plus intra-articular injections with optional extra sessions — the 'dose' is a package, and the exercise arm was unblinded by design; a 7–8 point separation from a saline-injection control is encouraging but saline injection itself is an active-feeling ritual with its own contextual effect.
cards.source: Rabago D et al. Dextrose prolotherapy for knee osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial. Annals of Family Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23690322. Registry ID: NCT00085722. cards.headline: Sit 2020: WOMAC pain difference −10.34 points (95% CI −19.20 to −1.49, P=0.022) for intra-articular dextrose versus saline at 52 weeks
cards.summary: Sit 2020: WOMAC pain difference −10.34 points (95% CI −19.20 to −1.49, P=0.022) for intra-articular dextrose versus saline at 52 weeks
cards.people: 76 patients with knee osteoarthritis at a Hong Kong university primary-care clinic, randomised 1:1 to intra-articular hypertonic dextrose prolotherapy or normal saline injections at weeks 0, 4, 8 and 16, with WOMAC, physical-function tests, pain visual-analogue scale and EuroQol-5D assessed to 52 weeks by linear mixed models.
cards.result: At 52 weeks the difference-in-difference estimates favoured dextrose for WOMAC pain (−10.34 points; 95% CI −19.20 to −1.49; P=0.022), WOMAC function (−9.55; −17.72 to −1.39; P=0.022), WOMAC composite (−9.65; −17.77 to −1.53; P=0.020) and pain visual-analogue score (−10.98; −21.36 to −0.61; P=0.038). Adherence and satisfaction were high and no adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind (patients blinded; injector necessarily aware), 76 patients, and wide intervals — the pain interval runs from a trivial −1.5 to a large −19.2 points; the record also prints an internally inconsistent EuroQol interval, so this shelf relies on its WOMAC outcomes only.
cards.source: Sit RWS et al. Efficacy of Intra-Articular Hypertonic Dextrose (Prolotherapy) for Knee Osteoarthritis: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Annals of Family Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32393559. cards.headline: Synthesis: two blinded saline-controlled trials, one direction — a felt benefit of roughly 8–10 WOMAC points at one year
cards.summary: Synthesis: two blinded saline-controlled trials, one direction — a felt benefit of roughly 8–10 WOMAC points at one year
cards.people: Two randomised blinded trials of dextrose prolotherapy versus saline injection in knee osteoarthritis: 90 US adults (Rabago 2013, combined extra-/intra-articular protocol) and 76 Hong Kong patients (Sit 2020, intra-articular protocol), each followed to 52 weeks.
cards.result: WOMAC composite change 15.3 versus 7.6 points (Rabago); WOMAC pain difference −10.34 points (Sit), with function and composite scores moving together in both trials and no adverse events reported in either. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No trial compares prolotherapy with corticosteroid or hyaluronic-acid injection, exercise therapy delivered in person, or weight loss — so 'better than saline' is the whole claim; structural (cartilage) effects were not measured. Tier C is not set: two concordant randomised blinded trials carry the claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rabago D et al. Annals of Family Medicine. 2013 (PMID: 23690322); Sit RWS et al. Annals of Family Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32393559).

shelves.title: Calf stretching for nocturnal leg cramps: one trial found 1.2 fewer cramps a night, the other — in quinine users — found nothing; the record splits by who was studied
shelves.question: In older adults with nocturnal leg cramps, do nightly calf and hamstring stretching exercises before sleep reduce cramp frequency and severity?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Stretching Exercises/methods · Physical Therapy Modalities · Severity of Illness Index · Sleep-Wake Transition Disorders/physiopathology/prevention & control/rehabilitation · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two randomised trials disagree, and their populations explain the split better than their methods do. In untreated older adults with nocturnal cramps (Hallegraeff JM et al., PMID: 22341378), six weeks of nightly calf and hamstring stretching cut cramp frequency by 1.2 more cramps per night than control (95% CI 0.6 to 1.8) and severity by 1.3 cm more on a 10-cm scale (0.9 to 1.7). In patients already prescribed quinine for night cramps (Coppin RJ et al., PMID: 15808033), a factorial trial found no significant effect of stretching advice on cramp numbers in the previous 4 weeks at 12 weeks (difference 1.95, 95% CI −3.01 to 6.90) or on symptom burden — while advice to stop quinine did let 26.5% more patients (13.3% to 39.7%) stay off quinine (odds ratio 3.32, 1.37–8.06) without major problems. PROPOSED SPLIT: stretching is a reasonable, harmless first try for untreated cramps on one positive trial; in established quinine users the trial evidence says it adds nothing measurable — the useful intervention there was a supervised trial off quinine.

cards.headline: Hallegraeff 2012: cramp frequency fell 1.2 more per night (95% CI 0.6–1.8) and severity 1.3 cm more (0.9–1.7) with nightly stretching at 6 weeks
cards.summary: Hallegraeff 2012: cramp frequency fell 1.2 more per night (95% CI 0.6–1.8) and severity 1.3 cm more (0.9–1.7) with nightly stretching at 6 weeks
cards.people: 80 adults aged over 55 years with nocturnal leg cramps who were not being treated with quinine, randomised (concealed allocation, intention-to-treat analysis) to nightly calf and hamstring stretching immediately before sleep for 6 weeks or to no specific stretching; cramp frequency and pain severity (10-cm visual analogue scale) were recorded in daily diaries; all participants completed the study.
cards.result: At 6 weeks, cramp frequency had decreased significantly more in the stretching group (mean difference 1.2 cramps per night; 95% CI 0.6 to 1.8), as had cramp severity (mean difference 1.3 cm; 95% CI 0.9 to 1.7 on the 10-cm scale).
cards.watchOut: An unblindable exercise intervention with self-recorded diary outcomes in 80 volunteers — expectation effects point in the same direction as the result — and the control group received no attention-matched activity; six weeks says nothing about persistence once stretching stops.
cards.source: Hallegraeff JM et al. Stretching before sleep reduces the frequency and severity of nocturnal leg cramps in older adults: a randomised trial. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2012. PMID: 22341378. Registry ID: NCT01421628. cards.headline: Coppin 2005: stretching advice changed nothing at 12 weeks (cramp difference 1.95, 95% CI −3.01 to 6.90) — but 26.5% more patients stayed off quinine after advice to stop (OR 3.32)
cards.summary: Coppin 2005: stretching advice changed nothing at 12 weeks (cramp difference 1.95, 95% CI −3.01 to 6.90) — but 26.5% more patients stayed off quinine after advice to stop (OR 3.32)
cards.people: 191 patients prescribed quinine for night cramps in 28 general practices in southern England, randomised in a 2×2 factorial design to advice or no advice on calf-stretching exercises, crossed with advice or no advice to stop quinine; outcomes (cramp frequency, symptom burden, quinine use) at 12 weeks were documented in 181 patients (95%).
cards.result: At 12 weeks there was no significant difference in the number of cramps in the previous 4 weeks for the exercise factor (1.95; 95% CI −3.01 to 6.90) or the quinine-cessation factor (3.45; −1.52 to 8.41), and no effect on symptom burden or cramp severity. However, 26.5% more patients advised to stop quinine reported taking no quinine in the previous week (95% CI 13.3% to 39.7%; odds ratio 3.32, 1.37–8.06), while stretching advice had no effect on quinine use (OR 0.73, 0.27–1.98).
cards.watchOut: Advice-to-stretch is a weaker intervention than supervised nightly stretching, adherence was self-reported, and these were prevalent quinine users whose cramps may be a selected, treatment-experienced phenotype — the null may be about the population or the delivery, not about stretching itself; the trial cannot distinguish those readings.
cards.source: Coppin RJ et al. Managing nocturnal leg cramps--calf-stretching exercises and cessation of quinine treatment: a factorial randomised controlled trial. British Journal of General Practice. 2005. PMID: 15808033. cards.headline: Synthesis: one positive trial in the untreated, one null trial in quinine users — prescribe the trial of stretching, and separately trial stopping quinine
cards.summary: Synthesis: one positive trial in the untreated, one null trial in quinine users — prescribe the trial of stretching, and separately trial stopping quinine
cards.people: Two randomised trials in older adults with nocturnal leg cramps: nightly stretching versus no stretching in 80 quinine-untreated adults (Hallegraeff 2012) and a 191-patient factorial trial of stretching advice and quinine cessation in established quinine users (Coppin 2005).
cards.result: Frequency: −1.2 cramps/night (0.6 to 1.8) favouring stretching in the untreated; no significant difference (1.95; −3.01 to 6.90) in quinine users. Severity: −1.3 cm favouring stretching in the untreated; null in quinine users. Quinine cessation: 26.5% more patients off quinine after advice to stop (OR 3.32). PROPOSED SPLIT, as in the balance above.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was blinded and both rely on self-report; the honest clinical sequence the pair supports is 'try stretching first if untreated; if already on quinine, a supervised stop is the evidence-backed experiment'. Tier C is not set: the split rests on two randomised trials read together.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hallegraeff JM et al. Journal of Physiotherapy. 2012 (PMID: 22341378); Coppin RJ et al. British Journal of General Practice. 2005 (PMID: 15808033).

shelves.title: Lumbar traction for low back pain: the sham-controlled trial found nothing at 12 weeks or 6 months, and the Cochrane review of 32 trials (2,762 people) found little or no difference on pain, function or return to work
shelves.question: In adults with low back pain, with or without sciatica, does lumbar traction — alone or added to physiotherapy — reduce pain and disability compared with sham traction, no treatment or other treatments?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain/therapy · Chronic Pain/therapy · Humans · Low Back Pain/complications/therapy · Pain Measurement · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sciatica/complications/therapy · Traction/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — this is one of the more thoroughly negative records in physical therapy. The Cochrane review (Wegner I et al., PMID: 23959683) pooled 32 randomised trials with 2,762 participants and found low- to moderate-quality evidence that traction makes little or no difference to pain intensity, functional status, global improvement or return to work versus placebo, sham traction or no treatment — in mixed back-pain populations, in back pain with sciatica, and for chronic pain without sciatica versus sham — with adverse effects (increased pain, aggravated neurological signs, subsequent surgery) reported in seven studies. The methodologically strongest single trial (Beurskens AJ et al., PMID: 9431610) compared high-dose motorised traction with sham low-dose traction in 151 patients, with patients and assessors blinded, and found no significant differences on any outcome at 12 weeks or 6 months — every 95% confidence interval included zero. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): traction, alone or added to physiotherapy, should not be sold as pain relief for low back pain on this record.

cards.headline: Wegner 2013 (Cochrane): 32 trials, 2,762 participants — little or no difference on pain, function, global improvement or return to work in every population and comparison
cards.summary: Wegner 2013 (Cochrane): 32 trials, 2,762 participants — little or no difference on pain, function, global improvement or return to work in every population and comparison
cards.people: 32 randomised trials (2,762 participants) of manual or machine-delivered traction for acute, subacute or chronic non-specific low back pain with or without sciatica, versus placebo, sham traction, reference treatments or no treatment, alone or combined with physiotherapy; 16 trials (57% of participants) were at low risk of bias; data were insufficient for statistical pooling, so effects were summarised descriptively by evidence quality.
cards.result: For mixed symptom patterns there was low- to moderate-quality evidence that traction may make little or no difference in pain intensity, functional status, global improvement or return to work versus placebo, sham or no treatment, and similarly when traction was added to physiotherapy or compared with other treatments. For low back pain with sciatica, low- to moderate-quality evidence indicated traction probably has no impact on pain, function or global improvement. For chronic pain without sciatica, moderate-quality evidence indicated traction probably makes little or no difference in pain versus sham. Adverse effects were reported in seven of 32 studies, including increased pain, aggravation of neurological signs and subsequent surgery; four studies reported none.
cards.watchOut: A descriptive (non-pooled) synthesis of mostly small, older trials with moderate-to-high risk of bias in many — the review's own caution is that shown effects are small and not clinically relevant, which supports 'no meaningful benefit' rather than a precise zero; specific traction devices or protocols invented after 2012 are outside this record.
cards.source: Wegner I et al. Traction for low-back pain with or without sciatica. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013. PMID: 23959683. cards.headline: Beurskens 1997: high-dose versus sham traction in 151 patients — no significant difference on any outcome at 12 weeks or 6 months; all confidence intervals included zero
cards.summary: Beurskens 1997: high-dose versus sham traction in 151 patients — no significant difference on any outcome at 12 weeks or 6 months; all confidence intervals included zero
cards.people: 151 patients with at least 6 weeks of non-specific low back pain, randomised to high-dose motorised continuous traction or sham (low-dose) traction delivered through a specially designed brace that tightened in the back so it felt like real traction; patients and the outcome assessor were blinded; outcomes included global perceived effect, main complaints, functional status, pain, range of motion, work absence and medical treatment, with very low loss to follow-up.
cards.result: Intention-to-treat analyses at 12 weeks and 6 months showed no statistically significant differences between high-dose and sham traction on any outcome measure — all 95% confidence intervals included zero — and other analyses showed the same results. The authors conclude the trial did not support the claim that traction is efficacious for low back pain.
cards.watchOut: One trial of one motorised protocol in subacute-to-chronic non-specific pain: it cannot exclude benefits of different forces, positions or patient subgroups (for example, acute radicular pain), which is why the shelf's LIKELY null leans on the 32-trial review for breadth and on this trial for rigour.
cards.source: Beurskens AJ et al. Efficacy of traction for nonspecific low back pain. 12-week and 6-month results of a randomized clinical trial. Spine. 1997. PMID: 9431610. cards.headline: Synthesis: breadth and rigour agree — no clinically relevant benefit, with occasional harm reports
cards.summary: Synthesis: breadth and rigour agree — no clinically relevant benefit, with occasional harm reports
cards.people: A Cochrane review of 32 randomised trials (2,762 participants; Wegner 2013) and the largest blinded sham-controlled trial within that literature (151 patients; Beurskens 1997).
cards.result: Pain, function, global improvement and return to work: little or no difference for traction versus sham, placebo, no treatment, other treatments, or physiotherapy alone, across acute-to-chronic pain with and without sciatica. Adverse effects (increased pain, worse neurology, later surgery) reported in 7 of 32 trials. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: The evidence is old (search to 2012) and heterogeneous in technique; the claim is about traction as tested — largely motorised or manual lumbar traction in unselected back pain — not about every manual-therapy manoeuvre that includes a traction component. Tier C is not set: the null rests on a full Cochrane review plus a concordant blinded trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wegner I et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23959683); Beurskens AJ et al. Spine. 1997 (PMID: 9431610).

shelves.title: Soy isoflavones do not preserve bone density after menopause: three placebo-controlled trials (202, 131 and 431 women) and a 1,433-woman meta-analysis all null
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with low bone density, do soy isoflavones reduce bone loss compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Bone Density/drug effects · Cognition/drug effects · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Isoflavones/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Lipids/blood · Middle Aged · Milk Proteins/pharmacology · Postmenopause/drug effects · Soybean Proteins/pharmacology/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — three concordant null trials plus a null pooling. Kreijkamp-Kaspers 2004 (PMID: 15238592) gave 202 postmenopausal women soy protein containing 99 mg isoflavones daily or milk protein for 12 months: bone mineral density of hip and lumbar spine did not differ significantly. Kenny 2009 (PMID: 19474141), in 131 older women randomised across soy protein and/or isoflavone tablets (105 mg aglycone equivalents) for 1 year, found no significant differences in BMD between groups. Tai 2012 (PMID: 21901480), the largest and longest, gave 431 women 300 mg/day isoflavones or placebo for 2 years: BMD differences were not significant at lumbar spine (p = 0.42) or total femur (p = 0.39), with bone loss proceeding in both groups. Ricci 2010 (PMID: 20673147) pooled 12 studies and 1,433 women: the lumbar-spine BMD difference was 9.86 mg/cm² (95% CI −2.64 to 22.36), not statistically significant. None of the records names a branded product or company. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): soy isoflavone mixtures, at doses up to 300 mg/day for up to 2 years, did not slow postmenopausal bone loss versus placebo.

cards.headline: Kreijkamp-Kaspers 2004 (JAMA): 99 mg isoflavones in soy protein for a year — hip and spine bone density no different from milk protein
cards.summary: Kreijkamp-Kaspers 2004 (JAMA): 99 mg isoflavones in soy protein for a year — hip and spine bone density no different from milk protein
cards.people: 202 healthy postmenopausal women aged 60 to 75 years from a population-based sample in the Netherlands, randomised to 25.6 g soy protein containing 99 mg isoflavones (52 mg genistein, 41 mg daidzein, 6 mg glycitein) or total milk protein powder daily for 12 months; 175 women were in the modified intention-to-treat analysis. No branded product or company is named in the record.
cards.result: Cognitive function, bone mineral density (hip and lumbar spine by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry), and plasma lipids did not differ significantly between the groups after a year, despite good adherence (median plasma genistein 615.1 nmol/L on soy versus 17.2 nmol/L on placebo).
cards.watchOut: Participants were healthy women aged 60–75, not women selected for low bone density or osteoporosis, and 12 months is short for a bone-density endpoint — the two later trials below cover longer exposure and women with bone loss.
cards.source: Kreijkamp-Kaspers S et al. Effect of soy protein containing isoflavones on cognitive function, bone mineral density, and plasma lipids in postmenopausal women: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2004. PMID: 15238592. cards.headline: Kenny 2009: soy protein, isoflavone tablets (105 mg), both, or neither for a year in 131 older women — no BMD difference in any arm
cards.summary: Kenny 2009: soy protein, isoflavone tablets (105 mg), both, or neither for a year in 131 older women — no BMD difference in any arm
cards.people: 131 healthy ambulatory women aged over 60 years randomised to one of four groups — soy protein (18 g) plus isoflavone tablets (105 mg isoflavone aglycone equivalents), soy protein plus placebo tablets, control protein plus isoflavone tablets, or control protein plus placebo tablets — for 1 year; 97 women completed the trial. No branded product or company is named in the record.
cards.result: No significant differences in bone mineral density were observed between groups from baseline to 1 year, and no difference in BMD change between equol producers and non-producers. The authors concluded soy protein and isoflavones, alone or together, should not be considered effective interventions for preserving skeletal health in older women.
cards.watchOut: Only 97 of 131 randomised women completed, and the four-arm split leaves each comparison small; its value is as a concordant null alongside the larger trials, not as a standalone answer.
cards.source: Kenny AM et al. Soy proteins and isoflavones affect bone mineral density in older women: a randomized controlled trial. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2009. PMID: 19474141. cards.headline: Tai 2012: 300 mg/day isoflavones for 2 years in 431 women with bone loss — spine p = 0.42, femur p = 0.39; bone loss continued in both groups
cards.summary: Tai 2012: 300 mg/day isoflavones for 2 years in 431 women with bone loss — spine p = 0.42, femur p = 0.39; bone loss continued in both groups
cards.people: 431 postmenopausal Taiwanese women aged 45–65 years with bone loss, randomised to 300 mg/day isoflavones (aglycone equivalents: 172.5 mg genistein plus 127.5 mg daidzein) or placebo for 2 years, all also receiving 600 mg calcium and 125 IU vitamin D3 daily; 200 of 217 (isoflavone) and 199 of 214 (placebo) completed. No branded product or company is named in the record.
cards.result: Differences in mean percentage change in bone mineral density were not statistically significant between isoflavone and placebo groups (lumbar spine, p = 0.42; total femur, p = 0.39), and a significant time trend of bone loss was observed at both sites (p < 0.001). Bone-marker differences were also not significant, despite markedly elevated serum isoflavone metabolite concentrations on treatment (p < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: This is the highest dose and longest duration in the set, in the population closest to the question (women with bone loss) — its null is the strongest single piece of evidence here; all women also received calcium and vitamin D, so the comparison is isoflavones added to standard supplementation.
cards.source: Tai TY et al. The effect of soy isoflavone on bone mineral density in postmenopausal Taiwanese women with bone loss: a 2-year randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study. cards.headline: Ricci 2010 meta-analysis: 12 studies, 1,433 women — lumbar-spine difference 9.86 mg/cm² (95% CI −2.64 to 22.36), not significant; isoflavone mixtures alone 0.73 (−2.79 to 4.25)
cards.summary: Ricci 2010 meta-analysis: 12 studies, 1,433 women — lumbar-spine difference 9.86 mg/cm² (95% CI −2.64 to 22.36), not significant; isoflavone mixtures alone 0.73 (−2.79 to 4.25)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Ricci 2010)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised placebo-controlled trials of phytoestrogens in perimenopausal and postmenopausal Western women (1990–2010); lumbar-spine BMD data from 12 studies including 1,433 subjects.
cards.result: The effect of phytoestrogens on lumbar-spine BMD was not statistically significant (mean difference 9.86 mg/cm², 95% CI −2.64 to 22.36) under a random-effects model. Excluding the single isolated-genistein study, analyses of isoflavone mixtures showed no bone-sparing effect (0.73, 95% CI −2.79 to 4.25), and no effect emerged with higher dose or longer duration.
cards.watchOut: The pooled point estimate leans on one isolated-genistein study the reviewers singled out as inconsistent with the mixture trials; the mixture-only estimate — the products women actually buy — is essentially zero.
cards.source: Ricci E et al. Soy isoflavones and bone mineral density in perimenopausal and postmenopausal Western women: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Women's Health. 2010. PMID: 20673147. cards.headline: Synthesis: doses from 99 to 300 mg/day, durations to 2 years, 764 women in the three trials plus 1,433 pooled — no significant bone-density benefit anywhere
cards.summary: Synthesis: doses from 99 to 300 mg/day, durations to 2 years, 764 women in the three trials plus 1,433 pooled — no significant bone-density benefit anywhere
cards.people: Three randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 764 postmenopausal women (Netherlands, United States, Taiwan) and one meta-analysis of 12 studies and 1,433 women.
cards.result: Hip and spine BMD: no significant difference (Kreijkamp-Kaspers 2004). Four-arm BMD comparison: no significant differences (Kenny 2009). Two-year high-dose trial: spine p = 0.42, femur p = 0.39 (Tai 2012). Pooled lumbar-spine difference: 9.86 mg/cm² (95% CI −2.64 to 22.36), not significant; mixtures alone 0.73 (−2.79 to 4.25) (Ricci 2010). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Bone density is a surrogate for fracture, and no trial here was powered for fractures — but a treatment that does not move the surrogate at any tested dose has no evidentiary path to a fracture claim. Tier C per this band's rule for every shelf.

shelves.title: PRP versus hyaluronic acid for knee osteoarthritis: a 34-trial meta-analysis favours PRP at 6–12 months on low-quality evidence — the two double-blind head-to-head trials found no difference at all
shelves.question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, do platelet-rich plasma injections reduce pain compared with hyaluronic acid injections?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Osteoarthritis, Knee/drug therapy · Platelet-Rich Plasma · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the pooled literature and the best individual trials point in different directions. A meta-analysis of 34 randomised trials (1,403 PRP knees, 1,426 control knees) found WOMAC scores favoured PRP over hyaluronic acid at 6 and 12 months (P<0.001 for both), while rating the quality of evidence low and noting superiority did not reach the minimal clinically important difference for all outcomes (Filardo 2021, PMID: 32551947). But the double-blind head-to-head trials do not reproduce it: Wang 2022 (PMID: 36013495, n=110, single-injection PRP versus crosslinked HA) found no significant between-group difference in WOMAC change at 1, 3 or 6 months, and Fossati 2024 (PMID: 39367905, n=174, three injections of PRP, HA, or both) found no significant differences among the groups on any outcome at 6 or 12 months (WOMAC p=0.45 and p=0.64). Note the separate question — PRP versus saline placebo — is homed at live shelf #457, where blinded trials were null; this shelf asks only whether PRP beats the active comparator HA. PROPOSED SPLIT: pooled small trials say yes at a year, the rigorous double-blind trials say no difference — paying a PRP premium over HA is not supported by the best evidence.

cards.headline: Filardo 2021: WOMAC favoured PRP over HA at 6 and 12 months (P<0.001) across 34 trials — with low quality of evidence and sub-MCID effects on some outcomes
cards.summary: Filardo 2021: WOMAC favoured PRP over HA at 6 and 12 months (P<0.001) across 34 trials — with low quality of evidence and sub-MCID effects on some outcomes
cards.people: 34 randomised trials of PRP injections for knee osteoarthritis, 1,403 knees in PRP groups and 1,426 in control groups (placebo, hyaluronic acid, steroids and other injectables), searched to January 2020; risk of bias per Cochrane guidelines, evidence graded with GRADE.
cards.result: WOMAC score favoured PRP with a statistically and clinically significant difference versus placebo at 12 months (P=0.02) and versus hyaluronic acid at 6 months (P<0.001) and 12 months (P<0.001). Against steroids, PRP was favoured on pain and function scores at 6 months. However, superiority did not reach the minimal clinically important difference for all outcomes, the quality of evidence was low, and the authors describe the improvement as partial, urging further research to confirm benefits and identify the best formulation.
cards.watchOut: The pooled PRP advantage emerges only at 6–12 months and pools many small, variably blinded trials with different PRP preparations; the placebo comparison inside this same analysis sits uneasily beside the null blinded placebo trials carded at live shelf #457, which is exactly why this shelf is scoped to the HA comparison.
cards.source: Filardo G et al. PRP Injections for the Treatment of Knee Osteoarthritis: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Cartilage. 2021. PMID: 32551947. cards.headline: Wang 2022: single-injection PRP versus crosslinked HA, double-blind — no significant difference in WOMAC change at 1, 3 or 6 months
cards.summary: Wang 2022: single-injection PRP versus crosslinked HA, double-blind — no significant difference in WOMAC change at 1, 3 or 6 months
cards.people: 110 patients with early-stage knee osteoarthritis randomised to a single intra-articular PRP injection (n=54) or a single injection of crosslinked hyaluronic acid (n=56; the record names the product HyajointPlus); primary outcome change in WOMAC score at 1, 3 and 6 months.
cards.result: Both groups improved significantly from baseline on most WOMAC measures by 6 months, but when the change in WOMAC score was compared between groups at 1, 3 and 6 months, no significant differences were found between PRP and HA at any follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Early-stage disease only, a single injection of each product, and follow-up to 6 months — the meta-analysis claims PRP's advantage grows at 12 months, beyond this trial's horizon. The HA tested is one specific crosslinked product; results may not transfer to every HA formulation.

cards.headline: Fossati 2024: PRP, HA and PRP+HA all improved, with no significant difference among groups on any outcome at 6 or 12 months (n=174)
cards.summary: Fossati 2024: PRP, HA and PRP+HA all improved, with no significant difference among groups on any outcome at 6 or 12 months (n=174)
cards.people: 174 patients with mild-to-moderate knee osteoarthritis randomised to three intra-articular injections, two weeks apart, of hyaluronic acid, PRP, or PRP combined with HA; assessed with WOMAC, KOOS, IKDC, VAS and Tegner scores at 3, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: All treatments reduced pain and improved function, but analysis of covariance showed no statistically significant differences among the three groups for any investigated outcome at 6 months (WOMAC p=0.45) or 12 months (p=0.64). Adverse events (p=0.49) and painkiller use (p=0.28 and p=0.56) also did not differ. The authors conclude the three options have comparable efficacy in mild-to-moderate knee OA.
cards.watchOut: No placebo or saline arm, so the trial cannot say whether any of the three beats an inert injection — it answers only the head-to-head question, and on that question it is the largest double-blind test and it is null, including at the 12-month point where the meta-analysis claims PRP pulls ahead.
cards.source: Fossati C et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: the average of many small trials favours PRP; the two trials built to answer this exact question, blinded, do not
cards.summary: Synthesis: the average of many small trials favours PRP; the two trials built to answer this exact question, blinded, do not
cards.people: One meta-analysis of 34 randomised trials (2,829 knees) and two double-blind head-to-head randomised trials totalling 284 patients with early or mild-to-moderate knee osteoarthritis, followed 6–12 months.
cards.result: Meta-analysis: WOMAC favours PRP over HA at 6 and 12 months (P<0.001), low-quality evidence, not always reaching the minimal clinically important difference. Double-blind trials: no significant between-group difference at 6 months (Wang, n=110) or at 6 and 12 months on any outcome (Fossati, n=174). PROPOSED SPLIT: if PRP has an edge over HA it is small, late and preparation-dependent; on current best evidence the two are interchangeable for symptoms.
cards.watchOut: PRP is not one product — platelet and leukocyte content vary by preparation, and neither this shelf nor live shelf #457 (PRP versus saline, null in blinded trials) supports claims of cartilage regeneration. Tier C: conflicting evidence with a mortality/CV claim absent but a direct cost implication (PRP is usually the more expensive injection).
cards.source: Synthesis of Filardo G et al. Cartilage. 2021 (PMID: 32551947); Wang YC et al. Medicina. 2022 (PMID: 36013495); Fossati C et al. Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery. 2024 (PMID: 39367905).

shelves.title: PRP for rotator-cuff tendinopathy: no better than saline at one year in the double-blind trial — better than dry needling in a smaller one, and a meta-analysis pools the two kinds of control into a positive answer
shelves.question: In adults with rotator-cuff tendinopathy, do platelet-rich plasma injections improve pain and function compared with corticosteroid or saline?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Therapy · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet-Rich Plasma · Rotator Cuff · Shoulder Pain/therapy · Tendinopathy/therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer flips with the comparator. Against saline placebo, the rigorous trial is null: Kesikburun 2013 (PMID: 23893418), a double-blind trial of 40 patients with chronic rotator-cuff tendinopathy, found no significant difference between PRP and saline on WORC, SPADI or pain scores at one year (P=0.174, 0.314 and 0.904), though both groups improved with their exercise programme. Against dry needling, PRP won: Rha 2013 (PMID: 23035005, n=39) found Shoulder Pain and Disability Index scores of 17.7 versus 29.5 at six months favouring PRP (P<0.05). A meta-analysis of eight RCTs (A Hamid 2021, PMID: 33970936) — four against saline, four against rehabilitation or dry needling — concluded PRP was effective for long-term pain control and function, pooling those unlike controls together. The candidate's corticosteroid comparison could not be verified as a discrete carded trial this session; the verified split is saline versus active-needling controls. PROPOSED SPLIT: PRP beats needling a tendon without injecting anything active; it has not beaten salt water.

cards.headline: Kesikburun 2013: PRP no more effective than saline at one year on WORC (P=0.174), SPADI (P=0.314) or pain (P=0.904) — both groups improved with exercise
cards.summary: Kesikburun 2013: PRP no more effective than saline at one year on WORC (P=0.174), SPADI (P=0.314) or pain (P=0.904) — both groups improved with exercise
cards.people: 40 patients aged 18–70 with shoulder pain for more than 3 months, MRI findings of rotator-cuff tendinopathy or partial rupture, and at least 50% pain relief from a diagnostic subacromial anaesthetic injection; randomised to one ultrasound-guided subacromial injection of 5 mL PRP (n=20) or 5 mL saline (n=20), both followed by a 6-week standard exercise programme; outcomes to one year.
cards.result: No significant difference between groups in WORC, SPADI or 100-mm pain scores at one-year follow-up (P=0.174, P=0.314, P=0.904 respectively), and similar results at 3, 6, 12 and 24 weeks. Within each group, scores improved significantly from baseline at every time point (P<0.001). There were no significant group-by-time interactions for range of motion.
cards.watchOut: Small (20 per arm) and a single PRP injection with one preparation; a modest true effect could hide inside it. But it is the only double-blind saline-controlled test here, and its point estimates give PRP nothing — the improvement patients feel is fully explained by the exercise programme, time, and the injection ritual itself.
cards.source: Kesikburun S et al. Platelet-rich plasma injections in the treatment of chronic rotator cuff tendinopathy: a randomized controlled trial with 1-year follow-up. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2013. PMID: 23893418. cards.headline: Rha 2013: PRP beat dry needling — SPADI 17.7 versus 29.5 at six months (P<0.05), with superiority from six weeks onward
cards.summary: Rha 2013: PRP beat dry needling — SPADI 17.7 versus 29.5 at six months (P<0.05), with superiority from six weeks onward
cards.people: 39 patients at a university rehabilitation hospital with a supraspinatus tendon lesion (tendinosis or partial tear under 1.0 cm, not a complete tear), randomised to two ultrasound-guided PRP injections or two dry-needling procedures four weeks apart; outcomes (SPADI, passive range of motion, physician global rating, ultrasound) to six months.
cards.result: The clinical effect of PRP was superior to dry needling from six weeks to six months after the initial injection (P<0.05). At six months the mean Shoulder Pain and Disability Index was 17.7 ± 3.7 in the PRP group versus 29.5 ± 3.8 in the dry-needling group (P<0.05). No severe adverse effects occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: Dry needling is not an inert placebo — needling itself can help or irritate a tendon — so this trial shows PRP beats one active procedure, not that PRP beats placebo. Thirty-nine patients, one centre, and the dry-needling arm's scores leave open whether needling underperformed rather than PRP overperformed.
cards.source: Rha DW et al. Comparison of the therapeutic effects of ultrasound-guided platelet-rich plasma injection and dry needling in rotator cuff disease: a randomized controlled trial. Clinical Rehabilitation. 2013. PMID: 23035005. cards.headline: A Hamid 2021: eight RCTs pooled — PRP 'safe and effective' for long-term pain and function, but half the controls were saline and half were rehabilitation or dry needling
cards.summary: A Hamid 2021: eight RCTs pooled — PRP 'safe and effective' for long-term pain and function, but half the controls were saline and half were rehabilitation or dry needling
cards.people: Eight randomised trials of PRP injection for rotator-cuff conditions published to December 2020; six at low risk of bias for randomisation, one unclear, one high. Four trials used normal saline controls; the other four used a rehabilitation programme or dry needling.
cards.result: Meta-analysis of the selected studies led the authors to conclude that PRP injection was a safe and effective intervention for long-term pain control and shoulder function in patients with rotator-cuff disorders. PRP techniques (preparation and injection protocol) varied across studies, as did the control interventions.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports no pooled effect size, and pooling saline-controlled trials with active-control trials averages two different questions — the saline-controlled subset contains the null Kesikburun trial carded above. Read this review as evidence PRP can beat doing-needling-or-exercise-alone comparisons, not as a verdict against placebo.
cards.source: A Hamid MS et al. Platelet-rich plasma for rotator cuff tendinopathy: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS ONE. 2021. PMID: 33970936. cards.headline: Synthesis: comparator decides the verdict — null against saline, positive against dry needling, positive in a meta-analysis that merges the two
cards.summary: Synthesis: comparator decides the verdict — null against saline, positive against dry needling, positive in a meta-analysis that merges the two
cards.people: Two small double-blind randomised trials (n=40 against saline with one-year follow-up; n=39 against dry needling with six-month follow-up) and one meta-analysis of eight RCTs with mixed controls.
cards.result: Versus saline: no significant difference on any score at any time point to one year. Versus dry needling: SPADI 17.7 versus 29.5 at six months (P<0.05). Pooled across unlike controls: authors conclude long-term benefit. PROPOSED SPLIT: PRP for rotator-cuff tendinopathy is unproven against placebo and modestly supported against an active needling comparator — the saline result should govern what patients are told.
cards.watchOut: No corticosteroid-controlled PRP trial was carded: the candidate's steroid comparison remains unverified this session and is flagged in the part summary. All trials are small and preparations differ; Tier C for this band.

shelves.title: Spinal manipulation for acute low back pain: it did not speed recovery by a single day against placebo manipulation (hazard ratio 1.01) — yet a JAMA meta-analysis pooling other comparators finds a modest 10 mm pain improvement at six weeks
shelves.question: In adults with acute non-specific low back pain, does spinal manipulative therapy reduce pain and speed recovery compared with sham manipulation or inert treatment?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen/therapeutic use · Acute Disease/therapy · Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Diclofenac/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Low Back Pain/drug therapy,therapy · Male · Manipulation, Spinal/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — against sham manipulation the answer is no; against the mixed bag of other comparators it is a modest yes. Hancock 2007 (PMID: 17993364), a 240-patient factorial trial in acute low back pain on top of advice and paracetamol, found spinal manipulative therapy did not appreciably reduce days to recovery versus placebo manipulation (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.31; p=0.955); 99% had recovered or were censored by 12 weeks regardless. Paige 2017 (PMID: 28399251), a JAMA systematic review of 26 RCTs, found moderate-quality evidence that manipulation was associated with a pooled pain improvement of −9.95 mm on a 100-mm scale (95% CI −15.6 to −4.3; 15 trials, 1,711 patients) and a function effect size of −0.39 (12 trials, 1,381 patients) at up to six weeks — with large heterogeneity the reviewers could not explain, and minor transient harms (increased pain, stiffness, headache) reported 50–67% of the time in large case series. The pragmatic question — manipulation added to usual care for established low back pain — is homed at live shelf #785; this shelf covers the acute, sham-controlled question only. PROPOSED SPLIT: no faster recovery than placebo manipulation, but a small short-term pain and function advantage over the range of alternatives trials have used.

cards.headline: Hancock 2007: hazard ratio 1.01 for recovery with manipulation versus placebo manipulation — neither manipulation nor diclofenac shortened acute back pain
cards.summary: Hancock 2007: hazard ratio 1.01 for recovery with manipulation versus placebo manipulation — neither manipulation nor diclofenac shortened acute back pain
cards.people: 240 community patients with acute low back pain who had seen their GP and received advice and paracetamol, allocated to four groups of 60: diclofenac plus placebo manipulation, spinal manipulative therapy plus placebo drug, both active treatments, or double placebo; primary outcome days to recovery from pain, followed 12 weeks.
cards.result: Neither diclofenac nor spinal manipulative therapy appreciably reduced the number of days until recovery compared with placebo drug or placebo manipulation (diclofenac hazard ratio 1.09, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.42, p=0.516; spinal manipulative therapy hazard ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.31, p=0.955). 237 patients (99%) had recovered or were censored by 12 weeks. Twenty-two patients had possible adverse reactions (gastrointestinal disturbance, dizziness, palpitations), split evenly between active and placebo diclofenac.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is speed of recovery, not pain intensity at a fixed week — a treatment could ease pain without shortening the episode and this trial would miss it (the meta-analysis card speaks to that outcome). 'Placebo manipulation' in a factorial GP-based trial is a credible sham, which is precisely why its null result carries weight.

cards.headline: Paige 2017 (JAMA): pooled pain improvement −9.95 mm and function effect −0.39 at up to six weeks, moderate-quality evidence — heterogeneity large and unexplained
cards.summary: Paige 2017 (JAMA): pooled pain improvement −9.95 mm and function effect −0.39 at up to six weeks, moderate-quality evidence — heterogeneity large and unexplained
cards.people: 26 eligible RCTs of spinal manipulative therapy for acute (six weeks or less) low back pain in ambulatory adults, versus sham or alternative treatments, with pain or function measured within six weeks; harms supplemented by observational studies.
cards.result: Fifteen RCTs (1,711 patients) provided moderate-quality evidence of a statistically significant association with pain improvement (pooled mean improvement −9.95 mm on the 100-mm visual analogue scale, 95% CI −15.6 to −4.3). Twelve RCTs (1,381 patients) provided moderate-quality evidence for function (pooled mean effect size −0.39, 95% CI −0.71 to −0.07). Heterogeneity was not explained by clinician type, manipulation type, study quality, or whether manipulation was given alone or in a package. No RCT reported a serious adverse event; minor transient events such as increased pain, muscle stiffness and headache were reported 50% to 67% of the time in large case series.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate mixes sham-controlled trials with trials against inert or active alternatives, and averages about 10 mm on a 100-mm scale — below many patients' threshold for a worthwhile difference — with large unexplained heterogeneity, meaning some settings likely see no effect at all. It does not contradict Hancock: it measures pain at weeks, not days to recovery.
cards.source: Paige NM et al. Association of Spinal Manipulative Therapy With Clinical Benefit and Harm for Acute Low Back Pain: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28399251. cards.headline: Synthesis: recovery speed — no; short-term pain scores versus assorted alternatives — a small yes
cards.summary: Synthesis: recovery speed — no; short-term pain scores versus assorted alternatives — a small yes
cards.people: One 240-patient sham-controlled factorial trial with a time-to-recovery outcome, and one meta-analysis of 26 RCTs (1,711 patients in the pain analysis) with pain and function outcomes to six weeks.
cards.result: Versus placebo manipulation: hazard ratio for recovery 1.01 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.31) — no effect. Pooled versus sham or alternative treatments: pain −9.95 mm (95% CI −15.6 to −4.3), function effect size −0.39, moderate-quality evidence, large heterogeneity. Harms: no serious events in RCTs; transient soreness, stiffness or headache in 50–67% in case series. PROPOSED SPLIT: patients should not be promised a shorter episode; a modest easing of pain over the first weeks is a fair, weaker claim.
cards.watchOut: Acute low back pain improves on its own in nearly everyone (99% recovered or censored by 12 weeks in Hancock), which compresses any treatment's room to show benefit; chronic and subacute manipulation questions live elsewhere (#785, #1486) and are not re-opened here. Tier C for this band.

shelves.title: Aquatic exercise for hip and knee osteoarthritis: pain and disability about 5 points better than control on a 0–100 scale in the Cochrane pool of 13 trials — small, short-term, and never tested against a blinded comparator
shelves.question: In adults with hip or knee osteoarthritis, does aquatic exercise improve pain and function compared with land-based exercise or control?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Balneology · Chronic Disease · Exercise · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Hydrotherapy/methods · Male · Osteoarthritis, Hip/therapy · Osteoarthritis, Knee/therapy · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Swimming · Water
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a consistent small short-term gain against non-exercise controls, with the land-based comparison essentially untested in the carded evidence. The Cochrane review (Bartels 2016, PMID: 27007113; 13 trials, 1,190 participants, mean programme 12 weeks) found aquatic exercise improved pain (SMD −0.31, 95% CI −0.47 to −0.15; 12 trials, 1,076 participants) and disability (SMD −0.32, −0.47 to −0.17) versus control, corresponding to about five points lower pain and disability scores on a 0–100 scale, with a small quality-of-life effect (SMD −0.25) and no serious adverse events — moderate-quality evidence. The largest single trial, Hinman 2007 (PMID: 17142642; n=71), found 72% of aquatic-therapy participants reported improved pain and 75% improved function versus 17% each in controls after six weeks, with benefits maintained six weeks later. This shelf covers structured exercise in water; passive spa/balneotherapy for knee OA and fibromyalgia is homed at pack #2699 and is not rebuilt here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pool-based exercise is a reasonable, low-harm way to buy a small short-term improvement — superiority over equivalent land exercise is asserted by enthusiasts, not shown here.

cards.headline: Bartels 2016 (Cochrane): pain SMD −0.31 and disability SMD −0.32 across 12 trials — about five points on a 0–100 scale, moderate-quality evidence, no serious adverse events
cards.summary: Bartels 2016 (Cochrane): pain SMD −0.31 and disability SMD −0.32 across 12 trials — about five points on a 0–100 scale, moderate-quality evidence, no serious adverse events
cards.people: 13 randomised trials, 1,190 participants with knee or hip osteoarthritis (75% female, average age 68 years, average BMI 29.4, mean OA duration 6.7 years), comparing aquatic exercise (mean duration 12 weeks) with control groups such as usual care, education, social attention, telephone contact or waiting list.
cards.result: Aquatic exercise caused a small short-term improvement in pain (SMD −0.31, 95% CI −0.47 to −0.15; 12 trials, 1,076 participants) and disability (SMD −0.32, 95% CI −0.47 to −0.17; 12 trials, 1,059 participants), and a small effect on quality of life (SMD −0.25, 95% CI −0.49 to −0.01; 10 trials, 971 participants). In absolute terms these correspond to scores about five points lower for pain and disability and seven points higher for quality of life on 0–100 scales versus control. No trial performed radiographic evaluation; no serious adverse events were reported in relation to aquatic exercise.
cards.watchOut: Controls were mostly non-exercise, so the pool cannot separate 'exercise helps' from 'water helps'; participants cannot be blinded to being in a pool, and effects are short-term — the review's own wording is 'small, short-term, and clinically relevant' at moderate quality, with no structural (radiographic) outcome anywhere.
cards.source: Bartels EM et al. Aquatic exercise for the treatment of knee and hip osteoarthritis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2016. PMID: 27007113. cards.headline: Hinman 2007: 72% reported better pain and 75% better function after six weeks of aquatic therapy, versus 17% each with no intervention
cards.summary: Hinman 2007: 72% reported better pain and 75% better function after six weeks of aquatic therapy, versus 17% each with no intervention
cards.people: 71 volunteers with symptomatic hip or knee osteoarthritis randomised to six weeks of aquatic physical therapy or no aquatic physical therapy; outcomes pain, physical function, activity, quality of life and muscle strength, with follow-up six weeks after treatment ended.
cards.result: The aquatic programme produced less pain and joint stiffness and greater physical function, quality of life and hip muscle strength than control. Seventy-two per cent of participants reported improvement in pain and 75% in function, compared with 17% (each) of controls. Benefits were maintained six weeks after therapy ended, and 84% of participants were continuing the programme independently.
cards.watchOut: A no-intervention control in an unblindable intervention — the authors themselves state it is unclear whether the benefits were intervention effects or a placebo response. Seventy-one patients, one programme; the responder percentages (72–75% versus 17%) are far larger than the Cochrane pooled effect, which is what small single trials often do.
cards.source: Hinman RS et al. Aquatic physical therapy for hip and knee osteoarthritis: results of a single-blind randomized controlled trial. Physical Therapy. 2007. PMID: 17142642. cards.summary: Synthesis: small, real-looking, short-term benefit versus doing nothing — the 'better than land' claim has no carded support
cards.people: One Cochrane review (13 trials, 1,190 participants) and one single-blind randomised trial (71 participants), in hip and/or knee osteoarthritis, with programmes of 6–12 weeks.
cards.result: Pooled: pain and disability each about five points better than control on 0–100 scales (SMD ≈ −0.31 to −0.32), quality of life slightly better, no serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prescribe the pool for adherence and joint unloading, not on proof it beats the gym.

shelves.title: Epidural steroids for sciatica from a herniated disc: a flicker of leg-pain relief at 3–6 weeks in two double-blind trials — no gain in function, and surgery rates identical at a year (about 25% in both arms)
shelves.question: In adults with sciatica from lumbar disc herniation, do epidural corticosteroid injections reduce leg pain and disability compared with placebo injections?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anti-Inflammatory Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Injections, Epidural/adverse effects · Intervertebral Disc Displacement/complications/surgery · Male · Methylprednisolone/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Methylprednisolone Acetate · Sciatica/drug therapy/etiology/physiopathology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — brief symptom relief, no durable benefit. In Carette S et al. (PMID: 9171065; 158 patients with sciatica from a herniated nucleus pulposus), epidural methylprednisolone improved leg pain more than saline at 6 weeks (P=0.03) but disability did not differ at 3 weeks (Oswestry change −8.0 versus −5.5; 95% CI for the difference −7.1 to 2.2) or at 3 months (−17.3 versus −15.4; 95% CI −9.3 to 5.4), and the cumulative probability of back surgery at 12 months was 25.8% versus 24.8% (P=0.90). The WEST trial (Arden NK et al., PMID: 16030082; 228 patients) found 75% disability improvement at 3 weeks in 12.5% on epidural triamcinolone versus 3.7% on placebo injections (number needed to treat 11.4) and no benefit at any point from 6 to 52 weeks, no gain in physical function or return to work, and no reduction in surgery. Two concordant double-blind trials say the injection buys a few weeks of partial relief and changes nothing else. PROPOSED SPLIT: transient leg-pain/disability benefit at 3–6 weeks; no benefit on function, work or surgery from 6 weeks to 1 year.

cards.headline: Carette 1997: leg pain better at 6 weeks (P=0.03), disability never significantly different, surgery by 12 months 25.8% versus 24.8% (P=0.90)
cards.summary: Carette 1997: leg pain better at 6 weeks (P=0.03), disability never significantly different, surgery by 12 months 25.8% versus 24.8% (P=0.90)
cards.people: 158 patients with sciatica due to a herniated nucleus pulposus and Oswestry disability scores above 20, randomised to up to three epidural injections of methylprednisolone acetate 80 mg or isotonic saline placebo, followed for 12 months.
cards.result: At 3 weeks the Oswestry score had improved by a mean of −8.0 on methylprednisolone and −5.5 on placebo (95% CI for the difference −7.1 to 2.2); at 3 months −17.3 versus −15.4 (95% CI −9.3 to 5.4) — not significant at either point. Leg-pain improvement was greater on methylprednisolone at 6 weeks (P=0.03), as were finger-to-floor distance (P=0.006) and sensory deficits (P=0.03) at 3 weeks. The cumulative probability of back surgery at 12 months was 25.8% versus 24.8% (P=0.90).
cards.watchOut: The positive findings are scattered single time points on secondary measures; the pre-specified disability outcome and the hard outcome patients care about — avoiding surgery — were null at every point.
cards.source: Carette S et al. Epidural corticosteroid injections for sciatica due to herniated nucleus pulposus. The New England journal of medicine. 1997. PMID: 9171065.
