cards.headline: WEST (Arden 2005): 75% disability improvement at 3 weeks in 12.5% versus 3.7% (NNT 11.4) — and no benefit at any point from 6 to 52 weeks
cards.summary: WEST (Arden 2005): 75% disability improvement at 3 weeks in 12.5% versus 3.7% (NNT 11.4) — and no benefit at any point from 6 to 52 weeks
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (Arden 2005, WEST)
cards.people: 228 patients with unilateral sciatica of 1–18 months' duration in four UK secondary pain clinics, randomised to three lumbar epidural injections of triamcinolone acetonide or interligamentous saline injections at 3-week intervals, followed for 12 months.
cards.result: At 3 weeks, 12.5% of the epidural group versus 3.7% of the placebo group achieved a 75% improvement in Oswestry disability (number needed to treat 11.4). No benefit was demonstrated from 6 to 52 weeks. Epidural injections did not improve physical function, hasten return to work or reduce the need for surgery, repeated injections were no better than a single injection, and no clinical predictors of response were found.
cards.watchOut: Even the 3-week win is a responder cut (75% improvement) reached by only one patient in eight; the majority in both arms still had significant pain and disability at the end of the study.
cards.source: Arden NK et al. A multicentre randomized controlled trial of epidural corticosteroid injections for sciatica: the WEST study. Rheumatology (Oxford, England). 2005. PMID: 16030082. cards.headline: Synthesis: two double-blind trials agree — weeks of partial relief, nothing durable, surgery untouched
cards.summary: Synthesis: two double-blind trials agree — weeks of partial relief, nothing durable, surgery untouched
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 386 patients with sciatica (Carette 1997, disc herniation confirmed; WEST 2005, clinical unilateral sciatica), each testing three epidural corticosteroid injections against placebo injections.
cards.result: Transient benefit: leg pain at 6 weeks (Carette, P=0.03) and 75% disability response at 3 weeks, 12.5% versus 3.7% (WEST). Durable outcomes: disability null at 3 months (Carette) and at 6–52 weeks (WEST); surgery 25.8% versus 24.8% at 12 months (Carette). PROPOSED SPLIT: brief symptom relief only; no functional or surgical benefit.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial used imaging-guided transforaminal technique, so advocates can claim the modern route was untested — but the burden of proof for the costlier technique sits with its proponents, and on the tested question the answer is consistent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Carette S et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1997 (PMID: 9171065); Arden NK et al. Rheumatology (Oxford, England). 2005 (PMID: 16030082).

shelves.title: Specific neck exercise for chronic neck pain: pain and disability fell versus control at 12 months in a 180-woman trial (P<0.001), and deep cervical flexor training added gains on top of conventional exercise in a 65-teacher trial
shelves.question: In adults with chronic neck pain, does specific neck exercise (deep cervical flexor training) reduce pain and disability compared with general exercise or control?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Chronic Disease · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Isometric Contraction · Middle Aged · Neck Muscles/physiology · Neck Pain/rehabilitation · Pain Measurement · Range of Motion, Articular · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — specific neck training beats advice and general activity; the deep-flexor-specific claim rests on smaller work. Ylinen J et al. (PMID: 12759322) randomised 180 women with chronic nonspecific neck pain to intensive isometric neck strength training, lighter neck endurance training, or a control group advised on aerobic and stretching exercise: at 12 months both training groups had decreased neck pain and disability compared with control (P<0.001), and maximal isometric neck strength improved in flexion by 110% in the strength group versus 28% in the endurance group and 10% in controls. Iqbal ZA et al. (PMID: 33521131) randomised 65 school teachers with neck pain to deep cervical flexor training with pressure biofeedback plus conventional exercises or conventional exercises alone, finding statistically significant additional improvement in muscle endurance, pain and disability at days 14 and 42. A systematic review of nine randomised trials of deep cervical flexor programmes (Amiri Arimi S et al., PMID: 28225440) found eight of nine supported low-load craniocervical flexion training for deep-flexor impairments, with one trial finding no difference against other cervical exercise. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): specific neck exercise reduces pain and disability versus control, with deep cervical flexor training a reasonable specific form.

cards.headline: Ylinen 2003: both neck training groups beat control on pain and disability at 12 months (P<0.001); flexion strength +110% (strength), +28% (endurance), +10% (control)
cards.summary: Ylinen 2003: both neck training groups beat control on pain and disability at 12 months (P<0.001); flexion strength +110% (strength), +28% (endurance), +10% (control)
cards.people: 180 female office workers aged 25–53 years with chronic nonspecific neck pain in Finland, randomised to intensive isometric neck strength training (n=60), lighter dynamic neck endurance training (n=60), or a control group (n=60) advised to do regular aerobic and stretching exercises; both training groups also did shoulder and upper-extremity dumbbell exercises; follow-up 12 months.
cards.result: At 12 months, neck pain and disability had decreased in both training groups compared with the control group (P<0.001). Maximal isometric neck strength improved in flexion by 110%, rotation by 76% and extension by 69% in the strength group; the respective improvements were 28%, 29% and 16% in the endurance group and 10%, 10% and 7% in controls. Range of motion also improved significantly in both training groups in rotation, and in the strength group in lateral flexion, flexion and extension.
cards.watchOut: Women office workers only, and the comparison is training versus advice — stretching and aerobic exercise alone, the usual self-care prescription, was the control that lost. The trial tests specific neck training, not the deep-flexor technique in isolation.
cards.source: Ylinen J et al. Active neck muscle training in the treatment of chronic neck pain in women: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2003. PMID: 12759322. cards.headline: Iqbal 2021: deep cervical flexor training with pressure biofeedback, added to conventional exercise, improved endurance, pain and disability significantly more by day 42 (65 teachers)
cards.summary: Iqbal 2021: deep cervical flexor training with pressure biofeedback, added to conventional exercise, improved endurance, pain and disability significantly more by day 42 (65 teachers)
cards.people: 65 school teachers aged 25–45 years with more than 5 years of teaching experience and neck pain, randomised to deep cervical flexor muscle training using pressure biofeedback plus conventional neck exercises, or conventional exercises only; pain (numeric rating scale), disability (Neck Disability Index) and deep-flexor endurance (craniocervical flexion test) measured at days 0, 14 and 42.
cards.result: Both groups improved, but the group receiving additional deep cervical flexor training showed a statistically significant improvement in muscle endurance, pain and disability compared with conventional exercise alone at days 14 and 42. (The record reports significance rather than the group means, so no absolute score changes are quoted here.) The trial was retrospectively registered.
cards.watchOut: Six weeks of follow-up, a single occupational group, retrospective registration, and no absolute effect sizes in the record — this card supports direction, not magnitude.
cards.source: Iqbal ZA et al. Efficacy of Deep Cervical Flexor Muscle Training on Neck Pain, Functional Disability, and Muscle Endurance in School Teachers: A Clinical Trial. BioMed research international. 2021. PMID: 33521131. Registry ID: NCT03537300. cards.headline: Amiri Arimi 2017: 8 of 9 randomised trials supported low-load craniocervical flexion training for deep-flexor impairments; 1 found no difference versus other cervical exercise
cards.summary: Amiri Arimi 2017: 8 of 9 randomised trials supported low-load craniocervical flexion training for deep-flexor impairments; 1 found no difference versus other cervical exercise
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Amiri Arimi 2017)
cards.people: 9 randomised trials (published 1990 to March 2016) of exercise programmes targeting the deep cervical flexor muscles in patients with chronic nonspecific neck pain, qualitatively assessed on the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale: four of moderate quality, five of good quality.
cards.result: Eight studies supported the effectiveness of specific low-load craniocervical flexion exercise on deep cervical flexor size, endurance, strength or activity; one study reported no significant difference between this exercise and other cervical exercise programmes. The reviewers conclude low-load craniocervical flexion exercise appears highly effective for deep-flexor impairments compared with other exercise types.
cards.watchOut: The reviewed outcomes are largely muscle-impairment measures (size, endurance, activation) rather than pain itself — the impairment improves more certainly than the symptom it is meant to explain.
cards.source: Amiri Arimi S et al. The Effect of Different Exercise Programs on Size and Function of Deep Cervical Flexor Muscles in Patients With Chronic Nonspecific Neck Pain: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials. American journal of physical medicine & rehabilitation. 2017. PMID: 28225440. cards.headline: Synthesis: specific neck training is one of rehabilitation's more consistent positives — the large trial is general neck training, the flexor-specific trials are small
cards.summary: Synthesis: specific neck training is one of rehabilitation's more consistent positives — the large trial is general neck training, the flexor-specific trials are small
cards.people: One examiner-blinded RCT of 180 women (Ylinen 2003), one RCT of 65 teachers testing deep cervical flexor training as an add-on (Iqbal 2021), and a systematic review of 9 deep-flexor RCTs (Amiri Arimi 2017).
cards.result: Pain and disability versus control at 12 months: significantly reduced in both training arms (P<0.001, Ylinen). Deep-flexor add-on: significant extra gains in endurance, pain and disability by day 42 (Iqbal). Reviewed RCTs: 8 of 9 favour low-load craniocervical flexion training for flexor impairments. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Exercise trials cannot blind participants, and the flexor-specific evidence leans on impairment outcomes and short follow-up; the durable 12-month pain result belongs to neck strength/endurance training broadly.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ylinen J et al. JAMA. 2003 (PMID: 12759322); Iqbal ZA et al. BioMed research international. 2021 (PMID: 33521131); Amiri Arimi S et al. American journal of physical medicine & rehabilitation. 2017 (PMID: 28225440).

shelves.title: Methotrexate in giant cell arteritis: three small trials disagreed, but pooled patient-level data show fewer relapses (hazard ratio 0.65 for a first relapse) and about 842 mg less prednisone over 48 weeks
shelves.question: In patients with giant-cell arteritis, does methotrexate reduce relapses and steroid dose compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Giant Cell Arteritis/drug therapy · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Methotrexate/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Placebos · Prednisone/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Recurrence · Sensitivity and Specificity · Statistics, Nonparametric
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — three small randomised trials, individually discordant, positive when pooled patient by patient. Jover JA et al. (PMID: 11177313) found at least one relapse in 45% on methotrexate plus prednisone versus 84.2% on prednisone alone (P=0.02), with a mean cumulative prednisone dose lower by 1,302 mg (95% CI 350 to 2,253; P=0.009). Hoffman GS et al. (PMID: 12115238), the largest trial at 98 patients, found treatment failure in 57.5% on methotrexate versus 77.3% on placebo (P=0.26) and no significant difference in cumulative corticosteroid dose. Spiera RF et al. (PMID: 11579707), with 21 patients, found no corticosteroid-sparing benefit. The individual patient data meta-analysis of all three (Mahr AD et al., PMID: 17665429; 161 patients) found hazard ratios of 0.65 for a first relapse (P=0.04) and 0.49 for a second relapse (P=0.02) — relative effects — a reduction in cumulative corticosteroid dose of 842 mg within 48 weeks (P<0.001), and a higher probability of sustained corticosteroid discontinuation for at least 24 weeks (hazard ratio 2.84, P=0.001), with no difference in dropout rates or adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive methotrexate modestly reduces relapse and steroid exposure in giant cell arteritis, on pooled small-trial evidence.

cards.headline: Jover 2001: at least one relapse in 45% on methotrexate plus prednisone versus 84.2% on prednisone alone (P=0.02); cumulative prednisone lower by a mean 1,302 mg
cards.summary: Jover 2001: at least one relapse in 45% on methotrexate plus prednisone versus 84.2% on prednisone alone (P=0.02); cumulative prednisone lower by a mean 1,302 mg
cards.people: 42 patients with new-onset, biopsy-proven giant cell arteritis at a university-based clinic, given high initial corticosteroid doses tapered quickly to withdrawal, with weekly methotrexate or placebo from the start of corticosteroid therapy for 24 months.
cards.result: Compared with prednisone plus placebo, prednisone plus methotrexate reduced the proportion of patients who experienced at least one relapse (45% versus 84.2%; P=0.02) and the proportion who experienced multiple relapses (P=0.004). Mean cumulative prednisone dose was 4,187 mg (SD 1,529) in the methotrexate group versus 5,489.5 mg (SD 1,396) in the placebo group (mean difference 1,302 mg, 95% CI 350 to 2,253; P=0.009). Overall rates and severity of adverse events were similar between groups; treatment was discontinued in three methotrexate patients with definite drug-related adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The smallest-but-one trial is the most positive — a pattern that invites caution — and its steroid taper was faster than in the other trials, which may be exactly the setting where a relapse-preventing adjunct shows its worth. Forty-two patients cannot settle a relapse question on their own.
cards.source: Jover JA et al. Combined treatment of giant-cell arteritis with methotrexate and prednisone. a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2001. PMID: 11177313. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hoffman 2002: treatment failure 57.5% on methotrexate versus 77.3% on placebo (P=0.26) — the largest trial found no significant benefit and no steroid sparing
cards.summary: Hoffman 2002: treatment failure 57.5% on methotrexate versus 77.3% on placebo (P=0.26) — the largest trial found no significant benefit and no steroid sparing
cards.people: 98 patients with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis enrolled over four years at 16 centres of the International Network for the Study of Systemic Vasculitides, treated with prednisone 1 mg/kg per day (maximum 60 mg) plus either methotrexate 0.15 mg/kg per week increased to 0.25 mg/kg per week (maximum 15 mg weekly; median dose achieved 15 mg per week) or placebo, with blinded assessment of disease status.
cards.result: Treatment failure (two distinct relapses, or persistence of disease activity after the first relapse despite increased corticosteroids) occurred in 57.5% of the methotrexate group (95% CI 41.6 to 73.4%) versus 77.3% of the placebo group (95% CI 61.9 to 92.8%) (P=0.26); in Cox regression, methotrexate was not associated with a reduced risk of treatment failure (relative risk 0.72, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.28). There were no significant differences in erythrocyte sedimentation rate elevations after initial remission, serious morbidity due to giant cell arteritis, cumulative corticosteroid dose, or treatment toxicity. Fewer methotrexate patients had relapse heralded by isolated polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms (1 case versus 5; P=0.05).
cards.watchOut: The point estimates lean methotrexate's way (57.5% versus 77.3% failure) but the trial is underpowered for them — 'not significant' here is not 'no effect'. Its null cumulative-dose result, though, is a direct counterweight to Jover's steroid-sparing claim at the individual-trial level.
cards.source: Hoffman GS et al. A multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of adjuvant methotrexate treatment for giant cell arteritis. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2002. PMID: 12115238. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Spiera 2001: 21 patients, no corticosteroid-sparing benefit — cumulative dose 6,469 mg on methotrexate versus 5,908 mg on placebo (p=0.6)
cards.summary: Spiera 2001: 21 patients, no corticosteroid-sparing benefit — cumulative dose 6,469 mg on methotrexate versus 5,908 mg on placebo (p=0.6)
cards.people: 21 patients with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis randomised to high-dose corticosteroids plus methotrexate starting at 7.5 mg per week (12 patients) or placebo (9 patients), with corticosteroids tapered by the treating physician and methotrexate or placebo increased by 2.5 mg per week for flares to a maximum of 20 mg per week.
cards.result: At completion there was no significant difference between methotrexate and placebo in cumulative corticosteroid dose (6,469 mg versus 5,908 mg; p=0.6), weeks to completion of steroids (68 versus 60; p=0.5), time to taper prednisone below 10 mg per day (23 versus 25 weeks; p=0.5), bone mineral density at one year, functional status (AIMS) or quality of life (SF-36). There was no late vision loss in either group and only one major treatment-responsive relapse, in a methotrexate-treated patient.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-one patients — this trial could not have detected the pooled effect even if real. Its value is as a reminder of how well both groups did with prompt tapering: few major corticosteroid side effects in either arm, which shrinks the headroom any adjunct can claim.
cards.source: Spiera RF et al. A prospective, double-blind, randomized, placebo controlled trial of methotrexate in the treatment of giant cell arteritis (GCA). Clinical and experimental rheumatology. 2001. PMID: 11579707. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mahr 2007 (individual patient data meta-analysis of all three trials): first-relapse hazard ratio 0.65 (P=0.04), second-relapse 0.49 (P=0.02), 842 mg less corticosteroid by 48 weeks
cards.summary: Mahr 2007 (individual patient data meta-analysis of all three trials): first-relapse hazard ratio 0.65 (P=0.04), second-relapse 0.49 (P=0.02), 842 mg less corticosteroid by 48 weeks
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis of 3 randomised trials (Mahr 2007)
cards.people: 161 patients with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis from the three randomised placebo-controlled trials (84 methotrexate, 77 placebo), treated with initial high-dose corticosteroids plus oral methotrexate 7.5–15 mg per week or placebo; mean follow-up 54.7 weeks (SD 39.2).
cards.result: Hazard ratios with methotrexate versus placebo were 0.65 for a first relapse (P=0.04) and 0.49 for a second relapse (P=0.02) — relative effects. The predicted numbers needed to treat to prevent one first or one second relapse up to 48 weeks were 3.6 (95% CI 2.2 to 56.8) and 4.7 (95% CI 3.3 to 21.9) respectively. Methotrexate reduced the cumulative corticosteroid dose by 842 mg within 48 weeks (P<0.001) and was associated with a higher probability of achieving sustained discontinuation of corticosteroids for at least 24 weeks (hazard ratio 2.84, P=0.001). Dropout rates and adverse events did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: The pooled significance rests heavily on the smallest, most positive trial, and the number-needed-to-treat confidence interval for a first relapse runs to 56.8 — the honest width of three trials totalling 161 patients. Methotrexate doses (7.5–15 mg weekly) were also lower than many clinicians now use.
cards.source: Mahr AD et al. Adjunctive methotrexate for treatment of giant cell arteritis: an individual patient data meta-analysis. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2007. PMID: 17665429. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: individually a draw, pooled a modest win — fewer relapses and less prednisone, at small-trial certainty
cards.summary: Synthesis: individually a draw, pooled a modest win — fewer relapses and less prednisone, at small-trial certainty
cards.people: Three randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 161 patients with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis (Jover 2001, Hoffman 2002, Spiera 2001), pooled at individual patient level (Mahr 2007).
cards.result: Relapse proportions in the positive trial: 45% versus 84.2% for at least one relapse. Treatment failure in the largest trial: 57.5% versus 77.3%, not significant. Pooled: first-relapse hazard ratio 0.65 (P=0.04), second-relapse 0.49 (P=0.02), cumulative corticosteroid dose lower by 842 mg within 48 weeks (P<0.001), sustained steroid discontinuation hazard ratio 2.84 (P=0.001); adverse events and dropouts no different. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C under this band's rules.
cards.watchOut: Every trial predates the tocilizumab era (live shelf #385 homes that question), so this shelf answers the older, still-common question of what methotrexate adds to steroids alone — not how it compares with IL-6 blockade. Vision loss, the outcome patients fear most, was too rare in these trials for any of them to address.

cards.search: synthesis: individually a draw, pooled a modest win — fewer relapses and less prednisone, at small-trial certainty synthesis: individually a draw, pooled a modest win — fewer relapses and less prednisone, at small-trial certainty in patients with giant-cell arteritis, does methotrexate reduce relapses and steroid dose compared with placebo? synthesis three randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trials totalling 161 patients with newly diagnosed giant cell arteritis (jover 2001, hoffman 2002, spiera 2001), pooled at individual patient level (mahr 2007). relapse proportions in the positive trial: 45% versus 84.2% for at least one relapse. treatment failure in the largest trial: 57.5% versus 77.3%, not significant. pooled: first-relapse hazard ratio 0.65 (p=0.04), second-relapse 0.49 (p=0.02), cumulative corticosteroid dose lower by 842 mg within 48 weeks (p<0.001), sustained steroid discontinuation hazard ratio 2.84 (p=0.001); adverse events and dropouts no different. proposed possible (benefit), tier c under this band's rules. every trial predates the tocilizumab era (live shelf #385 homes that question), so this shelf answers the older, still-common question of what methotrexate adds to steroids alone — not how it compares with il-6 blockade. vision loss, the outcome patients fear most, was too rare in these trials for any of them to address. synthesis of jover ja et al. annals of internal medicine. 2001 (pmid: 11177313); hoffman gs et al. arthritis and rheumatism. 2002 (pmid: 12115238); spiera rf et al. clinical and experimental rheumatology. 2001 (pmid: 11579707); mahr ad et al. arthritis and rheumatism. 2007 (pmid: 17665429).

shelves.title: PRP for acute hamstring injury: beat platelet-poor plasma by 5.7 days in one trial, matched no injection in the same trial, and matched placebo outright in the other — return to play is not reliably faster
shelves.question: In athletes with acute hamstring injury, does platelet-rich plasma speed return to play compared with placebo or rehabilitation alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Athletic Injuries/physiopathology/rehabilitation · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Test · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Isometric Contraction/physiology · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle, Skeletal/injuries · Platelet-Rich Plasma · Return to Sport/physiology · Secondary Prevention · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by comparator. In Hamilton 2015, a single platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection shortened return to play versus a platelet-poor plasma injection (adjusted difference −5.7 days, 95% CI −10.1 to −1.4; adjusted HR 2.29, 95% CI 1.30 to 4.04) but not versus no injection at all (−2.9 days, 95% CI −7.2 to 1.4; HR 1.48, p=0.15) — the platelet-poor injection arm, not PRP, looks like the outlier. In Reurink 2015, two PRP injections did not accelerate return to play versus saline placebo injections, and the 1-year re-injury rate was identical in effect terms (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.38 to 2.13; p=0.80). No trial showed a re-injury benefit at any time point, and no adverse effects were reported in Hamilton. Read together: an injection ritual plus intensive rehabilitation returns athletes when rehabilitation returns them; PRP itself has no dependable effect. PROPOSED SPLIT: PRP beat an active plasma comparator once, matched no treatment in the same trial, and matched placebo in the second trial — no reliable return-to-play or re-injury benefit.

cards.headline: Hamilton 2015: PRP returned players 5.7 days sooner than platelet-poor plasma — but no sooner than no injection (−2.9 days, p=0.189), and re-injury did not differ
cards.summary: Hamilton 2015: PRP returned players 5.7 days sooner than platelet-poor plasma — but no sooner than no injection (−2.9 days, p=0.189), and re-injury did not differ
cards.type: Randomised three-arm trial, double-blind for the injection arms (Hamilton 2015)
cards.people: 90 professional male athletes with MRI-positive acute hamstring injuries, randomised to a single intramuscular PRP injection, a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection, or no injection; all received an intensive standardised rehabilitation programme. Primary outcome was time to return to play, with re-injury at 2 and 6 months.
cards.result: Adjusted HR for return to play was 2.29 (95% CI 1.30 to 4.04; p=0.004) for PRP versus PPP, 1.48 (95% CI 0.869 to 2.520; p=0.15) for PRP versus no injection, and 1.57 for PPP versus no injection (p=0.13). Adjusted differences in time to return to sport: PRP versus PPP −5.7 days (95% CI −10.1 to −1.4; p=0.01); PRP versus no injection −2.9 days (95% CI −7.2 to 1.4; p=0.189); PPP versus no injection +2.8 days (p=0.210). There was no significant difference in the secondary outcome measures, including re-injury, and no adverse effects were reported. The authors conclude there is no benefit of a single PRP injection over intensive rehabilitation.
cards.watchOut: The three-arm design is the lesson: PRP only 'won' against the one comparator that itself trended slower than doing nothing, so the apparent 5.7-day gain is as consistent with PPP delaying recovery as with PRP accelerating it. A single injection was tested; multi-injection commercial protocols are an extrapolation.
cards.source: Hamilton B et al. Platelet-rich plasma does not enhance return to play in hamstring injuries: a randomised controlled trial. British journal of sports medicine. 2015. PMID: 26136179. cards.summary: Reurink 2015 (Dutch Hamstring Injection Therapy study): PRP did not accelerate return to play versus placebo, and 1-year re-injury was HR 0.89 (p=0.80)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, full report (Reurink 2015)
cards.people: 80 competitive and recreational athletes with acute hamstring muscle injuries in a multicentre trial, randomised to intramuscular PRP injections or placebo (saline) injections alongside rehabilitation. Primary outcome was time to return to play during 6 months of follow-up; this full report adds the secondary scores and 1-year re-injury follow-up of the trial first reported as a New England Journal of Medicine letter in 2014.
cards.result: PRP did not accelerate return to play (primary outcome, as reported in the earlier primary publication and restated in this report), and the 2-month re-injury rate did not differ. At 1 year there was no significant between-group difference in re-injury rate (HR 0.89; 95% CI 0.38 to 2.13; p=0.80) or in any other secondary outcome measure, including clinical and MRI parameters, patient satisfaction, and the hamstring outcome score.
cards.watchOut: The primary return-to-play figures themselves sit in the 2014 NEJM letter; this card is built from the full journal report fetched for this shelf, which states the primary result and carries the complete 1-year data. Two injections were used here versus one in Hamilton — the null is consistent across both schedules.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two double-blind trials, one comparator-dependent signal, no re-injury benefit — rehabilitation remains the treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: two double-blind trials, one comparator-dependent signal, no re-injury benefit — rehabilitation remains the treatment
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling 170 athletes with acute hamstring injury (90 professional men in Hamilton 2015; 80 competitive and recreational athletes in Reurink 2015), each testing PRP injections added to rehabilitation against an injection or no-injection comparator.
cards.result: Return to play: PRP faster than platelet-poor plasma by 5.7 days in Hamilton, but not faster than no injection in the same trial, and not faster than saline placebo in Reurink. Re-injury: no difference at 2 or 6 months in Hamilton and HR 0.89 (95% CI 0.38 to 2.13) at 1 year in Reurink. Harms: none reported in Hamilton. PROPOSED SPLIT: the only positive contrast is against a comparator that itself performed worst, so the shelf does not support PRP as a return-to-play treatment.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial-per-protocol evidence (one injection in Hamilton, two in Reurink) and return-to-play decisions are partly judgement calls even in blinded trials. Tier C is set: this band is held for the developer's personal verdict, and the split turns on comparator choice, which a reader should see rather than have averaged away.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hamilton B et al. British journal of sports medicine. 2015 (PMID: 26136179); Reurink G et al. British journal of sports medicine. 2015 (PMID: 25940636).

shelves.title: Upadacitinib versus adalimumab in psoriatic arthritis (SELECT-PsA 1): ACR20 at week 12 in 70.6% (15 mg) and 78.5% (30 mg) versus 65.0% on adalimumab — non-inferior at 15 mg, superior only at 30 mg
shelves.question: In patients with psoriatic arthritis, does upadacitinib beat adalimumab for joint response?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Adult · Antirheumatic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Arthritis, Psoriatic/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Heterocyclic Compounds, 3-Ring/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Humans · Janus Kinase Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Least-Squares Analysis · Liver Diseases/etiology · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for upadacitinib over placebo, and for parity-or-better against adalimumab. In SELECT-PsA 1 (McInnes IB et al., PMID: 33789011; 1,704 patients), ACR20 at week 12 was 70.6% on upadacitinib 15 mg, 78.5% on 30 mg, 36.2% on placebo (p<0.001 for both doses versus placebo) and 65.0% on adalimumab: the 15 mg difference versus adalimumab was 5.6 percentage points (95% CI −0.6 to 11.8; non-inferior, not superior), the 30 mg difference 13.5 points (95% CI 7.5 to 19.4; superior). In biologic-refractory disease (SELECT-PsA 2, Mease PJ et al., PMID: 33272960; 642 patients), ACR20 was 56.9% (15 mg) and 63.8% (30 mg) versus 24.1% on placebo (p<0.001). Serious infections through week 24 in SELECT-PsA 1: 1.2% (15 mg), 2.6% (30 mg), 0.9% (placebo), 0.7% (adalimumab). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): upadacitinib matches adalimumab at the licensed-style 15 mg dose and beats it only at 30 mg, where infections rise.

cards.headline: SELECT-PsA 1: ACR20 70.6% (15 mg) and 78.5% (30 mg) versus 36.2% placebo and 65.0% adalimumab at week 12
cards.summary: SELECT-PsA 1: ACR20 70.6% (15 mg) and 78.5% (30 mg) versus 36.2% placebo and 65.0% adalimumab at week 12
cards.people: 1,704 patients with psoriatic arthritis and inadequate response to non-biologic DMARDs, randomised 1:1:1:1 to upadacitinib 15 mg or 30 mg once daily, placebo, or adalimumab 40 mg every other week, for 24 weeks.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 12: 70.6% (15 mg), 78.5% (30 mg), 36.2% (placebo; p<0.001 for both upadacitinib doses) and 65.0% (adalimumab). Difference versus adalimumab: 5.6 percentage points (95% CI −0.6 to 11.8) for 15 mg and 13.5 points (95% CI 7.5 to 19.4) for 30 mg — both doses non-inferior, only 30 mg superior. Adverse events through week 24: 66.9%, 72.3%, 59.6% and 64.8% respectively; serious infections 1.2%, 2.6%, 0.9% and 0.7%.
cards.watchOut: The superiority claim belongs to the 30 mg dose, which also carried the highest serious-infection rate (2.6%); the 15 mg result is parity with adalimumab, not a win, and 24 weeks says nothing about structural damage or long-term safety.
cards.source: McInnes IB et al. Trial of Upadacitinib and Adalimumab for Psoriatic Arthritis. The New England journal of medicine. 2021. PMID: 33789011. Registry ID: NCT03104400. shelves.title: Best medicine for acute low back pain: NSAIDs beat placebo by 7.3 points on a 100-point pain scale — an effect the Cochrane authors call small and probably not clinically relevant; paracetamol was no better than placebo at all
shelves.question: What is the best medicine for back pain? For acute low back pain, scoped here to the drug class with the best trial record — non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) versus placebo — how much do they reduce pain and disability, and how do the other drug classes compare?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain/drug therapy · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/adverse effects · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Cyclooxygenase 2 Inhibitors/adverse effects · Cyclooxygenase 2 Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Disability Evaluation · Humans · Low Back Pain/drug therapy · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Placebos/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), small. Scoped to NSAIDs for acute low back pain, this is the honest answer to 'best medicine': NSAIDs are the best-supported drug class, and their average advantage over placebo is small — pain −7.29 points on a 0–100 scale (van der Gaag 2020, Cochrane, 32 trials, 5,356 participants) and disability −2.02 points on a 0–24 scale, with the review's authors concluding the effects are 'small and probably not clinically relevant'. A second meta-analysis of spinal pain (Machado 2017) puts it in patient terms: 6 people need treatment for 1 extra person to achieve a clinically important pain reduction, and gastrointestinal reactions were 2.5 times more common on NSAIDs. The Cochrane overview of all drug classes (Cashin 2023; 7 reviews, 103 studies, 22,238 participants) found no high- or moderate-certainty evidence that any drug gives a large or medium effect on pain in acute or chronic low back pain, and high-certainty evidence that paracetamol is no better than placebo for acute low back pain (pain MD 0.49, 95% CI −1.99 to 2.97). BOUNDARY: this shelf covers NSAIDs alone. Whether adding a muscle relaxant to an NSAID helps is a separate question, homed on Shelf #786 ('Muscle relaxants for acute low back pain: the null shelf'); its studies are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: van der Gaag 2020 (Cochrane review, 32 trials, 5,356 participants with acute low back pain): NSAIDs versus placebo — pain −7.29 points (0–100), disability −2.02 points (0–24), global improvement RR 1.40, adverse events RR 0.86
cards.summary: van der Gaag 2020 (Cochrane review, 32 trials, 5,356 participants with acute low back pain): NSAIDs versus placebo — pain −7.29 points (0–100), disability −2.02 points (0–24), global improvement RR 1.40, adverse events RR 0.86
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis (van der Gaag 2020)
cards.people: 5,356 participants aged 16 to 78 years with acute low back pain in 32 randomised trials, conducted mostly in Europe and North America, with follow-up from 1 day to 6 months; 7 studies were at low risk of bias and almost half were industry-funded.
cards.result: Short-term (up to 3 weeks) NSAIDs versus placebo: pain intensity (VAS 0–100) mean difference −7.29 (95% CI −10.98 to −3.61; moderate-quality evidence; 4 RCTs, N=815); disability (Roland Morris Disability Questionnaire 0–24) MD −2.02 (−2.89 to −1.15; high-quality evidence; 2 RCTs, N=471); global improvement RR 1.40 (1.12–1.75; low-quality evidence; 5 RCTs, N=1,201; I²=52%); adverse events RR 0.86 (0.63–1.18; very low-quality evidence; 6 RCTs, N=1,394); return to work at 7 days RR 1.48 (0.98–2.23; 1 RCT, N=266). Selective COX-2 inhibitors versus non-selective NSAIDs: pain MD −2.60 (−9.23 to 4.03; 2 RCTs, N=437) and adverse events RR 0.97 (0.63–1.50; N=444) — no clear difference. The authors conclude the magnitude of the NSAID effects is small and probably not clinically relevant.
cards.watchOut: The pain estimate rests on 4 trials and the disability estimate on 2, most trials did not register their protocols, and the adverse-event data cover short-term use only — these trials cannot answer questions about longer-term or rare harms of NSAIDs. 'Probably not clinically relevant' is the review authors' judgement against usual thresholds for a worthwhile change, not a claim of zero effect.
cards.source: van der Gaag WH, Roelofs PDDM, Enthoven WTM, van Tulder MW, Koes BW. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for acute low back pain. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020. PMID: 32297973. Registry ID: none in the record (Cochrane review). cards.headline: Machado 2017 (35 placebo-controlled trials in spinal pain): NNT 6 for one extra clinically important pain reduction; only 3 of 14 analyses even marginally above the clinical-importance threshold; gastrointestinal reactions 2.5 times more common
cards.summary: Machado 2017 (35 placebo-controlled trials in spinal pain): NNT 6 for one extra clinically important pain reduction; only 3 of 14 analyses even marginally above the clinical-importance threshold; gastrointestinal reactions 2.5 times more common
cards.people: 35 randomised placebo-controlled trials of NSAIDs for spinal pain — neck pain, low back pain and radicular pain, acute and chronic mixed (total participant number not documented in the abstract; median trial duration 7 days).
cards.result: NSAIDs reduced pain and disability versus placebo but with clinically unimportant effects: 6 participants (95% CI 4 to 10) needed to be treated with NSAIDs rather than placebo for one additional participant to achieve clinically important pain reduction (a between-group difference of 10 points on a 0–100 scale was the pre-set threshold for clinical importance). Across the different spinal-pain types, outcomes and time points, in only 3 of the 14 analyses were pooled effects marginally above that threshold. NSAIDs increased the risk of gastrointestinal reactions by 2.5 times (95% CI 1.2 to 5.2). The authors conclude there are no simple analgesics that provide clinically important effects for spinal pain over placebo.
cards.watchOut: Scope warning: this analysis pools all spinal pain — neck, radicular and chronic pain included — so it is broader than this shelf's acute low back pain question; the acute-specific numbers are on the Cochrane card. The abstract does not print the total number of participants (N not documented), and a median trial duration of 7 days says nothing about longer use.
cards.source: Machado GC, Maher CG, Ferreira PH, Day RO, Pinheiro MB, Ferreira ML. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for spinal pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Cashin 2023 (Cochrane overview, 7 reviews, 103 studies, 22,238 participants): no drug class gives a large or medium effect on low back pain — and for acute low back pain paracetamol equals placebo (pain MD 0.49, high certainty)
cards.summary: Cashin 2023 (Cochrane overview, 7 reviews, 103 studies, 22,238 participants): no drug class gives a large or medium effect on low back pain — and for acute low back pain paracetamol equals placebo (pain MD 0.49, high certainty)
cards.people: Adults with non-specific low back pain of any duration, across 7 Cochrane Reviews covering 103 randomised trials and 22,238 participants, and six drug classes: paracetamol, NSAIDs, muscle relaxants, benzodiazepines, opioids and antidepressants.
cards.result: For acute low back pain, paracetamol versus placebo showed high-certainty evidence of no difference in pain intensity (MD 0.49 on a 0–100 scale, 95% CI −1.99 to 2.97), disability (MD 0.05 on a 0–24 scale, −0.50 to 0.60) or adverse events (RR 1.07, 0.86–1.33). Muscle relaxants (versus placebo, a different comparison from adding one to an NSAID — see Shelf #786) showed a small pain benefit at moderate certainty with more adverse events (RR 1.50, 1.14–1.98). No included review addressed opioids for acute low back pain, and no antidepressant evidence was identified for acute low back pain. The authors' overall conclusion: no high- or moderate-certainty evidence that any investigated drug provides a large or medium effect on pain intensity for acute or chronic low back pain.
cards.watchOut: An overview re-presents the underlying Cochrane reviews — its NSAID numbers for acute low back pain are the same van der Gaag 2020 estimates carded above, not independent confirmation. Most of its component reviews predate 2021, and 'no large or medium effect' still leaves room for the small effects patients may or may not notice.

cards.headline: Synthesis: NSAIDs are the best-supported medicine for acute low back pain — and 'best' still means a small average effect, with paracetamol no better than placebo
cards.summary: Synthesis: NSAIDs are the best-supported medicine for acute low back pain — and 'best' still means a small average effect, with paracetamol no better than placebo
cards.people: Adults with acute non-specific low back pain choosing an over-the-counter or prescribed analgesic.
cards.result: The three syntheses agree. NSAIDs beat placebo by about 7 points on a 100-point pain scale and 2 points on a 24-point disability scale in the acute-specific Cochrane review; expressed per patient, about 6 people must take an NSAID for 1 extra person to get a clinically important pain reduction, while gastrointestinal reactions occur 2.5 times as often as on placebo. No rival class does better: paracetamol is indistinguishable from placebo at high certainty, and the overview of all classes found nothing with a large or medium effect. Boundary restated: muscle relaxants added to NSAIDs are Shelf #786's question, not this one.
cards.watchOut: Short trials (median 7 days in Machado) in mostly non-specific back pain: these averages hide wide individual variation, say little about sciatica-dominant pain or use beyond a few weeks, and cannot capture rare NSAID harms. A small average effect is not the same as no effect for the individual who responds.
cards.source: Synthesis of van der Gaag WH et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020 (PMID: 32297973); Machado GC et al. Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases. 2017 (PMID: 28153830); Cashin AG et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023 (PMID: 37014979).

shelves.title: Taking ibuprofen every day: cardiovascular events matched other NSAIDs in PRECISION, but ibuprofen was the worst of the three for blood pressure, kidneys and stomach lining
shelves.question: "Is it safe to take ibuprofen every day?" For a person taking ibuprofen daily for months or years — usually for arthritis or chronic pain — what does the long-term evidence show about heart, stomach, kidney and blood-pressure harm, and how does ibuprofen compare with celecoxib and naproxen?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the honest answer splits by organ system, and PRECISION (Nissen 2016, PMID: 27959716; 24,081 arthritis patients at increased cardiovascular risk, NCT00346216) is the anchor: at the doses actually used (mean ibuprofen 2,045 mg/day — a high, prescription-level dose), cardiovascular event rates were close across all three drugs (primary outcome: celecoxib 2.3%, naproxen 2.5%, ibuprofen 2.7%), so daily ibuprofen was not shown to be a cardiovascular outlier among NSAIDs. But ibuprofen was the worst of the three on two other systems: gastrointestinal events were significantly fewer on celecoxib than on ibuprofen (P=0.002) or naproxen (P=0.01), and renal events were significantly fewer on celecoxib than on ibuprofen (P=0.004) but not naproxen (P=0.19). The blood-pressure substudy (Ruschitzka 2017, PMID: 29020251; 444 patients) sharpens the renal/vascular picture: over 4 months, mean 24-hour systolic pressure changed by −0.3 mmHg on celecoxib, +1.6 on naproxen and +3.7 on ibuprofen, and new hypertension developed in 23.2% of previously normotensive ibuprofen patients versus 19.0% on naproxen and 10.3% on celecoxib. The older placebo-controlled record (CNT Collaboration, PMID: 23726390; 280 trials, 124,513 participants) supplies the absolute frame: ibuprofen carried the highest relative rate of upper gastrointestinal complications of the traditional NSAIDs (RR 3.97, 95% CI 2.22–7.10 — relative), a non-significant relative rate for major vascular events (RR 1.44, 0.89–2.33) and for major coronary events (RR 2.22, 1.10–4.48) in the NSAID-versus-placebo comparisons, all NSAIDs roughly doubled heart-failure risk, and the collaboration's absolute anchor — about 3 extra major vascular events per 1,000 patients treated for a year with a coxib or diclofenac, one of them fatal — shows that relative risks of this size translate into small absolute numbers for most people, but real ones. PROPOSED SPLIT: daily ibuprofen at arthritis doses is not uniquely dangerous to the heart among NSAIDs, but it is measurably the hardest of the three compared drugs on blood pressure, kidneys and gut — so 'safe every day' depends on dose, duration, and the taker's stomach, kidneys, blood pressure and other medicines. Shelf #330 covers strategies to prevent NSAID harm; this shelf prices the harm itself.

cards.headline: PRECISION (Nissen 2016; 24,081 patients): cardiovascular events were similar on celecoxib (2.3%), naproxen (2.5%) and ibuprofen (2.7%) — but ibuprofen had significantly more gastrointestinal events than celecoxib (P=0.002) and more renal events (P=0.004)
cards.summary: PRECISION (Nissen 2016; 24,081 patients): cardiovascular events were similar on celecoxib (2.3%), naproxen (2.5%) and ibuprofen (2.7%) — but ibuprofen had significantly more gastrointestinal events than celecoxib (P=0.002) and more renal events (P=0.004)
cards.people: 24,081 patients with osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis and increased cardiovascular risk, randomised to celecoxib, ibuprofen or naproxen, with low-dose aspirin permitted. Mean daily doses received: celecoxib 209 ± 37 mg, naproxen 852 ± 103 mg, ibuprofen 2,045 ± 246 mg. Mean duration of treatment was 20.3 ± 16.0 months and mean follow-up 34.1 ± 13.4 months. The primary composite outcome was death from cardiovascular causes (including haemorrhagic death), nonfatal myocardial infarction, or nonfatal stroke.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis the primary outcome occurred in 188 patients (2.3%) in the celecoxib group, 201 (2.5%) in the naproxen group and 218 (2.7%) in the ibuprofen group; hazard ratios were 0.93 (95% CI 0.76–1.13) for celecoxib versus naproxen and 0.85 (0.70–1.04) for celecoxib versus ibuprofen — relative measures, printed beside the absolute rates — with P<0.001 for noninferiority in both comparisons. In the on-treatment analysis the outcome occurred in 1.7%, 1.8% and 1.9% respectively. The rate of gastrointestinal events was significantly lower with celecoxib than with naproxen (P=0.01) or ibuprofen (P=0.002), and the rate of renal events was significantly lower with celecoxib than with ibuprofen (P=0.004) but not than with naproxen (P=0.19). The authors concluded that moderate-dose celecoxib was noninferior to ibuprofen or naproxen for cardiovascular safety.
cards.watchOut: Four limits. (1) Dose: the ibuprofen arm averaged about 2,000 mg/day — prescription-level, roughly five 400 mg tablets daily; PRECISION cannot price the risk of occasional or low-dose over-the-counter use. (2) Population: arthritis patients at increased cardiovascular risk, many on aspirin — not healthy young users. (3) There is no placebo arm: 'noninferior to other NSAIDs' is not 'as safe as taking nothing'. (4) The abstract reports the gastrointestinal and renal comparisons as significance levels without absolute event rates, so this card states the direction and significance honestly rather than inventing rates; dropout over 34 months was substantial, as in most long NSAID trials.

cards.headline: PRECISION-ABPM (Ruschitzka 2017; 444 patients): ibuprofen raised 24-hour systolic pressure by 3.7 mmHg over 4 months while celecoxib lowered it slightly (−0.3) — and 23.2% of normotensive ibuprofen patients developed new hypertension, versus 10.3% on celecoxib
cards.summary: PRECISION-ABPM (Ruschitzka 2017; 444 patients): ibuprofen raised 24-hour systolic pressure by 3.7 mmHg over 4 months while celecoxib lowered it slightly (−0.3) — and 23.2% of normotensive ibuprofen patients developed new hypertension, versus 10.3% on celecoxib
cards.type: Prespecified ambulatory blood-pressure substudy of PRECISION (Ruschitzka 2017)
cards.people: Prespecified ambulatory blood-pressure substudy of PRECISION: 444 patients (mean age 62 ± 10 years, 54% women, 92% osteoarthritis) randomised to celecoxib 100–200 mg twice daily, ibuprofen 600–800 mg three times daily, or naproxen 375–500 mg twice daily, with 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure measured at baseline and after 4 months of treatment. The primary endpoint was the change from baseline in mean 24-hour systolic blood pressure.
cards.result: At month 4, mean 24-hour systolic blood pressure had decreased by 0.3 mmHg (95% CI −2.25 to 1.74) on celecoxib, increased by 3.7 mmHg (95% CI 1.72 to 5.58) on ibuprofen, and increased by 1.6 mmHg (95% CI −0.40 to 3.57) on naproxen; the celecoxib-versus-ibuprofen difference was −3.9 mmHg (P=0.0009). Among patients normotensive at baseline, the incidence of new hypertension was significantly higher on ibuprofen (23.2%) and naproxen (19.0%) than on celecoxib (10.3%), with odds ratios of 0.39 (P=0.004) and 0.49 (P=0.03) for celecoxib versus ibuprofen and naproxen respectively (relative measures, printed beside the absolute percentages). The authors concluded that among NSAIDs, celecoxib was associated with the best blood-pressure outcome overall.
cards.watchOut: Again a high-dose comparison (ibuprofen 600–800 mg three times daily) over 4 months, in older arthritis patients — the +3.7 mmHg is what sustained high-dose ibuprofen did to this group, not a prediction for a 200 mg tablet taken twice a week. A 3–4 mmHg population-average rise is small for an individual reading but is exactly the size that, sustained, shifts stroke and heart-failure rates across millions of users; and the new-hypertension percentages (about 1 in 4 previously normotensive ibuprofen patients within 4 months) are the most patient-legible numbers on this shelf.

Differential blood pressure effects of ibuprofen, naproxen, and celecoxib in patients with arthritis: the PRECISION-ABPM (Prospective Randomized Evaluation of Celecoxib Integrated Safety Versus Ibuprofen or Naproxen) trial. European Heart Journal. 2017. PMID: 29020251. Registry ID: NCT00346216. cards.headline: CNT Collaboration 2013 (280 placebo-controlled trials, 124,513 participants): ibuprofen carried the highest relative rate of upper gastrointestinal complications (RR 3.97) of the traditional NSAIDs, and every NSAID roughly doubled heart-failure risk
cards.summary: CNT Collaboration 2013 (280 placebo-controlled trials, 124,513 participants): ibuprofen carried the highest relative rate of upper gastrointestinal complications (RR 3.97) of the traditional NSAIDs, and every NSAID roughly doubled heart-failure risk
cards.type: Individual-participant-data meta-analysis of randomised trials (CNT Collaboration 2013)
cards.people: Meta-analyses by the Coxib and Traditional NSAID Trialists' (CNT) Collaboration of individual participant data from randomised trials of a coxib, diclofenac, ibuprofen or naproxen versus placebo or versus another NSAID: 280 trials of NSAID versus placebo (124,513 participants, 68,342 person-years) and 474 trials of one NSAID versus another (229,296 participants, 165,456 person-years). Main outcomes: major vascular events, major coronary events, stroke, mortality, heart failure and upper gastrointestinal complications.
cards.result: All rate ratios are relative measures from the NSAID-versus-placebo comparisons. Major vascular events were increased by coxibs (RR 1.37, 95% CI 1.14–1.66) and diclofenac (1.41, 1.12–1.78), mainly from increased major coronary events (coxibs 1.76, 1.05–2.96; diclofenac 1.70, 1.19–2.41); ibuprofen also increased major coronary events (RR 2.22, 1.10–4.48; P=0.0253) but not major vascular events overall (1.44, 0.89–2.33; P=0.14), and naproxen did not increase major vascular events (0.93, 0.69–1.27). Vascular death was significantly increased by coxibs (1.58, 1.00–2.49) and diclofenac (1.65, 1.02–2.68), non-significantly by ibuprofen (1.90, 0.56–6.41), and not by naproxen (1.08, 0.48–2.47). Heart failure risk was roughly doubled by all NSAIDs. Upper gastrointestinal complications were increased by coxibs (RR 1.81, 1.17–2.81), diclofenac (1.89, 1.16–3.09), ibuprofen (3.97, 2.22–7.10) and naproxen (4.22, 2.71–6.56). In absolute terms, the collaboration estimated that of 1,000 patients allocated a coxib or diclofenac for a year, three more would have major vascular events, one of which would be fatal.
cards.watchOut: The trials pooled here are mostly short and often used high doses, in patients who needed regular anti-inflammatory treatment — the relative risks describe sustained therapeutic-dose exposure, not a tablet after a run. Ibuprofen's coronary signal (RR 2.22) rests on few events with a wide interval, and its overall vascular and vascular-death estimates were non-significant; precision for ibuprofen specifically is the weakest of the four drugs. Conversely, 'non-significant' is not 'safe': the point estimates for ibuprofen point the same way as the drugs whose harms are established. The printed absolute anchor (3 extra major vascular events per 1,000 patient-years) is for coxibs/diclofenac, offered as the scale of translation from relative to absolute — do not reassign it to ibuprofen.
cards.source: Coxib and Traditional NSAID Trialists' (CNT) Collaboration (Bhala N et al.). Vascular and upper gastrointestinal effects of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs: meta-analyses of individual participant data from randomised trials. Lancet. 2013. PMID: 23726390. Registry ID: none in the record (individual-participant-data meta-analysis). cards.headline: Synthesis: daily high-dose ibuprofen matched other NSAIDs on cardiovascular events in PRECISION but was worst for blood pressure, kidneys and gut — 'safe every day' has no single answer, only a dose-and-person answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: daily high-dose ibuprofen matched other NSAIDs on cardiovascular events in PRECISION but was worst for blood pressure, kidneys and gut — 'safe every day' has no single answer, only a dose-and-person answer
cards.people: PRECISION (24,081 arthritis patients at increased cardiovascular risk, mean ibuprofen dose 2,045 mg/day, NCT00346216), its ambulatory blood-pressure substudy (444 patients), and the CNT Collaboration's individual-participant meta-analyses (280 placebo-controlled trials, 124,513 participants; 474 head-to-head trials, 229,296 participants).
cards.result: Cardiovascular: primary event rates 2.3% (celecoxib), 2.5% (naproxen), 2.7% (ibuprofen) over ~34 months — no demonstrated ibuprofen excess among NSAIDs (PRECISION); versus placebo, ibuprofen's major-vascular estimate was non-significant (RR 1.44) while its major-coronary estimate was elevated (RR 2.22) (CNT). Blood pressure and kidney: +3.7 mmHg mean 24-hour systolic pressure and 23.2% new hypertension on ibuprofen versus −0.3 mmHg and 10.3% on celecoxib (PRECISION-ABPM); renal events significantly fewer on celecoxib than ibuprofen (P=0.004) (PRECISION). Gut: upper gastrointestinal complications RR 3.97 (relative) for ibuprofen versus placebo — the highest of the traditional NSAIDs (CNT); gastrointestinal events significantly fewer on celecoxib than ibuprofen (P=0.002) (PRECISION). PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — GAP-E (harm profile). Every card here studies sustained, mostly high-dose use in people with arthritis or trial-level indications; none of them measures the risk of intermittent low-dose over-the-counter ibuprofen in healthy people, and this shelf must not be quoted as if it did — nor the reverse: 'no evidence at low dose' is not evidence of no harm, because the harms are dose- and duration-related pharmacology. Risk concentrates in exactly the people most likely to take it daily: older age, prior ulcer or bleeding, kidney disease, heart failure, uncontrolled blood pressure, and concurrent anticoagulants, aspirin, corticosteroids or alcohol. Strategies to reduce NSAID harm (gastroprotection, drug choice, monitoring) are homed on Shelf #330; acute dental and other short-term pain relief is Shelf #5287.
cards.source: Synthesis of Nissen SE et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 2016 (PMID: 27959716); Ruschitzka F et al. European Heart Journal. 2017 (PMID: 29020251); Coxib and Traditional NSAID Trialists' (CNT) Collaboration. Lancet. 2013 (PMID: 23726390).

shelves.title: Baker's cyst: draining the cyst and injecting steroid eases knee pain for a few weeks — one small randomised trial (n=60) and small series only, and about 1 in 8 cysts needed draining again
shelves.question: How is a Baker's cyst treated? I have a swelling behind my knee — will draining it or injecting steroid help, and will it come back? Clinical question underneath: in adults with a symptomatic popliteal (Baker's) cyst, usually alongside knee osteoarthritis, does ultrasound-guided aspiration with corticosteroid injection (into the cyst or into the joint) improve pain, function and cyst size, and how often does the cyst recur?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Osteoarthritis, Knee/complications · Popliteal Cyst/diagnostic imaging · Popliteal Cyst/therapy · Suction · Triamcinolone · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the honest summary is that needle treatment of a Baker's cyst probably eases knee pain in the short term, but the evidence is one small randomised trial with only 4 weeks of follow-up plus small uncontrolled or partly controlled series, and nothing here tests surgery. In the randomised trial (Di Sante 2012, PMID: 22525511; 60 patients with knee osteoarthritis and a Baker's cyst), ultrasound-guided aspiration plus corticosteroid injection kept pain lower at 4 weeks while electrical 'horizontal therapy' alone did not, and the combination arm had the lowest pain scores — yet the cyst's maximum axial area did not shrink in any group (P=0.259). A 40-patient comparison (Bandinelli 2012, PMID: 22200813) found cyst diameters fell further when the steroid was injected directly into the aspirated cyst than into the joint (p<0.01 at 4 and 8 weeks). The largest series (Smith 2015, PMID: 26502415; 47 patients) reported WOMAC scores improving from 48.55 to 17.15 after aspiration, fenestration and steroid injection, with 6 of 47 (12.7%) needing re-aspiration for recurrence and no infections. Because most of this is short-term and partly uncontrolled, the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): aspiration with corticosteroid injection likely gives short-term pain relief; durability beyond a few weeks and the value of arthroscopic surgery on the underlying knee are not established by the studies carded here.

cards.headline: Di Sante 2012 (randomised, n=60): aspiration + steroid injection kept pain down at 4 weeks, adding electrical therapy scored lowest pain — but the cyst's axial area did not shrink in any group
cards.summary: Di Sante 2012 (randomised, n=60): aspiration + steroid injection kept pain down at 4 weeks, adding electrical therapy scored lowest pain — but the cyst's axial area did not shrink in any group
cards.people: 60 outpatients with knee osteoarthritis and an ultrasound-confirmed Baker's cyst, randomised to ultrasound-guided cyst aspiration plus corticosteroid injection (Group A, n=20), horizontal therapy (an electrical physical therapy; Group B, n=20), or both (Group C, n=20). Pain (visual analogue scale), WOMAC function and ultrasound cyst measurements were taken at baseline, 1 week and 4 weeks.
cards.result: Patients in Groups A and C, but not Group B (electrical therapy alone), maintained a lower pain level at 4 weeks than at baseline, with significantly lower pain scores in Group C (the combination). On ultrasound, the cyst's maximum axial area did not change with treatment in any of the three groups (P=0.259); sagittal area measurements were influenced by time (P<0.01). The authors concluded the combined treatment performed best for pain, function and cyst dimension.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up was only 4 weeks, groups were 20 patients each, and the headline cyst-size measure (axial area) was flat — the benefit shown is short-term pain relief, not cyst disappearance or durability. The trial says nothing about recurrence over months or years.
cards.source: Di Sante L et al. Ultrasound-guided aspiration and corticosteroid injection compared to horizontal therapy for treatment of knee osteoarthritis complicated with Baker's cyst: a randomized, controlled trial. European Journal of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine. 2012. PMID: 22525511. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bandinelli 2012 (n=40): injecting the steroid directly into the aspirated cyst shrank it more than injecting the same dose into the knee joint (p<0.01 at 4 and 8 weeks)
cards.summary: Bandinelli 2012 (n=40): injecting the steroid directly into the aspirated cyst shrank it more than injecting the same dose into the knee joint (p<0.01 at 4 and 8 weeks)
cards.people: 40 patients with knee osteoarthritis and a symptomatic Baker's cyst; all had ultrasound-guided aspiration of the cyst, then 40 mg triamcinolone acetonide injected either directly into the cyst (n=20) or intra-articularly into the knee (n=20). Cyst diameters (longitudinal, transverse, thickness) and clinical signs (Rauschning and Lindgren score) were followed by ultrasound at baseline and 2, 4 and 8 weeks.
cards.result: All ultrasound measures of the cyst and the clinical score decreased significantly after treatment compared with baseline (p<0.001) and then stayed stable between 2 and 8 weeks. At 4 and 8 weeks, cyst diameters were lower when the steroid had been injected directly into the cyst than when it was injected into the joint (p<0.01).
cards.watchOut: Small, short (8 weeks) and not described as randomised; it compares injection site, not injection versus no treatment, so it cannot show how much of the improvement was the procedure itself. No recurrence or longer-term outcomes were reported.
cards.source: Bandinelli F et al. Longitudinal ultrasound and clinical follow-up of Baker's cysts injection with steroids in knee osteoarthritis. Clinical Rheumatology. 2012. PMID: 22200813. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Smith 2015 (series, n=47): aspiration, fenestration and steroid injection cut WOMAC scores from 48.55 to 17.15; 12.7% needed re-aspiration for recurrence, no infections
cards.summary: Smith 2015 (series, n=47): aspiration, fenestration and steroid injection cut WOMAC scores from 48.55 to 17.15; 12.7% needed re-aspiration for recurrence, no infections
cards.people: 47 patients treated from 2008 to 2011 with ultrasound-guided aspiration, fenestration and injection (UGAFI) of symptomatic popliteal cysts: aspiration through a spinal needle, fenestration of the cyst walls and septations, then injection of 1 mL (40 mg) triamcinolone (Kenalog, as named in the paper) and 2 mL 0.5% bupivacaine (Sensorcaine, as named in the paper) into the decompressed cyst. Outcomes were pre- and post-treatment WOMAC scores, recurrence, complications, cyst complexity and size.
cards.result: Mean total WOMAC score improved from 48.55 before aspiration to 17.15 at final follow-up (P<0.0001), with pain improving from 10.68 to 3.94, stiffness from 4.51 to 1.77 and physical function from 31.34 to 12.17 (all P<0.0001). There were 6 reaspirations for recurrence (12.7%), 1 patient went on to unicompartmental knee arthroplasty, and there were no infections or other complications.
cards.watchOut: A single-arm retrospective series: with no comparison group, some of the large score improvement may reflect natural fluctuation, the underlying arthritis care, or expectation effects. The 12.7% figure counts only recurrences that came back for re-aspiration, so true recurrence is at least this high.
cards.source: Smith MK et al. Treatment of Popliteal (Baker) Cysts With Ultrasound-Guided Aspiration, Fenestration, and Injection: Long-term Follow-up. Sports Health. 2015. PMID: 26502415. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: needle treatment probably relieves Baker's cyst pain for weeks; whether it lasts, and whether surgery does better, is untested in the studies carded here
cards.summary: Synthesis: needle treatment probably relieves Baker's cyst pain for weeks; whether it lasts, and whether surgery does better, is untested in the studies carded here
cards.people: One randomised trial (60 patients, 4 weeks; Di Sante 2012), one prospective injection-site comparison (40 patients, 8 weeks; Bandinelli 2012) and one retrospective series (47 patients; Smith 2015) — 147 patients in total, all with cysts mostly alongside knee osteoarthritis.
cards.result: Aspiration plus corticosteroid injection beat electrical therapy alone on pain at 4 weeks in the only randomised trial, though cyst axial area did not shrink (P=0.259); direct intra-cyst injection shrank cyst diameters more than intra-articular injection (p<0.01); the largest series showed large WOMAC gains with 12.7% re-aspiration for recurrence and no infections. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for short-term symptom relief. Nothing carded here measures outcomes beyond 8 weeks in a controlled way, and no carded study tests arthroscopic or open surgery against needle treatment.
cards.watchOut: Boundary: this shelf covers needle treatment (aspiration/injection) of the cyst itself. Surgical and arthroscopic treatment aimed at the underlying knee pathology is a separate question and is not carded here — the one arthroscopy series identified during the build could not be retrieved in full, so no surgical numbers are stated rather than guessed. Tier C: small, short, partly uncontrolled evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Di Sante L et al. European Journal of Physical and Rehabilitation Medicine. 2012 (PMID: 22525511); Bandinelli F et al. Clinical Rheumatology. 2012 (PMID: 22200813); Smith MK et al. Sports Health. 2015 (PMID: 26502415).

shelves.title: Calcium citrate vs carbonate in PPI users: citrate absorbs far better in the fasting acid-free gut (0.452 vs 0.042), but PPI exposure itself did not reduce absorption and no bone-outcome trial exists
shelves.question: In adults with osteoporosis, does calcium citrate improve absorption and bone outcomes compared with calcium carbonate in people taking proton pump inhibitors?
shelves.mesh: Achlorhydria · Adult · Aged · Calcium · Calcium Carbonate · Calcium Radioisotopes · Citrates · Citric Acid · Fasting · Female · Humans · Intestinal Absorption · Male · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: For absorption under acid-free conditions the physiology evidence favours citrate strongly; for people actually taking proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), and for bone outcomes, there is no direct trial evidence at all. The classic experiment (Recker 1985, PMID: 4000241) compared the two salts in fasting patients with achlorhydria (n = 11): fractional absorption was 0.452 for citrate versus 0.042 for carbonate (P < 0.0001), while in normal subjects the salts did not differ (0.243 vs 0.225) — and carbonate taken with breakfast was absorbed normally even without acid. A direct PPI test (Hansen 2010, PMID: 20578215; 21 postmenopausal women) found 30 days of omeprazole 40 mg did not decrease fractional calcium absorption at all (20–23% across visits, P = .07), undercutting the premise that PPI use creates the achlorhydric fasting problem. A practice review (van der Velde 2014, PMID: 25147494) reports intestinal absorption of citrate about 24% better than carbonate overall, and states plainly that data comparing the salts during simultaneous PPI use are lacking. No study in any carded record measures bone density or fractures by calcium salt in PPI users. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) — citrate is absorbed far better than carbonate when fasting without gastric acid, but benefit in PPI users, and any bone-outcome benefit, is untested.

cards.headline: Recker 1985: in fasting patients with achlorhydria (n = 11), fractional calcium absorption was 0.452 from citrate vs 0.042 from carbonate (P < 0.0001); in normal subjects the salts did not differ, and carbonate with breakfast absorbed normally
cards.summary: Recker 1985: in fasting patients with achlorhydria (n = 11), fractional calcium absorption was 0.452 from citrate vs 0.042 from carbonate (P < 0.0001); in normal subjects the salts did not differ, and carbonate with breakfast absorbed normally
cards.people: 11 fasting patients with achlorhydria and 9 fasting normal subjects, each studied with both calcium forms using a modified double-isotope procedure with 0.25 g of calcium as carrier. The achlorhydric group N = 11 is printed here because it is small.
cards.result: Mean fractional absorption (± SD) in achlorhydria was 0.452 ± 0.125 for the pH-adjusted citrate form and 0.042 ± 0.021 for carbonate (P < 0.0001). In normal subjects, absorption was 0.243 ± 0.049 for citrate and 0.225 ± 0.108 for carbonate (not significant). Carbonate absorption in achlorhydria was significantly lower than in normal subjects and lower than citrate in either group; citrate absorption in achlorhydria was significantly higher than in normal subjects. Calcium carbonate given as part of a normal breakfast was absorbed completely normally in the achlorhydric subjects. The author concludes carbonate absorption is impaired in achlorhydria under fasting conditions and carbonate may not be the ideal supplement in older persons, in whom achlorhydria is common.
cards.watchOut: Achlorhydria from atrophic gastritis is not the same as pharmacological acid suppression, the measurements were fasting single-dose physiology in 20 people in 1985, and the breakfast result shows the carbonate defect disappears with food — the exact conditions of the PPI question were not tested.
cards.source: Recker RR et al. Calcium absorption and achlorhydria. The New England Journal of Medicine. 1985. PMID: 4000241. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Achlorhydria · Adult · Aged · Calcium · Calcium Carbonate · Calcium Radioisotopes · Citrates · Citric Acid · Fasting · Female · Humans · Intestinal Absorption · Male · Middle Aged

cards.headline: Hansen 2010: 30 days of omeprazole 40 mg/day did not decrease fractional calcium absorption in 21 postmenopausal women (20% and 18% at baseline visits, 23% on omeprazole; P = .07)
cards.summary: Hansen 2010: 30 days of omeprazole 40 mg/day did not decrease fractional calcium absorption in 21 postmenopausal women (20% and 18% at baseline visits, 23% on omeprazole; P = .07)
cards.type: Physiological absorption study with PPI exposure (Hansen 2010)
cards.people: 21 postmenopausal women (at least 5 years past menopause, mean age 58 ± 7 years) not previously taking acid suppressants, each undergoing three 24-hour inpatient fractional calcium absorption studies by the dual stable-isotope method — two baseline studies a month apart, then a third after 30 days of omeprazole 40 mg/day — with identical study meals. N = 21, printed here because it is small.
cards.result: Fractional calcium absorption (mean ± SD) was 20% ± 10% at visit 1, 18% ± 10% at visit 2, and 23% ± 10% after 30 ± 3 days of daily omeprazole (P = .07, ANOVA) — no decrease. Age, gastric pH, serum omeprazole levels, adherence and 25-hydroxyvitamin D were unrelated to the change in absorption; only the 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D level at visit 2 was associated with the change (P = .049). The authors conclude PPI-associated hypochlorhydria does not decrease fractional calcium absorption after 30 days of continuous use, and that fracture mechanisms should be sought elsewhere.
cards.watchOut: Thirty days of omeprazole in 21 women with standardised meals does not exclude an absorption effect of years of PPI therapy or in fasting supplement-takers, and the study did not randomise citrate against carbonate — it tests whether PPI exposure itself lowers absorption, and found it did not.
cards.source: Hansen KE et al. Do proton pump inhibitors decrease calcium absorption? Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2010. PMID: 20578215. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: van der Velde 2014: citrate absorption is reported about 24% better than carbonate overall, and data comparing the two salts during simultaneous PPI use are lacking — stated plainly in the record
cards.summary: van der Velde 2014: citrate absorption is reported about 24% better than carbonate overall, and data comparing the two salts during simultaneous PPI use are lacking — stated plainly in the record
cards.people: Systematic practice review of calcium and vitamin D supplementation for daily practice, covering physiological studies, guidelines, meta-analyses, randomised trials and cohort studies; no single patient cohort is reported in the record.
cards.result: The record reports no head-to-head effect size for citrate versus carbonate in PPI users, and states that such data are lacking. It reports that intestinal absorption of calcium citrate is approximately 24% better than that of calcium carbonate, independent of intake with meals, and recommends tailoring supplementation to need (usually 500 mg/day to reach a total intake of about 1,200 mg/day, with 800 IU/day vitamin D). No bone-density or fracture comparison by calcium salt is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: The 24% figure is the review's summary of general absorption comparisons, not a PPI-population result; the review is carded chiefly because it states the PPI-specific evidence gap plainly, which is the central fact for this shelf's question.
cards.source: van der Velde RY et al. Calcium and vitamin D supplementation: state of the art for daily practice. Food & Nutrition Research. 2014. PMID: 25147494. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: citrate beats carbonate on absorption only in the fasting, acid-free gut; PPI exposure itself did not reduce absorption in the direct test, and no bone-outcome comparison exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: citrate beats carbonate on absorption only in the fasting, acid-free gut; PPI exposure itself did not reduce absorption in the direct test, and no bone-outcome comparison exists
cards.people: The carded evidence: one small physiological study in achlorhydria and normal subjects (20 people total; achlorhydric subgroup n = 11), one small PPI-exposure absorption study (21 postmenopausal women), and one systematic practice review (no cohort N documented in the record). Total documented participants are 41, above the small-N stamp threshold; each small study's N is printed on its card face.
cards.result: Fasting achlorhydria: citrate 0.452 vs carbonate 0.042 fractional absorption (Recker 1985), abolished by taking carbonate with food. On omeprazole: absorption 23% vs 18–20% at baseline, no decrease (Hansen 2010). Review position: citrate about 24% better absorbed overall; PPI-specific head-to-head data lacking; no bone outcomes by salt (van der Velde 2014). PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) for absorption in acid-free fasting conditions only.
cards.watchOut: Nothing on this shelf measures bone mineral density, fractures or falls, and nothing randomises PPI users between the salts: recommending citrate to a PPI user rests on extrapolating 1985 achlorhydria physiology that the one direct PPI study did not confirm.
cards.source: Synthesis of Recker RR et al. New England Journal of Medicine. 1985 (PMID: 4000241); Hansen KE et al. Journal of Bone and Mineral Research. 2010 (PMID: 20578215); van der Velde RY et al. Food & Nutrition Research. 2014 (PMID: 25147494).
