shelves.title: Bisphosphonates in osteoporosis with CKD stage 3 (SPLIT): bone density improves, but fracture benefit is unproven in stage 3 CKD and safety signals are unresolved
shelves.question: In adults with osteoporosis and chronic kidney disease stage 3, are bisphosphonates safe and effective versus no antiresorptive treatment?
shelves.mesh: Bone Density Conservation Agents · Denosumab · Diphosphonates · Female · Humans · Osteoporosis · Raloxifene Hydrochloride · Renal Insufficiency, Chronic · Teriparatide
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides by outcome and by CKD substage, and the split is named in the stamp. For bone mineral density the direction is favourable: the AHRQ systematic review (Wilson 2017, PMID: 28395318; 13 trials, n = 9,850) found bisphosphonates may slow loss of BMD, and a large propensity-matched cohort in stage 3B+ CKD found femoral-neck BMD gaining 2.65% per year more in bisphosphonate users than in matched non-users (Robinson 2021, PMID: 33739919). For fractures — the outcome that matters — no carded source demonstrates a reduction in stage 3 CKD: Wilson rates fracture effects unclear; the individual-patient meta-analysis of ibandronate trials (Whitlock 2024, PMID: 39381071; 7,428 participants, 27.5% stage G3A and 3.0% G3B) found an overall fracture hazard ratio of 0.871 (95% CI 0.746 to 1.018) but an increased fracture risk in the small G3B subgroup (HR 3.862, 95% CI 1.156 to 12.903), and a 2023 meta-analysis of stage 3–5 CKD and transplant trials concluded there is no evidence these medications reduce fracture risk (Leng 2023, PMID: 37387531). On safety, the IPD analysis found no effect on eGFR over 12 months but more hypocalcaemia (HR 1.324); the cohort found a 12% relative excess of CKD progression (subdistribution HR 1.12) and no increase in acute kidney injury, hypocalcaemia or gastrointestinal events. PROPOSED SPLIT: BMD improves, fracture benefit is unproven in stage 3 CKD, and safety signals (hypocalcaemia, possible CKD progression, a G3B fracture signal) are unresolved — randomised fracture-outcome data in stage 3 CKD do not exist in the carded records.

cards.headline: Wilson 2017 (AHRQ review, 13 trials, n = 9,850): bisphosphonates may slow loss of bone mineral density in CKD, but their effects on fractures and safety are unclear — and only 3 trials covered stage 3–5 CKD or dialysis
cards.summary: Wilson 2017 (AHRQ review, 13 trials, n = 9,850): bisphosphonates may slow loss of bone mineral density in CKD, but their effects on fractures and safety are unclear — and only 3 trials covered stage 3–5 CKD or dialysis
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (at least 6 months of follow-up) of osteoporosis medications (bisphosphonates, teriparatide, raloxifene, denosumab) versus placebo, usual care, or active control in patients with CKD, searched December 2006 through December 2016: 13 trials (n = 9,850) comprising kidney transplant recipients (6 trials), patients with stage 3 to 5 CKD or receiving dialysis (3 trials), and postmenopausal women with CKD (4 trials).
cards.result: Evidence showed that bisphosphonates may slow loss of bone mineral density among transplant recipients (moderate strength of evidence), but their effects on fractures and safety in transplant recipients and others with CKD are unclear. Raloxifene may prevent vertebral fractures but may not improve BMD (low strength of evidence). Effects of teriparatide and denosumab on BMD and fractures are unclear (very low strength of evidence), and these medications may increase risk for some safety outcomes. The authors note unclear rigor of evidence, possible reporting biases, and scant evidence among patients with stage 3 to 5 CKD, and conclude that effects of osteoporosis medications on BMD, fracture risk, and safety among patients with CKD are not clearly established.
cards.watchOut: Most of this review's bisphosphonate BMD signal comes from transplant recipients, not stage 3 CKD — for this shelf's exact population the review itself calls the evidence scant, so it cannot carry a claim of fracture protection.
cards.source: Wilson LM et al. Benefits and Harms of Osteoporosis Medications in Patients With Chronic Kidney Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Annals of internal medicine. 2017. PMID: 28395318. Registry ID: none in the record. systematic review and meta-analysis (wilson 2017) systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (at least 6 months of follow-up) of osteoporosis medications (bisphosphonates, teriparatide, raloxifene, denosumab) versus placebo, usual care, or active control in patients with ckd, searched december 2006 through december 2016: 13 trials (n = 9,850) comprising kidney transplant recipients (6 trials), patients with stage 3 to 5 ckd or receiving dialysis (3 trials), and postmenopausal women with ckd (4 trials). evidence showed that bisphosphonates may slow loss of bone mineral density among transplant recipients (moderate strength of evidence), but their effects on fractures and safety in transplant recipients and others with ckd are unclear. raloxifene may prevent vertebral fractures but may not improve bmd (low strength of evidence). effects of teriparatide and denosumab on bmd and fractures are unclear (very low strength of evidence), and these medications may increase risk for some safety outcomes. the authors note unclear rigor of evidence, possible reporting biases, and scant evidence among patients with stage 3 to 5 ckd, and conclude that effects of osteoporosis medications on bmd, fracture risk, and safety among patients with ckd are not clearly established. most of this review's bisphosphonate bmd signal comes from transplant recipients, not stage 3 ckd — for this shelf's exact population the review itself calls the evidence scant, so it cannot carry a claim of fracture protection. wilson lm et al. benefits and harms of osteoporosis medications in patients with chronic kidney disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis. annals of internal medicine. 2017. pmid: 28395318. registry id: none in the record. mesh: bone density conservation agents · denosumab · diphosphonates · female · humans · osteoporosis · raloxifene hydrochloride · renal insufficiency, chronic · teriparatide

cards.headline: Whitlock 2024 (individual-patient meta-analysis of ibandronate trials, 7,428 women): fracture hazard ratio 0.871 overall, but 3.862 in the small stage G3B subgroup; no effect on eGFR, more hypocalcaemia (HR 1.324)
cards.summary: Whitlock 2024 (individual-patient meta-analysis of ibandronate trials, 7,428 women): fracture hazard ratio 0.871 overall, but 3.862 in the small stage G3B subgroup; no effect on eGFR, more hypocalcaemia (HR 1.324)
cards.type: Individual patient-level meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials (Whitlock 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and individual patient-level meta-analysis of randomised, placebo-controlled trials with 100 or more participants of bisphosphonate therapy for primary osteoporosis/osteopenia; individual data were available for 7 studies, all of ibandronate. Of 7,428 participants (5,010 ibandronate, 2,418 placebo), 100% were female and 98.6% white; mean eGFR was 69.1 mL/min/1.73 m2, with 14.5% stage G1, 54.9% G2, 27.5% G3A, 3.0% G3B and 0.2% G4 CKD; there were 740 fracture events.
cards.result: Ibandronate increased hip and lumbar spine bone mineral density and decreased the risk of fracture in the overall population (hazard ratio (HR) 0.871, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.746, 1.018) — a relative estimate whose confidence interval crosses 1 — but in patients with stage G3B CKD it increased the risk of fracture (HR 3.862, 95% CI 1.156, 12.903). Ibandronate did not impact eGFR over 12 months but increased the risk of hypocalcemia (calcium <2.00 mmol/L, approximately <8.0 mg/dL) (HR 1.324, 95% CI 1.056, 1.660), with no evidence of effect modification by CKD stage for safety (all tests of interaction p > 0.05). Limitations printed in the record: clinically significant heterogeneity, lack of long-term follow-up and bone biopsy results, and limited representation of stage G4 and G5 CKD.
cards.watchOut: Only one bisphosphonate (ibandronate), only women, and the stage 3 patients are mostly G3A — the G3B harm signal rests on 3.0% of participants, so it is a warning flag rather than proof of harm, and nothing here speaks to men or to other bisphosphonates.

cards.headline: Leng 2023 (meta-analysis of 27 studies in stage 3–5 CKD and transplant recipients): alendronate raised lumbar spine BMD in stage 3–4 CKD, but there is no evidence these medications reduce fracture risk
cards.summary: Leng 2023 (meta-analysis of 27 studies in stage 3–5 CKD and transplant recipients): alendronate raised lumbar spine BMD in stage 3–4 CKD, but there is no evidence these medications reduce fracture risk
cards.people: Meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials of osteoporosis medications in adult patients with stage 3–5 CKD or kidney transplant recipients, searched through October 21, 2022: 27 studies met the inclusion criteria and 19 were included in the meta-analysis, reporting BMD and T scores at 6 and 12 months, fracture risk, and adverse events.
cards.result: In stage 3–4 CKD patients, alendronate increased lumbar spine bone mineral density. In patients at stage 5 CKD undergoing hemodialysis, alendronate and raloxifene increased lumbar spine BMD. After 6 months, the BMD of kidney transplant recipients was significantly increased; however, there was no difference after 12 months, and the risk of fracture did not reduce. The authors conclude there is no evidence that these medications reduce the risk of fracture and their effect on BMD and fracture remains unproven, that the medications may increase the incidence of adverse events and their safety needs further evaluation, and that no definitive conclusion about efficacy and safety can be drawn in this population.
cards.watchOut: This analysis pools bisphosphonates with other drug classes and pools CKD stages 3–5 with transplant recipients, so its null fracture conclusion is about the mixed literature, not a clean stage-3 bisphosphonate test — but it is concordant with the other carded reviews that fracture benefit is unproven.
cards.source: Leng Y et al. Efficacy and safety of medications for osteoporosis in kidney transplant recipients or patients with chronic kidney disease: A meta-analysis. cards.headline: Robinson 2021 (propensity-matched cohort, stage 3B+ CKD): bisphosphonate users gained 2.65% per year more femoral-neck BMD, but hip fracture was not reduced (HR 1.25, attributed by the authors to confounding) and CKD progression was 12% relatively higher
cards.summary: Robinson 2021 (propensity-matched cohort, stage 3B+ CKD): bisphosphonate users gained 2.65% per year more femoral-neck BMD, but hip fracture was not reduced (HR 1.25, attributed by the authors to confounding) and CKD progression was 12% relatively higher
cards.people: New-user propensity score-matched cohort study using UK primary care records (Clinical Practice Research Datalink GOLD) linked to hospital records, plus Danish Odense University Hospital databases for the BMD work package; eligible patients had at least one eGFR measurement <45 ml/minute/1.73 m2 (stage 3B or worse), with work packages covering CKD progression, hip fracture, safety events (acute kidney injury, hypocalcaemia, hypophosphataemia, gastrointestinal events), and femoral-neck BMD change.
cards.result: Bisphosphonate use was associated with an excess risk of chronic kidney disease progression (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.12, 95% confidence interval 1.02 to 1.24) but did not increase the probability of the other safety outcomes studied. For hip fracture, results suggested bisphosphonate use increased fracture risk (hazard ratio 1.25, 95% confidence interval 1.13 to 1.39), but sensitivity analyses suggested this was related to unresolved confounding, and bias analyses suggested the findings were due to inappropriate adjustment for pre-treatment risk. Bisphosphonates improved bone mineral density, with an average 2.65% (95% confidence interval 1.32% to 3.99%) greater gain in femoral neck bone mineral density per year in users than in matched non-users. The authors conclude bisphosphonate therapy increased BMD but antifracture effectiveness was not demonstrated, and that randomised trial data are needed in stage 3B+ CKD.
cards.watchOut: Observational: bisphosphonate users differ from non-users in fracture risk and kidney trajectory (confounding by indication, which the authors themselves invoke for the fracture result), and the cohort is stage 3B+, one substage beyond this shelf's stage 3 question — it informs, but cannot settle, safety or efficacy.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in stage 3 CKD, bisphosphonates improve bone mineral density but no carded source shows fewer fractures, and safety is not fully settled (more hypocalcaemia; a possible CKD-progression signal; one small G3B fracture signal)
cards.summary: Synthesis: in stage 3 CKD, bisphosphonates improve bone mineral density but no carded source shows fewer fractures, and safety is not fully settled (more hypocalcaemia; a possible CKD-progression signal; one small G3B fracture signal)
cards.people: The carded evidence: an AHRQ systematic review of 13 trials (n = 9,850, only 3 trials in stage 3–5 CKD/dialysis), an individual-patient meta-analysis of 7 ibandronate trials (7,428 women; 27.5% G3A, 3.0% G3B), a meta-analysis of 27 studies in stage 3–5 CKD and transplant recipients (19 pooled), and a propensity-matched cohort in stage 3B+ CKD. Total carded participants exceed 17,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is that almost none of the randomised data were collected in stage 3 CKD for fracture outcomes, printed here.
cards.result: BMD: bisphosphonates may slow BMD loss (Wilson 2017), alendronate raised lumbar spine BMD in stage 3–4 CKD (Leng 2023), and users gained 2.65% per year more femoral-neck BMD than matched non-users (Robinson 2021). Fractures: overall HR 0.871 (95% CI 0.746 to 1.018) for ibandronate with HR 3.862 in the small G3B subgroup (Whitlock 2024); no fracture reduction demonstrated in the other reviews. Safety: no eGFR effect over 12 months but hypocalcaemia HR 1.324 (Whitlock 2024); CKD progression subdistribution HR 1.12 in the cohort, with no excess acute kidney injury or gastrointestinal events (Robinson 2021). PROPOSED SPLIT — BMD benefit versus unproven fracture benefit and unresolved safety in stage 3 CKD.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap on this shelf is a trial that does not exist in the carded records: a randomised, fracture-outcome trial of a bisphosphonate conducted in stage 3 CKD itself. Until one exists, BMD is a surrogate standing in for the outcome patients care about.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wilson LM et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28395318); Whitlock R et al. Canadian journal of kidney health and disease. 2024 (PMID: 39381071); Leng Y et al. Journal of investigative medicine : the official publication of the American Federation for Clinical Research. 2023 (PMID: 37387531); Robinson DE et al. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2021 (PMID: 33739919).

shelves.title: Baclofen versus tizanidine after stroke: no evidence baclofen is better — the only direct comparisons (270 patients, mixed multiple sclerosis and cerebrovascular lesions) found the two drugs equally effective on muscle tone
shelves.question: Does oral baclofen help post-stroke spasticity better than tizanidine?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anticonvulsants/therapeutic use · Baclofen/therapeutic use · Cerebrovascular Disorders/drug therapy · Clonidine/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Diazepam/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Multiple Sclerosis/drug therapy · Muscle Relaxants, Central/therapeutic use · Muscle Spasticity/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: There is no randomised trial of oral baclofen against tizanidine in post-stroke spasticity alone — that absence is the finding of this shelf, and the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) because of it. The only head-to-head synthesis (Groves 1998, PMID: 10186943) pooled individual patient data from ten double-blind comparative trials (270 patients) of tizanidine against baclofen (seven trials) or diazepam (three trials) in patients with multiple sclerosis or cerebrovascular lesions: on total and lower-body Ashworth scores the drugs reduced spasticity similarly, muscle strength was affected less by tizanidine, and investigators judged tizanidine better tolerated. Nothing in that record separates the cerebrovascular patients' results, so it cannot be quoted as a post-stroke result — it is printed that way on the card. The systematic review of oral antispastics in nonprogressive neurologic disease (Montané 2004, PMID: 15505149) is blunter about the whole field: twelve trials, 469 patients, only two direct drug-versus-drug comparisons, small and short trials of inadequate methodologic quality, evidence 'weak', efficacy 'marginal if any', and adverse effects (drowsiness, sedation, muscle weakness) common. The post-stroke-specific review (Olvey 2010, PMID: 21353101) confirms the gap from the other side: of 54 studies of upper-limb spasticity after stroke, 51 concerned botulinum toxin; the oral-drug record is a single tizanidine study and two intrathecal baclofen studies, with no oral head-to-head trial identified. A randomised trial of early baclofen after stroke (the Baclotox study, botulinum toxin versus oral baclofen) is in progress as a protocol, but it does not compare baclofen with tizanidine either. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): on current evidence baclofen is not shown to help post-stroke spasticity better than tizanidine; the two look equivalent where they have been compared at all, in mixed populations.

cards.headline: Groves 1998: pooling the head-to-head trials (270 patients with multiple sclerosis or cerebrovascular lesions), tizanidine and baclofen reduced spasticity similarly on Ashworth scores — baclofen was not better
cards.summary: Groves 1998: pooling the head-to-head trials (270 patients with multiple sclerosis or cerebrovascular lesions), tizanidine and baclofen reduced spasticity similarly on Ashworth scores — baclofen was not better
cards.type: Meta-analysis of double-blind comparative trials with individual patient data (Groves 1998)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of controlled, double-blind, randomised comparative studies with individual patient data, drawn from the European sponsor's trial records: ten trials involving 270 patients with multiple sclerosis or cerebrovascular lesions met the criteria (seven used baclofen as comparator, three used diazepam); outcomes were the Ashworth Rating Scale for muscle tone, muscle strength, and a global tolerability rating. The record does not report the cerebrovascular subgroup separately — printed on the face, because this shelf's question is specifically post-stroke.
cards.result: As measured by total and lower-body Ashworth scores, tizanidine had similar spasticity-reducing effects to both baclofen and diazepam. Muscle strength was affected less by tizanidine than by either comparator, and investigators judged tizanidine to have greater tolerability; muscle strength improved in all three treatment groups, most with tizanidine. The record reports no numerical effect size for the baclofen-versus-tizanidine tone comparison beyond this equivalence statement — printed plainly rather than estimated. Within the limits of these comparisons, the three drugs were equally effective in decreasing excessive muscle tone.
cards.watchOut: Sponsor-held trial records, a 1998 evidence base, and a mixed multiple-sclerosis/cerebrovascular population: this is the best head-to-head evidence available and it still cannot answer the post-stroke question directly.
cards.source: Groves L et al. Tizanidine treatment of spasticity: a meta-analysis of controlled, double-blind, comparative studies with baclofen and diazepam. Advances in therapy. 1998. PMID: 10186943. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Montané 2004: systematic review of oral antispastics — 12 trials, 469 patients, only two direct drug comparisons; the reviewers call the evidence weak and any efficacy marginal, with adverse effects common
cards.summary: Montané 2004: systematic review of oral antispastics — 12 trials, 469 patients, only two direct drug comparisons; the reviewers call the evidence weak and any efficacy marginal, with adverse effects common
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised controlled trials (Montané 2004)
cards.people: Systematic review of double-blind randomised controlled trials of oral antispastic drugs in nonprogressive neurologic disease: twelve studies (469 patients) — six on stroke, three on spinal cord diseases, three on cerebral palsy. Tizanidine was assessed in four trials (276 patients, 142 exposed), baclofen in three (70 patients, 55 exposed), dantrolene in four, diazepam in two and gabapentin in one; ten trials were placebo-controlled and only two were direct comparisons between drugs.
cards.result: Most trials were small, short and of inadequate methodologic quality; efficacy outcome variables were heterogeneous and only four reports described the magnitude of the antispastic effect. The incidence of adverse drug effects (drowsiness, sedation and muscle weakness) was high. The authors conclude that evidence on the efficacy of oral antispastic drugs in nonprogressive neurologic disease is weak, does not include evaluation of patients' quality of life, and that if any efficacy exists it is marginal. No baclofen-versus-tizanidine effect size is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: A 2004 verdict on an old trial base: it tells the reader how much weight the baclofen–tizanidine comparison can bear (very little), not which drug a given patient should take — tolerability and comorbidity decide that in practice.

systematic review of randomised controlled trials (montané 2004) systematic review of double-blind randomised controlled trials of oral antispastic drugs in nonprogressive neurologic disease: twelve studies (469 patients) — six on stroke, three on spinal cord diseases, three on cerebral palsy. tizanidine was assessed in four trials (276 patients, 142 exposed), baclofen in three (70 patients, 55 exposed), dantrolene in four, diazepam in two and gabapentin in one; ten trials were placebo-controlled and only two were direct comparisons between drugs. most trials were small, short and of inadequate methodologic quality; efficacy outcome variables were heterogeneous and only four reports described the magnitude of the antispastic effect. the incidence of adverse drug effects (drowsiness, sedation and muscle weakness) was high. the authors conclude that evidence on the efficacy of oral antispastic drugs in nonprogressive neurologic disease is weak, does not include evaluation of patients' quality of life, and that if any efficacy exists it is marginal. no baclofen-versus-tizanidine effect size is reported in the record. a 2004 verdict on an old trial base: it tells the reader how much weight the baclofen–tizanidine comparison can bear (very little), not which drug a given patient should take — tolerability and comorbidity decide that in practice. montané e et al. oral antispastic drugs in nonprogressive neurologic diseases: a systematic review. neurology. 2004. pmid: 15505149. registry id: none in the record. mesh: administration, oral · drug-related side effects and adverse reactions · humans · muscle spasticity/drug therapy/etiology · muscle weakness/chemically induced · nervous system diseases/complications · parasympatholytics/administration & dosage/adverse effects · quality of life · randomized controlled trials as topic/standards/statistics & numerical data · sleep stages/drug effects · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Olvey 2010: in post-stroke upper-limb spasticity specifically, 51 of 54 studies were botulinum toxin — the oral record is one tizanidine study and two intrathecal baclofen studies, with no oral baclofen-versus-tizanidine trial at all
cards.summary: Olvey 2010: in post-stroke upper-limb spasticity specifically, 51 of 54 studies were botulinum toxin — the oral record is one tizanidine study and two intrathecal baclofen studies, with no oral baclofen-versus-tizanidine trial at all
cards.type: Systematic review of post-stroke spasticity pharmacotherapy (Olvey 2010)
cards.people: Systematic review of clinical trials (1995–2010) of contemporary pharmacologic therapies for upper-limb spasticity after stroke: 113 articles identified, 54 studies included (23 randomised controlled trials and 31 open-label, nonrandomised or observational studies), of which 51 involved botulinum toxin treatment.
cards.result: Thirty-eight trials reported a significant reduction in spasticity with botulinum toxin versus baseline or placebo (P < 0.05), and one head-to-head study found botulinum toxin superior to oral tizanidine (P < 0.001). For the drugs in this shelf's question, the post-stroke record consists of one study of oral tizanidine reporting significant reductions in upper-limb spasticity after 16 weeks (P < 0.001) and two studies of intrathecal (not oral) baclofen reporting significant reductions after 12 months (all P < 0.001). No study comparing oral baclofen with tizanidine after stroke is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Intrathecal baclofen is a different treatment from oral baclofen (implanted pump, selected severe cases) and must not be read across to the oral comparison this shelf asks about.
cards.source: Olvey EL et al. Contemporary pharmacologic treatments for spasticity of the upper limb after stroke: a systematic review. Clinical therapeutics. 2010. PMID: 21353101. cards.headline: Synthesis: baclofen is not shown to be better than tizanidine after stroke — the drugs look equivalent on tone in mixed-population comparisons, and the post-stroke head-to-head trial does not exist
cards.summary: Synthesis: baclofen is not shown to be better than tizanidine after stroke — the drugs look equivalent on tone in mixed-population comparisons, and the post-stroke head-to-head trial does not exist
cards.people: The carded evidence: one individual-patient meta-analysis of the head-to-head trials (270 patients, multiple sclerosis or cerebrovascular lesions, not separated), one systematic review of oral antispastics in nonprogressive neurologic disease (12 trials, 469 patients, six of them stroke trials but only two drug-versus-drug comparisons in the whole set), and one post-stroke-specific systematic review (54 studies, no oral head-to-head). Review populations overlap, so no summed N is claimed; every component is small and old, which is what the stamp records.
cards.result: Tizanidine and baclofen had similar effects on Ashworth muscle-tone scores in the pooled head-to-head trials, with less effect on muscle strength and better judged tolerability for tizanidine (Groves 1998). The wider oral-antispastic literature is rated weak with marginal efficacy and common sedation and weakness (Montané 2004), and the post-stroke literature contains no oral baclofen-versus-tizanidine comparison (Olvey 2010). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): no basis to prefer baclofen over tizanidine for post-stroke spasticity on efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence in old, small, mixed-population trials is not proof of equivalence after stroke — it is the absence of a demonstrated difference, and individual patients still differ in sedation, weakness, liver monitoring (tizanidine) and withdrawal risk (baclofen), none of which these records quantify for stroke.
cards.source: Synthesis of Groves L et al. Advances in therapy. 1998 (PMID: 10186943); Montané E et al. Neurology. 2004 (PMID: 15505149); Olvey EL et al. Clinical therapeutics. 2010 (PMID: 21353101).

shelves.title: Gabapentin plus nortriptyline for neuropathic pain: better than either drug alone by 0.6–0.9 points in the one direct crossover trial
shelves.question: Does combining gabapentin with nortriptyline work better than either drug alone for neuropathic pain?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Amines · Analgesics · Antidepressive Agents, Tricyclic · Canada · Cross-Over Studies · Cyclohexanecarboxylic Acids · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Gabapentin · Humans · Least-Squares Analysis · Linear Models · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia · Nortriptyline · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). One double-blind crossover trial answers the question directly: in 47 analysed patients with diabetic polyneuropathy or postherpetic neuralgia, mean daily pain at maximum tolerated dose was 2.3 on the gabapentin–nortriptyline combination versus 3.2 on gabapentin alone and 2.9 on nortriptyline alone (combination lower by 0.9 points versus gabapentin, P = 0.001, and by 0.6 points versus nortriptyline, P = 0.02, on a 0–10 scale). The Cochrane review of combination pharmacotherapy found this was the only trial of this specific pairing (56 participants) among 21 combination studies, and — while several combinations beat their single agents — declined to recommend any one specific combination because trials were few, small and short. A second Gilron crossover trial of a different pairing (gabapentin plus morphine) found the same pattern — combination pain 3.06 versus 4.15 (gabapentin) and 3.70 (morphine) — supporting the combination principle without adding a second trial of this pairing. Dry mouth was the commonest adverse event on nortriptyline-containing treatment. A single direct trial caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the combination works better than either drug alone, by about 0.6–0.9 points on a 0–10 pain scale.

cards.headline: Gilron 2009: combination pain was 2.3 versus 3.2 on gabapentin alone and 2.9 on nortriptyline alone at maximum tolerated dose — significantly lower than either (56 randomised, 47 analysed; Ns on the face)
cards.summary: Gilron 2009: combination pain was 2.3 versus 3.2 on gabapentin alone and 2.9 on nortriptyline alone at maximum tolerated dose — significantly lower than either (56 randomised, 47 analysed; Ns on the face)
cards.people: Patients with diabetic polyneuropathy or postherpetic neuralgia and daily pain of at least 4/10, treated at one Canadian site: 56 randomised to sequences of oral gabapentin, nortriptyline and their combination, each for a 6-week period titrated to maximum tolerated dose; 45 completed all three periods and 47 completed at least two and were analysed for the primary outcome.
cards.result: Mean daily pain (0–10) was 5.4 (95% CI 5.0 to 5.8) at baseline and, at maximum tolerated dose, 3.2 (2.5 to 3.8) for gabapentin, 2.9 (2.4 to 3.4) for nortriptyline and 2.3 (1.8 to 2.8) for combination treatment. Pain on the combination was significantly lower than on gabapentin (−0.9, 95% CI −1.4 to −0.3, P = 0.001) or nortriptyline alone (−0.6, 95% CI −1.1 to −0.1, P = 0.02). The most common adverse event was dry mouth, significantly less frequent on gabapentin than on nortriptyline (P < 0.0001) or the combination (P < 0.0001). No serious adverse events were recorded.
cards.watchOut: One site, one trial, 47 analysed patients, and doses pushed to each person's maximum tolerated dose — a design that maximises the chance of showing a difference and may not match ordinary fixed-dose prescribing.
cards.source: Gilron I et al. Nortriptyline and gabapentin, alone and in combination for neuropathic pain: a double-blind, randomised controlled crossover trial. Lancet. 2009. PMID: 19796802. Registry ID: ISRCTN73178636. cards.headline: Chaparro 2012 (Cochrane): this pairing rests on exactly one trial (56 participants) — several combinations beat single agents, but the review recommends no specific combination
cards.summary: Chaparro 2012 (Cochrane): this pairing rests on exactly one trial (56 participants) — several combinations beat single agents, but the review recommends no specific combination
cards.people: Cochrane review of 21 randomised double-blind studies of two-drug combinations for neuropathic pain in adults, including four studies (578 participants) of an opioid with gabapentin or pregabalin, two (77 participants) of an opioid with a tricyclic, and one (56 participants) of gabapentin with nortriptyline — the Gilron 2009 trial carded above.
cards.result: Meta-analysis was possible for only one comparison — gabapentin plus opioid versus gabapentin alone (386 participants, two studies) — which showed modest but statistically significant superiority of the combination, with significantly more side-effect-related dropouts than gabapentin alone. For gabapentin plus nortriptyline the review rests on the single 56-participant trial and reports no separate pooled effect size for it; none is printed here. The authors conclude that multiple good-quality studies show superior efficacy of two-drug combinations, but the number of studies for any one combination, and limited trial size and duration, preclude recommending any one specific combination.
cards.watchOut: A review whose caution is the finding: most combinations pair drugs that share sedation and cognitive side effects, and dropout rates for combinations were similar or higher — efficacy gains can be bought with tolerability losses.
cards.source: Chaparro LE et al. Combination pharmacotherapy for the treatment of neuropathic pain in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2012. PMID: 22786518. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: 57 patients (35 with painful diabetic neuropathy, 22 with postherpetic neuralgia) in a randomised, double-blind, active placebo-controlled, four-period crossover trial of lorazepam (active placebo), sustained-release morphine, gabapentin and the gabapentin–morphine combination, each for 5 weeks; 41 completed the trial. This card is a different drug pairing, carded as support for the combination principle only.
cards.result: Mean daily pain at maximum tolerated dose was 5.72 at baseline, 4.49 with placebo, 4.15 with gabapentin, 3.70 with morphine and 3.06 with the gabapentin–morphine combination (P < 0.05 for the combination versus placebo, gabapentin and morphine). Short-Form McGill scores were 14.4 (placebo), 10.7 (gabapentin), 10.7 (morphine) and 7.5 (combination). Maximum tolerated doses of each drug were lower in combination than alone. The combination caused more constipation than gabapentin alone and more dry mouth than morphine alone.
cards.watchOut: Morphine is not nortriptyline: this card cannot substitute for a second trial of the shelf's own pairing, and it comes from the same research group as the anchor trial, so it is supportive rather than independent replication.

shelves.title: Tapentadol versus oxycodone for low back pain with a neuropathic component: SPLIT — the trial (against oxycodone/naloxone) favours tapentadol, routine-practice data favour the oxycodone combination
shelves.question: Does tapentadol work better than oxycodone for chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Opioid · Delayed-Action Preparations · Endpoint Determination · Female · Humans · Low Back Pain · Male · Middle Aged · Naloxone · Narcotic Antagonists · Neuralgia · Oxycodone · Pain Measurement · Phenols · Tapentadol
shelves.balance: SPLIT. First, a correction the shelf must carry: every head-to-head record fetched compares tapentadol prolonged release with oxycodone/naloxone prolonged release — a fixed oxycodone combination product — not with oxycodone alone, and no carded record tests tapentadol against plain oxycodone in this condition. In the one randomised trial (open-label, phase 3b/4, in opioid-naive patients with severe chronic low back pain and a neuropathic component), tapentadol was noninferior on pain change and, in confirmatory analysis, superior (97.5% repeated confidence interval for the difference −1.820 to −0.184; P = 0.003 for superiority), with significantly better neuropathic-symptom scores and gastrointestinal tolerability, and lower constipation and vomiting in its companion tolerability report. Against that, a blinded end-point analysis of German Pain Registry routine data (128 patients started on oxycodone/naloxone, 133 on tapentadol) found the composite benefit–risk end point significantly favoured oxycodone/naloxone (39.8% versus 25.6%; odds ratio 1.93, a relative measure; P = 0.014), driven by superior analgesic response rates at stricter thresholds. A sponsored open-label trial says tapentadol is better; routine-practice data say the oxycodone combination is at least as good. PROPOSED SPLIT (randomised trial: tapentadol benefit; routine-data analysis: oxycodone/naloxone benefit) — and the comparison actually tested is against oxycodone/naloxone, not oxycodone alone.

cards.headline: Baron 2016 (effectiveness): tapentadol PR was noninferior — and on confirmatory analysis superior — to oxycodone/naloxone PR for pain in severe chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component
cards.summary: Baron 2016 (effectiveness): tapentadol PR was noninferior — and on confirmatory analysis superior — to oxycodone/naloxone PR for pain in severe chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component
cards.people: Non-opioid-pretreated patients with severe chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component (average pain intensity at least 6/10; painDETECT positive or unclear), randomised open-label to twice-daily tapentadol PR 50 mg or oxycodone/naloxone PR 10 mg/5 mg, with 21-day titration (maximum twice-daily tapentadol PR 250 mg, or oxycodone/naloxone PR 40 mg/20 mg plus oxycodone PR 10 mg) then 9 weeks at target dose. The record does not state the total randomised N, and none is printed here.
cards.result: For the primary end point (change in average pain intensity from baseline to final evaluation), tapentadol PR was noninferior to oxycodone/naloxone PR (97.5% repeated confidence interval for tapentadol minus oxycodone/naloxone: −1.820 to −0.184; P < 0.001 for noninferiority), and the same interval yielded confirmatory evidence of superiority (P = 0.003). Improvements in painDETECT and Neuropathic Pain Symptom Inventory scores were significantly greater with tapentadol PR (all P ≤ 0.005). The record reports the between-group interval rather than each group's absolute pain change, so no absolute change is printed here.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, industry-era trial against a combination product whose naloxone component caps oxycodone dosing — not a test against oxycodone alone, and unblinded pain scores in a sponsored trial are exactly where expectation effects live.
cards.source: Baron R et al. Effectiveness of Tapentadol Prolonged Release (PR) Compared with Oxycodone/Naloxone PR for the Management of Severe Chronic Low Back Pain with a Neuropathic Component: A Randomized, Controlled, Open-Label, Phase 3b/4 Study. Pain Pract. 2016. PMID: 26095455. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Baron 2016 (tolerability): constipation and vomiting were significantly less frequent on tapentadol, and quality-of-life gains were significantly greater — the same trial's companion report
cards.summary: Baron 2016 (tolerability): constipation and vomiting were significantly less frequent on tapentadol, and quality-of-life gains were significantly greater — the same trial's companion report
cards.type: Randomised, controlled, open-label trial — tolerability report (Baron 2016)
cards.people: The same randomised, open-label trial population (severe chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component, opioid-naive), comparing tapentadol PR with oxycodone/naloxone PR over titration plus 9 weeks; the primary tolerability end point was change in the Patient Assessment of Constipation Symptoms (PAC-SYM) total score. Total randomised N is again not stated in the record.
cards.result: PAC-SYM change was noninferior for tapentadol (97.5% repeated confidence interval −0.259 to 0.121; upper limit below the 0.7 margin). Incidences of constipation and vomiting were significantly lower with tapentadol PR than with oxycodone/naloxone PR (P ≤ 0.045; the record gives no percentages, and none are printed here). Improvements in the SF-12 physical component summary and the EuroQol-5 Dimension health status index and health state assessment were significantly greater with tapentadol PR (P ≤ 0.024).
cards.watchOut: A companion report of the same trial, not a second trial: it deepens the tolerability picture (the comparison product contains naloxone specifically to protect the bowel, which makes the constipation result notable) but adds no independent patients.
cards.source: Baron R et al. Pain Pract. 2016. PMID: 26554630. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ueberall 2016: in routine-practice registry data the direction reversed — the composite benefit–risk response favoured oxycodone/naloxone, 39.8% versus 25.6% (odds ratio 1.93, relative)
cards.summary: Ueberall 2016: in routine-practice registry data the direction reversed — the composite benefit–risk response favoured oxycodone/naloxone, 39.8% versus 25.6% (odds ratio 1.93, relative)
cards.type: Blinded end-point analysis of registry routine data (Ueberall 2016)
cards.people: Blinded end-point analysis of randomly selected 12-week prospective open-label routine data from the German Pain Registry: adults with chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component who started oxycodone/naloxone (n = 128) or tapentadol (n = 133) in line with German prescribing information in 2015; baseline and pretreatment characteristics were comparable between the groups.
cards.result: The primary composite end point (at least 30% improvement in pain, pain-related disability and quality of life, plus normal bowel function, no central nervous system side effects and no adverse-event discontinuation) was formally noninferior for oxycodone/naloxone versus tapentadol and was reached significantly more often: 39.8% versus 25.6% (odds ratio 1.93, a relative measure; P = 0.014). At stricter response thresholds the analgesic advantage grew: at least 50% pain response in 67.2% versus 54.1% (P = 0.031) and at least 70% in 39.1% versus 15.8% (P < 0.001). Tolerability components (normal bowel function 68.0% versus 72.2%; no CNS side effects 91.4% versus 89.5%; completion without adverse-event discontinuation 93.0% versus 92.5%) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised: doctors chose the drug, so confounding by indication is unavoidable, and a composite end point can be carried by its softest components — but it is the only carded evidence from ordinary practice, and it points the other way.
cards.source: Ueberall MA et al. Efficacy and tolerability balance of oxycodone/naloxone and tapentadol in chronic low back pain with a neuropathic component: a blinded end point analysis of randomly selected routine data from 12-week prospective open-label observations. J Pain Res. 2016. PMID: 27881925. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — the randomised trial favours tapentadol, routine-practice data favour oxycodone/naloxone, and neither tested oxycodone alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — the randomised trial favours tapentadol, routine-practice data favour oxycodone/naloxone, and neither tested oxycodone alone
cards.people: The carded evidence: one open-label randomised trial reported in two papers (total N not stated in either record) and one registry routine-data analysis (261 patients). No carded record compares tapentadol with oxycodone alone in this condition.
cards.result: Trial: pain difference interval −1.820 to −0.184 favouring tapentadol, with less constipation and vomiting. Registry: composite response 39.8% (oxycodone/naloxone) versus 25.6% (tapentadol), odds ratio 1.93 relative. PROPOSED SPLIT (trial: tapentadol benefit; routine data: oxycodone/naloxone benefit).
cards.watchOut: Anyone citing this shelf for 'tapentadol beats oxycodone' is overstating twice over: the comparator was oxycodone/naloxone, and the only non-trial dataset found the opposite.
cards.source: Synthesis of Baron R et al. Pain Pract. 2016 (PMID: 26095455); Baron R et al. Pain Pract. 2016 (PMID: 26554630); Ueberall MA et al. J Pain Res. 2016 (PMID: 27881925).

shelves.title: Amitriptyline 10 mg at night in older adults: a sensible lowest-dose convention no trial has tested — and the drug's efficacy evidence is weaker than its reputation (MAYBE)
shelves.question: Should amitriptyline be started at 10 mg at night in older adults with neuropathic pain?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amitriptyline · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic · Antidepressive Agents, Tricyclic · Humans · Neuralgia · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) for the specific practice asked about. No carded record tests a 10 mg starting dose, at night, in older adults: that exact regimen is a prudence-based convention, not a trialled strategy, and this shelf says so plainly. What the evidence does show cuts in two directions. For efficacy, the Cochrane review of amitriptyline in neuropathic pain (17 studies, 1,342 participants) found no first- or second-tier evidence at all — only third-tier, very-low-quality evidence, with amitriptyline significantly better than placebo in only two of seven studies reporting usable data — while adverse events were commoner on amitriptyline (55% versus 36%; relative risk 1.5, 95% CI 1.3 to 1.8; number needed to harm 5.2). For the drug class, the NeuPSIG meta-analysis (Finnerup 2015) gives tricyclics the most favourable number needed to treat among first-line options and a strong first-line recommendation, without printing a starting dose in its record. For older adults specifically, the geriatric spine-pain review advises the lowest therapeutic doses for all analgesics in this age group and notes serotonin–noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors have a more favourable safety profile than tricyclics. A low, cautious start in an older adult is consistent with everything carded — but the 10 mg figure itself is untested, and even the underlying efficacy of amitriptyline is weaker than its reputation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): starting at 10 mg at night in older adults is a reasonable, harm-avoiding convention that no trial has directly tested.

cards.headline: Moore 2015 (Cochrane): amitriptyline's neuropathic-pain evidence is third-tier only — better than placebo in just two of seven usable studies — and adverse events hit 55% versus 36% on placebo
cards.summary: Moore 2015 (Cochrane): amitriptyline's neuropathic-pain evidence is third-tier only — better than placebo in just two of seven usable studies — and adverse events hit 55% versus 36% on placebo
cards.people: Cochrane review of 17 randomised, double-blind studies (1,342 participants) of amitriptyline versus placebo or another active treatment for at least 4 weeks in seven chronic neuropathic pain conditions; eight crossover studies (302 participants) and nine parallel-group studies (1,040 participants). The record does not single out older adults or a 10 mg starting dose.
cards.result: There was no first-tier or second-tier evidence for amitriptyline in any neuropathic pain condition; only third-tier evidence was available. In only two of seven studies reporting useful efficacy data was amitriptyline significantly better than placebo (very low quality evidence). More participants on amitriptyline experienced at least one adverse event: 55% versus 36% on placebo (relative risk 1.5, 95% CI 1.3 to 1.8; number needed to treat for an additional harmful outcome 5.2, 95% CI 3.6 to 9.1; low quality evidence). Serious adverse events were rare. The authors note that only a minority of people will achieve satisfactory pain relief with amitriptyline.
cards.watchOut: Most included studies were small and at high risk of bias; the review judges the drug's evidence, not any starting dose — it cannot tell a prescriber whether 10 mg is the right first step.
cards.source: Moore RA et al. Amitriptyline for neuropathic pain in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015. PMID: 26146793. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Finnerup 2015 (NeuPSIG): tricyclics carry a strong first-line recommendation and the most favourable NNT of the first-line classes — the class case for using amitriptyline at all
cards.summary: Finnerup 2015 (NeuPSIG): tricyclics carry a strong first-line recommendation and the most favourable NNT of the first-line classes — the class case for using amitriptyline at all
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis with GRADE recommendations (Finnerup 2015)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis by the Neuropathic Pain Special Interest Group of 229 randomised, double-blind studies of oral and topical pharmacotherapy for neuropathic pain, using number needed to treat (NNT) for 50% pain relief as the primary measure, with GRADE assessment. Analysis of publication bias suggested a 10% overstatement of treatment effects.
cards.result: Combined NNTs were 6.4 (95% CI 5.2 to 8.4) for serotonin–noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors, 7.7 (6.5 to 9.4) for pregabalin and 7.2 (5.9 to 9.2) for gabapentin; NNTs were lower (more favourable) for tricyclic antidepressants, strong opioids, tramadol and botulinum toxin A — the record states this ordering without printing the tricyclic point estimate, and none is invented here. Final evidence quality was moderate or high for all treatments except lidocaine patches. The panel made a strong recommendation for tricyclics, SNRIs, pregabalin and gabapentin as first-line treatments. The record prints no starting dose for any drug.
cards.watchOut: A class-level endorsement built largely on trials in younger and middle-aged adults: it supports choosing a tricyclic, and says nothing about how an older adult's first dose should be set.
cards.source: Finnerup NB et al. Pharmacotherapy for neuropathic pain in adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Lancet Neurol. 2015. PMID: 25575710. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Fu 2022: in older adults, geriatric pharmacotherapy reviews advise the lowest therapeutic doses — and rate SNRIs as having a more favourable safety profile than tricyclics
cards.summary: Fu 2022: in older adults, geriatric pharmacotherapy reviews advise the lowest therapeutic doses — and rate SNRIs as having a more favourable safety profile than tricyclics
cards.people: Narrative review of pharmacotherapy for spine-related pain in older adults, focused on drug metabolism and adverse drug reactions, built around 138 double-blind, placebo-controlled trials across analgesic classes, in a population with reduced liver and renal function, comorbidity and polypharmacy.
cards.result: The review found gabapentin and pregabalin had mixed evidence for neuropathic pain, while SNRIs had good evidence for neuropathic pain and a more favourable safety profile than tricyclic antidepressants. Its standing advice for older adults is that beneficial pharmacotherapy should employ the lowest therapeutic doses, with consideration of polypharmacy, decreased renal and hepatic metabolism and comorbid disorders. The record names no milligram starting dose for amitriptyline, and none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: Spine-related pain in older adults is the review's frame, not neuropathic pain alone, and 'lowest therapeutic dose' is a principle, not a tested 10 mg regimen — this card supports caution, not the specific number.
cards.source: Fu JL et al. Pharmacotherapy for Spine-Related Pain in Older Adults. Drugs Aging. 2022. PMID: 35754070. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the 10 mg night-time start in older adults is an untested convention — consistent with geriatric lowest-dose advice, resting on a drug whose own efficacy evidence is third-tier
cards.summary: Synthesis: the 10 mg night-time start in older adults is an untested convention — consistent with geriatric lowest-dose advice, resting on a drug whose own efficacy evidence is third-tier
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane review of amitriptyline itself (17 studies, 1,342 participants), the NeuPSIG class meta-analysis (229 studies) and a geriatric pharmacotherapy review (138 trials reviewed). No carded study enrolled older adults to compare starting doses, and no carded record prints a 10 mg starting dose.
cards.result: Amitriptyline: significantly better than placebo in only 2 of 7 usable studies (very low quality), adverse events 55% versus 36% (relative risk 1.5). Tricyclics as a class: strong first-line recommendation, most favourable NNT ordering. Older adults: lowest therapeutic doses advised. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for the specific 10 mg starting practice.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE here grades the dose question, not the clinician's caution: starting low in an older adult is plainly the safer course given a 55% adverse-event rate — the weakness is that neither the benefit at 10 mg nor the dose itself has been put to a trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moore RA et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015 (PMID: 26146793); Finnerup NB et al. Lancet Neurol. 2015 (PMID: 25575710); Fu JL et al. Drugs Aging. 2022 (PMID: 35754070).

shelves.title: Physical therapy after lumbar discectomy: SPLIT by timing — starting immediately made no difference, starting at 4–6 weeks modestly improved pain and function
shelves.question: Does early physical therapy after lumbar discectomy improve recovery compared with usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Intervertebral Disc · Intervertebral Disc Displacement · Lumbar Vertebrae · Male · Middle Aged · Orthopedic Procedures · Quality of Life · Referral and Consultation · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer divides by timing. Programmes started immediately after surgery were not more effective than their control interventions in the Cochrane review (22 trials, 2,503 participants), and the largest directly relevant randomised trial found referral for early rehabilitation (6–8 weeks of exercise therapy starting immediately after discharge) was neither more effective nor more cost-effective than no referral: no significant difference on any outcome at 26 weeks, including global perceived recovery (odds ratio 1.0, 95% CI 0.6 to 1.7, a relative measure) and functional status (mean difference 1.5, 95% CI −3.6 to 6.7). The same Cochrane review found the benefit sits later: exercise programmes starting four to six weeks after surgery beat no treatment for short-term pain (standardised mean difference −0.90, 95% CI −1.55 to −0.24; very low quality) and function (SMD −0.67, 95% CI −1.22 to −0.12; low quality), and physiotherapy from four to six weeks led to better function than no treatment or education only. A trial comparing two early exercise programmes (specific versus general trunk exercises, starting at two weeks) found no difference between them, with both groups improving. So 'early' rehabilitation in the first days adds nothing carded; rehabilitation begun at four to six weeks probably helps modestly. PROPOSED SPLIT (immediate start: the treatment made no difference; start at 4–6 weeks: benefit, low-quality evidence).

cards.headline: Oosterhuis 2017: early rehabilitation after disc surgery was neither more effective nor more cost-effective than no referral — no significant difference on any outcome at 26 weeks
cards.summary: Oosterhuis 2017: early rehabilitation after disc surgery was neither more effective nor more cost-effective than no referral — no significant difference on any outcome at 26 weeks
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial and economic evaluation (Oosterhuis 2017)
cards.people: Multicentre randomised controlled trial with economic evaluation in adults who had undergone discectomy for an MRI-confirmed herniated lumbar disc with corresponding nerve root compression: early rehabilitation (exercise therapy for 6–8 weeks, starting immediately after discharge) versus no referral, with outcomes at 3, 6, 9, 12 and 26 weeks. The record does not state the total randomised N, and none is printed here.
cards.result: There were no clinically relevant or statistically significant overall mean differences for any outcome: global perceived recovery odds ratio 1.0 (95% CI 0.6 to 1.7, a relative measure), functional status mean difference 1.5 (95% CI −3.6 to 6.7), leg pain 0.1 (−0.7 to 0.8), back pain 0.3 (−0.3 to 0.9), physical health −3.5 (−11.3 to 4.3) and mental health −4.1 (−9.4 to 1.3) — the treatment made no difference. At 26 weeks, quality-adjusted life years differed by 0.01 (95% CI −0.02 to 0.04) and societal costs by −€527 (95% CI −2846 to 1506); the maximum probability of cost-effectiveness was 0.75 at €32,000 per quality-adjusted life year.
cards.watchOut: The control was 'no referral', not a structured usual-care programme, and the trial's own record omits its sample size — its null is consistent across every outcome measured, which is its strength.
cards.source: Oosterhuis T et al. Early rehabilitation after lumbar disc surgery is not effective or cost-effective compared to no referral: a randomised trial and economic evaluation. J Physiother. 2017. PMID: 28668558. Registry ID: NTR3156. cards.headline: Oosterhuis 2014 (Cochrane): rehabilitation starting immediately after surgery was not more effective than controls — but exercise starting at 4–6 weeks beat no treatment for pain and function
cards.summary: Oosterhuis 2014 (Cochrane): rehabilitation starting immediately after surgery was not more effective than controls — but exercise starting at 4–6 weeks beat no treatment for pain and function
cards.people: Cochrane review of 22 randomised trials (2,503 participants; mean age 41.4 years) of rehabilitation after standard discectomy or microdiscectomy, clustered by start time: immediately after surgery (4 studies), four to six weeks after surgery (16 studies) or more than a year after surgery (2 studies). Mean programme duration was 12 weeks.
cards.result: Rehabilitation programmes that started immediately after surgery were not more effective than their control interventions, which included exercise. For programmes starting four to six weeks after surgery, pooled very-low-quality evidence (five trials, 272 participants) showed exercise more effective than no treatment for short-term pain (standardised mean difference −0.90, 95% CI −1.55 to −0.24) and low-quality evidence (four trials, 252 participants) showed better short-term functional status (SMD −0.67, 95% CI −1.22 to −0.12), with no difference in functional status at long-term follow-up (three trials, 226 participants; SMD −0.22, 95% CI −0.49 to 0.04). Low-quality evidence also showed physiotherapy from four to six weeks led to better function than no treatment or education only, and multidisciplinary rehabilitation led to faster return to work than usual care. None of the studies reported that exercise increased the reoperation rate. Overall evidence quality was low to very low, and no programme had high- or moderate-quality evidence.
cards.watchOut: The 4–6-week benefit rests on a few hundred participants and low-to-very-low-quality evidence with wide intervals; programme content varied so much that the review cannot say which rehabilitation, only roughly when.
cards.source: Oosterhuis T et al. Rehabilitation after lumbar disc surgery. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2014. PMID: 24627325. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hebert 2015: when rehabilitation did start early (at 2 weeks), specific trunk-muscle exercises and general trunk exercises produced identical outcomes — both groups simply improved (N = 61 on the face)
cards.summary: Hebert 2015: when rehabilitation did start early (at 2 weeks), specific trunk-muscle exercises and general trunk exercises produced identical outcomes — both groups simply improved (N = 61 on the face)
cards.people: 61 participants aged 18–60 scheduled for single-level lumbar discectomy, randomised two weeks after surgery to an 8-week multimodal exercise programme of either general trunk exercises (n = 32) or exercises specifically targeting the lumbar multifidus (n = 29); outcomes at 10 weeks and 6 months. Trial N = 61.
cards.result: There were no between-group differences in clinical or muscle function outcomes — disability (Oswestry Index), back and leg pain, global change, sciatica frequency and bothersomeness, and ultrasound-measured multifidus function all behaved the same in both groups, and participants in both groups improved on most measures. The record reports no effect sizes for the between-group comparisons, and none are printed here. The authors conclude that patient characteristics, clinician expertise and patient preference should direct exercise selection.
cards.watchOut: With no non-exercise control arm, this trial cannot say whether its early programme beat usual care — only that the fashionable specific-muscle version added nothing over general exercise.
cards.source: Hebert JJ et al. Early multimodal rehabilitation following lumbar disc surgery: a randomised clinical trial comparing the effects of two exercise programmes on clinical outcome and lumbar multifidus muscle function. Br J Sports Med. 2015. PMID: 24029724. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by timing — immediate rehabilitation made no difference; rehabilitation from 4–6 weeks modestly beat no treatment, on low-quality evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by timing — immediate rehabilitation made no difference; rehabilitation from 4–6 weeks modestly beat no treatment, on low-quality evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: a multicentre randomised trial of immediate referral versus no referral (N not stated in its record), the Cochrane synthesis of 22 trials (2,503 participants) and a 61-patient trial comparing two early exercise programmes.
cards.result: Immediate start: odds ratio for global recovery 1.0 and no significant difference on any outcome (Oosterhuis 2017); Cochrane concurs for immediately-started programmes. Start at 4–6 weeks: pain SMD −0.90 and function SMD −0.67 versus no treatment, low-to-very-low quality (Cochrane 2014). PROPOSED SPLIT (immediate: the treatment made no difference; 4–6 weeks: benefit).
cards.watchOut: 'Usual care' in these records ranges from no referral to education to exercise-containing controls; a service whose usual care already includes structured exercise should not expect the 4–6-week trial gains on top.

shelves.title: Opioid tapering in long-term high-dose therapy: SPLIT — pain may ease slightly but function does not improve, and tapering is associated with more overdose and mental-health crises
shelves.question: Does tapering opioids improve pain and function in patients on long-term high-dose therapy for chronic noncancer pain?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Analgesics · Chronic Pain · Drug Tapering · Pain Measurement · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT. On pain, the tapering literature leans favourable but is weak: a 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis (57 studies reviewed, 34 meta-analysed) found a beneficial overall effect of tapering (effect size 0.917, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.22) with significant improvement in pain intensity — but no statistically significant effect on physical functioning, mental-health or physical-health quality of life, or pain self-efficacy, and most included studies were poor quality (30 poor, 24 fair, 3 good). The one carded randomised trial of tapering off long-term therapy largely failed as an experiment: of 75 patients included, 40 dropped out before the tapering phase, and among the 15 tapered versus 20 controls, pain intensity stayed stable rather than improving. On harm, the largest carded dataset points the other way: in 113,618 patients on stable long-term higher-dose opioids (at least 50 morphine milligram equivalents daily), tapering was associated with 9.3 overdose events per 100 person-years versus 5.5 without tapering (adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.68, a relative measure) and 7.6 versus 3.3 mental-health-crisis events per 100 person-years (adjusted rate ratio 2.28), with risk rising with faster dose reduction — an observational association its authors flag as design-limited. So: pain may improve slightly or hold steady when doses come down, function does not demonstrably improve, and tapering as actually practised is associated with serious harms. PROPOSED SPLIT (pain: possible small benefit, low-quality evidence, function unchanged; tapering events: associated with increased overdose and mental-health crisis in observational data).

cards.headline: Wuyts 2024: tapering improved pain intensity in meta-analysis (effect size 0.917) — but physical functioning did NOT significantly improve, and 30 of 57 studies were poor quality
cards.summary: Wuyts 2024: tapering improved pain intensity in meta-analysis (effect size 0.917) — but physical functioning did NOT significantly improve, and 30 of 57 studies were poor quality
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies of pain-medication tapering in adults with chronic noncancer pain, searching to April 2024: 57 articles in the systematic review and 34 in the meta-analysis. Risk of bias was poor in 30 studies, fair in 24 and good in 3. Pain intensity was the most reported outcome (28 studies).
cards.result: A random-effects three-level meta-analysis found an overall effect size of 0.917 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.22; P < 0.001), indicating a beneficial effect of tapering, with statistically significant improvement after tapering for pain intensity, headache disability, headache days per month, anxiety, depression, pills consumed per month, days with medication intake per month, pain catastrophising and pain interference. No statistically significant effect was observed for physical functioning, mental health-related quality of life, opioid use, pain self-efficacy or physical health-related quality of life. The authors state the results must be interpreted with caution because of the high risk of bias of the included studies. The review is registered on PROSPERO as CRD42023416343, as printed in its record.
cards.watchOut: Mostly uncontrolled before–after studies: people who succeed in tapering are the people likeliest to report less pain anyway, and an effect size pooled from such designs cannot separate the taper from the selection.
cards.source: Wuyts E et al. Effectiveness of pain medication tapering in chronic pain patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Anaesth. 2024. PMID: 39358186. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Analgesics · Chronic Pain · Drug Tapering · Pain Measurement · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Kurita 2018: the randomised tapering trial mostly collapsed — 40 of 75 patients dropped out before tapering; in the 15 tapered, pain stayed stable rather than improving (Ns on the face)
cards.summary: Kurita 2018: the randomised tapering trial mostly collapsed — 40 of 75 patients dropped out before tapering; in the 15 tapered, pain stayed stable rather than improving (Ns on the face)
cards.people: Randomised clinical trial in chronic non-cancer pain patients on long-term opioid therapy: a medication stabilisation phase, then randomisation to stable treatment (control, n = 20) or a sequential opioid tapering-off programme (n = 15), assessed to 6 months. Of 274 patients screened, 75 were included and 40 dropped out before the tapering phase; 35 completed stabilisation.
cards.result: Patients who completed stabilisation (n = 35) had weak-to-moderate improvements in psychomotor function (P = 0.020), sleeping hours (P = 0.031), opioid withdrawal symptoms (P = 0.019), quality-of-life measures (P ≤ 0.043) and opioid misuse scores (P = 0.003). In the tapering phase, the taper group (n = 15) experienced stable pain intensity and felt significantly more rested at the third assessment than controls (n = 20) — pain did not improve, it held. The authors conclude the sequential tapering-off programme was not successful because of the vast number of dropouts and may be an unfeasible approach, while noting that stable pain in those tapered may encourage more refined programmes.
cards.watchOut: A 15-versus-20 comparison after more than half the included patients left cannot estimate a tapering effect; its real findings are feasibility (poor) and that stabilisation itself, before any taper, was where the measurable gains appeared.
cards.source: Kurita GP et al. Tapering off long-term opioid therapy in chronic non-cancer pain patients: A randomized clinical trial. Eur J Pain. 2018. PMID: 29754428. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Agnoli 2021: in 113,618 patients on stable higher-dose opioids, tapering was associated with more overdose (9.3 vs 5.5 per 100 person-years) and more mental-health crises (7.6 vs 3.3)
cards.summary: Agnoli 2021: in 113,618 patients on stable higher-dose opioids, tapering was associated with more overdose (9.3 vs 5.5 per 100 person-years) and more mental-health crises (7.6 vs 3.3)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort study of US claims data (2008–2019): adults prescribed stable long-term higher-dose opioids (mean at least 50 morphine milligram equivalents daily over a 12-month baseline), contributing 203,920 baseline periods; 113,618 patients in the final cohort. Tapering was defined as at least a 15% relative reduction in mean daily dose in any of six overlapping 60-day windows over 7 months, with follow-up to 12 months.
cards.result: Post-tapering periods had an adjusted incidence of 9.3 overdose events per 100 person-years versus 5.5 in non-tapered periods (adjusted incidence rate difference 3.8 per 100 person-years, 95% CI 3.0 to 4.6; adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.68, 95% CI 1.53 to 1.85 — a relative measure). Mental-health-crisis events (depression, anxiety, suicide attempt presenting to emergency or hospital care) were 7.6 versus 3.3 per 100 person-years (adjusted difference 4.3, 95% CI 3.2 to 5.3; adjusted rate ratio 2.28, 95% CI 1.96 to 2.65). Each 10% increase in maximum monthly dose-reduction velocity was associated with a rate ratio of 1.09 for overdose and 1.18 for mental-health crisis. The authors state interpretation is limited by the observational design.
cards.watchOut: Association is not causation: doses may have been tapered because patients were already deteriorating, and claims data cannot see illicit opioid use or the clinical conversation — but the size, dose-velocity gradient and seriousness of the outcomes mean the signal cannot be waved away.
cards.source: Agnoli A et al. Association of Dose Tapering With Overdose or Mental Health Crisis Among Patients Prescribed Long-term Opioids. JAMA. 2021. PMID: 34342618. Registry ID: none in the record. retrospective cohort study (agnoli 2021) retrospective cohort study of us claims data (2008–2019): adults prescribed stable long-term higher-dose opioids (mean at least 50 morphine milligram equivalents daily over a 12-month baseline), contributing 203,920 baseline periods; 113,618 patients in the final cohort. tapering was defined as at least a 15% relative reduction in mean daily dose in any of six overlapping 60-day windows over 7 months, with follow-up to 12 months. post-tapering periods had an adjusted incidence of 9.3 overdose events per 100 person-years versus 5.5 in non-tapered periods (adjusted incidence rate difference 3.8 per 100 person-years, 95% ci 3.0 to 4.6; adjusted incidence rate ratio 1.68, 95% ci 1.53 to 1.85 — a relative measure). mental-health-crisis events (depression, anxiety, suicide attempt presenting to emergency or hospital care) were 7.6 versus 3.3 per 100 person-years (adjusted difference 4.3, 95% ci 3.2 to 5.3; adjusted rate ratio 2.28, 95% ci 1.96 to 2.65). each 10% increase in maximum monthly dose-reduction velocity was associated with a rate ratio of 1.09 for overdose and 1.18 for mental-health crisis. the authors state interpretation is limited by the observational design. association is not causation: doses may have been tapered because patients were already deteriorating, and claims data cannot see illicit opioid use or the clinical conversation — but the size, dose-velocity gradient and seriousness of the outcomes mean the signal cannot be waved away. agnoli a et al. association of dose tapering with overdose or mental health crisis among patients prescribed long-term opioids. jama. 2021. pmid: 34342618. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · aged · analgesics, opioid · chronic pain · drug overdose · drug tapering · female · humans · male · mental health · middle aged · retrospective studies · substance withdrawal syndrome · young adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — pain may ease slightly or hold when doses fall (weak evidence), function does not improve, and tapering as practised is associated with overdose and mental-health harms
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — pain may ease slightly or hold when doses fall (weak evidence), function does not improve, and tapering as practised is associated with overdose and mental-health harms
cards.people: The carded evidence: a systematic review/meta-analysis of 57 tapering studies (34 meta-analysed, mostly poor quality), one small randomised tapering trial (75 included, 35 reaching the tapering phase) and one very large retrospective cohort (113,618 patients on at least 50 morphine milligram equivalents daily).
cards.result: Pain intensity improved after tapering in meta-analysis (effect size 0.917) with no significant effect on physical functioning (Wuyts 2024); pain was stable, not improved, in the randomised taper group (Kurita 2018); tapering was associated with overdose 9.3 versus 5.5 and mental-health crisis 7.6 versus 3.3 events per 100 person-years (Agnoli 2021). PROPOSED SPLIT (pain: possible small benefit, function unchanged; harms: increased in observational data).
cards.watchOut: Nothing carded supports forced or rapid tapering: the pain literature is low-quality and largely uncontrolled, the one trial could not retain its patients, and the harm gradient rises with tapering speed — pace and voluntariness are the variables the evidence keeps pointing at.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wuyts E et al. Br J Anaesth. 2024 (PMID: 39358186); Kurita GP et al. Eur J Pain. 2018 (PMID: 29754428); Agnoli A et al. JAMA. 2021 (PMID: 34342618).

shelves.title: Cannabis-based medicines for chronic neuropathic pain: a small real benefit for the tested standardised preparations (30% relief NNTB 11) with frequent nervous-system harms (NNTH 3)
shelves.question: Does cannabis-based medicine reduce chronic neuropathic pain compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic · Analgesics, Opioid · Cannabidiol · Chronic Pain · Codeine · Dronabinol · Humans · Medical Marijuana · Neuralgia · Numbers Needed To Treat · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a small benefit, product by product, with frequent harms. Cannabis-based products are not well regulated and differ by maker, so this shelf names the specific tested preparations exactly as the publications give them, and says plainly where they do not: the Cochrane review's trials tested a plant-derived tetrahydrocannabinol/cannabidiol oromucosal spray (10 studies — the spray is the nabiximols preparation, though the Cochrane record does not print a brand name or company), the synthetic tetrahydrocannabinol mimic nabilone (2 studies), inhaled herbal cannabis (2 studies) and plant-derived tetrahydrocannabinol as dronabinol (2 studies); no carded record names a manufacturer for these products. On benefit, 50% or greater pain relief was achieved by 21% on cannabis-based medicines versus 17% on placebo (risk difference 0.05; number needed to treat for benefit 20) and 30% or greater relief by 39% versus 33% (NNTB 11), on low-to-moderate quality evidence. The nabiximols-specific meta-analysis (9 trials, 1,289 participants) found a mean pain advantage of −0.40 points on an 11-point scale — statistically firm, clinically small. Harms are not small: nervous system adverse events in 61% versus 29% (number needed to harm 3), psychiatric disorders in 17% versus 5% (NNTH 10) and withdrawal for adverse events in 10% versus 5% (NNTH 25). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): cannabis-based medicines reduce chronic neuropathic pain slightly more than placebo for a minority of patients, at the cost of frequent nervous-system and psychiatric adverse effects, and results from one preparation must not be read across to unregulated products that differ by maker.

cards.headline: Mücke 2018 (Cochrane): 50% pain relief in 21% on cannabis-based medicines versus 17% on placebo (NNTB 20) — but nervous system adverse events in 61% versus 29% (NNTH 3)
cards.summary: Mücke 2018 (Cochrane): 50% pain relief in 21% on cannabis-based medicines versus 17% on placebo (NNTB 20) — but nervous system adverse events in 61% versus 29% (NNTH 3)
cards.people: Cochrane review of 16 randomised, double-blind studies with 1,750 participants with chronic neuropathic pain in adults, of 2 to 26 weeks' duration, each arm at least 10 participants. The tested preparations, as the record names them: an oromucosal spray with a plant-derived combination of tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) (10 studies), a synthetic cannabinoid mimicking THC (nabilone) (two studies), inhaled herbal cannabis (two studies) and plant-derived THC (dronabinol) (two studies), against placebo (15 studies) or dihydrocodeine (one study). The record names no brand or manufacturer for any product.
cards.result: Cannabis-based medicines may increase 50% or greater pain relief versus placebo: 21% versus 17% (risk difference 0.05, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.09; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome 20, 95% CI 11 to 100; 1,001 participants, eight studies, low-quality evidence). For 30% or greater relief: 39% versus 33% (risk difference 0.09, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.15; NNTB 11, 95% CI 7 to 33; 1,586 participants, ten studies, moderate quality). Withdrawals for adverse events were 10% versus 5% (risk difference 0.04; NNTH 25, 95% CI 16 to 50; moderate quality), with no enough evidence on serious adverse events (risk difference 0.01, 95% CI −0.01 to 0.03). Nervous system adverse events occurred in 61% versus 29% (risk difference 0.38; NNTH 3, 95% CI 2 to 6; low quality) and psychiatric disorders in 17% versus 5% (risk difference 0.10; NNTH 10, 95% CI 7 to 16; low quality). The authors conclude the potential benefits might be outweighed by the potential harms, and note no information on long-term risks.
cards.watchOut: Trials excluded people with a history of substance abuse and significant comorbidity and were mostly small — nine studies were at high risk of bias for study size — so both the benefit and the harm rates may differ in ordinary clinic populations.
cards.source: Mücke M et al. Cannabis-based medicines for chronic neuropathic pain in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018. PMID: 29513392. Registry ID: none in the record.
