cards.headline: Dykukha 2021: for the named product nabiximols (THC/CBD oromucosal spray), the pooled pain advantage over placebo was −0.40 points on an 11-point scale across 9 trials (1,289 participants)
cards.summary: Dykukha 2021: for the named product nabiximols (THC/CBD oromucosal spray), the pooled pain advantage over placebo was −0.40 points on an 11-point scale across 9 trials (1,289 participants)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of a named product (Dykukha 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of nine double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trials of nabiximols — the tetrahydrocannabinol/cannabidiol oromucosal spray — for chronic neuropathic pain, totalling 1,289 participants. Quality of evidence by GRADE was moderate; one study was at high risk of bias and five had some concerns. The record names the product (nabiximols) but no manufacturer.
cards.result: For change from baseline in mean pain score on 11-point numerical rating scales, nabiximols was superior to placebo: mean difference −0.40 (95% CI −0.59 to −0.21; fixed effect, P < 0.0001) or −0.44 (95% CI −0.70 to −0.19; random effects, P = 0.0006), a standardised mean difference of −0.21 to −0.26 — an incremental benefit over background analgesia that the authors themselves describe as a small effect size, calling for larger trials for definitive conclusions.
cards.watchOut: A −0.40-point average advantage on an 11-point scale is below what most patients can feel; responder analyses (the Cochrane card) are the fairer picture — a minority benefit meaningfully, most do not.
cards.source: Dykukha I et al. Nabiximols in Chronic Neuropathic Pain: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Placebo-Controlled Trials. Pain Med. 2021. PMID: 33561282. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: McDonagh 2022 (AHRQ): product type decides the answer — comparable-ratio THC:CBD spray probably gives a small improvement; high-THC synthetic products may improve pain but bring sedation and a large increase in dizziness
cards.summary: McDonagh 2022 (AHRQ): product type decides the answer — comparable-ratio THC:CBD spray probably gives a small improvement; high-THC synthetic products may improve pain but bring sedation and a large increase in dizziness
cards.people: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality systematic review of cannabis-based products for chronic pain: 18 randomised, placebo-controlled trials (1,740 participants) and 7 cohort studies (13,095 participants), mostly 1 to 6 months, 56% enrolling neuropathic pain. Products were categorised by THC-to-CBD ratio (high, comparable, low) and source (synthetic, extracted or purified, whole plant). The record names product categories and dronabinol in its indexing but no brand or manufacturer for the spray products.
cards.result: Sublingual spray with a comparable THC-to-CBD ratio (1.1:1) probably is associated with a small improvement in pain severity and overall function, and may be associated with a large increased risk for dizziness and sedation and a moderate increased risk for nausea. Synthetic products with high THC-to-CBD ratios (over 98% THC) may be associated with moderate improvement in pain severity and in achieving at least 30% improvement, with increased sedation and probably a large increased risk of dizziness. Extracted high-ratio products may be associated with a large increased risk of withdrawal due to adverse events and dizziness. Evidence for other products and for longer-term harms was not reported or was insufficient. The record reports these as graded qualitative effects without pooled numbers, and none are invented here.
cards.watchOut: This review covers chronic pain broadly, not neuropathic pain alone, and its central lesson is non-transferability: an effect shown for a standardised spray or a synthetic capsule says nothing about dispensary or herbal products of variable composition.
cards.source: McDonagh MS et al. Cannabis-Based Products for Chronic Pain : A Systematic Review. Ann Intern Med. 2022. PMID: 35667066. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Analgesics · Cannabinoids · Cannabis · Chronic Pain · Dizziness · Dronabinol · Humans

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but small placebo-beating effect for the tested, standardised preparations — 30% relief NNTB 11 — against nervous-system harms at NNTH 3; unregulated products are not covered by this evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but small placebo-beating effect for the tested, standardised preparations — 30% relief NNTB 11 — against nervous-system harms at NNTH 3; unregulated products are not covered by this evidence
cards.people: The carded evidence: the Cochrane neuropathic-pain review (16 studies, 1,750 participants), the nabiximols-specific meta-analysis (9 trials, 1,289 participants, overlapping with the Cochrane set) and the AHRQ chronic-pain review (18 trials, 1,740 participants, also overlapping). Unique participants across reviews cannot be summed because the reviews share trials; the underlying trial base is roughly 1,750 people in short studies.
cards.result: 50% relief 21% versus 17% (NNTB 20); 30% relief 39% versus 33% (NNTB 11); nabiximols mean pain difference −0.40 points; nervous system adverse events 61% versus 29% (NNTH 3); psychiatric disorders 17% versus 5% (NNTH 10). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — small effect, named preparations only.
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE is for the standardised preparations actually trialled (nabiximols-type THC/CBD spray, dronabinol, nabilone, and herbal cannabis as prepared in two small trials). Cannabis-based products are not well regulated and differ by maker; no carded record names a manufacturer, and nothing here licenses claims for unstandardised products.

shelves.title: Pregabalin dose in postherpetic neuralgia: 300 mg/day works slightly better than 150 mg/day (placebo-adjusted pain relief 1.07 versus 0.88 points) — a small average gain, with 600 mg/day stronger and less well tolerated
shelves.question: Does pregabalin 300 mg work better than 150 mg for postherpetic neuralgia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia, Postherpetic · Placebos · Pregabalin · Sleep Wake Disorders · Treatment Outcome · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a real but small dose advantage. Only one carded trial randomised postherpetic neuralgia (PHN) patients to both doses head-to-head: van Seventer 2006 (PMID: 16466610; 370 patients) found placebo-adjusted endpoint pain reductions of 0.88 points at 150 mg/day and 1.07 points at 300 mg/day — so 300 mg beat 150 mg by about 0.19 points on a 0–10 scale on average, while 600 mg/day reached 1.79 points. The other carded trials frame the doses rather than compare them: Dworkin 2003 (PMID: 12707429) dosed by renal function (300 or 600 mg/day) and beat placebo clearly (endpoint pain 3.60 versus 5.29; 50% pain reduction in 50% versus 20%), and Freynhagen 2005 (PMID: 15911152) showed flexible titration through 150–600 mg/day works, consistent with individual dose-finding rather than a fixed best dose. The cost of higher doses is tolerability: 13.5% of pregabalin patients in the dose-ranging trial withdrew for adverse events, led by dizziness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): yes, 300 mg/day works slightly better than 150 mg/day on average — a small increment that matters for some patients, bought with more dizziness and somnolence, which is why titration rather than a blanket 300 mg start is what the trials embody.

cards.headline: van Seventer 2006: the direct dose comparison — placebo-adjusted pain relief was 0.88 points at 150 mg/day, 1.07 at 300 mg/day and 1.79 at 600 mg/day, a dose-proportional gradient
cards.summary: van Seventer 2006: the direct dose comparison — placebo-adjusted pain relief was 0.88 points at 150 mg/day, 1.07 at 300 mg/day and 1.79 at 600 mg/day, a dose-proportional gradient
cards.people: 370 patients with postherpetic neuralgia randomised in a 13-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial to pregabalin 150, 300 or 600 mg/day (twice-daily dosing) or placebo; primary outcome was endpoint mean pain score from daily pain diaries.
cards.result: Pregabalin gave significant, dose-proportional pain relief at endpoint: difference from placebo in mean pain score was −0.88 at 150 mg/day (p = 0.0077), −1.07 at 300 mg/day (p = 0.0016) and −1.79 at 600 mg/day (p = 0.0003) — so 300 mg/day exceeded 150 mg/day by about 0.19 points of additional average relief. Weekly pain scores improved from week 1, and sleep interference improved in all pregabalin groups (p < 0.001). Among pregabalin-treated patients 13.5% withdrew for adverse events, most commonly dizziness (16 patients, 5.8%), somnolence (8, 2.9%) and ataxia (7, 2.5%).
cards.watchOut: The 300-versus-150 contrast is a between-arm difference of average effects (about 0.19 points), not a guarantee for any individual patient — averages conceal responders and nonresponders at both doses, and the trial was not powered as a 300-versus-150 superiority study.
cards.source: van Seventer R et al. Efficacy and tolerability of twice-daily pregabalin for treating pain and related sleep interference in postherpetic neuralgia: a 13-week, randomized trial. Current medical research and opinion. 2006. PMID: 16466610. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dworkin 2003: pregabalin dosed by renal function (300 mg/day if clearance 30–60, else 600 mg/day) beat placebo clearly — endpoint pain 3.60 versus 5.29, with 50% pain reduction in 50% versus 20%
cards.summary: Dworkin 2003: pregabalin dosed by renal function (300 mg/day if clearance 30–60, else 600 mg/day) beat placebo clearly — endpoint pain 3.60 versus 5.29, with 50% pain reduction in 50% versus 20%
cards.people: 173 patients with postherpetic neuralgia (pain for 3 or more months after rash healing) in a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled 8-week trial; pregabalin patients received 600 mg/day (creatinine clearance above 60 mL/min) or 300 mg/day (clearance 30–60 mL/min).
cards.result: Pregabalin-treated patients had greater pain decreases than placebo (endpoint mean scores 3.60 versus 5.29, p = 0.0001), significant from the first full day of treatment; 63% versus 25% achieved at least 30% pain reduction and 50% versus 20% at least 50% reduction (p = 0.001). Sleep, McGill Pain Questionnaire scores and global improvement also favoured pregabalin (p = 0.0001 to 0.001). Side effects were more frequent than with placebo but generally mild to moderate.
cards.watchOut: Dose was assigned by kidney function, not randomised between 150 and 300 mg — this trial proves the 300–600 mg/day range works in PHN but cannot rank 300 against 150, and its renal dosing is a reminder that dose comparisons ignore clearance at their peril.
cards.source: Dworkin RH et al. Pregabalin for the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Neurology. 2003. PMID: 12707429. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Freynhagen 2005: flexible titration (150–600 mg/day by response and tolerability) and a fixed 300-then-600 mg/day schedule both beat placebo — supporting titration to effect rather than a fixed dose for everyone
cards.summary: Freynhagen 2005: flexible titration (150–600 mg/day by response and tolerability) and a fixed 300-then-600 mg/day schedule both beat placebo — supporting titration to effect rather than a fixed dose for everyone
cards.people: 338 patients with chronic postherpetic neuralgia or painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy randomised to placebo (n = 65), flexible-dose pregabalin (150, 300, 450 and 600 mg/day with weekly escalation by response and tolerability; n = 141), or fixed-dose pregabalin (300 mg/day for 1 week, then 600 mg/day for 11 weeks; n = 132), over 12 weeks.
cards.result: Both pregabalin regimens significantly reduced endpoint mean pain score versus placebo (flexible P = 0.002; fixed P < 0.001) and improved pain-related sleep interference (P < 0.001). The most common adverse events were dizziness, peripheral oedema, weight gain and somnolence. The authors conclude that dosing aimed at an optimal balance of efficacy and tolerability provides significant pain relief and may reduce adverse-event discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: The population mixes postherpetic neuralgia with diabetic neuropathy and neither arm holds patients at 150 or 300 mg/day — it answers 'titrate or push?' rather than the shelf's exact 300-versus-150 question, and is carded as supporting context.
cards.source: Freynhagen R et al. Efficacy of pregabalin in neuropathic pain evaluated in a 12-week, randomised, double-blind, multicentre, placebo-controlled trial of flexible- and fixed-dose regimens. Pain. 2005. PMID: 15911152. cards.headline: Synthesis: 300 mg/day beats 150 mg/day by a small average margin (placebo-adjusted 1.07 versus 0.88 pain points) in the one direct dose-ranging trial — with 600 mg/day stronger still and adverse events the price of escalation
cards.summary: Synthesis: 300 mg/day beats 150 mg/day by a small average margin (placebo-adjusted 1.07 versus 0.88 pain points) in the one direct dose-ranging trial — with 600 mg/day stronger still and adverse events the price of escalation
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 370-patient dose-ranging PHN trial randomising 150, 300 and 600 mg/day against placebo (van Seventer 2006), one 173-patient renal-dosed trial of 300/600 mg/day (Dworkin 2003), and one 338-patient flexible/fixed-dose trial in mixed neuropathic pain (Freynhagen 2005). Total carded participants = 881, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Placebo-adjusted endpoint pain relief rose with dose: 0.88 points (150 mg/day), 1.07 (300 mg/day) and 1.79 (600 mg/day), all significant — a 300-over-150 advantage of about 0.19 points on average. The renal-dosed trial confirmed the 300–600 range beats placebo (endpoint pain 3.60 versus 5.29; 50% responders 50% versus 20%), and flexible titration also beat placebo. Adverse-event withdrawal was 13.5% on pregabalin in the dose-ranging trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — small dose advantage.
cards.watchOut: Responder-level data by dose are not printed in the fetched records, so the shelf can rank average relief by dose but cannot say how many more patients respond at 300 than at 150 mg — the honest claim is a small average gain, individually variable.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Seventer R et al. Current medical research and opinion. 2006 (PMID: 16466610); Dworkin RH et al. Neurology. 2003 (PMID: 12707429); Freynhagen R et al. Pain. 2005 (PMID: 15911152).

shelves.title: Corticosteroid injection for knee osteoarthritis: real but brief relief — clinically relevant for about 2–6 weeks, small to 13 weeks, and gone by 26 weeks
shelves.question: Does an intra-articular corticosteroid injection provide short-term relief in knee osteoarthritis, and how long does it last?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Cortex Hormones · Arthralgia · Humans · Hyaluronic Acid · Injections, Intra-Articular · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Pain Measurement · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Therapeutic Irrigation
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — short-term only, with the duration printed in the stamp. Three independent syntheses of the placebo-controlled trials agree on the shape of the effect: it is real early and gone by about 6 months. The Cochrane review (27 trials, 1,767 participants) found pain benefits that were moderate at 1–2 weeks (SMD −0.48), small to moderate at 4–6 weeks (SMD −0.41), small at 13 weeks (SMD −0.22) and absent at 26 weeks (SMD −0.07; Jüni 2015, PMID: 26490760). A duration-focused meta-analysis put the pooled effect at SMD −0.58 with an NNT of 5.1, approaching statistical insignificance at 4 months (Saltychev 2020, PMID: 31972612). The most clinically framed synthesis found the benefit reached the minimal clinically important difference only at short-term follow-up (6 weeks or less: pain mean difference −1.6, function −9.9), fell below it by mid-term, and showed no difference at 6 months or beyond (Bensa 2024, PMID: 38294103). Repeated scheduled injections and cartilage outcomes are a different question, homed on shelf #1481, and are not re-carded here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — short-term only: expect clinically relevant relief for roughly 2–6 weeks, a small residual benefit out to about 13 weeks, and no benefit by 26 weeks (the treatment made no difference at 6 months).

cards.headline: Jüni 2015 (Cochrane): pain benefit was moderate at 1–2 weeks (SMD −0.48), small at 13 weeks (−0.22) and absent at 26 weeks (−0.07) — the effect decays on a timetable
cards.summary: Jüni 2015 (Cochrane): pain benefit was moderate at 1–2 weeks (SMD −0.48), small at 13 weeks (−0.22) and absent at 26 weeks (−0.07) — the effect decays on a timetable
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Jüni 2015, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 27 randomised trials with 1,767 participants comparing intra-articular corticosteroids with control interventions (including placebo/sham) in knee osteoarthritis, with effects stratified by length of follow-up; evidence quality was graded low for all outcomes.
cards.result: For pain, benefits were moderate at 1 to 2 weeks after treatment (SMD −0.48, 95% CI −0.70 to −0.27), small to moderate at 4 to 6 weeks (SMD −0.41, −0.61 to −0.21), small at 13 weeks (SMD −0.22, −0.44 to 0.00), and there was no evidence of an effect at 26 weeks (SMD −0.07, −0.25 to 0.11). Function improved modestly (SMD −0.33, corresponding to a number needed to treat for benefit of 10). Participants on corticosteroids were 11% less likely in relative terms to experience adverse events, but confidence intervals included the null (relative risk 0.89, 0.64 to 1.23). The authors caution that whether benefits at 1–6 weeks are clinically important remains unclear given low-quality, heterogeneous evidence with small-study effects.
cards.watchOut: Effects were smaller in larger, better trials — trials randomising at least 50–100 participants per group showed lower treatment effects — so the pooled early benefit is probably an upper estimate, and the one trial with adequate bias protection in the review found no benefit at all.
cards.source: Juni P et al. Intra-articular corticosteroid for knee osteoarthritis. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 26490760. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Saltychev 2020: pooled pain effect SMD −0.58 with NNT 5.1 — and the effect approached statistical insignificance at 4 months
cards.summary: Saltychev 2020: pooled pain effect SMD −0.58 with NNT 5.1 — and the effect approached statistical insignificance at 4 months
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 randomised controlled studies of intra-articular corticosteroid injections versus placebo in knee osteoarthritis, with follow-ups from 1 to 26 weeks; risk of bias was low in five studies and high in three.
cards.result: The pooled standardised mean difference for pain was −0.58 (95% CI −0.88 to −0.27), with a number needed to treat of 5.1, and considerable heterogeneity. The pooled effect size approached the level of statistical insignificance at 4 months. The pooled relative risk of adverse effects was 0.95 (0.34 to 2.55) — not significant. The authors describe a mild-to-moderate effect on pain up to 3 months, longer than previously reported, varying substantially between patient groups.
cards.watchOut: Only eight trials, three at high risk of bias, with considerable heterogeneity — its 'up to 3 months' reading is the most generous of the three syntheses carded and still converges on nothing by 4–6 months.
cards.source: Saltychev M et al. The Magnitude and Duration of the Effect of Intra-articular Corticosteroid Injections on Pain Severity in Knee Osteoarthritis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. American journal of physical medicine & rehabilitation. 2020. PMID: 31972612. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bensa 2024: the benefit cleared the clinically-important threshold only at 6 weeks or less (pain −1.6, function −9.9) — below it by 3 months and no difference at 6 months (the treatment made no difference long-term)
cards.summary: Bensa 2024: the benefit cleared the clinically-important threshold only at 6 weeks or less (pain −1.6, function −9.9) — below it by 3 months and no difference at 6 months (the treatment made no difference long-term)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 randomised placebo-controlled trials (842 patients) of intra-articular corticosteroid injections in knee osteoarthritis, interpreting effects against minimal clinically important differences (pain VAS 1.4; WOMAC 9) at short-term (6 weeks or less), mid-term (over 6 weeks to 3 months) and long-term (6 months or more) follow-up.
cards.result: Corticosteroids beat placebo significantly at short-term follow-up (pain mean difference −1.6, p < 0.001; WOMAC −9.9, p < 0.001) and at mid-term (−1.3, p = 0.001; −4.9, p = 0.005), but the mean differences reached the minimal clinically important difference values only at the short-term follow-up; no difference was observed at long-term follow-up. Risk-of-bias and GRADE assessments found limited quality of evidence, and the authors question the indication for these injections on this basis.
cards.watchOut: Statistical significance outlasts clinical relevance here — mid-term differences are real but smaller than what patients can perceive as important, so quoting 'works for 3 months' without the clinical-importance qualifier would misstate this record.
cards.source: Bensa A et al. Intra-articular corticosteroid injections provide a clinically relevant benefit compared to placebo only at short-term follow-up in patients with knee osteoarthritis: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA. 2024. PMID: 38294103. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: yes, short-term relief is real — clinically relevant for about 2–6 weeks, small to about 13 weeks, and gone by 26 weeks in every synthesis carded
cards.summary: Synthesis: yes, short-term relief is real — clinically relevant for about 2–6 weeks, small to about 13 weeks, and gone by 26 weeks in every synthesis carded
cards.people: The carded evidence: three systematic reviews/meta-analyses of the randomised placebo-controlled literature (27 trials/1,767 participants; 8 trials; 11 trials/842 patients — overlapping trial sets, as syntheses of one literature must). No individual trial is re-carded; the repeated-injection cartilage question lives on shelf #1481.
cards.result: Pain effects by time: SMD −0.48 at 1–2 weeks, −0.41 at 4–6 weeks, −0.22 at 13 weeks and −0.07 (null) at 26 weeks (Cochrane); pooled SMD −0.58, NNT 5.1, fading toward insignificance at 4 months (Saltychev 2020); clinically important thresholds met only at 6 weeks or less, with no difference at 6 months or beyond (Bensa 2024). Adverse-effect rates did not differ significantly from placebo in the syntheses reporting them. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) — short-term only.
cards.watchOut: All three syntheses grade the underlying trial evidence as low quality with heterogeneity and small-study effects — LIKELY reflects three concordant syntheses of randomised trials, and the honest counselling number is weeks of relief, not months.
cards.source: Synthesis of Juni P et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015 (PMID: 26490760); Saltychev M et al. shelves.title: Tramadol for chronic low back pain beyond 12 weeks (split by duration): benefit is shown only in trials of about 13 weeks or less — beyond 12 weeks there is no placebo-controlled support, and the single 56-week trial's tramadol arm was null versus placebo
shelves.question: Is tramadol effective for chronic low back pain beyond 12 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesics, Opioid · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal · Chronic Pain · Female · Humans · Low Back Pain · Male · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT by trial duration, printed on the face. In trials lasting about 13 weeks or less, tramadol (alone in the Cochrane pooling, and as tramadol/acetaminophen in the two 91-day trials) beat placebo on pain by a small-to-moderate amount. Beyond 12 weeks the placebo-controlled evidence essentially disappears: the Cochrane reviewers state there are no placebo-controlled randomised trials supporting long-term opioid therapy for chronic low back pain, and in the one trial that ran 56 weeks, tramadol prolonged-release did not improve patients' global assessment or pain-interference scores versus placebo at week 16 (the placebo comparison ended at week 16). So the honest answer is: benefit is shown only up to about 3 months; effectiveness beyond 12 weeks is unproven, and the single long trial's tramadol arm was null against placebo. PROPOSED SPLIT (short trials: benefit; beyond 12 weeks: no benefit shown) — tramadol reduced pain more than placebo in trials of about 13 weeks or less, but no placebo-controlled evidence supports effectiveness beyond 12 weeks, and the one 56-week trial found tramadol made no difference versus placebo at week 16 on global and pain-interference measures.

cards.headline: Chaparro 2013 (Cochrane): tramadol beat placebo for pain (SMD −0.55) and function (SMD −0.18) across five trials with 1,378 participants — but the included trials were of short duration, and the review states there are no placebo-controlled trials supporting long-term opioid therapy for chronic low back pain
cards.summary: Chaparro 2013 (Cochrane): tramadol beat placebo for pain (SMD −0.55) and function (SMD −0.18) across five trials with 1,378 participants — but the included trials were of short duration, and the review states there are no placebo-controlled trials supporting long-term opioid therapy for chronic low back pain
cards.people: Adults with chronic low back pain in 15 randomised trials (5,540 participants) of non-injectable opioids for at least 4 weeks; tramadol was examined in five trials with 1,378 participants. Trials comparing different opioids only were excluded.
cards.result: Tramadol was better than placebo for pain (SMD −0.55, 95% CI −0.66 to −0.44; low quality evidence) and function (SMD −0.18, 95% CI −0.29 to −0.07; moderate quality evidence). The reviewers state that the included trials had high drop-out rates, were of short duration, and had limited interpretability of functional improvement, and conclude: 'There are no placebo-RCTs supporting the effectiveness and safety of long-term opioid therapy for treatment of CLBP.' One trial (1,583 participants) found tramadol may make little difference compared with celecoxib for pain relief (relative risk 0.82, 95% CI 0.76 to 0.90; very low quality evidence).
cards.watchOut: The pooled tramadol benefit comes from trials of at least 4 weeks that the reviewers themselves describe as short — it cannot be extrapolated past 12 weeks, which is exactly the period this shelf asks about.
cards.source: Chaparro LE et al. Opioids compared to placebo or other treatments for chronic low-back pain. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 23983011. cards.headline: Peloso 2004: the longest placebo-controlled tramadol-combination trial ran 91 days (about 13 weeks) — tramadol/acetaminophen lowered final pain scores versus placebo (47.4 vs 62.9 on a 100 mm scale) in 336 patients
cards.summary: Peloso 2004: the longest placebo-controlled tramadol-combination trial ran 91 days (about 13 weeks) — tramadol/acetaminophen lowered final pain scores versus placebo (47.4 vs 62.9 on a 100 mm scale) in 336 patients
cards.people: 338 outpatients with chronic low back pain requiring daily medication for 3 months or more and at least moderate pain (visual analogue score 40/100 mm or more) after washout; 336 received tramadol 37.5 mg/acetaminophen 325 mg (n = 167) or placebo (n = 169) for 91 days after a 10-day titration. Average daily tramadol dose was 158 mg.
cards.result: Mean final pain visual analogue scores were 47.4 with tramadol/acetaminophen versus 62.9 with placebo (P < 0.001), and mean final pain relief scores 1.8 versus 0.7 (P < 0.001). Roland Disability Questionnaire scores were significantly better with the combination, and more patients rated it 'very good' or 'good' (63.6% vs 25.2%; P < 0.001). Kaplan-Meier cumulative discontinuation for efficacy failure was 22.9% versus 54.7% (P < 0.001). The most common treatment-related adverse events were nausea (12.0%), dizziness (10.8%) and constipation (10.2%).
cards.watchOut: This is a combination product (tramadol plus acetaminophen), so the effect cannot be credited to tramadol alone — and at 91 days it only just crosses the 12-week line this shelf asks about; it says nothing about 6 or 12 months.
cards.source: Peloso PM et al. cards.headline: Ruoff 2003: a second 91-day trial of tramadol/acetaminophen in 318 patients also beat placebo on pain — final pain scores P = 0.015, with discontinuation for insufficient relief 22.1% versus 41.0%
cards.summary: Ruoff 2003: a second 91-day trial of tramadol/acetaminophen in 318 patients also beat placebo on pain — final pain scores P = 0.015, with discontinuation for insufficient relief 22.1% versus 41.0%
cards.people: 318 patients with at least moderate chronic lower back pain (pain visual analogue score 40 mm or more on a 100 mm scale; mean baseline 70.0 mm; mean age 53.9 years; 63.2% female) randomised to tramadol 37.5 mg/acetaminophen 325 mg up to 8 tablets daily (n = 161) or placebo (n = 157) for 91 days (intent-to-treat population).
cards.result: Tramadol/acetaminophen significantly improved final pain visual analogue scores (P = 0.015) and final Pain Relief Rating Scale scores (P < 0.001) versus placebo, and significantly improved Roland Disability Questionnaire scores (P ≤ 0.027) and the total Short-Form McGill Pain Questionnaire score (P = 0.021). Cumulative discontinuation for insufficient pain relief was 22.1% versus 41.0% (P < 0.001). Treatment-emergent adverse events in the combination group included nausea (13.0%), somnolence (12.4%) and constipation (11.2%). The record does not print the final mean pain scores themselves, only the P values — printed here as reported.
cards.watchOut: Same two limits as the other 91-day trial: a combination product rather than tramadol alone, and a duration (91 days) that barely exceeds 12 weeks — neither trial followed patients beyond about 3 months.

cards.headline: Markman 2022: in the only trial running well beyond 12 weeks (56 weeks of treatment), tramadol prolonged-release did NOT improve global assessment or pain-interference scores versus placebo at week 16 (the treatment made no difference on those measures)
cards.summary: Markman 2022: in the only trial running well beyond 12 weeks (56 weeks of treatment), tramadol prolonged-release did NOT improve global assessment or pain-interference scores versus placebo at week 16 (the treatment made no difference on those measures)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, secondary-measures analysis (Markman 2022; NCT02528253)
cards.people: Patients with chronic low back pain and a history of inadequate response to standard-of-care analgesics, randomised to placebo (up to week 16; n = 406), tanezumab 5 mg (n = 407), tanezumab 10 mg (n = 407), or oral tramadol prolonged-release 100–300 mg/day (n = 605), for 56 weeks of treatment with 24 weeks of safety follow-up (NCT02528253). This report analyses secondary measures: Patient's Global Assessment of low back pain, Brief Pain Inventory-short form, treatment satisfaction and treatment-impact questionnaires at weeks 16 and 56.
cards.result: Tramadol did not improve Patient's Global Assessment or Brief Pain Inventory-short form scores versus placebo at week 16. Most differences between tanezumab and tramadol at week 56 did not reach statistical significance. The record reports no effect size for tramadol versus placebo on these measures — it states the null plainly, and no number is invented here.
cards.watchOut: Tramadol was the active comparator in a tanezumab trial, not the experimental question, and placebo stopped at week 16 — so even this trial gives no placebo comparison beyond 16 weeks. It is nonetheless the only long-duration randomised tramadol evidence found, and on the measures reported it was null.
cards.source: Markman JD et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: tramadol's benefit for chronic low back pain is a short-trial finding (up to about 13 weeks); beyond 12 weeks there is no placebo-controlled support, and the single 56-week trial's tramadol arm made no difference versus placebo at week 16
cards.summary: Synthesis: tramadol's benefit for chronic low back pain is a short-trial finding (up to about 13 weeks); beyond 12 weeks there is no placebo-controlled support, and the single 56-week trial's tramadol arm made no difference versus placebo at week 16
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane pooling of five tramadol trials (1,378 participants, all short), two 91-day tramadol/acetaminophen trials (336 and 318 patients), and one 56-week trial with a 605-patient tramadol arm. The trials overlap (the 91-day trials sit inside the wider opioid reviews), so participants are not summed as if independent; the total evidence base is well over 30 people, and no small-N stamp labelling applies — the limitation is duration, not size, and it is printed here.
cards.result: Up to about 3 months: tramadol SMD −0.55 for pain versus placebo (Chaparro 2013); tramadol/acetaminophen final pain 47.4 vs 62.9 at 91 days (Peloso 2004) with a concordant second 91-day trial (Ruoff 2003). Beyond 12 weeks: no placebo-controlled trials support long-term use (Chaparro 2013), and tramadol did not improve global or pain-interference scores versus placebo at week 16 in the 56-week trial (Markman 2022). PROPOSED SPLIT (short trials: benefit; beyond 12 weeks: no benefit shown).
cards.watchOut: Do not read the short-trial benefit forward in time: every positive card on this shelf ends at or before about 13 weeks, and the two 91-day trials tested a tramadol/acetaminophen combination, not tramadol alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chaparro LE et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23983011); Peloso PM et al. The Journal of rheumatology. 2004 (PMID: 15570651); Ruoff GE et al. Clinical therapeutics. 2003 (PMID: 12809961); Markman JD et al. Pain and therapy. 2022 (PMID: 35962939).

shelves.title: Early gabapentin after herpes zoster: POSSIBLE (no benefit shown) for preventing postherpetic neuralgia — the one randomised trial was null (pain at 12 weeks 18.2% vs 9.5% on placebo)
shelves.question: Does early gabapentin after herpes zoster prevent postherpetic neuralgia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gabapentin · Herpes Zoster · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia, Postherpetic · Quality of Life · Sleep · Spain
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no benefit shown), stated plainly. The one randomised trial of the exact strategy — gabapentin started within 72 hours of rash onset, titrated to up to 1,800 mg/day for 5 weeks, on top of valaciclovir — found pain at 12 weeks in 18.2% of the gabapentin group versus 9.5% with placebo (P = 0.144): the treatment made no difference, and the point estimate ran the wrong way, with worse quality of life and sleep in the gabapentin group. The sibling gabapentinoid pregabalin, started during acute zoster in a small trial (N = 29, printed on its card), likewise made no difference to acute pain or to postherpetic neuralgia onset. Context: even antiviral treatment started within 72 hours does not significantly reduce postherpetic neuralgia incidence in the Cochrane pooling (relative risk 0.75 at 4 months, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.11), so prevention by early drug treatment is a high bar that gabapentin does not clear. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit shown): early gabapentin does not prevent postherpetic neuralgia in the randomised evidence.

cards.headline: Bulilete 2019: gabapentin started within 72 hours of rash onset did NOT prevent pain at 12 weeks — 18.2% with gabapentin vs 9.5% with placebo reported pain (P = 0.144; the treatment made no difference), and moderate-severe pain occurred only in the gabapentin group (12.1% vs 0%)
cards.summary: Bulilete 2019: gabapentin started within 72 hours of rash onset did NOT prevent pain at 12 weeks — 18.2% with gabapentin vs 9.5% with placebo reported pain (P = 0.144; the treatment made no difference), and moderate-severe pain occurred only in the gabapentin group (12.1% vs 0%)
cards.people: 98 patients older than 50 years presenting with herpes zoster within 72 hours of rash onset and moderate-severe pain (4 or more on a 10-point visual analogue scale), randomised in 17 primary-care centres in Mallorca, Spain, to gabapentin (started at 300 mg/day, titrated to a maximum of 1,800 mg/day, for 5 weeks) or placebo; all patients received valaciclovir for 7 days and analgesia if needed, with 7 further weeks of follow-up. 75 patients completed the study (33 gabapentin, 42 control).
cards.result: 18.2% of patients in the gabapentin group and 9.5% in the control group reported pain at 12 weeks (P = 0.144) — no significant difference, with the point estimate favouring placebo. Four patients in the gabapentin group (12.1%), but no patients in the placebo group, reported pain of 4 or more on the 10-point scale. Patients taking gabapentin reported worse health-related quality of life and poorer sleep quality, and three patients discontinued because of gabapentin adverse effects. The authors conclude that adding gabapentin to usual treatment within 72 hours of rash onset provided no significant relief from acute herpetic pain or prevention of postherpetic neuralgia.
cards.watchOut: Attrition was uneven (33 of the gabapentin group versus 42 controls completed), and the trial is small for a prevention outcome — but it is the only randomised test of this exact strategy, its result is null-to-harmful in direction, and nothing carded contradicts it.
cards.source: Bulilete O et al. Efficacy of gabapentin for the prevention of postherpetic neuralgia in patients with acute herpes zoster: A double blind, randomized controlled trial. PloS one. 2019. PMID: 31166976. Registry ID: ISRCTN79871784. cards.headline: Krcevski Skvarc 2010: the sibling gabapentinoid pregabalin, given for 3 weeks during acute zoster, also made no difference — no significant effect on acute pain or on development of postherpetic neuralgia, with significantly more dizziness and somnolence (small trial, N = 29, printed here)
cards.summary: Krcevski Skvarc 2010: the sibling gabapentinoid pregabalin, given for 3 weeks during acute zoster, also made no difference — no significant effect on acute pain or on development of postherpetic neuralgia, with significantly more dizziness and somnolence (small trial, N = 29, printed here)
cards.people: 29 outpatients with acute zoster pain for 7–14 days, in a prospective randomised double-blind placebo-controlled study, treated for 3 weeks with pregabalin 150–300 mg daily or placebo; pain was also treated with naproxen, tramadol or oxycodone as necessary. Small single study N = 29.
cards.result: There were no statistically significant differences between pregabalin and placebo in intensity of pain, allodynia, hyperalgesia, burning, prickling or tingling sensations, consumption of analgesics, quality of sleep or physical activity, and no significant difference in development of postherpetic neuralgia. Dizziness and somnolence occurred significantly more often with pregabalin. The record reports no effect sizes for the pain or neuralgia comparisons — the null is printed as reported, and no number is invented here.
cards.watchOut: Pregabalin is not gabapentin, and with 29 patients this trial could miss a modest effect — it is carded as class corroboration only; the shelf's answer rests on the gabapentin trial above.
cards.source: Krcevski Skvarc N et al. Effects of pregabalin on acute herpetic pain and postherpetic neuralgia incidence. Wiener klinische Wochenschrift. 2010. PMID: 20517672. cards.headline: Chen 2014 (Cochrane): even antiviral treatment started within 72 hours does not significantly reduce postherpetic neuralgia — aciclovir relative risk 0.75 at 4 months (95% CI 0.51 to 1.11) and 1.05 at 6 months across 1,211 trial participants
cards.summary: Chen 2014 (Cochrane): even antiviral treatment started within 72 hours does not significantly reduce postherpetic neuralgia — aciclovir relative risk 0.75 at 4 months (95% CI 0.51 to 1.11) and 1.05 at 6 months across 1,211 trial participants
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane, Chen 2014)
cards.people: Six randomised trials (1,211 participants) of antiviral treatment given within 72 hours of herpes zoster onset for preventing postherpetic neuralgia: five trials of oral aciclovir and one of oral famciclovir (419 participants). All patients in the gabapentin trial carded above received valaciclovir as background treatment, so this is the prevention backdrop against which gabapentin was tested.
cards.result: Based on three trials (609 participants), there was no significant difference between aciclovir and control in the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia four months after rash onset (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.51 to 1.11), nor at six months (relative risk 1.05, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.27; two trials, 476 participants). In the famciclovir trial, neither the 500 mg nor the 750 mg dose reduced herpetic neuralgia significantly. The reviewers conclude there is high-quality evidence that oral aciclovir does not reduce the incidence of postherpetic neuralgia significantly.
cards.watchOut: This card answers a neighbouring question (antivirals, not gabapentin): it is carded to show that the failure to prevent postherpetic neuralgia is not unique to gabapentin — no early drug treatment has cleared that bar — not as evidence about gabapentin itself.
cards.source: Chen N et al. Antiviral treatment for preventing postherpetic neuralgia. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 24500927. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: early gabapentin does not prevent postherpetic neuralgia in the randomised evidence — the one direct trial was null with the estimate running the wrong way (18.2% vs 9.5% in pain at 12 weeks), the class sibling pregabalin was also null, and even early antivirals do not significantly prevent the condition
cards.summary: Synthesis: early gabapentin does not prevent postherpetic neuralgia in the randomised evidence — the one direct trial was null with the estimate running the wrong way (18.2% vs 9.5% in pain at 12 weeks), the class sibling pregabalin was also null, and even early antivirals do not significantly prevent the condition
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised gabapentin prevention trial (98 randomised, 75 completing), one small randomised pregabalin trial in acute zoster (N = 29, printed on its card), and the Cochrane antiviral-prevention pooling (6 trials, 1,211 participants). Total carded participants exceed 1,300, so no small-N stamp labelling applies at shelf level; the smallest single study's N is printed on its face.
cards.result: Gabapentin: pain at 12 weeks 18.2% vs 9.5%, P = 0.144 (the treatment made no difference), moderate-severe pain 12.1% vs 0% (Bulilete 2019). Pregabalin: no significant difference in pain or postherpetic neuralgia development (Krcevski Skvarc 2010). Antivirals: relative risk 0.75 (95% CI 0.51 to 1.11) for neuralgia at 4 months (Chen 2014). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no benefit shown): early gabapentin after herpes zoster does not prevent postherpetic neuralgia.
cards.watchOut: Gabapentin remains an established treatment for established postherpetic neuralgia pain — this shelf is only about prevention when started during acute zoster, and the prevention claim is what the trials fail to support.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bulilete O et al. PloS one. 2019 (PMID: 31166976); Krcevski Skvarc N et al. Wiener klinische Wochenschrift. 2010 (PMID: 20517672); Chen N et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014 (PMID: 24500927).

shelves.title: Treat-to-target beats symptom-driven gout care in the first head-to-head strategy trial (GO TEST Overture): remission in 39.4% versus 24.0%, with reaching urate under 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L) associated with far fewer flares (27% versus 64% having at least one flare)
shelves.question: In adults with gout, does treat-to-target urate lowering reduce flare frequency versus treat-to-symptoms management?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Allopurinol/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Benzbromarone/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Febuxostat/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Gout/drug therapy,blood · Gout Suppressants/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Hyperuricemia/drug therapy,blood · Netherlands · Treatment Outcome · Uric Acid/blood
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — single strategy trial, printed on the face. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #681 covers nurse-led treat-to-target care versus general-practitioner usual care (the Nottingham trial); the uncovered slice carded here is the formal strategy comparison — treat-to-target against treat-to-symptoms management itself. The GO TEST Overture trial (Moses 2026; 308 adults with gout and hyperuricaemia not on urate-lowering therapy, in Dutch secondary care) randomised exactly that: structured urate-guided titration to a serum urate under 0.36 mmol/L (≈6.1 mg/dL) versus symptom-driven management in which starting urate-lowering therapy was discretionary. Remission during months 18–24 — a composite requiring no flares in that window, no tophi, low pain, and high patient global assessment — occurred in 39.4% versus 24.0% (absolute difference 15.4 percentage points, 95% CI 6.4 to 24.4; P = 0.024), with adverse events in 42% versus 53%. On flares specifically, the supporting individual-patient analysis of two earlier trials (Stamp 2022; 588 participants) found that patients whose average serum urate fell under 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L) had at least one flare in months 12–24 in 27% of cases versus 64% of non-responders (adjusted odds ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.51) and fewer flares per month (adjusted mean difference −1.41) — an association independent of the original randomised allocation, so supportive rather than randomised strategy evidence. The large US primary-care strategy trial designed to answer this question definitively (Solomon 2025, TRUST) has published its design only, with no results in the record. One completed strategy trial therefore caps the stamp. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): treat-to-target urate lowering reduces flares and improves disease control versus treat-to-symptoms management.

cards.headline: GO TEST Overture (Moses 2026): treat-to-target (urate under 0.36 mmol/L, ≈6.1 mg/dL) beat symptom-driven management on remission at months 18–24 — 39.4% versus 24.0% (difference 15.4 points) in 308 adults with gout
cards.summary: GO TEST Overture (Moses 2026): treat-to-target (urate under 0.36 mmol/L, ≈6.1 mg/dL) beat symptom-driven management on remission at months 18–24 — 39.4% versus 24.0% (difference 15.4 points) in 308 adults with gout
cards.type: Pragmatic randomised controlled strategy trial (Moses 2026, GO TEST Overture)
cards.people: 308 adults (87% male; mean age 65.9 years) with gout and hyperuricaemia (typically serum urate over 0.36 mmol/L, ≈6.1 mg/dL) not currently using urate-lowering therapy, at eight Dutch secondary-care rheumatology centres, randomised to a treat-to-target strategy (145) with structured urate-guided titration of oral urate-lowering therapy (first-line allopurinol; second-line febuxostat or benzbromarone) or to symptom-driven management (163) in which whether to start urate-lowering therapy, and its type and dose, were left to physician and patient discretion without a urate target. Open-label, pragmatic design.
cards.result: The primary outcome — remission during months 18–24, defined as absence of gout flares during months 18–24, no subcutaneous tophi at month 24, a patient-reported pain score under 2, and a patient global assessment score over 8 — occurred more often with treat-to-target than symptom-driven management (39.4% [57 of 145] vs 24.0% [39 of 163]; absolute difference 15.4 percentage points, 95% CI 6.4 to 24.4; P = 0.024). Adverse events occurred in 61 (42%) treat-to-target and 86 (53%) symptom-driven participants (difference −10.7 points, 95% CI −21.8 to 0.4; P = 0.060); no serious drug-related adverse events and no treatment-related deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a remission composite, not flare frequency alone: freedom from flares in months 18–24 is one of its four components, so the trial proves better overall disease control under treat-to-target, with the flare-specific numbers carried by the Stamp analysis below. Open-label and conducted in secondary care, where symptom-driven care may be more structured than in primary practice.
cards.source: Moses A et al. A treat-to-target strategy versus symptom-driven management of gout in the Netherlands (GO TEST Overture): a multicentre, open-label, pragmatic, superiority, randomised controlled trial. The Lancet Rheumatology. 2026. PMID: 41865749. Registry ID: EudraCT 2020-005721-82 (from the record). cards.headline: Stamp 2022: patients who reached average serum urate under 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L) had at least one flare in months 12–24 in 27% of cases versus 64% for non-responders (adjusted OR 0.29), and 1.41 fewer flares per month
cards.summary: Stamp 2022: patients who reached average serum urate under 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L) had at least one flare in months 12–24 in 27% of cases versus 64% for non-responders (adjusted OR 0.29), and 1.41 fewer flares per month
cards.type: Secondary individual-patient analysis of two randomised trials (Stamp 2022)
cards.people: 588 participants with gout from two randomised urate-lowering trials (Nottingham, UK, and New Zealand) with individual patient-level data; serum urate responders (343) were those whose average serum urate at 6, 9 and 12 months was under 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L), and non-responders numbered 245. Outcomes were assessed from 12 to 24 months.
cards.result: Significantly fewer serum urate responders had a gout flare between 12 and 24 months than non-responders (91 [27%] of 343 vs 156 [64%] of 245; adjusted odds ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.51; P < 0.0001), and the mean number of flares per participant per month was significantly lower in responders (adjusted mean difference −1.41, 95% CI −1.77 to −1.04; P < 0.0001). The association was independent of the original randomised treatment allocation. The authors conclude that achieving an average serum urate under 6 mg/dL (0.36 mmol/L) is associated with absence of flares and fewer flares in the subsequent 12 months, supporting a treat-to-target approach.
cards.watchOut: Responder status is achieved, not randomised: patients who reach target differ from those who do not (adherence, disease severity, drug tolerance), so the 27%-versus-64% contrast overstates what the strategy itself guarantees — it is carded as mechanistic support for the target, with the randomised strategy evidence on the GO TEST card.
cards.source: Stamp LK et al. Association between serum urate and flares in people with gout and evidence for surrogate status: a secondary analysis of two randomised controlled trials. The Lancet Rheumatology. 2022. PMID: 38288731. Registry ID: NCT01477346. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Solomon 2025 (TRUST design): the large US primary-care trial of treat-to-target serum urate versus treat-to-avoid-symptoms, with flares as the primary outcome, has published its design only — no results in the record
cards.summary: Solomon 2025 (TRUST design): the large US primary-care trial of treat-to-target serum urate versus treat-to-avoid-symptoms, with flares as the primary outcome, has published its design only — no results in the record
cards.type: Trial design paper, no results (Solomon 2025, TRUST)
cards.people: Design for a pragmatic randomised comparative-effectiveness trial in primary care: patients with known gout, elevated serum urate, and at least one flare in the previous 12 months. Of the first 1,381 patients found in primary-care records, 691 (50%) passed prescreening; potentially eligible participants had a median age of 67 years, 85% were men, median serum urate was 7.2 mg/dL, and 18% were taking low-dose allopurinol. No participants had been randomised in the record fetched.
cards.result: No outcome results are reported — this is a design paper. The treat-to-target arm will receive urate-lowering therapy (primarily allopurinol) titrated to maintain serum urate under 6 mg/dL with six months of flare prophylaxis; the treat-to-avoid-symptoms arm will receive week-long flare-treatment courses (colchicine, naproxen, or an oral glucocorticoid) without urate lowering. Gout flares, assessed every two weeks by masked staff with a validated questionnaire, are the primary outcome. Recruitment was underway at publication.
cards.watchOut: A design card is evidence about the state of the science, not about gout treatment: it is carded so the shelf does not pretend the definitive primary-care strategy trial has reported, and it must never be cited as a result.
cards.source: Solomon DH et al. The Design of a Randomized Controlled Active Comparator Strategy Trial for Gout: Treat to Target Serum Urate Versus Treat to Avoid Symptoms. ACR Open Rheumatology. 2025. PMID: 40126890. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

shelves.title: Tramadol in older adults with neuropathic pain: generally avoid — modest 4–6-week benefit, adverse events in 58%, a reproducible early hyponatraemia signal, and more fractures than codeine (though recorded falls did not differ)
shelves.question: Should tramadol be avoided in older adults with neuropathic pain because of hyponatremia and falls?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Opioid · Humans · Middle Aged · Neuralgia · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Tramadol
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only for the hyponatraemia and fracture outcomes. PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2696, which covers tramadol's benefit–harm balance in musculoskeletal and osteoarthritis pain; this shelf answers only the uncovered slice, older adults with neuropathic pain and the hyponatraemia/falls harms, and none of #2696's carded records is re-carded here. The benefit in neuropathic pain is modest and short-term: at least 50% relief in 53% versus 30% on placebo over 4–6 weeks (NNT 4.4, low-quality evidence), with adverse events in 58% versus 34% and adverse-event withdrawal in 16% versus 3% (Duehmke 2017, Cochrane). The hyponatraemia signal is consistent across designs and is concentrated at initiation: hospitalisation for severe hyponatraemia at an adjusted odds ratio of 2.34 in the first 90 days, with no increased risk in ongoing users (Falhammar 2019), and early laboratory hyponatraemia at a matched rate ratio of 1.57 versus acetaminophen alone (Lee 2023). On falls the record is more nuanced than the question assumes: the large tramadol-versus-codeine cohort found more fractures (hazard ratio 1.50; 12.26 vs 8.13 per 1,000 person-years) and higher mortality, but no significant difference in recorded falls (Xie 2021) — both facts are printed on the card. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only for harms: in older adults with neuropathic pain, tramadol's modest, short-lived benefit does not justify its adverse-event burden and early hyponatraemia risk, and it should generally be avoided.

cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Duehmke 2017, Cochrane)
cards.people: Cochrane review of six randomised double-blind studies (438 participants) of tramadol for chronic neuropathic pain (cancer or cancer treatment, postherpetic neuralgia, diabetic neuropathy, spinal cord injury, polyneuropathy); mean age 50 to 67 years; tramadol started at about 100 mg daily and titrated to a maximum of 400 mg daily or the maximum tolerated dose; treatment lasted 4 to 6 weeks.
cards.result: At least 50% pain relief was reported by 70 of 132 participants (53%) on tramadol versus 40 of 133 (30%) on placebo (relative risk 2.2, 95% CI 1.02 to 4.6; number needed to treat 4.4, 95% CI 2.9 to 8.8) — absolute rates 53% versus 30% as printed. Any adverse event was reported by 58% on tramadol versus 34% on placebo (relative risk 1.6, 1.2 to 2.1; number needed to harm 4.2), and adverse-event withdrawal by 16% versus 3% (relative risk 4.1, 2.0 to 8.4; number needed to harm 8.2). Only four serious adverse events were reported, with no deaths. The reviewers graded the benefit evidence low quality and adverse-event evidence low or very low quality, from small studies at risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: The trials were short (4–6 weeks), small and excluded people with significant comorbidity — precisely the older, frailer patients this shelf is about — and they predate long-term harm follow-up, so the trial record understates the real-world harm side of the balance.

cards.headline: Falhammar 2019: newly started tramadol was associated with hospitalisation for severe hyponatraemia at an adjusted odds ratio of 2.34 — while ongoing use showed no increased risk (adjusted odds ratio 0.70)
cards.summary: Falhammar 2019: newly started tramadol was associated with hospitalisation for severe hyponatraemia at an adjusted odds ratio of 2.34 — while ongoing use showed no increased risk (adjusted odds ratio 0.70)
cards.people: Swedish population-based case-control study: 14,359 people hospitalised with a principal diagnosis of hyponatraemia compared with 57,383 matched controls from the general population; multivariable logistic regression adjusted for co-medication, diseases, previous hospitalisations and socioeconomic factors.
cards.result: The unadjusted odds ratio for hospitalisation due to hyponatraemia was 2.45 (95% CI 2.26 to 2.66) for tramadol; after adjustment it fell to 1.17 (1.08 to 1.26). For newly initiated treatment (within 90 days) the adjusted odds ratio was 2.34 (95% CI 2.01 to 2.72), whereas for ongoing therapy it was 0.70 (0.61 to 0.80) — no increased risk. The authors note the association may be causal or may reflect pain, nausea or the underlying disease.
cards.watchOut: Case-control data cannot prove tramadol caused the hyponatraemia — the illness or pain prompting the prescription can lower sodium too — and the protective-looking estimate for ongoing use (0.70) most likely reflects depletion of susceptible patients early in treatment, not a benefit of staying on the drug.
cards.source: Falhammar H et al. Tramadol- and codeine-induced severe hyponatremia: A Swedish population-based case-control study. European Journal of Internal Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31416660. cards.headline: Lee 2023: hyponatraemia within 10 days of starting tramadol/acetaminophen occurred in 8.4% versus 4.2% on acetaminophen alone — a matched incidence rate ratio of 1.57
cards.summary: Lee 2023: hyponatraemia within 10 days of starting tramadol/acetaminophen occurred in 8.4% versus 4.2% on acetaminophen alone — a matched incidence rate ratio of 1.57
cards.people: Real-world hospital database study (OMOP common data model) of 30,999 patients taking tramadol/acetaminophen (n = 19,149) or acetaminophen alone (n = 11,850) from 2011 to 2020; 39.1% were aged over 65 years. New-onset hyponatraemia was defined as serum sodium under 135 mEq/L within 10 days of drug initiation; analyses included 1:1 propensity-score matching.
cards.result: Hyponatraemia developed in 1,613 of 19,149 patients (8.4%) on the tramadol combination versus 493 of 11,850 (4.2%) on acetaminophen alone. In the matched model the incidence rate was 6.8 per 1,000 person-days with tramadol/acetaminophen versus 4.3 per 1,000 person-days without tramadol — a rate ratio of 1.57 (95% CI 1.31 to 1.89). The extended-release tramadol formulation carried a significantly higher incidence than the immediate-release formulation in both crude and matched models.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is any sodium under 135 mEq/L within 10 days — mostly mild, laboratory-defined hyponatraemia in hospital patients, not the severe symptomatic events of the Swedish study — and residual confounding by the reason tramadol was prescribed remains possible despite matching.
cards.source: Lee YJ et al. Risk of Hyponatremia after Tramadol/Acetaminophen Single-Pill Combination Therapy: A Real-World Study Based on the OMOP-CDM Database. Drugs in R&D. 2023. PMID: 37507616. cards.headline: Xie 2021: versus codeine, new tramadol dispensing was associated with more fractures (hazard ratio 1.50; absolute rates 12.26 vs 8.13 per 1,000 person-years) and higher mortality — but the falls outcome itself did not differ significantly (printed plainly)
cards.summary: Xie 2021: versus codeine, new tramadol dispensing was associated with more fractures (hazard ratio 1.50; absolute rates 12.26 vs 8.13 per 1,000 person-years) and higher mortality — but the falls outcome itself did not differ significantly (printed plainly)
cards.people: Population-based propensity-matched cohort in a Catalan primary-care database covering about 6 million people: 368,960 patients (184,480 matched pairs; mean age 53.1 years, 57.3% women) with a new dispensation of tramadol or codeine between 2007 and 2017, followed for 1 year for mortality, cardiovascular events, fractures, falls, delirium, constipation, opioid abuse/dependence and sleep disorders.
cards.result: Compared with codeine, tramadol was associated with higher all-cause mortality (13.00 vs 5.61 per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 2.31, 95% CI 2.08 to 2.56; absolute rate difference 7.37 per 1,000 person-years), cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 1.15, 1.05 to 1.27) and fractures (12.26 vs 8.13 per 1,000 person-years; hazard ratio 1.50, 1.37 to 1.65; absolute rate difference 4.10 per 1,000 person-years). No significant difference was observed for the risk of falls, delirium, constipation, opioid abuse/dependence, or sleep disorders in the record.
cards.watchOut: This is a general adult primary-care population (mean age 53), not older adults with neuropathic pain specifically, and dispensing is not consumption; the fracture excess without a falls excess may reflect coding or confounding by indication rather than a falls mechanism — the shelf prints both facts rather than merging them.
cards.source: Xie J et al. Association of Tramadol vs Codeine Prescription Dispensation With Mortality and Other Adverse Clinical Outcomes. JAMA. 2021. PMID: 34665205. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for older adults with neuropathic pain the balance is unfavourable — modest short-term pain relief bought with frequent adverse events, a reproducible early hyponatraemia signal, and a fracture signal in comparative data, while the direct falls outcome was not significantly increased in the one large comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: for older adults with neuropathic pain the balance is unfavourable — modest short-term pain relief bought with frequent adverse events, a reproducible early hyponatraemia signal, and a fracture signal in comparative data, while the direct falls outcome was not significantly increased in the one large comparison
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of neuropathic-pain trials (438 participants, mean ages 50–67), one population case-control study of hyponatraemia hospitalisation (14,359 cases, 57,383 controls), one database cohort on early hyponatraemia (30,999 patients, 39% over 65) and one propensity-matched comparative cohort (368,960 patients). Total carded participants exceed 470,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Benefit: at least 50% pain relief in 53% versus 30% on placebo over 4–6 weeks (NNT 4.4), graded low quality (Duehmke 2017). Harms: any adverse event 58% versus 34% and adverse-event withdrawal 16% versus 3% in those same trials; hyponatraemia hospitalisation adjusted odds ratio 2.34 in the first 90 days (Falhammar 2019) and early hyponatraemia rate ratio 1.57 versus acetaminophen alone (Lee 2023); fractures hazard ratio 1.50 versus codeine with no significant difference in recorded falls (Xie 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only for the hyponatraemia and fracture outcomes: tramadol should generally be avoided in older adults with neuropathic pain.
cards.watchOut: No carded study enrolled older adults with neuropathic pain and measured hyponatraemia and falls together — the shelf assembles the harm picture from the neuropathic-pain trials plus general-population harm studies, and says so; the recommendation to avoid is a balance judgement on that assembled evidence, not a single trial's result.

shelves.title: Aerobic exercise for post-stroke fatigue (partial completion of #1522, which covers fitness and gait): interval training cut fatigue scores in a small trial and graded activity boosted fatigue-therapy response — POSSIBLE benefit, two small trials only
shelves.question: Does a structured aerobic exercise program reduce post-stroke fatigue?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Cardiorespiratory Fitness · Female · Fatigue · Stroke · Middle Aged · Male · Aged · Stroke Rehabilitation · Exercise Therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1522, which covers aerobic exercise in chronic stroke for fitness and gait (Macko 2005 treadmill trial, carded there and not re-carded here) but never measured fatigue. On the uncovered fatigue slice, the direct evidence is thin but concordant. A small 2026 randomised trial of home-based supervised cardiorespiratory interval training (Bråndal 2026, PMID: 42089147; 45 randomised) cut fatigue by 5.35 Swedish Fatigue Assessment Scale points versus usual care and raised peak oxygen uptake. A second randomised trial (Zedlitz 2012, PMID: 22308241) found that adding graded activity training to cognitive therapy produced clinical fatigue improvement in 58% versus 24% of patients with persistent post-stroke fatigue, though the activity component cannot be isolated from the cognitive therapy it was bundled with. The wider literature urges caution: the Cochrane review of post-stroke fatigue interventions (Wu 2015, PMID: 26133313) pooled no aerobic-exercise treatment trial and judged the evidence for every intervention insufficient, and an observational meta-analysis (Larsson 2023, PMID: 36622013) found only a weak association between fatigue and fitness (r = −0.24). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a structured aerobic programme probably reduces post-stroke fatigue, on one small direct trial plus one combined-intervention trial; larger and longer trials are still needed.

cards.headline: Bråndal 2026: home-based supervised cardiorespiratory interval training cut post-stroke fatigue by 5.35 points versus usual care and raised peak oxygen uptake by 4.48 mL/kg/min — in 45 randomised patients (small N on the face)
cards.summary: Bråndal 2026: home-based supervised cardiorespiratory interval training cut post-stroke fatigue by 5.35 points versus usual care and raised peak oxygen uptake by 4.48 mL/kg/min — in 45 randomised patients (small N on the face)
cards.people: 45 participants with post-stroke fatigue (Swedish Fatigue Assessment Scale score 28 or above), 1 to 7 months after stroke, randomised 1:1 at two centres to a home-based supervised cardiorespiratory interval training programme or to usual care with self-directed activity after early supported discharge; 43 completed the post-intervention assessment (22 training, 21 control). Mean age 64 years; 56% women. Randomised N = 45.
cards.result: The training programme was 35-minute cycling sessions three times a week at 70% to 80% of maximum heart rate for 8 weeks. In adjusted intention-to-treat analyses, fatigue at 8 weeks was lower with training than control (between-group mean difference −5.35 Swedish Fatigue Assessment Scale points, 95% CI −9.03 to −3.67; P < 0.001) and peak oxygen uptake was higher (+4.48 mL/kg per minute, 95% CI 3.41 to 5.54; P < 0.001). Adherence was 92% and no adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: A single small, open-label trial with an 8-week horizon: it was powered to detect a 9-point fatigue difference and found 5.35 points, and whether the benefit persists beyond the programme is unknown.
cards.source: Bråndal A et al. Home-Based Supervised Cardiorespiratory Interval Training Decreases Poststroke Fatigue and Improves Cardiorespiratory Fitness: A Randomized Controlled Trial. Stroke. 2026. PMID: 42089147. Registry ID: NCT03458884. cards.headline: Zedlitz 2012 (COGRAT): adding graded activity training to cognitive therapy produced clinical fatigue improvement in 58% versus 24% of stroke patients with persistent fatigue
cards.summary: Zedlitz 2012 (COGRAT): adding graded activity training to cognitive therapy produced clinical fatigue improvement in 58% versus 24% of stroke patients with persistent fatigue
cards.people: 83 stroke patients more than 4 months after stroke with persistent fatigue, recruited at 8 rehabilitation centres and randomly assigned after a 3-month qualification period to 12 weeks of cognitive therapy alone or cognitive therapy plus graded activity training (COGRAT); 73 completed treatment and 68 were available at follow-up.
cards.result: Both treatments significantly improved fatigue, but gains for the combined group exceeded cognitive therapy alone on the number of individuals showing clinical improvement on the Checklist Individual Strength fatigue subscale (improvement of 8 points or more: 58% versus 24%) and on physical endurance (partial eta-squared 0.20, P < 0.001). The authors conclude that a 12-week cognitive therapy programme can alleviate persistent fatigue after stroke, with the best results when it is augmented with graded activity training.
cards.watchOut: The graded activity was bundled with cognitive therapy and compared against cognitive therapy alone, so this trial shows activity training adds benefit inside a fatigue programme — it does not isolate a purely aerobic exercise effect.
cards.source: Zedlitz AM et al. Cognitive and graded activity training can alleviate persistent fatigue after stroke: a randomized, controlled trial. Stroke. 2012. PMID: 22308241. Registry ID: NTR2704. cards.headline: Wu 2015 (Cochrane): across 12 post-stroke fatigue trials the pooled benefit vanished in well-concealed trials — and no aerobic-exercise trial was among the pooled treatment comparisons
cards.summary: Wu 2015 (Cochrane): across 12 post-stroke fatigue trials the pooled benefit vanished in well-concealed trials — and no aerobic-exercise trial was among the pooled treatment comparisons
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of interventions to treat or prevent post-stroke fatigue: 12 trials with 703 participants; eight trials primarily investigated treating fatigue, of which six trials with seven comparisons (five pharmacological interventions, a fatigue education programme and a mindfulness-based stress reduction programme) provided data suitable for meta-analysis.
cards.result: Fatigue severity was lower in the intervention groups than the control groups (244 participants, pooled standardised mean difference −1.07, 95% CI −1.93 to −0.21), with significant heterogeneity (I-squared 87%). The beneficial effect was not seen in trials that had used adequate allocation concealment (two trials, 89 participants, SMD −0.38, 95% CI −0.80 to 0.04). The reviewers concluded there was insufficient evidence on the efficacy of any intervention to treat or prevent fatigue after stroke.
cards.watchOut: This review is carded as the state-of-the-field check, not as exercise evidence: none of its pooled treatment comparisons tested aerobic exercise, so it cannot confirm or refute the exercise trials above — it shows how fragile the fatigue-treatment literature was before them.
cards.source: Wu S et al. Interventions for post-stroke fatigue. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 26133313. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Antidepressive Agents · Drugs, Chinese Herbal · Fatigue · Female · Humans · Male · Mindfulness · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stress, Psychological · Stroke

cards.headline: Larsson 2023: higher post-stroke fatigue was only weakly associated with impaired fitness (meta r = −0.24) and not associated with physical activity — observational data only
cards.summary: Larsson 2023: higher post-stroke fatigue was only weakly associated with impaired fitness (meta r = −0.24) and not associated with physical activity — observational data only
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Larsson 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (cross-sectional or prospective) of post-stroke fatigue and its associations with physical activity and physical fitness: 32 unique studies with a total of 4,721 participants.
cards.result: There was moderate-certainty evidence of a weak association between higher post-stroke fatigue and impaired fitness (meta r = −0.24, 95% CI −0.33 to −0.15; n = 905, 7 studies), and very low-certainty evidence of no association between fatigue and physical activity (meta r = −0.09, 95% CI −0.34 to 0.161; n = 430, 3 studies). The authors note the results indicate fitness might protect against fatigue, and that randomised trials of exercise for fatigue are needed.
cards.watchOut: Association is not treatment effect: fatigued patients may simply be less able to exercise, so this card supports the rationale for aerobic training, not its efficacy.
cards.source: Larsson P et al. Association of post-stroke fatigue with physical activity and physical fitness: A systematic review and meta-analysis. International journal of stroke : official journal of the International Stroke Society. 2023. PMID: 36622013. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: structured aerobic training probably reduces post-stroke fatigue — one small direct interval-training trial and one graded-activity trial point the same way, against a literature the Cochrane review judged insufficient
cards.summary: Synthesis: structured aerobic training probably reduces post-stroke fatigue — one small direct interval-training trial and one graded-activity trial point the same way, against a literature the Cochrane review judged insufficient
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial of home-based cardiorespiratory interval training versus usual care in patients selected for post-stroke fatigue (45 randomised), one randomised trial of graded activity training added to cognitive therapy (83 randomised), one Cochrane review of fatigue interventions (12 trials, 703 participants, no exercise trial pooled) and one observational meta-analysis (32 studies, 4,721 participants). Unique participants in the two exercise trials total 128, so no small-N stamp labelling applies, but each trial is small and the limitation is printed on the faces.
cards.result: Interval training reduced fatigue by 5.35 points (95% CI −9.03 to −3.67) and raised peak oxygen uptake by 4.48 mL/kg per minute versus usual care (Bråndal 2026). Adding graded activity to cognitive therapy raised the proportion with clinical fatigue improvement from 24% to 58% (Zedlitz 2012). The Cochrane review found the overall fatigue-intervention evidence insufficient and its pooled benefit absent in adequately concealed trials (Wu 2015), and observational data link fatigue only weakly to fitness (Larsson 2023). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #1522 answers the fitness and gait question for aerobic exercise after stroke; this shelf answers only the fatigue outcome, and its two positive trials are small, short and — in one case — a combined intervention.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bråndal A et al. Stroke. 2026 (PMID: 42089147); Zedlitz AM et al. Stroke. 2012 (PMID: 22308241); Wu S et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015 (PMID: 26133313); Larsson P et al. International journal of stroke. 2023 (PMID: 36622013).
