shelves.title: Long-term opioids for neuropathic pain without functional gain (PARTIAL completion of #346): trials show pain relief but no functional improvement, and tapering usually leaves pain unchanged — continuation is not supported
shelves.question: Should opioids be continued long term for chronic neuropathic pain if function does not improve?
shelves.mesh: Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Nervous System Diseases/complications/drug therapy · Neuralgia/drug therapy · Pain/drug therapy/etiology · Pain Measurement/methods/statistics & numerical data · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #346, which covers long-term opioid versus non-opioid strategy in chronic back and joint pain; this shelf covers the slices #346 does not: neuropathic pain specifically, and the continuation question when function does not improve. The neuropathic-pain trial base (McNicol 2013, PMID: 23986501, Cochrane) reaches only 12 weeks: intermediate-term trials showed modest pain relief (at least 33% relief in 57% on opioid versus 34% on placebo) but opioids did not demonstrate improvement in many aspects of emotional or physical functioning — the trials show pain scores moving without function moving. No randomised trial tests continuation beyond 12 weeks. The tapering literature (Mackey 2020, PMID: 33145689) finds pain scores mostly unchanged or improved after dose reduction, with low confidence, and observational signals of overdose and suicidal ideation after reduction or discontinuation that mandate monitoring. A voluntary patient-centred tapering cohort (Darnall 2018, PMID: 29459978; 2–3-year follow-up, PMID: 33490845) reduced doses durably with pain intensity unchanged on average. None of the tapering studies was restricted to neuropathic pain — printed plainly, that is the remaining gap. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): continuing long-term opioids for chronic neuropathic pain when function does not improve — pain relief in trials is modest and function does not improve, while supervised tapering usually leaves pain unchanged.

cards.headline: McNicol 2013 (Cochrane): opioids beat placebo for neuropathic pain over ≤12 weeks (≥33% relief in 57% versus 34%) but did not improve emotional or physical functioning — and no trial ran longer
cards.summary: McNicol 2013 (Cochrane): opioids beat placebo for neuropathic pain over ≤12 weeks (≥33% relief in 57% versus 34%) but did not improve emotional or physical functioning — and no trial ran longer
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane; McNicol 2013)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 31 randomised trials of opioid agonists for central or peripheral neuropathic pain of any aetiology. Fourteen intermediate-term studies (lasting 12 weeks or less, most under 6 weeks) included 845 participants; 17 acute-exposure studies (under 24 hours) included 392 participants.
cards.result: In intermediate-term studies, at least 33% pain relief was achieved by 57% of participants on an opioid versus 34% on placebo (risk difference 0.25, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.37; number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome 4.0); at least 50% relief: 47% versus 30% (NNTB 5.9). However, the review states opioids did not demonstrate improvement in many aspects of emotional or physical functioning, as measured by validated questionnaires. Harms: constipation 34% versus 9% (NNTH 4.0), drowsiness 29% versus 14%, nausea 27% versus 9%; 13% withdrew for adverse events versus 4% on placebo. The reviewers warn the efficacy results are likely to overestimate benefit (small, short studies with dropout handling prone to bias) and that long-term efficacy, safety and quality-of-life effects are unestablished.
cards.watchOut: Every efficacy number here comes from trials of 12 weeks or less in a question about long-term continuation: the review can show what opioids do to pain and function in the short term, and its most important finding for this shelf is negative — functioning did not improve.
cards.source: McNicol ED et al. Opioids for neuropathic pain.. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. PMID: 23986501. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mackey 2020 (rapid review of dose reduction/discontinuation): pain scores mostly unchanged or improved after tapering, confidence low — and observational signals of overdose and suicidal ideation after reduction mean tapering must be monitored
cards.summary: Mackey 2020 (rapid review of dose reduction/discontinuation): pain scores mostly unchanged or improved after tapering, confidence low — and observational signals of overdose and suicidal ideation after reduction mean tapering must be monitored
cards.people: Rapid systematic review (an update of a 2017 review) of 49 studies of long-term opioid therapy dose reduction or discontinuation in patients with chronic pain, prioritising 19 studies most applicable to outpatients and Veteran populations. Not restricted to neuropathic pain — no neuropathic-specific tapering synthesis was found.
cards.result: Improvements in mean pain scores were common among patients tapering while participating in intensive multimodal pain interventions, and pain was mostly unchanged with less intensive or nonspecific co-interventions. The reviewers' confidence in these findings is low because of methodological limitations. Observational data suggest serious harms such as opioid overdose and suicidal ideation can occur following dose reduction or discontinuation, but their incidence at population level is unknown; the net balance of benefits and harms of dose reduction is unclear, and clinicians should closely monitor patients during tapering.
cards.watchOut: Low-confidence, largely observational evidence about chronic pain in general, not neuropathic pain in particular — and it cuts both ways: it does not show tapering harms pain, but it documents that forced or unmonitored discontinuation carries its own serious risks.
cards.source: Mackey K et al. Benefits and Harms of Long-term Opioid Dose Reduction or Discontinuation in Patients with Chronic Pain: a Rapid Review.. Journal of general internal medicine. 2020. PMID: 33145689. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Darnall 2018: voluntary, patient-centred opioid tapering in community outpatients was feasible without behavioural treatment — the record reports no outcome numbers, printed plainly
cards.summary: Darnall 2018: voluntary, patient-centred opioid tapering in community outpatients was feasible without behavioural treatment — the record reports no outcome numbers, printed plainly
cards.people: Education-intervention study of voluntary, patient-centred prescription opioid tapering in community outpatients with chronic pain, without behavioural treatment. The record's abstract is a single summary sentence and reports no participant number and no outcome values.
cards.result: No effect size, pain score, dose value or participant count is reported in the record fetched this session — the card is included because its 2–3-year follow-up (carded next) supplies the numbers, and the pair together are the longest prospective tapering evidence found. The record establishes only the study's design and setting: voluntary tapering, community outpatients, no behavioural treatment component.
cards.watchOut: A design-only card: nothing about whether tapering helped or harmed can be taken from this record alone, and the cohort's chronic pain was not restricted to neuropathic pain.
cards.source: Darnall BD et al. Patient-Centered Prescription Opioid Tapering in Community Outpatients With Chronic Pain.. JAMA internal medicine. 2018. PMID: 29459978. cards.headline: Darnall 2020 follow-up: 2–3 years after voluntary tapering, 95% of reachable patients had reduced their opioid dose and pain intensity was unchanged on average — but only 23 patients (44%) were reached, by self-report
cards.summary: Darnall 2020 follow-up: 2–3 years after voluntary tapering, 95% of reachable patients had reduced their opioid dose and pain intensity was unchanged on average — but only 23 patients (44%) were reached, by self-report
cards.people: Two-to-three-year telephone follow-up of a subset of the Darnall 2018 voluntary tapering cohort: 23 patients responded (44% of the original sample), reporting average pain intensity and current opioid use, converted to morphine equivalent daily dose. Small single-cohort N = 23, printed on the face.
cards.result: Since baseline, 20 (95%) of the followed patients had reduced their morphine equivalent daily dose, and 15 (71%) had reduced further between 4 months and the 2–3-year follow-up. There was no effect of time on change in pain intensity across baseline, 4 months and 2–3 years; 11 (52%) reported pain reduction since baseline and 5 (24%) reported increased pain intensity. Opioid use was self-reported and could not be verified against medical records.
cards.watchOut: Fewer than half the original patients were reached, outcomes are self-reported and unverified, and there is no comparison group: this shows durable dose reduction without average pain worsening is achievable in motivated volunteers — it does not show what happens when tapering is imposed.
cards.source: Darnall BD et al. Patient-centered prescription opioid tapering in community outpatients with chronic pain: 2- to 3-year follow-up in a subset of patients. JAMA internal medicine. 2020. PMID: 33490845. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: trials show pain relief without functional improvement over ≤12 weeks, and tapering usually leaves pain unchanged — continuation without functional gain is not supported, but tapering must be voluntary and monitored
cards.summary: Synthesis: trials show pain relief without functional improvement over ≤12 weeks, and tapering usually leaves pain unchanged — continuation without functional gain is not supported, but tapering must be voluntary and monitored
cards.people: The carded evidence: one Cochrane review of 31 neuropathic-pain trials (845 participants in intermediate-term studies), one rapid review of 49 dose-reduction studies in chronic pain generally, and one small voluntary tapering cohort with its 23-patient long-term follow-up. Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the 23-patient follow-up carries its N on its own face.
cards.result: Neuropathic pain: ≥33% relief 57% versus 34% (NNTB 4.0) over ≤12 weeks, with no demonstrated improvement in emotional or physical functioning and common harms (constipation NNTH 4.0). Dose reduction: pain mostly unchanged or improved (low confidence); serious harms after discontinuation are reported observationally at unknown incidence. Voluntary tapering: dose reductions durable at 2–3 years with pain intensity unchanged on average. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) for continuing long-term opioids when function does not improve.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap: no study — trial or taper — was restricted to neuropathic pain patients whose function had failed to improve, which is exactly this shelf's population; the answer is assembled from the neuropathic trial base plus general chronic-pain tapering evidence, and the shelf says so.
cards.source: Synthesis of McNicol ED et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013 (PMID: 23986501); Mackey K et al. Journal of general internal medicine. 2020 (PMID: 33145689); Darnall BD et al. JAMA internal medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29459978) and 2020 (PMID: 33490845).

shelves.title: Calcium plus vitamin D and hip fractures in community-dwelling older adults (PARTIAL): no prevention — 33 trials and two mega-trials are null, unlike the deficient nursing-home population on the home shelf
shelves.question: In older adults, does calcium plus vitamin D supplementation prevent hip fractures in community-dwelling people versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Calcium/therapeutic use · Dietary Supplements · Drug Therapy, Combination · Fractures, Bone/epidemiology · Fractures, Bone/prevention & control · Hip Fractures/epidemiology · Hip Fractures/prevention & control · Humans · Incidence · Independent Living · Middle Aged · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk · Vitamin D/therapeutic use · Vitamins/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1498. That shelf covers calcium plus vitamin D in nursing-home elderly women, where the deficient institutionalised population benefited; it does not cover the community-dwelling population. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: community-dwelling older adults. The evidence is concordantly null. A JAMA meta-analysis of 33 randomised trials with 51,145 community-dwelling participants older than 50 found combined calcium and vitamin D was not associated with hip fracture (relative risk 1.09; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39; absolute risk difference 0.00; Zhao 2017). The RECORD trial (5,292 people aged 70 or older after a low-trauma fracture) found no difference between combination treatment and placebo for new fractures (12.6% vs 13.4%; Grant 2005), and the Women's Health Initiative trial (36,282 postmenopausal women, 7 years) found a non-significant hip-fracture hazard ratio of 0.88 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.08) with significantly more kidney stones (HR 1.17; Jackson 2006). The deficiency-correcting nursing-home result on #1498 does not generalise to the replete community population. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit) — calcium plus vitamin D supplementation does not prevent hip fractures in community-dwelling older adults (the treatment made no difference in intention-to-treat analyses).

cards.headline: Zhao 2017 (JAMA): in 33 randomised trials with 51,145 community-dwelling older adults, combined calcium plus vitamin D was not associated with hip fracture (relative risk 1.09; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39)
cards.summary: Zhao 2017 (JAMA): in 33 randomised trials with 51,145 community-dwelling older adults, combined calcium plus vitamin D was not associated with hip fracture (relative risk 1.09; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Zhao 2017)
cards.people: 33 randomised clinical trials involving 51,145 participants, comparing calcium, vitamin D, or combined calcium and vitamin D supplements with placebo or no treatment for fracture incidence in community-dwelling adults older than 50 years; hip fracture was the primary outcome.
cards.result: There was no significant association of combined calcium and vitamin D with hip fracture compared with placebo or no treatment (relative risk 1.09; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39 — a relative measure; absolute risk difference 0.00; 95% CI −0.00 to 0.00). Calcium alone (RR 1.53; 95% CI 0.97 to 2.42) and vitamin D alone (RR 1.21; 95% CI 0.99 to 1.47) were likewise not associated with lower hip fracture risk, and no significant associations were found for nonvertebral, vertebral or total fractures. Subgroup analyses were generally consistent regardless of dose, sex, fracture history, dietary calcium intake and baseline serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration. The authors conclude the findings do not support routine use of these supplements for fracture prevention in community-dwelling older adults (the treatment made no difference to hip fractures).
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis of trials, not a single trial: its null pools the two large trials carded below with smaller ones, so the cards overlap by design and must not be added together as independent evidence.
cards.source: Zhao JG et al. Association Between Calcium or Vitamin D Supplementation and Fracture Incidence in Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 29279934. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: RECORD 2005: in 5,292 people aged 70 or older with a previous low-trauma fracture, calcium plus vitamin D did not differ from placebo for new fractures (12.6% vs 13.4%; hazard ratio for the interaction 1.01)
cards.summary: RECORD 2005: in 5,292 people aged 70 or older with a previous low-trauma fracture, calcium plus vitamin D did not differ from placebo for new fractures (12.6% vs 13.4%; hazard ratio for the interaction 1.01)
cards.people: 5,292 people aged 70 years or older (85% women) who were mobile before developing a low-trauma fracture, recruited in 21 UK hospitals and followed for 24–62 months in a factorial trial of 800 IU daily oral vitamin D3, 1,000 mg calcium, both combined, or placebo; the primary outcome was new low-energy fractures. These were community-dwelling older people managed as outpatients after a fracture (secondary prevention).
cards.result: 698 (13%) of 5,292 participants had a new low-trauma fracture, 183 (26%) of which were of the hip. The incidence of new low-trauma fractures did not differ significantly between participants allocated calcium and those not (331 [12.6%] of 2,617 vs 367 [13.7%] of 2,675; hazard ratio 0.94; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.09), between those allocated vitamin D3 and those not (353 [13.3%] of 2,649 vs 345 [13.1%] of 2,643; HR 1.02; 95% CI 0.88 to 1.19), or between combination treatment and placebo (165 [12.6%] of 1,306 vs 179 [13.4%] of 1,332; HR for interaction 1.01; 95% CI 0.75 to 1.36). The groups did not differ in all-new fractures, radiography-confirmed fractures, hip fractures, death, falls or quality of life (the treatment made no difference). By 24 months only 54.5% were still taking tablets, and compliance with calcium-containing tablets was significantly lower, partly because of gastrointestinal symptoms.
cards.watchOut: A secondary-prevention population (everyone had already fractured) and adherence fell to about half by 2 years — the null is a null for supplements as actually taken by community-dwelling older people, which is the question this shelf asks.
cards.source: Grant AM et al. cards.headline: WHI 2006: in 36,282 postmenopausal women, calcium plus vitamin D did not significantly reduce hip fracture over 7 years (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.08) — and increased kidney stones (HR 1.17)
cards.summary: WHI 2006: in 36,282 postmenopausal women, calcium plus vitamin D did not significantly reduce hip fracture over 7 years (hazard ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.08) — and increased kidney stones (HR 1.17)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, Women's Health Initiative (Jackson 2006)
cards.people: 36,282 community-dwelling postmenopausal women aged 50 to 79 years already enrolled in a Women's Health Initiative clinical trial, randomly assigned to 1,000 mg elemental calcium (as calcium carbonate) with 400 IU vitamin D3 daily or placebo, with fractures ascertained over an average follow-up of 7.0 years; bone density was measured at three centres.
cards.result: Hip bone density was 1.06% higher in the calcium plus vitamin D group than in the placebo group (P < 0.01). Intention-to-treat analysis gave a hazard ratio of 0.88 for hip fracture (95% CI 0.72 to 1.08 — a relative measure; the record prints no absolute hip-fracture rates), 0.90 for clinical spine fracture (0.74 to 1.10) and 0.96 for total fractures (0.91 to 1.02) — none statistically significant (the treatment made no difference to hip fractures in the primary analysis). The risk of renal calculi increased with calcium plus vitamin D (hazard ratio 1.17; 95% CI 1.02 to 1.34). Censoring women when they ceased to adhere reduced the hip-fracture hazard ratio to 0.71 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.97). Effects did not vary significantly by prerandomisation serum vitamin D levels.
cards.watchOut: The adherent-only analysis (HR 0.71) is the result readers most often quote — it is a secondary, adherence-censored analysis of a trial whose primary intention-to-treat result is null, and the same regimen significantly increased kidney stones.
cards.source: Jackson RD et al. Calcium plus vitamin D supplementation and the risk of fractures. The New England journal of medicine. 2006. PMID: 16481635. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT00000611. cards.headline: Synthesis: in community-dwelling older adults, calcium plus vitamin D does not prevent hip fractures — two very large trials and a 33-trial meta-analysis are concordantly null on intention-to-treat analysis
cards.summary: Synthesis: in community-dwelling older adults, calcium plus vitamin D does not prevent hip fractures — two very large trials and a 33-trial meta-analysis are concordantly null on intention-to-treat analysis
cards.people: The carded evidence: a meta-analysis of 33 randomised trials (51,145 community-dwelling participants older than 50), the RECORD factorial trial (5,292 people aged 70 or older after a low-trauma fracture) and the Women's Health Initiative trial (36,282 postmenopausal women followed 7 years). The meta-analysis includes the two trials, so participants overlap between cards by design; the unique randomised total exceeds 40,000, and no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Combined calcium and vitamin D showed no association with hip fracture in the pooled community-dwelling trials (relative risk 1.09; 95% CI 0.85 to 1.39; absolute risk difference 0.00; Zhao 2017). RECORD found no difference in new fractures for the combination versus placebo (12.6% vs 13.4%; Grant 2005), and the WHI found a non-significant hip-fracture hazard ratio of 0.88 with a significant increase in kidney stones (HR 1.17; Jackson 2006). The contrast with the nursing-home evidence on shelf #1498 — where the population was vitamin-D-deficient institutionalised women — is the clinical point: correcting deficiency in care homes is not the same intervention as supplementing the general community population. PROPOSED LIKELY (no benefit) — calcium plus vitamin D does not prevent hip fractures in community-dwelling older adults (the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: The one favourable number in this evidence base (WHI adherent-only HR 0.71) comes from censoring non-adherers, which breaks the randomised comparison; it is reported on its card, labelled as such, and does not move the stamp.
cards.source: Synthesis of Zhao JG et al. JAMA. 2017 (PMID: 29279934); Grant AM et al. Lancet (London, England). 2005 (PMID: 15885294); Jackson RD et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2006 (PMID: 16481635).

shelves.title: Capsaicin 8% patch vs pregabalin for postherpetic neuralgia (PARTIAL): longer relief unproven — no PHN head-to-head trial; the mixed-neuropathic-pain trial shows equal 8-week relief and faster onset, not longer duration
shelves.question: Does high-concentration capsaicin patch provide longer relief for postherpetic neuralgia than pregabalin?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Capsaicin/administration & dosage · Capsaicin/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia/drug therapy · Pain Management/methods · Pain Measurement/drug effects · Pregabalin/administration & dosage · Pregabalin/therapeutic use · Transdermal Patch · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2565. That shelf covers the 8% capsaicin patch versus control in postherpetic neuralgia; it does not card any comparison with pregabalin. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: the head-to-head with pregabalin, on duration of relief. The direct evidence is thin and off-target. The only head-to-head randomised trial (559 patients) enrolled peripheral neuropathic pain of mixed causes — not postherpetic neuralgia specifically, with no PHN subgroup in the record — and ran only 8 weeks: the patch was non-inferior to optimised pregabalin (≥30% pain decrease 55.7% vs 54.5%) with faster onset (median 7.5 vs 36.0 days) and fewer systemic adverse effects (Haanpää 2016; allodynia analysis, Cruccu 2018). Faster onset is not longer relief, and duration beyond 8 weeks was not compared. The PHN-specific comparative literature is a cost-effectiveness model that states no head-to-head studies were identified and whose results hinge on the assumed retreatment frequency (Armstrong 2011), and a network meta-analysis printing no direct capsaicin-versus-pregabalin estimate (Guo 2025). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — whether the patch's relief lasts longer than pregabalin's in postherpetic neuralgia is unproven on the carded evidence.

cards.headline: Haanpää 2016: the only carded head-to-head trial — in 559 patients with peripheral neuropathic pain (not postherpetic neuralgia specifically), the 8% capsaicin patch was non-inferior to pregabalin at 8 weeks (≥30% pain decrease in 55.7% vs 54.5%), with faster onset (median 7.5 vs 36.0 days) — duration beyond 8 weeks was not compared
cards.summary: Haanpää 2016: the only carded head-to-head trial — in 559 patients with peripheral neuropathic pain (not postherpetic neuralgia specifically), the 8% capsaicin patch was non-inferior to pregabalin at 8 weeks (≥30% pain decrease in 55.7% vs 54.5%), with faster onset (median 7.5 vs 36.0 days) — duration beyond 8 weeks was not compared
cards.type: Randomised open-label non-inferiority head-to-head trial, ELEVATE (Haanpää 2016)
cards.people: 559 patients with peripheral neuropathic pain, aged 18–80 years, randomly assigned to the capsaicin 8% patch (n = 282, single clinic application) or an optimised dose of oral pregabalin (n = 277), assessed for a ≥30% mean decrease in Numeric Pain Rating Scale score from baseline to week 8. The population was peripheral neuropathic pain of mixed causes; the record gives no postherpetic-neuralgia subgroup results.
cards.result: The capsaicin 8% patch was non-inferior to pregabalin for a ≥30% mean decrease in pain score from baseline to week 8 (55.7% vs 54.5%; odds ratio 1.03; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.50 — a relative measure, with the absolute responder proportions printed here). The proportion achieving optimal therapeutic effect at week 8 was 52.1% for the patch vs 44.8% for pregabalin (difference 7.3%; 95% CI −0.9% to 15.6%). Median time to onset of pain relief was significantly shorter with the patch (7.5 vs 36.0 days; hazard ratio 1.68; 95% CI 1.35 to 2.08; P < 0.0001). Treatment satisfaction was significantly greater with the patch. Treatment-emergent adverse events were mild to moderate and led to discontinuation only with pregabalin (n = 24); systemic adverse drug reactions ranged from 0 to 1.1% with the patch and 2.5 to 18.4% with pregabalin.
cards.watchOut: This trial answers a different question from this shelf's: mixed peripheral neuropathic pain rather than postherpetic neuralgia, and an 8-week horizon rather than duration of relief. Faster onset is not longer relief, and no PHN-specific numbers exist in the record — both limits are printed on the face because they decide what this shelf can claim.
cards.source: Haanpää M et al. Capsaicin 8% patch versus oral pregabalin in patients with peripheral neuropathic pain. European journal of pain (London, England). 2016. PMID: 26581442. cards.headline: Cruccu 2018: in the same head-to-head programme, the patch beat pregabalin on dynamic mechanical allodynia over 8 weeks — complete resolution in 24.1% vs 12.3% of the 488 patients who had allodynia at baseline
cards.summary: Cruccu 2018: in the same head-to-head programme, the patch beat pregabalin on dynamic mechanical allodynia over 8 weeks — complete resolution in 24.1% vs 12.3% of the 488 patients who had allodynia at baseline
cards.type: Randomised head-to-head trial, allodynia analysis of the same programme (Cruccu 2018)
cards.people: 488 patients with peripheral neuropathic pain who had dynamic mechanical allodynia at baseline (253 in the capsaicin 8% patch group and 235 in the pregabalin group), from the randomised, open-label, head-to-head 8-week study of a single patch application vs an optimised dose of pregabalin; area and intensity of allodynia and complete resolution were assessed. Same trial programme as the Haanpää 2016 card — participants overlap, printed on the face.
cards.result: From baseline to end of study, the change in allodynia intensity significantly favoured the capsaicin 8% patch over pregabalin (−0.63; 95% CI −1.04 to −0.23; P = 0.002), as did the change in allodynia area (−39.5 cm²; 95% CI −69.1 to −10.0; P = 0.009). A greater proportion of patients had complete resolution of allodynia with the patch than with pregabalin (24.1% vs 12.3%; P = 0.001 — absolute proportions as printed).
cards.watchOut: A secondary outcome (allodynia, not overall pain duration) in a subset of the same single trial programme — it strengthens the 'patch works at least as well at 8 weeks' reading and adds nothing about postherpetic neuralgia specifically or about relief lasting longer.
cards.source: Cruccu G et al. Superiority of capsaicin 8% patch versus oral pregabalin on dynamic mechanical allodynia in patients with peripheral neuropathic pain. European journal of pain (London, England). 2018. PMID: 29194851. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised head-to-head trial, allodynia analysis of the same programme (cruccu 2018) 488 patients with peripheral neuropathic pain who had dynamic mechanical allodynia at baseline (253 in the capsaicin 8% patch group and 235 in the pregabalin group), from the randomised, open-label, head-to-head 8-week study of a single patch application vs an optimised dose of pregabalin; area and intensity of allodynia and complete resolution were assessed. same trial programme as the haanpää 2016 card — participants overlap, printed on the face. from baseline to end of study, the change in allodynia intensity significantly favoured the capsaicin 8% patch over pregabalin (−0.63; 95% ci −1.04 to −0.23; p = 0.002), as did the change in allodynia area (−39.5 cm²; 95% ci −69.1 to −10.0; p = 0.009). a greater proportion of patients had complete resolution of allodynia with the patch than with pregabalin (24.1% vs 12.3%; p = 0.001 — absolute proportions as printed). a secondary outcome (allodynia, not overall pain duration) in a subset of the same single trial programme — it strengthens the 'patch works at least as well at 8 weeks' reading and adds nothing about postherpetic neuralgia specifically or about relief lasting longer. cruccu g et al. superiority of capsaicin 8% patch versus oral pregabalin on dynamic mechanical allodynia in patients with peripheral neuropathic pain. european journal of pain (london, england). 2018. pmid: 29194851. registry id: none in the record. mesh: administration, oral · administration, topical · adolescent · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · analgesics/administration & dosage · analgesics/therapeutic use · capsaicin/administration & dosage · capsaicin/therapeutic use · female · humans · hyperalgesia/drug therapy · male · middle aged · neuralgia/drug therapy · pregabalin/administration & dosage · pregabalin/therapeutic use · treatment outcome · young adult

cards.headline: Armstrong 2011: the postherpetic-neuralgia-specific comparison is a model, not a trial — it states plainly that no head-to-head studies were identified, and its capsaicin results hinge on the assumed retreatment frequency
cards.summary: Armstrong 2011: the postherpetic-neuralgia-specific comparison is a model, not a trial — it states plainly that no head-to-head studies were identified, and its capsaicin results hinge on the assumed retreatment frequency
cards.people: A 1-year Markov cost-effectiveness model for postherpetic neuralgia from a managed-care payer perspective, comparing the 8% capsaicin patch with tricyclic antidepressants, topical lidocaine patches, duloxetine, gabapentin and pregabalin; the efficacy parameter was the proportion of patients achieving at least 30% improvement in PHN pain, taken from separate clinical trials of each treatment. No patients were enrolled — this is a modelling study, printed on the face.
cards.result: The model's effectiveness results indicated the 8% capsaicin patch and topical lidocaine patch were significantly more effective than the oral PHN products, including pregabalin. Tricyclic antidepressants were least costly. The incremental cost-effectiveness ratio for the capsaicin patch overlapped with the lidocaine patch and was within the accepted threshold of cost per quality-adjusted life-year gained compared with tricyclics, duloxetine, gabapentin and pregabalin. The authors state the limitations directly: since no head-to-head studies were identified, the model used inputs from multiple clinical trials; a last-observation-carried-forward process was assumed to continue for the duration of the model; and the frequency of the capsaicin patch retreatment assumption significantly impacts its cost-effectiveness results. The record prints no comparative duration-of-relief estimate.
cards.watchOut: A model built from separate placebo-controlled trials cannot compare duration of relief between two active treatments — and its own key sensitivity is exactly the retreatment interval, i.e. how long one patch application lasts, which is the quantity this shelf's question asks about and no carded study measures head-to-head.
cards.source: Armstrong EP et al. Cost-effectiveness analysis of a new 8% capsaicin patch compared to existing therapies for postherpetic neuralgia. Current medical research and opinion. 2011. PMID: 21375358. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Guo 2025: across 38 PHN trials (8,621 participants), the 8% capsaicin patch significantly reduced pain intensity (mean difference −9.20) in indirect comparison — but the record prints no direct capsaicin-versus-pregabalin estimate and no duration outcome
cards.summary: Guo 2025: across 38 PHN trials (8,621 participants), the 8% capsaicin patch significantly reduced pain intensity (mean difference −9.20) in indirect comparison — but the record prints no direct capsaicin-versus-pregabalin estimate and no duration outcome
cards.type: Network meta-analysis of randomised trials in postherpetic neuralgia (Guo 2025)
cards.people: 38 randomised controlled trials enrolling 8,621 participants with postherpetic neuralgia, comparing pharmacotherapies in a Bayesian network meta-analysis; 9 studies (24%) were assessed at high risk of bias, 15 (39%) with some concerns and 14 (37%) at low risk of bias with the RoB 2.0 tool.
cards.result: The network meta-analysis showed the NGX-4010 8% capsaicin patch had a statistically significant effect on pain intensity (mean difference −9.20; 95% CI −12.0 to −6.60; the record does not state the comparator or scale for this estimate in the abstract). Amitriptyline plus pregabalin demonstrated the highest probability of clinical superiority (SUCRA = 0.92), and opioids had the highest adverse-event ranking (SUCRA = 0.87). The authors conclude capsaicin patches were more significant in relieving pain in PHN while calcium-channel modulators (the pregabalin class) were more comprehensive in clinical management, and that more high-quality articles are needed. No capsaicin-versus-pregabalin head-to-head estimate and no duration-of-relief outcome is printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: Network estimates are indirect — assembled through placebo comparators — and this one does not even print the direct contrast this shelf asks about; a quarter of its trials are at high risk of bias. It confirms both drugs relieve PHN pain; it cannot say whose relief lasts longer.
cards.source: Guo Z et al. Efficacy and safety of different medications compared for the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia: a network meta-analysis. Frontiers in pharmacology. 2025. PMID: 40808683. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: 'longer relief than pregabalin' is not established for postherpetic neuralgia — there is no PHN head-to-head trial; the one head-to-head trial (mixed neuropathic pain, 8 weeks) shows equal relief with faster onset for the patch
cards.summary: Synthesis: 'longer relief than pregabalin' is not established for postherpetic neuralgia — there is no PHN head-to-head trial; the one head-to-head trial (mixed neuropathic pain, 8 weeks) shows equal relief with faster onset for the patch
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised head-to-head trial programme in peripheral neuropathic pain (559 patients; 488 in the allodynia analysis — the same patients, counted once), one PHN cost-effectiveness model (no enrolled patients), and one PHN network meta-analysis (38 trials, 8,621 participants, indirect comparisons). Unique direct-comparison participants total 559, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: In the only direct comparison, the 8% patch was non-inferior to optimised pregabalin at 8 weeks (≥30% pain decrease 55.7% vs 54.5%), with faster onset (median 7.5 vs 36.0 days) and fewer systemic adverse effects (Haanpää 2016), and superior allodynia resolution (24.1% vs 12.3%; Cruccu 2018). For PHN specifically, the comparative literature is a model that states no head-to-head studies were identified and whose results hinge on the assumed retreatment frequency (Armstrong 2011), and an indirect network analysis printing no capsaicin-versus-pregabalin estimate (Guo 2025). Duration of relief beyond 8 weeks has never been compared in a carded record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — longer relief for PHN is unproven.
cards.watchOut: The honest gap: a single patch application is licensed and used on a roughly 3-monthly cycle while pregabalin is taken daily — that dosing fact is not evidence that relief lasts longer, and this shelf does not upgrade it into a finding.
cards.source: Synthesis of Haanpää M et al. European journal of pain (London, England). 2016 (PMID: 26581442); Cruccu G et al. European journal of pain (London, England). 2018 (PMID: 29194851); Armstrong EP et al. Current medical research and opinion. 2011 (PMID: 21375358); Guo Z et al. Frontiers in pharmacology. 2025 (PMID: 40808683).

shelves.title: Opioids for osteoarthritis in older adults (PARTIAL, observational only): falls and fractures consistently higher than with NSAIDs across three designs — a harm ledger with no offsetting pain advantage on the home shelf
shelves.question: Should opioids be avoided for chronic osteoarthritis pain in older adults because of falls and fractures?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/administration & dosage · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/adverse effects · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/complications · Cardiovascular Diseases/chemically induced · Cardiovascular Diseases/epidemiology · Comorbidity · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Cyclooxygenase 2 Inhibitors/administration & dosage · Cyclooxygenase 2 Inhibitors/adverse effects · Disease-Free Survival · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/epidemiology · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions/mortality · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Incidence · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Medicare · New Jersey/epidemiology · Odds Ratio · Osteoarthritis/complications · Pain/drug therapy · Pain/etiology · Pennsylvania/epidemiology · United States
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only. PARTIAL completion of live shelf #346. That shelf compares opioid with non-opioid strategies for pain in chronic back and joint pain generally (finding no opioid advantage); it does not isolate older adults or the falls-and-fractures outcome. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: opioids for chronic osteoarthritis pain in older adults, judged on falls and fractures. Three observational designs agree. In propensity-matched Medicare beneficiaries with arthritis (mean age 80), opioid initiators had a fracture hazard ratio of 4.47 versus non-selective NSAID initiators (Solomon 2010). In 13,354 osteoarthritis patients aged 65–89, a narcotic prescription carried odds ratios of 3.3 (vs COX-2 inhibitors) and 4.1 (vs NSAIDs) for falls/fractures, rising with the number of prescriptions (Rolita 2013). In 100,358 osteoarthritis patients, tramadol initiation carried hip-fracture hazard ratios of 1.4–1.6 versus NSAIDs — an absolute excess of about 2 hip fractures per 1,000 person-years (Li 2022). All of this is observational and confounding by frailty and pain severity cannot be excluded; but combined with the absence of a pain advantage on #346, it supports avoiding opioids as routine first-line treatment for osteoarthritis in older adults. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.

cards.headline: Solomon 2010: in older adults with arthritis (mean age 80), opioid initiators had over four times the fracture risk of non-selective NSAID initiators (hazard ratio 4.47; 95% CI 3.12 to 6.41) — observational only
cards.summary: Solomon 2010: in older adults with arthritis (mean age 80), opioid initiators had over four times the fracture risk of non-selective NSAID initiators (hazard ratio 4.47; 95% CI 3.12 to 6.41) — observational only
cards.type: Propensity-matched cohort study in Medicare beneficiaries (Solomon 2010)
cards.people: Medicare beneficiaries from Pennsylvania and New Jersey (mean age 80.0 years, almost 85% women) who initiated therapy with a non-selective NSAID, a selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitor (coxib), or an opioid between 1999 and 2005 for arthritis (osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, as printed in the record), matched on propensity scores across the three analgesic cohorts. The record does not print the total matched cohort size.
cards.result: Compared with non-selective NSAIDs, fracture risk was elevated with opioid use (hazard ratio 4.47; 95% CI 3.12 to 6.41 — a relative measure; the record prints no absolute fracture rates), while coxib and non-selective NSAID users had similar fracture risk. Opioids also carried elevated relative risk for cardiovascular events (HR 1.77; 95% CI 1.39 to 2.24), safety events requiring hospitalisation (HR 1.68; 95% CI 1.37 to 2.07) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.87; 95% CI 1.39 to 2.53) versus non-selective NSAIDs; gastrointestinal bleeding risk was similar for opioid users. The authors conclude opioid use exhibits an increased relative risk of many safety events compared with non-selective NSAIDs.
cards.watchOut: Propensity matching balances measured differences only: older patients prescribed opioids rather than NSAIDs may be frailer, in more pain, or have contraindications that themselves predict fracture — a hazard ratio of 4.47 is large, but from observational data it cannot be read as the drug's causal effect.
cards.source: Solomon DH et al. The comparative safety of analgesics in older adults with arthritis. Archives of internal medicine. 2010. PMID: 21149752. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rolita 2013: in 13,354 adults aged 65–89 with osteoarthritis, a narcotic prescription was associated with about 3–4 times the odds of a fall or fracture versus a COX-2 inhibitor (OR 3.3) or an NSAID (OR 4.1) — observational only
cards.summary: Rolita 2013: in 13,354 adults aged 65–89 with osteoarthritis, a narcotic prescription was associated with about 3–4 times the odds of a fall or fracture versus a COX-2 inhibitor (OR 3.3) or an NSAID (OR 4.1) — observational only
cards.type: Nested case-control study in an integrated health system (Rolita 2013)
cards.people: 13,354 individuals aged 65 to 89 with a diagnosis of osteoarthritis, in electronic medical records from an integrated health system in rural Pennsylvania (2001–2009); the incidence of falls and fractures was examined in relation to prescribed narcotics, COX-2 inhibitors and NSAIDs, with a comparison sample of individuals who did not fall matched 3:1 by age, sex and comorbidity.
cards.result: Narcotic analgesic prescriptions were associated with a significantly greater risk of falls and fractures. The likelihood of experiencing a fall/fracture was higher in participants prescribed narcotic analgesics than in those prescribed a COX-2 inhibitor (odds ratio 3.3; 95% CI 2.5 to 4.3 — a relative measure; the record prints no absolute fall/fracture rates) or an NSAID (OR 4.1; 95% CI 3.7 to 4.5). The number of narcotic prescriptions mattered (the study's title finding: a greater number of narcotic analgesic prescriptions for osteoarthritis was associated with more falls and fractures). The authors conclude that guidelines including first-line prescription of narcotics for osteoarthritis pain should be re-evaluated.
cards.watchOut: A case-control analysis of prescriptions, not randomised exposure: patients given more narcotic prescriptions plausibly had worse pain, worse mobility and more comorbidity — the dose pattern is consistent with harm and equally consistent with confounding by indication, and the design cannot separate them.
cards.source: Rolita L et al. Greater number of narcotic analgesic prescriptions for osteoarthritis is associated with falls and fractures in elderly adults. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2013. PMID: 23452054. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Li 2022: in 100,358 osteoarthritis patients, initiating tramadol — the opioid most often chosen as 'safer' — carried higher hip-fracture risk than diclofenac (HR 1.6; rate difference 1.9 per 1,000 person-years) or COX-2 inhibitors (HR 1.4; rate difference 1.7) within 1 year — observational only
cards.summary: Li 2022: in 100,358 osteoarthritis patients, initiating tramadol — the opioid most often chosen as 'safer' — carried higher hip-fracture risk than diclofenac (HR 1.6; rate difference 1.9 per 1,000 person-years) or COX-2 inhibitors (HR 1.4; rate difference 1.7) within 1 year — observational only
cards.people: 100,358 patients with osteoarthritis in British Columbia, Canada (mean age 68 years, 63% women), in a sequential propensity score-matched cohort study (2005–2013) comparing tramadol initiation with initiation of naproxen, diclofenac, cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors or codeine; outcomes within 1 year after initiation included all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, venous thromboembolism and hip fractures.
cards.result: Tramadol had a higher risk of hip fractures than diclofenac (hazard ratio 1.6; 95% CI 1.2 to 2.0 — a relative measure, with the absolute rate difference 1.9 per 1,000 person-years; 95% CI 0.4 to 3.4) and than cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors (HR 1.4; 95% CI 1.1 to 1.9; rate difference 1.7 per 1,000 person-years; 95% CI 0.2 to 3.3). All-cause mortality was also higher for tramadol than for NSAIDs (rate differences 3.3 to 8.1 per 1,000 person-years; HRs 1.2 to 1.5), and venous thromboembolism risk was higher than with diclofenac (HR 1.7; rate difference 2.2 per 1,000 person-years). No differences were observed between tramadol and codeine for any event (the record's closing sentence on NSAID comparisons for all events is internally inconsistent as printed and is not relied on here).
cards.watchOut: Tramadol is one opioid, and channeling runs both ways — it is preferentially prescribed to patients judged too frail for NSAIDs. The absolute excess (about 2 extra hip fractures per 1,000 person-years) is the number to carry away, not the relative 1.6.
cards.source: Li L et al. Association of tramadol with all-cause mortality, cardiovascular diseases, venous thromboembolism, and hip fractures among patients with osteoarthritis: a population-based study. Arthritis research & therapy. 2022. PMID: 35410440. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in older adults with osteoarthritis, opioid initiation is consistently associated with more falls and fractures than NSAID initiation — relative risks from 1.4 to 4.5 across three observational designs — supporting avoidance as first-line treatment, on observational evidence only
cards.summary: Synthesis: in older adults with osteoarthritis, opioid initiation is consistently associated with more falls and fractures than NSAID initiation — relative risks from 1.4 to 4.5 across three observational designs — supporting avoidance as first-line treatment, on observational evidence only
cards.people: The carded evidence: a propensity-matched Medicare cohort (mean age 80; total N not documented in the record), a nested case-control study in 13,354 osteoarthritis patients aged 65–89, and a propensity-matched population cohort of 100,358 osteoarthritis patients. All carded evidence is observational, printed in the stamp; participants total over 113,000 across the two studies that print Ns, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Opioid initiators had a fracture hazard ratio of 4.47 versus non-selective NSAID initiators (Solomon 2010); a narcotic prescription carried odds ratios of 3.3–4.1 for fall/fracture versus COX-2 inhibitors or NSAIDs (Rolita 2013); and tramadol initiation carried hip-fracture hazard ratios of 1.4–1.6 versus individual NSAIDs, an absolute excess of about 2 hip fractures per 1,000 person-years (Li 2022). Read with home shelf #346 — where opioids showed no pain advantage over non-opioid treatment — the ledger for older adults with osteoarthritis is harm without offsetting benefit. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: None of this is randomised: every estimate can be inflated by the frailty and pain severity that lead clinicians to choose opioids. The consistency across three designs, populations and comparators — and the absence of any efficacy advantage on #346 — is what the stamp rests on, and it is labelled observational so no reader mistakes it for trial evidence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Solomon DH et al. Archives of internal medicine. 2010 (PMID: 21149752); Rolita L et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2013 (PMID: 23452054); Li L et al. Arthritis research & therapy. 2022 (PMID: 35410440).

shelves.title: Low-dose naltrexone for fibromyalgia pain (PARTIAL, split): pooled small trials say yes, the largest trial says no — and the 'general population' evidence is still women-only
shelves.question: Does low-dose naltrexone help fibromyalgia pain?
shelves.mesh: Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Algorithms · Fibromyalgia/drug therapy · Naltrexone/adverse effects · Pain · Rheumatic Diseases · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1455. That shelf covers low-dose naltrexone in women with fibromyalgia only, from a single small positive crossover trial at 4.5 mg; this shelf covers the uncovered slice: the general fibromyalgia population and the wider trial literature. FLAG for the developer, printed on the cards: the wider literature does not in fact widen the population — every randomised trial in the carded records enrolled women only or almost only, and no trial in men was found in the records fetched this session, so the general-population answer is the women's evidence pooled, stated plainly. That pooled evidence splits. Two overlapping meta-analyses of the small trials find a pain benefit (mean difference −0.86 across 4 trials and 222 patients, Vatvani 2024; standardised mean difference −0.61 across 5 trials, Nazir 2025 — both pools include the home shelf's trial, which is NOT re-carded here). The largest double-blind trial, of 6 mg in 99 women, found no significant pain difference versus placebo (−0.34 points; P = 0.27; Due Bruun 2024), and a single-blind dose-response study in 25 women (Bruun-Plesner 2020) supplies the dose rationale without efficacy evidence. Tolerability was good throughout, with vivid dreams the consistent excess adverse effect. PROPOSED SPLIT (pooled small trials: benefit; largest trial: the treatment made no difference; population: women only in the carded trials).

cards.headline: Due Bruun 2024 (FINAL): the largest LDN fibromyalgia trial (99 women) — 6 mg naltrexone did not beat placebo on pain: between-group difference −0.34 points (95% CI −0.95 to 0.27; P = 0.27) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Due Bruun 2024 (FINAL): the largest LDN fibromyalgia trial (99 women) — 6 mg naltrexone did not beat placebo on pain: between-group difference −0.34 points (95% CI −0.95 to 0.27; P = 0.27) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, FINAL (Due Bruun 2024)
cards.people: 99 women aged 18–64 years diagnosed with fibromyalgia, randomised at a single Danish centre to low-dose naltrexone 6 mg once daily (n = 49) or identical placebo (n = 50) for 12 weeks; the primary outcome was change in pain intensity on an 11-point numeric rating scale, in the intention-to-treat population. Mean age was 50.6 years; no participants were lost to follow-up. N = 99 printed on the face.
cards.result: The mean change in pain intensity was −1.3 points (95% CI −1.7 to −0.8) in the naltrexone group and −0.9 (−1.4 to −0.5) in the placebo group, a between-group difference of −0.34 (−0.95 to 0.27; P = 0.27; Cohen's d 0.23) — not statistically significant (the treatment made no difference to pain in this trial). Discontinuations due to adverse events were 4 (8%) of 49 on naltrexone and 3 (6%) of 50 on placebo; 41 (84%) vs 43 (86%) had an adverse event, and one serious adverse event occurred in the placebo group. The authors conclude the study did not show 6 mg low-dose naltrexone was superior to placebo for relieving pain, while noting a possible memory-problems signal for future trials.
cards.watchOut: Women only, like every other carded trial here — this trial enlarges and contradicts the home shelf's small positive crossover trial, but it does not itself widen the population beyond women, and 6 mg is a higher dose than the 4.5 mg tested on the home shelf.
cards.source: Due Bruun K et al. Naltrexone 6 mg once daily versus placebo in women with fibromyalgia: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Rheumatology. 2024. PMID: 38258677. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04270877. cards.headline: Vatvani 2024: pooling 4 randomised trials (222 patients), low-dose naltrexone reduced pain scores versus placebo (mean difference −0.86; 95% CI −1.20 to −0.51) — a pooled result the largest single trial does not share
cards.summary: Vatvani 2024: pooling 4 randomised trials (222 patients), low-dose naltrexone reduced pain scores versus placebo (mean difference −0.86; 95% CI −1.20 to −0.51) — a pooled result the largest single trial does not share
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials with trial sequential analysis (Vatvani 2024)
cards.people: 4 randomised controlled trials with 222 fibromyalgia patients comparing low-dose naltrexone with placebo, from a search of Scopus, Medline, ClinicalTrials.gov and the Cochrane Library to 20 May 2024; pain scores, pressure pain threshold, the revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire, pain catastrophising and adverse events were pooled. The included trials are the small trials of this literature — predominantly or entirely women, as in the other cards; the record does not print a sex breakdown.
cards.result: Low-dose naltrexone was associated with a significant reduction in pain scores (mean difference −0.86; 95% CI −1.20 to −0.51; P < 0.001; I² = 33%) and a higher increment in pressure pain threshold (MD 0.17; 95% CI 0.08 to 0.25; P < 0.001; I² = 0%) versus placebo. The revised Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire and the Pain Catastrophizing Scale did not differ significantly between groups (the treatment made no difference on those measures). Low-dose naltrexone was associated with more vivid dreams and nausea, with no significant difference in serious adverse events, headache, diarrhoea or dizziness. The authors suggest efficacy for pain with a relatively good safety profile.
cards.watchOut: A pooled mean difference of −0.86 built from 222 patients in 4 small trials — a literature in which the single largest trial (99 patients, carded above) is null; small positive trials dominate meta-analyses of this shape, and trial sequential analysis cannot create patients the field has not randomised.
cards.source: Vatvani AD et al. Efficacy and safety of low-dose naltrexone for the management of fibromyalgia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials with trial sequential analysis. The Korean journal of pain. 2024. PMID: 39344363. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Nazir 2025: pooling 5 randomised trials, low-dose naltrexone was superior to placebo for pain (standardised mean difference −0.61; 95% CI −1.14 to −0.08) — with vivid dreams significantly more common (relative risk 2.41)
cards.summary: Nazir 2025: pooling 5 randomised trials, low-dose naltrexone was superior to placebo for pain (standardised mean difference −0.61; 95% CI −1.14 to −0.08) — with vivid dreams significantly more common (relative risk 2.41)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Nazir 2025)
cards.people: 5 randomised controlled trials comparing low-dose naltrexone with placebo in fibromyalgia patients, from PubMed, CENTRAL and ClinicalTrials.gov; dichotomous outcomes were reported as relative risks and continuous outcomes as standardised mean differences under a DerSimonian-and-Laird random-effects model, with trial quality assessed by the revised Cochrane Risk of Bias tool. The record does not print the pooled total participant number or a sex breakdown; the underlying trials are those of the cards above and the home shelf.
cards.result: Low-dose naltrexone was superior to placebo in alleviating pain in the primary analysis (standardised mean difference −0.61; 95% CI −1.14 to −0.08 — a relative standardised effect; the record prints no absolute pain rates) and in sensitivity analysis (SMD −0.87; 95% CI −1.28 to −0.46), but not in raising mechanical pain threshold (SMD 0.24; 95% CI −0.09 to 0.56). Headache incidence was not associated with low-dose naltrexone in the primary (relative risk 1.68; 95% CI 0.84 to 3.36) or sensitivity analysis (RR 0.98; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.34). Vivid dreams were significantly more common on treatment (RR 2.41; 95% CI 1.77 to 3.28). No serious adverse effects were reported in the treatment group. The authors conclude more randomised trials are needed.
cards.watchOut: This meta-analysis overlaps the Vatvani 2024 pool almost completely — the two reviews are not independent confirmations, and both inherit the same small, women-only trial base and the same tension with the largest trial's null result.
cards.source: Nazir MH et al. Efficacy and safety of low-dose naltrexone (LDN) in fibromyalgia: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Annals of medicine and surgery (2012). 2025. PMID: 40337423. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Bruun-Plesner 2020: the dose-finding study behind the 6 mg dose — in 25 evaluable women, the estimated effective dose was 3.88 mg for 50% of subjects and 5.40 mg for 95%, with wide individual variation
cards.summary: Bruun-Plesner 2020: the dose-finding study behind the 6 mg dose — in 25 evaluable women, the estimated effective dose was 3.88 mg for 50% of subjects and 5.40 mg for 95%, with wide individual variation
cards.people: Women with fibromyalgia aged 18–60 years referred to a public pain clinic at a Danish university hospital, in a single-blinded up-and-down dose-response study of low-dose naltrexone (test doses 0.75–6 mg in 0.75 mg steps); 27 subjects were included, 2 withdrawn, leaving 25 evaluable. N = 25 printed on the face. This study measured dose-response, not placebo-controlled efficacy.
cards.result: After inclusion of 25 evaluable subjects, the dose estimates were 3.88 mg for the dose effective in 50% of subjects (ED50) and 5.40 mg for 95% (ED95). As a secondary outcome, effects on 10 common fibromyalgia symptoms were evaluated; a high interindividual variation was observed both in baseline symptom presentation and in which symptoms were reduced. The authors conclude 4.5 mg — the dose used previously — seems a relevant test dose, and recommend that future studies include non-pain fibromyalgia symptoms as outcomes and be placebo-controlled randomised trials. The record reports no placebo comparison and no pain effect size.
cards.watchOut: A dose-ranging study in 25 women with no placebo arm: it explains where the doses on the other cards came from and contributes no efficacy evidence — it is carded so the shelf's dose story is complete, and it must never be cited as a positive trial.
cards.source: Bruun-Plesner K et al. Low-Dose Naltrexone for the Treatment of Fibromyalgia: Investigation of Dose-Response Relationships. Pain medicine (Malden, Mass.). 2020. PMID: 32068870. Registry ID: none in the record. single-blind dose-response trial (bruun-plesner 2020) women with fibromyalgia aged 18–60 years referred to a public pain clinic at a danish university hospital, in a single-blinded up-and-down dose-response study of low-dose naltrexone (test doses 0.75–6 mg in 0.75 mg steps); 27 subjects were included, 2 withdrawn, leaving 25 evaluable. n = 25 printed on the face. this study measured dose-response, not placebo-controlled efficacy. after inclusion of 25 evaluable subjects, the dose estimates were 3.88 mg for the dose effective in 50% of subjects (ed50) and 5.40 mg for 95% (ed95). as a secondary outcome, effects on 10 common fibromyalgia symptoms were evaluated; a high interindividual variation was observed both in baseline symptom presentation and in which symptoms were reduced. the authors conclude 4.5 mg — the dose used previously — seems a relevant test dose, and recommend that future studies include non-pain fibromyalgia symptoms as outcomes and be placebo-controlled randomised trials. the record reports no placebo comparison and no pain effect size. a dose-ranging study in 25 women with no placebo arm: it explains where the doses on the other cards came from and contributes no efficacy evidence — it is carded so the shelf's dose story is complete, and it must never be cited as a positive trial. bruun-plesner k et al. low-dose naltrexone for the treatment of fibromyalgia: investigation of dose-response relationships. pain medicine (malden, mass.). 2020. pmid: 32068870. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · female · fibromyalgia/drug therapy · humans · middle aged · naltrexone · outcome assessment, health care · pain clinics · single-blind method · treatment outcome · young adult

cards.headline: Synthesis: the pooled literature says low-dose naltrexone helps fibromyalgia pain; the largest and most rigorous single trial says it does not — and every randomised patient carded, here and on the home shelf, is a woman
cards.summary: Synthesis: the pooled literature says low-dose naltrexone helps fibromyalgia pain; the largest and most rigorous single trial says it does not — and every randomised patient carded, here and on the home shelf, is a woman
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised double-blind trial of 6 mg (99 women), two overlapping meta-analyses of the small-trial literature (4 trials, 222 patients; and 5 trials, pooled N not documented in the record), and one single-blind dose-response study (25 evaluable women, no placebo arm). Unique randomised participants are at least 222 and drawn almost entirely from the same small trials, so no small-N stamp labelling applies to the shelf total — the smallness of the underlying trials is printed on each card.
cards.result: Pooled across the small trials, low-dose naltrexone reduced pain (mean difference −0.86, Vatvani 2024; standardised mean difference −0.61, Nazir 2025). The largest single trial, testing the dose the dose-finding study pointed to (6 mg), found a between-group pain difference of −0.34 points that was not significant (P = 0.27; Due Bruun 2024). Tolerability was good in all reports, with vivid dreams the consistent excess adverse effect. On the population question: no carded trial enrolled men in any documented number, so the 'general population' evidence is, in fact, the women's evidence pooled. PROPOSED SPLIT (meta-analyses of small trials: benefit; largest double-blind trial: the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Two overlapping meta-analyses of the same handful of trials are one body of evidence, not two — and the home shelf's positive 31-woman crossover trial is inside both pools, which is why this shelf's split cannot be resolved by counting reviews.
cards.source: Synthesis of Due Bruun K et al. The Lancet. Rheumatology. 2024 (PMID: 38258677); Vatvani AD et al. The Korean journal of pain. 2024 (PMID: 39344363); Nazir MH et al. shelves.title: Early corticosteroid injection in frozen shoulder (PARTIAL completion of #3761): injection beat placebo on early pain, disability and range of motion, but by 12 months there was no difference
shelves.question: In adults with frozen shoulder, does early corticosteroid injection improve range of motion?
shelves.mesh: Bursitis/physiopathology/*therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Disability Evaluation · *Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Injections, Intra-Articular · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Management · Range of Motion, Articular · Severity of Illness Index · *Shoulder Joint · Treatment Outcome · Triamcinolone Acetonide/administration & dosage/*analogs & derivatives/*therapeutic use
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion — home live #3761 asks whether hydrodilatation beats corticosteroid injection or physiotherapy in frozen shoulder and cards the injection only as a comparator; this shelf asks the slice #3761 does not: whether an early corticosteroid injection itself, against placebo injection or no injection, improves range of motion. The direct evidence is old and small but consistent in direction and time course. In the only placebo-controlled trial (Carette 2003, 93 patients with adhesive capsulitis of under 1 year's duration), a single fluoroscopy-guided intra-articular corticosteroid injection improved pain-and-disability scores significantly more than saline injection by 6 weeks, with the steroid-plus-physiotherapy arm gaining the most range of motion, and the advantage was gone by 12 months. A 2017 meta-analysis of 5 studies (225 patients) found greater range-of-motion improvement with corticosteroid than placebo at both 0–8 and 9–24 weeks, while the pain advantage did not persist past 8 weeks. A primary-care randomised trial against physiotherapy (van der Windt 1998) shows the same early-speed pattern (77% vs 46% treatment success at 7 weeks, differences small by 26–52 weeks) but answers an injection-versus-physiotherapy question, not injection-versus-nothing. No carded record isolates an 'early versus late injection' comparison, so 'early' here means injection given in the first year of symptoms, as the trials enrolled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): an early corticosteroid injection speeds recovery of range of motion and pain in the first weeks to months, but by about a year outcomes converge with no injection (the treatment made no difference at 12 months in the placebo-controlled trial).

cards.headline: Carette 2003: a single early corticosteroid injection beat saline placebo on pain and disability by 6 weeks in adhesive capsulitis of under 1 year's duration — and steroid plus physiotherapy gained the most range of motion; by 12 months all groups were the same
cards.summary: Carette 2003: a single early corticosteroid injection beat saline placebo on pain and disability by 6 weeks in adhesive capsulitis of under 1 year's duration — and steroid plus physiotherapy gained the most range of motion; by 12 months all groups were the same
cards.people: 93 subjects with adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder of <1 year's duration, randomised to 4 groups: corticosteroid injection (triamcinolone hexacetonide 40 mg, fluoroscopy-guided) plus supervised physiotherapy; corticosteroid injection alone; saline injection plus supervised physiotherapy; or saline injection alone (placebo). All subjects were taught a home exercise programme and reassessed at 6 weeks, 3, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: At 6 weeks, total Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI) scores had improved significantly more in the two corticosteroid groups than in the two saline groups (P = 0.0004). Total range of active and passive motion increased in all groups, with the corticosteroid-plus-physiotherapy group having significantly greater improvement than the other 3 groups. At 3 months the corticosteroid groups still showed significantly greater SPADI improvement than the placebo-alone group. At 12 months, all groups had improved to a similar degree on all outcome measures (the treatment made no difference by 12 months).
cards.watchOut: The record reports significance levels for the range-of-motion differences rather than pooled degrees of motion gained, so the size of the early motion advantage cannot be stated in degrees from this record; the trial is small (93 patients across 4 arms) and two decades old.
cards.source: Carette S et al. Intraarticular corticosteroids, supervised physiotherapy, or a combination of the two in the treatment of adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder: a placebo-controlled trial. Arthritis and Rheumatism. 2003. PMID: 12632439. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wang 2017 meta-analysis: across 5 studies (225 patients), intra-articular corticosteroid improved range of motion more than placebo at both 0–8 and 9–24 weeks, while the pain advantage lasted only 0–8 weeks
cards.summary: Wang 2017 meta-analysis: across 5 studies (225 patients), intra-articular corticosteroid improved range of motion more than placebo at both 0–8 and 9–24 weeks, while the pain advantage lasted only 0–8 weeks
cards.people: Meta-analysis of 5 articles (4 randomised clinical trials) totalling 225 patients with adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder: 115 in injection groups and 110 in placebo groups, identified from 1,166 articles screened.
cards.result: Compared with placebo, intra-articular corticosteroid injections were more effective in reducing the pain score at 0 to 8 weeks, but there was no difference between the injection and control groups at 9 to 24 weeks. Improvement in range of motion in the injection group was greater than in the control group both at 0 to 8 weeks and at 9 to 24 weeks. The record reports the direction and significance of these pooled comparisons without printing pooled degree values for range of motion.
cards.watchOut: Five small studies and 225 patients is a thin base for a pooled claim, and the included trials vary in injection technique and co-therapy; the range-of-motion signal outlasting the pain signal should be read as suggestive, not settled.
cards.source: Wang W et al. Effectiveness of corticosteroid injections in adhesive capsulitis of shoulder: A meta-analysis. Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28700506. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: van der Windt 1998: in primary care, corticosteroid injections produced faster relief than physiotherapy (treatment success 77% vs 46% at 7 weeks), with differences small by 26–52 weeks — an injection-versus-physiotherapy trial, carded for the time course
cards.summary: van der Windt 1998: in primary care, corticosteroid injections produced faster relief than physiotherapy (treatment success 77% vs 46% at 7 weeks), with differences small by 26–52 weeks — an injection-versus-physiotherapy trial, carded for the time course
cards.people: 109 patients consulting general practitioners in 40 practices for a painful stiff shoulder, randomly allocated to 6 weeks of corticosteroid injections (53 patients) or physiotherapy (56 patients), with outcome assessments at 3, 7, 13, 26 and 52 weeks.
cards.result: At 7 weeks, 40 (77%) of 52 patients treated with injections were considered treatment successes compared with 26 (46%) of 56 treated with physiotherapy (difference between groups 31%, 95% confidence interval 14% to 48%). The difference in improvement favoured corticosteroids in nearly all outcome measures and was statistically significant early; at 26 and 52 weeks differences between the groups were comparatively small. Adverse reactions were generally mild, but among women receiving corticosteroids facial flushing was reported by 9 women and irregular menstrual bleeding by 6.
cards.watchOut: The enrolled condition was 'painful stiff shoulder' in primary care, not strictly diagnosed frozen shoulder, and the comparator was physiotherapy rather than no injection — this card supports the early-speed pattern only and is not direct evidence against no treatment.
cards.source: van der Windt DA et al. Effectiveness of corticosteroid injections versus physiotherapy for treatment of painful stiff shoulder in primary care: randomised trial. BMJ. 1998. PMID: 9804720. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: early corticosteroid injection speeds range-of-motion and pain recovery in frozen shoulder over the first weeks to months, but the advantage is temporary — by 12 months the placebo-controlled trial found no difference
cards.summary: Synthesis: early corticosteroid injection speeds range-of-motion and pain recovery in frozen shoulder over the first weeks to months, but the advantage is temporary — by 12 months the placebo-controlled trial found no difference
cards.people: The carded evidence: one placebo-controlled randomised trial in adhesive capsulitis of <1 year's duration (93 patients), one meta-analysis of injection versus placebo (5 studies, 225 patients), and one primary-care randomised trial of injection versus physiotherapy (109 patients). Total carded participants = 427, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: A single early injection improved pain and disability more than saline placebo at 6 weeks (P = 0.0004), with the largest range-of-motion gain when injection was combined with physiotherapy, and no between-group difference at 12 months (Carette 2003). Pooled across trials, range-of-motion improvement was greater with corticosteroid than placebo at 0–8 and 9–24 weeks, while pain relief separated only at 0–8 weeks (Wang 2017). Against physiotherapy, injections won early (77% vs 46% success at 7 weeks) and converged later (van der Windt 1998). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), time-limited as stated.
cards.watchOut: No carded study randomised patients by timing (early versus late injection): 'early' is inferred from trials enrolling patients within the first year of symptoms, and the shelf should not be cited as evidence that delaying an injection forfeits its benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Carette S et al. Arthritis and Rheumatism. 2003 (PMID: 12632439); Wang W et al. Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28700506); van der Windt DA et al. BMJ. 1998 (PMID: 9804720).

shelves.title: Osteoporosis treatment sequence (precedent-b build; ARCH/FRAME homed on live #92, STRUCTURE on pack #1828): anabolic first, then antiresorptive — the reverse order blunts the gains
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does an anabolic-first treatment sequence followed by an antiresorptive preserve bone density and prevent fractures better than starting with an antiresorptive first?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Bone Density · Bone Density Conservation Agents · Denosumab · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Substitution · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Middle Aged · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal · Single-Blind Method · Teriparatide
shelves.balance: FLAG — precedent (b) build: the slate's named anchors are already homed and are NOT re-carded here — ARCH and FRAME are carded on live shelf #92 and STRUCTURE is carded on pack #1828. This shelf is built only on the free sequence reports below, and the homed trials are cross-pointed, not re-used. What the free reports show: in DATA-Switch, women who went from teriparatide to denosumab kept gaining bone density (total hip +6.6% over 4 years), while women switched from denosumab to teriparatide gained less at the hip (+2.8%) and lost ground transiently at the radius — the antiresorptive-to-anabolic direction blunts or reverses gains at cortical sites. In ACTIVExtend, 18 months of the anabolic abaloparatide followed by alendronate produced far fewer vertebral fractures over 43 months than placebo followed by alendronate (0.9% vs 5.6%). And after a teriparatide course, following with denosumab preserved more spine density than following with a bisphosphonate (Niimi 2018). Together with the homed ARCH result on live #92 (romosozumab-then-alendronate beat alendronate alone on fractures), the direction is consistent: build first, then hold with an antiresorptive; starting with an antiresorptive attenuates the later anabolic response. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the anabolic-first sequence: the fracture evidence for sequencing itself rests mainly on one extension study plus the homed ARCH trial, and the direct switch evidence is bone-density based.

cards.headline: DATA-Switch 2015: teriparatide followed by denosumab kept building hip bone density (+6.6% over 4 years); switching from denosumab to teriparatide gained less (+2.8%) and lost radius density
cards.summary: DATA-Switch 2015: teriparatide followed by denosumab kept building hip bone density (+6.6% over 4 years); switching from denosumab to teriparatide gained less (+2.8%) and lost radius density
cards.people: Postmenopausal women with osteoporosis from the randomised DATA study (94 women originally assigned to 24 months of teriparatide, denosumab, or both); in DATA-Switch, 77 women completed at least one post-baseline visit after switching — teriparatide to denosumab (n=27), denosumab to teriparatide (n=27), or combination to denosumab alone (n=23) — with bone density followed to 48 months.
cards.result: Spine bone density rose in all groups by 48 months (+18.3% teriparatide-to-denosumab, +14.0% denosumab-to-teriparatide, +16.0% combination-to-denosumab; between-group differences not significant, p=0.13 for the head-to-head switch comparison). Total hip density diverged: +6.6% (95% CI 5.3 to 7.9) after teriparatide-to-denosumab versus +2.8% (1.3 to 4.2) after denosumab-to-teriparatide (p=0.0002). Radius density was unchanged after teriparatide-to-denosumab (0.0%) but fell after denosumab-to-teriparatide (−1.8%). The authors conclude that switching from teriparatide to denosumab continues to increase density, whereas switching from denosumab to teriparatide results in progressive or transient bone loss.
cards.watchOut: A small extension study (77 women analysed) with bone density, not fractures, as its outcome — it shows the direction of sequence effects at the hip and radius, but cannot by itself prove a fracture advantage for either order.
cards.source: Leder BZ et al. Denosumab and teriparatide transitions in postmenopausal osteoporosis (the DATA-Switch study): extension of a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2015. PMID: 26144908. Registry ID: NCT00926380.
