cards.headline: ACTIVExtend 2018: abaloparatide first, then alendronate, cut vertebral fractures over 43 months — 0.9% versus 5.6% for placebo first, then alendronate
cards.summary: ACTIVExtend 2018: abaloparatide first, then alendronate, cut vertebral fractures over 43 months — 0.9% versus 5.6% for placebo first, then alendronate
cards.people: Women with postmenopausal osteoporosis who completed the ACTIVE trial on the anabolic abaloparatide or placebo and enrolled in the extension: 558 from the abaloparatide group and 581 from the placebo group, all then given open-label alendronate for up to 24 months; outcomes counted over the full 43-month period.
cards.result: Over 43 months, new radiographic vertebral fractures occurred in 0.9% of the abaloparatide-then-alendronate group versus 5.6% of the placebo-then-alendronate group — an 84% relative risk reduction (P<0.001) — and Kaplan–Meier rates of nonvertebral, clinical and major osteoporotic fractures were also significantly lower with the anabolic-first sequence. Bone density gains from the anabolic phase increased further on alendronate. A supplemental analysis found no hip fractures in the anabolic-first group versus five in the placebo-first group. Adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is anabolic-first versus no-treatment-first, both followed by alendronate — it proves the anabolic course must come before (or at least not be skipped), but it is not a head-to-head against an antiresorptive-first sequence; that direct fracture comparison is the homed ARCH trial on live shelf #92.

cards.headline: Niimi 2018: after a teriparatide course, following with denosumab preserved more spine bone density (+4.3%) than following with a bisphosphonate (+0.5% to +1.3%)
cards.summary: Niimi 2018: after a teriparatide course, following with denosumab preserved more spine bone density (+4.3%) than following with a bisphosphonate (+0.5% to +1.3%)
cards.people: 300 Japanese patients who had completed daily teriparatide treatment, enrolled in a prospective randomised open-label 12-month trial of follow-on therapy: oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or minodronate) or denosumab 60 mg every 6 months.
cards.result: Lumbar spine bone density increased by 4.3% ± 3.5% on denosumab, versus 1.3% ± 5.1% on alendronate and 0.5% ± 4.6% on minodronate — significantly greater for denosumab than for either bisphosphonate. Femoral neck gains were smaller and did not differ significantly between groups (+1.4% denosumab, +0.7% alendronate, +0.2% minodronate). The anabolic gains were preserved or extended by every follow-on antiresorptive, most strongly by denosumab.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-country, bone-density outcomes over 12 months only, and minodronate is a Japan-market bisphosphonate; the card answers which antiresorptive best holds anabolic gains, not whether the sequence prevents fractures.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the sequence evidence points one way — anabolic first, antiresorptive second — with the direct fracture proof homed on live #92
cards.summary: Synthesis: the sequence evidence points one way — anabolic first, antiresorptive second — with the direct fracture proof homed on live #92
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised switch extension (77 women analysed), one large anabolic-then-antiresorptive extension (1,139 women enrolled), and one randomised follow-on trial (300 patients). Total carded participants exceed 1,500, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Switching from an anabolic to an antiresorptive continued to build or hold bone density (DATA-Switch hip +6.6%; Niimi spine +4.3% on denosumab), while switching from an antiresorptive to an anabolic blunted hip gains (+2.8%) and cost radius density (−1.8%). An anabolic-first sequence followed by alendronate prevented vertebral fractures versus a no-anabolic-first sequence (0.9% vs 5.6% over 43 months, ACTIVExtend). The head-to-head fracture trial of anabolic-first versus antiresorptive-only (ARCH) and the bisphosphonate-transition trial (STRUCTURE) are homed on live shelf #92 and pack #1828 respectively and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for anabolic-first sequencing.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial randomises women to anabolic-first versus antiresorptive-first and counts fractures in both arms; the sequence verdict combines switch studies, one extension, and the homed ARCH comparison — read it as a consistent direction, not a single decisive trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Leder BZ et al. Lancet (London, England). 2015 (PMID: 26144908); Bone HG et al. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2018 (PMID: 29800372); Niimi R et al. JBMR plus. 2018 (PMID: 30283910).

shelves.title: Screening and treating latent TB before anti-TNF therapy (GAP-E, observational): registry cases cluster where screening or prophylaxis was incomplete
shelves.question: In adults about to start anti-TNF therapy, does screening and treating latent tuberculosis prevent tuberculosis reactivation?
shelves.mesh: Adalimumab · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antirheumatic Agents · Comorbidity · Etanercept · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulin G · Immunosuppression Therapy · Incidence · Infliximab · Male · Middle Aged · Receptors, Tumor Necrosis Factor · Registries · Rheumatic Diseases · Risk · Risk Factors · Secondary Prevention · Spain · Tuberculosis · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha
shelves.balance: GAP-E, observational throughout — there is no randomised trial of tuberculosis screening before anti-TNF therapy, and the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE with the observational label on the face. The three national registries behind the guideline recommendations tell one coherent story. In Spain's BIOBADASER, after screening recommendations were disseminated, active tuberculosis still occurred at 172 per 100,000 patient-years, but the probability of developing it was 7 times higher when the recommendations were not followed (incidence rate ratio 7.09) — and the commonest failure was the two-step tuberculin skin test for latent infection. In France's RATIO registry, all 69 tuberculosis cases occurred in patients who had not received correct chemoprophylactic treatment, at a standardised incidence ratio of 12.2 against the background population. In the British BSRBR, all 40 tuberculosis cases occurred in the anti-TNF cohort and none in 3,232 DMARD-treated comparators. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): screening for and treating latent tuberculosis before anti-TNF therapy prevents most reactivation — the cases that still occur cluster where screening or prophylaxis was incomplete — but the size of the preventive effect has never been randomised.

cards.headline: BIOBADASER 2007: tuberculosis was 7 times more likely when latent-TB screening recommendations were not followed (incidence rate ratio 7.09)
cards.summary: BIOBADASER 2007: tuberculosis was 7 times more likely when latent-TB screening recommendations were not followed (incidence rate ratio 7.09)
cards.people: 5,198 patients treated with a TNF antagonist and registered in Spain's BIOBADASER registry after March 2002, when recommendations to prevent reactivation of latent tuberculosis infection had been disseminated; outcomes stratified by whether the recommendations were completely or incompletely followed (2,655 treatments followed them fully).
cards.result: Fifteen cases of active tuberculosis occurred (rate 172 per 100,000 patient-years, 95% CI 103–285). The probability of developing active tuberculosis was 7 times higher when the recommendations were not followed (incidence rate ratio 7.09, 95% CI 1.60–64.69). The major compliance failure was the two-step tuberculin skin test for latent infection. Cases occurred on all three available TNF antagonists.
cards.watchOut: Compliance with recommendations was not randomised: clinicians who skipped the two-step test may have differed in other ways, and the confidence interval on the 7-fold figure is very wide (1.60–64.69) because it rests on 15 cases.
cards.source: Gómez-Reino JJ et al. Risk of tuberculosis in patients treated with tumor necrosis factor antagonists due to incomplete prevention of reactivation of latent infection. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2007. PMID: 17530674. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: RATIO 2009: none of the 69 tuberculosis cases on anti-TNF therapy had received correct chemoprophylaxis (standardised incidence ratio 12.2)
cards.summary: RATIO 2009: none of the 69 tuberculosis cases on anti-TNF therapy had received correct chemoprophylaxis (standardised incidence ratio 12.2)
cards.people: All cases of tuberculosis arising over 3 years in French patients receiving anti-TNF monoclonal antibody therapy for any indication, collected by the prospective national RATIO registry: 69 cases (rheumatoid arthritis 40, spondylarthritides 18, inflammatory colitis 9, psoriasis 1, Behçet's disease 1), each matched to 2 anti-TNF-treated controls.
cards.result: The sex- and age-adjusted tuberculosis incidence was 116.7 per 100,000 patient-years, a standardised incidence ratio of 12.2 (95% CI 9.7–15.5) against the background population — higher on infliximab (SIR 18.6) and adalimumab (SIR 29.3) than on etanercept (SIR 1.8). None of the 69 patients had received correct chemoprophylactic treatment. Risk factors included the first year of treatment and being born in an endemic area — the pattern the authors read as reactivation of latent infection that screening and prophylaxis exist to catch.
cards.watchOut: 'None received correct chemoprophylaxis' is a case-series observation without a screened comparator arm — it shows where the failures clustered, not a measured preventive effect size; some cases will also have been new infections rather than reactivation.
cards.source: Tubach F et al. Risk of tuberculosis is higher with anti-tumor necrosis factor monoclonal antibody therapy than with soluble tumor necrosis factor receptor therapy: The three-year prospective French Research Axed on Tolerance of Biotherapies registry. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2009. PMID: 19565495. Registry ID: NCT00224562. cards.headline: BSRBR 2010: all 40 tuberculosis cases occurred in 10,712 anti-TNF-treated patients and none in 3,232 DMARD-treated comparators
cards.summary: BSRBR 2010: all 40 tuberculosis cases occurred in 10,712 anti-TNF-treated patients and none in 3,232 DMARD-treated comparators
cards.people: 10,712 patients with rheumatoid arthritis treated with anti-TNF therapy (3,913 etanercept, 3,295 infliximab, 3,504 adalimumab) in the British Society for Rheumatology Biologics Register, compared with 3,232 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis treated with traditional disease-modifying drugs, followed to April 2008.
cards.result: Forty cases of tuberculosis were reported, all in the anti-TNF cohort. Rates were higher for the monoclonal antibodies (adalimumab 144 and infliximab 136 events per 100,000 person-years) than for etanercept (39 per 100,000 person-years); adjusted incidence rate ratios versus etanercept were 4.2 (95% CI 1.4–12.4) for adalimumab and 3.1 (1.0–9.5) for infliximab. 62% of cases were extrapulmonary, 13 of 40 occurred after stopping treatment, and non-white ethnicity carried a sixfold increased risk.
cards.watchOut: This card quantifies the risk screening exists to prevent rather than the effect of screening itself; UK practice already included latent-TB screening for much of this period, so these rates are residual risk under screening, not the unscreened counterfactual.
cards.source: Dixon WG et al. Drug-specific risk of tuberculosis in patients with rheumatoid arthritis treated with anti-TNF therapy: results from the British Society for Rheumatology Biologics Register (BSRBR). Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2010. PMID: 19854715. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: registry evidence converges — reactivation happens where screening or prophylaxis was missed
cards.summary: Synthesis: registry evidence converges — reactivation happens where screening or prophylaxis was missed
cards.people: The carded evidence: three national registries — BIOBADASER (5,198 anti-TNF patients, Spain), RATIO (69 tuberculosis cases with matched controls, France) and BSRBR (10,712 anti-TNF patients plus 3,232 DMARD comparators, UK). All observational; no randomised trial of pre-treatment screening exists.
cards.result: BIOBADASER measured the screening contrast directly: tuberculosis was 7 times more likely when the latent-infection recommendations were not followed (IRR 7.09). RATIO found none of its 69 cases had received correct chemoprophylaxis, against a background standardised incidence ratio of 12.2. BSRBR found every case in the anti-TNF cohort and none in DMARD comparators. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (observational): screening and treating latent tuberculosis before anti-TNF therapy prevents tuberculosis reactivation in most patients; residual cases concentrate in incomplete screening, the first treatment year, and higher-risk drugs and ethnic backgrounds.
cards.watchOut: Observational registries cannot separate the effect of screening from the effect of the prophylactic treatment that follows a positive screen, nor from secular falls in tuberculosis incidence — the honest claim is prevention consistent across three health systems, not a randomised effect size.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gómez-Reino JJ et al. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2007 (PMID: 17530674); Tubach F et al. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2009 (PMID: 19565495); Dixon WG et al. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2010 (PMID: 19854715).

shelves.title: Fibromyalgia CBT (PARTIAL of live #391): small, consistent gains in pain, mood, fatigue and function — about 5 extra large pain responses per 100 treated
shelves.question: In fibromyalgia, does cognitive-behavioural therapy (including CBT for insomnia) improve pain, fatigue and function versus education or usual care?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Child · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Fibromyalgia · Humans · Negativism · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion: the live fibromyalgia family shelf (#391) homes the licensed drugs and exercise; this shelf asks only about structured psychological therapy as the tested intervention. Two Bernardy syntheses agree on a small, real benefit. The 2013 Cochrane review (23 studies, 2,031 patients, evidence graded low quality) found cognitive behavioural therapies (CBTs) reduced pain by 0.5 points on a 0–10 scale at end of treatment (standardised mean difference −0.29) and 0.6 points at long-term follow-up, with parallel small gains in negative mood and disability and no excess dropout (risk ratio 0.94). The 2018 updated systematic review (29 randomised trials, 2,509 patients) found CBTs gave at least 50% pain relief to 5 more patients per 100 than controls (risk difference 0.05, high-quality evidence), at least 20% quality-of-life improvement to 13 more per 100 (risk difference 0.13, moderate-quality), and small reductions in negative mood, disability and fatigue (standardised mean differences −0.43, −0.30 and −0.27). The specific programmes tested include CBT for insomnia (Edinger 2005: 57% of CBT patients met strict sleep-improvement criteria versus 17% on sleep-hygiene education and 0% on usual care, in a 47-patient trial) and an internet-delivered Web-Enhanced Behavioral Self-Management programme grounded in cognitive-behavioural pain principles (Williams 2010, 118 patients), which improved pain, physical functioning and global impression over standard care. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: CBT improves pain, fatigue, mood and function in fibromyalgia by small average amounts versus education or usual care — a benefit closer to the drugs' 'one patient in ten' scale than to a cure.

cards.headline: Bernardy 2013 Cochrane review: across 23 studies (2,031 patients), CBT cut pain by 0.5 points on a 0–10 scale at end of treatment and 0.6 at follow-up — small gains, low-quality evidence, no excess dropout
cards.summary: Bernardy 2013 Cochrane review: across 23 studies (2,031 patients), CBT cut pain by 0.5 points on a 0–10 scale at end of treatment and 0.6 at follow-up — small gains, low-quality evidence, no excess dropout
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of 23 randomised studies (Bernardy 2013)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of 23 randomised studies (24 CBT arms) of cognitive behavioural therapies in children, adolescents and adults with fibromyalgia; 2,031 patients (1,073 in CBT groups, 958 in control groups receiving waiting list, attention control, treatment as usual or other non-drug therapies).
cards.result: CBTs were superior to controls in reducing pain at end of treatment by 0.5 points on a 0–10 scale (standardised mean difference −0.29, 95% CI −0.49 to −0.17) and by 0.6 points at long-term follow-up (median 6 months; SMD −0.40, 95% CI −0.62 to −0.17); in reducing negative mood by 0.7 points at end of treatment (SMD −0.33) and 1.3 points at follow-up (SMD −0.43); and in reducing disability by 0.7 points (SMD −0.30) and 1.2 points at follow-up (SMD −0.52). Dropout for any reason did not differ (risk ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.65–1.35). Only two studies were without any risk of bias and the GRADE quality of evidence was low. The authors' conclusion: CBTs provided a small incremental benefit over control interventions.
cards.watchOut: Psychological-therapy trials cannot blind participants, and controls ranged from waiting list to active education — the pooled 0.5-point pain gain averages across those very different comparators, and the review itself grades the evidence low.

cochrane systematic review of 23 randomised studies (bernardy 2013) cochrane systematic review of 23 randomised studies (24 cbt arms) of cognitive behavioural therapies in children, adolescents and adults with fibromyalgia; 2,031 patients (1,073 in cbt groups, 958 in control groups receiving waiting list, attention control, treatment as usual or other non-drug therapies). cbts were superior to controls in reducing pain at end of treatment by 0.5 points on a 0–10 scale (standardised mean difference −0.29, 95% ci −0.49 to −0.17) and by 0.6 points at long-term follow-up (median 6 months; smd −0.40, 95% ci −0.62 to −0.17); in reducing negative mood by 0.7 points at end of treatment (smd −0.33) and 1.3 points at follow-up (smd −0.43); and in reducing disability by 0.7 points (smd −0.30) and 1.2 points at follow-up (smd −0.52). dropout for any reason did not differ (risk ratio 0.94, 95% ci 0.65–1.35). only two studies were without any risk of bias and the grade quality of evidence was low. the authors' conclusion: cbts provided a small incremental benefit over control interventions. psychological-therapy trials cannot blind participants, and controls ranged from waiting list to active education — the pooled 0.5-point pain gain averages across those very different comparators, and the review itself grades the evidence low. bernardy k et al. cognitive behavioural therapies for fibromyalgia. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013. pmid: 24018611. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adolescent · adult · child · cognitive behavioral therapy · fibromyalgia · humans · negativism · randomized controlled trials as topic

cards.headline: Bernardy 2018 updated meta-analysis: across 29 trials (2,509 patients), CBT gave ≥50% pain relief to 5 more patients per 100 than controls (risk difference 0.05, high-quality evidence)
cards.summary: Bernardy 2018 updated meta-analysis: across 29 trials (2,509 patients), CBT gave ≥50% pain relief to 5 more patients per 100 than controls (risk difference 0.05, high-quality evidence)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 randomised trials (Bernardy 2018)
cards.people: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of 29 randomised controlled trials (2,509 patients) of cognitive behavioural therapies, including acceptance-based CBTs, versus controls (waiting list, attention control, treatment as usual, or other active non-pharmacological therapies) in fibromyalgia syndrome, searched to May 2017.
cards.result: At end of therapy, CBTs were superior to controls for pain relief of 50% or greater (risk difference 0.05, 95% CI 0.02–0.07; high-quality evidence), improvement of health-related quality of life of 20% or greater (risk difference 0.13, 95% CI 0.00–0.26; moderate-quality evidence), and reductions in negative mood (SMD −0.43, 95% CI −0.62 to −0.24), disability (SMD −0.30, 95% CI −0.52 to −0.08) and fatigue (SMD −0.27, 95% CI −0.50 to −0.03), each rated high-quality evidence. Acceptability and safety did not differ significantly between CBTs and controls. The update did not change the previous review's major findings.
cards.watchOut: A risk difference of 0.05 for halving pain means about 20 patients treated for one extra large pain response — the average effect is small even where the evidence quality is rated high; this update overlaps the 2013 Cochrane trial set and is not an independent body of trials.
cards.source: Bernardy K et al. Efficacy, acceptability and safety of cognitive behavioural therapies in fibromyalgia syndrome - A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.headline: Edinger 2005: CBT for insomnia in fibromyalgia — 57% of CBT patients met strict sleep-improvement criteria versus 17% on sleep-hygiene education and 0% on usual care (N=47 enrolled)
cards.summary: Edinger 2005: CBT for insomnia in fibromyalgia — 57% of CBT patients met strict sleep-improvement criteria versus 17% on sleep-hygiene education and 0% on usual care (N=47 enrolled)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of CBT for insomnia (Edinger 2005; N=47)
cards.people: 47 patients with fibromyalgia and chronic insomnia complaints randomised to cognitive-behavioural therapy for insomnia, sleep-hygiene instructions (an education-style behavioural control), or usual fibromyalgia care alone; 42 completed baseline and entered treatment. The tested intervention was a structured CBT-for-insomnia protocol (stimulus control, sleep restriction and cognitive therapy elements as standard for CBT-I).
cards.result: Sleep logs showed CBT patients achieved nearly a 50% reduction in nocturnal wake time by study completion, versus 20% reductions on sleep hygiene and 3.5% on usual care. Eight of 14 CBT recipients (57%) met strict subjective sleep-improvement criteria, versus 2 of 12 (17%) on sleep hygiene and 0% on usual care, with comparable findings on actigraphy criteria. Sleep-hygiene patients showed favourable pain and mental well-being outcomes, most notably a subgroup that self-selected CBT strategies. The authors call CBT a promising intervention for sleep disturbance in fibromyalgia and call for larger trials.
cards.watchOut: A 47-patient, single-blind trial with 42 entering treatment: the 57%-versus-0% contrast rests on 14 CBT patients and 12 sleep-hygiene patients in the arms the report details, and its primary target was sleep, not pain — it supports the CBT-for-insomnia slice of this shelf's question, not a pain claim.

cards.headline: Williams 2010: an internet-delivered behavioural self-management programme (WEB-SM) built on cognitive-behavioural principles improved pain and physical functioning over standard care (N=118)
cards.summary: Williams 2010: an internet-delivered behavioural self-management programme (WEB-SM) built on cognitive-behavioural principles improved pain and physical functioning over standard care (N=118)
cards.people: 118 individuals with fibromyalgia randomised to standard care alone or standard care plus access to a Web-Enhanced Behavioral Self-Management programme (WEB-SM) — an internet-based exercise and behavioural self-management programme grounded in cognitive and behavioural pain-management principles — assessed at baseline and 6 months.
cards.result: Patients assigned to WEB-SM reported significantly greater improvement in pain, physical functioning and overall global impression of improvement than standard-care patients; secondary outcomes included fatigue, sleep, anxiety and depressive symptoms. Exercise and relaxation techniques were the most commonly used skills over the 6 months. The authors conclude a no-contact internet self-management intervention can be integrated into routine care with positive outcomes, while noting not everyone is expected to benefit.
cards.watchOut: WEB-SM bundles exercise with behavioural self-management, so its benefit cannot be credited to cognitive-behavioural techniques alone; the record's abstract reports significance without the absolute score changes, so no effect size is printed on this card.
cards.source: Williams DA et al. Internet-enhanced management of fibromyalgia: a randomized controlled trial. Pain. 2010. PMID: 20855168. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: CBT in fibromyalgia gives small average gains across pain, mood, fatigue and disability — consistent in two syntheses, with the insomnia-specific trial pointing the same way
cards.summary: Synthesis: CBT in fibromyalgia gives small average gains across pain, mood, fatigue and disability — consistent in two syntheses, with the insomnia-specific trial pointing the same way
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane review of 23 studies (2,031 patients), an updated meta-analysis of 29 trials (2,509 patients, overlapping trial set), a 47-patient CBT-for-insomnia trial, and a 118-patient internet behavioural self-management trial. The drug and exercise evidence for fibromyalgia is homed on live shelf #391 and is not re-carded here.
cards.result: Average pain relief is about half a point on a 0–10 scale (Cochrane), and 5 more patients per 100 achieve at least 50% pain relief on CBT than on controls (2018 update), with small concordant gains in negative mood (SMD −0.43), disability (−0.30) and fatigue (−0.27), and no acceptability or safety penalty. CBT for insomnia produced the largest single-trial contrast, on sleep outcomes, in a very small trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: CBT (including CBT for insomnia) improves pain, fatigue and function in fibromyalgia versus education or usual care, by small average amounts.
cards.watchOut: The two syntheses share most of their trials, so the carded evidence is effectively one trial literature read twice, plus two small programme trials; effect sizes are averages over responders and non-responders alike.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bernardy K et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2013 (PMID: 24018611); Bernardy K et al. European journal of pain (London, England). 2018 (PMID: 28984402); Edinger JD et al. Archives of internal medicine. 2005 (PMID: 16314551); Williams DA et al. Pain. 2010 (PMID: 20855168).

shelves.title: Chronic low back pain: transdermal and buccal buprenorphine beat placebo-switch in enriched-withdrawal trials — effects of 0.6–1.0 points in preselected responders
shelves.question: In chronic low back pain, do transdermal or buccal buprenorphine formulations reduce pain versus placebo in opioid-naïve and opioid-experienced patients?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Opioid · Buprenorphine · Double-Blind Method · Electrocardiography · Female · Humans · Low Back Pain · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: All three pivotal trials used enriched-enrolment randomised-withdrawal designs: patients first had to tolerate and respond to the drug in an open-label titration, and only those responders were randomised to continue it or switch to placebo — so every effect below is an effect in preselected responders, and the designs measure loss of benefit on withdrawal as much as benefit itself. The tested products are named because the formulation is the intervention: the buprenorphine transdermal system (Butrans, 7-day patch) and buccal buprenorphine film (Belbuca). In opioid-naïve patients, the transdermal trial (541 randomised) found week-12 pain scores lower on continued patch than placebo (treatment difference −0.58 on a 0–10 scale; P=.010), and the buccal trial in opioid-naïve patients (461 randomised) found pain rose less after randomisation on continued film than placebo (difference −0.67; P=.0012), with at least 30% pain reduction in 63% versus 47%. In opioid-experienced patients, the buccal trial (511 randomised) found the largest separation (difference −0.98; P<.001), with significantly more patients achieving 30% and 50% pain reductions on continued film. Nausea, constipation and vomiting were the common adverse events. Buprenorphine's opioid-use-disorder uses are homed on other shelves and are not this question. PROPOSED LIKELY (in enriched-withdrawal responders): continuing transdermal or buccal buprenorphine keeps chronic low back pain lower than switching to placebo, in both opioid-naïve and opioid-experienced patients — with average separations under one point on a 0–10 scale.

cards.headline: Steiner 2011 (Butrans transdermal, opioid-naïve): continuing the 7-day buprenorphine patch beat switching to placebo — week-12 pain difference −0.58 on a 0–10 scale (P=.010); 541 randomised after open-label run-in
cards.summary: Steiner 2011 (Butrans transdermal, opioid-naïve): continuing the 7-day buprenorphine patch beat switching to placebo — week-12 pain difference −0.58 on a 0–10 scale (P=.010); 541 randomised after open-label run-in
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, enriched-enrolment randomised-withdrawal (Steiner 2011, transdermal, opioid-naïve)
cards.people: Opioid-naïve patients with moderate-to-severe chronic low back pain who tolerated and responded to the buprenorphine transdermal system (BTDS; Butrans, 10 or 20 µg/hour 7-day patch) during an open-label run-in (541 of 1,024 entrants) were randomised double-blind to continue BTDS (n=257) or switch to matching placebo (n=284) for 12 weeks (NCT00490919).
cards.result: Patients continuing BTDS reported statistically significantly lower 'average pain over the last 24 hours' scores at week 12 than those switched to placebo (least-squares mean treatment difference −0.58, P=.010); sensitivity analyses and the secondary outcomes (sleep disturbance, supplemental analgesic tablet use) supported the result. During the double-blind phase, treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 55% on BTDS and 52% on placebo, with no unanticipated laboratory, vital-sign or ECG findings.
cards.watchOut: Only 53% of run-in entrants were randomised — everyone randomised had already shown they tolerated and responded to the patch, so −0.58 is the effect of continuing versus stopping in responders, not the expected effect of starting the patch in an unselected patient.
cards.source: Steiner DJ et al. Efficacy and safety of the seven-day buprenorphine transdermal system in opioid-naïve patients with moderate to severe chronic low back pain: an enriched, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study. Journal of pain and symptom management. 2011. PMID: 21945130. Registry ID: NCT00490919. cards.headline: Rauck 2016 (Belbuca buccal film, opioid-naïve): pain rose less on continued film than on placebo after randomisation (difference −0.67; P=.0012); ≥30% pain reduction in 63% vs 47%
cards.summary: Rauck 2016 (Belbuca buccal film, opioid-naïve): pain rose less on continued film than on placebo after randomisation (difference −0.67; P=.0012); ≥30% pain reduction in 63% vs 47%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, enriched-enrolment randomised-withdrawal (Rauck 2016, buccal, opioid-naïve)
cards.people: Opioid-naïve patients with moderate-to-severe chronic low back pain requiring around-the-clock analgesia (749 entered titration) were titrated openly to buccal buprenorphine film (BBUP; Belbuca, 150–450 µg every 12 hours) giving adequate, tolerated analgesia for at least 14 days, then randomised double-blind to continue BBUP (n=229) or switch to placebo (n=232) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Entry pain averaged 7.15 (SD 1.05) on a 0–10 numeric rating scale and fell to 2.81 (1.07) after titration. From randomisation to week 12, mean pain rose by 0.94 (1.85) on continued BBUP versus 1.59 (2.04) on placebo — a between-group difference of −0.67 (95% CI −1.07 to −0.26; P=.0012). At least 30% pain reduction was maintained by 63% on BBUP versus 47% on placebo (P=.0012). The most frequent adverse events on BBUP were nausea (10%), constipation (4%) and vomiting (4%).
cards.watchOut: As with every card on this shelf, the placebo group is a withdrawal group: part of the separation is pain returning when an effective drug is stopped, which overstates what starting the drug would add for a new patient.
cards.source: Rauck RL et al. Efficacy and tolerability of buccal buprenorphine in opioid-naive patients with moderate to severe chronic low back pain. Postgraduate medicine. 2016. PMID: 26634956. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gimbel 2016 (Belbuca buccal film, opioid-experienced): the largest separation — difference −0.98 (P<.001), with significantly more 30% and 50% pain reductions on continued film; 511 randomised
cards.summary: Gimbel 2016 (Belbuca buccal film, opioid-experienced): the largest separation — difference −0.98 (P<.001), with significantly more 30% and 50% pain reductions on continued film; 511 randomised
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, enriched-enrolment randomised-withdrawal (Gimbel 2016, buccal, opioid-experienced)
cards.people: Opioid-experienced patients (30–160 mg/day morphine-sulfate equivalents) with moderate-to-severe chronic low back pain on around-the-clock opioids, tapered to no more than 30 mg morphine equivalents, then titrated openly to buccal buprenorphine film (150–900 µg every 12 hours); responders were randomised double-blind to continue BBUP (n=254) or switch to placebo (n=257) for 12 weeks.
cards.result: Mean pain was 6.7 after the opioid taper and fell to 2.8 after BBUP titration. After randomisation, mean pain scores stayed lower on BBUP than placebo; the difference in mean change from baseline to week 12 was −0.98 (95% CI −1.32 to −0.64; P<.001). Significantly more BBUP patients achieved pain reductions of at least 30% and at least 50% (P<.001 for both; the record's abstract does not print the two percentages). The only adverse event reported more often on BBUP than placebo at 5% or more was vomiting (5.5% vs 2.3%).
cards.watchOut: Patients were tapered off their previous opioid before titration, so the trial tests switching stable opioid-treated patients to buccal buprenorphine — not adding it, and not starting opioids; generalising to either is a stretch.
cards.source: Gimbel J et al. Efficacy and tolerability of buccal buprenorphine in opioid-experienced patients with moderate to severe chronic low back pain: results of a phase 3, enriched enrollment, randomized withdrawal study. randomised controlled trial, enriched-enrolment randomised-withdrawal (gimbel 2016, buccal, opioid-experienced) opioid-experienced patients (30–160 mg/day morphine-sulfate equivalents) with moderate-to-severe chronic low back pain on around-the-clock opioids, tapered to no more than 30 mg morphine equivalents, then titrated openly to buccal buprenorphine film (150–900 µg every 12 hours); responders were randomised double-blind to continue bbup (n=254) or switch to placebo (n=257) for 12 weeks. mean pain was 6.7 after the opioid taper and fell to 2.8 after bbup titration. after randomisation, mean pain scores stayed lower on bbup than placebo; the difference in mean change from baseline to week 12 was −0.98 (95% ci −1.32 to −0.64; p<.001). significantly more bbup patients achieved pain reductions of at least 30% and at least 50% (p<.001 for both; the record's abstract does not print the two percentages). the only adverse event reported more often on bbup than placebo at 5% or more was vomiting (5.5% vs 2.3%). patients were tapered off their previous opioid before titration, so the trial tests switching stable opioid-treated patients to buccal buprenorphine — not adding it, and not starting opioids; generalising to either is a stretch. gimbel j et al. efficacy and tolerability of buccal buprenorphine in opioid-experienced patients with moderate to severe chronic low back pain: results of a phase 3, enriched enrollment, randomized withdrawal study. pain. 2016. pmid: 27434505. registry id: none in the record. mesh: administration, buccal · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · buprenorphine · chronic pain · disability evaluation · dose-response relationship, drug · double-blind method · female · follow-up studies · humans · low back pain · male · middle aged · morphine · narcotics · pain measurement · severity of illness index

cards.headline: Synthesis: in preselected responders, continuing either formulation beats switching to placebo in both opioid-naïve and opioid-experienced patients — by 0.6 to 1.0 points on a 0–10 scale
cards.summary: Synthesis: in preselected responders, continuing either formulation beats switching to placebo in both opioid-naïve and opioid-experienced patients — by 0.6 to 1.0 points on a 0–10 scale
cards.people: The carded evidence: three phase 3 enriched-enrolment randomised-withdrawal trials in moderate-to-severe chronic low back pain — transdermal patch in opioid-naïve patients (541 randomised), buccal film in opioid-naïve patients (461 randomised), and buccal film in opioid-experienced patients (511 randomised). Total randomised participants: 1,513, all preselected responders, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: All three trials favoured continuing buprenorphine over switching to placebo: −0.58 (transdermal, naïve; P=.010), −0.67 (buccal, naïve; P=.0012) and −0.98 (buccal, experienced; P<.001) points on 0–10 pain scales at 12 weeks, with responder-rate advantages where reported (63% vs 47% for ≥30% reduction, buccal naïve). PROPOSED LIKELY (within the enriched-withdrawal design): transdermal and buccal buprenorphine reduce chronic low back pain versus placebo in patients who have already tolerated and responded to them, whether opioid-naïve or opioid-experienced.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial randomised unselected patients to start buprenorphine versus placebo in parallel groups, and none compares these formulations with non-opioid care; the shelf answers the regulatory question the trials asked, in the population the enrichment produced.
cards.source: Synthesis of Steiner DJ et al. Journal of pain and symptom management. 2011 (PMID: 21945130); Rauck RL et al. Postgraduate medicine. 2016 (PMID: 26634956); Gimbel J et al. Pain. 2016 (PMID: 27434505).

shelves.title: Botulinum toxin A for peripheral neuropathic pain: pain fell more than on placebo in the trials and in the pooled analysis — small trials, moderate-quality evidence
shelves.question: In peripheral neuropathic pain, do botulinum toxin A injections reduce pain versus placebo injections?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Botulinum Toxins, Type A/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Injections, Subcutaneous · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia/drug therapy · Neuromuscular Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Outcome Assessment, Health Care
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the randomised evidence points the same way but is small. The largest trial (BOTNEP, 68 patients, two subcutaneous administrations up to 300 units, 12 weeks apart) found botulinum toxin A reduced mean weekly pain intensity over 24 weeks versus placebo (adjusted effect estimate −0.77, 95% CI −0.95 to −0.59). The earlier single-injection trial (29 patients with focal painful neuropathies and allodynia) found spontaneous-pain relief from week 2 to week 14. Pooling 10 randomised trials (505 patients), a 2022 meta-analysis found pain scores lower on botulinum toxin A by a mean difference of −1.87 points at 1 month and −1.38 at 3 months, with the largest effect in diabetic polyneuropathy, no demonstrated quality-of-life benefit, and no difference in adverse effects; the reviewers rated the evidence moderate quality. Neither trial record names a branded botulinum toxin A product or manufacturer, so no specific commercial product can be endorsed from this evidence — products differ by maker and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a real analgesic signal, carried by small trials, which is why neuropathic-pain guidance positions botulinum toxin A as a later-line, specialist option rather than a first-line drug.

cards.headline: BOTNEP 2016: two rounds of subcutaneous botulinum toxin A (up to 300 units) reduced pain over 24 weeks versus placebo (adjusted effect −0.77) in 68 randomised patients
cards.summary: BOTNEP 2016: two rounds of subcutaneous botulinum toxin A (up to 300 units) reduced pain over 24 weeks versus placebo (adjusted effect −0.77) in 68 randomised patients
cards.people: 68 patients aged 18–85 years with peripheral neuropathic pain at two clinics in France and one in Brazil, randomly assigned (34 per group) to two subcutaneous administrations of botulinum toxin A (up to 300 units) or placebo, 12 weeks apart; 66 patients (34 botulinum toxin A, 32 placebo) were included in the primary analysis. The record does not name a branded botulinum toxin A product or its manufacturer.
cards.result: Botulinum toxin A reduced self-reported mean weekly pain intensity over the 24 weeks from the first administration compared with placebo (adjusted effect estimate −0.77, 95% CI −0.95 to −0.59; p<0.0001). Pain on injection was the only adverse effect reported (19 of 34 [56%] on botulinum toxin A vs 17 of 32 [53%] on placebo); severe injection pain occurred in 10 (29%) versus 11 (34%). Allodynia and a limited thermal deficit may predict response, per the authors.
cards.watchOut: The largest trial on this shelf randomised only 68 patients, and its pain scale and effect estimate come from a mixed-model analysis rather than raw group means; the record names no branded product, so the result cannot be transferred automatically to any specific commercial toxin preparation.
cards.source: Attal N et al. Safety and efficacy of repeated injections of botulinum toxin A in peripheral neuropathic pain (BOTNEP): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2016. PMID: 26947719. Registry ID: NCT01251211. cards.headline: Ranoux 2008: a single intradermal botulinum toxin A injection (20–190 units) relieved spontaneous pain from week 2 to week 14 in 29 patients with focal painful neuropathies
cards.summary: Ranoux 2008: a single intradermal botulinum toxin A injection (20–190 units) relieved spontaneous pain from week 2 to week 14 in 29 patients with focal painful neuropathies
cards.people: 29 patients with focal painful neuropathies and mechanical allodynia, in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled design, receiving a one-time intradermal administration of botulinum toxin type A (20–190 units) into the painful area or placebo. The record does not name a branded botulinum toxin A product or its manufacturer.
cards.result: Botulinum toxin A, relative to placebo, was associated with persistent improvement in spontaneous pain intensity from 2 weeks after injection to 14 weeks; it also improved allodynia to brushing and cold pain thresholds without affecting perception thresholds. The number needed to treat for 50% pain relief was 3.03 at 12 weeks (a relative-derived measure reported by the authors). Neuropathic symptoms and general activity improved; most patients reported pain during the injections, with no further local or systemic side effects.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-nine patients, one injection, and a selected population — focal neuropathies with allodynia and preserved thermal sensation, the subgroup the authors themselves link to response; the finding may not extend to diffuse polyneuropathy without allodynia.
cards.source: Ranoux D et al. Botulinum toxin type A induces direct analgesic effects in chronic neuropathic pain. Annals of neurology. 2008. PMID: 18546285. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hary 2022 meta-analysis: across 10 randomised trials (505 patients), subcutaneous botulinum toxin A lowered pain by 1.87 points at 1 month and 1.38 at 3 months versus placebo — moderate-quality evidence
cards.summary: Hary 2022 meta-analysis: across 10 randomised trials (505 patients), subcutaneous botulinum toxin A lowered pain by 1.87 points at 1 month and 1.38 at 3 months versus placebo — moderate-quality evidence
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 randomised trials (Hary 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 10 randomised controlled trials including 505 patients, comparing subcutaneous botulinum toxin A injections with placebo injections for chronic peripheral neuropathic pain; primary endpoint pain at 1 month after injection.
cards.result: Pain scores were lower on botulinum toxin A at 1 month (mean difference −1.87, 95% CI −2.91 to −0.83) and at 3 months (mean difference −1.38, 95% CI −1.95 to −0.81). A subgroup analysis showed greater efficacy in diabetic polyneuropathy (mean difference −2.48, 95% CI −3.22 to −1.74). There was no impact on quality of life and no difference in adverse effects between botulinum toxin A and placebo. The evidence was rated moderate quality by GRADE.
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials are the same small literature carded above — the meta-analysis adds precision, not new patients — and the pain scales and injection protocols varied between trials; the diabetic-polyneuropathy subgroup effect rests on few trials.
cards.source: Hary V et al. Efficacy and safety of botulinum A toxin for the treatment of chronic peripheral neuropathic pain: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials and meta-analysis. European journal of pain (London, England). 2022. PMID: 35293078. Registry ID: none in the record (review registered PROSPERO CRD42021239108). cards.headline: Synthesis: two small positive trials and a concordant pooled analysis — a genuine but modestly evidenced analgesic effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small positive trials and a concordant pooled analysis — a genuine but modestly evidenced analgesic effect
cards.people: The carded evidence: one multicentre trial of repeated injections (68 randomised), one single-injection trial (29 patients), and one meta-analysis of 10 trials (505 patients, overlapping the trial literature).
cards.result: Every carded report favours botulinum toxin A over placebo for pain: BOTNEP's adjusted effect was −0.77 points over 24 weeks, and the pooled mean differences were −1.87 at 1 month and −1.38 at 3 months, with no excess adverse effects beyond injection pain and no demonstrated quality-of-life gain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent, but the trials are small and the pooled evidence is rated moderate quality, so the stamp stops at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: No carded record names the branded product or manufacturer tested, and botulinum toxin A products are not interchangeable unit-for-unit — the shelf supports the drug class as tested, not any named commercial preparation.

shelves.title: Vitamin D for knee osteoarthritis progression: no slowing of cartilage loss and no pain benefit in two dedicated trials or in the VITAL knee-pain analysis
shelves.question: Does vitamin D supplementation slow cartilage loss or reduce knee pain progression in knee osteoarthritis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Arthralgia/drug therapy · Cartilage/anatomy & histology,drug effects · Cholecalciferol/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Knee Joint · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/blood,drug therapy · Pain Measurement · Tasmania · Tibia · Victoria · Vitamin D/analogs & derivatives,blood · Vitamins/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the trials asked the question directly, raised blood vitamin D levels as intended, and found nothing. In the Tasmanian/Victorian trial (Jin 2016; the VIDEO programme), 413 patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis and low vitamin D (25-hydroxyvitamin D 12.5–60 nmol/L, ≈5–24 ng/mL) took monthly oral vitamin D3 50,000 IU or placebo for 2 years: blood levels rose by 40.6 nmol/L (≈16 ng/mL) more than on placebo, yet annual change in tibial cartilage volume and WOMAC pain did not differ, nor did cartilage defects or bone marrow lesions. The Boston trial (McAlindon 2013) titrated daily cholecalciferol 2,000 IU upward to push levels above 36 ng/mL in 146 patients for 2 years: knee pain fell similarly in both groups and cartilage volume fell by the same ~4.3% in both groups. The VITAL ancillary analysis (MacFarlane 2020) followed 1,398 US adults with chronic knee pain for a mean 5.3 years and found no difference in WOMAC pain, function or stiffness at any time point. The tested preparations were oral cholecalciferol (vitamin D3) — monthly 50,000 IU in Jin, daily 2,000 IU with dose escalation in McAlindon; the VITAL record does not state its dose, and no record names a branded product. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): supplementation corrects the blood level without changing the joint outcome.

cards.headline: Jin 2016 (VIDEO): monthly vitamin D3 50,000 IU for 2 years raised blood levels but did not slow tibial cartilage loss or improve WOMAC knee pain versus placebo in 413 patients
cards.summary: Jin 2016 (VIDEO): monthly vitamin D3 50,000 IU for 2 years raised blood levels but did not slow tibial cartilage loss or improve WOMAC knee pain versus placebo in 413 patients
cards.people: 413 participants (mean age 63.2 years; 50% women) with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis and low 25-hydroxyvitamin D (12.5–60 nmol/L, ≈5–24 ng/mL) in Tasmania and Victoria, Australia, randomly assigned to monthly oral vitamin D3 50,000 IU (n = 209) or identical placebo (n = 204) for 2 years; 340 (82.3%) completed the study. Primary outcomes were change in MRI tibial cartilage volume and change in WOMAC pain score (0–500). The record names the preparation as oral vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) and gives no brand name.
cards.result: 25-hydroxyvitamin D rose by 40.6 nmol/L (≈16 ng/mL) in the vitamin D group versus 6.7 nmol/L (≈2.7 ng/mL) on placebo (P < .001) over 2 years. There were no significant differences in annual change of tibial cartilage volume or WOMAC pain score, and no significant differences in change of tibiofemoral cartilage defects or bone marrow lesions — the treatment made no difference. At least one adverse event occurred in 56 vitamin D participants versus 37 placebo participants (P = .04).
cards.watchOut: This trial enrolled only patients with low vitamin D levels, so its null is the strongest version of the test — it cannot be read as leaving open a benefit in deficient patients; monthly bolus dosing is, however, a different exposure pattern from daily dosing, which the next card covers.
cards.source: Jin X et al. Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation on Tibial Cartilage Volume and Knee Pain Among Patients With Symptomatic Knee Osteoarthritis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2016. cards.headline: McAlindon 2013: daily cholecalciferol titrated to a blood level above 36 ng/mL for 2 years did not reduce knee pain or cartilage volume loss versus placebo in 146 patients
cards.summary: McAlindon 2013: daily cholecalciferol titrated to a blood level above 36 ng/mL for 2 years did not reduce knee pain or cartilage volume loss versus placebo in 146 patients
cards.people: 146 participants with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (mean age 62.4 years) at Tufts Medical Center, Boston, randomised to oral cholecalciferol 2,000 IU/day with dose escalation to raise serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D above 36 ng/mL, or placebo, for 2 years; 85% completed. Primary outcomes were WOMAC knee pain (0–20) and MRI cartilage volume loss. The record gives no brand name for the cholecalciferol.
cards.result: Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D rose by a mean 16.1 ng/mL in the treatment group versus 2.1 ng/mL on placebo (P < .001), as reported in the record. Knee pain decreased in both groups (−2.31 on treatment, −1.46 on placebo) with no significant difference at any time, and cartilage volume decreased by the same extent in both groups (about −4.3% in each; P = .96) — the treatment made no difference. No secondary clinical endpoint differed.
cards.watchOut: The smaller of the two dedicated trials, with slightly worse baseline pain and function in the treatment group; its null agrees with the larger trial, but on its own it could miss a small effect — the shelf's verdict rests on the concordance of all three carded reports.

randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (mcalindon 2013) 146 participants with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (mean age 62.4 years) at tufts medical center, boston, randomised to oral cholecalciferol 2,000 iu/day with dose escalation to raise serum 25-hydroxyvitamin d above 36 ng/ml, or placebo, for 2 years; 85% completed. primary outcomes were womac knee pain (0–20) and mri cartilage volume loss. the record gives no brand name for the cholecalciferol. serum 25-hydroxyvitamin d rose by a mean 16.1 ng/ml in the treatment group versus 2.1 ng/ml on placebo (p < .001), as reported in the record. knee pain decreased in both groups (−2.31 on treatment, −1.46 on placebo) with no significant difference at any time, and cartilage volume decreased by the same extent in both groups (about −4.3% in each; p = .96) — the treatment made no difference. no secondary clinical endpoint differed. the smaller of the two dedicated trials, with slightly worse baseline pain and function in the treatment group; its null agrees with the larger trial, but on its own it could miss a small effect — the shelf's verdict rests on the concordance of all three carded reports. mcalindon t et al. effect of vitamin d supplementation on progression of knee pain and cartilage volume loss in patients with symptomatic osteoarthritis: a randomized controlled trial. jama. 2013. pmid: 23299607. registry id: nct00306774. mesh: aged · cartilage/pathology · dietary supplements · disease progression · double-blind method · female · humans · knee joint/pathology · magnetic resonance imaging · male · middle aged · osteoarthritis, knee/complications,drug therapy,pathology · pain/etiology,prevention & control · treatment outcome · vitamin d/therapeutic use · vitamins/therapeutic use

cards.headline: MacFarlane 2020 (VITAL ancillary): in 1,398 US adults with chronic knee pain followed ~5.3 years, vitamin D did not improve WOMAC pain, function or stiffness at any time point
cards.summary: MacFarlane 2020 (VITAL ancillary): in 1,398 US adults with chronic knee pain followed ~5.3 years, vitamin D did not improve WOMAC pain, function or stiffness at any time point
cards.type: Randomised trial ancillary analysis (VITAL knee pain, MacFarlane 2020)
cards.people: Ancillary analysis of the double-blind, placebo-controlled VITAL trial (25,871 US adults randomised in a 2-by-2 factorial design to vitamin D or marine omega-3 fatty acids): the 1,398 participants with chronic knee pain before randomisation who returned at least one knee-pain questionnaire (mean age 67.7 years; 66% women; mean WOMAC pain 37 ± 19 on a 0–100 scale), followed for a mean 5.3 ± 0.7 years. The record does not state the vitamin D dose used in VITAL.
cards.result: WOMAC pain did not differ between the active vitamin D group and the vitamin D placebo group at any time point during follow-up, and the linear time-by-treatment interaction was not significant (P = 0.41); vitamin D also did not significantly affect WOMAC function or stiffness scores over time — the treatment made no difference.
cards.watchOut: VITAL enrolled a general older population, not clinic knee-OA patients, and this analysis covers participants who reported chronic knee pain rather than imaging-confirmed osteoarthritis; it answers the pain-progression half of the question at scale, while the structural half rests on the two dedicated trials above.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised reports, two dosing patterns, one answer — vitamin D does not slow cartilage loss or knee-pain progression
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised reports, two dosing patterns, one answer — vitamin D does not slow cartilage loss or knee-pain progression
cards.people: The carded evidence: two dedicated 2-year placebo-controlled trials in symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (413 and 146 patients) and one large trial ancillary analysis in chronic knee pain (1,398 participants, ~5.3 years).
cards.result: Cartilage volume loss was identical on vitamin D and placebo where it was measured (~4.3% over 2 years in McAlindon; no significant difference in Jin), and knee pain improved no more on vitamin D in any report, despite verified rises in blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — a concordant null across monthly bolus and daily titrated dosing.
cards.watchOut: The null is about osteoarthritis progression and knee pain; it says nothing about vitamin D for bone health, deficiency correction, or any non-joint indication, and the trials tested cholecalciferol preparations, not combination joint supplements.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jin X et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 26954409); McAlindon T et al. JAMA. 2013 (PMID: 23299607); MacFarlane LA et al. Arthritis & rheumatology (Hoboken, N.J.). 2020 (PMID: 32583982).

shelves.title: Canakinumab and osteoarthritis: an exploratory CANTOS signal for fewer hip/knee replacements (hazard ratio 0.58) that dedicated knee-OA trials of IL-1 inhibition did not confirm for pain — hypothesis-generating only
shelves.question: In knee osteoarthritis, was the interleukin-1β inhibition signal (canakinumab) for fewer joint replacements and less OA pain real?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip/statistics & numerical data · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/statistics & numerical data · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Incidence · Interleukin-18/antagonists & inhibitors · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Hip/drug therapy · Osteoarthritis, Knee/drug therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT (outcome), and hypothesis-generating throughout — this is an evidence question about whether a signal was real, and the honest answer is: not established. The signal comes from an exploratory analysis of CANTOS (Schieker 2020), a cardiovascular trial of canakinumab in 10,061 people after myocardial infarction — not an osteoarthritis trial and not a knee-OA population: pooled canakinumab doses were associated with fewer incident total hip or knee replacements (0.31 vs 0.54 events per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.42–0.80) and fewer osteoarthritis-related adverse events (hazard ratio 0.73). But CANTOS collected no structural joint outcomes and measured no OA pain endpoint, and the analysis was exploratory. Against it: randomised trials that actually enrolled knee-OA patients and targeted the IL-1 pathway read out negatively (Brom 2025 review of the programme), and a network meta-analysis of anti-inflammatory biologics in OA (Li 2022; 15 studies, 1,566 patients) found no biologic — canakinumab among them — superior to placebo for function or stiffness, with only etanercept and infliximab superior for knee pain in the conventional analysis. The slate's premise of a published canakinumab knee-OA phase 2 trial could not be verified as a journal report on PubMed this session; the dedicated-trial record reaches this shelf through the programme review and the network meta-analysis, which is itself a reason the stamp is capped. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome): POSSIBLE (benefit), hypothesis-generating only, for the joint-replacement signal; no demonstrated pain benefit in the population that actually has knee osteoarthritis.

cards.headline: Schieker 2020 (CANTOS exploratory): pooled canakinumab was associated with fewer incident hip or knee replacements (0.31 vs 0.54 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 0.58) — an exploratory analysis, not an OA trial
cards.summary: Schieker 2020 (CANTOS exploratory): pooled canakinumab was associated with fewer incident hip or knee replacements (0.31 vs 0.54 per 100 person-years; hazard ratio 0.58) — an exploratory analysis, not an OA trial
cards.type: Exploratory analysis of a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (CANTOS, Schieker 2020)
cards.people: Exploratory analysis of the randomised, double-blind CANTOS trial: 10,061 participants with previous myocardial infarction at 1,091 sites in 39 countries, randomly allocated to placebo or canakinumab 50 mg, 150 mg or 300 mg subcutaneously every 3 months; median follow-up 3.7 years. Outcomes were time to first incident total hip or knee replacement (THR/TKR) and osteoarthritis-related adverse events, ascertained blinded from trial databases. HYPOTHESIS-GENERATING: the parent trial was not designed to examine osteoarthritis efficacy and collected no structural joint outcomes.
cards.result: Hazard ratios for incident THR/TKR versus placebo were 0.60 (95% CI 0.38–0.95) for 50 mg, 0.53 (95% CI 0.33–0.84) for 150 mg and 0.60 (95% CI 0.38–0.93) for 300 mg; pooled incidence rates were 0.31 (canakinumab) versus 0.54 (placebo) events per 100 person-years (hazard ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.42–0.80; P = 0.001). The hazard ratio for osteoarthritis-related adverse events was 0.73 (95% CI 0.61–0.87). Similar findings appeared in participants with a history of osteoarthritis. The authors conclude the findings support further investigation of IL-1β inhibition for large-joint osteoarthritis.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory and post-randomisation in framing: CANTOS patients were post-myocardial-infarction patients, most without a knee-OA diagnosis; joint replacement is a decision-sensitive endpoint (surgery thresholds, survival, and competing risks can move it), OA pain was never an endpoint, and no imaging or structural outcome was collected — this card generates the hypothesis; it does not test it in knee OA.
cards.source: Schieker M et al. Effects of Interleukin-1β Inhibition on Incident Hip and Knee Replacement : Exploratory Analyses From a Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial. Annals of internal medicine. 2020. PMID: 32744862. Registry ID: NCT01327846. cards.headline: Li 2022 network meta-analysis: across 15 biologic trials in OA (1,566 patients), no biologic — canakinumab included — beat placebo on function or stiffness, and canakinumab was not among the agents superior for knee pain
cards.summary: Li 2022 network meta-analysis: across 15 biologic trials in OA (1,566 patients), no biologic — canakinumab included — beat placebo on function or stiffness, and canakinumab was not among the agents superior for knee pain
cards.type: Conventional and network meta-analysis of 15 randomised trials (Li 2022)
cards.people: Conventional and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 15 randomised controlled trials (1,566 patients with osteoarthritis) comparing anti-inflammatory biologic agents (including canakinumab, lutikizumab, anakinra, etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab, tocilizumab) with placebo or each other; outcomes were pain, physical function, stiffness and adverse events.
cards.result: In the conventional meta-analysis, only etanercept (standardised mean difference −0.47, 95% CI −0.89 to −0.05) and infliximab (standardised mean difference −2.04, 95% CI −2.56 to −1.52) were superior to placebo for knee pain; canakinumab was not shown superior to placebo. No significant differences were observed between biologics and placebo regarding physical function, stiffness, or risk of adverse events. The authors state the results must be interpreted cautiously and further randomised trials are warranted.
cards.watchOut: The included trials are small and the network is sparse — several comparisons rest on single small trials (the very large standardised effects for infliximab come from few patients); the card's weight is its negative finding for the class on function and stiffness, not its agent rankings.
cards.source: Li Y et al. Relative Efficacy and Safety of Anti-Inflammatory Biologic Agents for Osteoarthritis: A Conventional and Network Meta-Analysis. Journal of clinical medicine. 2022. PMID: 35887724. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Brom 2025 programme review: randomised trials of IL-1 inhibition in knee OA itself 'read out negatively' — the CANTOS joint-replacement signal stands unconfirmed by any dedicated OA trial
cards.summary: Brom 2025 programme review: randomised trials of IL-1 inhibition in knee OA itself 'read out negatively' — the CANTOS joint-replacement signal stands unconfirmed by any dedicated OA trial
cards.type: Narrative review of the IL-1-inhibitor knee-OA trial programme (Brom 2025)
cards.people: Narrative review of interventions with direct IL-1 pathway inhibitors in patients with knee osteoarthritis, plus key preclinical observations, written by a group including investigators from the CANTOS osteoarthritis analysis.
cards.result: The review states that randomised controlled studies using IL-1 inhibition as a treatment approach in knee OA have read out negatively, although trends for improvement in pain and impact on biomarkers could be observed; in contrast, the post-hoc CANTOS analysis showed a substantial reduction in joint-replacement incidence on canakinumab, and a similar post-hoc signal was reported from the LoDoCo2 low-dose colchicine cardiovascular trial. The authors propose the metabolic-phenotype subset of OA as the population in which IL-1 inhibition should be revisited.
cards.watchOut: A narrative review, not a systematic one, and several authors are CANTOS osteoarthritis investigators arguing to revisit their own signal — its value here is the plain statement that the dedicated knee-OA randomised trials were negative, which cuts against the authors' own proposal and is therefore the more credible for it.
cards.source: Brom M et al. Is It Time to Revisit the Role of Interleukin-1 Inhibitors in Osteoarthritis? Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy. 2025. PMID: 40458527. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one exploratory cardiovascular-trial signal versus negative dedicated knee-OA trials — the signal is possible, unconfirmed, and hypothesis-generating
cards.summary: Synthesis: one exploratory cardiovascular-trial signal versus negative dedicated knee-OA trials — the signal is possible, unconfirmed, and hypothesis-generating
cards.people: The carded evidence: one exploratory analysis of a 10,061-person cardiovascular outcomes trial (hip or knee replacement endpoint), one network meta-analysis of 15 small OA biologic trials (1,566 patients), and one narrative review of the IL-1 knee-OA programme.
cards.result: For joint replacement: pooled canakinumab hazard ratio 0.58 (95% CI 0.42–0.80) in CANTOS — a large, precise, but exploratory and population-mismatched signal. For OA pain and function in patients who actually have knee OA: dedicated IL-1-inhibition trials read out negatively, and no biologic beat placebo on function or stiffness in the network analysis. PROPOSED SPLIT (outcome), capped at POSSIBLE and labelled hypothesis-generating: the replacement signal may be real, but as of these reports it has never been confirmed in a trial designed to test it in knee osteoarthritis.
cards.watchOut: Quoting the CANTOS hazard ratio without its exploratory status and post-myocardial-infarction population is exactly the misreading this shelf exists to prevent; equally, the negative dedicated trials tested pain over months, not joint replacement over years, so the two halves of the split are not direct contradictions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Schieker M et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32744862); Li Y et al. Journal of clinical medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35887724); Brom M et al. Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy. 2025 (PMID: 40458527).

shelves.title: Lorecivivint for knee osteoarthritis: the phase 2a trial and both phase 3 trials (OA-10, OA-11) missed their primary pain endpoints — subgroup signals only
shelves.question: In knee osteoarthritis, does lorecivivint improve pain and function versus placebo injection?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Imidazoles/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Indazoles/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Injections, Intra-Articular · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee/drug therapy,physiopathology · Pain Measurement · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Protein Serine-Threonine Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · Protein-Tyrosine Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · Pyridines/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Wnt Signaling Pathway/drug effects · Dyrk Kinases
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — the programme was given three fair tests and missed all three primary endpoints. In the phase 2a dose-ranging trial (Yazici 2020; 455 patients, single 2 mL intra-articular injection of 0.03, 0.07 or 0.23 mg versus placebo), no dose beat placebo on week-13 WOMAC pain (changes −23.3, −23.5 and −21.3 versus −22.1 on placebo, on a 0–100 scale; every group, placebo included, improved by a clinically meaningful ≥20 points). The phase 3 programme — reported in the journal records as OA-10 and OA-11 — used the selected 0.07 mg dose: OA-10 (498 patients, 28 weeks) failed its week-12 Pain NRS primary endpoint and showed no significant differences on other efficacy endpoints; OA-11 (513 patients, 56 weeks) found week-12 pain change of −2.24 on lorecivivint versus −2.49 on placebo (p = 0.185) — numerically favouring placebo — with no discernible effects on other endpoints and no meaningful joint-space-width loss in either group. Positive findings exist only in subgroups: week-52 benefits in the phase 2a prespecified unilateral-symptom subgroup (and a post-hoc no-widespread-pain subgroup), and a post-hoc week-4 signal in OA-10's Kellgren–Lawrence grade 2 subgroup. The drug was well tolerated throughout. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on the question as asked — pain and function versus placebo injection in knee osteoarthritis overall.

cards.headline: Yazici 2020 phase 2a: no lorecivivint dose (0.03, 0.07 or 0.23 mg, single injection) beat placebo on week-13 WOMAC pain in 455 patients — the primary endpoint was not met
cards.summary: Yazici 2020 phase 2a: no lorecivivint dose (0.03, 0.07 or 0.23 mg, single injection) beat placebo on week-13 WOMAC pain in 455 patients — the primary endpoint was not met
cards.type: Phase IIa randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial (Yazici 2020)
cards.people: 455 subjects with moderately to severely symptomatic knee osteoarthritis in a 52-week, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging phase IIa trial, receiving a single 2 mL intra-articular injection of lorecivivint (0.03 mg, 0.07 mg or 0.23 mg) or placebo; efficacy was assessed by WOMAC pain and function subscales (0–100) and radiographic medial joint space width (JSW).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — significant improvement in WOMAC pain versus placebo at week 13 — was not met by any dose (mean change from baseline −23.3 ± 2.2 for 0.03 mg, −23.5 ± 2.1 for 0.07 mg, −21.3 ± 2.2 for 0.23 mg, and −22.1 ± 2.1 for placebo; each P > 0.05 versus placebo), and no dose significantly changed medial JSW versus placebo at week 52 in the full population. In the prespecified unilateral-symptoms subgroup and a post-hoc unilateral-without-widespread-pain subgroup, 0.07 mg did significantly improve week-52 WOMAC pain (between-group differences −8.73 and −11.21) and function, and increased medial JSW (0.39 mm and 0.42 mm). Lorecivivint appeared safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: The subgroup findings that carried the programme forward came from a prespecified subgroup and a post-hoc subgroup after a negative primary endpoint, in a trial where the placebo group itself improved by 22 points — exactly the setting in which subgroup signals most often fail to replicate, as the phase 3 cards show.

cards.headline: OA-10 phase 3 (2025): a single lorecivivint 0.07 mg injection failed the week-12 pain primary endpoint in 498 patients; no significant differences on any other efficacy endpoint
cards.summary: OA-10 phase 3 (2025): a single lorecivivint 0.07 mg injection failed the week-12 pain primary endpoint in 498 patients; no significant differences on any other efficacy endpoint
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (OA-10, Yazici 2025)
cards.people: 498 patients with ACR-defined knee osteoarthritis, Kellgren–Lawrence grades 2–3, and target-knee pain Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) ≥4 and ≤8, in a phase 3, 28-week, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of a single intra-articular injection of lorecivivint 0.07 mg versus vehicle placebo on day 1; 51.9% had Kellgren–Lawrence grade 3 severity. Primary endpoint was change from baseline in Pain NRS at week 12.
cards.result: In the full analysis set, lorecivivint failed to meet the primary endpoint versus placebo, and no significant treatment differences were noted in other efficacy endpoints (WOMAC Function, WOMAC Pain, Patient Global Assessment). A post-hoc analysis showed a nominally significant week-4 pain difference favouring lorecivivint in the Kellgren–Lawrence grade 2 subgroup only (p<0.05). Adverse-event incidence, seriousness and severity were similar across groups; lorecivivint was well tolerated despite not meeting the primary endpoint — the treatment made no difference on the tested outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The only positive note is a post-hoc, single-time-point (week 4), single-subgroup (grade 2) result at nominal significance — hypothesis-generating at best, and not a basis for claiming efficacy in early disease without a dedicated trial.
cards.source: Yazici Y et al. cards.headline: OA-11 phase 3 (2025): week-12 pain fell −2.24 on lorecivivint versus −2.49 on placebo (p = 0.185) in 513 patients — no discernible treatment effect on any endpoint over 56 weeks
cards.summary: OA-11 phase 3 (2025): week-12 pain fell −2.24 on lorecivivint versus −2.49 on placebo (p = 0.185) in 513 patients — no discernible treatment effect on any endpoint over 56 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (OA-11, Yazici 2025)
cards.people: 513 patients with ACR-criteria knee osteoarthritis, Kellgren–Lawrence grades 2–3, and medial joint space width 1.5–4 mm in the target knee (baseline mean 2.61 ± 0.7 mm), in a phase 3, 56-week, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of a single intra-articular lorecivivint 0.07 mg injection versus vehicle placebo on day 1. Primary endpoint was change from baseline in Pain NRS at week 12.
cards.result: Mean change from baseline in weekly average daily Pain NRS at week 12 was −2.24 (± 0.13) on lorecivivint versus −2.49 (± 0.13) on placebo (p = 0.185; 95% CI for the difference −0.12 to 0.62) — the primary endpoint was not met and the point estimate numerically favoured placebo. No discernible treatment effects were revealed on other endpoints (WOMAC Function, WOMAC Pain, Patient Global Assessment, medial joint space width); neither group showed meaningful medial JSW loss over 52 weeks. Adverse events were similar between groups — the treatment made no difference.
cards.watchOut: Because neither arm lost meaningful joint space over 52 weeks, this trial also could not test the disease-modification claim — a null pain result in a structurally stable population leaves the structure question unanswered rather than answered negatively.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three randomised trials, three missed primary pain endpoints — the overall answer is no demonstrated benefit over placebo injection
cards.summary: Synthesis: three randomised trials, three missed primary pain endpoints — the overall answer is no demonstrated benefit over placebo injection
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 2a dose-ranging trial (455 randomised), and two phase 3 trials of the selected 0.07 mg single injection (OA-10, 498 randomised; OA-11, 513 randomised) — 1,466 patients in total.
cards.result: Week-13 WOMAC pain (phase 2a) and week-12 Pain NRS (both phase 3 trials) all failed to separate lorecivivint from vehicle placebo; OA-11's point estimate favoured placebo (−2.24 vs −2.49). Function, global assessment and joint-space outcomes likewise showed no treatment effect in the full populations. Positive results are confined to subgroups (unilateral symptoms in phase 2a; Kellgren–Lawrence grade 2, week 4 only, post-hoc in OA-10). PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for pain and function in knee osteoarthritis overall.
cards.watchOut: A large placebo-injection response (~22 WOMAC points in phase 2a) runs through this whole programme; the subgroup hypotheses (unilateral symptoms, earlier structural grade) remain just that — hypotheses no confirmatory trial has yet tested as its primary question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yazici Y et al. Arthritis & rheumatology (Hoboken, N.J.). 2020 (PMID: 32432388); Yazici Y et al. Clinical and experimental rheumatology. 2025 (PMID: 39808288); Yazici Y et al. Clinical and experimental rheumatology. 2025 (PMID: 39808286).
