shelves.title: Bimekizumab in axial spondyloarthritis: ASAS40 at week 16 was 47.7% versus 21.4% in non-radiographic disease and 44.8% versus 22.5% in radiographic disease (BE MOBILE 1 and 2), sustained to 2 years
shelves.question: In axial spondyloarthritis, does bimekizumab improve disease activity versus placebo in both radiographic and non-radiographic disease?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Interleukin-17 · Non-Radiographic Axial Spondyloarthritis · Treatment Outcome · Spondylitis, Ankylosing/drug therapy · Spondylarthritis/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single programme. BE MOBILE 1 (non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis; 254 randomised) and BE MOBILE 2 (radiographic disease; 332 randomised) were parallel 52-week phase 3 trials of bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks versus placebo, with all patients on bimekizumab from week 16. At week 16 the primary ASAS40 endpoint was met in both: 47.7% on bimekizumab versus 21.4% on placebo in non-radiographic disease, and 44.8% versus 22.5% in radiographic disease (p < 0.001 for both), with all ranked secondary endpoints met, responses in both TNF-inhibitor-naive and inadequate-responder patients, and improvements in ASDAS states, high-sensitivity CRP and MRI inflammation (van der Heijde 2023). Week-52 results (Baraliakos 2024) show the week-16 gains sustained in bimekizumab-randomised patients, with placebo-switchers catching up; treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 75.0% (non-radiographic) and 75.5% (radiographic) of patients over 52 weeks, oral candidiasis was the most frequent fungal infection (7.4% and 6.1%), and uveitis and inflammatory bowel disease were uncommon. At 2 years in the open-label extension (Baraliakos 2025), over 50% of randomised patients held an ASAS40 response and about 60% reached ASDAS low disease activity, with no new safety signals. The axial sequencing question (IL-17 versus a second TNF inhibitor after TNF failure) is homed on pack 5455 and is not re-opened here; bimekizumab's psoriasis homes do not ask the axial question.

cards.headline: van der Heijde 2023 (BE MOBILE 1 and 2): ASAS40 at week 16 — 47.7% versus 21.4% (non-radiographic) and 44.8% versus 22.5% (radiographic), p < 0.001 in both trials
cards.summary: van der Heijde 2023 (BE MOBILE 1 and 2): ASAS40 at week 16 — 47.7% versus 21.4% (non-radiographic) and 44.8% versus 22.5% (radiographic), p < 0.001 in both trials
cards.type: Two parallel randomised double-blind phase 3 trials (BE MOBILE 1 and BE MOBILE 2)
cards.people: Patients with active axial spondyloarthritis in two parallel double-blind phase 3 trials: BE MOBILE 1 in non-radiographic disease (254 randomised, 1:1) and BE MOBILE 2 in radiographic disease (332 randomised, 2:1), treated with bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks or placebo, with all patients receiving bimekizumab from week 16; efficacy and adverse events reported to week 24.
cards.result: At week 16 the primary endpoint (ASAS40, at least 40% improvement) was reached by 47.7% on bimekizumab versus 21.4% on placebo in non-radiographic disease and 44.8% versus 22.5% in radiographic disease (p < 0.001 for both), and all ranked secondary endpoints were met in both trials. ASAS40 responses were similar in TNF-inhibitor-naive and TNF-inhibitor inadequate-responder patients, with improvements in ASDAS states, high-sensitivity CRP and MRI inflammation of the sacroiliac joints and spine. The most frequent adverse events on bimekizumab (over 3%) included nasopharyngitis, upper respiratory tract infection, pharyngitis, diarrhoea, headache and oral candidiasis; fungal infections (all localised) were more frequent than on placebo, with no major adverse cardiovascular events or active tuberculosis, and low rates of uveitis and adjudicated inflammatory bowel disease.
cards.watchOut: The placebo-controlled period is 16 weeks; after that every patient received bimekizumab, so longer-term comparisons are within-cohort, not against placebo. Trial registration numbers are not in this record; they appear in the week-52 report carded next.
cards.source: van der Heijde D et al. Efficacy and safety of bimekizumab in axial spondyloarthritis: results of two parallel phase 3 randomised controlled trials. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2023. PMID: 36649967. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Baraliakos 2024 (BE MOBILE week 52): week-16 gains were sustained to week 52, placebo-switchers caught up, and oral candidiasis affected 7.4% (non-radiographic) and 6.1% (radiographic)
cards.summary: Baraliakos 2024 (BE MOBILE week 52): week-16 gains were sustained to week 52, placebo-switchers caught up, and oral candidiasis affected 7.4% (non-radiographic) and 6.1% (radiographic)
cards.type: Randomised phase 3 trials, 52-week report (BE MOBILE 1 and 2)
cards.people: The BE MOBILE 1 (non-radiographic; NCT03928704) and BE MOBILE 2 (radiographic; NCT03928743) populations through the 36-week maintenance period, in which all patients received bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks from week 16.
cards.result: Improvements versus placebo at week 16 in ASAS40, ASDAS, high-sensitivity CRP and MRI inflammation were sustained to week 52 in bimekizumab-randomised patients, and responses in patients switching from placebo at week 16 were comparable by week 52. Over 52 weeks at least one treatment-emergent adverse event was reported in 183 (75.0%) patients with non-radiographic and 249 (75.5%) with radiographic disease; serious events occurred in 9 (3.7%) and 20 (6.1%). Oral candidiasis was the most frequent fungal infection (18 patients, 7.4%, non-radiographic; 20, 6.1%, radiographic); uveitis occurred in 3 (1.2%) and 7 (2.1%), and inflammatory bowel disease in 2 (0.8%) and 3 (0.9%).
cards.watchOut: No placebo group exists after week 16, so week-52 figures describe durability on treatment, not a controlled effect; candidiasis is the recurring class harm to counsel on.

cards.headline: Baraliakos 2025 (2-year open-label extension): over 50% of randomised patients held ASAS40 at week 104 and about 60% reached ASDAS low disease activity, with no new safety signals
cards.summary: Baraliakos 2025 (2-year open-label extension): over 50% of randomised patients held ASAS40 at week 104 and about 60% reached ASDAS low disease activity, with no new safety signals
cards.type: Open-label extension of two phase 3 trials, 2-year report
cards.people: Patients completing week 52 of BE MOBILE 1 and 2 who entered the open-label extension (NCT04436640), all receiving bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks; efficacy reported for all 586 randomised patients to week 104.
cards.result: In weeks 52–104, 70.8% (367 of 518) of extension patients reported at least one treatment-emergent adverse event; the most frequent were COVID-19 infection (exposure-adjusted incidence 25.2 per 100 patient-years), nasopharyngitis (11.0) and oral candidiasis (5.4), with fungal infections overall at 11.8 per 100 patient-years (mostly Candida, 6.8; most mild or moderate, none serious or systemic). Inflammatory bowel disease and uveitis rates were low and there were no major adverse cardiovascular events or deaths. At week 104 over 50% of randomised patients achieved ASAS40, approximately 60% achieved ASDAS low disease activity (under 2.1) and over 30% ASDAS inactive disease (under 1.3), with sustained MRI inflammation suppression (over 57% MRI remission).
cards.watchOut: Open-label, uncontrolled extension data in trial completers — survivorship and expectation effects apply; it supports durability and safety consistency, not the size of the treatment effect.
cards.source: Baraliakos X et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of bimekizumab in axial spondyloarthritis: 2-year results from two phase 3 studies. Rheumatology (Oxford, England). 2025. shelves.title: Bimekizumab in psoriatic arthritis: ACR50 at week 16 was 44% versus 10% in biologic-naive patients (BE OPTIMAL) and 43% versus 7% after TNF-inhibitor failure (BE COMPLETE), with strong skin clearance in both
shelves.question: In psoriatic arthritis, does bimekizumab improve joint and skin responses versus placebo, including after TNF-inhibitor failure?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Arthritis, Psoriatic/drug therapy · Adalimumab/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Antirheumatic Agents/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Biological Products/therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), single programme. In BE OPTIMAL (McInnes 2023; 852 randomised patients with active psoriatic arthritis naive to biologic DMARDs), ACR50 at week 16 was reached by 189 (44%) of 431 on bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks versus 28 (10%) of 281 on placebo (OR 7.1, 95% CI 4.6 to 10.9; p < 0.0001), similar to the adalimumab reference arm (46%), with all secondary hierarchical endpoints met and treatment-emergent adverse events in 60% versus 49% to week 16. In BE COMPLETE (Merola 2023; 400 randomised patients with prior inadequate response or intolerance to one or two TNF inhibitors), ACR50 was reached by 116 (43%) of 267 on bimekizumab versus 9 (7%) of 133 on placebo (adjusted OR 11.1, 5.4 to 23.0; p < 0.0001), and among patients with psoriasis over at least 3% body surface area, 121 (69%) of 176 on bimekizumab reached PASI 90. A 52-week post-hoc analysis across both trials (McInnes 2024) found ACR50 held at 54.4–54.7% (BE OPTIMAL) and 48.0–56.3% (BE COMPLETE) with or without methotrexate, with complete skin clearance (PASI 100) achieved in similar proportions regardless of methotrexate. So the TNF-failure half of the question is answered by its own trial, not extrapolated from the naive population. Bimekizumab's plaque-psoriasis homes (for example pack 4353) do not ask the psoriatic-arthritis question.

cards.headline: McInnes 2023 (BE OPTIMAL): ACR50 at week 16 in 44% on bimekizumab versus 10% on placebo (OR 7.1) in biologic-naive psoriatic arthritis, matching the adalimumab reference arm (46%)

cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with active reference (BE OPTIMAL)
cards.people: 852 adults with active psoriatic arthritis (CASPAR criteria for at least 6 months) naive to biologic DMARDs, at 135 sites in 14 countries, randomised to bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks (n = 431), placebo (n = 281) or adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks as an active reference (n = 140); placebo patients switched to bimekizumab at week 16; data presented to week 24.
cards.result: At week 16, ACR50 (at least 50% improvement in American College of Rheumatology criteria) was reached by 189 (44%) of 431 on bimekizumab versus 28 (10%) of 281 on placebo (OR 7.1, 95% CI 4.6 to 10.9; p < 0.0001) and by 64 (46%) of 140 on adalimumab; all secondary hierarchical endpoints were met. Treatment-emergent adverse events to week 16 were reported in 258 (60%) of 431 on bimekizumab, 139 (49%) of 281 on placebo and 83 (59%) of 140 on adalimumab.

cards.summary: McInnes 2024 (52-week analysis of BE OPTIMAL and BE COMPLETE): ACR50 held at about 54–55% and 48–56% at week 52, with complete skin clearance (PASI 100), regardless of methotrexate use
cards.type: Post-hoc 52-week analysis of two phase 3 trials and their extension
cards.people: Post-hoc analysis of patients from BE OPTIMAL (biologic-naive), BE COMPLETE (TNF-inhibitor inadequate responders/intolerant) and the BE VITAL open-label extension (NCT04009499), grouped by concomitant methotrexate at baseline; from week 16 placebo-randomised patients received bimekizumab.
cards.result: Through week 52, similar proportions of bimekizumab-treated patients achieved ACR50 with and without methotrexate (BE OPTIMAL: 54.4% with methotrexate, 54.7% without; BE COMPLETE: 56.3% with, 48.0% without), with similar proportions achieving complete skin clearance (PASI 100) and minimal disease activity in both methotrexate groups, and similar trends in placebo-to-bimekizumab switchers. Treatment-emergent adverse events through week 52 were similar between methotrexate subgroups (BE OPTIMAL 79.3% versus 78.8%; BE COMPLETE 62.5% versus 62.7%), and the safety profile was consistent with the prior bimekizumab profile. The record carries no MeSH list, so the fallback applies to this card.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and uncontrolled after week 16 (all patients on bimekizumab), with imputation for missing data — it speaks to durability and to the methotrexate question, not to the controlled effect size.

shelves.title: Central sensitisation and descending pain modulation (physiology): fibromyalgia patients show exaggerated wind-up and after-sensations, knee osteoarthritis patients show facilitated temporal summation, and conditioned pain modulation is impaired across chronic pain (pooled effect size 0.78)
shelves.question: What human experimental evidence supports central sensitisation and impaired descending pain modulation (conditioned pain modulation) in chronic pain states such as fibromyalgia and osteoarthritis?
shelves.mesh: Female · Fibromyalgia/physiopathology,psychology · Hand/physiopathology · Hot Temperature · Humans · Male · Pain/physiopathology · Pain Threshold · Psychophysics/methods · Reference Values · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong Review of Medical Physiology; Boron and Boulpaep Medical Physiology): nociceptive input is amplified or damped centrally — repeated C-fibre input progressively increases dorsal-horn responses (wind-up, the laboratory signature of central sensitisation), and a second, distant painful stimulus normally suppresses pain elsewhere through descending inhibitory pathways (the basis of conditioned pain modulation, CPM). The carded human experimental studies show both systems behaving abnormally in chronic pain. In fibromyalgia, Staud 2001 found wind-up was evoked in patients and controls but was greater in patients at every level: the first stimulus in a series already felt stronger, temporal summation within the series was larger (patients reached painful levels at interstimulus intervals of 2–5 seconds at which controls rarely reported pain), and after-sensations were greater, longer and more often painful. Staud 2014 (38 fibromyalgia patients, 33 controls) integrated three heat-pulse trains into a wind-up response function whose slope — the measure of central pain sensitivity — was significantly steeper in patients (p < 0.003), and whose after-sensations predicted clinical pain intensity (r = 0.4). For descending modulation, the Lewis 2012 systematic review and meta-analysis (30 studies; 778 patients, 664 controls) found a large pooled effect size of 0.78 for reduced CPM in chronic pain populations versus healthy controls. In knee osteoarthritis specifically, Petersen 2017 (133 severe knee osteoarthritis patients, 50 matched controls) found widespread pressure hyperalgesia and facilitated temporal summation (p < 0.02) with a trend to impaired CPM (p = 0.06). No animal studies are carded; animal mechanism appears only as the textbook framing above.

cards.headline: Staud 2001: fibromyalgia patients showed greater wind-up, reached pain at stimulus intervals (2–5 s) that rarely hurt controls, and had stronger, longer, more often painful after-sensations
cards.summary: Staud 2001: fibromyalgia patients showed greater wind-up, reached pain at stimulus intervals (2–5 s) that rarely hurt controls, and had stronger, longer, more often painful after-sensations
cards.type: Primary human experimental pain study (fibromyalgia versus controls)
cards.people: Patients with long-standing fibromyalgia syndrome and healthy control subjects, studied with repetitive thermal stimulation of the glabrous skin of the hands at varying interstimulus intervals, rating sensory magnitude during and after each series; the record does not state the group sizes, so this card prints N not documented for its groups.
cards.result: Wind-up was evoked in both groups, but the perceived magnitude of the first stimulus in a series was greater in fibromyalgia subjects, as was the amount of temporal summation within a series. Fibromyalgia subjects reported increases in sensory magnitude to painful levels at interstimulus intervals of 2–5 seconds, whereas pain was evoked infrequently in controls at intervals over 2 seconds. After the last stimulus, after-sensations were greater in magnitude, lasted longer and were more frequently painful in fibromyalgia subjects. The authors interpret this as psychophysical evidence that input to central nociceptive pathways is abnormally processed in fibromyalgia.
cards.watchOut: Group sizes are N not documented in the fetched record, and psychophysical ratings are subjective by design — the finding is the between-group pattern under identical stimulation, not an objective biomarker.
cards.source: Staud R et al. Abnormal sensitization and temporal summation of second pain (wind-up) in patients with fibromyalgia syndrome. Pain. 2001. PMID: 11240089. cards.headline: Staud 2014: the wind-up response-function slope (central pain sensitivity) was significantly steeper in 38 fibromyalgia patients than in 33 controls (p < 0.003), and after-sensations predicted clinical pain (r = 0.4)
cards.summary: Staud 2014: the wind-up response-function slope (central pain sensitivity) was significantly steeper in 38 fibromyalgia patients than in 33 controls (p < 0.003), and after-sensations predicted clinical pain (r = 0.4)
cards.type: Primary human experimental pain study (fibromyalgia versus controls)
cards.people: 33 normal controls and 38 fibromyalgia patients studied with 0.4 Hz heat-pulse trains to the hands at three stimulus intensities (44, 46 and 48 degrees C), with wind-up calculated as the difference between first and fifth pulse ratings and integrated into a wind-up response function; N = 71 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Wind-up difference scores accelerated linearly with stimulus intensity in both groups (p < 0.001), more in fibromyalgia than controls, spanning wind-down to wind-up. The slope of the wind-up response function, representing central pain sensitivity, was significantly steeper in fibromyalgia patients than controls (p < 0.003), and wind-up after-sensations at 15 and 30 seconds predicted clinical fibromyalgia pain intensity (Pearson r = 0.4; p < 0.04). The authors conclude the response-function method controls for individual pain sensitivity and better characterises central pain responding.
cards.watchOut: A methods-development study in one centre's volunteers; the clinical-pain correlation (r = 0.4) is modest, and wind-up is a laboratory model of central sensitisation, not a direct measure of spinal cord physiology in patients.
cards.source: Staud R et al. Slow temporal summation of pain for assessment of central pain sensitivity and clinical pain of fibromyalgia patients. PloS one. 2014. PMID: 24558475. primary human experimental pain study (fibromyalgia versus controls) 33 normal controls and 38 fibromyalgia patients studied with 0.4 hz heat-pulse trains to the hands at three stimulus intensities (44, 46 and 48 degrees c), with wind-up calculated as the difference between first and fifth pulse ratings and integrated into a wind-up response function; n = 71 printed on the face of this physiology card. wind-up difference scores accelerated linearly with stimulus intensity in both groups (p < 0.001), more in fibromyalgia than controls, spanning wind-down to wind-up. the slope of the wind-up response function, representing central pain sensitivity, was significantly steeper in fibromyalgia patients than controls (p < 0.003), and wind-up after-sensations at 15 and 30 seconds predicted clinical fibromyalgia pain intensity (pearson r = 0.4; p < 0.04). the authors conclude the response-function method controls for individual pain sensitivity and better characterises central pain responding. a methods-development study in one centre's volunteers; the clinical-pain correlation (r = 0.4) is modest, and wind-up is a laboratory model of central sensitisation, not a direct measure of spinal cord physiology in patients. staud r et al. slow temporal summation of pain for assessment of central pain sensitivity and clinical pain of fibromyalgia patients. plos one. 2014. pmid: 24558475. registry id: none in the record. mesh: analysis of variance · case-control studies · fibromyalgia/*physiopathology · hot temperature · humans · *models, biological · nociceptors/*physiology · pain/*physiopathology · pain measurement/*methods · surveys and questionnaires

cards.headline: Lewis 2012 (meta-analysis, 30 studies; 778 patients, 664 controls): conditioned pain modulation was reduced in chronic pain populations with a large pooled effect size of 0.78
cards.summary: Lewis 2012 (meta-analysis, 30 studies; 778 patients, 664 controls): conditioned pain modulation was reduced in chronic pain populations with a large pooled effect size of 0.78
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of human experimental studies
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 studies that used a standardised conditioned-pain-modulation protocol in a chronic pain population and a healthy control population (778 patients and 664 control participants in total).
cards.result: Across all studies there was a large effect size of 0.78 reflecting reduced conditioned pain modulation in the patient group; participant gender and age significantly influenced the effect size, while the type of outcome measure, test stimulus, conditioning stimulus and conditioning pain level did not. Risk-of-bias assessment found poor assessor blinding and weak control of confounders were common. The authors conclude conditioned pain modulation is impaired in populations with chronic pain, indicating dysfunction of endogenous pain modulatory mechanisms.
cards.watchOut: Protocols varied across the 30 studies and assessor blinding was often poor; the pooled effect establishes the direction and rough size of the CPM deficit, not a patient-level diagnostic test.
cards.source: Lewis GN et al. Conditioned pain modulation in populations with chronic pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. The journal of pain. 2012. PMID: 22981090. cards.headline: Petersen 2017: 133 severe knee osteoarthritis patients showed widespread pressure hyperalgesia and facilitated temporal summation (p < 0.02) versus 50 controls, with a trend to impaired CPM (p = 0.06)
cards.summary: Petersen 2017: 133 severe knee osteoarthritis patients showed widespread pressure hyperalgesia and facilitated temporal summation (p < 0.02) versus 50 controls, with a trend to impaired CPM (p = 0.06)
cards.type: Primary human experimental pain study (knee osteoarthritis versus controls)
cards.people: 133 patients with severe knee osteoarthritis and 50 age- and sex-matched asymptomatic controls, assessed by cuff and handheld pressure algometry around the knee and at a distant site, with temporal summation from 10 repetitive cuff stimulations and conditioned pain modulation measured as the change in pressure tolerance during tonic arm pain; N = 183 printed on the face of this physiology card.
cards.result: Patients demonstrated reduced mild pain detection threshold, pressure tolerance threshold and pressure pain thresholds (p < 0.01), facilitated temporal summation of pain (p < 0.02), and a trend toward impaired conditioned pain modulation (p = 0.06) compared with controls. Pressure hyperalgesia correlated negatively with age, while temporal summation and conditioned pain modulation showed no age association, which the authors read as these dynamic mechanisms being robust across age. (Senior author group: the Arendt-Nielsen pain-sensitisation programme.)
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional and in severe (largely pre-surgical) osteoarthritis; the CPM difference itself was a trend (p = 0.06) in this cohort — the strong CPM claim rests on the meta-analysis card, with this card showing the osteoarthritis pattern for hyperalgesia and temporal summation.
cards.source: Petersen KK et al. Age Interactions on Pain Sensitization in Patients With Severe Knee Osteoarthritis and Controls. The Clinical journal of pain. 2017. PMID: 28277434. cards.headline: Synthesis: exaggerated wind-up in fibromyalgia, facilitated summation in osteoarthritis, and impaired conditioned pain modulation across chronic pain — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: exaggerated wind-up in fibromyalgia, facilitated summation in osteoarthritis, and impaired conditioned pain modulation across chronic pain — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human evidence: two fibromyalgia psychophysics studies (one with N = 71 printed, one N not documented in its record), one knee-osteoarthritis cohort (N = 183) and a 30-study meta-analysis (778 patients, 664 controls).
cards.result: Three different experimental approaches converge: ascending amplification is exaggerated (wind-up and temporal summation larger in fibromyalgia and in knee osteoarthritis than in matched controls), and descending inhibition is weaker (conditioned pain modulation reduced across chronic pain conditions, pooled effect 0.78). This is the human experimental basis for the central-sensitisation account given in Ganong and in Boron and Boulpaep, which frame this shelf; no animal data are carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the existence of both phenomena in these conditions — not for any drug or procedure that claims to reverse them, which belongs on treatment shelves.
cards.watchOut: Established as group-level experimental phenomena; neither wind-up nor CPM is a validated individual diagnostic test, and effect sizes vary with protocol, age and sex matching, as the meta-analysis itself reports.
cards.source: Synthesis of Staud R et al. Pain. 2001 (PMID: 11240089); Staud R et al. PloS one. 2014 (PMID: 24558475); Lewis GN et al. The journal of pain. 2012 (PMID: 22981090); Petersen KK et al. shelves.title: Asfotase alfa in hypophosphatasia: survival 95% versus 42% at 1 year against historical controls — single-arm evidence in very small cohorts
shelves.question: In people with hypophosphatasia, does asfotase alfa, compared with supportive care/historical natural history, improve survival, respiratory function and skeletal mineralisation?
shelves.mesh: Alkaline Phosphatase/administration & dosage,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Biological Availability · Bone and Bones/diagnostic imaging,drug effects · Child, Preschool · Enzyme Replacement Therapy/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Hypophosphatasia/complications,drug therapy · Immunoglobulin G/administration & dosage,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Infant · Infant, Newborn · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Subcutaneous/adverse effects · Male · Radiography · Recombinant Fusion Proteins/administration & dosage,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Rickets/diagnostic imaging,drug therapy,etiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — an evidence question resting on single-arm studies against historical natural history, with small-N labelling throughout. Survival in perinatal/infantile disease was 95% versus 42% at 1 year and 84% versus 27% at 5 years against historical controls (Whyte 2016), rickets healed in 9 of the first 11 treated infants (Whyte 2012, where the product is published as ENB-0040), and older children gained sustained function over 5 years (JCI Insight 2016). The one randomised study (19 adolescents/adults) is a dose comparison with a biochemical co-primary endpoint. Effect sizes are large, but every comparison is historical or within-cohort.

cards.headline: Whyte 2012: in 11 infants and young children with life-threatening hypophosphatasia, the enzyme (published as ENB-0040, later asfotase alfa) healed rickets in 9 by 6 months, with improved pulmonary and physical function and no definite drug-related serious adverse events
cards.summary: Whyte 2012: in 11 infants and young children with life-threatening hypophosphatasia, the enzyme (published as ENB-0040, later asfotase alfa) healed rickets in 9 by 6 months, with improved pulmonary and physical function and no definite drug-related serious adverse events
cards.people: 11 infants and young children with life-threatening or debilitating perinatal or infantile hypophosphatasia, enrolled in a multinational open-label study; 10 completed 6 months of therapy and 9 completed 1 year. Single-arm — no concurrent control group. N=11 printed plainly: this cohort is at the reference floor and is carded under the small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: Healing of rickets at 6 months in 9 patients was accompanied by improvement in developmental milestones and pulmonary function. Plasma levels of the tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase substrates inorganic pyrophosphate and pyridoxal 5'-phosphate diminished. Serum parathyroid hormone rose as the skeleton healed, often requiring dietary calcium supplementation. There was no evidence of hypocalcaemia, ectopic calcification, or definite drug-related serious adverse events; low titres of anti-drug antibodies developed in four patients without evident clinical, biochemical or autoimmune abnormalities at 48 weeks.
cards.watchOut: Product naming, as published: the 2012 paper names the tested product ENB-0040 (bone-targeted recombinant human tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, Enobia Pharma) — the molecule later marketed as asfotase alfa. Single-arm, N=11: every number on this card is a within-cohort observation, not a comparison.
cards.source: Single-arm open-label trial (phase 2) | Whyte MP et al. N Engl J Med. 2012. PMID: 22397652. Registry ID: NCT00744042 (ClinicalTrials.gov, as printed in the record). cards.headline: Whyte 2016: against historical natural-history controls, survival was 95% versus 42% at 1 year and 84% versus 27% at 5 years; 76% of ventilated treated patients survived versus 5% of ventilated controls
cards.summary: Whyte 2016: against historical natural-history controls, survival was 95% versus 42% at 1 year and 84% versus 27% at 5 years; 76% of ventilated treated patients survived versus 5% of ventilated controls
cards.people: 37 treated patients with perinatal or infantile hypophosphatasia from two open-label phase 2 studies (median treatment duration 2.7 years; asfotase alfa 1 mg/kg six times weekly or 2 mg/kg three times weekly), compared with 48 historical controls of similar age and disease characteristics from a retrospective natural-history study. The treated group includes the Whyte 2012 cohort — the cards overlap and must not be added together.
cards.result: Survival at age 1 year was 95% in treated patients versus 42% in historical controls, and at age 5 years 84% versus 27% (P<0.0001, Kaplan-Meier log-rank). Among patients who required ventilatory assistance, 76% (16 of 21) of treated patients survived versus 5% (1 of 20) of historical controls; 75% (12 of 16) of the surviving ventilated treated patients were weaned from ventilatory support. The better respiratory outcome accompanied radiographic improvements in skeletal mineralisation.
cards.watchOut: Historical controls are not a randomised comparison: era effects, supportive-care improvements and selection into treatment can all inflate the contrast. The survival gap is very large, which is why the stamp is POSSIBLE rather than MAYBE, but it remains single-arm evidence.
cards.source: Single-arm trials compared with historical natural-history controls (phase 2) | Whyte MP et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2016. PMID: 26529632. cards.headline: Whyte 2016 (JCI Insight): in 12 children aged 6–12 years treated for 5 years, radiographic rickets measures improved significantly by 6 months and growth, strength, motor function and quality of life mostly reached age-matched normal values; pain and disability resolved for most
cards.summary: Whyte 2016 (JCI Insight): in 12 children aged 6–12 years treated for 5 years, radiographic rickets measures improved significantly by 6 months and growth, strength, motor function and quality of life mostly reached age-matched normal values; pain and disability resolved for most
cards.people: 12 children aged 6–12 years at baseline, substantially impaired by hypophosphatasia, treated with asfotase alfa subcutaneously and studied for 5 years; skeletal disease was quantified on two radiographic scales, including comparisons with serial radiographs from similarly affected historical control patients. Single-arm. N=12 printed plainly under the small-N labelling rule.
cards.result: The 6-month primary endpoint was met, with significant radiographic improvement. Growth, strength, motor function, agility and quality of life improved significantly, for most patients reaching normal values for age- and sex-matched peers and sustained at 5 years; for most, pain and disability resolved. Mild-to-moderate injection-site reactions were common and sometimes associated with lipohypertrophy. Low anti-asfotase alfa antibody titres were noted in all patients. No evidence emerged for clinically important ectopic calcification or treatment resistance.
cards.watchOut: N=12, single-arm, with radiographic (not clinical-event) comparison to historical controls; functional gains are within-cohort changes over 5 years of growth, so maturation itself contributes an unknown share.
cards.source: Single-arm open-label trial (phase 2) with historical-control radiographic comparison | Whyte MP et al. JCI Insight. 2016. PMID: 27699270. cards.headline: Kishnani 2019: the one randomised study — 19 adolescents and adults randomised to two asfotase alfa doses or no treatment for 6 months; substrate levels fell significantly for pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (P=0.0285) but not inorganic pyrophosphate (P=0.0715), and 6-minute walk distance rose from a median 355 m to 450 m over 5 years of treatment
cards.summary: Kishnani 2019: the one randomised study — 19 adolescents and adults randomised to two asfotase alfa doses or no treatment for 6 months; substrate levels fell significantly for pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (P=0.0285) but not inorganic pyrophosphate (P=0.0715), and 6-minute walk distance rose from a median 355 m to 450 m over 5 years of treatment
cards.people: 19 patients aged 13–66 years with (paediatric-onset) hypophosphatasia, randomised to asfotase alfa 0.3 mg/kg/day (n=7), 0.5 mg/kg/day (n=6) or no treatment (n=6) for a 6-month primary period, then all treated in a 4.5-year extension. Randomised but open-label and very small — N=19 printed plainly.
cards.result: Changes in plasma pyridoxal 5'-phosphate and inorganic pyrophosphate (co-primary measures) were greater in the combined asfotase alfa group than in controls at 6 months, reaching significance for pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (P=0.0285) but not inorganic pyrophosphate (P=0.0715); within-subject falls in both substrates over 5 years were significant. Mineralisation lag time on bone histomorphometry fell significantly at year 1; dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry bone mineral density did not differ between treated and control patients at 6 months. Median 6-minute walk distance increased from 355 m before treatment to 450 m at 5 years (n=13; P<0.05). There were no deaths; the most common adverse events were mild-to-moderate injection-site reactions.
cards.watchOut: The only randomised card is a 19-patient dose study whose untreated arm lasted 6 months and whose co-primary endpoint was biochemical, not clinical; the 5-year functional figures are single-arm extension data.
cards.source: Randomised open-label trial (phase 2) with extension | Kishnani PS et al. Bone. 2019. PMID: 30576866. Registry ID: NCT01163149 (as printed in the record; EudraCT 2010-019850-42). cards.headline: Synthesis: asfotase alfa is associated with markedly better survival and respiratory outcomes than natural history in severe infantile hypophosphatasia, and with sustained skeletal and functional improvement in older children — all from single-arm studies against historical controls, in very small cohorts
cards.summary: Synthesis: asfotase alfa is associated with markedly better survival and respiratory outcomes than natural history in severe infantile hypophosphatasia, and with sustained skeletal and functional improvement in older children — all from single-arm studies against historical controls, in very small cohorts
cards.people: Synthesis of Whyte 2012 (n=11 infants), Whyte 2016 survival comparison (37 treated versus 48 historical controls; includes the 2012 cohort), Whyte 2016 JCI Insight (n=12 children aged 6–12) and Kishnani 2019 (n=19 adolescents/adults, the one randomised study). No hypophosphatasia or asfotase home exists in the library — verified against the live ask-index and the built-pack tree this session.
cards.result: The pattern is consistent across cohorts: rickets healed radiographically in 9 of the first 11 infants; survival against historical controls was 95% versus 42% at 1 year and 84% versus 27% at 5 years, with most ventilated treated infants surviving and being weaned; children aged 6–12 gained growth, strength and motor function sustained over 5 years; and the small randomised adult/adolescent study showed substrate normalisation and better walking distance. The honest limits are on every face: no placebo-controlled trial exists in the severe paediatric disease, cohorts are 11–37 treated patients, the survival comparison is against historical controls, and the product was published as ENB-0040 in the founding study before being named asfotase alfa.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: small-N labelling applies to the whole pack — the largest treated cohort is 37 patients, and the cohorts overlap (the 2016 survival analysis includes the 2012 infants), so the treated total must not be summed across cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of Whyte MP et al. N Engl J Med. 2012 (PMID: 22397652; NCT00744042); Whyte MP et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2016 (PMID: 26529632); Whyte MP et al. JCI Insight. 2016 (PMID: 27699270; NCT00952484, NCT01203826); Kishnani PS et al. Bone. 2019 (PMID: 30576866; NCT01163149).

shelves.question: In long-term bisphosphonate users, what is the absolute risk of atypical femoral fracture, how does it change with treatment duration, and how quickly does it fall after stopping?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — a risk-quantification shelf, observational throughout, with absolutes on the face as commissioned. Incidence by duration (Dell 2012, Kaiser): 1.78 per 100,000/year at 0.1–1.9 years of use, rising to 113.1 per 100,000/year at 8–9.9 years. Black 2020 (196,129 women, 277 events) gives adjusted hazards of 8.86 (3–<5 years) and 43.51 (8+ years) versus <3 months and a rapid fall after discontinuation. The independent Danish case-cohort (Bauer 2024) concurs: HR 7.29 for 5–7 years versus <1 year, quick fall after stopping, 5-year NNH 1,424 against NNT 56 to prevent one hip fracture.

cards.headline: Black 2020 (Kaiser, 196,129 women): 277 atypical femur fractures occurred; risk rose steeply with duration (hazard ratio 8.86 at 3 to <5 years and 43.51 at 8+ years versus <3 months) and fell rapidly after discontinuation — while fracture prevention dwarfed the harm (after 3 years, 149 hip fractures prevented versus 2 atypical fractures in White women)
cards.summary: Black 2020 (Kaiser, 196,129 women): 277 atypical femur fractures occurred; risk rose steeply with duration (hazard ratio 8.86 at 3 to <5 years and 43.51 at 8+ years versus <3 months) and fell rapidly after discontinuation — while fracture prevention dwarfed the harm (after 3 years, 149 hip fractures prevented versus 2 atypical fractures in White women)
cards.people: 196,129 women aged 50 and older receiving bisphosphonates in the Kaiser Permanente Southern California system, followed 2007–2017; atypical femur fractures were radiographically adjudicated and risk factors taken from electronic health records. An observational cohort — the risk-quantification anchor for this shelf, with absolutes modelled by the authors.
cards.result: 277 atypical femur fractures occurred. After multivariable adjustment, risk increased with longer bisphosphonate use: hazard ratio (versus less than 3 months) 8.86 (95% CI 2.79–28.20) for 3 to under 5 years, rising to 43.51 (13.70–138.15) for 8 years or more — relative measures on a very low absolute baseline. Other risk factors included Asian versus White race (HR 4.84, 3.57–6.56), height, weight and glucocorticoid use. Bisphosphonate discontinuation was associated with a rapid decrease in atypical-fracture risk. In the authors' risk-benefit modelling over 1–10 years, decreases in osteoporotic and hip fractures far outweighed the atypical-fracture increase in White women and less so in Asian women: after 3 years of use, 149 hip fractures were prevented and 2 bisphosphonate-associated atypical fractures occurred in White women, compared with 91 prevented and 8 atypical in Asian women.
cards.watchOut: Women only, one health system, and the prevented-versus-caused counts are modelled, not counted head-to-head. The huge duration hazard ratios sit on a tiny absolute baseline — the next card's incidence rates are the numbers to quote.
cards.source: Prospective cohort study (health-system, radiographically adjudicated) | Black DM et al. N Engl J Med. 2020. PMID: 32813950. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Dell 2012 (Kaiser): the age-adjusted incidence of atypical femoral fracture rose from 1.78 per 100,000 per year with 0.1–1.9 years of bisphosphonate exposure to 113.1 per 100,000 per year with 8–9.9 years
cards.summary: Dell 2012 (Kaiser): the age-adjusted incidence of atypical femoral fracture rose from 1.78 per 100,000 per year with 0.1–1.9 years of bisphosphonate exposure to 113.1 per 100,000 per year with 8–9.9 years
cards.people: All femur fractures from 2007–2011 among 1,835,116 patients older than 45 in the Kaiser Southern California Healthy Bones Program; potential atypical fractures were identified by codes and adjudicated on radiographs, with bisphosphonate exposure from pharmacy records. 142 patients had atypical fractures, 128 of them bisphosphonate-exposed; 188,814 patients in the population had used bisphosphonates. Observational.
cards.result: The age-adjusted incidence of atypical fracture was 1.78 per 100,000 per year (95% CI 1.5–2.0) with bisphosphonate exposure of 0.1 to 1.9 years, and rose with duration to 113.1 per 100,000 per year (69.3–156.8) with exposure of 8 to 9.9 years. Mean duration of use among atypical-fracture patients was 5.5 years; there was no significant correlation of duration with age or bone density (mean T-score −2.1). The authors conclude incidence rises with longer use, remains far below the expected rate of hip fractures in elderly osteoporotic patients, and should be weighed when continuing bisphosphonates beyond 5 years.
cards.watchOut: The same Kaiser system as Black 2020, with an overlapping era — the two Kaiser cards are one evidence stream at two time windows, not independent replications. Incidence denominators are person-time in exposed strata, so the top stratum (113.1/100,000/year) rests on relatively few long-term users.
cards.source: Population cohort study (health-system, radiographically adjudicated) | Dell RM et al. J Bone Miner Res. 2012. PMID: 22836783. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Bauer 2024 (Denmark, case-cohort): 5–7 years of bisphosphonate use carried a 7-fold atypical-fracture hazard versus under 1 year (adjusted HR 7.29), risk fell quickly after discontinuation — and the 5-year number needed to harm was 1,424 against a number needed to treat of 56 to prevent one hip fracture; 31% of atypical fractures had no bisphosphonate exposure at all
cards.summary: Bauer 2024 (Denmark, case-cohort): 5–7 years of bisphosphonate use carried a 7-fold atypical-fracture hazard versus under 1 year (adjusted HR 7.29), risk fell quickly after discontinuation — and the 5-year number needed to harm was 1,424 against a number needed to treat of 56 to prevent one hip fracture; 31% of atypical fractures had no bisphosphonate exposure at all
cards.people: Population-based case-cohort study in the Danish national healthcare system: all 1.9 million Danish adults aged 50 and older, with 4,973 subtrochanteric or femoral-shaft fractures (2010–2015) compared against a random sample of 37,021; bisphosphonate use was collected from 1995–2015 and 4,769 fracture radiographs were reviewed blinded, identifying 189 atypical femoral fractures by established criteria. An independent (non-Kaiser) evidence stream.
cards.result: Compared with under 1 year of bisphosphonate use, 5 to 7 years of use was associated with a 7-fold increase in atypical femoral fracture (adjusted hazard ratio 7.29, 95% CI 3.07–17.30 — a relative measure), and the risk fell quickly after discontinuation. The 5-year number needed to harm for one atypical fracture was 1,424, while the 5-year number needed to treat to prevent one hip fracture was 56. Glucocorticoid and proton-pump-inhibitor use were independently associated with atypical-fracture risk. Notably, 31% of patients with an atypical fracture had no bisphosphonate exposure. The authors conclude the benefit of therapy in adults 50 and older dramatically exceeds the increased atypical-fracture risk.
cards.watchOut: Case-cohort design with radiographic adjudication — the strongest design carded — but atypical fractures also occur without bisphosphonates (31% here), so duration associations are not proof that every long-term user's fracture was drug-caused.
cards.source: Population-based case-cohort study (blinded radiographic review) | Bauer DC et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2024. PMID: 38198798. Registry ID: none in the record (observational study). cards.headline: Synthesis: atypical femoral fracture is a real, duration-dependent harm with very low absolute risk — about 2 per 100,000 per year in the first 2 years of use, rising to about 113 per 100,000 per year by 8–10 years, and falling rapidly when the drug is stopped
cards.summary: Synthesis: atypical femoral fracture is a real, duration-dependent harm with very low absolute risk — about 2 per 100,000 per year in the first 2 years of use, rising to about 113 per 100,000 per year by 8–10 years, and falling rapidly when the drug is stopped
cards.people: Synthesis of Black 2020 (Kaiser cohort, 196,129 women, 277 atypical fractures), Dell 2012 (Kaiser population incidence by duration) and Bauer 2024 (Danish case-cohort, 189 adjudicated atypical fractures). No shelf in the library poses atypical femoral fracture as its question — verified against the live ask-index and the built-pack tree this session; the bisphosphonate shelves cover efficacy and drug holidays (e.g. live #351) without this risk quantification.
cards.result: Three questions, three answers, all with absolutes on the face. How big is the risk? Very small: 277 events among 196,129 bisphosphonate-treated women over a decade (Black), an incidence of 1.78 per 100,000 per year early in treatment (Dell). How does it change with duration? Steeply: incidence reaches 113.1 per 100,000 per year at 8–9.9 years (Dell), with adjusted hazards of 8.86 at 3–5 years and 43.51 at 8+ years versus under 3 months (Black) and 7.29 for 5–7 years versus under 1 year in Denmark (Bauer). How fast does it fall after stopping? Rapidly — both Black and Bauer report a quick decline after discontinuation, though neither fetched record prints an exact half-life, so none is quoted. Set against benefit, the Danish 5-year numbers are 1,424 treated for one atypical fracture caused versus 56 treated to prevent one hip fracture; Black's modelling gives 149 hip fractures prevented versus 2 atypical fractures after 3 years in White women (91 versus 8 in Asian women, who carry higher atypical risk).
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: a risk-quantification shelf — all evidence observational, hence the POSSIBLE ceiling, but the duration gradient, the rapid fall after stopping, and two independent health systems (Kaiser and Denmark) make the shape of the risk about as firm as observational evidence gets. Exact post-discontinuation decay rates are not printed in the fetched records and are not invented here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Black DM et al. N Engl J Med. 2020 (PMID: 32813950); Dell RM et al. J Bone Miner Res. 2012 (PMID: 22836783); Bauer DC et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2024 (PMID: 38198798). Registry IDs: none in the records (observational studies).

shelves.title: Teriparatide in men with osteoporosis: spine BMD rose 5.9% (20 µg) and 9.0% (40 µg) in 437 men; vertebral fractures fell by about half in follow-up, with moderate/severe fractures down 83%
shelves.question: In men with osteoporosis at high fracture risk, does teriparatide, compared with placebo, increase bone mineral density and reduce vertebral fractures?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Animals · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Neoplasms/chemically induced · Bone Remodeling/drug effects · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoporosis/drug therapy,metabolism · Osteosarcoma/chemically induced · Rats · Rats, Inbred F344 · Teriparatide/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use,toxicity
shelves.balance: BMD benefit is consistent across both men's trials; the fracture evidence is one follow-up analysis and is graded POSSIBLE accordingly. Orwoll 2003 randomised 437 men with spine or hip BMD more than 2 SD below the young-adult male mean to placebo, teriparatide 20 µg or 40 µg daily; the trial was stopped at a median 11 months because of osteosarcomas in rat toxicology studies, yet spine BMD had already risen 5.9% and 9.0% (P<0.001 vs placebo for both) and femoral-neck BMD 1.5% and 2.9%. Kaufman 2005 followed 355 of those men for 30 months post-treatment (42 months total): incident vertebral fractures in the radiographed subset were 11.7% (placebo) vs 5.4% (20 µg) and 6.0% (40 µg) — a 51% relative risk reduction for combined teriparatide that did not reach significance (P=0.07), while moderate/severe fractures were significantly reduced by 83% (P=0.01, relative). The smaller independent Kurland 2000 trial (23 men with idiopathic osteoporosis, PTH(1-34) 400 IU/day as published) found a 13.5% lumbar-spine BMD gain vs no change on placebo (P<0.001), directionally concordant. Desk-check: the library's teriparatide shelves rest on the postmenopausal-women trials; the men question was unhomed (male-osteoporosis shelves cover other agents).

cards.headline: Orwoll 2003: teriparatide raised spine BMD 5.9% (20 µg) and 9.0% (40 µg) vs placebo in 437 men with osteoporosis
cards.summary: Orwoll 2003: teriparatide raised spine BMD 5.9% (20 µg) and 9.0% (40 µg) vs placebo in 437 men with osteoporosis
cards.people: Multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial: 437 men with spine or hip bone mineral density more than 2 SD below the young-adult male mean, randomised to daily self-injections of placebo, teriparatide 20 µg or teriparatide 40 µg, all with supplemental calcium and vitamin D. The study was stopped after a median of 11 months because routine rat toxicology studies found osteosarcomas.
cards.result: Spine BMD increased 5.9% (20 µg) and 9.0% (40 µg) above baseline (P<0.001 vs placebo for both), with separation from placebo by 3 months. Femoral-neck BMD rose 1.5% (20 µg; P=0.029) and 2.9% (40 µg; P<0.001); whole-body bone mineral content rose 0.6% and 0.9%; radial BMD did not change. Bone-formation markers rose early, followed by resorption markers. Adverse events were similar for placebo and 20 µg, and more frequent at 40 µg. Responses were similar regardless of gonadal status, age, baseline BMD, BMI, smoking or alcohol intake.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early at a median 11 months for a rat toxicology signal, so the exposure is shorter than the usual 18–24-month course, and the trial was powered for BMD, not fractures — the fracture answer comes from its follow-up report (card 2). The record's MeSH includes the rat osteosarcoma toxicology terms; those are animal data and are not carded as evidence here.

cards.people: Follow-up report of the Orwoll men's trial: 355 men treated with placebo or teriparatide 20 or 40 µg daily entered 30 months of post-treatment observation (42 months from baseline); lateral thoracolumbar radiographs at baseline and 18 months after discontinuation were available for 279 men. After discontinuation, some men received antiresorptive treatment, which prevented BMD decline.
cards.result: Incident vertebral fractures: 11.7% of placebo-assigned men vs 5.4% (20 µg) and 6.0% (40 µg). Combined teriparatide vs placebo: vertebral fracture risk reduced by 51% (relative; P=0.07, not significant). Moderate or severe vertebral fractures were reduced by 83% (relative; P=0.01). Lumbar-spine and total-hip BMD remained significantly above baseline 30 months after stopping (P≤0.001) and declined gradually off treatment unless an antiresorptive followed.
cards.watchOut: The fracture analysis is a follow-up of the same cohort as card 1 (not an independent trial), post-treatment antiresorptive use was not randomised, and the headline 51% figure is a relative reduction that did not reach significance — the shelf grades fracture benefit POSSIBLE, not LIKELY.

cards.headline: Kurland 2000: PTH(1-34) raised lumbar-spine BMD 13.5% vs no change on placebo in 23 men with idiopathic osteoporosis
cards.summary: Kurland 2000: PTH(1-34) raised lumbar-spine BMD 13.5% vs no change on placebo in 23 men with idiopathic osteoporosis
cards.people: 18-month randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial: 23 men aged 30–68 years (mean 50) with idiopathic osteoporosis, all receiving calcium 1,500 mg and vitamin D 400 IU daily; 10 randomised to PTH(1-34) 400 IU/day by daily subcutaneous injection (the dose and units as published) and 13 to vehicle.
cards.result: Lumbar-spine bone mass rose 13.5% on PTH(1-34) while the control group did not change (P<0.001); mean lumbar-spine T-score improved from −3.5 ± 0.2 to −2.4 ± 0.4 (the abstract's printed follow-up value is read as −2.4). Femoral-neck BMD rose 2.9% (P<0.05); the distal radius third site did not change. All bone-turnover markers rose on treatment (osteocalcin +230%, urinary N-telopeptide +375% by 12 months; P<0.001). Serum calcium, urinary calcium and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D did not change significantly in either group.
cards.watchOut: Very small (n=23) and in idiopathic (largely low-turnover) male osteoporosis with an IU-dosed preparation, not the standard 20 µg teriparatide pen — concordant BMD evidence only; it says nothing about fractures.
cards.source: Kurland ES et al. Parathyroid hormone as a therapy for idiopathic osteoporosis in men: effects on bone mineral density and bone markers. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2000. PMID: 10999788. cards.people: Men with osteoporosis: 437 in the Orwoll trial (355 followed by Kaufman) and 23 in the Kurland trial.
cards.result: Teriparatide increased spine BMD by roughly 6–9% over ~11 months in the large trial and by 13.5% over 18 months in the small one, with smaller hip gains and no radial gain in either. shelves.title: RANK/RANKL/osteoprotegerin (physiology): osteoblast-lineage cells set the resorption rate through one ratio — RANKL drives osteoclasts via RANK, osteoprotegerin is the decoy that soaks it up — and human genetics proves the set-point at both extremes: no osteoprotegerin means runaway turnover, activated RANK means focal osteolysis
shelves.question: How does the RANK/RANKL/osteoprotegerin system couple osteoclast and osteoblast activity in bone remodelling, and what human genetic/physiological evidence establishes the set-point?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Carrier Proteins/blood,physiology · Chromosomes, Human, Pair 8/genetics · Fatal Outcome · Female · *Gene Deletion · Genetic Markers · Glycoproteins/blood,deficiency,genetics,physiology · Homozygote · Humans · Infant · Male · Membrane Glycoproteins/blood,physiology · Molecular Sequence Data · Osteitis Deformans/genetics · Osteoprotegerin · Polymerase Chain Reaction · RANK Ligand · Receptor Activator of Nuclear Factor-kappa B · Receptors, Cytoplasmic and Nuclear/blood,deficiency,genetics,physiology · Receptors, Tumor Necrosis Factor/deficiency,genetics,physiology · Signal Transduction
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology, bone-remodelling sections). The historical anchor is Lacey and colleagues' 1998 discovery (Cell; PMID 9568710, verified by title search this session and not carded, because it is a molecular discovery paper rather than a human study) of osteoprotegerin ligand — the molecule now called RANKL — as the osteoblast-lineage cytokine that drives osteoclast differentiation and activation, with osteoprotegerin (OPG) as its decoy receptor. In the textbook account, remodelling is coupled through this single axis: osteoblast-lineage cells express RANKL, RANKL engages RANK on osteoclast precursors, osteoclasts form and resorb; OPG, secreted by the same lineage, binds RANKL and sets how much signal gets through — the RANKL/OPG ratio is the set-point. The carded human evidence tests every limb. Delete OPG entirely (homozygous TNFRSF11B deletion) and the result is juvenile Paget's disease — rapidly remodelling woven bone with undetectable OPG and markedly increased soluble RANKL (Whyte 2002) — and replacing OPG pharmacologically in two affected siblings suppressed resorption and rebuilt radial bone mass (Cundy 2005). Activate RANK itself by signal-peptide mutations and focal osteolysis follows (Hughes 2000). In ordinary physiology, oestrogen deficiency raises RANKL expression two- to three-fold on human marrow cells, tracking resorption markers (Eghbali-Fatourechi 2003). Denosumab, the anti-RANKL antibody, is the drug-shelf exploitation of this axis; this shelf is the physiology. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Whyte 2002: two patients with juvenile Paget's disease had a homozygous ~100 kb deletion of the osteoprotegerin gene (TNFRSF11B) — serum osteoprotegerin undetectable, soluble RANKL markedly increased (N = 2)
cards.summary: Whyte 2002: two patients with juvenile Paget's disease had a homozygous ~100 kb deletion of the osteoprotegerin gene (TNFRSF11B) — serum osteoprotegerin undetectable, soluble RANKL markedly increased (N = 2)
cards.type: Primary human genetic study (osteoprotegerin-deficiency cases, Whyte programme) — N = 2
cards.people: Two apparently unrelated Navajo patients with juvenile Paget's disease — an autosomal recessive osteopathy of rapidly remodelling woven bone, osteopenia, fractures and progressive skeletal deformity — evaluated by PCR amplification, direct sequencing and Southern blotting of genomic DNA for defects in TNFRSF11B, the gene encoding osteoprotegerin. N = 2, printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires.
cards.result: Both patients had a homozygous deletion of TNFRSF11B with identical break points on chromosome 8q24.2, spanning approximately 100 kb with neighbouring genes intact. Serum levels of osteoprotegerin were undetectable and soluble osteoclast differentiation factor (RANK ligand) was markedly increased. The paper's premise is the physiology: osteoprotegerin suppresses bone turnover by functioning as a decoy receptor for RANK ligand — remove the decoy completely and human bone turnover runs away. This is the loss-of-function experiment of nature that fixes OPG's place in the set-point.
cards.watchOut: N = 2 with a founder deletion — an experiment of nature, carded for what complete OPG absence does to the human set-point, not for any frequency or prognosis estimate. One patient's outcome was fatal (per the record's MeSH), underlining that this is the extreme end of the axis.
cards.source: Whyte MP et al. Osteoprotegerin deficiency and juvenile Paget's disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2002. PMID: 12124406. cards.headline: Hughes 2000: activating signal-peptide mutations in RANK (TNFRSF11A) in four families caused familial expansile osteolysis — the receptor limb of the axis, gain-of-function in humans
cards.summary: Hughes 2000: activating signal-peptide mutations in RANK (TNFRSF11A) in four families caused familial expansile osteolysis — the receptor limb of the axis, gain-of-function in humans
cards.type: Primary human genetic study (RANK gain-of-function families)
cards.people: Affected members of four families with familial expansile osteolysis or familial Paget disease of bone — autosomal dominant disorders of focal, increased bone remodelling with osteolytic lesions showing increased osteoblast and osteoclast activity — mapped by linkage to chromosome 18q21.2–21.3, the region containing TNFRSF11A, the gene encoding RANK. The record does not print the number of individual patients genotyped (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Two heterozygous insertion mutations in exon 1 of TNFRSF11A were identified — a duplication of 18 bases and a duplication of 27 bases — both affecting the signal peptide region of the RANK molecule. Expression of the recombinant mutant proteins showed perturbed expression and lack of normal signal-peptide cleavage, and both mutations caused an increase in RANK-mediated NF-κB signalling in vitro, consistent with activating mutations. A receptor that signals too readily produces focal runaway remodelling in humans — the mirror image of osteoprotegerin deficiency, at the receiving end of the same axis.
cards.watchOut: The NF-κB signalling assay is in-vitro supporting work inside a human genetics paper; the card's evidence is the human phenotype–genotype link. Familial expansile osteolysis is rare and focal — it demonstrates RANK's necessity in the circuit, not the behaviour of the common remodelling set-point, which the postmenopausal card addresses.
cards.source: Hughes AE et al. Mutations in TNFRSF11A, affecting the signal peptide of RANK, cause familial expansile osteolysis. Nature genetics. 2000. PMID: 10615125. cards.headline: Eghbali-Fatourechi 2003: early postmenopausal women expressed 2–3× more RANKL per marrow cell than premenopausal or oestrogen-treated women — and RANKL tracked bone-resorption markers
cards.summary: Eghbali-Fatourechi 2003: early postmenopausal women expressed 2–3× more RANKL per marrow cell than premenopausal or oestrogen-treated women — and RANKL tracked bone-resorption markers
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (marrow RANKL expression across oestrogen states, Khosla programme)
cards.people: 36 women in three groups of 12: premenopausal women (Group A), early postmenopausal women (Group B), and age-matched oestrogen-treated postmenopausal women (Group C). Bone marrow mononuclear cells expressing RANKL on their surface were isolated by two-colour flow cytometry using osteoprotegerin-Fc as the probe, and characterised as preosteoblastic marrow stromal cells, T lymphocytes or B lymphocytes; fluorescence intensity indexed surface RANKL concentration per cell.
cards.result: Fluorescence intensity — surface RANKL per cell — was increased in the early postmenopausal group over both the premenopausal and oestrogen-treated groups by two- to three-fold, for marrow stromal cells, T cells, B cells and total RANKL-expressing cells. In the merged groups, RANKL expression per cell correlated directly with the bone-resorption markers serum C-terminal telopeptide and urine N-telopeptide of type I collagen in all three cell types, and inversely with serum 17β-oestradiol for total RANKL-expressing cells. The authors conclude upregulation of RANKL on bone marrow cells is an important determinant of the increased bone resorption of oestrogen deficiency — the set-point being moved, in ordinary human physiology, by a hormone acting through RANKL.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional group comparison with a flow-cytometric index rather than an absolute RANKL concentration: it establishes direction and correlation with resorption markers in humans, complementing — and explicitly motivated by — rodent work the authors cite; the rodent data are not part of this card.
cards.source: Eghbali-Fatourechi G et al. Role of RANK ligand in mediating increased bone resorption in early postmenopausal women. The Journal of clinical investigation. 2003. PMID: 12697741. cards.headline: Cundy 2005: recombinant osteoprotegerin in two siblings with juvenile Paget's disease suppressed resorption, and radial bone mass rose 9% and 30% over 15 months (N = 2)
cards.summary: Cundy 2005: recombinant osteoprotegerin in two siblings with juvenile Paget's disease suppressed resorption, and radial bone mass rose 9% and 30% over 15 months (N = 2)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (osteoprotegerin replacement in genetic deficiency) — N = 2
cards.people: Two adult siblings with juvenile Paget's disease from inactivating mutations in the gene encoding osteoprotegerin, treated with once-weekly subcutaneous recombinant osteoprotegerin at 0.3–0.4 mg per kilogram of body weight, with bone resorption assessed by N-telopeptide excretion, radial bone mass measured, and skeletal bisphosphonate retention tracked. N = 2, printed on the face.
cards.result: Bone resorption was suppressed by the weekly recombinant osteoprotegerin doses. After 15 months of treatment, radial bone mass increased by 9% in one patient and 30% in the other (relative increases), skeletal bisphosphonate retention decreased by 37% and 55% respectively, and there was radiographic improvement. Apart from mild hypocalcaemia and hypophosphataemia, no apparent adverse events occurred. Replacing the missing decoy in humans re-imposed the set-point — the rescue experiment that completes the loss-of-function proof on the Whyte card.
cards.watchOut: N = 2, uncontrolled, in a rare genetic disease, and recombinant osteoprotegerin is not a clinical therapy: the card is carded as a physiological rescue experiment — proof that the decoy sets the human resorption rate — not as treatment evidence.
cards.source: Cundy T et al. Recombinant osteoprotegerin for juvenile Paget's disease. The New England journal of medicine. 2005. PMID: 16135836. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one ratio sets the resorption rate, and humans have been observed at every point on it
cards.summary: Synthesis: one ratio sets the resorption rate, and humans have been observed at every point on it
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology (bone-remodelling sections), with Lacey 1998 (PMID 9568710) as the discovery anchor in prose. No new data.
cards.result: Osteoblast-lineage cells couple formation to resorption through a single signalling ratio: RANKL presented to RANK on osteoclast precursors drives osteoclastogenesis; osteoprotegerin, the soluble decoy, determines how much RANKL gets through. Human evidence fixes each element: no OPG at all → unopposed turnover with undetectable OPG and markedly raised soluble RANKL (PMID 12124406), reversed by OPG replacement (PMID 16135836); a hyper-responsive RANK → focal osteolysis (PMID 10615125); and in everyday physiology oestrogen deficiency moves the set-point by raising marrow RANKL expression two- to three-fold, in step with resorption markers (PMID 12697741). PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

shelves.title: FGF23 and klotho (physiology): bone talks to kidney through one hormone — FGF23, acting only where klotho is present, orders phosphate excretion and switches off vitamin D activation — and humans break in both directions: too much FGF23 action wastes phosphate into rickets, too little calcifies soft tissue
shelves.question: How do FGF23 and klotho regulate phosphate excretion and vitamin D activation, and what happens to phosphate balance when this axis is disrupted in humans?
shelves.mesh: Abnormalities, Multiple/genetics · Amino Acid Sequence · Chromosomes, Human, Pair 12/genetics · DNA Mutational Analysis · Europe · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 · Fibroblast Growth Factors/deficiency,genetics,physiology · *Genes · *Genes, Dominant · Genetic Heterogeneity · Humans · Hypophosphatemia, Familial/genetics · Lod Score · Male · Molecular Sequence Data · Pedigree · Point Mutation · Reverse Transcriptase Polymerase Chain Reaction · Sequence Alignment · Sequence Homology, Amino Acid · United States
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology, phosphate-handling sections). In the textbook account, FGF23 is a hormone secreted by osteocytes that acts on the kidney only where its co-receptor klotho is expressed with an FGF receptor: it reduces proximal-tubule phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia) and suppresses 1α-hydroxylase, lowering 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and hence gut phosphate absorption — a bone-to-kidney negative-feedback loop for phosphate. Humans provide experiments of nature at every joint of that loop, and they are the carded evidence. FGF23 was identified as the ADHR gene: missense mutations at its proteolytic cleavage motif make it cleavage-resistant and overactive, wasting phosphate (ADHR Consortium 2000). The same molecule was cloned from a human tumour causing tumour-induced osteomalacia, a syndrome whose defining feature is that removing the tumour normalises phosphate metabolism (Shimada 2001). And when the co-receptor fails — a homozygous klotho mutation in a 13-year-old girl — FGF23 cannot signal, and the phenotype inverts: severe hyperphosphataemia with tumoral calcinosis despite elevated FGF23 (Ichikawa 2007). Excess action wastes phosphate; absent action retains it. The ferric carboxymaltose hypophosphataemia question built from slate row S4-1-29 is this axis operating iatrogenically, and burosumab treatment shelves (#1194 family) exploit it therapeutically; this shelf is the physiology. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: ADHR Consortium 2000: autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets is caused by missense mutations in FGF23 — the first mutations found in a human FGF gene
cards.summary: ADHR Consortium 2000: autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets is caused by missense mutations in FGF23 — the first mutations found in a human FGF gene
cards.type: Primary human genetic study (positional cloning in ADHR families, ADHR Consortium)
cards.people: Families with autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets (ADHR) — low serum phosphorus, rickets, osteomalacia, lower-extremity deformity, short stature, bone pain and dental abscesses — studied by positional cloning across a 4 Mb region containing 37 annotated genes. The record does not print the number of patients or families (N not documented in the record).
cards.result: Missense mutations were identified in a gene encoding a new member of the fibroblast growth factor family, FGF23 — the first mutations found in a human FGF gene. The mutations (subsequently localised to the RXXR proteolytic cleavage motif, as the Shimada record on this shelf sets out) render FGF23 resistant to cleavage and therefore overactive: a gain of FGF23 function produces isolated renal phosphate wasting with rickets in otherwise well humans. Together with the PHEX mutations of X-linked hypophosphataemia described in the same record, this established that inherited phosphate wasting is a hormone-excess problem, not a tubular-transporter problem.
cards.watchOut: A gene-discovery paper: it proves FGF23 causes human phosphate wasting but does not itself quantify phosphate excretion rates or vitamin D changes in the patients — the quantitative physiology is the textbook's account, and the direction of effect is what this card establishes.
cards.source: ADHR Consortium. Autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets is associated with mutations in FGF23. Nature genetics. 2000. PMID: 11062477. cards.headline: Shimada 2001: FGF23 cloned from a human tumour causing tumour-induced osteomalacia — the phosphaturic factor, identified in human tissue
cards.summary: Shimada 2001: FGF23 cloned from a human tumour causing tumour-induced osteomalacia — the phosphaturic factor, identified in human tissue
cards.type: Primary human study (identification of the causal factor from a human TIO tumour, Shimada programme)
cards.people: A tumour causing tumour-induced osteomalacia (TIO) — a paraneoplastic syndrome of hypophosphataemia from renal phosphate wasting in which, as the record states, removal of the responsible tumour normalises phosphate metabolism — from which tumour-specific cDNA clones abundantly expressed only in the tumour were isolated and characterised. The in-vivo reproduction experiments used recombinant FGF23 and FGF23-expressing cells in mice (animal work, flagged in the watch-out, not the card's human evidence).
cards.result: A 2,270-bp cDNA cloned from the tumour encoded fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) — the same gene mutated in ADHR. Analysis of the recombinant products showed proteolytic cleavage of FGF23 at the RXXR motif, and the ADHR missense mutations sit in that motif, plausibly preventing cleavage and enhancing biological activity. Two independent human routes — an inherited cleavage-resistant hormone and an acquired tumour secreting the normal hormone — converge on one conclusion: excess FGF23 action is sufficient to make the human kidney waste phosphate and produce osteomalacia.
cards.watchOut: The dose-response reproduction of TIO (serum phosphate falling within 12 hours of recombinant FGF23, hypophosphataemia with increased renal phosphate clearance from implanted cells, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) was performed in mice and is animal mechanistic support only, labelled as such here per the physiology rules; the card's human evidence is the identification of FGF23 as the factor a human TIO tumour overproduces, converging with the ADHR genetics.

Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. 2001. PMID: 11344269. cards.headline: Ichikawa 2007: a homozygous klotho mutation (H193R) in a 13-year-old girl caused severe tumoral calcinosis with hyperphosphataemia — FGF23 was elevated but could not act (N = 1)
cards.summary: Ichikawa 2007: a homozygous klotho mutation (H193R) in a 13-year-old girl caused severe tumoral calcinosis with hyperphosphataemia — FGF23 was elevated but could not act (N = 1)
cards.type: Primary human genetic study (klotho loss-of-function case, experiment of nature) — N = 1
cards.people: A 13-year-old girl with severe tumoral calcinosis including dural and carotid artery calcifications, found to carry a homozygous missense mutation (H193R) in the KLOTHO (KL) gene; expression and secretion of the mutant protein and its effect on FGF23 signalling were characterised in vitro as supporting work. N = 1, printed on the face as the physiology labelling rule requires.
cards.result: The patient exhibited marked hyperphosphataemia and hypercalcaemia with elevated serum parathyroid hormone and elevated FGF23 — the hormone was present in excess, yet phosphate was retained and soft tissue calcified: the signature of end-organ FGF23 resistance. Compared with wild-type, expression and secretion of H193R klotho were markedly reduced in vitro, diminishing FGF23's ability to signal via its cognate FGF receptors. The authors conclude this is the first evidence that loss-of-function mutations in human KL impair FGF23 bioactivity, underscoring klotho's essential role in FGF23-mediated phosphate and vitamin D homeostasis in humans. Without the co-receptor, the axis is off — whatever the hormone level.
cards.watchOut: A single case: it demonstrates necessity — that human FGF23 signalling requires klotho — and cannot support any statement about how common or how graded klotho variation is in the general population. Serum phosphate and calcium values are described qualitatively in the record ('marked') and are not given invented numbers here.
cards.source: Ichikawa S et al. A homozygous missense mutation in human KLOTHO causes severe tumoral calcinosis. The Journal of clinical investigation. 2007. PMID: 17710231. cards.headline: Synthesis: one hormone, one co-receptor, two opposite human diseases — the axis is the set-point for phosphate
cards.summary: Synthesis: one hormone, one co-receptor, two opposite human diseases — the axis is the set-point for phosphate
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded human studies, framed by Boron & Boulpaep, Medical Physiology (phosphate-handling sections). No new data.
cards.result: FGF23 from bone, acting through FGF receptors only where klotho is co-expressed in the kidney, increases phosphate excretion and suppresses vitamin D activation. Human experiments of nature bracket the set-point: cleavage-resistant FGF23 (ADHR, PMID 11062477) or tumour-secreted FGF23 (TIO, PMID 11344269) → renal phosphate wasting, hypophosphataemia, rickets/osteomalacia; a broken co-receptor (klotho H193R, PMID 17710231) → FGF23 resistance, hyperphosphataemia, ectopic calcification despite high FGF23. Measuring FGF23 without asking whether the axis can signal misreads the physiology — the same lesson the ferric-carboxymaltose phosphate story teaches clinically. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: This shelf does not cover FGF23 as a biomarker in chronic kidney disease, nor burosumab treatment (homed on the XLH treatment shelves) — it establishes the regulatory axis and what its disruption does to phosphate balance.
