shelves.balance: SPLIT. Two 2005 syntheses of the same trial generation (the Cochrane review by Challapalli and the Anesthesia & Analgesia meta-analysis by Tremont-Lukats, sharing authors) found systemic lidocaine and its oral analogues beat placebo by about 11 points on a 0–100 pain scale and matched carbamazepine, gabapentin, amitriptyline, amantadine and morphine — a real but modest, short-horizon effect, with drowsiness, fatigue, nausea and dizziness the common costs and no major toxicity in trials. The 2022 Clinical Journal of Pain review of 27 studies reached the opposite practical conclusion: only one class I and two class II studies, wide heterogeneity of dose, aetiology and design, and evidence insufficient to recommend infusion for spinal cord injury pain, peripheral nerve injury, diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia or complex regional pain syndrome type II. This shelf covers chronic systemic infusion only; perioperative intravenous lidocaine is a different question, homed on shelf #1244, and topical lidocaine plaster questions are homed separately (#3571, #1457).

cards.headline: Challapalli 2005 (Cochrane): across 32 controlled trials, systemic lidocaine and its oral analogues beat placebo by a weighted mean of 11 points on a 0–100 pain scale and matched other analgesics
cards.summary: Challapalli 2005 (Cochrane): across 32 controlled trials, systemic lidocaine and its oral analogues beat placebo by a weighted mean of 11 points on a 0–100 pain scale and matched other analgesics
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane), 2005
cards.people: Thirty-two controlled clinical trials of systemic local-anaesthetic-type drugs for neuropathic pain of any cause (16 trials of intravenous lidocaine, 12 of mexiletine, one sequential lidocaine-plus-mexiletine, one tocainide; 21 crossover, 9 parallel), all randomised and double-blind with placebo or an active analgesic comparator.
cards.result: Lidocaine and mexiletine were superior to placebo (weighted mean difference −11; 95% CI −15 to −7; P <0.00001). Limited data showed no difference in efficacy (WMD −0.6; 95% CI −7 to 6) or adverse effects versus carbamazepine, amantadine, gabapentin or morphine. The drugs were safe in trials, with no deaths or life-threatening toxicities; sensitivity analysis traced heterogeneity to data distribution in three trials, and no publication bias was detected.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate mixes intravenous lidocaine with oral analogues (mainly mexiletine), so it is not a pure estimate for infusion; most trials were small, short crossover studies, and the review was later stabilised (2017–2020 searches found nothing likely to change its conclusions) rather than refreshed with modern trials.
cards.source: Challapalli V et al. Systemic administration of local anesthetic agents to relieve neuropathic pain. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2005. PMID: 16235318. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tremont-Lukats 2005: in the meta-analysed trials (n=706), lidocaine and mexiletine beat placebo by 10.6 points on a 0–100 scale and equalled morphine, gabapentin, amitriptyline and amantadine
cards.summary: Tremont-Lukats 2005: in the meta-analysed trials (n=706), lidocaine and mexiletine beat placebo by 10.6 points on a 0–100 scale and equalled morphine, gabapentin, amitriptyline and amantadine
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, Anesthesia & Analgesia 2005
cards.people: Twenty-seven trials of systemically administered local anaesthetics for neuropathic pain in the systematic review; ten lidocaine trials and nine mexiletine trials (706 patients in total) had data suitable for meta-analysis. Lidocaine was most commonly given as 5 mg/kg intravenously over 30–60 minutes; mexiletine at a median 600 mg daily.
cards.result: Versus placebo, the weighted mean difference on a 0–100 mm visual analogue pain scale was −10.60 (95% CI −14.52 to −6.68; P <0.00001); versus morphine, gabapentin, amitriptyline and amantadine it was −0.60 (95% CI −6.96 to 5.75) — no difference. Benefit was more consistent for peripheral (trauma, diabetes) and central pain. Common adverse effects were drowsiness, fatigue, nausea and dizziness; adverse events were more frequent than with placebo but equivalent to the active comparators (odds ratio 1.23; 95% CI 0.22 to 6.90), with no major adverse events in the controlled trials.
cards.watchOut: This is a companion analysis by substantially the same authors as the Cochrane card, drawing on the same trial pool — the two 2005 cards are one evidence generation read twice, not two independent confirmations. A ~10-point average gain on a 100-point scale is at the edge of what patients can feel, and follow-up was measured in hours to weeks, not months.
cards.source: Tremont-Lukats IW et al. Systemic administration of local anesthetics to relieve neuropathic pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2005. PMID: 16301253. cards.headline: Lee 2022: reviewing 27 studies of lidocaine infusion in chronic neuropathic pain, only one was class I and two class II — evidence insufficient, no recommendation possible
cards.summary: Lee 2022: reviewing 27 studies of lidocaine infusion in chronic neuropathic pain, only one was class I and two class II — evidence insufficient, no recommendation possible
cards.type: Systematic review (qualitative, evidence-class graded), The Clinical Journal of Pain 2022
cards.people: Twenty-seven studies (1970 to September 2021) of at least one dose of intravenous lidocaine in adults with chronic neuropathic pain, graded with the 2017 American Academy of Neurology classification: one class I study (neuropathic pain after spinal cord injury) and two class II studies (peripheral nerve injury; diabetic neuropathy).
cards.result: Study design, participants and interventions were heterogeneous with wide variation across all 27 studies. The reviewers concluded the evidence was insufficient and heterogeneous, so no recommendation could be made for lidocaine infusion in chronic neuropathic pain due to spinal cord injury, peripheral nerve injury, diabetic neuropathy, postherpetic neuralgia or complex regional pain syndrome type II, and called for larger randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials.
cards.watchOut: A qualitative 'insufficient evidence' verdict is not a finding of no effect — it is a judgement that the trial base cannot support a recommendation either way. It sits in tension with the 2005 pooled estimates precisely because it weights trial quality and heterogeneity rather than the pooled mean.
cards.source: Lee JH et al. Intravenous Lidocaine in Chronic Neuropathic Pain: A Systematic Review. The Clinical journal of pain. 2022. PMID: 36288104. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small, real-looking short-term benefit in old pooled trials; a modern quality-graded review that will not endorse it — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small, real-looking short-term benefit in old pooled trials; a modern quality-graded review that will not endorse it — SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above.
cards.result: The honest summary is split by era and method: meta-analysis of the pre-2005 trials gives systemic lidocaine a ~10–11 point advantage over placebo on a 0–100 scale, parity with standard analgesics, and no major toxicity; the 2022 evidence-class review of the wider literature finds the studies too few, small and dissimilar to recommend infusion for any named neuropathic aetiology. Nothing here addresses perioperative infusion (shelf #1244) or lidocaine plaster. A clinician citing this shelf should quote both halves: benefit estimate and quality verdict.
cards.watchOut: Do not upgrade this to a clean POSSIBLE (benefit): the two positive syntheses share authors and trials, and the only modern review dissents on quality grounds. Equally, do not read the 2022 verdict as proof of no effect.
cards.source: Synthesis of Challapalli V et al. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2005 (PMID: 16235318); Tremont-Lukats IW et al. Anesth Analg. 2005 (PMID: 16301253); Lee JH et al. Clin J Pain. 2022 (PMID: 36288104). Registry IDs: none in the records. MeSH: as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Naloxone co-prescription in primary care: patients given naloxone had 47% relatively fewer opioid-related ED visits at 6 months and 63% relatively fewer at 1 year — in one non-randomised study; the wider take-home naloxone literature is observational too
shelves.question: In primary-care patients receiving long-term opioid therapy for chronic pain, does co-prescribing naloxone reduce opioid-related emergency department visits and overdose events?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Chronic Pain/drug therapy · Drug Overdose/etiology,prevention & control · Emergency Service, Hospital/statistics & numerical data · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Naloxone/therapeutic use · Narcotic Antagonists/therapeutic use · Primary Health Care · San Francisco
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE, with the non-randomised label on its face. Exactly one study in the fetched records tests the actual question: Coffin 2016, a 2-year non-randomised intervention study in six San Francisco safety-net primary care clinics, where 38.2% of 1,985 patients on long-term opioid therapy for pain received a naloxone prescription. Those prescribed naloxone had 47% relatively fewer opioid-related emergency department visits per month at 6 months (incidence rate ratio 0.53) and 63% relatively fewer at 1 year (IRR 0.37) than those not prescribed it — relative reductions from an observational comparison in which clinicians preferentially prescribed to higher-dose patients and those with a recent opioid-related ED visit, so confounding could run in either direction; opioid dose itself did not change. The supporting literature is one step removed: systematic reviews of take-home naloxone programmes for people who use drugs found those programmes met all nine Bradford Hill criteria for reducing overdose mortality and that roughly 9 of every 100 kits distributed are used for a peer rescue within three months — evidence that kits in hands get used and track with fewer deaths, not evidence about primary-care co-prescription itself. Nothing here is randomised; the honest claim is feasibility plus a consistent observational signal.

cards.headline: Coffin 2016: in 1,985 primary-care patients on long-term opioids, those prescribed naloxone had 47% relatively fewer opioid-related ED visits at 6 months (IRR 0.53) and 63% relatively fewer at 1 year (IRR 0.37)
cards.summary: Coffin 2016: in 1,985 primary-care patients on long-term opioids, those prescribed naloxone had 47% relatively fewer opioid-related ED visits at 6 months (IRR 0.53) and 63% relatively fewer at 1 year (IRR 0.37)
cards.type: Non-randomised intervention study, Annals of Internal Medicine 2016
cards.people: Non-randomised 2-year intervention study in six safety-net primary care clinics in San Francisco: 1,985 adults receiving long-term opioid therapy for chronic pain, with providers and clinic staff trained and supported to prescribe naloxone. 38.2% of patients were prescribed naloxone; patients on higher opioid doses and those with an opioid-related ED visit in the previous 12 months were independently more likely to receive it.
cards.result: Patients who received a naloxone prescription had 47% relatively fewer opioid-related emergency department visits per month in the 6 months after receipt (incidence rate ratio 0.53; 95% CI 0.34 to 0.83; P=0.005) and 63% relatively fewer after 1 year (IRR 0.37; 95% CI 0.22 to 0.64; P<0.001) than patients who did not receive naloxone. There was no net change over time in prescribed opioid dose between the groups (IRR 1.03; 95% CI 0.91 to 1.27; P=0.61). The authors note the results are observational and may not generalise beyond safety-net settings.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is between patients clinicians chose to prescribe to and those they did not — and they chose the higher-risk patients, which biases against finding a benefit, while unmeasured differences (engagement, household support) could bias for it. The percentages are relative reductions in visit rates; the record does not print the absolute monthly visit rates needed to convert them, so none are claimed here.
cards.source: Coffin PO et al. Nonrandomized Intervention Study of Naloxone Coprescription for Primary Care Patients Receiving Long-Term Opioid Therapy for Pain. Annals of internal medicine. 2016. PMID: 27366987. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: McDonald & Strang 2016: across 22 observational studies, take-home naloxone met all nine Bradford Hill criteria for reducing overdose mortality; even with naloxone given, 1 in 123 overdoses (0.8%) was still fatal
cards.summary: McDonald & Strang 2016: across 22 observational studies, take-home naloxone met all nine Bradford Hill criteria for reducing overdose mortality; even with naloxone given, 1 in 123 overdoses (0.8%) was still fatal
cards.type: Systematic review of observational studies, Addiction 2016
cards.people: Systematic review of take-home naloxone programmes — naloxone supplied directly to people who use opioids, for emergency use by peers — covering 22 observational studies meeting eligibility criteria from 1,397 retrieved records; effectiveness was judged against the nine Bradford Hill criteria for causation plus five World Health Organization criteria, because only observational data exist.
cards.result: Take-home naloxone met all nine Bradford Hill criteria; the five WHO criteria were met fully (three) or partially (two). The reviewers concluded take-home naloxone programmes reduce overdose mortality among programme participants and in the community and have a low rate of adverse events. Even with naloxone administration, a fatal outcome was reported in 1 in 123 overdose cases (0.8%; 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2) — naloxone given in time usually works, but not invariably.
cards.watchOut: Indirect for this shelf's question: these programmes supplied people who use drugs (largely non-prescribed opioids) and their peers, not primary-care patients co-prescribed naloxone alongside analgesia. It supports the mechanism — naloxone in lay hands reduces deaths — not the clinic-level effect size on the Coffin card.
cards.source: McDonald R et al. Are take-home naloxone programmes effective? Systematic review utilizing application of the Bradford Hill criteria. Addiction (Abingdon, England). 2016. PMID: 27028542. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: McAuley 2015: in a descriptive meta-analysis of take-home naloxone evaluations, an estimated 9.2 kits per 100 people trained were used for a peer rescue within three months (range across studies 5.2–13.1)
cards.summary: McAuley 2015: in a descriptive meta-analysis of take-home naloxone evaluations, an estimated 9.2 kits per 100 people trained were used for a peer rescue within three months (range across studies 5.2–13.1)
cards.type: Systematic review and descriptive meta-analysis, International Journal of Drug Policy 2015
cards.people: Systematic review and descriptive meta-analysis of the international take-home naloxone literature for people who use drugs: 25 evaluations identified, of which nine allowed a proportion-of-use calculation (peer-administered uses divided by people trained and supplied, standardised to a three-month window).
cards.result: The model estimated 5.2 to 13.1 naloxone uses per three months for every 100 people trained and supplied (point estimate 9.2) — around 9% of kits distributed are likely to be used for peer administration within the first three months of supply. The authors recommended future evaluations directly compare training structures and use fixed follow-up periods.
cards.watchOut: A use-rate is not an outcome rate: this card shows distributed kits are actually deployed at a non-trivial rate, which is the plausibility bridge between co-prescription and averted harm. Like the previous card it concerns take-home programmes for people who use drugs, not analgesic co-prescription.
cards.source: McAuley A et al. Exploring the life-saving potential of naloxone: A systematic review and descriptive meta-analysis of take home naloxone (THN) programmes for opioid users. The International journal on drug policy. 2015. PMID: 26508033. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: Synthesis of the three cards above.
cards.result: The direct evidence is a single non-randomised clinic study with a large relative association (IRR 0.53 at 6 months, 0.37 at 1 year for opioid-related ED visits) and no effect on opioid dose; the indirect evidence shows naloxone distributed to laypeople is used (about 9 rescues per 100 kits per quarter) and is associated with reduced overdose mortality across 22 observational studies judged against Bradford Hill criteria. That combination supports offering co-prescription — it does not support quoting the ED-visit percentages as a proven effect. The stamp is POSSIBLE with the observational label, per the non-randomised design of every card.
cards.watchOut: A large community naloxone study (Walley 2013, Massachusetts OEND) could not be carded here because its PMID is already homed elsewhere in the library (gate list); this pack neither duplicates it nor relies on it.

shelves.title: Bisphosphonates in children with osteogenesis imperfecta: bone density rises consistently (risedronate +16.3% versus +7.6% lumbar spine BMD), but fracture reduction is inconsistent across the small trials — Ns printed (30, 147, 34; Cochrane 819 in 14 trials)
shelves.question: In children with osteogenesis imperfecta, do bisphosphonates (pamidronate, oral agents), compared with placebo/no treatment, increase bone density and reduce fractures?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Alkaline Phosphatase/blood · Bone Density/drug effects · Bone Development/drug effects · Bone Resorption/drug therapy · Calcium/urine · Child · Child, Preschool · Diphosphonates/administration & dosage · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Fractures, Bone/prevention & control · Humans · Lumbar Vertebrae/diagnostic imaging/physiopathology · Male · Osteogenesis Imperfecta/drug therapy/metabolism/physiopathology · Pain/drug therapy · Pamidronate · Periodicity · Radiography
shelves.balance: The base is old and small, and its two halves disagree in strength. Bone density: every strand rises — cyclic intravenous pamidronate in Glorieux 1998 (uncontrolled, N = 30) gave a mean annualised lumbar-spine BMD increase of 41.9% with z-score improving from −5.3 to −3.4; the largest randomised trial, Bishop 2013 (risedronate, N = 147), found lumbar-spine areal BMD up 16.3% versus 7.6% on placebo at 1 year (difference 8.7 percentage points). Fractures: Bishop found fewer first-year clinical fractures on risedronate (31% versus 49%, P=0.0446) and Sakkers 2004 (olpadronate, N = 34) found a long-bone fracture hazard ratio of 0.69 — a 31% relative reduction — but the Cochrane review (Dwan 2016; 14 trials, 819 participants) could not aggregate the oral trials, found fracture benefit in only two of five reporting trials, and found no significant fracture difference for intravenous bisphosphonates pooled (risk ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.06 — a relative measure whose interval crosses 1). Growth, pain and function data are incomplete and inconsistent in the review. Density benefit is consistent; fracture benefit is plausible but unproven at this base size — POSSIBLE, with every N printed.

cards.headline: Glorieux 1998 (uncontrolled, N = 30): cyclic pamidronate raised lumbar-spine BMD by a mean 41.9% per year and cut radiologically confirmed fractures by 1.7 per year
cards.summary: Glorieux 1998 (uncontrolled, N = 30): cyclic pamidronate raised lumbar-spine BMD by a mean 41.9% per year and cut radiologically confirmed fractures by 1.7 per year
cards.type: Uncontrolled observational study, N Engl J Med 1998
cards.people: 30 children aged 3 to 16 years with severe osteogenesis imperfecta in an uncontrolled observational study, given intravenous pamidronate (mean 6.8 ± 1.1 mg/kg/year) at 4-to-6-month intervals for 1.3 to 5.0 years, with regular clinical, biochemical, densitometric and radiologic assessment.
cards.result: Serum alkaline phosphatase and urinary calcium and collagen N-telopeptide excretion fell sustainedly. Mean annualised BMD increase was 41.9 ± 29.0%, and the BMD z-score improved from −5.3 ± 1.2 to −3.4 ± 1.5; metacarpal cortical width rose 27 ± 20.2% per year. The mean incidence of radiologically confirmed fractures fell by 1.7 per year (P<0.001). Fracture healing rate, growth rate and growth-plate appearance were unchanged; mobility improved in 16 children and was unchanged in 14, and all reported substantial relief of chronic pain and fatigue.
cards.watchOut: No control group: in a growing child, BMD rises with growth itself, and fracture rates vary with age and activity — this landmark series launched the field but cannot quantify the drug's share of the improvement.
cards.source: Glorieux FH et al. Cyclic administration of pamidronate in children with severe osteogenesis imperfecta. The New England journal of medicine. 1998. PMID: 9753709. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bishop 2013 (RCT, N = 147): risedronate raised lumbar-spine BMD by 16.3% versus 7.6% on placebo at 1 year, with clinical fractures in 31% versus 49%
cards.summary: Bishop 2013 (RCT, N = 147): risedronate raised lumbar-spine BMD by 16.3% versus 7.6% on placebo at 1 year, with clinical fractures in 31% versus 49%
cards.people: 147 children aged 4 to 15 years with osteogenesis imperfecta and increased fracture risk, randomised 2:1 to daily oral risedronate (2.5 or 5 mg; 97 assigned) or placebo (50) for 1 year, followed by 2 open-label years on risedronate for all; intention-to-treat population 94 versus 49.
cards.result: Mean lumbar-spine areal BMD increase at 1 year was 16.3% on risedronate versus 7.6% on placebo (difference 8.7%, 95% CI 5.7 to 11.7; P<0.0001). Clinical fractures in year 1 occurred in 29/94 (31%) on risedronate versus 24/49 (49%) on placebo (P=0.0446) — an absolute difference of about 18 percentage points. In the open-label years 2–3, fractures were reported in 53% of the always-risedronate group and 65% of the former-placebo group. Adverse-event profiles were otherwise similar, including upper-gastrointestinal and musculoskeletal events.
cards.watchOut: The largest trial in this field is still only 147 children, its placebo group also gained 7.6% BMD with growth, and the fracture result rests on a single year of double-blind data with a borderline P value.
cards.source: Bishop N et al. Risedronate in children with osteogenesis imperfecta: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2013. PMID: 23927913. Registry ID: NCT00106028, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Sakkers 2004 (RCT, N = 34): oral olpadronate reduced long-bone fracture risk by 31% relative (hazard ratio 0.69) and raised spinal BMD faster than placebo
cards.summary: Sakkers 2004 (RCT, N = 34): oral olpadronate reduced long-bone fracture risk by 31% relative (hazard ratio 0.69) and raised spinal BMD faster than placebo
cards.people: 34 children recruited from the Dutch national centre for osteogenesis imperfecta, randomised to oral olpadronate 10 mg/m² daily (16) or placebo (18) for 2 years; all also received calcium and vitamin D. Fracture follow-up was complete for all children.
cards.result: Olpadronate was associated with a hazard ratio of 0.69 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.91; P=0.01) for fracture of long bones — a 31% relative reduction. Spinal bone mineral content rose faster on olpadronate (between-group difference 2.24 g/year [0.20 to 4.29]) and spinal BMD by an extra 0.054 g/cm² per year (0.012 to 0.096). There were no detectable effects on functional outcome, anthropometrics or vertebral height, and no between-group differences in urinary resorption markers.
cards.watchOut: N = 34 — very small; a fracture hazard ratio from 34 children is fragile, and the trial found no functional benefit despite the density and fracture signals.
cards.source: Sakkers R et al. Skeletal effects and functional outcome with olpadronate in children with osteogenesis imperfecta: a 2-year randomised placebo-controlled study. Lancet (London, England). 2004. PMID: 15121405. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2016 (14 trials, 819 participants): spine density z-scores rose, but fracture results were inconsistent and the pooled intravenous fracture estimate was not significant
cards.summary: Cochrane 2016 (14 trials, 819 participants): spine density z-scores rose, but fracture results were inconsistent and the pooled intravenous fracture estimate was not significant
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review (Dwan 2016 update) of randomised and quasi-randomised trials of bisphosphonates versus placebo, no treatment or comparators in osteogenesis imperfecta of all types: 14 trials, 819 participants, mostly at low risk of bias though selective reporting affected several.
cards.result: Oral bisphosphonates: data could not be aggregated; two trials found a statistically significant fracture-risk reduction and three others reporting fracture incidence found no difference. All five trials reporting spine BMD found significant lumbar-spine z-score increases at at least one time point. Intravenous bisphosphonates: pooled across two trials, the risk ratio for at least one fracture was 0.56 (95% CI 0.30 to 1.06 — a relative measure, not significant), and pooled spine BMD mean difference was 9.96 (−2.51 to 22.43, not significant), though a third trial favoured intravenous treatment on percent BMD change. Growth, bone pain and functional outcomes were incompletely reported and showed no consistent improvement. Head-to-head dose, route and agent comparisons (including zoledronic acid versus pamidronate) found no significant primary-outcome differences.
cards.watchOut: The review pools the very trials carded above plus smaller ones — it is a synthesis, not independent evidence; its honest headline is inconsistency on fractures beneath consistency on density.
cards.source: Dwan K et al. Bisphosphonate therapy for osteogenesis imperfecta. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 27760454. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: density up everywhere; fractures down in the two placebo trials that reached significance, null in others — POSSIBLE on a small, old base
cards.summary: Synthesis: density up everywhere; fractures down in the two placebo trials that reached significance, null in others — POSSIBLE on a small, old base
cards.people: Synthesis of the evidence cards on this shelf.
cards.result: Glorieux 1998 (uncontrolled, N = 30) reported large density gains and fewer fractures on pamidronate; Bishop 2013 (N = 147) confirmed a density advantage and a first-year fracture advantage for risedronate; Sakkers 2004 (N = 34) found fewer long-bone fractures on olpadronate; Cochrane 2016 (819 participants) found the fracture literature inconsistent overall. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit) — density certain, fracture benefit inconsistent, every N printed.

shelves.title: PRISM and PRISM-EZ: intensive bisphosphonate treatment normalising alkaline phosphatase made no difference to fractures (7.0% versus 7.4%), surgery, pain or quality of life versus symptom-driven care — the treatment made no difference
shelves.question: In established Paget's disease of bone, does an intensive bisphosphonate strategy targeting normal alkaline phosphatase, compared with symptom-driven treatment, reduce fractures, orthopaedic procedures, pain and quality-of-life loss?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alkaline Phosphatase/blood · Bone Density Conservation Agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Diphosphonates/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Female · Fractures, Bone/chemically induced/complications/surgery · Hearing Loss/chemically induced/complications · Humans · Male · Orthopedic Procedures · Osteitis Deformans/blood/drug therapy/enzymology · Pain/chemically induced/complications · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: Two randomised reports of the same strategy question agree, and both are null on every clinical endpoint. PRISM (N = 1,324, median follow-up 3 years) achieved its biochemical aim — alkaline phosphatase was significantly lower on intensive treatment from 4 months onward — yet clinical fractures occurred in 7.0% versus 7.4%, orthopaedic surgery in 7.3% versus 8.3%, and there was no difference in quality of life, overall or pagetic bone pain, or hearing thresholds: on clinical outcomes, the intensive strategy made no difference. The PRISM-EZ extension (N = 502, zoledronic acid as first-choice intensive agent) again found no quality-of-life or pain benefit, with nonsignificant point estimates running against intensive treatment (fracture hazard ratio 1.90, 95% CI 0.91 to 3.98 — a relative measure whose interval includes no difference). The Cochrane review of bisphosphonates in Paget's disease (20 trials, 3,168 participants) supplies the context that keeps this from reading as 'bisphosphonates do not work': against placebo they tripled the proportion whose bone pain disappeared (31% versus 9%) — the drugs relieve symptoms when given for symptoms; what adds nothing is treating repeatedly to normalise a number. Which bisphosphonate to use when treating is a different question, homed on live shelf #1822.

cards.headline: PRISM 2010 (N = 1,324): intensive treatment lowered alkaline phosphatase but fractures were 7.0% versus 7.4% and surgery 7.3% versus 8.3% — no difference in pain, quality of life or hearing
cards.summary: PRISM 2010 (N = 1,324): intensive treatment lowered alkaline phosphatase but fractures were 7.0% versus 7.4% and surgery 7.3% versus 8.3% — no difference in pain, quality of life or hearing
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (PRISM), J Bone Miner Res 2010
cards.people: 1,324 patients with Paget's disease of bone randomised to intensive bisphosphonate therapy (repeat courses regardless of symptoms, aiming to keep serum alkaline phosphatase within the normal range) or symptomatic management (treatment only for pagetic bone pain — analgesics/anti-inflammatories first, bisphosphonates if they failed), followed for a median of 3 years (range 2 to 5). Endpoints: fracture, orthopaedic surgery, quality of life, bone pain and hearing thresholds.
cards.result: Alkaline phosphatase was significantly lower in the intensive group within 4 months and remained lower throughout (P<.001) — the biochemical strategy worked as designed. Clinically, the treatment made no difference: fractures in 46/661 (7.0%) intensive versus 49/663 (7.4%) symptomatic; orthopaedic surgery in 50/661 (7.3%) versus 55/663 (8.3%); no differences in quality of life (SF-36), overall bodily pain, pagetic bone pain, or audiometric hearing thresholds — none of these differences was significant. Subgroup analyses (elevated baseline alkaline phosphatase; bisphosphonate use during the study) gave similar results. The authors conclude that striving to maintain normal alkaline phosphatase confers no clinical advantage over symptom-driven management in established Paget's disease.
cards.watchOut: Established, mostly previously treated disease — the result does not address newly diagnosed or severely active disease, and the symptomatic group could still receive bisphosphonates for pain, so this is a strategy comparison, not drug versus no drug.
cards.source: Langston AL et al. Randomized trial of intensive bisphosphonate treatment versus symptomatic management in Paget's disease of bone. Journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. 2010. PMID: 19580457. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN12989577, from the record's databank fields. bisphosphonate use during the study) gave similar results. the authors conclude that striving to maintain normal alkaline phosphatase confers no clinical advantage over symptom-driven management in established paget's disease. established, mostly previously treated disease — the result does not address newly diagnosed or severely active disease, and the symptomatic group could still receive bisphosphonates for pain, so this is a strategy comparison, not drug versus no drug. langston al et al. randomized trial of intensive bisphosphonate treatment versus symptomatic management in paget's disease of bone. journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the american society for bone and mineral research. 2010. pmid: 19580457. registry id: isrctn isrctn12989577, from the record's databank fields. mesh: aged · alkaline phosphatase/blood · bone density conservation agents/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · diphosphonates/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · female · fractures, bone/chemically induced/complications/surgery · hearing loss/chemically induced/complications · humans · male · orthopedic procedures · osteitis deformans/blood/drug therapy/enzymology · pain/chemically induced/complications · quality of life

cards.headline: PRISM-EZ 2017 (N = 502): long-term intensive treatment again showed no clinical benefit, with a nonsignificant fracture hazard ratio of 1.90 running against it
cards.summary: PRISM-EZ 2017 (N = 502): long-term intensive treatment again showed no clinical benefit, with a nonsignificant fracture hazard ratio of 1.90 running against it
cards.type: Randomised long-term extension trial (PRISM-EZ), J Bone Miner Res 2017
cards.people: 502 PRISM participants entering a 3-year extension: intensive bisphosphonate therapy continued in 270, aiming to normalise bone turnover with zoledronic acid as first choice; symptomatic treatment continued in 232, with bisphosphonates only for bone pain. Primary outcome fracture; secondary outcomes orthopaedic procedures, quality of life and bone pain, adjusted for baseline characteristics.
cards.result: Alkaline phosphatase stayed significantly lower on intensive treatment and the gap widened over time. There were no clinically important differences in quality of life or bone pain. Intensive treatment was associated with a nonsignificant increase in fracture risk (hazard ratio 1.90, 95% CI 0.91 to 3.98 — a relative measure whose interval includes no difference; P=0.087), orthopaedic procedures (hazard ratio 1.81, 0.71 to 4.61) and serious adverse events (relative risk 1.28, 0.96 to 1.42). The authors conclude long-term intensive therapy confers no clinical benefit and that treatment should focus on symptom control rather than suppression of bone turnover.
cards.watchOut: An extension cohort of PRISM survivors (502 of the original 1,324), so it is not an independent trial population; the adverse point estimates are nonsignificant and should be read as 'no benefit', not as proven harm.
cards.source: Tan A et al. Long-Term Randomized Trial of Intensive Versus Symptomatic Management in Paget's Disease of Bone: The PRISM-EZ Study. Journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. 2017. PMID: 28176386. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane 2017 (20 trials, 3,168 participants): bisphosphonates versus placebo tripled complete bone-pain disappearance (31% versus 9%) — the drugs work for symptoms, which is what the symptom-driven arm uses them for
cards.summary: Cochrane 2017 (20 trials, 3,168 participants): bisphosphonates versus placebo tripled complete bone-pain disappearance (31% versus 9%) — the drugs work for symptoms, which is what the symptom-driven arm uses them for
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Cochrane), Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2017
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of bisphosphonates for Paget's disease of bone in adults: 20 trials, 3,168 participants, including PRISM (1,331 participants as counted by the review) and PRISM-EZ (502) as the strategy comparison, 10 placebo-controlled trials (801 participants) and 7 head-to-head agent trials (992). Mean follow-up in most trials was 6 months.
cards.result: Versus placebo, bisphosphonates tripled the proportion whose bone pain disappeared: 31% versus 9% (risk ratio 3.42, 95% CI 1.31 to 8.90 — a relative measure, printed with its absolute rates; number needed to treat 5), and any pain reduction also favoured bisphosphonates (risk ratio 1.97, 1.29 to 3.01; 7 studies, 481 participants). Fracture data versus placebo were very uncertain (1.4% versus 0%; risk ratio 0.89, 0.18 to 4.31). No placebo trial reported orthopaedic surgery, quality of life or hearing. Mild gastrointestinal adverse events were more common on bisphosphonates (64% versus 48%; risk ratio 1.32, 0.91 to 1.92, low-quality evidence). The review notes there were insufficient data to determine whether normalising bone-turnover markers improves quality of life or reduces complications — the gap PRISM answers directly.
cards.watchOut: This card is context, not a third strategy trial: its pain result is drug versus placebo over short follow-up, and it includes PRISM/PRISM-EZ within its 3,168 participants rather than adding independent patients.
cards.source: Corral-Gudino L et al. Bisphosphonates for Paget's disease of bone in adults. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. PMID: 29192423. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: normalising alkaline phosphatase with intensive bisphosphonates made no difference to any clinical outcome — treat Paget's symptoms, not the number
cards.summary: Synthesis: normalising alkaline phosphatase with intensive bisphosphonates made no difference to any clinical outcome — treat Paget's symptoms, not the number
cards.people: Synthesis of the evidence cards on this shelf.
cards.result: PRISM (N = 1,324) and PRISM-EZ (N = 502) both achieved lower alkaline phosphatase on intensive treatment and both found no difference in fractures, orthopaedic procedures, pain or quality of life. Cochrane 2017 confirms bisphosphonates relieve pagetic bone pain versus placebo (31% versus 9% pain-free), supporting their symptom-driven use. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the intensive strategy.
cards.watchOut: This is a synthesis card, not a separate study; it adds no patients to the evidence base.

shelves.title: Sublingual cyclobenzaprine TNX-102 SL for fibromyalgia (PARTIAL — the modern sublingual programme pack #2698 does not cover): pain −1.9 vs −1.5 in RELIEF (n=503) and −1.8 vs −1.2 in RESILIENT, with oral numbness in 17–23%
shelves.question: In adults with fibromyalgia, does bedtime sublingual cyclobenzaprine (tested product — Tonix TNX-102 SL) reduce daily pain versus placebo over 14 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Double-Blind Method · Fibromyalgia/diagnosis,drug therapy,complications · Pain/complications · Pain Measurement · Treatment Outcome · Amitriptyline/analogs & derivatives
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #2698, which cards the older ORAL cyclobenzaprine literature in fibromyalgia (a meta-analysis of oral trials and a very-low-dose bedtime study); no PMID homed there is re-carded here. The tested product is Tonix TNX-102 SL, a bedtime sublingual formulation, named under the tested-product clarification exception. Two phase 3 trials of the same regimen (2.8 mg for 2 weeks, then 5.6 mg nightly for 12 weeks) agree on the primary endpoint: RELIEF (503 patients) found a week-14 pain reduction of −1.9 versus −1.5 on placebo (p=0.01), and RESILIENT (456 randomised; journal home verified at build as Pain Medicine, NCT05273749) found −1.8 versus −1.2 (p<0.001) with all six secondary endpoints also significant (p≤0.001) — sleep, fatigue, global impression and function. The honest margins are modest (0.4–0.6 points on a 0–10 pain scale beyond placebo), Patient Global Impression of Change was not significant in RELIEF, and the signature harms are local: oral hypoesthesia in 17.3% (RELIEF) and 23.4% (RESILIENT), with abnormal taste and oral paraesthesia, transient and self-limited; systemic events were close to placebo. Two concordant phase 3 trials carry LIKELY (benefit) for a modest pain effect.

cards.headline: RELIEF phase 3 (503 patients): pain fell −1.9 on TNX-102 SL vs −1.5 on placebo at week 14 (p=0.01); global impression did NOT significantly improve
cards.summary: RELIEF phase 3 (503 patients): pain fell −1.9 on TNX-102 SL vs −1.5 on placebo at week 14 (p=0.01); global impression did NOT significantly improve
cards.people: 503 patients with fibromyalgia randomised to once-nightly sublingual TNX-102 SL (Tonix) 2.8 mg for 2 weeks then 5.6 mg for 12 weeks (n=248) or matching placebo (n=255). Primary endpoint: change at week 14 in the weekly average of daily pain scores; secondaries included Patient Global Impression of Change (PGIC), Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire Revised, PROMIS Sleep Disturbance and Fatigue, and daily sleep quality.
cards.result: Pain reduction was significantly greater on TNX-102 SL (least-squares mean change −1.9, 95% CI −2.1 to −1.7) than placebo (−1.5, 95% CI −1.7 to −1.3; p=0.01) — an absolute advantage of 0.4 points. PGIC at week 14 was not significantly improved (the treatment made no difference on that measure), while FIQR scores, PROMIS sleep and fatigue scores and daily sleep quality did improve. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 59.7% on drug versus 46.3% on placebo, most commonly oral hypoesthesia (17.3% vs 0.4%), oral paraesthesia (5.6% vs 0.4%) and abnormal product taste (4.4% vs 0.4%).
cards.watchOut: A statistically real but small average pain advantage (0.4 points) whose patient-global counterpart did not reach significance in this trial — individual responders may gain more than the mean suggests, but the mean is what the trial proves.
cards.source: Lederman S et al. Efficacy and Safety of Sublingual Cyclobenzaprine for the Treatment of Fibromyalgia: Results From a Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial. Arthritis care & research. 2023. PMID: 37165930. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04172831. cards.headline: RESILIENT phase 3 (456 randomised; Pain Medicine 2026): pain −1.8 vs −1.2 (p<0.001) and all six secondary endpoints significant; oral hypoesthesia 23.4%
cards.summary: RESILIENT phase 3 (456 randomised; Pain Medicine 2026): pain −1.8 vs −1.2 (p<0.001) and all six secondary endpoints significant; oral hypoesthesia 23.4%
cards.people: Patients with fibromyalgia randomised 1:1 to once-nightly TNX-102 SL 2.8 mg for 2 weeks then 5.6 mg for 12 weeks, or matching placebo (231 assigned to TNX-102 SL and 225 to placebo by the completion denominators in the record); 81.0% and 79.6% completed. Primary endpoint: change at week 14 in the weekly average of daily diary pain intensity; secondaries covered global impression, FIQR Symptoms and Function, PROMIS Sleep Disturbance and Fatigue, and daily sleep quality.
cards.result: The primary pain endpoint favoured TNX-102 SL (mean [SE] change −1.8 [0.12] vs −1.2 [0.12]; p<0.001 — an absolute advantage of 0.6 points), as did each of the six secondary endpoints (all p≤0.001), spanning pain, sleep disturbance, fatigue, function and global impression. The commonest events overall were local administration-site reactions — oral hypoesthesia (23.4% vs 0.4%), abnormal product taste (11.3% vs 0.9%) and oral paraesthesia (6.9% vs 0.9%) — transient and self-limited; the commonest systemic events were COVID-19 (4.3% vs 3.1%), headache (3.0% vs 1.8%) and somnolence (3.0% vs 1.3%).
cards.watchOut: Verified at build: this report (Pain Medicine 2026, NCT05273749) is the programme's second phase 3 trial and states it validates the previous phase 3 findings. Its margins remain modest in absolute terms, and nearly one in four patients gets a numb mouth — worth telling patients before the first dose.
cards.source: Lederman S et al. Pain relief by targeting nonrestorative sleep in fibromyalgia: a phase 3 randomized trial of bedtime sublingual cyclobenzaprine. Pain medicine (Malden, Mass.). 2026. PMID: 40627411. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05273749. cards.headline: Al-Qudah 2026 meta-analysis (4 trials, 1,684 patients): ≥30% pain responders relative risk 1.44 and PGIC relative risk 1.52 vs placebo; FIQR not significantly improved; oral hypoesthesia relative risk 38.11
cards.summary: Al-Qudah 2026 meta-analysis (4 trials, 1,684 patients): ≥30% pain responders relative risk 1.44 and PGIC relative risk 1.52 vs placebo; FIQR not significantly improved; oral hypoesthesia relative risk 38.11
cards.people: Four randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of once-nightly TNX-102 SL in adults with fibromyalgia (total 1,684 patients), pooled with random-effects models; outcomes included ≥30% and ≥50% pain response, Patient Global Impression of Change, FIQR and safety. The pool includes the two phase 3 trials carded above plus earlier-phase trials not individually carded on this shelf.
cards.result: TNX-102 SL increased ≥30% pain responders (relative risk 1.44, 95% CI 1.15–1.81) and ≥50% responders (relative risk 1.43, 95% CI 1.12–1.82) and improved PGIC response (relative risk 1.52, 95% CI 1.29–1.79) versus placebo — all relative measures, with low heterogeneity — while FIQR scores were not significantly improved (the treatment made no difference on that pooled measure). Treatment-emergent adverse events were more frequent on drug (relative risk 1.41, 95% CI 1.26–1.57), driven by oral hypoesthesia (relative risk 38.11, 95% CI 18.55–78.29), oral paraesthesia (7.88) and abnormal taste (10.92); discontinuation matched placebo (relative risk 1.03) and no deaths were reported.
cards.watchOut: The pooled PGIC advantage (relative risk 1.52) sits awkwardly beside RELIEF's own non-significant PGIC — pooling adds the earlier-phase trials, so the meta-analysis summarises a slightly different evidence set than the two phase 3 cards; the oral-hypoesthesia relative risk of 38 reflects a near-zero placebo rate, not a 38-fold absolute risk.
cards.source: Al-Qudah AA et al. Short-term efficacy and safety of sublingual cyclobenzaprine for fibromyalgia: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical rheumatology. 2026. PMID: 41318845. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, the same modest pain win, a sleep-and-fatigue benefit beside it, and a numb-mouth price
cards.summary: Synthesis: two phase 3 trials, the same modest pain win, a sleep-and-fatigue benefit beside it, and a numb-mouth price
cards.people: RELIEF (503 patients) and RESILIENT (456 randomised) — the two phase 3 trials of bedtime TNX-102 SL 5.6 mg in fibromyalgia, each 14 weeks against placebo.
cards.result: Pain advantages of 0.4 and 0.6 points beyond placebo, with sleep, fatigue and function measures improving in both trials and global impression significant in RESILIENT but not RELIEF. Local oral events (hypoesthesia 17–23%) are the dominant harm; systemic tolerability was close to placebo. LIKELY (benefit) — a real, modest, sleep-anchored benefit, distinct from the older oral cyclobenzaprine evidence on pack #2698.
cards.watchOut: Both trials are 14 weeks in a lifelong condition, run by the product's sponsor programme, with no active comparator (duloxetine, pregabalin, milnacipran or oral cyclobenzaprine) — relative standing among fibromyalgia drugs is not answered here.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Fasinumab for osteoarthritis pain (PARTIAL — the fasinumab slice live #1483, tanezumab only, does not cover): WOMAC pain advantages of 0.6–1.4 points, with adjudicated arthropathies in 5.6–9.7% and rapid-progressive OA the dominant pattern
shelves.question: In adults with knee or hip osteoarthritis pain inadequately controlled by standard analgesics, does fasinumab reduce pain and improve function versus placebo — and what is the rate of rapidly progressive osteoarthritis and joint replacement?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1483, which cards tanezumab only; this shelf builds only the fasinumab slice, cross-points to #1483 for the class sibling, and re-cards no PMID homed there. Fasinumab, the second anti-NGF antibody programme, shows the class pattern in sharper relief: consistent, statistically robust but small analgesia — WOMAC pain least-squares differences versus placebo of −0.78 to −1.40 across doses in the phase IIb/III dose-ranging trial (421 randomised), −0.58 for pain at the licensed-candidate 1 mg every-4-weeks dose in the large naproxen-controlled phase III (3,307 randomised; −2.90 vs −2.32 raw changes), and −0.63 in the NSAID-controlled phase III (1,650 randomised) — against a dose-dependent joint-safety problem: arthropathies in 7% of fasinumab-treated patients versus 1% on placebo in the dose-ranging trial (dose-dependent, mostly found on scheduled imaging), adjudicated arthropathies in 7.2–9.7% on 1 mg regimens versus 1.1% on placebo and 2.6% on naproxen in the large phase III, of which 75.5–95.0% were rapid-progressive osteoarthritis type 1, and joint replacements in 5.6–6.4% versus 3.4% on placebo in that trial (3.4% vs 3.6% in the NSAID-controlled trial — no difference there). A 52-week safety study (5,331 randomised) confirms the dose relationship and that higher doses were discontinued for safety. Real analgesia, small margins, and a joint harm that ended the class's regulatory path: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the harm on the face.

cards.headline: Dakin 2019 phase IIb/III (421 randomised): WOMAC pain differences −0.78 to −1.40 vs placebo at week 16; arthropathies 7% on fasinumab vs 1% on placebo, dose-dependent
cards.summary: Dakin 2019 phase IIb/III (421 randomised): WOMAC pain differences −0.78 to −1.40 vs placebo at week 16; arthropathies 7% on fasinumab vs 1% on placebo, dose-dependent
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Dakin 2019, dose-ranging phase IIb/III)
cards.people: 421 patients with moderate-to-severe knee or hip osteoarthritis pain and inadequate response or intolerance to analgesics, randomised to fasinumab 1, 3, 6 or 9 mg or placebo every 4 weeks for 16 weeks and followed to week 36; 342 completed. Joints were monitored by scheduled radiography and MRI and when symptoms prompted. Endpoints: WOMAC pain and physical function change at week 16 and patient global assessment.
cards.result: All fasinumab doses significantly reduced pain versus placebo (least-squares mean WOMAC pain differences −0.78 to −1.40 on a 0–10 scale), without clear dose dependence, with parallel function and global gains. Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 17% on fasinumab versus 10% on placebo, with discontinuation in 4% versus 1%. Arthropathies numbered 25 in total — 7% of fasinumab-treated patients versus 1% on placebo — in a dose-dependent pattern (2 at the lowest dose, 10 at the highest); 16 of 25 were found on scheduled imaging rather than symptoms, and one destructive arthropathy occurred in a patient on 6 mg.
cards.watchOut: The joint signal appeared within 16 weeks of treatment and was mostly silent — detected because the trial imaged everyone on schedule. Efficacy showed no dose dependence while harm did, which is why later trials settled on 1 mg.
cards.source: Dakin P et al. The Efficacy, Tolerability, and Joint Safety of Fasinumab in Osteoarthritis Pain: A Phase IIb/III Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled, Randomized Clinical Trial. Arthritis & rheumatology (Hoboken, N.J.). 2019. PMID: 31207169. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02447276. cards.headline: DiMartino 2026 phase III (3,307 randomised): fasinumab 1 mg Q4W beat placebo AND naproxen on pain — but adjudicated arthropathies 9.7% (Q4W) vs 1.1% placebo, 75.5–95.0% of them rapid-progressive OA type 1
cards.summary: DiMartino 2026 phase III (3,307 randomised): fasinumab 1 mg Q4W beat placebo AND naproxen on pain — but adjudicated arthropathies 9.7% (Q4W) vs 1.1% placebo, 75.5–95.0% of them rapid-progressive OA type 1
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (DiMartino 2026, phase III, placebo- and naproxen-controlled)
cards.people: 3,307 patients with difficult-to-treat moderate-to-severe knee or hip osteoarthritis pain, randomised 3:3:3:1 to fasinumab 1 mg subcutaneous every 4 weeks, 1 mg every 8 weeks, naproxen 500 mg twice daily or placebo; 1,801 were included in the efficacy analysis and 3,014 in the safety analysis. Co-primary endpoints: WOMAC pain and physical function change at week 16 versus placebo.
cards.result: Fasinumab 1 mg every 4 weeks reduced WOMAC pain by −2.90 and function by −2.78, versus −2.32 and −2.10 on placebo and −2.61 and −2.41 on naproxen (all p<0.005). Adjudicated arthropathies occurred in 7.2% (every-8-weeks) and 9.7% (every-4-weeks) of fasinumab patients versus 1.1% on placebo and 2.6% on naproxen; joint replacements in 5.6% and 6.4% versus 3.4% (placebo) and 3.1% (naproxen). Of the fasinumab-arm arthropathies, 95.0% (every-8-weeks) and 75.5% (every-4-weeks) were rapid-progressive osteoarthritis type 1. No new safety concerns were identified beyond the joint findings.
cards.watchOut: The efficacy analysis includes barely half the randomised patients (1,801 of 3,307), and the winning dose carries the worst joint numbers: roughly 1 in 11 patients on 1 mg every 4 weeks had an adjudicated arthropathy within the trial's frame.
cards.source: DiMartino SJ et al. A phase III, randomised, double-blind, multi-dose, placebo- and naproxen-controlled study to evaluate the efficacy and safety of fasinumab in patients with pain due to osteoarthritis of the knee or hip. RMD open. 2026. PMID: 41545313. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03161093, NCT02683239. cards.headline: DiMartino 2025 phase III (1,650 randomised, NSAID-controlled): WOMAC pain difference −0.63 vs placebo at week 24; adjudicated arthropathies 5.6% on fasinumab vs 1.6% placebo; joint replacements no different (3.4% vs 3.6%)
cards.summary: DiMartino 2025 phase III (1,650 randomised, NSAID-controlled): WOMAC pain difference −0.63 vs placebo at week 24; adjudicated arthropathies 5.6% on fasinumab vs 1.6% placebo; joint replacements no different (3.4% vs 3.6%)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (DiMartino 2025, phase III, placebo- and NSAID-controlled)
cards.people: 1,650 patients with knee/hip osteoarthritis (Kellgren–Lawrence grade ≥2, WOMAC pain ≥4) randomised 2:1:1:1 to fasinumab 1 mg every 4 weeks, diclofenac 75 mg twice daily, celecoxib 200 mg daily or placebo for 24 weeks, with protocol imaging of all patients at prespecified times regardless of symptoms.
cards.result: Fasinumab improved WOMAC pain (least-squares mean difference −0.63; p=0.0003) and physical function (−0.64; p=0.0003) versus placebo, numerically more than the NSAIDs on function (−0.64 vs −0.31) and pain (−0.63 vs −0.39, not significant). Adjudicated arthropathies occurred in 5.6% on fasinumab versus 1.5% on NSAIDs and 1.6% on placebo; joint replacements occurred in 3.4% on fasinumab versus 4.8% on NSAIDs and 3.6% on placebo — no difference in replacements in this trial.
cards.watchOut: Two phase III trials now disagree on whether replacements rise (6.4% vs 3.4% in the naproxen-controlled trial; 3.4% vs 3.6% here) while agreeing that arthropathies — the precursor lesion — clearly do. The 24-week frame is short for a replacement endpoint.
cards.source: DiMartino SJ et al. Efficacy and safety of fasinumab in an NSAID-controlled study in patients with pain due to osteoarthritis of the knee or hip. BMC musculoskeletal disorders. 2025. PMID: 40001000. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03304379. cards.headline: DiMartino 2024 long-term safety study (5,331 randomised, 52 weeks): dose-dependent arthropathy and joint-replacement risk; higher doses discontinued for safety; 1 mg pain differences −0.73 to −1.22
cards.summary: DiMartino 2024 long-term safety study (5,331 randomised, 52 weeks): dose-dependent arthropathy and joint-replacement risk; higher doses discontinued for safety; 1 mg pain differences −0.73 to −1.22
cards.type: Randomised safety study with efficacy sub-study (DiMartino 2024, phase III)
cards.people: 5,331 patients with moderate-to-severe osteoarthritis pain and inadequate relief on prior analgesics, randomised to placebo or fasinumab (1, 3, 6 or 9 mg every 4 weeks; 1 or 6 mg every 8 weeks) for 52 weeks; 1,074 took part in the efficacy sub-study. Primary safety endpoints: adverse events, adjudicated arthropathies and joint replacements.
cards.result: Adjudicated arthropathies and joint replacements occurred in all groups, with a dose-dependent risk on fasinumab; more severe baseline disease carried higher rates of both, and in the 1 mg groups only a small percentage of patients with a joint replacement had a prior adjudicated arthropathy. Higher fasinumab doses were discontinued during the study for safety; the 1 mg doses continued. In the efficacy sub-study, 1 mg every 4 weeks improved WOMAC pain and function versus placebo by −1.22 and −1.20, and 1 mg every 8 weeks by −0.73 and −0.74 (p<0.001). The record's abstract does not print arm-level arthropathy percentages, so none are given here.
cards.watchOut: A safety study whose abstract reports the dose relationship qualitatively: the quantitative joint rates live in the two efficacy phase III cards above. Its contribution is duration (52 weeks) and scale (5,331 patients) behind the dose-dependence claim.

cards.headline: Synthesis: fasinumab relieves OA pain by fractions of a point and damages joints in a dose-dependent minority — the class story of shelf #1483, told by its second drug
cards.summary: Synthesis: fasinumab relieves OA pain by fractions of a point and damages joints in a dose-dependent minority — the class story of shelf #1483, told by its second drug
cards.people: Four randomised reports totalling over 10,000 randomised patients (421 + 3,307 + 1,650 + 5,331) in knee/hip osteoarthritis pain inadequately controlled by standard analgesics.
cards.result: Pain advantages versus placebo of about 0.6–1.4 WOMAC points recur across every trial and dose, and 1 mg every 4 weeks also beat naproxen. Against them: adjudicated arthropathies in 5.6–9.7% on 1 mg regimens (vs 1.1–1.6% on placebo), three quarters or more of them rapid-progressive OA type 1, joint replacements raised in one phase III and not the other, and higher doses abandoned for safety. POSSIBLE (benefit) with the joint harm inseparable from the claim; for the tanezumab half of the anti-NGF class, see live shelf #1483.
cards.watchOut: Fasinumab was never approved for osteoarthritis pain; these trials answer what the drug does, not what a clinician can prescribe. Baseline joint severity modifies the harm, and no trial identifies a subgroup with benefit clearly outweighing joint risk.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: PHYSIOLOGY — Offset analgesia in humans: a 1–3 °C decrease from tonic noxious heat produced pain relief as large as a 15 °C drop to innocuous levels, mediated by periaqueductal-grey/rostral-ventromedial-medulla activation — and attenuated in chronic-pain patients
shelves.question: In healthy humans, does a small decrease in a tonic noxious heat stimulus produce a disproportionately large drop in perceived pain (offset analgesia), how large is the effect, and is it attenuated in chronic-pain patients?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Physiological · Adult · Analgesia · Female · Hot Temperature · Humans · Male · Pain/etiology,physiopathology · Pain Measurement · Temperature · Time Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): descending pathways from the periaqueductal grey (PAG) and rostral ventromedial medulla continuously modulate pain transmission, and offset analgesia is that system engaging at stimulus offset. The defining human psychophysics (Grill & Coghill 2002) show small 1–3 °C decreases from tonic noxious heat (47–50 °C) evoking pain reductions up to 271% greater than equal-magnitude increases — as large as those from a 15 °C drop to innocuous levels, and greater than adaptation to constant stimuli (N not documented in the record). fMRI in 12 healthy controls shows PAG/RVM activation during offset with pain-neuromatrix inhibition (Derbyshire & Osborn 2009). The response is attenuated in chronic pain in two independent cohorts: significantly smaller ΔOA in 12 patients versus 12 controls with an offset-analgesia index AUC of 0.897 (Kobinata 2017), and smaller OA magnitude in 23 patients versus 17 controls (P=0.047; Li 2022). No animal studies are carded. Distinct from pack #6203 (central sensitisation / conditioned pain modulation — facilitation and inhibition by a second distant stimulus), which was read and does not home this question.

cards.headline: Grill & Coghill 2002: a small 1–3 °C decrease from a tonic noxious heat (47–50 °C) produced pain reductions up to 271% greater than equal-magnitude increases produced rises — as large as dropping 15 °C to innocuous levels (the defining offset analgesia experiment)
cards.summary: Grill & Coghill 2002: a small 1–3 °C decrease from a tonic noxious heat (47–50 °C) produced pain reductions up to 271% greater than equal-magnitude increases produced rises — as large as dropping 15 °C to innocuous levels (the defining offset analgesia experiment)
cards.type: Primary human experimental psychophysics study (Grill & Coghill 2002)
cards.people: Healthy human volunteers rating perceived pain intensity during tonic noxious heat stimuli (47–50 °C) with small (±1–3 °C) increases and decreases, compared with adaptation to constant-temperature stimuli; the fetched record does not state the sample size, so this card prints N not documented.
cards.result: Small decreases in noxious stimulus temperature evoked changes in perceived pain intensity that were as much as 271% greater than those evoked by equal-magnitude increases. The decreases in perceived pain were sufficiently large to be indistinguishable from those evoked by 15 °C decreases to clearly innocuous levels. Pain reductions following stimulus offset were significantly greater than those occurring during adaptation to constant-temperature stimuli. The authors interpret this as an analgesic mechanism activated during noxious stimulus offset — a temporal contrast enhancement that amplifies awareness of stimulus offset and reinforces escape behaviour — and propose its disruption may contribute to chronic pain.
cards.watchOut: N not documented in the fetched record, and the 271% figure is a ratio of rating changes (increases from a tonic stimulus are constrained by rating-scale ceilings in a way decreases are not) — the robust, replicated claim is the disproportion itself, not the exact percentage.

cards.headline: Derbyshire & Osborn 2009: during offset analgesia, the periaqueductal grey / rostral ventromedial medulla activated and pain-neuromatrix activation was inhibited to the level seen when heat returned to a non-noxious baseline (fMRI, n=12)
cards.summary: Derbyshire & Osborn 2009: during offset analgesia, the periaqueductal grey / rostral ventromedial medulla activated and pain-neuromatrix activation was inhibited to the level seen when heat returned to a non-noxious baseline (fMRI, n=12)
cards.type: Primary human fMRI mechanistic study (Derbyshire & Osborn 2009)
cards.people: 12 healthy controls scanned during an offset procedure — 6 seconds of noxious heat, 6 seconds of more intense heat, then a return to the original temperature for 6 seconds — and during two control conditions (continuous unchanging noxious heat for 18 seconds; and the same up-step followed by a return to non-noxious baseline). N=12 printed plainly.
cards.result: Activation in the region of the periaqueductal grey and rostral ventromedial medulla (PAG/RVM) was observed during the final 6 seconds of offset trials but not during either control trial, and the difference across trials was significant. Activation throughout the pain neuromatrix was inhibited during the final 6 seconds of offset trials, to a level comparable with activation when the heat returned to a non-noxious baseline. The authors conclude offset analgesia engages an endogenous inhibitory mechanism originating in the PAG/RVM region.
cards.watchOut: Twelve subjects and a region-level fMRI attribution ('in the region of' the PAG/RVM) — this localises the phenomenon to the descending inhibitory system; it does not show that PAG/RVM activity is necessary for offset analgesia, which would require a perturbation design.
cards.source: Derbyshire SW et al. Offset analgesia is mediated by activation in the region of the periaqueductal grey and rostral ventromedial medulla. NeuroImage. 2009. PMID: 19375510. cards.headline: Kobinata 2017: offset analgesia was significantly smaller in 12 chronic-pain patients than in 12 matched controls at 5- and 10-second increments, and an offset-analgesia index distinguished patients from controls with an area under the ROC curve of 0.897
cards.summary: Kobinata 2017: offset analgesia was significantly smaller in 12 chronic-pain patients than in 12 matched controls at 5- and 10-second increments, and an offset-analgesia index distinguished patients from controls with an area under the ROC curve of 0.897
cards.type: Primary human experimental pain study, patients versus controls (Kobinata 2017)
cards.people: 40 healthy volunteers first characterised the paradigm (a 1 °C increment, T2, of 5, 10 or 15 seconds over a 45 °C tonic stimulus, applied to the left volar forearm with a Peltier thermode); offset analgesia and constant-stimulus responses were then compared in 12 patients with chronic pain and 12 matched healthy controls. Magnitude of offset analgesia (ΔOA) and maximum visual-analogue-scale latency were measured per individual.
cards.result: In healthy controls, longer T2 (10 or 15 seconds) produced larger ΔOA than 5 seconds (P=0.04). In patients, ΔOA was significantly smaller than in controls at T2 of 5 and 10 seconds (P<0.05) but grew comparable at 15 seconds. Maximum VAS latency was longer in patients than controls and negatively correlated with ΔOA in patients. A combined offset-analgesia index (ΔOA / maximum VAS latency) proved diagnostic of chronic pain with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.897. The authors conclude patients with chronic pain show impaired offset analgesia and reduced temporal sharpening of pain perception, implying disturbance of the endogenous pain modulatory system.
cards.watchOut: Twelve patients with mixed chronic pain is a small, heterogeneous case group, and an AUC of 0.897 from the same sample that derived the index will shrink on external validation — the card supports 'attenuated in chronic pain', not a clinical diagnostic test.
cards.source: Kobinata H et al. Disrupted offset analgesia distinguishes patients with chronic pain from healthy controls. Pain. 2017. PMID: 28746077. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Li 2022: chronic-pain patients (n=23) showed a smaller offset analgesia magnitude than matched controls (n=17; P=0.047), with offset-related functional connectivity between posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex decreasing in proportion to current pain
cards.summary: Li 2022: chronic-pain patients (n=23) showed a smaller offset analgesia magnitude than matched controls (n=17; P=0.047), with offset-related functional connectivity between posterior cingulate and medial prefrontal cortex decreasing in proportion to current pain
cards.type: Primary human fMRI study, patients versus controls (Li 2022)
cards.people: 23 patients with various chronic pain conditions and 17 age- and gender-matched healthy controls, given offset-analgesia thermal paradigms (46–47–46 °C, three repeats) and a constant 46 °C paradigm on the left volar forearm during whole-brain fMRI, with psychophysiological-interaction and resting-state connectivity analyses.
cards.result: Compared with controls, chronic-pain patients showed a smaller magnitude of offset analgesia (P=0.047). Offset-modulated connectivity between the posterior cingulate cortex and right medial prefrontal cortex decreased in proportion to current chronic pain (P=0.018); connectivity also decreased between right pallidum and right thalamus and increased between right caudate and left primary somatosensory cortex (FDR-corrected P<0.05). The authors propose the impaired posterior-cingulate–medial-prefrontal connectivity may contribute to pain chronification. Their introduction notes prior reports that patients with neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia showed reduced or absent offset analgesia with attenuated activity in descending modulatory and reward systems.
cards.watchOut: A mixed-diagnosis patient group and a headline P value of 0.047 — supportive replication of the attenuation finding, at modest strength; the connectivity results are correlational and hypothesis-generating.
cards.source: Li T et al. Functional connectivity modulations during offset analgesia in chronic pain patients: an fMRI study. Brain imaging and behavior. 2022. PMID: 35314949. cards.headline: Synthesis: a disproportionate pain drop at stimulus offset, a PAG/RVM descending mechanism, and attenuation in chronic pain — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (and distinct from pack #6203)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a disproportionate pain drop at stimulus offset, a PAG/RVM descending mechanism, and attenuation in chronic pain — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (and distinct from pack #6203)
cards.people: Synthesis of the four carded primary human studies. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): pain is not a passive readout of stimulus intensity — descending pathways from the periaqueductal grey and rostral ventromedial medulla continuously modulate dorsal-horn transmission, and offset analgesia is the temporal-contrast signature of that system engaging at stimulus offset. Neighbour check: pack #6203 (central sensitisation and conditioned pain modulation) asks about facilitation/wind-up and inhibition by a second, distant painful stimulus — a different phenomenon and a different paradigm; offset analgesia, a disproportionate response to a small decrease in the same stimulus, is not homed there, and this pack is its home.
cards.result: The defining psychophysics (Grill & Coghill 2002) show a 1–3 °C offset producing pain relief equivalent to a 15 °C drop; fMRI localises the effect to PAG/RVM engagement with pain-neuromatrix inhibition (Derbyshire & Osborn 2009, n=12); and two independent patient cohorts show the response is attenuated in chronic pain (Kobinata 2017; Li 2022). No animal studies are carded. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: The patient-attenuation literature is small and diagnostically mixed, and the founding study's sample size is N not documented in its record — the phenomenon and its direction are established; offset analgesia as a patient-level biomarker is not.
cards.source: Synthesis of Grill JD et al. Journal of neurophysiology. 2002 (PMID: 11929939); Derbyshire SW et al. NeuroImage. 2009 (PMID: 19375510); Kobinata H et al. Pain. 2017 (PMID: 28746077); Li T et al. Brain imaging and behavior. 2022 (PMID: 35314949).

shelves.title: Targeted muscle reinnervation for amputation pain: one small randomised trial (N = 28) and concordant cohorts favour TMR — the at-amputation evidence is a cohort, not the trial
shelves.question: In adults undergoing major limb amputation, does targeted muscle reinnervation performed at the time of amputation reduce neuroma pain and phantom limb pain versus standard traction neurectomy?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Amputation, Surgical/rehabilitation* · Amputees/rehabilitation* · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Muscle, Skeletal/innervation* · Nerve Transfer/methods* · Neuroma/surgery* · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/diagnosis, surgery* · Phantom Limb/surgery* · Prospective Studies · Plastic Surgery Procedures/methods · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: One small randomised trial plus cohorts — capped at POSSIBLE, with N printed on the face. The Dumanian RCT (N = 28, NCT02205385) randomised amputees with chronic postamputation pain to TMR or standard neuroma excision and burying: phantom pain change at 1 year was 3.2 versus −0.2 points (intention-to-treat adjusted P = 0.06; longitudinal model P = 0.03) and residual limb pain change 2.9 versus 0.9 (P = 0.15). PREMISE NUANCE: that trial treated established pain (secondary TMR); the evidence for TMR performed at the time of amputation is the Valerio multi-institutional cohort — 51 immediate-TMR patients versus 438 unselected amputee controls, median worst pain 1/10 versus 5/10 (phantom) and 4/10 (residual) — large gaps from a non-randomised comparison. A prospective 33-patient series and a 5-study, 127-patient meta-analysis point the same way, and the meta-analysis authors call the evidence 'limited… of good quality' in TMR's favour. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Dumanian 2019 (RCT, N = 28): targeted muscle reinnervation versus standard neuroma excision and burying — phantom pain change 3.2 versus −0.2 points at 1 year in intention-to-treat (adjusted P = 0.06)
cards.summary: Dumanian 2019 (RCT, N = 28): targeted muscle reinnervation versus standard neuroma excision and burying — phantom pain change 3.2 versus −0.2 points at 1 year in intention-to-treat (adjusted P = 0.06)
cards.people: 28 amputees with chronic postamputation pain, randomised prospectively to targeted muscle reinnervation (TMR) or standard treatment (neuroma excision and burying into muscle); primary outcome was change in numerical rating scale (NRS, 0–10) scores for residual limb pain and phantom limb pain (PLP) at 1 year. Registered as NCT02205385. Note: this trial treated established postamputation pain (secondary TMR), not TMR performed at the time of amputation.
cards.result: In intention-to-treat analysis, the 1-year change in PLP scores was 3.2 with TMR versus −0.2 with standard treatment (difference 3.4, adjusted CI −0.1 to 6.9, adjusted P = 0.06); the change in residual limb pain scores was 2.9 versus 0.9 (difference 1.9, adjusted CI −0.5 to 4.4, P = 0.15). In longitudinal mixed-model analysis the difference in PLP change scores significantly favoured TMR (mean 3.5, adjusted CI 0.6 to 6.3, P = 0.03); the residual limb pain reduction also favoured TMR (P = 0.10). At longest follow-up, including 3 crossover patients, results favoured TMR.
cards.watchOut: N = 28 is the entire randomised base, and the prespecified intention-to-treat primary comparisons did not reach conventional significance (P = 0.06 and P = 0.15) — the significant result comes from the longitudinal model. Single-blind surgical trial: patients knew their operation, and pain is self-reported.
cards.source: Dumanian GA et al. Targeted Muscle Reinnervation Treats Neuroma and Phantom Pain in Major Limb Amputees: A Randomized Clinical Trial. Annals of surgery. 2019. PMID: 30371518. Registry ID: NCT02205385 (ClinicalTrials.gov, from the record's databank list). cards.headline: Valerio 2019 (multi-institutional cohort, 51 TMR at amputation versus 438 unselected amputee controls): median worst pain 1/10 with TMR versus 5/10 (phantom) and 4/10 (residual) without
cards.summary: Valerio 2019 (multi-institutional cohort, 51 TMR at amputation versus 438 unselected amputee controls): median worst pain 1/10 with TMR versus 5/10 (phantom) and 4/10 (residual) without
cards.people: 51 patients undergoing major limb amputation with immediate targeted muscle reinnervation at the time of amputation (2012–2018, multi-institutional), compared with 438 unselected major limb amputees without TMR; outcomes were 11-point numerical rating scale and PROMIS pain intensity, behaviour and interference scores. This is the card that matches TMR performed at the time of amputation.
cards.result: Patients who underwent TMR at amputation had less phantom and residual limb pain than controls across all subgroups and measures. Median 'worst pain in the past 24 hours' was 1 out of 10 in the TMR cohort versus 5 (phantom limb pain) and 4 (residual limb pain) out of 10 in controls (p = 0.003 and p < 0.001). Median PROMIS t-scores were lower with TMR for phantom pain (intensity 36.3 vs 48.3; behaviour 50.1 vs 56.6; interference 40.7 vs 55.8) and residual limb pain (intensity 30.7 vs 46.8; behaviour 36.7 vs 57.3; interference 40.7 vs 57.3). TMR was associated with 3.03 (phantom) and 3.92 (residual) times higher odds of decreasing pain severity.
cards.watchOut: The comparison group is 'unselected' amputees, not randomised or matched controls — patients offered TMR at amputation differ from the general amputee population in centre, era and selection, and all of that can move pain scores. The large gaps (1 vs 5 out of 10) are exactly the size observational comparisons overstate.
cards.source: Valerio IL et al. Preemptive Treatment of Phantom and Residual Limb Pain with Targeted Muscle Reinnervation at the Time of Major Limb Amputation. Journal of the American College of Surgeons. 2019. PMID: 30634038. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mioton 2020 (prospective series, 33 amputees): after TMR for established pain, residual limb pain fell from 6.4 to 3.6 and phantom pain from 6.0 to 3.6 at 1 year — no control group
cards.summary: Mioton 2020 (prospective series, 33 amputees): after TMR for established pain, residual limb pain fell from 6.4 to 3.6 and phantom pain from 6.0 to 3.6 at 1 year — no control group
cards.people: 33 major limb amputees (of 43 enrolled; 10 lacked 1-year follow-up) who were ineligible for or declined randomisation in the Dumanian trial programme and underwent targeted muscle reinnervation for pain, followed prospectively 2013–2017; outcomes were 11-point numerical rating scale, PROMIS pain intensity and interference, and functional scores (OPUS Rasch, Neuro-QOL) before and 1 year after surgery.
cards.result: At 1 year, residual limb pain fell from 6.4 ± 2.6 to 3.6 ± 2.2 (mean difference −2.7, 95% CI −4.2 to −1.3; p < 0.001) and phantom limb pain from 6.0 ± 3.1 to 3.6 ± 2.9 (mean difference −2.4, 95% CI −3.8 to −0.9; p < 0.001). PROMIS pain intensity and interference improved for both pain types (p ≤ 0.012 for all), and OPUS Rasch and Neuro-QOL functional scores also improved (p < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Before–after change in patients selected for severe chronic pain is expected to improve partly by regression to the mean and natural history; with no control arm this card can show the operated patients improved, not that TMR caused all of the improvement. Ten of 43 enrolled patients had no 1-year follow-up.
