cards.headline: Hagiga 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 5 studies, 127 patients): significantly better phantom and residual pain with TMR versus standard treatment at 12 months — 'limited evidence of good quality'
cards.summary: Hagiga 2023 (systematic review and meta-analysis, 5 studies, 127 patients): significantly better phantom and residual pain with TMR versus standard treatment at 12 months — 'limited evidence of good quality'
cards.people: Five studies (four in the quantitative meta-analysis) enrolling a total of 127 patients who underwent targeted muscle reinnervation after amputation, compared with standard treatment, with patient-reported pain outcomes to 12 months; protocol registered in PROSPERO (CRD42020218242, as reported in the record).
cards.result: The TMR group showed significantly better phantom limb pain on the numerical rating score, and significantly lower PROMIS pain intensity for phantom and residual limb pain, than standard treatment at 12 months. The authors' own conclusion: there is limited evidence of good quality favouring TMR in reducing postamputation phantom and residual limb pain compared with standard care, and randomised trials comparing surgical techniques are encouraged.
cards.watchOut: 127 patients across the whole quantitative literature, dominated by the single 28-patient RCT and its sibling cohorts from the same programme — the meta-analysis pools a very small, partly overlapping evidence base and cannot add certainty the primary studies do not have.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one small RCT (N = 28) plus concordant cohorts — direction consistent, certainty low; the at-amputation question rests on the cohort, not the trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small RCT (N = 28) plus concordant cohorts — direction consistent, certainty low; the at-amputation question rests on the cohort, not the trial
cards.people: One randomised trial of TMR for established postamputation pain (28 patients), one multi-institutional cohort of TMR at the time of amputation (51 vs 438 controls), one prospective single-arm series (33 patients) and a 5-study meta-analysis (127 patients).
cards.result: Randomised: phantom pain change favoured TMR by 3.4 points in intention-to-treat (P = 0.06), significant in the longitudinal model (P = 0.03). At amputation (cohort): median worst pain 1/10 with TMR versus 5/10 phantom and 4/10 residual in controls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), with the randomised N printed on the face.
cards.watchOut: Two different questions share this shelf: TMR as treatment for established neuroma/phantom pain (the RCT) and TMR as prevention at the time of amputation (the cohort). Quoting the trial's numbers for the prevention question, or the cohort's large gaps as if randomised, would each overstate the evidence.

shelves.title: VER-01 full-spectrum cannabis extract in chronic low back pain: pain fell 0.6 NRS points more than placebo in phase A, the randomised-withdrawal phase D missed its endpoint, and a head-to-head trial favoured VER-01 over opioids on constipation and pain
shelves.question: In adults with chronic low back pain, does the standardised full-spectrum cannabis extract VER-01, versus placebo, reduce pain intensity?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested product is VER-01, a standardised full-spectrum extract from Cannabis sativa DKJ127; the fetched records do not name its manufacturer, so none is printed, and these results must not be generalised to other cannabis preparations, which differ in composition. In the placebo-controlled phase 3 (n=820), 12-week pain fell 1.9 NRS points on VER-01 versus a mean difference of −0.6 points against placebo (p<0.001) — statistically clear, small on average — but the randomised-withdrawal phase D missed its primary endpoint (HR 0.75, p=0.288), so durability after stopping is not established by the design built to test it. Adverse events were commoner on VER-01 (83.3% vs 67.3%), mostly mild to moderate, with no signs of dependence or withdrawal reported. A second phase 3 (n=384) found VER-01 superior to a range of opioids on its primary gastrointestinal endpoint and modestly superior on pain over 6 months, though week-27 secondary endpoints alone were not significant. A 2026 systematic review of cannabinoids for low back pain found no class-wide effect and rested its chronic-low-back-pain conclusion substantially on this same VER-01 trial — corroboration of interpretation, not independent replication.

cards.headline: Phase 3 placebo-controlled trial, phase A (Karst 2025): pain difference −0.6 NRS points vs placebo (p<0.001); randomised-withdrawal phase D primary endpoint missed (HR 0.75, p=0.288)
cards.summary: Phase 3 placebo-controlled trial, phase A (Karst 2025): pain difference −0.6 NRS points vs placebo (p<0.001); randomised-withdrawal phase D primary endpoint missed (HR 0.75, p=0.288)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with randomised withdrawal (Karst 2025)
cards.people: 820 adults with chronic low back pain (VER-01 n=394; placebo n=426) in a multicentre phase 3 trial with a 12-week double-blind phase (phase A), a 6-month open-label extension (phase B), then either continuation (phase C) or randomised withdrawal (phase D). Phase A's primary endpoint was change in mean numeric rating scale (NRS) pain intensity; phase D's was time to treatment failure. Registered as NCT04940741.
cards.result: Phase A met its primary endpoint: mean pain reduction −1.9 NRS points on VER-01, a mean difference versus placebo of −0.6 (95% CI −0.9 to −0.3; p<0.001). The key secondary endpoint was also met in participants with a neuropathic pain component (NPSI mean difference −7.3; p=0.017). Phase D did not meet its primary endpoint (hazard ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.44–1.27; p=0.288), although pain rose more on placebo after withdrawal (mean difference 0.5; p=0.034). In phase A, adverse events occurred in 83.3% on VER-01 versus 67.3% on placebo (p<0.001), mostly mild to moderate and transient; no signs of dependence or withdrawal were reported.
cards.watchOut: Print the split plainly: a −0.6-point average advantage is below what most patients notice individually, and the phase designed to prove the effect persists — randomised withdrawal — missed. Open-label extension improvements (to −2.9 points) are uncontrolled and cannot be credited to the drug over time, expectancy and completer selection.

cards.headline: Phase 3 opioid-comparator trial (Meissner 2025): constipation relative risk 0.25 with VER-01 vs opioids; pain reduction over 6 months 2.50 vs 2.16 NRS points (difference 0.34, p=0.048)
cards.summary: Phase 3 opioid-comparator trial (Meissner 2025): constipation relative risk 0.25 with VER-01 vs opioids; pain reduction over 6 months 2.50 vs 2.16 NRS points (difference 0.34, p=0.048)
cards.type: Randomised, open comparator phase 3 trial versus opioids (Meissner 2025)
cards.people: 384 adults with chronic low back pain randomised 1:1 to VER-01 (n=192) or a range of commercially available opioids (n=192), with 3 weeks of titration, 24 weeks of treatment and 2 weeks of wash-out. The primary endpoint was the relative risk (labelled relative) of constipation after 27 weeks. Registered as NCT05610813 (EudraCT 2022-001358-41, as stated in the record).
cards.result: VER-01 patients were less likely to develop constipation (relative risk 0.25, 95% CI 0.09–0.69; p=0.007) and less likely to use laxatives (relative risk 0.34, 95% CI 0.18–0.65; p<0.001) — relative measures, printed as reported. Over 6 months, mean pain reduction was 2.50 NRS points on VER-01 versus 2.16 on opioids (mean difference 0.34, 95% CI 0.00–0.67; p=0.048), and sleep improved more on VER-01 (difference 0.45; p=0.009); however, secondary endpoints limited to week 27 alone were not significant.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was a heterogeneous range of opioids rather than a single drug or dose, the pain advantage (0.34 points) sits at the edge of significance with a confidence interval touching 0.00, and the cleaner result is the gastrointestinal one. A trial designed and powered around constipation should not be quoted as proof of superior analgesia.

cards.headline: Systematic review (Costa-Oliveira 2026): no class-wide cannabinoid effect for low back pain across 5 RCTs (1,072 participants) — the chronic-pain conclusion rests substantially on the VER-01 phase 3 carded above
cards.summary: Systematic review (Costa-Oliveira 2026): no class-wide cannabinoid effect for low back pain across 5 RCTs (1,072 participants) — the chronic-pain conclusion rests substantially on the VER-01 phase 3 carded above
cards.people: Five double-blind randomised trials (1,072 participants) of isolated cannabinoids, synthetic cannabinoids, vaporised cannabis products and standardised cannabis extracts for low back pain, migraine and medication-overuse headache, assessed with RoB 2 and GRADE; registered in PROSPERO as 582772, as printed in the record.
cards.result: The review found no support for a class-wide effect. In acute low back pain, a single 400-mg oral dose of cannabidiol was not superior to placebo. For chronic low back pain, the VER-01 phase 3 trial (carded above) showed improved pain intensity, disability, sleep quality and patient-reported outcomes versus placebo, and the review rated the VER-01 evidence moderate-certainty. THC-containing inhaled formulations carried more psychoactive adverse effects and possible functional unblinding.
cards.watchOut: This review adds interpretation, not patients: its chronic-low-back-pain content is the same VER-01 trial on the first card. It is carded because its class-level null — other cannabinoid preparations did not work — is exactly the guardrail against generalising VER-01's result to cannabis products generally.

cards.summary: Synthesis: VER-01 beats placebo by 0.6 NRS points at 12 weeks and opioids on constipation, but its withdrawal phase missed and no other group has replicated it
cards.people: Synthesis of the three reports carded on this shelf: the placebo-controlled phase 3 (n=820), the opioid-comparator phase 3 (n=384), and a systematic review whose chronic-low-back-pain evidence is substantially the first of these.
cards.result: The programme is internally consistent — small average pain benefit, better gastrointestinal tolerability than opioids, frequent mild-to-moderate adverse events — and externally unconfirmed: one sponsor programme, a missed withdrawal endpoint, and a systematic review that warns against extending the result to cannabinoids as a class.

shelves.title: ReActiv8 restorative neurostimulation for mechanical chronic low back pain: the sham-controlled primary endpoint was inconclusive (57.1% vs 46.6%, p=0.138), while an open-label trial vs medical management and 5-year follow-up favoured the device
shelves.question: In adults with refractory mechanical chronic low back pain and multifidus dysfunction who are not surgical candidates, does implanted restorative neurostimulation of the L2 medial branch (ReActiv8), versus sham or optimal medical management, improve pain and disability?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the central caveat on the face: in ReActiv8-B, the only sham-controlled trial (n=204), the primary responder endpoint at 120 days was inconclusive for superiority (57.1% vs 46.6%; difference 10.4%, 95% CI −3.3 to 24.1; p=0.138) — the blinded comparison did not prove the device beats sham. Prespecified secondary analyses favoured treatment, gains accrued after the sham group crossed over, and at 5 years the (by then uncontrolled) cohort showed large maintained improvements. The open-label RESTORE trial (n=203) found a large disability advantage over optimal medical management (ODI −19.7 vs −2.9 at 1 year), a design that cannot exclude expectancy and attention effects for an implanted device. The tested system is the ReActiv8 Restorative Neurostimulation system; the fetched records do not name its manufacturer, so none is printed. The population is narrow — refractory mechanical pain with a positive prone instability test indicating multifidus dysfunction and no surgical indication — and nothing here answers back pain generally. Serious procedure- or device-related adverse events were 3.9% in ReActiv8-B. Note: a two-year RESTORE report cited elsewhere was not found on PubMed this session; the carded RESTORE report is the 1-year publication.

cards.headline: ReActiv8-B sham-controlled trial (Gilligan 2021): primary responder endpoint inconclusive — 57.1% vs 46.6% at 120 days (difference 10.4%, 95% CI −3.3 to 24.1; p=0.138)
cards.summary: ReActiv8-B sham-controlled trial (Gilligan 2021): primary responder endpoint inconclusive — 57.1% vs 46.6% at 120 days (difference 10.4%, 95% CI −3.3 to 24.1; p=0.138)
cards.people: 204 adults with refractory mechanical chronic low back pain and a positive prone instability test indicating impaired multifidus control, implanted at 26 multidisciplinary centres and randomised to therapeutic (n=102) or low-level sham (n=102) stimulation of the medial branch of the dorsal ramus nerve, 30 minutes twice daily. The primary endpoint was the responder proportion (≥30% relief on the pain visual analogue scale without increased analgesics) at 120 days; after that assessment the sham group switched to therapeutic stimulation. Registered as NCT02577354.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was inconclusive in terms of treatment superiority: responders 57.1% on therapeutic stimulation versus 46.6% on sham (difference 10.4%, 95% CI −3.3 to 24.1; p=0.138). Prespecified secondary outcomes and analyses were consistent with a modest but clinically meaningful benefit at 120 days, and improvements continued to accrue in the combined cohort through 1 year after crossover. Serious procedure- or device-related adverse events occurred in 3.9%.
cards.watchOut: This is the only blinded test of the device, and it did not meet its primary endpoint — every favourable number elsewhere on this shelf comes from unblinded or post-crossover data. The sham itself (implantation plus low-level stimulation plus trial attention) produced a 46.6% responder rate, which is the context the 57.1% must be read against.

cards.headline: RESTORE trial (Schwab 2025): disability improved −19.7 vs −2.9 ODI points at 1 year versus optimal medical management (p<0.001) — open-label
cards.summary: RESTORE trial (Schwab 2025): disability improved −19.7 vs −2.9 ODI points at 1 year versus optimal medical management (p<0.001) — open-label
cards.type: Randomised, open-label trial versus optimal medical management (Schwab 2025)
cards.people: 203 patients (average age 47 years, average 11-year history of back pain) with chronic mechanical low back pain associated with multifidus dysfunction, no indication for or history of lumbar spine surgery, randomised at multiple centres to restorative neurostimulation with the ReActiv8 system or to optimal medical management (OMM). Primary endpoint: mean change in Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) at 1 year. Registered as NCT04803214.
cards.result: The primary endpoint favoured neurostimulation by a large margin: ODI change −19.7 (±1.4) versus −2.9 (±1.4) on OMM (p<0.001). Pain (NRS −3.6 vs −0.6) and quality of life (EQ-5D-5L 0.155 vs 0.008) also improved significantly more with the device (both p<0.001). The authors describe the therapy as safe and reversible; the abstract does not print adverse-event rates.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, implanted-device versus tablets-and-therapy: patients knew whether they had received an implant, and ODI and pain are self-reported — the design maximises expectancy effects in the device arm and disappointment effects in the control arm. The effect size is large enough to be interesting and the design weak enough that it cannot substitute for the missed sham-controlled endpoint.

cards.headline: ReActiv8-B 5-year follow-up (Gilligan 2024): pain VAS 7.3 → 2.4 cm and ODI 39.1 → 16.5 in the followed cohort — explicitly labelled follow-up report of the trial above, uncontrolled after crossover
cards.summary: ReActiv8-B 5-year follow-up (Gilligan 2024): pain VAS 7.3 → 2.4 cm and ODI 39.1 → 16.5 in the followed cohort — explicitly labelled follow-up report of the trial above, uncontrolled after crossover
cards.type: Five-year longitudinal follow-up of a randomised trial (Gilligan 2024) — explicitly labelled report of ReActiv8-B
cards.people: The ReActiv8-B cohort (N=204 implanted; n=126 assessed at 5 years) with refractory mechanical chronic low back pain and multifidus dysfunction; after the 120-day blinded phase all participants could receive therapeutic stimulation, so 5-year outcomes are a single-cohort follow-up analysed by intention-to-treat principles with mixed-effects modelling for missing data. Registered as NCT02577354 — the same trial as the first card.
cards.result: At 5 years, pain VAS had improved from 7.3 to 2.4 cm (−4.9; p<0.0001) and 71.8% of participants had a ≥50% pain reduction; ODI improved from 39.1 to 16.5 (−22.7; p<0.0001) with 61.1% improving by ≥20 points; EQ-5D-5L rose from 0.585 to 0.807. Of 52 participants on opioids at baseline who had a 5-year visit, 46% had discontinued and 23% had decreased intake. No lead migrations were observed, and the authors report a safety profile comparing favourably with other neurostimulator treatments.
cards.watchOut: Durability in a cohort where everyone eventually received the device, 126 of 204 remained at 5 years, and there is no parallel control: natural history, co-interventions, completer selection and the passage of 5 years are all inside these numbers. It shows benefit can persist in responders who stay in follow-up; it cannot show the device caused the persistence.

cards.type: Prospective observational cohort, post-market (Thomson 2021) — labelled observational
cards.people: 42 patients with longstanding chronic mechanical low back pain treated with restorative neurostimulation in a prospective post-market follow-up, assessed at 45, 90 and 180 days and at 1 and 2 years after device activation; 37 completed 2-year follow-up. Registered as NCT01985230.

cards.headline: Synthesis: an implanted therapy whose blinded trial missed, whose open-label trial hit by a wide margin, and whose long-term cohort kept its gains — in a narrowly selected minority of back-pain patients
cards.summary: Synthesis: an implanted therapy whose blinded trial missed, whose open-label trial hit by a wide margin, and whose long-term cohort kept its gains — in a narrowly selected minority of back-pain patients
cards.people: Synthesis of the four reports carded on this shelf: ReActiv8-B (n=204, sham-controlled) and its 5-year follow-up, the RESTORE trial versus medical management (n=203), and the ReActiv8-A post-market cohort (n=42).
cards.result: Read in design order, the evidence weakens as the controls loosen: inconclusive against sham at 120 days; strongly positive against unblinded medical management at 1 year; large maintained gains at 5 years without a control. The consistent thread is a real signal in carefully selected patients with demonstrated multifidus dysfunction; the unresolved question is how much of it is the stimulation itself.
cards.watchOut: POSSIBLE (benefit): the stamp is capped by the inconclusive sham-controlled primary endpoint. Quoting RESTORE or the 5-year figures without ReActiv8-B's p=0.138 misstates this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 34534176, 39812968, 38483366, 34478115). No additional source.

shelves.title: Pain reprocessing therapy for primary chronic back pain: 66% were pain-free or nearly so after 4 weeks vs 20% on placebo and 10% on usual care in the single pivotal trial — not yet independently replicated at scale
shelves.question: In adults with primary (nociplastic) chronic back pain, does pain reprocessing therapy, versus placebo injection or usual care, reduce pain intensity?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The tested intervention is the specific Pain Reprocessing Therapy protocol (Gordon/Ashar) — one physician telehealth session plus eight psychological sessions over 4 weeks teaching patients to reattribute pain to nondangerous brain processes — not generic pain psychology. In the Boulder Back Pain Study (n=151), 66% of the PRT group were pain-free or nearly pain-free (0–1 of 10) post-treatment versus 20% on open-label placebo injection and 10% on usual care, with mean pain 1.18 vs 2.84 vs 3.13, maintained at 1 year. Three qualifications belong on the face: the population was selected primary back pain with low-to-moderate baseline pain (mean 4.10 of 10) and disability, treated by experienced therapists in a university setting; the trial is single and not yet independently replicated at scale — the only independent randomised report is a 53-person feasibility pilot in chronic widespread pain, a different condition; and the 5-year follow-up report's PubMed record carries no abstract figures this session, so no 5-year numbers are printed. A secondary analysis supports the proposed mechanism: increases in mind-brain attribution mediated the treatment effect.

cards.headline: Boulder Back Pain Study (Ashar 2021): 66% pain-free or nearly pain-free after PRT vs 20% on placebo injection and 10% on usual care; mean pain 1.18 vs 2.84 vs 3.13
cards.summary: Boulder Back Pain Study (Ashar 2021): 66% pain-free or nearly pain-free after PRT vs 20% on placebo injection and 10% on usual care; mean pain 1.18 vs 2.84 vs 3.13
cards.people: 151 adults (54% female; mean age 41.1 years) with primary chronic back pain of mean 10.0 years' duration, mean baseline pain intensity 4.10 (SD 1.26) of 10 and disability 23.34 of 100, randomised in a university research setting to pain reprocessing therapy (1 telehealth physician session plus 8 psychological sessions over 4 weeks; n=50), open-label subcutaneous saline placebo injection (n=51) or usual care (n=50), with fMRI and 1-year follow-up. Registered as NCT03294148.
cards.result: At post-treatment, mean pain was 1.18 (SD 1.24) on PRT versus 2.84 (1.64) on placebo and 3.13 (1.45) on usual care (Hedges g −1.14 vs placebo and −1.74 vs usual care; p<0.001). Pain-free or nearly pain-free (pain 0–1 of 10): 33 of 50 (66%) on PRT, 10 of 51 (20%) on placebo, 5 of 50 (10%) on usual care. Effects were maintained at 1 year (mean pain 1.51 vs 2.79 vs 3.00). fMRI showed reduced evoked-pain responses in anterior midcingulate and anterior prefrontal cortex for PRT versus placebo.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes this large (g up to −1.74) in a single 151-person trial of a psychological treatment should be expected to shrink on replication: participants were selected for primary pain with low-to-moderate baseline severity, therapists were the protocol's own experts, and neither participants nor therapists could be blinded — the placebo arm was an open-label injection, not a matched psychological placebo.
cards.source: Boulder Back Pain Study — pain reprocessing therapy randomised trial (Ashar 2021) — Ashar YK et al. cards.headline: Secondary analysis (Ashar 2023): reattributing pain to mind-brain processes rose to 51% of attributions on PRT vs 8% on control and mediated pain relief — explicitly labelled secondary report of the Boulder trial
cards.summary: Secondary analysis (Ashar 2023): reattributing pain to mind-brain processes rose to 51% of attributions on PRT vs 8% on control and mediated pain relief — explicitly labelled secondary report of the Boulder trial
cards.type: Secondary (mechanism) analysis of a randomised trial (Ashar 2023)
cards.people: The same 151 Boulder trial participants, who listed their top three perceived causes of their pain in their own words before and after treatment; attributions were coded by masked raters as mind/brain-related or not, with automated natural-language scoring validated against the human coding. This is an explicitly labelled secondary analysis of the trial carded above, not a new trial.
cards.result: Mind/brain-related attributions rose from 10% at baseline to 51% of post-treatment attributions in the PRT group versus 8% in the control conditions (attribution-score effects g=1.95 vs placebo and g=2.06 vs usual care). Increases in mind-brain attribution were associated with pain reduction at post-treatment (standardised β −0.25; p=0.04) and mediated the PRT effect on 1-year pain intensity (β −0.35; p=0.05).
cards.watchOut: Mediation within a single trial shows the treatment moved its intended target and that movement tracked outcome — supportive of the mechanism, but the mediator was measured, not randomised, so confounding of the mediator–outcome link remains. It adds no new patients and no independent efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Secondary analysis of the Boulder trial — pain reattribution mechanism (Ashar 2023) — Ashar YK et al. Reattribution to Mind-Brain Processes and Recovery From Chronic Back Pain: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA network open. 2023. PMID: 37768666. cards.headline: Five-year follow-up (Ashar 2025): the Boulder cohort was followed to 5 years — the fetched record carries no abstract or outcome figures, so no 5-year numbers are printed
cards.summary: Five-year follow-up (Ashar 2025): the Boulder cohort was followed to 5 years — the fetched record carries no abstract or outcome figures, so no 5-year numbers are printed
cards.type: Five-year follow-up report of a randomised trial (Ashar 2025) — explicitly labelled follow-up report
cards.people: Participants of the Boulder Back Pain Study (n=151 randomised to PRT, placebo injection or usual care) followed to 5 years; the report is a secondary analysis of that randomised trial, published as a research letter in JAMA Psychiatry (pages 1049–1051, as printed in the record).
cards.result: The fetched PubMed record for this report contains no abstract text beyond a plain-language summary stating that it provides 5-year follow-up data for the three groups; it prints no outcome figures. Accordingly this card records the follow-up's existence and design only — any 5-year percentages quoted elsewhere are not confirmed by a fetched record this session and are deliberately not reproduced.

cards.type: Pilot randomised clinical trial — feasibility primary outcome (Sit 2026)
cards.people: 53 adults with chronic widespread pain (a nociplastic condition distinct from the back-pain population above), randomised 1:1 in Hong Kong to PRT (n=27; one evaluation/education session plus eight weekly 1-hour individual sessions) or psychoeducation control (n=26; four biweekly group sessions) over 12 weeks. cards.result: Feasibility was demonstrated: 416 people screened, 53 enrolled over 13 months, PRT attendance averaged 7.8 sessions, dropout was 11.1% on PRT versus 27.0% on control, and data retention was 85% at 8 weeks and 79% at 12 weeks. Favourable trends for PRT were observed in all secondary outcomes (pain intensity, interference, anxiety, depression, kinesiophobia, fatigue, quality of life) at 12 weeks; the abstract prints no efficacy effect sizes, so none are quoted.
cards.watchOut: A different condition (widespread pain, not back pain), a pilot powered for feasibility, and trends without figures: this card's value is that an independent group, in another country, could deliver the protocol and saw no contrary signal. cards.people: Synthesis of the four reports carded on this shelf: the Boulder trial (n=151), its reattribution secondary analysis and 5-year follow-up report, and an independent 53-person feasibility pilot in chronic widespread pain.
cards.result: The Boulder result is the strongest single-trial result for any psychological back-pain treatment in this library — two-thirds pain-free or nearly so at 4 weeks, maintained at 1 year — and it stands alone: every efficacy number traces to those 151 selected patients. shelves.title: Skeletal turnover (physiology): calcium-tracer kinetics put whole-skeleton remodelling at ~0.34 g of calcium turned over per day before the menopause, rising after it — and tetracycline-labelled iliac biopsies give a mineral apposition rate of 0.53 µm/day, formation rates of ~15%/year in younger women, and remodelling periods from 0.28 to 4.5 years
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how fast does the skeleton turn over — what do calcium-tracer kinetics and transiliac bone-biopsy histomorphometry measure as activation frequency and bone-remodelling period, and what fraction of the skeleton is replaced per year in young adults versus after menopause?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep — bone-physiology sections): the adult skeleton is continuously remodelled by coupled resorption and formation, and the textbook's account is that a measurable fraction of bone is replaced each year, faster in trabecular than cortical bone. This shelf's numbers come from the two classic human measurement traditions, which cross-check each other. Calcium-tracer kinetics under metabolic-balance conditions (Heaney 1978; 151 perimenopausal women) put premenopausal mineral accretion at 0.337 g/day and resorption at 0.358 g/day — near-balanced turnover of roughly a third of a gram of calcium a day — rising after the menopause in untreated women to 0.387 and 0.425 g/day, with a more negative computed skeletal balance (−0.038 vs −0.021 g/day); oestrogen-treated postmenopausal women matched the premenopausal values. Tetracycline-labelled transiliac biopsy histomorphometry (Recker 1988; 34 normal postmenopausal women recruited to define normal values) gives the tissue-level clock: mineral apposition rate 0.53 ± 0.08 µm/day, volume-based bone formation rate ranging 0.7–28%/year, and a remodelling period of 0.28–4.5 years. A head-to-head study (Eastell 1988; 12 younger vs 11 older normal women) found histomorphometric bone formation rate higher in the older group (31.1 ± 4.9 vs 15.1 ± 2.7%/year) while calcium-kinetic accretion did not differ (5.9 ± 1.0 vs 7.5 ± 1.2 in the record's units) — the methods disagree about the age direction, and the card prints that disagreement rather than smoothing it. This shelf is the quantitative-rate companion to pack #6301 (the RANK/RANKL/OPG molecular coupling set-point) and pack #6254 (calcium absorption); it cards none of their references and answers none of their questions. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Heaney 1978: calcium-kinetic remodelling in 151 normal perimenopausal women ran at 0.337 g/day accretion and 0.358 g/day resorption before the menopause — and rose to 0.387 / 0.425 g/day, with a worse balance, in untreated postmenopausal women (N = 151)
cards.summary: Heaney 1978: calcium-kinetic remodelling in 151 normal perimenopausal women ran at 0.337 g/day accretion and 0.358 g/day resorption before the menopause — and rose to 0.387 / 0.425 g/day, with a worse balance, in untreated postmenopausal women (N = 151)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (calcium-tracer kinetics and metabolic balance, Heaney programme)
cards.people: 151 normal perimenopausal women in three groups — premenopausal, untreated postmenopausal, and postmenopausal treated with oestrogen (mean dose 0.0188 mg equivalents of ethinyl estradiol) — with bone remodelling measured by a calcium-kinetic method; 15 of the women were also studied in paired fashion across the menopause.
cards.result: Premenopausal women exhibited remodelling rates of 0.337 g/day Ca for mineral accretion and 0.358 g/day Ca for mineral resorption, a computed skeletal balance of −0.021 g/day Ca. Oestrogen-treated postmenopausal women were essentially identical (0.332 and 0.351 g/day). Untreated postmenopausal women exhibited higher rates — 0.387 g/day accretion and 0.425 g/day resorption — with a computed balance of −0.038 g/day Ca, significantly higher turnover than either other group. The paired studies across menopause in 15 women showed a rise in remodelling rates virtually identical to the between-group differences. The authors interpret menopause as a partial release from an inhibition of skeletal resorption.
cards.watchOut: Whole-skeleton calcium flux in grams per day, not a percentage of bone replaced: converting it to a yearly skeletal fraction needs total skeletal calcium, which this record does not print — the percentage-per-year figures on this shelf come from the biopsy cards, measured differently.
cards.source: Heaney RP et al. Menopausal changes in bone remodeling. The Journal of laboratory and clinical medicine. 1978. PMID: 739174. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Recker 1988: normal postmenopausal iliac histomorphometry — mineral apposition rate 0.53 ± 0.08 µm/day, volume-based formation rate 0.7–28%/year, remodelling period 0.28–4.5 years (N = 34)
cards.summary: Recker 1988: normal postmenopausal iliac histomorphometry — mineral apposition rate 0.53 ± 0.08 µm/day, volume-based formation rate 0.7–28%/year, remodelling period 0.28–4.5 years (N = 34)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (transiliac biopsy histomorphometry normative cohort, Recker programme)
cards.people: 34 healthy postmenopausal women recruited solely to establish normal bone histomorphometry, given in vivo fluorochrome (tetracycline) labelling before transiliac bone biopsy; stained and unstained undecalcified sections were scored with a Merz grid, with results also grouped by ages 45–54, 55–64 and 65–74.
cards.result: The mineral apposition rate (MAR) was 0.53 ± 0.08 µm/day in cancellous bone — similar to previous cancellous reports but one-third less than in cortical bone — and MAR declined markedly with age. Double-label surface ranged widely, from 0.5 to 8.0% of bone surface. Using double-label surface as the mineralising surface, volume-based bone formation rate (BFR/BV) ranged from 0.7 to 28%/year, and the remodelling period (Rm.P) varied from 0.28 to 4.5 years; calculations using other mineralising-surface conventions are also presented in the paper. The spread is the finding: normal turnover is a wide range, not a point.
cards.watchOut: Iliac-crest cancellous bone in postmenopausal women: cortical bone turns over more slowly (the record's own MAR comparison), other skeletal sites differ, and the derived rates move with the mineralising-surface convention chosen — the paper prints the alternatives.
cards.source: Recker RR et al. Static and tetracycline-based bone histomorphometric data from 34 normal postmenopausal females. Journal of bone and mineral research. 1988. PMID: 3213608. cards.headline: Eastell 1988: histomorphometry said bone formation was higher in older normal women (31.1 vs 15.1%/year) while calcium kinetics said accretion was the same — a printed method disagreement (N = 23)
cards.summary: Eastell 1988: histomorphometry said bone formation was higher in older normal women (31.1 vs 15.1%/year) while calcium kinetics said accretion was the same — a printed method disagreement (N = 23)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (concurrent histomorphometry, calcium kinetics and markers, Riggs programme)
cards.people: 12 younger (30–41 years) and 11 older (55–73 years) normal women assessed concurrently by bone histomorphometry of iliac biopsy, calcium kinetics, and biochemical markers (serum bone Gla-protein/osteocalcin and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase).
cards.result: Bone formation was higher in the older women by serum bone Gla-protein (1.67 ± 0.07 vs 1.14 ± 0.10 nmol/L; P < 0.01), by serum bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (388 ± 42 vs 223 ± 22 nanokatal/L; P < 0.01), and by histomorphometric bone formation rate (31.1 ± 4.9 vs 15.1 ± 2.7%/year; P < 0.01) — but similar in the two groups when accretion was assessed by calcium kinetics (5.9 ± 1.0 vs 7.5 ± 1.2; P = NS, in the record's reported units). The authors attribute the discrepancy to age-related factors including reduced mineralisation of completed osteons and failure to correct for decreased total skeletal calcium in the older group, and conclude the data call into question the traditional belief that bone turnover decreases in older women.
cards.watchOut: Small groups (12 and 11) and the two gold-standard methods point in opposite directions on ageing: this card is carded precisely so the shelf does not print a single age trend the primary record contradicts.
cards.source: Eastell R et al. Bone formation rate in older normal women: concurrent assessment with bone histomorphometry, calcium kinetics, and biochemical markers. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 1988. PMID: 3262119. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the skeleton turns over at ~0.34 g of calcium a day before the menopause and faster after it; at tissue level a remodelling cycle takes ~0.3–4.5 years and formation replaces roughly 15%/year in younger women by biopsy — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: the skeleton turns over at ~0.34 g of calcium a day before the menopause and faster after it; at tissue level a remodelling cycle takes ~0.3–4.5 years and formation replaces roughly 15%/year in younger women by biopsy — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Carded human data: 151 perimenopausal women by calcium kinetics, 34 normal postmenopausal women by labelled iliac biopsy, and 23 normal women (12 younger, 11 older) by both methods concurrently (208 women in total).
cards.result: Two independent human measurement traditions describe the same system at different scales. Whole-skeleton tracer kinetics: accretion 0.337 and resorption 0.358 g Ca/day premenopausally, near balance (−0.021 g/day), rising after untreated menopause to 0.387/0.425 g/day with balance −0.038 g/day, and normalised by oestrogen. Tissue histomorphometry: mineral apposition 0.53 ± 0.08 µm/day, volume-based formation 0.7–28%/year across normal postmenopausal women, remodelling period 0.28–4.5 years; in younger women the biopsy formation rate was 15.1 ± 2.7%/year. Where the methods conflict — the direction of change with age — the conflict is printed on the Eastell card, not resolved by assertion. Activation frequency as a standalone normative number was not printed in any fetched record, so none is claimed; the remodelling period and formation rate are the carded expressions of the same clock. Cross-points: the molecular coupling that sets this rate is pack #6301 (RANK/RANKL/OPG); intestinal calcium absorption is pack #6254 — neither is duplicated here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: All carded cohorts are women, mostly peri- or postmenopausal, and the biopsy data are iliac cancellous bone: male, cortical and non-iliac turnover rates are not established by this shelf, and the textbook's single 'percent per year' figure should be read against the wide measured ranges printed here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Heaney RP et al. J Lab Clin Med. 1978 (PMID: 739174); Recker RR et al. J Bone Miner Res. 1988 (PMID: 3213608); Eastell R et al. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 1988 (PMID: 3262119). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall; Boron & Boulpaep (bone physiology) — framing, not evidence cards.

shelves.title: Dotinurad (selective URAT1 inhibitor) for gout and hyperuricaemia
shelves.question: In adults with gout and hyperuricaemia, does the selective URAT1 inhibitor dotinurad, compared with febuxostat or placebo, lower serum urate to target?
shelves.balance: The urate-lowering answer is consistent across the whole Japanese and Chinese programme. In the China phase 3 trial in gout (n=451), dotinurad 4 mg/day was superior to febuxostat 40 mg/day on the primary endpoint: 73.6% versus 38.1% reached serum urate ≤6.0 mg/dL at week 24. In Japan, phase 3 trials showed dotinurad titrated to 2 mg/day was non-inferior to febuxostat 40 mg/day (urate fall 41.82% versus 44.00%; n=203) and non-inferior to benzbromarone 50 mg/day (45.9% versus 43.8%; n=201), and the phase 2 dose-finding study (n=80) showed a clear dose-response against placebo (urate falls of 37.03%, 50.91% and 64.37% at 1, 2 and 4 mg versus 0.85% on placebo). SINGLE-REGION flag: all trials are from Japan (where dotinurad has been approved since 2020) and China; there is no trial programme outside East Asia. SURROGATE flag: every endpoint is serum urate — no trial measures gout flares, tophus resolution, kidney outcomes or cardiovascular events, so urate lowering is not equated here with flare prevention. Adverse-event profiles were similar to the comparators in each trial, with no noteworthy safety concerns raised in the phase 3 reports.

cards.summary: China phase 3 in gout (2025): dotinurad 4 mg beat febuxostat 40 mg — 73.6% versus 38.1% reached serum urate ≤6.0 mg/dL at week 24, n = 451
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind active-controlled trial, Arthritis & Rheumatology 2025
cards.people: 451 patients with gout in China, randomised 1:1 to oral dotinurad or febuxostat (441 in the full analysis set). The primary comparison was dotinurad titrated to 4 mg/day versus febuxostat 40 mg/day; a secondary comparison tested dotinurad 2 mg/day against febuxostat 40 mg/day at week 12.
cards.result: The responder rate (serum urate ≤6.0 mg/dL) at week 24 was significantly higher on dotinurad 4 mg/day than febuxostat 40 mg/day (73.6% vs 38.1%; adjusted difference 35.9 percentage points, 95% CI 27.4 to 44.4; P < 0.0001), and at week 12 dotinurad 2 mg/day was non-inferior to febuxostat 40 mg/day (55.5% vs 50.5%; adjusted difference 5.2%, 95% CI −3.7 to 14.2). Incidences of treatment-emergent adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: The comparator dose matters: febuxostat was fixed at 40 mg/day, a starting dose in many countries, so superiority here is against that dose, not against titrated febuxostat. Serum urate is a surrogate; flares were not the endpoint.
cards.source: Sun J, Wang Y, Cheng Y, et al. Efficacy and Safety of Dotinurad Versus Febuxostat for the Treatment of Gout: A Randomized, Multicenter, Double-Blind, Phase 3 Trial in China. Arthritis Rheumatol. 2025;77(12):1757-1766. PMID: 40417858. No registry ID appears in the fetched record. cards.headline: Japan phase 3 versus febuxostat (2020): dotinurad titrated to 2 mg was non-inferior to febuxostat 40 mg on urate lowering (41.82% vs 44.00%), n = 203
cards.summary: Japan phase 3 versus febuxostat (2020): dotinurad titrated to 2 mg was non-inferior to febuxostat 40 mg on urate lowering (41.82% vs 44.00%), n = 203
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial, Clinical and Experimental Nephrology 2020
cards.people: 203 Japanese patients with hyperuricaemia with or without gout, randomised to dotinurad (started at 0.5 mg/day, titrated to 2 mg/day) or febuxostat (started at 10 mg/day, titrated to 40 mg/day) over 14 weeks, in a forced-titration, double-blind, active-controlled design.
cards.result: The percent change in serum uric acid from baseline to the final visit was 41.82% on dotinurad and 44.00% on febuxostat (mean difference −2.17 percentage points, 95% CI −5.26 to 0.92); the lower limit sat above the −10% non-inferiority margin, demonstrating non-inferiority of dotinurad to febuxostat. The profiles of adverse events and adverse drug reactions raised no noteworthy safety concerns in either group.
cards.watchOut: A mixed population (hyperuricaemia with or without gout) and a non-inferiority design: the trial shows dotinurad is not worse than febuxostat by more than the margin, not that it is better. Fourteen weeks only.
cards.source: Hosoya T, Furuno K, Kanda S. A non-inferiority study of the novel selective urate reabsorption inhibitor dotinurad versus febuxostat in hyperuricemic patients with or without gout. cards.headline: Japan phase 3 versus benzbromarone (2020): dotinurad 2 mg was non-inferior to benzbromarone 50 mg (urate fall 45.9% vs 43.8%), n = 201
cards.summary: Japan phase 3 versus benzbromarone (2020): dotinurad 2 mg was non-inferior to benzbromarone 50 mg (urate fall 45.9% vs 43.8%), n = 201
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial, Clinical and Experimental Nephrology 2020
cards.people: 201 Japanese patients with hyperuricaemia with or without gout, randomised to dotinurad 2 mg (n=102) or benzbromarone 50 mg (n=99) once daily for 14 weeks, with dose escalation, in a double-blind parallel-group design.
cards.result: The mean percent change in serum uric acid from baseline to the final visit was 45.9% on dotinurad and 43.8% on benzbromarone; the 95% confidence interval for the difference (−1.27 to 5.37%) verified non-inferiority against the predefined margin. The incidence of adverse events and adverse drug reactions was comparable between the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Benzbromarone is itself a URAT1 inhibitor unavailable in many countries (hepatotoxicity history), so this comparison mainly establishes class-equivalent urate lowering. Mixed gout/hyperuricaemia population; urate endpoint only.
cards.source: Hosoya T, Sano T, Sasaki T, et al. Dotinurad versus benzbromarone in Japanese hyperuricemic patient with or without gout: a randomized, double-blind, parallel-group, phase 3 study. cards.headline: Japan early phase 2 dose-finding (2020): urate fell 37.03%, 50.91% and 64.37% at dotinurad 1, 2 and 4 mg versus 0.85% on placebo over 8 weeks, n = 80
cards.summary: Japan early phase 2 dose-finding (2020): urate fell 37.03%, 50.91% and 64.37% at dotinurad 1, 2 and 4 mg versus 0.85% on placebo over 8 weeks, n = 80
cards.type: Early phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-finding study, Clinical and Experimental Nephrology 2020
cards.people: 80 Japanese patients with hyperuricaemia with or without gout, randomised to dotinurad 1, 2 or 4 mg once daily, or placebo, for 8 weeks in a dose-escalation, double-blind, placebo-controlled design.
cards.result: The mean percent change in serum uric acid at the final visit was 37.03%, 50.91% and 64.37% at dotinurad 1, 2 and 4 mg versus 0.85% on placebo — a clear dose-response. The proportions reaching serum uric acid ≤6.0 mg/dL were 75.0%, 89.5% and 95.2% across the dose groups versus none on placebo. The incidence of adverse events was comparable among all groups and no serious adverse event was found.
cards.watchOut: Small (about 20 per arm) and short (8 weeks); its role is the placebo comparison and dose-response that the active-controlled phase 3 trials lack. 'None on placebo' reaching target reflects an 8-week window in untreated hyperuricaemia.
cards.source: Hosoya T, Sano T, Sasaki T, et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: dotinurad reliably lowers urate to target across four randomised trials — in East Asia, on a surrogate endpoint
cards.summary: Synthesis: dotinurad reliably lowers urate to target across four randomised trials — in East Asia, on a surrogate endpoint
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: China phase 3 in gout (451 randomised), Japan phase 3 versus febuxostat (203), Japan phase 3 versus benzbromarone (201) and Japan phase 2 dose-finding (80) — 935 randomised patients in total.
cards.result: Every comparison agrees: dotinurad lowers serum urate dose-dependently, far beyond placebo, at least as well as febuxostat 40 mg and benzbromarone 50 mg, and better than febuxostat 40 mg on target attainment at the 4 mg dose in gout. That concordance earns LIKELY for the urate question asked. The limits are equally clear: all evidence is Japanese or Chinese, the endpoint is a blood level rather than flares or outcomes, and the febuxostat comparator was a fixed 40 mg dose.
cards.watchOut: Do not convert urate lowering into a flare or kidney-outcome claim: no dotinurad trial has measured those endpoints. The newer URAT1 agent pozdeutinurad (AR882) is conference-abstract only and is not part of this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the four cards above (PMIDs 40417858, 31970593, 31980978, 31754882). No additional source.

shelves.title: Cannabinoids for fibromyalgia pain and sleep: small trials, split by outcome
shelves.question: In adults with fibromyalgia, do cannabinoids (nabilone, dronabinol/THC), versus placebo or amitriptyline, reduce pain and improve sleep?
shelves.mesh: Analgesics/therapeutic use · Anxiety/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Dronabinol/analogs & derivatives, therapeutic use · Fibromyalgia/complications · Humans · Middle Aged · Pain/drug therapy, etiology · Pain Measurement · Placebos · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The controlled evidence is three small trials that do not tell one story. For pain: Skrabek 2008 (n=40) found pharmaceutical nabilone improved pain and function scores at 4 weeks, with all benefit lost after washout; Ware 2010 (n=29) found no pain effect at all; van de Donk 2019 (n=20, single inhalations of defined pharmaceutical-grade varieties) found no variety beat placebo on spontaneous pain overall. For sleep: Ware 2010 found nabilone superior to low-dose amitriptyline (Insomnia Severity Index difference 3.2) over 2 weeks. The largest dataset, a 367-patient observational cohort, reports pain falling from a median 9.0 to 5.0 over 6 months with mostly mild adverse effects — but it has no control group and cannot estimate efficacy. Clarification exception applied in full: the tested products were pharmaceutical nabilone and named Bedrocan varieties of exactly known THC/CBD content; dispensary cannabis is not interchangeable with them. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Skrabek 2008 (nabilone RCT, N = 40): pain VAS fell 2.04 points and FIQ 12.07 points on pharmaceutical nabilone at 4 weeks (p<.02) — and all benefit was lost after washout
cards.summary: Skrabek 2008 (nabilone RCT, N = 40): pain VAS fell 2.04 points and FIQ 12.07 points on pharmaceutical nabilone at 4 weeks (p<.02) — and all benefit was lost after washout
cards.people: 40 patients with fibromyalgia, titrated on nabilone from 0.5 mg at bedtime to 1 mg twice daily over 4 weeks or matching placebo, with outcomes at 2 and 4 weeks and reassessment after a 4-week washout.
cards.result: At 4 weeks the nabilone group improved significantly on visual analogue pain (-2.04, p<.02), Fibromyalgia Impact Questionnaire (-12.07, p<.02) and anxiety (-1.67, p<.02); the placebo group did not improve. The nabilone group had more side effects per person at 2 and 4 weeks. After washout, the benefits were lost and scores returned to baseline (per the companion report of this trial).
cards.watchOut: Forty patients and 4 weeks: the largest controlled pain signal on this shelf is also short and small, the effect does not survive stopping the drug, and side effects (drowsiness, dry mouth, vertigo, ataxia in the trial reports) were commoner on nabilone. The tested product was pharmaceutical nabilone at defined doses — not dispensary cannabis.
cards.source: Skrabek RQ et al. Nabilone for the treatment of pain in fibromyalgia. J Pain. 2008. PMID: 17974490. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ware 2010 (nabilone versus amitriptyline crossover, N = 29 completers): sleep better on nabilone (Insomnia Severity Index difference 3.2) — pain unchanged (the treatment made no difference to pain, mood or quality of life)
cards.summary: Ware 2010 (nabilone versus amitriptyline crossover, N = 29 completers): sleep better on nabilone (Insomnia Severity Index difference 3.2) — pain unchanged (the treatment made no difference to pain, mood or quality of life)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind active-control crossover trial — N = 31 enrolled, 29 completed
cards.people: 31 patients with fibromyalgia and chronic insomnia (29 completed; 26 women, mean age 49.5 years), each receiving nabilone 0.5-1.0 mg at bedtime and amitriptyline 10-20 mg at bedtime for 2 weeks each, separated by a 2-week washout.
cards.result: Both drugs improved sleep, but nabilone was superior to amitriptyline on the Insomnia Severity Index (difference 3.2; 95% CI 1.2 to 5.3) and marginally better on sleep restfulness, though not on wakefulness. No effects on pain, mood or quality of life were observed (the treatment made no difference on those outcomes). Adverse events were mostly mild to moderate and more frequent with nabilone — dizziness, nausea and dry mouth commonest.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks per drug in 29 people, against a low-dose active comparator rather than placebo: this supports a short-term sleep claim only, and the same trial is a null for pain — which is why this shelf does not let the Skrabek pain result stand unqualified.
cards.source: Ware MA et al. The effects of nabilone on sleep in fibromyalgia: results of a randomized controlled trial. Anesth Analg. 2010. PMID: 20007734. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: van de Donk 2019 (inhaled pharmaceutical-grade cannabis, 4-way crossover, N = 20): no variety beat placebo on spontaneous or electrical pain overall; THC varieties raised pressure pain threshold; Bediol gave more 30% pain-score responders (90% versus 55%, p=0.01)
cards.summary: van de Donk 2019 (inhaled pharmaceutical-grade cannabis, 4-way crossover, N = 20): no variety beat placebo on spontaneous or electrical pain overall; THC varieties raised pressure pain threshold; Bediol gave more 30% pain-score responders (90% versus 55%, p=0.01)
cards.type: Experimental randomised placebo-controlled 4-way crossover trial — N = 20
cards.people: 20 chronic pain patients with fibromyalgia receiving, in random order, single vaporised inhalations of four pharmaceutical-grade cannabis varieties of exactly known content: Bedrocan (22.4 mg THC, <1 mg CBD), Bediol (13.4 mg THC, 17.8 mg CBD), Bedrolite (18.4 mg CBD, <1 mg THC) — all Bedrocan International BV, Veendam, the Netherlands — and a placebo variety with no THC or CBD; outcomes measured for 3 hours.
cards.result: None of the treatments had an effect greater than placebo on spontaneous or electrical pain responses overall. More participants on Bediol showed a 30% decrease in spontaneous pain scores than on placebo (90% versus 55%, p=0.01), with pain scores correlating with the magnitude of drug high. THC-containing varieties significantly increased pressure pain threshold versus placebo (p<0.01). Inhaled CBD raised THC plasma levels but diminished THC's analgesic effects.
cards.watchOut: A single-inhalation, 3-hour experimental study in 20 patients — it tests pharmacology, not treatment. Its headline is a null on spontaneous pain, and the responder contrast sits inside that null; quoting the 90% versus 55% without the overall null would misrepresent the trial. Product naming is exact here because the varieties are defined pharmaceutical preparations; dispensary cannabis of unknown content is not interchangeable with them.
cards.source: van de Donk T et al. An experimental randomized study on the analgesic effects of pharmaceutical-grade cannabis in chronic pain patients with fibromyalgia. Pain. 2019. PMID: 30585986. cards.headline: Sagy 2019 (prospective observational cannabis cohort, N = 367): pain intensity fell from a median 9.0 to 5.0 over 6 months, response rate 70.8% — uncontrolled, labelled as such
cards.summary: Sagy 2019 (prospective observational cannabis cohort, N = 367): pain intensity fell from a median 9.0 to 5.0 over 6 months, response rate 70.8% — uncontrolled, labelled as such
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort (observational — labelled as such) — N = 367
cards.people: 367 fibromyalgia patients (mean age 52.9 years; 82.0% women) treated with medical cannabis at a specialised clinic in Israel between 2015 and 2017 and willing to complete questionnaires, followed for 6 months; 28 patients (7.6%) stopped treatment before the 6-month follow-up.
cards.result: The 6-month response rate was 70.8%; pain intensity fell from a median of 9.0 at baseline to 5.0 (p<0.001), and 194 patients (81.1% of those assessed) achieved treatment response. Common adverse effects were mild: dizziness 7.9%, dry mouth 6.7%, gastrointestinal symptoms 5.4%. The authors state that standardisation of compounds and regimens is required.
cards.watchOut: No control group, self-selected clinic patients, questionnaire outcomes and non-standardised products: regression to the mean, expectancy and concurrent care can each produce a fall like this, so the cohort can describe tolerability but cannot estimate efficacy. It is carded for scale and safety context only, and it does not raise the stamp.
cards.source: Sagy I et al. Safety and efficacy of medical cannabis in fibromyalgia. J Clin Med. 2019. PMID: 31195754. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: one small positive pain RCT, one small sleep-positive/pain-null crossover, one experimental null, one uncontrolled cohort — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small positive pain RCT, one small sleep-positive/pain-null crossover, one experimental null, one uncontrolled cohort — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: 89 randomised patients across three small controlled trials (40 + 29 + 20) and 367 patients in an uncontrolled observational cohort.
cards.result: Pain: improved on nabilone in Skrabek 2008 (VAS -2.04 at 4 weeks, lost on washout); unchanged on nabilone in Ware 2010; not beaten versus placebo on spontaneous pain after single inhalations in van de Donk 2019. Sleep: better on nabilone than low-dose amitriptyline in Ware 2010 (ISI difference 3.2). The 367-patient cohort reports large uncontrolled improvements with mild adverse effects. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — the controlled record is three trials of 20-40 patients pointing in different directions by outcome, and the only large dataset has no comparator.
cards.watchOut: The tested products were pharmaceutical nabilone and defined pharmaceutical-grade cannabis varieties (named on the van de Donk card); consumer and dispensary cannabis products vary in content and are not what was tested, so current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. A 9-patient THC pilot from the same era sits below this library's reference floor and is not carded.
cards.source: Synthesis of Skrabek RQ et al. 2008 (PMID: 17974490), Ware MA et al. 2010 (PMID: 20007734), van de Donk T et al. 2019 (PMID: 30585986) and Sagy I et al. 2019 (PMID: 31195754), all carded above.

shelves.title: One bout of exercise blunts pain sensitivity: hypoalgesia is largest at the exercised part and scales with intensity
shelves.question: In healthy humans, how much does a single bout of aerobic or isometric exercise reduce experimental pain sensitivity, how long does the effect last, and how do intensity and muscle group (local vs remote) scale it?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Cold Temperature/adverse effects · Conditioning, Psychological* · Cross-Over Studies · Exercise* · Female · Humans · Isometric Contraction/physiology · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Threshold/physiology · Physical Stimulation/adverse effects · Pressure/adverse effects · Time Factors · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on endogenous pain modulation: a single bout of exercise produces exercise-induced hypoalgesia (EIH) — a generalised reduction in pain sensitivity during and for some time after exercise — distinct from conditioned pain modulation (a second noxious stimulus) and from offset analgesia, both of which have their own shelves in this library and are not duplicated here. The primary record fetched is concordant on the scaling rules: in 80 healthy adults, pressure pain thresholds rose at local and remote sites after all exercise conditions except low-intensity cycling, the response was larger in the exercising body part than in non-exercising parts for every condition, and high-intensity exercise produced greater responses than low-intensity exercise; isometric-exercise studies in 58 young adults showed raised pressure pain thresholds and reduced pain ratings after just 3 minutes of submaximal contraction, with an endocannabinoid (not opioid, by naltrexone blockade) mechanism signal. EIH in healthy humans is PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED; its attenuation in chronic-pain populations is the emerging clinical corollary, presented as such and not merged into the main claim.

cards.headline: Vaegter 2014: pressure pain thresholds rose at local and remote sites after exercise — larger at the exercising part, and larger after high- than low-intensity exercise (N = 80)
cards.summary: Vaegter 2014: pressure pain thresholds rose at local and remote sites after exercise — larger at the exercising part, and larger after high- than low-intensity exercise (N = 80)
cards.people: 80 healthy subjects (40 women), aged 18–65, in a randomised repeated-measures crossover study over 2 days: EIH was assessed with 2 intensities of aerobic cycling and 2 intensities of isometric contraction (arm and leg), with pressure pain thresholds recorded before, during, after and 15 minutes after exercise at sites local to and remote from the exercised extremity (N = 80).
cards.result: Pressure pain thresholds increased at local and remote sites after all exercise conditions except low-intensity bicycling. The EIH response was larger in the exercising body part than in non-exercising parts for all conditions, and high-intensity exercise produced greater EIH responses than low-intensity exercise. EIH after bicycling was higher in women than in men; responses after isometric exercise were comparable between sexes and unaffected by age. Effects were still measurable after exercise, including at the 15-minute assessment by design of the protocol.
cards.watchOut: The record reports direction and pattern (local > remote; high > low intensity) rather than a single pooled percentage rise in threshold — this shelf does not invent one. The comparison with conditioned pain modulation in the same study showed the two phenomena are not correlated, supporting their separation.
cards.source: Vaegter HB et al. Similarities between exercise-induced hypoalgesia and conditioned pain modulation in humans. Pain. 2014. PMID: 24076045. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Koltyn 2014: 3 minutes of submaximal isometric exercise raised pressure pain thresholds and lowered pain ratings in 58 young adults — and naltrexone did not block it
cards.summary: Koltyn 2014: 3 minutes of submaximal isometric exercise raised pressure pain thresholds and lowered pain ratings in 58 young adults — and naltrexone did not block it
cards.people: 58 healthy men and women (mean age 21 years) completing 3 sessions, with double-blind naltrexone (50 mg) or placebo before pain testing and 3 minutes of submaximal isometric exercise; heat temporal summation and pressure pain were tested before and after, with blood drawn for endocannabinoids (N = 58).
cards.result: Circulating endocannabinoids and related lipids increased significantly after exercise. Pressure pain thresholds increased significantly and pressure pain ratings decreased significantly after exercise, and temporal summation ratings were significantly lower. None of these pain changes differed between naltrexone and placebo conditions — evidence against an opioid mechanism and for a non-opioid (endocannabinoid-associated) mechanism for isometric EIH.
cards.watchOut: Young, healthy volunteers and a brief isometric protocol: the size and duration of EIH after longer aerobic exercise, and in older people, are separate measurements (see the other cards). Mechanism findings are associative — one lipid (docosahexaenoylethanolamine) was significantly associated with EIH.
cards.source: Koltyn KF et al. Mechanisms of exercise-induced hypoalgesia. The journal of pain. 2014. PMID: 25261342. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gomolka 2019: after 15 minutes of aerobic cycling, thresholds rose at the leg (local) in both sessions — reliability was fair locally and poor at the remote hand (N = 30)
cards.summary: Gomolka 2019: after 15 minutes of aerobic cycling, thresholds rose at the leg (local) in both sessions — reliability was fair locally and poor at the remote hand (N = 30)
cards.people: 30 healthy adults (15 women) performing 15 minutes of heart-rate-controlled aerobic cycling in two sessions, with pressure pain thresholds at the leg (local), back (semilocal) and hand (remote) before, immediately after and 15 minutes after exercise (N = 30).
cards.result: Thresholds increased significantly at the leg in both sessions (all P<0.001) and at the back in session 2 (P<0.001), indicating EIH still present at the post-exercise assessments including 15 minutes. Between-session reliability was fair for absolute changes at the leg (ICC 0.54) and back (ICC 0.40) but poor for percentage changes and at the hand (ICC <0.33), and responder agreement was not significant.
cards.watchOut: N = 30, labelled plainly, and a reliability study: its caution — that EIH measurement is only fairly reproducible locally and poorly reproducible remotely — belongs beside any clinical use of EIH as a test. The fair local reliability was shown in men in the authors' analysis.
cards.source: Gomolka S et al. Assessing Endogenous Pain Inhibition: Test-Retest Reliability of Exercise-Induced Hypoalgesia in Local and Remote Body Parts After Aerobic Cycling. cards.headline: Synthesis: EIH is real, intensity-scaled and locally largest in healthy humans; the chronic-pain attenuation is a separate, emerging corollary
cards.summary: Synthesis: EIH is real, intensity-scaled and locally largest in healthy humans; the chronic-pain attenuation is a separate, emerging corollary
cards.people: Three primary human experimental studies (Ns 80, 58 and 30) in healthy volunteers, framed by Guyton & Hall / Ganong on endogenous analgesia.
cards.result: Pressure pain thresholds rise after aerobic and isometric exercise at local and remote sites (exception: low-intensity cycling), larger locally and after high intensity; 3 minutes of isometric exercise suffices, with a non-opioid mechanism signal; the effect persists at least to the 15-minute post-exercise assessment in these protocols. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED in healthy humans. The attenuation or reversal of EIH in chronic-pain populations is presented in the balance as the emerging clinical corollary, not as part of the established claim.
cards.watchOut: Exact magnitudes vary by pain modality (pressure, heat, electrical), exercise dose and test site, and no record fetched supports a single headline percentage — the shelf deliberately reports the pattern and the protocol-specific findings instead.
cards.source: Synthesis of Vaegter HB et al. Pain. 2014; Koltyn KF et al. Journal of Pain. 2014; Gomolka S et al. Pain Medicine. 2019. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall / Ganong, as framing only.

shelves.title: Quantitative sensory testing profiles (physiology): thresholds are site- and age-dependent, pain thresholds are lower in women, and detection thresholds mostly do not differ by sex
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are normal quantitative sensory testing profiles - cold and warm detection and pain thresholds, mechanical detection and pain thresholds, vibration and pressure-pain thresholds - by body site, sex and decade of age, on the standardised DFNS protocol?
shelves.mesh: Pain Threshold · Sensation · Reference Values · Diagnostic Techniques, Neurological · Humans
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing (Ganong's Review of Medical Physiology; Boron & Boulpaep Medical Physiology): somatosensory receptors transduce thermal and mechanical stimuli whose detection and pain thresholds can be profiled psychophysically. The German Research Network on Neuropathic Pain (DFNS) standardised a 30-minute battery giving a complete profile for one region, and its normative programme is the anchor: 180 healthy subjects assessed bilaterally over face, hand and foot (Rolke 2006), extended to the trunk in 162 healthy subjects (Pfau 2014). The consistent findings across the carded cohorts: QST parameters are region-specific and age-dependent; pain thresholds are significantly lower in women than men while detection thresholds are generally independent of gender; the trunk is less sensitive than the hand on the upper back and more sensitive than the foot on the lower back; and side-to-side (relative) comparisons are 1.1 to 2.5 times more sensitive than absolute reference values. Independent cohorts agree in direction: 124 pain-free African American adults showed lower-body sites less sensitive than upper-body sites across thermal modalities, and 84 Italian adults tested with the Q-sense device showed all thermal measures affected by age, sex and site, with worse discrimination and higher heat-pain thresholds on the foot after age 40. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Rolke 2006 (DFNS protocol): reference values from 180 healthy subjects - thresholds are region-specific and age-dependent; pain thresholds lower in women
cards.summary: Rolke 2006 (DFNS protocol): reference values from 180 healthy subjects - thresholds are region-specific and age-dependent; pain thresholds lower in women
cards.people: 180 healthy subjects in the nationwide German multicentre DFNS programme, assessed bilaterally over face, hand and foot with the standardised quantitative sensory testing (QST) protocol: thermal detection and pain thresholds including paradoxical heat sensations, mechanical detection thresholds (von Frey filaments, 64 Hz tuning fork), mechanical pain thresholds (pinprick, blunt pressure), pinprick stimulus-response functions, dynamic mechanical allodynia, and wind-up ratio.
cards.result: QST parameters were region specific and age dependent. Pain thresholds were significantly lower in women than men; detection thresholds were generally independent of gender. Reference data were normalised as z-scores against region-, age- and gender-specific means. Side-to-side comparisons enhanced sensitivity by a factor of 1.1 to 2.5; relative comparisons across body regions offered no advantage over absolute reference values. Heat hypoalgesia, cold hypoalgesia and mechanical hyperesthesia can hardly be diagnosed from absolute values because confidence limits sit close to the possible data range.
cards.watchOut: Reference values are protocol-bound: they apply to the DFNS battery and its devices, and some loss-of-function signs cannot be diagnosed from absolute values at all - the protocol's own limit, stated by its authors.
cards.source: Rolke R et al.. Quantitative sensory testing in the German Research Network on Neuropathic Pain (DFNS): standardized protocol and reference values.. Pain. 2006. PMID: 16697110. cards.headline: Pfau 2014 (DFNS trunk extension): 162 healthy subjects - upper back less sensitive than hand, lower back more sensitive than foot; pressure pain the most sensitive parameter
cards.summary: Pfau 2014 (DFNS trunk extension): 162 healthy subjects - upper back less sensitive than hand, lower back more sensitive than foot; pressure pain the most sensitive parameter
cards.type: Normative cohort study (DFNS trunk reference data)
cards.people: 162 healthy subjects tested with the full DFNS QST profile on the back (trunk), extending the standard face/hand/foot sites, with profiles also recorded at standard sites for comparison.
cards.result: QST showed lower sensitivity on the upper back than the hand and higher sensitivity on the lower back than the foot, with no systematic difference between the trunk sites themselves. Age effects were significant for most parameters; the only significant gender difference was lower pressure pain thresholds in females. Abnormal thermal detection required temperature changes of more than 3.3-8.2 degrees C; for mechanical detection and pain, left-right differences were 1.5-2.3 times more sensitive than absolute values, and pressure pain threshold was the most sensitive parameter (side-to-side differences over 35% abnormal).
cards.watchOut: Cold pain confidence intervals extended mostly beyond safety cut-offs, so for cold pain only relative (side-difference) reference data are sufficiently sensitive - an absolute cold-pain 'normal range' is not established by this study.

cards.headline: Powell-Roach 2019: 124 pain-free African American adults - forearm cool detection 29.2 C, warm detection 34.5 C, heat pain 37.8 C; lower body less sensitive than upper
cards.summary: Powell-Roach 2019: 124 pain-free African American adults - forearm cool detection 29.2 C, warm detection 34.5 C, heat pain 37.8 C; lower body less sensitive than upper
cards.people: 124 pain-free African American adults aged 18-69 years (49% female), tested with thermal and mechanical QST including pain-intensity ratings, with prior pain experience and psychological status also measured.
cards.result: At the anterior forearm, cool detection was 29.2 C (SD 1.6), warm detection 34.5 C (SD 1.2), cold pain threshold 26.3 C (SD 5.0), heat pain threshold 37.8 C (SD 3.6), and mechanical pain threshold 16.7 (SD 22.2) grams of force. Women were more sensitive on warm detection (q = 0.027). Lower-body sites were less sensitive than upper-body sites across all thermal modalities (q < 0.003) but not for the mechanical modality.
cards.watchOut: A different protocol and device set from the DFNS battery, so its absolute values are not interchangeable with DFNS z-scores; thermal pain thresholds sat close to the adaptation temperature in this cohort, which the authors themselves note.
cards.source: Powell-Roach KL et al.. Thermal and mechanical quantitative sensory testing values among healthy African American adults.. Journal of pain research. 2019. PMID: 31496792. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Cosentino 2023 (Q-sense device): 84 Italian adults - every thermal measure depended on age, sex and site; foot discrimination worsened after 40
cards.summary: Cosentino 2023 (Q-sense device): 84 Italian adults - every thermal measure depended on age, sex and site; foot discrimination worsened after 40
cards.people: 84 healthy participants (42 men; aged 20-76 years) equally distributed across three age groups (18-39, 40-59, 60-80 years), tested with the Q-sense device at the supraorbital region, thenar hand and foot dorsum on the right side: warm and cold detection thresholds by method of limits and method of levels, and heat pain threshold by method of limits.
cards.result: All QST measures were affected by age, gender and tested site. At extra-trigeminal sites, females showed lower warm detection thresholds and higher cold detection thresholds, while males had higher heat pain thresholds. People over 40 showed worse sensory discrimination and increased heat pain thresholds on the foot. Age-related differences were more evident with the reaction-time-dependent method of limits than with the method of levels.
cards.watchOut: Thermal modalities only, on a different (Q-sense) device - its reference limits (2.5th-97.5th percentiles) serve that device, not the DFNS thermode; method of limits versus levels changes the age effect seen.

cards.headline: Synthesis: site and age move every threshold; sex moves pain thresholds - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.summary: Synthesis: site and age move every threshold; sex moves pain thresholds - PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED
cards.people: Healthy volunteers across four normative cohorts (180 DFNS face/hand/foot; 162 DFNS trunk; 124 African American adults; 84 Italian adults; total 550).
cards.result: On the standardised DFNS protocol, quantitative sensory profiles are region-specific and age-dependent, pain thresholds are lower in women while detection thresholds are largely sex-independent, and side-to-side differences are more sensitive than absolute cut-offs. Independent device cohorts reproduce the site and age pattern. Framing per Ganong and Boron & Boulpaep somatosensory physiology. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY - ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Normative values are protocol- and device-bound - DFNS, Q-sense and other batteries are not interchangeable, and cold-pain and some loss-of-function signs cannot be judged from absolute values alone.

shelves.title: Ianalumab in Sjögren's disease: phase 3 ESSDAI differences of about one point, no symptom benefit — a marginal systemic effect from the first programme to reach phase 3
shelves.question: In adults with primary Sjögren's disease with moderate-to-severe systemic activity, does the anti-BAFF-receptor antibody ianalumab, compared with placebo plus standard care, improve systemic disease activity (ESSDAI response)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Injection Site Reaction/epidemiology · Injections, Subcutaneous · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Severity of Illness Index · Sjogren's Syndrome/diagnosis,drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): Ianalumab 300 mg monthly produced a statistically significant but small extra fall in ESSDAI versus placebo in two phase 3 trials (−1.3 points, P=0.0496, NEPTUNUS-1, n=275; −1.0 points, P=0.04, NEPTUNUS-2, n=504), with no significant difference in ESSDAI response or in patient-reported symptom scores (SSSD/ESSPRI). The phase 2 programme points the same way (dose–response in the 190-patient dose-finding trial; sustained effect to 52 weeks; B-cell depletion with favourable trends in a 27-patient single-dose trial). A single manufacturer's programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the effect size — about 1 point on a 123-point index, without symptom benefit — is the central caveat. Hydroxychloroquine alone and rituximab in Sjögren's are homed on shelf #2716; symptomatic pilocarpine is shelf #1796 — neither is carded here.

cards.headline: NEPTUNUS-1 and NEPTUNUS-2 phase 3 (Mariette 2026): ianalumab monthly lowered ESSDAI by 1.3 and 1.0 points more than placebo at week 48 (P=0.0496 and P=0.04) — but ESSDAI response and symptom scores did not differ
cards.summary: NEPTUNUS-1 and NEPTUNUS-2 phase 3 (Mariette 2026): ianalumab monthly lowered ESSDAI by 1.3 and 1.0 points more than placebo at week 48 (P=0.0496 and P=0.04) — but ESSDAI response and symptom scores did not differ
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trials, two trials in one publication (Mariette 2026, NEPTUNUS-1/-2)
cards.people: Two 52-week double-blind placebo-controlled trials in active Sjögren's disease: NEPTUNUS-1, 275 patients randomised 1:1 to subcutaneous ianalumab 300 mg monthly or placebo; NEPTUNUS-2, 504 patients randomised 1:1:1 to ianalumab 300 mg monthly, ianalumab 300 mg every 3 months, or placebo. Primary endpoint: change in ESSDAI (0–123) at week 48.
cards.result: Monthly ianalumab beat placebo on change in ESSDAI by −1.3 points (95% CI −2.6 to 0.0; P=0.0496) in NEPTUNUS-1 and −1.0 points (95% CI −2.0 to 0.0; P=0.04) in NEPTUNUS-2. There were no significant differences in ESSDAI response (≥5-point reduction) or in change in SSSD or ESSPRI symptom scores at week 48. Serious adverse events were similar; nonserious injection-site and injection-related reactions were more common with ianalumab.
cards.watchOut: The ESSDAI differences are small (about 1 point on a 123-point scale), sit exactly on the significance boundary, and were not matched by any benefit on the responder endpoint or on patient-reported dryness, pain and fatigue — statistical significance here is not the same as a benefit patients can feel. One publication reporting two trials is counted as one report.
cards.source: Mariette X et al. Ianalumab for the Treatment of Patients with Sjögren's Disease. N Engl J Med. 2026. PMID: 42906087. Registry ID: NCT05350072 (NEPTUNUS-1) and NCT05349214 (NEPTUNUS-2).
