cards.headline: Phase 2b dose-finding trial (Bowman 2022): dose-related ESSDAI fall; the 300 mg dose differed from placebo by −1.92 points (95% CI −4.15 to 0.32; P=0.092)
cards.summary: Phase 2b dose-finding trial (Bowman 2022): dose-related ESSDAI fall; the 300 mg dose differed from placebo by −1.92 points (95% CI −4.15 to 0.32; P=0.092)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2b dose-finding trial (Bowman 2022)
cards.people: 190 patients aged 18–75 with primary Sjögren's syndrome, ESSDAI ≥6 and ESSPRI ≥5, at 56 centres in 19 countries, randomised 1:1:1:1 to subcutaneous placebo or ianalumab 5 mg, 50 mg or 300 mg every 4 weeks for 24 weeks. Primary outcome: change in ESSDAI at week 24, tested as a dose–response.
cards.result: A statistically significant dose–response for ESSDAI was seen in four of five prespecified models (P<0.025 in four; P=0.060 in one). The largest fall was at 300 mg: placebo-adjusted least-squares mean change −1.92 points (95% CI −4.15 to 0.32; P=0.092). Four serious adverse events occurred in three patients (pneumonia and gastroenteritis on placebo; appendicitis plus tubo-ovarian abscess in one patient on ianalumab 50 mg); there was no increase in infections.
cards.watchOut: The trial met its dose–response objective while the headline 300 mg pairwise comparison itself was not significant (P=0.092) — read the dose–response claim, not a proven dose effect, from this report.
cards.source: Bowman SJ et al. Safety and efficacy of subcutaneous ianalumab (VAY736) in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2b dose-finding trial. Lancet. 2022. PMID: 34861168. Registry ID: NCT02962895. cards.headline: Single-dose phase 2 trial (Dörner 2019): one infusion of ianalumab depleted B cells profoundly and showed a consistent favourable trend across ESSDAI and symptom measures in 27 patients
cards.summary: Single-dose phase 2 trial (Dörner 2019): one infusion of ianalumab depleted B cells profoundly and showed a consistent favourable trend across ESSDAI and symptom measures in 27 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 single-dose trial (Dörner 2019)
cards.people: 27 patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome and ESSDAI ≥6 at a single centre, randomised double-blind to a single intravenous infusion of ianalumab 3 mg/kg (n=6), 10 mg/kg (n=12) or placebo (n=9), with blinded outcomes to week 24.
cards.result: A similar favourable trend for ianalumab over placebo was seen on the primary clinical outcome (ESSDAI) and all secondary measures (ESSPRI, fatigue, quality of life, physician and patient global assessments), with rapid, profound and long-lasting B-cell depletion and falls in serum immunoglobulin light chains. Adverse effects were largely mild-to-moderate infusion reactions within 24 hours. No comparative effect estimate with a confidence interval is reported in the record — this is a signal-finding study.
cards.watchOut: Only 27 patients and no quantified treatment effect in the record — it supports biological activity, not clinical benefit, and its two dose arms (n=6 and n=12) are each at or near the reference floor.
cards.source: Dörner T et al. Treatment of primary Sjögren's syndrome with ianalumab (VAY736) targeting B cells by BAFF receptor blockade coupled with enhanced, antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Ann Rheum Dis. 2019. PMID: 30826774. Registry ID: none listed in the record. cards.summary: 52-week phase 2b results (Dörner 2025): efficacy was sustained to week 52 in patients who continued ianalumab 300 mg, in the same trial as the 24-week report
cards.type: Randomised phase 2b long-term (52-week) report of the dose-finding trial (Dörner 2025)
cards.people: The 190 patients of the phase 2b dose-finding trial (NCT02962895) followed beyond week 24: patients on 300 mg were re-randomised to continue 300 mg (n=43) or switch to placebo, patients on placebo switched to ianalumab 150 mg, and the 5 mg and 50 mg groups entered safety follow-up. 90 patients entered the second treatment period and 81 completed it.
cards.result: In patients who continued 300 mg, efficacy was sustained: change from week 24 to week 52 was −1.45 for ESSDAI, −0.46 for ESSPRI, −4.69 for patient global assessment and −6.86 for physician global assessment, with numerical improvement in stimulated salivary flow and autoantibody levels. Treatment-emergent adverse events were not dose-dependent except injection-site reactions; grade 3 neutrophil-count decreases occurred in three patients during post-treatment follow-up, without associated infection except one asymptomatic cytomegalovirus finding.
cards.watchOut: This is the same trial as the 24-week report, not an independent replication — after week 24 there is no continuing placebo group on the original doses, so the week-52 numbers are within-group changes, not controlled comparisons.
cards.source: Dörner T et al. Safety and Efficacy of Ianalumab in Patients With Sjögren's Disease: 52-Week Results From a Randomized, Placebo-Controlled, Phase 2b Dose-Ranging Study. Arthritis Rheumatol. 2025. PMID: 39557617. Registry ID: NCT02962895. cards.headline: Synthesis: ianalumab lowers ESSDAI by about a point more than placebo — a real but marginal systemic effect, with no demonstrated symptom benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: ianalumab lowers ESSDAI by about a point more than placebo — a real but marginal systemic effect, with no demonstrated symptom benefit
cards.people: Four publications: the NEPTUNUS-1/-2 phase 3 publication (779 patients across two trials), the phase 2b dose-finding trial at 24 weeks (190 patients) and its 52-week report, and a single-dose phase 2 trial (27 patients).
cards.result: Every controlled comparison points the same way on ESSDAI and none shows a symptom (ESSPRI/SSSD) or responder-endpoint benefit: phase 3 differences of −1.3 and −1.0 ESSDAI points, phase 2b −1.92 points at 300 mg. Harms are mainly injection reactions; serious adverse events were similar to placebo in phase 3. Ianalumab (a Novartis product) is the first systemic therapy programme in Sjögren's disease to reach phase 3 publication. The older systemic treatments for this disease — hydroxychloroquine alone and rituximab — are homed on shelf #2716 and are not carded here.
cards.watchOut: A single manufacturer's programme with no independent replication, and the phase 3 effect size is at the edge of what the ESSDAI can meaningfully register. Whether a ~1-point ESSDAI gain without symptom relief justifies a monthly B-cell-depleting injection is the open clinical question.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mariette X et al. N Engl J Med. 2026 (PMID: 42906087); Bowman SJ et al. Lancet. 2022 (PMID: 34861168); Dörner T et al. Ann Rheum Dis. 2019 (PMID: 30826774); Dörner T et al. Arthritis Rheumatol. 2025 (PMID: 39557617).

shelves.title: Abatacept in early Sjögren's syndrome (ASAP-III): no difference from placebo on ESSDAI or gland histology — open-label gains only
shelves.question: In adults with early active primary Sjögren's syndrome, does abatacept, compared with placebo, improve systemic disease activity and glandular function (ASAP-III programme)?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): In the single randomised trial (ASAP-III, 80 patients with early active primary Sjögren's syndrome), abatacept did not improve the primary ESSDAI endpoint versus placebo at week 24 (adjusted difference −1.3 points, 95% CI −4.1 to 1.6), and a biopsy substudy found virtually no effect on salivary gland inflammation. The 48-week open-label extension showed improvement (median ESSDAI 14.0 to 4.0; 73% CRESS responders), but with no control group it cannot establish benefit. A single small trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Hydroxychloroquine and rituximab in Sjögren's are homed on shelf #2716 and are not carded here.

cards.headline: ASAP-III primary trial (van Nimwegen 2020): abatacept did not beat placebo on ESSDAI at week 24 — adjusted difference −1.3 points (95% CI −4.1 to 1.6)
cards.summary: ASAP-III primary trial (van Nimwegen 2020): abatacept did not beat placebo on ESSDAI at week 24 — adjusted difference −1.3 points (95% CI −4.1 to 1.6)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled single-centre trial (van Nimwegen 2020, ASAP-III)
cards.people: 80 patients with early active primary Sjögren's syndrome (American-European Consensus Group criteria, positive salivary gland biopsy, diagnosis within 7 years, ESSDAI ≥5) at a single centre (Groningen, Netherlands), randomised 1:1 to weekly subcutaneous abatacept 125 mg or placebo for 24 weeks. Efficacy was analysed in 40 abatacept and 39 placebo patients.
cards.result: The primary outcome did not differ between groups: adjusted mean difference in ESSDAI at week 24 was −1.3 (95% CI −4.1 to 1.6). No deaths or treatment-related serious adverse events occurred. Adverse events occurred in 38 of 40 patients in each group (103 events on abatacept, including 46 infections and one serious event; 87 on placebo, including 49 infections and four serious events). The authors conclude abatacept cannot be recommended as standard care to reduce systemic disease activity in primary Sjögren's syndrome.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 80 patients; the confidence interval (−4.1 to 1.6) cannot exclude a moderate ESSDAI benefit, so this is a null result, not proof of no effect in every phenotype — the authors themselves call for study of specific subgroups.
cards.source: van Nimwegen JF et al. Abatacept treatment for patients with early active primary Sjögren's syndrome: a single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial (ASAP-III study). Lancet Rheumatol. 2020. PMID: 38263653. Registry ID: none listed in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: ASAP-III open-label extension (de Wolff 2022): after 48 weeks on abatacept, median ESSDAI fell from 14.0 to 4.0 and 73% were CRESS responders — with no control group
cards.summary: ASAP-III open-label extension (de Wolff 2022): after 48 weeks on abatacept, median ESSDAI fell from 14.0 to 4.0 and 73% were CRESS responders — with no control group
cards.type: Open-label extension of a randomised trial (de Wolff 2022, ASAP-III extension)
cards.people: The 40 patients treated with abatacept from baseline in ASAP-III, followed through the open-label extension in which all patients received abatacept from week 24 to week 48. Main inclusion criteria: American-European Consensus Group criteria, positive gland biopsy, disease duration ≤7 years, ESSDAI ≥5.
cards.result: In patients on abatacept for 48 weeks (n=40), median ESSDAI improved from 14.0 (IQR 9.0–16.8) at baseline to 4.0 (2.0–8.0) at week 48 (P<0.001), with 50% reaching low disease activity (ESSDAI <5). Median ESSPRI improved from 7.0 to 5.0 (P<0.001), dry-eye and laboratory measures improved, 73% were Composite of Relevant Endpoints for Sjögren's Syndrome (CRESS) responders at week 48, and further improvement occurred between weeks 24 and 48.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, uncontrolled follow-up of only the abatacept arm — improvement over 48 weeks mixes any drug effect with placebo response, regression to the mean and natural fluctuation, and it cannot overturn the blinded phase's null primary result.
cards.source: de Wolff L et al. Long-term abatacept treatment for 48 weeks in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome: The open-label extension phase of the ASAP-III trial. Semin Arthritis Rheum. 2022. PMID: 35091325. Registry ID: NCT02067910. MeSH: Abatacept/therapeutic use · Biopsy · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Sjogren's Syndrome/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Salivary gland biopsy analysis (Nakshbandi 2024): 24 weeks of abatacept had virtually no effect on salivary gland inflammation versus placebo in 41 biopsied patients
cards.summary: Salivary gland biopsy analysis (Nakshbandi 2024): 24 weeks of abatacept had virtually no effect on salivary gland inflammation versus placebo in 41 biopsied patients
cards.people: 41 patients from the ASAP-II and ASAP-III trials and an international abatacept trial who had a labial (n=13) or parotid (n=28) salivary gland biopsy at baseline and after 24 weeks of abatacept (n=25) or placebo (n=16).
cards.result: There were virtually no differences between abatacept and placebo in histopathological parameters of parotid and labial glands over 24 weeks. In labial glands only the number of IgA plasma cells/mm² differed over time (P=0.034); in parotid glands IgA plasma cells increased on abatacept (P=0.049) and CD20+ B cells/mm² increased on placebo (P=0.021). Baseline histopathology did not predict clinical (CRESS or ClinESSDAI) response to abatacept.
cards.watchOut: A small pooled biopsy substudy (41 patients across three trials, two gland sites) — underpowered for modest histological effects, but it gives no support to a glandular mechanism for any late clinical gain.
cards.source: Nakshbandi U et al. Abatacept use for 24 weeks has a limited effect on salivary gland inflammation in Sjögren's disease patients. Clin Exp Rheumatol. 2024. PMID: 39699866. Registry ID: none listed in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the blinded trial was null on its primary endpoint and on gland histology — the open-label improvement does not establish benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: the blinded trial was null on its primary endpoint and on gland histology — the open-label improvement does not establish benefit
cards.people: One randomised trial programme: ASAP-III (80 patients randomised; 40 continued on abatacept to 48 weeks) plus a 41-patient biopsy substudy pooled across three abatacept trials.
cards.result: Controlled evidence: ESSDAI difference −1.3 points (95% CI −4.1 to 1.6) at week 24 and no material change in salivary gland inflammation. Uncontrolled evidence: median ESSDAI 14.0 to 4.0 and 73% CRESS response after 48 weeks of open-label abatacept. Harms in the blinded phase were similar to placebo, with infections common in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The whole controlled base is one single-centre trial of 80 patients in early disease — it does not test abatacept in longstanding disease, severe systemic manifestations, or biomarker-selected subgroups, where the question remains genuinely open.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Nimwegen JF et al. Lancet Rheumatol. 2020 (PMID: 38263653); de Wolff L et al. Semin Arthritis Rheum. 2022 (PMID: 35091325); Nakshbandi U et al. Clin Exp Rheumatol. 2024 (PMID: 39699866).

shelves.title: Leflunomide plus hydroxychloroquine in Sjögren's disease: two small trials, the same ~4-point ESSDAI gain — a replicated pilot signal
shelves.question: In adults with primary Sjögren's syndrome, does the combination of leflunomide plus hydroxychloroquine, compared with placebo, improve systemic disease activity (ESSDAI)?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): Leflunomide 20 mg plus hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily beat placebo on ESSDAI by −4.35 points (P=0.0078) in RepurpSS-I (29 patients) and by −4.135 points (P=0.0012) in the replication trial RepurpSS-II (46 patients) — two concordant positive trials, but both small and from the same single centre, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. A pooled transcriptomic analysis suggests the benefit concentrates in one endotype. This shelf asks the combination question only: hydroxychloroquine alone (which failed in JOQUER) and rituximab are homed on shelf #2716 and are not carded here. Harms were mainly gastrointestinal discomfort and transient liver-enzyme rises.

cards.headline: RepurpSS-I (van der Heijden 2020): leflunomide plus hydroxychloroquine lowered ESSDAI by 4.35 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (P=0.0078) in 29 patients
cards.summary: RepurpSS-I (van der Heijden 2020): leflunomide plus hydroxychloroquine lowered ESSDAI by 4.35 points more than placebo at 24 weeks (P=0.0078) in 29 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2a trial (van der Heijden 2020, RepurpSS-I)
cards.people: 29 patients (28 women, 1 man) with primary Sjögren's syndrome, ESSDAI ≥5 and labial biopsy focus score ≥1, at a single centre (Utrecht, Netherlands), randomised 2:1 to leflunomide 20 mg plus hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily (n=21) or placebo (n=8) for 24 weeks. Primary endpoint: between-group difference in change in ESSDAI, adjusted for baseline.
cards.result: The adjusted mean difference in ESSDAI change was −4.35 points (95% CI −7.45 to −1.25; P=0.0078) favouring the combination. No serious adverse events occurred on the combination; two occurred on placebo (pancreatitis admission, nephrolithiasis admission). The commonest adverse events on the combination were gastrointestinal discomfort (52% vs 25%), modest transient alanine aminotransferase rises (48% vs 13%) and brief malaise/shivering episodes (43% vs 13%). One placebo patient who needed high-dose prednisone was excluded from the primary analysis.
cards.watchOut: Very small and single-centre, with only 8 placebo patients — the effect estimate is fragile, and the population (biopsy-positive, ESSDAI ≥5) is selected. A positive pilot, not a proven treatment.
cards.source: van der Heijden EHM et al. Leflunomide-hydroxychloroquine combination therapy in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome (RepurpSS-I): a placebo-controlled, double-blinded, randomised clinical trial. Lancet Rheumatol. 2020. PMID: 38273473. Registry ID: EudraCT 2014-003140-12. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: RepurpSS-II (Wong 2026): the combination replicated the ESSDAI effect — difference −4.135 points (P=0.0012) in 46 patients
cards.summary: RepurpSS-II (Wong 2026): the combination replicated the ESSDAI effect — difference −4.135 points (P=0.0012) in 46 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2b trial (Wong 2026, RepurpSS-II)
cards.people: 46 adults aged 18–75 with Sjögren's disease and ESSDAI ≥5 at a single centre (Utrecht, Netherlands), randomised 1:1 to leflunomide 20 mg plus hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily (n=21) or placebo (n=25) for 24 weeks, masked to week 24. 93% were female; median age 55 years. Primary endpoint: between-group difference in change in ESSDAI at week 24.
cards.result: The mean difference in ESSDAI at 24 weeks was −4.135 (95% CI −6.558 to −1.709; P=0.0012) favouring the combination — closely replicating RepurpSS-I. One serious adverse event occurred on treatment (hospital admission for myocardial infarction, judged probably unrelated). Adverse events were similar between groups; gastrointestinal discomfort was commonest (29% vs 16%). There were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Still single-centre (the same centre as RepurpSS-I) and only 46 patients, in systemically active disease — independent multicentre replication and evidence in low-activity/high-symptom patients are still missing.
cards.source: Wong WY et al. Repurposing leflunomide and hydroxychloroquine to treat Sjögren's disease (RepurpSS-II): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial. Lancet Rheumatol. 2026. PMID: 42161318. Registry ID: EudraCT 2020-001933-11. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2b trial (wong 2026, repurpss-ii) 46 adults aged 18–75 with sjögren's disease and essdai ≥5 at a single centre (utrecht, netherlands), randomised 1:1 to leflunomide 20 mg plus hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily (n=21) or placebo (n=25) for 24 weeks, masked to week 24. 93% were female; median age 55 years. primary endpoint: between-group difference in change in essdai at week 24. the mean difference in essdai at 24 weeks was −4.135 (95% ci −6.558 to −1.709; p=0.0012) favouring the combination — closely replicating repurpss-i. one serious adverse event occurred on treatment (hospital admission for myocardial infarction, judged probably unrelated). adverse events were similar between groups; gastrointestinal discomfort was commonest (29% vs 16%). there were no deaths. still single-centre (the same centre as repurpss-i) and only 46 patients, in systemically active disease — independent multicentre replication and evidence in low-activity/high-symptom patients are still missing. wong wy et al. repurposing leflunomide and hydroxychloroquine to treat sjögren's disease (repurpss-ii): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2b trial. lancet rheumatol. 2026. pmid: 42161318. registry id: eudract 2020-001933-11. mesh: adult · aged · female · humans · male · middle aged · antirheumatic agents/therapeutic use · double-blind method · drug repositioning · drug therapy, combination · hydroxychloroquine/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · leflunomide/therapeutic use · sjogren's syndrome/drug therapy · treatment outcome · adolescent · young adult

cards.headline: Transcriptomic stratification (Chevet 2026): response to the combination concentrated in one endotype (cluster 3) — cluster 2 ('healthy-like') patients responded to no therapy
cards.summary: Transcriptomic stratification (Chevet 2026): response to the combination concentrated in one endotype (cluster 3) — cluster 2 ('healthy-like') patients responded to no therapy
cards.type: Pooled transcriptomic secondary analysis of three randomised trials (Chevet 2026)
cards.people: Pooled analysis of three randomised trials in Sjögren's disease, including the hydroxychloroquine–leflunomide (RepurpSS-I) trial (n=18 with transcriptomic data), a rituximab trial (n=56) and abatacept trials (n=117); 170 patients were assigned to four whole-blood transcriptomic endotypes and response was measured with the Sjögren Tool for Assessing Response index.
cards.result: In pooled analyses, cluster 1 patients responded more to active treatment than placebo (61.5% vs 32.6%; P=0.016). Cluster 3 patients specifically benefited from hydroxychloroquine–leflunomide, whereas cluster 2 ('healthy-like') patients showed no significant response to any therapy. ESSDAI was higher in clusters 3 and 4 than in clusters 1 and 2 (P=0.003), while patient-reported symptoms were comparable across clusters.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc, hypothesis-generating stratification: the hydroxychloroquine–leflunomide limb contributes only 18 patients (a subset of RepurpSS-I), so the endotype claim needs prospective validation before it guides treatment choice.
cards.source: Chevet B et al. Transcriptomic stratification predicts response to rituximab, abatacept, or the association of hydroxychloroquine and leflunomide in 3 randomised controlled clinical trials of Sjögren's disease. Ann Rheum Dis. 2026. PMID: 41448992. Registry ID: none listed in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two small single-centre trials agree on a ~4-point ESSDAI gain for the combination — promising, cheap, and not yet independently replicated
cards.summary: Synthesis: two small single-centre trials agree on a ~4-point ESSDAI gain for the combination — promising, cheap, and not yet independently replicated
cards.people: Two randomised trials from one centre (RepurpSS-I, 29 patients; RepurpSS-II, 46 patients) plus a pooled transcriptomic analysis in which the combination's data come from 18 RepurpSS-I patients.
cards.result: ESSDAI differences were −4.35 points (P=0.0078) and −4.135 points (P=0.0012) — a consistent, clinically meaningful size, unlike hydroxychloroquine alone, which showed no benefit in the JOQUER trial homed on shelf #2716 (that shelf asks hydroxychloroquine alone and rituximab; the combination question is asked only here). Harms were mainly gastrointestinal upset and transient liver-enzyme rises. The transcriptomic analysis suggests benefit concentrates in particular endotypes.
cards.watchOut: Total randomised experience is 75 patients from a single centre, with 24-week follow-up and an activity-score endpoint — no data yet on glandular damage, lymphoma, fatigue-predominant disease, or longer-term leflunomide safety in this population.
cards.source: Synthesis of van der Heijden EHM et al. Lancet Rheumatol. 2020 (PMID: 38273473); Wong WY et al. Lancet Rheumatol. 2026 (PMID: 42161318); Chevet B et al. Ann Rheum Dis. 2026 (PMID: 41448992).

shelves.title: Secukinumab in giant cell arteritis: phase 2 promised, phase 3 missed its primary endpoint — a split record
shelves.question: In adults with giant cell arteritis, does secukinumab, compared with placebo plus a glucocorticoid taper, sustain remission?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Giant Cell Arteritis/drug therapy · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Double-Blind Method · Female · Male · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use,adverse effects,administration & dosage · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use,administration & dosage · Aged, 80 and over · Treatment Outcome · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: SPLIT: The evidence disagrees with itself. The phase 2 TitAIN trial (52 patients) found a large advantage (median sustained remission 70% vs 20% to week 28, Bayesian analysis), but the phase 3 GCAptAIN trial (353 patients) missed its primary endpoint (the treatment made no difference at conventional significance): sustained remission 25.6% on secukinumab 300 mg with a 26-week glucocorticoid taper versus 16.9% on placebo with a 52-week taper (difference 8.7 points, 95% CI −1.3 to 18.8; P=0.09). An Italian observational cohort (36 patients, labelled observational) reports high remission and steroid-sparing without a comparator. Interleukin-6 blockade in giant cell arteritis is homed on live shelf #385 and upadacitinib on live shelf #1812 — not carded here.

cards.headline: TitAIN phase 2 (Venhoff 2023): sustained remission to week 28 in a median 70% on secukinumab versus 20% on placebo (Bayesian analysis) in 52 patients
cards.summary: TitAIN phase 2 (Venhoff 2023): sustained remission to week 28 in a median 70% on secukinumab versus 20% on placebo (Bayesian analysis) in 52 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (Venhoff 2023, TitAIN)
cards.people: 52 patients aged 50 or older with new-onset or relapsing giant cell arteritis, biologic-naive and on glucocorticoids (prednisolone equivalent 25–60 mg/day), at 11 German centres, randomised 1:1 to secukinumab 300 mg (n=27) or placebo (n=25) subcutaneously, with prednisolone tapered to zero over 26 weeks in both groups. Primary endpoint: median proportion in sustained remission to week 28 (Bayesian analysis using a prior derived from an earlier tocilizumab trial).
cards.result: The median proportion in sustained remission to week 28 was 70% (95% credibility interval 52–85) on secukinumab versus 20% (12–30) on placebo. Adverse events occurred in 100% versus 96% of patients; the commonest were hypertension (22% vs 32%) and nasopharyngitis (19% vs 20%). Two patients died (one per group), neither death judged treatment-related. Four secukinumab and eight placebo patients discontinued by week 28.
cards.watchOut: A 52-patient proof-of-concept trial whose headline numbers are Bayesian medians informed by a prior borrowed from a tocilizumab trial — encouraging, but exactly the kind of small phase 2 result that phase 3 often shrinks.
cards.source: Venhoff N et al. Safety and efficacy of secukinumab in patients with giant cell arteritis (TitAIN): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial. Lancet Rheumatol. 2023. PMID: 38251601. Registry ID: NCT03765788. cards.headline: GCAptAIN phase 3 (Stone 2026): sustained remission at week 52 did not differ significantly — 25.6% on secukinumab 300 mg versus 16.9% on placebo (difference 8.7 points; P=0.09) (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint)
cards.summary: GCAptAIN phase 3 (Stone 2026): sustained remission at week 52 did not differ significantly — 25.6% on secukinumab 300 mg versus 16.9% on placebo (difference 8.7 points; P=0.09) (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Stone 2026, GCAptAIN)
cards.people: 353 patients with new-onset or relapsing giant cell arteritis analysed: secukinumab 300 mg (n=140), secukinumab 150 mg (n=98) or placebo (n=115). Secukinumab groups received a 26-week glucocorticoid taper; the placebo group received a 52-week taper. Primary outcome: sustained remission at week 52, secukinumab 300 mg versus placebo.
cards.result: Sustained remission at week 52 was 25.6% with secukinumab 300 mg versus 16.9% with placebo (marginal difference 8.7 percentage points, 95% CI −1.3 to 18.8; P=0.09) and 19.4% with secukinumab 150 mg versus 17.7% with placebo in the post-amendment comparison (difference 1.6 points, 95% CI −9.2 to 12.4). Adverse events occurred in 92.9%, 95.9% and 97.4% of the three groups; serious adverse events in 20.0%, 27.6% and 32.2%; serious infections in 5.0%, 9.2% and 6.1%.
cards.watchOut: The comparison is not taper-matched: secukinumab was tested with a faster (26-week) glucocorticoid taper against placebo with a 52-week taper, so the trial asks whether secukinumab can carry a faster taper — and on that question the primary endpoint was missed, though the confidence interval still includes a worthwhile benefit.
cards.source: Stone JH et al. Secukinumab for Giant Cell Arteritis. NEJM Evidence. 2026. PMID: 42234457. Registry ID: NCT04930094 (EudraCT 2020-004809-31). cards.headline: Italian real-world cohort (Iorio 2026, observational): 83.3% in clinical remission at 12 months and glucocorticoids stopped in 42.9% — in 36 uncontrolled, mostly relapsing patients
cards.summary: Italian real-world cohort (Iorio 2026, observational): 83.3% in clinical remission at 12 months and glucocorticoids stopped in 42.9% — in 36 uncontrolled, mostly relapsing patients
cards.people: Retrospective multicentre cohort of 36 patients with giant cell arteritis treated with secukinumab at 14 Italian centres with at least 6 months of follow-up (66.7% women; median age 74 years). 88.9% had previously relapsed and 72.2% had previously received tocilizumab.
cards.result: Clinical remission was observed in 85.2%, 80.6% and 83.3% at 3, 6 and 12 months; complete remission in 55.6%, 52.8% and 63.3%; glucocorticoid-free remission rose to 40.0% at 12 months (P=0.012). Median daily glucocorticoid dose fell from 8.7 mg at baseline to 0 mg at 12 months (P<0.001), and glucocorticoids were discontinued in 12 of 28 patients (42.9%). The 12-month retention rate was 77.0%. Adverse events occurred in 55.6% of patients; infections in 50.0% (21 episodes).
cards.watchOut: Observational and uncontrolled: patients selected for secukinumab (mostly after relapse or tocilizumab) who stayed on it are the ones counted at 12 months, so high remission rates are expected even for an ineffective drug — this cohort cannot rescue the negative phase 3 primary endpoint.
cards.source: Iorio L et al. Real-World Effectiveness and Safety of Secukinumab in Giant Cell Arteritis: An Italian Multicenter Cohort Study. Arthritis Care Res. 2026. PMID: 42765445. Registry ID: none listed in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: a strongly positive small phase 2, a negative phase 3 primary endpoint, and an encouraging uncontrolled cohort — the split is the answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: a strongly positive small phase 2, a negative phase 3 primary endpoint, and an encouraging uncontrolled cohort — the split is the answer
cards.people: Three reports: TitAIN phase 2 (52 patients), GCAptAIN phase 3 (353 patients) and an Italian retrospective cohort (36 patients).
cards.result: Phase 2 suggested a large remission advantage (median 70% vs 20% to week 28); phase 3 found a smaller, non-significant difference (25.6% vs 16.9%, P=0.09) under a faster glucocorticoid taper; the cohort shows high remission and steroid-sparing in routine use without a comparator. Established giant cell arteritis treatments are homed elsewhere — interleukin-6 blockade on live shelf #385 and upadacitinib (SELECT-GCA) on live shelf #1812 — and are not carded here.
cards.watchOut: The phase 3 confidence interval (−1.3 to 18.8 points) does not exclude a clinically useful effect, and the taper mismatch means the trial is not a pure drug-versus-placebo test — but as the evidence stands, benefit is unproven at phase 3 standard.
cards.source: Synthesis of Venhoff N et al. Lancet Rheumatol. 2023 (PMID: 38251601); Stone JH et al. NEJM Evidence. 2026 (PMID: 42234457); Iorio L et al. Arthritis Care Res. 2026 (PMID: 42765445).

shelves.title: Tocilizumab in Takayasu arteritis: hazard ratio 0.41 for relapse, primary endpoint narrowly missed — suggestive evidence in a rare disease
shelves.question: In adults with refractory Takayasu arteritis, does tocilizumab, compared with placebo (and in long-term follow-up, continued therapy), reduce relapse?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Japan · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Receptors, Interleukin-6/antagonists & inhibitors · Remission Induction · Takayasu Arteritis/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence): The only randomised trial, TAKT (36 Japanese patients with refractory Takayasu arteritis), favoured tocilizumab on time to relapse (hazard ratio 0.41) but missed its primary endpoint (95.41% CI 0.15 to 1.10; P=0.0596). Its 96-week open-label extension showed glucocorticoid doses roughly halving with mostly stable imaging, and a retrospective series (11 patients, labelled observational) plus a 211-patient literature pool (73% remission) point the same way. That is a consistent direction on very thin, largely uncontrolled evidence — 47 distinct patients in primary data — hence MAYBE (weak evidence). No Takayasu question is homed elsewhere in the library.

cards.headline: TAKT phase 3 (Nakaoka 2018): time to relapse favoured tocilizumab but the primary endpoint was missed — hazard ratio 0.41 (95.41% CI 0.15 to 1.10; P=0.0596) in 36 patients
cards.summary: TAKT phase 3 (Nakaoka 2018): time to relapse favoured tocilizumab but the primary endpoint was missed — hazard ratio 0.41 (95.41% CI 0.15 to 1.10; P=0.0596) in 36 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Nakaoka 2018, TAKT)
cards.people: 36 patients with Takayasu arteritis who had relapsed within the previous 12 weeks, induced into remission with oral glucocorticoids, then randomised 1:1 in Japan to weekly subcutaneous tocilizumab 162 mg (n=18) or placebo (n=18), with glucocorticoids tapered 10% per week from week 4. Primary endpoint: time to relapse (a composite of systemic symptoms, inflammation markers, vascular and ischaemic features). The per-protocol set was 16 versus 17 patients.
cards.result: Relapse occurred in 8 tocilizumab and 11 placebo patients. The hazard ratio for time to relapse was 0.41 (95.41% CI 0.15 to 1.10; P=0.0596) in the intention-to-treat population — the primary endpoint was not met — and 0.34 (95.41% CI 0.11 to 1.00; P=0.0345) in the per-protocol set. Secondary definitions of relapse were consistent. Serious adverse events occurred in one tocilizumab and two placebo patients; there were no serious infections and no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Only 36 patients and 19 relapses — the trial was stopped by event count, not by a fixed duration, and was underpowered: a hazard ratio of 0.41 is a large point estimate that the sample size could not confirm. Per-protocol significance does not repair a missed intention-to-treat primary endpoint.
cards.source: Nakaoka Y et al. Efficacy and safety of tocilizumab in patients with refractory Takayasu arteritis: results from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial in Japan (the TAKT study). Ann Rheum Dis. 2018. PMID: 29191819. Registry ID: JapicCTI-142616. randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (nakaoka 2018, takt) 36 patients with takayasu arteritis who had relapsed within the previous 12 weeks, induced into remission with oral glucocorticoids, then randomised 1:1 in japan to weekly subcutaneous tocilizumab 162 mg (n=18) or placebo (n=18), with glucocorticoids tapered 10% per week from week 4. primary endpoint: time to relapse (a composite of systemic symptoms, inflammation markers, vascular and ischaemic features). the per-protocol set was 16 versus 17 patients. relapse occurred in 8 tocilizumab and 11 placebo patients. the hazard ratio for time to relapse was 0.41 (95.41% ci 0.15 to 1.10; p=0.0596) in the intention-to-treat population — the primary endpoint was not met — and 0.34 (95.41% ci 0.11 to 1.00; p=0.0345) in the per-protocol set. secondary definitions of relapse were consistent. serious adverse events occurred in one tocilizumab and two placebo patients; there were no serious infections and no deaths. only 36 patients and 19 relapses — the trial was stopped by event count, not by a fixed duration, and was underpowered: a hazard ratio of 0.41 is a large point estimate that the sample size could not confirm. per-protocol significance does not repair a missed intention-to-treat primary endpoint. nakaoka y et al. efficacy and safety of tocilizumab in patients with refractory takayasu arteritis: results from a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial in japan (the takt study). ann rheum dis. 2018. pmid: 29191819. registry id: japiccti-142616. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · antibodies, monoclonal, humanized/adverse effects,therapeutic use · double-blind method · female · glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · humans · intention to treat analysis · japan · kaplan-meier estimate · male · middle aged · receptors, interleukin-6/antagonists & inhibitors · remission induction · takayasu arteritis/drug therapy · treatment outcome · young adult

cards.headline: TAKT final long-term results (Nakaoka 2020): over 96 weeks of open-label tocilizumab, glucocorticoid dose roughly halved and disease was stable or improved on imaging in 85.7%
cards.summary: TAKT final long-term results (Nakaoka 2020): over 96 weeks of open-label tocilizumab, glucocorticoid dose roughly halved and disease was stable or improved on imaging in 85.7%
cards.type: Open-label long-term extension of a randomised trial (Nakaoka 2020, TAKT final results)
cards.people: All 36 patients from the TAKT double-blind period entered the open-label extension on weekly subcutaneous tocilizumab 162 mg for up to 96 weeks or longer, with glucocorticoid tapering at investigators' discretion; 28 patients received tocilizumab for 96 weeks.
cards.result: Median glucocorticoid dose fell from 0.223 mg/kg/day at the pre-entry relapse to 0.131 mg/kg/day (IQR 0.099–0.207) at 48 weeks and 0.105 mg/kg/day (IQR 0.039–0.153) at 96 weeks; 46.4% of patients reduced to below 0.1 mg/kg/day (mean difference −0.120 mg/kg/day, 95% CI −0.154 to −0.087). Imaging showed disease improved in 17.9% and stable in 67.9% at 96 weeks, health-survey scores improved and were maintained, and no unexpected safety issues were reported.
cards.watchOut: The same 36 patients as the primary report, now uncontrolled — steroid tapering at clinician discretion in an open-label study will fall whether or not the drug works, so this report supports tolerability and feasibility, not efficacy.
cards.source: Nakaoka Y et al. Long-term efficacy and safety of tocilizumab in refractory Takayasu arteritis: final results of the randomized controlled phase 3 TAKT study. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2020. PMID: 31951279. Registry ID: JapicCTI-142616. cards.headline: Retrospective cohort and literature review (Li 2022, observational): 11 refractory patients improved on tocilizumab; across 211 published patients, 73% achieved remission
cards.summary: Retrospective cohort and literature review (Li 2022, observational): 11 refractory patients improved on tocilizumab; across 211 published patients, 73% achieved remission
cards.type: Retrospective observational cohort with literature review (Li 2022)
cards.people: Retrospective series of 11 patients with refractory Takayasu arteritis treated with tocilizumab at a single Chinese centre (2017–2020; median age 34 years), together with the authors' review of published tocilizumab experience in Takayasu arteritis from 2010 to 2021 (211 patients, 80% female, mean age 35 years).
cards.result: In the 11-patient series, median NIH activity score fell from 3 (range 2–5) at baseline to 1 (0–2) after 6 months (P<0.05) and ITAS-2010 from 8.5 (6–11) to 6 (1–10) (P<0.05); one patient (9%) relapsed on treatment, and after withdrawal one relapsed while nine (81%) were spared glucocorticoid use. In the literature review, 73% of 211 patients achieved remission after the last tocilizumab infusion, relapse occurred in 6% during treatment and 5% after withdrawal, and infection was the commonest adverse effect (reported in 50% of patients in the reviewed reports).
cards.watchOut: Observational throughout: the authors' own series is 11 patients, and the 211-patient literature pool is published-case experience, which systematically over-reports success. It is consistent with benefit and proves none.
cards.source: Li H et al. Efficacy of tocilizumab for refractory Takayasu arteritis: a retrospective study and literature review. Heart Vessels. 2022. PMID: 34750666. Registry ID: none listed in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small trial that narrowly missed, its uncontrolled extension, and supportive case experience — suggestive, not established
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small trial that narrowly missed, its uncontrolled extension, and supportive case experience — suggestive, not established
cards.people: Three reports covering 47 distinct patients in primary data (TAKT, 36 patients, reported twice; a retrospective series, 11 patients) plus a 211-patient literature pool.
cards.result: The only controlled comparison gives a hazard ratio of 0.41 for relapse with a confidence interval crossing 1 (P=0.0596). Long-term open-label treatment halved glucocorticoid doses with stable imaging in most patients, and observational experience reports remission in about three quarters. No other Takayasu arteritis question is homed anywhere in this library — this is a whole-disease gap filled with thin evidence.
cards.watchOut: Takayasu arteritis is rare and relapsing, and a definitive trial may never be much larger than TAKT — but on the current record the honest statement is that tocilizumab probably delays relapse, with the size of any effect poorly estimated (hazard ratio 0.41, CI 0.15 to 1.10).
cards.source: Synthesis of Nakaoka Y et al. Ann Rheum Dis. 2018 (PMID: 29191819); Nakaoka Y et al. Rheumatology (Oxford). 2020 (PMID: 31951279); Li H et al. Heart Vessels. 2022 (PMID: 34750666).

shelves.title: Dazukibart in dermatomyositis: skin activity down ~16 points versus placebo in phase 2 — large, rapid, and not yet phase 3
shelves.question: In adults with dermatomyositis, does the interferon-beta-specific monoclonal antibody dazukibart, compared with placebo, improve skin disease activity (CDASI) and muscle outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Dermatomyositis/drug therapy,immunology · Double-Blind Method · Middle Aged · Male · Female · Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized/therapeutic use,adverse effects,administration & dosage · Aged · Interferon-beta/therapeutic use,adverse effects,immunology · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult · Severity of Illness Index · Adolescent · Aged, 80 and over
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): In the single phase 2 programme (75 patients), dazukibart produced a large reduction in skin disease activity — pooled CDASI-A change −19.2 on 600 mg versus a placebo-adjusted difference of −16.3 points at week 12 (P<0.0001) — with significant improvement already by week 4 and persistence to week 76 in a small open-label extension. Muscle outcomes were secondary and rest on an 18-patient cohort, so the programme is skin-primary. Phase-2-only, single-programme evidence caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Intravenous immunoglobulin in dermatomyositis is homed on pack #2718 and is not carded here.

cards.headline: Phase 2 trial (Fiorentino 2025): dazukibart cut skin activity (CDASI-A) by 16.3 points more than placebo at week 12 in pooled skin-predominant disease (P<0.0001)
cards.summary: Phase 2 trial (Fiorentino 2025): dazukibart cut skin activity (CDASI-A) by 16.3 points more than placebo at week 12 in pooled skin-predominant disease (P<0.0001)
cards.people: 75 adults aged 18–80 with moderate-to-severe dermatomyositis at 25 sites in Germany, Hungary, Poland, Spain and the USA: skin-predominant disease (CDASI-A ≥14, at least one failed standard systemic treatment) in stages 1, 2 and 2a, and muscle-predominant disease in stage 3. Patients received intravenous dazukibart 150 mg (n=15), dazukibart 600 mg (n=37) or placebo (n=23) every 4 weeks, with treatment switches at week 12 in stages 2a and 3. Primary skin outcome: change in CDASI-A at week 12.
cards.result: In stage 1, mean CDASI-A change on dazukibart 600 mg was −18.8 (90% CI −21.8 to −15.8), a placebo-adjusted difference of −14.8 (90% CI −20.3 to −9.4; P<0.0001). In the pooled skin population, change was −19.2 on 600 mg (placebo-adjusted −16.3, 90% CI −20.4 to −12.1; P<0.0001) and −16.6 on 150 mg (placebo-adjusted −13.7, 90% CI −18.3 to −9.0; P<0.0001). Treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 80% (150 mg), 81% (600 mg) and 78% (placebo); infections were the commonest category. Serious adverse events were reported by four patients on 150 mg and one on placebo. One stage 3 patient died during follow-up from haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and macrophage activation syndrome.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 only, 75 patients in a multi-stage design with mid-trial treatment switches, and a skin-primary programme: the muscle-predominant cohort (18 patients) contributed safety data, not a powered muscle efficacy result. The single death (haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis/macrophage activation syndrome) occurred in a disease where that complication is itself a recognised risk.
cards.source: Fiorentino D et al. Efficacy, safety, and target engagement of dazukibart, an IFNβ specific monoclonal antibody, in adults with dermatomyositis: a multicentre, double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 2 trial. Lancet. 2025. PMID: 39798982. Registry ID: NCT03181893. cards.headline: Rapid-onset analysis (Aggarwal 2026): skin improvement was already significant by week 4 — at least 40% CDASI-A improvement in 53.3% (150 mg) and 42.9% (600 mg) versus 7.7% on placebo
cards.summary: Rapid-onset analysis (Aggarwal 2026): skin improvement was already significant by week 4 — at least 40% CDASI-A improvement in 53.3% (150 mg) and 42.9% (600 mg) versus 7.7% on placebo
cards.type: Prespecified secondary (rapid-onset) analysis of a randomised phase 2 trial (Aggarwal 2026)
cards.people: Prespecified secondary analysis of the same phase 2 trial (NCT03181893): skin-predominant cohort (n=57) and muscle-predominant cohort (n=18), assessing CDASI-A, itch (5D-itch), quality of life (DLQI), Total Improvement Score and core-set measures at weeks 1, 4 and 8, before the week-12 primary readout.
cards.result: In skin-predominant disease, placebo-adjusted CDASI-A improvement was already significant at week 4 (150 mg: −10.5, P=0.0006; 600 mg: −9.7, P=0.0004), itch improved by week 1 on 600 mg (−2.0; P=0.0359) and quality of life by week 4. A decrease of at least 40% in CDASI-A at week 4 occurred in 53.3% on 150 mg, 42.9% on 600 mg and 7.7% on placebo. In the muscle-predominant cohort (n=18, not powered), Total Improvement Score numerically favoured dazukibart 600 mg at week 4, creatine kinase fell significantly (P=0.0445), and minimal and major improvement were achieved by 77.8% and 22.2% on 600 mg versus 66.7% and 0% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: An early-timepoint re-analysis of the same 75-patient trial — speed of onset is useful clinically, but these are secondary looks at one small dataset, and the muscle cohort (18 patients) cannot support a muscle-efficacy claim.
cards.source: Aggarwal R et al. Rapid Onset of Response in Adults with Dermatomyositis Receiving Dazukibart: A Phase 2, Double-Blind, Randomized, Placebo-Controlled Study. Clin Cosmet Investig Dermatol. 2026. PMID: 42273013. Registry ID: NCT03181893. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Long-term extension (Vleugels 2026): skin gains held to week 76 in the small open-label extension — median CDASI-A change −23.5 in the pooled skin set (n=16)
cards.summary: Long-term extension (Vleugels 2026): skin gains held to week 76 in the small open-label extension — median CDASI-A change −23.5 in the pooled skin set (n=16)
cards.type: Open-label extension of a phase 2 trial (Vleugels 2026)
cards.people: Participants who completed the 24-week double-blind phase 2 study entered a 52-week open-label extension (combined duration 92 weeks). The long-term analysis covers patients who received at least one dose of dazukibart 600 mg in the extension: 9 from the skin-predominant cohort, 15 from the muscle-predominant cohort, and 16 in the pooled skin analysis set (baseline CDASI-A ≥14). Median age 49.5 years; 83% female; 96% White.
cards.result: Treatment-emergent adverse events were mild (55%), moderate (38%) or severe (7%), with no treatment-related serious adverse events or treatment discontinuations. At week 76, median CDASI-A change from baseline was −24.0 (range −33 to −12) in the skin-predominant group, −9.0 (−32 to 1) in the muscle-predominant group and −23.5 (−33 to −12) in the pooled skin set. In the muscle-predominant cohort, median Total Improvement Score at week 76 was 65.0 (range 2.5–95.0). Improvements persisted, slightly reduced, through the 16-week post-treatment follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Very small, uncontrolled extension subsets (9–16 patients per analysis set) drawn from trial completers — durability in responders who stayed on treatment, not evidence about the average patient. Counts here are the extension analysis sets, not the original randomised population.
cards.source: Vleugels RA et al. Long-Term Safety and Efficacy of Dazukibart in Dermatomyositis: Combined Phase II Results From Double-Blind and Open-Label Extension Studies. J Rheumatol. 2026. PMID: 42542380. Registry ID: NCT05192200 (extension) and NCT03181893. cards.headline: Synthesis: a large, rapid skin effect in one phase 2 programme — muscle benefit and phase 3 confirmation are still missing
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large, rapid skin effect in one phase 2 programme — muscle benefit and phase 3 confirmation are still missing
cards.people: One phase 2 programme (75 randomised patients) reported three times: the primary trial, a rapid-onset secondary analysis, and a small open-label extension.
cards.result: Skin activity fell by about 14–16 CDASI-A points more than placebo at week 12, with separation by week 4 and persistence to week 76 in extension patients. Muscle outcomes are secondary and rest on an 18-patient cohort. Harms were mainly infections at rates similar to placebo, with one death from haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis/macrophage activation syndrome during follow-up. Dazukibart is a Pfizer product. Intravenous immunoglobulin in dermatomyositis (ProDERM) is homed on pack #2718 and is not carded here.
cards.watchOut: A single sponsor's phase 2 programme with a skin-primary endpoint: the effect size is unusually large for dermatomyositis, which is precisely why phase 3 confirmation — and a powered muscle outcome — are needed before this is more than POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fiorentino D et al. Lancet. 2025 (PMID: 39798982); Aggarwal R et al. Clin Cosmet Investig Dermatol. 2026 (PMID: 42273013); Vleugels RA et al. J Rheumatol. 2026 (PMID: 42542380).

shelves.title: Rituximab in systemic sclerosis (DESIRES): skin score −8.44 points versus placebo — the strongest skin signal in the disease, from one small trial
shelves.question: In adults with systemic sclerosis, does rituximab, compared with placebo, improve skin thickening (modified Rodnan skin score) and lung function (DESIRES programme)?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): In the DESIRES trial (56 Japanese patients with systemic sclerosis and mRSS ≥10), rituximab improved skin thickening versus placebo at week 24 (mRSS change −6.30 vs +2.14; difference −8.44, 95% CI −11.00 to −5.88; P<0.0001), with further improvement after a second course in the open-label extension and sustained skin and lung gains in long-term follow-up. A single-country, investigator-initiated programme of 56 randomised patients caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Rituximab comparisons in connective-tissue-disease lung disease are homed on packs #3950 and #6841, and SSc lung treatments on live shelf #688 — not carded here. The primary report was re-verified by title search at build: PMID 38279402 is the DESIRES double-blind trial (Lancet Rheumatol 2021).

cards.headline: DESIRES double-blind trial (Ebata 2021): skin score improved on rituximab and worsened on placebo — mRSS change −6.30 versus +2.14 (difference −8.44; P<0.0001) in 56 patients
cards.summary: DESIRES double-blind trial (Ebata 2021): skin score improved on rituximab and worsened on placebo — mRSS change −6.30 versus +2.14 (difference −8.44; P<0.0001) in 56 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled investigator-initiated trial (Ebata 2021, DESIRES)
cards.people: 56 patients aged 20–79 with systemic sclerosis (2013 ACR/EULAR criteria) and modified Rodnan Skin Score (mRSS) of at least 10, at four hospitals in Japan, randomised 1:1 to intravenous rituximab 375 mg/m² (n=28) or placebo (n=28) once weekly for 4 weeks. Primary endpoint: absolute change in mRSS at week 24. 91% were women.
cards.result: Change in mRSS at week 24 was −6.30 on rituximab versus +2.14 on placebo (difference −8.44, 95% CI −11.00 to −5.88; P<0.0001). Adverse events occurred in 28 of 28 patients (100%) on rituximab and 23 of 26 (88%) on placebo; the commonest was upper respiratory infection (39% vs 38%). One serious adverse event leading to discontinuation occurred in each group (decreased serum albumin on rituximab; biliary enzyme increase on placebo). There were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: A single-country (Japan), investigator-initiated trial of 56 patients with a skin-score primary endpoint at 24 weeks — the effect is large, but the trial is small, and 22 of 28 placebo patients versus 27 of 28 rituximab patients completed follow-up, so attrition was uneven.
cards.source: Ebata S et al. Safety and efficacy of rituximab in systemic sclerosis (DESIRES): a double-blind, investigator-initiated, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Rheumatol. 2021. PMID: 38279402. Registry ID: NCT04274257 (and UMIN000030139). MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: DESIRES open-label extension (Ebata 2022): a second rituximab course deepened the gain (mRSS −8.88 by week 48), and patients switched from placebo improved once treated (−6.05)
cards.summary: DESIRES open-label extension (Ebata 2022): a second rituximab course deepened the gain (mRSS −8.88 by week 48), and patients switched from placebo improved once treated (−6.05)
cards.type: Open-label extension of a randomised trial (Ebata 2022, DESIRES extension)
cards.people: Patients completing the 24-week double-blind DESIRES phase received a further 24 weeks of open-label rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 weeks): 26 patients originally on rituximab and 20 originally on placebo entered the extension, and 24 and 19 respectively completed it. All endpoints were exploratory.
cards.result: In the rituximab–rituximab group, mRSS improved from baseline by −5.81 (SD 3.16) at week 24 and −8.88 (SD 3.10) at week 48. In the placebo–rituximab group, mRSS had worsened by week 24 (+2.14, SD 5.51) and improved after switching, reaching −6.05 (SD 4.43) at week 48. One serious adverse event occurred in each group during the extension (cholangitis; pneumococcal pneumonia). There were no deaths.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no continuing placebo group — the switchers' improvement is consistent with a drug effect (and mirrors the blinded result), but expectation and natural skin softening in systemic sclerosis cannot be excluded without a control.
cards.source: Ebata S et al. Safety and efficacy of rituximab in systemic sclerosis (DESIRES): open-label extension of a double-blind, investigators-initiated, randomised, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet Rheumatol. 2022. PMID: 38294008. Registry ID: NCT04274257 (and UMIN000030139). cards.headline: DESIRES long-term follow-up (Kuzumi 2023, observational cohort): skin and lung gains were sustained to a median 96 weeks in 29 patients who continued rituximab
cards.summary: DESIRES long-term follow-up (Kuzumi 2023, observational cohort): skin and lung gains were sustained to a median 96 weeks in 29 patients who continued rituximab
cards.type: Observational long-term cohort follow-up of a randomised trial (Kuzumi 2023)
cards.people: Single-centre cohort of 29 patients with systemic sclerosis (93% female; median age 48 years) who completed the DESIRES trial and continued rituximab, with complete data, followed for a median of 96 weeks. Post-hoc analysis of skin score, lung function and serum immunoglobulins by number of rituximab courses.
cards.result: Modified Rodnan Skin Score improved significantly after one course (median change −7, IQR −8.5 to −4; P<0.001) and percentage of predicted forced vital capacity after three courses (median change +1.85, IQR 0.13 to 5.68; P<0.001), both sustained during follow-up. High responders (mRSS improvement of at least 9; n=16) had greater falls in serum IgG and IgA than low responders (n=13), and the fall in IgA correlated with skin improvement (r=0.64; P<0.001). Low IgM, IgA and IgG were seen in 7, 1 and 1 patients respectively at last follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Observational follow-up of the 29 of 43 trial completers who chose to continue rituximab and had complete data — a responder-enriched group, so sustained benefit here is expected and cannot be generalised to all starters.
cards.source: Kuzumi A et al. Long-term Outcomes After Rituximab Treatment for Patients With Systemic Sclerosis: Follow-up of the DESIRES Trial With a Focus on Serum Immunoglobulin Levels. JAMA Dermatol. 2023. PMID: 36790794. Registry ID: none listed in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small Japanese trial programme with a large skin effect, sustained on continued treatment — promising and unreplicated
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small Japanese trial programme with a large skin effect, sustained on continued treatment — promising and unreplicated
cards.people: One investigator-initiated programme reported three times: the double-blind trial (56 patients), its open-label extension (46 patients) and a long-term cohort (29 patients).
cards.result: Skin score: −8.44 points versus placebo at week 24 (P<0.0001), deepening to −8.88 from baseline at week 48 after a second course, with lung function gains emerging after three courses in long-term follow-up. Harms were mainly infections at placebo-like rates in the blinded phase. Other systemic sclerosis questions are homed elsewhere — nintedanib and tocilizumab for SSc lung disease on live shelf #688, and rituximab against cyclophosphamide or added to mycophenolate in connective-tissue-disease lung disease on packs #3950 and #6841 — those comparisons are not carded here; this shelf asks rituximab versus placebo on skin disease.
cards.watchOut: A single-country, single-programme base of 56 randomised patients: the result is the strongest placebo-controlled skin signal in systemic sclerosis, and it still needs a larger, multicentre trial before it can carry more than POSSIBLE.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ebata S et al. Lancet Rheumatol. 2021 (PMID: 38279402); Ebata S et al. Lancet Rheumatol. 2022 (PMID: 38294008); Kuzumi A et al. JAMA Dermatol. 2023 (PMID: 36790794).

shelves.title: Olokizumab in rheumatoid arthritis (CREDO): three positive phase 3 trials, noninferior to adalimumab — effective, unapproved, long-term safety unknown
shelves.question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis with inadequate response to conventional or biologic DMARDs, does the anti-IL-6 monoclonal antibody olokizumab, compared with placebo or adalimumab, improve disease activity (CREDO programme)?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antirheumatic Agents/adverse effects · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/chemically induced,drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Humans · Interleukin-6 · Methotrexate · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit): Three phase 3 CREDO trials (2,444 patients) consistently show olokizumab 64 mg (every 2 or 4 weeks) plus methotrexate beating placebo on ACR20 at week 12 — CREDO-1: 63.6%/70.4% vs 25.9%; CREDO-2: 70.3%/71.4% vs 44.4%, with noninferiority to adalimumab; CREDO-3 (TNF-inadequate responders): 60.9%/59.6% vs 40.6%. The stamp stays at POSSIBLE because the programme is a single sponsor's, predominantly Russia/Eastern Europe in origin, limited to 24-week trials, and the drug is not FDA-approved, so long-term interleukin-6-class safety is uncharacterised. The interleukin-6 receptor blockers tocilizumab and sarilumab in rheumatoid arthritis are homed on pack #5446 and are not carded here.

cards.headline: CREDO-1 (Nasonov 2022): ACR20 at week 12 in 63.6% (every 2 weeks) and 70.4% (every 4 weeks) on olokizumab versus 25.9% on placebo (P<0.0001) in 428 patients
cards.summary: CREDO-1 (Nasonov 2022): ACR20 at week 12 in 63.6% (every 2 weeks) and 70.4% (every 4 weeks) on olokizumab versus 25.9% on placebo (P<0.0001) in 428 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Nasonov 2022, CREDO-1)
cards.people: 428 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate, in a 24-week multicentre double-blind trial, randomised 1:1:1 to subcutaneous olokizumab 64 mg every 2 weeks, olokizumab 64 mg every 4 weeks, or placebo, all plus methotrexate. Primary endpoint: ACR20 response at week 12.
cards.result: ACR20 responses were 63.6% on olokizumab every 2 weeks and 70.4% on olokizumab every 4 weeks versus 25.9% on placebo (P<0.0001 for both). All secondary endpoints (including DAS28-CRP below 3.2, HAQ-DI, ACR50 and Clinical Disease Activity Index remission) differed significantly in favour of olokizumab, with no discernible difference between the two regimens. Treatment-emergent serious adverse events were more frequent on olokizumab than placebo; infections were the commonest. No neutralising antidrug antibodies developed.
cards.watchOut: A 24-week trial with a 12-week symptom-and-signs primary endpoint — it establishes short-term disease-activity control, not structural protection, cardiovascular safety, or durability beyond the extension data.
cards.source: Nasonov E et al. Olokizumab, a monoclonal antibody against interleukin 6, in combination with methotrexate in patients with rheumatoid arthritis inadequately controlled by methotrexate: efficacy and safety results of a randomised controlled phase III study. Ann Rheum Dis. 2022. PMID: 34344706. Registry ID: NCT02760368. cards.headline: CREDO-2 (Smolen 2022, NEJM): olokizumab beat placebo (ACR20 70.3% and 71.4% vs 44.4%) and was noninferior to adalimumab in 1,648 patients
cards.summary: CREDO-2 (Smolen 2022, NEJM): olokizumab beat placebo (ACR20 70.3% and 71.4% vs 44.4%) and was noninferior to adalimumab in 1,648 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo- and active-controlled phase 3 trial (Smolen 2022, CREDO-2)
cards.people: 1,648 patients with rheumatoid arthritis and an inadequate response to methotrexate, randomised 2:2:2:1 to subcutaneous olokizumab 64 mg every 2 weeks (n=464), olokizumab every 4 weeks (n=479), adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks (n=462) or placebo (n=243), all continuing methotrexate, for 24 weeks. Primary endpoint: ACR20 at week 12, tested for superiority to placebo and noninferiority to adalimumab (margin −12 percentage points).
cards.result: ACR20 at week 12 occurred in 70.3% on olokizumab every 2 weeks (difference vs placebo 25.9 percentage points, 97.5% CI 17.1 to 34.1), 71.4% on olokizumab every 4 weeks (difference 27.0 points, 97.5% CI 18.3 to 35.2) and 66.9% on adalimumab (difference 22.5 points, 95% CI 14.8 to 29.8), versus 44.4% on placebo (P<0.001 for superiority of each olokizumab dose). Both olokizumab doses were noninferior to adalimumab (differences 3.4 points, 97.5% CI −3.5 to 10.2, and 4.5 points, 97.5% CI −2.2 to 11.2). Adverse events, most commonly infections, occurred in approximately 70% of olokizumab patients; anti-olokizumab antibodies were detected in 3.8% (every 2 weeks) and 5.1% (every 4 weeks).
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority to adalimumab on a 12-week ACR20 endpoint with a wide (−12 point) margin is not equivalence on outcomes that matter long-term, and the authors themselves call for larger, longer trials for efficacy and safety. The placebo ACR20 rate (44.4%) was high, which compresses the apparent advantage.
cards.source: Smolen JS et al. Olokizumab versus Placebo or Adalimumab in Rheumatoid Arthritis. N Engl J Med. 2022. PMID: 36001712. Registry ID: NCT02760407. cards.headline: CREDO-3 (Feist 2022): in TNF-inhibitor inadequate responders, ACR20 was 60.9% and 59.6% on olokizumab versus 40.6% on placebo (P<0.01) in 368 patients
cards.summary: CREDO-3 (Feist 2022): in TNF-inhibitor inadequate responders, ACR20 was 60.9% and 59.6% on olokizumab versus 40.6% on placebo (P<0.01) in 368 patients
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 3 trial (Feist 2022, CREDO-3)
cards.people: 368 patients with rheumatoid arthritis and prior inadequate response to tumour necrosis factor inhibitors, in a 24-week multicentre double-blind trial, randomised 2:2:1 to subcutaneous olokizumab 64 mg every 2 weeks, olokizumab every 4 weeks, or placebo, all plus methotrexate; placebo patients were re-randomised to olokizumab at week 16. Primary endpoint: ACR20 at week 12.
cards.result: ACR20 response rates were 60.9% on olokizumab every 2 weeks and 59.6% on olokizumab every 4 weeks versus 40.6% on placebo (P<0.01 for both comparisons). DAS28-CRP below 3.2 at week 12 also significantly favoured olokizumab, and improvements were maintained to week 24 and appeared after week 16 in placebo switchers. Treatment-emergent serious adverse events were dose-related: 7% on olokizumab every 2 weeks, 3.2% on olokizumab every 4 weeks and none on placebo.
cards.watchOut: The harder-to-treat TNF-inadequate population still shows a ~20-point ACR20 advantage, but serious treatment-emergent events were numerically higher on olokizumab (7% at the higher frequency versus none on placebo) in a trial too small and short to characterise interleukin-6-class harms.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials agree — olokizumab controls rheumatoid arthritis activity about as well as adalimumab at 12 weeks; long-term safety is the open question
cards.summary: Synthesis: three phase 3 trials agree — olokizumab controls rheumatoid arthritis activity about as well as adalimumab at 12 weeks; long-term safety is the open question
cards.people: Three phase 3 trials in the CREDO programme: CREDO-1 (428 methotrexate inadequate responders), CREDO-2 (1,648 patients, with an adalimumab arm) and CREDO-3 (368 TNF-inhibitor inadequate responders) — 2,444 patients in total.
cards.result: ACR20 advantages over placebo at week 12 were consistent: about +38 to +44 points in CREDO-1, +26 to +27 points in CREDO-2 and about +20 points in CREDO-3, with both dosing intervals (every 2 or every 4 weeks) effective and noninferiority to adalimumab shown in CREDO-2. Infections were the commonest harm, as expected for interleukin-6 blockade. Olokizumab blocks the interleukin-6 ligand itself, unlike the receptor blockers tocilizumab and sarilumab homed on pack #5446 — a distinct agent, not carded there. Olokizumab is not FDA-approved, and its programme originates predominantly from Russia and Eastern Europe.
cards.watchOut: All trials are 24 weeks with 12-week primary endpoints from one sponsor's programme: there is no long-term cardiovascular, malignancy or structural-outcome record comparable to the established interleukin-6 receptor blockers, which is why three positive phase 3 trials still cap at POSSIBLE for a drug without FDA approval or independent replication.

shelves.title: Grip-strength centiles across the life course: median grip peaks at 51 kg in men and 31 kg in women, holds to midlife, then declines — with developing-region norms about 0.85 SD below British centiles
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are grip-strength centiles across the life course by sex (peak, plateau and decline), harmonised across dynamometer studies — and how much do values vary between world regions?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Child · Child, Preschool · Cohort Studies · Cross-Sectional Studies · Databases, Factual · Female · Hand Strength · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Strength Dynamometer · Prevalence · Sarcopenia · United Kingdom · White People · Young Adult
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (skeletal-muscle physiology; textbook framing, not evidence). The carded base meets the row's condition of at least one primary normative cohort alongside the syntheses: a pooled primary-data analysis of twelve British general-population studies (49,964 participants), a primary population-based household-survey cohort from Brazil (N=3,050, Jamar dynamometer), and a global systematic review/meta-analysis of normative data (63 samples, 96,537 observations). All three agree on the life-course shape — rise to a peak in early adult life, maintenance through midlife, decline from midlife onwards, men stronger than women from adolescence — and on the size of the sex gap at peak (median 51 kg men versus 31 kg women in the British centiles). The honest regional caveat is quantified, not hand-waved: developed-region norms sit essentially on the British centiles (+0.12 SD), while developing-region norms sit clearly lower (−0.85 SD), so British cut-points travel across developed regions but not worldwide. Dynamometer type and test position were examined in sensitivity analyses in the British pooled analysis and did not change the findings; the primary Brazilian cohort used a single named device and protocol and is carded as such.

cards.headline: Dodds 2014: grip rises to a peak median of 51 kg in men (ages 29–39) and 31 kg in women (ages 26–42), holds through midlife, then declines — weak grip reaches 23% of men and 27% of women by age 80
cards.summary: Dodds 2014: grip rises to a peak median of 51 kg in men (ages 29–39) and 31 kg in women (ages 26–42), holds through midlife, then declines — weak grip reaches 23% of men and 27% of women by age 80
cards.people: 49,964 participants (26,687 female) contributing 60,803 grip-strength observations across twelve British general-population studies, ages 4 to 90 years; centile curves were produced across the life course.
cards.result: The pooled centiles show three periods: increase to a peak in early adult life, maintenance through midlife, and decline from midlife onwards. Males were on average stronger than females from adolescence onwards: peak median grip was 51 kg in males between ages 29 and 39, compared with 31 kg in females between ages 26 and 42. Weak grip, defined as at least 2.5 SD below the sex-specific peak mean, rose sharply with age, reaching a prevalence of 23% in males and 27% of females by age 80. Sensitivity analyses found the centiles robust to dynamometer type and to seated versus standing measurement position.
cards.watchOut: British, predominantly White general-population samples — the centiles are a developed-region reference; the global comparison card below shows they do not transfer unchanged to developing regions.

cards.headline: Schlüssel 2008 (primary population cohort, Brazil): mean right-hand grip 42.8 kg in men and 25.3 kg in women, peaking in the fourth decade and falling after age 40 in women and 50 in men
cards.summary: Schlüssel 2008 (primary population cohort, Brazil): mean right-hand grip 42.8 kg in men and 25.3 kg in women, peaking in the fourth decade and falling after age 40 in women and 50 in men
cards.people: 3,050 healthy adults aged 20 years and over (1,122 men and 1,928 women) from a representative household survey in Niterói, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; grip measured three times in both hands with a Jamar mechanical dynamometer, highest value analysed.
cards.result: Mean right-hand grip was 42.8 kg in men and 25.3 kg in women (left hand 40.9 and 24.0 kg). Grip increased with age to its highest values in the fourth decade of life, then decreased significantly after age 40 in women and after age 50 in men. Body mass index was associated with grip in both sexes, but only underweight men had significantly lower values. This single-protocol primary cohort independently reproduces the pooled British life-course shape — fourth-decade peak, midlife decline, large sex gap — in a non-British population.
cards.watchOut: One city, one device (Jamar mechanical dynamometer), best-of-three protocol — absolute values are protocol-bound; the cohort supports the life-course pattern and the sex gap, not a universal kilogram cut-point.

cards.headline: Dodds 2016 (global meta-analysis): developed-region grip norms match British centiles (+0.12 SD) but developing-region norms are clearly lower (−0.85 SD) — cut-points do not travel worldwide
cards.summary: Dodds 2016 (global meta-analysis): developed-region grip norms match British centiles (+0.12 SD) but developing-region norms are clearly lower (−0.85 SD) — cut-points do not travel worldwide
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 60 papers reporting 63 samples with age- and sex-stratified normative grip data, comprising 726 normative data items and 96,537 grip-strength observations across seven UN regions (44 of 63 samples from developed regions).
cards.result: Normative data were converted to Z-scores against the British life-course centiles. Developed-region data were broadly similar to the British reference, pooling at +0.12 SD (95% CI 0.07 to 0.17). Developing-region data were clearly lower, pooling at −0.85 SD (95% CI −0.94 to −0.76). The authors conclude British centiles and their weak-grip cut-points are supportable across developed regions, but different cut-points are needed in developing regions.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis of normative reports with differing devices and protocols, and developed regions dominate the sample count (44 of 63) — the developing-region estimate rests on fewer, more heterogeneous samples.

cards.headline: Synthesis: grip strength has a settled life-course centile shape — peak near 51 kg (men) and 31 kg (women), plateau to midlife, then decline — but the kilogram values are regional, not universal
cards.summary: Synthesis: grip strength has a settled life-course centile shape — peak near 51 kg (men) and 31 kg (women), plateau to midlife, then decline — but the kilogram values are regional, not universal
cards.people: Synthesis of Dodds 2014 (pooled British primary data, 49,964 participants), Schlüssel 2008 (primary Brazilian population cohort, N=3,050) and Dodds 2016 (global meta-analysis, 96,537 observations), framed by Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (textbook framing, not an evidence card).
cards.result: Three independent angles — pooled primary data, a single-protocol population cohort on another continent, and a worldwide meta-analysis — give the same physiology: grip rises through childhood and adolescence to an early-adult peak (British medians 51 kg in men, 31 kg in women), is maintained through midlife, and declines from midlife on, steeply enough that roughly a quarter of 80-year-olds fall at least 2.5 SD below the peak mean. Men are stronger than women at every adult age. The variation that matters clinically is regional: norms from developed regions sit on the British centiles (+0.12 SD), norms from developing regions sit about 0.85 SD lower, so a weak-grip threshold derived in Britain will over-label weakness where regional norms are lower. Device and position differences did not move the British centiles in sensitivity analyses, but each primary cohort's absolute values remain bound to its own protocol — compare a patient against centiles from a matching population and protocol, not against a single universal number.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis: two of the three carded reports share the Dodds group and the British reference dataset — the Brazilian primary cohort is the fully independent replication of the pattern, and regional transfer limits are part of the finding, not a footnote.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dodds RM et al. PLoS One. 2014 (PMID: 25474696); Schlüssel MM et al. Clin Nutr. 2008 (PMID: 18547686); Dodds RM et al. Age Ageing. 2016 (PMID: 26790455). Registry IDs: none in the records.
