shelves.title: Ozoralizumab in rheumatoid arthritis: ACR20 about 76–80% versus 37% on placebo plus methotrexate in the Japanese OHZORA trial; NATSUZORA tested it without methotrexate
shelves.question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate, does the anti-TNF multivalent NANOBODY compound ozoralizumab, compared with placebo plus methotrexate (and, in a second trial, without methotrexate), improve disease activity (OHZORA / NATSUZORA programme)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Antirheumatic Agents · Arthritis, Rheumatoid · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Methotrexate · Treatment Outcome · Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. In OHZORA (381 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite methotrexate), ozoralizumab 30 mg and 80 mg every 4 weeks plus methotrexate produced ACR20 responses at week 16 of 79.6% and 75.3% versus 37.3% on placebo plus methotrexate (P<0.001), with significantly more structural nonprogression at week 24. In NATSUZORA (140 patients), ozoralizumab without methotrexate was tested in an open-label randomised dose comparison — responses were high at week 24 and maintained to 52 weeks, but there was no placebo arm, and antidrug antibodies appeared in about 40% of patients. The integrated long-term analysis of both trials and their HOSHIZORA extension (521 enrolled; mean treatment duration 200 weeks) found no new safety concerns and maintained responses. The limits are printed on the face: this is a single-country (Japan) programme, the drug is approved there and not FDA-approved, only one trial is placebo-controlled, and no trial compares ozoralizumab with an established anti-TNF agent. Ozoralizumab is a single-source product of Taisho (named for clarification, as a product not approved or regulated outside Japan).

cards.headline: OHZORA phase II/III primary (Takeuchi 2022): ACR20 at week 16 in 79.6% (30 mg) and 75.3% (80 mg) versus 37.3% on placebo plus methotrexate
cards.summary: OHZORA phase II/III primary (Takeuchi 2022): ACR20 at week 16 in 79.6% (30 mg) and 75.3% (80 mg) versus 37.3% on placebo plus methotrexate
cards.type: Phase II/III randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 24 weeks
cards.people: 381 patients with rheumatoid arthritis whose disease remained active despite methotrexate, randomised to subcutaneous placebo, ozoralizumab 30 mg, or ozoralizumab 80 mg, each plus methotrexate, injected every 4 weeks for 24 weeks.
cards.result: ACR20 response at week 16 was 79.6% on ozoralizumab 30 mg and 75.3% on 80 mg versus 37.3% on placebo (P<0.001 for both). The proportion with structural nonprogression (change in Sharp/van der Heijde score ≤0 at week 24) was significantly higher in both ozoralizumab groups than on placebo, and some secondary endpoints improved from as early as day 3. Serious adverse events occurred in 4 patients in the 30 mg group and 5 in the 80 mg group; the authors reported acceptable tolerability with no new safety signals compared with other anti-TNF antibodies.
cards.watchOut: A single-country (Japan) trial in methotrexate inadequate responders; ozoralizumab is approved in Japan and is not FDA-approved. The 52-week report of this same OHZORA trial is a further report of this trial, not a second trial, and is not carded separately here.

cards.summary: NATSUZORA phase III (Tanaka 2023): ozoralizumab without methotrexate — randomised open-label dose comparison in 140 patients, responses high at week 24 and maintained to week 52
cards.type: Phase III randomised, open-label, multicentre dose-comparison trial (no placebo arm), 52 weeks
cards.people: 140 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis randomly allocated 2:1 to subcutaneous ozoralizumab 30 mg or 80 mg every 4 weeks for 52 weeks, without methotrexate co-administration.
cards.result: Both dose groups showed good clinical improvement: American College of Rheumatology response rates were high at week 24 and maintained through 52 weeks, improvements in other endpoints were seen from week 1, and efficacy assessments were similar between doses (the record's abstract reports the pattern without dose-specific response percentages). No deaths were reported; serious adverse events occurred in a total of 20 patients. Antidrug antibodies increased in approximately 40% of patients, and 27.7% of the 30 mg group were neutralising-antibody positive.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo or active comparator — this trial shows maintained response on treatment, not a placebo-controlled effect, and its immunogenicity rates (about 40% antidrug antibodies without methotrexate) are part of its result.
cards.source: Tanaka Y et al. Efficacy and safety of anti-TNF multivalent NANOBODY® compound 'ozoralizumab' without methotrexate co-administration in patients with active rheumatoid arthritis: A 52-week result of phase III, randomised, open-label trial (NATSUZORA trial). Modern rheumatology. 2023. PMID: 36201360. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Integrated long-term analysis (Tanaka 2024): OHZORA + NATSUZORA + HOSHIZORA extension — 521 enrolled, mean 200 weeks of treatment, no new safety concerns and ACR responses maintained
cards.summary: Integrated long-term analysis (Tanaka 2024): OHZORA + NATSUZORA + HOSHIZORA extension — 521 enrolled, mean 200 weeks of treatment, no new safety concerns and ACR responses maintained
cards.type: Integrated long-term safety/efficacy analysis of the OHZORA and NATSUZORA trials and their HOSHIZORA long-term extension (one programme)
cards.people: The OHZORA and NATSUZORA trials enrolled 521 patients in total; 401 entered the HOSHIZORA long-term extension and 279 completed it, with a mean treatment duration of 200 weeks and total exposure of 1419.34 person-years in all enrolled patients.
cards.result: Of the patients, 96.9% had at least one adverse event, mostly mild to moderate. One death was observed; no conspicuous adverse events emerged and no specific concerns in adverse events of special interest were found through long-term administration. American College of Rheumatology 20%, 50% and 70% response rates were maintained during the trials.
cards.watchOut: An integrated analysis of the same programme's trials and their extension — it adds duration and exposure, not an independent test of efficacy, and extension populations are survivors of the parent trials.
cards.source: Tanaka Y et al. Long-term safety and efficacy of anti-TNF multivalent VHH antibodies ozoralizumab in patients with rheumatoid arthritis. RMD open. 2024. PMID: 39179257. cards.summary: Synthesis: one Japanese programme — a clear placebo-controlled win with methotrexate, maintained responses without it, and clean long-term tolerability within programme limits; POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: OHZORA (381 patients, placebo-controlled with methotrexate), NATSUZORA (140 patients, open-label without methotrexate) and the integrated HOSHIZORA long-term analysis (521 enrolled across the programme).
cards.result: The placebo-controlled evidence is one trial: ACR20 separated from placebo by about 38–42 percentage points at week 16 with less structural progression. The no-methotrexate trial was open-label and dose-comparing only, and the long-term analysis is the same programme followed longer. A single-country, single-programme base caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: Ozoralizumab is a single-source product (Taisho, Japan; named here for clarification as a non-FDA-approved product) and is not approved outside Japan; antidrug and neutralising antibodies were commoner without methotrexate, and no trial here compares ozoralizumab with an established anti-TNF agent.

shelves.title: Mavrilimumab in rheumatoid arthritis: phase 2 DAS28-CRP response 55.7% versus 34.7% on placebo; long-term extension followed the pulmonary signal for 899 patient-years
shelves.question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis, does the anti-GM-CSF-receptor-α antibody mavrilimumab, compared with placebo (on background methotrexate), improve disease activity — and what did its long-term extension show about the pulmonary safety signal that defines this class?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antirheumatic Agents · Arthritis, Rheumatoid · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate · Middle Aged · Receptors, Granulocyte-Macrophage Colony-Stimulating Factor · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. Mavrilimumab, a human monoclonal antibody against the GM-CSF receptor α subunit, showed rapid, dose-related efficacy in phase 2: the primary DAS28-CRP response at week 12 was 55.7% on mavrilimumab versus 34.7% on placebo (p=0.003), reaching 66.7% at 100 mg, and a 51-patient Japanese phase IIa population report pointed the same way (75.0% at 30 mg and 100 mg versus 23.5% on placebo). The long-term report of two phase IIb studies and their open-label extension (442 patients, 899 patient-years, median 2.5 years) found sustained efficacy (DAS28-CRP <2.6 in 40.6% at week 122) and addressed the class-defining pulmonary watch: reductions in FEV1 or FVC occurred in roughly 3–6% of patients at weeks 74–104, were mostly transient, and were only infrequently associated with adverse events. The programme was discontinued after phase 2 and mavrilimumab was never marketed — this shelf records a positive but unfinished programme, in the precedent of other discontinued-programme shelves.

cards.headline: Phase 2 dose-ranging trial (Burmester 2013): DAS28-CRP response at week 12 in 55.7% on mavrilimumab versus 34.7% on placebo, on background methotrexate
cards.summary: Phase 2 dose-ranging trial (Burmester 2013): DAS28-CRP response at week 12 in 55.7% on mavrilimumab versus 34.7% on placebo, on background methotrexate
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial, 12 weeks
cards.people: Subjects with rheumatoid arthritis on stable background methotrexate, randomised to subcutaneous mavrilimumab 10 mg, 30 mg, 50 mg or 100 mg, or placebo, every other week for 12 weeks (the record's abstract does not state the total number randomised).
cards.result: The primary endpoint — a decrease of at least 1.2 in DAS28-CRP at week 12 — was met by 55.7% of mavrilimumab-treated subjects versus 34.7% on placebo (p=0.003); by dose, responses were 41.0% (10 mg, p=0.543), 61.0% (30 mg, p=0.011), 53.8% (50 mg, p=0.071) and 66.7% (100 mg, p=0.001). At 100 mg, DAS28-CRP remission (<2.6) was 23.1% versus 6.7% (p=0.016) and ACR20 was 69.2% versus 40.0% (p=0.005). Adverse events were generally mild or moderate; no significant hypersensitivity reactions, serious or opportunistic infections, or changes in pulmonary parameters were observed in this 12-week trial.
cards.watchOut: A 12-week phase 2 trial — its clean pulmonary readout is short-term only; the class-defining pulmonary question is addressed by the long-term report carded below, not by this trial.
cards.source: Burmester GR et al. Efficacy and safety of mavrilimumab in subjects with rheumatoid arthritis. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2013. PMID: 23234647. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Japanese-population phase IIa report (Takeuchi 2015): DAS28-CRP response 50.0% versus 23.5% on placebo in 51 Japanese subjects (p=0.081); 75.0% at the 30 mg and 100 mg doses (p=0.028)
cards.summary: Japanese-population phase IIa report (Takeuchi 2015): DAS28-CRP response 50.0% versus 23.5% on placebo in 51 Japanese subjects (p=0.081); 75.0% at the 30 mg and 100 mg doses (p=0.028)
cards.type: Phase IIa randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — Japanese-population report, 12 weeks plus 12-week follow-up
cards.people: 51 Japanese subjects with moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis (from a phase IIa study conducted in Japan and Europe) received mavrilimumab 10–100 mg or placebo subcutaneously every other week for 12 weeks.
cards.result: By week 12, more mavrilimumab- than placebo-treated subjects achieved a DAS28-CRP response (decrease >1.2): 50.0% versus 23.5% (p=0.081); the 30 mg and 100 mg groups each reached 75.0% versus 23.5% (p=0.028), and the 100 mg group also showed statistically significant HAQ-DI and ACR20 responses. Adverse events were mild to moderate, with one serious adverse event of pneumonia considered possibly treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: A 51-patient population report of one phase IIa study within the same programme — it supports the dose-response in a Japanese population; it is not an independent programme, and its headline comparison did not reach significance (p=0.081).
cards.source: Takeuchi T et al. Efficacy and safety of mavrilimumab in Japanese subjects with rheumatoid arthritis: findings from a Phase IIa study. Modern rheumatology. 2015. PMID: 24720551. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Long-term report (Burmester 2018): two phase IIb studies plus open-label extension — 442 patients, 899 patient-years; efficacy sustained to week 122 and pulmonary function changes mostly transient
cards.summary: Long-term report (Burmester 2018): two phase IIb studies plus open-label extension — 442 patients, 899 patient-years; efficacy sustained to week 122 and pulmonary function changes mostly transient
cards.type: Long-term safety/efficacy report of two phase IIb randomised studies and their open-label extension (one programme)
cards.people: 442 patients with rheumatoid arthritis received mavrilimumab across phase IIb study 1071 (inadequate response to DMARDs; mavrilimumab 30, 100 or 150 mg or placebo, plus methotrexate), study 1107 (inadequate response to anti-TNF agents and/or DMARDs; mavrilimumab 100 mg or golimumab 50 mg, plus methotrexate), and the open-label extension (mavrilimumab 100 mg every other week plus methotrexate). Cumulative exposure was 899 patient-years; median treatment duration 2.5 years.
cards.result: The commonest treatment-emergent adverse events were nasopharyngitis (7.68 per 100 patient-years) and bronchitis (5.68 per 100 patient-years). At weeks 74 and 104, 3.5% and 6.2% of patients showed a reduction in forced expiratory volume in 1 second, and 2.9% and 3.4% a reduction in forced vital capacity (>20% reduction from baseline to <80% predicted); most pulmonary changes were transient and only infrequently associated with adverse events. At week 122 on 100 mg every other week, 65.0% of patients had DAS28-CRP <3.2 and 40.6% had DAS28-CRP <2.6.
cards.watchOut: Extension-phase efficacy is measured in patients who stayed on treatment, and the pulmonary percentages are the observed signal the class is watched for — small, mostly transient, and not a pulmonary alveolar proteinosis epidemic, but not zero.
cards.source: Burmester GR et al. Mavrilimumab, a Fully Human Granulocyte-Macrophage Colony-Stimulating Factor Receptor α Monoclonal Antibody: Long-Term Safety and Efficacy in Patients With Rheumatoid Arthritis. Arthritis & rheumatology (Hoboken, N.J.). 2018. PMID: 29361199. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01712399 (the open-label extension), from the record. cards.headline: Phase 1 first-in-human study (Burmester 2011): single intravenous doses in 32 patients — safety and pharmacodynamic activity (SOCS3 suppression), no DAS28 change overall
cards.summary: Phase 1 first-in-human study (Burmester 2011): single intravenous doses in 32 patients — safety and pharmacodynamic activity (SOCS3 suppression), no DAS28 change overall
cards.type: Phase 1 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-escalation study (programme support)
cards.people: 32 subjects with rheumatoid arthritis on stable methotrexate received single intravenous escalating doses of mavrilimumab (0.01–10.0 mg/kg) or placebo.
cards.result: Adverse events were mild or moderate and similar across cohorts; one subject at 10.0 mg/kg had moderate face and neck urticaria during infusion that resolved with symptomatic treatment. Pharmacodynamic activity was confirmed at 1.0 and 3.0 mg/kg by suppression of suppressor of cytokine signalling 3 mRNA transcripts, and acute-phase reactants fell in subjects with elevated baseline values. No significant change in DAS28 was seen in any cohort overall; in the subgroup with baseline DAS28 >3.2, mean DAS28 was significantly reduced at 4 weeks.
cards.watchOut: A single-dose phase 1 study carded as programme support for safety and mechanism — it is not efficacy evidence and its subgroup DAS28 finding is exploratory.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a discontinued phase 2 programme — real dose-related efficacy over 12 weeks and sustained responses in extension, with a small, mostly transient pulmonary-function signal; POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: a discontinued phase 2 programme — real dose-related efficacy over 12 weeks and sustained responses in extension, with a small, mostly transient pulmonary-function signal; POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the phase 2 dose-ranging trial, the 51-patient Japanese phase IIa population report, the long-term report of two phase IIb studies plus extension (442 patients, 899 patient-years), and the 32-patient phase 1 study — all one programme.
cards.result: Every randomised comparison favoured mavrilimumab on DAS28-CRP response, with the clearest effects at 100 mg, and extension data show responses maintained past two years in patients who continued. The programme was discontinued after phase 2 and the drug was never marketed, so there is no phase 3 confirmation and no current clinical role — the shelf records what the evidence showed. A discontinued phase 2 programme caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Iguratimod in rheumatoid arthritis: ACR20 53.8% versus 17.2% on placebo, 69.5% versus 30.7% added to methotrexate, and non-inferior to methotrexate alone in the 911-patient SMILE trial
shelves.question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis, does the oral immunomodulator iguratimod, compared with placebo or salazosulfapyridine, and added to methotrexate in methotrexate inadequate responders, improve disease activity?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antirheumatic Agents · Arthritis, Rheumatoid · Chromones · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate · Middle Aged · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. Iguratimod, an oral immunomodulator approved as a DMARD in Japan and China (not FDA/EMA-approved — flagged on the face), has three concordant randomised trials. Against placebo and salazosulfapyridine in 376 patients, ACR20 was 53.8% versus 17.2% on placebo (P<0.001) and non-inferior to salazosulfapyridine. Added to methotrexate in 253 inadequate responders, ACR20 at week 24 was 69.5% versus 30.7% (P<0.001). In SMILE (911 methotrexate-naïve patients with early RA), iguratimod monotherapy and iguratimod plus methotrexate both achieved higher ACR20 at week 52 than methotrexate alone (77.4% and 77.1% versus 65.9%), with non-inferiority on radiographic progression for monotherapy but no radiographic superiority. No trial compares iguratimod with a biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD, and all evidence is single-region — that is what holds the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Phase 3 trial (Hara 2007): ACR20 in 53.8% on iguratimod versus 17.2% on placebo, and not inferior to salazosulfapyridine (63.1% versus 57.7%) in 376 patients
cards.summary: Phase 3 trial (Hara 2007): ACR20 in 53.8% on iguratimod versus 17.2% on placebo, and not inferior to salazosulfapyridine (63.1% versus 57.7%) in 376 patients
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel-group controlled trial versus placebo and salazosulfapyridine, 28 weeks
cards.people: 376 Japanese patients with active rheumatoid arthritis received iguratimod, placebo, or salazosulfapyridine for 28 weeks.
cards.result: ACR20 response was 53.8% on iguratimod versus 17.2% on placebo (P<0.001), and iguratimod was not inferior to salazosulfapyridine (63.1% versus 57.7%; 95% confidence interval for the rate difference −7.9% to 18.7%). Iguratimod began to show its effect within 8 weeks and was effective even in patients who had responded poorly to previous DMARDs. There was no statistically significant difference in the incidence of adverse reactions between iguratimod and salazosulfapyridine.
cards.watchOut: The placebo comparison ran against a low placebo response (17.2%), and the active-comparator arm used salazosulfapyridine, an older conventional DMARD — this trial does not compare iguratimod with methotrexate or any biologic.

cards.headline: Add-on trial (Ishiguro 2013): iguratimod plus methotrexate — ACR20 at week 24 in 69.5% versus 30.7% on placebo plus methotrexate in 253 inadequate responders
cards.summary: Add-on trial (Ishiguro 2013): iguratimod plus methotrexate — ACR20 at week 24 in 69.5% versus 30.7% on placebo plus methotrexate in 253 inadequate responders
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled add-on trial, 24 weeks
cards.people: 253 Japanese patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite stable methotrexate (6 or 8 mg/week) were randomised 2:1 to iguratimod (25 mg/day for 4 weeks, then 50 mg/day) or placebo, each added to methotrexate.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24 was 69.5% on iguratimod versus 30.7% on placebo (P<0.001), with significant improvements also in ACR50, ACR70, HAQ Disability Index, DAS28 <3.2, and rheumatoid factor. The commonest adverse events were decreased blood iron, nasopharyngitis and decreased lymphocytes, mild or moderate in severity; no deaths occurred.
cards.watchOut: Background methotrexate doses (6–8 mg/week) are lower than those used in many other countries' practice, which may affect how the add-on effect generalises.
cards.source: Ishiguro N et al. Concomitant iguratimod therapy in patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite stable doses of methotrexate: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. cards.headline: SMILE study (Du 2025): 911 patients with early RA — iguratimod monotherapy and iguratimod plus methotrexate both beat methotrexate alone on ACR20 at week 52 (77.4% and 77.1% versus 65.9%)
cards.summary: SMILE study (Du 2025): 911 patients with early RA — iguratimod monotherapy and iguratimod plus methotrexate both beat methotrexate alone on ACR20 at week 52 (77.4% and 77.1% versus 65.9%)
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised non-inferiority trial, 52 weeks (28 centres, China)
cards.people: 911 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis naïve to methotrexate were randomised 1:1:1 to methotrexate monotherapy (10–15 mg weekly, n=293), iguratimod monotherapy (25 mg twice daily, n=297), or iguratimod plus methotrexate (n=305) for 52 weeks.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 52 was 77.44% on iguratimod monotherapy, 77.05% on iguratimod plus methotrexate, and 65.87% on methotrexate monotherapy. Non-inferiority of iguratimod monotherapy to methotrexate was established for ACR20 (difference 11.57%; 95% CI 4.35–18.79%; P<0.001) and for change in van der Heijde-modified total Sharp score (−0.37; 95% CI −1.22 to 0.47; P=0.022); iguratimod monotherapy was also superior to methotrexate on ACR20 (P=0.002) but not on the Sharp score, and the combination was superior on ACR20 (P=0.003) but not on the Sharp score (P=0.091). The difference in adverse-event incidence between groups was not statistically significant.
cards.watchOut: A non-inferiority design against methotrexate monotherapy in early, methotrexate-naïve disease — a different population from the inadequate-responder trials above, and the radiographic differences did not reach superiority.
cards.source: Du F et al. The SMILE study: Study of long-term methotrexate and iguratimod combination therapy in early rheumatoid arthritis. Chinese medical journal. 2025. PMID: 39056160. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01548001, from the record. cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the phase 3 placebo/salazosulfapyridine trial (376 patients), the methotrexate add-on trial (253 patients), and the SMILE early-RA trial (911 patients).

shelves.title: Denosumab for rheumatoid arthritis erosions: erosion progression slowed on methotrexate in phase 2 and pooled phase 3 data — but no effect on joint-space narrowing or disease activity
shelves.question: In adults with rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, does adding the anti-RANKL antibody denosumab, compared with placebo, slow bone erosion and joint-space narrowing — without improving synovitis or disease activity?
shelves.mesh: Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Antirheumatic Agents · Arthritis, Rheumatoid · Bone Density · Denosumab · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate · Middle Aged · RANK Ligand
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — for structural protection only. Adding denosumab to methotrexate slowed bone erosion in every randomised report: in the phase 2 MRI trial (218 patients), MRI erosion score rose by 0.06 on denosumab 180 mg versus 1.75 on placebo at 6 months (P=0.007); in DRIVE (350 Japanese patients), modified Sharp erosion change at 12 months was 0.09–0.27 across dosing intervals versus 0.99 on placebo; and in the pooled DRIVE + DESIRABLE analysis (909 patients), total Sharp progression was 0.66–0.88 versus 1.50 on placebo, driven entirely by the erosion component. The honest balance is the dissociation itself, printed on the face: no report found an effect on joint-space narrowing, synovitis, or measures of RA disease activity (the treatment made no difference to disease activity), which is why denosumab was never approved for RA. Its osteoporosis questions are homed elsewhere in the library and are not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Phase 2 trial (Cohen 2008): denosumab on methotrexate cut MRI erosion progression at 6 months (mean change 0.06 on 180 mg, P=0.007, versus 1.75 on placebo) — with no effect on joint-space narrowing or disease activity
cards.summary: Phase 2 trial (Cohen 2008): denosumab on methotrexate cut MRI erosion progression at 6 months (mean change 0.06 on 180 mg, P=0.007, versus 1.75 on placebo) — with no effect on joint-space narrowing or disease activity
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 12 months
cards.people: 218 patients with rheumatoid arthritis receiving methotrexate received subcutaneous placebo (n=75), denosumab 60 mg (n=71), or denosumab 180 mg (n=72) every 6 months for 12 months.
cards.result: At 6 months, the increase in MRI erosion score was 0.13 on denosumab 60 mg (P=0.118) and 0.06 on 180 mg (P=0.007) versus 1.75 on placebo. A significant difference in modified Sharp erosion score was seen at 6 months for 180 mg (P=0.019) and at 12 months for both doses (60 mg P=0.012; 180 mg P=0.007). Denosumab caused sustained suppression of bone-turnover markers. There was no evidence of an effect on joint space narrowing or on measures of RA disease activity, and adverse-event rates were comparable with placebo.
cards.watchOut: The dissociation is the finding: structural protection without any anti-inflammatory or disease-activity effect — the reason denosumab was never approved for rheumatoid arthritis. Endpoints are imaging scores, not symptoms or function.
cards.source: Cohen SB et al. Denosumab treatment effects on structural damage, bone mineral density, and bone turnover in rheumatoid arthritis: a twelve-month, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase II clinical trial. cards.headline: DRIVE phase 2 (Takeuchi 2016): 350 Japanese patients — modified Sharp erosion change at 12 months 0.99 on placebo versus 0.27 / 0.14 / 0.09 across denosumab dosing intervals (all significant), again with no joint-space-narrowing effect
cards.summary: DRIVE phase 2 (Takeuchi 2016): 350 Japanese patients — modified Sharp erosion change at 12 months 0.99 on placebo versus 0.27 / 0.14 / 0.09 across denosumab dosing intervals (all significant), again with no joint-space-narrowing effect
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-interval trial, 12 months
cards.people: 350 Japanese patients with rheumatoid arthritis of 6 months to <5 years' duration, on methotrexate with calcium and vitamin D, randomised to placebo or denosumab 60 mg every 6, 3, or 2 months.
cards.result: Mean change in modified Sharp erosion score at 12 months was 0.99 on placebo versus 0.27 (every 6 months, p=0.0082), 0.14 (every 3 months, p=0.0036) and 0.09 (every 2 months, p<0.0001) on denosumab — a dose-interval gradient. Denosumab also significantly inhibited the increase in modified total Sharp score, increased bone mineral density, and showed no obvious evidence of an effect on joint space narrowing. Safety profiles showed no apparent difference from placebo.
cards.watchOut: A radiographic-endpoint trial in a single-country population with early RA; structural scores over 12 months are a surrogate for long-term joint damage, not a measured clinical outcome.

cards.headline: Pooled DRIVE + DESIRABLE analysis (Tanaka 2020): 909 patients — total Sharp progression reduced by denosumab (0.88 and 0.66 versus 1.50 on placebo), driven entirely by the erosion component; no effect on joint-space narrowing
cards.summary: Pooled DRIVE + DESIRABLE analysis (Tanaka 2020): 909 patients — total Sharp progression reduced by denosumab (0.88 and 0.66 versus 1.50 on placebo), driven entirely by the erosion component; no effect on joint-space narrowing
cards.type: Pooled patient-level analysis of the DRIVE phase 2 and DESIRABLE phase 3 randomised trials (overlaps the DRIVE card above)
cards.people: 909 patients with rheumatoid arthritis pooled from DRIVE (methotrexate-based background) and DESIRABLE (any DMARD background), randomised to denosumab 60 mg every 6 months, every 3 months, or placebo, followed 12 months.
cards.result: Change in van der Heijde-modified total Sharp score at 12 months was 0.88 (every 6 months, p=0.0024) and 0.66 (every 3 months, p=0.0002) versus 1.50 on placebo. The reduction was due to the erosion score (0.44 and 0.20 versus 0.98 on placebo); no effect was observed on the joint-space narrowing score. Anti-CCP antibody status, glucocorticoid use and baseline erosion score showed significant interactions, with denosumab particularly effective in anti-CCP-positive patients.
cards.watchOut: This pooled analysis re-uses the DRIVE patients carded above and adds the DESIRABLE phase 3 population — it is a programme-level summary, not a third independent trial, and it still shows no effect on joint-space narrowing or (by design) on synovitis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: denosumab reliably slows bone erosion in RA without touching synovitis, disease activity or joint-space narrowing — structural protection only; POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: denosumab reliably slows bone erosion in RA without touching synovitis, disease activity or joint-space narrowing — structural protection only; POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the phase 2 MRI/Sharp trial (218 patients), the DRIVE phase 2 trial (350 patients), and the pooled DRIVE + DESIRABLE analysis (909 patients, overlapping DRIVE).
cards.result: Across doses, countries and imaging methods, adding denosumab to methotrexate-based therapy reduced erosion progression versus placebo, with a dose-interval gradient in DRIVE, while joint-space narrowing and disease activity measures consistently showed no effect (the treatment made no difference to synovitis or disease activity). The stamp is POSSIBLE for the structural claim only: the endpoints are radiographic surrogates, no trial shows a symptom, function or disability benefit, and denosumab is not approved for rheumatoid arthritis.
cards.watchOut: Denosumab's osteoporosis use is homed elsewhere in the library and is not re-carded here; rebound bone loss after denosumab discontinuation, known from the osteoporosis setting, was not assessed in these 12-month RA trials.

shelves.title: Deucravacitinib in systemic lupus erythematosus: PAISLEY phase 2 — SRI-4 in 58% versus 34% on placebo at the 3 mg twice-daily dose (one trial, reported three ways)
shelves.question: In adults with active systemic lupus erythematosus, does the oral TYK2 inhibitor deucravacitinib, compared with placebo plus standard therapy, improve disease activity (SRI-4 / BICLA response; PAISLEY programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · TYK2 Kinase · Treatment Outcome · Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic · Double-Blind Method · Severity of Illness Index · Heterocyclic Compounds
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. The SLE evidence for deucravacitinib is one trial, printed on the face: PAISLEY (363 adults with active SLE) found SRI-4 response at week 32 of 58% on 3 mg twice daily (odds ratio 2.8; P<0.001) and 50% on 6 mg twice daily (P=0.02) versus 34% on placebo, with the 12 mg once-daily dose at 45% (nominal P=0.08); BICLA, CLASI-50, low-disease-activity and joint-count responses also favoured deucravacitinib. The trial's own patient-reported-outcomes report found larger pain and fatigue improvements on deucravacitinib at week 48, and its pharmacodynamic analysis showed rapid, sustained suppression of interferon-pathway markers — supportive, but the same 363 patients, not independent confirmation. Infections and cutaneous events were commoner on deucravacitinib; serious adverse events were comparable. Phase 3 (POETYK SLE) was designed but unreported at the time of these reports, so no phase 3 claim is made. Deucravacitinib in plaque psoriasis is homed on live shelf #1155 and in psoriatic arthritis on pack #6989; this shelf asks only the unasked SLE slice and re-cards none of their evidence.

cards.headline: PAISLEY phase 2 primary (Morand 2023): SRI-4 at week 32 in 58% (3 mg twice daily), 50% (6 mg twice daily) and 45% (12 mg once daily) versus 34% on placebo in 363 patients with active SLE
cards.summary: PAISLEY phase 2 primary (Morand 2023): SRI-4 at week 32 in 58% (3 mg twice daily), 50% (6 mg twice daily) and 45% (12 mg once daily) versus 34% on placebo in 363 patients with active SLE
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (PAISLEY), primary endpoint at week 32, secondary outcomes to week 48
cards.people: 363 adults with active systemic lupus erythematosus from 162 sites in 17 countries, randomised 1:1:1:1 to deucravacitinib 3 mg twice daily, 6 mg twice daily, 12 mg once daily, or placebo, on standard therapy.
cards.result: SRI-4 response at week 32 was 34% on placebo versus 58% on deucravacitinib 3 mg twice daily (odds ratio 2.8; 95% CI 1.5–5.1; P<0.001), 50% on 6 mg twice daily (odds ratio 1.9; 95% CI 1.0–3.4; P=0.02), and 45% on 12 mg once daily (odds ratio 1.6; 95% CI 0.8–2.9; nominal P=0.08). Response rates for BICLA, CLASI-50, Lupus Low Disease Activity State and joint counts were also higher with deucravacitinib. Adverse-event rates were similar across groups except higher infections and cutaneous events (including rash and acne) with deucravacitinib; serious adverse-event rates were comparable, with no deaths, opportunistic or tuberculosis infections, major adverse cardiovascular events, or thrombotic events.
cards.watchOut: One phase 2 trial: the highest dose did not significantly beat placebo on the primary endpoint, and the phase 3 POETYK SLE trials were still unreported when these reports were published — no phase 3 claim is made on this shelf.

Arthritis & rheumatology (Hoboken, N.J.). 2023. PMID: 36369798. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03252587, from the record. cards.headline: PAISLEY patient-reported outcomes (Mosca 2025): same trial — pain fell 2.2–2.3 points versus 1.3 on placebo and fatigue 5.9–7.3 versus 3.4 points at week 48
cards.summary: PAISLEY patient-reported outcomes (Mosca 2025): same trial — pain fell 2.2–2.3 points versus 1.3 on placebo and fatigue 5.9–7.3 versus 3.4 points at week 48
cards.type: Patient-reported-outcomes report of the PAISLEY phase 2 trial (same single trial as the card above)
cards.people: The same 363 patients with active SLE randomised in PAISLEY (placebo n=90; deucravacitinib 3 mg twice daily n=91; 6 mg twice daily n=93; 12 mg once daily n=89), assessing pain (Numeric Rating Scale), PROMIS Fatigue Short Form 7a and SF-36 to week 48.
cards.result: At week 48, pain decreased by 1.3 points on placebo versus 2.2–2.3 points across deucravacitinib dose groups, and fatigue scores decreased by 3.4 points versus 5.9–7.3 points. Mean SF-36 physical scores were 41.5 on placebo versus at least 44.6 on deucravacitinib, and mental scores 45.2 versus at least 46.3; a greater proportion on deucravacitinib reported clinically meaningful SF-36 improvements. Regardless of treatment group, SRI-4 and BICLA responders reported greater pain and fatigue improvements than non-responders.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory endpoints from the same single trial, with control-based pattern imputation for missing data — supportive of the primary result, not independent confirmation of it.

cards.headline: PAISLEY pharmacodynamic analysis (Kahlenberg 2026): same trial — deucravacitinib rapidly and sustainably reduced interferon levels and IFN-responsive gene expression versus placebo
cards.summary: PAISLEY pharmacodynamic analysis (Kahlenberg 2026): same trial — deucravacitinib rapidly and sustainably reduced interferon levels and IFN-responsive gene expression versus placebo
cards.type: Pharmacodynamic / biomarker analysis of the PAISLEY phase 2 trial (same single trial as the cards above)
cards.people: Whole-blood transcripts, serum proteins, blood cell subsets and antibody profiles from the 363 PAISLEY patients with SLE, with up to 60 demographically matched healthy volunteer samples; all analyses were descriptive.
cards.result: At screening, 42 genes and 75 proteins were differentially expressed in SLE versus healthy volunteers. Deucravacitinib produced rapid and sustained reductions in interferon (IFN) levels and expression of IFN-responsive genes, IFN-inducible proteins, B-cell pathway markers and serological biomarkers, and increases in complement 3 and 4 expression, with similar kinetics versus placebo. The IFN signature score fell in both IFN-high and IFN-low subgroups, and anti-double-stranded DNA antibody titres fell in the IFN-high subgroup.
cards.watchOut: A mechanistic, descriptive analysis of the same trial — it shows the drug engaged its target pathways; biomarker movement is not itself a clinical outcome, and this report adds no new patients.
cards.source: Kahlenberg JM et al. Pharmacodynamic analysis of TYK2 inhibition by deucravacitinib: results from the phase 2 PAISLEY SLE trial in patients with active systemic lupus erythematosus. cards.summary: Synthesis: one phase 2 trial (PAISLEY) reported three ways — clinical response, patient-reported benefit and interferon-pathway suppression all point the same way; phase 3 unreported; POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above — all reports of the single PAISLEY phase 2 trial (363 patients): its primary report, its patient-reported-outcomes report, and its pharmacodynamic analysis.
cards.result: Within one trial, SRI-4 separated from placebo by 11–24 percentage points (significant at the two lower doses), pain and fatigue improved more on deucravacitinib, and interferon-pathway biomarkers fell as the mechanism predicts. A single phase 2 trial caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and the trial base is one trial however many reports it has generated. Deucravacitinib in plaque psoriasis is homed on live shelf #1155 and in psoriatic arthritis on pack #6989; neither is re-carded here — this shelf asks only the SLE question.
cards.watchOut: Phase 3 (POETYK SLE) results were unreported at the time of these publications; infection and cutaneous adverse events were commoner on deucravacitinib, and longer-term TYK2-inhibitor safety in SLE is not settled by a 48-week phase 2 trial.

shelves.title: Enpatoran in lupus (WILLOW): skin cohort met its dose-response endpoint (CLASI-A, p=0.0002) while the systemic SLE cohort missed its primary dose-response objective (p=0.14) — SPLIT
shelves.question: In adults with systemic lupus erythematosus or cutaneous lupus erythematosus with active skin disease, does the oral TLR7/8 inhibitor enpatoran, compared with placebo plus standard care, improve systemic disease activity and skin activity (WILLOW programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic · Lupus Erythematosus, Cutaneous · Severity of Illness Index · Toll-Like Receptor 7 · Toll-Like Receptor 8 · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT. WILLOW is one phase 2 basket trial reported by cohort, and the cohorts answer different questions in different populations — they are not merged on this shelf. In Cohort A (102 participants with cutaneous lupus or SLE with active skin disease), enpatoran produced a significant, dose-dependent improvement in skin activity at week 16 (CLASI-A change −64 to −72 percentage points across doses versus −44 on placebo; p=0.0002 for dose-response). In Cohort B (354 participants with moderate-to-severe SLE), BICLA response at week 24 was numerically higher at every dose (49–58% versus 39% on placebo) but the trial did not meet its primary objective of a statistically significant dose-response relationship (p=0.14). A 25-patient phase Ib study adds clean tolerability and dose-dependent interferon-gene-signature suppression, as programme support only. Enpatoran is an oral TLR7/8 inhibitor from a single source (Merck KGaA, named for clarification); the evidence is phase 2 only.

cards.headline: WILLOW Cohort B (Morand 2026): moderate-to-severe SLE — BICLA at week 24 in 58% / 49% / 49% across enpatoran doses versus 39% on placebo, but the primary dose-response objective was NOT met (p=0.14)
cards.summary: WILLOW Cohort B (Morand 2026): moderate-to-severe SLE — BICLA at week 24 in 58% / 49% / 49% across enpatoran doses versus 39% on placebo, but the primary dose-response objective was NOT met (p=0.14)
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-finding basket trial — Cohort B (systemic lupus), 24 weeks
cards.people: 354 participants aged 18–75 with moderate-to-severe active SLE, with or without cutaneous manifestations, on stable background medication, randomised across 132 centres in 22 countries to placebo (95) or enpatoran 25 mg (71), 50 mg (74) or 100 mg (114), all twice daily for 24 weeks, with glucocorticoids tapered to no more than 5 mg/day prednisone-equivalent from weeks 2–12; 353 were in the efficacy full analysis set (335 female, 95%).
cards.result: The study did not meet its primary objective of identifying a statistically significant dose-response relationship for enpatoran in BICLA response rate at week 24 (p=0.14) — on its primary analysis, the treatment made no difference that met the prespecified dose-response test. BICLA response rates were numerically higher at every dose than placebo: 58% (41/71) on 25 mg (odds ratio 2.2; 95% CI 1.1–4.0), 49% (36/74) on 50 mg (odds ratio 1.5; 95% CI 0.8–2.8) and 49% (56/114) on 100 mg (odds ratio 1.6; 95% CI 0.9–2.8) versus 39% (37/94) on placebo. The commonest treatment-emergent adverse event was diarrhoea; serious adverse events occurred in 1–4% across enpatoran groups and 3% on placebo.
cards.watchOut: Cohort B's population (moderate-to-severe systemic disease) is different from Cohort A's skin-predominant population — the two cohorts are reported separately on this shelf and their results are not merged. The flat, non-monotonic dose pattern (the lowest dose numerically highest) is part of why the dose-response test failed.

cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-finding basket trial — Cohort A (cutaneous lupus / SLE with skin disease), 24 weeks
cards.people: 102 participants aged 18–75 with cutaneous lupus erythematosus only, or SLE with mild or no extra-cutaneous activity, and CLASI-A score at least 8, randomised 1:1:1:1 to placebo or enpatoran 25, 50 or 100 mg twice daily for 24 weeks with standard of care; 100 were analysed for efficacy (placebo 26; 25 mg 23; 50 mg 25; 100 mg 26).
cards.result: At week 16, enpatoran had a significant, dose-dependent effect on CLASI-A score (p=0.0002 for the dose-response relationship): adjusted mean changes from baseline were −64 percentage points (25 mg), −68 (50 mg) and −72 (100 mg) versus −44 percentage points on placebo. The commonest treatment-emergent adverse event was upper respiratory tract infection; serious adverse events occurred in one placebo, one 100 mg and two 25 mg participants, and none on 50 mg.
cards.watchOut: A skin-activity endpoint (CLASI-A) in a skin-predominant population — this cohort does not show benefit on systemic lupus activity, which is Cohort B's separate and negative-on-primary question.
cards.source: Morand EF et al. cards.headline: Phase Ib multiple-ascending-dose study (Witte 2025): 25 patients with SLE/CLE — safety-primary; tolerability clean and interferon gene signature suppressed dose-dependently
cards.summary: Phase Ib multiple-ascending-dose study (Witte 2025): 25 patients with SLE/CLE — safety-primary; tolerability clean and interferon gene signature suppressed dose-dependently
cards.type: Phase Ib randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled multiple-ascending-dose study (third report; safety-primary, not a load-bearing efficacy card)
cards.people: 25 patients with active SLE/CLE randomised 3:1 to enpatoran (n=19) or placebo (n=6) across four dose cohorts for 12/24 weeks; 80% female, median age 44 years.
cards.result: By week 12, treatment-emergent adverse events were reported by 42% of patients across the enpatoran dose groups and 33% on placebo; 96% of events were mild or moderate and there were no serious treatment-emergent adverse events. Enpatoran pharmacokinetics were dose-proportional (peak at 1–2 hours; half-life 6–10 hours). Greater reductions in SLEDAI-2000, Physician's Global Assessment and 28-joint count were observed at week 24 with enpatoran versus placebo, with rapid, dose-dependent and reversible suppression of the interferon gene signature.
cards.watchOut: A 25-patient safety and pharmacokinetic study — its clinical-response observations are preliminary and are carded as programme support only, not as efficacy evidence.

cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by cohort — a significant dose-dependent skin benefit in Cohort A, a missed primary dose-response objective in systemic Cohort B, and a clean small phase Ib; SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by cohort — a significant dose-dependent skin benefit in Cohort A, a missed primary dose-response objective in systemic Cohort B, and a clean small phase Ib; SPLIT
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: WILLOW Cohort B (354 randomised, systemic SLE), WILLOW Cohort A (102 randomised, skin-predominant CLE/SLE), and the phase Ib study (25 patients) — one basket programme, two distinct populations.
cards.result: The split is the result: in skin-predominant disease, enpatoran's effect on CLASI-A was significant and dose-dependent (p=0.0002); in moderate-to-severe systemic SLE, BICLA rates were numerically higher at all doses but the prespecified dose-response primary objective was not met (p=0.14). Tolerability was acceptable in both cohorts and in the phase Ib study. Enpatoran is a single-source product of Merck KGaA (named for clarification); the programme is phase 2 only, with a long-term extension ongoing.
cards.watchOut: Phase 2 only, one basket trial reported by cohort — neither cohort's result should be read onto the other's population, and the systemic claim awaits a trial designed around a single dose and a conventional primary comparison.

shelves.title: Bimagrumab in inclusion body myositis (RESILIENT): no difference in 6-minute walk distance at any dose, deterioration in all groups over 2 years — muscle mass rose, function did not
shelves.question: In adults with sporadic inclusion body myositis, does the activin-receptor-IIB antibody bimagrumab, compared with placebo, improve walking performance and slow functional decline (RESILIENT programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myositis, Inclusion Body · Treatment Outcome · Walk Test
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). RESILIENT (251 adults with sporadic inclusion body myositis) found no difference in 6-minute walk distance at week 52 at any bimagrumab dose versus placebo (+17.6 m, p=0.22; +18.6 m, p=0.19; −1.3 m, p=0.93). Its long-term extension (211 participants) showed progressive deterioration in all groups over 2 years and was terminated early because the core trial had missed its endpoint. A 10-patient long-term safety cohort showed the programme's characteristic dissociation: lean body mass rose 6.9% while walk distance declined. This is a failed programme, presented in the failed-programme precedent: the drug did what it was built to do to muscle mass and made no difference to walking or strength. Bimagrumab in type 2 diabetes with obesity is homed on live shelf #1095 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: RESILIENT phase 2b/3 primary (Hanna 2019): 251 patients — 6-minute walk distance at week 52 did not differ at any dose (the treatment made no difference: +17.6 m, p=0.22; +18.6 m, p=0.19; −1.3 m, p=0.93)
cards.summary: RESILIENT phase 2b/3 primary (Hanna 2019): 251 patients — 6-minute walk distance at week 52 did not differ at any dose (the treatment made no difference: +17.6 m, p=0.22; +18.6 m, p=0.19; −1.3 m, p=0.93)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b trial (RESILIENT), 52 weeks
cards.people: 251 adults aged 36–85 with sporadic inclusion body myositis meeting modified 2010 Medical Research Council criteria, at 38 academic sites, randomised 1:1:1:1 to intravenous bimagrumab 10 mg/kg (63), 3 mg/kg (63) or 1 mg/kg (63), or placebo (62), every 4 weeks for at least 48 weeks.
cards.result: The primary outcome — change in 6-minute walk distance (6MWD) at week 52 — did not differ between any bimagrumab dose and placebo (least-squares mean differences: 10 mg/kg +17.6 m, 99% CI −19.6 to 54.8, p=0.22; 3 mg/kg +18.6 m, p=0.19; 1 mg/kg −1.3 m, p=0.93): the treatment made no difference to walking performance. At least one adverse event occurred in 100% of each bimagrumab group and 98% on placebo; falls were the most frequent event (76–87% across groups). The most frequent bimagrumab-associated events were muscle spasms (40–68% versus 21% on placebo) and diarrhoea (32–52% versus 18%). Two deaths occurred, neither considered related to bimagrumab, and no significant cardiac effects were recorded.
cards.watchOut: RESILIENT is the largest randomised trial conducted in inclusion body myositis and its null is a well-powered one — the confidence intervals exclude a large walking benefit at the tested doses, though the 10 mg/kg interval does not exclude a modest one.
cards.source: Hanna MG et al. Safety and efficacy of intravenous bimagrumab in inclusion body myositis (RESILIENT): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b trial. The Lancet. Neurology. 2019. PMID: 31397289. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01925209, from the record. cards.headline: RESILIENT long-term extension (Amato 2021): 211 participants followed to 2 years — progressive deterioration in 6-minute walk distance in all groups, no clinical benefit; extension terminated early
cards.summary: RESILIENT long-term extension (Amato 2021): 211 participants followed to 2 years — progressive deterioration in 6-minute walk distance in all groups, no clinical benefit; extension terminated early
cards.type: Long-term extension of RESILIENT (double-blind period, then open-label period), up to 104 weeks
cards.people: 211 participants who completed RESILIENT entered the extension, continuing their core-study assignment (bimagrumab 10, 3 or 1 mg/kg, or placebo, intravenously every 4 weeks).
cards.result: Mean change in 6-minute walk distance was highly variable but indicated progressive deterioration from weeks 24–104 in all treatment groups, including placebo — extended bimagrumab treatment did not provide clinical benefit in mobility (the treatment made no difference over 2 years). At least one treatment-emergent adverse event occurred in 91.0% of the pooled bimagrumab group and 89.1% on placebo; falls were commonest, and serious adverse-event incidence was comparable (18.6% versus 14.5%). The extension was terminated early because the core study had not met its primary endpoint. The report rates this as Class IV evidence of no meaningful functional benefit.
cards.watchOut: An extension of a negative trial, terminated early — it confirms the direction of the primary result over a longer horizon rather than testing a new hypothesis.
cards.source: Amato AA et al. Efficacy and Safety of Bimagrumab in Sporadic Inclusion Body Myositis: Long-term Extension of RESILIENT. Neurology. 2021. PMID: 33597289. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02573467, from the record. cards.headline: Long-term safety report (Sivakumar 2020): 10 adults on bimagrumab 10 mg/kg for up to 2 years — muscle mass rose (lean body mass +6.9% at week 76) while walk distance progressively declined
cards.summary: Long-term safety report (Sivakumar 2020): 10 adults on bimagrumab 10 mg/kg for up to 2 years — muscle mass rose (lean body mass +6.9% at week 76) while walk distance progressively declined
cards.type: Open-label long-term extension safety/tolerability study (small cohort, n=10)
cards.people: 10 adults with sporadic inclusion body myositis who had completed a single-dose core study received bimagrumab 10 mg/kg intravenously every 4 weeks for up to 104 weeks; mean age 70.1 years. All 10 discontinued (7 because the study was terminated early; 3 for adverse events — myocardial infarction, oesophageal carcinoma and dementia, none considered treatment-related).
cards.result: The most common adverse events were muscle spasms and falls (both 9 of 10), diarrhoea (6 of 10), and acne and skin eruption (both 5 of 10). Thigh muscle volume rose 4.1% at week 8 and 4.5% at week 16, and lean body mass increased and was sustained at +6.9% at week 76 — but mean 6-minute walk distance progressively declined to week 76, handgrip showed only a modest numerical increase, and quadriceps strength did not significantly change: muscle mass grew without clinical improvement.
cards.watchOut: Only 10 patients, open-label, from a separate single-dose core study — carded for the long-term safety picture and the mass-versus-function dissociation, not as efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Sivakumar K et al. Long-term safety and tolerability of bimagrumab (BYM338) in sporadic inclusion body myositis. Neurology. 2020. PMID: 32690797. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02250443, from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a failed programme — bimagrumab grew muscle mass but made no difference to walking or strength in RESILIENT, its extension, or long-term follow-up; LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a failed programme — bimagrumab grew muscle mass but made no difference to walking or strength in RESILIENT, its extension, or long-term follow-up; LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: RESILIENT (251 patients), its long-term extension (211 patients), and a 10-patient long-term safety cohort — one programme.
cards.result: The programme's randomised primary test was cleanly negative at all three doses, the 2-year extension showed deterioration in every group, and the small long-term cohort reproduced the pattern in miniature: lean mass up about 7%, walking down. The concordant null across the programme's reports supports LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for walking performance and functional decline in sporadic inclusion body myositis. Bimagrumab's body-composition question in type 2 diabetes with obesity is homed on live shelf #1095 and is not re-carded here; this shelf asks only the inclusion-body-myositis question.
cards.watchOut: The null is for the tested intravenous doses and durations in established sporadic IBM; it does not address earlier disease, other activin-pathway agents, or combination approaches.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hanna MG et al. The Lancet. Neurology. 2019. PMID: 31397289; Amato AA et al. Neurology. 2021. PMID: 33597289; Sivakumar K et al. Neurology. 2020. PMID: 32690797. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Netakimab in axial spondyloarthritis: ASAS20 up to 90.9% versus 42.9% on placebo in phase 2, ASTERA phase 3 subgroup-consistent, and 85.5% two-year real-world retention (observational) — all Russian evidence
shelves.question: In adults with active radiographic axial spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis), does the anti-IL-17A antibody netakimab, compared with placebo, improve disease activity (ASTERA programme) — and what does Russian real-world use show on retention and safety?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Humans · Interleukin-17 · Spondylitis, Ankylosing · Axial Spondyloarthritis · C-Reactive Protein · Sacroiliitis · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. Netakimab, a humanised anti-IL-17A antibody approved in Russia (single-source Biocad product, named for clarification), beat placebo in its phase 2 dose-finding trial (89 patients): ASAS20 at week 16 was 72.7%, 81.8% and 90.9% across doses versus 42.9% on placebo, with superiority confirmed at 80 and 120 mg. The ASTERA phase 3 programme (228 randomised) is represented in PubMed-indexed journals by a post-hoc analysis showing effectiveness regardless of baseline CRP or MRI sacroiliac inflammation — a title search this session located no primary ASTERA publication in a PubMed-indexed journal, and that gap is printed on the face. The real-world limb is observational and labelled as such: the LIBRA cohort (137 patients) showed 90.4% retention at 1 year and 85.5% at 2 years, with sustained BASDAI/ASDAS-CRP reductions and treatment-related adverse events in about 5–6%. All evidence is single-country (Russia), and the real-world reports sit in a low-visibility translated journal.

cards.summary: Phase 2 dose-finding trial (Erdes 2020): ASAS20 at week 16 in 72.7% / 81.8% / 90.9% across netakimab doses versus 42.9% on placebo in 89 patients; superiority confirmed at 80 and 120 mg
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled dose-finding trial, to week 16
cards.people: 89 adults with active ankylosing spondylitis despite NSAID treatment, randomised to subcutaneous netakimab 40, 80 or 120 mg, or placebo, at weeks 0, 1, 2 and every 2 weeks thereafter until week 12, with the primary endpoint at week 16.
cards.result: ASAS20 response at week 16 was 72.73% on 40 mg, 81.82% on 80 mg and 90.91% on 120 mg versus 42.86% on placebo; superiority to placebo was confirmed for the 80 mg and 120 mg doses against the prespecified 10% clinically non-meaningful margin. The most frequent adverse events were lymphocytosis, neutropenia and asymptomatic bacteriuria; no dose-dependent toxicity or serious adverse events were observed. The 120 mg dose was selected for phase 3.
cards.watchOut: A small, short dose-finding trial — its very high top-dose response rate (90.91%) comes from a small dose group and should be read against the phase 3 programme below, not on its own.
cards.source: Erdes S et al. Primary efficacy of netakimab, a novel interleukin-17 inhibitor, in the treatment of active ankylosing spondylitis in adults. Clinical and experimental rheumatology. 2020. PMID: 31025924. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Antibodies, Monoclonal, Humanized · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Interleukin-17 · Spondylitis, Ankylosing · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: ASTERA phase 3 post-hoc analysis (Mazurov 2023): 228 randomised — netakimab effective regardless of baseline CRP or MRI sacroiliac inflammation in the 114-patient treated subanalysis
cards.summary: ASTERA phase 3 post-hoc analysis (Mazurov 2023): 228 randomised — netakimab effective regardless of baseline CRP or MRI sacroiliac inflammation in the 114-patient treated subanalysis
cards.type: Post-hoc subgroup analysis of the ASTERA phase 3 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (16-week data)
cards.people: 228 adults with active radiographic axial spondyloarthritis in ASTERA received subcutaneous netakimab 120 mg or placebo at weeks 0, 1, 2 and every other week thereafter; the subanalysis covers 114 netakimab-treated patients with available baseline CRP and sacroiliac MRI, grouped by CRP (<5 versus ≥5 mg/L), MRI sacroiliitis (SPARCC <2 versus ≥2), and peripheral arthritis.
cards.result: At week 16, improvement in all outcomes was similar for MRI-inflammation-negative and -positive patients, except change in the ASspi-MRI-a score, which was significantly greater in MRI-positive patients. Netakimab was effective regardless of baseline CRP and peripheral arthritis; in patients with CRP at least 5 mg/L a more pronounced decline in disease activity was observed, with a trend to the most prominent ASDAS-CRP and BASDAI improvement at CRP above 20 mg/L.
cards.watchOut: This is a post-hoc subgroup analysis, not the ASTERA primary report: a title search of PubMed this session located no primary ASTERA publication in a PubMed-indexed journal — the phase 3 record available to card is this post-hoc analysis, and it reports within-treated-patient subgroup patterns rather than the trial's primary placebo comparison.
cards.source: Mazurov VI et al. Clinical and experimental rheumatology. 2023. PMID: 36062743. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03447704, stated in the record. cards.headline: LIBRA real-world study, 1-year results (Erdes 2024): observational — 137 patients, 90.4% still on netakimab at 52 weeks, BASDAI and ASDAS-CRP significantly down (observational, no comparator)
cards.summary: LIBRA real-world study, 1-year results (Erdes 2024): observational — 137 patients, 90.4% still on netakimab at 52 weeks, BASDAI and ASDAS-CRP significantly down (observational, no comparator)
cards.type: Multicentre observational (real-world) post-registration study — LIBRA, first-year results; labelled observational
cards.people: 137 patients with ankylosing spondylitis (93 men, 44 women; mean age 42.3 years; 34.3% previously treated with biologic DMARDs, mainly TNF inhibitors) prescribed netakimab in routine practice at 23 centres in the Russian Federation, recruited August 2020 to December 2021, with retrospective first-visit data and prospective visits at 12, 24 and 52 weeks.
cards.result: At 52 weeks, 90.4% (95% CI 85.4–95.7) of patients continued netakimab. BASDAI and ASDAS-CRP decreased significantly from baseline at all time points. Treatment-related adverse events were reported in 7 patients (5.1%); two patients stopped netakimab for adverse events (terminal ileitis and chronic colitis).
cards.watchOut: Observational and single-arm: retention and within-patient score changes in routine practice cannot separate drug effect from selection and natural course — this card is labelled observational and is not randomised evidence.
cards.source: Erdes S et al. Real-World Retention Rate, Effectiveness, and Safety of Netakimab in the Treatment of Patients with Ankylosing Spondylitis: First Year Results of the LIBRA Post-Registration Safety Study. Doklady. Biochemistry and biophysics. 2024. PMID: 39196530. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: LIBRA real-world study, 2-year results (Erdes 2026): same 137-patient cohort — retention 85.5% at 104 weeks, 74% in low disease activity or inactive disease (observational, no comparator)
cards.summary: LIBRA real-world study, 2-year results (Erdes 2026): same 137-patient cohort — retention 85.5% at 104 weeks, 74% in low disease activity or inactive disease (observational, no comparator)
cards.type: Multicentre observational (real-world) study — LIBRA, two-year results of the same cohort as the card above; labelled observational
cards.people: The same 137 patients with ankylosing spondylitis at 23 Russian centres, followed to 104 weeks (median observation 104 weeks, range 1–137); 21 patients (15.3%) withdrew before the final visit, mainly for loss to follow-up (5.1%) and treatment inefficacy (4.4%).
cards.result: At 104 weeks, 85.5% (95% CI 79.7–91.8) of patients continued netakimab; retention was 88.7% in biologic-naïve and 78.9% in biologic-experienced patients (p=0.16). BASDAI fell about threefold in the first 3 months and twofold over the first year, with slower further reduction in year 2; by week 104, 52.9% had low disease activity and 21.3% inactive disease by ASDAS. Treatment-related adverse events were reported in 8 patients (6.0%).
cards.watchOut: The two-year report of the same observational cohort as the one-year card — one cohort reported twice, not two cohorts; the same observational limits apply.

cards.headline: Synthesis: positive phase 2 and phase 3 programme signals plus high real-world retention — all single-country (Russia), with the phase 3 primary report not located in PubMed-indexed journals and the real-world limb observational; POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: positive phase 2 and phase 3 programme signals plus high real-world retention — all single-country (Russia), with the phase 3 primary report not located in PubMed-indexed journals and the real-world limb observational; POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the phase 2 dose-finding trial (89 patients), the ASTERA phase 3 post-hoc analysis (228 randomised; 114 treated patients subanalysed), and the LIBRA observational cohort (137 patients, reported at 1 and 2 years).
cards.result: Randomised evidence shows a dose-related ASAS20 win over placebo in phase 2 and subgroup-consistent effectiveness in the ASTERA post-hoc analysis; observational LIBRA data show 85.5% two-year retention with sustained score reductions. Observational evidence is capped at POSSIBLE and labelled as such, the ASTERA primary publication was not located in PubMed-indexed journals this session, and all evidence is single-country (Russia, where netakimab — a single-source Biocad product, named for clarification — is approved). That combination holds the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: The real-world reports appear in a low-visibility translated journal (Doklady. Biochemistry and biophysics); retention in a post-registration study of patients already prescribed the drug is a selected measure and should not be compared directly with trial response rates.
cards.source: Synthesis of Erdes S et al. Clinical and experimental rheumatology. 2020. PMID: 31025924; Mazurov VI et al. Clinical and experimental rheumatology. 2023. PMID: 36062743; Erdes S et al. shelves.title: Pentosan polysulfate in knee osteoarthritis: synovial biomarker changes in a phase 2 injectable trial, a positive 2005 intramuscular pilot (n=114), and an uncontrolled oral pilot — MAYBE (weak evidence)
shelves.question: In adults with painful knee osteoarthritis, does pentosan polysulfate sodium (oral or subcutaneous), compared with placebo, reduce knee pain and improve function?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Double-Blind Method · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Biomarkers · Pentosan Sulfuric Polyester · Synovial Fluid · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Aged · Treatment Outcome · Injections, Subcutaneous
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). The knee-osteoarthritis evidence for pentosan polysulfate is three small reports, each in a different route, and they are not merged on this shelf. The modern phase 2 trial (61 participants) tested subcutaneous injectable pentosan (iPPS; no brand or manufacturer named in the publication) against placebo with synovial-fluid biomarkers as the primary endpoint: the cartilage-degradation marker ARGS fell significantly versus placebo at day 56 and day 168, while pain outcomes were secondary. The only placebo-controlled pain evidence is a 2005 randomised pilot (114 patients, verified from the record) of four weekly intramuscular injections, positive on stiffness duration, pain at rest and patient global assessment but on only 3 of 7 direct assessments. The oral evidence is a single-arm, open-label pilot in 38 patients taking the named product Elmiron®, in which pain fell without any comparator — labelled single-arm on its card. Pentosan in bladder pain syndrome is homed on live shelf #917 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Phase 2 subcutaneous iPPS biomarker trial (Skerrett 2026): 61 patients — synovial ARGS fell significantly versus placebo (day 56 −56.6%, p=0.028; day 168 −74.0%, p=0.024); the primary endpoint was biomarkers, not pain
cards.summary: Phase 2 subcutaneous iPPS biomarker trial (Skerrett 2026): 61 patients — synovial ARGS fell significantly versus placebo (day 56 −56.6%, p=0.028; day 168 −74.0%, p=0.024); the primary endpoint was biomarkers, not pain
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled exploratory biomarker trial, 39 days of treatment with 365-day follow-up
cards.people: 61 participants with moderate to severe knee osteoarthritis pain randomised 1:1:1 to twice-weekly subcutaneous injectable pentosan polysulfate sodium (iPPS), once-weekly iPPS, or placebo for 39 days. The publication names the tested product only as subcutaneous injectable pentosan polysulfate sodium (iPPS) — no brand or manufacturer is named in the record.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was change in synovial fluid biomarkers at day 56. Versus placebo, the cartilage-degradation marker ARGS fell by 56.60% (p=0.028) at day 56 and remained significantly reduced at day 168 (−74.01%, p=0.024); COMP changes were not significant (−23.60% at day 56, confidence interval crossing zero), the cartilage-degradation inhibitor TIMP-1 rose 10.55% (interval crossing zero), TNF-α and βNGF changes were not significant, and serum CTX-I rose significantly (35.74%, p=0.022 at day 56). Clinical responses were secondary endpoints through day 365. iPPS was well tolerated, with no serious related adverse events or adverse events of special interest. Percent changes here are relative biomarker changes as reported by the trial.
cards.watchOut: An exploratory biomarker trial: it shows biological activity in synovial fluid, not demonstrated pain or function benefit — the pain question rests on the two pilot reports below, and the subcutaneous injectable formulation is a different route from the oral product in the third card; their results are not merged.
cards.source: Skerrett DL et al. Effects of pentosan polysulfate sodium on synovial fluid biomarkers in moderate to severe knee osteoarthritis: an exploratory, phase 2, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Arthritis research & therapy. 2026. PMID: 41588475. Registry ID: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry ACTRN12621000136808, stated in the record. cards.headline: Randomised pilot (Ghosh 2005): 114 patients — four weekly intramuscular pentosan injections improved stiffness duration and pain at rest versus control for up to 24 weeks
cards.summary: Randomised pilot (Ghosh 2005): 114 patients — four weekly intramuscular pentosan injections improved stiffness duration and pain at rest versus control for up to 24 weeks
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial, 4 weeks of treatment with follow-up to 24 weeks
cards.people: 114 patients aged at least 18 with knee osteoarthritis at a single Australian centre (83 women, 31 men; mean age 63.3 years), randomised to sodium pentosan polysulfate 3 mg/kg intramuscularly once weekly for 4 weeks (n=54) or Ringer's solution control (n=60). N=114 verified from the record — the pilot clears the ≥10-patient floor.
cards.result: Significant between-group differences were found in 3 of 7 direct clinical assessments: duration of joint stiffness (at 4, 8, 12 and 16 weeks, all P≤0.015), pain at rest (at 8, 12, 16 and 24 weeks, all P≤0.017), and patient global assessment (at 4, 8, 12, 16 and 24 weeks, all P<0.006). Trial continuation rates were higher on pentosan at 8, 12 and 24 weeks (all P<0.05), and the aggregate activities-of-daily-living score improved significantly at weeks 8 and 12 (both P=0.02). Mild bruising at the injection site occurred in under 1% of patients in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A 2005 single-centre pilot with many endpoints and time points — 3 of 7 direct assessments were positive, so selective-reporting and multiplicity cautions apply; the route here was intramuscular, different again from the subcutaneous and oral routes in the other cards.
cards.source: Ghosh P et al. Effects of pentosan polysulfate in osteoarthritis of the knee: A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot study. Current therapeutic research, clinical and experimental. 2005. PMID: 24678076. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Single-arm open-label oral pilot (Liu 2023): 38 patients — knee pain NRS fell from 6.39 to 3.63 at week 16 on oral pentosan (Elmiron®); no comparator (labelled single-arm)
cards.summary: Single-arm open-label oral pilot (Liu 2023): 38 patients — knee pain NRS fell from 6.39 to 3.63 at week 16 on oral pentosan (Elmiron®); no comparator (labelled single-arm)
cards.type: Single-arm, open-label, prospective non-randomised pilot study; labelled as such
cards.people: 38 participants (mean age 62.2 years) with painful knee osteoarthritis and primary hypercholesterolaemia took oral pentosan polysulfate sodium 10 mg/kg once every 4 days for 5 weeks, for two cycles separated by 5 weeks without medication. The tested product is named in the publication as Elmiron® (named here per the clarification exception for a specific tested product).
cards.result: Knee pain on the numerical rating scale fell significantly from 6.39 at baseline to 4.18 at week 6, 3.63 at week 16 and 4.38 at week 26 (all P<0.001, within-patient comparisons). The commonest adverse events were positive faecal occult blood tests, headache and diarrhoea.

cards.headline: Synthesis: three small reports, three different routes — biomarker activity subcutaneously, a positive 2005 intramuscular pilot, and an uncontrolled oral pilot; MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: three small reports, three different routes — biomarker activity subcutaneously, a positive 2005 intramuscular pilot, and an uncontrolled oral pilot; MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: the phase 2 subcutaneous biomarker trial (61 participants), the 2005 randomised intramuscular pilot (114 patients), and the single-arm oral pilot (38 participants) — 213 people in total across three different formulations/routes.
cards.result: No single formulation has more than one small report: the modern trial's primary endpoint was synovial biomarkers (ARGS significantly reduced; pain was secondary), the only placebo-controlled pain evidence is a 2005 pilot positive on 3 of 7 assessments, and the oral evidence is single-arm. That is the definition of MAYBE (weak evidence) on this shelf, and the routes — subcutaneous injectable, intramuscular, oral — are kept separate on the face rather than merged into one pentosan effect.
cards.watchOut: Pentosan's bladder pain syndrome / interstitial cystitis question is homed on live shelf #917 and is not re-carded here. Pentosan is an anticoagulant-like compound; bleeding-related events (such as the positive faecal occult blood tests in the oral pilot) are the safety watch, and none of these small reports can size that risk.
cards.source: Synthesis of Skerrett DL et al. Arthritis research & therapy. 2026. PMID: 41588475; Ghosh P et al. Current therapeutic research, clinical and experimental. 2005. shelves.title: Abaloparatide in men with osteoporosis (ATOM): lumbar spine BMD rose 8.48% versus 1.17% on placebo over 12 months in the single men's trial
shelves.question: In men with osteoporosis, does abaloparatide, compared with placebo, increase bone mineral density (ATOM programme)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Humans · Bone Density · Bone Density Conservation Agents/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Femur Neck · Osteoporosis/drug therapy · Parathyroid Hormone-Related Protein/pharmacology/therapeutic use · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — this shelf asks only the men's question. The companion shelf for postmenopausal women (the ACTIVE trial) is a separate home (pack #1820) and is not re-carded here; this shelf rests entirely on ATOM, the single randomised trial in men, reported in several publications that are distinct reports of ONE trial of 228 men — the trial base is single and the face says so. In ATOM, 12 months of daily abaloparatide 80 micrograms raised lumbar spine BMD by 8.48% versus 1.17% on placebo, with smaller gains at total hip (2.14% versus 0.01%) and femoral neck (2.98% versus 0.15%), all P<0.0001. A prespecified response-rates report found a >3% BMD gain at all three sites in 31.9% of abaloparatide men versus 1.5% on placebo at month 12, and a bone-turnover-marker report found early PINP rises correlated with the 12-month spine BMD gain (r=0.614 at 3 months). BMD is a surrogate endpoint: ATOM was not powered for fractures and reports no fracture outcome, so no fracture claim is made for men on this shelf. The stamp caps at POSSIBLE because the evidence is one trial and a surrogate endpoint.

cards.headline: ATOM primary (Czerwinski 2022): lumbar spine BMD +8.48% on abaloparatide versus +1.17% on placebo at 12 months; total hip +2.14% versus +0.01%; femoral neck +2.98% versus +0.15% (all P<0.0001)
cards.summary: ATOM primary (Czerwinski 2022): lumbar spine BMD +8.48% on abaloparatide versus +1.17% on placebo at 12 months; total hip +2.14% versus +0.01%; femoral neck +2.98% versus +0.15% (all P<0.0001)
cards.type: Phase 3, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (ATOM) — primary report
cards.people: 228 men aged 40 to 85 years with osteoporosis (mean age 68.3 years; mean lumbar spine BMD T-score -2.1) were randomised 2:1 to daily subcutaneous abaloparatide 80 micrograms (n=149) or placebo (n=79) for 12 months. Primary endpoint: change from baseline in lumbar spine BMD.
cards.result: BMD gains were greater with abaloparatide than placebo at every site: lumbar spine least squares mean percentage change 8.48 (SE 0.54) versus 1.17 (0.72); total hip 2.14 (0.27) versus 0.01 (0.35); femoral neck 2.98 (0.34) versus 0.15 (0.45); all P<0.0001. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events (at least 5%) were injection site reaction, dizziness, nasopharyngitis, arthralgia, bronchitis, hypertension and headache, with a safety profile the authors describe as consistent with previous studies.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 228 men, 12 months, and a surrogate endpoint: BMD change is not a fracture outcome, and ATOM was not powered for fractures. The placebo arm also gained spine BMD (+1.17%), so the drug-attributable gain is the between-group difference, not the headline 8.48%.
cards.source: Czerwinski E et al. The Efficacy and Safety of Abaloparatide-SC in Men With Osteoporosis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. J Bone Miner Res. 2022. PMID: 36190391. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03512262, named in the record's abstract.
