cards.headline: ATOM response rates (Dhaliwal 2024): a >3% BMD gain at all three sites in 31.9% of abaloparatide men versus 1.5% on placebo at month 12 (P<0.0001)
cards.summary: ATOM response rates (Dhaliwal 2024): a >3% BMD gain at all three sites in 31.9% of abaloparatide men versus 1.5% on placebo at month 12 (P<0.0001)
cards.type: Prespecified secondary analysis of the ATOM randomised trial — same trial as the primary card, not an independent trial
cards.people: The same 228 men randomised in ATOM (abaloparatide 80 micrograms or placebo); this prespecified analysis counted men achieving percent BMD gains of >0%, >3% and >6% at lumbar spine, total hip and femoral neck at months 3, 6 and 12, and shifts in T-score category at month 12 (denominators are the men with measurements at each visit, e.g. 119 abaloparatide and 66 placebo at month 12 for the three-site analysis).
cards.result: Significantly more abaloparatide than placebo men gained >3% BMD at all three anatomical sites at month 6 (18/122 [14.8%] versus 1/70 [1.4%], P=.002) and month 12 (38/119 [31.9%] versus 1/66 [1.5%], P<.0001). At month 3, more abaloparatide men had a >3% lumbar spine gain (82/134 [61.2%] versus 21/68 [30.9%], P<.0001). A greater proportion of abaloparatide men improved T-score category from osteoporosis to low BMD or normal.
cards.watchOut: A responder re-expression of the same trial's BMD data — it adds no new patients and no fracture information, and visit denominators shrink over time, so the percentages describe men still measured, not all 228 randomised.
cards.source: Dhaliwal R et al. Response rates for lumbar spine, total hip, and femoral neck bone mineral density in men treated with abaloparatide: results from the ATOM study. JBMR Plus. 2024. PMID: 38505522. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03512262, named in the record's abstract. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: ATOM bone-turnover markers (Eastell 2025): PINP rises at 1–12 months correlated with 12-month spine BMD gain (r=0.485 to 0.632, all P<0.0001); uncoupling index favoured formation from month 1
cards.summary: ATOM bone-turnover markers (Eastell 2025): PINP rises at 1–12 months correlated with 12-month spine BMD gain (r=0.485 to 0.632, all P<0.0001); uncoupling index favoured formation from month 1
cards.type: Randomised-trial biomarker analysis of the ATOM trial — same trial as the primary card, not an independent trial
cards.people: Men from the randomised phase 3 ATOM study treated with abaloparatide or placebo; correlations were computed between changes in fasting PINP and serum CTX at months 1, 3, 6 and 12 and percent BMD change at month 12, with the uncoupling index (formation minus resorption balance) compared against 12-month results for women in the separate ACTIVE trial.
cards.result: In abaloparatide-treated men, PINP increases at 1 month (r=0.485), 3 months (r=0.614), 6 months (r=0.632) and 12 months (r=0.521) were highly correlated (all P<.0001) with 12-month lumbar spine BMD increases. Mean uncoupling index on abaloparatide exceeded placebo from month 1 (2.26 versus -0.25) and correlated with 12-month spine BMD in men (3-month UI r=0.453, P<.001) and in women (r=0.252, P<.01), more strongly in men.
cards.watchOut: A mechanistic correlation inside one trial: marker rises track BMD, but neither the markers nor BMD are fracture outcomes, and the cross-trial comparison with women is a statistical contrast between two separate trials, not a randomised comparison.
cards.source: Eastell R et al. Bone turnover markers predict changes in bone mineral density in men treated with abaloparatide: results from the abaloparatide for the treatment of men with osteoporosis (ATOM) study. shelves.title: Six-minute walk distance: median 576 m in healthy men and 494 m in women aged 40–80 (Enright), mean 571 ± 90 m across seven countries with real geographic variation, and 631 ± 93 m in healthy 50–85-year-olds on a 50-m corridor
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what distance is walked in six minutes — the reference equations (Enright) and the seven-country reference standards for the 6-minute walk test — by age, sex, height and weight, and how large is the learning effect between a first and second test?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Exercise Test/standards · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen Consumption/physiology · Reference Values · Regression Analysis · Sex Factors · Walking/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing for the walk test is general (Guyton & Hall ch. 84; Boron & Boulpaep exercise physiology) — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature and says so. Three primary cohorts built the normative base. Enright & Sherrill (1998) tested 290 healthy adults aged 40–80 on the standardised protocol: median distance 576 m in men and 494 m in women, with sex-specific equations in height, age and weight explaining about 40% of the variance (relative share of variance, printed as reported). The seven-country study (Casanova 2011) tested 444 adults at 10 centres: mean 571 ± 90 m, men walking 30 m more than women, strong age decline — but centre-to-centre variability wide enough (adjusted r² 0.09–0.73 across centres) that the authors do not recommend routine use of a single pooled equation, offering age-specific standard curves instead. In healthy 50–85-year-olds on a 50-m corridor (Troosters 1999), distance averaged 631 ± 93 m, 84 m greater in men, with age, height, sex and weight explaining 66% of variability. Corridor length and encouragement protocol change distances, so values are carded per-protocol. On the learning effect: none of the three carded records quantifies a first-to-second-test gain in its abstract — the shelf states that gap plainly rather than borrowing a number from elsewhere.

cards.headline: Enright & Sherrill 1998: median 6-minute walk distance 576 m (men) and 494 m (women) in 290 healthy adults aged 40–80, with the original sex-specific reference equations
cards.summary: Enright & Sherrill 1998: median 6-minute walk distance 576 m (men) and 494 m (women) in 290 healthy adults aged 40–80, with the original sex-specific reference equations
cards.type: Human normative cohort (classic primary dataset, standardised protocol), Am J Respir Crit Care Med 1998
cards.people: 117 healthy men and 173 healthy women aged 40–80 years, given the standardised 6-minute walk test, with oxygen saturation, pulse rate and Borg dyspnoea score measured before and at the end of the walk.
cards.result: The median distance walked was 576 m for men and 494 m for women; distance was significantly less in older and heavier subjects of both sexes and in shorter men. The sex-specific regression equations explained about 40% of the variance in distance (relative share, as reported): for men, 6MWD = (7.57 × height in cm) − (5.02 × age) − (1.76 × weight in kg) − 309 m; for women, 6MWD = (2.11 × height in cm) − (2.29 × weight in kg) − (5.78 × age) + 667 m. The authors propose the equations for computing percent-predicted distance for a patient performing the test for the first time on the standardised protocol.
cards.watchOut: ~60% of the variance in healthy walking distance is unexplained by age, sex, height and weight — percent-predicted from these equations carries wide individual scatter, and the equations were framed by their authors for a first test on the standardised protocol, not for serial testing.
cards.source: Enright PL, Sherrill DL. Reference equations for the six-minute walk in healthy adults. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 1998. PMID: 9817683. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration era). cards.headline: Casanova 2011: across seven countries, mean 6MWD was 571 ± 90 m (range 380–782), men walked 30 m more than women — and centre variability was wide enough that a single pooled equation is not recommended
cards.summary: Casanova 2011: across seven countries, mean 6MWD was 571 ± 90 m (range 380–782), men walked 30 m more than women — and centre variability was wide enough that a single pooled equation is not recommended
cards.type: Human normative cohort (multinational primary dataset, 10 centres), Eur Respir J 2011
cards.people: 444 healthy subjects (238 men) aged 40–80 years from seven countries (10 centres), prospectively measured for 6-minute walk distance, height, weight, spirometry, heart rate and maximal heart rate during the test, Borg dyspnoea score and oxygen saturation.
cards.result: Mean ± SD distance was 571 ± 90 m (range 380–782 m); males walked 30 m more than females (P < 0.001). A multiple regression model including age, sex, height, weight and percent-predicted maximal heart rate explained an adjusted r² of 0.38 — but performance varied sharply by centre (adjusted r² 0.09–0.73), so the authors do not recommend routine use of the pooled equation. Age reduced distance significantly and independently of centre, and the study's deliverable is age-specific reference standard curves for men and women rather than one universal equation.
cards.watchOut: Geographic variation is a measured finding here, not noise to be averaged away: applying another country's equation imports its centre effect. Corridor and encouragement protocols were those of the participating centres — the per-protocol caution on this shelf applies to this card most of all.
cards.source: Casanova C et al. The 6-min walk distance in healthy subjects: reference standards from seven countries. Eur Respir J. 2011. PMID: 20525717. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Troosters 1999: in 51 healthy adults aged 50–85 on a 50-m corridor, 6MWD averaged 631 ± 93 m — 84 m greater in men — with age, height, sex and weight explaining 66% of variability
cards.summary: Troosters 1999: in 51 healthy adults aged 50–85 on a 50-m corridor, 6MWD averaged 631 ± 93 m — 84 m greater in men — with age, height, sex and weight explaining 66% of variability
cards.type: Human normative cohort (primary dataset, elderly, 50-m corridor), Eur Respir J 1999
cards.people: 51 healthy volunteers aged 50–85 years, free of diseases that could interfere with walking performance; tests performed in a quiet 50-m hospital corridor with encouragement every 30 seconds to keep walking as quickly as possible.
cards.result: Walking distance averaged 631 ± 93 m and was 84 m greater in men than women (P < 0.001). Distance correlated with age (r = −0.51, P < 0.01) and height (r = 0.54, P < 0.01); in stepwise multiple regression, age, height, sex and weight were independent contributors explaining 66% of the variability (relative share, as reported) — a tighter fit than the broader-age cohorts, in a narrower elderly band on a long corridor.
cards.watchOut: N = 51 and a 50-m corridor — longer than the 30-m course common in clinics, with fewer turns; distances on shorter corridors run lower for the same person, so this card's 631 m must not be used as the expectation for a short-corridor test.
cards.source: Troosters T et al. Six minute walking distance in healthy elderly subjects. Eur Respir J. 1999. PMID: 10515400. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy 6-minute walk distance centres near 570–580 m in middle-aged men and ~495 m in women, falls steeply with age — and the equation, corridor and country move the 'normal' line by tens of metres
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy 6-minute walk distance centres near 570–580 m in middle-aged men and ~495 m in women, falls steeply with age — and the equation, corridor and country move the 'normal' line by tens of metres
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human cohorts above (Enright & Sherrill 1998; Casanova 2011; Troosters 1999), framed by Guyton & Hall ch. 84 as textbook framing.
cards.result: The anchors agree on structure and roughly on level: men outwalk women by 30 m in the multinational cohort and by 84 m in the elderly single-centre cohort; age is the dominant negative determinant everywhere; height and weight enter every equation. Enright's equations remain the reference standard for a first standardised test (median 576 m men, 494 m women, ages 40–80), Casanova's seven-country data replace blind equation use with age-specific curves and a warning about geographic variation, and Troosters shows what a long corridor and an elderly-only sample do to the numbers (631 ± 93 m). LEARNING EFFECT — stated plainly: the question asks how large the gain is between a first and a second test, and none of the three carded records quantifies it in its fetched abstract; Enright's equations were explicitly framed for first-time performance. This shelf therefore does not print a learning-effect number rather than borrow one unverified — a full-text pull of the standardisation literature is the route to that figure.
cards.watchOut: Percent-predicted values are only as valid as the match between the patient's corridor, encouragement and population and the equation's — a mismatch of any one can shift interpretation by more than most treatment effects measured with this test.
cards.source: Synthesis of Enright PL, Sherrill DL, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 1998 (PMID: 9817683); Casanova C et al., Eur Respir J 2011 (PMID: 20525717); Troosters T et al., Eur Respir J 1999 (PMID: 10515400). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Usual gait speed: pooled mean 0.92 m/s at mean age 73.5 across 34,485 older adults in nine cohorts — each 0.1 m/s faster carries a pooled hazard ratio of 0.88 for death, and decade means run from 1.43 m/s (men in their 40s) down to 0.94 m/s (women in their 80s)
shelves.question: In community-dwelling older adults, what is usual gait speed by age and sex — the pooled nine-cohort distributions — and what speeds mark the transitions to disability and survival risk?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cohort Studies · Female · Gait · Geriatric Assessment/methods · Humans · Life Expectancy · Male · Reference Values · Survival Analysis · Walking/physiology
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing is thin (Guyton & Hall ch. 84 and the motor-control chapters) — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary cohort literature and says so. The pooled analysis (Studenski 2011) combined individual data from nine cohorts: 34,485 community-dwelling adults aged 65+, mean age 73.5, mean gait speed 0.92 (SD 0.27) m/s; gait speed predicted survival across the whole range, with a pooled hazard ratio of 0.88 per 0.1 m/s faster (a relative measure, labelled as such wherever used here) — at age 75, predicted 10-year survival spanned 19–87% in men and 35–91% in women across the speed range. The descriptive meta-analysis (Bohannon & Williams Andrews 2011) pooled 23,111 healthy adults from 41 articles: decade means from 143.4 cm/s (1.43 m/s) in men aged 40–49 down to 94.3 cm/s (0.94 m/s) in women aged 80–99. The population-representative NHANES analysis (Bohannon 2008, n=1,923 aged 50+) found slower, more representative speeds — 3.26 ft/s (≈0.99 m/s) over 8 feet and 3.29 ft/s (≈1.00 m/s) over 20 feet — with the two course lengths effectively interchangeable (r = 0.933). Course length and protocol are carded per-study: a short-course standing-start speed is not a long-course usual-pace speed.

cards.headline: Studenski 2011: pooled nine cohorts, 34,485 adults aged 65+ — mean gait speed 0.92 (0.27) m/s, and each 0.1 m/s faster carried a pooled hazard ratio of 0.88 (relative) for death
cards.summary: Studenski 2011: pooled nine cohorts, 34,485 adults aged 65+ — mean gait speed 0.92 (0.27) m/s, and each 0.1 m/s faster carried a pooled hazard ratio of 0.88 (relative) for death
cards.type: Human normative cohort analysis (pooled individual data, nine cohorts), JAMA 2011
cards.people: 34,485 community-dwelling older adults aged 65 years or older (mean age 73.5 (SD 5.9) years; 59.6% women; 79.8% white) with baseline gait speed data, pooled at individual level from nine cohort studies collected between 1986 and 2000, followed for 6 to 21 years; 17,528 deaths occurred.
cards.result: Mean (SD) gait speed was 0.92 (0.27) m/s. Overall 5-year survival was 84.8% and 10-year survival 59.7%. Gait speed was associated with survival in all studies: the pooled hazard ratio was 0.88 per 0.1 m/s of gait speed (95% CI 0.87–0.90; P < 0.001) — a relative hazard, printed as such — with significant survival increments across the full range of speeds, not only below a threshold. At age 75, predicted 10-year survival across the observed speed range ran from 19% to 87% in men and from 35% to 91% in women; prediction from age, sex and gait speed was as accurate as prediction from age, sex, mobility aids and self-reported function, or from chronic conditions and clinical measures combined.
cards.watchOut: The survival gradient is an association in observational cohorts — gait speed integrates health status rather than causing the survival difference, and the pooled cohorts used their own walk protocols, so 0.92 m/s is a pooled mean across protocols, not a single-protocol constant.
cards.source: Studenski S et al. Gait speed and survival in older adults. JAMA. 2011. PMID: 21205966. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Cohort Studies · Female · Gait · Geriatric Assessment/methods · Humans · Life Expectancy · Male · Survival Analysis · United States/epidemiology

cards.headline: Bohannon & Williams Andrews 2011: meta-analysis of 41 articles and 23,111 healthy adults — usual gait speed from 143.4 cm/s (men, 40s) to 94.3 cm/s (women, 80–99), homogeneous within age–sex strata
cards.summary: Bohannon & Williams Andrews 2011: meta-analysis of 41 articles and 23,111 healthy adults — usual gait speed from 143.4 cm/s (men, 40s) to 94.3 cm/s (women, 80–99), homogeneous within age–sex strata
cards.type: Human normative synthesis of primary cohorts (descriptive meta-analysis), Physiotherapy 2011
cards.people: 23,111 apparently healthy adults pooled from 41 articles in which gait speed was documented at a normal (usual) pace over courses of 3 to 30 m, with summary data included only from strata of at least 10 participants within a gender-and-decade group.
cards.result: Gait speed was homogeneous within age-and-sex strata. Mean speed ranged from 143.4 cm/second (1.43 m/s) for men aged 40 to 49 years down to 94.3 cm/second (0.94 m/s) for women aged 80 to 99 years — a decline of roughly a third across the adult age span (relative comparison of the printed stratum means), with men faster than women within each decade. The authors offer the consolidated strata as the standard against which an individual's speed can be judged limited or not.
cards.watchOut: Courses ran 3–30 m at usual pace; the authors caution the values may not serve as a standard when gait is measured over short distances from a standing 'go' command or with a turn involved — protocol first, comparison second.
cards.source: Bohannon RW, Williams Andrews A. Normal walking speed: a descriptive meta-analysis. Physiotherapy. 2011. PMID: 21820535. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bohannon 2008 (NHANES): in a population-representative sample of 1,923 adults aged 50+, mean gait speed was 3.26 ft/s (≈0.99 m/s) over 8 feet and 3.29 ft/s (≈1.00 m/s) over 20 feet — slower than clinic-cohort norms, and the two courses agreed at r = 0.933
cards.summary: Bohannon 2008 (NHANES): in a population-representative sample of 1,923 adults aged 50+, mean gait speed was 3.26 ft/s (≈0.99 m/s) over 8 feet and 3.29 ft/s (≈1.00 m/s) over 20 feet — slower than clinic-cohort norms, and the two courses agreed at r = 0.933
cards.type: Human normative cohort (population-representative primary dataset, NHANES), J Geriatr Phys Ther 2008
cards.people: 1,923 individuals aged 50 years and older from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey 2001–2002, a population-based sample, with gait speed measured over 8 and 20 feet alongside age, stature, adiposity and isokinetic knee extension force.
cards.result: Mean gait speeds were 3.26 ft/s over 8 feet and 3.29 ft/s over 20 feet (≈0.99 and ≈1.00 m/s) — statistically different (P = 0.002) but not meaningfully so, and strongly correlated (r = 0.933, P < 0.001), so the shorter course is justifiable. Age, stature, knee extension force and waist circumference each correlated significantly with speed over both distances, and multiple regression (age, gender, knee extension force, waist circumference, stature) predicted speed with R = 0.459 (8 feet) and R = 0.506 (20 feet). The author notes these population estimates are slower than many previously published values but may be more representative.
cards.watchOut: Short courses (8 and 20 feet) from a standing start include acceleration, which lowers the computed speed versus a flying-start usual-pace course — part of why these representative values sit below the meta-analytic strata, and a further reason protocol must travel with the number.
cards.source: Bohannon RW. Population representative gait speed and its determinants. J Geriatr Phys Ther. 2008. PMID: 19856549. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: usual gait speed falls from ~1.4 m/s in the 40s to ~0.9 m/s in the 80s, men run faster than women at every age, and speed stratifies survival smoothly — there is no single cliff, only a gradient read against age, sex and protocol
cards.summary: Synthesis: usual gait speed falls from ~1.4 m/s in the 40s to ~0.9 m/s in the 80s, men run faster than women at every age, and speed stratifies survival smoothly — there is no single cliff, only a gradient read against age, sex and protocol
cards.people: Synthesis of the three carded human reports above (Studenski 2011; Bohannon & Williams Andrews 2011; Bohannon 2008), with textbook framing from Guyton & Hall noted as thin in the balance.
cards.result: The three sources interlock. Level and slope: decade means descend from 143.4 cm/s (men, 40s) to 94.3 cm/s (women, 80–99) in the healthy-adult meta-analysis, and the pooled older-adult mean is 0.92 m/s at mean age 73.5 (Studenski). Representativeness: an unselected population sample walks slower than research cohorts (≈0.99–1.00 m/s at 50+, NHANES) — whose norm you use decides whose speed counts as slow. Meaning: survival rises smoothly with speed across the whole range (pooled hazard ratio 0.88 per 0.1 m/s, a relative measure), so the disability and risk 'transitions' the question asks about are gradients with clinically used landmarks along them, not natural breakpoints in these data — at 75, the speed range spans 19–87% (men) and 35–91% (women) predicted 10-year survival. Protocol discipline (course length, standing vs flying start) is the price of using any of these numbers.
cards.watchOut: None of the carded records derives a disability-transition threshold as a measured breakpoint; any single cut-off quoted in practice is a convention laid over the Studenski gradient and should be labelled as such, exactly as with the FeNO limits on the neighbouring shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Studenski S et al., JAMA 2011 (PMID: 21205966); Bohannon RW, Williams Andrews A, Physiotherapy 2011 (PMID: 21820535); Bohannon RW, J Geriatr Phys Ther 2008 (PMID: 19856549). Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Timed Up and Go reference values by decade in healthy older adults
shelves.question: In healthy older adults, what are reference values for the Timed Up and Go test by decade (60s–90s) — the descriptive meta-analysis norms — and how wide is the normal range before a time counts as slow?
shelves.mesh: Reference Values · Geriatric Assessment · Locomotion · Postural Balance/physiology · Age Factors · Sex Factors · Reproducibility of Results
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing is thin for this test: Guyton & Hall's exercise and motor-control chapters frame mobility generally, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, as its slate row directs). The carded record is concordant. Bohannon's descriptive meta-analysis of 21 studies gives mean Timed Up and Go (TUG) times of 8.1 seconds in the 60s, 9.2 seconds in the 70s and 11.3 seconds from 80 to 99 years, with a time above the upper 95% confidence limit counting as worse than average. The primary cohorts behave the same way: Steffen's 96 community-dwelling elders showed the same age-related slowing with very high test–retest reliability (ICC 0.95–0.97), Vereeck's 318 asymptomatic adults found TUG times rising with age yet still at or under 10 seconds even in older subjects, and a dedicated oldest-old cohort (mean age 90.3 years) averaged 12.6 seconds. So the normal range widens with age — roughly 8 seconds in the 60s to roughly 11–13 seconds in the 80s and 90s — and a single young-adult cut-off mislabels healthy old people as slow. Chair height and exact course protocol were not stated in the fetched records and are a standing source of between-study spread, which the wide confidence interval at 80–99 years (10.0–12.7 seconds) reflects.

cards.headline: Bohannon 2006 meta-analysis (21 studies): mean Timed Up and Go 8.1 s in the 60s, 9.2 s in the 70s and 11.3 s at 80–99 years
cards.summary: Bohannon 2006 meta-analysis (21 studies): mean Timed Up and Go 8.1 s in the 60s, 9.2 s in the 70s and 11.3 s at 80–99 years
cards.people: Twenty-one studies of apparently healthy elders consolidated in a descriptive meta-analysis; the pooled mean covers individuals at least 60 years of age, with age-stratified means for the 60–69, 70–79 and 80–99 year bands.
cards.result: The mean (95% confidence interval) TUG time for individuals at least 60 years of age was 9.4 (8.9–9.9) seconds. By age band: 8.1 (7.1–9.0) seconds for 60 to 69 year olds, 9.2 (8.2–10.2) seconds for 70 to 79 years, and 11.3 (10.0–12.7) seconds for 80 to 99 years. The author proposes that patients whose performance exceeds the upper limit of the reported confidence intervals be considered to have worse than average performance.
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies differed in their particulars (the author says so plainly), and the record does not state a single chair height or course protocol — the decade means are a standard to compare against, not a pass/fail line, and the 80–99 band pools three decades into one wide interval.

cards.headline: Steffen 2002: in 96 community-dwelling elders (61–89 years) TUG performance declined with age in both sexes, with test–retest ICC 0.95–0.97
cards.summary: Steffen 2002: in 96 community-dwelling elders (61–89 years) TUG performance declined with age in both sexes, with test–retest ICC 0.95–0.97
cards.people: 96 community-dwelling elderly people (61–89 years of age) with independent functioning, analysed by gender and by age cohort (60–69, 70–79 and 80–89 years); TUG was measured alongside the Six-Minute Walk Test, Berg Balance Scale and comfortable/fast gait speeds.
cards.result: The TUG (with the 6-minute walk and gait speeds) showed high test–retest reliability (ICC [2,1] = .95–.97), and mean scores showed a trend of age-related decline for both male and female subjects. The record's abstract reports that means, standard deviations and 95% confidence intervals were calculated for each cohort but does not print the per-cohort TUG seconds, so no cohort value is quoted here.
cards.watchOut: A modest single sample (N = 96) split across six age-by-sex cells, so its cell means are imprecise; its durable contributions are the reliability figure and the confirmation, in a primary cohort, of the meta-analysis's age gradient.
cards.source: Steffen TM et al. Age- and gender-related test performance in community-dwelling elderly people: Six-Minute Walk Test, Berg Balance Scale, Timed Up & Go Test, and gait speeds. cards.headline: Vereeck 2008: in 318 asymptomatic adults TUG times rose with age, yet even older subjects should complete the test in 10 seconds or less; women performed poorer
cards.summary: Vereeck 2008: in 318 asymptomatic adults TUG times rose with age, yet even older subjects should complete the test in 10 seconds or less; women performed poorer
cards.people: 318 asymptomatic adults undergoing a clinical balance battery (standing balance, tandem gait, dynamic gait index and the Timed Up and Go test), analysed for age and gender effects.
cards.result: Linear regression equations indicated that for both men and women, timed up and go test times increased with age, but even older subjects should perform the TUG in 10 seconds or less. Women performed significantly poorer on the TUG (and on tandem Romberg with eyes closed at the 30-second limit) than men.
cards.watchOut: This cohort's '10 seconds or less even when older' bound sits in some tension with the meta-analysis mean of 11.3 seconds at 80–99 years — the samples differ (asymptomatic volunteers versus pooled study samples), which is exactly why a range, not a single cut-off, is the honest summary for the oldest ages.

cards.headline: Kafri 2019 oldest-old: mean TUG 12.6 (SD 6.9) seconds at a mean age of 90.3 years in 45 independently ambulating assisted-living residents
cards.summary: Kafri 2019 oldest-old: mean TUG 12.6 (SD 6.9) seconds at a mean age of 90.3 years in 45 independently ambulating assisted-living residents
cards.people: 45 individuals aged 85 years and over (mean age 90.3, SD 3.7 years) living in an assisted living facility and ambulating independently; balance was tested with the mini-BESTest and the Timed Up and Go test, function with the Late-Life Function and Disability Instrument.
cards.result: The mean TUG time was 12.6 (6.9) seconds, alongside a mean mini-BESTest score of 69.8% (18.6%). Notably, fallers and nonfallers in this oldest-old sample differed significantly across almost all outcome measures except the TUG (and two mini-BESTest domains).
cards.watchOut: N = 45 from one assisted-living facility — a selected, independently ambulating subgroup of the 90s, not a population sample; the wide standard deviation (6.9 s) is itself the finding: by the 90s the normal spread is very wide, and in this sample TUG did not separate fallers from nonfallers.

cards.headline: Synthesis: Timed Up and Go slows by roughly a second a decade — about 8 s in the 60s, 9 s in the 70s, 11 s in the 80s and around 12–13 s in the 90s — and the normal range widens as it slows
cards.summary: Synthesis: Timed Up and Go slows by roughly a second a decade — about 8 s in the 60s, 9 s in the 70s, 11 s in the 80s and around 12–13 s in the 90s — and the normal range widens as it slows
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: Bohannon's 21-study descriptive meta-analysis, Steffen's 96 community-dwelling elders, Vereeck's 318 asymptomatic adults, and Kafri's 45 oldest-old residents (mean age 90.3 years).
cards.result: All four reports agree on the shape: TUG time rises steadily with age and the spread around the mean widens. The meta-analytic decade means (8.1 s, 9.2 s, 11.3 s) are the working reference values; the primary cohorts confirm the gradient, the high test–retest reliability (ICC 0.95–0.97), a small female disadvantage, and a 90s mean near 12.6 s. A time beyond the age band's upper confidence limit is the record's own definition of worse-than-average performance. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the decade gradient and its widening range are concordant across the meta-analysis and the primary cohorts.
cards.watchOut: Chair height, armrest use, footwear and encouragement were not standardised across the underlying studies and are not stated in the fetched records; a clinic comparing its own patients against these values should use one fixed local protocol. Values for the 90s rest on a single small facility cohort.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bohannon RW. Journal of geriatric physical therapy. 2006 (PMID: 16914068); Steffen TM et al. Physical therapy. 2002 (PMID: 11856064); Vereeck L et al. shelves.title: Five-times sit-to-stand and 30-second chair-stand reference values by age and sex
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are reference values for the five-times sit-to-stand test (and the 30-second chair-stand count) by age and sex — the pooled 14-country analysis and national cohort norms?
shelves.mesh: Reference Values · Exercise Test/methods · Geriatric Assessment/methods · Muscle Strength/physiology · Age Factors · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing thin, as the slate row directs: Guyton & Hall's exercise/motor chapters frame mobility generally; the row rests on the primary measurement literature). Three large normative datasets agree on the shape of five-times sit-to-stand (FTSST) performance: fastest in the 50s (median about 9–10 seconds), slowing steadily to a median of about 15 seconds by the late 80s and 90s, with women slower than men at every age and a very wide spread in old age (in the English cohort, the 5th-to-95th performance span at 85+ runs from about 26 seconds down to about 10 seconds in women). A younger adult cohort (Chile, 18–80 years) extends the curve downward: medians of about 7–8 seconds in the 20s rising to 11–13 seconds at 70–80. The companion 30-second chair-stand count rests on a much thinner base — its founding validation study (76 older adults) established reliability and validity against leg-press strength but the fetched record does not print decade mean counts, so this shelf gives the 30-second test's measurement credentials, not invented counts. Note the percentile convention in the two GeroScience reports: their 5th percentile is the SLOWEST time and their 95th the fastest, the reverse of the usual direction, and the cards print them exactly as reported.

cards.headline: Grgic 2026 pooled SHARE analysis (45,470 people, 14 countries): five-times sit-to-stand median 10 s (women) and 9 s (men) in the 50s, slowing to a median of 15 s at 85+
cards.summary: Grgic 2026 pooled SHARE analysis (45,470 people, 14 countries): five-times sit-to-stand median 10 s (women) and 9 s (men) in the 50s, slowing to a median of 15 s at 85+
cards.people: 45,470 participants aged 50 years and over from the 5th wave of the Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe (14 European countries); weighted percentiles (5th to 95th) calculated by age band and sex. In this report the 5th percentile is the slowest performance and the 95th the fastest.
cards.result: For females, the best performance was at 50–54 years (5th percentile = 18 s; 50th = 10 s; 95th = 6 s) and the worst at 85–89 and ≥90 years (5th = 28 s; 50th = 15 s; 95th = 9 s). For males, the best was at 55–59 years (5th = 18 s; 50th = 9 s; 95th = 5 s) and the worst at ≥90 years (5th = 26 s; 50th = 15 s; 95th = 9 s). Performance was poorer in females and in older age groups throughout.
cards.watchOut: Survey participants aged 50+ are a general population, not screened healthy volunteers, so these percentiles describe the population distribution — including people with disease — rather than a 'healthy-only' range; the reversed percentile direction (5th = slowest) must not be misread as the fastest 5%.
cards.source: Grgic J et al. Reference values for the five-times-sit-to-stand test: a pooled analysis including 45,470 participants from 14 countries. GeroScience. 2026. PMID: 40875134. cards.headline: Grgic 2026 English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (7,658 people): FTSST span 15.6–5.6 s (women, 50s) widening to 26.3–9.8 s at 85+
cards.summary: Grgic 2026 English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (7,658 people): FTSST span 15.6–5.6 s (women, 50s) widening to 26.3–9.8 s at 85+
cards.people: Adults aged 50 years and over (female n = 4,234; male n = 3,424) from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing; weighted percentiles from the 5th to the 95th calculated for gait speed, five-times-sit-to-stand, balance and handgrip strength. As in the companion report, the span is printed slowest-to-fastest.
cards.result: Best FTSST performance was at 50–54 and 55–59 years (female P5–95: 15.6–5.6 s; male P5–95: 14.1–5.5 s) and worst at ≥85 years (female P5–95: 26.3–9.8 s; male P5–95: 23.4–8.6 s). The same cohort's gait-speed and grip values follow the same age pattern (cross-point: grip centiles are a separate shelf's question and are not carded here).
cards.watchOut: English population sample, again not a screened-healthy subset; the FTSST figures corroborate the 14-country pooled values closely, which is their main value here — two independent large datasets landing on the same medians and the same widening spread.

cards.headline: Torres-Castro 2025 Chilean cohort (463 healthy adults, 18–80 years): five-repetition sit-to-stand median 7.4 s (women) and 7.8 s (men) in the 20s, rising to 11.3 s and 13.0 s at 70–80

cards.people: 463 healthy adults (269 women) aged 18–80 years enrolled at five sites across Chile in a multicentre cross-sectional study; time to complete five repetitions recorded with anthropometry, physical activity and smoking history.
cards.watchOut: The men's medians are not perfectly monotonic (30–39 years faster than 18–29), a small-cell artefact to read as noise around a rising trend, not physiology; this is the only carded cohort screened as healthy and the only one covering ages under 50, so the young-adult end of the curve rests on it alone.

cards.headline: Jones 1999: the 30-second chair-stand test is reliable (test–retest ICC 0.84 men, 0.92 women) and tracks leg-press strength (r = 0.78 men, 0.71 women) in 76 community-dwelling older adults
cards.summary: Jones 1999: the 30-second chair-stand test is reliable (test–retest ICC 0.84 men, 0.92 women) and tracks leg-press strength (r = 0.78 men, 0.71 women) in 76 community-dwelling older adults
cards.type: Founding validation study of the 30-second chair-stand test (Jones 1999)
cards.people: 76 community-dwelling older adults (mean age 70.5 years) who each performed two 30-second chair-stand tests and two maximum leg-press tests on separate days 2–5 days apart.
cards.result: Test–retest intraclass correlations were .84 for men and .92 for women, with no significant change between days. Chair-stand performance correlated moderately highly with maximum weight-adjusted leg-press performance (r = .78 men, .71 women), and performance decreased significantly across the 60s, 70s and 80s age groups (P < .01) and was lower in low-active than high-active participants (P < .0001). The record's abstract does not print mean chair-stand counts by decade, so no counts are quoted here.
cards.watchOut: N = 76 and a validation design, not a normative survey: this card establishes that the 30-second count measures lower-body strength reliably — it does not by itself define normal counts by decade, and any decade count table must come from a larger normative record, not from this study.

cards.headline: Synthesis: five-times sit-to-stand takes a median of about 9–10 s in the 50s and about 15 s by the late 80s, women slower than men, with a wide old-age spread; the 30-second count is validated but its normative base is thinner
cards.summary: Synthesis: five-times sit-to-stand takes a median of about 9–10 s in the 50s and about 15 s by the late 80s, women slower than men, with a wide old-age spread; the 30-second count is validated but its normative base is thinner
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the 14-country SHARE pooled analysis (45,470 participants), the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing analysis (7,658), the Chilean healthy-adult cohort (463, ages 18–80), and the 30-second chair-stand validation study (76 older adults).
cards.result: Two very large population datasets and one screened-healthy cohort draw the same curve: FTSST time rises from roughly 7–8 seconds in young adults and 9–10 seconds (median) in the 50s to a median of about 15 seconds at 85+, with women slower at every age and the between-person spread roughly doubling by old age. The 30-second chair-stand count is a reliable, leg-strength-valid measure whose performance falls by decade, but its decade norms are not established by the carded record. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the five-times test's age/sex distribution; the 30-second count's normative distribution remains the thinner limb and is labelled as such.
cards.watchOut: Chair height, armrest use and whether arms were folded are protocol variables the fetched abstracts do not standardise; percentile direction in the two GeroScience reports runs slowest-first (5th percentile = slowest time) and is printed as reported. Population percentiles (SHARE, ELSA) include people with disease; the Chilean cohort is the screened-healthy comparator.

shelves.title: Bone turnover marker reference intervals: serum P1NP and CTX (IOF/IFCC analytes)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for the bone turnover markers used as the IOF/IFCC reference analytes — serum P1NP (formation) and serum CTX (resorption) — by sex, menopausal status and age, and how large are their circadian and fasting-related swings?
shelves.mesh: Biomarkers/blood · Bone Remodeling/physiology · Collagen Type I/blood · Procollagen/blood · Reference Values · Premenopause/blood · Sex Characteristics
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, parathyroid hormone, calcitonin and bone physiology; Ganong, endocrine control of bone). The IOF/IFCC reference analytes — serum P1NP for formation and serum CTX for resorption — have solid reference intervals, but they are assay- and population-specific, and that specificity is the shelf's core content. The largest intervals come from the Study of Health in Pomerania (1,939 people, IDS-iSYS platform): in men the intervals narrow with age (P1NP 31.1–95.9 ng/mL at 25–29 years falling to 15.7–68.1 ng/mL at 75–79; CTX 0.12–0.83 falling to 0.05–0.58 ng/mL), in premenopausal women (30–54) P1NP was 19.3–76.3 ng/mL and CTX 0.05–0.67 ng/mL, and in postmenopausal women (50–79) both ran higher (P1NP 18.2–102.3; CTX 0.09–1.05 ng/mL). The young-premenopausal reference study (637 women aged 30–39 across four countries) found significant country differences — P1NP and serum β-CTX higher in France — that largely disappeared once smoking, contraceptive-pill use, exercise, cycle timing and vitamin D were allowed for: behaviour and sampling conditions move these markers. The Danish assay comparison (2,308 fasting samples) is the caution: the two automated platforms (IDS-iSYS and Roche Cobas) disagreed significantly for both markers (P1NP mean difference −3 µg/L with limits of agreement −19 to +14; CTX mean difference 13 ng/L, limits −187 to +214, with a systematic concentration-dependent bias), so intervals and monitoring must stay on one assay. CTX sampling in the carded record was fasting; the size of CTX's circadian and food-related swings is part of the textbook account of sampling discipline, but no fetched record here quantifies those swings, so no swing number is printed.

cards.headline: Michelsen 2013 Study of Health in Pomerania (1,939 people, IDS-iSYS): age-specific P1NP and CTX reference intervals — men's P1NP 31.1–95.9 ng/mL at 25–29 years narrowing to 15.7–68.1 at 75–79; postmenopausal women's CTX up to 1.05 ng/mL
cards.summary: Michelsen 2013 Study of Health in Pomerania (1,939 people, IDS-iSYS): age-specific P1NP and CTX reference intervals — men's P1NP 31.1–95.9 ng/mL at 25–29 years narrowing to 15.7–68.1 at 75–79; postmenopausal women's CTX up to 1.05 ng/mL
cards.people: A healthy reference population of 1,107 men and 382 premenopausal and 450 postmenopausal women from the first follow-up of the Study of Health in Pomerania; serum intact P1NP, bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (BAP) and CTX measured on the IDS-iSYS automated system; the reference interval is the central 95% range, age-specific in men by quantile regression and age-independent in women.
cards.result: In men, P1NP and CTX intervals decreased with age (25–29 years: P1NP 31.1–95.9 ng/mL, CTX 0.12–0.83 ng/mL; 75–79 years: P1NP 15.7–68.1 ng/mL, CTX 0.05–0.58 ng/mL) while BAP barely changed (7.4–27.7 ng/mL at 25–29; 7.6–24.4 ng/mL at 75–79). Premenopausal women (30–54 years): P1NP 19.3–76.3 ng/mL, BAP 6.0–22.7 ng/mL, CTX 0.05–0.67 ng/mL. Postmenopausal women (50–79 years): P1NP 18.2–102.3 ng/mL, BAP 8.1–31.6 ng/mL, CTX 0.09–1.05 ng/mL.
cards.watchOut: One platform (IDS-iSYS) and one north-German population: the intervals are the best large-sample numbers in the carded record, but the Danish card below shows the other major platform reads differently, so these ng/mL limits must not be applied to Roche Cobas results.
cards.source: Michelsen J et al. Reference intervals for serum concentrations of three bone turnover markers for men and women. Bone. 2013. PMID: 24076251. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Glover 2009 (637 healthy premenopausal women aged 30–39, four countries): IFCC-method 95% reference intervals for P1NP and serum β-CTX — with country differences that behaviour and cycle timing largely explained
cards.summary: Glover 2009 (637 healthy premenopausal women aged 30–39, four countries): IFCC-method 95% reference intervals for P1NP and serum β-CTX — with country differences that behaviour and cycle timing largely explained
cards.type: Multinational reference-interval study, young premenopausal women (Glover 2009)
cards.people: 637 eligible healthy women aged 30–39 years (mean 34.6) with regular cyclic menses, from the United Kingdom, France, Belgium and the United States (participants in the HORIZON-PFT study); serum bone alkaline phosphatase, serum P1NP, serum β-CTX and urinary NTX measured, with two-sided 95% reference intervals estimated by the International Federation of Clinical Chemistry method.
cards.result: Serum β-CTX was significantly higher in France than in the United Kingdom (P = 0.01), and P1NP was higher in France (P < 0.001) and Belgium (P = 0.02) than in the United Kingdom, and higher in France than in the United States (P < 0.01). Low bone turnover markers were associated with nonsmoking, use of a contraceptive pill, exercise, being close to ovulation, and high 25-hydroxyvitamin D; countries differed in these characteristics, and once they were allowed for in the model, the country differences were attenuated or removed. The record's abstract establishes the intervals by the IFCC method but does not print their numerical limits, so none are quoted here.
cards.watchOut: This is the young-premenopausal anchor population for the IOF/IFCC markers — deliberately narrow (30–39, regular cycles) — so its intervals must not be stretched to adolescents, older premenopausal women or women on hormonal contraception without thought; the ovulation-timing association also means cycle day is a real sampling variable in this group.
cards.source: Glover SJ et al. Establishing a reference interval for bone turnover markers in 637 healthy, young, premenopausal women from the United Kingdom, France, Belgium, and the United States. cards.headline: Jørgensen 2017 Danish Health2006 (2,308 fasting samples): the two automated CTX/P1NP platforms disagree significantly — P1NP mean difference −3 µg/L (limits −19 to +14), CTX 13 ng/L (limits −187 to +214) — so intervals are assay-specific
cards.summary: Jørgensen 2017 Danish Health2006 (2,308 fasting samples): the two automated CTX/P1NP platforms disagree significantly — P1NP mean difference −3 µg/L (limits −19 to +14), CTX 13 ng/L (limits −187 to +214) — so intervals are assay-specific
cards.people: 2,308 individuals (1,250 males, 1,058 females; age range 24–76 years) from the Health2006 study, excluding those on anti-osteoporotic treatment (hormonal-contraceptive users included); fasting sera analysed for CTX and P1NP on both the automated IDS-iSYS analyser and the automated Roche Cobas e411 analyser.
cards.result: There was significant disagreement between the two P1NP assays (mean difference −3 µg/L, limits of agreement −19 to +14; P < 0.001) and between the two CTX assays (mean difference 13 ng/L, limits of agreement −187 to +214; P < 0.001), with a systematic bias for CTX: at low values Cobas read higher than iSYS, and at higher concentrations iSYS read increasingly higher than Cobas. The authors propose three reference intervals per sex (men: 25–29, 30–39 and 40–80 years; women: 25–29, over 30 premenopausal, and over 30 postmenopausal) — per assay, with the numerical limits in the full text rather than the record's abstract — and conclude that monitoring samples must be run on the same assay and that harmonisation is highly warranted.
cards.watchOut: Limits of agreement of −187 to +214 ng/L for CTX are wide against typical CTX values of a few hundred ng/L — a patient switched between platforms mid-monitoring can appear to change turnover by assay artefact alone; fasting sampling was this study's discipline, and non-fasting or afternoon samples add the circadian/food variation the intervals do not cover.
cards.source: Jørgensen NR et al. Comparison of two automated assays of BTM (CTX and P1NP) and reference intervals in a Danish population. Osteoporosis international. 2017. PMID: 28455749. cards.headline: Synthesis: P1NP and CTX reference intervals are established per assay and population — men narrow with age, postmenopausal women run highest — but the two automated platforms disagree enough that no platform-free interval exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: P1NP and CTX reference intervals are established per assay and population — men narrow with age, postmenopausal women run highest — but the two automated platforms disagree enough that no platform-free interval exists
cards.people: Synthesis of the carded reports: the Pomeranian reference population (1,939 people, IDS-iSYS), the four-country young-premenopausal study (637 women) and the Danish two-platform comparison (2,308 fasting samples).
cards.result: Read together: formation (P1NP) and resorption (CTX) intervals are widest and highest in postmenopausal women (CTX to 1.05 ng/mL), narrower and falling with age in men, and shifted by smoking, contraceptive use, exercise, cycle timing and vitamin D in young women. The Danish comparison caps the claim: with significant, concentration-dependent disagreement between IDS-iSYS and Roche Cobas, an interval is only valid for its own assay, and serial monitoring must never cross platforms. No fetched record quantified CTX's circadian or post-prandial swing size, so this shelf asserts the sampling discipline (fasting samples, as in the Danish study) without printing an unverified swing number. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the intervals are robust within their assay/population frames, but cross-assay harmonisation — the step that would make one universal interval possible — is outstanding on the carded record.
cards.watchOut: Bone turnover markers answer 'how fast is bone turning over', not 'how dense is the bone' — a value inside the reference interval does not exclude osteoporosis, and a value outside it does not diagnose a cause. Renal function, recent fracture and time of day all move CTX in particular; the carded intervals come from fasting, bone-disease-free reference samples.

synthesis synthesis of the carded reports: the pomeranian reference population (1,939 people, ids-isys), the four-country young-premenopausal study (637 women) and the danish two-platform comparison (2,308 fasting samples). read together: formation (p1np) and resorption (ctx) intervals are widest and highest in postmenopausal women (ctx to 1.05 ng/ml), narrower and falling with age in men, and shifted by smoking, contraceptive use, exercise, cycle timing and vitamin d in young women. the danish comparison caps the claim: with significant, concentration-dependent disagreement between ids-isys and roche cobas, an interval is only valid for its own assay, and serial monitoring must never cross platforms. no fetched record quantified ctx's circadian or post-prandial swing size, so this shelf asserts the sampling discipline (fasting samples, as in the danish study) without printing an unverified swing number. proposed physiology — emerging: the intervals are robust within their assay/population frames, but cross-assay harmonisation — the step that would make one universal interval possible — is outstanding on the carded record. bone turnover markers answer 'how fast is bone turning over', not 'how dense is the bone' — a value inside the reference interval does not exclude osteoporosis, and a value outside it does not diagnose a cause. renal function, recent fracture and time of day all move ctx in particular; the carded intervals come from fasting, bone-disease-free reference samples. synthesis of michelsen j et al. bone. 2013 (pmid: 24076251); glover sj et al. journal of bone and mineral research. 2009 (pmid: 18665786); jørgensen nr et al. osteoporosis international. 2017 (pmid: 28455749), all carded above. textbook framing: guyton & hall textbook of medical physiology (parathyroid hormone, calcitonin and bone physiology); ganong review of medical physiology (endocrine control of bone).

shelves.title: Peficitinib in rheumatoid arthritis: ACR20 56–64% vs 22–24% on placebo across two Asian phase 3 trials, with less joint damage in RAJ4 — a Japan-approved, single-region JAK programme
shelves.question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis (including methotrexate inadequate responders), does the oral pan-JAK inhibitor peficitinib (ASP015K), compared with placebo on background therapy, improve disease activity (RAJ programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adamantane · Adult · Aged · Antirheumatic Agents · Arthritis, Rheumatoid · Double-Blind Method · Drug Substitution · Female · Herpes Zoster · Humans · Immunosuppressive Agents · Infections · Janus Kinase Inhibitors · Japan · Male · Methotrexate · Middle Aged · Niacinamide · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Peficitinib 100 mg and 150 mg once daily beat placebo consistently across the RAJ programme: ACR20 responses of 58.6% and 64.4% versus 21.8% in RAJ4 (methotrexate inadequate responders, with methotrexate), 56.6% and 56.3% versus 24.2% in the 2024 Asian phase 3 trial, and a dose-related ACR20 advantage as monotherapy in the phase IIb trial, with less radiographic progression in RAJ4 (modified total Sharp score change 1.62 and 1.03 versus 3.37 on placebo). Patient- and physician-reported outcomes from RAJ3 and RAJ4 moved the same way. The whole programme is single-region (Japan/Asia; peficitinib is approved in Japan and is not FDA- or EMA-approved), and the harms are the JAK-class harms seen in the trials themselves — serious infections and herpes zoster were more frequent on peficitinib. The wider JAK-class cardiovascular and malignancy warnings (from ORAL Surveillance) are homed on the library's JAK-inhibitor shelves and are cross-pointed here, not re-carded. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: RAJ4 phase 3 RCT (Takeuchi 2019): peficitinib 100/150 mg + methotrexate beat placebo on ACR20 (58.6% and 64.4% vs 21.8%) and slowed joint damage in Japanese methotrexate inadequate responders
cards.summary: RAJ4 phase 3 RCT (Takeuchi 2019): peficitinib 100/150 mg + methotrexate beat placebo on ACR20 (58.6% and 64.4% vs 21.8%) and slowed joint damage in Japanese methotrexate inadequate responders
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (RAJ4), peficitinib + methotrexate vs placebo + methotrexate
cards.people: 519 Japanese patients with rheumatoid arthritis and an inadequate response to methotrexate, randomised 1:1:1 to placebo, peficitinib 100 mg once daily or peficitinib 150 mg once daily, all with methotrexate, for 52 weeks (placebo non-responders switched to peficitinib at week 12, the rest at week 28).
cards.result: ACR20 response at week 12/early termination was 58.6% (100 mg) and 64.4% (150 mg) versus 21.8% on placebo (both p<0.001). Mean change in van der Heijde-modified total Sharp score at week 28/early termination was 1.62 (100 mg) and 1.03 (150 mg) versus 3.37 on placebo (both p<0.001) — less structural progression on peficitinib. Peficitinib was associated with haematological and biochemical parameter changes and an increased incidence of serious infections and herpes zoster-related disease. One death from suicide occurred in a patient in the placebo group after switching to peficitinib 100 mg.
cards.watchOut: Japanese population only, and the placebo arm was switched to peficitinib from week 12/28, so the placebo comparison is a 12-week comparison for symptoms and 28 weeks for structure; longer-term placebo-controlled data do not exist in this programme.

cards.headline: Asian phase 3 RCT (Yang 2024): peficitinib 100/150 mg beat placebo on ACR20 (56.6% and 56.3% vs 24.2%) in patients with inadequate response or intolerance to methotrexate
cards.summary: Asian phase 3 RCT (Yang 2024): peficitinib 100/150 mg beat placebo on ACR20 (56.6% and 56.3% vs 24.2%) in patients with inadequate response or intolerance to methotrexate
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, peficitinib + non-biologic DMARDs vs placebo + DMARDs
cards.people: 385 Asian patients with rheumatoid arthritis and an inadequate response or intolerance to methotrexate, from mainland China, Korea and Taiwan, randomised 1:1:1 to once-daily placebo (n=128), peficitinib 100 mg (n=129) or peficitinib 150 mg (n=128) in combination with non-biologic DMARDs; placebo patients switched to peficitinib at week 24.
cards.result: ACR20 response at week 24/early termination was 56.6% (100 mg) and 56.3% (150 mg) versus 24.2% on placebo — odds ratios 4.14 (95% CI 2.42 to 7.08) and 4.07 (95% CI 2.38 to 6.96), both p<0.001. No additional benefit was observed with the higher dose. Herpes zoster-related disease (herpes zoster and varicella) was more frequent on peficitinib than placebo (incidence rate 6.7 vs 3.7 per 100 patient-years), with no dose dependency observed.
cards.watchOut: Single-region (Asian) population, as with the whole peficitinib programme; the record carries no MeSH terms, so none are printed.

cards.headline: Phase IIb monotherapy RCT (Takeuchi 2016): peficitinib alone showed a dose-related ACR20 advantage over placebo at 50, 100 and 150 mg over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Phase IIb monotherapy RCT (Takeuchi 2016): peficitinib alone showed a dose-related ACR20 advantage over placebo at 50, 100 and 150 mg over 12 weeks
cards.type: Phase IIb double-blind placebo-controlled dose-finding randomised trial, peficitinib monotherapy vs placebo
cards.people: 281 Japanese adults with moderate to severe rheumatoid arthritis and active disease, not on concomitant DMARD therapy, randomised equally to once-daily placebo or peficitinib 25, 50, 100 or 150 mg for 12 weeks (mean age 53.0 years, 81.1% female, 25.3% had previously used anti-TNF therapy).
cards.result: Peficitinib 50, 100 and 150 mg each showed statistically significantly higher ACR20 response rates than placebo at week 12, with response rates increasing up to 150 mg and a statistically significant dose response. Treatment-emergent adverse event incidence was similar across groups (placebo 64.3%; peficitinib 25 mg 70.9%, 50 mg 64.9%, 100 mg 52.7%, 150 mg 67.2%); nasopharyngitis, increased blood creatine phosphokinase and diarrhoea were more frequent on peficitinib. No serious infections were reported; herpes zoster occurred in four patients (two each on 25 mg and 100 mg).
cards.watchOut: A 12-week dose-finding trial, not a registration trial; it supports the dose response but the efficacy weight of this shelf rests on the two phase 3 trials.

cards.summary: Patient- and physician-reported outcomes (Tanaka 2021): peficitinib improved pain, physical function and work productivity versus placebo across RAJ3 and RAJ4 (1,025 patients pooled)

cards.people: 1,025 patients from two randomised placebo-controlled phase 3 trials (RAJ3 and RAJ4) of Asian patients with rheumatoid arthritis and an inadequate response to prior DMARDs, receiving peficitinib 100 mg, peficitinib 150 mg or placebo, alone or with DMARDs (RAJ3) or with methotrexate (RAJ4).

shelves.title: Diacerein in knee osteoarthritis: no better than placebo in the 2026 trial, non-inferior to celecoxib in DISSCO — with diarrhoea in up to 39% and a retracted older trial fenced out
shelves.question: In adults with painful knee osteoarthritis, does the oral IL-1α/β inhibitor (SYSADOA) diacerein, compared with placebo or celecoxib, reduce knee pain and improve function?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Anthraquinones · Female · Double-Blind Method · Middle Aged · Male · Anti-Inflammatory Agents · Pain Measurement · Aged · Magnetic Resonance Imaging · Treatment Outcome · Australia · Interleukin-1beta
shelves.balance: The evidence splits by comparator. Against placebo, the best and newest test is negative: the 2026 multicentre randomised trial in patients selected for an inflammatory phenotype (effusion-synovitis on MRI) found no greater improvement in knee pain with diacerein than placebo over 24 weeks (between-group difference −1.3 mm on a 0–100 mm scale). Against an active comparator, the large DISSCO trial found diacerein non-inferior to celecoxib for pain and function over 6 months — a result compatible with a modest symptom effect, with a small effect shared with placebo response, or with celecoxib itself being modest in that population. The remaining reports (generic versus branded diacerein; a small diacerein + celecoxib combination study) have no placebo arm and cannot settle efficacy. Diarrhoea is the consistent harm (38.6% vs 22.3% on placebo in the 2026 trial; 10.2% vs 3.7% versus celecoxib in DISSCO), and diacerein is not marketed in the US. RETRACTION FENCE: the Pavelka et al. 2007 diacerein knee-OA trial (PMID 18050202) is a Retracted Publication and is deliberately NOT carded here; older meta-analyses that pool it should be read with that stated. Proposed stamp: SPLIT.

cards.headline: Randomised clinical trial (Aitken 2026): diacerein did NOT improve knee pain versus placebo over 24 weeks in knee OA with effusion-synovitis (−1.3 mm difference on a 0–100 mm scale)
cards.summary: Randomised clinical trial (Aitken 2026): diacerein did NOT improve knee pain versus placebo over 24 weeks in knee OA with effusion-synovitis (−1.3 mm difference on a 0–100 mm scale)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised clinical trial, diacerein vs placebo
cards.people: 262 participants with clinical knee osteoarthritis, substantial knee pain and effusion-synovitis on MRI, randomised 1:1 at 4 Australian centres to diacerein 50 mg once daily for 2 weeks then 50 mg twice daily to 24 weeks, or identical placebo (mean age 54.9 years, 56.1% female); 231 (88.2%) completed the trial.
cards.result: Knee pain (visual analogue scale 0–100 mm; minimal clinically important improvement 15 mm) changed by −19.9 mm on diacerein versus −18.6 mm on placebo — a between-group mean difference of −1.3 mm (95% CI −9.8 to 7.3), i.e. no greater improvement with diacerein. Gastrointestinal adverse events occurred in 55 participants (41.7%) on diacerein versus 33 (25.4%) on placebo, most commonly diarrhoea (51 [38.6%] vs 29 [22.3%]); urine colour change was observed in 13 participants (9.8%) on diacerein. The authors concluded the findings do not support diacerein for treating knee pain in this population.
cards.watchOut: Patients were selected for an inflammatory phenotype (effusion-synovitis on MRI) — the population in which an interleukin-1β blocker was most expected to work — which makes the negative result harder to explain away, though it also limits generalisation to non-inflammatory knee OA.
cards.source: Aitken D et al. Diacerein for Knee Osteoarthritis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2026. PMID: 41770553. Registry ID: ACTRN12618001656224. cards.headline: DISSCO equivalence RCT (Pelletier 2020): diacerein was non-inferior to celecoxib for knee OA pain over 6 months (WOMAC pain difference 0.7, meeting the non-inferiority margin), with more diarrhoea
cards.summary: DISSCO equivalence RCT (Pelletier 2020): diacerein was non-inferior to celecoxib for knee OA pain over 6 months (WOMAC pain difference 0.7, meeting the non-inferiority margin), with more diarrhoea
cards.type: International multicentre double-blind non-inferiority (equivalence) randomised trial, diacerein vs celecoxib
cards.people: 380 patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis (Kellgren-Lawrence grade 2–3, pain ≥4 on a 10-cm VAS), randomised to 6 months of diacerein 50 mg once daily for 1 month then twice daily (n=187) or celecoxib 200 mg once daily (n=193); the per-protocol population was 140 (diacerein) and 148 (celecoxib).
cards.result: Adjusted mean change in WOMAC pain score (0–50 cm) at 6 months was −11.1 with diacerein and −11.8 with celecoxib; the intergroup difference was 0.7 (95% CI −1.8 to 3.2; P=0.597), meeting the non-inferiority margin, with similar intention-to-treat results and no significant differences on other outcomes. Treatment-related adverse events were low and balanced overall, but diarrhoea was more frequent with diacerein (10.2% vs 3.7%), mild-to-moderate in all but one case and resolving completely.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority to celecoxib without a placebo arm cannot distinguish a real symptom effect of both drugs from a shared placebo/contextual response — read alongside the negative placebo-controlled 2026 trial above.
cards.source: Pelletier JP et al. An international, multicentre, double-blind, randomized study (DISSCO): effect of diacerein vs celecoxib on symptoms in knee osteoarthritis. Rheumatology (Oxford, England). 2020. PMID: 32521015. Registry ID: NCT02688400. cards.headline: Generic vs branded diacerein RCT (Jaruthien 2024): both formulations improved pain VAS and performance measures by 24 weeks, branded faster — a formulation comparison with no placebo arm
cards.summary: Generic vs branded diacerein RCT (Jaruthien 2024): both formulations improved pain VAS and performance measures by 24 weeks, branded faster — a formulation comparison with no placebo arm
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, generic diacerein vs branded diacerein (formulation comparison; specific products named in the publication: generic Diaceric® and branded Artrodar®)
cards.people: 94 randomised patients with mild to moderate knee osteoarthritis (47 generic diacerein 50 mg daily, 47 branded diacerein 50 mg daily), followed to 24 weeks with no patients lost to follow-up; 79.8% female, mean ages 63.2 and 64.8 years, Kellgren-Lawrence grade II most common.
cards.result: At 24 weeks both groups had significantly improved visual analogue scale pain, with improvement 12 weeks earlier in the branded group; performance measures (5-time sit-to-stand and 3-minute walk test) improved significantly from 12 weeks in both groups, while WOMAC and SF-12 improvements were not significant; no serious adverse events occurred in either group. The authors concluded generic diacerein had similar efficacy to branded diacerein at 24 weeks.
cards.watchOut: No placebo or untreated arm: within-group improvement over 24 weeks is expected in knee OA trials from natural fluctuation and contextual effects, so this report speaks to formulation equivalence, not to whether diacerein works.
cards.source: Jaruthien N et al. Efficacy of generic versus branded diacerein for treatment of knee osteoarthritis: A randomized control trial. Medicine. 2024. PMID: 39654215. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Combination RCT (Youn 2023) — COMBINATION study: diacerein + celecoxib versus each agent alone (71 patients) — all groups improved, no significant between-group difference in VAS change
cards.summary: Combination RCT (Youn 2023) — COMBINATION study: diacerein + celecoxib versus each agent alone (71 patients) — all groups improved, no significant between-group difference in VAS change
cards.type: Double-blind randomised trial of a COMBINATION (diacerein + celecoxib) vs diacerein alone vs celecoxib alone — labelled a combination study
cards.people: 71 subjects with knee osteoarthritis randomly assigned to diacerein + celecoxib, diacerein + placebo, or celecoxib + placebo, with the primary outcome the change in visual analogue scale pain score at 12 weeks.
cards.result: The combination group showed a significant within-group decrease in VAS, as did both monotherapy groups; there was no significant difference between groups, although the combination group's absolute VAS decrease was greater. At 4 weeks the combination group showed significantly greater improvement in WOMAC stiffness and physical function categories than the other groups. No serious adverse events occurred; most adverse events were mild and resolved without specific treatment.
cards.watchOut: Small (71 subjects across three arms) and a combination study: it cannot isolate diacerein's own effect and is carded as supporting context only, not as a diacerein-versus-control efficacy report.
cards.source: Youn S et al. Efficacy and safety of diacerein and celecoxib combination therapy for knee osteoarthritis: A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled prospective study. cards.headline: Synthesis: against placebo diacerein failed its best test (2026 trial, no pain benefit); against celecoxib it was non-inferior (DISSCO) — a split record, with diarrhoea the consistent harm and one older trial fenced out as retracted
cards.summary: Synthesis: against placebo diacerein failed its best test (2026 trial, no pain benefit); against celecoxib it was non-inferior (DISSCO) — a split record, with diarrhoea the consistent harm and one older trial fenced out as retracted
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The only modern placebo-controlled trial (262 patients with inflammatory-phenotype knee OA) found a −1.3 mm between-group pain difference (95% CI −9.8 to 7.3) — no benefit. The large active-comparator trial found diacerein non-inferior to celecoxib on WOMAC pain. The formulation and combination reports have no placebo arm and add no efficacy resolution. Diarrhoea occurred in 38.6% on diacerein versus 22.3% on placebo (2026 trial). FENCED AND NOT CARDED: the Pavelka et al. 2007 diacerein knee-OA randomised trial (PMID 18050202, Arthritis Rheum 2007) is typed Retracted Publication (retraction notice PMID 37337725) — it is excluded from this shelf and from any count, and older meta-analyses pooling it inherit that problem.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Oral salmon calcitonin in knee osteoarthritis: a failed programme — two phase 3 trials (2,206 patients) showed no structural benefit and no claimable symptom benefit
shelves.question: In adults with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis, does oral salmon calcitonin, compared with placebo, improve pain/function and slow structural progression?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Aged · Biomarkers · Bone Density Conservation Agents · Calcitonin · Collagen Type I · Collagen Type II · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Knee Joint · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Peptide Fragments · Peptides · Radiography · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A failed development programme. The two phase 3 trials (1,176 and 1,030 patients, reported together) missed their structural endpoint in both studies — no significant treatment effect on joint space narrowing at 24 months — and the symptom (WOMAC) effect seen in one trial could not be claimed significant under the hierarchical testing procedure, so oral salmon calcitonin never gained an OA indication. The earlier phase 2 trial (53 randomised, 41 completing) showed a functional-score and biomarker signal at 1 mg, and a 2021 post-hoc endotype analysis found no overall treatment effect on progression, with a hypothesis-generating subgroup pattern only. Nasal salmon calcitonin for postmenopausal osteoporosis (live #1829) is a different formulation and question, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Proposed stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Two phase 3 trials in one publication (Karsdal 2015): oral salmon calcitonin showed NO significant effect on joint space narrowing in either trial (1,176 and 1,030 patients) over 24 months
cards.summary: Two phase 3 trials in one publication (Karsdal 2015): oral salmon calcitonin showed NO significant effect on joint space narrowing in either trial (1,176 and 1,030 patients) over 24 months
cards.type: Two phase 3 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trials reported in ONE publication (labelled as such), oral salmon calcitonin vs placebo
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind multicentre placebo-controlled trials (CSMC021C2301, enrolling 1,176 patients, and CSMC021C2302, enrolling 1,030 patients) in patients with painful knee osteoarthritis with structural damage (Kellgren and Lawrence 2–3), randomised 1:1 to oral salmon calcitonin 0.8 mg twice daily (formulated with a 5-CNAC carrier) or placebo for 24 months. This card reports BOTH trials, as the publication does.
cards.result: At the 24-month endpoint there was no statistically significant treatment effect on joint space narrowing in either study. In CSMC021C2301 there was a treatment effect on WOMAC (pain, function, stiffness and total scores) and on biomarkers of bone and joint metabolism, but because of the hierarchical testing procedure that effect was not claimed statistically significant. The authors concluded that this formulation of oral salmon calcitonin did not provide reproducible clinical benefits in symptomatic knee osteoarthritis.
cards.watchOut: Two trials, one paper — the trial base is two, not one, but the reports must not be double-counted either: both missed the structural co-primary endpoint, which is why the programme was abandoned and oral calcitonin was never approved for osteoarthritis.
cards.source: Karsdal MA et al. Treatment of symptomatic knee osteoarthritis with oral salmon calcitonin: results from two phase 3 trials. Osteoarthritis and cartilage. 2015. PMID: 25582279. Registry ID: NCT00486434 and NCT00704847. cards.headline: Phase 2 RCT (Manicourt 2006): oral salmon calcitonin 1 mg improved function scores and lowered joint-metabolism biomarkers over 84 days — in 53 randomised patients, 41 completing
cards.summary: Phase 2 RCT (Manicourt 2006): oral salmon calcitonin 1 mg improved function scores and lowered joint-metabolism biomarkers over 84 days — in 53 randomised patients, 41 completing
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, oral salmon calcitonin 0.5/1 mg vs placebo
cards.people: Patients with knee osteoarthritis randomised to placebo (n=18), salmon calcitonin 0.5 mg daily (n=17) or salmon calcitonin 1 mg daily (n=18) for 84 days; 41 patients completed (13 in the 0.5 mg group, 14 in each of the other groups).
cards.result: On day 84, pain scores fell significantly and similarly in the placebo and 1 mg groups, while a significant reduction in the Lequesne function score was observed only in the two calcitonin groups. Biomarker levels did not fall significantly on placebo, whereas both calcitonin groups showed significant reductions in MMP-3 and hyaluronan, and the 1 mg group also in CTX-II, C2C and MMP-13. The authors suggested 1 mg oral salmon calcitonin might be a useful agent in knee OA — a suggestion the phase 3 programme (card above) did not confirm.
cards.watchOut: Small and short (53 randomised, 41 completing, 84 days), with biomarker and function-score outcomes — hypothesis-generating only, and superseded by the two negative phase 3 trials.
cards.source: Manicourt DH et al. Oral salmon calcitonin reduces Lequesne's algofunctional index scores and decreases urinary and serum levels of biomarkers of joint metabolism in knee osteoarthritis. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2006. PMID: 17009253. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Endotype post-hoc analysis (Luo 2021): low cartilage-formation (PRO-C2) patients progressed faster; there was NO significant overall effect of salmon calcitonin on joint space narrowing before stratification
cards.summary: Endotype post-hoc analysis (Luo 2021): low cartilage-formation (PRO-C2) patients progressed faster; there was NO significant overall effect of salmon calcitonin on joint space narrowing before stratification
cards.type: Post-hoc exploratory (Level III) endotype analysis of a cohort and a phase 3 trial subcohort — a programme analysis, not an independent treatment trial
cards.people: Knee osteoarthritis subjects from a New York University cohort (n=106) and a subcohort of the phase 3 oral salmon calcitonin trial SMC021-2301 (n=147), with serum/plasma PRO-C2 (type II collagen formation) measured and radiographic medial joint space narrowing assessed over 24 months.
cards.result: In both cohorts, subjects with low PRO-C2 had greater joint space narrowing than those with high PRO-C2 (mean difference 0.65 mm between very-low and high quartiles, p=0.002; 3.4-fold higher risk of progression, 95% CI 1.4 to 8.6). There was no significant effect of salmon calcitonin treatment, versus placebo, on joint space narrowing over 2 years before stratification by baseline PRO-C2; after stratification, there were proportionately fewer progressors in the calcitonin arm of the very-low/low PRO-C2 group than the moderate/high group (chi-squared 6.5, p=0.011).
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and exploratory: the subgroup pattern is a hypothesis about who might respond, not evidence that oral calcitonin works — the unstratified treatment comparison in the same analysis was not significant, matching the negative phase 3 primaries.
cards.source: Luo Y et al. A low cartilage formation and repair endotype predicts radiographic progression of symptomatic knee osteoarthritis. Journal of orthopaedics and traumatology : official journal of the Italian Society of Orthopaedics and Traumatology. 2021. PMID: 33687578. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the phase 3 programme (2,206 patients across two trials) found no structural benefit and no claimable symptom benefit — oral salmon calcitonin for knee OA is a failed programme, against a small phase 2 signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: the phase 3 programme (2,206 patients across two trials) found no structural benefit and no claimable symptom benefit — oral salmon calcitonin for knee OA is a failed programme, against a small phase 2 signal
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across CSMC021C2301 (n=1,176) and CSMC021C2302 (n=1,030), oral salmon calcitonin 0.8 mg twice daily had no statistically significant effect on joint space narrowing at 24 months in either trial, and the one WOMAC signal could not be claimed under hierarchical testing. The phase 2 trial (n=53) and the post-hoc endotype analysis do not overturn that: the endotype paper itself reports no significant overall treatment effect. Oral calcitonin was never approved for osteoarthritis.

cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
