shelves.title: Strontium ranelate in knee osteoarthritis: SEKOIA (one trial) slowed joint space narrowing by 0.10–0.14 mm over 3 years — a single-trial shelf for a drug later withdrawn in Europe
shelves.question: In adults with knee osteoarthritis, does strontium ranelate, compared with placebo, slow structural progression (joint-space narrowing) and improve symptoms (SEKOIA programme)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antirheumatic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Organometallic Compounds · Osteoarthritis, Knee · Radiography · Thiophenes · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: ONE trial, several reports — printed here on the face, as the row directs. SEKOIA (1,683 randomised; 1,371 in the intention-to-treat population) found strontium ranelate slowed joint space narrowing over 3 years versus placebo by 0.14 mm (1 g/day) and 0.10 mm (2 g/day) — statistically significant but absolutely small differences — with fewer radiological progressors, and a symptom responder advantage at 2 g/day only (≥20% WOMAC pain improvement 58% vs 47%). The MRI, responder and meniscal-extrusion reports are all analyses of this same SEKOIA population, not independent trials. Strontium ranelate was restricted and then withdrawn in Europe over cardiovascular safety and was never FDA-approved; its osteoporosis question (SOTI/TROPOS) is homed at live #1823, cross-pointed here and not re-carded. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-trial.

cards.headline: SEKOIA phase 3 RCT (Reginster 2013): strontium ranelate slowed joint space narrowing vs placebo over 3 years (differences 0.14 mm at 1 g/day and 0.10 mm at 2 g/day), with symptom benefit at 2 g/day
cards.summary: SEKOIA phase 3 RCT (Reginster 2013): strontium ranelate slowed joint space narrowing vs placebo over 3 years (differences 0.14 mm at 1 g/day and 0.10 mm at 2 g/day), with symptom benefit at 2 g/day
cards.type: Phase 3 international double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial (SEKOIA — the single trial behind every card on this shelf)
cards.people: Patients with knee osteoarthritis (Kellgren and Lawrence grade 2 or 3, joint space width 2.5–5 mm) randomised to strontium ranelate 1 g/day (n=558), 2 g/day (n=566) or placebo (n=559); the intention-to-treat population included 1,371 patients. Primary endpoint: radiographic change in joint space width (medial tibiofemoral compartment) over 3 years.
cards.result: Joint space width degradation was smaller on strontium ranelate than placebo (1 g/day −0.23 [SD 0.56] mm; 2 g/day −0.27 [SD 0.63] mm; placebo −0.37 [SD 0.59] mm); treatment–placebo differences were 0.14 mm (SE 0.04; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.23; p<0.001) for 1 g/day and 0.10 mm (SE 0.04; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.19; p=0.018) for 2 g/day, with fewer radiological progressors on strontium ranelate (p<0.001 and p=0.012). At 2 g/day there were greater reductions in total WOMAC score (p=0.045) and pain subscore (p=0.028). The drug was reported as well tolerated in the trial.
cards.watchOut: SINGLE-TRIAL base: every other card on this shelf is an analysis of SEKOIA's own patients. The structural differences (0.10–0.14 mm over 3 years) are small in absolute terms, and strontium ranelate was later restricted and withdrawn in Europe over cardiovascular safety and never FDA-approved — the trial's 'well tolerated' wording is not the last word on safety.

cards.headline: SEKOIA quantitative-MRI analysis (Pelletier 2015): strontium ranelate 2 g/day reduced cartilage volume loss on the plateaus and bone marrow lesion progression in the medial compartment (MRI subset, n=330)
cards.summary: SEKOIA quantitative-MRI analysis (Pelletier 2015): strontium ranelate 2 g/day reduced cartilage volume loss on the plateaus and bone marrow lesion progression in the medial compartment (MRI subset, n=330)
cards.type: Quantitative-MRI substudy analysis of the SEKOIA phase 3 trial (same trial as the primary card — not independent evidence)
cards.people: A subset of SEKOIA patients (modified intention-to-treat n=330: strontium ranelate 1 g/day 113, 2 g/day 105, placebo 112) with MRIs at baseline, 12, 24 and 36 months assessing cartilage volume and bone marrow lesions — the same SEKOIA trial population as the primary card, not a new trial.
cards.result: Strontium ranelate 2 g/day significantly decreased cartilage volume loss on the plateaus at 12 (p=0.002) and 36 (p=0.003) months versus placebo. In patients with medial-compartment bone marrow lesions at baseline, the bone marrow lesion score at 36 months was decreased in both treatment groups versus placebo (1 g/day p=0.002; 2 g/day p=0.001), and cartilage volume loss significantly decreased with 2 g/day (p=0.023) in the plateau. In the medial femur and plateau, 1 g/day — but not 2 g/day — had more cartilage volume loss than placebo, an internal inconsistency in the dose pattern.
cards.watchOut: A substudy of one-third of SEKOIA's patients with multiple compartment- and dose-specific comparisons (Bonferroni-adjusted); it supports the primary structural finding but adds no independent trial weight.

cards.headline: SEKOIA responder analysis (Bruyère 2014): at 2 g/day, more patients achieved clinically meaningful pain and function responses than on placebo (e.g. ≥20% WOMAC pain improvement 58% vs 47%); no symptom effect at 1 g/day
cards.summary: SEKOIA responder analysis (Bruyère 2014): at 2 g/day, more patients achieved clinically meaningful pain and function responses than on placebo (e.g. ≥20% WOMAC pain improvement 58% vs 47%); no symptom effect at 1 g/day
cards.type: Responder analysis of the SEKOIA phase 3 trial (same trial as the primary card — not independent evidence)
cards.people: SEKOIA patients receiving strontium ranelate 2 g/day (n=454), 1 g/day (n=445) or placebo (n=472) over 3 years, assessed with WOMAC subscores and minimal perceptible / minimal clinically important improvement and modified OMERACT-OARSI responder definitions; premature withdrawals were counted as non-responders. Same SEKOIA trial as the primary card.
cards.result: There was no significant symptom effect at 1 g/day. At 2 g/day, strontium ranelate beat placebo on ≥20% improvement in WOMAC pain (58% vs 47%, P=0.002) and on minimal perceptible improvement responses for WOMAC pain (52% vs 40%, P<0.001), stiffness (47% vs 39%, P=0.009) and physical function (46% vs 37%, P=0.009), and on OMERACT-OARSI-like response (44% vs 35%, P=0.004); the ≥50% WOMAC pain improvement difference (42% vs 36%, P=0.083) was not significant.
cards.watchOut: Responder analyses of a single trial, across many thresholds and time points: they describe the symptom side of SEKOIA's 2 g/day result, they do not replicate it.
cards.source: Bruyère O et al. Clinically meaningful effect of strontium ranelate on symptoms in knee osteoarthritis: a responder analysis. Rheumatology (Oxford, England). 2014. PMID: 24667161. cards.headline: SEKOIA meniscal-extrusion analysis (Roubille 2015): meniscal extrusion and bone marrow lesions together predicted faster structural progression on placebo; strontium 2 g/day showed less cartilage volume loss in the extrusion subgroup on MRI but not on X-ray joint space width
cards.summary: SEKOIA meniscal-extrusion analysis (Roubille 2015): meniscal extrusion and bone marrow lesions together predicted faster structural progression on placebo; strontium 2 g/day showed less cartilage volume loss in the extrusion subgroup on MRI but not on X-ray joint space width
cards.type: Structural subgroup analysis of the SEKOIA phase 3 trial MRI substudy (same trial as the primary card — not independent evidence)
cards.people: Patients from the SEKOIA quantitative-MRI substudy (strontium ranelate 1 g/day n=113, 2 g/day n=105, placebo n=112), stratified by medial-compartment meniscal extrusion and bone marrow lesions, assessed at 36 months with X-ray joint space width and quantitative MRI. Same SEKOIA trial as the primary card.
cards.result: On placebo, patients with meniscal extrusion (n=26) lost more joint space width (p=0.002) and cartilage volume than those without (n=86). Strontium ranelate 2 g/day showed a reduction in structural progression on quantitative MRI — less cartilage volume loss in the plateaus in extrusion-positive patients (n=15, p=0.007) — but not on joint space width. The authors presented the combined extrusion/bone-marrow-lesion risk pattern as the study's novel finding.
cards.watchOut: Very small strata (extrusion-positive placebo n=26; treated extrusion subgroup n=15) and an MRI-only treatment signal with no X-ray counterpart — exploratory subgroup evidence within a single trial.
cards.source: Roubille C et al. Meniscal extrusion promotes knee osteoarthritis structural progression: protective effect of strontium ranelate treatment in a phase III clinical trial. shelves.title: Colchicine in Behçet's syndrome: two placebo trials favour it for ulcers, erythema nodosum and arthritis — benefit concentrated in women in the 2-year trial, and no long-term sparing of immunosuppressives
shelves.question: In people with Behçet's syndrome, does colchicine, compared with placebo, reduce mucocutaneous (oral/genital ulcer, erythema nodosum) and articular manifestations?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Arthritis · Behcet Syndrome · Colchicine · Double-Blind Method · Erythema Nodosum · Female · Folliculitis · Humans · Male · Sex Factors · Treatment Outcome · Ulcer
shelves.balance: An old, small trial base that points modestly in colchicine's favour for mucocutaneous and articular disease. The 2-year double-blind trial (116 randomised) found benefit concentrated in women — fewer genital ulcers, erythema nodosum lesions and arthritic joints — with an arthritis benefit in men but no genital-ulcer or erythema nodosum benefit in men. The larger crossover trial (169 patients) found the overall disease activity index improved on colchicine and worsened on placebo, with no significant sex difference. The long-term survey of the 2001 trial cohort found early colchicine did not reduce later immunosuppressive use. One further anchor, the Aktulga et al. 1980 double-blind study (PMID 6778795), was REFUSED at build because its PubMed record carries an empty abstract, and is recorded as refused on the Synthesis card, not carded. Eye and major-organ Behçet disease are outside this question — they are immunosuppression territory — and adverse effects in the 2001 trial were similar between groups. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Double-blind RCT (Yurdakul 2001): colchicine reduced genital ulcers, erythema nodosum and arthritis in women, and arthritis in men, over 2 years — benefit was sex-specific
cards.summary: Double-blind RCT (Yurdakul 2001): colchicine reduced genital ulcers, erythema nodosum and arthritis in women, and arthritis in men, over 2 years — benefit was sex-specific
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, colchicine vs placebo (2 years)
cards.people: 116 patients with Behçet's syndrome (60 male, 56 female) with active mucocutaneous disease without eye or major organ involvement, randomised to placebo or colchicine 1–2 mg/day (adjusted to body weight) in a double-blind trial for 2 years; 84 patients (72%; 45 male, 39 female) completed the study. Primary outcome: sustained absence of any lesions during treatment (complete response).
cards.result: Kaplan-Meier analyses showed significantly more complete responses on colchicine for genital ulcers (P=0.004), erythema nodosum (P=0.004) and arthritis (P=0.033) among women, and for arthritis (P=0.012) among men. Mean numbers of genital ulcers (P=0.001), erythema nodosum lesions (P=0.002) and arthritic joints (P=0.014) were lower on colchicine in women, and mean arthritic joints lower in men (P=0.026); there was no demonstrated benefit in men for genital ulcers or erythema nodosum. Adverse effects were similar in both groups. The authors noted the sex pattern might reflect less severe disease among the women.
cards.watchOut: Pre-registration-era trial with 28% not completing, analysed separately by sex: the headline benefit is a women-only result for ulcers and erythema nodosum, and patients with eye or major-organ disease were excluded — it says nothing about sight-threatening Behçet disease.
cards.source: Yurdakul S et al. A double-blind trial of colchicine in Behçet's syndrome. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2001. PMID: 11710724. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Crossover RCT (Davatchi 2009): colchicine improved the overall disease activity index (3.35 to 2.75) while placebo worsened it (3.17 to 3.63); the colchicine–placebo difference was highly significant
cards.summary: Crossover RCT (Davatchi 2009): colchicine improved the overall disease activity index (3.35 to 2.75) while placebo worsened it (3.17 to 3.63); the colchicine–placebo difference was highly significant
cards.type: Randomised double-blind controlled crossover trial, colchicine vs placebo (4 months per period)
cards.people: 169 patients with Behçet's disease without major organ involvement, fulfilling the International Criteria for Behçet's Disease, randomised in a double-blind controlled crossover trial to colchicine or placebo for 4 months, then swapped to the other treatment for a further 4 months; the primary outcome was the overall disease activity index (IBDDAM).
cards.result: On placebo, IBDDAM worsened from 3.17 to 3.63 (P=0.08); on colchicine it improved from 3.35 to 2.75 (P<0.0001). Oral aphthosis, genital aphthosis, pseudofolliculitis and erythema nodosum improved significantly with colchicine but not with placebo, and the between-treatment difference in IBDDAM was highly significant (F=14.674, P=0.00016). Unlike the 2001 trial, the difference between males and females was not significant (F=0.181, P=0.67).
cards.watchOut: A crossover design with 4-month periods in a relapsing disease — carry-over and period effects are inherent risks — and, like the 2001 trial, it excluded major-organ disease.
cards.source: Davatchi F et al. Colchicine versus placebo in Behçet's disease: randomized, double-blind, controlled crossover trial. Modern rheumatology. 2009. PMID: 19597921. cards.type: Long-term follow-up survey of the Yurdakul 2001 randomised trial cohort (programme follow-up report — not independent comparative evidence)
cards.people: Patients who had participated in the double-blind placebo-controlled colchicine trial carded above (Yurdakul 2001), evaluated 16.6 ± 1.1 years later for immunosuppressive use during the post-trial period; 90 of the original 116 patients could be contacted. A follow-up report OF that trial, not a new trial.
cards.result: 28 of 90 patients (31%) received immunosuppressives during the post-trial period, 14 of them from the colchicine arm. Post-trial colchicine use and cumulative duration were similar between patients who did and did not receive immunosuppressives. The authors concluded that continuous colchicine use, even when started early, does not seem to decrease the use of immunosuppressives in the long term.
cards.watchOut: A survey of contactable survivors (90 of 116) nearly two decades on, with post-trial treatment uncontrolled: it tests a long-term disease-modification hypothesis, not colchicine's short-term symptom effect.
cards.source: Hamuryudan V et al. Colchicine in Behçet syndrome: a longterm survey of patients in a controlled trial. The Journal of rheumatology. 2014. PMID: 24532830. cards.headline: Synthesis: two placebo-controlled trials (116 and 169 patients) favour colchicine for mucocutaneous and articular Behçet manifestations — with a sex-specific pattern in one and no long-term reduction in immunosuppressive use

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Yurdakul 2001 found fewer genital ulcers, erythema nodosum lesions and arthritic joints on colchicine in women, and fewer arthritic joints in men, over 2 years; Davatchi 2009 found the disease activity index improved on colchicine and worsened on placebo in a crossover trial, without a significant sex difference. The ~17-year follow-up found no reduction in later immunosuppressive use from early colchicine. REFUSAL RECORDED: Aktulga et al. 1980 (PMID 6778795, Haematologica), a double-blind colchicine study in Behçet's disease named as an anchor for this shelf, was refused at build because its PubMed record carries an EMPTY abstract — no numbers could be verified from the record, so it is not carded and not counted. The trial base is old (2001, 2009) and modest, and excludes eye and major-organ disease.

shelves.title: Benzbromarone in gout: beats low-dose febuxostat and probenecid on urate target attainment in three randomised trials — a withdrawn-in-several-markets drug with a hepatotoxicity history
shelves.question: In adults with gout, does the uricosuric benzbromarone, compared with febuxostat or probenecid, lower serum urate to target — and at what hepatic cost?
shelves.mesh: Male · Humans · Febuxostat · Benzbromarone · Uric Acid · Hyperuricemia · Gout Suppressants · Prospective Studies · Gout · Treatment Outcome · Allopurinol
shelves.balance: On the surrogate that decides these trials — reaching serum urate target — benzbromarone performs at least as well as its comparators at the doses tested: clearly better than low-dose febuxostat 20 mg in men with renal uric-acid underexcretion (61% vs 32% reaching <6 mg/dL at 12 weeks), essentially equal to low-dose febuxostat in a second Chinese trial (35.7% vs 39.5% reaching <360 μmol/L, ≈6.0 mg/dL), and better than probenecid after allopurinol failure (92% vs 65% reaching ≤0.30 mmol/L, ≈5.0 mg/dL). The comparators are low, non-titrated doses, so these are comparisons against weak versions of the alternatives, and urate target is a surrogate, not flares or tophi. The harm side leads with history: benzbromarone was withdrawn in several markets over hepatotoxicity and is unavailable in the US; within these short trials, transaminase elevation was actually more frequent on febuxostat in the 2022 trial (15% vs 4%), but 12-week trials cannot exclude the rare severe liver injury that drove the withdrawals. Use is single-region (Japan/China/Europe legacy). The dotinurad shelf's benzbromarone-comparator trial is homed elsewhere (pack #6829) and is not re-carded here. Proposed stamp: POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Comparative-effectiveness RCT (Yan 2022): low-dose benzbromarone 25 mg beat low-dose febuxostat 20 mg for urate target attainment in underexcretion gout (61% vs 32% reaching <6 mg/dL)
cards.summary: Comparative-effectiveness RCT (Yan 2022): low-dose benzbromarone 25 mg beat low-dose febuxostat 20 mg for urate target attainment in underexcretion gout (61% vs 32% reaching <6 mg/dL)
cards.type: Prospective randomised single-centre open-label comparative-effectiveness trial, low-dose benzbromarone vs low-dose febuxostat
cards.people: 196 men with gout and renal uric acid underexcretion (fractional excretion of urate <5.5% and uric acid excretion ≤600 mg/day/1.73 m²), randomised at a single centre to low-dose benzbromarone 25 mg daily or low-dose febuxostat 20 mg daily for 12 weeks; all participants received daily urine alkalisation with oral sodium bicarbonate.
cards.result: More participants on benzbromarone achieved the serum urate target of <6 mg/dL than on febuxostat (61% compared to 32%, P<0.001). Rates of adverse events, including gout flares and urolithiasis, did not differ between groups, except greater transaminase elevation in the febuxostat group (4% for benzbromarone compared to 15% for febuxostat, P=0.008). The authors concluded low-dose benzbromarone had superior urate-lowering efficacy and similar safety in relatively young and healthy patients with underexcretion-type gout.
cards.watchOut: Men only, single centre, open-label, 12 weeks, and the febuxostat comparator was a fixed low dose (20 mg) with no titration — superiority over low-dose febuxostat is not superiority over febuxostat as usually dosed; all patients also received sodium bicarbonate alkalisation.
cards.source: Yan F et al. Superiority of Low-Dose Benzbromarone to Low-Dose Febuxostat in a Prospective, Randomized Comparative Effectiveness Trial in Gout Patients With Renal Uric Acid Underexcretion. Arthritis & rheumatology (Hoboken, N.J.). 2022. PMID: 35795968. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Randomised controlled trial (Liang 2019): low-dose benzbromarone 25 mg and low-dose febuxostat 20 mg performed similarly (target urate reached by 35.7% vs 39.5%) in Chinese primary gout
cards.summary: Randomised controlled trial (Liang 2019): low-dose benzbromarone 25 mg and low-dose febuxostat 20 mg performed similarly (target urate reached by 35.7% vs 39.5%) in Chinese primary gout
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled open-label trial, low-dose febuxostat vs low-dose benzbromarone (1:1)
cards.people: 240 male patients with primary gout at a dedicated gout clinic in China, randomised 1:1 to febuxostat 20 mg daily or benzbromarone 25 mg daily for 12 weeks; 214 completed (105 febuxostat, 109 benzbromarone). Target serum uric acid was <360 μmol/L (≈6.0 mg/dL).
cards.result: After 12 weeks, 39.5% on febuxostat and 35.7% on benzbromarone achieved target serum uric acid, and urate fell by 156.83 μmol/L (≈2.6 mg/dL) and 163.99 μmol/L (≈2.8 mg/dL) respectively. Baseline urate and renal function predicted target attainment; both drugs worked better in patients with baseline urate <540 μmol/L (≈9.1 mg/dL). Gout flares occurred in 22.85% on febuxostat and 33.94% on benzbromarone, and the drugs were reported as well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, men only, retrospectively registered, and again both drugs at fixed low doses for 12 weeks — a low-dose comparison in one Chinese clinic population, with flare rates numerically higher on benzbromarone.
cards.source: Liang N et al. Baseline urate level and renal function predict outcomes of urate-lowering therapy using low doses of febuxostat and benzbromarone: a prospective, randomized controlled study in a Chinese primary gout cohort. Arthritis research & therapy. 2019. PMID: 31477161. Registry ID: ChiCTR1800019352. cards.headline: Two-stage RCT (Reinders 2009): after allopurinol failure, benzbromarone 200 mg/day reached urate target in 92% vs 65% on probenecid 2 g/day
cards.summary: Two-stage RCT (Reinders 2009): after allopurinol failure, benzbromarone 200 mg/day reached urate target in 92% vs 65% on probenecid 2 g/day
cards.type: Prospective multicentre open-label two-stage randomised controlled trial; stage 2: benzbromarone vs probenecid after allopurinol failure
cards.people: 96 patients with gout and normal renal function enrolled in stage 1 (allopurinol 300 mg/day for 2 months); 62 entered stage 2 and were randomised to benzbromarone 200 mg/day (27 patients; 24 analysable) or probenecid 2 g/day (35 patients; 31 analysable) for a further 2 months, because they could not tolerate allopurinol or had not reached the target serum urate ≤0.30 mmol/L (≈5.0 mg/dL). Stage-2 arms are ≥10 patients per arm, as the row required confirming at build.
cards.result: In stage 1, allopurinol lowered serum urate by a mean 35% (SD 11%), but only 20 of 82 analysable patients (24%) reached target and 9 (11%) stopped for adverse drug reactions. In stage 2, treatment was successful in 22 of 24 patients (92%) on benzbromarone versus 20 of 31 (65%) on probenecid (p=0.03), with mean urate decreases from baseline of 64% (SD 9%) versus 50% (SD 7%) (p<0.001). The authors concluded benzbromarone 200 mg/day was more effective and better tolerated than probenecid 2 g/day in this setting.
cards.watchOut: The benzbromarone dose here (200 mg/day) is eight times the 25 mg low dose of the Chinese trials, the stage-2 sample is small (24 vs 31 analysable), treatment lasted 2 months, and all patients had normal renal function — not the impaired-renal-function population in which uricosurics are hardest to use.
cards.source: Reinders MK et al. Efficacy and tolerability of urate-lowering drugs in gout: a randomised controlled trial of benzbromarone versus probenecid after failure of allopurinol. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2009. PMID: 18250112. Registry ID: ISRCTN21473387. cards.headline: Synthesis: benzbromarone lowers urate to target at least as reliably as low-dose febuxostat or probenecid in three randomised comparisons — on a surrogate endpoint, at non-titrated comparator doses, for a drug withdrawn in several markets over hepatotoxicity
cards.summary: Synthesis: benzbromarone lowers urate to target at least as reliably as low-dose febuxostat or probenecid in three randomised comparisons — on a surrogate endpoint, at non-titrated comparator doses, for a drug withdrawn in several markets over hepatotoxicity
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Target attainment was 61% vs 32% against low-dose febuxostat in underexcretion gout (n=196), 35.7% vs 39.5% against low-dose febuxostat in a second trial (n=240 randomised), and 92% vs 65% against probenecid after allopurinol failure (stage 2, 24 vs 31 analysable). No trial here reports flare or tophus outcomes as its primary result, none exceeds 12 weeks at the low doses, and none can assess the rare severe hepatotoxicity that led to benzbromarone's withdrawal in several markets and its unavailability in the US.

shelves.title: Eldecalcitol in osteoporosis: ONE phase 3 trial (n=1,054) in three reports — vertebral fractures 13.4% vs 17.5% versus alfacalcidol, an active comparator (no placebo trial)
shelves.question: In adults with osteoporosis, does the active vitamin D3 analogue eldecalcitol, compared with alfacalcidol, reduce vertebral and non-vertebral fractures?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Density · Bone Remodeling · Cholecalciferol · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hormones · Humans · Incidence · Japan · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Osteoporotic Fractures · Risk Factors · Spinal Fractures · Treatment Outcome · Vitamin D
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) versus an active comparator — on a ONE-TRIAL programme, printed on the face: all three carded reports are publications of a single Japanese phase 3 trial of 1,054 patients (the primary report plus two post-hoc analyses), so the trial base is one, however many reports it generated. In that trial, eldecalcitol 0.75 μg daily reduced incident vertebral fractures versus alfacalcidol 1.0 μg daily over 3 years (13.4% vs 17.5%; hazard ratio 0.74, a relative measure). The post-hoc reports add WHO-defined fragility fractures (18.6% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio 0.70, relative) and severe vertebral fractures (3.8% vs 6.7%). The comparator is another active vitamin D analogue, not placebo, so this is a within-class comparison. Increases in serum and urinary calcium were more frequent on eldecalcitol — hypercalcaemia monitoring is the class harm. Single-region evidence (Japan; approved there).

cards.headline: Phase 3 RCT — primary report (Matsumoto 2011): eldecalcitol reduced vertebral fractures versus alfacalcidol over 3 years (13.4% vs 17.5%; hazard ratio 0.74, relative) in 1,054 patients
cards.summary: Phase 3 RCT — primary report (Matsumoto 2011): eldecalcitol reduced vertebral fractures versus alfacalcidol over 3 years (13.4% vs 17.5%; hazard ratio 0.74, relative) in 1,054 patients
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind active-comparator superiority trial — the single trial of this programme (primary report)
cards.people: 1,054 osteoporotic patients aged 46–92 years were randomised 1:1 to oral eldecalcitol 0.75 μg daily (n=528) or alfacalcidol 1.0 μg daily (n=526) for 3 years, stratified by site and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D; patients with low levels (<50 nmol/L) received 400 IU/day vitamin D3 supplementation. The primary endpoint was incident vertebral fractures.
cards.result: After 36 months the incidence of vertebral fractures was lower on eldecalcitol: 13.4% versus 17.5% (hazard ratio 0.74; predefined 90% CI 0.56 to 0.97 — a relative effect; the absolute difference was 4.1 percentage points). Eldecalcitol reduced bone-turnover markers and increased bone mineral density more strongly than alfacalcidol. A post-hoc analysis within this report found fewer wrist fractures (1.1% vs 3.6%; hazard ratio 0.29, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.77, relative). Increases in serum and urinary calcium were more frequent on eldecalcitol, with no difference in glomerular filtration rate.
cards.watchOut: ONE-TRIAL PROGRAMME: this is the only randomised trial of eldecalcitol for fractures; the two cards below are post-hoc analyses of this same trial population (n=1,054), not independent trials. The comparator is alfacalcidol, an active analogue — there is no placebo comparison.
cards.source: Matsumoto T et al. A new active vitamin D3 analog, eldecalcitol, prevents the risk of osteoporotic fractures--a randomized, active comparator, double-blind study. Bone. 2011. PMID: 21784190. Registry ID: NCT00144456. cards.headline: Post-hoc analysis of the SAME phase 3 trial (Nakamura 2013): WHO-defined osteoporotic fractures 18.6% vs 25.2% (hazard ratio 0.70, relative) and FRAX major fractures 11.1% vs 16.3% (hazard ratio 0.66, relative) — not a second trial
cards.summary: Post-hoc analysis of the SAME phase 3 trial (Nakamura 2013): WHO-defined osteoporotic fractures 18.6% vs 25.2% (hazard ratio 0.70, relative) and FRAX major fractures 11.1% vs 16.3% (hazard ratio 0.66, relative) — not a second trial
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of the single phase 3 trial carded above (same programme, same patients — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The same 1,054 patients from the phase 3 trial carded above; this report re-analysed that trial's data using the WHO Technical Report definition of osteoporotic fractures and the FRAX major osteoporotic fracture definition, and examined prespecified fracture risk factors.
cards.result: Eldecalcitol reduced WHO-defined osteoporotic fractures compared with alfacalcidol (18.6% vs 25.2%; hazard ratio 0.70, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.93 — a relative effect; absolute difference 6.6 percentage points) and FRAX major osteoporotic fractures (11.1% vs 16.3%; hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.94, relative). Prevalent vertebral fractures, two or more prevalent vertebral fractures, and total hip BMD T-score below −2.5 were the risk factors for new fractures showing significant between-treatment differences.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc re-analysis of the one trial, using alternative fracture definitions: it widens the fracture picture but adds no new patients and no independent confirmation.
cards.source: Nakamura T et al. Eldecalcitol is more effective for the prevention of osteoporotic fractures than alfacalcidol. Journal of Bone and Mineral Metabolism. 2013. PMID: 23575909. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Post-hoc analysis of the SAME phase 3 trial (Hagino 2013): severe (Grade 3) vertebral fractures 3.8% vs 6.7% on eldecalcitol vs alfacalcidol; quality of life improved in both groups without significant between-group differences — not a second trial
cards.summary: Post-hoc analysis of the SAME phase 3 trial (Hagino 2013): severe (Grade 3) vertebral fractures 3.8% vs 6.7% on eldecalcitol vs alfacalcidol; quality of life improved in both groups without significant between-group differences — not a second trial
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of the single phase 3 trial carded above (same programme, same patients — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The same 1,054 patients from the phase 3 trial carded above, randomised to eldecalcitol 0.75 μg or alfacalcidol 1.0 μg daily for 3 years in Japan; this report re-evaluated incident vertebral fractures by spinal location and severity (semi-quantitative method) and health-related quality of life (SF-36).
cards.result: Vertebral fractures at the lower spine (T11–L4) were less frequent on eldecalcitol (P=0.029), and severe Grade 3 vertebral fractures occurred in 3.8% on eldecalcitol versus 6.7% on alfacalcidol (P=0.036; absolute difference 2.9 percentage points). Both treatments improved health-related quality of life, with no significant differences in individual scores between groups during the trial.
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc severity and quality-of-life analyses of the one trial: the quality-of-life comparison itself showed no significant between-group difference, and none of this is a second trial.
cards.source: Hagino H et al. Eldecalcitol reduces the risk of severe vertebral fractures and improves the health-related quality of life in patients with osteoporosis. Journal of Bone and Mineral Metabolism. 2013. PMID: 23129180. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ONE trial (n=1,054) reported three times — eldecalcitol beat alfacalcidol on vertebral fractures (13.4% vs 17.5%) and, post hoc, on broader fracture definitions and severe vertebral fractures, with more calcium increases
cards.summary: Synthesis: ONE trial (n=1,054) reported three times — eldecalcitol beat alfacalcidol on vertebral fractures (13.4% vs 17.5%) and, post hoc, on broader fracture definitions and severe vertebral fractures, with more calcium increases
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf — three publications of a single phase 3 programme.
cards.result: The primary report showed a vertebral-fracture advantage for eldecalcitol over the active comparator alfacalcidol over 3 years (hazard ratio 0.74, relative; absolute 13.4% vs 17.5%). The two post-hoc reports of the same patients are consistent (WHO-defined fractures hazard ratio 0.70, relative; severe vertebral fractures 3.8% vs 6.7%) but are not replication. There is no placebo-controlled fracture trial and no second trial, so the finding rests on a single Japanese trial against another vitamin D analogue, with a higher incidence of increased serum and urinary calcium on eldecalcitol.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Posturography norms are per-platform: balance improves to ~45 then reverses (N = 914 percentiles), RombergLab equilibrium score 0.72 ± 0.22 (N = 350), and sway velocity is the most informative parameter
shelves.question: In healthy humans, what are force-plate posturography norms — centre-of-pressure sway path, velocity, area and frequency-domain measures, eyes open and closed, firm and foam surfaces — by age and sex, and how much does sway increase with normal ageing?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, vestibular sensations / motor control; Ganong, hearing and equilibrium. That framing is general — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. The fragmentation objection that once sank this question is answered by carding PER PLATFORM AND PER PARAMETER SET, never pooling one 'normal sway' number across systems: a 914-person European plantar-pressure percentile cohort (balance improves to ~45 years, then reverses), a 350-participant multicentre RombergLab global equilibrium score (0.72 ± 0.22, falling with age and height), virtual-surround dynamic posturography in 50 adults (matching published norms except SOT condition 4 and adaptation), pressure-platform sway in 106 young women (9.50 mm frontal, 13.00 mm sagittal), frequency-domain spectra in 30 elderly vs 30 young adults, and a >850-experiment parameter comparison naming mean displacement velocity the most informative measure. Cross-points in prose only: the built VEMP and vHIT/caloric shelves are vestibular-reflex measures, and the timed unipedal-stance shelf (#7252) is the bedside companion — neither is re-carded here. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: European percentile cohort (N = 914, ages 7-86): posturography percentile curves on a plantar-pressure platform — balance improves to about age 45, then reverses (Patti 2018)
cards.summary: European percentile cohort (N = 914, ages 7-86): posturography percentile curves on a plantar-pressure platform — balance improves to about age 45, then reverses (Patti 2018)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population posturography percentile cohort, plantar-pressure platform)
cards.people: 914 healthy subjects aged 7.0-85.99 years from various European countries, recruited by random cluster sampling stratified by age; posturography on a plantar pressure platform with a standardised measurement method; percentile curves (25th, 50th, 75th and interquartile range) by distance-weighted least squares. The cohort spans childhood as well as adult life — the adult bands are the normative limb for this shelf.
cards.result: Balance improved with age up to approximately 45 years, then the trend reversed in older age. Oscillations on the sagittal plane (y-mean) changed with advancing age: young people had more retro-podalic (rear-foot) support than older people, and balance shifted forward in elderly people. The authors propose these standardised-protocol values as normative posturography values for similar populations.
cards.watchOut: One platform and one protocol only: percentile curves from a plantar-pressure platform do not transfer to force-plate or dynamic systems, and the cohort includes children (from age 7), so paediatric bands must not be read as adult norms.
cards.source: Patti A et al. Postural control and balance in a cohort of healthy people living in Europe: An observational study. Medicine. 2018. PMID: 30593180. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: RombergLab open-source posturography (multicentre, N = 350): global equilibrium score mean 0.72 (SD 0.22), falling with age and height (Domènech-Vadillo 2019)
cards.summary: RombergLab open-source posturography (multicentre, N = 350): global equilibrium score mean 0.72 (SD 0.22), falling with age and height (Domènech-Vadillo 2019)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (multicentre normative dataset, open-source computerised posturography / low-cost force platform)
cards.people: 350 healthy participants in a multicentre prospective descriptive study; static postural stability measured with the modified clinical test of sensory interaction on balance, using RombergLab open-source software connected to a low-cost force platform; confidence ellipse area per condition combined into a global equilibrium score (GES), with cluster analysis for influencing factors.
cards.result: Mean (SD) GES was 0.72 (0.22). Age (P < 0.01), height (P < 0.01) and recruitment centre (P < 0.05) influenced GES; cluster analysis produced 16 groups stratified by age and height, and GES decreased with age and with height (P < 0.005). After correction for age and height, centre no longer influenced GES. The authors built these GES values into RombergLab v1.3 as its healthy reference.
cards.watchOut: The GES is a composite specific to this software and its sensory-interaction protocol — it is not interchangeable with sway path, velocity or area numbers from other platforms, and centre effects appeared before age/height correction.
cards.source: Domènech-Vadillo E et al. Normative data for static balance testing in healthy individuals using open source computerized posturography. European archives of oto-rhino-laryngology : official journal of the European Federation of Oto-Rhino-Laryngological Societies (EUFOS) : affiliated with the German Society for Oto-Rhino-Laryngology - Head and Neck Surgery. 2019. PMID: 30327905. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Computerised dynamic posturography with a virtual visual surround (N = 50, ages 20-69): most outcomes match published norms, SOT condition 4 and adaptation differ (Trueblood 2018)
cards.summary: Computerised dynamic posturography with a virtual visual surround (N = 50, ages 20-69): most outcomes match published norms, SOT condition 4 and adaptation differ (Trueblood 2018)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (age-based normative data, dynamic posturography with virtual visual surround)
cards.people: 50 healthy adults divided into five age groups (ages 20-69), tested on a computerised dynamic posturography (CDP) system using a full-field dynamic virtual visual surround (not a mechanically movable surround): sensory organization test (SOT), motor control test (MCT) and adaptation test (ADT); repeatability assessed in 5 subjects aged 23-30 on two days one week apart.
cards.result: Most outcomes were comparable to published normative CDP values, with notable differences in SOT condition 4 and in ADT — attributed to the virtual surround having a more compelling effect on balance even when stationary. SOT composite and conditions 4-6, all MCT translations and ADT toes-up showed moderate to good repeatability (r = 0.60 to 0.99). Age-group and gender differences were not substantial.
cards.watchOut: N = 50 across five age bands is a small normative base per band, and a virtual-surround system's norms must not be applied to traditional movable-surround CDP (or vice versa) — SOT condition 4 is exactly where they diverge.
cards.source: Trueblood PR et al. Age-based normative data for a computerized dynamic posturography system that uses a virtual visual surround environment. Acta oto-laryngologica. 2018. PMID: 29390922. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Standard reference values in 106 healthy young women (ages 21-30): average sway 9.50 mm frontal and 13.00 mm sagittal on a pressure platform (Ohlendorf 2019)
cards.summary: Standard reference values in 106 healthy young women (ages 21-30): average sway 9.50 mm frontal and 13.00 mm sagittal on a pressure platform (Ohlendorf 2019)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (standard reference values, pressure platform, young women)
cards.people: 106 healthy German women aged 21-30 years (mean 25, SD 2.7; mean BMI 21.1, SD 2.61 kg/m²), measured on a pressure-measuring platform in habitual standing; weight distribution and postural sway recorded, with median, tolerance range and confidence intervals calculated.
cards.result: Load distribution between right and left foot was 49.91% : 50.09%; the forefoot carried less load than the rear foot (33.3% : 66.67%), and the right rear foot carried the most body weight (34.34%). Average body sway was 9.50 mm in the frontal plane and 13.00 mm in the sagittal plane. The authors judge the values representative of young German women of this age.
cards.watchOut: Young women only, habitual standing on one pressure platform: these millimetre sway values are a sex- and age-specific limb of the norms, not a general adult standard, and platform-derived sway is not a force-plate centre-of-pressure path.
cards.source: Ohlendorf D et al. Standard reference values of the postural control in healthy young female adults in Germany: an observational study. BMJ open. 2019. PMID: 31175196. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Body-sway power spectra: 30 elderly vs 30 young adults — peak and mean power frequencies higher in the elderly, especially front-to-back (Demura 2006)
cards.summary: Body-sway power spectra: 30 elderly vs 30 young adults — peak and mean power frequencies higher in the elderly, especially front-to-back (Demura 2006)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (frequency-domain body-sway comparison, elderly vs young)
cards.people: 30 healthy elderly people and 30 young adults; body-sway time series and sway-velocity time series during static upright standing, analysed by power spectrum in three international-standard bands (A: 0.02-0.2 Hz, B: 0.2-2.0 Hz, C: 2.0-10.0 Hz). Classic small study — its Ns are printed here on the face.
cards.result: Peak frequency and mean power frequency were higher in elderly persons, the difference marked in the front-back direction. A significant age-group difference across the three bands was found only in the front-back direction: young adults were higher in the low-frequency A band for the sway time series, the elderly higher in the high-frequency C band for sway-velocity. Almost all power in both groups lay in the low-frequency band; the authors argue healthy people's frequency characteristics cannot be properly evaluated by the international standard sections written to screen disorders.
cards.watchOut: N = 30 per group and a frequency-domain parameter set only: these spectra describe how sway is composed, not how much sway is normal — do not read them as sway-size norms.
cards.source: Demura S et al. Comparison of power spectrum characteristics of body sway during a static upright standing posture in healthy elderly people and young adults. Perceptual and motor skills. 2006. PMID: 16826669. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Which sway parameter discriminates best? Over 850 force-platform experiments: mean displacement velocity was the most informative parameter (Raymakers 2005)
cards.summary: Which sway parameter discriminates best? Over 850 force-platform experiments: mean displacement velocity was the most informative parameter (Raymakers 2005)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (methodological comparison of force-plate sway parameters)
cards.people: Over 850 experiments on a Kistler static force platform (60 s of quiet barefoot standing, sampling 10 Hz) in young healthy subjects (n = 10, age 21-45), healthy elderly (n = 38, age 61-78) and two elderly groups with stability problems (n = 10 and n = 21, age 65-89), under eyes-open fixation, eyes closed, standing on plastic foam, and a modified Stroop cognitive task. Only the healthy groups anchor the norms here.
cards.result: Parameters compared included mean displacement velocity, maximal x/y range, movement area, planar deviation, the Riley phase-plane parameter and Collins diffusion-stabilogram parameters, with important overlap among groups and conditions. Mean displacement velocity showed the most consistent differences between test situations, health conditions and age ranges, but was not affected by the extra cognitive task in healthy old people. Standardised displacement parameters (SDs, planar deviation) discriminated less well than actual range or velocity; the diffusion critical time interval added distinct information (cognitive-task effect in old subjects on a firm surface, not on foam), and a new parameter (sum of maximal deviation time) completely discriminated frail elderly when vision was suppressed.
cards.watchOut: A parameter-choice study, not a normative table: its healthy young group is only n = 10, and its lesson — that the parameter chosen changes the answer — is why this shelf cards each platform's parameter set separately rather than pooling one 'normal sway' number.
cards.source: Raymakers JA et al. The assessment of body sway and the choice of the stability parameter(s). Gait & posture. 2005. PMID: 15536033. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: force-plate sway norms exist only per platform and per parameter set — large cohorts agree sway worsens after mid-life, but no single 'normal sway' number survives across systems
cards.summary: Synthesis: force-plate sway norms exist only per platform and per parameter set — large cohorts agree sway worsens after mid-life, but no single 'normal sway' number survives across systems
cards.people: Synthesis of the six primary reports carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (vestibular sensations and motor control) and Ganong (hearing and equilibrium); that framing is general, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature. The population spine is the 914-person European percentile cohort (balance improves to ~45 years, then reverses; support shifts forward with age; Patti 2018) and the 350-participant multicentre RombergLab dataset (global equilibrium score 0.72 ± 0.22, decreasing with age and height; Domènech-Vadillo 2019). Dynamic posturography with a virtual surround (N = 50) mostly reproduces published norms except SOT condition 4 and adaptation (Trueblood 2018). Parameter-specific limbs: sway of 9.50 mm frontal / 13.00 mm sagittal in 106 young women on a pressure platform (Ohlendorf 2019); higher sway power frequencies in 30 elderly vs 30 young adults (Demura 2006); and, across >850 experiments, mean displacement velocity as the most consistently discriminating parameter (Raymakers 2005). Cross-points, not re-carded here: the built vestibular-evoked (VEMP) and video head-impulse / caloric shelves measure vestibular reflexes, not force-plate sway. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age direction and per-platform norms; the fragmentation across platforms is printed on the face, not smoothed away.
cards.watchOut: Never pool parameters across platforms: a RombergLab global equilibrium score, a plantar-pressure percentile, a CDP SOT composite and a Kistler sway velocity are four different measurements that happen to share the word 'sway'.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Unipedal stance norms: time falls significantly with age in both eye conditions across 549 adults, a 1,000-person lifespan dataset and 240 Iranian adults — with no overall sex effect
shelves.question: In healthy adults, how long can a single-leg (unipedal) stance be held, eyes open and eyes closed — mean and best-of-three times by decade and sex — and at what age does the eyes-closed time collapse?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analysis of Variance · Confidence Intervals · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Postural Balance/physiology · Prospective Studies · Reference Values · Vision, Ocular · Aging/physiology · Anthropometry · Child · Child, Preschool · Exercise Test · Lower Extremity/growth & development,physiology · Motor Skills/physiology · Muscle Strength/physiology · Range of Motion, Articular/physiology · Walking/physiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, motor control / vestibular chapters — thin framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. Three primary normative datasets: 549 healthy adults in six age groups with mean and best-of-3 eyes-open and eyes-closed times (significant age decline, no gender effect, ICC 0.994/0.998 for best-of-3); a 1,000-person lifespan reference dataset (ages 3-101) carrying single-leg stance eyes closed among 12 functional measures; and 240 healthy Iranian adults in six age bands confirming age-specific declines. One commissioning-row anchor was refused at build: Furlanetto 2022's seven protocols contain no stance test (recorded on the Synthesis card), and a verified stance dataset was carded in its place. This is the timed bedside test — distinct from the instrumented force-plate shelf #7248 — and its ceiling effect in the young is printed on the face. Cross-points (gait speed, Timed Up and Go, sit-to-stand shelves) are prose only. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: The anchor norms: 549 healthy adults across six age groups (18-39 to 80+) — unipedal stance time falls significantly with age, eyes open and closed, with no gender effect (Springer 2007)
cards.summary: The anchor norms: 549 healthy adults across six age groups (18-39 to 80+) — unipedal stance time falls significantly with age, eyes open and closed, with no gender effect (Springer 2007)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative values, unipedal stance test, eyes open and closed)
cards.people: 549 healthy subjects aged 18 years or older at a tertiary care medical centre, in a prospective mixed-model study; unipedal stance test (UPST) performed with eyes open and eyes closed, with mean and best-of-3 times documented for males and females in six age groups (18-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, 70-79, 80+); inter-rater reliability tested.
cards.result: There was a significant age-dependent decrease in UPST time under both conditions (eyes open and eyes closed). Performance was age-specific and not related to gender. Inter-rater reliability for the best-of-3 trials was excellent: intraclass correlation coefficient 0.994 (95% CI 0.989-0.996) for eyes open and 0.998 (95% CI 0.996-0.999) for eyes closed. The fetched record reports the age pattern and the per-group normative tables' existence; it does not print the per-decade times themselves, and this card claims no specific seconds values.
cards.watchOut: Best-of-3 and mean-of-3 are different norms, and a clinic's ceiling (many protocols stop the clock at 30 or 45 s) truncates young adults' scores — compare a patient only against the same trial rule and stopping rule used here.
cards.source: Springer BA et al. Normative values for the unipedal stance test with eyes open and closed. Journal of geriatric physical therapy (2001). 2007. PMID: 19839175. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lifespan reference dataset (N = 1,000, ages 3-101): single-leg stance with eyes closed among 12 functional measures with age- and sex-stratified reference values (McKay 2017)
cards.summary: Lifespan reference dataset (N = 1,000, ages 3-101): single-leg stance with eyes closed among 12 functional measures with age- and sex-stratified reference values (McKay 2017)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (lifespan functional reference values, including single-leg stance eyes closed)
cards.people: 1,000 healthy individuals aged 3-101 years; twelve functional outcome measures collected, including single-leg stance with eyes closed (within a balance battery with the Star Excursion Balance Test and tandem stance, eyes open and closed), the 6-minute walk test, chair stands, jumping, stepping reaction time and dexterity tests; correlations and multiple regression for demographic, anthropometric, strength and flexibility influences.
cards.result: Age- and sex-stratified reference values were generated for all measures. Functional performance increased through childhood and adolescence, plateaued during adulthood and declined in older adulthood. Balance did not differ between the sexes (men generally performed better at gross motor tasks, women at dexterous tasks). Height was the most consistent correlate in children; lower-limb muscle strength was a major determinant in adolescents and adults; in older adults, age, lower-limb strength and joint flexibility explained up to 63% of the variance in functional measures.
cards.watchOut: Only the eyes-closed single-leg stance limb belongs to this shelf, and the cohort spans ages 3-101 — the adult strata are the normative limb here; the dataset's purpose (tracking neuromuscular decline) means its youngest bands are developmental, not adult, norms.
cards.source: McKay MJ et al. Reference values for developing responsive functional outcome measures across the lifespan. Neurology. 2017. PMID: 28330961. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Iranian normative cohort (240 healthy adults in six age groups, 18-29 to 70+): significant age-specific declines in single-leg stance, with sex differences at 18-29 and at 60+ (Nakhostin-Ansari 2022)
cards.summary: Iranian normative cohort (240 healthy adults in six age groups, 18-29 to 70+): significant age-specific declines in single-leg stance, with sex differences at 18-29 and at 60+ (Nakhostin-Ansari 2022)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (normative single-leg stance values, healthy Iranian adults)
cards.people: 240 healthy Iranian adults (120 men, 120 women) in six age groups (18-29, 30-39, 40-49, 50-59, 60-69, ≥70 years), cross-sectional; functional reach, single-leg stance (SLS), timed up and go (TUG) and dual-task TUG performed per the Persian version of BESTest instructions; normative values reported across age groups and genders. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: There were significant age-specific declines in balance performance across the tests. Gender affected performance in the 18-29 group and in older adults (≥60 years), where males performed better than females; on TUG and dual-task TUG, men and women performed similarly at ages 60-69 (P > 0.05). The authors present the age- and gender-banded normative values as the reference for estimating an individual's balance performance.
cards.watchOut: A single-population cohort normed under BESTest instructions: stance-time norms depend on instructions, footwear/surface conventions and stopping rules, so these bands complement — and do not replace — the Springer and McKay references.
cards.source: Nakhostin-Ansari A et al. Normative values of functional reach test, single-leg stance test, and timed "UP and GO" with and without dual-task in healthy Iranian adults: A cross-sectional study. Annals of medicine and surgery (2012). 2022. PMID: 36045774. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: unipedal stance time is an age measurement, not a sex measurement — it falls decade by decade (549 adults; 1,000-person lifespan dataset; 240 Iranian adults), and the eyes-closed condition is where ageing shows first and hardest
cards.summary: Synthesis: unipedal stance time is an age measurement, not a sex measurement — it falls decade by decade (549 adults; 1,000-person lifespan dataset; 240 Iranian adults), and the eyes-closed condition is where ageing shows first and hardest
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary reports carded above. Refusal recorded: Furlanetto et al. 2022 (PMID 34516997), listed in the commissioning row as a seven-protocol functional-test reference study (296 healthy subjects aged 20-80), was fetched this session and REFUSED for this shelf — its seven protocols are the 4-metre gait speed test (usual and maximal), the sit-to-stand test (5 repetitions, 30 seconds, 1 minute) and the Timed Up and Go (usual and maximal); it contains no single-leg / unipedal stance test, so it cannot card stance norms. The third stance dataset carded instead is Nakhostin-Ansari 2022 (PMID 36045774), fetched and gate-checked this session.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (motor control / vestibular chapters — thin framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature). The anchor is Springer 2007: 549 healthy adults, six age groups, mean and best-of-3 times for eyes open and eyes closed, a significant age-dependent decrease in both conditions, no gender relation, and near-perfect inter-rater reliability for best-of-3 (ICC 0.994 open, 0.998 closed). The lifespan dataset (McKay 2017, N = 1,000, ages 3-101) places single-leg stance eyes closed in the same arc — rise through youth, adult plateau, older-age decline — with balance not differing between the sexes and lower-limb strength a major determinant in adults. The Iranian cohort (Nakhostin-Ansari 2022, N = 240) confirms significant age-specific declines, with sex differences appearing at 18-29 and ≥60. Cross-points in prose only: the instrumented force-plate norms are shelf #7248, and the built gait-speed, Timed Up and Go and sit-to-stand shelves are this test's mobility companions — none re-carded here. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: The ceiling effect in the young is real: a healthy 25-year-old's eyes-open time is usually the protocol's stopping limit, not their ability — the informative comparisons are the eyes-closed condition and the older decades.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.question: In healthy adults, what distance is walked on the incremental shuttle walk test — reference values and prediction equations by age, sex, height and weight — and how large is the learning effect between the first and second test?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 84 (sports physiology); Boron & Boulpaep, exercise physiology — general framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. Three large primary datasets (862 Indian adults aged 17-75; 590 Japanese adults; 199 Singaporean adults aged 21-80) agree that ISWT distance falls steeply with age and is higher in men, each publishing its own reference equation (R² 0.50-0.74) — and the Singapore study demonstrates that foreign equations mispredict its population, so equations are carded per population, never pooled. All three used the standard two-trial protocol; no fetched record quantifies the learning effect numerically, and none is claimed. Distinct from the built 6-minute walk shelf (self-paced, submaximal): cross-point in prose only. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Singapore reference values (199 healthy adults, ages 21-80): median ISWT distance 660 m (IQR 440-850), with a five-variable prediction equation explaining 74% of variance (Azman 2023)
cards.summary: Singapore reference values (199 healthy adults, ages 21-80): median ISWT distance 660 m (IQR 440-850), with a five-variable prediction equation explaining 74% of variance (Azman 2023)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (ISWT normative reference values and regression equations, healthy Asian adults)
cards.people: 199 healthy community-dwelling Singaporeans (114 women, 85 men) aged 21-80 years, convenience-sampled; two ISWT trials per standard protocol, with incremental shuttle walk distance (ISWD), heart rate, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, modified Borg dyspnoea and perceived exertion recorded.
cards.result: Overall median ISWD was 660.0 m (IQR 440.0-850.0). Age-stratified values as reported fell steeply with age: 780.0 m (IQR 670.0-960.0) at ages 21-39, 480.0 m (IQR 438.0-650.0) at 40-59, and 430.0 m (IQR 350.0-450.0) at 60-80. Gender, age, weight, height and heart-rate change were the most significant determinants (P < 0.001). Reference equation: ISWD (m) = 651.4 × height (m) + 89.7 × gender (male = 1, female = 0) − 6.31 × age (years) − 3.61 × weight (kg) + 2.54 × HR change (bpm); R² = 0.741. Previously published ISWT equations could not accurately predict ISWD in this Singaporean population. Each subject performed two trials; the fetched record does not quantify a first-to-second-trial learning effect, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: A Singaporean equation for a Singaporean population: the authors themselves show foreign equations mispredict here — population, like protocol, is part of the reference.
cards.source: Azman MZB et al. Normative reference values, determinants and regression equations for the incremental shuttle walk test (ISWT) in healthy Asian population aged 21 to 80 years. PloS one. 2023. PMID: 37669286. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Indian reference values (862 healthy adults, ages 17-75): men walk 807.9 m at 17-40 years vs 478.2 m past 65; women 709.2 m vs 441.3 m (Agarwal 2016)
cards.summary: Indian reference values (862 healthy adults, ages 17-75): men walk 807.9 m at 17-40 years vs 478.2 m past 65; women 709.2 m vs 441.3 m (Agarwal 2016)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (ISWT reference values and predictive equation, healthy Indian adults)
cards.people: 862 healthy Indian adults aged 17-75 years (convenience sample), grouped as young adulthood (17-40), middle adulthood (40-65) and old adulthood (>65 years), by gender; ISWT performed per Sally Singh's standard protocol. This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: Average distance walked fell with age in both sexes: women 709.2 m (17-40), 556.4 m (40-65) and 441.3 m (>65); men 807.9 m, 639.6 m and 478.2 m in the same groups. Stepwise regression identified age and gender as the key variables correlating with ISWD; the predictive equation as printed is ISWD = 740.351 − (5.676 × age) + (99.007 × gender), and easily measurable variables explained 68% of the variance (as reported).
cards.watchOut: The equation is quoted exactly as printed in the record, including its combined age-and-gender form; three broad age bands (not decades) are the resolution of these norms, and a convenience sample is not a population sample.
cards.source: Agarwal B et al. Incremental shuttle walk test: Reference values and predictive equation for healthy Indian adults. Lung India : official organ of Indian Chest Society. 2016. PMID: 26933305. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Japanese reference equation (590 healthy adults): median ISWD 640 m [490-793]; age, gender and height explain 50% of variability (Itaki 2018)
cards.summary: Japanese reference equation (590 healthy adults): median ISWD 640 m [490-793]; age, gender and height explain 50% of variability (Itaki 2018)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (ISWT reference equation, healthy Japanese adults)
cards.people: 590 healthy Japanese subjects (237 men); ISWT performed twice, with gender, age, height, weight and BMI recorded; stepwise multiple regression for the reference equation.
cards.result: Subjects walked a median 640 m [490-793] on the ISWT. ISWD correlated with age (r = −0.51), gender (r = 0.56), weight (r = 0.39) and height (r = 0.62), all P < 0.001, but not with BMI (r = −0.01, P = 0.74). Age, gender and height were independent contributors, explaining 50% of variability. Reference equation: ISWD (m) = −4.894 − 4.107 × age (years) + 131.115 × gender (male = 1) + 4.895 × height (cm). Performing the test twice is the standard protocol's built-in guard against the learning effect; the fetched record does not report a numeric first-vs-second difference, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Half the variability is unexplained by age, sex and height (R² = 50%): an individual's predicted distance is a band, not a point — the equation grades exercise intolerance, it does not grade a person precisely.
cards.source: Itaki M et al. Reference equation for the incremental shuttle walk test in Japanese adults. Respiratory investigation. 2018. PMID: 30392537. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ISWT distance falls steeply and predictably with age in all three populations (862 Indian, 590 Japanese, 199 Singaporean adults) — but each population needs its own equation, and Singapore's authors show foreign equations mispredict their cohort
cards.summary: Synthesis: ISWT distance falls steeply and predictably with age in all three populations (862 Indian, 590 Japanese, 199 Singaporean adults) — but each population needs its own equation, and Singapore's authors show foreign equations mispredict their cohort
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary reports carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall, ch. 84 (sports physiology) and Boron & Boulpaep (exercise physiology) — general framing; this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature. The three datasets agree on the structure: distance falls with age and is higher in men, with age, sex and height (and, in Singapore, weight and heart-rate change) carrying the prediction — R² 0.74 in Singapore (Azman 2023), 68% of variance in India (Agarwal 2016), 50% in Japan (Itaki 2018). Absolute values differ by population: Indian men aged 17-40 average 807.9 m against a Japanese overall median of 640 m and a Singapore median of 660 m — protocol-identical tests, population-specific norms. All three studies performed two trials per subject per the standard protocol; none of the fetched records quantifies the first-to-second learning effect numerically, and this shelf claims no learning-effect size. Distinct from the built 6-minute walk reference shelf: the ISWT is externally paced and maximal, the 6MWT self-paced and submaximal — different tests, different equations, cross-pointed here in prose only. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Do not import an equation across populations: the Singapore study is itself the demonstration that published foreign equations mispredict a local cohort.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Fostamatinib in rheumatoid arthritis (OSKIRA): modest ACR20 benefit, no radiographic benefit, a negative biologic-failure trial — programme discontinued after phase III
shelves.question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis (including methotrexate and TNF-inhibitor inadequate responders), does the oral spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) inhibitor fostamatinib, compared with placebo (on background therapy, or as monotherapy), improve disease activity (OSKIRA programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aminopyridines · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/drug therapy · Diarrhea/chemically induced · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Hypertension/chemically induced · Intracellular Signaling Peptides and Proteins/antagonists & inhibitors · Male · Methotrexate/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Morpholines · Oxazines/therapeutic use · Protein-Tyrosine Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · Pyridines/therapeutic use · Pyrimidines · Syk Kinase · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a discontinued programme with a genuinely divided record. On the benefit side, fostamatinib on background methotrexate beat placebo on ACR20 in phase III (OSKIRA-1: 49.0% and 44.4% vs 34.2%; OSKIRA-3, TNF inadequate responders: 36.2% vs 21.1% for the 100 mg twice-daily regimen only) and as short-term monotherapy (OSKIRA-4, week 6). On the other side: OSKIRA-1's radiographic co-primary endpoint was negative (no slowing of joint damage), the phase II trial in biologic inadequate responders was negative on its primary endpoint (ACR20 38% vs 37%), every monotherapy regimen was inferior to adalimumab at week 24, and the authors of OSKIRA-1 themselves called the benefit statistically but not clinically significant. Harms were consistent — hypertension (24-hour ambulatory systolic +2.9 mm Hg vs placebo; blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg at ≥1 visit in ~42–52% vs ~19–27%), diarrhoea and neutropenia. The sponsors stopped developing fostamatinib in RA after phase III; it was never marketed for RA (it is marketed only for chronic immune thrombocytopenia).

cards.headline: OSKIRA-1 phase III (Weinblatt 2014): fostamatinib on background methotrexate met ACR20 at week 24 (49.0% and 44.4% vs 34.2% on placebo) but did NOT slow radiographic damage — authors called the benefit statistically but not clinically significant
cards.summary: OSKIRA-1 phase III (Weinblatt 2014): fostamatinib on background methotrexate met ACR20 at week 24 (49.0% and 44.4% vs 34.2% on placebo) but did NOT slow radiographic damage — authors called the benefit statistically but not clinically significant
cards.type: Phase III multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (OSKIRA-1), fostamatinib + methotrexate vs placebo + methotrexate in methotrexate inadequate responders
cards.people: 918 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis and an inadequate response to methotrexate, randomised 1:1:1 to fostamatinib 100 mg twice daily for 52 weeks, fostamatinib 100 mg twice daily for 4 weeks then 150 mg once daily, or placebo for 24 weeks then fostamatinib (all on background methotrexate).
cards.result: At week 24 the ACR20 response was 49.0% (100 mg twice daily) and 44.4% (100 mg twice daily then 150 mg once daily) versus 34.2% on placebo (P<0.001 and P=0.006) — absolute differences of about 15 and 10 percentage points. The co-primary radiographic endpoint was NOT met: change in modified total Sharp/van der Heijde score did not differ significantly from placebo (P=0.25 and P=0.17). The most common adverse events were hypertension (15.8%, 15.1% and 3.9% across the three groups) and diarrhoea (13.9%, 15.1% and 3.9%); blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg at ≥1 visit occurred in 44.2%, 41.6% and 19.3%. The authors concluded the ACR20 improvements were statistically significant but not clinically significant, at a lower level than in the phase II programme.
cards.watchOut: A positive symptom endpoint with a negative structural (radiographic) co-primary endpoint: this trial does not show fostamatinib prevents joint damage.
cards.source: Weinblatt ME et al. Effects of fostamatinib, an oral spleen tyrosine kinase inhibitor, in rheumatoid arthritis patients with an inadequate response to methotrexate: results from a phase III, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study. Arthritis & rheumatology. 2014. PMID: 25223724. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: OSKIRA-3 phase III (Genovese 2014): in TNF-antagonist inadequate responders only the 100 mg twice-daily regimen beat placebo on ACR20 (36.2% vs 21.1%); the stepped-down regimen did not (27.8%) — and the sponsors then stopped developing fostamatinib in RA
cards.summary: OSKIRA-3 phase III (Genovese 2014): in TNF-antagonist inadequate responders only the 100 mg twice-daily regimen beat placebo on ACR20 (36.2% vs 21.1%); the stepped-down regimen did not (27.8%) — and the sponsors then stopped developing fostamatinib in RA
cards.type: Phase III multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (OSKIRA-3), fostamatinib + methotrexate vs placebo + methotrexate in TNF-antagonist inadequate responders
cards.people: 323 adults with active rheumatoid arthritis and an inadequate response to a single TNF-α antagonist, on background methotrexate, randomised to fostamatinib 100 mg twice daily (n=105), fostamatinib 100 mg twice daily for 4 weeks then 150 mg once daily (n=108), or placebo (n=110) for 24 weeks.
cards.result: ACR20 at week 24 was achieved by 36.2% on continuous 100 mg twice daily (P=0.004 vs placebo) but only 27.8% on the stepped-down regimen (P=0.168), versus 21.1% on placebo. Frequently reported adverse events were diarrhoea, hypertension and headache; blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg at ≥1 visit occurred in 46.7%, 51.9% and 26.6%. There were 2 deaths (1 in the stepped-down fostamatinib group, 1 on placebo). The report states that, because of the efficacy and safety results of the phase III programme, the companies developing fostamatinib decided not to study it further in rheumatoid arthritis.
cards.watchOut: The hardest-to-treat population in the programme (prior TNF failure) and the smallest absolute benefit (about 15 percentage points, one regimen only).
cards.source: Genovese MC et al. A phase III, multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study of 2 dosing regimens of fostamatinib in patients with rheumatoid arthritis with an inadequate response to a tumor necrosis factor-α antagonist. The Journal of rheumatology. 2014. PMID: 25225285. Registry ID: NCT01197755. cards.headline: Phase II (Weinblatt 2010, NEJM): the result that launched the programme — ACR20 67% (100 mg twice daily) and 57% (150 mg once daily) vs 35% on placebo at month 6 in methotrexate inadequate responders, with diarrhoea, hypertension and neutropenia already visible
cards.summary: Phase II (Weinblatt 2010, NEJM): the result that launched the programme — ACR20 67% (100 mg twice daily) and 57% (150 mg once daily) vs 35% on placebo at month 6 in methotrexate inadequate responders, with diarrhoea, hypertension and neutropenia already visible
cards.type: Phase II multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, fostamatinib (R788) + methotrexate vs placebo + methotrexate
cards.people: 457 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis despite long-term methotrexate, in a 6-month double-blind placebo-controlled phase II trial of the Syk inhibitor R788 (fostamatinib).
cards.result: ACR20 at month 6 was 67% on 100 mg twice daily and 57% on 150 mg once daily versus 35% on placebo (P<0.001 for both); ACR50 was 43% and 32% versus 19%, and ACR70 28% and 14% versus 10%. A clinically significant effect was noted by the end of the first week. Adverse effects included diarrhoea (19% on the 100 mg dose vs 3% on placebo), upper respiratory infections (14% vs 7%) and neutropenia (6% vs 1%). Systolic blood pressure rose by approximately 3 mm Hg by month 1 (versus a 2 mm Hg fall on placebo), and 23% of fostamatinib patients versus 7% on placebo required starting or changing antihypertensive therapy.
cards.watchOut: Phase II effect sizes were NOT reproduced in phase III (compare OSKIRA-1: 49.0% vs 34.2%) — the classic phase II-to-III shrinkage, printed here so the early result is not read as the programme's true effect.
cards.source: Weinblatt ME et al. An oral spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) inhibitor for rheumatoid arthritis. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20879879. Registry ID: NCT00665925. cards.headline: Phase II in biologic inadequate responders (Genovese 2011): NEGATIVE on its primary endpoint — ACR20 38% on fostamatinib 100 mg twice daily vs 37% on placebo at month 3, against a high placebo response
cards.summary: Phase II in biologic inadequate responders (Genovese 2011): NEGATIVE on its primary endpoint — ACR20 38% on fostamatinib 100 mg twice daily vs 37% on placebo at month 3, against a high placebo response
cards.type: Phase II multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, fostamatinib vs placebo in biologic inadequate responders
cards.people: 219 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis in whom biologic agents had failed, in a 3-month multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase II trial of R788 (fostamatinib disodium).
cards.result: There was no difference in the primary endpoint: ACR20 at month 3 was 38% on fostamatinib 100 mg twice daily versus 37% on placebo, and ACR50 and ACR70 also did not differ significantly. Differences appeared only in secondary endpoints (C-reactive protein level and MRI synovitis score). The authors note baseline differences between groups (steroid use, prior biologic use, MRI synovitis) and a high placebo response, with exploratory analysis suggesting the placebo response was partly driven by patients entering with raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate but normal C-reactive protein.
cards.watchOut: A frankly negative randomised trial in the biologic-failure population — it must be weighed alongside, not underneath, the positive methotrexate-population trials.

cards.headline: OSKIRA-4 phase IIb monotherapy (Taylor 2015): fostamatinib alone beat placebo on DAS28-CRP at week 6 in two of three regimens, but every fostamatinib regimen was inferior to adalimumab monotherapy at week 24
cards.summary: OSKIRA-4 phase IIb monotherapy (Taylor 2015): fostamatinib alone beat placebo on DAS28-CRP at week 6 in two of three regimens, but every fostamatinib regimen was inferior to adalimumab monotherapy at week 24
cards.type: Phase IIb randomised placebo- and active-controlled trial (OSKIRA-4), fostamatinib monotherapy vs placebo and vs adalimumab monotherapy
cards.people: 279 patients with rheumatoid arthritis not currently taking disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, randomised to three fostamatinib monotherapy regimens, adalimumab 40 mg every 2 weeks monotherapy, or placebo (placebo for 6 weeks, then switch to fostamatinib).
cards.result: Fostamatinib significantly improved DAS28-CRP from baseline versus placebo at week 6 in the 100 mg twice-daily arm and the 100 mg twice-daily then 150 mg once-daily arm, but not in the 100 mg twice-daily then 100 mg once-daily arm. At week 24 fostamatinib was significantly less effective than adalimumab on DAS28-CRP. Adverse events were consistent with previous studies, including hypertension and diarrhoea.
cards.watchOut: Monotherapy evidence only, over 6 weeks against placebo; the week-24 comparison that matters clinically — against adalimumab — went against fostamatinib.
cards.source: Taylor PC et al. OSKIRA-4: a phase IIb randomised, placebo-controlled study of the efficacy and safety of fostamatinib monotherapy. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2015. PMID: 25074688. Registry ID: NCT01264770.
