cards.headline: OSKIRA-ABPM harm report (Kitas 2014): 24-hour ambulatory monitoring confirmed a real blood-pressure effect — mean systolic +2.9 mm Hg and diastolic +3.5 mm Hg versus placebo at 28 days, resolving within a week of stopping
cards.summary: OSKIRA-ABPM harm report (Kitas 2014): 24-hour ambulatory monitoring confirmed a real blood-pressure effect — mean systolic +2.9 mm Hg and diastolic +3.5 mm Hg versus placebo at 28 days, resolving within a week of stopping
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial (OSKIRA-ABPM), fostamatinib vs placebo — ambulatory blood-pressure harm quantification for the OSKIRA programme
cards.people: 135 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis randomised to fostamatinib 100 mg twice daily (n=68) or placebo (n=67) for 28 days, with ambulatory, clinic and home blood-pressure measurement (a report OF the OSKIRA programme, quantifying its principal harm — not a separate efficacy trial).
cards.result: Fostamatinib increased 24-hour mean systolic blood pressure by 2.9 mm Hg (P=0.023) and diastolic blood pressure by 3.5 mm Hg (P<0.001) versus placebo; clinic and home measurements agreed with ambulatory monitoring. One week after discontinuation, clinic blood pressure had returned to baseline.
cards.watchOut: A harm-quantification report of the same programme, carded and labelled as such; it adds no efficacy evidence. The blood-pressure rise is modest on average but was accompanied in the efficacy trials by roughly double the rate of visits with blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg.
cards.source: Kitas GD et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: a complete, discontinued programme — real but modest symptom benefit in methotrexate inadequate responders, no radiographic benefit, a negative trial in biologic inadequate responders, inferiority to adalimumab as monotherapy, and a consistent hypertension/diarrhoea/neutropenia harm profile; development in RA was abandoned after phase III
cards.summary: Synthesis: a complete, discontinued programme — real but modest symptom benefit in methotrexate inadequate responders, no radiographic benefit, a negative trial in biologic inadequate responders, inferiority to adalimumab as monotherapy, and a consistent hypertension/diarrhoea/neutropenia harm profile; development in RA was abandoned after phase III
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across the carded OSKIRA record: phase II promised ACR20 responses of 67% vs 35% (Weinblatt 2010), but phase III delivered 49.0%/44.4% vs 34.2% with no significant slowing of radiographic damage (OSKIRA-1), 36.2% vs 21.1% for one regimen only in TNF inadequate responders (OSKIRA-3), and a negative primary endpoint in biologic inadequate responders (38% vs 37%; Genovese 2011). As monotherapy fostamatinib beat placebo short-term but was inferior to adalimumab at week 24 (OSKIRA-4). Harms were consistent throughout: hypertension (blood pressure ≥140/90 mm Hg at ≥1 visit in ~42–52% on fostamatinib vs ~19–27% on placebo; +2.9/+3.5 mm Hg on 24-hour ambulatory monitoring, reversible on stopping), diarrhoea and neutropenia. Fostamatinib was never marketed for rheumatoid arthritis and is marketed only for chronic immune thrombocytopenia (its separate shelf); nothing in this record supports resurrecting it for RA.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Iguratimod in primary Sjögren syndrome: small Chinese RCT base — ESSPRI benefit vs placebo; primary endpoint missed vs hydroxychloroquine (REBUILD)
shelves.question: In adults with primary Sjögren syndrome (Sjögren disease), does the oral immunomodulator iguratimod, compared with placebo (or hydroxychloroquine), improve patient-reported dryness/fatigue (ESSPRI), disease activity (ESSDAI) and glandular measures?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use,adverse effects,administration & dosage · Biomarkers · Chromones/therapeutic use,adverse effects,administration & dosage · Hydroxychloroquine/therapeutic use,administration & dosage,adverse effects · Immunosuppressive Agents/therapeutic use,adverse effects,administration & dosage · Severity of Illness Index · Sjogren's Syndrome/drug therapy,diagnosis · Sulfonamides · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, single-region evidence. One small placebo-controlled RCT (66 patients) found iguratimod improved the patient-reported ESSPRI and several activity measures more than placebo over 24 weeks. Against hydroxychloroquine, the multicentre RCT (78 patients) MISSED its primary endpoint (SSRI-30 57.9% vs 40.0%, P=0.114) but favoured iguratimod on secondary STAR and ESSDAI responder rates and on IgG reduction, with more frequent but mostly mild adverse events (60.6% vs 37.8%). An open-label pilot (N=27, labelled as such) and a mechanistic B-cell comparison complete the base. All trials are from China; iguratimod is approved there and in Japan as a DMARD and is not FDA/EMA-approved — printed on the face. A retracted iguratimod-combination report (PMID 34805398) is fenced and is not carded or counted here.

cards.headline: Multicentre RCT vs hydroxychloroquine (Chen 2025): primary endpoint MISSED — SSRI-30 response 57.9% on iguratimod vs 40.0% on hydroxychloroquine (P=0.114) — but composite STAR and ESSDAI responder rates and IgG reduction favoured iguratimod
cards.summary: Multicentre RCT vs hydroxychloroquine (Chen 2025): primary endpoint MISSED — SSRI-30 response 57.9% on iguratimod vs 40.0% on hydroxychloroquine (P=0.114) — but composite STAR and ESSDAI responder rates and IgG reduction favoured iguratimod
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial, iguratimod vs hydroxychloroquine (active comparator, no placebo arm)
cards.people: 78 patients with active primary Sjögren syndrome randomised 1:1 to iguratimod 25 mg twice daily (n=38) or hydroxychloroquine 0.2 g twice daily (n=40) for 24 weeks; 66 patients (31 iguratimod, 35 hydroxychloroquine) completed the study (China).
cards.result: The primary endpoint, Sjögren's Syndrome Responder Index-30 (SSRI-30) response at week 24, was numerically higher on iguratimod (57.9% vs 40.0%) but NOT statistically significant (P=0.114) — absolute difference about 18 percentage points. Key secondary responder endpoints did favour iguratimod: STAR response 39.5% vs 15.0% (P=0.015) and ESSDAI response 21.1% vs 5.0% (P=0.034), and IgG reduction was greater (P=0.046). Adverse events were more frequent with iguratimod (60.6% vs 37.8%) but were mostly mild.
cards.watchOut: An active-comparator trial whose PRIMARY endpoint was not significant; the positive findings are secondary endpoints and should be read as such. No placebo arm, so neither drug's absolute effect is measured here.
cards.source: Chen X et al. Efficacy and safety of iguratimod in patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome: a multicentre randomised controlled trial. RMD open. 2025. PMID: 41423293. Registry ID: NCT04981145. cards.headline: Placebo-controlled RCT (Shao 2021): iguratimod improved the patient-reported ESSPRI more than placebo over 24 weeks (P=0.016), with better Schirmer test, ESR and IgG — the trial the earlier slate count missed
cards.summary: Placebo-controlled RCT (Shao 2021): iguratimod improved the patient-reported ESSPRI more than placebo over 24 weeks (P=0.016), with better Schirmer test, ESR and IgG — the trial the earlier slate count missed
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, iguratimod vs placebo
cards.people: 66 patients with primary Sjögren syndrome randomised 2:1 to oral iguratimod or matching placebo for 24 weeks.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, the EULAR Sjögren's Syndrome Patient Reported Index (ESSPRI), improved more with iguratimod than placebo (P=0.016). Mental discomfort visual analogue score, patient global assessment, Schirmer's test values, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and immunoglobulin G also improved more with iguratimod (all P<0.05). Adverse events were reported in 13.6% of the iguratimod group. Serum B-cell activating factor (BAFF) levels and plasma-cell proportions fell significantly on iguratimod, and plasma-cell proportions correlated positively with serum IgG and BAFF.
cards.watchOut: A single small trial (66 patients) carries the placebo-controlled evidence for this shelf; effect sizes for ESSPRI are reported as significance levels, not magnitudes, in the record carded here.
cards.source: Shao Q et al. Efficacy and safety of iguratimod on patients with primary Sjögren's syndrome: a randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Scandinavian journal of rheumatology. 2021. cards.type: Open-label single-arm pilot study (no comparator), iguratimod in early primary Sjögren syndrome
cards.people: 27 disease-modifying-antirheumatic-drug-naive women with early primary Sjögren syndrome (revised American-European Consensus Group criteria), treated open-label with iguratimod 25 mg twice daily for 24 weeks. N=27 — printed on the face per the small-base labelling rule.
cards.result: ESSDAI decreased significantly (median 5 at baseline versus 2 at weeks 12 and 24; P<0.01), as did IgG (median 26.6 to 21.4 g/L; P<0.01) and rheumatoid factor (median 119.9 to 83.8 IU/mL; P<0.01). ESSPRI, salivary and lacrimal gland function, fatigue and health-related quality of life did NOT change during treatment. One patient experienced thrombocytopenia; no other serious adverse effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: OPEN-LABEL and uncontrolled with N=27: within-patient changes cannot be attributed to iguratimod (regression to the mean and natural fluctuation are unconstrained), and the patient-reported index did not improve. Supportive only — never load-bearing for this shelf.

cards.headline: Regulatory B-cell comparison vs hydroxychloroquine (Zou 2025): after 6 months both drugs lowered ESSDAI/ESSPRI and fatigue scores; iguratimod lowered IgG more and raised CD19+CD5+CD1d+ regulatory B cells — a mechanistic comparison, labelled as such
cards.summary: Regulatory B-cell comparison vs hydroxychloroquine (Zou 2025): after 6 months both drugs lowered ESSDAI/ESSPRI and fatigue scores; iguratimod lowered IgG more and raised CD19+CD5+CD1d+ regulatory B cells — a mechanistic comparison, labelled as such
cards.type: Randomised comparison, iguratimod vs hydroxychloroquine — mechanistic (regulatory B-cell) programme support, single centre
cards.people: 60 patients with primary Sjögren syndrome at a single hospital (Mianyang Central Hospital, recruited December 2020 to December 2022), randomised to iguratimod 25 mg twice daily or hydroxychloroquine 0.2 g twice daily, each with prednisone ≤10 mg/day, for 6 months.
cards.result: After 6 months, IgG and ESSPRI were significantly lower in the iguratimod group than the hydroxychloroquine group, and CD19+CD5+CD1d+ B cells were significantly higher (P<0.05). Within the iguratimod group, IgG, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, B lymphocytes, ESSDAI, ESSPRI and fatigue (FACIT) scores all fell significantly from baseline and regulatory B cells rose; within the hydroxychloroquine group, C-reactive protein, ESR, ESSDAI, ESSPRI and FACIT fell with no significant change in regulatory B cells. The authors conclude iguratimod was superior for IgG reduction and affects peripheral B-lymphocyte populations.
cards.watchOut: Labelled mechanistic programme support: a small single-centre comparison whose distinctive contribution is immunology (regulatory B cells), not a powered clinical-endpoint result; both groups also received low-dose prednisone.
cards.source: Zou JM et al. Comparison of the effect of iguratimod and hydroxychloroquine on regulatory B cells in the treatment of primary Sjögren's syndrome. Frontiers in medicine. 2025. PMID: 40678132. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: a small, single-region (China) base — one small placebo-controlled RCT positive on patient-reported dryness/fatigue, one active-comparator RCT that missed its primary endpoint but favoured iguratimod on secondary composite/activity measures, one open-label pilot (N=27) and one mechanistic comparison; promising, not established
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small, single-region (China) base — one small placebo-controlled RCT positive on patient-reported dryness/fatigue, one active-comparator RCT that missed its primary endpoint but favoured iguratimod on secondary composite/activity measures, one open-label pilot (N=27) and one mechanistic comparison; promising, not established
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The placebo-controlled evidence is one 66-patient RCT (Shao 2021) in which ESSPRI and several secondary measures improved more on iguratimod than placebo. The larger comparative trial (Chen 2025, n=78 vs hydroxychloroquine) missed its primary SSRI-30 endpoint (57.9% vs 40.0%, P=0.114) while favouring iguratimod on STAR and ESSDAI responder rates and IgG reduction, with more (mostly mild) adverse events (60.6% vs 37.8%). The open-label pilot (n=27, women with early disease) showed ESSDAI and IgG falls but no change in ESSPRI or gland function, and the B-cell comparison (n=60) is mechanistic support. All evidence is from China, where iguratimod is approved as a DMARD (also Japan); it is not FDA- or EMA-approved. A retracted iguratimod-combination report exists in this literature and is deliberately NOT carded on this shelf (see watch-out).
cards.watchOut: A retracted iguratimod report (PMID 34805398, typed Retracted Publication) is fenced and has NOT been carded or counted anywhere on this shelf. See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Tripterygium wilfordii glycosides in rheumatoid arthritis (TRIFRA): not inferior to methotrexate in one open-label Chinese programme; herb-rule and toxicity limits on the face
shelves.question: In adults with active rheumatoid arthritis, do Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F (tripterygium glycosides) preparations — alone compared with methotrexate, or added to methotrexate or a TNF inhibitor — improve disease activity and slow radiographic progression (TRIFRA programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antirheumatic Agents/therapeutic use · Arthritis, Rheumatoid/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Methotrexate/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Phytotherapy · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome · Tripterygium
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — with the herb rule and single-region limits printed on the face. In the TRIFRA programme (China, open-label, assessor-blinded), Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F monotherapy was not inferior to methotrexate (ACR50 at week 24: 55.1% vs 46.4%) and the combination was better (76.8%), with comparable radiographic progression at 2 years. Combination evidence is mixed: TwHF + a TNF-receptor fusion protein beat methotrexate + the same agent at week 12 (ACR50 57.1% vs 41.3%), but adalimumab + TwHF was no better than adalimumab + methotrexate at week 24. HERB RULE: tripterygium glycoside preparations are not FDA-approved and differ by maker; none of the carded publications names a branded product or manufacturer in its record — the preparation is described only as Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F (20 mg three times daily in TRIFRA) — and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. Reproductive toxicity (infertility/amenorrhoea; irregular menstruation was seen in TRIFRA), hepatotoxicity and gastrointestinal harm lead the harm side. All evidence is single-region (China).

cards.headline: TRIFRA primary (Lv 2015): Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F monotherapy was not inferior to methotrexate on ACR50 at week 24 (55.1% vs 46.4%) and the combination was better than methotrexate alone (76.8%); irregular menstruation was the visible reproductive-harm signal
cards.summary: TRIFRA primary (Lv 2015): Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F monotherapy was not inferior to methotrexate on ACR50 at week 24 (55.1% vs 46.4%) and the combination was better than methotrexate alone (76.8%); irregular menstruation was the visible reproductive-harm signal
cards.type: Multicentre open-label randomised controlled trial (TRIFRA), Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F vs methotrexate vs the combination
cards.people: 207 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis (DMARD-naive) in a multicentre open-label randomised trial (China), allocated 1:1:1 to methotrexate 12.5 mg once weekly, Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F 20 mg three times daily, or both; monotherapy patients with <30% DAS28 reduction at week 12 were switched to the combination. 174 of 207 (84.1%) completed 24 weeks. Preparation as published: Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F (TwHF) 20 mg three times daily — the publication carded here does not name a branded product or manufacturer in its record, so none is stated; see the shelf-level herb-rule note.
cards.result: ACR50 at week 24 (intention-to-treat) was 46.4% (32/69) on methotrexate, 55.1% (38/69) on TwHF and 76.8% (53/69) on the combination (TwHF vs methotrexate P=0.014 for the non-inferiority/superiority comparison as reported; combination vs methotrexate P<0.001). ACR20, ACR70, Clinical Disease Activity Index good responses, EULAR good response, remission and low-disease-activity rates showed similar patterns; Health Assessment Questionnaire and SF-36 scores improved in all arms without significant between-arm differences. Irregular menstruation developed in 7 women in the TwHF group, 3 in the methotrexate group and 5 in the combination group (TwHF vs methotrexate P=0.216). The authors concluded TwHF monotherapy was not inferior to, and the combination better than, methotrexate monotherapy.
cards.watchOut: Herb rule (applies to every card on this shelf): Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F preparations are not FDA-approved and preparations differ by maker. This trial was OPEN-LABEL (assessors blinded, patients not), and non-inferiority here rests on a single trial programme. The preparation is described by plant and dose only in the record carded; no branded product/company is documented there.
cards.source: Lv QW et al. Comparison of Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F with methotrexate in the treatment of active rheumatoid arthritis (TRIFRA): a randomised, controlled clinical trial. Annals of the rheumatic diseases. 2015. PMID: 24733191. Registry ID: NCT01613079. cards.headline: TRIFRA 2-year follow-up (Zhou 2018): the disease-activity advantage persisted at year 2 (ACR50 58.0% TwHF vs 46.4% methotrexate) and radiographic progression was comparable between groups — but only 109 of 207 patients completed 2 years
cards.summary: TRIFRA 2-year follow-up (Zhou 2018): the disease-activity advantage persisted at year 2 (ACR50 58.0% TwHF vs 46.4% methotrexate) and radiographic progression was comparable between groups — but only 109 of 207 patients completed 2 years
cards.type: 2-year follow-up report of the TRIFRA randomised trial (same trial as the primary card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The 207 DMARD-naive patients randomised in TRIFRA (methotrexate vs Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F vs the combination), followed to year 2; 109 completed the 2-year follow-up. Radiographs were scored independently by two radiologists blinded to treatment. Preparation as in the primary TRIFRA report (TwHF 20 mg three times daily); no branded product or manufacturer is named in this record either.
cards.result: At year 2 (intention-to-treat), ACR50 was 46.4% on methotrexate, 58.0% on TwHF and 50.7% on the combination (TwHF vs methotrexate P=0.004), with similar patterns for ACR20, ACR70, good responses, remission and low disease activity; per-protocol analysis agreed. Changes in total Sharp score, joint erosion and joint-space narrowing over 2 years were comparable among the three groups (P≥0.05) and tracked changes in DAS28. Adverse events were similar in the three groups. Withdrawal numbers and adherence to the initial regimens were similar across groups.
cards.watchOut: Herb rule (applies to every card on this shelf): Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F preparations are not FDA-approved and preparations differ by maker. A follow-up report OF the TRIFRA trial, labelled as such — not a second trial. Nearly half the randomised patients did not complete 2 years, so the year-2 estimates rest on a depleted cohort.
cards.source: Zhou YZ et al. Comparison of the impact of Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F and Methotrexate treatment on radiological progression in active rheumatoid arthritis: 2-year follow up of a randomized, non-blinded, controlled study. Arthritis research & therapy. 2018. PMID: 29636089. Registry ID: NCT01613079. cards.headline: Phase IV combination trial (Zhang 2023): Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F PLUS a TNF inhibitor beat methotrexate plus TNF inhibitor on ACR50 at week 12 (57.1% vs 41.3%) — a COMBINATION study, not tripterygium-alone evidence
cards.summary: Phase IV combination trial (Zhang 2023): Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F PLUS a TNF inhibitor beat methotrexate plus TNF inhibitor on ACR50 at week 12 (57.1% vs 41.3%) — a COMBINATION study, not tripterygium-alone evidence
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind triple-dummy phase IV trial — COMBINATION study (Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F + TNF inhibitor), with TwHF-alone and methotrexate-alone arms
cards.people: 504 patients with active rheumatoid arthritis at 14 tertiary rheumatology centres in China, randomised in a double-blind triple-dummy phase IV trial to Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F + recombinant human TNF receptor–IgG Fc fusion protein (rhTNFR-Fc) (n=126), methotrexate + rhTNFR-Fc (n=126), TwHF alone (n=126) or methotrexate alone (n=126). Preparation as published: Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F combined with rhTNFR-Fc; the record carded does not name a branded TwHF product or manufacturer.
cards.result: ACR50 at week 12 was 57.1% (72/126) with TwHF + rhTNFR-Fc, 41.3% (52/126) with methotrexate + rhTNFR-Fc, 23.0% (29/126) with TwHF alone and 26.2% (33/126) with methotrexate alone (TwHF + rhTNFR-Fc vs each other group, all P<0.05). There was no statistical difference in serious adverse events or adverse events leading to discontinuation across the groups. The authors concluded TwHF + rhTNFR-Fc was superior to methotrexate-based treatment for active RA with a similar safety profile.
cards.watchOut: Herb rule (applies to every card on this shelf): Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F preparations are not FDA-approved and preparations differ by maker. COMBINATION evidence: the headline comparison is TwHF plus a TNF inhibitor, and must never be quoted as a tripterygium-alone effect. Note the TwHF-alone arm (23.0%) did not beat methotrexate alone (26.2%) in this shorter, different-population trial — unlike TRIFRA.

cards.headline: Adalimumab combination RCT (Luo 2024): adalimumab + Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F was NO better than adalimumab + methotrexate on low disease activity or remission at week 24 — a COMBINATION study with a null head-to-head result
cards.summary: Adalimumab combination RCT (Luo 2024): adalimumab + Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F was NO better than adalimumab + methotrexate on low disease activity or remission at week 24 — a COMBINATION study with a null head-to-head result
cards.type: Multicentre open-label randomised controlled trial — COMBINATION study (adalimumab + Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F vs adalimumab + methotrexate)
cards.people: 64 patients with rheumatoid arthritis and inadequate response to methotrexate, in a multicentre open-label randomised trial (China), assigned 1:1 to adalimumab + Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F or adalimumab + methotrexate for 24 weeks; 53 of 64 (82.8%) completed. Preparation as published: Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F combined with adalimumab; no branded TwHF product or manufacturer is named in the record carded.
cards.result: By intention-to-treat, outcomes were comparable: low disease activity was achieved by 43.8% (TwHF combination) versus 46.9% (methotrexate combination) (P=0.802), and the second reported rate pair (28.1% vs 31.3%, P=0.784) likewise did not differ; per-protocol analysis agreed. Adverse-event incidence was comparable between groups. The authors concluded there were no significant differences in efficacy or safety, and that TwHF might be an alternative for patients intolerant to methotrexate.
cards.watchOut: Herb rule (applies to every card on this shelf): Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F preparations are not FDA-approved and preparations differ by maker. COMBINATION evidence, open-label, and small (64 randomised): a null comparison against the standard combination, useful as a substitute-for-methotrexate signal only, not as evidence of added benefit.

cards.headline: Synthesis: in the TRIFRA programme tripterygium glycosides matched (and on ACR50 exceeded) methotrexate as monotherapy with comparable 2-year radiographic progression; the combination evidence is mixed — superior added to a TNF-receptor fusion protein at 12 weeks, no better than methotrexate added to adalimumab at 24 weeks — and the whole base is Chinese, open-label in its pivotal trial, with reproductive and other toxicity that constrains use
cards.summary: Synthesis: in the TRIFRA programme tripterygium glycosides matched (and on ACR50 exceeded) methotrexate as monotherapy with comparable 2-year radiographic progression; the combination evidence is mixed — superior added to a TNF-receptor fusion protein at 12 weeks, no better than methotrexate added to adalimumab at 24 weeks — and the whole base is Chinese, open-label in its pivotal trial, with reproductive and other toxicity that constrains use
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Monotherapy: TRIFRA (207 patients, open-label) found ACR50 at week 24 of 55.1% on Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F versus 46.4% on methotrexate (combination 76.8%), sustained at year 2 (58.0% vs 46.4%) with comparable radiographic progression — one programme, one country, assessor-blinded only. Combinations: TwHF + rhTNFR-Fc beat methotrexate + rhTNFR-Fc at week 12 (ACR50 57.1% vs 41.3%; Zhang 2023), while adalimumab + TwHF was no better than adalimumab + methotrexate at week 24 (Luo 2024). Harms visible in these records centre on reproductive toxicity (irregular menstruation in the TwHF arms of TRIFRA), with hepatotoxicity and gastrointestinal harm the recognised class concerns for tripterygium preparations; adverse events were otherwise reported as similar across arms. HERB RULE, stated plainly: none of the four publications carded here names a branded tripterygium glycoside product or its manufacturer in the record — the tested preparation is described only as Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F (20 mg three times daily in TRIFRA) — and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness from the preparations tested.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. All four reports are from China (single-region evidence).
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Prasterone (DHEA) in women with SLE: one positive trial, one subgroup-only steroid-sparing result — androgenic harms; never approved for lupus
shelves.question: In women with systemic lupus erythematosus, does oral prasterone (dehydroepiandrosterone, DHEA), compared with placebo plus standard therapy, improve disease activity and reduce corticosteroid requirements?
shelves.mesh: Adjuvants, Immunologic/therapeutic use · Adult · Dehydroepiandrosterone/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Lupus Erythematosus, Systemic/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — a women-only programme (1995–2004, never approved for SLE) with one positive, one subgroup-only and one small pilot result. Petri 2004 (381 women) found prasterone 200 mg/day improved or stabilised disease without deterioration in 58.5% versus 44.5% on placebo among women with active disease (P=0.017, ≈14 percentage points, on a composite counting stabilisation as response). Petri 2002's corticosteroid-sparing endpoint MISSED overall (55% vs 41%, P=0.110) and was significant only in the active-disease subgroup (51% vs 29%, P=0.031). The first trial was small (N=28). Harms are androgenic — acne (33% vs 14%), hirsutism (16% vs 2%) — with HDL cholesterol lowering. The sex restriction is printed on the face: there is no trial evidence in men.

cards.headline: First RCT (van Vollenhoven 1995): DHEA 200 mg/day for 3 months — SLEDAI, patient/physician assessments and prednisone dose moved favourably versus placebo (patient assessment P=0.022 adjusted); small (N=28) and short
cards.summary: First RCT (van Vollenhoven 1995): DHEA 200 mg/day for 3 months — SLEDAI, patient/physician assessments and prednisone dose moved favourably versus placebo (patient assessment P=0.022 adjusted); small (N=28) and short
cards.type: Double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial, prasterone (DHEA) vs placebo in women with SLE
cards.people: 28 women with mild to moderate systemic lupus erythematosus in a double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial of dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) 200 mg/day or placebo for 3 months; corticosteroid doses were adjusted as clinically indicated. N=28 — a small trial, printed on the face.
cards.result: In the DHEA group the SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI) score, patient's and physician's overall assessments of disease activity, and concurrent prednisone dosage decreased, while small increases were seen on placebo; the between-group difference in patient's assessment was statistically significant (P=0.022, adjusted). Lupus flares occurred more frequently in the placebo group (P=0.053). Mild acne was a frequent side effect of DHEA. The authors concluded DHEA may be useful in mild to moderate SLE and that further studies were warranted.
cards.watchOut: N=28 over 3 months: hypothesis-generating only — the two larger trials below carry this shelf. Women only, as is the whole prasterone-in-SLE base.

cards.headline: Corticosteroid-sparing RCT (Petri 2002): the overall primary comparison MISSED significance (responders 55% on prasterone 200 mg vs 41% on placebo, P=0.110) — significance appeared only in the subgroup with active disease at baseline (51% vs 29%, P=0.031)
cards.summary: Corticosteroid-sparing RCT (Petri 2002): the overall primary comparison MISSED significance (responders 55% on prasterone 200 mg vs 41% on placebo, P=0.110) — significance appeared only in the subgroup with active disease at baseline (51% vs 29%, P=0.031)
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled multicentre trial, prasterone 100/200 mg vs placebo — corticosteroid-requirement endpoint
cards.people: 191 women with systemic lupus erythematosus receiving prednisone 10–30 mg/day, in a double-blind randomised trial of placebo, prasterone 100 mg/day or prasterone 200 mg/day for 7–9 months; corticosteroid doses were reduced by algorithm when SLEDAI was stable or improved. A responder sustained prednisone ≤7.5 mg/day for at least the last 2 months with stable or reduced disease activity.
cards.result: Responder rates were 41% (placebo), 44% (prasterone 100 mg) and 55% (prasterone 200 mg) — the 200 mg versus placebo comparison was NOT significant overall (P=0.110). Among the 137 women with active disease at baseline (SLEDAI >2), responder rates were 29% (placebo, n=45), 38% (100 mg, n=47) and 51% (200 mg, n=45), which WAS significant for 200 mg versus placebo (P=0.031). Acne was the most common adverse event but was generally mild; other clinical and laboratory changes primarily reflected androgenic effects.
cards.watchOut: Read the two numbers together: the trial's overall result is negative (P=0.110) and the positive result is a baseline-activity SUBGROUP — subgroup significance after an overall miss is weaker evidence, and it is labelled as such here and in the balance.
cards.source: Petri MA et al. Effects of prasterone on corticosteroid requirements of women with systemic lupus erythematosus: a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. cards.headline: Disease-activity RCT (Petri 2004): in women with active disease at baseline, 58.5% on prasterone 200 mg/day improved or stabilised without deterioration vs 44.5% on placebo (P=0.017); acne 33% and hirsutism 16% on prasterone
cards.summary: Disease-activity RCT (Petri 2004): in women with active disease at baseline, 58.5% on prasterone 200 mg/day improved or stabilised without deterioration vs 44.5% on placebo (P=0.017); acne 33% and hirsutism 16% on prasterone
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, prasterone 200 mg vs placebo plus standard therapy in women with active SLE
cards.people: 381 women with active systemic lupus erythematosus at 27 centres, randomised to prasterone 200 mg/day plus standard therapy or placebo plus standard therapy for up to 12 months (standard therapy: prednisone ≤10 mg/day, antimalarials and immunosuppressives at stable doses). Responders had no clinical deterioration plus improvement or stabilisation on SLEDAI, the Systemic Lupus Activity Measure, patient global assessment and the Krupp Fatigue Severity Scale.
cards.result: Among women with clinically active disease at baseline (SLEDAI >2), 86 of 147 (58.5%) on prasterone were responders versus 65 of 146 (44.5%) on placebo (P=0.017) — an absolute difference of about 14 percentage points. Acne was reported in 33% on prasterone versus 14% on placebo, and hirsutism in 16% versus 2% (both P<0.05), mostly mild and rarely requiring withdrawal; myalgias (22% vs 36%) and oral stomatitis (15% vs 23%) were less frequent on prasterone. High-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides and C3 complement fell significantly on prasterone, while testosterone (and, less, estradiol) rose — the androgenic/lipid harm profile printed on the face.
cards.watchOut: The responder definition is a composite of stabilisation as well as improvement ('improved or stabilised without deterioration'), which inflates responder rates in both arms — the between-group difference (≈14 points) is the interpretable number. Women only; prednisone at entry was capped at ≤10 mg/day, unlike the 2002 trial.
cards.source: Petri MA et al. Effects of prasterone on disease activity and symptoms in women with active systemic lupus erythematosus. Arthritis and rheumatism. 2004. PMID: 15452837. cards.headline: Synthesis: a women-only, 1995–2004 programme that was never approved for SLE — one small positive pilot RCT, one corticosteroid-sparing trial negative overall but positive in its active-disease subgroup, and one larger trial positive on a stabilisation composite in active disease; androgenic effects and HDL lowering are the price
cards.summary: Synthesis: a women-only, 1995–2004 programme that was never approved for SLE — one small positive pilot RCT, one corticosteroid-sparing trial negative overall but positive in its active-disease subgroup, and one larger trial positive on a stabilisation composite in active disease; androgenic effects and HDL lowering are the price
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Van Vollenhoven 1995 (n=28, 3 months) pointed favourably. Petri 2002 (n=191, steroid-dependent women) missed its overall responder comparison (55% vs 41% on prasterone 200 mg vs placebo, P=0.110) and reached significance only in women with active disease at baseline (51% vs 29%, P=0.031). Petri 2004 (n=381) found more responders on prasterone 200 mg among women with active baseline disease (58.5% vs 44.5%, P=0.017) on a composite that counts stabilisation as response. Harms across the programme are androgenic — acne (33% vs 14% in 2004), hirsutism (16% vs 2%), voice change is the recognised class concern — plus significant falls in HDL cholesterol. Every trial enrolled women only, the programme is two decades old, and prasterone was never approved for systemic lupus erythematosus (its approved use is the intravaginal formulation for dyspareunia, a different question homed elsewhere in the library).

shelves.title: Ipriflavone in postmenopausal osteoporosis: JAMA 2001 found no bone-loss or fracture benefit — and lymphocytopenia in 13.2%
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does the isoflavone ipriflavone, compared with placebo (with calcium), prevent bone loss and reduce vertebral fractures?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Analysis of Variance · Biomarkers · Bone Density · Bone Remodeling · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Isoflavones/adverse effects,metabolism,therapeutic use · Lymphopenia/chemically induced · Middle Aged · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/drug therapy,metabolism,prevention & control · Prospective Studies · Spinal Fractures/epidemiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) on efficacy, with a harm signal — a negative-result shelf. The large JAMA 2001 trial (474 postmenopausal women, 3 years) found ipriflavone did NOT prevent bone loss at any site (lumbar spine annual change 0.1% vs 0.8% on placebo, P=0.14), did not change bone-resorption markers, and produced identical or near-identical new vertebral fracture counts — while 13.2% of treated women developed subclinical lymphocytopenia. The older, smaller Italian reports (Agnusdei 1997, two trials, 149 enrolled; Maugeri 1994, 100 enrolled) reported forearm/radial BMD gains, but they are peripheral-site, largely within-group analyses that the JAMA trial supersedes. Ipriflavone is a synthetic isoflavone marketed as a drug in some countries and as a supplement in others; no carded record names a branded tested product.

cards.headline: JAMA RCT (Alexandersen 2001): NEGATIVE — ipriflavone did not prevent bone loss at any site over 3 years, vertebral fracture counts were identical or nearly so, and 13.2% developed subclinical lymphocytopenia
cards.summary: JAMA RCT (Alexandersen 2001): NEGATIVE — ipriflavone did not prevent bone loss at any site over 3 years, vertebral fracture counts were identical or nearly so, and 13.2% developed subclinical lymphocytopenia
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (JAMA 2001), ipriflavone vs placebo with calcium
cards.people: 474 postmenopausal women aged 45–75 years with bone mineral density <0.86 g/cm², at 4 centres in Belgium, Denmark and Italy (1994–1998), randomised to ipriflavone 200 mg three times daily (n=234) or placebo (n=240); all received calcium 500 mg/day. Product as published: oral ipriflavone 200 mg three times daily; no branded product is named in the record carded.
cards.result: On intention-to-treat analysis at 36 months, annual percentage change in lumbar spine BMD was 0.1% on ipriflavone versus 0.8% on placebo (P=0.14), with no significant difference at any other site, and biochemical markers of bone resorption were also similar between groups (urinary hydroxyproline/creatinine 20.13 vs 20.67 mg/g, P=0.96; urinary CrossLaps/creatinine 268 vs 268 mg/mol, P=0.81). The number of women with new vertebral fracture was identical or nearly so in the two groups at all time points. Lymphocyte concentrations fell significantly on ipriflavone: 31 women (13.2%) developed subclinical lymphocytopenia, 29 of them during treatment; of those 29, 15 (52%) had recovered spontaneously by 1 year and 22 (81%) by 2 years. The authors concluded ipriflavone does not prevent bone loss or affect bone-metabolism markers, and induces lymphocytopenia in a significant number of women.
cards.watchOut: The largest and most rigorous trial on this shelf, and it is frankly negative on efficacy with a real harm signal — it dominates the balance against the two older, smaller positive reports below.
cards.source: Alexandersen P et al. Ipriflavone in the treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2001. PMID: 11255425. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Established-osteoporosis trials report (Agnusdei 1997): two Italian 2-year trials (149 enrolled, 111 completed) — forearm BMD rose on ipriflavone, urinary hydroxyproline fell, and fewer incident vertebral fractures were observed than on placebo
cards.summary: Established-osteoporosis trials report (Agnusdei 1997): two Italian 2-year trials (149 enrolled, 111 completed) — forearm BMD rose on ipriflavone, urinary hydroxyproline fell, and fewer incident vertebral fractures were observed than on placebo
cards.type: Report of two multicentre double-blind randomised trials plus a pooled long-term safety review, ipriflavone vs placebo with calcium
cards.people: 149 elderly osteoporotic women aged 65–79 years with prevalent vertebral fractures, enrolled in two Italian multicentre double-blind 2-year studies, randomised to oral ipriflavone 200 mg three times daily at meals or matching placebo, plus calcium 1 g/day; 111 women completed 2 years. Product as published: oral ipriflavone (i.p.) 200 mg three times daily; no branded product is named in the record carded. This card reports the two trials TOGETHER as published, plus the report's pooled long-term safety review.
cards.result: Forearm bone mineral density (dual photon absorptiometry) increased significantly on ipriflavone, with a significant between-treatment difference in both studies (the placebo groups lost only a little bone, probably because of the calcium supplement). Urinary hydroxyproline fell significantly on ipriflavone, suggesting reduced bone turnover, and a reduction in incident vertebral fractures was observed versus control; bone pain and mobility improved significantly in one study. The same report's safety review covered 2,769 patients treated with ipriflavone (3,132 patient-years across 60 studies in Italy, Japan and Hungary): adverse reactions occurred in 14.5% on ipriflavone versus 16.1% on placebo, mainly gastrointestinal, with few reversible laboratory changes.
cards.watchOut: A combined report of two trials (numbers pooled as published, not two separate cards) using forearm BMD — a weaker site than spine/hip — from the pre-JAMA era; its fracture observation is not a powered fracture endpoint. Superseded in weight by the JAMA 2001 trial above.
cards.source: Agnusdei D et al. Efficacy of ipriflavone in established osteoporosis and long-term safety. Calcified tissue international. 1997. PMID: 9263613. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Senile-osteoporosis trial (Maugeri 1994): 2-year double-blind trial — BMD rose from baseline on ipriflavone and fell on placebo; only 2 new fractures in the ipriflavone group (100 enrolled, 84 completed)
cards.summary: Senile-osteoporosis trial (Maugeri 1994): 2-year double-blind trial — BMD rose from baseline on ipriflavone and fell on placebo; only 2 new fractures in the ipriflavone group (100 enrolled, 84 completed)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised trial, ipriflavone vs placebo with calcium in senile osteoporosis
cards.people: 100 women over 65 years with osteoporosis and at least one previous vertebral fracture, in a multicentre double-blind randomised trial (1990–1993) of ipriflavone 200 mg three times daily (41 completers) or placebo (43 completers), all with oral calcium 1 g/day; 84 women completed. Product as published: ipriflavone 3 × 200 mg/day; no branded product is named in the record carded, and this record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.result: Bone mineral density (distal radius) increased significantly from starting values in the ipriflavone group throughout the study (P<0.05), while the placebo group showed decreased BMD by the end of the study (P<0.05); pain decreased rapidly and analgesic intake dropped on ipriflavone, with decreases in calciuria, hydroxyprolinuria, alkaline phosphatase, osteocalcin and parathyroid hormone values. Only two new fractures occurred in the ipriflavone group during the trial (the record carded does not state the placebo-group fracture count, so no fracture comparison is claimed here).
cards.watchOut: Within-group (versus baseline) significance at a peripheral site, in 84 completers, from 1994 — the weakest design-and-era combination on this shelf; carded to complete the record the slate row assembled, and given no weight against JAMA 2001.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a negative-result shelf — the one large rigorous trial (JAMA 2001, n=474) found no bone-loss prevention, no fracture benefit and a 13.2% subclinical lymphocytopenia rate; the older smaller Italian reports of BMD gains were not confirmed
cards.summary: Synthesis: a negative-result shelf — the one large rigorous trial (JAMA 2001, n=474) found no bone-loss prevention, no fracture benefit and a 13.2% subclinical lymphocytopenia rate; the older smaller Italian reports of BMD gains were not confirmed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Alexandersen 2001 (JAMA; 474 women, 3 years) is decisive in size and rigour: no significant BMD difference at spine, hip or forearm, similar bone-resorption markers, identical or near-identical new vertebral fracture counts, and a lymphocytopenia signal (31 of 234 women, 13.2%, developed subclinical lymphocytopenia on ipriflavone). The earlier reports — Agnusdei 1997 (two Italian trials, 149 enrolled, forearm BMD gains and an unpowered fracture observation) and Maugeri 1994 (100 enrolled, within-group radial BMD gains) — are smaller, older, peripheral-site and largely within-group analyses, and do not outweigh JAMA. Ipriflavone is a synthetic isoflavone marketed as a drug in some countries and as a supplement in others; no carded record names a branded tested product. The honest reading of the whole base is that ipriflavone does not prevent postmenopausal bone loss.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Bazedoxifene monotherapy for osteoporotic fractures: vertebral benefit (42% relative at 3 years) from ONE phase III programme; no overall nonvertebral benefit (PARTIAL vs #1341)
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, does bazedoxifene 20 mg daily (monotherapy), compared with placebo (and raloxifene as active control), reduce new vertebral and nonvertebral fractures? (The bazedoxifene + conjugated estrogens combination question is homed separately at live shelf #1341 and is not asked here.)
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Density · Bone and Bones/pathology · Female · Fractures, Bone/drug therapy · Humans · Indoles/therapeutic use · Lumbar Vertebrae/pathology · Middle Aged · Osteoporosis/drug therapy · Placebos · Postmenopause · Selective Estrogen Receptor Modulators/pharmacology · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for vertebral fractures, from a SINGLE phase III programme (printed on the face). Bazedoxifene 20 mg/day reduced new vertebral fractures versus placebo at 3 years (2.3% vs 4.1% — a 42% relative risk reduction, ≈1.8 percentage points absolute), sustained in the programme's 5-year (4.5% vs 6.8%; 35% relative) and 7-year (7.6% vs 9.9%; 30.4% relative) extensions. Nonvertebral fractures were NOT significantly reduced in the primary population at any time point; the nonvertebral signal appears only in higher-risk subgroups in post-hoc/FRAX-stratified analyses (significant at ≥20% baseline 10-year fracture probability). SERM-class harms (venous thromboembolism, hot flushes/vasodilatation, leg cramps) were more frequent than on placebo. PARTIAL slice: live shelf #1341 covers only the bazedoxifene + conjugated estrogens tissue-selective estrogen complex for menopausal hot flushes and endometrial protection — this shelf asks the monotherapy osteoporosis question that #1341 does not, and the combination evidence is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Phase III primary (Silverman 2008): bazedoxifene 20 mg cut new vertebral fractures versus placebo (2.3% vs 4.1% over 3 years — a 42% relative risk reduction, ≈1.8 percentage points absolute); nonvertebral fractures were NOT significantly reduced in the whole population
cards.summary: Phase III primary (Silverman 2008): bazedoxifene 20 mg cut new vertebral fractures versus placebo (2.3% vs 4.1% over 3 years — a 42% relative risk reduction, ≈1.8 percentage points absolute); nonvertebral fractures were NOT significantly reduced in the whole population
cards.type: Phase III randomised double-blind placebo- and active-controlled trial (single phase III programme — primary report), bazedoxifene monotherapy vs placebo and vs raloxifene
cards.people: 6,847 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis aged 55–85 years in the intention-to-treat population of a 3-year randomised double-blind placebo- and active-controlled trial (core study N=7,492) of bazedoxifene 20 mg/day, bazedoxifene 40 mg/day, raloxifene 60 mg/day or placebo. This shelf cards the bazedoxifene MONOTHERAPY question only (see the cross-point in the balance).
cards.result: New vertebral fractures at 36 months occurred in 2.3% on bazedoxifene 20 mg, 2.5% on bazedoxifene 40 mg and 2.3% on raloxifene versus 4.1% on placebo (all P<0.05) — relative risk reductions of 42%, 37% and 42% respectively, i.e. about 1.8 percentage points absolute for the 20 mg dose. The treatment effect was similar with or without a prevalent vertebral fracture (interaction P=0.89). Nonvertebral fracture incidence did NOT differ significantly from placebo overall; in a POST-HOC subgroup of higher-risk women (n=1,772; femoral neck T-score ≤−3.0 and/or ≥1 moderate/severe or multiple mild vertebral fractures), bazedoxifene 20 mg showed 50% and 44% relative reductions in nonvertebral fracture risk versus placebo (P=0.02) and raloxifene (P=0.05) — labelled post-hoc here and on the face. Bazedoxifene significantly improved BMD and reduced bone-turnover markers (P<0.001 vs placebo). Vasodilatation, leg cramps and venous thromboembolic events were more frequent on bazedoxifene and raloxifene than placebo.
cards.watchOut: ONE-TRIAL PROGRAMME: this and the two extension cards below are one phase III trial and its extensions, not three trials. The nonvertebral benefit is confined to a post-hoc higher-risk subgroup; the primary-population nonvertebral result was not significant.
cards.source: Silverman SL et al. Efficacy of bazedoxifene in reducing new vertebral fracture risk in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis: results from a 3-year, randomized, placebo-, and active-controlled clinical trial. Journal of bone and mineral research. 2008. PMID: 18665787. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: 5-year extension (Silverman 2012): vertebral benefit sustained (4.5% on bazedoxifene 20 mg vs 6.8% on placebo — a 35% relative risk reduction); nonvertebral benefit again only in the higher-risk subgroup, and only the pooled bazedoxifene doses reached significance (34% relative reduction)
cards.summary: 5-year extension (Silverman 2012): vertebral benefit sustained (4.5% on bazedoxifene 20 mg vs 6.8% on placebo — a 35% relative risk reduction); nonvertebral benefit again only in the higher-risk subgroup, and only the pooled bazedoxifene doses reached significance (34% relative reduction)
cards.type: 2-year extension report of the same phase III programme (years 4–5) — not an independent trial
cards.people: 4,216 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis enrolled in a 2-year extension of the 3-year core trial (same single phase III programme as the primary card above); the raloxifene arm was discontinued after 3 years and women on bazedoxifene 40 mg were transitioned to 20 mg after 4 years. Five-year results are reported for bazedoxifene 20 mg, bazedoxifene 40/20 mg and placebo.
cards.result: At 5 years, new vertebral fractures occurred in 4.5% on bazedoxifene 20 mg and 3.9% on 40/20 mg versus 6.8% on placebo (P<0.05) — relative risk reductions of 35% and 40% (≈2.3 and ≈2.9 percentage points absolute). Nonvertebral fracture incidence was similar among groups overall. In the higher-risk subgroup (n=1,324), bazedoxifene 20 mg reduced nonvertebral fracture risk by 37% relative to placebo (P=0.06, not significant); the combined bazedoxifene 20 + 40/20 mg analysis reached significance (34% relative reduction, P<0.05). Bazedoxifene significantly increased BMD and reduced bone turnover versus placebo (P<0.05) and was generally safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: EXTENSION of the primary trial, labelled as such: the analysed population is the subset who entered the extension, and the nonvertebral finding remains subgroup-bound (P=0.06 for the licensed 20 mg dose alone).

(the bazedoxifene + conjugated estrogens combination question is homed separately at live shelf #1341 and is not asked here.) 2-year extension report of the same phase iii programme (years 4–5) — not an independent trial 4,216 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis enrolled in a 2-year extension of the 3-year core trial (same single phase iii programme as the primary card above); the raloxifene arm was discontinued after 3 years and women on bazedoxifene 40 mg were transitioned to 20 mg after 4 years. five-year results are reported for bazedoxifene 20 mg, bazedoxifene 40/20 mg and placebo. at 5 years, new vertebral fractures occurred in 4.5% on bazedoxifene 20 mg and 3.9% on 40/20 mg versus 6.8% on placebo (p<0.05) — relative risk reductions of 35% and 40% (≈2.3 and ≈2.9 percentage points absolute). nonvertebral fracture incidence was similar among groups overall. in the higher-risk subgroup (n=1,324), bazedoxifene 20 mg reduced nonvertebral fracture risk by 37% relative to placebo (p=0.06, not significant); cards.headline: 7-year extension (Palacios 2015): cumulative vertebral fractures still lower on bazedoxifene (6.4% pooled / 7.6% for 20 mg vs 9.9% on placebo — relative reductions 36.5% and 30.4%); NO effect on overall nonvertebral fractures at 7 years
cards.summary: 7-year extension (Palacios 2015): cumulative vertebral fractures still lower on bazedoxifene (6.4% pooled / 7.6% for 20 mg vs 9.9% on placebo — relative reductions 36.5% and 30.4%); NO effect on overall nonvertebral fractures at 7 years
cards.type: Second extension report of the same phase III programme (years 6–7) — not an independent trial
cards.people: 1,530 women in the second 2-year extension (years 6–7) of the same phase III programme; during extension I women on bazedoxifene 40 mg had transitioned to 20 mg, and in extension II all bazedoxifene-treated women continued on 20 mg.
cards.result: At 7 years the cumulative incidence of new vertebral fractures was 6.4% in the pooled bazedoxifene group and 7.6% in the bazedoxifene 20 mg group versus 9.9% on placebo (relative risk reductions 36.5% and 30.4%, both P<0.001; ≈3.5 and ≈2.3 percentage points absolute). Bazedoxifene had NO effect on the overall incidence of nonvertebral fractures (11.2% pooled, 12.0% for 20 mg, 10.8% placebo). Lumbar spine BMD changes were +2.95%, +2.73% and +2.19% respectively, and total hip BMD fell less on bazedoxifene (−1.15% and −1.19%) than placebo (−2.53%; P≤0.002). Safety and tolerability remained favourable across 7 years, with similar adverse events, serious adverse events and discontinuations across groups.
cards.watchOut: By year 7 the analysed cohort (1,530 women) is a survivor subset of the original 7,492 — long-term extension estimates carry attrition bias in both directions and are printed with that limit.

cards.headline: FRAX-stratified analysis (Kaufman 2013): bazedoxifene's fracture benefit grew with baseline FRAX probability — nonvertebral and all-clinical fracture reductions were significant only at ≥20% 10-year fracture probability (hazard ratios ≈0.45 and ≈0.38–0.41); a POST-HOC analysis of the same trial
cards.summary: FRAX-stratified analysis (Kaufman 2013): bazedoxifene's fracture benefit grew with baseline FRAX probability — nonvertebral and all-clinical fracture reductions were significant only at ≥20% 10-year fracture probability (hazard ratios ≈0.45 and ≈0.38–0.41); a POST-HOC analysis of the same trial
cards.type: Post-hoc FRAX-stratified analysis of the same phase III programme — not an independent trial
cards.people: Data from the same pivotal phase III osteoporosis trial (bazedoxifene 20, 40 and 20/40 mg and raloxifene 60 mg versus placebo), re-analysed by baseline 10-year fracture probability (FRAX) using Cox regression — a post-hoc programme analysis, labelled as such, not a new trial.
cards.result: Hazard ratios for vertebral, nonvertebral and all clinical fractures versus placebo DECREASED with increasing baseline FRAX probability for bazedoxifene, while raloxifene's remained generally constant. Bazedoxifene significantly reduced vertebral fracture risk in every FRAX subgroup (HR 0.22–0.66), and at ≥20.0% 10-year fracture probability it significantly reduced nonvertebral fractures (HR 0.45, 0.44 and 0.45 for the 20, 40 and 20/40 mg doses) and all clinical fractures (HR 0.38, 0.41 and 0.40). Raloxifene's vertebral reductions were significant only at lower fracture probabilities and its nonvertebral/all-clinical reductions in no subgroup.
cards.watchOut: POST-HOC and subgroup-based: it explains WHERE the nonvertebral signal lives (higher baseline risk) but cannot upgrade it to a primary-population result.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ONE phase III programme, reported four ways — bazedoxifene 20 mg reduces vertebral fractures (42% relative, ≈1.8 points absolute at 3 years; sustained at 5 and 7 years) with no overall nonvertebral fracture benefit; the nonvertebral signal is confined to higher-risk women in post-hoc/subgroup analyses
cards.summary: Synthesis: ONE phase III programme, reported four ways — bazedoxifene 20 mg reduces vertebral fractures (42% relative, ≈1.8 points absolute at 3 years; sustained at 5 and 7 years) with no overall nonvertebral fracture benefit; the nonvertebral signal is confined to higher-risk women in post-hoc/subgroup analyses
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Silverman 2008 (primary, 6,847 in the intention-to-treat population): vertebral fractures 2.3% vs 4.1% on placebo; nonvertebral fractures not significantly different overall. Silverman 2012 (5-year extension, 4,216 women): vertebral 4.5% vs 6.8%; nonvertebral benefit only in the higher-risk subgroup and significant only for pooled doses. Palacios 2015 (7-year extension, 1,530 women): vertebral 7.6% (20 mg) vs 9.9%; no overall nonvertebral effect. Kaufman 2013 (post-hoc FRAX analysis): benefit concentrated at ≥20% baseline 10-year fracture probability. Harms are SERM-class: more vasodilatation (hot flushes), leg cramps and venous thromboembolic events than placebo in the primary trial. The trial base must be read as a SINGLE programme — four publications, one randomised cohort — and this shelf is the monotherapy slice only: the bazedoxifene + conjugated estrogens combination for menopausal symptoms is a different question, homed at live shelf #1341, and SERM-class evidence is cross-pointed there and to the raloxifene shelves rather than re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Palovarotene in FOP: negative small RCT; open-label MOVE vs natural history (post-hoc benefit, futility at 12 months) — growth-plate closure in ~1 in 3 children
shelves.question: In adults and children with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), does oral palovarotene, compared with placebo (phase 2) or with natural-history comparators (phase 3 MOVE), reduce new heterotopic ossification?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Myositis Ossificans/drug therapy · Ossification, Heterotopic/diagnostic imaging,drug therapy · Pyrazoles/therapeutic use · Stilbenes/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the design asymmetry is printed on the face. The only randomised placebo-controlled trial (phase 2, 40 patients) was NOT significant on its primary endpoint (responders 100%/88.9% on palovarotene vs 88.9% on placebo, P=0.17) or on CT heterotopic-ossification volume. The efficacy case rests on the phase 3 MOVE trial — OPEN-LABEL and SINGLE-ARM, analysed against an external natural-history cohort (97 vs 101): post-hoc 18-month analyses suggested 54–60% relative reductions in annualised new HO volume, but the prespecified 12-month analysis met futility criteria and the month-48 comparison was not significant (46.4% relative, nominal P=0.0585). Retinoid harms lead the harm side: ≥1 retinoid-associated adverse event in 97.0%, and premature physeal (growth-plate) closure in 36.8% of children under 14 (30.0% of under-18s by month 48), with computational signals of vertebral bone weakening. Single-source product: palovarotene (Ipsen, Sohonos), named per the clarification exception.

cards.headline: Phase 2 RCT (Pignolo 2022): the only placebo-controlled trial — responder rates at week 6 were 100% (10/5 mg), 88.9% (5/2.5 mg) and 88.9% on PLACEBO (trend P=0.17, not significant); new HO volume by CT was numerically lower on palovarotene (also not significant)
cards.summary: Phase 2 RCT (Pignolo 2022): the only placebo-controlled trial — responder rates at week 6 were 100% (10/5 mg), 88.9% (5/2.5 mg) and 88.9% on PLACEBO (trend P=0.17, not significant); new HO volume by CT was numerically lower on palovarotene (also not significant)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial, palovarotene vs placebo at flare-up
cards.people: 40 patients with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva aged 7–53 years experiencing a flare-up, in a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled phase 2 trial: cohort 1 (≥15 years) randomised 3:1 to palovarotene 10/5 mg (10 mg weeks 1–2, then 5 mg weeks 3–6) or placebo; cohort 2 (≥6 years) randomised 3:3:2 to palovarotene 10/5 mg, palovarotene 5/2.5 mg or placebo. Pooled: placebo n=10, palovarotene 5/2.5 mg n=9, palovarotene 10/5 mg n=21. Product: palovarotene (Ipsen, Sohonos) — single-source product, named per the clarification exception.
cards.result: The primary endpoint (proportion of responders — no/minimal new heterotopic ossification at the flare-up region by plain radiograph at week 6, per-protocol) was 100% on palovarotene 10/5 mg, 88.9% on 5/2.5 mg and 88.9% on placebo (Cochran-Armitage trend P=0.17 — NOT significant). At week 12 responders were 95.0%, 88.9% and 77.8% (P=0.15). Week-12 least-squares mean new HO volume by CT was 3.8 × 10³ mm³ (10/5 mg), 1.3 × 10³ mm³ (5/2.5 mg) and 18.0 × 10³ mm³ (placebo), with pairwise P≤0.12 versus placebo — again not significant. Palovarotene was well tolerated; no patient discontinued or required dose reduction, and one had a dose interruption for raised lipase. The authors state the findings were not statistically significant but support further evaluation.
cards.watchOut: Small (40 patients, only 10 on placebo) and formally NEGATIVE on its primary endpoint — the placebo responder rate (88.9%) shows how often flare-ups settle without new bone, which is exactly why the uncontrolled phase 3 comparison below cannot be read at face value.

cards.headline: Phase 3 MOVE, 18-month interim (Pignolo 2023): OPEN-LABEL, single-arm — mean annualised new HO volume 60% lower than an external natural-history cohort in post-hoc analyses (54% relative reduction, nominal P=0.039 by weighted model); the prespecified primary analysis had earlier met FUTILITY criteria, and premature physeal closure occurred in 36.8% of children under 14
cards.summary: Phase 3 MOVE, 18-month interim (Pignolo 2023): OPEN-LABEL, single-arm — mean annualised new HO volume 60% lower than an external natural-history cohort in post-hoc analyses (54% relative reduction, nominal P=0.039 by weighted model); the prespecified primary analysis had earlier met FUTILITY criteria, and premature physeal closure occurred in 36.8% of children under 14
cards.type: Open-label single-arm phase 3 trial (MOVE) analysed against an external natural-history cohort — NOT a concurrent placebo control; 18-month interim, post-hoc analyses
cards.people: 97 MOVE participants aged ≥4 years with post-baseline whole-body CT versus 101 untreated natural-history-study participants, in the 18-month interim analysis. Palovarotene dosing: chronic 5 mg once daily; flare-up 20 mg for 4 weeks then 10 mg for ≥8 weeks (weight-adjusted if skeletally immature). Product: palovarotene (Ipsen, Sohonos).
cards.result: The prespecified Bayesian compound Poisson analysis WITH square-root transformation gave a 65.4% probability of any reduction in new HO versus natural history; WITHOUT transformation the probability was 99.4%, and mean annualised new HO volume was 60% lower in MOVE than the natural-history cohort (a relative reduction; the weighted linear mixed-effects model gave a 54% relative reduction, nominal P=0.039). The 12-month interim analysis had met futility criteria and dosing was paused; an independent Data Monitoring Committee recommended continuation, and the 18-month analyses were POST HOC. All palovarotene-treated patients reported ≥1 adverse event, 97.0% reported ≥1 retinoid-associated event, and 29.3% reported ≥1 serious adverse event — including premature physeal closure/epiphyseal disorder in 21 of 57 (36.8%) patients aged <14 years. Post-hoc computational analyses also showed decreased vertebral BMD, content and strength and increased vertebral fracture risk on palovarotene.
cards.watchOut: DESIGN ASYMMETRY, printed on the face: MOVE has no concurrent control arm — every efficacy number is a comparison with a separate natural-history cohort, several analyses are post hoc, and the trial's own prespecified 12-month analysis met futility. The growth-plate harm in children (36.8% under 14) is a first-order part of the balance.

flare-up 20 mg for 4 weeks then 10 mg for ≥8 weeks (weight-adjusted if skeletally immature). product: palovarotene (ipsen, sohonos). the prespecified bayesian compound poisson analysis with square-root transformation gave a 65.4% probability of any reduction in new ho versus natural history; without transformation the probability was 99.4%, and mean annualised new ho volume was 60% lower in move than the natural-history cohort (a relative reduction; the weighted linear mixed-effects model gave a 54% relative reduction, nominal p=0.039). the 12-month interim analysis had met futility criteria and dosing was paused; an independent data monitoring committee recommended continuation, and the 18-month analyses were post hoc. all palovarotene-treated patients reported ≥1 adverse event, 97.0% reported ≥1 retinoid-associated event, and 29.3% reported ≥1 serious adverse event — including premature physeal closure/epiphyseal disorder in 21 of 57 (36.8%) patients aged <14 years. post-hoc computational analyses also showed decreased vertebral bmd, content and strength and increased vertebral fracture risk on palovarotene. design asymmetry, printed on the face: move has no concurrent control arm — every efficacy number is a comparison with a separate natural-history cohort, several analyses are post hoc, and the trial's own prespecified 12-month analysis met futility. the growth-plate harm in children (36.8% under 14) is a first-order part of the balance. pignolo rj et al. reduction of new heterotopic ossification (ho) in the open-label, phase 3 move trial of palovarotene for fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (fop). journal of bone and mineral research. 2023. pmid: 36583535. registry id: nct03312634 (move); cards.headline: MOVE month-48 report (Pignolo 2026): long-term exploratory analyses — mean annualised new HO volume numerically 46.4% lower than natural history but NOT significant (nominal P=0.0585); premature physeal closure in 24 of 80 patients under 18 (30.0%), all under 14
cards.summary: MOVE month-48 report (Pignolo 2026): long-term exploratory analyses — mean annualised new HO volume numerically 46.4% lower than natural history but NOT significant (nominal P=0.0585); premature physeal closure in 24 of 80 patients under 18 (30.0%), all under 14
cards.type: Month-48 exploratory post-hoc report of the open-label MOVE programme (same trial as the card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: Post-baseline HO measurements in 97 palovarotene-treated MOVE patients and 101 untreated natural-history patients, over 48 months including time on and off treatment (exploratory, post-hoc analyses of the same MOVE programme as the card above — not a new trial). 80 MOVE patients were aged <18 years, treated for a mean of 166.0 weeks.
cards.result: Across 48 months, mean annualised new HO volume was numerically lower (46.4% relative) in palovarotene-treated patients than untreated patients, but the difference was NOT significant (nominal P=0.0585). In patients who paused and stopped, or paused and restarted, annualised new HO volume appeared lower on treatment than off (significance not assessed). Proportions of patients with new HO and numbers of affected body regions were similar between treated and untreated patients (significance not assessed); flare-up rates were consistent with published literature. Adverse events were predominantly retinoid-associated mucocutaneous events. Premature physeal closure occurred in 24 of 80 patients aged <18 years (30.0%), all aged <14 years. Computational analyses showed a significantly increased risk of radiographically observed, asymptomatic new vertebral deformities on palovarotene. The authors state these exploratory analyses reaffirm the month-18 findings but must be interpreted with caution. This record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.watchOut: Exploratory and post hoc with a non-significant headline comparison at 48 months; the paediatric growth-plate signal persists (30.0% of under-18s). Long duration does not cure the absence of a concurrent control.
cards.source: Pignolo RJ et al. Palovarotene impact on fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP): data from month 48 of the phase III MOVE trial. JBMR plus. 2026. PMID: 42770123. Registry ID: NCT03312634. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: the randomised trial was small and formally negative; the efficacy case rests on an open-label single-arm phase 3 trial compared with natural history, whose prespecified analysis met futility and whose supportive analyses are post hoc — set against retinoid harms including premature growth-plate closure in roughly a third of treated children
cards.summary: Synthesis: the randomised trial was small and formally negative; the efficacy case rests on an open-label single-arm phase 3 trial compared with natural history, whose prespecified analysis met futility and whose supportive analyses are post hoc — set against retinoid harms including premature growth-plate closure in roughly a third of treated children
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Phase 2 (40 patients, placebo-controlled): no significant benefit on the primary responder endpoint (placebo itself 88.9%) or on CT HO volume. MOVE phase 3 (97 treated vs 101 natural-history): post-hoc 18-month analyses suggested 54–60% relative reductions in annualised new HO volume, but the prespecified 12-month analysis met futility, dosing was paused, and the month-48 headline comparison was not significant (46.4% relative, nominal P=0.0585). Harms: near-universal retinoid-associated adverse events (97.0% at 18 months), premature physeal closure in 21/57 (36.8%) of under-14s at 18 months and 24/80 (30.0%) of under-18s by month 48, and computational signals of reduced vertebral bone strength and new vertebral deformities. Palovarotene (Ipsen, Sohonos) is approved in several countries for FOP; the approval rested on the month-18 interim dataset. The design asymmetry — one small negative RCT plus one uncontrolled programme — is the shelf's central fact.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Garetosmab in FOP: OPTIMA phase 3 — 19 new lesions on placebo vs 1–2 on garetosmab; LUMINA-1 missed its primary endpoint but suppressed new lesions
shelves.question: In adults with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP), does the activin-A-blocking antibody garetosmab, compared with placebo, reduce new heterotopic ossification lesions and flare-ups (LUMINA-1 / OPTIMA programme)?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Female · Humans · Male · Young Adult · Activins/antagonists & inhibitors · Antibodies, Monoclonal/therapeutic use,adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Myositis Ossificans/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two genuine randomised trials in an ultra-rare disease (total randomised N=107, printed on the face). OPTIMA phase 3 (63 adults) found 19 new heterotopic bone lesions on placebo versus 1 on garetosmab 3 mg/kg and 2 on 10 mg/kg at week 56 (rate ratios 0.06 and 0.10, both significant; no deaths). LUMINA-1 phase 2 (44 adults) MISSED its primary PET-CT lesion-activity endpoint (P=0.0741) but suppressed new lesions, with no new lesions after placebo patients crossed over (0% vs 40.9%, P=0.0027); all patients had treatment-emergent adverse events (epistaxis, madarosis, skin abscesses) and 5 deaths (11.4%) occurred in its open-label period — considered unlikely related, causality not excludable. The flare-up analysis is post-hoc and labelled as such. Adults only; single-source product (Regeneron), named per the clarification exception.

cards.headline: LUMINA-1 phase 2 RCT (Di Rocco 2023): primary PET-CT lesion-activity endpoint MISSED (P=0.0741) — but new heterotopic ossification lesions were suppressed, and no placebo patient who crossed over to garetosmab developed a new lesion (0% vs 40.9%, P=0.0027); 5 deaths in the open-label period (11.4%), causality not excludable
cards.summary: LUMINA-1 phase 2 RCT (Di Rocco 2023): primary PET-CT lesion-activity endpoint MISSED (P=0.0741) — but new heterotopic ossification lesions were suppressed, and no placebo patient who crossed over to garetosmab developed a new lesion (0% vs 40.9%, P=0.0027); 5 deaths in the open-label period (11.4%), causality not excludable
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (LUMINA-1), garetosmab vs placebo in adults with FOP (N=44)
cards.people: 44 adults with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva randomised to intravenous garetosmab 10 mg/kg (n=20) or placebo (n=24) every 4 weeks for 28 weeks (period 1), followed by a 28-week open-label garetosmab period (n=43). Product: garetosmab (Regeneron) — single-source product, named per the clarification exception. FOP is ultra-rare; trial sizes are small by necessity and each N is printed on its card.
cards.result: The primary efficacy endpoint in period 1 (total lesion activity by PET-CT) was NOT met (P=0.0741). However, development of new HO lesions was suppressed in period 1, so the period 2 primary endpoint was prospectively changed to the number of new HO lesions versus period 1: no placebo patient crossing over to garetosmab developed new HO lesions (0% in period 2 versus 40.9% in period 1; P=0.0027). All patients had at least one treatment-emergent adverse event in period 1, notably epistaxis, madarosis (eyelash loss) and skin abscesses. Five deaths (5 of 44; 11.4%) occurred in the open-label period; they were considered unlikely to be related, but the report states causality cannot be ruled out.
cards.watchOut: N=44 — small by necessity in an ultra-rare disease, but small nonetheless: the randomised period's own primary endpoint missed, the new-lesion result leans on a prospectively changed period-2 endpoint, and the 5 open-label deaths (11.4%) are part of the record, not a footnote.
cards.source: Di Rocco M et al. Garetosmab in fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial. Nature medicine. 2023. PMID: 37770652. cards.headline: OPTIMA phase 3 RCT (Papa 2026): new heterotopic bone lesions 19 on placebo versus 1 (3 mg/kg) and 2 (10 mg/kg) on garetosmab at week 56 — rate ratios 0.06 and 0.10 (both significant); no deaths
cards.summary: OPTIMA phase 3 RCT (Papa 2026): new heterotopic bone lesions 19 on placebo versus 1 (3 mg/kg) and 2 (10 mg/kg) on garetosmab at week 56 — rate ratios 0.06 and 0.10 (both significant); no deaths
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (OPTIMA), garetosmab vs placebo in adults with FOP (N=63)
cards.people: 63 adults aged ≥18 years with FOP at 18 sites in 16 countries/regions, randomised 1:1:1 to monthly intravenous placebo (n=21), garetosmab 3 mg/kg (n=19) or garetosmab 10 mg/kg (n=23); mean age 26.6 years, 60% women. 62 participants completed 56 weeks. Product: garetosmab (Regeneron).
cards.result: The total number of new heterotopic bone lesions at week 56 was 19 on placebo versus 1 on garetosmab 3 mg/kg (rate ratio 0.06, 95% CI 0.00–0.73; P=0.027) and 2 on garetosmab 10 mg/kg (rate ratio 0.10, 95% CI 0.01–0.76; P=0.026) — relative reductions of roughly 94% and 90% in lesion rate, on small absolute lesion counts (19 vs 1 vs 2). Treatment-emergent adverse events of special interest occurred in 1 of 21 (5%) on placebo, 0 of 19 on 3 mg/kg and 4 of 23 (17%) on 10 mg/kg, all considered treatment-related. No deaths occurred. The authors conclude garetosmab substantially reduced new lesions and was generally well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: N=63 with only 22 total new lesions across all arms: the relative effect is large and significant, but the absolute event count is small, follow-up is 56 weeks, and the trial is in adults only — no paediatric efficacy or safety data are in this record.
cards.source: Papa R et al. Efficacy and safety of garetosmab, an activin A-blocking antibody, in fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (OPTIMA): a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. The Lancet. 2026. cards.headline: LUMINA-1 post-hoc flare-up analysis (Keen 2024): POST-HOC — 71% of placebo patients flared over 28 weeks and flares tracked with more new bone; garetosmab shortened median flare duration (15.0 vs 48.0 days) and reduced flare severity
cards.summary: LUMINA-1 post-hoc flare-up analysis (Keen 2024): POST-HOC — 71% of placebo patients flared over 28 weeks and flares tracked with more new bone; garetosmab shortened median flare duration (15.0 vs 48.0 days) and reduced flare severity
cards.type: Post-hoc analysis of the LUMINA-1 randomised trial (same programme as the phase 2 card — not an independent trial)
cards.people: The 44 adults of LUMINA-1 (same trial as the phase 2 card above), in a post-hoc analysis of patient-reported flare-ups (any 2 of: new pain, swelling, joint stiffness, decreased movement, perceived HO) across the 28-week placebo-controlled period and the open-label periods — labelled post-hoc here and on the face.
cards.result: Flare-ups were experienced by 71% (17/24) of placebo-treated patients; 59% (10/17) of those developed a new HO lesion irrespective of flare-up location, and only 24% of flare-ups location-matched a new lesion. Of 29 new HO lesions in the placebo cohort by week 28, 12 (41%) were at the site of a new or ongoing flare-up, and placebo patients with a prior flare-up formed more new bone (median new HO volume 16.6 vs 3.2 cm³). Garetosmab had previously been shown to reduce flare-up frequency in period 1; in this analysis it also reduced median flare duration (15.0 vs 48.0 days) and flare severity versus placebo, with numerically less corticosteroid use (40.0% vs 58.3%).
cards.watchOut: POST-HOC by the authors' own description, and of the same trial already carded: it characterises flare-ups and generates the flare-duration/severity findings — it is not a third trial and is not counted as one.
cards.source: Keen R et al.
