Journal of bone and mineral research. 2024. PMID: 39216107. Registry ID: NCT03188666. cards.headline: LUMINA-1 imaging programme report (González Trotter 2025): CT-only imaging performed similarly to PET/CT for detecting new HO lesions (patients with new lesions 14/44 by PET/CT vs 12/44 by CT only; kappa 0.46) — a methods report OF the LUMINA-1 programme, carded to complete the record
cards.summary: LUMINA-1 imaging programme report (González Trotter 2025): CT-only imaging performed similarly to PET/CT for detecting new HO lesions (patients with new lesions 14/44 by PET/CT vs 12/44 by CT only; kappa 0.46) — a methods report OF the LUMINA-1 programme, carded to complete the record
cards.type: Post-hoc imaging-methods comparison within the LUMINA-1 programme (same trial as the phase 2 card — not independent efficacy evidence)
cards.people: The 44 LUMINA-1 participants, whose baseline-to-week-28 PET/CT and CT-only scans were independently reviewed by two blinded reader sets plus an adjudicator (a report OF the LUMINA-1 programme, not a separate trial).
cards.result: The number of patients with new lesions was 14/44 (31.8%) by PET/CT and 12/44 (27.3%) by CT only; aggregate new-lesion counts/volumes were very similar between modalities in both treatment groups (placebo: 27 lesions/245.0 cm³ by PET/CT vs 37/261.8 cm³ by CT only; garetosmab: 3/21.3 cm³ vs 1/0.1 cm³). Mean new lesions per patient were 0.68 (SD 1.57) by PET/CT versus 0.86 (SD 1.95) by CT only, with moderate agreement for identifying patients with new lesions (kappa 0.46, 95% CI 0.17–0.74). The authors conclude CT-only imaging is a viable option for assessing new HO in FOP trials.
cards.watchOut: A measurement-methods report: it supports using CT alone in future FOP trials and incidentally re-displays the lesion contrast between arms, but it adds no independent efficacy evidence.
cards.source: González Trotter D et al. Comparison of PET/CT versus CT only in the assessment of new heterotopic ossification bone lesions in patients with fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva. cards.headline: Synthesis: two genuine randomised trials — phase 2 missed its imaging-activity primary endpoint but suppressed new lesions (with 5 open-label deaths, causality not excludable), and phase 3 OPTIMA showed a large, significant reduction in new lesions (19 on placebo vs 1–2 on garetosmab) over 56 weeks in adults; total randomised N is 107 in an ultra-rare disease

cards.result: LUMINA-1 (n=44): primary PET-CT lesion-activity endpoint missed (P=0.0741); new-lesion suppression in period 1 and 0% new lesions after crossover versus 40.9% before (P=0.0027); adverse events in all patients (epistaxis, madarosis, skin abscesses) and 5 deaths (11.4%) in the open-label period, considered unlikely related but not excludable. OPTIMA (n=63): 19 new lesions on placebo versus 1 (3 mg/kg) and 2 (10 mg/kg) on garetosmab at week 56 (rate ratios 0.06 and 0.10), adverse events of special interest in 0–17% on garetosmab versus 5% on placebo, and no deaths. The post-hoc flare analysis (labelled) and the imaging-methods report (labelled) complete the LUMINA-1 record without adding independent trials. Evidence is adults-only; the served total randomised base is 44 + 63 = 107 patients — small in absolute terms because FOP is ultra-rare, and printed here rather than hidden.

shelves.title: Setrusumab in osteogenesis imperfecta: ASTEROID missed its primary BMD endpoint (strength estimates up ~3%, no fracture difference) — phase 3 fenced (press-only)
shelves.question: In adults with osteogenesis imperfecta, does the sclerostin-neutralising antibody setrusumab (BPS804), compared with placebo or baseline, increase bone mineral density and bone formation (ASTEROID programme)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Osteogenesis Imperfecta/drug therapy,diagnostic imaging,pathology,physiopathology · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Adult · Bone Density/drug effects · Aged · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — ONE development programme (BPS804/setrusumab) reported across phase 2 publications and imaging/biopsy substudies, with SURROGATE endpoints only (printed on the face). ASTEROID phase 2b (110 adults) MISSED its primary endpoint (no change in radial trabecular volumetric BMD at 12 months); modelled bone-strength estimates rose ~3% at 8–20 mg/kg, and annualised fracture rates did NOT differ between doses. The phase 2a study was open-label with N=14. The timelapse and bone-matrix reports are ASTEROID substudies, labelled as such. PHASE 3 FENCE: the phase 3 programme's fracture endpoints were reported missed in a December 2025 topline press release with no journal publication — it is fenced, never carded or counted on this shelf, and no fracture benefit is claimed.

cards.headline: ASTEROID phase 2b (Glorieux 2024): primary endpoint MISSED — no change in radial trabecular volumetric BMD at 12 months; estimated bone strength rose (failure load +3.17% on 20 mg/kg; stiffness +3.06%/+3.19% on 8/20 mg/kg); fracture rates did not differ between doses
cards.summary: ASTEROID phase 2b (Glorieux 2024): primary endpoint MISSED — no change in radial trabecular volumetric BMD at 12 months; estimated bone strength rose (failure load +3.17% on 20 mg/kg; stiffness +3.06%/+3.19% on 8/20 mg/kg); fracture rates did not differ between doses
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial (ASTEROID), setrusumab vs placebo in adults with OI
cards.people: 110 adults with osteogenesis imperfecta type I, III or IV (pathogenic COL1A1/A2 variant, recent fragility fracture), randomised 1:1:1:1 to setrusumab 2, 8 or 20 mg/kg or placebo by monthly intravenous infusion for 12 months; placebo patients were subsequently reassigned to open-label setrusumab 20 mg/kg, so only the double-blind dose groups are reported. Product: setrusumab (BPS804).
cards.result: At 12 months there was NO change in radial trabecular volumetric BMD (the primary endpoint; P>0.05). Mean failure load (micro-finite-element bone-strength estimate) increased significantly in the 20 mg/kg group (+3.17%, SE 1.26%) and stiffness increased in the 8 mg/kg (+3.06%, SE 1.70%) and 20 mg/kg (+3.19%, SE 1.29%) groups from baseline. Gains were similar across OI types. There were NO significant differences in annualised fracture rates between doses. Two adults in the 20 mg/kg group experienced related serious adverse reactions. The authors conclude setrusumab benefited estimates of bone strength and provides the basis for phase 3 evaluation.
cards.watchOut: SURROGATE endpoints throughout: the primary BMD endpoint was negative and the positive findings are modelled bone-strength estimates; no fracture benefit was shown. One programme (ASTEROID) — the two cards below are its substudies, labelled as such.

cards.headline: Phase 2a (Glorieux 2017): 21-week open-label dose-escalation — bone-formation markers rose sharply (P1NP +84%) and lumbar spine aBMD rose 4% on BPS804 (setrusumab); N=14 total (9 treated, 5 reference) — printed on the face
cards.summary: Phase 2a (Glorieux 2017): 21-week open-label dose-escalation — bone-formation markers rose sharply (P1NP +84%) and lumbar spine aBMD rose 4% on BPS804 (setrusumab); N=14 total (9 treated, 5 reference) — printed on the face
cards.type: Phase 2a open-label randomised dose-escalation trial with untreated reference group, BPS804 (setrusumab) in adults with moderate OI (N=14)
cards.people: 14 adults with moderate osteogenesis imperfecta (BPS804 group n=9, mean age 30.7 years, mean aBMD Z-score −2.6; untreated reference group n=5, mean age 27.4 years, Z-score −2.2), receiving three escalating infusions (5, 10, 20 mg/kg, each 2 weeks apart) or no treatment, over 21 weeks. N=14 — a very small study, printed on the face per the small-base labelling rule.
cards.result: By day 43 in the BPS804 group, procollagen type 1 N-propeptide (P1NP) rose 84% (P<0.001), P1CP 53% (P=0.003), bone-specific alkaline phosphatase 59% (P<0.001) and osteocalcin 44% (P=0.012) versus baseline (reference group: +6%, +5%, −13% and −19%, mostly non-significant); CTX-1 fell 44% on BPS804 versus −7% on reference. Lumbar spine areal BMD rose 4% by day 141 on BPS804 (P=0.038) versus 1% on reference (P=0.138). There were 32 adverse events in nine patients, none suspected treatment-related, and no treatment-related fractures. The authors concluded BPS804 stimulates bone formation, reduces resorption and increases lumbar spine aBMD in moderate OI.
cards.watchOut: N=14, open-label, 21 weeks, biomarker endpoints: first-in-OI pharmacology, never load-bearing. Its role on this shelf is to show where the programme started; the ASTEROID card above carries the comparative evidence.

cards.headline: ASTEROID timelapse HR-pQCT substudy (Hosseinitabatabaei 2025): a SUBSTUDY of ASTEROID (78 participants' longitudinal scans) — dose-dependent increases in bone formation and resorption on setrusumab by timelapse imaging; primarily a methods paper (measurement error <1% with the chosen method)
cards.summary: ASTEROID timelapse HR-pQCT substudy (Hosseinitabatabaei 2025): a SUBSTUDY of ASTEROID (78 participants' longitudinal scans) — dose-dependent increases in bone formation and resorption on setrusumab by timelapse imaging; primarily a methods paper (measurement error <1% with the chosen method)
cards.type: Timelapse HR-pQCT imaging substudy/methods report of the ASTEROID phase 2b trial (same programme as the ASTEROID card — not an independent trial)
cards.people: Adults with osteogenesis imperfecta in the ASTEROID phase 2b trial: 29 same-day repeated scans used to optimise the timelapse method, and longitudinal scans (baseline, 6, 12, 18, 24 months) from 78 participants treated with setrusumab (anabolic) or zoledronic acid (anti-catabolic) within the ASTEROID programme — labelled a substudy of ASTEROID, not an independent trial. This record carries no registry ID for the substudy itself.
cards.result: For grayscale input images with 3D registration, a density threshold of 200 mgHA/cm³ with Gaussian noise reduction gave measurement errors <1% (binary images gave errors of ~13% and ~8% on first- and second-generation scanners). Timelapse analysis then showed a dose-dependent increase in bone formation AND resorption with setrusumab treatment; zoledronic acid shifted changes in favour of formation, though no zoledronic-acid change reached statistical significance. The authors present the method as a non-invasive imaging biomarker for future studies.
cards.watchOut: A methods-and-biomarker substudy OF ASTEROID: it shows bone remodelling moved, in both directions (formation and resorption rose), and adds no fracture or independent efficacy evidence.
cards.source: Hosseinitabatabaei S et al. Non-invasive quantification of bone (re)modeling dynamics in adults with osteogenesis imperfecta treated with setrusumab using timelapse high-resolution peripheral-quantitative computed tomography. cards.headline: ASTEROID bone-matrix substudy (Rummler 2024): a SUBSTUDY of ASTEROID — transiliac biopsies after 6 months of setrusumab showed bone matrix mineralisation and collagen orientation NOT adversely affected; inter-label bone modulus and hardness were lower on setrusumab than in untreated OI
cards.summary: ASTEROID bone-matrix substudy (Rummler 2024): a SUBSTUDY of ASTEROID — transiliac biopsies after 6 months of setrusumab showed bone matrix mineralisation and collagen orientation NOT adversely affected; inter-label bone modulus and hardness were lower on setrusumab than in untreated OI
cards.type: Bone-matrix biopsy substudy of the ASTEROID phase 2b trial (same programme as the ASTEROID card — not an independent trial)
cards.people: Tetracycline-labelled transiliac biopsies from three groups — controls with no metabolic bone disease, individuals with osteogenesis imperfecta, and individuals with OI after 6 months of setrusumab in the ASTEROID trial — examined by histomorphometry, nanoindentation, Raman spectroscopy, second-harmonic-generation imaging, quantitative backscattered electron imaging and small-angle X-ray scattering. Labelled a substudy of ASTEROID, not an independent trial; the record does not state the biopsy-group sizes, so none is printed here.
cards.result: Collagen orientation did not differ between groups. Bone mineral density distribution and Raman spectra indicated the OI groups had greater mean mineralisation, greater relative mineral content and lower crystallinity than controls, and setrusumab did NOT alter this. Modulus and hardness were LOWER in the inter-label (newly formed) bone of the setrusumab-treated OI group than in the untreated OI group. The authors conclude setrusumab increases bone mass while not adversely affecting bone matrix properties in OI, and note OI bone fragility may stem from organisation at higher length scales than the matrix itself.
cards.watchOut: A safety-of-matrix substudy: 'not adversely affected' is its claim, on biopsy material from an unstated number of participants — it cannot support an efficacy claim, and the lower modulus/hardness in newly formed bone is recorded here rather than smoothed over.
cards.source: Rummler M et al. Bone matrix properties in adults with osteogenesis imperfecta are not adversely affected by setrusumab-a sclerostin neutralizing antibody. Journal of bone and mineral research. 2024. PMID: 38982734. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: ONE programme (BPS804/setrusumab) — a 14-patient open-label phase 2a biomarker study and the ASTEROID phase 2b trial, whose primary BMD endpoint was negative, whose bone-strength estimates rose, and which showed no fracture-rate difference; the phase 3 programme is FENCED (press-release only, fracture endpoints reported missed) and is not carded or counted

shelves.title: Teriparatide in adults with osteogenesis imperfecta: BMD up (alone, mainly type I) but TOPaZ combination did not reduce fractures (HR 0.97)
shelves.question: In adults with osteogenesis imperfecta, does teriparatide (in the TOPaZ trial, combined with zoledronic acid, compared with standard care; and in an earlier trial, compared with placebo) increase bone mineral density and reduce fractures?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — BMD and fractures point in different directions, across two trials asking different questions (printed on the face). Teriparatide ALONE (Orwoll 2014, 79 adults, placebo-controlled) raised lumbar spine BMD (+6.1% vs +2.8%) and hip BMD (+2.6% vs −2.4%) over 18 months, with the response essentially confined to type I OI and NO difference in self-reported fractures. Teriparatide PLUS zoledronic acid (TOPaZ, JAMA 2026, 349 adults, vs standard care) did NOT reduce adjudicated incident fractures (36.9% vs 36.4%; HR 0.97) despite significantly greater BMD gains — a combination result that must never be worded as a teriparatide-alone effect. Fracture outcomes are secondary/surrogate-limited in the alone trial (BMD primary) and null-primary in TOPaZ. The third card is a biomarker report of the 2014 trial's lineage (verified before carding, per the row's stop-condition), not an independent trial.

cards.headline: TOPaZ RCT (Hald 2026, JAMA): teriparatide PLUS zoledronic acid did NOT reduce fractures versus standard care (36.9% vs 36.4% with incident fractures; HR 0.97) despite significantly greater BMD gains — a COMBINATION result, never a teriparatide-alone effect
cards.summary: TOPaZ RCT (Hald 2026, JAMA): teriparatide PLUS zoledronic acid did NOT reduce fractures versus standard care (36.9% vs 36.4% with incident fractures; HR 0.97) despite significantly greater BMD gains — a COMBINATION result, never a teriparatide-alone effect
cards.type: Multicentre open-label randomised clinical trial (TOPaZ), teriparatide followed by zoledronic acid vs standard care in adults with OI (N=349 evaluable)
cards.people: 349 evaluable adults with a clinical diagnosis of osteogenesis imperfecta at 27 referral centres (350 randomised: 176 to teriparatide + zoledronic acid, 174 to standard care, 1 withdrew), mean age 43.7 years, 53.9% women; most had type I OI from type 1 collagen gene variants. The active group received teriparatide 20 µg daily by subcutaneous injection for 2 years followed by one 5 mg zoledronic acid infusion; in standard care, bisphosphonates and other bone-targeted medicines were allowed but teriparatide and other anabolics were prohibited. Trial conducted May 2017 to March 2025, open-label with blinded fracture adjudication.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — participants with imaging-proven incident fractures — occurred in 65 of 176 (36.9%) on teriparatide + zoledronic acid versus 63 of 173 (36.4%) on standard care (absolute risk reduction −1.57%, 95% CI −9.90% to +5.89%; hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.68–1.38): NO fracture reduction. Lumbar spine and total hip BMD increased significantly more with teriparatide + zoledronic acid than standard care, and several quality-of-life measures favoured the active group. Adverse events were similar in both groups. The authors conclude the BMD gain without fracture benefit suggests reduced bone QUALITY, rather than low bone density, drives fracture in OI.
cards.watchOut: COMBINATION caveat, binding on any quotation of this shelf: TOPaZ tested teriparatide PLUS zoledronic acid against standard care (which itself could include bisphosphonates) — its null fracture result is a combination result and must never be worded as a teriparatide-alone effect. Open-label treatment (fracture adjudication was blinded).
cards.source: Hald JD et al. Teriparatide Plus Zoledronic Acid for Osteogenesis Imperfecta: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2026. PMID: 42133304. Registry ID: ISRCTN15313991. cards.headline: Teriparatide-alone RCT (Orwoll 2014): lumbar spine aBMD +6.1% vs +2.8% and total hip +2.6% vs −2.4% on placebo at 18 months — but self-reported fractures did NOT differ, and the anabolic response was essentially confined to type I OI (no benefit in types III/IV)
cards.summary: Teriparatide-alone RCT (Orwoll 2014): lumbar spine aBMD +6.1% vs +2.8% and total hip +2.6% vs −2.4% on placebo at 18 months — but self-reported fractures did NOT differ, and the anabolic response was essentially confined to type I OI (no benefit in types III/IV)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, teriparatide alone vs placebo in adults with OI (N=79)
cards.people: 79 adults with osteogenesis imperfecta randomised to teriparatide 20 µg daily or placebo for 18 months in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial — the teriparatide-ALONE evidence on this shelf.
cards.result: Lumbar spine areal BMD rose 6.1% (±1.0%) on teriparatide versus 2.8% (±1.0%) on placebo (P<0.05) and total hip areal BMD rose 2.6% versus −2.4% (P<0.001). Vertebral volumetric BMD and estimated strength improved on teriparatide (+18% ±6% and +15% ±3%) but declined on placebo (−5.0% ±6% and −2.0% ±3%; P<0.05 for both). P1NP rose 135% (±14%) and urinary NTx 64% (±10%) on teriparatide. The P1NP response was less pronounced in severe (type III/IV) OI, type I patients showed robust BMD increases, and there was NO observed benefit in type III/IV OI. There was no difference in self-reported fractures between the groups.
cards.watchOut: BMD was the primary endpoint and fractures were self-reported and secondary — this trial shows an anabolic BMD effect (in type I disease), not fracture protection. N=79 across all OI types, so the type III/IV subgroup is small.
cards.source: Orwoll ES et al. Evaluation of teriparatide treatment in adults with osteogenesis imperfecta. The Journal of clinical investigation. 2014. PMID: 24463451. Registry ID: NCT00131469. cards.headline: Collagen-biomarker report OF the 2014 trial's lineage (Nicol 2021): in type I OI, teriparatide raised biomarkers of collagens II–VI; in types III/IV the responses were blunted — a biomarker report of the Orwoll trial programme, verified as that trial's lineage (18-month teriparatide vs placebo, type I vs III/IV strata)
cards.summary: Collagen-biomarker report OF the 2014 trial's lineage (Nicol 2021): in type I OI, teriparatide raised biomarkers of collagens II–VI; in types III/IV the responses were blunted — a biomarker report of the Orwoll trial programme, verified as that trial's lineage (18-month teriparatide vs placebo, type I vs III/IV strata)
cards.type: Collagen-biomarker report of the Orwoll 2014 teriparatide-in-OI trial lineage (same trial programme as the card above — not an independent trial)
cards.people: Individuals with type I and types III/IV osteogenesis imperfecta treated with an 18-month course of teriparatide or placebo in the trial programme reported by Orwoll 2014 (the card above) — this report's design (18 months, teriparatide vs placebo, type I vs III/IV strata, prior collagen-I biomarker reporting from the same therapy course) matches that trial, and the lineage was verified from the record before carding, as the commissioning row required. A comparison group of postmenopausal women without OI treated with teriparatide is also reported. Labelled a biomarker report — not an independent trial.
cards.result: In type I OI, teriparatide increased serum biomarkers of collagens II, III, IV, V and VI. In types III/IV OI these biomarker responses were BLUNTED, as previously reported for collagen I biomarkers during the same teriparatide therapy. In postmenopausal women without OI, teriparatide had no effect on the collagen II, V and VI biomarkers assessed. The authors interpret this as teriparatide having abnormal, widespread effects on extracellular-matrix collagen homeostasis in OI, likely from skeletal and extra-skeletal tissues.
cards.watchOut: Biomarkers only: no BMD, strength or fracture data. Its value here is mechanistic corroboration of the type I versus III/IV divide seen in the parent trial. Lineage stop-condition: this card was carded ONLY because its record verifies the 18-month teriparatide-vs-placebo, type-stratified lineage of the 2014 trial; had that failed, this shelf would have stopped at two reports.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two trials, two different questions — teriparatide ALONE raises BMD in adults with OI (mainly type I; fractures self-reported, no difference), while teriparatide PLUS zoledronic acid in TOPaZ did not reduce adjudicated fractures versus standard care despite larger BMD gains; BMD and fracture outcomes point in different directions in OI
cards.summary: Synthesis: two trials, two different questions — teriparatide ALONE raises BMD in adults with OI (mainly type I; fractures self-reported, no difference), while teriparatide PLUS zoledronic acid in TOPaZ did not reduce adjudicated fractures versus standard care despite larger BMD gains; BMD and fracture outcomes point in different directions in OI
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Orwoll 2014 (n=79, teriparatide alone vs placebo, 18 months): spine aBMD +6.1% vs +2.8%, hip +2.6% vs −2.4%, vertebral strength estimates up — with no difference in self-reported fractures and no observed benefit in type III/IV OI; its biomarker lineage report (Nicol 2021, labelled) shows the same type I versus III/IV divide across collagens II–VI. TOPaZ (Hald 2026, n=349, teriparatide followed by zoledronic acid vs standard care): incident fractures 36.9% vs 36.4% (HR 0.97) — no fracture reduction despite significantly greater BMD increases, leading its authors to invoke bone quality over density. Fracture outcomes in both trials are secondary or (in TOPaZ) a null primary; no report on this shelf shows teriparatide, alone or combined, reducing fractures in adults with OI.

shelves.title: 2-minute walk test norms: healthy Chinese mean 199.1 m (973 adults), NIH Toolbox personalised percentiles in 1,385 US adults, obesity limb mean 176 m — equations explain only ~a third of variance
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what distance is walked in two minutes — reference equations and percentile values for the 2-minute walk test by age, sex and height — and how do the equations from different populations compare?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anthropometry · Body Weight · China · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Healthy Volunteers · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Walk Test/standards · Walking · Young Adult · United States · Walk Test · Cross-Sectional Studies · Independent Living · Asian People · Exercise Test/methods · Obesity · Walk Test/methods
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, ch. 84 (sports physiology) and Boron & Boulpaep, exercise physiology — the framing is general, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary measurement literature, and says so. Two large healthy-adult datasets anchor the row: 973 healthy Chinese adults aged 18–85 (mean 2-minute walk distance 199.1 ± 25.81 m; age and height the independent predictors, explaining only about a third of the variance) and 1,385 healthy community-dwelling US adults from the NIH Toolbox study, whose personalised (age, sex, height neighbours-based) reference values were slightly more precise than smooth age-based values (average interquartile range 149 ft (≈45 m) vs 158 ft (≈48 m); agreement ICC 0.96). A third dataset (295 middle-aged and elderly Chinese adults WITH OBESITY, mean 176 ± 20 m) is carded as an obesity limb only, never merged into the healthy norms, per the commissioning row. The stamp is graded down because the equations are population-specific, the predictors explain only ~28–35% of the variance, and corridor/encouragement protocol moves distances — there is no single universal 2-minute distance. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING. Cross-points: the 6-minute walk reference shelf and the incremental shuttle walk shelf (#7253) are different tests with different reference sets, not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Healthy Chinese reference equations (Zhang 2018): 973 healthy adults aged 18–85 walked a mean 199.1 ± 25.81 m in two minutes; age and height predict distance but explain only 35% (men) and 34% (women) of its variance
cards.summary: Healthy Chinese reference equations (Zhang 2018): 973 healthy adults aged 18–85 walked a mean 199.1 ± 25.81 m in two minutes; age and height predict distance but explain only 35% (men) and 34% (women) of its variance
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (2-minute walk reference equations, healthy Chinese adults)
cards.people: 973 healthy Chinese volunteers aged 18–85 years; each performed two 2-minute walk tests under a standardised protocol and the longer distance was analysed; sex-specific reference equations were derived by stepwise multiple regression on age, height and weight.
cards.result: Mean 2-minute walk distance for all participants was 199.1 ± 25.81 m. Age and height were the independent factors influencing distance in both sexes, explaining 35% of the variance in men and 34% in women — that is, about two-thirds of the variation between healthy people is NOT captured by the equations. The study's product is the pair of sex-specific reference equations for healthy Chinese adults, intended as the reference standard for settings where the 6-minute test is impractical.
cards.watchOut: Population- and protocol-bound: a single-country (China) equation set from the better of two walks; applying it to other populations or to a single-walk protocol misreads the reference.
cards.source: Zhang J et al. Two-minute walk test: Reference equations for healthy adults in China. PloS one. 2018. PMID: 30092036. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: NIH Toolbox personalised reference values (Kittelson 2023): 1,385 healthy US adults aged 18–85 — neighbours-based values (age, sex, height) slightly more precise than age-only smooth models (interquartile range 149 ft (≈45 m) vs 158 ft (≈48 m); ICC 0.96)

cards.type: Primary human physiology study (2-minute walk personalised reference values, NIH Toolbox, healthy US adults)
cards.people: 1,385 healthy, community-dwelling adult participants aged 18–85 years from the National Institutes of Health Toolbox study sites across the United States; cross-sectional analysis developing Two-Minute Walk Test reference values by two methods — generalised additive models for location, scale and shape (smooth function of age) and a semiparametric neighbours-based approach accounting for age, sex and height.
cards.result: Both methods gave accurate coverage of realised values and agreed closely overall (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.96), though they differed case by case. The neighbours-based (personalised) values were more precise by interquartile range (average 149 ft, 95% CI 146 to 152 ft; ≈45 m) than the age-based values (158 ft, 95% CI 155 to 162 ft; ≈48 m), with similar interdecile ranges (369 ft (≈112 m) vs 374 ft (≈114 m)). Height adjustment mattered most for people at extremes of height. The fetched record reports precision and coverage, not a single mean distance, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: A percentile-generating method paper: its deliverable is a way to compute an individual's expected range, and its widths (an interquartile span of about 45 m) show how wide 'normal' is for this test even in a large healthy sample.
cards.source: Kittelson AJ et al. Personalized Reference Values for the Two-Minute Walk Test: An Analysis of Cross-Sectional Data From the National Institutes of Health Toolbox Study. Archives of physical medicine and rehabilitation. 2023. PMID: 37037295. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Obesity limb, carded separately (Zhang 2022): 295 middle-aged and elderly Chinese adults with obesity walked a mean 176 ± 20 m in two minutes — age and BMI predict distance (28% men, 32% women of variance); NOT a healthy-norm anchor
cards.summary: Obesity limb, carded separately (Zhang 2022): 295 middle-aged and elderly Chinese adults with obesity walked a mean 176 ± 20 m in two minutes — age and BMI predict distance (28% men, 32% women of variance); NOT a healthy-norm anchor
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (2-minute walk reference equations, Chinese adults with obesity — population limb)
cards.people: 295 middle-aged and elderly Chinese individuals with obesity (body mass index above 30 kg/m2, the group the healthy equations of Zhang 2018 did not cover); two 2-minute walk tests performed, the longer distance analysed, and obesity-specific reference equations derived by stepwise regression. Carded as a population limb only, per the commissioning row — never merged into the healthy norms above.
cards.result: Mean 2-minute walk distance was 176 ± 20 m — about 23 m below the healthy Chinese mean of the companion study. Age and body mass index were the independent predictors, explaining 28% of the variance in men and 32% in women. The equations are offered for evaluating functional capacity and monitoring treatment in middle-aged and elderly Chinese people with obesity.
cards.watchOut: Different denominator: these are reference equations FOR people with obesity, so a distance 'normal' on this limb would be low against the healthy equations — the two must never be averaged or interchanged.
cards.source: Zhang J et al. Two-minute walk distance reference equations for middle-aged and elderly Chinese individuals with obesity. PloS one. 2022. PMID: 36001629. cards.headline: Synthesis: healthy 2-minute walk distance centres near 199 m in the large Chinese dataset, US personalised percentiles agree closely between methods, and obesity lowers the centre to about 176 m — but equations explain only about a third of healthy variation, so the test's reference values are population- and protocol-specific
cards.summary: Synthesis: healthy 2-minute walk distance centres near 199 m in the large Chinese dataset, US personalised percentiles agree closely between methods, and obesity lowers the centre to about 176 m — but equations explain only about a third of healthy variation, so the test's reference values are population- and protocol-specific
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above (973 healthy Chinese adults; 1,385 healthy US adults; 295 Chinese adults with obesity).
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (sports physiology) and Boron & Boulpaep (exercise physiology) — framing general; the shelf rests on the primary measurement literature. The healthy anchors agree that age and height (and, in the US analysis, sex via the neighbours method) set the expected distance, and that the spread around expectation is wide: interquartile spans of about 45–48 m in the NIH Toolbox analysis and only 34–35% of variance explained by the Chinese equations. The obesity limb sits clearly lower (mean 176 ± 20 m). The 6-minute walk and incremental shuttle walk tests (the latter at shelf #7253) have their own reference sets and are cross-points, not substitutes. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: two healthy datasets are large and concordant in method, but every equation is bound to its population and to the better-of-two-walks standardised protocol, and no equation predicts an individual's distance tightly.
cards.watchOut: Corridor length, encouragement and practice walks move 2-minute distances; a value below an equation's prediction is a prompt to look for a cause, not a diagnosis by itself.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: 1-minute sit-to-stand norms (PARTIAL to #7161): sea-level medians 38 reps in the 20s falling to 23–24 in the 70s (Chile, n=499; Portugal, n=546), high-altitude equations kept as a separate limb (n=400)
shelves.question: In healthy adults, how many repetitions of the one-minute sit-to-stand test are performed — reference values by age and sex at sea level and at high altitude — and how do they relate to the five-times and 30-second variants?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Adult · Chile · Middle Aged · Reference Values · Aged · Adolescent · Young Adult · Aged, 80 and over · Cross-Sectional Studies · Exercise Test/methods,standards · Exercise/physiology · Portugal · Body Mass Index · Exercise Test · Sex Factors · Age Factors · Altitude · Exercise Test/methods · Linear Models · Sitting Position
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: as for the companion walk-test shelf, Guyton & Hall's exercise/motor chapters frame mobility generally — the framing is thin, and this shelf rests on the primary measurement literature, and says so. PARTIAL home: pack #7161 asks the FIVE-TIMES sit-to-stand time and the 30-SECOND chair-stand count; the 1-minute repetition-count protocol — the variant used in respiratory and cardiac clinics — is not its question, and only that unasked slice is carded here, with #7161 cross-pointed. Stop-condition check: the row required a third primary healthy reference dataset beyond the two verified at mining (Chilean sea-level, n=499; high-altitude, n=400); a third was verified this session from its fetched record — Vilarinho 2024, 546 Portuguese adults without disabilities — so the condition is MET. The three datasets agree on shape: medians/counts fall steadily with age (Chilean medians 38 repetitions at 18–29 years falling to 23–24 at 70–80 years, lower limits of normality 15–17 in the oldest group), the Portuguese equation subtracts 0.34 repetitions per year of age, and the high-altitude equations are carded as a SEPARATE limb — altitude and sea-level norms are never merged. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: all three datasets are from 2024–2025, each is population-bound, and none has been replicated across protocols. The Short Physical Performance Battery shelf (which embeds the five-times variant only) is a further cross-point, not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Sea-level reference values (Otto-Yáñez 2025): 499 healthy Chilean adults — median 1-minute sit-to-stand 38 repetitions at 18–29 years (lower limit of normality 27–28) falling to 23 (men) and 24 (women) at 70–80 years (LLN 15–17)
cards.summary: Sea-level reference values (Otto-Yáñez 2025): 499 healthy Chilean adults — median 1-minute sit-to-stand 38 repetitions at 18–29 years (lower limit of normality 27–28) falling to 23 (men) and 24 (women) at 70–80 years (LLN 15–17)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (1-minute sit-to-stand reference values, healthy Chilean adults, sea level)
cards.people: Multicentre cross-sectional study at six locations in Chile: 499 healthy adults aged 18–80 years (57.5% women, n=287); anthropometry, physical activity, smoking status and Borg ratings recorded alongside the number of repetitions performed in the 1-minute sit-to-stand test; reference values determined by sex and age range.
cards.result: Median repetitions fell steadily with age in both sexes. In men, the median (and lower limit of normality) ranged from 38 repetitions (LLN 27) at 18–29 years to 23 repetitions (LLN 15) at 70–80 years. In women, the median ranged from 38 repetitions (LLN 28) at 18–29 years to 24 repetitions (LLN 17) at 70–80 years. These are the first reference values for the healthy Chilean population.
cards.watchOut: One country's sea-level norms, with a relatively high mean body mass index (27.3 ± 4.1 kg/m2) in the sample: chair height and population fitness move repetition counts, so these medians are a reference, not a universal pass mark.
cards.source: Otto-Yáñez M et al. One-minute sit-to-stand test: Reference values for the Chilean population. PloS one. 2025. PMID: 39879255. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Third primary dataset — the row's stop-condition (Vilarinho 2024): 546 Portuguese adults without disabilities aged 18–95 — reference equation 1MSTS = 61.53 − (0.34 × age) − (3.57 × sex) − (0.33 × BMI), r² = 26%
cards.summary: Third primary dataset — the row's stop-condition (Vilarinho 2024): 546 Portuguese adults without disabilities aged 18–95 — reference equation 1MSTS = 61.53 − (0.34 × age) − (3.57 × sex) − (0.33 × BMI), r² = 26%
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (1-minute and 5-times sit-to-stand reference values, Portuguese adults)
cards.people: Cross-sectional study in Portugal: 546 adult community volunteers without disabilities, age range 18–95 years, 58% female; age, sex, height, weight, body mass index, smoking and physical activity recorded; participants performed three repetitions of the 1-minute sit-to-stand and the 5-times sit-to-stand tests and the best was analysed; normative values provided by sex for each age decade. Verified from its fetched record this session as the third primary healthy dataset the commissioning row required.
cards.result: The reference equation for the 1-minute test was 1MSTS = 61.53 − (0.34 × age) − (3.57 × sex) − (0.33 × BMI), explaining 26% of the variance — that is, repetitions fall by about a third of a repetition per year of age, are lower in the sex coded positive in the equation and fall as BMI rises, while about three-quarters of individual variation lies outside the equation. The companion 5-times equation was 5TSTS = 3.89 + (0.10 × age) − (0.96 × physical activity), r² = 27% — the five-times protocol itself is homed at pack #7161 and is cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.watchOut: Best-of-three attempts and a volunteer sample spanning 18–95 years: decade norms from volunteers without disabilities describe the willing and able, and the equation's sex coding is as printed in the record.
cards.source: Vilarinho R et al. Reference values for the 1-minute sit-to-stand and 5 times sit-to-stand tests to assess functional capacity: a cross-sectional study. Physiotherapy. 2024. PMID: 38875841. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: High-altitude limb, carded separately (Morales-Satan 2025): 400 healthy adults aged 18–80 living at high altitude — predictive equations by sex (men: 19.833 − 0.168×age + 0.204×height − 0.122×weight; women: 27.845 − 0.198×age + 0.145×height − 0.094×weight); never merged with sea-level norms
cards.summary: High-altitude limb, carded separately (Morales-Satan 2025): 400 healthy adults aged 18–80 living at high altitude — predictive equations by sex (men: 19.833 − 0.168×age + 0.204×height − 0.122×weight; women: 27.845 − 0.198×age + 0.145×height − 0.094×weight); never merged with sea-level norms
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (1-minute sit-to-stand reference values, high-altitude residents — separate limb)
cards.people: Multicentre cross-sectional study in two high-altitude cities: 400 healthy adults aged 18–80 years (58% women); anthropometry, physical activity and smoking recorded with the number of 1-minute sit-to-stand repetitions; multiple linear regression used to generate sex-specific predictive equations. Carded as the altitude limb only, per the commissioning row.
cards.result: The predictive equations were: men, 1minSTST = 19.833 − (age × 0.168) + (height × 0.204) − (weight × 0.122); women, 1minSTST = 27.845 − (age × 0.198) + (height × 0.145) − (weight × 0.094) — repetitions fall with age and weight and rise with height in both sexes. The study established the first reference values for the healthy population aged 18–80 years living at high altitude; the fetched record presents the equations rather than decade medians, and this card claims no decade values.
cards.watchOut: Altitude is the variable: these equations describe acclimatised high-altitude residents and must not be applied to sea-level patients, nor the sea-level cards above to altitude residents.
cards.source: Morales-Satan M et al. One-minute sit-to-stand test reference values in people living at high altitudes. Colombia medica (Cali, Colombia). 2025. PMID: 40585476. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: three primary healthy datasets (499 Chilean sea-level; 546 Portuguese; 400 high-altitude) agree the 1-minute count falls steadily with age — from medians of 38 in the twenties to 23–24 in the seventies at sea level — and this shelf cards only the 1-minute protocol that pack #7161 does not ask
cards.summary: Synthesis: three primary healthy datasets (499 Chilean sea-level; 546 Portuguese; 400 high-altitude) agree the 1-minute count falls steadily with age — from medians of 38 in the twenties to 23–24 in the seventies at sea level — and this shelf cards only the 1-minute protocol that pack #7161 does not ask
cards.people: Synthesis of the three primary datasets carded above.
cards.result: Framing thin (Guyton & Hall exercise/motor chapters); the measurement literature carries the shelf. Sea-level medians in Chile run from 38 repetitions at 18–29 years to 23 (men) and 24 (women) at 70–80 years, with lower limits of normality of 15–17 in the oldest group; the Portuguese equation independently gives a decline of 0.34 repetitions per year of age with lower counts at higher BMI; the high-altitude equations show the same age/weight/height structure in a separate population that must not be pooled with sea-level values. Pack #7161 (five-times time and 30-second count) and the Short Physical Performance Battery (five-times variant) are cross-points. PHYSIOLOGY — EMERGING: the three datasets are recent (2024–2025), population-bound and not yet cross-validated against each other's protocols, as printed on the cards.
cards.watchOut: Chair height, arm use and encouragement change counts materially; compare a patient only against the protocol and population limb that matches how the test was actually done.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, motor control chapters (thin framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative literature, and says so). Three large community cohorts give the composite 0–12 Short Physical Performance Battery distribution: Tromsø (7,474 Norwegians aged ≥40; mean 11.4, SD 1.3, with a hard ceiling in every age group), Yishun, Singapore (538 adults aged 21–90; means 11.6 in men and 11.5 in women, most adults scoring the maximum) and SABE, Colombia (4,211 adults aged ≥60; mean 8.73, SD 2.0 — a genuinely older, lower-scoring population, not a contradiction). The score is ordinal with a ceiling: the distribution, not the mean alone, is the content, and protocol variants (4-m vs 8-ft gait course) are carded per study. The battery's components are homed separately (gait speed, five-times sit-to-stand pack #7161, single-leg stance) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Tromsø reference values (Bergland 2019): 7,474 community-dwelling Norwegians aged ≥40 — mean SPPB 11.4 (SD 1.3), men 0.28 points higher than women, main decline from the mid-sixties, ceiling effects in every age group
cards.summary: Tromsø reference values (Bergland 2019): 7,474 community-dwelling Norwegians aged ≥40 — mean SPPB 11.4 (SD 1.3), men 0.28 points higher than women, main decline from the mid-sixties, ceiling effects in every age group
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (SPPB normative reference values, Tromsø Study)
cards.people: 7,474 home-dwelling participants (53.2% women) aged 40 years or older in the 7th wave of the Tromsø Study, Norway; SPPB comprising a timed 4-m walk, a timed repeated chair sit-to-stand test and 10-s balance tests (side-by-side, semi-tandem and full-tandem).
cards.result: The mean SPPB total score for the entire sample was 11.4 (SD 1.3) points; on average the total score was 0.28 points greater in men than in women (P < 0.001), with significant sex differences in all age groups (40–49, 50–59, 60–69, 70–74, 75–79 and 80+ years). The main decline in physical function occurred in the mid-sixties, slightly earlier in women than in men. Ceiling effects were observed in all age groups, and the authors provide age-specific percentiles (5th to 95th) and conclude the battery should be reported as the total sum score plus the registered chair-stand and 4-m walk times.
cards.watchOut: Ceiling by construction: a mean of 11.4 out of 12 in a ≥40 population means the battery cannot discriminate among fitter younger adults — read the percentile distribution, not the mean alone.
cards.source: Bergland A et al. Norwegian reference values for the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB): the Tromsø Study. BMC geriatrics. 2019. PMID: 31395008. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Yishun reference values (Lee 2021): 538 Singaporean adults aged 21–90 — mean SPPB 11.6 (SD 1.1) in men and 11.5 (SD 1.2) in women, with at least half of adults aged 21–80 at the maximum score; the gait course here is 8 ft, not 4 m
cards.summary: Yishun reference values (Lee 2021): 538 Singaporean adults aged 21–90 — mean SPPB 11.6 (SD 1.1) in men and 11.5 (SD 1.2) in women, with at least half of adults aged 21–80 at the maximum score; the gait course here is 8 ft, not 4 m
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (SPPB normative reference values, Yishun study)
cards.people: 538 community-dwelling Singaporean adults (57.8% women) aged 21–90 years in the Yishun study; SPPB with an 8-ft gait-speed course, five-times repeated chair sit-to-stand and balance subtests.
cards.result: Mean SPPB score was 11.6 (SD 1.1) in men and 11.5 (SD 1.2) in women; the majority of participants (at least 50%) aged 21–80 years achieved the maximum SPPB score. Total and subtest scores generally decreased with age (all P < 0.001) but did not differ between the sexes. Among adults aged ≥60, the optimal cut-off discriminating sarcopenia under the criteria tested was SPPB ≤11 points (and gait-speed subtest ≤1.0 m/s) in both sexes — a discrimination cut-off from this cohort, not a universal disability threshold.
cards.watchOut: Protocol variant on the face: this cohort timed an 8-ft gait course while Tromsø timed 4 m — subtest times are not interchangeable between the two protocols, even though both yield a 0–12 composite.
cards.source: Lee SY et al. SPPB reference values and performance in assessing sarcopenia in community-dwelling Singaporeans - Yishun study. BMC geriatrics. 2021. PMID: 33781211. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SABE Colombia normative values (Ramírez-Vélez 2020): 4,211 adults aged ≥60 — mean SPPB 8.73 (SD 2.0), men 0.85 points higher than women, with age-specific percentiles from the LMS method
cards.summary: SABE Colombia normative values (Ramírez-Vélez 2020): 4,211 adults aged ≥60 — mean SPPB 8.73 (SD 2.0), men 0.85 points higher than women, with age-specific percentiles from the LMS method
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (SPPB normative values, SABE Colombia)
cards.people: 4,211 community-dwelling Colombian adults (57.3% women) aged 60 years or older in the Health and Well-being and Aging Survey in Colombia (SABE), 2015, who completed the SPPB with anthropometric measurements.
cards.result: The mean SPPB total score for the entire sample was 8.73 (2.0) points — far below the Norwegian and Singaporean means, in a sample restricted to ages ≥60. On average the total score was 0.85 points greater in men than in women (P < 0.001), with significant sex differences in all three age groups (60–69, 70–79, 80+ years). Age-specific percentiles (3rd to 97th) were calculated by the LMS method; age, body mass, height, body mass index and calf circumference contributed significantly to walking speed after adjustment.
cards.watchOut: The lower mean is a sampling-frame effect (≥60 only, a general older population) — do not read the gap between 8.73 and the Tromsø 11.4 as a country effect without the age structures, which differ by design.
cards.source: Ramírez-Vélez R et al. Normative Values for the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) and Their Association With Anthropometric Variables in Older Colombian Adults. The SABE Study, 2015. Frontiers in medicine. 2020. PMID: 32154258. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: the SPPB composite sits at its ceiling (means 11.4–11.6) in mixed-age community samples and falls to a mean of 8.73 in a ≥60-only population — the distribution and the age structure, per protocol, are the reference values
cards.summary: Synthesis: the SPPB composite sits at its ceiling (means 11.4–11.6) in mixed-age community samples and falls to a mean of 8.73 in a ≥60-only population — the distribution and the age structure, per protocol, are the reference values
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (motor control; thin framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary normative literature). Tromsø (Bergland 2019; 7,474 adults ≥40; 4-m gait course) gives mean 11.4 (SD 1.3) with ceiling effects in every age group and the main decline from the mid-sixties; Yishun (Lee 2021; 538 adults 21–90; 8-ft gait course) gives 11.6 in men and 11.5 in women with most adults at the maximum; SABE Colombia (Ramírez-Vélez 2020; 4,211 adults ≥60) gives 8.73 (2.0), where the conventional ≤9 / ≤10 disability-risk zone is therefore common rather than exceptional. Men score modestly higher in the two large cohorts (+0.28 and +0.85 points). The composite is this shelf's question; its components are homed separately — gait speed, the five-times sit-to-stand (pack #7161) and single-leg stance — and are cross-pointed, not re-carded here. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: three large community cohorts with published percentile distributions, bound to their protocols as printed on each card.
cards.watchOut: Never merge subtest times across the 4-m and 8-ft gait protocols, and never quote a mean SPPB without the sample's age range: the same battery yields 11.4 or 8.73 depending on who was sampled.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: DXA T-score reference: the primary NHANES III dataset itself (14,646 adults) carded; Irish BMD matches it, Swedish 25-year-olds sit +0.54 SD above manufacturer reference, and reference choice once swung femoral-neck osteoporosis from 2.3% to 27.6% of patients
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are DXA bone-mineral-density reference values — the young-adult mean and SD at the femoral neck and lumbar spine from which T-scores are calculated, and the BMD distribution by age, sex and ancestry in population samples — and how much does the choice of reference population (NHANES III vs manufacturer vs country-specific) reclassify who has osteoporosis?

shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, bone / calcium metabolism chapters (framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary densitometry-reference literature, and says so). STOP-CONDITION MET, as printed on the face: the primary NHANES III young-adult proximal-femur reference dataset itself is carded (Looker 1998 — 14,646 US adults from both NHANES III phases, whose non-Hispanic white total-femur data were selected as the reference database for femur standardisation), alongside three further reports (total 4). Around it: Irish proximal-femur BMD proved broadly similar to the NHANES III Caucasian reference (DXA-HIP, 6,729 adults); Swedish 25-year-old women sat ABOVE manufacturer and NHANES III references (Peak-25, n=1,061), arguing for country-specific young-adult data; and in over 2,000 patients the choice of standardisation plus reference set swung femoral-neck osteoporosis classification from 2.3% to 27.6%. This shelf reports reference data and reclassification only — treatment thresholds live on the osteoporosis shelves. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: PRIMARY NHANES III reference dataset (Looker 1998): proximal-femur BMD in 14,646 US adults aged ≥20 from both NHANES III phases (1988–1994), by age, sex and race/ethnicity — the non-Hispanic white total-femur data selected as the reference database for femur standardisation
cards.summary: PRIMARY NHANES III reference dataset (Looker 1998): proximal-femur BMD in 14,646 US adults aged ≥20 from both NHANES III phases (1988–1994), by age, sex and race/ethnicity — the non-Hispanic white total-femur data selected as the reference database for femur standardisation
cards.type: Primary population physiology dataset (NHANES III proximal-femur BMD reference data, both phases)
cards.people: 14,646 men and women aged 20 years and older in the nationally representative NHANES III sample (1988–1994, both phases); dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry bone mineral density, bone mineral content and scanned area in four proximal-femur regions (femur neck, trochanter, intertrochanter and total), provided separately by age and sex for non-Hispanic whites, non-Hispanic blacks and Mexican Americans. This is the primary dataset from which the young-adult (20–29 year) reference means and SDs behind femoral T-scores are drawn.
cards.result: This updated report (both phases, superseding the phase-1-only report) found non-Hispanic whites in the southern United States had slightly lower BMD than in other regions, but not enough to prevent pooling. The updated BMD data for the total femur region in non-Hispanic whites have been selected as the reference database for femur standardisation efforts by the International Committee on Standards in Bone Measurements. The fetched abstract describes the dataset, its strata and its reference role; it does not print the young-adult mean and SD values themselves, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: Every femoral T-score inherits this dataset's young non-Hispanic white stratum: a T-score is a distance from these 1988–1994 US volunteers, measured on era densitometers — cross-calibration to a modern scanner is part of the measurement, not a detail.
cards.source: Looker AC et al. Updated data on proximal femur bone mineral levels of US adults. Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA. 1998. PMID: 9850356. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: DXA-HIP, Ireland (E 2021): proximal-femur BMD in 6,729 healthy Irish adults broadly similar to the NHANES III Caucasian reference, especially in middle age — supporting NHANES III T- and Z-scores for Irish adults
cards.summary: DXA-HIP, Ireland (E 2021): proximal-femur BMD in 6,729 healthy Irish adults broadly similar to the NHANES III Caucasian reference, especially in middle age — supporting NHANES III T- and Z-scores for Irish adults
cards.type: Primary population physiology dataset (Irish DXA-HIP proximal-femur BMD vs NHANES III reference)
cards.people: 6,729 healthy Irish Caucasian adults (88% women, 5,923 of 6,729) selected from 36,321 adults who had a screening DXA scan (GE Lunar) at three centres in the west of Ireland, excluding bone disease, major fracture risk factors and osteoporosis medication; the majority aged 40–89 years. White female NHANES III T-scores were calculated across each decade and compared with published NHANES III Caucasian data.
cards.result: Proximal-femur BMD of healthy Irish men and women was broadly similar to that of the NHANES III reference population, especially in middle-aged adults; results differed for very young and very old adults, likely reflecting small sample size and referral bias. The authors conclude the results support using the NHANES III reference population to calculate proximal-femur T-scores and Z-scores for establishing the presence or prevalence of osteoporosis in Ireland.
cards.watchOut: A screening-referral sample (only 18.5% of scanned adults met the healthy criteria, and 88% were women): the similarity verdict is strongest exactly where the sample is densest — middle age — and weakest at the young ages that define the reference itself.
cards.source: E E et al. How does proximal femur BMD of healthy Irish adults compare to NHANES III? Results of the DXA-HIP Project. Archives of osteoporosis. 2021. PMID: 34773128. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Peak-25, Sweden (Callréus 2014): 1,061 women aged 25 — standardised BMD 1.5–8.3% higher at the femoral neck than comparison cohorts, with manufacturer-reference Z-scores of +0.54 (femoral neck), +0.47 (total hip) and +0.32 (lumbar spine); country-specific young-adult reference data argued for
cards.summary: Peak-25, Sweden (Callréus 2014): 1,061 women aged 25 — standardised BMD 1.5–8.3% higher at the femoral neck than comparison cohorts, with manufacturer-reference Z-scores of +0.54 (femoral neck), +0.47 (total hip) and +0.32 (lumbar spine); country-specific young-adult reference data argued for
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (young-adult DXA reference data, Peak-25 cohort, women aged 25)
cards.people: 1,061 women of the population-based Peak-25 cohort in Sweden (age 25.5 ± 0.2 years); BMD measured at all sites by DXA, standardised (sBMD) and compared with NHANES III and other equivalent cohorts, with Z-scores calculated from DXA manufacturer-supplied reference values.
cards.result: Against manufacturer reference values, Z-scores were 0.54 ± 0.98 (femoral neck), 0.47 ± 0.96 (total hip) and 0.32 ± 1.03 (lumbar spine) — that is, these healthy 25-year-olds sat about half a standard deviation ABOVE the reference they would be scored against. Standardised BMD was higher than in other equivalently aged European and North American cohorts (femoral neck 1.5%–8.3%; total hip 3.9%–9.2%; lumbar spine 2.4%–6.5%), except trochanter sBMD, which was 2.5% lower than NHANES III. Correlation between DXA sites was strong (r = 0.62–0.94). The authors argue country-specific young-adult reference data are warranted, because non-regional reference data could contribute to misdiagnosed osteoporosis in elderly women.
cards.watchOut: Women only, at a single age (25): this card measures how far a real young-adult population can sit from the reference mean — it cannot itself supply a male or multi-age reference.

cards.headline: Reclassification experiment (Simmons 1997): in over 2,000 patients, changing standardisation method and reference set together swung osteoporosis classification from 9.6% to 21.1% at the spine and from 2.3% to 27.6% at the femoral neck
cards.summary: Reclassification experiment (Simmons 1997): in over 2,000 patients, changing standardisation method and reference set together swung osteoporosis classification from 9.6% to 21.1% at the spine and from 2.3% to 27.6% at the femoral neck
cards.type: Primary measurement study (effect of standardisation and reference values on DXA patient classification)
cards.people: Over 2,000 patients classified by T-score for spine and femur DXA under competing combinations: two standardisation methods (International DXA Standardization Committee and the European Community COMAC-BME group) combined with young reference data from the major DXA manufacturers, the COMAC-BME group and NHANES III.
cards.result: The two standardisation techniques produced dissimilar classifications (kappa = 0.34–0.90), especially for the femoral neck, with up to 24.3% of patients reclassified from osteopenic to normal and 18.6% reclassified from osteoporotic to osteopenic when the standardisation method was changed. Considering reference data and standardisation together, the number classified as osteoporotic varied from 9.6% to 21.1% for the postero-anterior spine L2–4 region and from 2.3% to 27.6% for the femoral neck, with agreement between classifications ranging from very poor to excellent (kappa = 0.02–0.98). The authors conclude creating standardised reference data must be a priority.
cards.watchOut: A 1997 experiment from the pre-standardisation era: its percentages measure the bad old system, not today's — but it remains the clearest quantification of why the reference set is a clinical decision, and modern cross-calibration exists because of results like these.
cards.source: Simmons A et al. The effects of standardization and reference values on patient classification for spine and femur dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry. cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (bone / calcium metabolism; brief framing — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary densitometry-reference literature). The stop-condition for this row is met on the face: the primary NHANES III proximal-femur reference dataset itself is carded (Looker 1998, PMID 9850356; 14,646 adults, both phases), with three further reports, four in total. DXA-HIP (E 2021; 6,729 Irish adults) finds the NHANES III Caucasian reference transportable to Ireland; Peak-25 (Callréus 2014; 1,061 Swedish women aged 25) finds a young population sitting above manufacturer references (Z +0.54 at the femoral neck), arguing for country-specific data; Simmons 1997 (over 2,000 patients) quantifies the stakes — reference and standardisation choices together moved femoral-neck osteoporosis prevalence between 2.3% and 27.6%. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: the reference architecture (NHANES III young-adult mean and SD at the proximal femur) is the settled international standard, and its population limits are documented on the cards, not hidden.
cards.watchOut: A T-score never travels alone: state the site, the scanner family and the reference set. This shelf makes no treatment recommendation — who to treat lives on the osteoporosis shelves.

shelves.title: Trabecular bone score norms: peak ≈1.42 in young adults, falling 0.27%/year in women vs 0.11%/year in men (Thai data), with Japanese women below Caucasian women at every age
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the trabecular bone score (TBS) of the lumbar spine — its mean, spread and age-related decline by sex and ancestry — and how much does the choice of reference population move the values against which an individual's bone microarchitecture is judged?

shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED. Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, bone / calcium metabolism chapters (framing brief — rests chiefly on the primary densitometry-reference literature, and says so). Four population datasets on three continents tell one story: lumbar trabecular bone score peaks in young adulthood (peak mean ≈1.42 in both Thai and Iranian data) and declines with age — slowly in men (≈0.11%/year in Thai data) and faster in women (≈0.27%/year; a 16.0% linear fall from age 45 to 90 in US white women), with absolute levels differing by ancestry (Japanese women lower than Caucasian women at every age, the gap widening to age 65). TBS is a texture index from the spine DXA image, NOT bone mineral density — the DXA BMD / T-score reference shelf is the cross-point, not re-carded here. Every curve is software-version-bound (TBS iNsight, Med-Imaps) and the version is carded beside the data.

cards.headline: JPOS normative values in 3,069 Japanese women: mean TBS 1.187 ± 0.137, a three-piece age curve (little change young, rapid mid-life loss, slow late loss) explaining 70.7% of variance — lower than Caucasian women at every age (Iki 2015)
cards.summary: JPOS normative values in 3,069 Japanese women: mean TBS 1.187 ± 0.137, a three-piece age curve (little change young, rapid mid-life loss, slow late loss) explaining 70.7% of variance — lower than Caucasian women at every age (Iki 2015)
cards.type: Primary physiology / normative study (population-based, Japanese women)
cards.people: 4,550 women aged 15–79 randomly selected from 7 areas of Japan; after excluding under-20s and conditions affecting bone metabolism, 3,069 women with at least two assessable L1–L4 vertebrae were analysed. Mean age 48.7 ± 16.8 years, BMI 22.9 ± 3.4, spine aBMD 0.888 ± 0.169 g/cm². TBS from spine DXA using TBS iNsight software (Med-Imaps, France).
cards.result: A three-piece linear regression of TBS on age explained 70.7% of total variance: very small age-related change in the youngest segment, rapid loss in the middle segment, and small loss in the oldest segment. TBS was lower in Japanese women than in Caucasian women across all age ranges, with the difference increasing with age up through 65 years.
cards.watchOut: Women only, one ancestry, one software generation: the curve defines Japanese female norms and itself demonstrates why Caucasian curves cannot be borrowed for Asian populations.
cards.source: Iki M et al. Age-related normative values of trabecular bone score (TBS) for Japanese women: the Japanese Population-based Osteoporosis (JPOS) study. Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA. 2015. PMID: 25149857. cards.headline: Thai reference values in 1,372 adults aged 20–90: peak TBS 1.42 ± 0.08 (women, 30–49) and 1.42 ± 0.09 (men, 30–59); decline to age 90 of 13.4% in women (0.27%/year) vs 5.6% in men (0.11%/year) (Pongchaiyakul 2023)
cards.summary: Thai reference values in 1,372 adults aged 20–90: peak TBS 1.42 ± 0.08 (women, 30–49) and 1.42 ± 0.09 (men, 30–59); decline to age 90 of 13.4% in women (0.27%/year) vs 5.6% in men (0.11%/year) (Pongchaiyakul 2023)
cards.type: Primary physiology / normative study (Thai community-dwelling adults, both sexes)
cards.people: 1,372 community-dwelling Thai adults (799 women, 58.2%; mean age 57.25 ± 17.35 years) who underwent BMD testing at Srinagarind Hospital, Khon Kaen; narrow fan-beam DXA, L1–L4 TBS by iNsight software. Of the sample, 34.7% had lumbar osteopenia and 17.7% osteoporosis by T-score — a clinic-tested, not purely healthy, sample, labelled as such.
cards.result: Age- and sex-stratified L1–L4 TBS peaked at 1.42 ± 0.08 in females aged 30–49 years and 1.42 ± 0.09 in males aged 30–59 years. The rate of TBS reduction from ages 30 to 90 was 13.4% (0.27%/year) for females and 5.6% (0.11%/year) for males.
cards.watchOut: Participants were people referred for BMD testing, over a third of them osteopenic — the peak-age values are the normative content; late-age means mix in bone disease prevalence.
cards.source: Pongchaiyakul C et al. Reference Value of Dual X-Ray Absorptiometry-Derived Lumbar Spine Trabecular Bone Score in the Thai Population. cards.summary: Iranian reference values in 691 healthy adults: mean TBS 1.420 ± 0.094 in men (peak age 30.0) and 1.428 ± 0.070 in women (peak 24.5) — degraded microarchitecture at TBS ≤1.231 (men) and ≤1.287 (women) (Shafiee 2020)
cards.type: Primary physiology / normative study (healthy Iranian adults, both sexes)
cards.people: 691 healthy Iranian adults aged ≥18 (381 men, 310 women) from urban Bushehr, selected by multistage age- and sex-stratified cluster random sampling; L1–L4 TBS from spine DXA images using TBS iNsight software (Discovery WI, Hologic Inc, USA). This record carries no MeSH terms (see source line).
cards.result: Two standard deviations below the mean were 1.326 in men and 1.357 in women. The proposed categories: in men, TBS ≥1.326 normal, 1.231–1.326 partially degraded, ≤1.231 degraded microarchitecture; in women, ≥1.357 normal, 1.287–1.357 partially degraded, ≤1.287 degraded.
cards.watchOut: The category cut-points are this population's mean-minus-SD construction, not fracture-validated universal thresholds — they move with the reference population, which is this shelf's core teaching point.

cards.headline: Age-adjusted TBS curve in 619 non-Hispanic US white women aged 30–90: little change 30–45, then a linear 16.0% fall (−2.47 T-score units) from 45 to 90, with the loss rate rising 50% after age 65 (Simonelli 2014)
cards.summary: Age-adjusted TBS curve in 619 non-Hispanic US white women aged 30–90: little change 30–45, then a linear 16.0% fall (−2.47 T-score units) from 45 to 90, with the loss rate rising 50% after age 65 (Simonelli 2014)
cards.type: Primary physiology / normative study (non-Hispanic US white women)
cards.people: 619 non-Hispanic US white women aged 30–90 from 3 geographically dispersed US facilities, all with L1–L4 aBMD Z-score within ±2 SD; women with fractures, osteoporosis treatment or illness affecting bone metabolism were excluded. Prodigy DXA devices (GE-Lunar); TBS by Med-Imaps.
cards.result: TBS at L1–L4 was weakly inversely correlated with BMI (r = −0.17) and weight (r = −0.16) and not correlated with height. TBS decreased significantly with age for all vertebral combinations: a linear decrease of 16.0% (−2.47 T-score) at L1–L4 between ages 45 and 90 (vs −2.34 for aBMD), with the microarchitectural loss rate increasing after age 65 by 50% (−0.004 to −0.006 per year). Little change was seen between ages 30 and 45. The cohort's aBMD normative data did not differ from manufacturer Lunar norms (P = 0.30), indirectly validating the cohort.
cards.watchOut: A deliberately BMD-normal cohort (Z-score within ±2 SD, no fractures): the curve describes texture decline in women selected to have normal density — exactly the dissociation between TBS and BMD the measurement exists to show.
cards.source: Simonelli C et al. Creation of an age-adjusted, dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry-derived trabecular bone score curve for the lumbar spine in non-Hispanic US White women. Journal of clinical densitometry : the official journal of the International Society for Clinical Densitometry. 2014. PMID: 24582086. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (bone / calcium metabolism) — framing brief; the shelf rests on the primary densitometry literature. Japanese women (n=3,069) sit lower than Caucasian women at every age with a three-piece decline curve; Thai adults (n=1,372) peak at 1.42 in both sexes and lose 0.27%/year (women) vs 0.11%/year (men); healthy Iranians (n=691) peak at 1.420 (men) / 1.428 (women) with degraded-microarchitecture cut-points of ≤1.231 and ≤1.287 respectively; US white women (n=619) show a 16.0% fall from 45 to 90 accelerating after 65. TBS falls with age while BMD T-scores are age-referenced by construction — that contrast is core content. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the age/sex pattern; every absolute value remains bound to its population and TBS software version.
cards.watchOut: TBS is software-version-dependent (Med-Imaps algorithm generations) and scanner-dependent — never apply one population's cut-points to a patient scanned on a different device/software generation without the cross-calibration the US study performed.

shelves.title: HR-pQCT normative centiles: lifespan curves from 1,072 Hong Kong and 863 mainland Chinese adults (XtremeCT II) — trabecular parameters peak near 20, cortical loss after 50; young-adult references from Franco-Swiss and Canadian cohorts
shelves.question: In healthy adults and young adults, what are the normative values and centile curves for high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT) at the distal radius and tibia — volumetric bone mineral density, cortical and trabecular microarchitecture and finite-element bone-strength estimates — by age, sex, skeletal site and population, and how much do scanner generation and population move them?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Distribution · Aged · Bone Density · Cross-Sectional Studies · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Radius · Reference Standards · Tibia · Young Adult
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, bone and calcium-metabolism chapters — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary HR-pQCT reference literature, and says so. Four independent cohorts: Hong Kong lifespan centile curves in 1,072 adults aged 20-79 (Zhu 2018); mainland Chinese lifespan centiles in 863 adults aged 20-80 on the second-generation XtremeCT II scanner (Yu 2020 — the two Chinese populations are counted separately as published: different sampling frames and scanner generations); a Franco-Swiss young-women reference subset of 43 women aged 22-27 derived by discriminant analysis from 339 women (Koy 2022); and a Canadian youth reference cohort of 251 young adults aged 16-29 (Burt 2014). The shared pattern: trabecular and strength parameters peak around age 20 and decline steadily, while cortical loss comes mainly after 50 and is faster in women around menopause. First- and second-generation scanner values are NOT interchangeable and the generation is carded per dataset. DXA areal BMD / T-score reference data and trabecular bone score are different measurements, homed in their own rows and not re-carded. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the lifespan centile structure, with the scanner-generation and young-cohort limits on the face.

cards.headline: Hong Kong normative standards (Zhu 2018): sex-specific HR-pQCT centile curves from 1,072 ambulatory Chinese adults aged 20-79 — cortical loss only from mid-adulthood (faster in women), trabecular loss earlier and gradual
cards.summary: Hong Kong normative standards (Zhu 2018): sex-specific HR-pQCT centile curves from 1,072 ambulatory Chinese adults aged 20-79 — cortical loss only from mid-adulthood (faster in women), trabecular loss earlier and gradual
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (HR-pQCT normative centile curves, Hong Kong lifespan cohort)
cards.people: 1,072 ambulatory Chinese men (n=544) and women (n=528) aged 20-79 years, recruited from Hong Kong communities, free of conditions and medications affecting bone metabolism and with no fragility-fracture history; age-stratified cross-sectional design, with centile curves built by generalised additive models for location, scale and shape using age as the only explanatory variable.
cards.result: The centile curves reflect age-related change in density, microarchitecture and estimated bone strength, and yield expected values, percentiles, Z-scores and T-scores (T-scores calculated against the population with peak values) for a defined sex, age and percentile. In both sexes, loss of cortical bone was evident only in mid-adulthood — particularly in women, more rapidly, probably concurrent with menopause onset — whereas loss of trabecular bone was subtle, gradual, or occurred at an earlier age. The authors present the curves as a standard describing a norm or desirable target for clinical judgement, trial entry criteria and fracture-risk assessment.
cards.watchOut: A first-generation-scanner-era lifespan cohort: its absolute values should not be applied to second-generation XtremeCT II scans (next card) without the generation caveat, and the curves are Hong Kong Chinese norms, not global norms.
cards.source: Zhu TY et al. Normative Standards for HRpQCT Parameters in Chinese Men and Women. Journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. 2018. PMID: 29893993. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mainland Chinese centiles (Yu 2020): 863 healthy adults aged 20-80 on the second-generation XtremeCT II — trabecular and strength parameters peaked at 20 and declined steadily; most cortical loss came after 50, and cortical porosity changed most
cards.summary: Mainland Chinese centiles (Yu 2020): 863 healthy adults aged 20-80 on the second-generation XtremeCT II — trabecular and strength parameters peaked at 20 and declined steadily; most cortical loss came after 50, and cortical porosity changed most
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (HR-pQCT normative centile curves, mainland Chinese lifespan cohort, second-generation scanner)
cards.people: 863 healthy Chinese men and women aged 20-80 years scanned with the latest-generation scanner (Scanco XtremeCT II, Scanco Medical AG, Brüttisellen, Switzerland, named in the record); volumetric BMD, bone geometry, microarchitecture and bone strength evaluated at the distal radius and tibia, with age-, site- and sex-specific centile curves built by generalised additive models.
cards.result: Most trabecular and bone-strength parameters reached their peak at 20 years of age, regardless of sex and site, then declined steadily thereafter; most cortical bone loss was observed after age 50. Among the measures, cortical porosity changed most dramatically, and overall changes were more notable at the radius than the tibia and among women than men. Expected values for a defined age and percentile or Z-score are provided for clinical use. The authors present the data as the first normative HR-pQCT reference for the Chinese mainland population.
cards.watchOut: Second-generation scanner values are not interchangeable with first-generation values (previous card): the scanner generation is part of the reference, and this cohort is counted separately from the Hong Kong cohort as published — different sampling frame and generation.
cards.source: Yu F et al. Age-, Site-, and Sex-Specific Normative Centile Curves for HR-pQCT-Derived Microarchitectural and Bone Strength Parameters in a Chinese Mainland Population.
