cards.headline: Franco-Swiss young-women reference (Koy 2022): microarchitecture already declines before age 30; the optimal-bone-profile reference subset is 43 women aged 22-27 drawn from 339 women
cards.summary: Franco-Swiss young-women reference (Koy 2022): microarchitecture already declines before age 30; the optimal-bone-profile reference subset is 43 women aged 22-27 drawn from 339 women
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (HR-pQCT reference values, Franco-Swiss young adult women)
cards.people: 339 women aged 19-41 years with body mass index above 18 and below 30 kg/m2, living in Geneva (Switzerland), Lyon and Saint-Étienne (France), all with HR-pQCT at the non-dominant distal radius and tibia; a discriminant analysis identified the optimal bone profile at ages 22-27, and 43 participants in that band form the reference dataset with median values and percentiles.
cards.result: Microarchitectural parameters begin to decline before the age of 30 years. Based on the discriminant analysis, the optimal bone profile in this population was observed between 22 and 27 years, and the 43 participants in that range were used to establish the reference dataset. The authors present this as the first reference dataset of HR-pQCT measurements using specific age bounds in a Franco-Swiss female cohort at the distal radius and tibia.
cards.watchOut: Women-only and young-adult only: this is a peak-bone-mass reference subset of 43 women, deliberately selected for optimal bone status — it is not a lifespan curve and its percentiles describe an optimal subset, not the general young female population.
cards.source: Koy EHS et al. Reference microarchitectural values measured by HR-pQCT in a Franco-Swiss cohort of young adult women. Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA. 2022. PMID: 34642812. cards.headline: Canadian youth reference cohort (Burt 2014): 251 young adults aged 16-29 — radius parameters stable across the band; at the tibia, female density and strength peaked at 16-19 and fell by 29
cards.summary: Canadian youth reference cohort (Burt 2014): 251 young adults aged 16-29 — radius parameters stable across the band; at the tibia, female density and strength peaked at 16-19 and fell by 29
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (HR-pQCT youth reference cohort, radius and tibia)
cards.people: 251 participants (158 women) aged 16-29 years, grouped in 5-year brackets (16-19, 20-24, 25-29), assessed with HR-pQCT and finite-element analysis at the distal radius and tibia for microstructural and strength parameters.
cards.result: Men had higher total area and BMD, trabecular BMD and (at the radius) trabecular number, cortical thickness and porosity, and failure load, but lower cortical BMD than women (p<0.05). Within sex, parameters remained stable for men; in women they appeared to peak at 16-19 years at the tibia — tibia bone strength and trabecular BMD were highest at 16-19 (p<0.05) and tibia cortical porosity lowest at 16-19 (p<0.001). At the radius, all parameters except cortical BMD (which rose with age) were stable between 16 and 29 in both sexes, and no peak values were found at the radius for either sex.
cards.watchOut: Young-adult only (16-29): a peak-bone-mass reference, not a lifespan curve — and the female tibia peak at 16-19 sits uneasily beside the mainland cohort's peak-at-20 pattern, a between-cohort difference printed rather than smoothed over.
cards.source: Burt LA et al. Bone microarchitecture and strength of the radius and tibia in a reference population of young adults: an HR-pQCT study. Archives of osteoporosis. 2014. PMID: 24862979. cards.people: Synthesis of the four cohorts carded above.
cards.result: Framed by Guyton & Hall (bone / calcium metabolism; framing brief — this shelf rests chiefly on the primary HR-pQCT reference literature). Hong Kong (1,072 adults, 20-79) and mainland China (863 adults, 20-80, XtremeCT II) independently produce the same age structure: trabecular and strength parameters peak around 20 and decline steadily, cortical loss concentrates after 50 and runs faster in women. The Franco-Swiss reference (43 women aged 22-27 selected from 339) and the Canadian youth cohort (251 aged 16-29) supply the peak-bone-mass end in non-Chinese populations. DXA areal density and trabecular bone score are different measurements with their own homes, not re-carded here. PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for the centile structure in the populations studied; scanner generation and population remain part of every numeric value.
cards.watchOut: First- vs second-generation scanner values are not interchangeable; two of the four cohorts are young-adult only and are labelled as such on their cards.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Serum urate population distributions: median 5.16 mg/dL (about 307 µmol/L) in 3,099 healthy Mexico City adults, 95% interval to 7.98 mg/dL (about 475 µmol/L); Hangzhou indirect intervals shift by season; 13.2% hyperuricaemia in Brazil
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what is the population distribution of serum urate — mean, spread, reference interval and the fraction above the conventional hyperuricaemia thresholds (6.8 mg/dL, and sex-specific thresholds as published) — by sex, age and population, and how do directly recruited healthy cohorts compare with big-data (indirect) laboratory intervals?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Male · Reference Values · Uric Acid/blood · Cross-Sectional Studies · Adult · Middle Aged · Hyperuricemia/epidemiology,blood · Seasons · Sex Factors · Age Factors · Big Data
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, renal and purine-metabolism sections — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary population literature, and says so. This is a DISTRIBUTION row, not a treat-to-target row; renal urate HANDLING (fractional excretion physiology) is a different, mechanism question homed in its own row and not re-carded. Three independent populations plus one historical supporting limb: Mexico City Tlalpan 2020 (3,099 directly recruited healthy adults — median urate 5.16 mg/dL (about 307 µmol/L), central 95% interval 3.05 to 7.98 mg/dL (about 181 to 475 µmol/L), hyperuricaemia prevalence 16.5%); Hangzhou big-data indirect intervals (749,739 adult results — intervals shift by season, sex and age, e.g. winter/spring men 18-44: 262-539 µmol/L, i.e. about 4.4-9.1 mg/dL); a Brazilian population study (1,346 individuals — hyperuricaemia prevalence 13.2% at thresholds of 6.8 mg/dL (about 404 µmol/L) in men and 5.4 mg/dL (about 321 µmol/L) in women, as published); and the 1984 Reykjavik cohort of middle-aged men as a historical supporting limb whose fetched abstract prints no urate centile values, so none are claimed from it. Direct (healthy-cohort) and indirect (big-data laboratory) intervals are different kinds of number and are never merged on this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.

cards.headline: Tlalpan 2020, Mexico City (Miranda-Mendoza 2025): 3,099 healthy adults — median serum urate 5.16 mg/dL (about 307 µmol/L), central 95% interval 3.05-7.98 mg/dL (about 181-475 µmol/L); men 6.39 vs women 4.60 mg/dL; hyperuricaemia 16.5%
cards.summary: Tlalpan 2020, Mexico City (Miranda-Mendoza 2025): 3,099 healthy adults — median serum urate 5.16 mg/dL (about 307 µmol/L), central 95% interval 3.05-7.98 mg/dL (about 181-475 µmol/L); men 6.39 vs women 4.60 mg/dL; hyperuricaemia 16.5%
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (direct healthy-cohort serum urate reference values)
cards.people: 3,099 healthy adults (64.6% women) from the Tlalpan 2020 cohort in Mexico City, in a cross-sectional analysis excluding participants with chronic disease, abnormal blood pressure or glucose, or exposure to urate-altering medications; urate analysed overall and stratified by sex.
cards.result: Median serum urate was 5.16 mg/dL (about 307 µmol/L; interquartile range 4.32-6.15 mg/dL, about 257-366 µmol/L), with a central 95% reference interval of 3.05 to 7.98 mg/dL (about 181 to 475 µmol/L). Medians differed significantly by sex: 4.60 mg/dL (about 274 µmol/L; IQR 3.99-5.28) in women and 6.39 mg/dL (about 380 µmol/L; IQR 5.61-7.09) in men. Hyperuricaemia prevalence was 16.5% overall — 28.4% in men and 10.0% in women. The authors present these as sex-specific reference values for a healthy Mexican adult population.
cards.watchOut: A directly recruited healthy cohort — the cleanest kind of reference interval, but a single city's population; the male upper limit (7.98 mg/dL overall interval) sits well above the conventional 6.8 mg/dL (about 404 µmol/L) hyperuricaemia threshold, which is a distribution fact, not a treatment target.
cards.source: Miranda-Mendoza H et al. Establishing reference values for serum urate in healthy adults from Mexico City: Data from the Tlalpan 2020 cohort. Reumatologia clinica. 2025. PMID: 41047197. cards.headline: Hangzhou big-data indirect intervals (Chen 2025): 749,739 adult urate results — reference intervals shift by season: winter/spring men 18-44, 262-539 µmol/L (about 4.4-9.1 mg/dL); women 18-44, 175-385 µmol/L (about 2.9-6.5 mg/dL)
cards.summary: Hangzhou big-data indirect intervals (Chen 2025): 749,739 adult urate results — reference intervals shift by season: winter/spring men 18-44, 262-539 µmol/L (about 4.4-9.1 mg/dL); women 18-44, 175-385 µmol/L (about 2.9-6.5 mg/dL)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (indirect big-data serum urate reference intervals)
cards.people: 749,739 serum urate results from adults aged 18 years and over in Hangzhou, eastern coastal China, over 2021-2022, analysed by indirect statistical methods to derive reference intervals, with seasonal, sex and age effects examined and differences from the manufacturer's ranges assessed by reference change value.
cards.result: In winter/spring, intervals were: men 18-44 years, 262-539 µmol/L (about 4.4-9.1 mg/dL); women 18-44, 175-385 µmol/L (about 2.9-6.5 mg/dL); men 45 and over, 243-525 µmol/L (about 4.1-8.8 mg/dL); women 45 and over, 185-406 µmol/L (about 3.1-6.8 mg/dL). In summer/autumn: men 18-44, 273-552 µmol/L (about 4.6-9.3 mg/dL); women 18-44, 185-395 µmol/L (about 3.1-6.6 mg/dL); men 45 and over, 250-537 µmol/L (about 4.2-9.0 mg/dL); women 45 and over, 192-410 µmol/L (about 3.2-6.9 mg/dL). A significant difference from the manufacturer's range was observed for men, but not for women. Seasonal fluctuation is therefore part of the interval, not noise around it.
cards.watchOut: Indirect intervals are statistical extractions from routine laboratory results (including results from people tested for a reason), not measurements in screened-healthy volunteers — a different kind of number from the Tlalpan card, never merged with it. The sheer N (749,739 results, not 749,739 people) does not cure that.

cards.headline: Brazilian population study (Rodrigues 2012): 1,346 individuals — hyperuricaemia prevalence 13.2% at thresholds of 6.8 mg/dL (about 404 µmol/L) in men and 5.4 mg/dL (about 321 µmol/L) in women, as published
cards.summary: Brazilian population study (Rodrigues 2012): 1,346 individuals — hyperuricaemia prevalence 13.2% at thresholds of 6.8 mg/dL (about 404 µmol/L) in men and 5.4 mg/dL (about 321 µmol/L) in women, as published
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (population-based serum urate distribution, Brazil)
cards.people: 1,346 individuals in a Brazilian population-based study of the distribution of serum uric acid and its relationship with demographic and cardiovascular variables; hyperuricaemia was defined as at least 6.8 mg/dL for men and at least 5.4 mg/dL for women, as published, and metabolic syndrome by NCEP ATP III criteria.
cards.result: Hyperuricaemia prevalence was 13.2%. The association of serum uric acid with cardiovascular risk factors was sex-specific: in women, higher urate was associated with increasing body mass index even after adjustment for age and systolic blood pressure; in men, the urate–HDL cholesterol relationship was mediated by BMI. Triglycerides, waist circumference and systolic pressure explained 11%, 4% and 1% of urate variability in men; waist circumference and triglycerides explained 9% and 1% in women. Compared with the first urate quartile, men and women in the fourth quartile had 3.29-fold and 4.18-fold higher metabolic-syndrome risk (relative measures, as published). Abdominal obesity and hypertriglyceridaemia were the main factors associated with hyperuricaemia.
cards.watchOut: A general population sample (not a screened-healthy cohort), and its sex-specific thresholds are the study's own definitions — the 13.2% prevalence is not comparable with Tlalpan's 16.5% without aligning thresholds and exclusions, and this shelf does not align them.
cards.source: Rodrigues SL et al. Gender distribution of serum uric acid and cardiovascular risk factors: population based study. Arquivos brasileiros de cardiologia. 2012. PMID: 22146989. shelves.title: Topiroxostat in hyperuricaemia ± gout (3 Japanese trials): urate −36.3% vs −34.3% on allopurinol (non-inferior), dose-response vs placebo — biochemical endpoint only, no flare-outcome trial, single-region (Japan)
shelves.question: In Japanese adults with hyperuricaemia with or without gout, does the selective xanthine-oxidoreductase inhibitor topiroxostat, compared with placebo or allopurinol, lower serum urate?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Allopurinol/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Gout/drug therapy · Gout Suppressants/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Hyperuricemia/drug therapy · Japan · Male · Middle Aged · Nitriles/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Pyridines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome · Uric Acid/blood · Xanthine Oxidase/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for serum urate lowering only, on single-region (Japan) evidence. In the phase 3 double-blind trial, topiroxostat 120 mg/day reduced serum urate by −36.3% versus −34.3% on allopurinol 200 mg/day over 16 weeks (percent change from baseline), and non-inferiority was proved. The phase 2b study confirmed a dose-response, with a −44.8% reduction at 160 mg/day; the phase 2a study showed a dose-dependent reduction from 40 to 120 mg/day, with a mean percent change of −30.8% at 120 mg/day versus +1.6% on placebo over 8 weeks. SINGLE-REGION FLAG: all evidence is Japanese; topiroxostat is approved in Japan and is not FDA/EMA-approved. Serum urate is a biochemical endpoint — NO flare-outcome trial is in this base, so nothing here shows topiroxostat prevents gout attacks. Percent changes are printed as the abstracts print them (percent change from baseline).

cards.headline: Phase 3 active-controlled RCT (Hosoya 2016): topiroxostat 120 mg/day non-inferior to allopurinol 200 mg/day — serum urate percent change −36.3% vs −34.3% over 16 weeks
cards.summary: Phase 3 active-controlled RCT (Hosoya 2016): topiroxostat 120 mg/day non-inferior to allopurinol 200 mg/day — serum urate percent change −36.3% vs −34.3% over 16 weeks
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre randomised double-blind double-dummy active-controlled trial, topiroxostat vs allopurinol
cards.people: 206 Japanese patients with hyperuricaemia with or without gout (entry serum urate ≥416.4 μmol/L [≈7.0 mg/dL] for gout patients, with higher thresholds for asymptomatic hyperuricaemia), randomised to topiroxostat 120 mg/day or allopurinol 200 mg/day for 16 weeks with stepwise dose increases; 203 patients (98 topiroxostat, 105 allopurinol) received at least one dose and had serum urate assessed; 99% were men, mean age 53.0 years.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, percent change in serum urate from baseline to the final visit, was −36.3 ± 12.7% on topiroxostat versus −34.3 ± 11.1% on allopurinol; non-inferiority of topiroxostat was proved against the predefined margin (95% CI −5.3 to 1.3%). Overall incidences of adverse events and adverse drug reactions were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority against allopurinol on a biochemical endpoint, in an almost entirely male Japanese population; no gout-flare outcome was measured. Percent changes are percent change from baseline, as the abstract prints them.

cards.headline: Phase 2b RCT (Hosoya 2017): dose-response for urate lowering confirmed across placebo, topiroxostat 120 and 160 mg/day and allopurinol — a −44.8% reduction at 160 mg/day over 16 weeks
cards.summary: Phase 2b RCT (Hosoya 2017): dose-response for urate lowering confirmed across placebo, topiroxostat 120 and 160 mg/day and allopurinol — a −44.8% reduction at 160 mg/day over 16 weeks
cards.type: Phase 2b randomised double-blind controlled study, topiroxostat vs placebo and allopurinol
cards.people: 157 Japanese patients with hyperuricaemia with or without gout, randomised to placebo, topiroxostat 120 mg/day, topiroxostat 160 mg/day or allopurinol 200 mg/day for 16 weeks.
cards.result: A dose-response relationship for serum urate lowering was confirmed across placebo and the topiroxostat doses; at the end of administration the lowering rate was −44.8% in the topiroxostat 160 mg/day group. No significant difference in the incidence of adverse events was observed among all groups, including allopurinol. (The fetched abstract prints no per-group values for the other arms, and none are claimed here.)
cards.watchOut: The headline figure is for the 160 mg/day dose — above the 120 mg/day dose of the phase 3 trial. Biochemical endpoint only; single-region (Japan) evidence.
cards.source: Hosoya T et al. Clinical efficacy and safety of topiroxostat in Japanese hyperuricemic patients with or without gout: a randomized, double-blinded, controlled phase 2b study. cards.headline: Phase 2a exploratory RCT (Hosoya 2016): dose-dependent urate reduction from 40 to 120 mg/day (P<0.001) — mean percent change −30.8% at 120 mg/day vs +1.6% on placebo over 8 weeks (between-group difference −32.4%)
cards.summary: Phase 2a exploratory RCT (Hosoya 2016): dose-dependent urate reduction from 40 to 120 mg/day (P<0.001) — mean percent change −30.8% at 120 mg/day vs +1.6% on placebo over 8 weeks (between-group difference −32.4%)
cards.type: Exploratory phase 2a multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging study, topiroxostat vs placebo
cards.people: 187 Japanese men with hyperuricaemia with or without gout, randomised to placebo or topiroxostat 40, 60, 80 or 120 mg/day for 8 weeks; 186 received at least one dose.
cards.result: A dose-dependent serum urate reduction from 40 to 120 mg/day was demonstrated (P<0.001, Jonckheere–Terpstra test). Mean percent change at the final visit was −30.8% in the 120 mg group versus +1.6% on placebo (between-group difference −32.4%, 95% CI −38.9% to −25.9%; P<0.001). Overall adverse-event incidences in the topiroxostat groups were comparable to placebo; gouty arthritis incidences were not statistically but numerically higher in the 80 and 120 mg groups.
cards.watchOut: An 8-week exploratory study in men only; the numerically higher gouty-arthritis incidence at the higher doses is the expected early-treatment flare pattern of urate lowering and is printed here, not hidden. Biochemical endpoint only.
cards.source: Hosoya T et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: three Japanese randomised reports form one urate-lowering programme — non-inferior to allopurinol at phase 3, dose-responsive at phase 2 — but the endpoint is serum urate throughout and no flare-outcome trial exists in this base
cards.summary: Synthesis: three Japanese randomised reports form one urate-lowering programme — non-inferior to allopurinol at phase 3, dose-responsive at phase 2 — but the endpoint is serum urate throughout and no flare-outcome trial exists in this base
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (206 + 157 + 187 randomised patients, all in Japan).
cards.result: Topiroxostat lowered serum urate dose-dependently versus placebo in the phase 2a study (−30.8% at 120 mg/day vs +1.6% on placebo at 8 weeks) and phase 2b study (−44.8% at 160 mg/day at 16 weeks), and was non-inferior to allopurinol 200 mg/day in phase 3 (−36.3% vs −34.3% at 120 mg/day over 16 weeks). The ETUDE albuminuria study of topiroxostat is a diabetic-nephropathy question and is not carded here. Topiroxostat is approved in Japan and is not FDA/EMA-approved. Nothing in this base measures gout flares, tophi or any clinical outcome — the claim is urate lowering only.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; percent changes are percent change from baseline as the abstracts print them, and the phase 3 population was 99% male.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Gabapentin for neuropathic pain: modest benefit in postherpetic neuralgia (two trials) and painful diabetic neuropathy (one trial) — limbs labelled, never pooled
shelves.question: In adults with postherpetic neuralgia or painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy, does gabapentin (titrated to up to 3,600 mg/day) reduce daily pain versus placebo, and at what dizziness/somnolence cost?
shelves.mesh: Acetates · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Amines · Analgesics · Anticonvulsants · Cyclohexanecarboxylic Acids · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gabapentin · Herpes Zoster · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Neuralgia · Pain Measurement · Quality of Life · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — real but modest, in two labelled indication limbs that are never pooled. Postherpetic neuralgia (two trials, 229 and 334 randomised): gabapentin reduced daily pain 6.3→4.2 versus 6.5→6.0 on placebo (Rowbotham) and improved pain scores by −34.5%/−34.4% at 1,800/2,400 mg versus −15.7% on placebo, a difference of about 18.8 percentage points (Rice & Maton). Painful diabetic neuropathy (one trial, 165 randomised): end-point pain 3.9 versus 5.1 (Backonja). In absolute terms the advantage is about 1–2 points on an 11-point scale beyond placebo. The consistent price is dizziness and somnolence — 24% and 23% versus 4.9% and 6% in the diabetic-neuropathy trial — concentrated in titration and most consequential in the elderly PHN population.

cards.headline: PHN limb — Rowbotham 1998 RCT: gabapentin (titrated to up to 3,600 mg/day) reduced postherpetic neuralgia pain from 6.3 to 4.2 on an 11-point scale versus 6.5 to 6.0 on placebo over 8 weeks (P<.001)
cards.summary: PHN limb — Rowbotham 1998 RCT: gabapentin (titrated to up to 3,600 mg/day) reduced postherpetic neuralgia pain from 6.3 to 4.2 on an 11-point scale versus 6.5 to 6.0 on placebo over 8 weeks (P<.001)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled parallel-group trial, gabapentin in postherpetic neuralgia — PHN limb (never pooled with the diabetic-neuropathy limb)
cards.people: 229 subjects with postherpetic neuralgia randomised at 16 US outpatient centres (113 gabapentin, 116 placebo) to a 4-week titration to a maximum of 3,600 mg/day gabapentin or matching placebo, maintained at the maximum tolerated dose for a further 4 weeks. Concomitant tricyclic antidepressants and/or narcotics were continued if stabilised before entry. Completion: 78.8% on gabapentin, 81.9% on placebo.
cards.result: By intention-to-treat analysis, average daily pain score fell significantly more on gabapentin: from 6.3 to 4.2 points, versus 6.5 to 6.0 points on placebo (P<.001) — an absolute between-group difference of about 1.6 points on an 11-point scale. Secondary pain measures and pain-related sleep interference also improved with gabapentin (P<.001), and many Short Form-36 and Profile of Mood States measures favoured gabapentin (P≤.01). Somnolence, dizziness, ataxia, peripheral oedema and infection were all more frequent on gabapentin, but withdrawals were comparable (15, 13.3%, on gabapentin vs 11, 9.5%, on placebo).
cards.watchOut: An 8-week trial with forced titration to high doses; the PHN population is elderly, in whom the dizziness, ataxia and somnolence seen here carry fall risk that a short trial undercounts. No registry ID is in the PubMed record (pre-registration era).
cards.source: Rowbotham et al. Gabapentin for the treatment of postherpetic neuralgia: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 1998. PMID: 9846778. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Diabetic-neuropathy limb — Backonja 1998 RCT: gabapentin monotherapy reduced painful diabetic neuropathy pain to an end-point mean of 3.9 versus 5.1 on placebo (from baselines of 6.4 and 6.5; P<.001), with dizziness in 24% vs 4.9% and somnolence in 23% vs 6%
cards.summary: Diabetic-neuropathy limb — Backonja 1998 RCT: gabapentin monotherapy reduced painful diabetic neuropathy pain to an end-point mean of 3.9 versus 5.1 on placebo (from baselines of 6.4 and 6.5; P<.001), with dizziness in 24% vs 4.9% and somnolence in 23% vs 6%
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, gabapentin monotherapy in painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy — diabetic-neuropathy limb (never pooled with the PHN limb)
cards.people: 165 patients with a 1- to 5-year history of pain attributed to diabetic peripheral neuropathy and a minimum 40-mm pain score on the Short-Form McGill visual analogue scale, randomised at 20 outpatient sites to gabapentin titrated from 900 to 3,600 mg/day or maximum tolerated dose (n=84) or placebo (n=81) for 8 weeks. Completion: 83% on gabapentin, 80% on placebo.
cards.result: By intention-to-treat analysis, mean daily pain at end point was significantly lower on gabapentin (baseline 6.4, end point 3.9; n=82) than placebo (baseline 6.5, end point 5.1; n=80) (P<.001) — an absolute end-point difference of 1.2 points on an 11-point scale. All secondary pain measures were significantly better on gabapentin, as were sleep interference, Short Form-36 and Profile of Mood States measures. Adverse events significantly more frequent on gabapentin were dizziness (20 patients, 24%, vs 4, 4.9%; P<.001) and somnolence (19, 23%, vs 5, 6%; P=.003); confusion was also more frequent (7, 8%, vs 1, 1.2%; P=.06).
cards.watchOut: An 8-week monotherapy trial — it does not address gabapentin as add-on therapy, longer-term use, or glycaemic outcomes. The absolute pain advantage (1.2 points) is modest and bought with dizziness or somnolence in roughly one patient in four. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.
cards.source: Backonja et al. Gabapentin for the symptomatic treatment of painful neuropathy in patients with diabetes mellitus: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 1998. PMID: 9846777. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: PHN limb — Rice & Maton 2001 RCT: gabapentin 1,800 and 2,400 mg/day improved final pain scores by −34.5% and −34.4% versus −15.7% on placebo (differences of about 18.8 percentage points), with dizziness and somnolence commonest, concentrated in titration
cards.summary: PHN limb — Rice & Maton 2001 RCT: gabapentin 1,800 and 2,400 mg/day improved final pain scores by −34.5% and −34.4% versus −15.7% on placebo (differences of about 18.8 percentage points), with dizziness and somnolence commonest, concentrated in titration
cards.type: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, gabapentin 1,800 or 2,400 mg/day in postherpetic neuralgia — PHN limb (never pooled with the diabetic-neuropathy limb)
cards.people: 334 men and women aged at least 18 years (mean 73) with postherpetic neuralgia, randomised to gabapentin 1,800 or 2,400 mg/day or placebo in three divided doses with a forced titration schedule, over 7 weeks. The primary outcome was change in average daily pain diary score from the baseline week to the final week.
cards.result: From week 1, pain scores improved significantly more with gabapentin: the final difference versus baseline was −34.5% at 1,800 mg and −34.4% at 2,400 mg compared with −15.7% on placebo; the difference versus placebo was 18.8 percentage points (95% CI 10.9 to 26.8; P<0.01) at 1,800 mg and 18.7 points (10.7 to 26.7; P<0.01) at 2,400 mg — the two doses were indistinguishable. Sleep interference diaries showed a similar pattern, and significantly more gabapentin patients reported >50% reduction in pain intensity, with clinician and patient global impressions, Short Form-McGill scores and several Short Form-36 domains also favouring gabapentin. The most common adverse events were dizziness and somnolence, particularly during the titration phase.
cards.watchOut: The percentage improvements are relative to each group's own baseline pain; the placebo-subtracted difference is about 19 percentage points, and the two doses did not differ — there is no gain shown above 1,800 mg/day in this trial. Mean age 73: sedation and dizziness in this age group are the practical limit. No registry ID is in the PubMed record.
cards.source: Rice et al. Gabapentin in postherpetic neuralgia: a randomised, double blind, placebo controlled study. Pain. 2001. PMID: 11690735. Registry ID: none in the record. the difference versus placebo was 18.8 percentage points (95% ci 10.9 to 26.8; p<0.01) at 1,800 mg and 18.7 points (10.7 to 26.7; p<0.01) at 2,400 mg — the two doses were indistinguishable. sleep interference diaries showed a similar pattern, and significantly more gabapentin patients reported >50% reduction in pain intensity, with clinician and patient global impressions, short form-mcgill scores and several short form-36 domains also favouring gabapentin. the most common adverse events were dizziness and somnolence, particularly during the titration phase. the percentage improvements are relative to each group's own baseline pain; the placebo-subtracted difference is about 19 percentage points, and the two doses did not differ — there is no gain shown above 1,800 mg/day in this trial. mean age 73: sedation and dizziness in this age group are the practical limit. no registry id is in the pubmed record. rice et al. gabapentin in postherpetic neuralgia: a randomised, double blind, placebo controlled study. pain. 2001. pmid: 11690735. registry id: none in the record. mesh: acetates · adult · aged · aged, 80 and over · amines · analgesics · cyclohexanecarboxylic acids · double-blind method · female · gabapentin · herpes zoster · humans · male · middle aged · neuralgia · pain measurement · patient satisfaction · quality of life · treatment outcome · gamma-aminobutyric acid

cards.headline: Synthesis: two indications, carded as labelled limbs and never pooled — in postherpetic neuralgia, two trials (n=229 and n=334) show gabapentin beating placebo by about 1.6 points on an 11-point pain scale and by about 19 percentage points of relative pain improvement respectively; in painful diabetic neuropathy, one trial (n=165) shows an end-point advantage of 1.2 points; the effect is real and modest in both, and the price in all three trials is dizziness and somnolence in roughly a fifth to a quarter of patients

shelves.title: Odanacatib (LOFT): fractures halved (vertebral 3.7% vs 7.8%; hip 0.8% vs 1.6%) but stroke rose (HR 1.32) — development abandoned, never marketed
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women (and, in a separate trial, men) with osteoporosis, does the cathepsin K inhibitor odanacatib, compared with placebo, reduce fractures — and what cardiovascular harm ended its development (the LOFT programme)?

shelves.balance: Discontinued agent — the flag leads: odanacatib was NEVER marketed; its sponsor abandoned development on the benefit–risk balance printed in the LOFT report itself, and the stroke signal leads this balance rather than following the fracture win. LOFT (16,071 randomised postmenopausal women) succeeded on fractures: radiographic vertebral fractures 3.7% vs 7.8% (HR 0.46), hip fractures 0.8% vs 1.6% (HR 0.53) and non-vertebral fractures 5.1% vs 6.7% (HR 0.77), all P < 0.0001 — hazard ratios are relative measures, printed beside their absolute rates. Against that, stroke occurred in 1.7% vs 1.3% (HR 1.32, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.70; P = 0.034), and with the LOFT Extension data the cardiovascular composite (cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke) reached HR 1.17 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.36) with stroke at HR 1.37. The other two reports are bone-density (surrogate) trials only — a 2-year phase 2 dose-ranging study (lumbar spine BMD +5.5% and total-hip +3.2% on 50 mg weekly vs −0.2% and −0.9% on placebo) and a phase 3 trial in 292 men (lumbar spine BMD difference +5.6% at 24 months) — only LOFT answers the fracture question, and that distinction is printed on each card.

cards.headline: LOFT + LOFT Extension (McClung 2019): odanacatib halved vertebral fractures (3.7% vs 7.8%, HR 0.46) and hip fractures (0.8% vs 1.6%, HR 0.53) in 16,071 women — but stroke rose (1.7% vs 1.3%, HR 1.32, P = 0.034), and the sponsor abandoned development
cards.summary: LOFT + LOFT Extension (McClung 2019): odanacatib halved vertebral fractures (3.7% vs 7.8%, HR 0.46) and hip fractures (0.8% vs 1.6%, HR 0.53) in 16,071 women — but stroke rose (1.7% vs 1.3%, HR 1.32, P = 0.034), and the sponsor abandoned development
cards.type: Phase 3 multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled event-driven randomised trial (LOFT) plus double-blind Extension, odanacatib vs placebo
cards.people: 16,071 postmenopausal women aged at least 65 years (postmenopausal at least 5 years) with osteoporosis, randomised at 388 clinics in 40 countries to oral odanacatib 50 mg once weekly (8,043) or placebo (8,028); median follow-up 36.5 months in LOFT, extending to a total median of 47.6 months for the 8,257 women who entered the double-blind LOFT Extension.
cards.result: In LOFT, cumulative incidences on odanacatib vs placebo were: radiographic vertebral fractures 3.7% (251/6,770) vs 7.8% (542/6,910), HR 0.46 (95% CI 0.40 to 0.53); hip fractures 0.8% (65/8,043) vs 1.6% (125/8,028), HR 0.53 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.71); non-vertebral fractures 5.1% (412/8,043) vs 6.7% (541/8,028), HR 0.77 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.87) — all P < 0.0001, hazard ratios being relative measures printed beside the absolute rates. The harm: stroke 1.7% (136/8,043) vs 1.3% (104/8,028), HR 1.32 (95% CI 1.02 to 1.70; P = 0.034), with no increase in myocardial infarction (HR 0.82); the cardiovascular composite in LOFT alone was HR 1.12 (95% CI 0.95 to 1.34; P = 0.18). With Extension data included, the composite of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction or stroke became significantly higher on odanacatib (5.0% vs 4.3%; HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.36; P = 0.029), as did stroke (2.3% vs 1.7%; HR 1.37, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.71; P = 0.0051). The authors record that, on the overall benefit–risk balance, the sponsor decided to no longer pursue development of odanacatib.
cards.watchOut: The fracture benefit and the stroke harm are both real on these numbers and neither cancels the other arithmetically: the trial's own sponsor read the balance as unfavourable, which is why this drug was never marketed — any presentation of LOFT as a fracture win alone misstates the record.
cards.source: McClung MR et al. Odanacatib for the treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis: results of the LOFT multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial and LOFT Extension study. The lancet. Diabetes & endocrinology. 2019. PMID: 31676222. Registry ID: NCT00529373. cards.headline: Phase 2 dose-ranging (Bone 2010): 2 years of weekly odanacatib raised lumbar spine BMD by 5.5% and total-hip BMD by 3.2% at the 50 mg dose vs −0.2% and −0.9% on placebo — a BMD (surrogate) trial, not a fracture trial
cards.summary: Phase 2 dose-ranging (Bone 2010): 2 years of weekly odanacatib raised lumbar spine BMD by 5.5% and total-hip BMD by 3.2% at the 50 mg dose vs −0.2% and −0.9% on placebo — a BMD (surrogate) trial, not a fracture trial
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind placebo-controlled dose-ranging randomised trial (2 years), odanacatib vs placebo — BMD endpoint
cards.people: Postmenopausal women with low bone mineral density (T-scores −2.0 to −3.5 at the lumbar spine or femoral sites), randomised to placebo or odanacatib 3, 10, 25 or 50 mg once weekly for 1 year with a 1-year extension on the same assignment; all received vitamin D with calcium as needed. The fetched record prints no randomised N, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: Twenty-four months of treatment produced progressive, dose-related BMD increases. At the 50 mg dose, lumbar spine BMD increased 5.5% and total-hip BMD 3.2%, whereas placebo values were essentially unchanged (−0.2% and −0.9%). Biochemical markers of bone turnover changed in a dose-related manner, and safety and tolerability were generally similar to placebo with no dose-related trends in adverse experiences.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate-endpoint dose-ranging trial with no fracture outcome and no N in the fetched record: it explains how the LOFT dose was chosen, and its clean tolerability at this size and duration could not — and did not — exclude the stroke signal that only the 16,071-woman outcomes trial could see.
cards.source: Bone HG et al. Odanacatib, a cathepsin-K inhibitor for osteoporosis: a two-year study in postmenopausal women with low bone density. Journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. 2010. PMID: 19874198. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phase 3 in men (Binkley 2021): odanacatib raised lumbar spine BMD by 5.6% vs placebo at 24 months in 292 men with osteoporosis (all BMD sites P < 0.01) — a BMD (surrogate) trial whose report states development was stopped over the LOFT stroke risk
cards.summary: Phase 3 in men (Binkley 2021): odanacatib raised lumbar spine BMD by 5.6% vs placebo at 24 months in 292 men with osteoporosis (all BMD sites P < 0.01) — a BMD (surrogate) trial whose report states development was stopped over the LOFT stroke risk
cards.type: Phase 3 double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial in men (24 months), odanacatib vs placebo — BMD endpoint
cards.people: 292 men (mean age 68.8 years) with idiopathic osteoporosis or osteoporosis due to hypogonadism, randomised 1:1 to odanacatib 50 mg once weekly or placebo for 24 months (phase 3, double-blind); all received vitamin D3 5,600 IU weekly and calcium supplementation as needed.
cards.result: Versus placebo, odanacatib increased BMD from baseline at the lumbar spine by 5.6%, total hip by 2.0%, femoral neck by 1.7% and trochanter by 2.1% (all P < 0.01), with large falls in bone-resorption markers (urinary NTX/creatinine −68%, serum CTX −77%; both P < 0.001) and smaller falls in formation markers. The safety profile, including cardiovascular events, was similar between groups in this 292-man trial. The report states plainly that increased risk of stroke in another study (LOFT) stopped further odanacatib development.
cards.watchOut: BMD only, in 292 men: far too small and too short to see a stroke signal of LOFT's size, so its similar cardiovascular-event profile is no reassurance against LOFT — the fracture question in men was never tested in an outcomes trial.

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Only one report answers the fracture question: LOFT, in 16,071 postmenopausal women, where odanacatib roughly halved vertebral and hip fractures in relative terms on the absolute rates printed on its card, while increasing stroke (1.7% vs 1.3%; HR 1.32) — a signal that strengthened with the Extension data (stroke HR 1.37; cardiovascular composite HR 1.17) and on which the sponsor stopped development, as the LOFT report itself records. The phase 2 dose-ranging trial (Bone 2010) and the men's phase 3 trial (Binkley 2021, n=292) are BMD trials that support the mechanism and the dose; neither tests fractures and neither could detect the harm. The further LOFT reports (hip-fracture incidence; 5-year bone structure) are reports of the same trial — programme support only, not carded. This shelf is a historical record of a discontinued programme, not a treatment option.
cards.watchOut: Relative fracture reductions must always travel with their absolute rates and with the stroke signal; see the LOFT card for both.

shelves.balance: Never-marketed agent — this flag leads. Arzoxifene's fracture trial succeeded on vertebral fractures and invasive breast cancer, and still no product was marketed. The venous-thromboembolism increase (0.7 percentage points absolute; 2.3-fold relative) is printed beside the fracture win, and nonvertebral fractures were NOT significantly reduced. Only GENERATIONS answers the fracture question; the other three anchors (NEXT vs raloxifene, the phase 2 dose-ranging trial, FOUNDATION) are bone-mineral-density / bone-turnover surrogate trials, and that distinction is printed on each card. Relative reductions are labelled relative, with the absolute differences the abstracts give printed alongside. PROPOSED STAMP: SPLIT.

cards.headline: GENERATIONS outcomes trial (Cummings 2011): vertebral fractures 2.3 percentage points lower at 3 years (41% relative risk reduction) and invasive breast cancer 1.3 points lower over 4 years (56% relative reduction) — but VTE up 0.7 points (2.3-fold relative) and NO significant decrease in nonvertebral fractures
cards.summary: GENERATIONS outcomes trial (Cummings 2011): vertebral fractures 2.3 percentage points lower at 3 years (41% relative risk reduction) and invasive breast cancer 1.3 points lower over 4 years (56% relative reduction) — but VTE up 0.7 points (2.3-fold relative) and NO significant decrease in nonvertebral fractures
cards.type: Randomised blinded fracture and breast-cancer outcomes trial (GENERATIONS), arzoxifene vs placebo
cards.people: Postmenopausal women aged 60–85 years with osteoporosis (femoral neck or lumbar spine BMD T-score −2.5 or less, or a vertebral fracture) or low bone mass (T-score −1.0 or less and above −2.5), randomised double-blind to arzoxifene 20 mg or placebo daily; primary endpoints were new vertebral fracture in the osteoporosis subgroup and invasive breast cancer in the overall population. The fetched record prints no randomised N, and none is claimed on this card.
cards.result: After 3 years, the cumulative incidence of vertebral fractures in the osteoporosis subgroup was 2.3 percentage points lower on arzoxifene than placebo — a 41% relative risk reduction (95% CI 0.45 to 0.77; P < .001). Over 4 years, invasive breast cancer incidence was reduced by 1.3 percentage points — a 56% relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.44, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.76; P < .001). There was no significant decrease in nonvertebral fracture risk. Venous thromboembolic events increased by 0.7 percentage points — a 2.3-fold relative increase (95% CI 1.5 to 3.7).
cards.watchOut: The fracture win is vertebral only: nonvertebral fractures — the fractures that drive hip-fracture morbidity — were not significantly reduced, and the VTE increase is a class-typical harm printed in the same abstract. GENERATIONS' companion reports (gynaecological effects; breast-cancer incidence) are further reports of this same trial and are not carded as separate evidence.
cards.source: Cummings SR et al. Arzoxifene for prevention of fractures and invasive breast cancer in postmenopausal women. Journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. 2011. PMID: 20658564. Registry ID: NCT00088010. cards.headline: NEXT head-to-head vs raloxifene (Kendler 2012): lumbar spine BMD rose +2.75% on arzoxifene vs +1.66% on raloxifene at 12 months, with greater hip gains and turnover suppression — and fewer hot flushes (7.0% vs 16.7%)
cards.summary: NEXT head-to-head vs raloxifene (Kendler 2012): lumbar spine BMD rose +2.75% on arzoxifene vs +1.66% on raloxifene at 12 months, with greater hip gains and turnover suppression — and fewer hot flushes (7.0% vs 16.7%)
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised double-blind head-to-head BMD trial (NEXT), arzoxifene vs raloxifene
cards.people: 320 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis randomised to arzoxifene 20 mg/day (158) or raloxifene 60 mg/day (162) for 12 months, all receiving daily calcium and vitamin D; mean age 63 years, mean lumbar spine BMD T-score −2.9.
cards.result: At 12 months the increase in lumbar spine BMD was greater on arzoxifene than raloxifene (+2.75% versus +1.66%), as were femoral-neck and total-hip BMD gains (P < 0.05), and arzoxifene suppressed bone-turnover markers to a greater extent at 3, 6 and 12 months (P < 0.05). New or worsening hot flushes were reported less often on arzoxifene (7.0% versus 16.7%; P < 0.05); nasopharyngitis (10.1% versus 2.5%) and bronchitis (5.1% versus 0%) were reported more often. No cases of endometrial polyps, hyperplasia or cancer were reported. The authors note that, on the fracture-outcome findings, the BMD difference did not translate into improved fracture efficacy.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate-endpoint (BMD) comparison against another SERM, not a fracture trial: beating raloxifene on BMD is not evidence of beating it on fractures, as the authors themselves state.
cards.source: Kendler DL et al. Arzoxifene versus raloxifene: effect on bone and safety parameters in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis. Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA. 2012. PMID: 21374068. cards.headline: Phase 2 dose-ranging trial (Downs 2010): all arzoxifene doses (5–40 mg) significantly reduced bone-turnover markers vs placebo and increased lumbar spine BMD over 6 months, generally more than raloxifene
cards.summary: Phase 2 dose-ranging trial (Downs 2010): all arzoxifene doses (5–40 mg) significantly reduced bone-turnover markers vs placebo and increased lumbar spine BMD over 6 months, generally more than raloxifene
cards.type: Phase 2 randomised double-blind dose-ranging trial, arzoxifene vs raloxifene and placebo in low bone mass
cards.people: 219 postmenopausal women with low bone mass (T-score between −1 and −2.5; mean age 59 years), randomised double-blind to arzoxifene 5, 10, 20 or 40 mg, raloxifene 60 mg or placebo daily for 6 months, all receiving daily calcium.
cards.result: All arzoxifene doses significantly reduced osteocalcin (the primary endpoint), type 1 collagen C-telopeptide, bone-specific alkaline phosphatase and procollagen type I amino-terminal propeptide versus placebo, and increased lumbar spine BMD; effects were generally greater than raloxifene's, with 20 and 40 mg/day appearing optimal for turnover suppression and no clear dose effect overall. Arzoxifene decreased cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and fibrinogen versus placebo. Endometrial thickness change did not differ significantly from placebo or raloxifene, and no endometrial hyperplasia or adenocarcinoma was observed.
cards.watchOut: Six months, turnover markers and BMD only: a dose-finding surrogate study that cannot speak to fractures or to longer-term endometrial or thrombotic safety.
cards.source: Downs RW et al. Effects of arzoxifene on bone, lipid markers, and safety parameters in postmenopausal women with low bone mass. Osteoporosis international : a journal established as result of cooperation between the European Foundation for Osteoporosis and the National Osteoporosis Foundation of the USA. 2010. PMID: 19798460. cards.headline: FOUNDATION trial (Bolognese 2009): arzoxifene 20 mg raised lumbar spine BMD +2.9% and total-hip BMD +2.2% vs placebo over 2 years, with no endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma
cards.summary: FOUNDATION trial (Bolognese 2009): arzoxifene 20 mg raised lumbar spine BMD +2.9% and total-hip BMD +2.2% vs placebo over 2 years, with no endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma
cards.type: Phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled BMD and endometrial-safety trial (FOUNDATION), arzoxifene in normal-to-low bone mass
cards.people: 331 postmenopausal women with normal to low bone mass in a 2-year randomised, placebo-controlled trial of arzoxifene 20 mg/day versus placebo (the FOUNDATION study).
cards.result: Compared with placebo, arzoxifene significantly increased lumbar spine BMD (+2.9%) and total-hip BMD (+2.2%) and decreased biochemical markers of bone metabolism. There was no evidence of endometrial hyperplasia or carcinoma on central review of baseline and follow-up biopsies, no significant between-group change in endometrial thickness on transvaginal ultrasound, and no significant difference in uterine polyps or vaginal bleeding. Vulvovaginal mycotic infection was the only adverse event significantly increased versus placebo; hot flushes did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: A BMD (surrogate) trial in women with normal-to-low bone mass — a lower-risk population than GENERATIONS' osteoporosis subgroup — and 2 years is too short and 331 women too few to characterise fracture or VTE effects.
cards.source: Bolognese M et al. Effects of arzoxifene on bone mineral density and endometrium in postmenopausal women with normal or low bone mass. The Journal of clinical endocrinology and metabolism. 2009. PMID: 19351734. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one outcomes trial that split — vertebral fractures and breast cancer down, clots up, nonvertebral fractures unchanged — over three BMD surrogate trials; never marketed
cards.summary: Synthesis: one outcomes trial that split — vertebral fractures and breast cancer down, clots up, nonvertebral fractures unchanged — over three BMD surrogate trials; never marketed
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (GENERATIONS outcomes trial, randomised N not printed in its record; NEXT n=320; phase 2 n=219; FOUNDATION n=331).
cards.result: GENERATIONS is the only fracture evidence: vertebral fracture incidence 2.3 percentage points lower (41% relative risk reduction) and invasive breast cancer 1.3 points lower (56% relative reduction; HR 0.44), against no significant nonvertebral-fracture reduction and a 0.7-point absolute increase in venous thromboembolic events (2.3-fold relative). The three supporting trials consistently show arzoxifene raising BMD and suppressing turnover at least as much as raloxifene, with a neutral endometrial picture — surrogate support only. Despite the vertebral and breast results, arzoxifene was never marketed. The stamp is SPLIT: benefit and harm are both in the single outcomes trial.
cards.watchOut: Do not let the BMD trials upgrade the fracture claim: the head-to-head BMD advantage over raloxifene explicitly did not translate into improved fracture efficacy, and the nonvertebral null and the VTE increase travel with every citation of GENERATIONS.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Soluble α-Klotho reference intervals: 4 datasets — levels fall with age (founding range 239–1,266 pg/mL), but two assays on the same samples do not correlate, so intervals are assay-specific
shelves.question: In healthy adults, what are the reference intervals for soluble α-Klotho in serum — the central range by age and sex — how steeply do levels fall with age, and how far apart are the intervals given by different immunoassays measuring nominally the same protein?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging · Animals · Antibodies, Monoclonal · Calcium · Child · Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay · Female · Fibroblast Growth Factor-23 · Glucuronidase · Humans · Klotho Proteins · Male · Mice · Middle Aged · Mutation · Fibroblast Growth Factors · Health · Immunoassay · Reference Values · Regression Analysis · Solubility · Statistics, Nonparametric · Young Adult · Cross-Sectional Studies · Insulin-Like Growth Factor I · Biomarkers · Acromegaly · Glomerular Filtration Rate · Pituitary Neoplasms · Insulin-Like Growth Factor Binding Protein 3 · Adenoma
shelves.balance: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall, mineral / ageing-related sections, and Boron & Boulpaep — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Four independent adult datasets (N = 142, 120, 346 and 890) agree that soluble α-Klotho falls with age and shows no, or only a slight, sex difference (population medians 678 pg/mL in women vs 651 pg/mL in men). The defining problem is assay discordance: in the 120-adult head-to-head, two immunoassays did not correlate and neither recognised the other's standard (TRF medians 61 ng/mL in men / 99 ng/mL in women vs ELISA mean 472 pg/mL), so intervals are assay-specific to an unusual degree and units differ by three orders of magnitude as published, never converted silently. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (age gradient and assay-specificity consistent across 4 datasets; no universal interval exists).

cards.headline: Founding sandwich-ELISA dataset (142 healthy adults): serum soluble α-Klotho 239–1,266 pg/mL, mean 562 ± 146 pg/mL, falling with age and creatinine, unrelated to sex or mineral indices
cards.summary: Founding sandwich-ELISA dataset (142 healthy adults): serum soluble α-Klotho 239–1,266 pg/mL, mean 562 ± 146 pg/mL, falling with age and creatinine, unrelated to sex or mineral indices
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (founding sandwich-ELISA reference values, 142 healthy adults)
cards.people: 142 healthy adult volunteers (66 men; mean age 61.1 ± 18.5 years) in the study that first established a sandwich ELISA for circulating soluble α-Klotho; renal function, mineral-metabolism indices, age and sex were related to levels. The same paper's 39 children (952 ± 282 pg/mL) are a paediatric limb and are NOT counted as an adult dataset.
cards.result: Serum soluble α-Klotho in healthy adults ranged from 239 to 1,266 pg/mL (mean ± SD 562 ± 146 pg/mL). Levels were not modified by gender or indices of mineral metabolism, but were inversely related to creatinine and to age. In a multivariate analysis including children and adults, soluble α-Klotho correlated negatively with age and calcium and positively with inorganic phosphate.
cards.watchOut: The founding assay's own range: later assays give materially different numbers for nominally the same protein (next card), so this interval must never be printed without its assay.
cards.source: Yamazaki Y et al. Establishment of sandwich ELISA for soluble alpha-Klotho measurement: Age-dependent change of soluble alpha-Klotho levels in healthy subjects. Biochemical and biophysical research communications. 2010. PMID: 20599764. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Assay-discordance dataset (120 healthy adults): two immunoassays do not correlate and neither recognises the other's standard — TRF median 61 ng/mL (men) / 99 ng/mL (women) vs ELISA mean 472 pg/mL, each with its own reference interval
cards.summary: Assay-discordance dataset (120 healthy adults): two immunoassays do not correlate and neither recognises the other's standard — TRF median 61 ng/mL (men) / 99 ng/mL (women) vs ELISA mean 472 pg/mL, each with its own reference interval
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (two-immunoassay comparison with assay-specific reference intervals, 120 healthy adults) — the assay-discordance card
cards.people: 120 healthy adults aged 19–66 years whose stored sera were assayed for Klotho by both a time-resolved fluorescence immunoassay (TRF) and an ELISA (IBL), with age, gender and other clinical and laboratory characteristics recorded.
cards.result: Serum Klotho levels were significantly higher by TRF than by ELISA and no correlation was found between the assays; no signal was obtained in either assay when the standard curve was switched between them. TRF median was 61 ng/mL in men (2.5–97.5% reference limits 11–181 ng/mL) and 99 ng/mL in women (19–316 ng/mL), while the ELISA gave a mean of 472 pg/mL (reference limits 204–741 pg/mL) with no difference between genders. By TRF, levels were independently associated with estimated GFR and body weight; by ELISA, with age. The authors conclude the protein exists in different forms recognised differently by the assays, whose biomarker value must be evaluated separately, and they derived assay-specific reference intervals for both.

cards.headline: Population dataset (890 adults aged 20–89): median 678 pg/mL in women vs 651 pg/mL in men, weak negative age correlation, positive correlations with eGFR and IGF-I, LMS-derived reference intervals
cards.summary: Population dataset (890 adults aged 20–89): median 678 pg/mL in women vs 651 pg/mL in men, weak negative age correlation, positive correlations with eGFR and IGF-I, LMS-derived reference intervals
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset (population reference intervals by LMS method, 890 adults)
cards.people: 890 adults from a population sample (435 men, 455 women; aged 20–89 years) with soluble α-Klotho measured cross-sectionally; associations with sex, age, body-mass index, waist-hip ratio, eGFR, IGF-I and IGFBP-3, glucose, lipid, calcium and liver metabolism, fasting and estrogen status were analysed, and reference intervals calculated using LMS quantile regression with a Box-Cox transformation. (The same paper's pituitary-adenoma patient groups are not reference data and are not carded.)
cards.result: Across all ages, soluble α-Klotho (median [interquartile range]) was slightly but significantly higher in women than men — 678 (537–859) vs 651 (537–812) pg/mL; P = 0.01 — suggesting an estrogen impact. It showed a weak negative correlation with age and positive correlations with eGFR and IGF-I (P < 0.001 for both); correlations with glucose, liver and calcium metabolism and fasting duration were negligible. The authors describe soluble α-Klotho as a stable GH-sensitive biomarker less impacted by biological variables than IGF-I or IGFBP-3.
cards.watchOut: The largest dataset, but its sex difference is small and its age correlation explicitly weak — it refines, and partly softens, the steeper age story of the founding dataset; its LMS intervals belong to its own assay and population.
cards.source: Schweizer JROL et al. Soluble alpha klotho-impact of biological variables and reference intervals for adults. European journal of endocrinology. 2025. PMID: 40338072. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall (mineral / ageing-related sections) and Boron & Boulpaep — the framing is brief, and this shelf rests chiefly on the primary reference-interval literature, and says so. Four independent adult datasets: the founding sandwich ELISA (142 adults; 239–1,266 pg/mL, mean 562 ± 146 pg/mL, inversely related to age and creatinine); the two-immunoassay comparison (120 adults; assays uncorrelated, neither recognising the other's standard — TRF medians 61 ng/mL in men and 99 ng/mL in women vs ELISA mean 472 pg/mL, limits 204–741 pg/mL — with assay-specific intervals for both); the 346-adult ELISA study (seniors lowest, negative age association, no sex difference; no numeric interval in its abstract); and the 890-adult population study (medians 678 pg/mL in women vs 651 pg/mL in men, weak negative age correlation, LMS intervals). Every dataset exceeds the ~10-human reference floor (smallest N = 120). Cross-point only: pack #6303 (FGF23–Klotho mechanism) asks a different question and shares no dataset.
cards.watchOut: Never print an interval without its assay: the ng/mL (TRF) and pg/mL (ELISA) scales differ by method, not by a conversion this shelf performs.

shelves.title: Cyclical etidronate: vertebral fractures 29.5 vs 62.9 per 1,000 patient-years (Watts) — but Cochrane 2024 finds little to no difference; no nonvertebral evidence
shelves.question: In postmenopausal women with established osteoporosis, does intermittent cyclical etidronate, compared with placebo or sodium fluoride, increase spinal bone density and reduce new vertebral fractures?

shelves.balance: SPLIT — the superseded first-generation drug leads. Etidronate was the first bisphosphonate used for osteoporosis and has been displaced by agents with nonvertebral and hip fracture data; it has NO nonvertebral fracture evidence. Two 1990 NEJM trials were positive on their own terms — Watts (429 women): spinal density +4.2% / +5.2% and vertebral fractures 29.5 vs 62.9 per 1,000 patient-years; Storm (only 66 women): vertebral mineral content +5.3% vs −2.7% — but the fluoride head-to-head (118 women, heavy dropout) gave etidronate less density gain and a higher vertebral fracture count (19 vs 6), and the current Cochrane synthesis (2024) finds little to no difference on clinical fractures. The withdrawn 2007 Cochrane version is fenced and cited nowhere on this shelf.

cards.headline: Watts multicentre trial (1990): spinal bone density rose +4.2% and +5.2% in the two cyclical-etidronate groups, and new vertebral fractures ran at 29.5 vs 62.9 per 1,000 patient-years (P = 0.043) — a relative halving, rates printed beside it
cards.summary: Watts multicentre trial (1990): spinal bone density rose +4.2% and +5.2% in the two cyclical-etidronate groups, and new vertebral fractures ran at 29.5 vs 62.9 per 1,000 patient-years (P = 0.043) — a relative halving, rates printed beside it
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled multicentre trial (4-group cyclical design), 2 years
cards.people: 429 women with postmenopausal osteoporosis and 1–4 vertebral compression fractures plus radiographic osteopenia, in a 2-year double-blind multicentre study with a 4-group design: phosphate or placebo on days 1–3, etidronate 400 mg or placebo on days 4–17, and supplemental calcium 500 mg on days 18–91 of each 91-day cycle, repeated eight times.
cards.result: After 2 years, spinal bone density increased significantly in the two etidronate groups (+4.2 ± 0.8% and +5.2 ± 0.7%; P < 0.017). The rate of new vertebral fractures was reduced by half in etidronate-treated patients vs those not receiving etidronate (29.5 vs 62.9 fractures per 1,000 patient-years; P = 0.043) — a relative halving of a rate, with the absolute rates printed here. The effect was largest in the subgroup with the lowest baseline spinal density (42.3 vs 132.7 per 1,000 patient-years; P = 0.004). Phosphate added no apparent benefit, and there were no significant adverse effects of treatment, as published.
cards.watchOut: 1990-era vertebral evidence only: fractures are vertebral, rates are per patient-year rather than proportions of women, and the largest effect is a lowest-baseline-density subgroup — no nonvertebral or hip fracture evidence exists in this trial.
cards.source: Watts NB et al. Intermittent cyclical etidronate treatment of postmenopausal osteoporosis. The New England journal of medicine. 1990. PMID: 2113611. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Storm trial (1990): vertebral bone mineral content rose +5.3% (95% CI 2.0 to 8.6) on cyclical etidronate and fell −2.7% on placebo over 150 weeks (between-group difference 8.0 percentage points, P < 0.01); fracture rates from week 60 to 150 were 6 vs 54 per 100 patient-years (P = 0.023)
cards.summary: Storm trial (1990): vertebral bone mineral content rose +5.3% (95% CI 2.0 to 8.6) on cyclical etidronate and fell −2.7% on placebo over 150 weeks (between-group difference 8.0 percentage points, P < 0.01); fracture rates from week 60 to 150 were 6 vs 54 per 100 patient-years (P = 0.023)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, cyclical etidronate, 150 weeks
cards.people: 66 women with postmenopausal osteoporosis randomised in equal numbers, double-blind, to oral etidronate 400 mg/day for 2 weeks followed by 13 weeks off, repeated 10 times over 150 weeks, or placebo; both groups received daily calcium and vitamin D throughout. The bone-mineral-content analysis is reported in 20 patients per group, as published.
cards.result: Vertebral bone mineral content increased significantly after 150 weeks on etidronate (+5.3%; 95% CI 2.0 to 8.6; n = 20) and decreased on placebo (−2.7%; 95% CI −7.3 to 1.9; n = 20), a between-group difference of 8.0 percentage points (P < 0.01; 95% CI 2.4 to 13.6). Fracture rates differed significantly for weeks 60–150 (6 vs 54 fractures per 100 patient-years; P = 0.023). No adverse clinical, biochemical or bone-histomorphometric effects were observed.
cards.watchOut: Only 66 women randomised and 20 per group in the density analysis: the 6 vs 54 per 100 patient-years fracture contrast rests on very small absolute event counts in the later study period, and is supportive of — not independent confirmation beyond — the larger Watts trial.
cards.source: Storm T et al. Effect of intermittent cyclical etidronate therapy on bone mass and fracture rate in women with postmenopausal osteoporosis. The New England journal of medicine. 1990. cards.headline: Head-to-head vs sodium fluoride (Guañabens 2000): lumbar density rose more on fluoride (+8.5%) than on cyclical etidronate (+3.6%; P = 0.01 between groups); the proportion of women with new vertebral fractures did not differ (17% vs 16%), although the fracture count was higher on etidronate (19 vs 6, P = 0.05)
cards.summary: Head-to-head vs sodium fluoride (Guañabens 2000): lumbar density rose more on fluoride (+8.5%) than on cyclical etidronate (+3.6%; P = 0.01 between groups); the proportion of women with new vertebral fractures did not differ (17% vs 16%), although the fracture count was higher on etidronate (19 vs 6, P = 0.05)
cards.type: Randomised head-to-head trial, cyclical etidronate + calcium vs sodium fluoride + calcium, 3 years
cards.people: 118 postmenopausal women with at least one vertebral fracture randomised for 3 years to enteric-coated sodium fluoride 25 mg twice daily plus calcium 1,000 mg/day, or intermittent etidronate 400 mg/day for 14 days followed by calcium 1,000 mg/day for 76 days per cycle. Only 47 women in the etidronate group and 31 in the fluoride group completed the trial — heavy dropout, printed as published.
cards.result: At 36 months, mean lumbar bone density change was +8.5 ± 2.04% on fluoride (P = 0.001) vs +3.6 ± 0.84% on etidronate (P < 0.001), significantly higher on fluoride (P = 0.01 between groups); femoral neck density changed non-significantly in both groups. There was no significant difference in the cumulative proportion of women with new vertebral fractures (fluoride 16% vs etidronate 17%), but the number of new vertebral fractures was significantly lower on fluoride (6 vs 19 fractures; P = 0.05). Nonvertebral fracture patient counts were similar. Side effects (mainly gastrointestinal symptoms and lower-extremity pain) were frequent on fluoride; etidronate was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Against an active comparator, etidronate lost on density and on fracture count while tying on the proportion of women fracturing — and with only 78 of 118 women completing, every estimate here is attrition-fragile. Fluoride is itself a superseded therapy; this card compares two first-generation agents, neither against a modern standard.

cards.people: The 2024 update of the Cochrane review of intermittent/cyclic etidronate for primary and secondary prevention of osteoporotic fractures in postmenopausal women: 30 eligible randomised trials, 26 (2,770 women) with extractable data — 9 primary-prevention and 17 secondary-prevention studies. Carded as programme support only, as the commissioning row directs; the withdrawn 2007 version of this review is fenced and is NOT carded or cited anywhere on this shelf.
cards.result: For the etidronate 400 mg/day vs placebo comparison: in secondary prevention (4 studies, 667 women at higher fracture risk), etidronate may make little or no difference to non-vertebral fractures (risk ratio 1.07, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.58 — a relative measure; absolute risk 0.9% more, 95% CI 3.8% fewer to 8.1% more), and the evidence was very uncertain for hip and wrist fractures; clinical vertebral fractures were not reported in those studies. In primary prevention (9 studies, 740 women), etidronate probably results in little to no difference in non-vertebral fractures (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.61) and serious adverse events. The update echoes the previous version's key finding: etidronate probably makes or may make little to no difference to vertebral and non-vertebral fractures for both primary and secondary prevention. The reviewers had concerns about at least one risk-of-bias domain in every study.
cards.watchOut: FENCE APPLIED: the 2007 version of this Cochrane review is typed WITHDRAWN and is cited nowhere on this shelf; only this current (2024) version is carded. The review's pooled null on clinical fractures sits in tension with the 1990 trials' radiographic vertebral-fracture rates — both print, neither is suppressed.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a superseded first-generation drug — two 1990 NEJM trials found vertebral fracture-rate reductions and spinal density gains, the fluoride head-to-head favoured the comparator on fracture count, and the current Cochrane synthesis finds little to no difference on clinical fractures; there is no nonvertebral fracture evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: a superseded first-generation drug — two 1990 NEJM trials found vertebral fracture-rate reductions and spinal density gains, the fluoride head-to-head favoured the comparator on fracture count, and the current Cochrane synthesis finds little to no difference on clinical fractures; there is no nonvertebral fracture evidence
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The superseded first-generation drug leads: etidronate was the first bisphosphonate used for osteoporosis and has been displaced by agents with nonvertebral and hip fracture data. Its own record is vertebral and spinal-density only, from 1990: Watts (429 women) — density +4.2% / +5.2% and vertebral fractures 29.5 vs 62.9 per 1,000 patient-years; Storm (66 women) — vertebral mineral content +5.3% vs −2.7% and late fracture rates 6 vs 54 per 100 patient-years. Against sodium fluoride (118 women, heavy dropout), etidronate gained less density (+3.6% vs +8.5%) and accumulated more vertebral fractures by count (19 vs 6) with no difference in the proportion of women fracturing (17% vs 16%). The current Cochrane synthesis (2024; the withdrawn 2007 version is fenced and uncited) pools little to no difference on clinical vertebral and non-vertebral fractures. The cyclical schedule is part of the question, not a detail: continuous (non-cyclical) etidronate impairs mineralisation.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: percent density gains and per-patient-year fracture rates are always printed with their absolute denominators and study sizes.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for vertebral fractures only, and that qualifier leads. BONE, the programme's only placebo-controlled fracture trial (2,946 randomised, 3 years), found new vertebral fractures in 4.7% (daily) and 4.9% (intermittent) on oral ibandronate vs 9.6% on placebo — 62% and 50% relative reductions, about 5 percentage points absolute — and NO nonvertebral fracture benefit in the overall population (9.1% / 8.9% vs 8.2%); the abstract reports none and this shelf implies none. MOBILE (monthly oral) and DIVA (quarterly IV) are BMD (surrogate) non-inferiority trials against the daily regimen: they establish that monthly oral and IV dosing match daily dosing on density, nothing more.

cards.headline: BONE fracture trial (Chesnut 2004): new vertebral fractures in 4.7% (daily) and 4.9% (intermittent) on oral ibandronate vs 9.6% on placebo over 3 years — 62% and 50% relative reductions (P = 0.0001 and P = 0.0006), ≈5 percentage points absolute; nonvertebral fractures did NOT differ (9.1% / 8.9% vs 8.2%)
cards.summary: BONE fracture trial (Chesnut 2004): new vertebral fractures in 4.7% (daily) and 4.9% (intermittent) on oral ibandronate vs 9.6% on placebo over 3 years — 62% and 50% relative reductions (P = 0.0001 and P = 0.0006), ≈5 percentage points absolute; nonvertebral fractures did NOT differ (9.1% / 8.9% vs 8.2%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled fracture trial (BONE), daily and intermittent oral ibandronate, 3 years
cards.people: 2,946 postmenopausal women with osteoporosis (lumbar spine T-score ≤ −2.0 in at least one vertebra) and 1–4 prevalent vertebral fractures, randomised double-blind to oral ibandronate 2.5 mg daily, intermittent ibandronate 20 mg every other day for 12 doses every 3 months, or placebo, for 3 years.
cards.result: New morphometric vertebral fractures occurred in 4.7% (daily) and 4.9% (intermittent) vs 9.6% (placebo) — relative reductions of 62% (P = 0.0001) and 50% (P = 0.0006), i.e. about 5 percentage points absolute. Clinical vertebral fractures were also relatively reduced (49% and 48%, relative measures). Lumbar spine BMD at 3 years rose 6.5% (daily), 5.7% (intermittent) and 1.3% (placebo). Nonvertebral fracture incidence did NOT differ (9.1% daily, 8.9% intermittent, 8.2% placebo; not significant) in this overall low-risk population; a post-hoc analysis in a higher-risk subgroup (femoral neck T-score < −3.0) found a 69% relative reduction in nonvertebral fractures on daily ibandronate (P = 0.012) — a post-hoc subgroup result, printed as such. Ibandronate was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Vertebral-only antifracture evidence — the flag leads: the programme's only placebo-controlled fracture trial won on vertebral fractures and showed no nonvertebral benefit in the overall population; the nonvertebral subgroup finding is post-hoc and must never be printed as a trial result.

cards.headline: MOBILE monthly-dosing trial (Miller 2005): lumbar spine BMD rose 3.9% on daily oral ibandronate vs 4.3%, 4.1% and 4.9% on monthly regimens at 1 year — all monthly regimens non-inferior to daily, the 150 mg monthly regimen superior on BMD

cards.type: Randomised double-blind non-inferiority trial (MOBILE), monthly vs daily oral ibandronate — BMD endpoint, 1-year report
cards.people: 1,609 women with postmenopausal osteoporosis randomised double-blind to oral ibandronate 2.5 mg daily, or monthly regimens of 50/50 mg (single doses on consecutive days), 100 mg or 150 mg, in a 2-year non-inferiority trial; this is the 1-year report.
cards.result: After 1 year, lumbar spine BMD increased by 3.9% (daily), 4.3% (50/50 mg monthly), 4.1% (100 mg monthly) and 4.9% (150 mg monthly). All monthly regimens were proven non-inferior to daily, and the 150 mg regimen superior, on BMD; hip BMD gains were similar across monthly regimens and larger than with daily dosing. Serum C-telopeptide fell similarly on all regimens, and all were similarly well tolerated. No fracture outcomes are reported in this 1-year BMD report.
cards.watchOut: A BMD (surrogate) non-inferiority trial against the daily regimen, not a fracture trial: it establishes that monthly oral dosing matches daily dosing on density, nothing more — the fracture claim for every regimen on this shelf traces back to BONE alone.

cards.headline: DIVA intravenous trial (Eisman 2008): lumbar spine BMD rose 6.4% (IV 2 mg every 2 months) and 6.3% (IV 3 mg every 3 months) vs 4.8% on daily oral ibandronate over 2 years (P < 0.001) — non-inferior and superior on BMD, with similar C-telopeptide suppression (53.4–59.9%)
cards.summary: DIVA intravenous trial (Eisman 2008): lumbar spine BMD rose 6.4% (IV 2 mg every 2 months) and 6.3% (IV 3 mg every 3 months) vs 4.8% on daily oral ibandronate over 2 years (P < 0.001) — non-inferior and superior on BMD, with similar C-telopeptide suppression (53.4–59.9%)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind double-dummy non-inferiority trial (DIVA), IV vs daily oral ibandronate — BMD endpoint, 2 years
cards.people: 1,395 women aged 55–80 years, ≥5 years since menopause, with osteoporosis (mean lumbar spine T-score < −2.5 and ≥ −5.0), randomised double-blind double-dummy to IV ibandronate 2 mg every 2 months or 3 mg every 3 months (plus daily oral placebo) or daily oral ibandronate 2.5 mg (plus IV placebo), with vitamin D 400 IU and calcium 500 mg throughout, for 2 years.
cards.result: At 2 years, the 2- and 3-monthly IV regimens achieved statistically non-inferior and also superior increases in lumbar spine BMD vs daily oral (6.4% and 6.3% vs 4.8%; P < 0.001), with greater increases also in proximal femur BMD. Serum C-telopeptide was reduced to a similar extent in all arms (53.4–59.9%). The tolerability profile of the IV regimens was similar to daily oral therapy. No fracture outcomes are reported.
cards.watchOut: Again a BMD (surrogate) non-inferiority comparison against daily oral dosing, not a fracture trial and not placebo-controlled: quarterly IV dosing matching daily oral dosing on density does not extend the fracture evidence beyond BONE's vertebral result.

cards.result: Vertebral-only antifracture evidence — the flag leads. BONE (2,946 randomised, 3 years) reduced new vertebral fractures to 4.7% (daily) and 4.9% (intermittent) vs 9.6% on placebo (62% and 50% relative reductions, about 5 percentage points absolute), with no nonvertebral fracture difference in the overall population (9.1% / 8.9% vs 8.2%) and only a post-hoc higher-risk-subgroup nonvertebral signal. MOBILE (1,609 randomised; 1-year report) and DIVA (1,395 randomised; 2 years) are BMD non-inferiority trials against the daily regimen — monthly oral 150 mg (spine BMD +4.9% vs +3.9% daily) and IV 2 mg every 2 months / 3 mg every 3 months (+6.4% / +6.3% vs +4.8% daily) match or exceed daily dosing on the density surrogate. They establish dosing flexibility, not additional fracture protection, and no card on this shelf implies a nonvertebral or hip benefit.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards: every fracture number traces to BONE; MOBILE and DIVA numbers are density changes against an active daily comparator.

shelves.title: Straight-leg raising for lumbar disc herniation: 3 overlapping syntheses — sensitive but not specific (crossed test the reverse), with pooled specificity depending on population
shelves.question: In patients with low-back pain and leg pain, how accurately do the straight-leg-raising (Lasègue) test and the crossed straight-leg-raising test identify radiculopathy due to lumbar disc herniation against imaging or surgical findings — what pooled sensitivity and specificity does the Cochrane review find for each test in surgical populations, what did the earlier systematic review pool, and why does the pain-provocation review reach inconsistent conclusions across its seven studies? (Base: 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — counted as syntheses, never as independent cohorts.)
