shelves.balance: This shelf rests on 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 3 syntheses, not 3 independent cohorts. The specificity disagreement between syntheses (pooled 0.28 in surgical populations in the Cochrane review vs 0.52 in the older mixed review) is population- and reference-standard-dependent and is the content: no single pooled specificity prints without its population. Only one primary-care study exists inside the Cochrane set, so no card presents the surgical-population figures as primary-care performance. This is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf.

cards.headline: SLR synthesis 1 of 3 — Cochrane review of physical examination for lumbar radiculopathy (van der Windt 2010; 16 cohort and 3 case-control studies): in surgical populations (disc-herniation prevalence 58–98%) the straight leg raise showed pooled sensitivity 0.92 (95% CI 0.87 to 0.95) with widely varying specificity (pooled 0.28, 0.18 to 0.40), while the crossed straight leg raise showed pooled specificity 0.90 (0.85 to 0.94) with sensitivity 0.28 (0.22 to 0.35)
cards.summary: SLR synthesis 1 of 3 — Cochrane review of physical examination for lumbar radiculopathy (van der Windt 2010; 16 cohort and 3 case-control studies): in surgical populations (disc-herniation prevalence 58–98%) the straight leg raise showed pooled sensitivity 0.92 (95% CI 0.87 to 0.95) with widely varying specificity (pooled 0.28, 0.18 to 0.40), while the crossed straight leg raise showed pooled specificity 0.90 (0.85 to 0.94) with sensitivity 0.28 (0.22 to 0.35)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (synthesis 1 of 3; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: Patients with low-back pain and sciatica; tests compared with diagnostic imaging (MRI, CT, myelography) or findings at surgery; 16 cohort studies (median N = 126) and 3 case-control studies; only one study was in a primary-care population. One of 3 overlapping syntheses — never an independent cohort.
cards.result: Most physical tests in isolation performed poorly. Straight leg raise in surgical populations: pooled sensitivity 0.92 (95% CI 0.87 to 0.95), specificity widely varying (0.10 to 1.00; pooled 0.28, 0.18 to 0.40); studies using imaging showed more heterogeneity and poorer sensitivity. Crossed straight leg raise: pooled specificity 0.90 (0.85 to 0.94), sensitivity 0.28 (0.22 to 0.35). Combining positive tests increased specificity, but few studies presented combination data.
cards.watchOut: These are surgical-population figures (prevalence 58–98%) — never present them as primary-care performance; only one primary-care study exists in this set.

cards.headline: SLR synthesis 2 of 3 — earlier systematic review (Vroomen 1999; 37 studies, 1965–1994): the straight leg raise was the only sign consistently reported sensitive for sciatica due to disc herniation, with pooled sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.52; the crossed straight leg raise was the only sign shown specific (pooled 0.30 / 0.84)
cards.summary: SLR synthesis 2 of 3 — earlier systematic review (Vroomen 1999; 37 studies, 1965–1994): the straight leg raise was the only sign consistently reported sensitive for sciatica due to disc herniation, with pooled sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.52; the crossed straight leg raise was the only sign shown specific (pooled 0.30 / 0.84)
cards.type: Systematic review (synthesis 2 of 3; primary-study sets overlap)
cards.people: Studies of history and physical examination in patients suspected of sciatica due to disc herniation; 37 studies meeting selection criteria, read independently by three readers with a standard quality scoring list. One of 3 overlapping syntheses — never an independent cohort.
cards.result: Pain distribution seemed the only useful history item. Straight leg raise pooled sensitivity 0.85 and specificity 0.52; crossed straight leg raise pooled sensitivity 0.30 and specificity 0.84. There was considerable disagreement on other neurological signs. The reviewers warn the studies carry important biases and methodological drawbacks, so sensitivity was probably overestimated and specificity underestimated.

cards.type: Systematic review of the pain-provocation definition (synthesis 3 of 3; primary-study sets overlap)
cards.people: Studies in which a positive straight leg raise was defined by a pain response, with standardised reference standards, reporting both sensitivity and specificity for lumbar disc herniation, radiculopathy and/or sciatica; 7 studies, 3 rated high quality on QUADAS. cards.result: Sensitivity and specificity varied among the 7 studies: 4 suggested a pain response is sensitive, 3 suggested it is specific. shelves.title: ACL bedside examination: 3 overlapping syntheses — Lachman most valid (85–87% / 94%), pivot shift very specific but insensitive except acutely, lever sign entering the acute evidence
shelves.question: In patients with suspected anterior cruciate ligament injury, how accurately do the bedside knee examinations — the Lachman test, the pivot shift test, the anterior drawer test and the lever sign — detect ACL rupture against arthroscopy or MRI: what pooled sensitivity and specificity do the meta-analyses assign to the Lachman test, how specific but insensitive is the pivot shift, and how do the tests perform when the injury is acute? (Base: 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — counted as syntheses, never as independent cohorts.)

shelves.balance: This shelf rests on 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 3 syntheses, not 3 independent cohorts. Acuity is the key moderator and prints with every figure: the pivot shift's sensitivity more than doubles from 24% in mixed series to 0.55 in the acute-only synthesis, and the anterior drawer's good figures are chronic-only in the oldest synthesis. Examination under anaesthesia is a different test condition inside some primary studies, and no pooled figure prints as awake-examination performance without that caveat. This is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf.

cards.headline: ACL synthesis 1 of 3 (Benjaminse 2006, meta-analysis — 28 studies): the Lachman test was the most valid test (pooled sensitivity 85% (95% CI 83% to 87%), specificity 94% (92% to 95%)); the pivot shift was very specific (98% (96% to 99%)) but insensitive (24% (21% to 27%)); the anterior drawer performed well only in chronic conditions (92% / 91%)
cards.summary: ACL synthesis 1 of 3 (Benjaminse 2006, meta-analysis — 28 studies): the Lachman test was the most valid test (pooled sensitivity 85% (95% CI 83% to 87%), specificity 94% (92% to 95%)); the pivot shift was very specific (98% (96% to 99%)) but insensitive (24% (21% to 27%)); the anterior drawer performed well only in chronic conditions (92% / 91%)
cards.type: Meta-analysis (synthesis 1 of 3; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: Studies of clinical examination accuracy for ACL rupture against arthroscopy, arthrotomy or MRI; 28 studies, results heterogeneous. One of 3 overlapping syntheses — never an independent cohort.
cards.result: Lachman: pooled sensitivity 85% (95% CI 83 to 87%), specificity 94% (92 to 95%). Pivot shift: specificity 98% (96 to 99%), sensitivity 24% (21 to 27%) — very specific in both acute and chronic conditions per the authors. Anterior drawer: sensitivity 92% (88 to 95%) and specificity 91% (87 to 94%) in chronic conditions, but not in acute conditions. The authors recommend performing both the Lachman and the pivot shift when ACL injury is suspected.
cards.watchOut: The anterior drawer's good figures are chronic-only here — never quote 92% / 91% for an acute injury. Some primary studies examined under anaesthesia, a different test condition from the awake bedside examination.

cards.result: Lachman was the most sensitive test: pooled sensitivity 87.1% (95% CI 0.84 to 0.90), lowest negative likelihood ratio 0.17 (0.11 to 0.25, labelled as such). Pivot shift was the most specific: pooled specificity 97.5% (0.95 to 0.99), highest positive likelihood ratio 16.00 (7.34 to 34.87, labelled as such). The authors recommend the pivot shift for confirming and the Lachman for ruling out ACL rupture.

cards.result: Pooled sensitivities / specificities in the acute setting: Lachman 0.79 / 0.91, anterior drawer 0.78 / 0.91, pivot shift 0.55 / 0.96, lever sign 0.82 / 0.88. Lever sign had the lowest negative likelihood ratio (0.21) and pivot shift the highest positive likelihood ratio (11.60), both labelled as such. Area under the curve exceeded 0.70 for all four tests. The authors conclude the lever sign and pivot shift are useful for diagnosing ACL injuries acutely.
cards.watchOut: Journal note: the slate row named the Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine; the PubMed record fetched this session gives International journal of sports physical therapy — the record governs the source line. Acuity changes the ranking: the pivot shift's sensitivity is 0.55 here vs 24% in mixed series.

shelves.title: Serum osteocalcin reference values in healthy adults (PHYS, 3 datasets, 3 named assays): medians and intervals differ by platform and menopausal status — no merged interval
shelves.question: What are the reference intervals for serum osteocalcin (the osteoblast-derived bone-formation marker) in healthy adults — what medians does the German population study report for men, premenopausal and postmenopausal women on the IDS-iSYS N-Mid assay, what interval does the Chinese male cohort derive on the Elecsys assay, and what interval do healthy premenopausal ASEAN women show on the cobas assay? (PHYSIOLOGY: assay dependence is the headline; no merged interval.)
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · China · Ethnicity · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Osteocalcin/blood/standards · Physical Examination · Reference Values · Young Adult · Female · Biomarkers/blood · Bone Remodeling/physiology · Asia, Southeastern · Databases, Factual · Procollagen/blood · Osteocalcin/blood · Peptide Fragments/blood · Collagen Type I/blood · Southeast Asian People
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — no intervention stamp applies. Assay dependence is the headline: three named assay platforms give three different distributions (medians vs intervals as published), and no merged osteocalcin interval is printed. On the IDS-iSYS N-Mid assay (Study of Health in Pomerania; 1,107 men, 545 premenopausal and 498 postmenopausal women) medians were 15.4 ng/mL in men, 14.4 in premenopausal women and 18.6 in postmenopausal women — menopausal status moves the distribution materially within one study and prints. On the Elecsys assay (COBAS 6000 E601), 2,018 healthy Han Chinese men gave an interval of 12.49–43.94 ng/mL. On the cobas assay, 746 healthy premenopausal ASEAN women gave 9.0–33.0 µg/L (= 9.0–33.0 ng/mL), falling to 3.5–27.0 µg/L when women in their 20s were excluded. The male-only and female-only datasets do not cross-validate each other's sex, which prints. Specific assays are named per the standing product rule. Framing: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED for assay- and menopause-dependence of the distribution.

cards.headline: Dataset 1 of 3 (Hannemann 2013, BMC Endocrine Disorders — Study of Health in Pomerania; 1,107 men, 545 premenopausal and 498 postmenopausal women; IDS-iSYS N-Mid osteocalcin assay — the named assay prints): median osteocalcin was 15.4 ng/mL in men, 14.4 ng/mL in premenopausal women and 18.6 ng/mL in postmenopausal women
cards.summary: Dataset 1 of 3 (Hannemann 2013, BMC Endocrine Disorders — Study of Health in Pomerania; 1,107 men, 545 premenopausal and 498 postmenopausal women; IDS-iSYS N-Mid osteocalcin assay — the named assay prints): median osteocalcin was 15.4 ng/mL in men, 14.4 ng/mL in premenopausal women and 18.6 ng/mL in postmenopausal women
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — osteocalcin medians and reference intervals, IDS-iSYS N-Mid assay (dataset 1 of 3)
cards.people: A healthy reference population selected from the first follow-up of the Study of Health in Pomerania, Germany: 1,107 men aged 25–79, 545 premenopausal women aged 25–54 and 498 postmenopausal women aged 50–79. Serum osteocalcin measured with the IDS-iSYS N-Mid Osteocalcin assay on the IDS-iSYS Automated System (Immunodiagnostic Systems) — the specific assay named per the standing product rule. This record carries no MeSH in PubMed; its source line says so, and the shelf's top-level MeSH is taken from the other two datasets.
cards.result: Median (1st–3rd quartile) serum osteocalcin was 15.4 ng/mL (12.0–19.4) in men, 14.4 ng/mL (11.3–18.5) in premenopausal women and 18.6 ng/mL (13.6–25.6) in postmenopausal women. Concentrations were highest in men and premenopausal women aged 25–29, stable during midlife, and rose again after 65 years in men and at the transition to menopause in women. Concentrations were lower in women taking oral contraceptives or postmenopausal hormone replacement, and in subjects with diabetes or BMI <18 or >30 kg/m². Age-specific reference intervals (central 95%) were calculated by quantile regression for men and premenopausal women, and irrespective of age for postmenopausal women — the abstract reports the medians carded here; no interval is reconstructed from them.
cards.watchOut: Medians, not intervals, are what this abstract prints — the two are never interchanged on this shelf. The menopause shift within one study on one assay (14.4 → 18.6 ng/mL) is the cleanest menopause comparison available here, and prints as a median shift, not an interval shift.
cards.source: Hannemann A et al. Reference intervals for serum osteocalcin concentrations in adult men and women from the study of health in Pomerania. BMC endocrine disorders. 2013. PMID: 23497286. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Dataset 2 of 3 (Qin 2014, Clinical Laboratory — FAMHES cohort, 2,018 healthy Han Chinese men; Elecsys electrochemiluminescence assay on the COBAS 6000 E601 module — the named platform prints): the osteocalcin reference interval was 12.49–43.94 ng/mL
cards.summary: Dataset 2 of 3 (Qin 2014, Clinical Laboratory — FAMHES cohort, 2,018 healthy Han Chinese men; Elecsys electrochemiluminescence assay on the COBAS 6000 E601 module — the named platform prints): the osteocalcin reference interval was 12.49–43.94 ng/mL
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — osteocalcin reference interval, Elecsys assay, Chinese men (dataset 2 of 3)
cards.people: 2,018 healthy Han Chinese men from the Fangchenggang Area Male Health and Examination Survey (September–December 2009), with serum osteocalcin by electrochemiluminescence immunoassay on a COBAS 6000 system E601 (Elecsys module) analyser — the specific platform named per the standing product rule. A male-only dataset: it does not cross-validate the female datasets, which prints.
cards.result: Osteocalcin data were not normally distributed; after log-transformation they took a normal pattern. The reference interval for serum osteocalcin was 12.49–43.94 ng/mL. No difference was noted between non-smokers and smokers (P = 0.629) or non-drinkers and drinkers (P = 0.748). Osteocalcin varied with age (r = −0.371, P < 0.001) and BMI (r = −0.331, P < 0.001), and age- and BMI-dependent intervals were calculated.
cards.watchOut: An interval (12.49–43.94 ng/mL) on Elecsys against medians on IDS-iSYS: the two expressions and the two assays differ together, so no cross-assay numeric comparison is drawn from pairing them.
cards.source: Qin X et al. Reference interval for osteocalcin in Chinese Han ethnic males from the Fangchenggang Area Male Health and Examination Survey. Clinical laboratory. 2014. PMID: 25134387. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dataset 3 of 3 (Lee 2024, Bone — ASEAN healthy cohort, 746 premenopausal women aged 20–44 across five Southeast Asian countries; cobas modular analyser — the named platform prints): the osteocalcin reference interval was 9.0–33.0 µg/L (= 9.0–33.0 ng/mL)
cards.summary: Dataset 3 of 3 (Lee 2024, Bone — ASEAN healthy cohort, 746 premenopausal women aged 20–44 across five Southeast Asian countries; cobas modular analyser — the named platform prints): the osteocalcin reference interval was 9.0–33.0 µg/L (= 9.0–33.0 ng/mL)
cards.type: Primary human physiology dataset — osteocalcin reference interval, cobas assay, ASEAN premenopausal women (dataset 3 of 3)
cards.people: 746 healthy premenopausal women aged 20–44 from five ASEAN countries (Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam), with bone turnover markers on cobas modular analyser systems (Roche Diagnostics) — the specific platform named per the standing product rule. A female-only, premenopausal dataset: it does not cross-validate the male dataset, which prints. Only this dataset's osteocalcin limb is carded here; its P1NP/CTX limbs belong to pack #7169's territory and are not carded.
cards.result: The reference interval (central 95% range) for osteocalcin was 9.0–33.0 μg/L. (The same paper's intervals for CTX, 128–811 ng/L, and P1NP, 22.8–96.5 μg/L, belong to the built P1NP/CTX territory and are stated here only to identify the paper — not carded as this shelf's data.) Singaporeans had the highest median CTX, and Thais and Filipinos significantly higher P1NP and osteocalcin, in the cross-country comparison. Markers decreased with age at 20–29 and plateaued after 30; excluding participants in their 20s, the osteocalcin interval was 3.5–27.0 µg/L, as published.
cards.watchOut: The interval moves materially when women in their 20s are excluded (9.0–33.0 → 3.5–27.0 µg/L): age-band composition is part of the interval, and both versions print. µg/L and ng/mL are numerically identical for osteocalcin — the equivalence is stated, not converted.
